citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and let $d\ge1$ be a finite integer. An
$\mathbb R^d$-valued process $B=(B_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **standard
$d$-dimensional Brownian motion** if:

1. $B_0=0$ almost surely;
2. for every finite list $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_n$, the vector increments
   $$B_{t_j}-B_{t_{j-1}},\qquad 1\le j\le n,$$
   are mutually independent and have laws
   $N_d(0,(t_j-t_{j-1})I_d)$; and
3. there is one measurable event $A$ with $P(A)=1$ such that
   $t\mapsto B_t(\omega)$ is continuous from $[0,\infty)$ to
   $\mathbb R^d$ for every $\omega\in A$.

Equivalently, its $d$ coordinate processes $B^\alpha=(B_t^\alpha)_{t\ge0}$
are independent standard one-dimensional Brownian motions. Here independence
of the processes means the following precise assertion. Put
$I=[0,\infty)$ and equip $\mathbb R^I$ with its cylinder sigma-algebra. The
maps
$$ \Phi_\alpha:\Omega\longrightarrow\mathbb R^I, \qquad \Phi_\alpha(\omega)(t)=B_t^\alpha(\omega), \qquad 1\le\alpha\le d, $$
are independent random elements.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and let $d\ge1$ be a finite integer. An
$\mathbb R^d$-valued process $B=(B_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **standard
$d$-dimensional Brownian motion** if:

1. $B_0=0$ almost surely;
2. for every finite list $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_n$, the vector increments
   $$B_{t_j}-B_{t_{j-1}},\qquad 1\le j\le n,$$
   are mutually independent and have laws
   $N_d(0,(t_j-t_{j-1})I_d)$; and
3. there is one measurable event $A$ with $P(A)=1$ such that
   $t\mapsto B_t(\omega)$ is continuous from $[0,\infty)$ to
   $\mathbb R^d$ for every $\omega\in A$.

Equivalently, its $d$ coordinate processes $B^\alpha=(B_t^\alpha)_{t\ge0}$
are independent standard one-dimensional Brownian motions. Here independence
of the processes means the following precise assertion. Put
$I=[0,\infty)$ and equip $\mathbb R^I$ with its cylinder sigma-algebra. The
maps
$$ \Phi_\alpha:\Omega\longrightarrow\mathbb R^I, \qquad \Phi_\alpha(\omega)(t)=B_t^\alpha(\omega), \qquad 1\le\alpha\le d, $$
are independent random elements.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Let
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space with a continuous-time
filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. All processes here
are real-valued and indexed by $[0,\infty)$. AC is inherited from the cited
continuous-time-filtration interface, whose separate martingale clause uses
conditional expectation. Once the filtered probability space and stopping
times are given, the progressive and predictable constructions below make no
additional choice: they use only generated sigma-algebras and product
rectangles.

1. **Progressively measurable.** A process $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **progressively measurable** relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when for every
   $t\ge0$ the restricted map
   $[0,t]\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$, $(s,\omega)\mapsto X_s(\omega)$, is
   measurable for the product sigma-algebra
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$
   [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]].

2. **Time-zero and interval generators.** On the product space
   $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$, let $\mathcal P$ be the sigma-algebra generated by
   the family
   $$\mathcal G:=\bigl\{(s,u]\times A:\ 0\le s<u<\infty,\ A\in\mathcal F_s\bigr\}\ \cup\ \bigl\{\{0\}\times A:\ A\in\mathcal F_0\bigr\}.$$
   The interval generators with $s=0$ are included, so $(0,u]\times A$ with
   $A\in\mathcal F_0$ is a generator. The sigma-algebra $\mathcal P$ exists by
   [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]] and is called the
   **predictable sigma-algebra**. A process $H=(H_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **predictable** when the map $(s,\omega)\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is
   $\mathcal P$-measurable. For a finite horizon $T>0$ we write
   $\mathcal P_T$ for the sigma-algebra on $[0,T]\times\Omega$ generated by the
   same family restricted to $u\le T$ together with the time-zero generators;
   this is the trace of $\mathcal P$ on $[0,T]\times\Omega$. Indeed, the
   trace of an interval generator is empty when $s\ge T$, and otherwise is
   $(s,\min(u,T)]\times A$, while time-zero generators are unchanged.
   Conversely every listed finite-horizon generator is such a trace.

3. **Sections, adaptedness, and null sets.** Two structural conventions are
   used repeatedly and are part of the definition.
   (a) Every generator is a measurable rectangle of
   $\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$, hence
   $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$; the time-zero
   generator $\{0\}\times A$ has $dt\otimes P$-measure zero for every $A$. A
   set in $\mathcal P$ has its section at each fixed time $s$ in $\mathcal F_s$:
   sets with that section property form a sigma-algebra, and each generator
   has the property by the increasing-filtration condition. Its section at
   each fixed $\omega$ is Borel in time, by the same sigma-algebra argument.
   (b) If a process is predictable then it is progressively measurable: for
   $s\le t$ the section $\omega\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is $\mathcal F_s$-measurable
   $\subseteq\mathcal F_t$-measurable, and the progressive-measurability claim
   is the restriction of the joint map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$; the restriction
   of a $\mathcal P$-measurable map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$ is measurable for
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$ because every generator with $u\le t$
   lies in that product sigma-algebra and the generators with $u>t$ have
   intersection with $[0,t]\times\Omega$ of the form $(s,t]\times A$ with
   $s<t$ and $A\in\mathcal F_s$, or the empty set when $s\ge t$.
   The time-zero generators also lie in
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$.

The family $\mathcal G$ need not itself contain the whole space, but a finite intersection
of generators is empty or again a generator, or a time-zero generator, because
$(s,u]\cap(s',u']=(s\vee s',u\wedge u']$ and $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_{s\vee s'}$
whenever $A\in\mathcal F_s$, $A'\in\mathcal F_{s'}$, while
$\{0\}\times A$ is disjoint from every interval generator, including
$(0,u]\times A'$. Two time-zero generators intersect in
$\{0\}\times(A\cap A')$ with $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_0$.
Thus the family consisting of the whole space
together with finite intersections of generators is a pi-system generating
$\mathcal P$; this is the structural fact used by the density theorem below.

Because predictability is a measurability requirement for the joint map, it is
preserved by pointwise limits, products and linear combinations of predictable
processes. A deterministic function $h$ of time defines a predictable process
exactly when $h$ is Borel measurable: the sets $C$ for which
$C\times\Omega\in\mathcal P$ form a sigma-algebra containing the intervals
$(s,u]$ and $\{0\}$, hence all Borel sets. Conversely, take any fixed
$\omega\in\Omega$ (a probability space is nonempty) and use the Borel
time-section property from 3(a) on every inverse image of an open set.
This single choice uses no choice axiom. In particular the
indicators $1_{[0,u]}$ and $1_{(0,u]}$ are predictable for every deterministic
$u\ge0$, and the process $s\mapsto 1_{s\le\tau(\omega)}$ for a stopping time
$\tau$ [[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]] is predictable, since
$$\{(s,\omega):s>\tau(\omega)\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}(q,\infty)\times\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}\bigcup_{n>q}(q,n]\times\{\tau<q\}$$
is a countable union of generators: for rational $q>0$ one has
$\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q'<q,\ q'\in\mathbb Q}\{\tau\le q'\}\in\mathcal F_q$. The
complement of that set inside $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$ is the event of the
indicator, so $1_{[0,\tau]}$ is predictable; its left-continuity in the time
variable is the visual form of the same computation.

No completeness of the filtration and no right continuity of $(\mathcal F_t)$
is used or assumed. Apart from the inherited ambient assumption just recorded,
the constructions in this definition are choice-free.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]], and fix a probability space
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ with a continuous-time filtration
$(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]] and a standard
Brownian motion $B$ [[def-brownian-motion]] on it. **Standing hypothesis
(H).** $B$ is adapted to $(\mathcal F_t)$ and for all $0\le s<t$ the increment
$B_t-B_s$ is independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and has law $N(0,t-s)$. The raw
natural filtration and the usual augmented natural filtration
[[def-natural-and-usual-augmented-brownian-filtrations]] both satisfy (H) for a
standard Brownian motion, by
[[thm-brownian-future-path-markov-property]]; for a general filtration, (H) is
part of the data and is not automatic. Every statement in this development
names (H) when it is used.

Throughout, fix a finite horizon $T>0$. An **elementary predictable Brownian
integrand** on $[0,T]$ is a process of the form
$$H_s(\omega)=\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\xi_k(\omega)\,1_{(t_k,t_{k+1}]}(s),\qquad s\in[0,T],$$
where $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_m=T$ is a finite partition of $[0,T]$, each
$\xi_k$ is a bounded real $\mathcal F_{t_k}$-measurable random variable, and
the values at the partition points are irrelevant because the intervals are
left-open and right-closed. The **mesh** of the representation is
$\max_k(t_{k+1}-t_k)$, and the **supremum norm** of the representation is
$\max_k\|\xi_k\|_\infty$. The integrand itself is the process $H$; a second
list of the same name with different coefficients is the same elementary
integrand only if the two processes coincide in the almost-everywhere sense
made precise below.

The following properties are part of the definition and are used at once.

1. **Predictability.** $H$ is predictable
   [[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]]. Indeed, for a
   Borel set $\Gamma\subseteq\mathbb R$,
   $$\{H\in\Gamma\}=Z_\Gamma\cup\bigcup_{k=0}^{m-1}\bigl((t_k,t_{k+1}]\times\{\xi_k\in\Gamma\}\bigr), \qquad Z_\Gamma:=\begin{cases}\{0\}\times\Omega,&0\in\Gamma,\\\varnothing,&0\notin\Gamma,\end{cases}$$
   a finite union of generators of the predictable sigma-algebra because
   $\{\xi_k\in\Gamma\}\in\mathcal F_{t_k}$ and
   $\{0\}\times\Omega$ is a time-zero generator. Consequently $H$ is progressively
   measurable and measurable for the product sigma-algebra
   $\mathcal B([0,T])\otimes\mathcal F$, and $H$ belongs to
   $L^2([0,T]\times\Omega,\mathrm dt\otimes P)$: with
   $c:=\max_k\|\xi_k\|_\infty<\infty$ one has
   $E\int_0^TH_s^2\,ds\le c^2T<\infty$.

2. **Endpoint and null-set conventions.** Replacing the intervals by
   $(t_k,t_{k+1}]$ makes the value at $s=0$ zero for every elementary
   integrand. More generally, if two elementary integrands agree for all
   $s\in[0,T]$ except at finitely many deterministic times, then they agree
   $(\mathrm dt\otimes P)$-almost everywhere, since a finite set of times is
   Lebesgue-null and Tonelli computes
   $\mathrm dt\otimes P(\{u\}\times\Omega)=0$. All integrands and all
   integrals below are therefore elements of the quotient spaces of
   $L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)$ and $L^2(P)$; a claim about a process is a claim
   about its almost-everywhere class unless a representative is explicitly
   named, and path statements name the continuous representative.

3. **Deterministic coefficients.** If every $\xi_k$ is a deterministic real
   number, $H$ is a deterministic step function on $[0,T]$, so the elementary
   integrands include all step functions with deterministic coefficients. These
   are the integrands for which the integral is a Gaussian variable below.

The Axiom of Choice is declared because the Brownian construction and the
conditional-expectation interface used in items 6, 7 and 13 assume it; the
definition itself, including the predictability computation of clause 1, uses
no choice. The countable-choice obligations inherited from that interface are declared
as dependencies of this item.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and work under the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]: a filtered probability space
with a standard Brownian motion $B$ adapted to the filtration, with increments
$B_t-B_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ of law $N(0,t-s)$. Fix $T>0$ and an
elementary predictable integrand
$$H_s=\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\xi_k\,1_{(t_k,t_{k+1}]}(s),\qquad 0=t_0<\cdots<t_m=T,$$
with bounded $\mathcal F_{t_k}$-measurable coefficients $\xi_k$. The **Ito
integral of $H$ against $B$** is the process
$$I_t(H):=\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\xi_k\bigl(B_{t\wedge t_{k+1}}-B_{t\wedge t_k}\bigr),\qquad 0\le t\le T,$$
also written $\int_0^tH_s\,dB_s$ or $(H\cdot B)_t$. The sum is finite and is
evaluated with the Brownian path of the given representative; on the event
where $t\mapsto B_t$ is continuous it is continuous in $t$, and $I_0(H)=0$
because $0\wedge t_k=0$ for every $k$.

Three conventions are part of the definition.

1. **Adaptedness and continuity.** For fixed $t$, each summand
   $\xi_k(B_{t\wedge t_{k+1}}-B_{t\wedge t_k})$ is $\mathcal F_t$-measurable:
   if $t<t_k$, the Brownian difference and hence the summand are zero; if
   $t\ge t_k$, then $\mathcal F_{t_k}\subseteq\mathcal F_t$, while
   $B_{t\wedge u}$ is $\mathcal F_t$-measurable for every $u$ because
   $t\wedge u\le t$. Thus
   $I(H)$ is adapted. For each fixed $\omega$ the map
   $t\mapsto B_{t\wedge t_{k+1}}(\omega)-B_{t\wedge t_k}(\omega)$ is continuous
   outside the single exceptional null set of (H) on which the Brownian path is
   discontinuous; the finite sum is therefore continuous on the same event.

2. **Linearity on a common refinement.** If $H$ and $K$ are elementary
   integrands and a partition refines both representations, then the defining
   sums of $H$, $K$, $H+K$ and $aH$ are taken over that common partition, and
   the finite sums give $I_t(H+K)=I_t(H)+I_t(K)$ and $I_t(aH)=aI_t(H)$ for real
   $a$ identically. In particular $I_t(H)-I_t(K)=I_t(H-K)$ for the
   elementary integrand $H-K$ represented on that refinement. This is a
   rearrangement of finitely many terms, not a limiting statement.

3. **Dependence on the representation is temporary.** The definition attaches
   $I_t(H)$ to a *chosen* elementary representation.
   [[lem-elementary-ito-integral-is-independent-of-the-step-representation]] proves that
   two representations that agree $(\mathrm dt\otimes P)$-almost everywhere
   produce the same random variables almost surely at each fixed time, so that
   $I_t(H)$ is a function of the $(\mathrm dt\otimes P)$-class of $H$ alone.
   Until then, every statement about an elementary integrand names the
   representation it uses.

The Axiom of Choice is declared because the standing hypothesis (H) is part of
the Brownian interface of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]], which assumes it; the
definition of the finite sum uses no choice. The countable-choice obligations
inherited from that interface are declared as dependencies of this item.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Fix a horizon $T>0$ and let
$\mathcal P_T$ be the predictable sigma-algebra on $[0,T]\times\Omega$
[[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]]. Let $H$ be a
predictable process with
$$E\int_0^TH_s^2\,ds=\int_{[0,T]\times\Omega}H^2\,d(\mathrm dt\otimes P)<\infty ,$$
so that $H$ is an element of the quotient space
$L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)$ over $\mathcal P_T$; its class is what is integrated.
The **Ito integral** $\int_0^TH_s\,dB_s$, also written $H\cdot B$ or $I_T(H)$,
is defined as follows.

1. **Construction.** By the density theorem
   [[thm-density-of-elementary-predictable-processes-in-predictable-l2]] there
   is a sequence $(H^n)$ of bounded elementary predictable integrands
   [[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]] with
   $\|H^n-H\|_{L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)}\to0$. For such a sequence the
   elementary integrals $I_T(H^n)$
   [[def-ito-integral-of-an-elementary-predictable-process]] form a Cauchy
   sequence in $L^2(P)$: by the elementary isometry
   [[thm-ito-isometry-for-elementary-integrands]] and the well-definedness of
   the elementary integral,
   $$E\bigl(I_T(H^n)-I_T(H^m)\bigr)^2=E\int_0^T(H^n-H^m)^2ds=\|H^n-H^m\|^2_{L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)} ,$$
   and the right-hand side tends to $0$. Since $L^2(P)$ is complete
   [[thm-riesz-fischer-completeness-of-l-p]], the classes $I_T(H^n)$ converge
   in $L^2(P)$; the limit is a class in $L^2(P)$, and
   $$\int_0^TH_s\,dB_s:=\lim_{n\to\infty}I_T(H^n)\qquad\text{in }L^2(P).$$
   The limit is a random variable only up to almost-sure equality; statements
   about it are statements about that class. The limit does not depend on the
   chosen sequence: if another elementary sequence $K^n\to H$ is used, then
   the elementary isometry and linearity give
   $$\|I_T(H^n)-I_T(K^n)\|_{L^2(P)} =\|H^n-K^n\|_{L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)} \le\|H^n-H\|_2+\|K^n-H\|_2\longrightarrow0,$$
   so the two $L^2(P)$ limits agree.

2. **Integrals at a time.** For $t\in[0,T]$ put
   $\int_0^tH_s\,dB_s:=\int_0^TH_s1_{[0,t]}(s)\,dB_s$, the construction of
   clause 1 applied to the truncated process $H1_{[0,t]}$. That process is
   predictable: $H$ is $\mathcal P_T$-measurable and $1_{[0,t]}$ is a
   deterministic predictable indicator, so the product is
   $\mathcal P_T$-measurable; and it is square-integrable because
   $|H1_{[0,t]}|\le|H|$ pointwise. The same construction applied to $H$
   itself gives $t=T$. The family
   $\bigl(\int_0^tH\,dB\bigr)_{t\in[0,T]}$ is a family of $L^2(P)$-classes
   indexed by $t$; its continuous version is supplied by item 13, and no path
   property is asserted by this definition.

3. **Consistency with elementary integrands.** If $H$ is itself elementary,
   then the constant sequence $H^n:=H$ is admissible in clause 1, so
   $\int_0^TH\,dB$ is the limit of the constant sequence of elementary sums,
   namely the elementary sum $I_T(H)$ of
   [[def-ito-integral-of-an-elementary-predictable-process]]. The same argument
   with $H1_{[0,t]}$ in place of $H$, and the finite telescoping of the
   elementary sum over a refinement containing $t$, gives
   $\int_0^tH\,dB=I_t(H)$ for every $t\in[0,T]$. In particular the general
   definition extends, rather than replaces, the elementary definition.

4. **Linearity in the integrand is not asserted here.** Clause 1 defines each
   integral separately from an arbitrary approximating sequence; the linear and
   isometric properties of the extension are item 12. Until item 12 is proved,
   linearity may be used only for elementary integrands, where it is part of
   [[def-ito-integral-of-an-elementary-predictable-process]].

5. **Comparison with deterministic Riemann integration.** The integral is a
   stochastic integral: the integrand is paired with the Brownian path through
   left-endpoint sums and an $L^2(P)$ limit. This definition does not assert
   convergence of arbitrary tagged Riemann--Stieltjes sums for a general
   predictable integrand. Particular integrands can have a pathwise
   interpretation: for $H\equiv1$ every tagged sum telescopes to $B_T-B_0$,
   which is also its Ito integral by clause 3 (the value at time zero is
   irrelevant to its product-measure class). The notation $\int_0^TH\,dB$
   here always refers to the $L^2(P)$-class defined above.

The Axiom of Choice is declared because the construction selects an
approximating sequence and uses the completeness and conditional-expectation
interfaces that assume it; the inherited obligations are declared as
dependencies of this item. An alternative construction that avoids selecting the sequence is
not needed, because clause 1 shows every sequence gives the same class.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Let $H$ be a predictable
process with $E\int_0^TH_s^2ds<\infty$ for every finite $T$. Then there is an
adapted process $M=(M_t)_{t\ge0}$ with continuous paths such that
$M_t=\int_0^tH_s\,dB_s$ almost surely for every $t\ge0$
[[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]], and $M$ is a
square-integrable martingale relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$
[[def-continuous-time-adapted-process-and-martingale]]: $EM_t^2=E\int_0^tH_s^2ds<\infty$
for every $t$. Any two such continuous versions agree at every time on one
measurable event of probability one; in particular the continuous version is
unique in this common-full-measure-event sense, and it is the only continuous
square-integrable martingale whose value at each deterministic $t$ is the
integral class.

This conclusion is deliberately distinguished from the exact definition of
indistinguishability in
[[def-law-modification-and-indistinguishability-of-processes]]. On a
noncomplete probability space the full equality set, although it contains the
measurable probability-one event constructed below, need not itself be
measurable. On a complete probability space the two notions coincide, because
the complement of the equality set is then a measurable subset of a null set.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

The map $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[def-real-numbers]]) is an embedding of ordered
fields. Every real is approximated by rationals: for $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and
rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $q \in \mathbb{Q}$ with
$|x - \hat q| < \hat\varepsilon$. Consequently, strictly between any two
reals lies a rational.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Let
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space with a continuous-time
filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. All processes here
are real-valued and indexed by $[0,\infty)$. AC is inherited from the cited
continuous-time-filtration interface, whose separate martingale clause uses
conditional expectation. Once the filtered probability space and stopping
times are given, the progressive and predictable constructions below make no
additional choice: they use only generated sigma-algebras and product
rectangles.

1. **Progressively measurable.** A process $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **progressively measurable** relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when for every
   $t\ge0$ the restricted map
   $[0,t]\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$, $(s,\omega)\mapsto X_s(\omega)$, is
   measurable for the product sigma-algebra
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$
   [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]].

2. **Time-zero and interval generators.** On the product space
   $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$, let $\mathcal P$ be the sigma-algebra generated by
   the family
   $$\mathcal G:=\bigl\{(s,u]\times A:\ 0\le s<u<\infty,\ A\in\mathcal F_s\bigr\}\ \cup\ \bigl\{\{0\}\times A:\ A\in\mathcal F_0\bigr\}.$$
   The interval generators with $s=0$ are included, so $(0,u]\times A$ with
   $A\in\mathcal F_0$ is a generator. The sigma-algebra $\mathcal P$ exists by
   [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]] and is called the
   **predictable sigma-algebra**. A process $H=(H_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **predictable** when the map $(s,\omega)\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is
   $\mathcal P$-measurable. For a finite horizon $T>0$ we write
   $\mathcal P_T$ for the sigma-algebra on $[0,T]\times\Omega$ generated by the
   same family restricted to $u\le T$ together with the time-zero generators;
   this is the trace of $\mathcal P$ on $[0,T]\times\Omega$. Indeed, the
   trace of an interval generator is empty when $s\ge T$, and otherwise is
   $(s,\min(u,T)]\times A$, while time-zero generators are unchanged.
   Conversely every listed finite-horizon generator is such a trace.

3. **Sections, adaptedness, and null sets.** Two structural conventions are
   used repeatedly and are part of the definition.
   (a) Every generator is a measurable rectangle of
   $\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$, hence
   $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$; the time-zero
   generator $\{0\}\times A$ has $dt\otimes P$-measure zero for every $A$. A
   set in $\mathcal P$ has its section at each fixed time $s$ in $\mathcal F_s$:
   sets with that section property form a sigma-algebra, and each generator
   has the property by the increasing-filtration condition. Its section at
   each fixed $\omega$ is Borel in time, by the same sigma-algebra argument.
   (b) If a process is predictable then it is progressively measurable: for
   $s\le t$ the section $\omega\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is $\mathcal F_s$-measurable
   $\subseteq\mathcal F_t$-measurable, and the progressive-measurability claim
   is the restriction of the joint map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$; the restriction
   of a $\mathcal P$-measurable map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$ is measurable for
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$ because every generator with $u\le t$
   lies in that product sigma-algebra and the generators with $u>t$ have
   intersection with $[0,t]\times\Omega$ of the form $(s,t]\times A$ with
   $s<t$ and $A\in\mathcal F_s$, or the empty set when $s\ge t$.
   The time-zero generators also lie in
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$.

The family $\mathcal G$ need not itself contain the whole space, but a finite intersection
of generators is empty or again a generator, or a time-zero generator, because
$(s,u]\cap(s',u']=(s\vee s',u\wedge u']$ and $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_{s\vee s'}$
whenever $A\in\mathcal F_s$, $A'\in\mathcal F_{s'}$, while
$\{0\}\times A$ is disjoint from every interval generator, including
$(0,u]\times A'$. Two time-zero generators intersect in
$\{0\}\times(A\cap A')$ with $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_0$.
Thus the family consisting of the whole space
together with finite intersections of generators is a pi-system generating
$\mathcal P$; this is the structural fact used by the density theorem below.

Because predictability is a measurability requirement for the joint map, it is
preserved by pointwise limits, products and linear combinations of predictable
processes. A deterministic function $h$ of time defines a predictable process
exactly when $h$ is Borel measurable: the sets $C$ for which
$C\times\Omega\in\mathcal P$ form a sigma-algebra containing the intervals
$(s,u]$ and $\{0\}$, hence all Borel sets. Conversely, take any fixed
$\omega\in\Omega$ (a probability space is nonempty) and use the Borel
time-section property from 3(a) on every inverse image of an open set.
This single choice uses no choice axiom. In particular the
indicators $1_{[0,u]}$ and $1_{(0,u]}$ are predictable for every deterministic
$u\ge0$, and the process $s\mapsto 1_{s\le\tau(\omega)}$ for a stopping time
$\tau$ [[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]] is predictable, since
$$\{(s,\omega):s>\tau(\omega)\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}(q,\infty)\times\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}\bigcup_{n>q}(q,n]\times\{\tau<q\}$$
is a countable union of generators: for rational $q>0$ one has
$\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q'<q,\ q'\in\mathbb Q}\{\tau\le q'\}\in\mathcal F_q$. The
complement of that set inside $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$ is the event of the
indicator, so $1_{[0,\tau]}$ is predictable; its left-continuity in the time
variable is the visual form of the same computation.

No completeness of the filtration and no right continuity of $(\mathcal F_t)$
is used or assumed. Apart from the inherited ambient assumption just recorded,
the constructions in this definition are choice-free.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

1. For $1\le p<\infty$, the rule
   $$\|[f]\|_p:=\|f\|_p\qquad([f]\in L^p(\mu))$$
   is well defined on the quotient classes.
2. For $p=\infty$, the rule
   $$\|[f]\|_\infty:=\|f\|_\infty\qquad([f]\in L^\infty(\mu))$$
   is well defined.
3. In either case, with the quotient vector-space operations of
   [[prop-quotient-vector-space-operations-and-projection]], the resulting pair
   $(L^p(\mu),\|\cdot\|_p)$ is a normed space in the sense of
   [[def-norm-and-normed-space]].

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: For every Borel set $C\subseteq\mathbb R$, $H^{-1}(C)$ is the finite union of the predictable rectangles $(t_k,t_{k+1}]\times\{\xi_k\in C\}$, together with $\{0\}\times\Omega$ when $0\in C$; hence [F2] makes $H$ predictable. The intervals partition $(0,T]$, and [F3] makes the time-zero endpoint irrelevant to the product integral, so $E\int_0^T H_s^2ds=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}(t_{k+1}-t_k)E|\xi_k|^2<\infty$.

For $n\ge1$, clip each coefficient by $\xi_{k,n}=(-n)\vee(\xi_k\wedge n)$ and put $H^n_s=\sum_k\xi_{k,n}1_{(t_k,t_{k+1}]}(s)$. Each $H^n$ is bounded and elementary by [F3]. Since $|\xi_{k,n}-\xi_k|^2\le |\xi_k|^2 1_{\{|\xi_k|>n\}}$ and $E|\xi_k|^2<\infty$, [F7] applied to $|\xi_k|^2 1_{\{|\xi_k|\le n\}}\uparrow |\xi_k|^2$ gives $E|\xi_{k,n}-\xi_k|^2\to0$. The finite partition then gives $\|H^n-H\|_{L^2(dt\otimes P)}^2=\sum_k(t_{k+1}-t_k)E|\xi_{k,n}-\xi_k|^2\to0$.

For each fixed $t\in[0,T]$, [F5] defines $\int_0^tH_s\,dW_s$ as an $L^2(P)$ limit of the elementary integrals of $H^n1_{[0,t]}$. By [F4] those approximants are $S_t^n=\sum_k\xi_{k,n}(W_{t\wedge t_{k+1}}-W_{t\wedge t_k})$. Hence $S_t^n\to\int_0^tH_s\,dW_s$ in $L^2(P)$.

Put $\delta_k(t)=(t\wedge t_{k+1})-(t\wedge t_k)\ge0$. When $\delta_k(t)=0$ the increment in the $k$th summand vanishes. When $\delta_k(t)>0$, [F1] gives its $N(0,\delta_k(t))$ law, [F11] gives second moment $\delta_k(t)$, and [A1] makes it independent of $\xi_{k,n}-\xi_k$. Thus the $L^2$ norm of that summand's difference between $S_t^n$ and $S_t$ is $\sqrt{\delta_k(t)}\,\|\xi_{k,n}-\xi_k\|_2$. The triangle inequality [F10] and the finite number of intervals imply $S_t^n\to S_t$ in $L^2(P)$. Since also $S_t^n\to\int_0^tH_s\,dW_s$ by step 2.1, the triangle inequality gives $\|S_t-\int_0^tH_s\,dW_s\|_2=0$, and separation [F10] makes these classes equal almost surely.

Extend $H$ by zero after $T$; [F9] makes this extension predictable and its energy stays finite on every finite horizon. The process $S$ has continuous paths on the common Brownian continuity event [F12], because it is a finite sum of fixed random coefficients times stopped Brownian increments. Let $M$ be the continuous integral version supplied by [F6]. Step 3.1 gives $M_t=S_t$ almost surely at each $t$ in the countable dense set of [F8]; intersecting those measurable probability-one events with the continuity events and using continuity gives equality for every $t\in[0,T]$ on one measurable probability-one event. Assume the Axiom of Choice and let $d\ge1$ be a finite integer. An
$\mathbb R^d$-valued process $B=(B_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **standard
$d$-dimensional Brownian motion** if:

1. $B_0=0$ almost surely;
2. for every finite list $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_n$, the vector increments
   $$B_{t_j}-B_{t_{j-1}},\qquad 1\le j\le n,$$
   are mutually independent and have laws
   $N_d(0,(t_j-t_{j-1})I_d)$; and
3. there is one measurable event $A$ with $P(A)=1$ such that
   $t\mapsto B_t(\omega)$ is continuous from $[0,\infty)$ to
   $\mathbb R^d$ for every $\omega\in A$.

Equivalently, its $d$ coordinate processes $B^\alpha=(B_t^\alpha)_{t\ge0}$
are independent standard one-dimensional Brownian motions. Here independence
of the processes means the following precise assertion. Put
$I=[0,\infty)$ and equip $\mathbb R^I$ with its cylinder sigma-algebra. The
maps
$$ \Phi_\alpha:\Omega\longrightarrow\mathbb R^I, \qquad \Phi_\alpha(\omega)(t)=B_t^\alpha(\omega), \qquad 1\le\alpha\le d, $$
are independent random elements.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and use the finite-dimensional Brownian-motion
convention of [[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]]. Let the state dimension
$d$ and noise dimension $m$ be positive finite integers, and fix $T>0$ and
$N\in\mathbb N$ with $N\ge1$. Set $h=T/N>0$ and $t_k=kh$ for
$0\le k\le N$. Let
$b:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ and
$\sigma:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}$ be jointly Borel.
Write $|\cdot|$ for the Euclidean norm and $\|\cdot\|_F$ for the Frobenius
norm. Suppose finite constants $L,K$ satisfy, for every $s,t\in[0,T]$ and
$x,y\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$|b(t,x)-b(t,y)|+\|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(t,y)\|_F\le L|x-y|,$$
$$|b(t,x)|^2+\|\sigma(t,x)\|_F^2\le K^2(1+|x|^2),$$
and
$$|b(t,x)-b(s,x)|+\|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(s,x)\|_F\le K(1+|x|)|t-s|^{1/2}.$$
Let $W$ be an adapted standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion on a filtered
probability space, with $W_t-W_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and law
$N_m(0,(t-s)I_m)$ whenever $0\le s<t\le T$. Let $X_0$ be
$\mathcal F_0$-measurable, independent of future Brownian increments, and
$\mathbb E|X_0|^2<\infty$.

The **Euler–Maruyama algorithm** takes these data as input and returns
$Y_0,\ldots,Y_N$:

1. Set $Y_0=X_0$.
2. For $k=0,\ldots,N-1$, form $\Delta W_k=W_{t_{k+1}}-W_{t_k}$ and set
   $$Y_{k+1}=Y_k+b(t_k,Y_k)h+\sigma(t_k,Y_k)\Delta W_k.$$

The output is the grid approximation for the coefficient pair $(b,\sigma)$.
The companion step-process and interpolation definition uses this same grid
and endpoint convention.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: The law in [F1] has the representation $\sqrt{\delta}Z$ with $Z$ realized as in [F3]. By [F4] each coordinate has density $e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}$. Its $p$th absolute moment is finite: the integral on $[-1,1]$ is finite, and for $|x|\ge1$ the function $|x|^pe^{-x^2/4}$ is bounded, so $|x|^pe^{-x^2/2}\le C_pe^{-x^2/4}$. The finite-dimensional inequality $|Z|^p\le m^{p/2-1}\sum_{j=1}^m|Z_j|^p$ then gives $\mathbb E|Z|^p<\infty$ and $\mathbb E(|\sigma_s(U)(W_{s+\delta}-W_s)|^p\mid\mathcal F_s)\le c_{p,m}\delta^{p/2}\|\sigma_s(U)\|_F^p$. For $\delta=0$ the increment is zero.

For $\phi(x)=|x|^p$, direct differentiation gives $\|D^2\phi(x)\|\le C_p|x|^{p-2}$ for $p\ge2$. Apply the one-dimensional Taylor formula with integral remainder to $r\mapsto\phi(U+rR)$, where $R=\delta b_s(U)+\sigma_s(U)(W_{s+\delta}-W_s)$. The triangle inequality and $(a+b)^q\le C_q(a^q+b^q)$ for $q\ge0$ yield $\phi(U+R)\le\phi(U)+D\phi(U)R+C_p(|U|^{p-2}|R|^2+|R|^p)$.

The drift term in $V-U$ is $\mathcal F_s$-measurable and the Brownian increment is conditionally centered with covariance $\delta I_m$. Therefore the cross term has conditional expectation zero and $\mathbb E(|V-U|^2\mid\mathcal F_s)=\delta^2|b_s(U)|^2+\delta\|\sigma_s(U)\|_F^2\le C_{2,m,K}\delta(1+|U|^2)$. This also holds for $\delta=0$.

The coefficient growth assumption [F2] and $\delta\le1$ give $|b_s(U)|^p+\|\sigma_s(U)\|_F^p\le C_{p,K}(1+|U|^p)$. Conditional centering gives $\mathbb E(R\mid\mathcal F_s)=\delta b_s(U)$. By the growth bound and $|a+b|^2\le2|a|^2+2|b|^2$, $\mathbb E(|R|^2\mid\mathcal F_s)\le2K^2(\delta^2+\delta)(1+|U|^2)\le4K^2\delta(1+|U|^2)$. For the $p$th moment, $|a+b|^p\le2^{p-1}(|a|^p+|b|^p)$ and step 1.1 give $\mathbb E(|R|^p\mid\mathcal F_s)\le C_{p,m,K}(\delta^p+\delta^{p/2})(1+|U|^p)\le C_{p,m,K}\delta(1+|U|^p)$, since $p\ge2$ and $\delta\le1$. Also $|D\phi(U)\cdot\delta b_s(U)|\le C_{p,K}\delta(1+|U|^p)$. Substituting these bounds into step 1.2 and using $|U|^{p-2}(1+|U|^2)\le2(1+|U|^p)$ proves $\mathbb E(|V|^p\mid\mathcal F_s)\le(1+C_{p,m,K}\delta)|U|^p+C_{p,m,K}\delta$. The AC assumption is inherited from the cited Brownian and normal-law interfaces; these finite-dimensional estimates make no choice.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and use the finite-dimensional Brownian-motion
convention of [[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]]. Let the state dimension
$d$ and noise dimension $m$ be positive finite integers, and fix $T>0$ and
$N\in\mathbb N$ with $N\ge1$. Set $h=T/N>0$ and $t_k=kh$ for
$0\le k\le N$. Let
$b:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ and
$\sigma:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}$ be jointly Borel.
Write $|\cdot|$ for the Euclidean norm and $\|\cdot\|_F$ for the Frobenius
norm. Suppose finite constants $L,K$ satisfy, for every $s,t\in[0,T]$ and
$x,y\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$|b(t,x)-b(t,y)|+\|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(t,y)\|_F\le L|x-y|,$$
$$|b(t,x)|^2+\|\sigma(t,x)\|_F^2\le K^2(1+|x|^2),$$
and
$$|b(t,x)-b(s,x)|+\|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(s,x)\|_F\le K(1+|x|)|t-s|^{1/2}.$$
Let $W$ be an adapted standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion on a filtered
probability space, with $W_t-W_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and law
$N_m(0,(t-s)I_m)$ whenever $0\le s<t\le T$. Let $X_0$ be
$\mathcal F_0$-measurable, independent of future Brownian increments, and
$\mathbb E|X_0|^2<\infty$.

The **Euler–Maruyama algorithm** takes these data as input and returns
$Y_0,\ldots,Y_N$:

1. Set $Y_0=X_0$.
2. For $k=0,\ldots,N-1$, form $\Delta W_k=W_{t_{k+1}}-W_{t_k}$ and set
   $$Y_{k+1}=Y_k+b(t_k,Y_k)h+\sigma(t_k,Y_k)\Delta W_k.$$

The output is the grid approximation for the coefficient pair $(b,\sigma)$.
The companion step-process and interpolation definition uses this same grid
and endpoint convention.

Let $p\ge2$, $0\le\delta\le1$, and $s\ge0$ with $s+\delta\le T$. Let
$U$ be an $\mathcal F_s$-measurable $\mathbb R^d$-valued random variable
with $\mathbb E|U|^p<\infty$. Assume $W_{s+\delta}-W_s$ is independent of
$\mathcal F_s$ with law $N_m(0,\delta I_m)$. Let
$b_s:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ and
$\sigma_s:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}$ be measurable and satisfy
$$|b_s(x)|^2+\|\sigma_s(x)\|_F^2\le K^2(1+|x|^2).$$
Set $V=U+\delta b_s(U)+\sigma_s(U)(W_{s+\delta}-W_s)$. There is a
constant $C_{p,m,K}$, independent of $s,\delta,U$, such that
$$\mathbb E(|V|^p\mid\mathcal F_s)\le (1+C_{p,m,K}\delta)|U|^p+C_{p,m,K}\delta$$
and
$$\mathbb E(|V-U|^2\mid\mathcal F_s)\le C_{2,m,K}\delta(1+|U|^2).$$
The first estimate controls a grid step and, with
$\delta=t-t_k$, the interpolated value on one grid interval. The second
estimate is the interpolation increment bound. The global state-Lipschitz
and time-Hölder assumptions of [[alg-euler-maruyama]] are not needed for
these one-step bounds; the uniform linear-growth bound is enough.

Use the data and grid of [[alg-euler-maruyama]], and let
$Y_0,\ldots,Y_N$ be its recursion. The left-endpoint map is
$$\eta_h(t)=\max\{t_k:t_k\le t\},\qquad 0\le t\le T.$$
The right-continuous step process is
$$\bar Y_t=Y_k\quad(t_k\le t<t_{k+1}),\qquad \bar Y_T=Y_N.$$
The continuous interpolation is the pathwise process
$$Y_t=Y_k+b(t_k,Y_k)(t-t_k)+\sigma(t_k,Y_k)(W_t-W_{t_k})\quad(t_k\le t\le t_{k+1}).$$
At a shared grid endpoint the formulas agree because the recursion gives
$Y_{k+1}=Y_k+b(t_k,Y_k)h+\sigma(t_k,Y_k)(W_{t_{k+1}}-W_{t_k})$.
In particular $Y_{t_k}=Y_k$ for every $k$, including $Y_T=Y_N$.

For stochastic integration, define the predictable left-endpoint version by
$\bar Y^-_0=Y_0$ and $\bar Y^-_s=Y_k$ on $(t_k,t_{k+1}]$, and set
$\eta_h^-(0)=0$ and $\eta_h^-(s)=t_k$ on $(t_k,t_{k+1}]$. Its coefficient
integrands use the same fixed left endpoints. When the recursion is adapted,
each coordinate of $\bar Y^-$ and each coefficient composition is a
predictable finite-step process: on $(t_k,t_{k+1}]$ its value is
$\mathcal F_{t_k}$-measurable. These coefficients need not be bounded, so the
integrands need not be elementary in the bounded-coefficient sense of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Values at the finitely many
grid points do not change either integral. Once square integrability is
established, [[lem-square-integrable-predictable-step-ito-integral-is-finite-sum]]
identifies each finite-coordinate Itô integral of
[[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]] with its
finite-sum version, giving the equivalent formula
$$Y_t=X_0+\int_0^t b(\eta_h^-(s),\bar Y^-_s)\,ds+\sum_{j=1}^m\int_0^t \sigma_{\cdot j}(\eta_h^-(s),\bar Y^-_s)\,dW_s^j.$$
where $\eta_h^-(s)=t_k$ on $(t_k,t_{k+1}]$ and
$\sigma_{\cdot j}$ denotes column $j$ of the matrix.

The justified-by theorem
[[thm-euler-maruyama-uniform-moment-and-increment-bounds]] establishes the
required integrability and well-definedness under the stated coefficient and
initial-moment conditions.

For every real $x$,
$$1+x\le\exp(x).$$
Consequently, if $0\le p\le1$ and $m\in\mathbb N$, then
$$ (1-p)^m\le\exp(-mp). $$

Assume AC. Fix $T>0$ and a finite partition $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_N=T$.
Let $W$ be a scalar Brownian motion adapted to $(\mathcal F_t)$, with
$W_t-W_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and distributed as $N(0,t-s)$ for
every $0\le s<t\le T$. If each $\xi_k$ is real-valued,
$\mathcal F_{t_k}$-measurable and square-integrable, then the predictable
step process
$$H_s=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\xi_k1_{(t_k,t_{k+1}]}(s)$$
is square-integrable. Every continuous version of its Itô integral agrees, at every time on one
measurable event of probability one, with
$$S_t=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\xi_k\bigl(W_{t\wedge t_{k+1}}-W_{t\wedge t_k}\bigr),\qquad 0\le t\le T.$$
If the probability space is complete, this agreement is indistinguishability.
The coefficients need not be bounded.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and let $d\ge1$ be a finite integer. An
$\mathbb R^d$-valued process $B=(B_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **standard
$d$-dimensional Brownian motion** if:

1. $B_0=0$ almost surely;
2. for every finite list $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_n$, the vector increments
   $$B_{t_j}-B_{t_{j-1}},\qquad 1\le j\le n,$$
   are mutually independent and have laws
   $N_d(0,(t_j-t_{j-1})I_d)$; and
3. there is one measurable event $A$ with $P(A)=1$ such that
   $t\mapsto B_t(\omega)$ is continuous from $[0,\infty)$ to
   $\mathbb R^d$ for every $\omega\in A$.

Equivalently, its $d$ coordinate processes $B^\alpha=(B_t^\alpha)_{t\ge0}$
are independent standard one-dimensional Brownian motions. Here independence
of the processes means the following precise assertion. Put
$I=[0,\infty)$ and equip $\mathbb R^I$ with its cylinder sigma-algebra. The
maps
$$ \Phi_\alpha:\Omega\longrightarrow\mathbb R^I, \qquad \Phi_\alpha(\omega)(t)=B_t^\alpha(\omega), \qquad 1\le\alpha\le d, $$
are independent random elements.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Let
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space with a continuous-time
filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. All processes here
are real-valued and indexed by $[0,\infty)$. AC is inherited from the cited
continuous-time-filtration interface, whose separate martingale clause uses
conditional expectation. Once the filtered probability space and stopping
times are given, the progressive and predictable constructions below make no
additional choice: they use only generated sigma-algebras and product
rectangles.

1. **Progressively measurable.** A process $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **progressively measurable** relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when for every
   $t\ge0$ the restricted map
   $[0,t]\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$, $(s,\omega)\mapsto X_s(\omega)$, is
   measurable for the product sigma-algebra
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$
   [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]].

2. **Time-zero and interval generators.** On the product space
   $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$, let $\mathcal P$ be the sigma-algebra generated by
   the family
   $$\mathcal G:=\bigl\{(s,u]\times A:\ 0\le s<u<\infty,\ A\in\mathcal F_s\bigr\}\ \cup\ \bigl\{\{0\}\times A:\ A\in\mathcal F_0\bigr\}.$$
   The interval generators with $s=0$ are included, so $(0,u]\times A$ with
   $A\in\mathcal F_0$ is a generator. The sigma-algebra $\mathcal P$ exists by
   [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]] and is called the
   **predictable sigma-algebra**. A process $H=(H_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **predictable** when the map $(s,\omega)\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is
   $\mathcal P$-measurable. For a finite horizon $T>0$ we write
   $\mathcal P_T$ for the sigma-algebra on $[0,T]\times\Omega$ generated by the
   same family restricted to $u\le T$ together with the time-zero generators;
   this is the trace of $\mathcal P$ on $[0,T]\times\Omega$. Indeed, the
   trace of an interval generator is empty when $s\ge T$, and otherwise is
   $(s,\min(u,T)]\times A$, while time-zero generators are unchanged.
   Conversely every listed finite-horizon generator is such a trace.

3. **Sections, adaptedness, and null sets.** Two structural conventions are
   used repeatedly and are part of the definition.
   (a) Every generator is a measurable rectangle of
   $\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$, hence
   $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$; the time-zero
   generator $\{0\}\times A$ has $dt\otimes P$-measure zero for every $A$. A
   set in $\mathcal P$ has its section at each fixed time $s$ in $\mathcal F_s$:
   sets with that section property form a sigma-algebra, and each generator
   has the property by the increasing-filtration condition. Its section at
   each fixed $\omega$ is Borel in time, by the same sigma-algebra argument.
   (b) If a process is predictable then it is progressively measurable: for
   $s\le t$ the section $\omega\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is $\mathcal F_s$-measurable
   $\subseteq\mathcal F_t$-measurable, and the progressive-measurability claim
   is the restriction of the joint map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$; the restriction
   of a $\mathcal P$-measurable map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$ is measurable for
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$ because every generator with $u\le t$
   lies in that product sigma-algebra and the generators with $u>t$ have
   intersection with $[0,t]\times\Omega$ of the form $(s,t]\times A$ with
   $s<t$ and $A\in\mathcal F_s$, or the empty set when $s\ge t$.
   The time-zero generators also lie in
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$.

The family $\mathcal G$ need not itself contain the whole space, but a finite intersection
of generators is empty or again a generator, or a time-zero generator, because
$(s,u]\cap(s',u']=(s\vee s',u\wedge u']$ and $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_{s\vee s'}$
whenever $A\in\mathcal F_s$, $A'\in\mathcal F_{s'}$, while
$\{0\}\times A$ is disjoint from every interval generator, including
$(0,u]\times A'$. Two time-zero generators intersect in
$\{0\}\times(A\cap A')$ with $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_0$.
Thus the family consisting of the whole space
together with finite intersections of generators is a pi-system generating
$\mathcal P$; this is the structural fact used by the density theorem below.

Because predictability is a measurability requirement for the joint map, it is
preserved by pointwise limits, products and linear combinations of predictable
processes. A deterministic function $h$ of time defines a predictable process
exactly when $h$ is Borel measurable: the sets $C$ for which
$C\times\Omega\in\mathcal P$ form a sigma-algebra containing the intervals
$(s,u]$ and $\{0\}$, hence all Borel sets. Conversely, take any fixed
$\omega\in\Omega$ (a probability space is nonempty) and use the Borel
time-section property from 3(a) on every inverse image of an open set.
This single choice uses no choice axiom. In particular the
indicators $1_{[0,u]}$ and $1_{(0,u]}$ are predictable for every deterministic
$u\ge0$, and the process $s\mapsto 1_{s\le\tau(\omega)}$ for a stopping time
$\tau$ [[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]] is predictable, since
$$\{(s,\omega):s>\tau(\omega)\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}(q,\infty)\times\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}\bigcup_{n>q}(q,n]\times\{\tau<q\}$$
is a countable union of generators: for rational $q>0$ one has
$\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q'<q,\ q'\in\mathbb Q}\{\tau\le q'\}\in\mathcal F_q$. The
complement of that set inside $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$ is the event of the
indicator, so $1_{[0,\tau]}$ is predictable; its left-continuity in the time
variable is the visual form of the same computation.

No completeness of the filtration and no right continuity of $(\mathcal F_t)$
is used or assumed. Apart from the inherited ambient assumption just recorded,
the constructions in this definition are choice-free.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Fix a horizon $T>0$ and let
$\mathcal P_T$ be the predictable sigma-algebra on $[0,T]\times\Omega$
[[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]]. Let $H$ be a
predictable process with
$$E\int_0^TH_s^2\,ds=\int_{[0,T]\times\Omega}H^2\,d(\mathrm dt\otimes P)<\infty ,$$
so that $H$ is an element of the quotient space
$L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)$ over $\mathcal P_T$; its class is what is integrated.
The **Ito integral** $\int_0^TH_s\,dB_s$, also written $H\cdot B$ or $I_T(H)$,
is defined as follows.

1. **Construction.** By the density theorem
   [[thm-density-of-elementary-predictable-processes-in-predictable-l2]] there
   is a sequence $(H^n)$ of bounded elementary predictable integrands
   [[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]] with
   $\|H^n-H\|_{L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)}\to0$. For such a sequence the
   elementary integrals $I_T(H^n)$
   [[def-ito-integral-of-an-elementary-predictable-process]] form a Cauchy
   sequence in $L^2(P)$: by the elementary isometry
   [[thm-ito-isometry-for-elementary-integrands]] and the well-definedness of
   the elementary integral,
   $$E\bigl(I_T(H^n)-I_T(H^m)\bigr)^2=E\int_0^T(H^n-H^m)^2ds=\|H^n-H^m\|^2_{L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)} ,$$
   and the right-hand side tends to $0$. Since $L^2(P)$ is complete
   [[thm-riesz-fischer-completeness-of-l-p]], the classes $I_T(H^n)$ converge
   in $L^2(P)$; the limit is a class in $L^2(P)$, and
   $$\int_0^TH_s\,dB_s:=\lim_{n\to\infty}I_T(H^n)\qquad\text{in }L^2(P).$$
   The limit is a random variable only up to almost-sure equality; statements
   about it are statements about that class. The limit does not depend on the
   chosen sequence: if another elementary sequence $K^n\to H$ is used, then
   the elementary isometry and linearity give
   $$\|I_T(H^n)-I_T(K^n)\|_{L^2(P)} =\|H^n-K^n\|_{L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)} \le\|H^n-H\|_2+\|K^n-H\|_2\longrightarrow0,$$
   so the two $L^2(P)$ limits agree.

2. **Integrals at a time.** For $t\in[0,T]$ put
   $\int_0^tH_s\,dB_s:=\int_0^TH_s1_{[0,t]}(s)\,dB_s$, the construction of
   clause 1 applied to the truncated process $H1_{[0,t]}$. That process is
   predictable: $H$ is $\mathcal P_T$-measurable and $1_{[0,t]}$ is a
   deterministic predictable indicator, so the product is
   $\mathcal P_T$-measurable; and it is square-integrable because
   $|H1_{[0,t]}|\le|H|$ pointwise. The same construction applied to $H$
   itself gives $t=T$. The family
   $\bigl(\int_0^tH\,dB\bigr)_{t\in[0,T]}$ is a family of $L^2(P)$-classes
   indexed by $t$; its continuous version is supplied by item 13, and no path
   property is asserted by this definition.

3. **Consistency with elementary integrands.** If $H$ is itself elementary,
   then the constant sequence $H^n:=H$ is admissible in clause 1, so
   $\int_0^TH\,dB$ is the limit of the constant sequence of elementary sums,
   namely the elementary sum $I_T(H)$ of
   [[def-ito-integral-of-an-elementary-predictable-process]]. The same argument
   with $H1_{[0,t]}$ in place of $H$, and the finite telescoping of the
   elementary sum over a refinement containing $t$, gives
   $\int_0^tH\,dB=I_t(H)$ for every $t\in[0,T]$. In particular the general
   definition extends, rather than replaces, the elementary definition.

4. **Linearity in the integrand is not asserted here.** Clause 1 defines each
   integral separately from an arbitrary approximating sequence; the linear and
   isometric properties of the extension are item 12. Until item 12 is proved,
   linearity may be used only for elementary integrands, where it is part of
   [[def-ito-integral-of-an-elementary-predictable-process]].

5. **Comparison with deterministic Riemann integration.** The integral is a
   stochastic integral: the integrand is paired with the Brownian path through
   left-endpoint sums and an $L^2(P)$ limit. This definition does not assert
   convergence of arbitrary tagged Riemann--Stieltjes sums for a general
   predictable integrand. Particular integrands can have a pathwise
   interpretation: for $H\equiv1$ every tagged sum telescopes to $B_T-B_0$,
   which is also its Ito integral by clause 3 (the value at time zero is
   irrelevant to its product-measure class). The notation $\int_0^TH\,dB$
   here always refers to the $L^2(P)$-class defined above.

The Axiom of Choice is declared because the construction selects an
approximating sequence and uses the completeness and conditional-expectation
interfaces that assume it; the inherited obligations are declared as
dependencies of this item. An alternative construction that avoids selecting the sequence is
not needed, because clause 1 shows every sequence gives the same class.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: The recursion starts from $X_0\in L^p$. If $Y_k$ is $\mathcal F_{t_k}$-measurable and in $L^p$, the one-step estimate [L2] applies with $U=Y_k$ and $\delta=h$, so $Y_{k+1}$ is in $L^p$. Since $W_{t_{k+1}}-W_{t_k}$ is measurable at $t_{k+1}$ and independent of $\mathcal F_{t_k}$, the recursion also makes $Y_{k+1}$ $\mathcal F_{t_{k+1}}$-measurable. Induction gives adapted grid values with finite $p$th moments.

In particular the grid values are square-integrable. On each interval, $\bar Y^-_s=Y_k$ and the coefficient vectors $b(t_k,Y_k)$ and $\sigma_{\cdot j}(t_k,Y_k)$ are $\mathcal F_{t_k}$-measurable. The growth bound gives $E\int_0^T\bigl(|b(\eta_h^-(s),\bar Y^-_s)|^2+\|\sigma(\eta_h^-(s),\bar Y^-_s)\|_F^2\bigr)ds\le K^2\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}h(1+E|Y_k|^2)<\infty.$ Each scalar coordinate integrand is therefore predictable and square-integrable, although its coefficients need not be bounded. By [F3], its Itô integral has the finite-sum version; the ordinary drift integral is the corresponding finite sum as well. These are exactly the recursion and interpolation formulas in [L1]. For each $t\in[t_k,t_{k+1}]$, $Y_k$ is $\mathcal F_t$-measurable and $W_t-W_{t_k}$ is $\mathcal F_t$-measurable, so the interpolation is adapted. Brownian path continuity and the endpoint recursion make it continuous.

Put $u_k=\mathbb E|Y_k|^p$. The one-step estimate [L2] gives $u_{k+1}\le(1+C_ph)u_k+C_ph$, hence $1+u_{k+1}\le(1+C_ph)(1+u_k)$. Iteration and [F2] yield $1+u_k\le(1+C_ph)^k(1+u_0)\le\exp(C_pkh)(1+\mathbb E|X_0|^p)\le\exp(C_pT)(1+\mathbb E|X_0|^p)$. This bound is uniform in $k$ and $h$.

For $t\in[t_k,t_{k+1})$, apply [L2]'s first one-step estimate with $U=Y_k$ and $\delta=t-t_k\le h$ to obtain $\mathbb E|Y_t|^p\le(1+C_p\delta)\mathbb E|Y_k|^p+C_p\delta$. The step process equals $Y_k$ there. The grid estimate from step 2.2 therefore gives the two asserted uniform pointwise moment bounds; at $T$, $Y_T=\bar Y_T=Y_N$ is covered by the grid bound.

With $p=2$, [L2]'s second one-step estimate gives $\mathbb E(|Y_t-\bar Y_t|^2\mid\mathcal F_{t_k})\le C_{2,m,K}(t-t_k)(1+|Y_k|^2)$ on each grid interval. Taking expectations, using step 2.2, and using $t-t_k\le h$ proves $\mathbb E|Y_t-\bar Y_t|^2\le C_{T,K,d,m}h(1+\mathbb E|X_0|^2)$. At grid endpoints the difference is zero by [L1].

The induction and estimates use only finite Brownian increments and the explicitly given hypotheses; [A1] is inherited from the interfaces, not spent as a choice principle. A conclusion for a larger $p$ requires $X_0\in L^p$; it does not follow from $X_0\in L^2$ alone.

Proof steps 1.1 and 2.2 start at k=0 and allow N=1; step 3.1 includes Y_T=Y_N, so a single grid interval is covered.
Proof step 1.1 and recursion F1 keep Y_k=X_0 when b=sigma=0; step 3.2 then has zero interpolation increment. No nonexistent step2.2 is needed.

The theorem asserts moment and increment inequalities, not an if-and-only-if statement.

Lp implies L2; growth and the finite grid imply coefficient energy. Repaired finite-sum lemma supplies exactly the version identity used in step 2.1; common-event equality suffices, no full equality-set measurability is required. citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and use the finite-dimensional Brownian-motion
convention of [[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]]. Let the state dimension
$d$ and noise dimension $m$ be positive finite integers, and fix $T>0$ and
$N\in\mathbb N$ with $N\ge1$. Set $h=T/N>0$ and $t_k=kh$ for
$0\le k\le N$. Let
$b:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ and
$\sigma:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}$ be jointly Borel.
Write $|\cdot|$ for the Euclidean norm and $\|\cdot\|_F$ for the Frobenius
norm. Suppose finite constants $L,K$ satisfy, for every $s,t\in[0,T]$ and
$x,y\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$|b(t,x)-b(t,y)|+\|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(t,y)\|_F\le L|x-y|,$$
$$|b(t,x)|^2+\|\sigma(t,x)\|_F^2\le K^2(1+|x|^2),$$
and
$$|b(t,x)-b(s,x)|+\|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(s,x)\|_F\le K(1+|x|)|t-s|^{1/2}.$$
Let $W$ be an adapted standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion on a filtered
probability space, with $W_t-W_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and law
$N_m(0,(t-s)I_m)$ whenever $0\le s<t\le T$. Let $X_0$ be
$\mathcal F_0$-measurable, independent of future Brownian increments, and
$\mathbb E|X_0|^2<\infty$.

The **Euler–Maruyama algorithm** takes these data as input and returns
$Y_0,\ldots,Y_N$:

1. Set $Y_0=X_0$.
2. For $k=0,\ldots,N-1$, form $\Delta W_k=W_{t_{k+1}}-W_{t_k}$ and set
   $$Y_{k+1}=Y_k+b(t_k,Y_k)h+\sigma(t_k,Y_k)\Delta W_k.$$

The output is the grid approximation for the coefficient pair $(b,\sigma)$.
The companion step-process and interpolation definition uses this same grid
and endpoint convention.

Use the data and grid of [[alg-euler-maruyama]], and let
$Y_0,\ldots,Y_N$ be its recursion. The left-endpoint map is
$$\eta_h(t)=\max\{t_k:t_k\le t\},\qquad 0\le t\le T.$$
The right-continuous step process is
$$\bar Y_t=Y_k\quad(t_k\le t<t_{k+1}),\qquad \bar Y_T=Y_N.$$
The continuous interpolation is the pathwise process
$$Y_t=Y_k+b(t_k,Y_k)(t-t_k)+\sigma(t_k,Y_k)(W_t-W_{t_k})\quad(t_k\le t\le t_{k+1}).$$
At a shared grid endpoint the formulas agree because the recursion gives
$Y_{k+1}=Y_k+b(t_k,Y_k)h+\sigma(t_k,Y_k)(W_{t_{k+1}}-W_{t_k})$.
In particular $Y_{t_k}=Y_k$ for every $k$, including $Y_T=Y_N$.

For stochastic integration, define the predictable left-endpoint version by
$\bar Y^-_0=Y_0$ and $\bar Y^-_s=Y_k$ on $(t_k,t_{k+1}]$, and set
$\eta_h^-(0)=0$ and $\eta_h^-(s)=t_k$ on $(t_k,t_{k+1}]$. Its coefficient
integrands use the same fixed left endpoints. When the recursion is adapted,
each coordinate of $\bar Y^-$ and each coefficient composition is a
predictable finite-step process: on $(t_k,t_{k+1}]$ its value is
$\mathcal F_{t_k}$-measurable. These coefficients need not be bounded, so the
integrands need not be elementary in the bounded-coefficient sense of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Values at the finitely many
grid points do not change either integral. Once square integrability is
established, [[lem-square-integrable-predictable-step-ito-integral-is-finite-sum]]
identifies each finite-coordinate Itô integral of
[[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]] with its
finite-sum version, giving the equivalent formula
$$Y_t=X_0+\int_0^t b(\eta_h^-(s),\bar Y^-_s)\,ds+\sum_{j=1}^m\int_0^t \sigma_{\cdot j}(\eta_h^-(s),\bar Y^-_s)\,dW_s^j.$$
where $\eta_h^-(s)=t_k$ on $(t_k,t_{k+1}]$ and
$\sigma_{\cdot j}$ denotes column $j$ of the matrix.

The justified-by theorem
[[thm-euler-maruyama-uniform-moment-and-increment-bounds]] establishes the
required integrability and well-definedness under the stated coefficient and
initial-moment conditions.

Assume the coefficient, filtered Brownian-motion, and initial-value
hypotheses of [[alg-euler-maruyama]] on a uniform grid with $0<h\le1$ and
$N=T/h\in\mathbb N$, with $\mathbb E|X_0|^p<\infty$ for a fixed finite
$p\ge2$. Let $Y_k$, $\bar Y$,
and $Y_t$ be the recursion, step process, and continuous interpolation of
[[def-euler-maruyama-step-process-and-continuous-interpolation]]. Then the
step process has a predictable representative, the interpolation formula
is well-defined, and $Y$ is adapted and continuous. There is a constant
$C_{p,T,L,K,d,m}$ independent of $h$ such that
$$\max_{0\le k\le N}\mathbb E|Y_k|^p+\sup_{0\le t\le T}\mathbb E|\bar Y_t|^p+\sup_{0\le t\le T}\mathbb E|Y_t|^p\le C_{p,T,L,K,d,m}(1+\mathbb E|X_0|^p).$$
For every $t\in[0,T]$,
$$\mathbb E|Y_t-\bar Y_t|^2\le C_{T,K,d,m}h(1+\mathbb E|X_0|^2).$$
These are pointwise-in-time moment bounds; no claim is made about
$\mathbb E\sup_{t\le T}|Y_t|^p$. The estimates hold under the shared
half-Hölder time-modulus contract, although this proof uses only the
uniform linear-growth bound and the Brownian increment assumptions.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Fix a horizon $T>0$ and let
$\mathcal P_T$ be the predictable sigma-algebra on $[0,T]\times\Omega$
[[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]]. Let $H$ be a
predictable process with
$$E\int_0^TH_s^2\,ds=\int_{[0,T]\times\Omega}H^2\,d(\mathrm dt\otimes P)<\infty ,$$
so that $H$ is an element of the quotient space
$L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)$ over $\mathcal P_T$; its class is what is integrated.
The **Ito integral** $\int_0^TH_s\,dB_s$, also written $H\cdot B$ or $I_T(H)$,
is defined as follows.

1. **Construction.** By the density theorem
   [[thm-density-of-elementary-predictable-processes-in-predictable-l2]] there
   is a sequence $(H^n)$ of bounded elementary predictable integrands
   [[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]] with
   $\|H^n-H\|_{L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)}\to0$. For such a sequence the
   elementary integrals $I_T(H^n)$
   [[def-ito-integral-of-an-elementary-predictable-process]] form a Cauchy
   sequence in $L^2(P)$: by the elementary isometry
   [[thm-ito-isometry-for-elementary-integrands]] and the well-definedness of
   the elementary integral,
   $$E\bigl(I_T(H^n)-I_T(H^m)\bigr)^2=E\int_0^T(H^n-H^m)^2ds=\|H^n-H^m\|^2_{L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)} ,$$
   and the right-hand side tends to $0$. Since $L^2(P)$ is complete
   [[thm-riesz-fischer-completeness-of-l-p]], the classes $I_T(H^n)$ converge
   in $L^2(P)$; the limit is a class in $L^2(P)$, and
   $$\int_0^TH_s\,dB_s:=\lim_{n\to\infty}I_T(H^n)\qquad\text{in }L^2(P).$$
   The limit is a random variable only up to almost-sure equality; statements
   about it are statements about that class. The limit does not depend on the
   chosen sequence: if another elementary sequence $K^n\to H$ is used, then
   the elementary isometry and linearity give
   $$\|I_T(H^n)-I_T(K^n)\|_{L^2(P)} =\|H^n-K^n\|_{L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)} \le\|H^n-H\|_2+\|K^n-H\|_2\longrightarrow0,$$
   so the two $L^2(P)$ limits agree.

2. **Integrals at a time.** For $t\in[0,T]$ put
   $\int_0^tH_s\,dB_s:=\int_0^TH_s1_{[0,t]}(s)\,dB_s$, the construction of
   clause 1 applied to the truncated process $H1_{[0,t]}$. That process is
   predictable: $H$ is $\mathcal P_T$-measurable and $1_{[0,t]}$ is a
   deterministic predictable indicator, so the product is
   $\mathcal P_T$-measurable; and it is square-integrable because
   $|H1_{[0,t]}|\le|H|$ pointwise. The same construction applied to $H$
   itself gives $t=T$. The family
   $\bigl(\int_0^tH\,dB\bigr)_{t\in[0,T]}$ is a family of $L^2(P)$-classes
   indexed by $t$; its continuous version is supplied by item 13, and no path
   property is asserted by this definition.

3. **Consistency with elementary integrands.** If $H$ is itself elementary,
   then the constant sequence $H^n:=H$ is admissible in clause 1, so
   $\int_0^TH\,dB$ is the limit of the constant sequence of elementary sums,
   namely the elementary sum $I_T(H)$ of
   [[def-ito-integral-of-an-elementary-predictable-process]]. The same argument
   with $H1_{[0,t]}$ in place of $H$, and the finite telescoping of the
   elementary sum over a refinement containing $t$, gives
   $\int_0^tH\,dB=I_t(H)$ for every $t\in[0,T]$. In particular the general
   definition extends, rather than replaces, the elementary definition.

4. **Linearity in the integrand is not asserted here.** Clause 1 defines each
   integral separately from an arbitrary approximating sequence; the linear and
   isometric properties of the extension are item 12. Until item 12 is proved,
   linearity may be used only for elementary integrands, where it is part of
   [[def-ito-integral-of-an-elementary-predictable-process]].

5. **Comparison with deterministic Riemann integration.** The integral is a
   stochastic integral: the integrand is paired with the Brownian path through
   left-endpoint sums and an $L^2(P)$ limit. This definition does not assert
   convergence of arbitrary tagged Riemann--Stieltjes sums for a general
   predictable integrand. Particular integrands can have a pathwise
   interpretation: for $H\equiv1$ every tagged sum telescopes to $B_T-B_0$,
   which is also its Ito integral by clause 3 (the value at time zero is
   irrelevant to its product-measure class). The notation $\int_0^TH\,dB$
   here always refers to the $L^2(P)$-class defined above.

The Axiom of Choice is declared because the construction selects an
approximating sequence and uses the completeness and conditional-expectation
interfaces that assume it; the inherited obligations are declared as
dependencies of this item. An alternative construction that avoids selecting the sequence is
not needed, because clause 1 shows every sequence gives the same class.

Assume the Axiom of Choice as required by the stochastic-integral interfaces
below. Fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$ and finite integers $d,m\ge1$. Work on
a complete filtered probability space
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{0\le t\le T},P)$ whose filtration is
right-continuous and contains every $P$-null subset of $\mathcal F$ in
$\mathcal F_0$ (the usual conditions).

Let $W=(W_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ be a standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion
[[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]] adapted to this filtration, with
$W_t-W_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and distributed as
$N_m(0,(t-s)I_m)$ for $0\le s<t\le T$. Let
$X_0:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$ be $\mathcal F_0$-measurable, satisfy
$E|X_0|^2<\infty$, and be independent of the future Brownian increments.
Explicitly, $X_0$ is independent of the sigma-algebra
$\sigma(W_t-W_0:0\le t\le T)$.

Continuity of a process means continuity on one measurable event of
probability one. We use an everywhere-continuous adapted representative: if
the chosen process is continuous only on such an event $A$, replace it off $A$
by its initial value. Since $A^c$ is a null set and the filtration is complete,
$A^c\in\mathcal F_0$; the replacement preserves adaptedness and changes the
SDE identity only on a null event, hence preserves it up to
indistinguishability.

The drift and diffusion coefficients are jointly Borel maps
$$b:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d,\qquad \sigma:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}.$$
For nonnegative finite constants $L,K$, assume for every $t\in[0,T]$ and
$x,y\in\mathbb R^d$ that
$$|b(t,x)-b(t,y)|+\|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(t,y)\|_F\le L|x-y|,$$
$$|b(t,x)|+\|\sigma(t,x)\|_F\le K(1+|x|).$$
Here $|\cdot|$ is the Euclidean norm and
$\|A\|_F^2=\sum_{i=1}^d\sum_{k=1}^m|A^{ik}|^2$ is the Frobenius norm.

For an adapted continuous candidate $X:[0,T]\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$,
the vector Itô equation
$$X_t=X_0+\int_0^t b(s,X_s)\,ds+\left(\sum_{k=1}^m\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}(s,X_s)\,dW_s^k\right)_{i=1}^d,\qquad 0\le t\le T.$$
uses a pathwise Lebesgue integral for the drift and, in each coordinate, the
localized Itô integral from
[[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]], clause 2. Require
$\int_0^T|b(s,X_s)|ds<\infty$ and
$\int_0^T\|\sigma(s,X_s)\|_F^2ds<\infty$ almost surely; these are the local
coefficient-integrability conditions in that definition. When a coordinate
integrand has finite expected energy, its integral is the square-integrable
Itô integral of [[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]];
the Picard estimates below establish that stronger condition for every input
in $\mathcal H_T$. Equality of processes means
equality for every $t$ on one measurable event of probability one, that is,
indistinguishability
[[def-law-modification-and-indistinguishability-of-processes]]. A **strong
solution on $[0,T]$** is an adapted continuous process satisfying this
integral equation indistinguishably. No moment bound is included in the
definition; the existence theorem proves its $L^2$ path-sup bound.
The usual-filtration, continuity, and finite-coordinate conventions agree
with the multidimensional class of continuous Brownian Itô processes
[[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]. This definition makes no ellipticity,
transition-density, forward-equation, or time-reversal assertion.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Let $H$ be a predictable
process with $E\int_0^TH_s^2ds<\infty$ for every finite $T$. Then there is an
adapted process $M=(M_t)_{t\ge0}$ with continuous paths such that
$M_t=\int_0^tH_s\,dB_s$ almost surely for every $t\ge0$
[[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]], and $M$ is a
square-integrable martingale relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$
[[def-continuous-time-adapted-process-and-martingale]]: $EM_t^2=E\int_0^tH_s^2ds<\infty$
for every $t$. Any two such continuous versions agree at every time on one
measurable event of probability one; in particular the continuous version is
unique in this common-full-measure-event sense, and it is the only continuous
square-integrable martingale whose value at each deterministic $t$ is the
integral class.

This conclusion is deliberately distinguished from the exact definition of
indistinguishability in
[[def-law-modification-and-indistinguishability-of-processes]]. On a
noncomplete probability space the full equality set, although it contains the
measurable probability-one event constructed below, need not itself be
measurable. On a complete probability space the two notions coincide, because
the complement of the equality set is then a measurable subset of a null set.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: The functions $b=1$ and $\sigma=1$ are jointly Borel, globally Lipschitz in state with constant $0$, and satisfy the stated linear-growth bound with a finite $K$. Their time increments vanish, so the required half-Hölder time modulus holds. The deterministic initial value $X_0=0$ is $\mathcal F_0$-measurable, independent of future Brownian increments, and has every finite moment.

From [F1], induction gives $Y_k=kh+W_{kh}$. Substituting the coefficients into [F2] gives $Y_t=kh+(t-kh)+W_{kh}+W_t-W_{kh}=t+W_t$ on every interval. By [F4], at every fixed time the candidate path $X_t=t+W_t$ satisfies the integral equation. The continuous-version theorem [F6] and equality at all rational times identify these processes indistinguishably; hence [F5] makes this adapted continuous candidate a strong solution. Any strong solution with the same data equals $t+W_t$ directly from the constant-coefficient equation, so this is the exact path.

The initial value $X_0=0$ has every finite moment. Applying [F3] for each finite $p\ge2$ therefore proves finite moments of the grid, step, and interpolated processes uniformly in $n$ and $t\le1$. The explicit identity $Y_t=t+W_t$ from step 1.2 also identifies the exact path. AC in [A1] is inherited from the cited interfaces; no choice enters these computations.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and use the finite-dimensional Brownian-motion
convention of [[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]]. Let the state dimension
$d$ and noise dimension $m$ be positive finite integers, and fix $T>0$ and
$N\in\mathbb N$ with $N\ge1$. Set $h=T/N>0$ and $t_k=kh$ for
$0\le k\le N$. Let
$b:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ and
$\sigma:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}$ be jointly Borel.
Write $|\cdot|$ for the Euclidean norm and $\|\cdot\|_F$ for the Frobenius
norm. Suppose finite constants $L,K$ satisfy, for every $s,t\in[0,T]$ and
$x,y\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$|b(t,x)-b(t,y)|+\|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(t,y)\|_F\le L|x-y|,$$
$$|b(t,x)|^2+\|\sigma(t,x)\|_F^2\le K^2(1+|x|^2),$$
and
$$|b(t,x)-b(s,x)|+\|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(s,x)\|_F\le K(1+|x|)|t-s|^{1/2}.$$
Let $W$ be an adapted standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion on a filtered
probability space, with $W_t-W_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and law
$N_m(0,(t-s)I_m)$ whenever $0\le s<t\le T$. Let $X_0$ be
$\mathcal F_0$-measurable, independent of future Brownian increments, and
$\mathbb E|X_0|^2<\infty$.

The **Euler–Maruyama algorithm** takes these data as input and returns
$Y_0,\ldots,Y_N$:

1. Set $Y_0=X_0$.
2. For $k=0,\ldots,N-1$, form $\Delta W_k=W_{t_{k+1}}-W_{t_k}$ and set
   $$Y_{k+1}=Y_k+b(t_k,Y_k)h+\sigma(t_k,Y_k)\Delta W_k.$$

The output is the grid approximation for the coefficient pair $(b,\sigma)$.
The companion step-process and interpolation definition uses this same grid
and endpoint convention.

Assume the coefficient, filtered Brownian-motion, and initial-value
hypotheses of [[alg-euler-maruyama]] on a uniform grid with $0<h\le1$ and
$N=T/h\in\mathbb N$, with $\mathbb E|X_0|^p<\infty$ for a fixed finite
$p\ge2$. Let $Y_k$, $\bar Y$,
and $Y_t$ be the recursion, step process, and continuous interpolation of
[[def-euler-maruyama-step-process-and-continuous-interpolation]]. Then the
step process has a predictable representative, the interpolation formula
is well-defined, and $Y$ is adapted and continuous. There is a constant
$C_{p,T,L,K,d,m}$ independent of $h$ such that
$$\max_{0\le k\le N}\mathbb E|Y_k|^p+\sup_{0\le t\le T}\mathbb E|\bar Y_t|^p+\sup_{0\le t\le T}\mathbb E|Y_t|^p\le C_{p,T,L,K,d,m}(1+\mathbb E|X_0|^p).$$
For every $t\in[0,T]$,
$$\mathbb E|Y_t-\bar Y_t|^2\le C_{T,K,d,m}h(1+\mathbb E|X_0|^2).$$
These are pointwise-in-time moment bounds; no claim is made about
$\mathbb E\sup_{t\le T}|Y_t|^p$. The estimates hold under the shared
half-Hölder time-modulus contract, although this proof uses only the
uniform linear-growth bound and the Brownian increment assumptions.
