Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Let
$X_t=X_0+\int_0^tb_s\,ds+\int_0^t\sigma_s\,dB_s$ be a real continuous Brownian
Ito process [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]], under its usual-filtration
conditions, and let
$f\in C^{1,2}([0,\infty)\times\mathbb R)$, meaning that $f$, its first time
derivative $\partial_tf$ and its first two space derivatives
$\partial_xf,\partial^2_{x}f$ exist and are continuous on
$[0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$. Then, up to indistinguishability, for every
$t\ge0$
$$f(t,X_t)=f(0,X_0)+\int_0^t\Bigl(\partial_tf+b\,\partial_xf+\tfrac12\sigma^2\partial^2_xf\Bigr)(s,X_s)\,ds+\int_0^t\sigma_s\,\partial_xf(s,X_s)\,dB_s,$$
For the displayed integrands use the following representative convention.
Intersect the measurable full events of continuity of $X$, validity of its
decomposition, and local integrability of its coefficients at integer horizons.
Its complement is an $\mathcal F_0$-measurable null event by the usual
conditions. Replace $X,X_0,b,\sigma$ by zero there. This preserves the
decomposition up to indistinguishability and all coefficient classes, and
makes $X$ continuous everywhere and its coefficient path integrals locally
finite everywhere. All integrands below refer to these representatives.
The stochastic integral is the localized Ito integral of the predictable
locally square-integrable process $\sigma_s\partial_xf(s,X_s)$
[[thm-localized-ito-integral]] and the Lebesgue integral is the pathwise
integral of the progressively measurable process
$s\mapsto(\partial_tf+b\partial_xf+\tfrac12\sigma^2\partial^2_xf)(s,X_s)$,
which is pathwise integrable and finite almost surely for every $t$. In differential notation,
$df(t,X_t)=(\partial_tf+b\partial_xf+\tfrac12\sigma^2\partial^2_xf)(t,X_t)\,dt+\sigma_t\partial_xf(t,X_t)\,dB_t$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Fix $T>0$ and let
$h\in L^2[0,T]$ be deterministic, choose a Borel representative of its
Lebesgue-equivalence class, and set $h(s,\omega):=h(s)$. This process is
predictable with finite energy. Then the Ito integral
$\int_0^Th_s\,dB_s$
[[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]] is centered
normal with variance $\int_0^Th^2ds$: its law is $N(0,\int_0^Th^2ds)$ in the
convention of [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]], where $N(0,0)$ is the
Dirac law at $0$. More generally, for deterministic $h_1,\dots,h_d\in L^2[0,T]$
the vector of integrals is jointly Gaussian in the sense of
[[def-multivariate-normal-law]]: its law is $N_d(0,\Sigma)$ with
$$\Sigma_{jk}=\int_0^Th_j(s)h_k(s)\,ds .$$
In particular the covariance of the pair is
$\operatorname{Cov}(\int h_jdB,\int h_kdB)=\int h_jh_k$, the integrals are
uncorrelated exactly when $\int h_jh_k=0$, and integrals of deterministic
integrands with disjoint supports are independent.

Assume AC. If $X$ has law $N(m,\sigma^2)$ with $\sigma\ge0$, then $\varphi_X(t)=\exp(imt-\sigma^2t^2/2)$ for every real $t$. Moreover $\mathbb EX=m$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\sigma^2$, including $\sigma=0$.

Use the data and grid of [[alg-euler-maruyama]], and let
$Y_0,\ldots,Y_N$ be its recursion. The left-endpoint map is
$$\eta_h(t)=\max\{t_k:t_k\le t\},\qquad 0\le t\le T.$$
The right-continuous step process is
$$\bar Y_t=Y_k\quad(t_k\le t<t_{k+1}),\qquad \bar Y_T=Y_N.$$
The continuous interpolation is the pathwise process
$$Y_t=Y_k+b(t_k,Y_k)(t-t_k)+\sigma(t_k,Y_k)(W_t-W_{t_k})\quad(t_k\le t\le t_{k+1}).$$
At a shared grid endpoint the formulas agree because the recursion gives
$Y_{k+1}=Y_k+b(t_k,Y_k)h+\sigma(t_k,Y_k)(W_{t_{k+1}}-W_{t_k})$.
In particular $Y_{t_k}=Y_k$ for every $k$, including $Y_T=Y_N$.

For stochastic integration, define the predictable left-endpoint version by
$\bar Y^-_0=Y_0$ and $\bar Y^-_s=Y_k$ on $(t_k,t_{k+1}]$, and set
$\eta_h^-(0)=0$ and $\eta_h^-(s)=t_k$ on $(t_k,t_{k+1}]$. Its coefficient
integrands use the same fixed left endpoints. When the recursion is adapted,
each coordinate of $\bar Y^-$ and each coefficient composition is a
predictable finite-step process: on $(t_k,t_{k+1}]$ its value is
$\mathcal F_{t_k}$-measurable. These coefficients need not be bounded, so the
integrands need not be elementary in the bounded-coefficient sense of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Values at the finitely many
grid points do not change either integral. Once square integrability is
established, [[lem-square-integrable-predictable-step-ito-integral-is-finite-sum]]
identifies each finite-coordinate Itô integral of
[[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]] with its
finite-sum version, giving the equivalent formula
$$Y_t=X_0+\int_0^t b(\eta_h^-(s),\bar Y^-_s)\,ds+\sum_{j=1}^m\int_0^t \sigma_{\cdot j}(\eta_h^-(s),\bar Y^-_s)\,dW_s^j.$$
where $\eta_h^-(s)=t_k$ on $(t_k,t_{k+1}]$ and
$\sigma_{\cdot j}$ denotes column $j$ of the matrix.

The justified-by theorem
[[thm-euler-maruyama-uniform-moment-and-increment-bounds]] establishes the
required integrability and well-definedness under the stated coefficient and
initial-moment conditions.

Assume the coefficient, filtered Brownian-motion, and initial-value
hypotheses of [[alg-euler-maruyama]] on a uniform grid with $0<h\le1$ and
$N=T/h\in\mathbb N$, with $\mathbb E|X_0|^p<\infty$ for a fixed finite
$p\ge2$. Let $Y_k$, $\bar Y$,
and $Y_t$ be the recursion, step process, and continuous interpolation of
[[def-euler-maruyama-step-process-and-continuous-interpolation]]. Then the
step process has a predictable representative, the interpolation formula
is well-defined, and $Y$ is adapted and continuous. There is a constant
$C_{p,T,L,K,d,m}$ independent of $h$ such that
$$\max_{0\le k\le N}\mathbb E|Y_k|^p+\sup_{0\le t\le T}\mathbb E|\bar Y_t|^p+\sup_{0\le t\le T}\mathbb E|Y_t|^p\le C_{p,T,L,K,d,m}(1+\mathbb E|X_0|^p).$$
For every $t\in[0,T]$,
$$\mathbb E|Y_t-\bar Y_t|^2\le C_{T,K,d,m}h(1+\mathbb E|X_0|^2).$$
These are pointwise-in-time moment bounds; no claim is made about
$\mathbb E\sup_{t\le T}|Y_t|^p$. The estimates hold under the shared
half-Hölder time-modulus contract, although this proof uses only the
uniform linear-growth bound and the Brownian increment assumptions.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. If $0\le s,t$ and a real random variable
$X_t-X_s$ has law $N(0,|t-s|)$, then, for every integer $m\ge1$,
$$E|X_t-X_s|^{2m}=c_m|t-s|^m,$$
where
$$c_m=E|Z|^{2m}=(2m-1)!!=1\cdot3\cdots(2m-1)<\infty$$
for $Z\sim N(0,1)$. In particular, when $m\ge2$, this is the moment hypothesis
of the one-parameter Kolmogorov criterion with
$\alpha=2m$, $\beta=m-1$, and $C_T=c_m$.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d,m\ge1$ be finite, fix $T>0$, and work on
the complete usual filtered probability space of
[[def-ito-sde-and-strong-solution]]. Take $0<h\le1$ with $N=T/h\in\mathbb N$.
Let $W$ be an adapted standard
$m$-dimensional Brownian motion with increments independent of the current
filtration. Use Euclidean state norms and the Frobenius matrix norm, and write
$A:B=\operatorname{tr}(A^{\mathsf T}B)$. Let
$b:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ and
$\sigma:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}$ be jointly Borel,
globally Lipschitz in state, of uniform linear growth, and satisfy the
half-Hölder time modulus in [[alg-euler-maruyama]]. Let $X_0$ be
$\mathcal F_0$-measurable, independent of $\sigma(W_t-W_0:0\le t\le T)$, with
$\mathbb E|X_0|^p<\infty$ for some $p\ge2q+8$, where $q\ge0$ is finite;
when $q=0$, use the convention $|x|^q=1$.
Let $X$ be the exact strong solution and $Y^h,\bar Y^h$ the continuous
Euler interpolation and step process of
[[def-euler-maruyama-step-process-and-continuous-interpolation]].

For a bounded Borel payoff $\varphi:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$, define
$$u(t,x)=\mathbb E\bigl[\varphi(X_T^{t,x})\bigr],$$
where $X^{t,x}$ is the unique shifted strong solution started from $x$ at time
$t$, supplied by [[thm-global-strong-well-posedness-for-lipschitz-ito-sdes]]. Set
$$L_t v(x)=b(t,x)\cdot\nabla v(x)+\tfrac12\bigl(\sigma(t,x)\sigma(t,x)^{\mathsf T}\bigr):D_x^2v(x).$$
Assume $u(T,x)=\varphi(x)$ and $(\partial_t+L_t)u=0$ on
$[0,T)\times\mathbb R^d$. A multi-index is $\alpha=(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_d)$
with nonnegative integer entries and $|\alpha|=\sum_i\alpha_i$. Assume every
mixed derivative
$\partial_t^jD_x^\alpha u$ with $0\le j\le2$ and $|\alpha|\le4$ exists,
is continuous, and satisfies
$$|\partial_t^jD_x^\alpha u(t,x)|\le C_u(1+|x|^q)$$
for a common constant $C_u$. Finally, assume the exact and Euler processes
have uniform pointwise moments of order $p$ on $[0,T]$; the Euler bounds are
provided by [[thm-euler-maruyama-uniform-moment-and-increment-bounds]] and the
exact bound by the P-SDE-01 moment contract. Then
$$\bigl|\mathbb E\varphi(X_T)-\mathbb E\varphi(Y_N^h)\bigr|\le C h,$$
where $C$ is independent of $h$. The theorem is conditional on the stated
backward regularity; it does not derive that regularity from coefficient or
payoff smoothness.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Apply [F1] to $e^tX_t$. The drift terms cancel, so $X_t=\int_0^t e^{-(t-s)}dW_s.$ For a solution started at $(t,x)$, the same calculation gives $X_1^{t,x}=r(t)x+\int_t^1 e^{-(1-s)}dW_s.$ By [F2], the last integral is $N(0,(1-r(t)^2)/2)$.

Since $r'=r$ and $A(t):=e^{-(1-r(t)^2)/4}$ satisfies $A'/A=r^2/2$, direct differentiation gives $u_t=A\left(\frac{r^2}{2}\cos(rx)-rx\sin(rx)\right), \qquad u_x=-Ar\sin(rx), \qquad u_{xx}=-Ar^2\cos(rx).$ For the generator $L=-x\partial_x+\frac12\partial_{xx}$, these formulas imply $(\partial_t+L)u=0$. Every mixed derivative $\partial_t^j\partial_x^ku$ with $j\le2$, $k\le4$ is a finite sum of bounded smooth coefficient functions times $x^a\sin(rx)$ or $x^a\cos(rx)$ with $a\le2$; hence it is bounded by $C(1+|x|^2)$. The backward contract holds with $q=2$.

By [F3], for that normal variable $Z$, $\mathbb E e^{iZ}=e^{-(1-r^2)/4}$. Taking the real part after multiplying by $e^{irx}$ gives $\mathbb E\cos(X_1^{t,x}) =e^{-(1-r(t)^2)/4}\cos(r(t)x)=u(t,x).$ Thus $u$ is the stated backward value function and $u(1,x)=\cos x$.

The exact process is centered normal at each time with variance $(1-e^{-2t})/2\le1/2$ by [F2], so [F6] at order $12$ gives $E|X_t|^{12}=11!!\{(1-e^{-2t})/2\}^6\le11!!/64$ uniformly in $t\in[0,1]$, including $t=0$. For the Euler process, $b(x)=-x$ is globally Lipschitz with linear growth, $\sigma(x)=1$ is globally Lipschitz with linear growth, the time modulus is zero, and $X_0=0$ has every moment. Applying [F5] at $p=12$ therefore gives uniform pointwise 12th moments for $Y^h$ and $\bar Y^h$. The threshold is $p=12=2q+8$.

The payoff is bounded and $1$-Lipschitz. By [F4], the interpolation agrees with the Euler recursion at $T$, so the conclusion of [F7] applies to $Y_N^h$. Steps 2.1–2.2 verify its backward regularity and moment premises, giving $|\mathbb E\cos(X_1)-\mathbb E\cos(Y_N^h)|\le Ch$. AC is inherited through [A1].

Assume the Axiom of Choice and let $d\ge1$ be a finite integer. An
$\mathbb R^d$-valued process $B=(B_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **standard
$d$-dimensional Brownian motion** if:

1. $B_0=0$ almost surely;
2. for every finite list $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_n$, the vector increments
   $$B_{t_j}-B_{t_{j-1}},\qquad 1\le j\le n,$$
   are mutually independent and have laws
   $N_d(0,(t_j-t_{j-1})I_d)$; and
3. there is one measurable event $A$ with $P(A)=1$ such that
   $t\mapsto B_t(\omega)$ is continuous from $[0,\infty)$ to
   $\mathbb R^d$ for every $\omega\in A$.

Equivalently, its $d$ coordinate processes $B^\alpha=(B_t^\alpha)_{t\ge0}$
are independent standard one-dimensional Brownian motions. Here independence
of the processes means the following precise assertion. Put
$I=[0,\infty)$ and equip $\mathbb R^I$ with its cylinder sigma-algebra. The
maps
$$ \Phi_\alpha:\Omega\longrightarrow\mathbb R^I, \qquad \Phi_\alpha(\omega)(t)=B_t^\alpha(\omega), \qquad 1\le\alpha\le d, $$
are independent random elements.

Assume AC. If $X$ has law $N(m,\sigma^2)$ with $\sigma\ge0$, then $\varphi_X(t)=\exp(imt-\sigma^2t^2/2)$ for every real $t$. Moreover $\mathbb EX=m$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\sigma^2$, including $\sigma=0$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and use the finite-dimensional Brownian-motion
convention of [[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]]. Let the state dimension
$d$ and noise dimension $m$ be positive finite integers, and fix $T>0$ and
$N\in\mathbb N$ with $N\ge1$. Set $h=T/N>0$ and $t_k=kh$ for
$0\le k\le N$. Let
$b:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ and
$\sigma:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}$ be jointly Borel.
Write $|\cdot|$ for the Euclidean norm and $\|\cdot\|_F$ for the Frobenius
norm. Suppose finite constants $L,K$ satisfy, for every $s,t\in[0,T]$ and
$x,y\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$|b(t,x)-b(t,y)|+\|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(t,y)\|_F\le L|x-y|,$$
$$|b(t,x)|^2+\|\sigma(t,x)\|_F^2\le K^2(1+|x|^2),$$
and
$$|b(t,x)-b(s,x)|+\|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(s,x)\|_F\le K(1+|x|)|t-s|^{1/2}.$$
Let $W$ be an adapted standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion on a filtered
probability space, with $W_t-W_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and law
$N_m(0,(t-s)I_m)$ whenever $0\le s<t\le T$. Let $X_0$ be
$\mathcal F_0$-measurable, independent of future Brownian increments, and
$\mathbb E|X_0|^2<\infty$.

The **Euler–Maruyama algorithm** takes these data as input and returns
$Y_0,\ldots,Y_N$:

1. Set $Y_0=X_0$.
2. For $k=0,\ldots,N-1$, form $\Delta W_k=W_{t_{k+1}}-W_{t_k}$ and set
   $$Y_{k+1}=Y_k+b(t_k,Y_k)h+\sigma(t_k,Y_k)\Delta W_k.$$

The output is the grid approximation for the coefficient pair $(b,\sigma)$.
The companion step-process and interpolation definition uses this same grid
and endpoint convention.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d,m\ge1$ be finite, fix $T>0$, and work on
the complete usual filtered probability space of
[[def-ito-sde-and-strong-solution]]. Let $0<h\le1$ with $N=T/h\in\mathbb N$.
Use Euclidean state norms and the Frobenius matrix norm. Let $W$ be an adapted
standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion whose increments are independent of
the current filtration. Let
$b:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ and
$\sigma:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}$ be jointly Borel,
and suppose finite nonnegative constants $L,K$ satisfy, for all $s,t\in[0,T]$ and
$x,y\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$|b(t,x)-b(t,y)|+\|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(t,y)\|_F\le L|x-y|,$$
$$|b(t,x)|^2+\|\sigma(t,x)\|_F^2\le K^2(1+|x|^2),$$
and
$$|b(t,x)-b(s,x)|+\|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(s,x)\|_F \le K(1+|x|)|t-s|^{1/2}.$$
Let $X_0$ be $\mathcal F_0$-measurable, independent of
$\sigma(W_t-W_0:0\le t\le T)$, with $\mathbb E|X_0|^2<\infty$. Let $X$ be the exact continuous
strong solution with
$$\mathbb E\sup_{t\le T}|X_t|^2<\infty,$$
and let $Y^h,\bar Y^h$ be the continuous Euler interpolation and left-endpoint
step process of
[[def-euler-maruyama-step-process-and-continuous-interpolation]]. The
uniform pointwise moment and interpolation-increment bounds of
[[thm-euler-maruyama-uniform-moment-and-increment-bounds]] then imply that a
constant $C$, independent of $h$, satisfies
$$\mathbb E\sup_{0\le t\le T}|X_t-Y_t^h|^2\le Ch.$$
Thus the grid-point root-mean-square error is $O(h^{1/2})$. The constant may
depend on $T,d,m,L,K$ and the exact-solution supremum-moment bound supplied by
the P-SDE-01 existence theorem.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: The target equation has terminal value $X_1=W_1$. By [F1]–[F2], $\mathbb E\cos(X_1)=\operatorname{Re}\mathbb E e^{iW_1}=e^{-1/2}.$ The learned Euler recursion is $\widehat Y_{k+1}=\widehat Y_k+(\pi/2)h+\Delta W_k$. Summing its $N$ increments gives $\widehat Y_N=\frac\pi2 Nh+\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\Delta W_k=\frac\pi2+W_1,$ which is exactly $\widehat X_1$ for every $h=1/N$. Thus the discretization error relative to the learned equation is zero.

By [F2] and the addition formula, $\mathbb E\cos(\widehat X_1) =\operatorname{Re}\left(e^{i\pi/2}\mathbb E e^{iW_1}\right)=0.$ Therefore the absolute expectation bias relative to the target is $|0-e^{-1/2}|=e^{-1/2}>0$ for every step size, so it persists as $h\to0$. The solver theorem [F4] controls error to the learned SDE solution; it supplies no bound on the difference between the learned and target drifts. AC is inherited through [A1].

Verification step 1.1 gives exactly zero discretization error to the learned SDE for every h, while step 2.1 proves the target expectation bias is e^(-1/2)>0.
Example: one-dimensional Brownian motion drives both scalar equations; the finite sum in Verification step 1.1 also works for N=1.
Example fixes X_0=hat X_0=0 deterministically and sigma=1, and the exact constant learned drift pi/2 makes the solver terminal value exact.
Verification step 1.1 sums N increments over [0,1] to W_1; the step-size limit in step 2.1 preserves the positive bias instead of removing it.
Verification step 2.1 explicitly attributes AC to A1 and the normal characteristic-function interface; neither model nor its coupling is selected from a family.

finite_checks.claim: For N=2, Euler is exact for the constant learned drift and the cosine payoff bias relative to the target is e^(−1/2).
finite_checks.result: Summing two updates gives Yhat2=π/2+W1. The target cosine mean is e^(−1/2), while the learned cosine mean is Re(i e^(−1/2))=0; the absolute bias is e^(−1/2)>0.

Assume AC and the finite-$L^2$ coefficient and initial-value hypotheses of
[[thm-euler-maruyama-strong-rate-for-square-integrable-initial-data]]. Fix an
integer refinement factor $M\ge2$ and a fine step $h$ with $0<h\le1/M$,
$T/h\in\mathbb N$, and $T/(Mh)\in\mathbb N$. Construct the fine and coarse
Euler paths with the same initial value and Brownian motion. The coarse
Brownian increment over each coarse interval is, by definition, the sum of
the $M$ fine Brownian increments in that interval. Let $X_T$ be the common
exact solution, and let $\varphi:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be globally
Lipschitz with constant $L_\varphi$. Then constants independent of $h$ satisfy
$$\mathbb E|Y_T^h-Y_T^{Mh}|^2\le C_M h,$$
$$\operatorname{Var}\bigl(\varphi(Y_T^h)-\varphi(Y_T^{Mh})\bigr)\le C_ML_\varphi^2h, \qquad |\mathbb E\varphi(X_T)-\mathbb E\varphi(Y_T^h)|\le C L_\varphi h^{1/2}.$$
Thus the Lipschitz-payoff Euler level pair has correction variance exponent
$\beta=1$ and strong-error bias exponent $\alpha=1/2$. If, in addition,
$\varphi$ is bounded and its backward value function satisfies the hypotheses
of [[thm-euler-maruyama-weak-order-one-under-backward-regularity]], then the
bias bound improves to $|\mathbb E\varphi(X_T)-\mathbb E\varphi(Y_T^h)|\le Ch$,
so $\alpha=1$ while $\beta=1$ remains. With fixed dimension, fixed $M$, and
unit-cost coefficient and payoff evaluations, one coupled fine/coarse sample
has work $O(h^{-1})$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Let
$X_t=X_0+\int_0^tb_s\,ds+\int_0^t\sigma_s\,dB_s$ be a real continuous Brownian
Ito process [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]], under its usual-filtration
conditions, and let
$f\in C^{1,2}([0,\infty)\times\mathbb R)$, meaning that $f$, its first time
derivative $\partial_tf$ and its first two space derivatives
$\partial_xf,\partial^2_{x}f$ exist and are continuous on
$[0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$. Then, up to indistinguishability, for every
$t\ge0$
$$f(t,X_t)=f(0,X_0)+\int_0^t\Bigl(\partial_tf+b\,\partial_xf+\tfrac12\sigma^2\partial^2_xf\Bigr)(s,X_s)\,ds+\int_0^t\sigma_s\,\partial_xf(s,X_s)\,dB_s,$$
For the displayed integrands use the following representative convention.
Intersect the measurable full events of continuity of $X$, validity of its
decomposition, and local integrability of its coefficients at integer horizons.
Its complement is an $\mathcal F_0$-measurable null event by the usual
conditions. Replace $X,X_0,b,\sigma$ by zero there. This preserves the
decomposition up to indistinguishability and all coefficient classes, and
makes $X$ continuous everywhere and its coefficient path integrals locally
finite everywhere. All integrands below refer to these representatives.
The stochastic integral is the localized Ito integral of the predictable
locally square-integrable process $\sigma_s\partial_xf(s,X_s)$
[[thm-localized-ito-integral]] and the Lebesgue integral is the pathwise
integral of the progressively measurable process
$s\mapsto(\partial_tf+b\partial_xf+\tfrac12\sigma^2\partial^2_xf)(s,X_s)$,
which is pathwise integrable and finite almost surely for every $t$. In differential notation,
$df(t,X_t)=(\partial_tf+b\partial_xf+\tfrac12\sigma^2\partial^2_xf)(t,X_t)\,dt+\sigma_t\partial_xf(t,X_t)\,dB_t$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Let $H$ be a predictable
process on $[0,T]$, where $T\ge0$, with $E\int_0^TH_s^2ds<\infty$. Extend $H$ by zero after $T$ when applying the global continuous-version theorem, and let
$M_t=\int_0^tH_s\,dB_s$ be the continuous version of
[[thm-ito-integral-process-has-a-continuous-martingale-version]]. Then
$$E\sup_{0\le t\le T}|M_t|^2\le4\,E\int_0^TH_s^2\,ds .$$
The left-hand side is finite and does not depend on the chosen version, since
any two continuous versions are indistinguishable. Every continuous version of
the integral process satisfies the same bound. The path supremum in this
expectation means its measurable version $S_D=\sup_{q\in D}|M_q|$ on the
countable scaled dyadic grid $D$ (including both endpoints). Continuity
identifies it with the path supremum on a measurable event of probability one.
Indistinguishability here uses that full-event convention, as in the cited
continuous-version theorem, without assuming completeness of the filtration.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and let $d\ge1$ be a finite integer. An
$\mathbb R^d$-valued process $B=(B_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **standard
$d$-dimensional Brownian motion** if:

1. $B_0=0$ almost surely;
2. for every finite list $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_n$, the vector increments
   $$B_{t_j}-B_{t_{j-1}},\qquad 1\le j\le n,$$
   are mutually independent and have laws
   $N_d(0,(t_j-t_{j-1})I_d)$; and
3. there is one measurable event $A$ with $P(A)=1$ such that
   $t\mapsto B_t(\omega)$ is continuous from $[0,\infty)$ to
   $\mathbb R^d$ for every $\omega\in A$.

Equivalently, its $d$ coordinate processes $B^\alpha=(B_t^\alpha)_{t\ge0}$
are independent standard one-dimensional Brownian motions. Here independence
of the processes means the following precise assertion. Put
$I=[0,\infty)$ and equip $\mathbb R^I$ with its cylinder sigma-algebra. The
maps
$$ \Phi_\alpha:\Omega\longrightarrow\mathbb R^I, \qquad \Phi_\alpha(\omega)(t)=B_t^\alpha(\omega), \qquad 1\le\alpha\le d, $$
are independent random elements.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: The coefficients are $b(x)=-x$ and $\sigma(x)=1$. They are globally Lipschitz with constant $1$, satisfy $|b(x)|^2+|\sigma(x)|^2=x^2+1$, and are time independent, so the shared coefficient and time-modulus conditions hold. Applying [F2] to $e^tX_t$ gives $X_t=e^{-t}\int_0^t e^s dW_s$. Applying [F2] to $e^tW_t$ then gives $X_t=\int_0^t e^{-(t-s)}dW_s =W_t-\int_0^t e^{-(t-s)}W_sds.$ Hence $\sup_{t\le1}|X_t|\le2\sup_{t\le1}|W_t|$, and [F3] gives $\mathbb E\sup_{t\le1}|X_t|^2\le16<\infty$.

The payoff satisfies [A2]. Applying [F1] yields $\operatorname{Var}(\cos(Y_1^h)-\cos(Y_1^{2h}))\le Ch, \qquad |\mathbb E\cos(X_1)-\mathbb E\cos(Y_1^h)|\le C\sqrt h,$ and work $O(h^{-1})$ per coupled path pair. These rates correspond to $(\alpha,\beta)=(1/2,1)$ for this payoff.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be measurable spaces,
let $\pi$ be a probability measure on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$, and let
$K:\Theta\times\mathcal A\to[0,1]$ be a probability kernel. For
$C\in\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal A$, write
$C_\theta=\{x\in\mathcal X:(\theta,x)\in C\}$ and set
$$J(C)=\int_\Theta K(\theta,C_\theta)\,\pi(d\theta).$$
Then $J$ is a probability measure on the product sigma-algebra, and for every
nonnegative product-measurable $h$,
$$\int_{\Theta\times\mathcal X}h(\theta,x)\,J(d\theta,dx)=\int_\Theta\left(\int_\mathcal Xh(\theta,x)\,K(\theta,dx)\right)\pi(d\theta).$$
In particular, $J(A\times B)=\int_AK(\theta,B)\,\pi(d\theta)$ for
$A\in\mathcal T$ and $B\in\mathcal A$.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and let
$(S,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space. A **random element** of $S$ is a measurable
map
$$X:(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to(S,\Sigma)$$
in the sense of [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]].

When $S=\mathbb R$ and $\Sigma=\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$ from
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra]], the map $X$ is a **real random variable**.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element. Its
**law** or **distribution** is the set function
$$\mathbb P_X:\Sigma\to[0,+\infty],\qquad \mathbb P_X(B):=\mathbb P(X^{-1}(B)).$$

Thus the law of $X$ records the probability of each measurable target set by
pulling it back to an event in the original probability space.

Assume AC. Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ be a measurable random element with standard-Borel target, and let $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ be any sub-sigma-algebra. There exists a regular conditional distribution of $X$ given $\mathcal G$. Every section is a probability measure, including at exceptional sample points, and no countable-generation or completeness assumption on $\mathcal G$ is required.

For this necessarily nonempty target, the construction also supplies a bimeasurable bijection $c:E\to B$ onto a Borel set $B\subseteq[0,1]$, and a countable algebra $\mathcal A$ which generates $\mathcal S$, separates points, and determines finite measures.

Let a proper Bayesian model be given, and let $J$ be its joint prior-predictive probability on $(\Theta\times\mathsf Y,\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal Y)$, supplied by [[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]]. More generally, let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,Q)$ be any probability space carrying parameter and data random elements $X:\Omega\to\Theta$ and $Y:\Omega\to\mathsf Y$ whose joint law is $J$ ([[def-probability-measure]], [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]], [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]). A **posterior regular conditional distribution (posterior RCD)** is a regular conditional distribution of $X$ given $\sigma(Y)$, in the sense of [[def-regular-conditional-distribution]]. It is a kernel indexed by the sample point $\omega\in\Omega$. The canonical realization is $\Omega=\Theta\times\mathsf Y$ with $Q=J$ and coordinate maps $X(\theta,y)=\theta$, $Y(\theta,y)=y$.

A **data-indexed posterior kernel** is a probability kernel $\Pi_{\cdot}$ from $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ to $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ ([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]) for which $\omega\mapsto\Pi_{Y(\omega)}$ is a conditional law of $X$ given $Y$ ([[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]]). Equivalently, for every $A\in\mathcal T$ and $B\in\mathcal Y$,
$$Q(X\in A,\ Y\in B)=\int_B\Pi_y(A)\,Q_Y(dy),$$
where $Q_Y$ is the data marginal (equal to $J_Y$). This kernel is indexed by data values, not sample points.

The definition asserts no existence of either conditional kernel. Values of a data-indexed version on a measurable $J_Y$-null set are not fixed by the conditional-law identities; replacing them there by a fixed probability preserves those identities. A dominated-density construction is a separate route: [[thm-bayes-formula-for-dominated-kernels]] requires a proper prior, a sigma-finite data measure, and a specified jointly measurable sampling density, and fills fibres whose marginal density is zero or infinite with the prior. It does not require the data space to be standard Borel.

derivations.claim: By [F1], the model's prior and sampling kernel define the joint probability $J$ on the canonical product space. The given random elements $X,Y$ have this same joint law, and [F2] supplies the random-element and pushforward-law meanings used for this realization.

The target $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ is standard Borel and AC is assumed. Apply [F3] to $(\Omega,\mathcal F,Q)$, the given random element $X$, and the sub-sigma-algebra $\mathcal G=\sigma(Y)$. It gives an RCD of $X$ given $\sigma(Y)$; by [F4] this is the stated posterior RCD. The RCD theorem places no standard-Borel condition on $\mathsf Y$.

Step 2.1 invokes RCD existence without dividing by a data-event probability or evidence value; null-data values remain version-dependent.
Step 2.1 uses only the standard-Borel target condition, which includes singleton parameter spaces.
The model in step 1.1 may have a point-mass prior or a deterministic sampling kernel; no nondegeneracy premise is used.
Statement: the conditioning input is sigma(Y), an arbitrary sub-sigma-algebra rather than an interval; step 2.1 imposes no endpoint or standard-Borel data restriction.
Step 2.1 uses AC exactly through the standard-Borel RCD existence theorem; no weaker choice principle is substituted.

boundaries.reason: Statement: AC and a standard-Borel parameter imply existence of a sample-point RCD in step 2.1; no necessary-condition characterization is claimed.
Statement: existence of an RCD is not asserted to imply standard Borelness or AC; the conclusion is solely the sufficient-hypothesis existence result in step 2.1.

risk_review.notes: Reviewed Statement, F1-F4 and both proof steps with current joint-law, random-element, law, posterior-definition and standard-Borel RCD existence suppliers. F3 applies on the arbitrary given probability space, with measurable X, standard-Borel parameter target, G=sigma(Y) subset F and explicitly assumed AC; no condition on the observation space is required. F4 originally restricted the posterior terminology to the canonical realization, contrary to the actual definition; repaired that citation to include every realization with joint law J. This is a nonfatal citation defect: F3 already proves the full existence claim and the directly cited definition supplies the terminology. No change to Statement, dependencies or proof inference. Empty sample/parameter spaces excluded by probabilities, singleton and deterministic cases allowed, no divisions or simultaneous eventwise version selections.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be measurable spaces,
let $\pi$ be a probability measure on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$, and let
$K:\Theta\times\mathcal A\to[0,1]$ be a probability kernel. For
$C\in\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal A$, write
$C_\theta=\{x\in\mathcal X:(\theta,x)\in C\}$ and set
$$J(C)=\int_\Theta K(\theta,C_\theta)\,\pi(d\theta).$$
Then $J$ is a probability measure on the product sigma-algebra, and for every
nonnegative product-measurable $h$,
$$\int_{\Theta\times\mathcal X}h(\theta,x)\,J(d\theta,dx)=\int_\Theta\left(\int_\mathcal Xh(\theta,x)\,K(\theta,dx)\right)\pi(d\theta).$$
In particular, $J(A\times B)=\int_AK(\theta,B)\,\pi(d\theta)$ for
$A\in\mathcal T$ and $B\in\mathcal A$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
([[def-measurable-space]]). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and let
$(S,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space. A **random element** of $S$ is a measurable
map
$$X:(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to(S,\Sigma)$$
in the sense of [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]].

When $S=\mathbb R$ and $\Sigma=\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$ from
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra]], the map $X$ is a **real random variable**.

Assume AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let a proper Bayesian model have joint prior-predictive law $J$, and let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,Q)$ be any probability space carrying parameter and data random elements $X,Y$ whose joint law is $J$ ([[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]], [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]). If $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ is standard Borel ([[def-standard-borel-space]]), then a posterior RCD of $X$ given $\sigma(Y)$ exists. The data space $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ need only be measurable. In particular, the claim applies to the canonical product realization supplied by [[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]].

Assume AC. Let $X$ and $Y$ take values in nonempty standard-Borel spaces $(E,\mathcal S)$ and $(T,\mathcal T)$ on a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$. Let $L$ be a specified regular conditional distribution of $X$ given $\sigma(Y)$, everywhere a probability kernel. There is a probability kernel $K:T\to E$ such that $L(\omega,\cdot)=K(Y(\omega),\cdot)$ simultaneously outside a single null set. In fact, with the stated everywhere-kernel convention, the construction below gives this equality for every $\omega$. Consequently K is a conditional law of X given Y.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ and $Y:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(T,\mathcal T)$ be measurable random elements. A **conditional law of X given Y** is a probability kernel $K:(T,\mathcal T)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ such that $\omega\mapsto K(Y(\omega),\cdot)$ is a regular conditional distribution of X given $\sigma(Y)$ in [[def-regular-conditional-distribution]]. Thus for every $A\in\mathcal S$ and $H\in\sigma(Y)$,
$$\int_H K(Y(\omega),A)\,dP=P(H\cap\{X\in A\}).$$

Composition with Y makes each evaluation $\sigma(Y)$-measurable, and every section remains a probability by [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. The notation $P(X\in A\mid Y=y)=K(y,A)$ refers to a chosen kernel; it is not a ratio involving the possibly zero probability $P(Y=y)$.

Write $P_Y(B)=P(Y^{-1}(B))$ for the law in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]. If a specified countable family $\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal S$ determines probability measures, two conditional laws K,L agree as measures outside a single $\mathcal T$-measurable $P_Y$-null set. Indeed for each $A\in\mathcal C$ the measurable discrepancy $D_A=\{y:K(y,A)\ne L(y,A)\}$ has null inverse image under Y by [[lem-conditional-expectation-is-unique-almost-surely]]. Hence $P_Y(D_A)=0$ by the law definition; the countable union $D$ is null by [[thm-finite-and-countable-subadditivity-of-measures]], and off D the determining property gives equality of measures. This uses a supplied determining family and makes no AC assertion about obtaining one.

Values on a measurable $P_Y$-null subset may be replaced by a specified fixed probability on E without changing these identities. The inverse image of that subset is measurable null, and all event evaluations are bounded, so the modified event integrals agree. Empty-event evaluations remain zero and whole-target evaluations remain one. Existence on standard-Borel spaces is proved separately; the definition alone does not assert a conditional kernel exists.

Assume AC. Let $\lambda$ be a probability on $(E\times T,\mathcal S\otimes\mathcal T)$, where E and T are standard-Borel spaces, and let $\beta(B)=\lambda(E\times B)$ be its second marginal. There is a probability kernel $K:(T,\mathcal T)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ such that

$$\lambda(A\times B)=\int_B K(y,A)\,\beta(dy)\quad(A\in\mathcal S,\ B\in\mathcal T).$$

It is unique as a kernel outside a single measurable $\beta$-null set. For every nonnegative product-measurable $f:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$,

$$\int f(x,y)\,\lambda(d(x,y))=\int_T\left(\int_E f(x,y)K(y,dx)\right)\beta(dy).$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The word **proper** means that the prior is a probability measure. A sigma-finite improper prior is not a proper Bayesian model in this definition; fixed-data posterior normalizers for such priors are handled separately.

Let a proper Bayesian model be given, and let $J$ be its joint prior-predictive probability on $(\Theta\times\mathsf Y,\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal Y)$, supplied by [[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]]. A **data-indexed posterior kernel** is a probability kernel $\Pi_{\cdot}$ from $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ to $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ ([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]) for which $\omega\mapsto\Pi_{Y(\omega)}$ is a conditional law of $X$ given $Y$ ([[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]]). Equivalently, for every $A\in\mathcal T$ and $B\in\mathcal Y$,
$$Q(X\in A,\ Y\in B)=\int_B\Pi_y(A)\,Q_Y(dy),$$
where $Q_Y$ is the data marginal (equal to $J_Y$). This kernel is indexed by data values, not sample points.

Values of a data-indexed version on a measurable $J_Y$-null set are not fixed by the conditional-law identities; replacing them there by a fixed probability preserves those identities. A dominated-density construction is a separate route: [[thm-bayes-formula-for-dominated-kernels]] requires a proper prior, a sigma-finite data measure, and a specified jointly measurable sampling density, and fills fibres whose marginal density is zero or infinite with the prior. It does not require the data space to be standard Borel.

In a proper Bayesian model, suppose both parameter and data spaces $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ are standard Borel ([[def-standard-borel-space]]). There is a data-indexed posterior probability kernel $y\mapsto\Pi_y$ such that, for all $A\in\mathcal T$ and $B\in\mathcal Y$,
$$J(A\times B)=\int_B\Pi_y(A)\,J_Y(dy),\qquad J_Y(B)=\int_\Theta K(\theta,B)\,\Pi(d\theta).$$
The composition $\Pi_{Y(\omega)}$ is a posterior RCD. Any two data-indexed posterior kernels agree as probability measures outside one measurable $J_Y$-null set. On any measurable $J_Y$-null set, the conditional-law identities do not select a pointwise value: replacing the kernel there by the prior $\Pi$ preserves the identities.

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges ([[def-series]]) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

A measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$ is **standard Borel** if there are a Polish space $P$ and a bijection $h:E\to P$ such that $A\in\mathcal E$ exactly when $h[A]$ is Borel in $P$. Thus the measurable structure is part of the datum; no particular compatible Polish topology on $E$ is selected.

A topological space is **Polish** when it is separable ([[def-separable-space]]) and completely metrizable: its topology is induced by some complete metric ([[lem-complete-remetrisation]]). No particular compatible complete metric or countable dense subset is part of the structure.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

normalizer only; it does not by itself define a prior-predictive probability or
a conditional law.

When the data are described by a dominated experiment, the dominating measure
and its sigma-finiteness are as in
[[def-dominated-statistical-experiment]]. A family of pointwise likelihood
sections is not assumed to be jointly measurable in parameter and data; that
additional condition must be supplied separately whenever Tonelli is used.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T,\Pi)$ be a measure space, let $L_y:\Theta\to[0,+\infty]$
be measurable for a fixed datum $y$, and put
$Z:=\int_\Theta L_y\,d\Pi$. For a finite positive constant $c$, the set
function
$$A\longmapsto c\int_A L_y\,d\Pi$$
is a probability measure if and only if $0<Z<+\infty$ and $c=Z^{-1}$. In
particular, if $Z=0$ or $Z=+\infty$, no finite positive scaling makes the
fiberwise update a probability measure.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n$ is sigma-finite ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]):
   the cubes $(-k,k]^n$ are Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n\big((-k,k]^n\big) = (2k)^n < +\infty$, they increase with $k$, and
   their union over $k \in \mathbb{N}$ is $\mathbb{R}^n$.
2. Every bounded subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has $\lambda_n^*(E) < +\infty$; a bounded
   Lebesgue measurable set therefore has finite measure, and every compact
   subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is Lebesgue measurable of finite measure.
Let $\mu$ be a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. If $A,B\in\mathcal A$ and $A\subseteq B$, then $\mu(A)\le\mu(B)$.
Assume AC. The function $\phi(x)=e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}$ is positive and Borel measurable on $\mathbb R$, with Lebesgue integral one.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. For $E \in \mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$, define

$$(\mu \times \nu)(E) := \int_X \nu(E_x)\,d\mu = \int_Y \mu(E^y)\,d\nu.$$

The two displayed integrals are well-defined by
[[prop-sigma-finite-section-measure-functions-are-measurable]] and equal by
[[thm-iterated-section-measures-agree-on-product-measurable-sets]]. This is the
**product measure** of $\mu$ and $\nu$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $n,m\ge1$. Every continuous map
$f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is Borel measurable in
the sense of [[def-borel-and-lebesgue-measurable-function-on-rn]].

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then

$$\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n) \;\subseteq\; \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n) :$$

every Borel subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]) is Lebesgue
measurable ([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]). In
particular every open set, every closed set and every countable intersection of
open sets is Lebesgue measurable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and define
$$\nu_f(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu \qquad (A\in\mathcal A).$$
Then $\nu_f$ is a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

derivations.claim: By [A1] and [F6], countable choice is available for [F3]. The boxes $E_k=(-k,k]$ have finite measure $2k$ and cover $\mathbb R$ by [F3], so $\lambda$ is sigma-finite. Since $E_k\subseteq\mathbb R$, [F4] gives $\lambda(\mathbb R)\ge2k$ for every $k$, hence $\lambda(\mathbb R)=+\infty$ and the flat prior is improper.

Fix $\mu$ and set $T(x)=(x-\mu)/\sigma$. This is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism of $\mathbb R$ with inverse $t\mapsto\mu+\sigma t$ and $|T'(x)|=1/\sigma$. The formula for $q_\mu$ is continuous in $x$, hence Borel by [F12] and Lebesgue measurable by [F15]. Since $\phi$ is also Lebesgue measurable by [F5, F15], [F7] gives $\int_{\mathbb R}q_\mu\,d\lambda=\int_{\mathbb R}\phi\,d\lambda=1$. The set function $P_\mu(A)=\int_Aq_\mu\,d\lambda$ is a measure by [F16], and its total mass one makes it a probability by [F17]. For a Borel $A$, apply [F7] to $f=\mathbf1_Aq_\mu$ and $S(z)=\mu+\sigma z$: $$N(\mu,\sigma^2)(A)=\int \mathbf1_A(S(z))\phi(z)\,d\lambda(z)=\int_A q_\mu(x)\,d\lambda(x),$$ since $\sigma q_\mu(S(z))=\phi(z)$ and [F14] defines $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ as this affine pushforward. Thus each coordinate law has the stated density.

Put $S=\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\bar y)^2$. Expanding and using $\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)=0$ gives $\sum_i(y_i-\mu)^2=S+n(\mu-\bar y)^2$. Hence $L_{\mathbf y}(\mu)=(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-n/2}e^{-S/(2\sigma^2)}e^{-n(\mu-\bar y)^2/(2\sigma^2)}$. This is continuous in $\mu$, hence Borel by [F12] and $\mathcal L(\mathbb R)$-measurable by [F15]; therefore its evidence integral is defined by [F1].

For $k\ge1$, recursively form the finite product data measure $
u_k=\lambda^{\otimes k}$ on $\mathcal L(\mathbb R)^{\otimes k}$ using [F8] and [F9]. Starting from the sigma-finite $\lambda$, [F10] ensures that each $
u_k$ exists and is sigma-finite. The coordinate projections are measurable by [F8], so each pullback of $q_\mu$ is measurable by step 1.2; finite multiplication is continuous, making $f_k(y_1,\ldots,y_k)=\prod_{i=1}^kq_\mu(y_i)$ product-measurable. Step 1.2 gives $\int f_1\,d
u_1=1$. If $\int f_k\,d
u_k=1$, the recursive product definition and Tonelli [F11] give $\int f_{k+1}\,d
u_{k+1}=\int f_k\,d
u_k\int q_\mu\,d\lambda=1$. Thus $P_{\mu,n}(E):=\int_E f_n\,d
u_n$ is a measure by [F16] and a probability by [F17]. For measurable rectangles $E=A_1	imes\cdots	imes A_n$, repeated Tonelli gives $P_{\mu,n}(E)=\prod_{i=1}^nP_\mu(A_i)$. The product measure theorem [F10], iterated over the finite factors, identifies $P_{\mu,n}$ as the product of the one-coordinate laws. Therefore these coordinates are independent and $L_{\mathbf y}(\mu)$ is their joint density.

Set $T(\mu)=\sqrt n(\mu-\bar y)/\sigma$, a $C^1$ diffeomorphism of $\mathbb R$ with inverse $u\mapsto\bar y+\sigma u/\sqrt n$ and derivative $\sqrt n/\sigma$. Since $e^{-u^2/2}=\sqrt{2\pi}\,\phi(u)$ is nonnegative and Lebesgue measurable by [F5, F15], [F7] gives $\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-n(\mu-\bar y)^2/(2\sigma^2)}\,d\lambda(\mu)=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}\sqrt{2\pi}$. Integrating the factorization in step 1.3 against the flat prior gives $Z(\mathbf y)=(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-n/2}e^{-S/(2\sigma^2)}\frac{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}{\sqrt n}$, which is strictly positive and finite for every finite data vector.

Dividing step 1.3 by the finite positive evidence in step 2.2 gives $h(\mu)=\frac{\sqrt n}{\sigma}\phi\!\left(\frac{\sqrt n(\mu-\bar y)}{\sigma}\right)$, the displayed Lebesgue density. Put $s=\sigma/\sqrt n>0$; $S(z)=\bar y+sz$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism with inverse $\mu\mapsto(\mu-\bar y)/s$. For every Borel $A$, [F14] defines $N(\bar y,s^2)$ as this pushforward; [F7] applied to $f=\mathbf1_Ah$, which is Lebesgue measurable by [F12, F13, F15], gives $$\int_Ah(\mu)\,d\lambda(\mu)=\int\mathbf1_A(S(z))h(S(z))s\,d\lambda(z)=\int\mathbf1_A(S(z))\phi(z)\,d\lambda(z)=N(\bar y,s^2)(A).$$ The update on the full Lebesgue sigma-algebra is a probability by [F2]. If $n=0$ were allowed, its empty-product likelihood would be $1$ and the evidence would be $\lambda(\mathbb R)=+\infty$ by step 1.1, so no normalized update would exist.

boundaries.evidence: Step 3.1 states that the excluded n=0 likelihood is one and its evidence is infinite by step 1.1.
Step 2.2 proves strictly positive evidence for every finite data vector under n>=1 and sigma^2>0.
Steps 2.2 and 3.1 include n=1; the posterior is N(y_1,sigma^2).

boundaries.reason: The example assumes sigma^2>0, so the degenerate zero-variance model is excluded.
The parameter and data domains are real spaces without interval endpoints.

Example fixes n>=1 and positive known variance, then proves positive finite evidence and the normal posterior; no equivalence characterizes flat priors by normal posteriors.
Verification step 3.1 derives the density by division and separately records that n=0 gives infinite evidence; it does not infer a unique prior from the posterior normal density.

risk_review.notes: Read all six verification steps and all 21 direct dependency statements/definitions. Countable choice follows from assumed AC; Lebesgue sigma-finiteness and unbounded box masses establish an improper prior. The affine diffeomorphisms have positive nonzero derivatives; measurable Gaussian densities integrate to one. Recursive product measures and Tonelli apply to nonnegative product-measurable coordinate densities and give the product sampling probability. The completed-square cross term vanishes, and Z=(2*pi*sigma^2)^(-n/2)*exp(-S/(2*sigma^2))*sigma*sqrt(2*pi)/sqrt(n) is finite positive. Division yields the stated density; its Borel restriction is the affine normal pushforward. n=1 and excluded n=0 are explicitly checked, and sigma^2=0 is excluded. Independently checked BDA3 sections 2.5 (printed pp. 40-42) and 2.8 (pp. 51-52); no conditional-law inference from the improper prior is made. Reader/refuter have no findings; no defect found.

citations.quote:
Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ be a measurable parameter space, let $\Pi$ be a
sigma-finite measure on it, and fix a data value $y$. Let
$L_y:\Theta\to[0,+\infty]$ be a $\mathcal T$-measurable function. Define its
**evidence normalizer** by
$$Z_\Pi(y):=\int_\Theta L_y(\theta)\,\Pi(d\theta)\in[0,+\infty].$$
Only when $0<Z_\Pi(y)<+\infty$ define the **fiberwise posterior update** by
$$\Pi_y(A):=\frac{\int_A L_y(\theta)\,\Pi(d\theta)}{Z_\Pi(y)}\qquad(A\in\mathcal T).$$
The definition makes no quotient at zero or infinite evidence. A prior is
**proper** when $\Pi(\Theta)=1$, as in
[[def-bayesian-model-as-prior-and-sampling-kernel]]. We call a sigma-finite
prior **improper** when $\Pi(\Theta)=+\infty$; the formula also applies to
other sigma-finite measures. For an improper prior, $Z_\Pi(y)$ is a fiberwise
normalizer only; it does not by itself define a prior-predictive probability or
a conditional law.

When the data are described by a dominated experiment, the dominating measure
and its sigma-finiteness are as in
[[def-dominated-statistical-experiment]]. A family of pointwise likelihood
sections is not assumed to be jointly measurable in parameter and data; that
additional condition must be supplied separately whenever Tonelli is used.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T,\Pi)$ be a measure space, let $L_y:\Theta\to[0,+\infty]$
be measurable for a fixed datum $y$, and put
$Z:=\int_\Theta L_y\,d\Pi$. For a finite positive constant $c$, the set
function
$$A\longmapsto c\int_A L_y\,d\Pi$$
is a probability measure if and only if $0<Z<+\infty$ and $c=Z^{-1}$. In
particular, if $Z=0$ or $Z=+\infty$, no finite positive scaling makes the
fiberwise update a probability measure.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space ([[def-measure-space]]).

- The measure $\mu$ is **finite** if $\mu(X)<+\infty$.
- It is **sigma-finite** if there is a sequence $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$ such that $X=\bigcup_nE_n$ and $\mu(E_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$.
- It is **semifinite** if, whenever $E\in\mathcal A$ and $\mu(E)>0$, there is $F\in\mathcal A$ with $F\subseteq E$ and $0<\mu(F)<+\infty$.

The last condition is automatic when $0<\mu(E)<+\infty$, by taking $F=E$; its substantive case is $\mu(E)=+\infty$.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and define
$$\nu_f(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu \qquad (A\in\mathcal A).$$
Then $\nu_f$ is a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) and let
$\varepsilon \in F$ with $\varepsilon > 0$. Then there is a natural number
$n \ge 1$ such that

$$\frac{1}{n \cdot 1_F} < \varepsilon ,$$

where $n \cdot 1_F$ is the canonical natural of $F$ ([[thm-of-archimedean]]) and
$1/(n \cdot 1_F)$ is its multiplicative inverse ([[def-field]]). As is standard
we abbreviate $n \cdot 1_F$ to $n$ and write the conclusion $1/n < \varepsilon$.

This is the **reciprocal form** of the Archimedean property.
[[thm-of-archimedean]] on its own delivers only the assertion that the canonical
naturals are cofinal, $x < n \cdot 1_F$; the form actually used in analysis, that
the reciprocals of the naturals get below every positive bound, is the statement
above, and it is recorded separately so that no proof has to reconstruct the
inversion step in passing.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then

$$\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n) \;\subseteq\; \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n) :$$

every Borel subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]) is Lebesgue
measurable ([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]). In
particular every open set, every closed set and every countable intersection of
open sets is Lebesgue measurable.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n$ is sigma-finite ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]):
   the cubes $(-k,k]^n$ are Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n\big((-k,k]^n\big) = (2k)^n < +\infty$, they increase with $k$, and
   their union over $k \in \mathbb{N}$ is $\mathbb{R}^n$.
2. Every bounded subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has $\lambda_n^*(E) < +\infty$; a bounded
   Lebesgue measurable set therefore has finite measure, and every compact
   subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is Lebesgue measurable of finite measure.

derivations.claim: By [A1] and [F7], countable choice is available for [F3], [F4], [F10], and [F11]. Write $f(p)=1/[p(1-p)]$ on $(0,1)$. For any continuous $g:(0,1)\to\mathbb R$ and open $U\subseteq\mathbb R$, continuity makes $g^{-1}(U)$ open in the subspace $(0,1)$, so $g^{-1}(U)=O\cap(0,1)$ for some open $O\subseteq\mathbb R$. This intersection is open in $\mathbb R$, hence Borel by [F9] and Lebesgue measurable by [F10]. Thus $g$ is measurable for the restricted Lebesgue sigma-algebra. This applies to $f$ and to every binomial likelihood section, which is a polynomial. By [F11], Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R$ is a measure; its restriction to the measurable interval $(0,1)$ is a measure as well. Thus [F5] defines the prior measure $\Pi(A)=\int_A f\,d\lambda$. For each $p\in(0,1)$, let $\varepsilon=\min\{p,1-p,1/3\}>0$; by [F8] choose $k\ge1$ with $1/k<\varepsilon$. Then $k\ge3$ and $p\in E_k=[1/k,1-1/k]$, so these sets cover $(0,1)$. On $E_k$, $f(p)\le k^2$. Their Lebesgue lengths are at most one by [F4], so homogeneity and monotonicity [F6] give $\Pi(E_k)\le k^2<\infty$; [F3] makes this a sigma-finite prior. It is not finite: on each disjoint interval $I_j=(2^{-j-1},2^{-j}]$, $j\ge1$, one has $f(p)\ge1/p\ge2^j$ and $\lambda(I_j)=2^{-j-1}$ by [F4]. Homogeneity and monotonicity [F6] give $\Pi(I_j)=\int_{I_j}f\,d\lambda\ge1/2$. By [F5], $\Pi$ is a measure, so the prior mass of the union of the first $m$ such intervals is at least $m/2$ for every $m$. Hence $\Pi((0,1))=+\infty$ and the prior is improper.

For $y=0$, put $
u_0(A):=\int_A L_0\,d\Pi$; it is a measure by [F5], and $Z(0)=
u_0((0,1))$ by [F1]. The likelihood is $L_0(p)= inom n0(1-p)^n=(1-p)^n$, so on each $I_j$ from step 1.1, $p\le1/2$ gives $L_0(p)\ge2^{-n}$. Also $\Pi(I_j)\ge1/2$ by step 1.1. Monotonicity and homogeneity [F6] therefore give $
u_0(I_j)\ge2^{-n-1}$. The intervals are pairwise disjoint, so measure additivity gives $
u_0( igcup_{j=1}^m I_j)\ge m2^{-n-1}$; since this union is contained in $(0,1)$, countable additivity gives $
u_0((0,1))\ge m2^{-n-1}$ for every $m$. Thus $Z(0)=+\infty$ and [F1] leaves the quotient undefined.

For $y=n$, put $
u_n(A):=\int_A L_n\,d\Pi$; it is a measure by [F5], and $Z(n)=
u_n((0,1))$ by [F1]. Here $L_n(p)= inom nn p^n=p^n$. On each reflected interval $J_j=[1-2^{-j},1-2^{-j-1})$, $j\ge1$, one has $p\ge1/2$, so $L_n(p)\ge2^{-n}$. Also $f(p)\ge1/(1-p)\ge2^j$ there and $\lambda(J_j)=2^{-j-1}$ by [F4], so $\Pi(J_j)\ge1/2$ by [F6]. Monotonicity and homogeneity [F6] give $
u_n(J_j)\ge2^{-n-1}$. The intervals are pairwise disjoint, and additivity followed by nonnegativity on their complement gives $Z(n)=
u_n((0,1))\ge m2^{-n-1}$ for every $m$. Thus $Z(n)=+\infty$ and [F1] leaves this quotient undefined. By [F2], neither endpoint fiber admits a normalized posterior probability.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

For $p,q>0$, define $B(p,q)=\int_0^1t^{p-1}(1-t)^{q-1}\,dt$.

The integral is improper at both endpoints. The exact convergence theorem [[thm-real-beta-integral-convergence]] proves that it exists precisely for the displayed positive parameters and therefore discharges the definition's existence obligation.
For $p,q>0$, $B(p,q)=\Gamma(p)\Gamma(q)/\Gamma(p+q)$.
Let $s$ be real. The Euler integral $\int_0^\infty t^{s-1}e^{-t}\,dt$ converges if and only if $s>0$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $a<b$ and let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be
bounded and Riemann integrable. Then $f$ is Lebesgue measurable on $[a,b]$ and
is integrable there, and its Lebesgue integral equals its Riemann integral:
$$\int_{[a,b]} f\,d\lambda_1=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx.$$

This is the point at which the completeness of Lebesgue measure is used
essentially: the proof obtains a Borel function equal to $f$ almost everywhere,
and measurability of $f$ itself is then a completeness statement.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $p,q$ be real. The Beta integral converges if and only if $p>0$ and $q>0$.

Here the Beta integral means $\int_0^1t^{p-1}(1-t)^{q-1}\,dt$.

For $a>0$, the function $x\mapsto a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and
$$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$
For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with
$$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$

Fix $n \ge 1$ and let $\lambda_n^*$ be the Lebesgue outer set function on $\mathbb{R}^n$
([[def-lebesgue-outer-measure]]). A set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is
**Lebesgue measurable** when

$$\lambda_n^*(A) \;=\; \lambda_n^*(A \cap E) \;+\; \lambda_n^*(A \setminus E) \qquad \text{for every } A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n .$$

This formula makes sense before any outer-measure theorem is invoked. Under
countable choice, [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-is-an-outer-measure-agreeing-with-volume]]
makes $\lambda_n^*$ an outer measure, and the displayed condition is then exactly
Carathéodory measurability in the sense of [[def-caratheodory-measurable-set]].

The family of Lebesgue measurable sets is written $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$,
and **Lebesgue measure** is the restriction

$$\lambda_n \;:=\; \lambda_n^*\!\restriction_{\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)} .$$

On the real line the subscript is dropped and $\lambda := \lambda_1$.

The quantifier over every test set $A$ is part of the condition, and no
hypothesis on $E$ is imposed before it is tested. That
$\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra and that $\lambda_n$ is a complete
measure on it are not part of this definition: they are proved, under the Axiom
of Countable Choice, in [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]], which is
recorded in this item's `justified_by` because it is a statement about the
objects introduced here. Until that theorem the symbols $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$
and $\lambda_n$ name a family of sets and a restricted set function, nothing more.
For $s>0$, define $\Gamma(s)=\int_0^\infty t^{s-1}e^{-t}\,dt$.

For $a>0$ and $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$a^x:=\exp(x\log a).$$
For the supplementary zero-base convention, define $0^x:=0$ when $x>0$.

The expressions $0^0$ and $0^x$ for $x<0$ are left undefined. Negative bases are not assigned arbitrary real powers.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. **Nonnegativity.** If $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $\int_a^b f \ge 0$.
2. **Monotonicity.** If $f(x) \le g(x)$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $$\int_a^b f \;\le\; \int_a^b g .$$
3. **Two-sided bound.** If $m \le f(x) \le M$ for every $x \in [a,b]$, with
   $m, M$ real, then
   $$m\,(b-a) \;\le\; \int_a^b f \;\le\; M\,(b-a) .$$

**Equality in claim 1 does not force $f$ to vanish.** A nonnegative integrable
function with integral $0$ may be positive at infinitely many points; that is
[[fs-nonnegative-integrable-with-zero-integral-vanishes]] on the previous page's
companion. Under the additional hypothesis of continuity the conclusion does
hold, and that is [[thm-nonnegative-continuous-with-zero-integral-vanishes]]
below.

**Claim 2 is stated for $a < b$ and is not orientation-invariant.** With the
convention of [[def-oriented-integral]], $f \le g$ gives
$\int_u^v f \le \int_u^v g$ when $u \le v$ and the reverse inequality when
$u \ge v$, since both sides change sign together.

Changing a finite lower endpoint of $\int_a^\infty f$, a finite upper endpoint of $\int_{-\infty}^b f$, or a compact truncation beside a finite singular endpoint neither creates nor destroys improper convergence. The values change by the corresponding oriented proper integral.

Consequently, convergence and value in the definitions of an interior-singularity integral and a whole-line integral are independent of the chosen finite split point.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and
   $\lambda_n$ is a measure on it ([[def-measure]]);
2. the measure space $(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n), \lambda_n)$ is
   complete ([[def-complete-measure-space]]), and every $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   with $\lambda_n^*(S) = 0$ is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(S) = 0$;
3. every elementary set is Lebesgue measurable and
   $\lambda_n(A) = \mu_0(A)$ for every $A \in \mathcal{E}_n$; in particular
   $\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ for every half-open box $B$,
   $\lambda_n(\varnothing) = 0$ and $\lambda_n(\mathbb{R}^n) = +\infty$.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then

$$\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n) \;\subseteq\; \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n) :$$

every Borel subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]) is Lebesgue
measurable ([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]). In
particular every open set, every closed set and every countable intersection of
open sets is Lebesgue measurable.

derivations.claim: Fix $s>0$ and put $h_s(t)=t^{s-1}e^{-t}$ for $t>0$. For $1\le t\le2$, [F12] gives $0\le\log t\le\log2$, so $(s-1)\log t\ge\min\{0,(s-1)\log2\}$. By [F11] and [F13], $h_s(t)\ge c_s:=\exp(\min\{0,(s-1)\log2\})\exp(-2)>0$. The function $h_s$ is continuous on $[1,2]$ by [F8] and [F13], hence bounded and Riemann integrable by [F5]. The lower integral bound [F14] therefore gives $\int_1^2 h_s(t)\,dt\ge c_s(2-1)=c_s>0$.

By [F3] and [F10], $\Gamma(s)$ is finite. The integrand $h_s$ is positive on $(0,\infty)$ by [F11] and [F13]. Every compact truncation integral on either side of $[1,2]$ is nonnegative by [F14], and its finite improper limit is nonnegative as well. Splitting at $1$ and $2$ by [F15] gives $\Gamma(s)=\int_0^1h_s+\int_1^2h_s+\int_2^\infty h_s\ge\int_1^2h_s\ge c_s>0$. Thus $0<\Gamma(s)<\infty$ for every $s>0$, with strict positivity proved here rather than inferred from convergence alone.

Apply step 2.2 with $s=\alpha,\beta,\alpha+\beta$. The identity in [F2] expresses $B(\alpha,\beta)$ as a quotient of finite positive numbers, hence $0<B(\alpha,\beta)<\infty$. Together with step 2.1 this proves the displayed Lebesgue integral identity and its endpoint bounds.

routine_steps.claim: By [F8], $f(p)=p^{\alpha-1}(1-p)^{\beta-1}$ is continuous and hence Borel and Lebesgue measurable on $(0,1)$ with the measure in [F9]. For each integer $m\ge3$, one has $1/m<1-1/m$, so its restriction to $[1/m,1-1/m]$ is continuous, hence bounded and Riemann integrable by [F5], and [F4] identifies its Lebesgue integral with its Riemann integral. The indicators of these intervals increase pointwise to one, so the truncated functions increase to $f$.
routine_steps.justification: For m>=3 the restriction of f to C_m=[1/m,1-1/m] is continuous and bounded Riemann integrable. F4 gives its relative Lebesgue measurability and integral identity; F4 full proof L7 supplies measurability of C_m. Its zero extension has preimage equal to its relative preimage inside C_m, joined with the measurable complement precisely when the tested Borel set contains 0. Thus each zero extension is measurable. C_m increases to (0,1); positivity gives increasing truncations. Threshold preimages of their limit are countable unions of measurable sets, giving the measurability needed for F6. Continuous-to-Borel measurability in the opening clause also follows directly from open preimages. This is the actual native batch-40 routine completion, independently checked on current sources; source step1.1 remains unedited.

routine_steps.claim: By [F6], the Lebesgue integral of $f$ is the limit of the truncated integrals from step 1.1. The same truncations define the improper integral in [F1], which converges by [F7]; therefore the limit is $B(\alpha,\beta)$.
routine_steps.justification: For m>=3 split the proper integral over C_m at1/2 by additivity of bounded integrable restrictions. The left compact integrals tend to the finite left-end improper integral and the right compact integrals tend to the finite right-end improper integral, as defined by F1 and proved convergent separately in F7. The sum of these two finite limits is B(alpha,beta); hence the diagonal truncation limit equals B. F6 identifies the same limit with the nonnegative Lebesgue integral.
