The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: By [A1] and [F2], Countable Choice holds, so the change-of-variables theorem [F3] applies. For $\sigma>0$, the map $T(x)=m+\sigma x$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism of $\mathbb R$ with derivative $\sigma$.

For any Borel set $B\subseteq\mathbb R$, apply [F3] to the nonnegative Borel function $y\mapsto\mathbf1_B(y)\phi((y-m)/\sigma)/\sigma$. The change of variables gives $\int_B\frac1\sigma\phi((y-m)/\sigma)\,dy=\int_{\mathbb R}\mathbf1_B(m+\sigma x)\phi(x)\,dx=N(m,\sigma^2)(B)$, where the last equality is the pushforward identity in [F1]. Therefore the displayed function is a density on every Borel set, proving the statement.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. $f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ be measurable for the Borel sigma-algebra on
the extended real line. Products of functions use

abbreviates $\underline c\odot_X f$ for the constant function $\underline c$.
The magnitude function is $|f|=\max(f,-f)$ as in
[[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]]. Then:

1. $cf$ is measurable for every real scalar $c$;
2. $\max(f,g)$, $\min(f,g)$, $|f|$, $f^+$, and $f^-$ are measurable;
3. if the partial pointwise sum $f+g$ is defined at every point, then it is measurable;
4. the pointwise product $fg:=f\odot_X g$ is measurable.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

If $f:X\to Y$ is continuous between topological spaces, then
$f^{-1}[B]\in\mathcal B(X)$ for every $B\in\mathcal B(Y)$.

$$\nu_f(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu \qquad (A\in\mathcal A).$$
Then $\nu_f$ is a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

$m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification

$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ generating $\mathcal A$, and let $\mu,\nu$ be measures on $(X,\mathcal A)$ that agree on $\mathcal P$. Suppose there is an increasing sequence $(P_n)$ in $\mathcal P$ with

$$X=\bigcup_nP_n,\qquad \mu(P_n)=\nu(P_n)<+\infty\quad(n\in\mathbb N).$$

Then $\mu=\nu$ on $\mathcal A$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
one has
$$\mathcal B(\mathbb R^m)\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n) = \mathcal B(\mathbb R^{m+n}).$$

$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

On every product rectangle, the density measure $\ell(\mu,\cdot)\,d\lambda_n$ has the product of the $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ marginal probabilities by [F9] and [F10]; conditional independence gives the same rectangle values, so [F11] identifies it with the conditional sample law. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC. Let $X\in\mathbb R^d$ and $Y\in\mathbb R^m$, with $d,m\ge1$, be
jointly multivariate normal with mean $(a,b)$ and positive-semidefinite block
covariance
$$\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}A&C\\C^T&B\end{pmatrix},$$
where $B$ is positive definite. Then
$$S=A-CB^{-1}C^T$$
is positive semidefinite, and for every $y\in\mathbb R^m$ the probability law
$$K(y,\cdot)=N_d\!\left(a+CB^{-1}(y-b),S\right)$$
is defined. The map $K$ is a probability kernel and is a conditional law of
$X$ given $Y$: for all Borel $E\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ and
$F\subseteq\mathbb R^m$,
$$\mathbb P(X\in E,Y\in F)=\int_F K(y,E)\,\mathbb P_Y(dy).$$
The covariance $A$ and the conditional covariance $S$ may be singular.
Positive definiteness of $B$ is required; no pseudoinverse formula for
singular $B$ is asserted.

Computing covariances from $\operatorname{Cov}(Z)=I_2$ gives $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$, $C=\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}$, and $B=(2)$. Since $\det A=0$, the state covariance is singular.

The observed block $B=(2)$ is positive definite. Its inverse is $(1/2)$, so $A-CB^{-1}C^T=\begin{pmatrix}1/2&1/2\\1/2&1/2\end{pmatrix}$ and $CB^{-1}(y-0)=(y/2,y/2)$. The conditional covariance is also singular, with determinant zero.

Apply [F2] with these blocks. It gives the displayed conditional Gaussian kernel for every $y$, despite singularity of $A$ and the conditional covariance; no inverse or pseudoinverse of either is used.

> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\in\mathbb N_0$, $a,b>0$, and
$\lambda\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(a,b)$ in shape-rate convention. Conditional
on $\lambda$, let $Y_1,\ldots,Y_n$ be independent with
$Y_i\sim\operatorname{Pois}(e_i\lambda)$ for $i=1,\ldots,n$, where each fixed
exposure $e_i\ge0$.
The data space $\mathbb N_0^n$ has counting measure. If some $e_i=0$ but
$y_i>0$, the likelihood and evidence are zero and no posterior quotient is
defined. Otherwise put $E=\sum_i e_i$, $S=\sum_i y_i$, and
$$c(\mathbf e,\mathbf y)=\prod_{i:e_i>0}\frac{e_i^{y_i}}{y_i!},$$
with the empty product one. Then
$$m(\mathbf y)=c(\mathbf e,\mathbf y)\, \frac{b^a\Gamma(a+S)}{\Gamma(a)(b+E)^{a+S}}\in(0,\infty),$$
and the posterior is $\operatorname{Gamma}(a+S,b+E)$. This includes all-zero
exposures with zero counts, for which the posterior equals the prior.
For every natural number $n$, $\Gamma(n+1)=n!$.

The same identity applied to $(\theta,z)\mapsto g(z)$ gives the displayed integral formula.

Fix $B\in\mathcal Z$. The function $\theta\mapsto Q_\theta(B)$ is $\mathcal T$-measurable by [F2], so $(y,\theta)\mapsto Q_\theta(B)$ is $\mathcal Y\otimes\mathcal T$-measurable as the composition with the measurable coordinate projection. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same

$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

On $E_y$, $|z|\le 1+z^2$ gives a finite first absolute moment, so $\mu(\theta)$ is finite and measurable by [F4]. Expanding the square in the variance definition [F3] gives $v(\theta)=s_2(\theta)-\mu(\theta)^2\ge0$, hence $\mu(\theta)^2\le s_2(\theta)$; therefore $\mu$ is square-integrable under $\Pi_y$ and $v$ is integrable.

For the joint-model hypotheses in the Statement, let $B$ be a measurable future event and $G\in\mathcal G$. The function $\theta\mapsto Q_\theta(B)$ is measurable by [F9]. Apply [F5] to the posterior conditional law and this bounded function to obtain $\int_G Q^{\mathrm{pred}}_Y(B)\,dP=\int_G Q_X(B)\,dP$. Since $G\in\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal H$, apply [F5] again to the conditional law $Q_X$ to get $\int_G Q_X(B)\,dP=P(G\cap\{Z\in B\})$. By [F2], the mixture has probability-measure sections and measurable evaluations; these event identities therefore make $Q^{\mathrm{pred}}_Y$ a regular conditional distribution of $Z$ given $\mathcal G$ under [F6].

By [F1], $Q_y^{\mathrm{pred}}$ is the mixture defined from $Q_\theta$ and $\Pi_y$. Apply [F2] to $g(z)=z^2$ to obtain $\int z^2Q_y^{\mathrm{pred}}(dz)=\int s_2\,d\Pi_y<\infty$. Apply [F2] to $|z|$ and use $|z|\le1+z^2$ to see that $Q_y^{\mathrm{pred}}$ has finite first absolute moment. Applying [F2] to the nonnegative positive and negative parts of $z$ and subtracting their finite integrals gives $\int zQ_y^{\mathrm{pred}}(dz)=\int\mu\,d\Pi_y$.

Apply [F5] to $z$ and $z^2$ under $Q_X$. Writing $m:=\mu(X)$ and $s:=s_2(X)$, their conditional-integration identities give $\mathbb E[1_A Z]=\mathbb E[1_A m]$ and $\mathbb E[1_A Z^2]=\mathbb E[1_A s]$ for every $A\in\mathcal H$, and $\mathbb E[s]=\mathbb E[Z^2]<\infty$. Applying [F5] to $s_2$ under $\Pi_Y$ gives a conditional version of $s$ with expectation $\mathbb E[s]$; hence $D:=\{y:\int s_2(\theta)\Pi_y(d\theta)<\infty\}$ has full probability. Thus $\mathbb E[1_A mZ]=\mathbb E[1_A m^2]$, and expansion gives $\mathbb E[1_A(Z-m)^2]=\mathbb E[1_A(s-m^2)]=\mathbb E[1_Av(X)]$ for every $A\in\mathcal H$. This proves eventwise that $m$ is the conditional-mean version of $Z$ and $v(X)$ is the conditional-variance version given $\mathcal H$.

On $E_y$, $s_2=v+\mu^2$, and off $E_y$ the set is $\Pi_y$-null. By [F3] and step 2.1, $\operatorname{Var}_{Q_y^{\mathrm{pred}}}(Z)=\int s_2\,d\Pi_y-(\int\mu\,d\Pi_y)^2=\int v\,d\Pi_y+\int\mu^2\,d\Pi_y-(\int\mu\,d\Pi_y)^2=\int v\,d\Pi_y+\operatorname{Var}_{\Pi_y}(\mu)$. A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be an increasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$, so $E_n\subseteq E_{n+1}$. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\sup_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

No finiteness hypothesis is required.

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a decreasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$. If $\mu(E_{n_0})<+\infty$ for some $n_0$, then

$$\mu\left(\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\inf_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

Write $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ for the image of $\mathbb{Q}$ in $\mathbb{R}$
under the canonical embedding $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]), the
set usually written $\mathbb{Q}$ once the identification is made, and put
$X := \mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ for the irrationals. Then:

1. $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$, that is,
   $\overline{\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}} = \mathbb{R}$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]);
2. $X$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$;
3. every nonempty open subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is uncountable
   ([[def-countable]]).

Claim 2 is not a symmetry of claim 1: the rationals are dense because they are
*constructed* to approximate, whereas the irrationals are dense because there are
too many points in any interval for a countable set to exhaust it, which is why
claim 3 is proved alongside and used for it.

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

**No choice principle is used.** The one place where a reader expects a choice,
"pick a representative $a/b$ of each rational", is exactly where
[[lem-rat-positive-denominator]] applies: every rational *has* a representative
with positive denominator, so the map $(a,b) \mapsto [(a,b)]$ defined on
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is already **surjective** onto $\mathbb{Q}$,
and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).

The map $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[def-real-numbers]]) is an embedding of ordered
fields. Every real is approximated by rationals: for $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and
rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $q \in \mathbb{Q}$ with
$|x - \hat q| < \hat\varepsilon$. Consequently, strictly between any two
reals lies a rational.

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded below. Then $S$ has a
greatest lower bound in $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-infimum]]), and it is given by

$$\inf S = -\sup(-S), \qquad \text{where } -S = \{-s : s \in S\}.$$

In particular the complete ordered field $\mathbb{R}$ has the
greatest-lower-bound property, which is therefore not an extra axiom: it is a
consequence of the least-upper-bound property.

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ and $\ell \in \mathbb{R}$. Then $\ell$ is a
**greatest lower bound**, or **infimum**, of $S$ if both of the following hold:

- $\ell$ is a lower bound of $S$ ([[def-bounded-set]]), that is, $\ell \le s$ for
  every $s \in S$;
- $\ell' \le \ell$ for every lower bound $\ell'$ of $S$.

Written out in one line:

$$\ell \text{ is an infimum of } S \iff \big[(\forall s \in S)\, \ell \le s\big] \text{ and } \big[(\forall \ell' \in \mathbb{R})\, \big((\forall s \in S)\, \ell' \le s\big) \Rightarrow \ell' \le \ell\big].$$

An infimum, when it exists, is unique ([[lem-sup-unique]]), so we may write
$\inf S$ for it.
Let $\mu$ be a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. If $A,B\in\mathcal A$ and $A\subseteq B$, then $\mu(A)\le\mu(B)$.

Every complete ordered field $F$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) is Archimedean:
for every $x \in F$ there is a natural number $n \ge 1$ with $x < n \cdot 1_F$,
where $n \cdot 1_F$ is the canonical natural of the ordered field $F$
([[def-ordered-field]]). Equivalently, the canonical naturals are cofinal in $F$.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) and let
$\varepsilon \in F$ with $\varepsilon > 0$. Then there is a natural number
$n \ge 1$ such that

$$\frac{1}{n \cdot 1_F} < \varepsilon ,$$

where $n \cdot 1_F$ is the canonical natural of $F$ ([[thm-of-archimedean]]) and
$1/(n \cdot 1_F)$ is its multiplicative inverse ([[def-field]]). As is standard
we abbreviate $n \cdot 1_F$ to $n$ and write the conclusion $1/n < \varepsilon$.

This is the **reciprocal form** of the Archimedean property.
[[thm-of-archimedean]] on its own delivers only the assertion that the canonical
naturals are cofinal, $x < n \cdot 1_F$; the form actually used in analysis, that
the reciprocals of the naturals get below every positive bound, is the statement
above, and it is recorded separately so that no proof has to reconstruct the
inversion step in passing.

Let $F$ be an ordered field, with field structure as in [[def-field]], and for
$n \ge 1$ let $n \cdot 1_F$ denote the canonical natural number
$\underbrace{1_F + \cdots + 1_F}_{n}$, defined recursively by $1 \cdot 1_F = 1_F$
and $(n+1) \cdot 1_F = n \cdot 1_F + 1_F$. Then for every $n \ge 1$:

- $n \cdot 1_F > 0$ and $(n+1) \cdot 1_F > n \cdot 1_F$;
- the map $n \mapsto n \cdot 1_F$ is strictly increasing, hence injective, on $\{1, 2, 3, \dots\}$;
- $(m+n) \cdot 1_F = m \cdot 1_F + n \cdot 1_F$ and $(mn) \cdot 1_F = (m \cdot 1_F)(n \cdot 1_F)$ for all $m, n \ge 1$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) with positive cone $P$, and
let $a, b \in F$.

1. If $a > 0$ then $a^{-1} > 0$.
2. If $0 < a < b$ then $0 < b^{-1} < a^{-1}$.

The Cauchy-sequence reals $\mathbb{R}_C$ have the **least-upper-bound property**:
every nonempty $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}_C$ that is bounded above has a least upper
bound $\sup S \in \mathbb{R}_C$. Hence, together with [[thm-reals-ordered-field]],
$\mathbb{R}_C$ is a **complete ordered field** ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]).

derivations.claim: Fix $y$. By [F8, F10], the sets $(-\infty,n]$ increase to $\mathbb R$, so [F2] gives $F_y(n)\uparrow1$ and some natural $n$ satisfies $F_y(n)\ge u$. By [F4] choose a rational $r>n$; then [F7] gives $F_y(r)\ge u$, so $S_y=\{r\in\mathbb Q:F_y(r)\ge u\}$ is nonempty. Again by [F8, F10], the sets $(-\infty,-n]$ decrease to the empty set; [F3] gives some natural $m$ with $F_y(-m)<u$. Choose a rational $s<-m$ by [F4]. For any rational $r\le s$, [F7] gives $F_y(r)\le F_y(-m)<u$, so every member of $S_y$ exceeds $s$ and $S_y$ is bounded below. Hence [F6, F10] gives its real infimum $q_u(y)$.

For each $c\in\mathbb R$, the infimum definition and nonemptiness give $\{y:q_u(y)<c\}=\bigcup_{\substack{r\in\mathbb Q\\r<c}}\{y:F_y(r)\ge u\}.$ Each set on the right is measurable by [F1], and the union is countable by [F5], so $q_u$ is measurable.

Suppose $\Pi_y((-\infty,q_u(y)])<u$. By [F9], the sets $(-\infty,q_u(y)+1/n]$ decrease to $(-\infty,q_u(y)]$; they have finite measure by [F1], so [F3] gives an $n$ with $F_y(q_u(y)+1/n)<u$. By [F4], choose rational $r$ with $q_u(y)<r<q_u(y)+1/n$. Then [F7] gives $F_y(r)\le F_y(q_u(y)+1/n)<u$. Consequently no member of $S_y$ is at most $r$, so $r$ is a lower bound of $S_y$. Then $q_u(y)=\inf S_y\ge r>q_u(y)$, a contradiction; therefore $u\le\Pi_y((-\infty,q_u(y)])$.

Suppose $\Pi_y((-\infty,q_u(y)))>u$. By [F9], the sets $(-\infty,q_u(y)-1/n]$ increase to $(-\infty,q_u(y))$, so [F2] gives an $n$ with $F_y(q_u(y)-1/n)>u$. By [F4], choose rational $r$ with $q_u(y)-1/n<r<q_u(y)$. Then [F7] gives $F_y(r)\ge F_y(q_u(y)-1/n)>u$, so $r\in S_y$, contradicting that $q_u(y)$ is a lower bound of $S_y$. Thus $\Pi_y((-\infty,q_u(y)))\le u$. Combining with step 2.2 proves the CDF bracket.

**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library

Let $\pi$ be a prior probability on $(E,\mathcal S)$ and let $Q:E\to T$ be a probability kernel dominated by a sigma-finite measure $\nu$ on $(T,\mathcal T)$, with specified nonnegative jointly measurable density $\ell:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$:
$$Q(\theta,B)=\int_B\ell(\theta,y)\,\nu(dy)\quad\text{for every }\theta\in E,\ B\in\mathcal T.$$

Define $m(y)=\int_E\ell(\theta,y)\,\pi(d\theta)$. Under the joint law with density $\ell$ relative to $\pi\times\nu$, a conditional law of the parameter given the observation is
$$K(y,A)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\int_A\ell(\theta,y)\,\pi(d\theta)}{m(y)},&0<m(y)<\infty,\\ \pi(A),&m(y)=0\text{ or }m(y)=\infty.\end{cases}$$

The observation marginal is $m\,d\nu$, and the filled fibres have marginal mass zero. This is a choice-free assertion about the explicit kernel and event identities.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

supplier_interfaces.excerpt:
Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Real $L^2(\Omega,\mathcal G,P|_{\mathcal G})$ embeds isometrically as a closed subspace of real $L^2(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$. For $X\in L^2(P)$, $U=E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ is its orthogonal projection onto this subspace. It uniquely minimizes $E[(X-Z)^2]$ over $Z\in L^2(\mathcal G)$ as an almost-sure class.

derivations.claim: The absolute loss $L(\theta,a)=|\theta-a|$ is continuous on $\mathbb R^2$, hence product-Borel measurable as required by [F2]. The function $(y,\theta)\mapsto|\theta|$ is product-measurable, so [F4] makes its posterior integral measurable and hence $D_1$ a measurable data domain. Fix $y\in D_1$ and a median $m$. For any $a>m$, put $d=a-m$ and partition $\mathbb R$ into $A=(-\infty,m]$, $B=(m,a)$, and $C=[a,\infty)$. On these three sets respectively, $|\theta-a|-|\theta-m|$ equals $d$, $a+m-2\theta$, and $-d$. On $B$, $a+m-2\theta\ge-d$. If $a<m$, put $d=m-a$ and partition into $A=(-\infty,a]$, $B=(a,m)$, and $C=[m,\infty)$. On these sets the loss difference is respectively $-d$, $2\theta-a-m$, and $d$; on $B$, $2\theta-a-m\ge-d$. Hence $\rho_y(a)-\rho_y(m)\ge d\{-\Pi_y(A)-\Pi_y(B)+\Pi_y(C)\}=d\{2\Pi_y(C)-1\}\ge0$ by the second median condition [F1]. Equality holds when $a=m$. derivations.claim: Since the parameter and action spaces are finite with all subsets measurable, the zero–one loss is product-measurable as required by [F1]. For $j=1,\ldots,k$, put $p_j(y)=\Pi_y(\{j\})$. By [F2], every $p_j$ is measurable. The zero–one posterior risk of action $j$ is $\rho_y(j)=\sum_{\ell\ne j}p_\ell(y)=1-p_j(y).$ Thus the risk is minimized exactly by maximizing $p_j(y)$.

Since $k\ge1$ is finite, the nonempty finite list $p_1(y),\ldots,p_k(y)$ has a maximum. Define $j^*(y)$ to be the least index attaining it. For each $j$, $\{y:j^*(y)=j\}=\bigcap_{\ell>j}\{y:p_j(y)\ge p_\ell(y)\}\ \cap\ \bigcap_{\ell<j}\{y:p_j(y)>p_\ell(y)\}.$ Both intersections are finite, and each set is measurable because the $p_\ell$ are measurable; hence $j^*$ is measurable. $$s_2(\theta)=\int_{\mathbb R}z^2\,Q_\theta(dz),$$and assume $\int_\Theta s_2(\theta)\,\Pi_y(d\theta)<\infty$. On the full-measure set $E_y=\{\theta:s_2(\theta)<\infty\}$, define$$\mu(\theta)=\int z\,Q_\theta(dz),\qquad v(\theta)=\operatorname{Var}_{Q_\theta}(Z),$$and set $\mu=v=0$ off $E_y$ when integrating them against $\Pi_y$. $$\operatorname{Var}_{Q_y^{\mathrm{pred}}}(Z)=\int v(\theta)\,\Pi_y(d\theta)+\operatorname{Var}_{\Pi_y}(\mu).$$
These kernel identities are choice-free. For the conditional interpretation, suppose a joint probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ carries measurable random elements $Y$ (data), $X$ (parameter), and $Z$ (future observation). Let $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal H\subseteq\mathcal F$ be sub-sigma-algebras such that $Y$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable and $X$ is $\mathcal H$-measurable. Thus the future law given the information in $\mathcal H$ is assumed to depend on it through $X$ alone. If $\mathbb E[Z^2]<\infty$, then $Q^{\mathrm{pred}}_Y$ is a regular conditional distribution of $Z$ given $\mathcal G$, and the displayed identities give the corresponding conditional-mean and conditional-variance versions almost surely. For a fixed data fiber $y$ and action $a$, define the **posterior risk** only when
$$\rho_y(a):=\int_\Theta L(\theta,a)\,\Pi_y(d\theta)<\infty.$$
A **pointwise Bayes action** at $y$ is a finite-risk action attaining the minimum among all finite-risk actions. On a declared measurable data domain $D$, a **Bayes action rule** is a measurable map $\delta:D\to\mathsf A$ whose finite posterior risk attains that minimum at every $y\in D$. This definition makes no assertion that finite-risk actions or measurable minimizing rules always exist. It therefore does not infer a Bayes action merely from the existence of an infimum. $$\Pi_y((-\infty,m])\ge \tfrac12\quad\text{and}\quad\Pi_y([m,\infty))\ge\tfrac12.$$

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ be measurable spaces and let $y\mapsto\Pi_y$ be a supplied posterior probability kernel. For $\alpha\in[0,1]$, a set-valued rule $C$ is **graph-measurable** when
$$\{(y,\theta)\in\mathsf Y\times\Theta:\theta\in C(y)\}\in\mathcal Y\otimes\mathcal T.$$
It is a **posterior credible set at level $1-\alpha$** when it is graph-measurable and
$$\Pi_y(C(y))\ge 1-\alpha\qquad\text{for every }y\text{ in its declared data domain}.$$
The posterior-mass function is measurable by integration of the indicator of the membership graph against the kernel. If a density is available relative to a specified dominating measure, a highest-posterior-density region selects parameter values with largest density; such regions need not be intervals and may be disconnected or nonunique.

Let $\Pi_y$ be a posterior probability kernel on $\mathbb R$ and let $0<\alpha<1$. Define $C_\alpha(y)=[q_{\alpha/2}(y),q_{1-\alpha/2}(y)]$ using the quantiles from [[lem-measurable-posterior-quantile-and-cdf-bracketing]]. Then $C_\alpha$ is graph-measurable and $\Pi_y(C_\alpha(y))\ge1-\alpha$ for every $y$. Thus equal-tailed posterior quantile intervals are one kind of credible set.

Therefore the posterior densities are $p(\theta\mid Y=1)=2\theta$ and $p(\theta\mid Y=0)=2(1-\theta)$; each conditional law integrates to one and satisfies the defining conditioning identity.

Their CDFs on $[0,1]$ are $F_1(x)=x^2$ and $F_0(x)=1-(1-x)^2$. Hence the central 95% intervals are $C(1)=[\sqrt{0.025},\sqrt{0.975}]$ and $C(0)=[1-\sqrt{0.975},1-\sqrt{0.025}]$. Each has posterior mass $0.975-0.025=0.95$, also in accordance with [F1, F2].

For fixed true $\theta_0=0.005$, $\sqrt{0.025}>0.005$ because $0.025>0.005^2$. Also $1-\sqrt{0.975}>0.005$ because $0.975<0.995^2$. Thus $\theta_0$ lies below the lower endpoint of both possible intervals, so $P_{\theta_0}\{\theta_0\in C(Y)\}=0$, not $0.95$. This verifies that posterior credibility is not a frequentist coverage guarantee.

Let $(S,\Sigma)$ and $(T_i,\Tau_i)$ for $i<n$ be measurable spaces, with
$n<\infty$, and let $K_i:S\to T_i$ be probability kernels with the same
source. There is a unique probability kernel
$$K:S\to\prod_{i<n}T_i$$
whose evaluation on every measurable rectangle is
$$K(s,\prod_{i<n}B_i)=\prod_{i<n}K_i(s,B_i).$$
For $n=0$, the target is the empty-product singleton and $K$ is its point
mass. For $n>0$, the product sigma-algebra is the recursive finite product
sigma-algebra.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and define
$$\nu_f(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu \qquad (A\in\mathcal A).$$
Then $\nu_f$ is a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ generating $\mathcal A$, and let $\mu,\nu$ be measures on $(X,\mathcal A)$ that agree on $\mathcal P$. Suppose there is an increasing sequence $(P_n)$ in $\mathcal P$ with

$$X=\bigcup_nP_n,\qquad \mu(P_n)=\nu(P_n)<+\infty\quad(n\in\mathbb N).$$

Then $\mu=\nu$ on $\mathcal A$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space ([[def-measure-space]]). Equip
$\overline{\mathbb R}$ ([[def-extended-reals]]) with its order topology and let
$\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$ be the corresponding Borel sigma-algebra
([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]).

A function $f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ is **measurable** when
$f^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal A$ for every $B\in\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$.

Equivalently, it is enough to require
$$\{x\in X:f(x)>a\}\in\mathcal A \qquad \text{for every } a\in\mathbb R,$$
because the rays $(a,+\infty]$ generate $\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$.

Write $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ for the image of $\mathbb{Q}$ in $\mathbb{R}$
under the canonical embedding $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]), the
set usually written $\mathbb{Q}$ once the identification is made, and put
$X := \mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ for the irrationals. Then:

1. $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$, that is,
   $\overline{\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}} = \mathbb{R}$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]);
2. $X$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$;
3. every nonempty open subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is uncountable
   ([[def-countable]]).

Claim 2 is not a symmetry of claim 1: the rationals are dense because they are
*constructed* to approximate, whereas the irrationals are dense because there are
too many points in any interval for a countable set to exhaust it, which is why
claim 3 is proved alongside and used for it.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

derivations.claim: The product kernel $K$ is a probability kernel by [F1]. Construct the finite product measure recursively: the one-factor case is $\nu_0$, and each next product is sigma-finite by [F2] applied to the preceding sigma-finite product and the next $\nu_j$. By [F7], each coordinate pullback $(s,t)\mapsto f_j(s,t_j)$ is measurable on $S\times\prod_{j<n}T_j$. For two nonnegative extended-measurable functions $u,v$ and $a\ge0$, $$\{uv>a\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q,\ q>0}\{u>q\}\cap\{v>a/q\};$$ when $uv>a$, one can choose a positive rational $q$ with $a/v<q<u$, with the evident choice of any $0<q<u$ when $a=0$; this also covers infinite factors and excludes a zero factor under the stated $0\cdot\infty=0$ convention. For $a<0$ the superlevel set is the whole domain. Thus finite multiplication preserves measurability by [F6], and $f$ is jointly measurable.

Fix $s$ and define $\lambda_s(A)=\int_A f(s,t)\,
u(dt)$. By [F4], $\lambda_s$ is a measure. Repeated Tonelli [F3] and the probability-kernel density identities give $$\lambda_s\!\left(\prod_{j<n}T_jight)=\int\prod_{j<n}f_j(s,t_j)\,d
u=\prod_{j<n}\int f_j(s,t_j)\,
u_j(dt_j)=\prod_{j<n}K_j(s,T_j)=1.$$ Hence $\lambda_s$ is a probability measure.

For a measurable rectangle $R=\prod_{j<n}B_j$, repeated Tonelli and the density identities yield $$\lambda_s(R)=\prod_{j<n}\int_{B_j}f_j(s,t_j)\,\nu_j(dt_j)=\prod_{j<n}K_j(s,B_j)=K(s,R),$$ where the last equality is [F1]. Rectangles form a generating pi-system containing the whole product. Both measures are probabilities by step 1.2 and [F1], so the constant exhaustion by the whole product has common finite mass one. [F5] therefore gives $\lambda_s=K(s,\cdot)$ on the full product sigma-algebra. This holds for every $s$, proving the density assertion.

Fix a finite group count $m\ge1$, a standard Borel hyperparameter space
$(H,\mathcal H)$, and a standard Borel parameter space $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$.
Let $\Pi$ be a probability measure on $(H,\mathcal H)$ and let
$$G:H\times\mathcal T\to[0,1]$$
be a probability kernel. For each $j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$, let
$(\mathcal Y_j,\mathcal A_j)$ be a measurable observation space, let $\nu_j$
be a sigma-finite measure on it, and let $K_j$ be a probability kernel from
$(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ to $(\mathcal Y_j,\mathcal A_j)$ with a specified
jointly measurable density $f_j:\Theta\times\mathcal Y_j\to[0,\infty]$:
$$K_j(\theta,B)=\int_B f_j(\theta,y_j)\,\nu_j(dy_j)\qquad(B\in\mathcal A_j).$$

The **finite-group hierarchical model** is the following specified kernel
construction. First draw $\eta\sim\Pi$. Conditional on $\eta$, draw
$\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_m$ from the finite product kernel
$$G_\eta^{\otimes m}(d\theta_1\cdots d\theta_m)=\bigotimes_{j=1}^mG_\eta(d\theta_j).$$
Thus the group parameters are conditionally independent and have the same
conditional law $G_\eta$. Conditional on the parameter tuple, draw the group
observations from the product kernel $\bigotimes_{j=1}^mK_j(\theta_j,\cdot)$.
The product-kernel laws are probability kernels by
[[lem-finite-products-of-probability-kernels]]. For each fixed $\eta$, the
coordinate maps under $G_\eta^{\otimes m}$ are independent random elements,
so their joint law is the finite product law
([[thm-independent-random-elements-have-product-joint-law]]).

Put $\Xi=H\times\Theta^m$ with its finite product sigma-algebra. The proper
latent prior $P_0$ on $\Xi$ is
$$P_0(d\eta,d\theta_1\cdots d\theta_m)=\Pi(d\eta)\prod_{j=1}^mG_\eta(d\theta_j),$$
well-defined by [[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]]. For
$\xi=(\eta,\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_m)\in\Xi$, lift each observation kernel
to the common source $\Xi$ by
$$M_j(\xi,B)=K_j(\theta_j,B)\qquad(B\in\mathcal A_j).$$
The coordinate projection $\xi\mapsto\theta_j$ is measurable, so the kernel
definition shows that each $M_j$ is a probability kernel. Its specified
jointly measurable density is $(\xi,y_j)\mapsto f_j(\theta_j,y_j)$, by
composition with the same measurable coordinate projection. Let
$\mathcal Y=\prod_{j=1}^m\mathcal Y_j$,
$\nu=\bigotimes_{j=1}^m\nu_j$, and $y=(y_1,\ldots,y_m)$. The observation
kernel from $\Xi$ has jointly measurable density
$$L_y(\eta,\theta_1\cdots\theta_m)=\prod_{j=1}^m f_j(\theta_j,y_j)$$
with respect to $\nu$, by [[lem-finite-products-of-dominated-kernels-have-product-density]].
Its **evidence** is the possibly extended nonnegative number
$$Z(y)=\int_\Xi L_y(\eta,\theta_1\cdots\theta_m)\,P_0(d\eta,d\theta_1\cdots d\theta_m).$$
The normalized likelihood measure is called a pointwise joint posterior on a
fiber only when $0<Z(y)<\infty$; no quotient is formed at zero or infinite
evidence.

For each group, $\theta\mapsto K_j(\theta,\cdot)$ is a parametric statistical
model in the sense of [[def-parametric-statistical-model]], with its
parameter-measurable kernel representation as in
[[def-parameter-measurable-statistical-model-as-markov-kernel]]. Here
“conditionally independent given $\eta$” is shorthand for the explicit
finite product-kernel specification above. The library's random-element
conditional-independence terminology is defined in
[[def-conditional-independence-given-a-sigma-algebra]]; its
conditional-expectation-class convention assumes AC. The finite
product-kernel definition here does not use that class convention or any
choice axiom.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be measurable spaces,
let $\pi$ be a probability measure on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$, and let
$K:\Theta\times\mathcal A\to[0,1]$ be a probability kernel. For
$C\in\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal A$, write
$C_\theta=\{x\in\mathcal X:(\theta,x)\in C\}$ and set
$$J(C)=\int_\Theta K(\theta,C_\theta)\,\pi(d\theta).$$
Then $J$ is a probability measure on the product sigma-algebra, and for every
nonnegative product-measurable $h$,
$$\int_{\Theta\times\mathcal X}h(\theta,x)\,J(d\theta,dx)=\int_\Theta\left(\int_\mathcal Xh(\theta,x)\,K(\theta,dx)\right)\pi(d\theta).$$
In particular, $J(A\times B)=\int_AK(\theta,B)\,\pi(d\theta)$ for
$A\in\mathcal T$ and $B\in\mathcal A$.
Every finite product of standard Borel spaces, with its finite product sigma-algebra, is standard Borel.

Assume AC. Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ be a measurable random element with standard-Borel target, and let $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ be any sub-sigma-algebra. There exists a regular conditional distribution of $X$ given $\mathcal G$. Every section is a probability measure, including at exceptional sample points, and no countable-generation or completeness assumption on $\mathcal G$ is required.

For this necessarily nonempty target, the construction also supplies a bimeasurable bijection $c:E\to B$ onto a Borel set $B\subseteq[0,1]$, and a countable algebra $\mathcal A$ which generates $\mathcal S$, separates points, and determines finite measures.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Put $\Xi=H\times\Theta^m$ with its finite product sigma-algebra. The model definition supplies the proper latent prior $P_0$ on $\Xi$ and the probability kernel from $\Xi$ to the product observation space $\mathcal Y$; apply [F2] to obtain the joint probability law $P_0(d\xi)K(\xi,dy)$ on $\Xi\times\mathcal Y$. Let $\Omega=\Xi\times\mathcal Y$ with this law and let $\xi$ and $Y$ be the coordinate projections. By [F5], both projections are measurable.

The target $\Xi$ is standard Borel by [F3], since $H$ and $\Theta$ are standard Borel and there are finitely many factors. The coordinate map $\xi:\Omega\to\Xi$ is a measurable random element, and $\sigma(Y)$ is a sub-sigma-algebra of the canonical product sigma-algebra. By [F4] under [A1], $\xi$ has a regular conditional distribution given $\sigma(Y)$. The definition of a regular conditional distribution requires every section to be a probability measure, including at exceptional sample points. The theorem asserts no normalization formula on a fixed observation fiber.

boundaries.reason: Statement imports m>=1 and proper probability kernels from the hierarchical model; the latent standard-Borel target supports P_0 and cannot be empty on this canonical probability space.

boundaries.evidence: Statement distinguishes RCD existence from a normalized posterior on zero-evidence fibers.
The RCD definition requires probability sections at every sample point; step 2.1 invokes that property.
Statement admits point-mass hyperpriors and group-parameter kernels; proof step 2.1 needs only a standard-Borel latent target under AC, so deterministic latent coordinates still have an RCD.
Statement explicitly separates RCD existence from normalized likelihood values at Z=0 or infinity; proof step 2.1 guarantees probability sections even at exceptional sample points without a quotient.
Statement assumes AC, and step 2.1 uses it only to apply the standard-Borel RCD existence theorem.

boundaries.reason: Statement concludes RCD existence under AC and the standard-Borel hierarchy, not an iff characterization of measurable spaces admitting disintegration.
Proof applies standard-Borel existence only in the forward direction; having some RCD is not asserted to imply a standard-Borel latent target.

risk_review.notes: Reviewed both proof steps and all seven direct dependency statements/definitions. The canonical joint law uses proper P0 and a probability observation kernel. Coordinate maps are measurable; the finite latent target H x Theta^m is standard Borel. The cited RCD theorem requires AC and a standard-Borel target, but allows an arbitrary conditioning sub-sigma-algebra, so arbitrary observation spaces cause no gap. The target is nonempty because its proper prior exists. Every section is a probability under the exact RCD definition; this does not identify exceptional pointwise evidence fibers. No extra measurable factorization or normalization claimed. No reader/refuter finding or defect.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $(S,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space. For each $j<n$, let
$K_j$ be a probability kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T_j,\Tau_j)$, let
$\nu_j$ be sigma-finite on $(T_j,\Tau_j)$, and let
$f_j:S\times T_j\to[0,\infty]$ be a specified
jointly measurable function such that
$$K_j(s,B)=\int_B f_j(s,t_j)\,\nu_j(dt_j)\qquad(B\in\Tau_j).$$
On the finite product spaces, let $K=\bigotimes_{j<n}K_j$ be the product
probability kernel, let $\nu=\bigotimes_{j<n}\nu_j$, and put
$$f(s,t)=\prod_{j<n}f_j(s,t_j),$$
using the extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=0$. Then $f$ is jointly
measurable and, for every $s\in S$, it is a density of $K(s,\cdot)$

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be measurable spaces,
let $\pi$ be a probability measure on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$, and let
$K:\Theta\times\mathcal A\to[0,1]$ be a probability kernel. For
$C\in\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal A$, write
$C_\theta=\{x\in\mathcal X:(\theta,x)\in C\}$ and set
$$J(C)=\int_\Theta K(\theta,C_\theta)\,\pi(d\theta).$$

Let $\pi$ be a prior probability on $(E,\mathcal S)$ and let $Q:E\to T$ be a probability kernel dominated by a sigma-finite measure $\nu$ on $(T,\mathcal T)$, with specified nonnegative jointly measurable density $\ell:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$:
$$Q(\theta,B)=\int_B\ell(\theta,y)\,\nu(dy)\quad\text{for every }\theta\in E,\ B\in\mathcal T.$$

$$K(y,A)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\int_A\ell(\theta,y)\,\pi(d\theta)}{m(y)},&0<m(y)<\infty,\\ \pi(A),&m(y)=0\text{ or }m(y)=\infty.\end{cases}$$

derivations.claim: By [F1] and [F3], the latent prior $P_0$ is a probability measure and the model kernel gives a joint probability law for the latent tuple and the observations. By [F2], that observation kernel is dominated by the sigma-finite product measure $\nu$ with the specified jointly measurable density $L(\xi,y)=\prod_j f_j(\theta_j,y_j)$. Thus all hypotheses of [F4] apply with prior $P_0$ and likelihood density $L$.

The resulting evidence is $m(y)=\int_\Xi L_y(\xi)P_0(d\xi)=Z(y)$. On every fiber with $0<Z(y)<\infty$, [F4] gives the probability measure $P_y(A)=Z(y)^{-1}\int_A L_y\,dP_0$ and the conditional-event identities. On fibers with zero or infinite evidence [F4] uses the probability filler $P_0$, so its kernel remains a regular conditional distribution there without dividing by zero or infinity. The same theorem says these filled fibers have prior-predictive measure zero.

boundaries.evidence: Statement posterior formula at A=empty has numerator zero and positive finite denominator, giving P_y(empty)=0; its P_0 filler also assigns zero to empty.
Statement and step 2.1 use the prior filler instead of a quotient when evidence is zero.
Step 2.1 obtains a probability posterior by dividing by finite positive evidence.
Statement allows a point-mass proper latent prior P_0=delta_xi; at every positive finite evidence fiber the weighted quotient stays delta_xi, while exceptional fibers use the same prior filler.
Statement and step 2.1 fill both zero and infinite evidence fibers with P0.

boundaries.reason: Proof step 2.1 chooses the already supplied prior P_0 as its specified filler; it neither selects a latent point nor invokes a family of conditional-law representatives.
Statement gives the normalized posterior and specified exceptional-fiber filler; it does not characterize all posterior versions by an iff assertion.
Proof step 2.1 does not infer positive finite evidence from arbitrary conditional-law existence: the prior filler already yields a probability section on exceptional fibers.

finite_checks.claim: For a singleton latent space with prior mass 1 and likelihood value c in (0,infinity), the normalized posterior is the singleton point mass.
finite_checks.result: The evidence is c and the normalized likelihood-weighted prior has total mass c/c=1.

risk_review.notes: Reviewed steps 1.1-2.1 against model, product-density lemma, prior-kernel joint law and dominated Bayes theorem Statements. The supplied likelihood is jointly measurable on Xi x Y and dominates every kernel section against the sigma-finite finite product measure. P0 is a probability, so all Bayes hypotheses hold; Z is exactly its evidence m. Each positive finite fiber is normalized, while P0 is the probability filler on Z=0 or infinity. Those fibers have prior-predictive mass zero (infinite densities can occur only on nu-null sets since total integral is one). No quotient or canonical posterior uniqueness on exceptional fibers is asserted. No AC is used in this density derivation and no reader/refuter defect.

$f_j:S\times T_j\to[0,\infty]$ be a specified
jointly measurable function such that

Assume the finite-group hierarchical model of
[[def-hierarchical-bayesian-model]]. Write $P_0$ for its proper prior on
$\Xi=H\times\Theta^m$, let $L_y(\xi)$ be its specified product likelihood
density with respect to the finite product measure $\nu$, and define
$$Z(y)=\int_\Xi L_y(\xi)\,P_0(d\xi).$$
For every observation $y$ with $0<Z(y)<\infty$, the measure
$$P_y(A)=\frac{\int_A L_y(\xi)\,P_0(d\xi)}{Z(y)}\qquad(A\in\mathcal H\otimes\mathcal T^{\otimes m})$$

prior-predictive law; no quotient is formed on either exceptional fiber.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume AC. Let $\mu\sim N(\mu_0,\tau_0^2)$ with $\tau_0^2>0$, and, conditional
on $\mu$, let $Y_1,\ldots,Y_n$ be IID $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ with known
$\sigma^2>0$ and $n\ge1$. The sampling data use the Borel sigma-algebra on
$\mathbb R^n$ with $n$-dimensional Lebesgue measure. For every
$y_{1:n}\in\mathbb R^n$, define
$$V_n=(\tau_0^{-2}+n\sigma^{-2})^{-1},\qquad \mu_n=V_n\left(\frac{\mu_0}{\tau_0^2} +\frac{n\bar y}{\sigma^2}\right),\qquad \bar y=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^ny_i.$$
The evidence is finite and positive, and the posterior is $N(\mu_n,V_n)$.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ generating $\mathcal A$, and let $\mu,\nu$ be measures on $(X,\mathcal A)$ that agree on $\mathcal P$. Suppose there is an increasing sequence $(P_n)$ in $\mathcal P$ with

$$X=\bigcup_nP_n,\qquad \mu(P_n)=\nu(P_n)<+\infty\quad(n\in\mathbb N).$$

Then $\mu=\nu$ on $\mathcal A$.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces, and let
$$f : X \times Y \to \overline{\mathbb R}$$
be $(\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B,\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R}))$-measurable.
Then $f_x : Y \to \overline{\mathbb R}$ is $\mathcal B$-measurable for every
$x \in X$, and $f^y : X \to \overline{\mathbb R}$ is $\mathcal A$-measurable
for every $y \in Y$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $(S,\Sigma)$ and $(T_i,\Tau_i)$ for $i<n$ be measurable spaces, with
$n<\infty$, and let $K_i:S\to T_i$ be probability kernels with the same
source. There is a unique probability kernel
$$K:S\to\prod_{i<n}T_i$$
whose evaluation on every measurable rectangle is
$$K(s,\prod_{i<n}B_i)=\prod_{i<n}K_i(s,B_i).$$
For $n=0$, the target is the empty-product singleton and $K$ is its point
mass. For $n>0$, the product sigma-algebra is the recursive finite product
sigma-algebra.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Fix a group $j$ and specialize [F5] to one observation: identify its parameter with $\theta_j$, set $\mu_0=\mu$, $\tau_0^2=\tau^2$, $n=1$, $y_1=\bar y_j$, and $\sigma^2=s_j^2$. The model and pointwise density specification in [F1] supply this normal prior and the canonical normal likelihood density used by [F5], while [A1] and [A2] verify the choice and positive-variance hypotheses of [F5]. The theorem gives a finite positive group evidence and posterior variance $V_j=(1/\tau^2+1/s_j^2)^{-1}$ and mean $\hat\theta_j=V_j(\mu/\tau^2+\bar y_j/s_j^2)$, as stated.

For each group put $\mu_j(A)=\int_A f_j(\theta,\bar y_j)N(\mu,\tau^2)(d\theta)$ and let $m_j=\mu_j(\mathbb R)>0$. By [F5] and step 1.1, $\mu_j/m_j=Q_j=N(\hat\theta_j,V_j)$. Apply [F3] to the hierarchy with the proper point-mass hyperprior at the fixed $(\mu,\tau^2)$. Its latent prior on $\mathbb R^m$ is the product of the group priors by [F1], and its likelihood density is $\prod_j f_j(\theta_j,\bar y_j)$ by [F2]. Repeated Tonelli [F4] shows that the normalized posterior assigns each measurable rectangle $\prod_j A_j$ mass $\prod_j\mu_j(A_j)/\prod_jm_j=\prod_jQ_j(A_j)$, the rectangle mass of $\bigotimes_jQ_j$ by [F9]. By [F8], rectangles form a generating pi-system. Both are probability measures agreeing on it; the constant exhaustion by the full space has common finite mass one, so [F6] makes them equal. This proves conditional independence and the displayed formula for every group.

Now suppose $(\mu,\tau^2)$ is random with a proper hyperprior supported on $H$. For fixed observed summaries, put $M_j((\mu,\tau^2),A)=\int_A f_j(\theta,\bar y_j)N(\mu,\tau^2)(d\theta)$. The factor $f_j(\cdot,\bar y_j)$ is measurable by the section fact [F8]; composing it with the parameter-coordinate projection shows that $(\eta,\theta)\mapsto1_A(\theta)f_j(\theta,\bar y_j)$ is product-measurable. Since $G_\eta=N(\mu,\tau^2)$ is a probability kernel, [F7] makes $M_j(\cdot,A)$ measurable. Hence $m_j=M_j(\cdot,\mathbb R)$ and $Q_j(A)=M_j(\cdot,A)/m_j$ are measurable, with $m_j>0$ by step 1.1. Repeated Tonelli [F4] and the full-posterior formula [F3] give, for measurable $C\subseteq H$ and $A_1,\ldots,A_m\subseteq\mathbb R$, $P_y(C\times\prod_jA_j)=Z(y)^{-1}\int_C\prod_jM_j((\mu,\tau^2),A_j)\,\Pi(d\mu,d\tau^2)$. Taking every $A_j=\mathbb R$ shows $\Pi_y(C)=Z(y)^{-1}\int_C\prod_jm_j\,d\Pi$. Taking only $A_j=A$ and all other sets equal to $\mathbb R$ therefore gives $P_y(\theta_j\in A)=\int_HQ_j(A)\,\Pi_y(d\mu,d\tau^2)$. By [F5] and step 1.1, $Q_j=N(\hat\theta_j,V_j)$, so the group posterior is its conditional normal law averaged over the full hyperparameter posterior. If $\Pi_y$ is a point mass, this mixture equals its single conditional normal component; in general it need not equal a plug-in law.

citations.quote:
Assume the finite-group hierarchical model of
[[def-hierarchical-bayesian-model]]. Write $P_0$ for its proper prior on
$\Xi=H\times\Theta^m$, let $L_y(\xi)$ be its specified product likelihood
density with respect to the finite product measure $\nu$, and define
$$Z(y)=\int_\Xi L_y(\xi)\,P_0(d\xi).$$
For every observation $y$ with $0<Z(y)<\infty$, the measure
$$P_y(A)=\frac{\int_A L_y(\xi)\,P_0(d\xi)}{Z(y)}\qquad(A\in\mathcal H\otimes\mathcal T^{\otimes m})$$
is the joint posterior law of the latent tuple. Defining $P_y=P_0$ when
$Z(y)=0$ or $Z(y)=\infty$ gives a regular conditional distribution under the
prior-predictive law; no quotient is formed on either exceptional fiber.

Fix a finite group count $m\ge1$, a standard Borel hyperparameter space
$(H,\mathcal H)$, and a standard Borel parameter space $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$.
Let $\Pi$ be a probability measure on $(H,\mathcal H)$ and let
$$G:H\times\mathcal T\to[0,1]$$
be a probability kernel. For each $j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$, let
$(\mathcal Y_j,\mathcal A_j)$ be a measurable observation space, let $\nu_j$
be a sigma-finite measure on it, and let $K_j$ be a probability kernel from
$(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ to $(\mathcal Y_j,\mathcal A_j)$ with a specified
jointly measurable density $f_j:\Theta\times\mathcal Y_j\to[0,\infty]$:
$$K_j(\theta,B)=\int_B f_j(\theta,y_j)\,\nu_j(dy_j)\qquad(B\in\mathcal A_j).$$

The **finite-group hierarchical model** is the following specified kernel
construction. First draw $\eta\sim\Pi$. Conditional on $\eta$, draw
$\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_m$ from the finite product kernel
$$G_\eta^{\otimes m}(d\theta_1\cdots d\theta_m)=\bigotimes_{j=1}^mG_\eta(d\theta_j).$$
Thus the group parameters are conditionally independent and have the same
conditional law $G_\eta$. Conditional on the parameter tuple, draw the group
observations from the product kernel $\bigotimes_{j=1}^mK_j(\theta_j,\cdot)$.
The product-kernel laws are probability kernels by
[[lem-finite-products-of-probability-kernels]]. For each fixed $\eta$, the
coordinate maps under $G_\eta^{\otimes m}$ are independent random elements,
so their joint law is the finite product law
([[thm-independent-random-elements-have-product-joint-law]]).

Put $\Xi=H\times\Theta^m$ with its finite product sigma-algebra. The proper
latent prior $P_0$ on $\Xi$ is
$$P_0(d\eta,d\theta_1\cdots d\theta_m)=\Pi(d\eta)\prod_{j=1}^mG_\eta(d\theta_j),$$
well-defined by [[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]]. For
$\xi=(\eta,\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_m)\in\Xi$, lift each observation kernel
to the common source $\Xi$ by
$$M_j(\xi,B)=K_j(\theta_j,B)\qquad(B\in\mathcal A_j).$$
The coordinate projection $\xi\mapsto\theta_j$ is measurable, so the kernel
definition shows that each $M_j$ is a probability kernel. Its specified
jointly measurable density is $(\xi,y_j)\mapsto f_j(\theta_j,y_j)$, by
composition with the same measurable coordinate projection. Let
$\mathcal Y=\prod_{j=1}^m\mathcal Y_j$,
$\nu=\bigotimes_{j=1}^m\nu_j$, and $y=(y_1,\ldots,y_m)$. The observation
kernel from $\Xi$ has jointly measurable density
$$L_y(\eta,\theta_1\cdots\theta_m)=\prod_{j=1}^m f_j(\theta_j,y_j)$$
with respect to $\nu$, by [[lem-finite-products-of-dominated-kernels-have-product-density]].
Its **evidence** is the possibly extended nonnegative number
$$Z(y)=\int_\Xi L_y(\eta,\theta_1\cdots\theta_m)\,P_0(d\eta,d\theta_1\cdots d\theta_m).$$
The normalized likelihood measure is called a pointwise joint posterior on a
fiber only when $0<Z(y)<\infty$; no quotient is formed at zero or infinite
evidence.

For each group, $\theta\mapsto K_j(\theta,\cdot)$ is a parametric statistical
model in the sense of [[def-parametric-statistical-model]], with its
parameter-measurable kernel representation as in
[[def-parameter-measurable-statistical-model-as-markov-kernel]]. Here
“conditionally independent given $\eta$” is shorthand for the explicit
finite product-kernel specification above. The library's random-element
conditional-independence terminology is defined in
[[def-conditional-independence-given-a-sigma-algebra]]; its
conditional-expectation-class convention assumes AC. The finite
product-kernel definition here does not use that class convention or any
choice axiom.

Let $\mathcal Y=\prod_{j=1}^m\mathcal Y_j$ be the data space and
$\mathcal Y_+=\{y\in\mathcal Y:0<Z(y)<\infty\}$ its measurable subset of
positive finite evidence fibers. Write $P_y$ for the full latent probability
kernel supplied by
[[thm-hierarchical-posterior-normalization-on-positive-finite-evidence]], and
set $\Lambda_y:=P_y$ for every $y\in\mathcal Y$. On $\mathcal Y_+$ this is
the normalized joint posterior; off $\mathcal Y_+$ it is the prior filler
$P_0$, so no likelihood quotient is formed there. For an already observed
group $j$, its **current-group posterior predictive law** for a future
observation with the same conditional observation kernel is
$$Q^{\mathrm{cur}}_{j,y}(A)=\int_\Xi K_j(\theta_j,A)\,\Lambda_y(d\eta,d\theta_1\cdots d\theta_m).$$

For a new group, specify a probability kernel $K_{\mathrm{new}}$ from
$(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ to a future observation space
$(\widetilde{\mathcal Y},\widetilde{\mathcal A})$. Its **new-group posterior
predictive law** is
$$Q^{\mathrm{new}}_y(A)=\int_\Xi\left[\int_\Theta K_{\mathrm{new}}(\theta,A)\,G_\eta(d\theta)\right]\,\Lambda_y(d\eta,d\theta_1\cdots d\theta_m).$$
For $y\in\mathcal Y_+$, if $\Lambda_y^\eta$ denotes the hyperparameter
marginal of $\Lambda_y$, the joint posterior law of
$(\eta,\theta_{\mathrm{new}})$ used here is
$\Lambda_y^\eta(d\eta)G_\eta(d\theta_{\mathrm{new}})$. Thus the new-group
prediction first draws a new latent parameter from $G_\eta$ and then draws its
observation from $K_{\mathrm{new}}$. On $\mathcal Y_+$ both formulas average
over the joint posterior and retain uncertainty about unknown hyperparameters.
On exceptional fibers they reduce to prior-predictive laws because
$\Lambda_y=P_0$.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $K$ be a specified regular conditional distribution of $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ given $\mathcal G$. For measurable $f:E\to[0,\infty]$, the measurable function $I_f(\omega)=\int f(x)K(\omega,dx)$ satisfies

$$\int_H I_f\,dP=\int_H f(X)\,dP\qquad(H\in\mathcal G).$$

This assertion is choice-free. Under AC, it says $I_f=E[f(X)\mid\mathcal G]$ as nonnegative almost-sure classes. If $f:E\to\mathbb R$ is measurable and $E|f(X)|<\infty$, put $D=\{I_{|f|}<\infty\}$. Then $D\in\mathcal G$, $P(D)=1$, and the signed integral on $D$, extended by zero off $D$, is a real integrable conditional-expectation version of $f(X)$. Its identification with the AC-based conditional-expectation class uses AC only for that class convention.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be measurable spaces,
let $\pi$ be a probability measure on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$, and let
$K:\Theta\times\mathcal A\to[0,1]$ be a probability kernel. For
$C\in\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal A$, write
$C_\theta=\{x\in\mathcal X:(\theta,x)\in C\}$ and set
$$J(C)=\int_\Theta K(\theta,C_\theta)\,\pi(d\theta).$$
Then $J$ is a probability measure on the product sigma-algebra, and for every
nonnegative product-measurable $h$,
$$\int_{\Theta\times\mathcal X}h(\theta,x)\,J(d\theta,dx)=\int_\Theta\left(\int_\mathcal Xh(\theta,x)\,K(\theta,dx)\right)\pi(d\theta).$$
In particular, $J(A\times B)=\int_AK(\theta,B)\,\pi(d\theta)$ for
$A\in\mathcal T$ and $B\in\mathcal A$.

Let $(S,\Sigma)$ and $(T_i,\Tau_i)$ for $i<n$ be measurable spaces, with
$n<\infty$, and let $K_i:S\to T_i$ be probability kernels with the same
source. There is a unique probability kernel
$$K:S\to\prod_{i<n}T_i$$
whose evaluation on every measurable rectangle is
$$K(s,\prod_{i<n}B_i)=\prod_{i<n}K_i(s,B_i).$$
For $n=0$, the target is the empty-product singleton and $K$ is its point
mass. For $n>0$, the product sigma-algebra is the recursive finite product
sigma-algebra.

derivations.claim: Fix a current group $j$ and $y\in\mathcal Y$. For each measurable future-event set $A$, the formula $Q^{\mathrm{cur}}_{j,y}(A)=\int K_j(\theta_j,A)\,P_y(d\xi)$ gives zero on $A=\varnothing$ and one on the full observation space by [F1] and [F2]. If $(A_k)_{k\ge0}$ are disjoint, then $K_j(\theta_j,\bigcup_kA_k)=\lim_N\sum_{k\le N}K_j(\theta_j,A_k)$; [F4] passes this increasing limit through the $P_y$ integral and gives countable additivity. The integrand is measurable in $\xi$ by the kernel definition and coordinate projection, so [F3] makes $y\mapsto Q^{\mathrm{cur}}_{j,y}(A)$ measurable against the posterior kernel $y\mapsto P_y$. Thus each $Q^{\mathrm{cur}}_j$ is a probability kernel from $\mathcal Y$ to $\mathcal Y_j$.

For a new group, define $R_\eta(A)=\int K_{\mathrm{new}}(\theta,A)G_\eta(d\theta)$. The empty-set and whole-space evaluations are zero and one. For disjoint $(A_k)$, countable additivity of each $K_{\mathrm{new}}(\theta,\cdot)$ and [F4] pass the increasing partial sums through the $G_\eta$ integral; hence $R_\eta$ is a probability measure. [F3] makes $\eta\mapsto R_\eta(A)$ measurable, so $R$ is a probability kernel. Mixing $R_\eta(A)$ over $P_y$ through the measurable coordinate $\eta$ and repeating the countable-additivity argument shows that $Q^{\mathrm{new}}_y(A)$ is a probability measure and [F3] makes its evaluations measurable in $y$. Thus $Q^{\mathrm{new}}$ is a probability kernel from $\mathcal Y$ to $\widetilde{\mathcal Y}$. Its integral through the marginal $P_y^\eta$ is the same iterated-kernel law.

For either prediction let $H(\xi,A)$ be its conditional future-event probability given the latent tuple: $K_j(\theta_j,A)$ for a current group, or $R_\eta(A)$ for a new group. Steps 1.1–1.2 make $H$ a probability kernel. In the stipulated extension, [F7] ensures that the product of the observation kernel and this future kernel is a probability kernel from $\Xi$ to the product of data and future-observation spaces; applying [F6] with prior $P_0$ gives a joint probability law on $(\xi,Y,\widetilde Y)$. Because every section of $H$ has total mass one, marginalizing out $\widetilde Y$ leaves the original joint law of $(\xi,Y)$, so [F1] still supplies its posterior conditional law $P_y$. For data event $B$ and future event $A$, the triple law gives $P(Y\in B,\widetilde Y\in A)=E[1_{\{Y\in B\}}H(\xi,A)]$. Applying the event identity in [F5] to $H(\xi,A)$ turns the right side into $\int_B\int H(\xi,A)\,P_y(d\xi)\,P_Y(dy)=\int_B Q_y(A)\,P_Y(dy)$. This verifies the conditional-event identity for every data event $B$ and proves that both predictive kernels are the conditional laws of the future observations. Since $P_y=P_0$ off $\mathcal Y_+$, their exceptional-fiber predictions are the prior-predictive laws.

boundaries.evidence: Proof steps 1.1 and 1.2 explicitly evaluate both predictive set functions at A=empty and obtain zero before proving countable additivity.
Statement and step 2.1 show predictions on zero-evidence fibers use the prior predictive law.
Steps 1.1 and 2.1 verify total mass one for current and new-group predictions.

Proof steps 1.1 and 1.2 require only probability kernels, so deterministic current or new latent kernels remain admissible; a point-mass posterior reduces the corresponding outer integral to evaluation at its atom.
Statement and step 2.1 handle both zero and infinite evidence fibers with the prior filler.

boundaries.reason: Proof constructs R_eta by an integral and the triple joint law by finite products; its prior filler is fixed by F1, and no measurable selection from possible future values is required.
Statement establishes probability-kernel and conditional-law properties under the specified future sampling model; it does not characterize all possible predictive kernels by an equivalence.
Proof step 2.1 verifies conditioning-event identities for the constructed triple law; it does not recover a unique latent hierarchy from a conditional future law.

finite_checks.claim: If the posterior gives equal mass to two latent states and both future Bernoulli kernels assign probability 1/2 to {1}, the predictive probability of {1} is 1/2.
finite_checks.result: The kernel mixture is (1/2)(1/2)+(1/2)(1/2)=1/2; the same normalization holds on a prior-filler fiber.

Assume AC. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma>0$, the normal law $N(m,\sigma^2)$
of [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]] has Lebesgue density
$$g_{m,\sigma}(y)=\frac1\sigma\frac{e^{-((y-m)/\sigma)^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}e^{-(y-m)^2/(2\sigma^2)}.$$
Assume AC. The function $\phi(x)=e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}$ is positive and Borel measurable on $\mathbb R$, with Lebesgue integral one.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ be a measurable parameter space, let $\Pi$ be a
sigma-finite measure on it, and fix a data value $y$. Let
$L_y:\Theta\to[0,+\infty]$ be a $\mathcal T$-measurable function. Define its
**evidence normalizer** by
$$Z_\Pi(y):=\int_\Theta L_y(\theta)\,\Pi(d\theta)\in[0,+\infty].$$
Only when $0<Z_\Pi(y)<+\infty$ define the **fiberwise posterior update** by
$$\Pi_y(A):=\frac{\int_A L_y(\theta)\,\Pi(d\theta)}{Z_\Pi(y)}\qquad(A\in\mathcal T).$$
The definition makes no quotient at zero or infinite evidence. A prior is
**proper** when $\Pi(\Theta)=1$, as in
[[def-bayesian-model-as-prior-and-sampling-kernel]]. We call a sigma-finite
prior **improper** when $\Pi(\Theta)=+\infty$; the formula also applies to
other sigma-finite measures. For an improper prior, $Z_\Pi(y)$ is a fiberwise
normalizer only; it does not by itself define a prior-predictive probability or
a conditional law.

When the data are described by a dominated experiment, the dominating measure
and its sigma-finiteness are as in
[[def-dominated-statistical-experiment]]. A family of pointwise likelihood
sections is not assumed to be jointly measurable in parameter and data; that
additional condition must be supplied separately whenever Tonelli is used.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T,\Pi)$ be a measure space, let $L_y:\Theta\to[0,+\infty]$
be measurable for a fixed datum $y$, and put
$Z:=\int_\Theta L_y\,d\Pi$. For a finite positive constant $c$, the set
function
$$A\longmapsto c\int_A L_y\,d\Pi$$
is a probability measure if and only if $0<Z<+\infty$ and $c=Z^{-1}$. In
particular, if $Z=0$ or $Z=+\infty$, no finite positive scaling makes the
fiberwise update a probability measure.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: The prior is sigma-finite: the sets $E_n=[1/n,n]$ increase to $(0,\infty)$ and $\Pi(E_n)=\int_{1/n}^n dt/t=2\log n<\infty$. Integrating out $\theta$ gives the evidence at fixed $t$, $m(0\mid t)=\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{e^{-\theta^2/(2t)}}{\sqrt{2\pi t}}\frac{e^{-\theta^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\,d\theta=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi(1+t)}}$. Indeed, the exponent is $-(1+t^{-1})\theta^2/2$; the substitution $z=\sqrt{1+t^{-1}}\,\theta$ reduces the integral to the unit normal integral [F2]. It is positive and finite for every $t>0$.

The evidence-weighted density of $t$ is $q(t)=1/(t\sqrt{2\pi(1+t)})$ by [A2] and step 1.1. For each $k\ge0$, let $I_k=(2^{-(k+1)},2^{-k})$. On $I_k\subset(0,1)$, $q(t)\ge1/(t\sqrt{4\pi})$ and $1/t\ge2^k$, while the interval has length $2^{-(k+1)}$. Hence $\int_{I_k}q(t)\,dt\ge1/(2\sqrt{4\pi})$, uniformly in $k$.
