Fix a finite group count $m\ge1$, a standard Borel hyperparameter space
$(H,\mathcal H)$, and a standard Borel parameter space $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$.
Let $\Pi$ be a probability measure on $(H,\mathcal H)$ and let
$$G:H\times\mathcal T\to[0,1]$$
be a probability kernel. For each $j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$, let
$(\mathcal Y_j,\mathcal A_j)$ be a measurable observation space, let $\nu_j$
be a sigma-finite measure on it, and let $K_j$ be a probability kernel from
$(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ to $(\mathcal Y_j,\mathcal A_j)$ with a specified
jointly measurable density $f_j:\Theta\times\mathcal Y_j\to[0,\infty]$:
$$K_j(\theta,B)=\int_B f_j(\theta,y_j)\,\nu_j(dy_j)\qquad(B\in\mathcal A_j).$$

The **finite-group hierarchical model** is the following specified kernel
construction. First draw $\eta\sim\Pi$. Conditional on $\eta$, draw
$\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_m$ from the finite product kernel
$$G_\eta^{\otimes m}(d\theta_1\cdots d\theta_m)=\bigotimes_{j=1}^mG_\eta(d\theta_j).$$
Thus the group parameters are conditionally independent and have the same
conditional law $G_\eta$. Conditional on the parameter tuple, draw the group
observations from the product kernel $\bigotimes_{j=1}^mK_j(\theta_j,\cdot)$.
The product-kernel laws are probability kernels by
[[lem-finite-products-of-probability-kernels]]. For each fixed $\eta$, the
coordinate maps under $G_\eta^{\otimes m}$ are independent random elements,
so their joint law is the finite product law
([[thm-independent-random-elements-have-product-joint-law]]).

Put $\Xi=H\times\Theta^m$ with its finite product sigma-algebra. The proper
latent prior $P_0$ on $\Xi$ is
$$P_0(d\eta,d\theta_1\cdots d\theta_m)=\Pi(d\eta)\prod_{j=1}^mG_\eta(d\theta_j),$$
well-defined by [[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]]. For
$\xi=(\eta,\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_m)\in\Xi$, lift each observation kernel
to the common source $\Xi$ by
$$M_j(\xi,B)=K_j(\theta_j,B)\qquad(B\in\mathcal A_j).$$
The coordinate projection $\xi\mapsto\theta_j$ is measurable, so the kernel
definition shows that each $M_j$ is a probability kernel. Its specified
jointly measurable density is $(\xi,y_j)\mapsto f_j(\theta_j,y_j)$, by
composition with the same measurable coordinate projection. Let
$\mathcal Y=\prod_{j=1}^m\mathcal Y_j$,
$\nu=\bigotimes_{j=1}^m\nu_j$, and $y=(y_1,\ldots,y_m)$. The observation
kernel from $\Xi$ has jointly measurable density
$$L_y(\eta,\theta_1\cdots\theta_m)=\prod_{j=1}^m f_j(\theta_j,y_j)$$
with respect to $\nu$, by [[lem-finite-products-of-dominated-kernels-have-product-density]].
Its **evidence** is the possibly extended nonnegative number
$$Z(y)=\int_\Xi L_y(\eta,\theta_1\cdots\theta_m)\,P_0(d\eta,d\theta_1\cdots d\theta_m).$$
The normalized likelihood measure is called a pointwise joint posterior on a
fiber only when $0<Z(y)<\infty$; no quotient is formed at zero or infinite
evidence.

For each group, $\theta\mapsto K_j(\theta,\cdot)$ is a parametric statistical
model in the sense of [[def-parametric-statistical-model]], with its
parameter-measurable kernel representation as in
[[def-parameter-measurable-statistical-model-as-markov-kernel]]. Here
“conditionally independent given $\eta$” is shorthand for the explicit
finite product-kernel specification above. The library's random-element
conditional-independence terminology is defined in
[[def-conditional-independence-given-a-sigma-algebra]]; its
conditional-expectation-class convention assumes AC. The finite
product-kernel definition here does not use that class convention or any
choice axiom.

Assume the finite-group hierarchical model of
[[def-hierarchical-bayesian-model]]. Write $P_0$ for its proper prior on
$\Xi=H\times\Theta^m$, let $L_y(\xi)$ be its specified product likelihood
density with respect to the finite product measure $\nu$, and define
$$Z(y)=\int_\Xi L_y(\xi)\,P_0(d\xi).$$
For every observation $y$ with $0<Z(y)<\infty$, the measure
$$P_y(A)=\frac{\int_A L_y(\xi)\,P_0(d\xi)}{Z(y)}\qquad(A\in\mathcal H\otimes\mathcal T^{\otimes m})$$
is the joint posterior law of the latent tuple. Defining $P_y=P_0$ when
$Z(y)=0$ or $Z(y)=\infty$ gives a regular conditional distribution under the
prior-predictive law; no quotient is formed on either exceptional fiber.

Assume the normal specialization of [[def-hierarchical-bayesian-model]] with
parameter space $\Theta=\mathbb R$ and hyperparameter space
$H=\mathbb R\times(0,\infty)$. Fix $\mu\in\mathbb R$ and $\tau^2>0$.
Conditional on $(\mu,\tau^2)$, let the
group parameters be independent with $\theta_j\sim N(\mu,\tau^2)$. Let the
observed group summaries be conditionally independent with
$\bar Y_j\mid\theta_j\sim N(\theta_j,s_j^2)$, where each known $s_j^2>0$. In this normal specialization, the supplied
likelihood-density version is the canonical normal density at every parameter
and observation value:
$$f_j(\theta,y)=(2\pi s_j^2)^{-1/2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{(y-\theta)^2}{2s_j^2}\right)\qquad(\theta,y\in\mathbb R).$$
Then, conditional on $(\mu,\tau^2,\bar Y_1=\bar y_1,\ldots,\bar Y_m=\bar y_m)$,
the $\theta_j$ are independent and
$$\theta_j\sim N(\hat\theta_j,V_j),\qquad\hat\theta_j=\frac{\bar y_j/s_j^2+\mu/\tau^2}{1/s_j^2+1/\tau^2},\qquad V_j=\left(1/s_j^2+1/\tau^2\right)^{-1}.$$
If $(\mu,\tau^2)$ is unknown with a proper hyperprior supported on
$\mathbb R\times(0,\infty)$, let $P_y$ be the full posterior kernel from
[[thm-hierarchical-posterior-normalization-on-positive-finite-evidence]] and,
on each positive finite evidence fiber, define its hyperparameter marginal on
Borel $C\subseteq H$ by $\Pi_y(C):=P_y(C\times\mathbb R^m)$. The posterior law of
$\theta_j$ is the mixture of these conditional normal laws over $\Pi_y$;
replacing $\mu,\tau^2$ by point estimates need not give this posterior. No normalized
hyperparameter posterior is asserted on a zero or infinite evidence fiber.

Assume AC. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma>0$, the normal law $N(m,\sigma^2)$
of [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]] has Lebesgue density
$$g_{m,\sigma}(y)=\frac1\sigma\frac{e^{-((y-m)/\sigma)^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}e^{-(y-m)^2/(2\sigma^2)}.$$
Assume AC. The function $\phi(x)=e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}$ is positive and Borel measurable on $\mathbb R$, with Lebesgue integral one.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: The specified model supplies the prior and sampling kernels [F1]; their densities are given by [F4]. For fixed $t>0$, multiply the two densities and integrate over $\theta$. The integrand is $(2\pi\sqrt t)^{-1}\exp(-(1+t^{-1})\theta^2/2)$. Substituting $z=\sqrt{1+t^{-1}}\,\theta$ and using [F5] for the unit normal integral gives the marginal evidence $m_t(0)=1/\sqrt{2\pi(1+t)}$, which is positive and finite for $t=1,4$.

The two prior masses are equal, so [F2] gives posterior odds $P(t=1\mid y=0)/P(t=4\mid y=0)=m_1(0)/m_4(0)=\sqrt{5/2}>1$. Thus the posterior mode is $t=1$, and the posterior weights $w=P(t=1\mid y=0)$ and $1-w$ are both strictly between zero and one.
By [F3], $\theta\mid t=1,y=0\sim N(0,1/2)$ and $\theta\mid t=4,y=0\sim N(0,4/5)$. The full posterior is their mixture with weights $w$ and $1-w$, so its second moment is $w/2+(1-w)4/5>1/2$.

Plugging in the posterior mode $t=1$ gives only $N(0,1/2)$, whose second moment is $1/2$. This differs from the full posterior's second moment in step 3.1, so the plug-in posterior is not the full posterior mixture.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.1 checks both two-point hyperparameter evidences are strictly positive.

Verification step 2.1 proves both posterior weights are strictly between zero and one, so the full posterior is not a single-component degenerate mixture; step 3.1 distinguishes it by its strictly larger second moment.

finite_checks.claim: For t in {1,4} and y=0, the evidence ratio m_1(0)/m_4(0)=sqrt(5/2)>1 and the conditional posterior variances are 1/2 and 4/5.
finite_checks.result: Both hyperparameter posterior weights are strictly positive, so the mixture variance exceeds 1/2 while the mode plug-in variance is 1/2.

derivations.claim: Set $a_j=\tau^2/(\tau^2+s_j^2)$. Algebra in [F1] gives $\hat\theta_j=a_j\bar y_j+(1-a_j)\mu$ and $V_j=\tau^2s_j^2/(\tau^2+s_j^2)$. Since both variances are positive, $0<a_j<1$, so for finite positive $\tau^2$ the group mean uses both its own data and the population mean.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. For $m\in\mathbb R$, $\sigma\ge0$, and a real random variable
$X$ with law $N(m,\sigma^2)$,
$$E[X]=m,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(X)=\sigma^2.$$

If $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is a finite pairwise-independent family of square-integrable real random variables on a common probability space, then
$$\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\sum_{i\in I}X_i\right)=\sum_{i\in I}\operatorname{Var}(X_i).$$
Pairwise independence, rather than mutual independence, is sufficient. In particular, the original finite-probability-space case is included, with pairwise atom independence as in the finite-valued convention. The empty sum has variance zero.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. For each $i$, let
$g_i:(S_i,\Sigma_i)\to(T_i,\mathcal T_i)$ be measurable. Then the family
$(g_i\circ X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability
space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

derivations.claim: Put $\bar\epsilon_i=r^{-1}\sum_j\epsilon_{ij}$. By [F1], every error has mean zero and variance $\sigma^2$; [F6] gives $\mathbb E[\bar\epsilon_i]=0$. By [F2], the variance of $\sum_j\epsilon_{ij}$ is $r\sigma^2$, and the variance definition [F4] gives $\operatorname{Var}(\bar\epsilon_i)=r^{-2}r\sigma^2=\sigma^2/r$. Since $a_i$ is independent of the error vector, [F3] makes $a_i$ independent of $\bar\epsilon_i$. Thus [F2] gives $\operatorname{Var}(\bar Y_{i\cdot})=\tau^2+\sigma^2/r$, and [F6] gives $\mathbb E[\bar Y_{i\cdot}]=\mu$. Applying [F3] to the independent group blocks shows that the group means are independent by [F7].

For any numbers $x_1,\ldots,x_k$ with mean $\bar x$, expansion gives $\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2=\sum_i(x_i-\mu)^2-k(\bar x-\mu)^2$. Apply this with $x_i=\bar Y_{i\cdot}$. By [F2], $\operatorname{Var}(\bar Y_{\cdot\cdot})=(\tau^2+\sigma^2/r)/k$; [F4], [F5], and [F6] therefore give $\mathbb E\sum_i(\bar Y_{i\cdot}-\bar Y_{\cdot\cdot})^2=(k-1)(\tau^2+\sigma^2/r)$. $i\in I$, let $(\Theta_i,\mathcal T_i)$ be a measurable parameter space, let
$\Pi_i$ be a probability measure ([[def-probability-measure]]) on it, and let
$Q_i$ be a sampling kernel for a statistical experiment
([[def-statistical-experiment]]) on one common data space
$(\mathcal Y,\mathcal A)$. Assume the experiments are dominated
([[def-dominated-statistical-experiment]]) by the same supplied sigma-finite
measure $\mu$. Fix a specified likelihood density
([[def-likelihood-density]])
$f_i:\Theta_i\times\mathcal Y\to[0,\infty]$ such that
$$Q_i(\theta,B)=\int_B f_i(\theta,y)\,\mu(dy)\qquad(B\in\mathcal A).$$
Require that each $f_i$ is jointly measurable in parameter and data; separate
likelihood versions do not imply this joint measurability. Assign prior model
weights $w_i>0$ with $\sum_iw_i=1$. The **marginal likelihood**, or **model
evidence**, at $y$ is the possibly extended value
$$m_i(y):=\int_{\Theta_i} f_i(\theta,y)\,\Pi_i(d\theta)\in[0,\infty].$$
This is the BCS-02 evidence normalizer
([[def-posterior-evidence-normalizer-and-fiberwise-update]]) specialized to a
proper model prior, and is the prior-predictive density relative to the
specified common data measure. For models $i,j$ whose evidences at $y$ are both finite and positive,
the **Bayes factor for $j$ against $i$** is
$$BF_{ji}(y):=\frac{m_j(y)}{m_i(y)}.$$
The corresponding prior model odds are $w_j/w_i$. No Bayes factor is defined
here using an arbitrarily scaled improper parameter prior.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T,\Pi)$ be a measure space, let $L_y:\Theta\to[0,+\infty]$
be measurable for a fixed datum $y$, and put
$Z:=\int_\Theta L_y\,d\Pi$. For a finite positive constant $c$, the set
function
$$A\longmapsto c\int_A L_y\,d\Pi$$
is a probability measure if and only if $0<Z<+\infty$ and $c=Z^{-1}$. In
particular, if $Z=0$ or $Z=+\infty$, no finite positive scaling makes the
fiberwise update a probability measure.

Let $\pi$ be a prior probability on $(E,\mathcal S)$ and let $Q:E\to T$ be a probability kernel dominated by a sigma-finite measure $\nu$ on $(T,\mathcal T)$, with specified nonnegative jointly measurable density $\ell:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$:
$$Q(\theta,B)=\int_B\ell(\theta,y)\,\nu(dy)\quad\text{for every }\theta\in E,\ B\in\mathcal T.$$

Define $m(y)=\int_E\ell(\theta,y)\,\pi(d\theta)$. Under the joint law with density $\ell$ relative to $\pi\times\nu$, a conditional law of the parameter given the observation is
$$K(y,A)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\int_A\ell(\theta,y)\,\pi(d\theta)}{m(y)},&0<m(y)<\infty,\\ \pi(A),&m(y)=0\text{ or }m(y)=\infty.\end{cases}$$

be dominated by the fixed sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$. For each
$\theta$, the Radon–Nikodym theorem gives the almost-everywhere class
$dP_\theta/d\mu$; a sigma-finite exhaustion for $\mu$ is also finite for the
probability measure $P_\theta$. Under AC, select simultaneously a
finite-valued measurable nonnegative representative $p_\theta$ from each
class. The nonnegative version exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].

$$L_x:\Theta\to[0,+\infty),\qquad L_x(\theta):=p_\theta(x),$$
is the **likelihood at $x$**. This is a function on the parameter labels, not
a probability distribution on $\Theta$. No sigma-algebra on $\Theta$ or
measurability of $L_x$ is implied. Each density is determined only
$\mu$-almost everywhere; there is no canonical pointwise version and, for
arbitrary uncountable $\Theta$, no common exceptional null set is asserted.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $k,r\ge2$, let $\mu\in\mathbb R$, $\tau^2\ge0$, and $\sigma^2>0$.
For $i=1,\ldots,k$, let the group blocks
$U_i=(a_i,\boldsymbol\epsilon_i)$ be independent random elements on one
probability space, where $\boldsymbol\epsilon_i=(\epsilon_{i1},\ldots,\epsilon_{ir})$.
Within each block, $a_i$ and $\boldsymbol\epsilon_i$ are independent and the
coordinates of $\boldsymbol\epsilon_i$ are mutually independent. Assume
$a_i\sim N(0,\tau^2)$ and
$\epsilon_{ij}\sim N(0,\sigma^2)$. Put
$Y_{ij}=\mu+a_i+\epsilon_{ij}$,
$\bar Y_{i\cdot}=r^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^rY_{ij}$, and
$\bar Y_{\cdot\cdot}=k^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^k\bar Y_{i\cdot}$. Define
$$MSB=\frac{r}{k-1}\sum_{i=1}^k(\bar Y_{i\cdot}-\bar Y_{\cdot\cdot})^2,\qquad MSW=\frac{1}{k(r-1)}\sum_{i=1}^k\sum_{j=1}^r(Y_{ij}-\bar Y_{i\cdot})^2.$$
Then
$$\mathbb E[MSB]=\sigma^2+r\tau^2,\qquad \mathbb E[MSW]=\sigma^2.$$
Equating these two population moments to the observed mean squares gives the
raw method-of-moments estimates
$$\widehat{\sigma^2}_{\rm MOM}=MSW,\qquad \widehat{\tau^2}_{\rm MOM}=\frac{MSB-MSW}{r}.$$
The second estimate is not constrained to be nonnegative.

Assume AC. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma>0$, the normal law $N(m,\sigma^2)$
of [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]] has Lebesgue density
$$g_{m,\sigma}(y)=\frac1\sigma\frac{e^{-((y-m)/\sigma)^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}e^{-(y-m)^2/(2\sigma^2)}.$$

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

The map from the four observations to $(MSB-MSW)/2$ is a polynomial divided by the fixed positive integer $2$, hence continuous. At the displayed table its value is $-1$ by step 1.1, so some open neighborhood of the table still has negative estimates. The latent vector $(a_1,a_2,\epsilon_{11},\epsilon_{12},\epsilon_{21},\epsilon_{22})=(0,0,-1,1,-1,1)$ maps to that table. Since every coordinate has a strictly positive normal density by [F2], an open rectangle around this latent vector has positive probability by independence [F3]; it can be chosen inside the preimage of the negative-estimate neighborhood. Thus negative estimates occur with positive probability even when $\tau^2>0$, so replacing them by zero changes the estimator and does not prove a structural zero.

([[def-likelihood-density]])
$f_i:\Theta_i\times\mathcal Y\to[0,\infty]$ such that
$$Q_i(\theta,B)=\int_B f_i(\theta,y)\,\mu(dy)\qquad(B\in\mathcal A).$$
Require that each $f_i$ is jointly measurable in parameter and data; separate
likelihood versions do not imply this joint measurability. Assign prior model
weights $w_i>0$ with $\sum_iw_i=1$. The **marginal likelihood**, or **model
evidence**, at $y$ is the possibly extended value
$$m_i(y):=\int_{\Theta_i} f_i(\theta,y)\,\Pi_i(d\theta)\in[0,\infty].$$
This is the BCS-02 evidence normalizer
([[def-posterior-evidence-normalizer-and-fiberwise-update]]) specialized to a
proper model prior, and is the prior-predictive density relative to the
specified common data measure. For models $i,j$ whose evidences at $y$ are both finite and positive,
the **Bayes factor for $j$ against $i$** is
$$BF_{ji}(y):=\frac{m_j(y)}{m_i(y)}.$$
The corresponding prior model odds are $w_j/w_i$. No Bayes factor is defined
here using an arbitrarily scaled improper parameter prior.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ be a measurable parameter space, let $\Pi$ be a
sigma-finite measure on it, and fix a data value $y$. Let
$L_y:\Theta\to[0,+\infty]$ be a $\mathcal T$-measurable function. Define its
**evidence normalizer** by
$$Z_\Pi(y):=\int_\Theta L_y(\theta)\,\Pi(d\theta)\in[0,+\infty].$$
Only when $0<Z_\Pi(y)<+\infty$ define the **fiberwise posterior update** by
$$\Pi_y(A):=\frac{\int_A L_y(\theta)\,\Pi(d\theta)}{Z_\Pi(y)}\qquad(A\in\mathcal T).$$
The definition makes no quotient at zero or infinite evidence. A prior is
**proper** when $\Pi(\Theta)=1$, as in
[[def-bayesian-model-as-prior-and-sampling-kernel]]. We call a sigma-finite
prior **improper** when $\Pi(\Theta)=+\infty$; the formula also applies to
other sigma-finite measures. For an improper prior, $Z_\Pi(y)$ is a fiberwise
normalizer only; it does not by itself define a prior-predictive probability or
a conditional law.

When the data are described by a dominated experiment, the dominating measure
and its sigma-finiteness are as in
[[def-dominated-statistical-experiment]]. A family of pointwise likelihood
sections is not assumed to be jointly measurable in parameter and data; that
additional condition must be supplied separately whenever Tonelli is used.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n$ is sigma-finite ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]):
   the cubes $(-k,k]^n$ are Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n\big((-k,k]^n\big) = (2k)^n < +\infty$, they increase with $k$, and
   their union over $k \in \mathbb{N}$ is $\mathbb{R}^n$.
2. Every bounded subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has $\lambda_n^*(E) < +\infty$; a bounded
   Lebesgue measurable set therefore has finite measure, and every compact
   subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is Lebesgue measurable of finite measure.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

Assume AC. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma>0$, the normal law $N(m,\sigma^2)$
of [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]] has Lebesgue density
$$g_{m,\sigma}(y)=\frac1\sigma\frac{e^{-((y-m)/\sigma)^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}e^{-(y-m)^2/(2\sigma^2)}.$$

derivations.claim: By [A1, F3, F4], $\lambda$ is sigma-finite, so $\Pi_c=c\lambda$ is sigma-finite. By [F5], $\Pi_c([-n,n])=2cn$ for every positive integer $n$, hence $\Pi_c(\mathbb R)=+\infty$ and it is improper in the sense of [F2]. By [F6], its formal likelihood integral is $\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{c}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{(y-\theta)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)d\theta$. The substitution $z=(y-\theta)/\sigma$ has absolute Jacobian $\sigma$, so this equals $c\int_{\mathbb R}(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-z^2/2}\,dz=c$. This value is positive and finite for every fixed $c>0$, but $\Pi_c(\mathbb R)=+\infty$, so it is not an evidence under [F1].

For the two copies of the same normal-location likelihood specified above, with model-specific constants $c_1,c_2>0$, the formal ratio is $c_2/c_1$ by step 1.1. Rescaling either improper prior changes this ratio arbitrarily while leaving its unnormalized density proportional to Lebesgue measure; hence no generic Bayes factor is defined by these improper priors.

Fix a finite group count $m\ge1$, a standard Borel hyperparameter space
$(H,\mathcal H)$, and a standard Borel parameter space $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$.
Let $\Pi$ be a probability measure on $(H,\mathcal H)$ and let
$$G:H\times\mathcal T\to[0,1]$$
be a probability kernel. For each $j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$, let
$(\mathcal Y_j,\mathcal A_j)$ be a measurable observation space, let $\nu_j$
be a sigma-finite measure on it, and let $K_j$ be a probability kernel from
$(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ to $(\mathcal Y_j,\mathcal A_j)$ with a specified
jointly measurable density $f_j:\Theta\times\mathcal Y_j\to[0,\infty]$:
$$K_j(\theta,B)=\int_B f_j(\theta,y_j)\,\nu_j(dy_j)\qquad(B\in\mathcal A_j).$$

The **finite-group hierarchical model** is the following specified kernel
construction. First draw $\eta\sim\Pi$. Conditional on $\eta$, draw
$\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_m$ from the finite product kernel
$$G_\eta^{\otimes m}(d\theta_1\cdots d\theta_m)=\bigotimes_{j=1}^mG_\eta(d\theta_j).$$
Thus the group parameters are conditionally independent and have the same
conditional law $G_\eta$. Conditional on the parameter tuple, draw the group
observations from the product kernel $\bigotimes_{j=1}^mK_j(\theta_j,\cdot)$.
The product-kernel laws are probability kernels by
[[lem-finite-products-of-probability-kernels]]. For each fixed $\eta$, the
coordinate maps under $G_\eta^{\otimes m}$ are independent random elements,
so their joint law is the finite product law
([[thm-independent-random-elements-have-product-joint-law]]).

Put $\Xi=H\times\Theta^m$ with its finite product sigma-algebra. The proper
latent prior $P_0$ on $\Xi$ is
$$P_0(d\eta,d\theta_1\cdots d\theta_m)=\Pi(d\eta)\prod_{j=1}^mG_\eta(d\theta_j),$$
well-defined by [[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]]. For
$\xi=(\eta,\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_m)\in\Xi$, lift each observation kernel
to the common source $\Xi$ by
$$M_j(\xi,B)=K_j(\theta_j,B)\qquad(B\in\mathcal A_j).$$
The coordinate projection $\xi\mapsto\theta_j$ is measurable, so the kernel
definition shows that each $M_j$ is a probability kernel. Its specified
jointly measurable density is $(\xi,y_j)\mapsto f_j(\theta_j,y_j)$, by
composition with the same measurable coordinate projection. Let
$\mathcal Y=\prod_{j=1}^m\mathcal Y_j$,
$\nu=\bigotimes_{j=1}^m\nu_j$, and $y=(y_1,\ldots,y_m)$. The observation
kernel from $\Xi$ has jointly measurable density
$$L_y(\eta,\theta_1\cdots\theta_m)=\prod_{j=1}^m f_j(\theta_j,y_j)$$
with respect to $\nu$, by [[lem-finite-products-of-dominated-kernels-have-product-density]].
Its **evidence** is the possibly extended nonnegative number
$$Z(y)=\int_\Xi L_y(\eta,\theta_1\cdots\theta_m)\,P_0(d\eta,d\theta_1\cdots d\theta_m).$$
The normalized likelihood measure is called a pointwise joint posterior on a
fiber only when $0<Z(y)<\infty$; no quotient is formed at zero or infinite
evidence.

For each group, $\theta\mapsto K_j(\theta,\cdot)$ is a parametric statistical
model in the sense of [[def-parametric-statistical-model]], with its
parameter-measurable kernel representation as in
[[def-parameter-measurable-statistical-model-as-markov-kernel]]. Here
“conditionally independent given $\eta$” is shorthand for the explicit
finite product-kernel specification above. The library's random-element
conditional-independence terminology is defined in
[[def-conditional-independence-given-a-sigma-algebra]]; its
conditional-expectation-class convention assumes AC. The finite
product-kernel definition here does not use that class convention or any
choice axiom.

Assume the finite-group hierarchical model of
[[def-hierarchical-bayesian-model]]. Write $P_0$ for its proper prior on
$\Xi=H\times\Theta^m$, let $L_y(\xi)$ be its specified product likelihood
density with respect to the finite product measure $\nu$, and define
$$Z(y)=\int_\Xi L_y(\xi)\,P_0(d\xi).$$
For every observation $y$ with $0<Z(y)<\infty$, the measure
$$P_y(A)=\frac{\int_A L_y(\xi)\,P_0(d\xi)}{Z(y)}\qquad(A\in\mathcal H\otimes\mathcal T^{\otimes m})$$
is the joint posterior law of the latent tuple. Defining $P_y=P_0$ when
$Z(y)=0$ or $Z(y)=\infty$ gives a regular conditional distribution under the
prior-predictive law; no quotient is formed on either exceptional fiber.

Assume a finite-group hierarchy as in
[[def-hierarchical-bayesian-model]], with hyperparameter $\eta\in H$, group
parameters $\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_m$, conditional probability kernel
$G_\eta$ ([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]) on the group-parameter
space, and specified jointly measurable
likelihood density
$$L_y(\theta_{1:m})=\prod_{j=1}^m f_j(\theta_j,y_j)$$
against the common product data measure. For fixed $\eta$, define its
**marginal likelihood**
$$m(y\mid\eta):=\int_{\Theta^m}L_y(\theta_{1:m})\,G_\eta^{\otimes m}(d\theta_{1:m})\in[0,\infty].$$
Where the function $\eta\mapsto m(y\mid\eta)$ is finite-valued and attains a
positive finite maximum, a **Type-II maximum marginal likelihood choice** is
any
$$\widehat\eta(y)\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\eta\in H}m(y\mid\eta).$$
This definition does not assert that a maximum exists. A data-indexed choice
requires a selected measurable maximizer on its domain.

Only when $0<m(y\mid\widehat\eta(y))<\infty$ define the corresponding
**empirical-Bayes plug-in posterior** on a measurable
$A\subseteq\Theta^m$ by
$$\Pi_{\widehat\eta(y),y}(A):=\frac{\int_A L_y(\theta_{1:m})\,G_{\widehat\eta(y)}^{\otimes m}(d\theta_{1:m})}{m(y\mid\widehat\eta(y))}.$$
The finite-positive condition makes this a probability update by
[[prop-fiberwise-posterior-propriety-iff-finite-positive-evidence]].

Under a proper hyperprior $H_0$, at a data fiber with finite positive joint evidence
$0<Z(y):=\int_Hm(y\mid\eta)H_0(d\eta)<\infty$, full Bayes instead retains the posterior law of
$\eta$ jointly with the group parameters, as in
[[thm-hierarchical-posterior-normalization-on-positive-finite-evidence]].
Integrating over a shared uncertain hyperparameter can induce dependence
between group parameters, while a plug-in update fixes that hyperparameter at
one selected value; special cases can leave the groups independent. This
definition asserts no generic empirical-Bayes risk, consistency, dominance,
or credible-coverage guarantee.

A measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$ is **standard Borel** if there are a Polish space $P$ and a bijection $h:E\to P$ such that $A\in\mathcal E$ exactly when $h[A]$ is Borel in $P$. Thus the measurable structure is part of the datum; no particular compatible Polish topology on $E$ is selected.

derivations.claim: The finite discrete spaces are standard Borel by [F4]. The two-point hyperprior is proper, $G_0=\delta_0$ and $G_1=\delta_1$ are probability kernels, and each singleton observation measure $\nu_j$ is finite, hence sigma-finite. Its observation kernel has the specified density $f_j(\theta_j,*)=1$, jointly measurable on the finite product space. Thus the hierarchy in [F1] is well-defined and its joint evidence is $Z(*)=1$. By [F2], the full posterior equals the prior: it assigns probability $1/2$ to $(\eta,\theta_1,\theta_2)=(0,0,0)$ and $1/2$ to $(1,1,1)$.

For either fixed $\eta$, the conditional marginal likelihood is $m(*\mid\eta)=1$, so both values attain the maximum. The map from the singleton data space to $\eta=0$ is measurable, hence [F3] permits the plug-in choice $\widehat\eta(*)=0$; its posterior is $\delta_0\otimes\delta_0$.

Under the full posterior in step 1.1, $\Pr(\theta_1=1)=\Pr(\theta_2=1)=1/2$ but $\Pr(\theta_1=1,\theta_2=1)=1/2\ne1/4$. Therefore the group parameters are dependent after the shared hyperparameter is integrated out, and the full posterior differs from the plug-in posterior in step 2.1.

boundaries.reason: Example fixes exactly two groups and singleton observation spaces, each carrying mass one; these observation spaces are singletons rather than empty spaces.

boundaries.evidence: Step 2.1 explicitly chooses eta_hat(*)=0; zero is an admissible hyperparameter label, not a zero evidence, since m(*|0)=1.
Step 1.1 calculates Z(*)=1 and step 2.1 has m(*|eta)=1 at both hyperparameter values. Thus the unit endpoint is attained, contrary to the old credibility boilerplate.
Example defines G_eta=delta_eta, so conditional group laws are degenerate. Step 3.1 nevertheless computes marginal dependence: joint probability 1/2 differs from the product 1/4.
Step 1.1 gives posterior mass zero to the two unequal group tuples and mass 1/2 to each equal tuple; step 2.1 plug-in mass is one at (0,0).
Step 2.1 verifies both eta labels attain the same maximum and explicitly selects the measurable constant map eta_hat(*)=0 on the singleton data space.

boundaries.reason: Example exhibits dependence after mixing in one finite hierarchy; it does not claim that all hyperparameter uncertainty necessarily induces dependence.
Example compares one explicit full posterior with one explicit plug-in posterior; it offers no characterization of all cases in which those posteriors differ.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the finite dominated model setup of
[[def-marginal-likelihood-and-bayes-factor]]. Fix a data value $y$ such that
$0<m_i(y)<\infty$ for every $i\in I$. A version of the posterior model
probabilities at this fiber is
$$\Pr(M=i\mid y)=\frac{w_i m_i(y)}{\sum_{\ell\in I}w_\ell m_\ell(y)}.$$
For any two models $i,j\in I$, the posterior odds satisfy
$$\frac{\Pr(M=j\mid y)}{\Pr(M=i\mid y)}=\frac{w_j}{w_i}\,BF_{ji}(y).$$
The displayed version uses the specified jointly measurable density
representatives; no quotient is formed if an evidence is zero or infinite.

Let $I=\{1,\ldots,N\}$ with $N\ge2$ be a finite model index set. For each
$i\in I$, let $(\Theta_i,\mathcal T_i)$ be a measurable parameter space, let
$\Pi_i$ be a probability measure ([[def-probability-measure]]) on it, and let
$Q_i$ be a sampling kernel for a statistical experiment
([[def-statistical-experiment]]) on one common data space
$(\mathcal Y,\mathcal A)$. Assume the experiments are dominated
([[def-dominated-statistical-experiment]]) by the same supplied sigma-finite
measure $\mu$. Fix a specified likelihood density
([[def-likelihood-density]])
$f_i:\Theta_i\times\mathcal Y\to[0,\infty]$ such that
$$Q_i(\theta,B)=\int_B f_i(\theta,y)\,\mu(dy)\qquad(B\in\mathcal A).$$
Require that each $f_i$ is jointly measurable in parameter and data; separate
likelihood versions do not imply this joint measurability. Assign prior model
weights $w_i>0$ with $\sum_iw_i=1$. The **marginal likelihood**, or **model
evidence**, at $y$ is the possibly extended value
$$m_i(y):=\int_{\Theta_i} f_i(\theta,y)\,\Pi_i(d\theta)\in[0,\infty].$$
This is the BCS-02 evidence normalizer
([[def-posterior-evidence-normalizer-and-fiberwise-update]]) specialized to a
proper model prior, and is the prior-predictive density relative to the
specified common data measure. For models $i,j$ whose evidences at $y$ are both finite and positive,
the **Bayes factor for $j$ against $i$** is
$$BF_{ji}(y):=\frac{m_j(y)}{m_i(y)}.$$
The corresponding prior model odds are $w_j/w_i$. No Bayes factor is defined
here using an arbitrarily scaled improper parameter prior.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

Fix $n \ge 1$ and let $\lambda_n^*$ be the Lebesgue outer set function on $\mathbb{R}^n$
([[def-lebesgue-outer-measure]]). A set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is
**Lebesgue measurable** when

$$\lambda_n^*(A) \;=\; \lambda_n^*(A \cap E) \;+\; \lambda_n^*(A \setminus E) \qquad \text{for every } A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n .$$

This formula makes sense before any outer-measure theorem is invoked. Under
countable choice, [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-is-an-outer-measure-agreeing-with-volume]]
makes $\lambda_n^*$ an outer measure, and the displayed condition is then exactly
Carathéodory measurability in the sense of [[def-caratheodory-measurable-set]].

The family of Lebesgue measurable sets is written $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$,
and **Lebesgue measure** is the restriction

$$\lambda_n \;:=\; \lambda_n^*\!\restriction_{\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)} .$$

On the real line the subscript is dropped and $\lambda := \lambda_1$.

The quantifier over every test set $A$ is part of the condition, and no
hypothesis on $E$ is imposed before it is tested. That
$\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra and that $\lambda_n$ is a complete
measure on it are not part of this definition: they are proved, under the Axiom
of Countable Choice, in [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]], which is
recorded in this item's `justified_by` because it is a statement about the
objects introduced here. Until that theorem the symbols $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$
and $\lambda_n$ name a family of sets and a restricted set function, nothing more.

derivations.claim: By [A1, F3], $\lambda([0,1])=1$, so the uniform prior is proper. Under $M_0$, $m_0(0)=1$. Under $M_1$, its density is $1$ on $[0,1]$, so $m_1(0)=\int_0^1(1-\theta)\,d\theta=1/2$. Both evidences are finite and positive, and [F1] gives $\Pr(M_0\mid y=0)=w_0/(w_0+w_1/2)>0$.

By [F3], the degenerate closed interval $[0,0]=\{0\}$ is Lebesgue measurable and has measure zero; [F4] identifies this measure as $\lambda$. Thus the uniform prior assigns the singleton mass $\int_{\{0\}}1\,d\lambda=0$. The separate model atom in step 1.1 instead gives $\theta=0$ prior weight $w_0$ and positive posterior probability.

risk_review.notes: Independently read the complete Definition and all eight actual dependency statements. Supplied finite nonnegative densities make every square root meaningful; strict threshold preimages prove square-root measurability and the arithmetic closure theorem gives the squared difference. be dominated by the fixed sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$. For each
$\theta$, the Radon–Nikodym theorem gives the almost-everywhere class
$dP_\theta/d\mu$; a sigma-finite exhaustion for $\mu$ is also finite for the
probability measure $P_\theta$. Under AC, select simultaneously a
finite-valued measurable nonnegative representative $p_\theta$ from each
class. The nonnegative version exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].

$$L_x:\Theta\to[0,+\infty),\qquad L_x(\theta):=p_\theta(x),$$

a probability distribution on $\Theta$. No sigma-algebra on $\Theta$ or

arbitrary uncountable $\Theta$, no common exceptional null set is asserted.

> ([[def-choice-function]]).

all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space and let $P,Q$ be probability measures ([[def-probability-measure]]) on it, both dominated by a specified common sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$ as in [[def-dominated-statistical-experiment]]. $$h(P,Q):=\left(\int \bigl(\sqrt p-\sqrt q\bigr)^2\,d\mu\right)^{1/2}.$$

The square roots are measurable: for every real $r$, $\{\sqrt p>r\}$ is the whole space if $r<0$ and equals $\{p>r^2\}$ if $r\ge0$, and the same holds for $q$ ([[thm-threshold-characterisations-of-real-and-extended-real-measurability]]). The arithmetic and lattice rules make the nonnegative integrand measurable ([[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]). It is integrable because $(\sqrt p-\sqrt q)^2\le p+q$ and the integral is additive on nonnegative functions ([[cor-additivity-of-the-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]), so its integral is at most $P(\mathsf X)+Q(\mathsf X)=2$.

The generic density-selection convention [[def-likelihood-density]] assumes the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. When $p$ and $q$ are explicitly given, this displayed integral requires no further choice.

Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
$(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **total variation
distance** is

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}\bigl|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\bigr| .$$

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in
$[-1,1]$, because both measures have total mass one; hence the set being
maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.
The empty event and the whole space give the values $0$ and
$|\mu(E)-\nu(E)|=0$, so the distance is zero when $\mu=\nu$, and it is symmetric

measurable space where the decomposition is attained. On a countable state

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space ([[def-measure-space]]).

- The measure $\mu$ is **finite** if $\mu(X)<+\infty$.
- It is **sigma-finite** if there is a sequence $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$ such that $X=\bigcup_nE_n$ and $\mu(E_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$.
- It is **semifinite** if, whenever $E\in\mathcal A$ and $\mu(E)>0$, there is $F\in\mathcal A$ with $F\subseteq E$ and $0<\mu(F)<+\infty$.

The last condition is automatic when $0<\mu(E)<+\infty$, by taking $F=E$; its substantive case is $\mu(E)=+\infty$.

the extended real line. Products of functions use

abbreviates $\underline c\odot_X f$ for the constant function $\underline c$.

2. $\max(f,g)$, $\min(f,g)$, $|f|$, $f^+$, and $f^-$ are measurable;
3. if the partial pointwise sum $f+g$ is defined at every point, then it is measurable;
4. the pointwise product $fg:=f\odot_X g$ is measurable.

$$\int g\,d(f\,d\mu)=\int gf\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. If $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ are measurable, then

derivations.claim: By [A1], [F3], and [F4], take finite-valued nonnegative densities $p=dP/d\mu$ and $q=dQ/d\mu$ for a common sigma-finite dominator $\mu$. Define $\rho(A):=P(A)+Q(A)$. For disjoint measurable $A_k$, countable additivity of $P,Q$ and regrouping nonnegative series give $\rho(\bigcup_kA_k)=\sum_k\rho(A_k)$; also $\rho(\varnothing)=0$ and $\rho(\mathsf X)=2$. Thus $\rho$ is a finite, hence sigma-finite, measure by [F6]. Additivity of the nonnegative integral [F10] gives $\rho(A)=\int_A(p+q)\,d\mu$, with $p+q$ measurable by [F7].

Using $p,q$ against $\mu$, the set $B:=\{p\ge q\}$ is measurable by [F7,F8]. On $B$, $p=(p-q)+q$, so additivity [F10] gives $\delta:=P(B)-Q(B)=\int_B(p-q)\,d\mu\ge0$. On $B^c$, $q=(q-p)+p$ and the total masses are one, hence $\int_{B^c}(q-p)\,d\mu=Q(B^c)-P(B^c)=\delta$. Additivity then gives $\int|p-q|\,d\mu=2\delta$. For any measurable $A$, the difference on $A\cap B$ lies in $[0,\delta]$ by monotonicity [F10], while the difference on $A\cap B^c$ lies in $[-\delta,0]$; thus $|P(A)-Q(A)|\le\delta$, and $A=B$ attains $\delta$. Therefore [F2] gives $\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}=\delta=\tfrac12\int|p-q|\,d\mu$.

On $\{p+q>0\}$ define $\bar p=p/(p+q)$ and $\bar q=q/(p+q)$, and set both to zero on $\{p+q=0\}$. For $r<0$, $\{\bar p>r\}$ is the whole space; for $r\ge0$, it is $\{p+q>0\}\cap\{p-r(p+q)>0\}$. Thus [F7,F8] make $\bar p$ measurable, and the same argument applies to $\bar q$. Since $p=q=0$ where $p+q=0$, [F9] gives $\int_A\bar p\,d\rho=\int_A\bar p(p+q)\,d\mu=P(A)$ and $\int_A\bar q\,d\rho=Q(A)$ for every measurable $A$. Hence $\bar p,\bar q$ are finite-valued density representatives of $P,Q$ against $\rho$.

Pointwise $|p-q|=|\sqrt p-\sqrt q|(\sqrt p+\sqrt q)$. Hölder [F5] therefore gives $\int|p-q|\,d\mu\le h(P,Q)\bigl(\int(\sqrt p+\sqrt q)^2\,d\mu\bigr)^{1/2}$. The squared second factor is $2+2\int\sqrt{pq}\,d\mu\le4$, since [F5] applied to $\sqrt p,\sqrt q$ bounds their product integral by $1$. Step 1.2 now gives $\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}\le h(P,Q)$.

Write $H_\lambda(P,Q)^2$ for the defining Hellinger integral computed from supplied densities against a common dominator $\lambda$. Applying [F1] and [F9] to the densities in step 2.1 gives $H_\rho(P,Q)^2=\int(\sqrt{\bar p}-\sqrt{\bar q})^2\,d\rho=\int_{\{p+q>0\}}(\sqrt p-\sqrt q)^2\,d\mu=H_\mu(P,Q)^2$, because both original densities vanish where $p+q=0$. For any measure $\alpha$ and finite-valued nonnegative densities $f,g$ of the same finite measure $\Lambda$ with respect to $\alpha$, they agree $\alpha$-almost everywhere: on $E_m:=\{f\ge g+1/m\}$, equality of their density integrals gives $0=\int_{E_m}(f-g)\,d\alpha\ge\alpha(E_m)/m$, so $\alpha(E_m)=0$. Since $\{f>g\}=\bigcup_{m\ge1}E_m$, and the same argument with $f,g$ swapped handles $\{g>f\}$, this proves uniqueness almost everywhere. Thus changing supplied representatives against a fixed dominator does not change the Hellinger integral.

u, ar q_
u$ against the same finite measure $ho=P+Q$. The uniqueness argument in step 3.1 gives $ ar p_

u= ar q$ $ho$-almost everywhere. The same density-change calculation as in step 3.1 therefore identifies the Hellinger integral against $

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Suppose an experiment on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ also has a measurable
parameter space $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ ([[def-measurable-space]]). A
**Markov kernel** (or **probability kernel**) representation is a function
$$
K:\Theta\times\mathcal A\to[0,1]
$$
such that, for every $\theta\in\Theta$, the set function
$A\mapsto K(\theta,A)$ is a probability measure on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$,
and, for every $A\in\mathcal A$ and every Borel set $C\subseteq[0,1]$,
$$
\{\theta\in\Theta:K(\theta,A)\in C\}\in\mathcal T.
$$
Here the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,1]$ is generated by its relatively open
subsets $U\cap[0,1]$, where $U$ is open in $\mathbb R$. Thus the second
condition says that each event-probability map $\theta\mapsto K(\theta,A)$ is
measurable. The kernel represents the given experiment exactly when
$K(\theta,A)=P_\theta(A)$ for every $\theta$ and $A$
([[def-statistical-experiment]], [[def-probability-measure]]).

This is an optional parameter-measurable version of a model. An arbitrary
experiment does not include a measurable structure on $\Theta$ or imply this
kernel condition.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
([[def-measurable-space]]). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces, and let
$$f : X \times Y \to \overline{\mathbb R}$$
be $(\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B,\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R}))$-measurable.
Then $f_x : Y \to \overline{\mathbb R}$ is $\mathcal B$-measurable for every
$x \in X$, and $f^y : X \to \overline{\mathbb R}$ is $\mathcal A$-measurable
for every $y \in Y$.

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). It is
**dominated** by a supplied positive measure $\mu$ on
$(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ when $\mu$ is sigma-finite
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]) and
$P_\theta\ll\mu$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$
([[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]).
The dominating measure is part of the specified setup. This condition adds no
measurable structure on $\Theta$ and no measurability of
$\theta\mapsto P_\theta$.

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be dominated by the fixed sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$. For each
$\theta$, the Radon–Nikodym theorem gives the almost-everywhere class
$dP_\theta/d\mu$; a sigma-finite exhaustion for $\mu$ is also finite for the
probability measure $P_\theta$. Under AC, select simultaneously a
finite-valued measurable nonnegative representative $p_\theta$ from each
class. The nonnegative version exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].

For fixed observed $x\in\mathcal X$, the function
$$L_x:\Theta\to[0,+\infty),\qquad L_x(\theta):=p_\theta(x),$$
is the **likelihood at $x$**. This is a function on the parameter labels, not
a probability distribution on $\Theta$. No sigma-algebra on $\Theta$ or
measurability of $L_x$ is implied. Each density is determined only
$\mu$-almost everywhere; there is no canonical pointwise version and, for
arbitrary uncountable $\Theta$, no common exceptional null set is asserted.

Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
([[def-probability-measure]]). Absolute continuity $P\ll Q$ has the convention
of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If
$P\not\ll Q$, define $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and
let $r=dP/dQ$ be a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative of its
Radon–Nikodym class; such a representative exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].
On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This
function is measurable: for $a\ge0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r>\exp(a)\}$, and for
$a<0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r=0\}\cup\{r>\exp(a)\}$, by the inverse and
monotonicity properties of the natural logarithm
([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]). These are
measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since
$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$ by
[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$
The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,
$$0\le \frac{\log s}{s}=\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{u}\le\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{\sqrt u}\le\frac2{\sqrt s}.$$
Thus $t\log t\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$; here $L=\log$ by
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and
[[def-integral-logarithm]]. On $(0,\infty)$, $\psi$ is a product of continuous
functions by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $\psi$ is continuous on
$[0,\infty)$ and $\psi(r)$ is measurable by
[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts
([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]],
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

For $0<t\le1$, the function $-t\log t$ has derivative $-\log t-1$ and
maximum $1/e$ at $t=1/e$: $e=\exp(1)>1$ by
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $1/e=\exp(-1)$ by
[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and $\log(1/e)=-1$ by
[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and the inverse definition. The mean value
theorem gives increase before and decrease after this point
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]],
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).
At $t=0$ the negative part is zero. Since $Q$ is a probability measure,
$$\int \psi(r)^-\,dQ\le\frac1e.$$
The change-of-measure identity of [[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]],
applied to $\ell^-$ gives $\int\ell^-\,dP=\int\psi(r)^-\,dQ\le1/e$,
so $\int\ell\,dP$ is well-defined; applying it to both positive and negative
parts gives
$$D(P\|Q)=\int\ell\,dP=\int\psi(r)\,dQ=\int r\log r\,dQ,$$
with $0\log0:=0$ and a finite negative part. Therefore the extended integral
is well-defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.

This convention is directional: the first argument must be absolutely
continuous with respect to the second for the integral formula to apply.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $\pi$ be a prior probability on $(E,\mathcal S)$ and let $Q:E\to T$ be a probability kernel dominated by a sigma-finite measure $\nu$ on $(T,\mathcal T)$, with specified nonnegative jointly measurable density $\ell:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$:
$$Q(\theta,B)=\int_B\ell(\theta,y)\,\nu(dy)\quad\text{for every }\theta\in E,\ B\in\mathcal T.$$

Define $m(y)=\int_E\ell(\theta,y)\,\pi(d\theta)$. Under the joint law with density $\ell$ relative to $\pi\times\nu$, a conditional law of the parameter given the observation is
$$K(y,A)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\int_A\ell(\theta,y)\,\pi(d\theta)}{m(y)},&0<m(y)<\infty,\\ \pi(A),&m(y)=0\text{ or }m(y)=\infty.\end{cases}$$

The observation marginal is $m\,d\nu$, and the filled fibres have marginal mass zero. This is a choice-free assertion about the explicit kernel and event identities.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. For each $i$, let
$g_i:(S_i,\Sigma_i)\to(T_i,\mathcal T_i)$ be measurable. Then the family
$(g_i\circ X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent.

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$
For IID real $(X_n)_{n\ge1}$ with $\mathbb E|X_1|<\infty$, $S_n/n\to\mu=\mathbb EX_1$ almost surely.

Let $Y$ be a measurable real random variable on a probability space with $0\le Y\le1$ almost surely. Then, for every $\lambda\in\mathbb R$,

$$\mathbb E\exp\{\lambda(Y-\mathbb EY)\}\le \exp(\lambda^2/8).$$

This proof uses only finite product and scalar integral arguments; it does not assume the Axiom of Choice.

For all $x,y\in\mathbb R$ and $0\le t\le1$,
$$\exp((1-t)x+ty)\le(1-t)\exp x+t\exp y.$$
If $0<t<1$, equality holds exactly when $x=y$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $f\in L^1(\mathbb P)$
be real-valued, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval containing $f(x)$ for
almost every $x$, and let $\varphi:I\to\mathbb R$ be convex with
$\varphi\circ f\in L^1(\mathbb P)$. Then
$$\varphi\!\left(\int f\,d\mathbb P\right)\le\int\varphi(f)\,d\mathbb P.$$

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

Let $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be events in a probability space. If
$$\sum_{n=0}^\infty \mathbb P(A_n)<+\infty,$$
then
$$\mathbb P(A_n\ \mathrm{i.o.})=0.$$

No independence hypothesis is needed.

Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
$(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **total variation
distance** is

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}\bigl|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\bigr| .$$

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in
$[-1,1]$, because both measures have total mass one; hence the set being
maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.
The empty event and the whole space give the values $0$ and
$|\mu(E)-\nu(E)|=0$, so the distance is zero when $\mu=\nu$, and it is symmetric
in $\mu$ and $\nu$. This convention carries no factor $1/2$ in the supremum;
it is therefore not the total variation norm of the signed measure $\mu-\nu$,
which is twice the quantity above when that signed measure is considered on a
measurable space where the decomposition is attained. On a countable state
space with its power-set sigma-algebra the supremum equals the half-$\ell^1$
sum $\tfrac12\sum_{x\in E}|\mu(\{x\})-\nu(\{x\})|$; that identity is proved in
[[lem-total-variation-half-l1-formula-on-a-countable-space]], not assumed here.

Assume AC. For probability measures $P,Q$ on one measurable space, with
$$\|P-Q\|_{\rm TV}:=\sup_{A}|P(A)-Q(A)|,$$
the event-supremum convention without a factor $1/2$,
$$\|P-Q\|_{\rm TV}\le\sqrt{\frac12D(P\|Q)}.$$
If $P\not\ll Q$, the right side is $+\infty$ by the definition of KL
divergence.

Assume AC for the imported density-representative convention. Let $P,Q$ be probability laws on a measurable space, both dominated by one specified common sigma-finite positive measure. Then the root-L2 Hellinger distance from [[def-hellinger-distance-for-dominated-laws]] is independent of the choice of common dominating measure. With the library convention $\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A}|P(A)-Q(A)|$ from [[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]],

$$\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}\le h(P,Q),\qquad h(P,Q)^2\le 2\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}.$$

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ generating $\mathcal A$, and let $\mu,\nu$ be measures on $(X,\mathcal A)$ that agree on $\mathcal P$. Suppose there is an increasing sequence $(P_n)$ in $\mathcal P$ with

$$X=\bigcup_nP_n,\qquad \mu(P_n)=\nu(P_n)<+\infty\quad(n\in\mathbb N).$$

Then $\mu=\nu$ on $\mathcal A$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space and let
$f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ be measurable for the Borel sigma-algebra on
the extended real line. Products of functions use
$\odot_X$ from [[def-measurable-pointwise-extended-real-product]], and $cf$
abbreviates $\underline c\odot_X f$ for the constant function $\underline c$.
The magnitude function is $|f|=\max(f,-f)$ as in
[[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]]. Then:

1. $cf$ is measurable for every real scalar $c$;
2. $\max(f,g)$, $\min(f,g)$, $|f|$, $f^+$, and $f^-$ are measurable;
3. if the partial pointwise sum $f+g$ is defined at every point, then it is measurable;
4. the pointwise product $fg:=f\odot_X g$ is measurable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and define
$$\nu_f(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu \qquad (A\in\mathcal A).$$
Then $\nu_f$ is a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges ([[def-series]]) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

derivations.claim: For $n\ge1$ put $L_n(\theta,x_{1:n})=\prod_{i=1}^np(\theta,x_i)$ and $Z_n(x_{1:n})=\int_\Theta L_n(\theta,x_{1:n})\,\Pi(d\theta)$. The coordinate maps into $\Theta\times\mathsf X$ are measurable by the product sigma-algebra definition [F20]; joint measurability of $p$ and closure under finite products [F23] make $L_n$ product-measurable. For each fixed $\theta$, repeated Tonelli [F6, F21] and $\int p(\theta,x)\,d\mu=1$ give $\int L_n(\theta,\cdot)\,d\mu^n=1$. By [F24], $L_n(\theta,\cdot)d\mu^n$ is a measure. On every measurable rectangle $\prod_{i=1}^n A_i$, repeated Tonelli and the density identity give mass $\prod_iP_\theta(A_i)$; this is also the rectangle mass of $P_\theta^n$ by [F8, F10]. Rectangles generate the product sigma-algebra [F20], and both are probability measures, so [F22], using the whole sample space as a finite-measure exhaustion, identifies these measures. Tonelli over $\Pi$ and $\mu^n$ now gives $\int Z_n\,d\mu^n=1$, hence $Z_n<\infty$ $\mu^n$-almost everywhere and $P_0^n$-almost surely.

Fix $0<a<b$, choose measurable $B_a\subseteq\{\theta:D(P_0\|P_\theta)<a\}$ with $\Pi(B_a)>0$, and let $\Pi_a$ be the normalized restriction of $\Pi$ to $B_a$. For each $\theta\in B_a$, finite KL gives $P_0\ll P_\theta$. Define $r_\theta=p_0/p(\theta,\cdot)$ where $p(\theta,\cdot)>0$ and zero elsewhere. Since $P_0(\{p(\theta,\cdot)=0\})=0$, direct integration of the two supplied densities gives $\int_A r_\theta\,dP_\theta=P_0(A)$ for every measurable $A$, so $r_\theta$ is a Radon–Nikodym derivative. Define $Z_\theta=\log(p(\theta,\cdot)/p_0)$ where both densities are positive and zero elsewhere; then $Z_\theta=-\log r_\theta$ $P_0$-almost surely. For $u\ge1$, [F19] gives $\log u\le u$, so $\mathbb E_0Z_\theta^+\le\int_{\{p(\theta,x)>p_0(x)\}}p(\theta,x)\,d\mu\le1$. Pinsker [F17] gives $D(P_0\|P_\theta)\ge0$, and [F5] yields $\mathbb E_0Z_\theta^-=D(P_0\|P_\theta)+\mathbb E_0Z_\theta^+\le a+1$. Thus $\mathbb E_0|Z_\theta|\le a+2$.

Fix $\eta>0$ with $V_\eta\ne\varnothing$, and let $\alpha_n=P_0^n\phi_n$ and $\beta_n=\sup_{\theta\in V_\eta}P_\theta^n(1-\phi_n)$. The two summable series imply $\alpha_n,\beta_n\to0$. Choose $m\ge1$ with $\alpha_m<1/4$ and $\beta_m<1/4$. For $\ell=\lfloor n/m\rfloor$, group the first $\ell m$ observations into disjoint consecutive blocks of length $m$. By [F8, F10] the block vectors are independent and identically distributed under each fixed IID law; [F9] makes $Y_j:=\phi_m(\text{block }j)$ independent $[0,1]$ random variables. Their means are at most $1/4$ under $P_0$ and at least $3/4$ under every $P_\theta$ with $\theta\in V_\eta$. Let $\widetilde\phi_n=\mathbf1\{\ell^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^\ell Y_j>1/2\}$ for $\ell\ge1$, and $0$ otherwise.

Since $P_0=P_{\theta_0}\ll\mu$, $p_0(X_i)>0$ for every sampled coordinate almost surely. On this event define the relative evidence $D_n=Z_n(X_{1:n})/\prod_{i=1}^np_0(X_i)$; it is finite $P_0^n$-almost surely by step 1.1.

Let $u(\theta,x)=p(\theta,x)/p_0(x)$ when both densities are positive and $0$ otherwise; the lift of $p_0$ to $\Theta\times\mathsf X$ is measurable by [F2,F20], and the piecewise quotient is measurable by [F23,F25]. Extend $Z(\theta,x)=\log u(\theta,x)$ on $u>0$ by $0$ on $u=0$. For every real $s$, its upper threshold is $\{u>\exp(s)\}$ if $s\ge0$ and $\{u=0\}\cup\{u>\exp(s)\}$ if $s<0$; [F27,F29] and [F25] therefore make $Z$ product-measurable. For each $\theta\in B_a$, [F5] identifies $D(P_0\|P_\theta)=-\mathbb E_0Z_\theta$; applying [F6] to the positive and negative parts shows that these section integrals, and hence $\theta\mapsto D(P_0\|P_\theta)$ on $B_a$, are measurable. Tonelli [F6] and the uniform bound in step 1.2 show $G(x):=\int Z(\theta,x)\,\Pi_a(d\theta)$ is finite for $P_0$-almost every $x$ and integrable, with $\mathbb E_0G=-\kappa$ where $\kappa:=\int D(P_0\|P_\theta)\,\Pi_a(d\theta)\le a$. For each $\theta\in B_a$, $P_0\{x:p(\theta,x)=0\}=0$; Tonelli [F6] applied to the measurable indicator of this set implies $\Pi_a\{\theta:p(\theta,X_i)=0\}=0$ almost surely for each coordinate $i$. Intersecting these probability-one events over all $i$, $\exp(\sum_{i=1}^nZ(\theta,X_i))=\prod_{i=1}^np(\theta,X_i)/p_0(X_i)$ for $\Pi_a$-almost every $\theta$ and every $n$. Set $G=0$ on the measurable $P_0$-null set where the integral is not finite.

For $\ell\ge1$, [F26] writes the exponential of the centered sum as a product; the finite product law [F10] and Tonelli [F6] factor its expectation, and [F12] bounds each factor by $e^{\lambda^2/8}$. Thus $\mathbb E\exp\{\lambda\sum_{j=1}^\ell(Y_j-\mathbb EY_j)\}\le e^{\ell\lambda^2/8}$. Under $P_0$, rejection requires an upward deviation greater than $\ell/4$; Markov [F15] with $\lambda=1$ gives $P_0^n\widetilde\phi_n\le e^{-\ell/8}$. Under every $P_\theta$ in $V_\eta$, nonrejection requires a downward deviation at least $\ell/4$; Markov with $\lambda=-1$ gives $P_\theta^n(1-\widetilde\phi_n)\le e^{-\ell/8}$. Since $\ell\ge n/m-1$, both errors are at most $e^{1/8}e^{-cn}$ for $c:=1/(8m)$ and all $n\ge m$.

The variables $G(X_i)$ are IID by [F8, F9] and integrable by step 2.2. The strong law [F11] gives $n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nG(X_i)\to-\kappa$; because $\kappa\le a<b$, eventually $\sum_iG(X_i)>-nb$. Tonelli and the bound in step 1.2 also give $\int\sum_i|Z_\theta(X_i)|\,\Pi_a(d\theta)<\infty$ for $P_0^n$-almost every sample; the exponential is integrable by step 1.1. By step 2.2, the likelihood ratio in $D_n$ agrees with $\exp(\sum_iZ_\theta(X_i))$ for $\Pi_a$-almost every $\theta$, so $D_n\ge\Pi(B_a)\int\exp(\sum_iZ_\theta(X_i))\,\Pi_a(d\theta)$. Jensen [F13, F14] bounds this integral below by $\exp(\sum_iG(X_i))$, giving $D_n\ge\Pi(B_a)e^{-nb}$ eventually.

On $\{p_0(X_i)>0\text{ for }1\le i\le n\}$, define $A_n:=(1-\widetilde\phi_n)\int_{V_\eta}\prod_{i=1}^n[p(\theta,X_i)/p_0(X_i)]\,\Pi(d\theta)$, and set $A_n=0$ otherwise. The product-density identity in step 1.1 and Tonelli [F6] imply $\mathbb E_{P_0^n}A_n=\int_{V_\eta}P_\theta^n((1-\widetilde\phi_n)\mathbf1_{\{p_0(X_i)>0\,\forall i\}})\,\Pi(d\theta)\le e^{1/8}e^{-cn}$ for $n\ge m$, by step 2.3 and $\Pi(V_\eta)\le1$.

On valid posterior fibres, split the likelihood numerator over the test and its complement. The posterior formula [F7] gives $\Pi_n(V_\eta\mid X_{1:n})\le\widetilde\phi_n+A_n/D_n$. Step 3.1 ensures the denominator is finite and positive for all sufficiently large $n$ almost surely.

Choose $0<a<b<c$ and use step 3.1 with these radii. Since $c>0$ and $c-b>0$, [F27] gives $e^{-c},e^{-(c-b)}\in(0,1)$; [F28] makes the corresponding geometric series finite. For each $r>0$, Markov [F15] gives $\sum_{n\ge m}P_0^n(e^{nb}A_n>r)\le r^{-1}e^{1/8}\sum_{n\ge m}e^{-n(c-b)}<\infty$. Borel–Cantelli [F16], first for $r=1/k$ and then by countability, gives $e^{nb}A_n\to0$ almost surely. The type-I bound from step 2.3 is also summable, so [F16] gives $\widetilde\phi_n\to0$ almost surely. Combining these limits with $D_n\ge\Pi(B_a)e^{-nb}$ from step 3.1 and step 4.1 proves $\Pi_n(V_\eta\mid X_{1:n})\to0$ almost surely.
The consistency conclusion holds simultaneously for all $\eta>0$: intersect the probability-one events for positive rational $q$; for any $\eta>0$ choose rational $q<\eta$, so $V_\eta\subseteq V_q$.

For each $\theta$ with finite KL, Pinsker [F17] and the local comparison [F18] give $h(P_0,P_\theta)^2\le2\sqrt{D(P_0\|P_\theta)/2}$, hence $h(P_0,P_\theta)^4\le2D(P_0\|P_\theta)$. The parameter map $\theta\mapsto h(P_0,P_\theta)^2$ is measurable: [F25] makes both square-root sections measurable, [F23] makes their squared difference product-measurable, and Tonelli [F6] makes its $\mu$-integral measurable in $\theta$. Thus every Hellinger ball is measurable. Taking a positive-measure KL subset $B_{\eta^4/2}$ places it inside $\{\theta:h(P_0,P_\theta)<\eta\}$, proving positive prior mass.

boundaries.evidence: If V_eta is empty its posterior mass is zero; step 1.3 fixes the nonempty case for the testing argument.

Steps 1.1 and 3.1 establish finite positive relative evidence eventually P0-almost surely; the filler convention covers invalid fibres before then. Step 3.2 sets A_n=0 when a truth-density coordinate is zero, a P0^n-null event.
Step 1.3 defines the amplified test as zero when the block count ell=0 for n<m; the exponential estimates in step 2.3 discard these finitely many indices.
Step 7.1 handles zero KL and zero Hellinger distance; the KL-to-Hellinger inequality remains valid at zero.
Statement requires eta>0; steps 1.2 and 5.1 choose strict 0<a<b<c, and step 7.1 handles the strict Hellinger ball using KL radius eta^4/2.
Statement makes inherited AC explicit; step 1.2 uses the positive-prior measurable KL subset supplied by the KL-support hypothesis, with no arbitrary density selection.

risk_review.notes: Independently read all twelve proof steps, the complete Statement, and every one of the 35 actual supplier statements. Joint finite normalized densities and sigma-finite factors justify repeated Tonelli; finite product laws follow by equality on rectangles and the probability-measure uniqueness supplier. Finite KL gives P0<<Ptheta and log ratio integrability: E Z+<=1 and E Z-<=a+1; Tonelli therefore gives integrable G and its mean -kappa>=-a on the positive-prior measurable KL subset. The likelihood zeros are removed only on a Pi_a x P0 null set; countably many sample coordinates preserve the probability-one event. Jensen applies because the log sum and exponential are integrable on each relevant fibre; SLLN yields D_n>=Pi(B_a)exp(-nb) eventually for b>a. Summability allows one block size with both errors<1/4; independent bounded block tests and the supplied MGF yield both amplified errors <=exp(1/8)exp(-n/(8m)), including the nonrejection equality endpoint. Tested numerator integration is an inequality, retaining the p0-positive indicator, so it does not silently assume Ptheta<<P0. Choose 0<a<b<c, then Markov and BC give the numerator/denominator ratio to zero and eventual finite-positive evidence under the true law; prior-predictive nullness alone is not used for that conclusion. Empty complements are trivial; countable rational radii handle simultaneous eta. Pinsker gives h^4<=2 KL; square-root threshold measurability and Tonelli give measurable Hellinger balls with positive mass. Quotient measurability in 2.2 follows directly from thresholds {p-r p0>0} on the positive locus, an immediate elementary inference from F23/F25, with no additional supplier needed. The forward definition of A_n in 4.1 unambiguously supplies its use in 3.2. AC inheritance is explicit. Source checks: Kleijn §7.3 Theorems 7.5/7.8 and full proofs, PDF pp.41-44; KvdV §4.1 Lemma 4.1 and Corollaries 4.1/4.2, printed pp.376-379. The extracted Corollary 4.2 endpoint reads 1; local exclusion limit 0 is independently derived and agrees with preceding Corollary 4.1, rather than importing that apparent source typo.
