citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

An estimand $\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0$ is **identifiable** in a parametric
model $\mathsf P$ when
$$
P_\theta=P_\eta\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\psi(\theta)=\psi(\eta)\qquad(\theta,\eta\in\Theta),
$$
or equivalently when $\psi$ is constant on each set of parameter values with
the same sampling law ([[def-parametric-statistical-model]],
[[def-observational-equivalence]], [[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]]).
The model is **identifiable** when its identity target
$\operatorname{id}_\Theta:\Theta\to\Theta$ is identifiable, equivalently
when $\mathsf P$ is injective.

Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
([[def-probability-measure]]). Absolute continuity $P\ll Q$ has the convention
of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If
$P\not\ll Q$, define $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and
let $r=dP/dQ$ be a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative of its
Radon–Nikodym class; such a representative exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].
On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This
function is measurable: for $a\ge0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r>\exp(a)\}$, and for
$a<0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r=0\}\cup\{r>\exp(a)\}$, by the inverse and
monotonicity properties of the natural logarithm
([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]). These are
measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since
$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$ by
[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$
The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,
$$0\le \frac{\log s}{s}=\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{u}\le\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{\sqrt u}\le\frac2{\sqrt s}.$$
Thus $t\log t\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$; here $L=\log$ by
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and
[[def-integral-logarithm]]. On $(0,\infty)$, $\psi$ is a product of continuous
functions by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $\psi$ is continuous on
$[0,\infty)$ and $\psi(r)$ is measurable by
[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts
([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]],
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

For $0<t\le1$, the function $-t\log t$ has derivative $-\log t-1$ and
maximum $1/e$ at $t=1/e$: $e=\exp(1)>1$ by
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $1/e=\exp(-1)$ by
[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and $\log(1/e)=-1$ by
[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and the inverse definition. The mean value
theorem gives increase before and decrease after this point
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]],
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).
At $t=0$ the negative part is zero. Since $Q$ is a probability measure,
$$\int \psi(r)^-\,dQ\le\frac1e.$$
The change-of-measure identity of [[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]],
applied to $\ell^-$ gives $\int\ell^-\,dP=\int\psi(r)^-\,dQ\le1/e$,
so $\int\ell\,dP$ is well-defined; applying it to both positive and negative
parts gives
$$D(P\|Q)=\int\ell\,dP=\int\psi(r)\,dQ=\int r\log r\,dQ,$$
with $0\log0:=0$ and a finite negative part. Therefore the extended integral
is well-defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.

This convention is directional: the first argument must be absolutely
continuous with respect to the second for the integral formula to apply.

Assume AC for the imported density-representative convention. Let $P,Q$ be probability laws on a measurable space, both dominated by one specified common sigma-finite positive measure. Then the root-L2 Hellinger distance from [[def-hellinger-distance-for-dominated-laws]] is independent of the choice of common dominating measure. With the library convention $\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A}|P(A)-Q(A)|$ from [[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]],

$$\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}\le h(P,Q),\qquad h(P,Q)^2\le 2\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}.$$

Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
$(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **total variation
distance** is

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}\bigl|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\bigr| .$$

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in
$[-1,1]$, because both measures have total mass one; hence the set being
maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.
The empty event and the whole space give the values $0$ and
$|\mu(E)-\nu(E)|=0$, so the distance is zero when $\mu=\nu$, and it is symmetric
in $\mu$ and $\nu$. This convention carries no factor $1/2$ in the supremum;
it is therefore not the total variation norm of the signed measure $\mu-\nu$,
which is twice the quantity above when that signed measure is considered on a
measurable space where the decomposition is attained. On a countable state
space with its power-set sigma-algebra the supremum equals the half-$\ell^1$
sum $\tfrac12\sum_{x\in E}|\mu(\{x\})-\nu(\{x\})|$; that identity is proved in
[[lem-total-variation-half-l1-formula-on-a-countable-space]], not assumed here.

Let $\pi$ be a prior probability on $(E,\mathcal S)$ and let $Q:E\to T$ be a probability kernel dominated by a sigma-finite measure $\nu$ on $(T,\mathcal T)$, with specified nonnegative jointly measurable density $\ell:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$:
$$Q(\theta,B)=\int_B\ell(\theta,y)\,\nu(dy)\quad\text{for every }\theta\in E,\ B\in\mathcal T.$$

Define $m(y)=\int_E\ell(\theta,y)\,\pi(d\theta)$. Under the joint law with density $\ell$ relative to $\pi\times\nu$, a conditional law of the parameter given the observation is
$$K(y,A)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\int_A\ell(\theta,y)\,\pi(d\theta)}{m(y)},&0<m(y)<\infty,\\ \pi(A),&m(y)=0\text{ or }m(y)=\infty.\end{cases}$$

The observation marginal is $m\,d\nu$, and the filled fibres have marginal mass zero. This is a choice-free assertion about the explicit kernel and event identities.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). It is
**dominated** by a supplied positive measure $\mu$ on
$(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ when $\mu$ is sigma-finite
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]) and
$P_\theta\ll\mu$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$
([[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]).
The dominating measure is part of the specified setup. This condition adds no
measurable structure on $\Theta$ and no measurability of
$\theta\mapsto P_\theta$.

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be dominated by the fixed sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$. For each
$\theta$, the Radon–Nikodym theorem gives the almost-everywhere class
$dP_\theta/d\mu$; a sigma-finite exhaustion for $\mu$ is also finite for the
probability measure $P_\theta$. Under AC, select simultaneously a
finite-valued measurable nonnegative representative $p_\theta$ from each
class. The nonnegative version exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].

For fixed observed $x\in\mathcal X$, the function
$$L_x:\Theta\to[0,+\infty),\qquad L_x(\theta):=p_\theta(x),$$
is the **likelihood at $x$**. This is a function on the parameter labels, not
a probability distribution on $\Theta$. No sigma-algebra on $\Theta$ or
measurability of $L_x$ is implied. Each density is determined only
$\mu$-almost everywhere; there is no canonical pointwise version and, for
arbitrary uncountable $\Theta$, no common exceptional null set is asserted.

Suppose an experiment on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ also has a measurable
parameter space $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ ([[def-measurable-space]]). A
**Markov kernel** (or **probability kernel**) representation is a function
$$
K:\Theta\times\mathcal A\to[0,1]
$$
such that, for every $\theta\in\Theta$, the set function
$A\mapsto K(\theta,A)$ is a probability measure on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$,
and, for every $A\in\mathcal A$ and every Borel set $C\subseteq[0,1]$,
$$
\{\theta\in\Theta:K(\theta,A)\in C\}\in\mathcal T.
$$
Here the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,1]$ is generated by its relatively open
subsets $U\cap[0,1]$, where $U$ is open in $\mathbb R$. Thus the second
condition says that each event-probability map $\theta\mapsto K(\theta,A)$ is
measurable. The kernel represents the given experiment exactly when
$K(\theta,A)=P_\theta(A)$ for every $\theta$ and $A$
([[def-statistical-experiment]], [[def-probability-measure]]).

This is an optional parameter-measurable version of a model. An arbitrary
experiment does not include a measurable structure on $\Theta$ or imply this
kernel condition.

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges ([[def-series]]) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

derivations.claim: Let $\mathsf X=\{0,1\}$ with counting measure, let $\Theta=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ with its power-set sigma-algebra, and put $\delta_k=(k+2)^{-2}$ for $k\ge1$. Define $P_0=\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2)$ and $P_k=\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2+\delta_k)$. Every mass is strictly between zero and one, and the map $k\mapsto P_k$ is injective because the $\delta_k$ are distinct. Thus the model is identifiable by [F1]. The parameter and observation spaces are discrete, so every event-probability section is measurable by [F9] and every function on their countable product, including the pointwise Bernoulli density, is jointly measurable. The counting measure is sigma-finite and the displayed densities are normalized, so this is a dominated model by [F8].

Give the true parameter $0$ prior mass zero and set $\Pi(\{k\})=2^{-k}$ for $k\ge1$. By [F10] these masses sum to one, so [F12] makes $\Pi$ a probability. For $\delta=\delta_k$, the explicit densities and [F2] give $D(P_0\|P_k)=\tfrac12\log\frac{1/2}{1/2+\delta}+\tfrac12\log\frac{1/2}{1/2-\delta}=-\tfrac12\log(1-4\delta^2)$. For $0<x<1$, [F11] gives $0\le-\log(1-x)=\int_{1-x}^1dt/t\le x/(1-x)$; hence $0\le D(P_0\|P_k)\le2\delta_k^2/(1-4\delta_k^2)\to0$. Every KL neighborhood of $P_0$ therefore contains some $P_k$ with prior mass $2^{-k}>0$.

Put $d(P_j,P_k)=1$ for distinct model laws and $d(P_j,P_j)=0$. This is a metric: if the endpoints in a triangle inequality differ, at least one adjacent pair differs and the sum of its two distances is at least one; if they agree, the left side is zero. Thus the parameter complement is $V_{1/2}=\{k\ge1\}$. For every finite data vector, all $P_k^n(x_{1:n})>0$ and are at most one, so the evidence $\sum_{k\ge1}2^{-k}P_k^n(x_{1:n})$ is finite and positive. By [F5], the posterior is supported on $\{k\ge1\}$; consequently $\Pi_n(V_{1/2}\mid x_{1:n})=1$ for every data vector and every $n$.

Let $\rho_k=\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}}\sqrt{P_0(\{x\})P_k(\{x\})}$. Then $0\le\rho_k\le1$, since $h(P_0,P_k)^2=2-2\rho_k$ is an integral of a square. The IID product law [F6, F7] and distributivity give product affinity $\rho_k^n$, so $h(P_0^n,P_k^n)^2=2(1-\rho_k^n)\le n\,2(1-\rho_k)=n h(P_0,P_k)^2$, since $1-r^n=(1-r)\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}r^j\le n(1-r)$ for $0\le r\le1$. Also $\|P_0-P_k\|_{\rm TV}=\delta_k$: the four events in $\{0,1\}$ have probability differences $0,\delta_k,-\delta_k,0$. Thus [F3] gives $\|P_0^n-P_n^n\|_{\rm TV}\le h(P_0^n,P_n^n)\le\sqrt{2n\delta_n}\to0$.

Write $\Delta_n(x)=P_0^n(\{x\})-P_n^n(\{x\})$ on the finite sample space. Since $\sum_x\Delta_n(x)=0$, the positive and negative sums each have magnitude $\|P_0^n-P_n^n\|_{\rm TV}$: the event $\{x:\Delta_n(x)>0\}$ attains the positive sum, and every event sum lies between the negative and positive sums. For any randomized test $0\le\phi_n\le1$, it follows term-by-term that $|P_0^n\phi_n-P_n^n\phi_n|=|\sum_x\phi_n(x)\Delta_n(x)|\le\|P_0^n-P_n^n\|_{\rm TV}$. Hence $\sup_{k\ge1}P_k^n(1-\phi_n)\ge P_n^n(1-\phi_n)\ge1-P_0^n\phi_n-\|P_0^n-P_n^n\|_{\rm TV}$. If the type-I error tends to zero, step 2.3 makes this uniform type-II lower bound tend to one. No tests with both errors tending to zero exist for this complement, although the model is identifiable and the prior has KL support.
Steps 1.1 and 2.1 establish identifiability and KL support, while steps 2.2, 2.3, and 3.1 establish posterior inconsistency and absence of uniformly consistent tests. This refutes the statement.

boundaries.evidence: Step 2.1 identifies V_{1/2} exactly as the nontruth support {k>=1}, so the counterexample complement is nonempty.
Step 2.1 shows every likelihood is strictly positive and bounded by one, so evidence is positive and at most one for every data vector.
Steps 1.1–1.2 define all one-observation laws and establish positive prior mass in every KL neighborhood.

boundaries.reason: The family consists of distinct Bernoulli laws; no degenerate law is used in the counterexample.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.1 uses success probabilities strictly between zero and one, avoiding zero likelihoods at both sample outcomes.
The countable model, densities and prior are explicit; axiom use is inherited only from the imported general definitions.

boundaries.reason: The counterexample refutes a sufficiency claim and asserts no equivalence.

risk_review.notes: Read all six authored steps and all fifteen supplier statements. The explicit countable Bernoulli family has 0<1/2+delta_k<1, distinct positive delta_k=(k+2)^(-2), joint measurability on countable discrete spaces and counting domination. Prior masses 2^(-k), k>=1, sum to 1 while omitting truth 0. Directional KL equals -log(1-4delta_k^2)/2 and tends to zero via the stated integral bound. The discrete law metric has measurable complement {k>=1}; all likelihoods are positive and <=1, so every finite evidence is in (0,1] and the posterior stays on that complement. Product affinity gives h(product)^2<=n h(single)^2<=2n delta_k, and k=n makes TV tend to zero. The finite signed-mass argument applies even to randomized tests and forces uniform type-II error toward 1 when type-I tends to 0. This is a counterexample for an arbitrary law metric, not a claim of failure in TV or weak topology. Inherited AC is explicit, with no local choice. Reader/refuter report no finding. No defect or published supplier issue.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

An estimand $\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0$ is **identifiable** in a parametric
model $\mathsf P$ when
$$
P_\theta=P_\eta\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\psi(\theta)=\psi(\eta)\qquad(\theta,\eta\in\Theta),
$$
or equivalently when $\psi$ is constant on each set of parameter values with
the same sampling law ([[def-parametric-statistical-model]],
[[def-observational-equivalence]], [[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]]).
The model is **identifiable** when its identity target
$\operatorname{id}_\Theta:\Theta\to\Theta$ is identifiable, equivalently
when $\mathsf P$ is injective.

Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
([[def-probability-measure]]). Absolute continuity $P\ll Q$ has the convention
of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If
$P\not\ll Q$, define $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and
let $r=dP/dQ$ be a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative of its
Radon–Nikodym class; such a representative exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].
On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This
function is measurable: for $a\ge0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r>\exp(a)\}$, and for
$a<0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r=0\}\cup\{r>\exp(a)\}$, by the inverse and
monotonicity properties of the natural logarithm
([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]). These are
measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since
$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$ by
[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$
The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,
$$0\le \frac{\log s}{s}=\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{u}\le\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{\sqrt u}\le\frac2{\sqrt s}.$$
Thus $t\log t\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$; here $L=\log$ by
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and
[[def-integral-logarithm]]. On $(0,\infty)$, $\psi$ is a product of continuous
functions by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $\psi$ is continuous on
$[0,\infty)$ and $\psi(r)$ is measurable by
[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts
([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]],
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

For $0<t\le1$, the function $-t\log t$ has derivative $-\log t-1$ and
maximum $1/e$ at $t=1/e$: $e=\exp(1)>1$ by
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $1/e=\exp(-1)$ by
[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and $\log(1/e)=-1$ by
[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and the inverse definition. The mean value
theorem gives increase before and decrease after this point
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]],
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).
At $t=0$ the negative part is zero. Since $Q$ is a probability measure,
$$\int \psi(r)^-\,dQ\le\frac1e.$$
The change-of-measure identity of [[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]],
applied to $\ell^-$ gives $\int\ell^-\,dP=\int\psi(r)^-\,dQ\le1/e$,
so $\int\ell\,dP$ is well-defined; applying it to both positive and negative
parts gives
$$D(P\|Q)=\int\ell\,dP=\int\psi(r)\,dQ=\int r\log r\,dQ,$$
with $0\log0:=0$ and a finite negative part. Therefore the extended integral
is well-defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.

This convention is directional: the first argument must be absolutely
continuous with respect to the second for the integral formula to apply.

Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
$(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **total variation
distance** is

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}\bigl|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\bigr| .$$

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in
$[-1,1]$, because both measures have total mass one; hence the set being
maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.
The empty event and the whole space give the values $0$ and
$|\mu(E)-\nu(E)|=0$, so the distance is zero when $\mu=\nu$, and it is symmetric
in $\mu$ and $\nu$. This convention carries no factor $1/2$ in the supremum;
it is therefore not the total variation norm of the signed measure $\mu-\nu$,
which is twice the quantity above when that signed measure is considered on a
measurable space where the decomposition is attained. On a countable state
space with its power-set sigma-algebra the supremum equals the half-$\ell^1$
sum $\tfrac12\sum_{x\in E}|\mu(\{x\})-\nu(\{x\})|$; that identity is proved in
[[lem-total-variation-half-l1-formula-on-a-countable-space]], not assumed here.

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Let $Y$ be a measurable real random variable on a probability space with $0\le Y\le1$ almost surely. Then, for every $\lambda\in\mathbb R$,

$$\mathbb E\exp\{\lambda(Y-\mathbb EY)\}\le \exp(\lambda^2/8).$$

This proof uses only finite product and scalar integral arguments; it does not assume the Axiom of Choice.

Assume AC for the imported general Kullback–Leibler divergence and likelihood-density conventions. Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ be a measurable parameter space with a proper prior probability $\Pi$. Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an observation space with sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$. Suppose $\theta\mapsto P_\theta$ is a parameter-measurable probability kernel, every $P_\theta$ is dominated by $\mu$, and the truth is well-specified: $P_0=P_{\theta_0}$ for some $\theta_0\in\Theta$. Assume a specified nonnegative function $p:\Theta\times\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ is jointly measurable and, for every $\theta\in\Theta$ and $A\in\mathcal A$, $P_\theta(A)=\int_Ap(\theta,x)\,\mu(dx)$ with $\int p(\theta,x)\,\mu(dx)=1$. Write $p_0(x)=p(\theta_0,x)$.

Assume KL support at $P_0$: for every $\epsilon>0$ there is a measurable $B_\epsilon\subseteq\{\theta:D(P_0\|P_\theta)<\epsilon\}$ with $\Pi(B_\epsilon)>0$. Let $d$ be a metric on the model laws and require $V_\eta:=\{\theta:d(P_\theta,P_0)>\eta\}$ to be measurable for each $\eta>0$. For each $\eta$ with $V_\eta\ne\varnothing$, suppose there are measurable tests $\phi_n:\mathsf X^n\to[0,1]$ such that

$$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}P_0^n\phi_n<\infty,\qquad \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\sup_{\theta\in V_\eta}P_\theta^n(1-\phi_n)<\infty.$$

For each $A\in\mathcal T$, define the posterior by

$$\Pi_n(A\mid x_{1:n})=\frac{\int_A\prod_{i=1}^np(\theta,x_i)\,\Pi(d\theta)}{\int_\Theta\prod_{i=1}^np(\theta,x_i)\,\Pi(d\theta)}$$

on fibres with finite positive denominator, and use $\Pi$ as the fixed probability filler otherwise. Then, for any IID sequence with common law $P_0$, $\Pi_n(V_\eta\mid X_{1:n})\to0$ almost surely for every fixed $\eta>0$.

For the root-L2 Hellinger distance of [[def-hellinger-distance-for-dominated-laws]], every Hellinger ball about $P_0$ is measurable as a parameter set and has positive prior mass. Moreover, $h(P_0,P_\theta)^4\le2D(P_0\|P_\theta)$ under the library event-supremum total-variation convention; thus $D(P_0\|P_\theta)<\eta^4/2$ implies $h(P_0,P_\theta)<\eta$.

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges ([[def-series]]) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$

([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]) and

([[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]).

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space and let $P,Q$ be probability measures ([[def-probability-measure]]) on it, both dominated by a specified common sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$ as in [[def-dominated-statistical-experiment]]. For supplied finite-valued nonnegative measurable density representatives $p=dP/d\mu$ and $q=dQ/d\mu$ in the convention of [[def-likelihood-density]], the **root-L2 Hellinger distance** is

$$h(P,Q):=\left(\int \bigl(\sqrt p-\sqrt q\bigr)^2\,d\mu\right)^{1/2}.$$

The square roots are measurable: for every real $r$, $\{\sqrt p>r\}$ is the whole space if $r<0$ and equals $\{p>r^2\}$ if $r\ge0$, and the same holds for $q$ ([[thm-threshold-characterisations-of-real-and-extended-real-measurability]]). The arithmetic and lattice rules make the nonnegative integrand measurable ([[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]). It is integrable because $(\sqrt p-\sqrt q)^2\le p+q$ and the integral is additive on nonnegative functions ([[cor-additivity-of-the-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]), so its integral is at most $P(\mathsf X)+Q(\mathsf X)=2$.

The generic density-selection convention [[def-likelihood-density]] assumes the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. When $p$ and $q$ are explicitly given, this displayed integral requires no further choice.

Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
$(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **total variation
distance** is

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}\bigl|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\bigr| .$$

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in
$[-1,1]$, because both measures have total mass one; hence the set being
maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.
The empty event and the whole space give the values $0$ and
$|\mu(E)-\nu(E)|=0$, so the distance is zero when $\mu=\nu$, and it is symmetric
in $\mu$ and $\nu$. This convention carries no factor $1/2$ in the supremum;
it is therefore not the total variation norm of the signed measure $\mu-\nu$,
which is twice the quantity above when that signed measure is considered on a
measurable space where the decomposition is attained. On a countable state
space with its power-set sigma-algebra the supremum equals the half-$\ell^1$
sum $\tfrac12\sum_{x\in E}|\mu(\{x\})-\nu(\{x\})|$; that identity is proved in
[[lem-total-variation-half-l1-formula-on-a-countable-space]], not assumed here.

Assume AC for the imported density-representative convention. Let $P,Q$ be probability laws on a measurable space, both dominated by one specified common sigma-finite positive measure. Then the root-L2 Hellinger distance from [[def-hellinger-distance-for-dominated-laws]] is independent of the choice of common dominating measure. With the library convention $\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A}|P(A)-Q(A)|$ from [[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]],

$$\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}\le h(P,Q),\qquad h(P,Q)^2\le 2\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}.$$

derivations.claim: The densities are $p(0)=1,p(1)=0$ and $q(0)=0,q(1)=1$, so $\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}}|p(x)-q(x)|=2$. The four measurable events have probability differences $0,1,-1,0$, hence the supremum in [F2] is $1$.

By [F1], $h(P,Q)^2=(\sqrt1-\sqrt0)^2+(\sqrt0-\sqrt1)^2=2$, so $h(P,Q)=\sqrt2$. Therefore $h(P,Q)^2=2\,\mathrm{TV}(P,Q)$, attaining equality in the upper comparison in [F3]; the lower comparison reads $1\le\sqrt2$.

citations.quote: A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$

Let $n\ge1$, let $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ be independent real random variables on a
common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then
   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$
   in $[0,+\infty]$. In this finite product of expectations, a zero factor
   makes the product zero even when another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise
   multiplication has its usual extended nonnegative meaning.
2. If every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable
   and the same factorization holds in $\mathbb R$.

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space and let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int f\,d\mu=0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad f=0 \text{ almost everywhere.}$$

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space and let
$f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ be measurable for the Borel sigma-algebra on
the extended real line. Products of functions use
$\odot_X$ from [[def-measurable-pointwise-extended-real-product]], and $cf$
abbreviates $\underline c\odot_X f$ for the constant function $\underline c$.
The magnitude function is $|f|=\max(f,-f)$ as in
[[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]]. Then:

1. $cf$ is measurable for every real scalar $c$;
2. $\max(f,g)$, $\min(f,g)$, $|f|$, $f^+$, and $f^-$ are measurable;
3. if the partial pointwise sum $f+g$ is defined at every point, then it is measurable;
4. the pointwise product $fg:=f\odot_X g$ is measurable.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$, $(Y,\mathcal{B})$, and $(Z,\mathcal{C})$ be measurable
spaces. If $f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Y,\mathcal{B})$ is measurable and
$g : (Y,\mathcal{B}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable, then
$g \circ f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable.

In particular, if $f$ is measurable and $g$ is a Borel measurable function on
its codomain, then $g \circ f$ is measurable.

derivations.claim: If $m=0$, then $S_m=V=0$, so the zero-variance clause holds. Suppose $m\ge1$, fix one centered variable $Z$ with $|Z|\le b$, and let $\sigma^2=\mathbb E[Z^2]$. For every integer $k\ge2$, the power functions are Borel and $x\mapsto e^{\lambda x}$ is continuous by [F9], so their compositions with $Z$ are measurable by [F10]; the almost-sure bound gives integrability of each power. Thus $|\mathbb E[Z^k]|\le\mathbb E[|Z|^k]\le b^{k-2}\sigma^2$. For fixed real $\lambda$, the exponential series converges uniformly on $[-b,b]$: its tail is bounded by $\sum_{k>N}(|\lambda|b)^k/k!\to0$. Since $|Z|\le b$ almost surely, this uniform convergence and finite linearity [F2] permit termwise expectation in [F3], and the centered first-order term vanishes.

For $k\ge2$, $k!\ge2\cdot3^{k-2}$, by induction from $2!=2$ and the fact that each next factor is at least $3$. If $|\lambda|b<3$, [F3] and step 1.1 therefore give $\mathbb E e^{\lambda Z}\le1+\sigma^2\sum_{k\ge2}\frac{|\lambda|^k b^{k-2}}{k!}\le1+\frac{\lambda^2\sigma^2}{2(1-|\lambda|b/3)}\le\exp\!\left(\frac{\lambda^2\sigma^2}{2(1-|\lambda|b/3)}\right),$ where the last inequality follows from $1+x\le e^x$ for $x\ge0$, which follows termwise from [F3].

For $0<\lambda<3/b$, repeated use of [F4] gives $e^{\lambda S_m}=\prod_{i=1}^m e^{\lambda Z_i}$. Each $Z_i$ is measurable, scalar multiplication preserves measurability by [F10], and $x\mapsto e^x$ is Borel by [F9], so the factors are measurable by composition. They are nonnegative functions of the independent variables, so [F5] and step 2.1 yield $\mathbb E e^{\lambda S_m}=\prod_{i=1}^m\mathbb E e^{\lambda Z_i}\le\exp\!\left(\frac{\lambda^2V}{2(1-\lambda b/3)}\right).$

If $V>0$, take $\lambda=t/(V+bt/3)$; then $0<\lambda b/3=bt/(3V+bt)<1$. The finite sum $S_m$ and its threshold event are measurable by [F10]. Since [F9] makes $e^x$ increasing, on $\{S_m\ge t\}$ one has $e^{\lambda S_m}\ge e^{\lambda t}$. Markov [F6] and step 3.1 give $\mathbb P(S_m\ge t)\le\exp\!\left(\frac{\lambda^2V}{2(1-\lambda b/3)}-\lambda t\right)=\exp\!\left(-\frac{t^2}{2(V+bt/3)}\right).$

Applying step 4.1 to $-Z_1,\ldots,-Z_m$ gives the lower-tail bound, since this family remains independent, centered, bounded by $b$, and has the same total second moment $V$. If $V=0$, each nonnegative $Z_i^2$ has expectation zero, so [F7] makes every $Z_i=0$ almost surely; their finite sum is then zero almost surely.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
([[def-probability-measure]]). Absolute continuity $P\ll Q$ has the convention
of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If
$P\not\ll Q$, define $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and
let $r=dP/dQ$ be a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative of its
Radon–Nikodym class; such a representative exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].
On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This
function is measurable: for $a\ge0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r>\exp(a)\}$, and for
$a<0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r=0\}\cup\{r>\exp(a)\}$, by the inverse and
monotonicity properties of the natural logarithm
([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]). These are
measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since
$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$ by
[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$
The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,
$$0\le \frac{\log s}{s}=\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{u}\le\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{\sqrt u}\le\frac2{\sqrt s}.$$
Thus $t\log t\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$; here $L=\log$ by
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and
[[def-integral-logarithm]]. On $(0,\infty)$, $\psi$ is a product of continuous
functions by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $\psi$ is continuous on
$[0,\infty)$ and $\psi(r)$ is measurable by
[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts
([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]],
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

For $0<t\le1$, the function $-t\log t$ has derivative $-\log t-1$ and
maximum $1/e$ at $t=1/e$: $e=\exp(1)>1$ by
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $1/e=\exp(-1)$ by
[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and $\log(1/e)=-1$ by
[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and the inverse definition. The mean value
theorem gives increase before and decrease after this point
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]],
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).
At $t=0$ the negative part is zero. Since $Q$ is a probability measure,
$$\int \psi(r)^-\,dQ\le\frac1e.$$
The change-of-measure identity of [[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]],
applied to $\ell^-$ gives $\int\ell^-\,dP=\int\psi(r)^-\,dQ\le1/e$,
so $\int\ell\,dP$ is well-defined; applying it to both positive and negative
parts gives
$$D(P\|Q)=\int\ell\,dP=\int\psi(r)\,dQ=\int r\log r\,dQ,$$
with $0\log0:=0$ and a finite negative part. Therefore the extended integral
is well-defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.

This convention is directional: the first argument must be absolutely
continuous with respect to the second for the integral formula to apply.

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). It is
**dominated** by a supplied positive measure $\mu$ on
$(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ when $\mu$ is sigma-finite
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]) and
$P_\theta\ll\mu$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$
([[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]).

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be dominated by the fixed sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$. For each
$\theta$, the Radon–Nikodym theorem gives the almost-everywhere class

probability measure $P_\theta$. Under AC, select simultaneously a
finite-valued measurable nonnegative representative $p_\theta$ from each
class. The nonnegative version exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].

For fixed observed $x\in\mathcal X$, the function
$$L_x:\Theta\to[0,+\infty),\qquad L_x(\theta):=p_\theta(x),$$
is the **likelihood at $x$**. This is a function on the parameter labels, not
a probability distribution on $\Theta$. No sigma-algebra on $\Theta$ or

([[def-probability-measure]]). Absolute continuity $P\ll Q$ has the convention
of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If
$P\not\ll Q$, define $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and
let $r=dP/dQ$ be a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative of its
Radon–Nikodym class; such a representative exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].
On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This
function is measurable: for $a\ge0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r>\exp(a)\}$, and for
$a<0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r=0\}\cup\{r>\exp(a)\}$, by the inverse and
monotonicity properties of the natural logarithm
([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]). These are
measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since
$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$ by
[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$
The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,
$$0\le \frac{\log s}{s}=\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{u}\le\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{\sqrt u}\le\frac2{\sqrt s}.$$
Thus $t\log t\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$; here $L=\log$ by
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and
[[def-integral-logarithm]]. On $(0,\infty)$, $\psi$ is a product of continuous
functions by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $\psi$ is continuous on
$[0,\infty)$ and $\psi(r)$ is measurable by
[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts
([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]],
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

For $0<t\le1$, the function $-t\log t$ has derivative $-\log t-1$ and
maximum $1/e$ at $t=1/e$: $e=\exp(1)>1$ by
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $1/e=\exp(-1)$ by
[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and $\log(1/e)=-1$ by
[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and the inverse definition. The mean value
theorem gives increase before and decrease after this point
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]],
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).
At $t=0$ the negative part is zero. Since $Q$ is a probability measure,
$$\int \psi(r)^-\,dQ\le\frac1e.$$
The change-of-measure identity of [[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]],
applied to $\ell^-$ gives $\int\ell^-\,dP=\int\psi(r)^-\,dQ\le1/e$,
so $\int\ell\,dP$ is well-defined; applying it to both positive and negative
parts gives
$$D(P\|Q)=\int\ell\,dP=\int\psi(r)\,dQ=\int r\log r\,dQ,$$
with $0\log0:=0$ and a finite negative part. Therefore the extended integral
is well-defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.

This convention is directional: the first argument must be absolutely
continuous with respect to the second for the integral formula to apply.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $f\in L^1(\mathbb P)$
be real-valued, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval containing $f(x)$ for
almost every $x$, and let $\varphi:I\to\mathbb R$ be convex with
$\varphi\circ f\in L^1(\mathbb P)$. Then
$$\varphi\!\left(\int f\,d\mathbb P\right)\le\int\varphi(f)\,d\mathbb P.$$

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. For each $i$, let
$g_i:(S_i,\Sigma_i)\to(T_i,\mathcal T_i)$ be measurable. Then the family
$(g_i\circ X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

If $X$ is a square-integrable real random variable and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(|X-\mathbb E[X]|\ge a)\le\frac{\operatorname{Var}(X)}{a^2}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space and let
$f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ be measurable for the Borel sigma-algebra on
the extended real line. Products of functions use
$\odot_X$ from [[def-measurable-pointwise-extended-real-product]], and $cf$
abbreviates $\underline c\odot_X f$ for the constant function $\underline c$.
The magnitude function is $|f|=\max(f,-f)$ as in
[[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]]. Then:

1. $cf$ is measurable for every real scalar $c$;
2. $\max(f,g)$, $\min(f,g)$, $|f|$, $f^+$, and $f^-$ are measurable;
3. if the partial pointwise sum $f+g$ is defined at every point, then it is measurable;
4. the pointwise product $fg:=f\odot_X g$ is measurable.

For a finite family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ of square-integrable real random variables on one common probability space,
$$\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\sum_{i\in I}X_i\right)=\sum_{i\in I}\operatorname{Var}(X_i)+2\sum_{\{i,j\}\subseteq I}\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j).$$
Equivalently, it is $\sum_{i,j\in I}\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j)$. The empty sum has variance zero, and the singleton formula is the identity.
The original finite-probability-space case is included, since every real random variable there is square-integrable and the covariance/variance definitions agree with the finite centered-product/square formulas.
In the first display, the second sum is over two-element subsets of $I$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ be independent real random variables on a
common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then
   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$
   in $[0,+\infty]$. In this finite product of expectations, a zero factor
   makes the product zero even when another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise
   multiplication has its usual extended nonnegative meaning.
2. If every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable
   and the same factorization holds in $\mathbb R$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$, $(Y,\mathcal{B})$, and $(Z,\mathcal{C})$ be measurable
spaces. If $f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Y,\mathcal{B})$ is measurable and
$g : (Y,\mathcal{B}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable, then
$g \circ f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable.

In particular, if $f$ is measurable and $g$ is a Borel measurable function on
its codomain, then $g \circ f$ is measurable.

If $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable and $\int f\,d\mu<+\infty$, then
$f(x)<+\infty$ for almost every $x$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space and let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int f\,d\mu=0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad f=0 \text{ almost everywhere.}$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. The **measure with density $f$ relative
to $\mu$** is the measure
$$f\,d\mu:\mathcal A\to[0,+\infty],\qquad (f\,d\mu)(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu,$$
whose measure property is supplied by
[[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mu$ be a positive measure and let $
u$ be a signed measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. Assume there is an increasing measurable exhaustion $(X_n)$ with $ igcup_nX_n=X$, $\mu(X_n)<+\infty$, and $|
u|(X_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$. If $
u\ll\mu$, then there exists a measurable real-valued function $f$, unique up to $\mu$-almost-everywhere equality, such that
$$
u(E)=\int_Ef\,d\mu\qquad(E\in\mathcal A).$$
If in addition $|
u|(X)<+\infty$, then $f\in L^1(\mu)$.

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

derivations.claim: Define $k(\theta,x)=p_0(x)\log(p_0(x)/p_\theta(x))$ as $0$ when $p_0=0$ and as $+\infty$ when $p_0>0,p_\theta=0$. The sets $\{p_0=0\}$, $\{p_0>0,p_\theta=0\}$, and $\{p_0>0,p_\theta>0\}$ are product-measurable; on the last set the logarithm is a difference of measurable logarithms by [F13]–[F14]. Thus $k^+$ and $k^-$ are product-measurable by [F10]. Where $p_\theta>p_0>0$, setting $u=p_0/p_\theta\in(0,1)$ gives $-u\log u\le1/e$, so $k^-\le p_\theta/e$ and $\int k^-d\mu\le1/e$. If $P_0\ll P_\theta$, then $P_0\{p_\theta=0\}=0$; [F17] gives $p_0=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere there. Consequently, for every measurable $A$, the function $r_\theta=p_0/p_\theta$ on $\{p_\theta>0\}$ and $0$ otherwise satisfies $\int_A r_\theta\,dP_\theta=\int_{A\cap\{p_\theta>0\}}p_0d\mu=P_0(A)$. By [F18], it is a Radon–Nikodym derivative, so [F3] identifies $\mathrm{KL}(P_0\Vert P_\theta)=\int k(\theta,x)d\mu$. Conversely, if $P_0\{p_\theta=0\}=0$, then every $P_\theta$-null set $A$ has $p_\theta=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $A$, hence $P_0(A)=0$; thus failure of $P_0\ll P_\theta$ implies $P_0\{p_\theta=0\}>0$. In that case the same integral is $+\infty$, again equal to [F3]. Finally, Tonelli [F4] makes the integrals of $k^+$ and $k^-$ measurable in $\theta$; the latter is finite, so their difference gives a measurable extended-real KL map. For the log-square coordinate, the specified ratio conventions and [F10], [F13], [F14] give a nonnegative product-measurable integrand, whose section integral is measurable by [F4]. Hence $K_n\in\mathcal T$.

Set $Y_{\theta,i}:=p_\theta(X_i)/p_0(X_i)$ when $p_0(X_i)>0$ and $0$ otherwise. This is a measurable function of $X_i$ by [F10, F14]. Since $P_0\{p_0=0\}=\int_{\{p_0=0\}}p_0\,d\mu=0$, change of density using [F1, F2] gives $\mathbb E_{P_0}Y_{\theta,i}=\int_{\{p_0>0\}}p_\theta\,d\mu\le1$. For each fixed $\theta$, the $Y_{\theta,i}$ are independent measurable transforms of the IID coordinates; [F6, F7, F12] therefore give $\mathbb E_{P_0^n}\prod_iY_{\theta,i}\le1$. Joint measurability and Tonelli [F4] imply $\mathbb E_{P_0^n}D_n\le1$, so [F15] gives $D_n<\infty$ almost surely.

By [A1, F3], every $\theta\in K_n$ satisfies $P_0\ll P_\theta$, so $P_0\{p_\theta=0\}=0$. For each fixed $\theta$, the IID sample therefore has $\prod_i p_\theta(X_i)>0$ almost surely. Apply Tonelli [F4] to the zero-product indicator on $K_n\times\mathsf X^n$ with the product of the prior conditioned on K_n and the n-fold sampling law: for $P_0^n$-almost every sample, the conditional prior measure of parameters with zero product is zero. Hence the product likelihood is positive for prior-almost every $\theta\in K_n$, and [F17] implies its integral over the positive-mass set $K_n$ is positive. On the full-probability event where each $p_0(X_i)>0$, this implies $D_n>0$.

Write $\bar\Pi_n=\Pi(\cdot\mid K_n)$ and define the jointly measurable extended-real function $\ell(\theta,x)$ by the ratio conventions in the Statement: it is zero on $\{p_0=0\}$, equals $\log(p_\theta/p_0)$ where $p_0,p_\theta>0$, and is $-\infty$ where $p_0>0,p_\theta=0$; the stated arithmetic and Borel-composition facts [F10, F13, F14] justify this measurability. This avoids assuming a common $P_0$-full set on which all densities in an uncountable family are positive. For every $\theta\in K_n$, finite KL gives $P_0\ll P_\theta$, so $\ell(\theta,\cdot)$ is finite $P_0$-almost everywhere; the local second-moment condition gives $\mathbb E_{P_0}\ell(\theta,X_1)^2\le\epsilon_n^2$. Holder [F16] on the probability space yields $\mathbb E_{P_0}|\ell(\theta,X_1)|\le\epsilon_n$, and the directional convention [F3] gives $\mathbb E_{P_0}\ell(\theta,X_1)=-\mathrm{KL}(P_0\Vert P_\theta)\ge-\epsilon_n^2$. Tonelli [F4] applied to the positive and negative parts therefore makes $Z(x):=\int\ell(\theta,x)\,\bar\Pi_n(d\theta)$ finite almost everywhere, measurable after assigning zero on the null exceptional set, and integrable with $\mathbb E_{P_0}Z(X_1)\ge-\epsilon_n^2$. Tonelli also gives $\mathbb E_{P_0}\int\ell(\theta,X_1)^2\,\bar\Pi_n(d\theta)\le\epsilon_n^2$; for $P_0$-almost every $x$, Jensen [F5] for $z\mapsto z^2$ gives $Z(x)^2\le\int\ell(\theta,x)^2\,\bar\Pi_n(d\theta)$. Hence $\mathbb E_{P_0}Z(X_1)^2\le\epsilon_n^2$.

Set $Z_i:=Z(X_i)$. By [F6] and [F7], the $Z_i$ are IID; [F8] and step 1.4 imply $\operatorname{Var}(Z_i)\le\epsilon_n^2$, so the centered variables are square-integrable and integrable. For $i\ne j$, the centered variables are independent measurable transforms of independent coordinates, so [F12] factors their product expectation and their covariance is zero. Applying [F11] to their finite sum therefore gives $\operatorname{Var}(n^{-1}\sum_i Z_i)=n^{-2}\sum_i\operatorname{Var}(Z_i)\le\epsilon_n^2/n$.

The mean of $n^{-1}\sum_i Z_i$ is at least $-\epsilon_n^2$ and its variance is at most $\epsilon_n^2/n$, by independence in step 2.1. Thus the event $n^{-1}\sum_iZ_i<-2\epsilon_n^2$ forces a deviation from its mean of at least $\epsilon_n^2$. Chebyshev [F9] yields $P_0^n\!\left\{n^{-1}\sum_iZ_i<-2\epsilon_n^2\right\}\le\frac1{n\epsilon_n^2}.$

By Tonelli [F4] and the local second-moment bound, for $P_0^n$-almost every sample each of the finitely many functions $\theta\mapsto\ell(\theta,X_i)$ is square-integrable under $\bar\Pi_n$; Cauchy–Schwarz [F16] makes their sum integrable. Step 1.3 and the $P_0^n$-full event where each $p_0(X_i)>0$ ensure that $\exp(\sum_i\ell(\theta,X_i))=\prod_i p_\theta(X_i)/p_0(X_i)$ for $\bar\Pi_n$-almost every $\theta$. Step 1.2 bounds the integrated exponential by the finite $D_n/\Pi(K_n)$, so Jensen [F5] applies to that sum and the exponential. On the complementary event, it gives $D_n\ge\Pi(K_n)\int\exp\!\left(\sum_i\ell(\theta,X_i)\right)\bar\Pi_n(d\theta)\ge\Pi(K_n)\exp\!\left(\sum_iZ_i\right)\ge e^{-(C+2)n\epsilon_n^2}.$ Combining with step 3.1 proves the probability bound.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.3 treats the local set as a positive-prior-mass set, which is guaranteed by the premise.

boundaries.reason: Statement: epsilon_n is required to be strictly positive; zero rate is excluded.

boundaries.evidence: Statement and steps 1.1–4.1 allow n=1; asymptotic large-n conditions are not assumed here.
Step 4.1 yields D_n=1 when the prior is concentrated at the truth.

boundaries.reason: Statement: there is no interval parameter or endpoint case.

boundaries.evidence: The statement supplies a jointly measurable density family; only the imported KL convention carries AC.

boundaries.reason: Statement uses KL/log-square prior mass to imply a lower bound on D_n with a Chebyshev probability guarantee; it is a sufficient-condition result.
Statement does not infer the KL neighborhood prior mass from a large likelihood denominator, nor equate denominator bounds with posterior contraction.

finite_checks.name: prior concentrated at the true density
finite_checks.calculation: Every likelihood ratio is 1, so D_n=1. The local KL and log-square moments are zero and the prior mass condition holds for every C>0; hence the claimed lower bound is at most 1.

risk_review.notes: Reviewed all seven steps and all 22 exact dependency statements. Joint finite-valued densities and sigma-finite mu permit Tonelli for KL positive/negative parts (negative integral <=1/e) and the log square, so K_n is measurable. Positive KL mass gives positive D_n by Tonelli without a common exceptional null set; expectation <=1 gives finiteness. Conditional-prior log average has second moment <=epsilon_n^2, independent sample averaging variance <=epsilon_n^2/n, and Chebyshev plus Jensen gives threshold exp(-(C+2)n epsilon_n^2). n>=1, epsilon_n>0 and positive mass are explicit; the probability lower bound may be negative for small n but remains valid. AC is explicitly inherited from directional KL/RN, with no density selection. Reader product-law citation is accurate. Kleijn Lemma 6.4.5 and full proof, printed p.184, checked.

citations.quote:
Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $p,q:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ be measurable densities with $\int p\,d\mu=\int q\,d\mu=1$. They define probability laws $P(B)=\int_Bp\,d\mu$ and $Q(B)=\int_Bq\,d\mu$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **root-L2 Hellinger distance**, with the root-L2 normalization, is
$$h(P,Q):=\left(\int_{\mathsf X}(\sqrt p-\sqrt q)^2\,d\mu\right)^{1/2}.$$

The dominating measure $\mu$ is fixed throughout a use of this definition. Changing either density on a $\mu$-null set does not change the value, since the integrand changes only on a null set. This definition does not assert that separate choices of density versions are jointly measurable in an additional parameter.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $f,g\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$, then
   $$\|f+g\|_p\le\|f\|_p+\|g\|_p.$$
2. If $f,g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\|f+g\|_\infty\le\|f\|_\infty+\|g\|_\infty.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
$(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **total variation
distance** is

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}\bigl|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\bigr| .$$

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in
$[-1,1]$, because both measures have total mass one; hence the set being
maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.
The empty event and the whole space give the values $0$ and
$|\mu(E)-\nu(E)|=0$, so the distance is zero when $\mu=\nu$, and it is symmetric
in $\mu$ and $\nu$. This convention carries no factor $1/2$ in the supremum;
it is therefore not the total variation norm of the signed measure $\mu-\nu$,
which is twice the quantity above when that signed measure is considered on a
measurable space where the decomposition is attained. On a countable state
space with its power-set sigma-algebra the supremum equals the half-$\ell^1$
sum $\tfrac12\sum_{x\in E}|\mu(\{x\})-\nu(\{x\})|$; that identity is proved in
[[lem-total-variation-half-l1-formula-on-a-countable-space]], not assumed here.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space and let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int f\,d\mu=0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad f=0 \text{ almost everywhere.}$$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space and let
$f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ be measurable for the Borel sigma-algebra on
the extended real line. Products of functions use
$\odot_X$ from [[def-measurable-pointwise-extended-real-product]], and $cf$
abbreviates $\underline c\odot_X f$ for the constant function $\underline c$.
The magnitude function is $|f|=\max(f,-f)$ as in
[[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]]. Then:

1. $cf$ is measurable for every real scalar $c$;
2. $\max(f,g)$, $\min(f,g)$, $|f|$, $f^+$, and $f^-$ are measurable;
3. if the partial pointwise sum $f+g$ is defined at every point, then it is measurable;
4. the pointwise product $fg:=f\odot_X g$ is measurable.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$, $(Y,\mathcal{B})$, and $(Z,\mathcal{C})$ be measurable
spaces. If $f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Y,\mathcal{B})$ is measurable and
$g : (Y,\mathcal{B}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable, then
$g \circ f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable.

In particular, if $f$ is measurable and $g$ is a Borel measurable function on
its codomain, then $g \circ f$ is measurable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. If $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ are measurable, then
$$\int(f+g)\,d\mu=\int f\,d\mu+\int g\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: Since $p,q$ are measurable, [F8] makes $\sqrt p,\sqrt q$ measurable and [F7] makes their difference and absolute value measurable. Their unit integrals put both roots in $L^2(\mu)$. The triangle inequality in [F2] gives symmetry, nonnegativity, and the triangle inequality for $h$. If $h(P,Q)=0$, [F5] gives $\sqrt p=\sqrt q$ almost everywhere, hence $p=q$ almost everywhere and $P=Q$. Conversely, put $g=p-q\in L^1(\mu)$ by [F6]. If $P=Q$, then for every measurable $A$, $\int g\mathbf1_A\,d\mu=\int p\mathbf1_A\,d\mu-\int q\mathbf1_A\,d\mu=P(A)-Q(A)=0$ by [F6]. For each integer $m\ge1$, the set $E_m:=\{g\ge1/m\}$ is measurable by [F8]. Define $u_m:=g\mathbf1_{E_m}$; it is nonnegative and measurable by [F7], and linearity gives $\int u_m\,d\mu=0$. By [F5], $u_m=0$ almost everywhere; since $u_m\ge1/m$ on $E_m$, $\mu(E_m)=0$. Applying the same argument to $(q-p)\mathbf1_{\{q-p\ge1/m\}}$ shows $\mu(\{g\le-1/m\})=0$. Since $\{g\ne0\}$ is the countable union of these null sets, $p=q$ almost everywhere and $h(P,Q)=0$. Thus $h$ is a metric on these laws.

Put $g:=p-q$ and $A:=\{x:g(x)\ge0\}$, which is measurable by [F7, F8]. Since $\int g\,d\mu=0$, the positive and negative parts have equal integral, so $\int_Ag\,d\mu=\frac12\int|g|\,d\mu$. For every measurable $B$, positivity of $g$ on $A$ and nonpositivity on $A^c$, together with monotonicity [F9], give $\int_{A^c}g\le\int_Bg\le\int_Ag$; equality in the absolute supremum is attained at $A$ (or $A^c$). Thus [F4] gives $\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\rm TV}=\frac12d_1(P,Q)$.

The functions in the pointwise inequality are measurable by [F7, F8]. If $p\ge q$, then $(\sqrt p-\sqrt q)^2\le p-q$, because $0\le(\sqrt p-\sqrt q)/(\sqrt p+\sqrt q)\le1$ when the denominator is positive; the case $q\ge p$ is symmetric, and when both vanish the inequality is zero on both sides. Monotonicity [F9] and [F1] give $h(P,Q)^2\le d_1(P,Q)$.

By [F7, F8], the displayed products and sums of square roots are measurable. Factor $|p-q|=|\sqrt p-\sqrt q|(\sqrt p+\sqrt q)$. By [F3], $d_1(P,Q)\le h(P,Q)\lVert\sqrt p+\sqrt q\rVert_2$. Also $\lVert\sqrt p+\sqrt q\rVert_2^2=2+2\int\sqrt{pq}\,d\mu\le4$, again by [F3] and the unit $L^2$ norms. Hence $d_1(P,Q)\le2h(P,Q)$, and step 1.2 gives $\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\rm TV}\le h(P,Q)$.
