citations.quote:
Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). It is
**dominated** by a supplied positive measure $\mu$ on
$(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ when $\mu$ is sigma-finite
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]) and
$P_\theta\ll\mu$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$
([[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]).
The dominating measure is part of the specified setup. This condition adds no
measurable structure on $\Theta$ and no measurability of
$\theta\mapsto P_\theta$.

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be dominated by the fixed sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$. For each
$\theta$, the Radon–Nikodym theorem gives the almost-everywhere class
$dP_\theta/d\mu$; a sigma-finite exhaustion for $\mu$ is also finite for the
probability measure $P_\theta$. Under AC, select simultaneously a
finite-valued measurable nonnegative representative $p_\theta$ from each
class. The nonnegative version exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].

For fixed observed $x\in\mathcal X$, the function
$$L_x:\Theta\to[0,+\infty),\qquad L_x(\theta):=p_\theta(x),$$
is the **likelihood at $x$**. This is a function on the parameter labels, not
a probability distribution on $\Theta$. No sigma-algebra on $\Theta$ or
measurability of $L_x$ is implied. Each density is determined only
$\mu$-almost everywhere; there is no canonical pointwise version and, for
arbitrary uncountable $\Theta$, no common exceptional null set is asserted.

Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
$(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **total variation
distance** is

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}\bigl|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\bigr| .$$

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in
$[-1,1]$, because both measures have total mass one; hence the set being
maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.
The empty event and the whole space give the values $0$ and
$|\mu(E)-\nu(E)|=0$, so the distance is zero when $\mu=\nu$, and it is symmetric
in $\mu$ and $\nu$. This convention carries no factor $1/2$ in the supremum;
it is therefore not the total variation norm of the signed measure $\mu-\nu$,
which is twice the quantity above when that signed measure is considered on a
measurable space where the decomposition is attained. On a countable state
space with its power-set sigma-algebra the supremum equals the half-$\ell^1$
sum $\tfrac12\sum_{x\in E}|\mu(\{x\})-\nu(\{x\})|$; that identity is proved in
[[lem-total-variation-half-l1-formula-on-a-countable-space]], not assumed here.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$, $m\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $\Sigma$ be a real symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then its law has Lebesgue density
$$f_{m,\Sigma}(x)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\det(\Sigma)^{-1/2} \exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(x-m)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-m)\right), \qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$

For each positive integer $n$, let $(\Omega_n,\mathcal A_n,P_n)$ be a probability space and let $X_n:\Omega_n\to\mathbb R^d$ be measurable into the Borel sigma-algebra generated by the Euclidean open sets, where $d\ge1$ is fixed and $\mathbb R^d$ has the Euclidean norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]], [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]], [[def-probability-measure]]). The spaces and measures may depend on $n$; no common probability space is required.

Write $X_n=o_P(1)$ if for every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$P_n(\|X_n\|_2>\varepsilon)\longrightarrow0.$$
Write $X_n=O_P(1)$, or say that $(X_n)$ is bounded in probability, if for every $\eta>0$ there is $M>0$ such that
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty}P_n(\|X_n\|_2>M)\le\eta.$$
For real-valued variables on one common probability space, $o_P(1)$ is convergence in probability to zero as defined in [[def-convergence-in-probability]].

The norms and tail probabilities are part of the definition. Independence is not implicit in either notation.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Let $Q_n$ be the posterior law of $H_n$. The contraction premise implies that $(Q_n)$ is tight in probability: for every $\eta,\varepsilon>0$ there is a finite $R$ such that $\limsup_nP_{0,n}\{Q_n(\|h\|_2>R)>\eta\}<\varepsilon$. Otherwise there would be $\eta,\varepsilon>0$ and increasing radii $R_k\to\infty$ with indices $n_k$ for which $P_{0,n_k}\{Q_{n_k}(\|h\|_2>R_k)>\eta\}>\varepsilon$. Define $M_n=R_k$ for $n_k\le n<n_{k+1}$, with any positive initial values. Then $M_n\to\infty$ and the assumed contraction fails along $n_k$, a contradiction.

The supplied common-dominator density setup [F1, F2] makes the posterior likelihood ratio well-defined on the stated $P_{0,n}$-full set. Fix $R>0$ and put $K_R=\{h:\|h\|_2\le R\}$. Since $\theta^*$ is interior and $\delta_n\to0$, $\theta^*+\delta_nK_R\subset\Theta$ for all sufficiently large $n$. Relative to Lebesgue measure on $K_R$, the unnormalized posterior density for $H_n$ is proportional to $q_n(h)=\exp(\ell_n(\theta^*+\delta_nh))\pi(\theta^*+\delta_nh)$; the Jacobian $\delta_n^d$ cancels on conditioning on $K_R$. Set $g_n(h)=\exp(h^T\Delta_n-\tfrac12h^TVh)$. By compact-uniform LAN and continuity of $\pi$ at $\theta^*$, $q_n(h)/g_n(h)=\pi(\theta^*)(1+o_{P_{0,n}}(1))$ uniformly on $K_R$. Completing the square gives $g_n$ proportional to the density in [F5] with mean $V^{-1}\Delta_n$ and covariance $V^{-1}$. If $w_n=q_n/g_n$ and $\bar w_n=\int_{K_R}w_n\,dG_n^{K_R}$, where $G_n^{K_R}$ is the Gaussian law conditioned on $K_R$, the two conditional densities have ratio $w_n/\bar w_n$. Uniform convergence $w_n/\pi(\theta^*)\to1$ implies $\bar w_n/\pi(\theta^*)\to1$, so $\sup_{K_R}|w_n/\bar w_n-1|=o_{P_{0,n}}(1)$ and their total-variation distance tends to zero.

By [F6] and the assumed $\Delta_n=O_{P_{0,n}}(1)$, the Gaussian means $V^{-1}\Delta_n$ are bounded in probability. For any fixed bound on the mean, its Gaussian probability outside $K_R$ is at most the centered $N_d(0,V^{-1})$ probability outside a ball whose radius tends to infinity with $R$. For integers $m\ge1$, the sets $F_m=\{z:\|z\|_2>m\}$ decrease to the empty set, and $F_m=\bigsqcup_{k\ge m}(F_k\setminus F_{k+1})$. Countable additivity makes $P(F_m)$ the tail of a convergent nonnegative series, so it tends to zero. Hence the Gaussian tails are tight in probability as $R\to\infty$.

For any two probability measures $P,Q$ and measurable $K$, their restrictions conditioned on $K$ satisfy $\|P-Q\|_{\rm TV}\le \|P(\cdot\mid K)-Q(\cdot\mid K)\|_{\rm TV}+2P(K^c)+2Q(K^c)$ whenever both conditioning probabilities are positive. Indeed, for any event $A$, split it into $A\cap K$ and $A\cap K^c$, compare the two conditional masses on $K$, and use $|P(K)-Q(K)|\le P(K^c)+Q(K^c)$. Choose $R$ so the posterior tail from step 1.1 and Gaussian tail from step 1.3 are arbitrarily small in probability; the conditional distance tends to zero for this fixed $R$ by step 1.2. Letting the tail tolerance decrease to zero proves the asserted full total-variation convergence under [F3].

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be a parametric
model, let $\Theta$ be open in $\mathbb R^d$, and let a supplied sigma-finite
measure $\mu$ dominate every $P_\theta$
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]], [[def-dominated-statistical-experiment]]).
Supply as part of the setup a family of nonnegative finite-valued measurable
functions $p_\theta:\mathcal X\to[0,\infty)$ satisfying
$P_\theta(A)=\int_Ap_\theta\,d\mu$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$
([[def-measure-with-density]]). Thus each $p_\theta$ integrates to one.
The density family is supplied, rather than selected from domination alone;
no choice principle, joint measurability in $(\theta,x)$, or common
exceptional null set is asserted. A supplied extended-valued probability
density can be made finite-valued by setting it to zero on its measurable
infinite-value set, which has measure zero because its integral is one.
The QMD condition is unchanged by replacing any supplied density by an
almost-everywhere equal version: for each fixed $h$, the norm in the
condition below changes only on the union of two null sets.
At an interior point $\theta_0$, the model is
**quadratic-mean differentiable (QMD)** with score $s_{\theta_0}$ if
$s_{\theta_0}:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^d$ is measurable,
$\mathbb E_{\theta_0}\|s_{\theta_0}(X)\|^2<\infty$, and
$$
\int\left(\sqrt{p_{\theta_0+h}}-\sqrt{p_{\theta_0}}- \tfrac12 h^Ts_{\theta_0}\sqrt{p_{\theta_0}}\right)^2d\mu=o(\|h\|^2)
$$
as $h\to0$ with $\theta_0+h\in\Theta$. Values of the score on
$\{p_{\theta_0}=0\}$ do not affect this condition. The Fisher information
associated with this QMD score is
$I_{\theta_0}=\mathbb E_{\theta_0}[s_{\theta_0}s_{\theta_0}^T]$; it may be
singular. QMD is an $L^2(\mu)$ condition and does not assert pointwise
differentiability of $p_\theta$ or local mutual absolute continuity of
$P_\theta$ and $P_{\theta_0}$.

Assume AC and the hypotheses of [[def-qmd-path]]. Write $p_0=p_{\theta_0}$,
$p_u=p_{\theta_0+u}$, and $P_0=P_{\theta_0}$. Let
$$\alpha(u):=P_{\theta_0+u}(p_0=0),\qquad \beta(u):=P_0(p_u=0).$$
Then $\alpha(u)=o(\|u\|_2^2)$ and $\beta(u)=o(\|u\|_2^2)$ as $u\to0$.

Assume AC and [[def-qmd-path]] at $\theta_0$ with score $s$ and information $I$.
Let $h_n\to h$ in $\mathbb R^d$, put $u_n=h_n/\sqrt n$, and write
$P_0=P_{\theta_0}$ and $P_{u_n}=P_{\theta_0+u_n}$. On
$S=\{p_{\theta_0}>0\}$ define, for all sufficiently large $n$,
$$q_n(x)=\frac{\mathbf1_S(x)p_{\theta_0+u_n}(x)} {(1-\alpha_n)p_{\theta_0}(x)},\qquad \alpha_n=P_{u_n}(S^c).$$
Then $q_n$ is a probability density relative to $P_0$. For IID
$X_1,\ldots,X_n\sim P_0$, let $L_n=\prod_{i=1}^nq_n(X_i)$ and
$\Delta_n=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^ns(X_i)$. Under $P_0^{\otimes n}$,
$$\log L_n=h_n^T\Delta_n-\tfrac12h^TIh+o_P(1),\qquad P_0^{\otimes n}(L_n=0)\to0.$$
Moreover, if $\bar P_n=q_nP_0$ is the normalized absolutely continuous
component of $P_{u_n}$ relative to $P_0$, then
$$\|P_{u_n}^{\otimes n}-\bar P_n^{\otimes n}\|_{\rm TV}\to0.$$
No full likelihood ratio for $P_{u_n}^{\otimes n}$ is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\{P_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\subseteq
\mathbb R^d\}$ be dominated by a common sigma-finite measure, with $\Theta$
open, and suppose the model is QMD at an interior $\theta_0$ with score $s$
and information $I=E_{\theta_0}[ss^T]$. Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be IID
$P_{\theta_0}$, and for each fixed local sequence $h_n\to h$ set
$u_n=h_n/\sqrt n$. Then the local product laws
$P_{\theta_0+u_n}^{\otimes n}$ admit mean-one likelihood-ratio proxies
$L_n$ relative to $P_{\theta_0}^{\otimes n}$ such that
$$\left\|P_{\theta_0+u_n}^{\otimes n}-L_nP_{\theta_0}^{\otimes n}\right\|_{\rm TV} \to0,$$
and under $P_{\theta_0}^{\otimes n}$,
$$\log L_n=h_n^T\Delta_n-\tfrac12h^TIh+o_P(1),\qquad \Delta_n=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^ns(X_i)\Rightarrow N_d(0,I).$$
Thus the IID QMD experiment is LAN in the proxy sense of
[[def-lan-experiment]]. This assertion does not claim that the full local
product law has a Radon–Nikodym derivative relative to the base law.

Assume AC. For each $n$, let $X^{(n)}$ have law $P_{0,n}$ on a measurable
space, and let $\Theta\subset\mathbb R^d$ be open, $d\ge1$. Suppose a
supplied sigma-finite measure $\mu_n$ dominates $P_{0,n}$ and the model laws
$P_{n,\theta}$, and suppose jointly measurable finite-valued densities
$p_{0,n}$ and $p_{n,\theta}$ are supplied. Fix an interior point
$\theta^*\in\Theta$ with $p_{n,\theta^*}(X^{(n)})>0$
$P_{0,n}$-almost surely. Let the prior be a proper Lebesgue density $\pi$
continuous and strictly positive on a neighbourhood of $\theta^*$, and assume
the displayed likelihood integral is finite and positive almost surely so it
defines the posterior
$$\Pi_n(A\mid X^{(n)})=\frac{\int_Ap_{n,\theta}(X^{(n)})\pi(\theta)\,d\theta}{\int_\Theta p_{n,\theta}(X^{(n)})\pi(\theta)\,d\theta}.$$
For $\delta_n>0$ with $\delta_n\to0$, write
$$\ell_n(\theta)=\log\frac{p_{n,\theta}(X^{(n)})}{p_{n,\theta^*}(X^{(n)})}.$$
Assume $V$ is a fixed symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix,
$\Delta_n=O_{P_{0,n}}(1)$, and for every compact $K\subset\mathbb R^d$,
$$\sup_{h\in K}\left|\ell_n(\theta^*+\delta_nh)-h^T\Delta_n+\tfrac12h^TVh\right|=o_{P_{0,n}}(1).$$
Also assume that for every deterministic sequence $M_n\to\infty$,
$$\Pi_n\!\left(\|\theta-\theta^*\|_2>\delta_nM_n\mid X^{(n)}\right)=o_{P_{0,n}}(1).$$
Then the posterior law of $H_n=\delta_n^{-1}(\theta-\theta^*)$ satisfies
$$\left\|\Pi_n(H_n\in\cdot\mid X^{(n)})-N_d(V^{-1}\Delta_n,V^{-1})\right\|_{\rm TV}=o_{P_{0,n}}(1),$$
where $\|P-Q\|_{\rm TV}=\sup_A|P(A)-Q(A)|$ over measurable sets. The
LAN condition concerns likelihood-density ratios on the $P_{0,n}$-full set
where the denominator is positive; it does not assert a Radon–Nikodym
derivative for the entire local model law.

derivations.claim: By [A1, F1, F2], $\alpha(u)=o(\|u\|_2^2)$ and $\beta(u)=o(\|u\|_2^2)$. For fixed compact $H$ with $\|h\|_2\le R$, this little-$o$ relation is uniform over $\|u\|_2\le R/\sqrt n$: $n\sup_{h\in H}\alpha(h/\sqrt n)\to0$ and $n\sup_{h\in H}\beta(h/\sqrt n)\to0$.

Under $P_0$, each observation lies in $S$ almost surely. On $S$, the actual density ratio is $p_{\theta^*+u}/p_0=(1-\alpha(u))q_u$. For $\alpha\le1/2$, $|\log(1-\alpha)|\le2\alpha$, so step 1.1 gives $\sup_{h\in H}\left|n\log(1-\alpha(h/\sqrt n))\right|\le2n\sup_{h\in H}\alpha(h/\sqrt n)\longrightarrow0.$ Thus the actual posterior likelihood ratios have the same compact-uniform LAN expansion as the normalized proxy. The zero-overlap bound in step 1.1 is recorded separately; compact-uniform positivity is supplied by the proxy-LAN hypothesis, not inferred from pointwise QMD.

For each local $u$, write $P_{\theta^*+u}=(1-\alpha(u))\bar P_u+\alpha(u)S_u$, where $\bar P_u=q_uP_0$ is supported on $S$ and $S_u$ is the normalized restriction to $S^c$ when $\alpha(u)>0$. In the product mixture, the all-$\bar P_u$ component has weight $(1-\alpha(u))^n$ and every other component is supported outside $S^n$. Hence $\|P_{\theta^*+u}^{\otimes n}-\bar P_u^{\otimes n}\|_{\rm TV}=1-(1-\alpha(u))^n\le n\alpha(u).$ Step 1.1 makes this $o(1)$ uniformly for $h\in H$. This comparison is between probability laws and does not identify a full Radon–Nikodym derivative for $P_{\theta^*+u}^{\otimes n}$.

Step 2.1 supplies the compact-uniform LAN premise for the actual posterior likelihood ratios; the prior, evidence, and posterior-rate hypotheses are those of [F5]. For each $n$, the iid product experiment is dominated by the finite product of the common sigma-finite dominator, with product densities formed from the supplied jointly measurable versions; iterated integration on rectangles and uniqueness of product measures identify these as the densities of the iid laws. Thus the actual ratios in step 2.1 are the likelihood ratios required by [F5]. Applying [F5] with $\delta_n=n^{-1/2}$ proves the BvM limit. The fixed-sequence assertion [F4] alone would not justify the compact supremum used here.

citations.quote: Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

For each positive integer $n$, let $(\Omega_n,\mathcal A_n,P_n)$ be a probability space and let $X_n:\Omega_n\to\mathbb R^d$ be measurable into the Borel sigma-algebra generated by the Euclidean open sets, where $d\ge1$ is fixed and $\mathbb R^d$ has the Euclidean norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]], [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]], [[def-probability-measure]]). The spaces and measures may depend on $n$; no common probability space is required.

Write $X_n=o_P(1)$ if for every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$P_n(\|X_n\|_2>\varepsilon)\longrightarrow0.$$
Write $X_n=O_P(1)$, or say that $(X_n)$ is bounded in probability, if for every $\eta>0$ there is $M>0$ such that
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty}P_n(\|X_n\|_2>M)\le\eta.$$
For real-valued variables on one common probability space, $o_P(1)$ is convergence in probability to zero as defined in [[def-convergence-in-probability]].

Let $d\ge1$ and $n\ge1$, let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be IID with law $P$, and let
$f_t:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable for $t$ in a neighbourhood of
$0\in\mathbb R^d$. Assume $f_0=0$ and that on one $P$-full set
$$|f_t(x)-f_s(x)|\le M(x)\|t-s\|_2$$
for all such $s,t$, where $M\ge0$ is measurable and $P M^2<\infty$. For
$P_nf=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nf(X_i)$, both displayed sample-path suprema have measurable versions; expectations
below are taken using these versions. There is a finite constant $C_d$, depending only on $d$, such that for every
radius $r$ whose closed ball is in the parameter neighbourhood,
$$E\sup_{\|t\|_2\le r}|\sqrt n(P_n-P)f_t|\le C_d r(PM^2)^{1/2}.$$
Moreover, for $0<\varepsilon\le r$,
$$E\sup_{\substack{\|s\|_2,\|t\|_2\le r\\\|t-s\|_2\le\varepsilon}}|\sqrt n(P_n-P)(f_t-f_s)|\le C_d\varepsilon\sqrt{\log(e r/\varepsilon)}(PM^2)^{1/2}.$$

derivations.claim: Define the log-ratio class to be zero off the common measurable full set of the log-Lipschitz bound, as in [F3]; this changes no integral or almost-sure sample path and makes its suprema measurable. On that full set put $f_t=\log(p_{\theta^*+t}/p_{\theta^*})$ and $r_t=f_t-t^Ts$. Along every coordinate direction $e_j$, $f_{ae_j}/a\to s_j$ in $P_0$-probability as $a\to0$, while the envelope gives $|f_{ae_j}/a|\le M$. Dominated convergence along almost-surely convergent subsequences therefore gives $E_0s_j=\lim_{a\to0}E_0f_{ae_j}/a=0$, since the contrast expansion makes the last numerator $O(a^2)$. The same subsequence argument applied to the directional difference quotients and the common envelope gives $|s_j|\le M$ almost surely for every coordinate, hence $\|s\|_2\le\sqrt d M$ and $E_0\|s\|_2^2<\infty$.

The contrast expansion is uniform after the local substitution: for fixed $R$, $\sup_{\|h\|_2\le R}\left|nE_0f_{h/\sqrt n}+\tfrac12h^TVh\right|\longrightarrow0,$ because the remainder divided by $\|t\|_2^2$ tends to zero uniformly over $0<\|t\|_2\le R/\sqrt n$.

Differentiability in probability says $r_t/\|t\|_2\to0$ in $P_0$-probability. The bound $|r_t|/\|t\|_2\le M+\|s\|_2\le(1+\sqrt d)M$ and $E_0M^2<\infty$ imply $E_0r_t^2=o(\|t\|_2^2)$ by dominated convergence along every sequence $t\to0$. Also $|r_t-r_u|\le L\|t-u\|_2$ on the common full set, where $L=(1+\sqrt d)M$. Fix $R>0$ and $0<\varepsilon\le R$, and choose a finite $\varepsilon$-net $H_\varepsilon$ of the radius-$R$ ball. For each fixed $h\in H_\varepsilon$, independence gives $E_0\left|n(P_n-P_0)r_{h/\sqrt n}\right|^2=n\,\operatorname{Var}_0(r_{h/\sqrt n})\le nE_0r_{h/\sqrt n}^2\longrightarrow0.$ Because the net is finite, the maximum of these centered sums tends to zero in probability. For any $h$ in the ball choose $h_\varepsilon\in H_\varepsilon$ with $\|h-h_\varepsilon\|_2\le\varepsilon$. The modulus bound [F3], applied to $r_t$ with envelope $L$ on radius $R/\sqrt n$ and distance $\varepsilon/\sqrt n$, gives $E_0\sup_{\substack{\|h\|_2,\|h'\|_2\le R\\\|h-h'\|_2\le\varepsilon}}\left|n(P_n-P_0)(r_{h/\sqrt n}-r_{h'/\sqrt n})\right|\le C_d\|L\|_{L^2(P_0)}\varepsilon\sqrt{\log(eR/\varepsilon)}.$ For fixed $\varepsilon$, the finite-net maximum vanishes as $n\to\infty$; Markov's inequality bounds the remaining modulus probability by a constant times $\varepsilon\sqrt{\log(eR/\varepsilon)}$, which tends to zero as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. Therefore $\sup_{\|h\|_2\le R}\left|n(P_n-P_0)r_{h/\sqrt n}\right|=o_{P_0}(1).$

For $\|h\|_2\le R$, decompose $\sum_{i=1}^nf_{h/\sqrt n}(X_i)=nE_0f_{h/\sqrt n}+h^TS_n+n(P_n-P_0)r_{h/\sqrt n},$ where $E_0s=0$ from step 1.1. Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be IID from $P_0$ on a measurable space, and let
$\Theta\subset\mathbb R^d$ be open, $d\ge1$. Suppose a sigma-finite measure
$\mu$ and jointly measurable finite-valued densities $p_0,p_\theta$ are
supplied, with $P_0(dx)=p_0(x)\mu(dx)$, $P_\theta(dx)=p_\theta(x)\mu(dx)$,
and $p_{\theta^*}>0$ $P_0$-almost surely. Define the directional contrast
$$K(\theta)=E_0\log\frac{p_0(X)}{p_\theta(X)}.$$
Assume $K$ is finite near an interior point $\theta^*$, $\theta^*$ is a
finite minimizer of $K$, and, for $t\to0$,
$$E_0\log\frac{p_{\theta^*}(X)}{p_{\theta^*+t}(X)}=\tfrac12t^TVt+o(\|t\|_2^2)$$
for a fixed symmetric positive-definite matrix $V$. Assume also that a
measurable random vector $s(X)\in\mathbb R^d$ satisfies
$$\frac{\log p_{\theta^*+t}(X)-\log p_{\theta^*}(X)-t^Ts(X)}{\|t\|_2}\longrightarrow0$$
in $P_0$-probability as $t\to0$ through nonzero vectors, and that on a
neighbourhood $U$ of $\theta^*$ there is a common $P_0$-almost-sure bound
$$\left|\log\frac{p_{\theta_1}(X)}{p_{\theta_2}(X)}\right|\le M(X)\|\theta_1-\theta_2\|_2\qquad(\theta_1,\theta_2\in U),$$
where $M\ge0$ and $E_0M^2<\infty$. Then $E_0s=0$ and
$I=E_0[ss^T]$ is finite. With $S_n=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^ns(X_i)$ and
$\Delta_n=V^{-1}S_n$, for every compact $H\subset\mathbb R^d$,
$$\sup_{h\in H}\left|\sum_{i=1}^n\log\frac{p_{\theta^*+h/\sqrt n}(X_i)}{p_{\theta^*}(X_i)}-h^TS_n+\tfrac12h^TVh\right|=o_{P_0}(1).$$
Suprema and convergence in probability use measurable versions obtained by
setting the log-ratio class to zero off its common measurable full set.
In particular $\Delta_n=O_{P_0}(1)$. No equality between $I$ and $V$ is
assumed; under misspecification they generally differ.

Assume AC. For each $n$, let $X^{(n)}$ have law $P_{0,n}$ on a measurable
space, and let $\Theta\subset\mathbb R^d$ be open, $d\ge1$. Suppose a
supplied sigma-finite measure $\mu_n$ dominates $P_{0,n}$ and the model laws
$P_{n,\theta}$, and suppose jointly measurable finite-valued densities
$p_{0,n}$ and $p_{n,\theta}$ are supplied. Fix an interior point
$\theta^*\in\Theta$ with $p_{n,\theta^*}(X^{(n)})>0$
$P_{0,n}$-almost surely. Let the prior be a proper Lebesgue density $\pi$
continuous and strictly positive on a neighbourhood of $\theta^*$, and assume
the displayed likelihood integral is finite and positive almost surely so it
defines the posterior
$$\Pi_n(A\mid X^{(n)})=\frac{\int_Ap_{n,\theta}(X^{(n)})\pi(\theta)\,d\theta}{\int_\Theta p_{n,\theta}(X^{(n)})\pi(\theta)\,d\theta}.$$
For $\delta_n>0$ with $\delta_n\to0$, write
$$\ell_n(\theta)=\log\frac{p_{n,\theta}(X^{(n)})}{p_{n,\theta^*}(X^{(n)})}.$$
Assume $V$ is a fixed symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix,
$\Delta_n=O_{P_{0,n}}(1)$, and for every compact $K\subset\mathbb R^d$,
$$\sup_{h\in K}\left|\ell_n(\theta^*+\delta_nh)-h^T\Delta_n+\tfrac12h^TVh\right|=o_{P_{0,n}}(1).$$
Also assume that for every deterministic sequence $M_n\to\infty$,
$$\Pi_n\!\left(\|\theta-\theta^*\|_2>\delta_nM_n\mid X^{(n)}\right)=o_{P_{0,n}}(1).$$
Then the posterior law of $H_n=\delta_n^{-1}(\theta-\theta^*)$ satisfies
$$\left\|\Pi_n(H_n\in\cdot\mid X^{(n)})-N_d(V^{-1}\Delta_n,V^{-1})\right\|_{\rm TV}=o_{P_{0,n}}(1),$$
where $\|P-Q\|_{\rm TV}=\sup_A|P(A)-Q(A)|$ over measurable sets. The
LAN condition concerns likelihood-density ratios on the $P_{0,n}$-full set
where the denominator is positive; it does not assert a Radon–Nikodym
derivative for the entire local model law.

derivations.claim: By [F1], take $\delta_n=n^{-1/2}$ and use $S_n$ as the central vector $\Delta_n$ in [F2]. The local LAN theorem supplies the required compact-uniform expansion with curvature $V$ and proves $S_n=O_{P_0}(1)$; [F2] therefore centers the Gaussian at $V^{-1}S_n$.

For each $n$, the iid sample experiment is dominated by the finite product $\mu^{\otimes n}$, with densities $p_{0,n}(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\prod_i p_0(x_i)$ and $p_{n,\theta}(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\prod_i p_\theta(x_i)$. Iterated integration gives the product-law formula on measurable rectangles, so uniqueness of product measures identifies these as densities of $P_0^{\otimes n}$ and $P_\theta^{\otimes n}$. Thus the LAN expansion in [F1] is the log-likelihood ratio for this iid experiment. The prior, evidence, interior-point, and parameter-tail hypotheses in the Statement are exactly the remaining hypotheses of [F2]. Applying [F2] gives the claimed total-variation limit.

For each positive integer $n$, let $(\Omega_n,\mathcal A_n,P_n)$ be a probability space and let $X_n:\Omega_n\to\mathbb R^d$ be measurable into the Borel sigma-algebra generated by the Euclidean open sets, where $d\ge1$ is fixed and $\mathbb R^d$ has the Euclidean norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]], [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]], [[def-probability-measure]]). The spaces and measures may depend on $n$; no common probability space is required.

Write $X_n=o_P(1)$ if for every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$P_n(\|X_n\|_2>\varepsilon)\longrightarrow0.$$
Write $X_n=O_P(1)$, or say that $(X_n)$ is bounded in probability, if for every $\eta>0$ there is $M>0$ such that
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty}P_n(\|X_n\|_2>M)\le\eta.$$
For real-valued variables on one common probability space, $o_P(1)$ is convergence in probability to zero as defined in [[def-convergence-in-probability]].

The norms and tail probabilities are part of the definition. Independence is not implicit in either notation.

Let $d\ge1$ and $n\ge1$, let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be IID with law $P$, and let
$f_t:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable for $t$ in a neighbourhood of
$0\in\mathbb R^d$. Assume $f_0=0$ and that on one $P$-full set
$$|f_t(x)-f_s(x)|\le M(x)\|t-s\|_2$$
for all such $s,t$, where $M\ge0$ is measurable and $P M^2<\infty$. For
$P_nf=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nf(X_i)$, both displayed sample-path suprema have measurable versions; expectations
below are taken using these versions. There is a finite constant $C_d$, depending only on $d$, such that for every
radius $r$ whose closed ball is in the parameter neighbourhood,
$$E\sup_{\|t\|_2\le r}|\sqrt n(P_n-P)f_t|\le C_d r(PM^2)^{1/2}.$$
Moreover, for $0<\varepsilon\le r$,
$$E\sup_{\substack{\|s\|_2,\|t\|_2\le r\\\|t-s\|_2\le\varepsilon}}|\sqrt n(P_n-P)(f_t-f_s)|\le C_d\varepsilon\sqrt{\log(e r/\varepsilon)}(PM^2)^{1/2}.$$

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be a finite integer. Let $(X_k)_{k\ge1}$ be iid $\mathbb R^d$-valued random vectors with $\mathbb E\|X_1\|^2<\infty$, mean m and covariance Sigma. Then $$n^{-1/2}\sum_{k=1}^n(X_k-m)\Rightarrow N_d(0,\Sigma).$$ The covariance may be singular.

Let all random vectors with index $n$ be defined on a common probability space for that $n$; the spaces may vary with $n$. In any fixed finite-dimensional Euclidean space, the following rules hold:

1. If $U_n=o_P(1)$ and $V_n=o_P(1)$, then $U_n+V_n=o_P(1)$. If $U_n=O_P(1)$ and $V_n=O_P(1)$, then $U_n+V_n=O_P(1)$.
2. For positive integers $p,q,r$, let $B:\mathbb R^p\times\mathbb R^q\to\mathbb R^r$ be a fixed map for which there is a constant $C\ge0$ with $\|B(u,v)\|_2\le C\|u\|_2\|v\|_2$ for all $u,v$. Assume in each application that $B(U_n,V_n)$ is a random vector on the same probability space as $U_n,V_n$, for every $n$. If $U_n=o_P(1)$ and $V_n=O_P(1)$, or conversely, then $B(U_n,V_n)=o_P(1)$. If both are $O_P(1)$, then $B(U_n,V_n)=O_P(1)$.
3. If $X_n\Rightarrow X$ in $\mathbb R^d$, then $X_n=O_P(1)$.

The last conclusion is finite-dimensional boundedness in probability. No independence or Axiom of Choice is assumed.

Let $d,k,m\ge1$ be fixed. For each $n$, let $X_n\in\mathbb R^d$ and $Y_n\in\mathbb R^k$ be random vectors on one probability space; the probability space may vary with $n$. Let $X\in\mathbb R^d$ be a random vector on any probability space, and let $c\in\mathbb R^k$ be constant. If $X_n\Rightarrow X$ and $Y_n-c=o_P(1)$, then
$$ (X_n,Y_n)\Rightarrow(X,c). $$
Consequently, for every continuous $h:\mathbb R^{d+k}\to\mathbb R^m$, $h(X_n,Y_n)\Rightarrow h(X,c)$. No independence between $X_n$ and $Y_n$ is required.

Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
$(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **total variation
distance** is

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}\bigl|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\bigr| .$$

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in
$[-1,1]$, because both measures have total mass one; hence the set being
maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.
The empty event and the whole space give the values $0$ and
$|\mu(E)-\nu(E)|=0$, so the distance is zero when $\mu=\nu$, and it is symmetric
in $\mu$ and $\nu$. This convention carries no factor $1/2$ in the supremum;
it is therefore not the total variation norm of the signed measure $\mu-\nu$,
which is twice the quantity above when that signed measure is considered on a
measurable space where the decomposition is attained. On a countable state
space with its power-set sigma-algebra the supremum equals the half-$\ell^1$
sum $\tfrac12\sum_{x\in E}|\mu(\{x\})-\nu(\{x\})|$; that identity is proved in
[[lem-total-variation-half-l1-formula-on-a-countable-space]], not assumed here.

Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Write $f_t=\log(p_{\theta^*+t}/p_{\theta^*})$. Positive definiteness of $V$ and the contrast expansion in [F1] give constants $c,\rho>0$ with $E_0f_t\le-c\|t\|_2^2$ for $\|t\|_2\le\rho$. Use the measurable versions from [F3], obtained by zero extension off the common log-Lipschitz full set. The log-Lipschitz envelope and [F3] give $E_0\sup_{\|t\|\le r}|G_nf_t|\le C r$ for $r\le\rho$, where $G_n=\sqrt n(P_n-P_0)$ and $C=C_d(E_0M^2)^{1/2}$.

Let $\eta_n=n(\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}P_n\log p_\theta-P_n\log p_{\widehat\theta_n})$. The assumption gives $\eta_n=o_{P_0}(1)$ by [F2]. For fixed $A\ge1$, set $r_j=2^jA/\sqrt n$ and consider shells $r_j\le\|\widehat\theta_n-\theta^*\|_2\le2r_j$ with $2r_j\le\rho$. On such a shell, approximate maximization implies $nP_nf_{\widehat\theta_n-\theta^*}\ge-\eta_n$, while step 1.1 bounds the mean term above by $-cnr_j^2$. On $\{\eta_n\le cA^2/2\}$ this forces $\sup_{\|t\|\le2r_j}|G_nf_t|\ge(c/2)\sqrt n r_j^2$. For nonnegative $Z$ and $a>0$, $a\mathbf1_{\{Z\ge a\}}\le Z$ implies $P_0(Z\ge a)\le E_0Z/a$; apply this to the supremum and threshold above, then step 1.1 gives $C'/(\sqrt n r_j)=C'/(2^jA)$. Summing over the shells, using consistency to remove $\|\widehat\theta_n-\theta^*\|>\rho/4$, and then taking $A\to\infty$ proves $\sqrt n(\widehat\theta_n-\theta^*)=O_{P_0}(1)$.

Set $\widehat h_n=\sqrt n(\widehat\theta_n-\theta^*)$ and $h_n^*=V^{-1}S_n$. By [F4] the score sums converge in distribution; [F5] makes $S_n$ and $h_n^*$ bounded in probability. Step 2.1 gives the same for $\widehat h_n$. Since $\theta^*$ is interior, $\theta^*+h_n^*/\sqrt n\in\Theta$ with probability tending to one.

On any fixed ball containing $\widehat h_n$ and $h_n^*$ with probability arbitrarily close to one, [F1] expands both log likelihoods uniformly. Approximate maximization then gives $Q_n(\widehat h_n)\ge Q_n(h_n^*)-o_{P_0}(1),\qquad Q_n(h)=h^TS_n-\tfrac12h^TVh.$ Completing the square gives $Q_n(h_n^*)-Q_n(\widehat h_n)=\tfrac12(\widehat h_n-h_n^*)^TV(\widehat h_n-h_n^*)\ge\tfrac12\lambda_{\min}(V)\|\widehat h_n-h_n^*\|_2^2$. Hence $\widehat h_n-h_n^*=o_{P_0}(1)$.

By [F1], $V^{-1}s(X_i)$ is centered, iid, and has covariance $V^{-1}IV^{-1}$. Applying the multivariate CLT [F4] to these vectors gives $h_n^*=V^{-1}S_n\Rightarrow N_d(0,V^{-1}IV^{-1})$, including when this covariance is singular. Then [F6] and step 4.1 give $\widehat h_n\Rightarrow N_d(0,V^{-1}IV^{-1})$. This is the sandwich sampling covariance; it need not equal the posterior covariance $V^{-1}$.

For each $n$, the iid sample experiment is dominated by the finite product $\mu^{\otimes n}$, with densities $p_{0,n}(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\prod_i p_0(x_i)$ and $p_{n,\theta}(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\prod_i p_\theta(x_i)$. Iterated integration gives the product-law formula on measurable rectangles, so uniqueness of product measures identifies these as densities of $P_0^{\otimes n}$ and $P_\theta^{\otimes n}$. Their likelihood ratio is the sum in the LAN conclusion of [F1]. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.
Assume AC. The function $\phi(x)=e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}$ is positive and Borel measurable on $\mathbb R$, with Lebesgue integral one.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
$(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **total variation
distance** is

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}\bigl|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\bigr| .$$

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in
$[-1,1]$, because both measures have total mass one; hence the set being
maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.
The empty event and the whole space give the values $0$ and
$|\mu(E)-\nu(E)|=0$, so the distance is zero when $\mu=\nu$, and it is symmetric
in $\mu$ and $\nu$. This convention carries no factor $1/2$ in the supremum;
it is therefore not the total variation norm of the signed measure $\mu-\nu$,
which is twice the quantity above when that signed measure is considered on a
measurable space where the decomposition is attained. On a countable state
space with its power-set sigma-algebra the supremum equals the half-$\ell^1$
sum $\tfrac12\sum_{x\in E}|\mu(\{x\})-\nu(\{x\})|$; that identity is proved in
[[lem-total-variation-half-l1-formula-on-a-countable-space]], not assumed here.

citations.quote: A topological space is **Polish** when it is separable ([[def-separable-space]]) and completely metrizable: its topology is induced by some complete metric ([[lem-complete-remetrisation]]). No particular compatible complete metric or countable dense subset is part of the structure.

A topological space $X$ is **separable** if some at most countable subset $D\subseteq X$ is dense in $X$ ([[def-dense-top]], [[def-countable]]). Equivalently, every nonempty open subset of $X$ meets $D$.

1. $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ with the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]) is a complete metric space
   ([[def-complete-metric-space]]).
2. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on
   $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ is complete.

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited and is not decoration.**
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] defines $\mathbb{R}^n$ and its three metrics only for
$n \ge 1$, because at $n = 0$ the metric $d_\infty$ would be a maximum over the
empty index set. Every statement about $\mathbb{R}^n$ in this library carries the
hypothesis, and this one does too.

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

**No choice principle is used.** The one place where a reader expects a choice,
"pick a representative $a/b$ of each rational", is exactly where
[[lem-rat-positive-denominator]] applies: every rational *has* a representative
with positive denominator, so the map $(a,b) \mapsto [(a,b)]$ defined on
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is already **surjective** onto $\mathbb{Q}$,
and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).

The map $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[def-real-numbers]]) is an embedding of ordered
fields. Every real is approximated by rationals: for $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and
rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $q \in \mathbb{Q}$ with
$|x - \hat q| < \hat\varepsilon$. Consequently, strictly between any two
reals lies a rational.

A measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$ is **standard Borel** if there are a Polish space $P$ and a bijection $h:E\to P$ such that $A\in\mathcal E$ exactly when $h[A]$ is Borel in $P$. Thus the measurable structure is part of the datum; no particular compatible Polish topology on $E$ is selected.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be non-negative. Then there exists a unique non-negative operator
$R:V\to V$ such that

$$R^2=T.$$

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then $$\Phi_X(t):=\mathbb E e^{it\cdot X}=\exp(it\cdot m-t^T\Sigma t/2)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R^d).$$ This transform uniquely determines the law, including singular Sigma.

Let $(E_i,\mathcal E_i)_{i\in I}$ be measurable spaces. A family
$(\mu_F)_{F\Subset I}$, indexed by all finite subsets of $I$, is a **consistent family of finite-dimensional
distributions** when each $\mu_F$ is a probability measure on
$\bigotimes_{i\in F}\mathcal E_i$, with the finite unordered product
sigma-algebra of [[def-coordinate-maps-and-cylinder-sigma-algebra]], and for
every pair of finite sets $F\subseteq G\subseteq I$ the pushforward of
$\mu_G$ under the restriction $p_{G,F}(x)=x|_F$ equals $\mu_F$; equivalently,
$\mu_G(p_{G,F}^{-1}(A))=\mu_F(A)$ for every
$A\in\bigotimes_{i\in F}\mathcal E_i$. The restriction is measurable since
inverse images of coordinate generators are coordinate generators. The empty
support carries the unique probability measure on the singleton empty product.

Reordering means choosing a different enumeration of the **same** finite set
$F$. If $e:[n]\to F$ is an enumeration, its displayed ordered law is the
pushforward of $\mu_F$ under $r_e(x)=(x_{e(0)},\ldots,x_{e(n-1)})$.
For another enumeration $e'$, the coordinate permutation $r_{e'}\circ r_e^{-1}$
pushes this ordered law to the one displayed using $e'$. This is automatic
from these definitions and does not require equal laws on different subsets
of $I$, or invariance under permutations of a fixed ordered product.
In particular, consistency is data about
every finite joint law, not merely the one-coordinate marginals.

The measurable space $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$ with its usual
topology is standard Borel.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For any set $I$, standard-Borel coordinate spaces $(E_i,\mathcal E_i)$, and consistent finite-dimensional laws $(\mu_F)_{F\Subset I}$, there is a unique probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathcal C_I$ whose $F$-coordinate marginal is $\mu_F$ for each finite $F$.

For measurable spaces $(E_i,\mathcal E_i)_{i\in I}$, put
$E=\prod_{i\in I}E_i$. For finite $F\subseteq I$, let
$\pi_F:E\to\prod_{i\in F}E_i$ be restriction to $F$ (the singleton empty
product when $F=\varnothing$). On $\prod_{i\in F}E_i$, write $q_i$ for the
$i$th coordinate map and define

$$\bigotimes_{i\in F}\mathcal E_i:=\sigma\{q_i^{-1}(A):i\in F,\ A\in\mathcal E_i\}.$$

For $F=\varnothing$ this is the two-set sigma-algebra on the singleton. If
$e:[n]\to F$ is any enumeration, coordinate relabelling identifies this
sigma-algebra with the recursively defined finite product sigma-algebra of
[[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]: both are
generated by the same coordinate inverse images. Thus the notation is
independent of the enumeration.

A **finite-coordinate cylinder** is $\pi_F^{-1}(A)$ for
$A\in\bigotimes_{i\in F}\mathcal E_i$. The **cylinder sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal C_I:=\sigma\{\pi_F^{-1}(A):F\subseteq I\text{ finite},\ A\in\bigotimes_{i\in F}\mathcal E_i\}.$$

This is the product sigma-algebra on the arbitrary product; the empty-support cylinder is either $\varnothing$ or $E$.

For $t\in I$, let $X_t:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(E_t,\mathcal E_t)$ be a random element. The family $X=(X_t)_{t\in I}$ is a **stochastic process**. For an ordered tuple of distinct times $(t_1,\ldots,t_n)$, its finite-dimensional distribution is the pushforward law of $(X_{t_1},\ldots,X_{t_n})$ on $\prod_{j<n}E_{t_{j+1}}$. These laws, including their coordinate order, form a consistent family under deletion and permutation of times.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. A real stochastic process
$X=(X_t)_{t\in I}$ [[def-stochastic-process-and-finite-dimensional-distributions]]
is a **Gaussian process** if, for every integer $n\ge 1$, every time list
$t_1,\ldots,t_n\in I$, and every $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in\mathbb R$, the random
variable
$$
\sum_{j=1}^n a_jX_{t_j}
$$
has a normal law $N(m,\sigma^2)$ for some $m\in\mathbb R$ and
$\sigma\ge0$. Variance zero is allowed, so constant linear combinations are
included.

Equivalently, for every such time list the evaluation vector
$(X_{t_1},\ldots,X_{t_n})$ has a possibly singular multivariate normal law in
the sense of [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]. Indeed, that definition says
exactly that every scalar projection of the vector is normal. This also covers
repeated times, zero coefficients, and singular covariance matrices; no
distinct-time convention is needed for this definition.

Choice is declared because the library's scalar and multivariate normal-law
interfaces construct their probability laws and independent standard-normal
realizations under AC. The equivalence itself is only an unpacking of the
finite-dimensional projection definition and makes no further selection.

derivations.claim: For each nonempty finite $F\subseteq T$, use AC to choose an enumeration $e_F:\{1,\ldots,n\}\to F$. Set $a_i=m(e_F(i))$ and $\Sigma_{ij}=k(e_F(i),e_F(j))$. Positive semidefiniteness of $k$ makes $\Sigma$ positive semidefinite; [F1] supplies its positive square root and [F2] gives the possibly singular law $N_n(a,\Sigma)$. Push this law to $\mathbb R^F$ by relabelling coordinate $i$ as $e_F(i)$. A different enumeration changes both the mean and covariance by the same permutation; [F3] shows that the relabelled law is unchanged. For $F=\varnothing$, take the unique law on the singleton empty product.

If $F\subseteq G$ are finite, the characteristic function of the restriction pushforward of the $G$-law at $u\in\mathbb R^F$ is $ \exp\!\left(i\sum_{t\in F}u_t m(t)-\frac12\sum_{s,t\in F}u_su_t k(s,t)\right). $ This is also the characteristic function of the $F$-law. By [F3] the two pushforward laws agree, so the family constructed in step 1.1 is consistent in the sense of [F4]. The empty marginal is the singleton law.

Each coordinate space $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$ is standard Borel by [F5]. The consistent family from step 2.1 therefore satisfies [F6], which gives a unique probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathcal C_T$ with exactly these finite-coordinate marginals.

Define $X_t(x)=x(t)$ on $(\mathbb R^T,\mathcal C_T,\mu)$. By [F7] these coordinates are measurable, and step 3.1 gives each finite evaluation vector the stated multivariate normal law. Every finite linear combination is a scalar projection of such a vector, hence is normal by [F2]. Thus [F8] makes $X$ a Gaussian process. Its one- and two-coordinate laws give mean $m$ and covariance $k$, including zero-variance coordinates and singular finite covariance matrices.

The extension in step 3.1 is unique on $\mathcal C_T$. It supplies no topology or probability law on a path-continuous or Banach-valued function space, so no such regularity or tightness conclusion is included.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. A real stochastic process
$X=(X_t)_{t\in I}$ [[def-stochastic-process-and-finite-dimensional-distributions]]
is a **Gaussian process** if, for every integer $n\ge 1$, every time list

has a normal law $N(m,\sigma^2)$ for some $m\in\mathbb R$ and
$\sigma\ge0$. Variance zero is allowed, so constant linear combinations are
included.

Equivalently, for every such time list the evaluation vector
$(X_{t_1},\ldots,X_{t_n})$ has a possibly singular multivariate normal law in
the sense of [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]. Indeed, that definition says

Choice is declared because the library's scalar and multivariate normal-law
interfaces construct their probability laws and independent standard-normal
realizations under AC. The equivalence itself is only an unpacking of the

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $m\ge1$ be finite, let $d_j\ge1$, and let
$Z_j$ for $1\le j\le m$ be mutually independent random elements of
$\mathbb R^{d_j}$. Suppose $Z_j\sim N_{d_j}(a_j,\Sigma_j)$, where each
$\Sigma_j$ is symmetric positive semidefinite. Put
$D=\sum_{j=1}^m d_j$, $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$,
$a=(a_1,\ldots,a_m)$, and
$\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(\Sigma_1,\ldots,\Sigma_m)$. Then
$$Z\sim N_D(a,\Sigma).$$
No covariance block needs to be invertible.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC. Let $X\in\mathbb R^d$ and $Y\in\mathbb R^m$, with $d,m\ge1$, be
jointly multivariate normal with mean $(a,b)$ and positive-semidefinite block
covariance
$$\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}A&C\\C^T&B\end{pmatrix},$$
where $B$ is positive definite. Then
$$S=A-CB^{-1}C^T$$
is positive semidefinite, and for every $y\in\mathbb R^m$ the probability law
$$K(y,\cdot)=N_d\!\left(a+CB^{-1}(y-b),S\right)$$
is defined. The map $K$ is a probability kernel and is a conditional law of
$X$ given $Y$: for all Borel $E\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ and
$F\subseteq\mathbb R^m$,
$$\mathbb P(X\in E,Y\in F)=\int_F K(y,E)\,\mathbb P_Y(dy).$$
The covariance $A$ and the conditional covariance $S$ may be singular.
Positive definiteness of $B$ is required; no pseudoinverse formula for
singular $B$ is asserted.

Let $n\ge 1$ and let $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$, with the real case obtained by
restricting scalars to $\mathbb R$. Then the following are equivalent:

1. $A$ has a Cholesky factorisation $A=LL^*$ with $L$ lower triangular and
   positive real diagonal.
2. $A$ is Hermitian positive definite.

When these conditions hold, the factor $L$ is unique.

Let $F$ be a field, let $n\ge 1$, and let $b\in F^n$.

If $L=(\ell_{ij})\in M_n(F)$ is lower triangular with every diagonal entry
$\ell_{ii}\ne 0$, the **forward substitution solve** of $Lx=b$ is the recursive
construction

$$x_i:=\frac{1}{\ell_{ii}}\left(b_i-\sum_{j<i}\ell_{ij}x_j\right)\qquad(0\le i<n).$$If $U=(u_{ij})\in M_n(F)$ is upper triangular with every diagonal entry $u_{ii}\ne 0$, the **backward substitution solve** of $Ux=b$ is the recursive construction$$x_i:=\frac{1}{u_{ii}}\left(b_i-\sum_{j>i}u_{ij}x_j\right)\qquad(n-1\ge i\ge 0).$$

The triangular vocabulary is from
[[def-triangular-and-diagonal-matrices-over-a-commutative-ring]]. The matrix
product convention from [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]] is the one
used when later items rewrite these recursions as matrix equations.

Let $F$ be a field, let $n\ge 1$, and let $b\in F^n$.

1. If $L\in M_n(F)$ is lower triangular with nonzero diagonal, the forward
   substitution recursion of
   [[def-forward-and-back-substitution-for-triangular-systems]] produces the
   unique solution of $Lx=b$.
2. If $U\in M_n(F)$ is upper triangular with nonzero diagonal, the backward
   substitution recursion produces the unique solution of $Ux=b$.

Each solve uses exactly $n$ divisions,
$\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ multiplications, and $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ additions or
subtractions, hence $O(n^2)$ scalar operations.

derivations.claim: By [F1], the concatenated finite evaluation vector $U=(f_{X_*},f_X)$ is multivariate normal with mean $(m_*,m_X)$ and covariance $ \begin{pmatrix}K_{**}&K_{*X}\\K_{X*}&K_{XX}\end{pmatrix}. $ This remains valid when either list has repetitions.

The vector $\epsilon$ is multivariate normal with mean zero and covariance $R$. Each coordinate of $U$ is a measurable function of the process coordinates, so $\sigma(U)\subseteq\sigma(f)$. By [F2] and the independence hypothesis, $\sigma(\epsilon)$ is independent of $\sigma(f)$ and hence of $\sigma(U)$. Applying [F3] to $U$ and $\epsilon$ shows that $Z=(f_{X_*},f_X,\epsilon)$ is jointly multivariate normal with block-diagonal covariance between $U$ and $\epsilon$.

Apply the linear map $(u,v,e)\mapsto(u,v+e)$ to $Z$. Every scalar projection of the result is a scalar projection of $Z$, hence is normal by [F4]; its mean is $(m_*,m_X)$. The Gaussian vectors have finite second moments, so independence and $E\epsilon=0$ give $\operatorname{Cov}(f_{X_*},\epsilon)=0$ and $\operatorname{Cov}(Y)=K_{XX}+R=C$. By step 1.1, $\operatorname{Cov}(f_{X_*},f_X)=K_{*X}$, so $(f_{X_*},Y)$ is jointly Gaussian with covariance $ \begin{pmatrix}K_{**}&K_{*X}\\K_{X*}&C\end{pmatrix}. $

Apply [F5] with $A=K_{**}$, cross-covariance $K_{*X}$, and observed covariance $B=C\succ0$. The result is a probability-kernel version for every $y$, with the displayed mean and Schur-complement covariance; [F5] also proves this covariance is positive semidefinite even if singular.

If $\eta_*$ is present, it is jointly independent of the process and $\epsilon$ by hypothesis. By [F3], the stack $(f_{X_*},f_X,\epsilon,\eta_*)$ is jointly Gaussian. The linear map $(u,v,e,h)\mapsto(u+h,v+e)$ has mean $(m_*,m_X)$, cross-covariance $K_{*X}$, observed covariance $C$, and prediction covariance $K_{**}+R_*$. Applying [F5] to this pair gives the stated noisy-prediction law.

By [F6], write $C=LL^T$. For any right-hand side $b$, solve $Lz=b$ by forward substitution and $L^Tu=z$ by backward substitution; [F8] gives both unique solutions. Then $Cu=L(L^Tu)=Lz=b$, so $u=C^{-1}b$. Applying this to $b=y-m_X$ and, column by column, to $K_{X*}$ evaluates both formula terms without forming the inverse.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a set, let $m:T\to\mathbb R$, and let
$k:T\times T\to\mathbb R$ be symmetric and positive semidefinite, meaning that
for every finite list $t_1,\ldots,t_n\in T$ and every $a\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$\sum_{i,j=1}^n a_i a_j k(t_i,t_j)\ge0.$$
There is a unique probability measure $\mu$ on the cylinder sigma-algebra
$\mathcal C_T$ of $\mathbb R^T$ whose marginal on each finite-coordinate space
$\mathbb R^F$, for $F\subseteq T$ finite, is the Gaussian law with mean
$(m(t))_{t\in F}$ and covariance matrix $(k(s,t))_{s,t\in F}$. The coordinate
process $X_t(x)=x(t)$ is Gaussian, has mean function $m$, and has covariance
kernel $k$. This construction gives only the cylinder-space process; it
asserts no sample-path continuity, joint measurability in $(t,x)$, or tight
Banach-valued law.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. Then the following are
equivalent:

1. the family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent;
2. for every natural number $n\ge1$, every choice of distinct indices
   $i_0,\dots,i_{n-1}\in I$, and every choice of measurable sets
   $B_k\in\Sigma_{i_k}$,
   $$\mathbb P\bigl(X_{i_0}\in B_0,\dots,X_{i_{n-1}}\in B_{n-1}\bigr)=\prod_{k<n}\mathbb P(X_{i_k}\in B_k).$$

For measurable spaces $(E_i,\mathcal E_i)_{i\in I}$, put
$E=\prod_{i\in I}E_i$. For finite $F\subseteq I$, let
$\pi_F:E\to\prod_{i\in F}E_i$ be restriction to $F$ (the singleton empty
product when $F=\varnothing$). On $\prod_{i\in F}E_i$, write $q_i$ for the
$i$th coordinate map and define

$$\bigotimes_{i\in F}\mathcal E_i:=\sigma\{q_i^{-1}(A):i\in F,\ A\in\mathcal E_i\}.$$

For $F=\varnothing$ this is the two-set sigma-algebra on the singleton. If
$e:[n]\to F$ is any enumeration, coordinate relabelling identifies this
sigma-algebra with the recursively defined finite product sigma-algebra of
[[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]: both are
generated by the same coordinate inverse images. Thus the notation is
independent of the enumeration.

A **finite-coordinate cylinder** is $\pi_F^{-1}(A)$ for
$A\in\bigotimes_{i\in F}\mathcal E_i$. The **cylinder sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal C_I:=\sigma\{\pi_F^{-1}(A):F\subseteq I\text{ finite},\ A\in\bigotimes_{i\in F}\mathcal E_i\}.$$

This is the product sigma-algebra on the arbitrary product; the empty-support cylinder is either $\varnothing$ or $E$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Assume AC and let $f=(f_t)_{t\in T}$ be a real Gaussian process with mean
$m$ and covariance kernel $k$; when $m$ and $k$ are specified as a prior,
the canonical cylinder-space process exists by
[[thm-gaussian-process-exists-from-mean-and-positive-semidefinite-covariance-kernel]].
Let $X=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in T^n$ and $X_*=(x_1^*,\ldots,x_p^*)\in T^p$,
where $n,p\ge1$ and repeated indices are allowed. Write
$f_X=(f_{x_i})_{i=1}^n$, $f_{X_*}=(f_{x_j^*})_{j=1}^p$,
$m_X=(m(x_i))_{i=1}^n$, and $m_*=(m(x_j^*))_{j=1}^p$. For finite lists
$A=(a_i)$ and $B=(b_j)$, define
$K_{AB}=(k(a_i,b_j))_{i,j}$.

Let $\epsilon\sim N_n(0,R)$ be independent of the process, where $R$ is
symmetric positive semidefinite, and set $Y=f_X+\epsilon$. Assume the
observed covariance $C=K_{XX}+R$ is positive definite. Then a version of the
conditional law of $f_{X_*}$ given $Y=y$ is, for every $y\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$N_p\!\left(m_*+K_{*X}C^{-1}(y-m_X),\;K_{**}-K_{*X}C^{-1}K_{X*}\right).$$
The displayed conditional covariance is positive semidefinite and may be
singular; $K_{XX}$ and $K_{**}$ may also be singular. If a prediction-noise
vector $\eta_*\sim N_p(0,R_*)$ jointly independent of the process and
$\epsilon$ is added to $f_{X_*}$, with $R_*$ symmetric positive semidefinite,
the conditional mean is unchanged and
$R_*$ is added to the conditional covariance. The displayed kernel is a
version defined at every $y$; conditional-law versions are determined only
$P_Y$-almost surely.

For computation, the occurrences of $C^{-1}v$ mean solving $Cu=v$. Since
$C$ is positive definite, its Cholesky factorization and forward/back
substitution evaluate these solves without forming $C^{-1}$.

derivations.claim: For every finite coefficient list on $T$, the constant kernel has quadratic form $(\sum_i a_i)^2\ge0$. The noise matrix is positive definite because $u^2+uv+v^2=(u+v/2)^2+3v^2/4>0$ for $(u,v)\ne(0,0)$. By [F1] there is a cylinder-space GP law $\mu$ and [F2] gives the noise law. Their product probability exists by [F3]; its process and noise coordinates are measurable by [F5] and independent by [F4]. Thus this is a model satisfying the theorem's noise assumption.

The observed and test covariance blocks are $K_{XX}=J_2$, $K_{cX}=(1,1)$, and $K_{cc}=1$. Thus $C=J_2+R=\begin{pmatrix}2&3/2\\3/2&2\end{pmatrix}$, which is positive definite since its quadratic form is $2(u+3v/4)^2+7v^2/8$. Direct multiplication gives $C^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}8/7&-6/7\\-6/7&8/7\end{pmatrix}$.
Since $m_X=(1,-1)$, $m_c=2$, and $y-m_X=(-1,2)$, $C^{-1}(y-m_X)=(-20/7,22/7)$ and $K_{cX}C^{-1}(y-m_X)=2/7$. The posterior mean in [F6] is therefore $2+2/7=16/7$.

Also $C^{-1}K_{Xc}=(2/7,2/7)^T$, so $K_{cX}C^{-1}K_{Xc}=4/7$. The posterior variance is $1-4/7=3/7$, proving the displayed conditional-kernel value. This is the value of the all-$y$ kernel version specified in [F6] at $y=(0,1)$; the theorem does not make conditional-law values pointwise unique.

Their product probability exists by [F3]; its process and noise random elements are measurable by [F5] and independent by [F4].

Hence it is positive definite and $C^{-1}=\frac13\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}$. For the repeated test list, $K_{*X}=K_{**}=J_2$. Since $C$ is positive definite, the hypotheses of [F6] hold.

The prior observation covariance and conditional predictive covariance are both singular, whereas the matrix inverted by the formula is the positive-definite observed covariance $C$. This verifies why singular prior and predictive blocks are permitted under the stated condition.

Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a set, let $m:T\to\mathbb R$, and let
$k:T\times T\to\mathbb R$ be symmetric and positive semidefinite, meaning that
for every finite list $t_1,\ldots,t_n\in T$ and every $a\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$\sum_{i,j=1}^n a_i a_j k(t_i,t_j)\ge0.$$
There is a unique probability measure $\mu$ on the cylinder sigma-algebra
$\mathcal C_T$ of $\mathbb R^T$ whose marginal on each finite-coordinate space
$\mathbb R^F$, for $F\subseteq T$ finite, is the Gaussian law with mean
$(m(t))_{t\in F}$ and covariance matrix $(k(s,t))_{s,t\in F}$. The coordinate
process $X_t(x)=x(t)$ is Gaussian, has mean function $m$, and has covariance
kernel $k$. This construction gives only the cylinder-space process; it
asserts no sample-path continuity, joint measurability in $(t,x)$, or tight
Banach-valued law.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. Then the following are
equivalent:

1. the family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent;
2. for every natural number $n\ge1$, every choice of distinct indices
   $i_0,\dots,i_{n-1}\in I$, and every choice of measurable sets
   $B_k\in\Sigma_{i_k}$,
   $$\mathbb P\bigl(X_{i_0}\in B_0,\dots,X_{i_{n-1}}\in B_{n-1}\bigr)=\prod_{k<n}\mathbb P(X_{i_k}\in B_k).$$

For measurable spaces $(E_i,\mathcal E_i)_{i\in I}$, put
$E=\prod_{i\in I}E_i$. For finite $F\subseteq I$, let
$\pi_F:E\to\prod_{i\in F}E_i$ be restriction to $F$ (the singleton empty
product when $F=\varnothing$). On $\prod_{i\in F}E_i$, write $q_i$ for the
$i$th coordinate map and define

$$\bigotimes_{i\in F}\mathcal E_i:=\sigma\{q_i^{-1}(A):i\in F,\ A\in\mathcal E_i\}.$$

For $F=\varnothing$ this is the two-set sigma-algebra on the singleton. If
$e:[n]\to F$ is any enumeration, coordinate relabelling identifies this
sigma-algebra with the recursively defined finite product sigma-algebra of
[[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]: both are
generated by the same coordinate inverse images. Thus the notation is
independent of the enumeration.

A **finite-coordinate cylinder** is $\pi_F^{-1}(A)$ for
$A\in\bigotimes_{i\in F}\mathcal E_i$. The **cylinder sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal C_I:=\sigma\{\pi_F^{-1}(A):F\subseteq I\text{ finite},\ A\in\bigotimes_{i\in F}\mathcal E_i\}.$$

This is the product sigma-algebra on the arbitrary product; the empty-support cylinder is either $\varnothing$ or $E$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Assume AC and let $f=(f_t)_{t\in T}$ be a real Gaussian process with mean
$m$ and covariance kernel $k$; when $m$ and $k$ are specified as a prior,
the canonical cylinder-space process exists by
[[thm-gaussian-process-exists-from-mean-and-positive-semidefinite-covariance-kernel]].
Let $X=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in T^n$ and $X_*=(x_1^*,\ldots,x_p^*)\in T^p$,
where $n,p\ge1$ and repeated indices are allowed. Write
$f_X=(f_{x_i})_{i=1}^n$, $f_{X_*}=(f_{x_j^*})_{j=1}^p$,
$m_X=(m(x_i))_{i=1}^n$, and $m_*=(m(x_j^*))_{j=1}^p$. For finite lists
$A=(a_i)$ and $B=(b_j)$, define
$K_{AB}=(k(a_i,b_j))_{i,j}$.

Let $\epsilon\sim N_n(0,R)$ be independent of the process, where $R$ is
symmetric positive semidefinite, and set $Y=f_X+\epsilon$. Assume the
observed covariance $C=K_{XX}+R$ is positive definite. Then a version of the
conditional law of $f_{X_*}$ given $Y=y$ is, for every $y\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$N_p\!\left(m_*+K_{*X}C^{-1}(y-m_X),\;K_{**}-K_{*X}C^{-1}K_{X*}\right).$$
The displayed conditional covariance is positive semidefinite and may be
singular; $K_{XX}$ and $K_{**}$ may also be singular. If a prediction-noise
vector $\eta_*\sim N_p(0,R_*)$ jointly independent of the process and
$\epsilon$ is added to $f_{X_*}$, with $R_*$ symmetric positive semidefinite,
the conditional mean is unchanged and
$R_*$ is added to the conditional covariance. The displayed kernel is a
version defined at every $y$; conditional-law versions are determined only
$P_Y$-almost surely.

For computation, the occurrences of $C^{-1}v$ mean solving $Cu=v$. Since
$C$ is positive definite, its Cholesky factorization and forward/back
substitution evaluate these solves without forming $C^{-1}$.

citations.quote: A topological space $X$ is **separable** if some at most countable subset $D\subseteq X$ is dense in $X$ ([[def-dense-top]], [[def-countable]]). Equivalently, every nonempty open subset of $X$ meets $D$.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $X$ be a real or
complex Banach space. An $X$-valued **measurable simple function** is a function
$s:\Omega\to X$ having a representation

$$s=\sum_{j=1}^{m}x_j\mathbf 1_{A_j},$$

where $m\geq 0$, the sets $A_j\in\mathcal A$ are pairwise disjoint, and the
vectors $x_j\in X$ are distinct and nonzero. The value of $s$ off
$\bigcup_jA_j$ is $0$. The empty representation is therefore the zero
function.

The simple function is **integrable** when $\mu(A_j)<\infty$ for every nonzero
coefficient $x_j$. Its integral over $E\in\mathcal A$ is

$$\int_E s\,d\mu:=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\mu(E\cap A_j)x_j.$$

In particular, $\int s\,d\mu$ means $\int_\Omega s\,d\mu$. Requiring finite
measure only for the nonzero level sets avoids the undefined product
$0\cdot\infty$. The next lemma proves that the displayed value does not depend
on the chosen disjoint representation.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and $X$ a real or complex
Banach space. A function $f:\Omega\to X$ is **strongly measurable** (or
**Bochner measurable**) if there are measurable $X$-valued simple functions
$s_n$ and a measurable null set $N$ such that

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\|s_n(\omega)-f(\omega)\|=0$$

for every $\omega\in\Omega\setminus N$.

This is a norm-convergence condition. It is not, by definition, merely Borel
measurability of $f$ or measurability of every scalar function $x^*\circ f$.
Changing $f$ on a null set preserves strong measurability: enlarge $N$ by that
null set and retain the same approximants.

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a decreasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$. If $\mu(E_{n_0})<+\infty$ for some $n_0$, then

$$\mu\left(\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\inf_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

Let $\mu$ be a measure and let $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be measurable. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k).$$

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ one also has

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k<m}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k<m}\mu(E_k),$$

including $m=0$, where both sides are $0$.

derivations.claim: Choose a countable dense sequence $(d_j)_{j\ge1}$ in $B$. For each $n\ge1$, assign $\omega$ to the first index $j$ for which $\|f(\omega)-d_j\|<2^{-n}$; such an index exists by density. The resulting sets $A_{n,j}$ form a measurable countable partition: each is the preimage of an open ball under $f$, with the finitely many earlier preimages removed.

Since the partial unions $\bigcup_{j\le N}A_{n,j}$ increase to $\Omega$, [F3] gives an integer $N_n$ for which the omitted tail has measure at most $2^{-2n}$. Define $s_n=d_j$ on $A_{n,j}$ for $j\le N_n$, and $s_n=0$ on the omitted tail. Then $s_n$ is a finite-valued measurable simple function.

The tail events $T_n=\bigcup_{j>N_n}A_{n,j}$ satisfy $\sum_nP(T_n)\le\sum_n2^{-2n}<\infty$. By [F4], for every $N$, $P(\bigcup_{n\ge N}T_n)\le\sum_{n\ge N}2^{-2n}$; continuity from above makes the probability of belonging to infinitely many $T_n$ equal to zero. Outside that null set, for all sufficiently large $n$ the point is not in $T_n$, and then $\|s_n(\omega)-f(\omega)\|<2^{-n}$. Thus $s_n\to f$ almost everywhere, which is strong measurability by [F2].

citations.quote: A topological space $X$ is **separable** if some at most countable subset $D\subseteq X$ is dense in $X$ ([[def-dense-top]], [[def-countable]]). Equivalently, every nonempty open subset of $X$ meets $D$.

Work over ZF. The **real dominated-extension principle**, denoted **HB**, is the following assertion:

For every real vector space $X$, every sublinear functional $p:X\to\mathbb R$ in the sense of [[def-sublinear-functional]], every real linear subspace $M\le X$ in the sense of [[def-linear-subspace]], and every real linear functional $g:M\to\mathbb R$ in the sense of [[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]],
$$\bigl(\forall m\in M,\ g(m)\le p(m)\bigr)\ \Longrightarrow\ \exists F:X\to\mathbb R\ \bigl(F\text{ is real linear},\ F|_M=g,\ \forall x\in X,\ F(x)\le p(x)\bigr).$$

This names an additional principle; it does not assert a proof of HB in ZF. Subsequent results explicitly state when they assume HB. Neither topology nor completeness is part of this assertion. The subspace may be $\{0\}$ or all of $X$. Sublinearity at scalar zero gives $p(0)=0$, and a linear functional has value zero at zero.

Assume HB and let $X$ be a real or complex normed space. For each $x\ne0$ there is $f\in X^*$ with $\|f\|=1$ and $f(x)=\|x\|$, a positive real number also in the complex case. Hence $X^*$ separates distinct points, and
$$\|x\|=\max_{f\in X^*,\ \|f\|\le1}|f(x)|\qquad(x\in X).$$
The formula includes $x=0$ and the zero space. Moreover, if $H\subseteq X^*$ has norm-dense scalar-linear span and $h(x)=0$ for all $h\in H$, then $x=0$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: If $B=\{0\}$, take the constant zero sequence. Otherwise let $D$ be a countable dense subset of $B$. The normalized set $\{d/\|d\|:d\in D,\ d\ne0\}$ is countable and dense in the unit sphere: for $\|x\|=1$ and $d\to x$, eventually $d\ne0$ and $\|d/\|d\|-x\|\le2\|d-x\|$. Enumerate it as $(x_j)$. By [F2] and [A1], choose $\ell_j\in B^*$ with $\|\ell_j\|=1$ and $\ell_j(x_j)=1$ for each $j$.

For every $x\in B$ and every $j$, $|\ell_j(x)|\le\|x\|$, so the supremum is at most $\|x\|$. If $x\ne0$, choose unit vectors $x_{j_k}\to x/\|x\|$. Then $\ell_{j_k}(x/\|x\|)\ge 1-\|x_{j_k}-x/\|x\|\|\to1$, so $\sup_j|\ell_j(x)|\ge\|x\|$. The zero vector gives equality directly.
