Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$, $m\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $\Sigma$ be a real symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then its law has Lebesgue density
$$f_{m,\Sigma}(x)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\det(\Sigma)^{-1/2} \exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(x-m)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-m)\right), \qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $m\ge1$ be finite, let $d_j\ge1$, and let
$Z_j$ for $1\le j\le m$ be mutually independent random elements of
$\mathbb R^{d_j}$. Suppose $Z_j\sim N_{d_j}(a_j,\Sigma_j)$, where each
$\Sigma_j$ is symmetric positive semidefinite. Put
$D=\sum_{j=1}^m d_j$, $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$,
$a=(a_1,\ldots,a_m)$, and
$\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(\Sigma_1,\ldots,\Sigma_m)$. Then
$$Z\sim N_D(a,\Sigma).$$
No covariance block needs to be invertible.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Phi(x)=P(Z\le x)$ for $Z\sim N(0,1)$. Then $\Phi$ is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$, with $\lim_{x\to-\infty}\Phi(x)=0$ and $\lim_{x\to+\infty}\Phi(x)=1$.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval and let $f:X\times I\to\mathbb C$
be such that:

1. for every $t\in I$, the function $x\mapsto f(x,t)$ is integrable;
2. for almost every $x$, the map $t\mapsto f(x,t)$ is differentiable on $I$;
3. for every $t\in I$, the function
   $$x\mapsto \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t),$$
   extended by zero where the derivative is undefined, is measurable;
4. there are a measurable null set $N$ and a nonnegative measurable function
   $g$ with
   $$\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$$
   and
   $$\left|\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t)\right|\le g(x)$$
   for every $t\in I$ and every $x\in X\setminus N$.

Then
$$F(t):=\int f(x,t)\,d\mu(x)$$
is differentiable on $I$, and
$$F'(t)=\int \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t)\,d\mu(x),$$
with the same zero extension in the last integral.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. For $F,G\in AC[a,b]$,
$$\int_a^bFG'+\int_a^bF'G=F(b)G(b)-F(a)G(a).$$

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. For $F:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$, the following are equivalent:

1. $F$ is absolutely continuous.
2. $F'$ exists almost everywhere, $F'\in L^1[a,b]$, and
$$F(x)-F(a)=\int_a^xF'(t)\,dt\quad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume countable choice. If $P$ is Polish and $\mu$ is a Borel probability measure on $P$, then for every Borel $A\subseteq P$ and $\varepsilon>0$ there is a compact $K\subseteq A$ with $\mu(A\setminus K)<\varepsilon$.

Let $\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ satisfy

$$ \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \varphi(x)\,dx = 1. $$

For $\varepsilon > 0$, define

$$ \varphi_\varepsilon(x) := \varepsilon^{-n}\varphi(x/\varepsilon) \qquad(x \in \mathbb{R}^n). $$

The family $(\varphi_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ is the **mollifier family
generated by $\varphi$**.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex with at least two elements
([[def-interval]]), let $f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$
([[def-continuity-real]]) and injective
([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]), and let $g : f[I] \to I$ be the
inverse of $f : I \to f[I]$ supplied by [[thm-continuous-inverse]]. Let
$c \in I$ and put $b := f(c)$.

Then $c$ is a limit point of $I$ and $b$ is a limit point of $f[I]$, so that
$f'(c)$ and $g'(b)$ are meaningful symbols ([[def-derivative]]), and, assuming
$f$ is differentiable at $c$:

1. if $f'(c) \ne 0$, then $g$ is differentiable at $b$ and
   $$g'(b) \;=\; \frac{1}{f'(c)} ;$$
2. if $f'(c) = 0$, then $g$ is **not** differentiable at $b$.

**The two claims together say that the inverse inherits differentiability
exactly where the derivative does not vanish.** Nothing is asserted at a point
of $f[I]$ that is not of the form $f(c)$ with $f$ differentiable at $c$, and
nothing is asserted about $g$ being differentiable *on* a set.

**No compactness and no boundedness is assumed.** $I$ may be open, half-open or
unbounded; all that is used of it is order-convexity and the presence of two
distinct points, the latter being exactly what makes every point of $I$ a limit
point of $I$ ([[def-derivative]]).

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on the closed bounded interval $[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-continuity-real]]), and let $y \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$f(a) \le y \le f(b) \qquad \text{or} \qquad f(b) \le y \le f(a) .$$

Then there is $c \in [a,b]$ with $f(c) = y$.

**The construction is canonical, so no choice principle is used.** The bisection
below tests the left half first and takes the right half only when the left one
has been ruled out, so the passage from one interval to the next is a *function*
of that interval, and [[thm-recursion]] applies with nothing selected. This is
the same discipline the library uses wherever a sequence is built one term at a
time.

**Completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ is what does the work.** The bisection produces a
nested sequence of closed bounded intervals whose lengths tend to $0$, and it is
[[thm-nested-interval-property]] — hence the least-upper-bound property — that
supplies the point. Over an ordered field that is not complete the theorem
fails; the witness for that, stated for an arbitrary ordered field and worked
over $\mathbb{Q}$, is
[[cex-evt-and-ivt-fail-over-a-non-complete-field]], which states its own
$\varepsilon$-$\delta$ continuity inline and is not an instance of this page's
definition.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ and $b_0, \dots, b_{n-1}$ be
reals, with finite sums as in [[def-finite-sum]]. Then

$$\Big(\sum_{k<n} a_k b_k\Big)^{2} \;\le\; \Big(\sum_{k<n} a_k^{2}\Big)\Big(\sum_{k<n} b_k^{2}\Big),$$

and, in root form ([[thm-of-square-roots]]),

$$\Big|\sum_{k<n} a_k b_k\Big| \;\le\; \sqrt{\sum_{k<n} a_k^{2}} \; \sqrt{\sum_{k<n} b_k^{2}}.$$

Equality holds in the first display if and only if the two lists are
proportional, in the symmetric sense that there is a pair
$(\lambda, \mu) \ne (0,0)$ of reals with $\lambda a_k = \mu b_k$ for every
$k < n$.

**No root is used in the proof of the squared form.** That form is an identity
plus a sign argument in the ordered field, and the root form is only a
restatement of it through the monotonicity of squaring on the nonnegatives
([[lem-of-square-monotone]]); the root enters nowhere but the last step, where
that restatement is made and [[thm-of-square-roots]] is what supplies the
square-root symbol. This matters here, because it makes the squared
inequality independent of the existence theorem for roots.

Let $a\le b$ and $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]). The function $f$ is
**absolutely continuous** on $[a,b]$ if for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is
$\delta>0$ such that every finite family of subintervals
$[u_j,v_j]\subseteq[a,b]$, indexed by $j<m$, whose open interiors are pairwise
disjoint and which satisfies

$$\sum_{j<m}(v_j-u_j)<\delta$$

also satisfies

$$\sum_{j<m}|f(v_j)-f(u_j)|<\varepsilon.$$

Finite sums and the empty sum are those of [[def-finite-sum]] and
[[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. For $m=0$ both sums are $0$, so the condition is
automatic. On $[a,a]$ every permitted interval is a singleton and every endpoint
increment is $0$ ([[def-abs-value]]), so every function on that singleton is
absolutely continuous. Absolute continuity implies ordinary continuity
([[def-continuity-real]]); that implication is proved next rather than built into
the definition.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$, $m\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $\Sigma$ be a real symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then its law has Lebesgue density
$$f_{m,\Sigma}(x)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\det(\Sigma)^{-1/2} \exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(x-m)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-m)\right), \qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $m\ge1$ be finite, let $d_j\ge1$, and let
$Z_j$ for $1\le j\le m$ be mutually independent random elements of
$\mathbb R^{d_j}$. Suppose $Z_j\sim N_{d_j}(a_j,\Sigma_j)$, where each
$\Sigma_j$ is symmetric positive semidefinite. Put
$D=\sum_{j=1}^m d_j$, $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$,
$a=(a_1,\ldots,a_m)$, and
$\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(\Sigma_1,\ldots,\Sigma_m)$. Then
$$Z\sim N_D(a,\Sigma).$$
No covariance block needs to be invertible.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. > $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval and let $f:X\times I\to\mathbb C$

1. for every $t\in I$, the function $x\mapsto f(x,t)$ is integrable;
2. for almost every $x$, the map $t\mapsto f(x,t)$ is differentiable on $I$;
3. for every $t\in I$, the function
   $$x\mapsto \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t),$$
   extended by zero where the derivative is undefined, is measurable;
4. there are a measurable null set $N$ and a nonnegative measurable function
   $g$ with
   $$\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$$
   and
   $$\left|\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t)\right|\le g(x)$$
   for every $t\in I$ and every $x\in X\setminus N$.

$$F(t):=\int f(x,t)\,d\mu(x)$$
is differentiable on $I$, and
$$F'(t)=\int \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t)\,d\mu(x),$$

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. For $F,G\in AC[a,b]$,
$$\int_a^bFG'+\int_a^bF'G=F(b)G(b)-F(a)G(a).$$

$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ generating $\mathcal A$, and let $\mu,\nu$ be measures on $(X,\mathcal A)$ that agree on $\mathcal P$. Suppose there is an increasing sequence $(P_n)$ in $\mathcal P$ with

$$X=\bigcup_nP_n,\qquad \mu(P_n)=\nu(P_n)<+\infty\quad(n\in\mathbb N).$$

The map $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[def-real-numbers]]) is an embedding of ordered
fields. Every real is approximated by rationals: for $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and
rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $q \in \mathbb{Q}$ with
$|x - \hat q| < \hat\varepsilon$. Consequently, strictly between any two
reals lies a rational.

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

**No choice principle is used.** The one place where a reader expects a choice,
"pick a representative $a/b$ of each rational", is exactly where
[[lem-rat-positive-denominator]] applies: every rational *has* a representative
with positive denominator, so the map $(a,b) \mapsto [(a,b)]$ defined on
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is already **surjective** onto $\mathbb{Q}$,
and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).

If $A$ and $B$ are at most countable ([[def-countable]]) then so is
$A \times B$.

**No choice principle is used**: the two enumerations are given, and the
enumeration of the product is written down from them.

A topological space $X$ is **separable** if some at most countable subset $D\subseteq X$ is dense in $X$ ([[def-dense-top]], [[def-countable]]). Equivalently, every nonempty open subset of $X$ meets $D$.

derivations.claim: For every $x\in B$ and $r>0$, the given norming identity gives the identity $B(x,r)=\bigcup_{\substack{q\in\mathbb Q\\0\le q<r}} \ \bigcap_{j\ge1}\{y:|\ell_j(y-x)|\le q\}.$ If $\|y-x\|<r$, use [F2] to choose rational $q$ between that norm and $r$; conversely, membership in one intersection implies $\|y-x\|\le q<r$. Thus every open ball belongs to $\sigma(\ell_j:j\ge1)$. By [F3], fix a countable dense set $D\subseteq B$. The balls $B(d,s)$ with $d\in D$ and positive rational $s$ form a countable family by [F2]. For any open $U$ and $y\in U$, take $a>0$ with $B(y,a)\subseteq U$, choose $d\in D$ with $\|d-y\|<a/4$, and choose rational $s$ with $a/4<s<a/2$ by [F2]. Then $y\in B(d,s)\subseteq B(y,a)\subseteq U$. Thus this family is a base, and every open set is the union of its members contained in that set, a countable union. All those balls are in $\sigma(\ell_j)$ by the first part, so every open set is in that sigma-algebra. Conversely each continuous linear $\ell_j$ is Borel measurable, giving the reverse inclusion; hence it is the Borel sigma-algebra.

The finite-coordinate cylinder sets form a pi-system generating $\sigma(\ell_j:j\ge1)$. The assumed equality of finite-dimensional pushforwards makes $\mu$ and $\nu$ agree on each such cylinder. The cylinder pi-system contains $B$, and both probabilities assign it mass one; the constant exhaustion by $B$ meets [F1], which gives equality on the generated Borel sigma-algebra.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. **$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume AC, DC, and countable choice, and let $\gamma_d$ be standard Gaussian
measure on $\mathbb R^d$. For every
$g\in C^2(\mathbb R^d)$ bounded above and below by positive constants, with
bounded first and second derivatives,
$$\operatorname{Ent}_{\gamma_d}(g) :=\int g\log g\,d\gamma_d -\left(\int g\,d\gamma_d\right)\log\left(\int g\,d\gamma_d\right) \le \frac12\int\frac{|\nabla g|^2}{g}\,d\gamma_d.$$

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$, $m\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $\Sigma$ be a real symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then its law has Lebesgue density
$$f_{m,\Sigma}(x)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\det(\Sigma)^{-1/2} \exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(x-m)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-m)\right), \qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval and let $f:X\times I\to\mathbb C$
be such that:

1. for every $t\in I$, the function $x\mapsto f(x,t)$ is integrable;
2. for almost every $x$, the map $t\mapsto f(x,t)$ is differentiable on $I$;
3. for every $t\in I$, the function
   $$x\mapsto \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t),$$
   extended by zero where the derivative is undefined, is measurable;
4. there are a measurable null set $N$ and a nonnegative measurable function
   $g$ with
   $$\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$$
   and
   $$\left|\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t)\right|\le g(x)$$
   for every $t\in I$ and every $x\in X\setminus N$.

Then
$$F(t):=\int f(x,t)\,d\mu(x)$$
is differentiable on $I$, and
$$F'(t)=\int \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t)\,d\mu(x),$$
with the same zero extension in the last integral.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

Assume $L>0$. The function $q(\lambda)=\psi(\lambda)/\lambda$ extends continuously to $q(0)=0$ because $\psi(0)=\psi'(0)=0$. Its derivative on $(0,\infty)$ is $q'(\lambda)=(\lambda\psi'(\lambda)-\psi(\lambda))/\lambda^2\le L^2/2$ by step 1.1. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be a real vector space, let
$M \subseteq X$ be a linear subspace, let
$p:X \to \mathbb{R}$ be sublinear, and let $f:M \to \mathbb{R}$ be linear with
$f(m) \le p(m)$ for every $m \in M$. Then there exists a linear functional
$F:X \to \mathbb{R}$ such that $F|_M=f$ and $F(x) \le p(x)$ for every $x \in X$.

Work over ZF. The **real dominated-extension principle**, denoted **HB**, is the following assertion:

For every real vector space $X$, every sublinear functional $p:X\to\mathbb R$ in the sense of [[def-sublinear-functional]], every real linear subspace $M\le X$ in the sense of [[def-linear-subspace]], and every real linear functional $g:M\to\mathbb R$ in the sense of [[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]],
$$\bigl(\forall m\in M,\ g(m)\le p(m)\bigr)\ \Longrightarrow\ \exists F:X\to\mathbb R\ \bigl(F\text{ is real linear},\ F|_M=g,\ \forall x\in X,\ F(x)\le p(x)\bigr).$$

This names an additional principle; it does not assert a proof of HB in ZF. Subsequent results explicitly state when they assume HB. Neither topology nor completeness is part of this assertion. The subspace may be $\{0\}$ or all of $X$. Sublinearity at scalar zero gives $p(0)=0$, and a linear functional has value zero at zero.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then $$\Phi_X(t):=\mathbb E e^{it\cdot X}=\exp(it\cdot m-t^T\Sigma t/2)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R^d).$$ This transform uniquely determines the law, including singular Sigma.

Assume HB and countable choice. Let $B$ be a real separable Banach space. There is a sequence
$(\ell_j)_{j\ge1}\subseteq B^*$ with $\|\ell_j\|=1$ such that
$$\|x\|=\sup_{j\ge1}|\ell_j(x)|\qquad(x\in B).$$
If $B=\{0\}$, the conclusion is interpreted using the zero functional and the
supremum is $0$.

Let $B$ be a separable Banach space, and let $(\ell_j)_{j\ge1}\subseteq B^*$ satisfy the norming identity $\|x\|=\sup_{j\ge1}|\ell_j(x)|$ for every $x\in B$. If Borel probabilities $\mu,\nu$ on $B$ have equal finite-dimensional pushforwards under every finite subfamily of $(\ell_j)$, then $\mu=\nu$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ generating $\mathcal A$, and let $\mu,\nu$ be measures on $(X,\mathcal A)$ that agree on $\mathcal P$. Suppose there is an increasing sequence $(P_n)$ in $\mathcal P$ with

$$X=\bigcup_nP_n,\qquad \mu(P_n)=\nu(P_n)<+\infty\quad(n\in\mathbb N).$$

Then $\mu=\nu$ on $\mathcal A$.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. Then the following are
equivalent:

1. the family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent;
2. for every natural number $n\ge1$, every choice of distinct indices
   $i_0,\dots,i_{n-1}\in I$, and every choice of measurable sets
   $B_k\in\Sigma_{i_k}$,
   $$\mathbb P\bigl(X_{i_0}\in B_0,\dots,X_{i_{n-1}}\in B_{n-1}\bigr)=\prod_{k<n}\mathbb P(X_{i_k}\in B_k).$$

derivations.claim: On $(B\times B,\mathcal B(B)\otimes\mathcal B(B),\mu\otimes\mu)$ let $W(x,y)=x$ and $W'(x,y)=y$ be the coordinate copies. The product-measure rectangle formula makes them independent. A countable dense subset of $B$ and rational-radius balls give a countable base, and products of base sets give one for $B\times B$, so [F5] identifies the product sigma-algebra with $\mathcal B(B\times B)$. The coordinate projections are continuous, hence Borel; the maps $(x,y)\mapsto(x+y)/\sqrt2$ and $(x,y)\mapsto(x-y)/\sqrt2$ are continuous as well, so [F5] makes $U=(W+W')/\sqrt2$ and $V=(W-W')/\sqrt2$ Borel random elements. For any finite list of functionals used on either $U$ or $V$, the corresponding vectors from $W$ and $W'$ are independent centered Gaussian vectors, so [F6] makes their stack multivariate Gaussian. The finite coordinate vector of $(U,V)$ is a linear image of that stack, hence is also centered multivariate Gaussian.

Centering and independence give, for all $\ell,m\in B^*$, $E[\ell(U)m(V)]=\tfrac12(E[\ell(W)m(W)]-E[\ell(W)m(W')]+E[\ell(W')m(W)]-E[\ell(W')m(W')])=0$. Independence and centering give $E[\ell(U)m(U)]=E[\ell(W)m(W)]$ and $E[\ell(V)m(V)]=E[\ell(W)m(W)]$. Thus each finite coordinate vector of $U$ or $V$ is centered Gaussian with the same covariance as the corresponding vector of $W$, so [F2] gives matching finite laws.

By [A2], the HB and countable-choice hypotheses of [F1] and [F4] hold. The zero mixed covariances from step 2.1 let [F1] make $U,V$ independent, while [F4] upgrades their matching finite norming-coordinate laws to equality of Borel laws with $W$. Thus $U,V$ are independent copies of $W$.

Let $p(r)=P(\|W\|>r)$. By [F3] and $\|W\|<\infty$ almost surely, $p(r)\to0$ as $r\to\infty$; choose $s>0$ with $q:=1-p(s)>0$. For $r>s$, the event $\{\|W\|>r,\ \|W'\|\le s\}$ has probability $p(r)q$. On it, $\sqrt2\,U=W+W'$ and $\sqrt2\,V=W-W'$ imply $\|U\|>(r-s)/\sqrt2$ and $\|V\|>(r-s)/\sqrt2$, by the reverse triangle inequality. Since $U,V$ are independent copies by step 3.1, $p(r)q\le p((r-s)/\sqrt2)^2.$

Choose $r_0>s$ with $p(r_0)<q$, and define $r_{n+1}=\sqrt2\,r_n+s$. If $p(r_0)=0$, then $W$ is bounded almost surely and the theorem follows immediately. Otherwise put $\theta=p(r_0)/q\in(0,1)$. Iterating step 4.1 gives $p(r_n)\le q\,\theta^{2^n}$. The explicit recurrence solution is $r_n=(r_0+c)2^{n/2}-c$, where $c=s/(\sqrt2-1)$. Hence for all sufficiently large $n$, $r_n$ is bounded below by a positive multiple of $2^{n/2}$ and $r_{n+1}\le2r_n$. If $r_n<t\le r_{n+1}$, then $p(t)\le p(r_n)\le q e^{-|\log\theta|2^n}\le C e^{-b t^2}$ for constants $C,b>0$ independent of $n$. Thus $P(\|W\|>t)\le C e^{-b t^2}$ for all sufficiently large $t$.

Choose $0<a<b/3$. Partition according to $\|W\|\le r_N$ and the intervals $r_n<\|W\|\le r_{n+1}$ for sufficiently large fixed $N$. On the $n$th interval, $e^{a\|W\|^2}\le e^{a r_{n+1}^2}$, while step 5.1 bounds its probability by $C e^{-b r_n^2}$. Since $r_{n+1}^2/r_n^2\to2$, the resulting series is bounded for large $n$ by a constant times $e^{-(b-3a)r_n^2}$ and converges. The initial bounded interval contributes finitely. Therefore $E e^{a\|W\|^2}<\infty$, and then $\|W\|^2\le c_a e^{a\|W\|^2}$ for a finite constant $c_a$ proves the second claim.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be a real vector space, let
$M \subseteq X$ be a linear subspace, let
$p:X \to \mathbb{R}$ be sublinear, and let $f:M \to \mathbb{R}$ be linear with
$f(m) \le p(m)$ for every $m \in M$. Then there exists a linear functional
$F:X \to \mathbb{R}$ such that $F|_M=f$ and $F(x) \le p(x)$ for every $x \in X$.

Work over ZF. The **real dominated-extension principle**, denoted **HB**, is the following assertion:

For every real vector space $X$, every sublinear functional $p:X\to\mathbb R$ in the sense of [[def-sublinear-functional]], every real linear subspace $M\le X$ in the sense of [[def-linear-subspace]], and every real linear functional $g:M\to\mathbb R$ in the sense of [[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]],
$$\bigl(\forall m\in M,\ g(m)\le p(m)\bigr)\ \Longrightarrow\ \exists F:X\to\mathbb R\ \bigl(F\text{ is real linear},\ F|_M=g,\ \forall x\in X,\ F(x)\le p(x)\bigr).$$

This names an additional principle; it does not assert a proof of HB in ZF. Subsequent results explicitly state when they assume HB. Neither topology nor completeness is part of this assertion. The subspace may be $\{0\}$ or all of $X$. Sublinearity at scalar zero gives $p(0)=0$, and a linear functional has value zero at zero.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $W$ be a centered Borel Gaussian random
element in a real separable Banach space $B$. There is a constant $a>0$ such
that
$$E\exp(a\|W\|^2)<\infty.$$
In particular, $E\|W\|^2<\infty$.

Assume HB and countable choice. Let $B$ be a real separable Banach space. There is a sequence
$(\ell_j)_{j\ge1}\subseteq B^*$ with $\|\ell_j\|=1$ such that
$$\|x\|=\sup_{j\ge1}|\ell_j(x)|\qquad(x\in B).$$
If $B=\{0\}$, the conclusion is interpreted using the zero functional and the
supremum is $0$.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be non-negative. Then there exists a unique non-negative operator
$R:V\to V$ such that

$$R^2=T.$$

Assume AC. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then $$\Phi_X(t):=\mathbb E e^{it\cdot X}=\exp(it\cdot m-t^T\Sigma t/2)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R^d).$$ This transform uniquely determines the law, including singular Sigma.

Assume AC, DC, and countable choice. Let $Z\sim\gamma_d$ be standard Gaussian
on $\mathbb R^d$ and let
$f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be $L$-Lipschitz. If $L>0$, then for every $r>0$,
$$P\{f(Z)\ge E f(Z)+r\}\le e^{-r^2/(2L^2)}.$$
If $L=0$, the probability on the left is zero.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be an increasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$, so $E_n\subseteq E_{n+1}$. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\sup_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

No finiteness hypothesis is required.

derivations.claim: By [F1], $\sigma^2\le E\|W\|^2<\infty$. Choose a countable norming family $(\ell_j)_{j\ge1}$ from [F2], and let $F_n=\max_{1\le j\le n}|\ell_j(W)|$. Then $F_n\uparrow\|W\|$ and $EF_n\to E\|W\|$ by [F5].
If $\sigma>0$ and $r=0$, the probability is at most $1=e^0$, which is the required bound.

Suppose $\sigma>0$ and $r>0$. The vector $(\ell_1(W),\ldots,\ell_n(W))$ is centered Gaussian. By [F3] it has the law of $AZ$ for a matrix $A$ and a standard Gaussian vector $Z$. The function $z\mapsto\max_{j\le n}|(Az)_j|$ is $\max_j\|\operatorname{row}_j(A)\|_2$-Lipschitz, and $\|\operatorname{row}_j(A)\|_2^2=E[\ell_j(W)^2]\le\sigma^2$. Applying [F4] gives $P(F_n>EF_n+r)\le e^{-r^2/(2\sigma^2)}$. Since $EF_n\le E\|W\|$, the event $\{F_n>E\|W\|+r\}$ is contained in that tail event.
If $\sigma>0$ and $r>0$, the events $\{F_n>E\|W\|+r\}$ increase to $\{\|W\|>E\|W\|+r\}$. Continuity from below [F6] and step 2.1 give the claimed bound.

If $\sigma=0$, each $\ell_j(W)$ has zero variance, so countably many probability-one equalities give $\ell_j(W)=0$ for every $j$ almost surely; [F2] then gives $W=0$ almost surely. Hence the displayed tail probability is zero for every $r\ge0$.

derivations.claim: For $\ell\in B^*$, the map $\omega\mapsto\ell(W(\omega))W(\omega)$ is Borel as the composition of $W$ with the continuous map $x\mapsto\ell(x)x$. It is strongly measurable by [F2], and $\|\ell(W)W\|\le\|\ell\|\|W\|^2$ is integrable by [F1]. Hence [F3] defines $C\ell=E[\ell(W)W]$ as a Bochner integral.

By [F1], $E|\ell(W)|^2\le\|\ell\|^2E\|W\|^2<\infty$ for every $\ell\in B^*$; Cauchy–Schwarz [F6] therefore makes $E|m(W)\ell(W)|$ finite. Applying $m\in B^*$ to the Bochner integral using [F4] gives $m(C\ell)=E[m(W)\ell(W)]$. Thus $Q(\ell,m)=m(C\ell)$ is a finite symmetric bilinear form, nonnegative on the diagonal. Again by [F6], $|Q(\ell,m)|\le Q(\ell,\ell)^{1/2}Q(m,m)^{1/2}$, so $Q(\ell,\ell)=0$ implies $Q(\ell,m)=0$ for every $m$; therefore $N$ is the radical of $Q$ and the quotient form is an inner product.

If $\ell\in N$, step 2.1 gives $m(C\ell)=0$ for every $m$, so $C\ell=0$ by [F5]. Conversely, if $C\ell=0$, taking $m=\ell$ in step 2.1 gives $Q(\ell,\ell)=0$, hence $\ell\in N$. Therefore $[\ell]\mapsto C\ell$ is well-defined and injective on $B^*/N$.

By [F3] and [F6], $\|C\ell\|\le E(|\ell(W)|\|W\|) \le Q(\ell,\ell)^{1/2}(E\|W\|^2)^{1/2}.$ So the map on the quotient is bounded and extends uniquely to its Hilbert completion because $B$ is complete. For every $m\in B^*$, the identity $m(C\ell)=\langle[\ell],[m]\rangle_H$ from step 2.1 extends by continuity to $m(iu)=\langle u,[m]\rangle_H$. If $iu=0$, then $u$ is orthogonal to the dense subspace $B^*/N$, so $u=0$. The extension is injective, proving all claims.

Let $z_h=J(u)$ and choose $[\ell_n]\to u$ in the quotient completion; put $Z_n=\ell_n(W)$. Since $L^2(\mu)$ is formed from Borel-measurable functions on $(B,\mathcal B(B),\mu)$, choose a Borel-measurable representative $z_h$ of its class. Approximation in $L^2$ gives uniqueness up to $\mu$-null sets, with $\|Z_n-z_h\|_2\to0$. For fixed $\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_m\in B^*$, set $Y_n=(Z_n,\ell_1(W),\ldots,\ell_m(W))$ and $Y=(z_h,\ell_1(W),\ldots,\ell_m(W))$. Each $Y_n$ is centered multivariate Gaussian by [F2]. Cauchy–Schwarz [F5] gives $E|Z_n-z_h|\le\|Z_n-z_h\|_2\to0$, $|E[Z_n\ell_j(W)]-E[z_h\ell_j(W)]|\le\|Z_n-z_h\|_2\|\ell_j(W)\|_2\to0$, and $|E[Z_n^2]-E[z_h^2]|\le\|Z_n-z_h\|_2(\|Z_n\|_2+\|z_h\|_2)\to0$. For each $t=(s,t_1,\ldots,t_m)$, $|E e^{it\cdot Y_n}-E e^{it\cdot Y}|\le |s|E|Z_n-z_h|\to0$. By [F2], $E e^{it\cdot Y_n}=e^{-t^\mathsf T\Sigma_n t/2}$, so the characteristic function of $Y$ is $e^{-t^\mathsf T\Sigma t/2}$, the characteristic function of $N(0,\Sigma)$. Uniqueness in [F2] proves that $Y$ is jointly Gaussian. Finally, its mixed covariances satisfy $\operatorname{Cov}(z_h,\ell_j(W))=\lim_n\langle[\ell_n],[\ell_j]\rangle_H=\langle u,[\ell_j]\rangle_H=\ell_j(h)$ by [F1].

Choose a countable norming family $(\ell_j)_{j\ge1}$ for $B$ using [A1, A2], and put $D=\exp(z_h-\|h\|_H^2/2)$. By [F2], for every finite subvector $L=(\ell_1(W),\ldots,\ell_m(W))$, the joint vector $(z_h,L)$ is a linear image of a finite standard Gaussian vector. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be a real vector space, let
$M \subseteq X$ be a linear subspace, let
$p:X \to \mathbb{R}$ be sublinear, and let $f:M \to \mathbb{R}$ be linear with
$f(m) \le p(m)$ for every $m \in M$. Then there exists a linear functional
$F:X \to \mathbb{R}$ such that $F|_M=f$ and $F(x) \le p(x)$ for every $x \in X$.

Work over ZF. The **real dominated-extension principle**, denoted **HB**, is the following assertion:

For every real vector space $X$, every sublinear functional $p:X\to\mathbb R$ in the sense of [[def-sublinear-functional]], every real linear subspace $M\le X$ in the sense of [[def-linear-subspace]], and every real linear functional $g:M\to\mathbb R$ in the sense of [[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]],
$$\bigl(\forall m\in M,\ g(m)\le p(m)\bigr)\ \Longrightarrow\ \exists F:X\to\mathbb R\ \bigl(F\text{ is real linear},\ F|_M=g,\ \forall x\in X,\ F(x)\le p(x)\bigr).$$

This names an additional principle; it does not assert a proof of HB in ZF. Subsequent results explicitly state when they assume HB. Neither topology nor completeness is part of this assertion. The subspace may be $\{0\}$ or all of $X$. Sublinearity at scalar zero gives $p(0)=0$, and a linear functional has value zero at zero.

Assume AC. For $d\ge1$, let $\gamma_d$ be standard Gaussian measure on $\mathbb R^d$,
let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be Borel, and let
$A+rB_2^d=\{a+ru:a\in A,\ |u|\le1\}$. Then for every $r\ge0$,
$$\gamma_{d,*}(A+rB_2^d)\ge \Phi\!\left(\Phi^{-1}(\gamma_d(A))+r\right),$$
where $\gamma_{d,*}(S)=\sup\{\gamma_d(K):K\subseteq S,\ K\text{ compact}\}$ is Gaussian inner measure, and $\Phi^{-1}(0)=-\infty$, $\Phi^{-1}(1)=+\infty$.

Assume AC. Let $W$ be a centered Borel Gaussian random element in a real separable
Banach space $B$, with law $\mu$. For $\ell\in B^*$ define
$$C\ell=E[\ell(W)W]\in B,\qquad Q(\ell,m)=E[\ell(W)m(W)]\quad(\ell,m\in B^*).$$
The **Cameron–Martin reproducing-kernel Hilbert space** $H$ is the completion
of $B^*/N$ in the inner product induced by $Q$, where
$N=\{\ell\in B^*:Q(\ell,\ell)=0\}$. The canonical map sends the class of
$\ell$ to $C\ell$ and extends continuously to an injective map $i:H\to B$;
we identify $H$ with its image in $B$ and use the completed Hilbert norm
$\|\cdot\|_H$. The preceding construction is well-defined by
[[thm-banach-gaussian-covariance-rkhs-is-well-defined]].

The term *RKHS* here denotes this covariance-induced Hilbert space of shifts
inside $B$; it is not the space of all continuous functions on an arbitrary
index set.

Assume AC. Under the hypotheses and notation of
[[def-banach-gaussian-covariance-operator-and-rkhs]], each $C\ell$ exists as a
Bochner integral; $Q$ is a finite positive-semidefinite bilinear form;
$N=\{\ell:Q(\ell,\ell)=0\}$ is its nullspace; and the induced map from the
completion of $B^*/N$ to $B$ is continuous and injective. Thus the definition
identifies a Hilbert space of shifts in $B$.

Assume AC. Let $\mu$ be a centered tight Borel Gaussian law on a real separable Banach
space $B$, and let $H\subset B$ be its covariance RKHS. The closed Hilbert
unit ball
$$H_1=\{h\in H:\|h\|_H\le1\}$$
is compact in the Banach norm.

Assume countable choice. If $P$ is Polish and $\mu$ is a Borel probability measure on $P$, then for every Borel $A\subseteq P$ and $\varepsilon>0$ there is a compact $K\subseteq A$ with $\mu(A\setminus K)<\varepsilon$.

A topological space $X$ is **separable** if some at most countable subset $D\subseteq X$ is dense in $X$ ([[def-dense-top]], [[def-countable]]). Equivalently, every nonempty open subset of $X$ meets $D$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a decreasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$. If $\mu(E_{n_0})<+\infty$ for some $n_0$, then

$$\mu\left(\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\inf_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

Assume HB and let $X$ be a real or complex normed space. For each $x\ne0$ there is $f\in X^*$ with $\|f\|=1$ and $f(x)=\|x\|$, a positive real number also in the complex case. Hence $X^*$ separates distinct points, and
$$\|x\|=\max_{f\in X^*,\ \|f\|\le1}|f(x)|\qquad(x\in X).$$
The formula includes $x=0$ and the zero space. Moreover, if $H\subseteq X^*$ has norm-dense scalar-linear span and $h(x)=0$ for all $h\in H$, then $x=0$.

Set $G=\sum_{j=1}^m\varphi_j(W)e_j$ and $S=T\circ i|_Q$. The vector of coefficients is standard Gaussian on $Q$ because its covariance matrix is the identity. For each $i$, $[\ell_i]=\sum_j\langle[\ell_i],e_j\rangle_H e_j$; by the covariance quotient and [F2], the residual $\ell_i(W)-\ell_i(iG)$ has variance $\|[\ell_i]-\sum_j\langle[\ell_i],e_j\rangle_H e_j\|_H^2=0$. Hence $T(W)=S(G)$ almost surely. The map $S$ is injective: if $S(q)=0$, then $\langle q,[\ell_i]\rangle_H=0$ for every $i$, and these classes span $Q$, so $q=0$.

Now let $A\subseteq B$ be Borel with $0<\mu(A)<1$, and fix $ eta<\Phi^{-1}(\mu(A))$. By [F4] choose compact $K\subseteq A$ with $\mu(K)>\Phi( eta)$. For each $x
otin K$ and $y\in K$, [F7] gives $\ell_y\in B^*$ with $\ell_y(x)
e\ell_y(y)$. The open sets $U_y=\{z:|\ell_y(z)-\ell_y(y)|<|\ell_y(x)-\ell_y(y)|/3\}$ cover $K$; compactness gives a finite subcover $U_{y_1},\ldots,U_{y_q}$. For every $z\in K$, some $i$ has $z\in U_{y_i}$, which forces $\ell_{y_i}(z)
e\ell_{y_i}(x)$. Thus the finite coordinate map $T_x=(\ell_{y_1},\ldots,\ell_{y_q})$ satisfies $T_x(x)
otin T_x(K)$. The cylinder $F_x=T_x^{-1}(T_x(K))$ is closed, contains $K$, and excludes $x$, since $T_x(K)$ is compact. The open complements $B\setminus F_x$ cover $B\setminus K$. By [F5] this cover has a countable subcover: for every basis element meeting $B\setminus K$ and contained in a cover member, countable choice selects one such member; every point is covered by one selected member. If the subcover is finite, repeat one member to index it by $j\ge1$.

If $m=0$, then $T(W)=0$ almost surely, so $\mu(F)$ is zero or one; the endpoint convention, $0\in H_1$, and inner regularity [F4] give the claimed inequality. If $m>0$, define $E=S^{-1}(M)\subset Q$. It is closed and $\mu(F)=\gamma_Q(E)$. For $r\ge0$, $E_r=E+r(Q\cap H_1)$ is closed because its second summand is compact. Thus [F4] identifies its inner and ordinary Gaussian measures, and [F1] gives $\gamma_Q(E_r)\ge\Phi(\Phi^{-1}(\gamma_Q(E))+r)$. Let $C_r=T^{-1}(S(E_r))$, a closed finite-coordinate cylinder because $S$ is a linear isomorphism from finite-dimensional $Q$ onto the closed subspace $S(Q)$; injectivity of $S$ and $T(W)=S(G)$ give $\mu(C_r)=\gamma_Q(E_r)$. If $y\in C_r$, write $T(y)=S(u+v)$ with $u\in E$ and $v\in r(Q\cap H_1)$. Then $T(y-i(v))=S(u)\in M$, so $y-i(v)\in F$ and $y\in F+rH_1$. Each $G_n$ is a closed finite-coordinate cylinder because it is a finite intersection of such cylinders; the sequence decreases, $\bigcap_nG_n=K$, and $\mu(G_n)\ge\mu(K)>\Phi(\beta)$. Applying step 2.1 yields $\mu_*(G_n+rH_1)\ge\Phi(\beta+r)$. The set $G_n+rH_1$ is closed: if $a_j+h_j$ converges with $a_j\in G_n$ and $h_j\in rH_1$, compactness [F3] gives a convergent subsequence of $h_j$, after which closedness of $G_n$ gives a limit representation. Thus [F4] gives equality of its inner and ordinary measures.

The closed sets $G_n+rH_1$ decrease and their intersection is $K+rH_1$. Indeed, if $x=a_n+h_n$ with $a_n\in G_n$ and $h_n\in rH_1$ for every $n$, compactness [F3] gives a subsequence $h_{n_j}\to h\in rH_1$; then $a_{n_j}\to x-h$, and for each fixed $N$ the tail belongs to the closed set $G_N$, so $x-h\in K$. The reverse inclusion is immediate. Continuity from above [F6] gives $\mu(K+rH_1)\ge\Phi(\beta+r)$. Since $K\subseteq A$, $\mu_*(A+rH_1)\ge\Phi(\beta+r)$. Letting $\beta\uparrow\Phi^{-1}(\mu(A))$ proves the interior-probability case. If $\mu(A)=0$ the right side is zero; if $\mu(A)=1$, inner regularity [F4] and $0\in H_1$ give $\mu_*(A+rH_1)=1$.

Assume AC and countable choice. Let $\mu$ be a centered tight Borel Gaussian law on a real separable Banach
space $B$, with covariance RKHS $H$, and let $w_0\in\overline H^{\,B}$. For
$\varepsilon>0$, write
$\varepsilon B^\circ=\{x\in B:\|x\|_B<\varepsilon\}$ and define the
**concentration function**
$$\phi_{w_0}(\varepsilon) =\inf_{\substack{h\in H\\\|h-w_0\|_B<\varepsilon}} \left\{\|h\|_H^2-\log\mu(\varepsilon B^\circ)\right\}.$$
The feasible set is nonempty because $w_0$ lies in the Banach-norm closure of
$H$. Also $\mu(\varepsilon B^\circ)>0$ because $0\in\operatorname{supp}\mu$;
thus the logarithm is finite. The value is finite and nonnegative. The support assertion used here is
[[thm-support-of-banach-gaussian-is-closure-of-rkhs]].

Assume AC and countable choice. Let $W$ be a centered Borel Gaussian random
element in a real separable
Banach space $B$, with law $\mu$ and covariance RKHS $H\subseteq B$. For
$h\in H$, let $z_h$ be the $L^2(\mu)$-limit of the coordinate functions
$\ell(x)$ representing a sequence of classes $[\ell]\to i^{-1}h$ in the
completion $H$. The limit has a Borel-measurable version and does not depend
on the approximating sequence. If $\mu_h$ denotes the law of $W+h$, then
$$\frac{d\mu_h}{d\mu}(x) =\exp\!\left(z_h(x)-\frac12\|h\|_H^2\right).$$
In particular, $\mu_h$ and $\mu$ are equivalent. If $h=C\ell$ for
$\ell\in B^*$, then $z_h(x)=\ell(x)$ $\mu$-almost surely and
$\|h\|_H^2=E[\ell(W)^2]$; these formulas are independent of the choice of
representative $\ell$.

Assume AC and countable choice. Let $\mu$ be a centered tight Borel Gaussian law on a real separable Banach
space $B$, with covariance RKHS $H$ and unit ball $H_1$. For every Borel set
$A\subseteq B$ and $r\ge0$,
$$\mu_*(A+rH_1)\ge \Phi\!\left(\Phi^{-1}(\mu(A))+r\right),$$
where $\mu_*(S)=\sup\{\mu(K):K\subseteq S,\ K\text{ compact}\}$ is the inner
measure and $\Phi^{-1}(0)=-\infty$, $\Phi^{-1}(1)=+\infty$. When
$A+rH_1$ is Borel, its inner measure equals its ordinary $\mu$-measure.

space $B$, and let $H\subset B$ be its covariance RKHS. The closed Hilbert

$$H_1=\{h\in H:\|h\|_H\le1\}$$
is compact in the Banach norm.

By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Assume countable choice. If $P$ is Polish and $\mu$ is a Borel probability measure on $P$, then for every Borel $A\subseteq P$ and $\varepsilon>0$ there is a compact $K\subseteq A$ with $\mu(A\setminus K)<\varepsilon$.

A topological space $X$ is **separable** if some at most countable subset $D\subseteq X$ is dense in $X$ ([[def-dense-top]], [[def-countable]]). Equivalently, every nonempty open subset of $X$ meets $D$.

The map $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[def-real-numbers]]) is an embedding of ordered
fields. Every real is approximated by rationals: for $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and
rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $q \in \mathbb{Q}$ with
$|x - \hat q| < \hat\varepsilon$. Consequently, strictly between any two
reals lies a rational.

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).

If $A$ and $B$ are at most countable ([[def-countable]]) then so is
$A \times B$.

**No choice principle is used**: the two enumerations are given, and the
enumeration of the product is written down from them.

Let $X,Y$ be second-countable topological spaces and give $X\times Y$ the
product topology. Then
$$\mathcal B(X\times Y)=\mathcal B(X)\otimes\mathcal B(Y).$$

Banach space $B$, with law $\mu$ and covariance RKHS $H\subseteq B$. For
$h\in H$, let $z_h$ be the $L^2(\mu)$-limit of the coordinate functions
$\ell(x)$ representing a sequence of classes $[\ell]\to i^{-1}h$ in the
completion $H$. The limit has a Borel-measurable version and does not depend
on the approximating sequence. If $\mu_h$ denotes the law of $W+h$, then
$$\frac{d\mu_h}{d\mu}(x) =\exp\!\left(z_h(x)-\frac12\|h\|_H^2\right).$$

$\ell\in B^*$, then $z_h(x)=\ell(x)$ $\mu$-almost surely and
$\|h\|_H^2=E[\ell(W)^2]$; these formulas are independent of the choice of
representative $\ell$.

Assume HB and countable choice. Let $B$ be a real separable Banach space. There is a sequence
$(\ell_j)_{j\ge1}\subseteq B^*$ with $\|\ell_j\|=1$ such that
$$\|x\|=\sup_{j\ge1}|\ell_j(x)|\qquad(x\in B).$$
If $B=\{0\}$, the conclusion is interpreted using the zero functional and the
supremum is $0$.

Let $B$ be a separable Banach space, and let $(\ell_j)_{j\ge1}\subseteq B^*$ satisfy the norming identity $\|x\|=\sup_{j\ge1}|\ell_j(x)|$ for every $x\in B$. If Borel probabilities $\mu,\nu$ on $B$ have equal finite-dimensional pushforwards under every finite subfamily of $(\ell_j)$, then $\mu=\nu$.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

A pseudometric $d$ on a set $T$ is a nonnegative symmetric function $d:T\times T\to[0,\infty)$ with $d(t,t)=0$ and $d(s,t)\le d(s,u)+d(u,t)$; distinct points may have distance zero. For a nonempty subset $\mathcal F\subseteq T$ and $\epsilon>0$, the covering number $N(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)$ is the least finite $k$ for which there are centers $f_1,\ldots,f_k\in\mathcal F$ such that every $f\in\mathcal F$ satisfies $d(f,f_j)\le\epsilon$ for some $j$. It is $+\infty$ if no finite cover exists. Set $N(\epsilon,\varnothing,d)=1$.

The packing number $D(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)$ is the largest size of a finite subset $\{f_1,\ldots,f_k\}\subseteq\mathcal F$ whose distinct members have pairwise distance strictly greater than $\epsilon$. If the sizes of such finite subsets are unbounded, put $D=+\infty$; put $D(\epsilon,\varnothing,d)=0$. These conventions give the radius comparison proved in [[lem-packing-covering-number-comparison]]. The metric entropy is $H(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d):=\log N(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)$ for nonempty classes, with $\log(+\infty)=+\infty$.

For a probability measure $Q$ on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ and a measurable real function $g$, set $\|g\|_{Q,r}:=(\int |g|^r\,dQ)^{1/r}$ for $1\le r<\infty$ when the integral is finite, using the real-power convention, including $0^{1/r}=0$, of [[def-real-power]]. If the integral is $+\infty$, define $\|g\|_{Q,r}:=+\infty$ directly. The function $|g|$ is measurable by [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]], and [[lem-real-power-preserves-measurability]] makes $|g|^r$ measurable, so this nonnegative extended integral is well-defined. On a class of functions with finite such norms, $d_{Q,r}(f,g):=\|f-g\|_{Q,r}$ is a pseudometric: nonnegativity, symmetry, and zero diagonal follow from the absolute value, and the triangle inequality is [[thm-minkowski-inequality-for-integrals]]. Functions that agree $Q$-almost everywhere have distance zero. We write $N(\epsilon,\mathcal F,L^r(Q))$ for this covering number.

For measurable real endpoints $\ell\le u$ $Q$-almost everywhere, the bracket $[\ell,u]$ is the set of measurable functions $f$ satisfying $\ell\le f\le u$ $Q$-almost everywhere. Its $L^r(Q)$ width is $\|u-\ell\|_{Q,r}$. The bracketing number $N_{[]} (\epsilon,\mathcal F,L^r(Q))$ is the least number of such brackets of width at most $\epsilon$ that cover $\mathcal F$, or $+\infty$ if no finite cover exists; for the empty class set it equal to $1$. Centers of metric covers are in $\mathcal F$; bracket endpoints need not be.

derivations.claim: The hypothesis [F1] implies $p\ge e^{-t}>0$, because every candidate $h$ has $\|h\|_H^2\ge0$. Fix $h\in H$. Take a countable norming family for $B$ and append the scalar coordinate $z_h$; this is a countable norming family for $B\times\mathbb R$ with the maximum product norm. By [F7], each finite coordinate vector is centered Gaussian and hence invariant under negation, so countable law determination makes the joint law symmetric under $(x,z)\mapsto(-x,-z)$. Thus, since $\varepsilon B^\circ$ is symmetric, $\int_{\varepsilon B^\circ}e^{-z_h(x)}\,d\mu(x) =\int_{\varepsilon B^\circ}\cosh(z_h(x))\,d\mu(x) \ge p.$ The Cameron–Martin identity [F2] for $-h$ now gives $\mu(h+\varepsilon B^\circ)\ge e^{-\|h\|_H^2/2}p$.

For each $\delta>0$, choose $h\in H$ with $\|h-w_0\|_B<\varepsilon$ and $\|h\|_H^2-\log p<\phi_{w_0}(\varepsilon)+\delta\le t+\delta$. Since $\|h\|_H^2/2-\log p\le\|h\|_H^2-\log p<t+\delta$, and $h+\varepsilon B^\circ\subset w_0+2\varepsilon B^\circ$, step 1.1 gives $\mu\{\|W-w_0\|_B<2\varepsilon\}\ge e^{-t-\delta}$. Letting $\delta\downarrow0$ proves the small-ball lower bound.

Let $b=\Phi^{-1}(e^{-Ct})<0$ and $M=-2b>0$, and set $B_n=\varepsilon B^\circ+MH_1$. This is open, hence measurable. Since $p\ge e^{-t}$ and $C>1$, monotonicity of $\Phi^{-1}$ gives $\Phi^{-1}(p)>b$. By [F3], $\mu(B_n)\ge \Phi(\Phi^{-1}(p)+M) >\Phi(-b)=1-e^{-Ct}.$ The set $B_n$ is open and therefore Borel, so [F6] identifies its inner measure with $\mu(B_n)$. Thus $\mu(B\setminus B_n)\le e^{-Ct}$.

Choose a maximal finite set $\{h_1,\ldots,h_N\}\subset MH_1$ with pairwise distances greater than $2\varepsilon$; such a set exists and covers $MH_1$ by closed $2\varepsilon$-balls because $MH_1$ is compact by [F4]. The open balls $h_i+\varepsilon B^\circ$ are disjoint. Step 1.1 and $\|h_i\|_H\le M$ imply each has $\mu$-measure at least $e^{-M^2/2}p$. Hence $N e^{-M^2/2}p\le1$ and $\log N\le M^2/2-\log p\le M^2/2+t$. Every point of $B_n$ is $x+h$ with $x\in\varepsilon B^\circ$ and $h\in MH_1$, so it lies within $3\varepsilon$ of some $h_i$. Also $h_i=0+h_i\in B_n$ because $0\in\varepsilon B^\circ$. Thus these are admissible centers in the covering-number convention [F8], and $N(3\varepsilon,B_n,\|\cdot\|_B)\le N$.

Completing the square in the standard normal density [F5] gives $E e^{-\lambda Z}=e^{\lambda^2/2}$. For $x\ge0$, on $\{Z\le-x\}$ one has $e^{-xZ}\ge e^{x^2}$, so $\Phi(-x)=P(Z\le-x)\le e^{-x^2}E e^{-xZ}=e^{-x^2/2}$. With $x=\sqrt{2Ct}$ this gives $\Phi(-\sqrt{2Ct})\le e^{-Ct}=\Phi(b)$, hence $-\sqrt{2Ct}\le b<0$ and $b^2\le2Ct$. Consequently $\log N(3\varepsilon,B_n,\|\cdot\|_B)\le2b^2+t\le4Ct+t\le5Ct\le6Ct$, using $C>1$. Step 2.2 supplies the complement bound and step 2.1 the small-ball bound. Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a set, let $m:T\to\mathbb R$, and let
$k:T\times T\to\mathbb R$ be symmetric and positive semidefinite, meaning that
for every finite list $t_1,\ldots,t_n\in T$ and every $a\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$\sum_{i,j=1}^n a_i a_j k(t_i,t_j)\ge0.$$
There is a unique probability measure $\mu$ on the cylinder sigma-algebra
$\mathcal C_T$ of $\mathbb R^T$ whose marginal on each finite-coordinate space
$\mathbb R^F$, for $F\subseteq T$ finite, is the Gaussian law with mean
$(m(t))_{t\in F}$ and covariance matrix $(k(s,t))_{s,t\in F}$. The coordinate
process $X_t(x)=x(t)$ is Gaussian, has mean function $m$, and has covariance
kernel $k$. This construction gives only the cylinder-space process; it
asserts no sample-path continuity, joint measurability in $(t,x)$, or tight
Banach-valued law.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a decreasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$. If $\mu(E_{n_0})<+\infty$ for some $n_0$, then

$$\mu\left(\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\inf_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

Let $\mu$ be a measure and let $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be measurable. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k).$$

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ one also has

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k<m}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k<m}\mu(E_k),$$

including $m=0$, where both sides are $0$.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ generating $\mathcal A$, and let $\mu,\nu$ be measures on $(X,\mathcal A)$ that agree on $\mathcal P$. Suppose there is an increasing sequence $(P_n)$ in $\mathcal P$ with

$$X=\bigcup_nP_n,\qquad \mu(P_n)=\nu(P_n)<+\infty\quad(n\in\mathbb N).$$

Then $\mu=\nu$ on $\mathcal A$.

Assume AC. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then $$\Phi_X(t):=\mathbb E e^{it\cdot X}=\exp(it\cdot m-t^T\Sigma t/2)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R^d).$$ This transform uniquely determines the law, including singular Sigma.

derivations.claim: For any finite list of indices $t_i$ and real coefficients $a_i$, $\sum_{i,j}a_i a_j k(t_i,t_j)=\sum_t(\sum_{i:t_i=t}a_i)^2\ge0$, so $k$ is positive semidefinite. By [F1], its zero-mean cylinder law has marginal $N_d(0,I_d)$ on every set of $d$ distinct coordinates. The independent standard-normal vector in [F2] also has law $N_d(0,I_d)$. Their characteristic functions agree by [F6], whose uniqueness assertion identifies the two laws. Thus every finite family of distinct coordinates is independent and standard normal.

Fix $N$. For $M\ge N$, finite-coordinate independence gives $P(|Z_k|\le1\text{ for all }N\le k\le M)=(1-q)^{M-N+1}$. These events decrease as $M\to\infty$, so [F3] shows $P(|Z_k|\le1\text{ for every }k\ge N)=0$. The event that only finitely many $|Z_k|$ exceed $1$ is the countable union over $N$ of these null events; [F4] makes that union null, so almost surely infinitely many coordinates satisfy $|Z_k|>1$.

Infinitely many terms of $\sum_k Z_k^2$ exceed $1$, hence the sum diverges almost surely. The set $\ell^2\subset\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$ is cylinder-measurable because it equals $\bigcup_{m\ge1}\bigcap_{N\ge1}\{\sum_{k\le N}x_k^2\le m\}$; its cylinder probability is therefore zero by step 2.1. If an $\ell^2$-valued Borel random element had these finite-coordinate laws, its coordinate map into $\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$ would be measurable for the cylinder sigma-algebra, so its pushforward would agree with the given cylinder law on every finite-coordinate cylinder. By [F5], the two probability measures are equal; but the pushforward assigns probability one to $\ell^2$, contradicting its zero cylinder probability. Thus no Borel $\ell^2$-valued random element, and in particular no tight Borel $\ell^2$ prior, has these finite-coordinate laws.

The map $z\mapsto(z,2z)$ is continuous, so its pushforward of the standard normal law is a Borel probability on $B$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.

Work over ZF. The **real dominated-extension principle**, denoted **HB**, is the following assertion:

For every real vector space $X$, every sublinear functional $p:X\to\mathbb R$ in the sense of [[def-sublinear-functional]], every real linear subspace $M\le X$ in the sense of [[def-linear-subspace]], and every real linear functional $g:M\to\mathbb R$ in the sense of [[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]],
