derivations.claim: The kernel $K$ in [F2] is a probability kernel because, for fixed $(F,\sigma,x)$, $A\mapsto F(A)$ is a probability measure, while for fixed Borel $A$, $(F,\sigma,x)\mapsto F(A)$ is measurable by the evaluation sigma-algebra. The integrand $(\sigma,x,z)\mapsto(\sigma\sqrt{2\pi})^{-1}\exp(-(x-z)^2/(2\sigma^2))$ is continuous on $(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^2$ and hence product-measurable. Therefore [F3] makes its integral against $K$ jointly measurable.

The integrand is strictly positive, so its integral against a probability measure is positive. It is bounded above by $(\sigma\sqrt{2\pi})^{-1}$, so the integral is finite and has the stated upper bound.

By [F4], $\int_{\mathbb R}p_{F,\sigma}(x)\,dx=\int_{\mathbb R}\left(\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-(x-z)^2/(2\sigma^2)}\,dx\right)F(dz)=\int_{\mathbb R}1\,F(dz)=1,$ where the inner integral is one by [F1] and $F$ has total mass one. Thus $p_{F,\sigma}$ is a probability density.

For every Borel set $B\subseteq\mathbb R$, Tonelli [F4] gives $\int_Bp_{F,\sigma}(x)\,dx=\int_{\mathbb R}\left(\int_B\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-(x-z)^2/(2\sigma^2)}\,dx\right)F(dz)$. The inner integral is $N(z,\sigma^2)(B)$ by [F1], so the right side is the convolution measure $(F*N(0,\sigma^2))(B)$ by its definition. Hence this density represents the convolution law in the Statement.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This

measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since
$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$ by
[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$

[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and

[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts

[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $1/e=\exp(-1)$ by
[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and $\log(1/e)=-1$ by

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

derivations.claim: Put $u=p/q$ on $\{q>0\}$. The absolute-continuity premise gives $p=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $\{q=0\}$. Define $g(u)=(\sqrt u-1)^2$ and $a(u)=(u\log u-u+1)/g(u)$, $b(u)=u(\log u)^2/g(u)$ for $u\ne1$, with their limiting values at $u=1$ and $u=0$. At zero, set $s=1/u$; for $s\ge1$, [F3] gives $0\le\log s\le\int_1^s t^{-3/4}dt\le4s^{1/4}$. Hence $u\log u=-(\log s)/s\to0$ and $u(\log u)^2=(\log s)^2/s\le16s^{-1/2}\to0$, so $a(0)=1$ and $b(0)=0$. At one, $\log u/(u-1)\to1$ by [F3], $g(u)/(u-1)^2=1/(\sqrt u+1)^2\to1/4$, and $u(\log u)^2/(u-1)^2\to1$. Also $u\log u-u+1=\int_1^u\log t\,dt$, so $[u\log u-u+1]/(u-1)^2\to1/2$; therefore $a(1)=2$ and $b(1)=4$. Thus $a,b$ are continuous on $[0,2]$ and bounded there.

For $u\ge2$, $g(u)=u(1-u^{-1/2})^2\ge u(1-2^{-1/2})^2$, while $0\le u\log u-u+1\le u\log u$ and $u(\log u)^2$ retain their displayed forms. Hence $a(u)\le C\log u$ and $b(u)\le C(\log u)^2$ for a universal $C$. Combining with step 1.1, for every $0\le u\le R$, $u\log u-u+1\le Cg(u)(1+\log^+R),\qquad u(\log u)^2\le Cg(u)(1+\log^+R)^2.$

Integrating the first inequality in step 2.1 against $q\,d\mu$ gives the KL bound, since $\int q(u\log u-u+1)d\mu=\int p\log(p/q)d\mu$ by $\int p=\int q=1$ and [F2]. Integrating the second gives the log-square bound. Finally $\int qg\,d\mu=h^2$ by [F1], so both right sides have the claimed factors of $h^2$.

Assume AC. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma>0$, the normal law $N(m,\sigma^2)$
of [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]] has Lebesgue density
$$g_{m,\sigma}(y)=\frac1\sigma\frac{e^{-((y-m)/\sigma)^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}e^{-(y-m)^2/(2\sigma^2)}.$$

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval and let $f:X\times I\to\mathbb C$
be such that:

1. for every $t\in I$, the function $x\mapsto f(x,t)$ is integrable;
2. for almost every $x$, the map $t\mapsto f(x,t)$ is differentiable on $I$;
3. for every $t\in I$, the function
   $$x\mapsto \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t),$$
   extended by zero where the derivative is undefined, is measurable;
4. there are a measurable null set $N$ and a nonnegative measurable function
   $g$ with
   $$\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$$
   and
   $$\left|\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t)\right|\le g(x)$$
   for every $t\in I$ and every $x\in X\setminus N$.

Then
$$F(t):=\int f(x,t)\,d\mu(x)$$
is differentiable on $I$, and
$$F'(t)=\int \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t)\,d\mu(x),$$
with the same zero extension in the last integral.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $u, v : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at
every point of $[a,b]$ as functions on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]). Suppose
$u'$ and $v'$ are integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then $uv'$
and $u'v$ are integrable and

$$\int_a^b u\,v' \;=\; u(b)v(b) - u(a)v(a) \;-\; \int_a^b u'\,v .$$

**The integrability of $u'$ and $v'$ is a hypothesis, not a formality.** Without
it the two integrals in the display need not exist at all, and the identity is
then not false but ill-formed; that is
the false statement that deletes it on the companion
page. The hypothesis is automatic when $u$ and $v$ are continuously
differentiable, since a continuous function on $[a,b]$ is integrable
([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]).

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: At every zero of the nonnegative differentiable function $p$, $p'=0$. At each accumulation point of its zero set, differentiation along zeros of $p'$ gives $p''=0$; isolated zeros form a countable set. Thus $p''=0$ almost everywhere on $\{p=0\}$. Put $r=p''/p$ on $\{p>0\}$ and zero elsewhere. Then $p''=rp$ almost everywhere, $\int r^2p=J$, and [F2] gives $\int|p''|\le\sqrt J$. Both $p$ and $p''$ are continuous and compactly supported.

Let $P_t f=f*\phi_{\sqrt t}$ for $t>0$. Direct differentiation of [F1] gives $\partial_t\phi_{\sqrt t}=\tfrac12\partial_x^2\phi_{\sqrt t}$. For fixed $x$ and $0<\varepsilon<t$, the differentiated integrand in $P_sp(x)$ is bounded on $s\in[\varepsilon,t]$ and the compact support of $p$ by $C_{x,\varepsilon,t}|p(z)|$; differentiation under the integral [F5] and two integrations by parts [F6] therefore give $\partial_sP_s p=\tfrac12P_s p''$. The boundary terms vanish because $p,p'$ have compact support. Dominated convergence [F9] makes $s\mapsto P_s p''(x)$ continuous on $[\varepsilon,t]$, so [F7] integrates the derivative there. Gaussian approximate identities converge uniformly on continuous compactly supported functions: split their convolution integral at $|z|\le\delta$, where uniform continuity controls the integrand difference, and its complement, whose normal mass tends to zero by scaling and integrability of [F1]. Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ consequently yields $p-P_t p=-\tfrac12\int_0^tP_s p''\,ds$ pointwise; the omitted integral over $[0,\varepsilon]$ tends to zero because $|P_sp''(x)|\le\|p''\|_\infty$.

Fix $t>0$ and put $q=P_t p$. It is positive everywhere because $p$ is a nonzero nonnegative density and the Gaussian kernel is positive; Tonelli [F3] and $\int\phi_{\sqrt t}=1$ show $q$ integrates to one. For $0<s\le t$, the Gaussian formula gives $\phi_{\sqrt t}(z)\ge\sqrt{s/t}\,\phi_{\sqrt s}(z)$ for every $z$, hence $q\ge\sqrt{s/t}P_s p$. Applying [F2] inside the convolution and then [F3] gives $|P_s p''|^2\le(P_s p)P_s(r^2p)$ and therefore $\int |P_s p''|^2/q\le\sqrt{t/s}\int P_s(r^2p)=\sqrt{t/s}J$. These inequalities remain valid if one of the pointwise nonnegative integrals is infinite.

Apply [F2] to the time integral in step 2.1 with weights $w(s)=(t/s)^{1/4}$. Since $\int_0^t w(s)ds=4t/3$, it gives $|p-q|^2\le\tfrac14(4t/3)\int_0^t w(s)^{-1}|P_s p''|^2ds$. Divide by $q$, integrate and use [F3] and step 2.2. The result is $\int(p-q)^2/q\le\tfrac14(4t/3)J\int_0^t(t/s)^{1/4}ds=(4/9)t^2J$. In particular all these weighted integrals are finite.

For $u>0$, the function $u-1-\log u$ has value zero at $1$ and derivative $(u-1)/u$, so $\log u\le u-1$ and $u\log u-u+1\le(u-1)^2$. For $t\ge1$, $t-t^{-1}-2\log t$ has value zero at $1$ and derivative $(t-1)^2/t^2\ge0$; replacing $t$ by $1/t$ gives $2|\log t|\le|t-t^{-1}|$ also for $0<t<1$. With $u=t^2$, this yields $u(\log u)^2\le(u-1)^2$. At $u=0$, use the conventions $u\log u=u(\log u)^2=0$, for which both inequalities hold. Apply these pointwise bounds to $u=p/q$ and integrate against $q$. Since $p,q$ integrate to one, [F4] identifies the first integral as KL; its negative part is integrable because $u\log u\ge-e^{-1}$. Both requested logarithmic quantities are at most the chi-square integral from step 3.1. Taking $t=\sigma^2$ proves the Statement.

Let $\mathcal P(\mathbb R)$ be the probability measures on the Borel sets of
$\mathbb R$, equipped with the evaluation sigma-algebra, and let $\sigma>0$.
For $F\in\mathcal P(\mathbb R)$ define
$$p_{F,\sigma}(x):=\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{(x-z)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)F(dz).$$
Then $(F,\sigma,x)\mapsto p_{F,\sigma}(x)$ is jointly measurable,
$0<p_{F,\sigma}(x)\le(\sigma\sqrt{2\pi})^{-1}$ for every $(F,\sigma,x)$,
and $\int_{\mathbb R}p_{F,\sigma}(x)\,dx=1$. In particular it is the
Lebesgue density of the convolution of $F$ with $N(0,\sigma^2)$.

Assume AC. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma>0$, the normal law $N(m,\sigma^2)$
of [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]] has Lebesgue density
$$g_{m,\sigma}(y)=\frac1\sigma\frac{e^{-((y-m)/\sigma)^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}e^{-(y-m)^2/(2\sigma^2)}.$$

The **monic probabilists' Hermite polynomials** are the polynomials $H_m\in\mathbb R[x]$ defined by
$$H_0=1,\qquad H_1(x)=x,\qquad xH_m(x)=H_{m+1}(x)+m\,H_{m-1}(x)\quad(m\ge1).$$
The recurrence is solved for the higher polynomial, $H_{m+1}(x)=xH_m(x)-mH_{m-1}(x)$, so it determines $H_m$ uniquely by induction on $m$. Each $H_m$ is monic of degree $m$: $H_2=x^2-1$, $H_3=x^3-3x$ and $H_4=x^4-6x^2+3$; in general $H_m(x)=m!\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor m/2\rfloor}\frac{(-1/2)^j x^{m-2j}}{j!\,(m-2j)!}$.

Under the AC assumption of the Gaussian-law supplier, these are the monic orthogonal polynomials for the standard normal law of [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]]: they form an orthogonal system for the measure $(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}dx$; orthogonality and the expansion of monomials in this system are proved separately on this page. The moments of that law are those of [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]], and the polynomial calculus used below is that of [[def-derivative]]. The defining property used in this batch is the recurrence; no choice principle is used.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Assume AC. For $m\in\mathbb R$, $\sigma\ge0$, and a real random variable
$X$ with law $N(m,\sigma^2)$,
$$E[X]=m,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(X)=\sigma^2.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $u, v : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at
every point of $[a,b]$ as functions on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]). Suppose
$u'$ and $v'$ are integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then $uv'$
and $u'v$ are integrable and

$$\int_a^b u\,v' \;=\; u(b)v(b) - u(a)v(a) \;-\; \int_a^b u'\,v .$$

**The integrability of $u'$ and $v'$ is a hypothesis, not a formality.** Without
it the two integrals in the display need not exist at all, and the identity is
then not false but ill-formed; that is
the false statement that deletes it on the companion
page. The hypothesis is automatic when $u$ and $v$ are continuously
differentiable, since a continuous function on $[a,b]$ is integrable
([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]).

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Partition $[-A,A]$ into $K\le 2A/\sigma+1$ consecutive Borel intervals $I_i$ of length at most $\sigma$, with left endpoints $a_i$. Ignore intervals of zero $F$-mass and let $G_i$ be the law of $W_i=(Z-a_i)/\sigma$ conditional on $Z\in I_i$. Let $\ell_i$ be the length of $I_i$ and put $b_i=\ell_i/\sigma\le1$, so $G_i$ is supported on $[0,b_i]$. Approximate the moment vector $(\int w\,dG_i,\ldots,\int w^m dG_i)$ by finite sums obtained from partitions of $[0,b_i]$; it is therefore in the closure of the convex hull of the compact moment curve $w\mapsto(w,\ldots,w^m)$ on that interval. Every finite convex combination with more than $m+1$ points can be reduced: affine dependence supplies coefficients $c_j$, not all zero, with $\sum c_j=0$ and $\sum c_jx_j=0$; moving the weights along this relation until one becomes zero preserves nonnegativity and the represented point, so iteration gives at most $m+1$ points. Thus the convex hull is the continuous image of a compact set consisting of $m+1$ curve points and simplex weights; it is compact and closed. The moment vector belongs to it, giving a probability $G'_i$ on at most $m+1$ points of $[0,b_i]$ matching the first $m$ moments of $G_i$.

The Hermite recurrence [F3] and differentiation of $\phi$ give $\phi^{(r)}=(-1)^rH_r\phi$ for every integer $r\ge0$. The case $r=0$ is immediate. If it holds at orders $r$ and $r-1$, differentiating $H_r$'s recurrence gives $H'_{r+1}=H_r+xH'_r-rH'_{r-1}=H_r+r(xH_{r-1}-(r-1)H_{r-2})=(r+1)H_r$; the base cases $H'_0=0$ and $H'_1=1$ start this induction. Thus differentiating $(-1)^rH_r\phi$ gives $(-1)^{r+1}H_{r+1}\phi$. Since $H_r$ is monic, $H_r^{(r)}=r!$. Apply integration by parts [F7] repeatedly on $[-T,T]$ and let $T\to\infty$; the boundary terms vanish because each derivative is a polynomial times the Gaussian. This gives $\int H_r^2\phi=(-1)^r\int H_r\phi^{(r)}=\int H_r^{(r)}\phi=r!$. Cauchy--Schwarz [F4] therefore gives $\|\phi^{(r)}\|_1\le\sqrt{r!}$. Also $\phi^{(r)}$ tends to zero at $-\infty$, so [F8] on $[-T,x]$, followed by $T\to\infty$, gives $|\phi^{(r)}(x)|\le\int_{-\infty}^x|\phi^{(r+1)}(t)|dt\le\sqrt{(r+1)!}$ and $\|\phi^{(r)}\|_\infty\le\sqrt{(r+1)!}$.

Repeated application of [F8] gives the Taylor integral remainder for $w\mapsto\phi(x-w)$ through degree $m-1$: $R_m(x,w)=\frac{(-w)^m}{(m-1)!}\int_0^1(1-t)^{m-1}\phi^{(m)}(x-tw)\,dt$. By translation invariance and Tonelli [F6], $\|R_m(\cdot,w)\|_1\le w^m\|\phi^{(m)}\|_1/m!\le1/\sqrt{m!}$; the same formula gives $\|R_m(\cdot,w)\|_\infty\le w^m\|\phi^{(m)}\|_\infty/m!\le\sqrt{m+1}/\sqrt{m!}$ by step 1.2. Moment matching in step 1.1 cancels the polynomial terms after integration against $G_i-G'_i$. Integrating the remainder bounds against these two probability laws gives $\|p_{G_i,1}-p_{G'_i,1}\|_1,\|p_{G_i,1}-p_{G'_i,1}\|_\infty\le2\sqrt{m+1}/\sqrt{m!}$. The bound $\log(m!)=\sum_{k=1}^m\log k\ge\int_1^m\log x\,dx=m\log m-m+1$ shows this error is at most $\eta$ when $m=\lceil c\log(e/\eta)\rceil$ for a sufficiently large universal $c$, with $\eta\in(0,1/2)$ absorbed by increasing $c$.

Let $
u_i$ and $
u_i'$ be the pushforwards of $G_i$ and $G_i'$, respectively, under $w\mapsto a_i+\sigma w$, and set $F'=\sum_iF(I_i)
u_i'$. Since $G'_i$ is supported on $[0,b_i]$, every $
u_i'$ is supported in the closure of $I_i$, so $F'$ is a discrete probability measure on $[-A,A]$ with at most $K(m+1)\le C(A/\sigma\vee1)\log(e/\eta)$ support points. Translation and scaling give $p_{
u_i,\sigma}(x)=\sigma^{-1}p_{G_i,1}((x-a_i)/\sigma)$ and the same identity for $
u_i'$ and $G_i'$. Summing these component errors with weights $F(I_i)$ shows the $L^1$ error is at most $\eta$ and the supremum error at most $\eta/\sigma$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
([[def-probability-measure]]). Absolute continuity $P\ll Q$ has the convention
of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If
$P\not\ll Q$, define $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and
let $r=dP/dQ$ be a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative of its
Radon–Nikodym class; such a representative exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].
On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This
function is measurable: for $a\ge0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r>\exp(a)\}$, and for
$a<0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r=0\}\cup\{r>\exp(a)\}$, by the inverse and
monotonicity properties of the natural logarithm
([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]). These are
measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since
$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$ by
[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$
The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,
$$0\le \frac{\log s}{s}=\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{u}\le\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{\sqrt u}\le\frac2{\sqrt s}.$$
Thus $t\log t\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$; here $L=\log$ by
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and
[[def-integral-logarithm]]. On $(0,\infty)$, $\psi$ is a product of continuous
functions by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $\psi$ is continuous on
$[0,\infty)$ and $\psi(r)$ is measurable by
[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts
([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]],
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

For $0<t\le1$, the function $-t\log t$ has derivative $-\log t-1$ and
maximum $1/e$ at $t=1/e$: $e=\exp(1)>1$ by
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $1/e=\exp(-1)$ by
[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and $\log(1/e)=-1$ by
[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and the inverse definition. The mean value
theorem gives increase before and decrease after this point
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]],
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).
At $t=0$ the negative part is zero. Since $Q$ is a probability measure,
$$\int \psi(r)^-\,dQ\le\frac1e.$$
The change-of-measure identity of [[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]],
applied to $\ell^-$ gives $\int\ell^-\,dP=\int\psi(r)^-\,dQ\le1/e$,
so $\int\ell\,dP$ is well-defined; applying it to both positive and negative
parts gives
$$D(P\|Q)=\int\ell\,dP=\int\psi(r)\,dQ=\int r\log r\,dQ,$$
with $0\log0:=0$ and a finite negative part. Therefore the extended integral
is well-defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.

This convention is directional: the first argument must be absolutely
continuous with respect to the second for the integral formula to apply.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ be a measurable parameter space, $\Pi$ a prior probability measure on it, and $p_\theta$ a jointly measurable family of finite-valued probability densities relative to one fixed sigma-finite measure $\mu$. Let $P_0$ have finite-valued density $p_0$ relative to $\mu$, and let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be IID with law $P_0$. Assume the Axiom of Choice for the imported directional KL convention ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). The jointly measurable density family is explicit input, so no arbitrary-index selection of versions is used here. In the expression below, the weighted log terms are set to zero on $\{p_0=0\}$; on $\{p_0>0,p_\theta=0\}$ the log ratio is $-\infty$ and its square is $+\infty$. For $\epsilon_n>0$, define
$$K_n:=\left\{\theta:\mathrm{KL}(P_0\Vert P_\theta)\le\epsilon_n^2,\quad \int\left[\log\frac{p_\theta}{p_0}\right]^2p_0\,d\mu\le\epsilon_n^2\right\}.$$
Joint measurability and Tonelli make $K_n$ measurable, as verified below. If $\Pi(K_n)\ge e^{-Cn\epsilon_n^2}$ for $C>0$ and $\mathrm{KL}(P_0\Vert P_\theta)$ uses the direction in [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]], then, defining the ratio to be zero on the $P_0$-null set where $p_0=0$, the likelihood denominator
$$D_n:=\int_\Theta\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{p_\theta(X_i)}{p_0(X_i)}\,\Pi(d\theta)$$
is finite and positive $P_0^n$-almost surely and
$$P_0^n\!\left\{D_n\ge e^{-(C+2)n\epsilon_n^2}\right\}\ge1-\frac1{n\epsilon_n^2}.$$

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $p,q:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ be measurable densities with $\int p\,d\mu=\int q\,d\mu=1$. They define probability laws $P(B)=\int_Bp\,d\mu$ and $Q(B)=\int_Bq\,d\mu$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **root-L2 Hellinger distance**, with the root-L2 normalization, is
$$h(P,Q):=\left(\int_{\mathsf X}(\sqrt p-\sqrt q)^2\,d\mu\right)^{1/2}.$$

The dominating measure $\mu$ is fixed throughout a use of this definition. Changing either density on a $\mu$-null set does not change the value, since the integrand changes only on a null set. This definition does not assert that separate choices of density versions are jointly measurable in an additional parameter.

For probability densities $p,q$ relative to one fixed measure $\mu$, define $h$ as in [[def-hellinger-distance-between-density-laws]] and set $d_1(P,Q):=\int|p-q|\,d\mu$. Then $h$ is a metric on the induced probability laws and
$$h(P,Q)^2\le d_1(P,Q)=2\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\rm TV},\qquad d_1(P,Q)\le2h(P,Q),$$
where library total variation is the event supremum $\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\rm TV}=\sup_{A\in\mathcal A}|P(A)-Q(A)|$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). It is
**dominated** by a supplied positive measure $\mu$ on
$(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ when $\mu$ is sigma-finite
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]) and
$P_\theta\ll\mu$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$
([[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]).
The dominating measure is part of the specified setup. This condition adds no
measurable structure on $\Theta$ and no measurability of
$\theta\mapsto P_\theta$.

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be dominated by the fixed sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$. For each
$\theta$, the Radon–Nikodym theorem gives the almost-everywhere class
$dP_\theta/d\mu$; a sigma-finite exhaustion for $\mu$ is also finite for the
probability measure $P_\theta$. Under AC, select simultaneously a
finite-valued measurable nonnegative representative $p_\theta$ from each
class. The nonnegative version exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].

For fixed observed $x\in\mathcal X$, the function
$$L_x:\Theta\to[0,+\infty),\qquad L_x(\theta):=p_\theta(x),$$
is the **likelihood at $x$**. This is a function on the parameter labels, not
a probability distribution on $\Theta$. No sigma-algebra on $\Theta$ or
measurability of $L_x$ is implied. Each density is determined only
$\mu$-almost everywhere; there is no canonical pointwise version and, for
arbitrary uncountable $\Theta$, no common exceptional null set is asserted.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $n\ge1$, let $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ be independent real random variables on a
common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then
   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$
   in $[0,+\infty]$. In this finite product of expectations, a zero factor
   makes the product zero even when another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise
   multiplication has its usual extended nonnegative meaning.
2. If every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable
   and the same factorization holds in $\mathbb R$.

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. The **measure with density $f$ relative
to $\mu$** is the measure
$$f\,d\mu:\mathcal A\to[0,+\infty],\qquad (f\,d\mu)(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu,$$
whose measure property is supplied by
[[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]].

A pseudometric $d$ on a set $T$ is a nonnegative symmetric function $d:T\times T\to[0,\infty)$ with $d(t,t)=0$ and $d(s,t)\le d(s,u)+d(u,t)$; distinct points may have distance zero. For a nonempty subset $\mathcal F\subseteq T$ and $\epsilon>0$, the covering number $N(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)$ is the least finite $k$ for which there are centers $f_1,\ldots,f_k\in\mathcal F$ such that every $f\in\mathcal F$ satisfies $d(f,f_j)\le\epsilon$ for some $j$. It is $+\infty$ if no finite cover exists. Set $N(\epsilon,\varnothing,d)=1$.

The packing number $D(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)$ is the largest size of a finite subset $\{f_1,\ldots,f_k\}\subseteq\mathcal F$ whose distinct members have pairwise distance strictly greater than $\epsilon$. If the sizes of such finite subsets are unbounded, put $D=+\infty$; put $D(\epsilon,\varnothing,d)=0$. These conventions give the radius comparison proved in [[lem-packing-covering-number-comparison]]. The metric entropy is $H(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d):=\log N(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)$ for nonempty classes, with $\log(+\infty)=+\infty$.

For a probability measure $Q$ on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ and a measurable real function $g$, set $\|g\|_{Q,r}:=(\int |g|^r\,dQ)^{1/r}$ for $1\le r<\infty$ when the integral is finite, using the real-power convention, including $0^{1/r}=0$, of [[def-real-power]]. If the integral is $+\infty$, define $\|g\|_{Q,r}:=+\infty$ directly. The function $|g|$ is measurable by [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]], and [[lem-real-power-preserves-measurability]] makes $|g|^r$ measurable, so this nonnegative extended integral is well-defined. On a class of functions with finite such norms, $d_{Q,r}(f,g):=\|f-g\|_{Q,r}$ is a pseudometric: nonnegativity, symmetry, and zero diagonal follow from the absolute value, and the triangle inequality is [[thm-minkowski-inequality-for-integrals]]. Functions that agree $Q$-almost everywhere have distance zero. We write $N(\epsilon,\mathcal F,L^r(Q))$ for this covering number.

For measurable real endpoints $\ell\le u$ $Q$-almost everywhere, the bracket $[\ell,u]$ is the set of measurable functions $f$ satisfying $\ell\le f\le u$ $Q$-almost everywhere. Its $L^r(Q)$ width is $\|u-\ell\|_{Q,r}$. The bracketing number $N_{[]} (\epsilon,\mathcal F,L^r(Q))$ is the least number of such brackets of width at most $\epsilon$ that cover $\mathcal F$, or $+\infty$ if no finite cover exists; for the empty class set it equal to $1$. Centers of metric covers are in $\mathcal F$; bracket endpoints need not be.

derivations.claim: Put $x_n=n\epsilon_n^2$, $y_n=n\delta_n^2$, and let $D_n$ be the likelihood denominator relative to $p_0^n$. By [F1], on an event $\Omega_n$ with $P_0^n(\Omega_n^c)\le y_n^{-1}$, $D_n\ge e^{-(C_0+2)y_n}$.

Write $T_n=\sum_j\sqrt{N_{n,j}\pi_{n,j}}$ and $s_n=e^{-x_n}T_n$, so $s_n\to0$. Fix $K>2(C_0+3)$ and split indices into active $J_n^+=\{j:\pi_{n,j}\ge e^{-Kx_n}\}$ and small-mass $J_n^-$. Since $N_{n,j}\ge1$, $\sum_{J_n^-}\pi_{n,j}\le e^{-Kx_n/2}T_n=e^{(1-K/2)x_n}s_n$. For active $j$, $\sqrt{N_{n,j}\pi_{n,j}}\le T_n=e^{x_n}s_n$, hence $\log(N_{n,j}/\pi_{n,j})\le(2+2K)x_n$ for all sufficiently large $n$.

Fix a sufficiently large constant $M$. If $M\epsilon_n\ge\sqrt2$, then the alternative is empty because Hellinger distance is at most $\sqrt2$, and the desired posterior mass is zero for this $n$. For the remaining $n$, choose, by [A1], a finite $\epsilon_n$-cover with centers in each active stratum's density image, as allowed by [F9]. Discard centers whose closed $\epsilon_n$-ball meets no density in the stratum with $h(p_\theta,p_0)>M\epsilon_n$; at most $N_{n,j}$ centers remain, and they cover that alternative. For every retained center $q$, the triangle inequality gives $h(q,p_0)>(M-1)\epsilon_n$. Set $m_n=\left\lceil\frac{2\log 8}{(M-1)^2\epsilon_n^2}\right\rceil$. On a block of $m_n$ observations define $T_q=\mathbf1\{\prod_iq(X_i)>\prod_i p_0(X_i)\}$. On rejection, $p_0^{\otimes m_n}\le\sqrt{p_0^{\otimes m_n}q^{\otimes m_n}}$, so its type-I error is at most the product affinity; on acceptance, $q^{\otimes m_n}\le\sqrt{p_0^{\otimes m_n}q^{\otimes m_n}}$, so its type-II error under $q$ has the same bound. By [F2], this affinity is $(1-h^2(q,p_0)/2)^{m_n}\le e^{-m_nh^2(q,p_0)/2}\le1/8$.

If $h(p_\theta,q)\le\epsilon_n$, product affinity gives $h^2(P_\theta^{m_n},Q^{m_n})=2\left[1-\left(1-h^2(p_\theta,q)/2\right)^{m_n}\right]\le m_n\epsilon_n^2$, using $1-(1-u)^m\le mu$ for $u\in[0,1]$; [F3] bounds their total variation by $\sqrt{m_n}\epsilon_n$. Since $M\epsilon_n<\sqrt2$, $\epsilon_n^2<2/M^2$ and $m_n\epsilon_n^2\le\frac{2\log8}{(M-1)^2}+\frac{2}{M^2}\le1/64$ for sufficiently large $M$. The total variation is then at most $1/8$. Therefore the block test in step 1.3 rejects with probability at least $3/4$ under every $p_\theta$ in the alternative and at most $1/8$ under $p_0$.

Divide $L_n=\lfloor n/m_n\rfloor$ disjoint blocks and let $Y_k$ be their block-test indicators. Under each IID law the indicators are independent by [F6]; their means are at most $a=1/8$ under $P_0$ and at least $b=3/4$ under every alternative by step 2.1. For independent Bernoulli variables with means at most $a$, exponential Markov [F7] gives $P_0(L_n^{-1}\sum Y_k\ge t)\le e^{-L_nD(t\Vert a)}$; with means at least $b$, the negative-exponential bound gives $P_\theta(L_n^{-1}\sum Y_k<t)\le e^{-L_nD(t\Vert b)}$, where $D(t\Vert u)=t\log(t/u)+(1-t)\log((1-t)/(1-u))$. These bounds follow by bounding each moment generating function by $1-u+ue^\lambda$ (using $u=a$ for $\lambda>0$, $u=b$ for $\lambda<0$) and optimizing over $\lambda$.

The function $D(t\Vert a)-D(t\Vert b)$ is affine and strictly increasing on $[a,b]$, is negative at $a$, and equals $D(b\Vert a)>0$ at $b$. Let $t_*$ be its unique zero. By AC [A1], for each active $j$ choose $t_j\in[t_*,b]$ such that $L_n\{D(t_j\Vert a)-D(t_j\Vert b)\}=\log(N_{n,j}/\pi_{n,j})$. This is possible after increasing $M$: writing $A=2\log 8$, $M\epsilon_n<\sqrt2$ implies $A/((M-1)^2\epsilon_n^2)>2$ for sufficiently large $M$, so the ceiling in $m_n$ costs at most a fixed factor; since $n\epsilon_n^2\to\infty$, the floor in $L_n$ also costs at most a fixed factor eventually. Hence $L_n\ge cM^2x_n$ for a universal $c>0$, while step 1.2 bounds the right side by $(2+2K)x_n$. Define $\phi_{n,j}$ as the maximum of the block-majority tests over its retained centers (or zero if there are none), using threshold $t_j$. Continuity on $[t_*,b]$ and positivity of both divergences at $t_*$ give a constant $c_*>0$ such that $(D(t\Vert a)+D(t\Vert b))/2\ge c_*$ there. The null union bound and step 3.1 give $P_0^n(\phi_{n,j}=1)\le\sqrt{N_{n,j}\pi_{n,j}}e^{-c_*L_n}$; the same Chernoff bound for a center within $\epsilon_n$ of each alternative gives $\sup_{\theta\in S_{n,j}:h(p_\theta,p_0)>M\epsilon_n}P_\theta^n(\phi_{n,j}=0)\le\sqrt{N_{n,j}/\pi_{n,j}}e^{-c_*L_n}$ by step 2.1.

Let $\phi_n$ be one on the countable union of the rejection events of $\phi_{n,j}$ over $j\in J_n^+$ and zero otherwise; it is measurable as a countable union of measurable events. The union bound and step 4.1 give $P_0^n(\phi_n=1)\le T_ne^{-c_*L_n}$. For the tested likelihood numerator on an active stratum, Tonelli [F4], the jointly measurable likelihood interface [F5] and change of density give $E_0[(1-\phi_n)\int_{\{\theta\in S_{n,j}:h(p_\theta,p_0)>M\epsilon_n\}}\prod_i\frac{p_\theta(X_i)}{p_0(X_i)}\,\Pi_n(d\theta)]\le\pi_{n,j}\sup_{\theta\text{ in the set}}P_\theta^n(1-\phi_{n,j})\le\sqrt{N_{n,j}\pi_{n,j}}e^{-c_*L_n}.$

Write $d_n=e^{-(C_0+2)y_n}$. For the active numerator $R_n^+$, step 5.1 gives $P_0^n(\phi_n=1)\le T_ne^{-c_*L_n}$ and $E_0[(1-\phi_n)R_n^+]\le T_ne^{-c_*L_n}$. Thus, for every fixed $\zeta>0$, $P_0^n(R_n^+/D_n>\zeta)\le P_0^n(D_n<d_n)+T_ne^{-c_*L_n}+\zeta^{-1}d_n^{-1}T_ne^{-c_*L_n}$. This tends to zero for sufficiently large $M$, since $T_n=e^{x_n}s_n$, $y_n\le x_n$, $L_n\ge cM^2x_n$, and $s_n\to0$. For the small-mass numerator $R_n^-$, [F8] and Tonelli give $E_0[R_n^-]\le\sum_{J_n^-}\pi_{n,j}\le e^{-Kx_n/2}T_n$; hence its posterior mass tends to zero in probability by Markov and the denominator event, because $e^{(C_0+2)y_n}e^{-Kx_n/2}T_n\le s_ne^{(C_0+3-K/2)x_n}\to0$ when $K>2(C_0+3)$.

The posterior outside the $M\epsilon_n$-ball is the union of its active-stratum part, its small-mass-stratum part, and the sieve complement. Step 6.1 sends the first two parts to zero in probability, and the sieve-complement term tends to zero by hypothesis.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

There is a universal constant $C$ such that, for $A,\sigma>0$,
$0<\eta<1/2$, and every probability measure $F$ supported on $[-A,A]$,
there is a discrete probability measure $F'$ on $[-A,A]$ with at most
$$C(A/\sigma\vee1)\log(e/\eta)$$
support points and
$$\|p_{F,\sigma}-p_{F',\sigma}\|_1\le\eta,\qquad \|p_{F,\sigma}-p_{F',\sigma}\|_\infty\le\eta/\sigma.$$

For probability densities $p,q$ relative to one fixed measure $\mu$, define $h$ as in [[def-hellinger-distance-between-density-laws]] and set $d_1(P,Q):=\int|p-q|\,d\mu$. Then $h$ is a metric on the induced probability laws and
$$h(P,Q)^2\le d_1(P,Q)=2\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\rm TV},\qquad d_1(P,Q)\le2h(P,Q),$$
where library total variation is the event supremum $\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\rm TV}=\sup_{A\in\mathcal A}|P(A)-Q(A)|$.

Assume AC. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma>0$, the normal law $N(m,\sigma^2)$
of [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]] has Lebesgue density
$$g_{m,\sigma}(y)=\frac1\sigma\frac{e^{-((y-m)/\sigma)^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}e^{-(y-m)^2/(2\sigma^2)}.$$

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $p,q:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ be measurable densities with $\int p\,d\mu=\int q\,d\mu=1$. They define probability laws $P(B)=\int_Bp\,d\mu$ and $Q(B)=\int_Bq\,d\mu$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **root-L2 Hellinger distance**, with the root-L2 normalization, is
$$h(P,Q):=\left(\int_{\mathsf X}(\sqrt p-\sqrt q)^2\,d\mu\right)^{1/2}.$$

The dominating measure $\mu$ is fixed throughout a use of this definition. Changing either density on a $\mu$-null set does not change the value, since the integrand changes only on a null set. This definition does not assert that separate choices of density versions are jointly measurable in an additional parameter.

Assume AC. For $m\in\mathbb R$, $\sigma\ge0$, and a real random variable
$X$ with law $N(m,\sigma^2)$,
$$E[X]=m,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(X)=\sigma^2.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

derivations.claim: Put $K:=\lceil C_0(A/\tau\vee1)\log(e/\epsilon)\rceil$. By [F1], every $p_{F,\sigma}\in\mathcal P_{A,\tau}$ is within $L^1$ distance $\epsilon^2/C_1$ of a mixture with at most $K$ atoms, for a fixed sufficiently large $C_1$. Pad shorter mixtures by zero-weight atoms.

Differentiating the density in [F3] gives $\|\partial_z\phi_\sigma(\cdot-z)\|_1=\sigma^{-1}E|Z|\le\sigma^{-1}$, since $2|Z|\le1+Z^2$ and $E Z^2=1$ by [F5], and $\|\partial_\sigma\phi_\sigma(\cdot-z)\|_1=\sigma^{-1}E|Z^2-1|\le2\sigma^{-1}$ for $Z\sim N(0,1)$. Integrating these derivatives along the location and scale segments by [F7] yields $\|\phi_\sigma(\cdot-z)-\phi_\sigma(\cdot-z')\|_1\le |z-z'|/\sigma$ and $\|\phi_\sigma-\phi_{\sigma'}\|_1\le2|\sigma-\sigma'|/(\sigma\wedge\sigma')$. For the first class use a scale grid in $[\tau,2\tau]$; for an actual band, instead grid $[\tau,\min\{2\tau,s_n\}]$, omitting $2\tau$ when that endpoint is excluded. In either case choose grid mesh at most $c_2\tau\epsilon^2$, with every grid point admitted by the corresponding scale constraint. Use a location grid in $[-A,A]$ with mesh at most $c_2\tau\epsilon^2$ and an $L^1$ grid on the $K$-simplex of mesh at most $c_2\epsilon^2$. Replacing the scale, locations and weights changes the mixture density in $L^1$ by at most $C c_2\epsilon^2$: integrate the componentwise location and scale bounds against the finite mixing weights, and use Tonelli [F6] for the componentwise integrals. Choose $c_2$ so this plus the approximation from step 1.1 is at most $\epsilon^2/4$. Thus the resulting finite set, with centers in the class being covered, is an $L^1$ cover of radius $\epsilon^2/4$, hence an $h$-cover of radius $\epsilon/2$ by [F2].

The scale grid has at most $C\epsilon^{-2}$ points and the location grid at most $C(1+A/(\tau\epsilon^2))$ points. Rounding each of the first $K-1$ weights down to a mesh proportional to $\epsilon^2/K$ leaves the last weight nonnegative after setting it to make the sum one, gives at most $(CK/\epsilon^2)^K$ weight vectors, and changes their $L^1$ distance by at most $2c_2\epsilon^2$. Therefore the logarithm of the cover size is at most $C\log(e/\epsilon)+K\left[\log\!\left(\frac{C(A/\tau\vee1)}{\epsilon^2}\right)+\log\!\left(\frac{CK}{\epsilon^2}\right)\right]\le C(A/\tau\vee1)\left[\log\!\left(\frac{C(A/\tau\vee1)}{\epsilon}\right)\right]^2.$ The constructed finite set is an $h$-net of radius $\epsilon/2$, hence also a net of radius $\epsilon$; its cardinality therefore bounds the covering number and proves the first bound.

If $r:=F([-A,A]^c)=0$, then $F$ already belongs to the compact-location class. If $0<r\le\rho<1$, let $F_A$ and $F_{A^c}$ be the normalized restrictions to $[-A,A]$ and its complement. Then $p_{F,\sigma}=(1-r)p_{F_A,\sigma}+r p_{F_{A^c},\sigma}$, so $\|p_{F,\sigma}-p_{F_A,\sigma}\|_1\le2r$ by integrating the mixture densities (Tonelli [F6]). By [F2], $h(p_{F,\sigma},p_{F_A,\sigma})\le\sqrt{2r}$; the triangle inequality in [F4] then transfers the cover to the tail-constrained class. The scale grid is restricted as in step 2.1, so every center has $F([-A,A]^c)=0$ and satisfies the band and cutoff constraints. For sufficiently small universal $c$, $\rho\le c\epsilon^2$ makes the truncation error at most $\epsilon/2$, so the radius-$\epsilon/2$ cover from steps 2.1 and 3.1 becomes a radius-$\epsilon$ cover after the constant rescaling used in the entropy bound.

all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$ be a standard Borel space and let $\alpha$ be a
finite nonzero measure on it. Write $\mathcal P(\mathsf X)$ for the set of
probability measures on $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$, equipped with the
**evaluation sigma-algebra**
$$\sigma\bigl(\{G\mapsto G(A):A\in\mathcal A\}\bigr).$$
For a probability law $P$ on this space, let $G$ be the coordinate random
probability measure $G(\omega)=\omega$. Call $P$ a **Dirichlet-process law
with base measure** $\alpha$ if, for every finite measurable partition
$(A_1,\ldots,A_k)$ of $\mathsf X$, the vector
$(G(A_1),\ldots,G(A_k))$ has the Dirichlet distribution with parameters
$(\alpha(A_1),\ldots,\alpha(A_k))$ after zero-parameter cells are omitted;
each omitted zero-base cell has mass zero. If the partition has one
positive-parameter cell, its mass is one. The finite-partition specification
determines at most one law on the evaluation sigma-algebra. When such a law
exists, denote it by $DP(\alpha)$; the construction theorem on this page
proves existence.

The Dirichlet distribution here has the positive-parameter density and
one-category convention of [[def-dirichlet-distribution]]. The definition
asserts no weak topology, support statement, or density-contraction result.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$ be a standard Borel
space and let $\alpha$ be a finite nonzero measure on it. Then there is a
measurable random probability measure $G$ whose law on the evaluation
sigma-algebra of $\mathcal P(\mathsf X)$ is $DP(\alpha)$. For every finite
measurable partition $(A_1,\ldots,A_k)$, the unnormalized increments are
independent with
$\Gamma(A_j)\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(\alpha(A_j),1)$ when
$\alpha(A_j)>0$, and $\Gamma(A_j)=0$ almost surely when $\alpha(A_j)=0$.
Consequently the normalized masses have the finite-partition Dirichlet laws
in [[def-dirichlet-process]]. These laws determine the probability law on
$\mathcal P(\mathsf X)$ uniquely.

The construction uses the Poisson random measure with intensity
$$\mu(dx,dt)=\alpha(dx)t^{-1}e^{-t}\,dt\quad\text{on }\mathsf X\times(0,\infty),$$
and normalizes its weighted projection onto $\mathsf X$. It does not assume a
gamma-process existence theorem.

Assume Countable Choice. For $k\ge2$ and $\alpha_j>0$, the **Dirichlet distribution**
$\operatorname{Dirichlet}(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_k)$ is the probability law
on the open probability simplex with density
$$\frac{\Gamma(\alpha_+)}{\prod_j\Gamma(\alpha_j)} \prod_jp_j^{\alpha_j-1}$$
relative to $dp_1\cdots dp_{k-1}$, with $p_k=1-\sum_{j<k}p_j$. Its
normalization is [[thm-dirichlet-density-normalization]]. For $k=1$, define
the law to be the point mass at $p_1=1$. All coordinates of the parameter
vector must be strictly positive.

For $s>0$, define $\Gamma(s)=\int_0^\infty t^{s-1}e^{-t}\,dt$.

The integral is improper at both $0$ and $+\infty$. Its convergence for every $s>0$, and its failure for $s\le0$, are proved in [[thm-real-gamma-euler-integral-convergence]], which justifies the definition on exactly the displayed domain. The integrand is positive, so $\Gamma(s)>0$ throughout $(0,\infty)$.
Let $s$ be real. The Euler integral $\int_0^\infty t^{s-1}e^{-t}\,dt$ converges if and only if $s>0$.
For every $s>0$, $\Gamma(s+1)=s\Gamma(s)$, and $\Gamma(1)=1$.
The real Gamma function is smooth on $(0,\infty)$. For every natural $k$ and every $s>0$, $\Gamma^{(k)}(s)=\int_0^\infty(\log t)^kt^{s-1}e^{-t}\,dt$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$ be a standard Borel
space and let $\alpha$ be a finite nonzero measure on it. Then there is a
measurable random probability measure $G$ whose law on the evaluation
sigma-algebra of $\mathcal P(\mathsf X)$ is $DP(\alpha)$. For every finite
measurable partition $(A_1,\ldots,A_k)$, the unnormalized increments are
independent with
$\Gamma(A_j)\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(\alpha(A_j),1)$ when
$\alpha(A_j)>0$, and $\Gamma(A_j)=0$ almost surely when $\alpha(A_j)=0$.
Consequently the normalized masses have the finite-partition Dirichlet laws
in [[def-dirichlet-process]]. These laws determine the probability law on
$\mathcal P(\mathsf X)$ uniquely.

The construction uses the Poisson random measure with intensity
$$\mu(dx,dt)=\alpha(dx)t^{-1}e^{-t}\,dt\quad\text{on }\mathsf X\times(0,\infty),$$
and normalizes its weighted projection onto $\mathsf X$. It does not assume a
gamma-process existence theorem.

Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
([[def-probability-measure]]). Absolute continuity $P\ll Q$ has the convention
of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If
$P\not\ll Q$, define $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and
let $r=dP/dQ$ be a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative of its
Radon–Nikodym class; such a representative exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].
On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This
function is measurable: for $a\ge0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r>\exp(a)\}$, and for
$a<0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r=0\}\cup\{r>\exp(a)\}$, by the inverse and
monotonicity properties of the natural logarithm
([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]). These are
measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since
$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$ by
[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$
The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,
$$0\le \frac{\log s}{s}=\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{u}\le\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{\sqrt u}\le\frac2{\sqrt s}.$$
Thus $t\log t\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$; here $L=\log$ by
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and
[[def-integral-logarithm]]. On $(0,\infty)$, $\psi$ is a product of continuous
functions by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $\psi$ is continuous on
$[0,\infty)$ and $\psi(r)$ is measurable by
[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts
([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]],
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

For $0<t\le1$, the function $-t\log t$ has derivative $-\log t-1$ and
maximum $1/e$ at $t=1/e$: $e=\exp(1)>1$ by
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $1/e=\exp(-1)$ by
[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and $\log(1/e)=-1$ by
[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and the inverse definition. The mean value
theorem gives increase before and decrease after this point
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]],
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).
At $t=0$ the negative part is zero. Since $Q$ is a probability measure,
$$\int \psi(r)^-\,dQ\le\frac1e.$$
The change-of-measure identity of [[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]],
applied to $\ell^-$ gives $\int\ell^-\,dP=\int\psi(r)^-\,dQ\le1/e$,
so $\int\ell\,dP$ is well-defined; applying it to both positive and negative
parts gives
$$D(P\|Q)=\int\ell\,dP=\int\psi(r)\,dQ=\int r\log r\,dQ,$$
with $0\log0:=0$ and a finite negative part. Therefore the extended integral
is well-defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.

This convention is directional: the first argument must be absolutely
continuous with respect to the second for the integral formula to apply.

Let $\mathcal P(\mathbb R)$ be the probability measures on the Borel sets of
$\mathbb R$, equipped with the evaluation sigma-algebra, and let $\sigma>0$.
For $F\in\mathcal P(\mathbb R)$ define
$$p_{F,\sigma}(x):=\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{(x-z)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)F(dz).$$
Then $(F,\sigma,x)\mapsto p_{F,\sigma}(x)$ is jointly measurable,
$0<p_{F,\sigma}(x)\le(\sigma\sqrt{2\pi})^{-1}$ for every $(F,\sigma,x)$,
and $\int_{\mathbb R}p_{F,\sigma}(x)\,dx=1$. In particular it is the
Lebesgue density of the convolution of $F$ with $N(0,\sigma^2)$.

There is a universal constant $C$ such that, for $A,\sigma>0$,
$0<\eta<1/2$, and every probability measure $F$ supported on $[-A,A]$,
there is a discrete probability measure $F'$ on $[-A,A]$ with at most
$$C(A/\sigma\vee1)\log(e/\eta)$$
support points and
$$\|p_{F,\sigma}-p_{F',\sigma}\|_1\le\eta,\qquad \|p_{F,\sigma}-p_{F',\sigma}\|_\infty\le\eta/\sigma.$$

Assume AC, let $\alpha$ be a finite nonzero measure of total mass $m$, and
let $F\sim DP(\alpha)$. Consider a finite partition
$(U_0,U_1,\ldots,U_N)$ with $\alpha(U_0)=0$ or
$0<\alpha(U_0)\le m$. Write $\alpha_j=\alpha(U_j)$ for $j\ge1$, and assume
$$a\eta^b\le\alpha_j\le1\quad(1\le j\le N),\qquad 0<\eta<1/4,\qquad N\eta\le1/4,$$
for fixed $a,b>0$. For every $w=(w_1,\ldots,w_N)$ in the probability
simplex, there are constants $c,C>0$ depending only on $a,b,m,\alpha(U_0)$
such that
$$\Pr\!\left\{\sum_{j=1}^N|F(U_j)-w_j|+F(U_0)\le3\eta,\quad \min_{1\le j\le N}F(U_j)\ge\eta^2/2\right\}\ge C\exp\{-cN\log(e/\eta)\}.$$
For any compact $J\subset(0,m]$, the constants may instead depend only on
$a,b,m,J$ and are uniform over $\alpha(U_0)\in J$.
When $\alpha(U_0)=0$, the zero-base cell has $F(U_0)=0$ almost surely and is
omitted from the Dirichlet vector.

Let $p,q$ be probability densities relative to one measure $\mu$, assume
$p\,d\mu\ll q\,d\mu$, let
$h^2:=\int(\sqrt p-\sqrt q)^2d\mu$, and suppose
$R:=\operatorname*{ess,sup}_{q\,d\mu}(p/q)<\infty$, with $p/q=0$ on
$\{q=0,p=0\}$. Then $p\ll q$ and for a universal constant $C$,
$$\mathrm{KL}(p\,d\mu\Vert q\,d\mu)\le C h^2(1+\log^+R),\qquad \int p\left[\log(p/q)\right]^2d\mu\le C h^2(1+\log^+R)^2.$$
The logarithm is assigned value zero on $\{p=0\}$; the moment integrand is
also set to zero there.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$ be a standard Borel space and let $\alpha$ be a
finite nonzero measure on it. Write $\mathcal P(\mathsf X)$ for the set of
probability measures on $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$, equipped with the
**evaluation sigma-algebra**
$$\sigma\bigl(\{G\mapsto G(A):A\in\mathcal A\}\bigr).$$
For a probability law $P$ on this space, let $G$ be the coordinate random
probability measure $G(\omega)=\omega$. Call $P$ a **Dirichlet-process law
with base measure** $\alpha$ if, for every finite measurable partition
$(A_1,\ldots,A_k)$ of $\mathsf X$, the vector
$(G(A_1),\ldots,G(A_k))$ has the Dirichlet distribution with parameters
$(\alpha(A_1),\ldots,\alpha(A_k))$ after zero-parameter cells are omitted;
each omitted zero-base cell has mass zero. If the partition has one
positive-parameter cell, its mass is one. The finite-partition specification
determines at most one law on the evaluation sigma-algebra. When such a law
exists, denote it by $DP(\alpha)$; the construction theorem on this page
proves existence.

The Dirichlet distribution here has the positive-parameter density and
one-category convention of [[def-dirichlet-distribution]]. The definition
asserts no weak topology, support statement, or density-contraction result.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$ be a standard Borel
space and let $\alpha$ be a finite nonzero measure on it. Then there is a
measurable random probability measure $G$ whose law on the evaluation
sigma-algebra of $\mathcal P(\mathsf X)$ is $DP(\alpha)$. For every finite
measurable partition $(A_1,\ldots,A_k)$, the unnormalized increments are
independent with
$\Gamma(A_j)\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(\alpha(A_j),1)$ when
$\alpha(A_j)>0$, and $\Gamma(A_j)=0$ almost surely when $\alpha(A_j)=0$.
Consequently the normalized masses have the finite-partition Dirichlet laws
in [[def-dirichlet-process]]. These laws determine the probability law on
$\mathcal P(\mathsf X)$ uniquely.

The construction uses the Poisson random measure with intensity
$$\mu(dx,dt)=\alpha(dx)t^{-1}e^{-t}\,dt\quad\text{on }\mathsf X\times(0,\infty),$$
and normalizes its weighted projection onto $\mathsf X$. It does not assume a
gamma-process existence theorem.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $p,q:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ be measurable densities with $\int p\,d\mu=\int q\,d\mu=1$. They define probability laws $P(B)=\int_Bp\,d\mu$ and $Q(B)=\int_Bq\,d\mu$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **root-L2 Hellinger distance**, with the root-L2 normalization, is
$$h(P,Q):=\left(\int_{\mathsf X}(\sqrt p-\sqrt q)^2\,d\mu\right)^{1/2}.$$

The dominating measure $\mu$ is fixed throughout a use of this definition. Changing either density on a $\mu$-null set does not change the value, since the integrand changes only on a null set. This definition does not assert that separate choices of density versions are jointly measurable in an additional parameter.

For probability densities $p,q$ relative to one fixed measure $\mu$, define $h$ as in [[def-hellinger-distance-between-density-laws]] and set $d_1(P,Q):=\int|p-q|\,d\mu$. Then $h$ is a metric on the induced probability laws and
$$h(P,Q)^2\le d_1(P,Q)=2\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\rm TV},\qquad d_1(P,Q)\le2h(P,Q),$$
where library total variation is the event supremum $\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\rm TV}=\sup_{A\in\mathcal A}|P(A)-Q(A)|$.

Assume AC. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma>0$, the normal law $N(m,\sigma^2)$
of [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]] has Lebesgue density
$$g_{m,\sigma}(y)=\frac1\sigma\frac{e^{-((y-m)/\sigma)^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}e^{-(y-m)^2/(2\sigma^2)}.$$

Assume AC. For $m\in\mathbb R$, $\sigma\ge0$, and a real random variable
$X$ with law $N(m,\sigma^2)$,
$$E[X]=m,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(X)=\sigma^2.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim: Since $G$ is a probability on $(0,\infty)=\bigcup_{m\ge1}[1/m,m]$, choose $0<s_-<s_+<\infty$ with $g:=G([s_-,s_+])>0$. Put $\sigma_-=s_-\sigma_n$. Apply the moment-matching proof of [F2] to the law $P_0$ at scale $\sigma_-$, restricting each compact moment curve to $K$ intersected with the closure of its partition interval. The same convex-hull reduction and remainder bounds then give a finite discrete probability $F_n$ supported on $K$ with at most $C\sigma_n^{-1}\log n$ atoms and $\|p_{F_n,\sigma_-}-p_{P_0,\sigma_-}\|_1\le\eta_n$, where $\eta_n:=\sigma_n^8$.

Choose an open neighborhood $V$ of $K$ on which the density of $\alpha$ is bounded above and below by positive constants. By compactness, choose a fixed finite union $D$ of disjoint compact intervals with $K\subset\operatorname{int}D\subset D\subset V$. Move each atom of $F_n$ to a nearest point of a lattice of mesh $\eta_n\sigma_-$, merge coincident atoms, and call the resulting law $\widetilde F_n$. Each atom moves by at most $\eta_n\sigma_-/2$; for every $\sigma\ge\sigma_-$ this changes the mixture in $L^1$ by at most $\eta_n/2$, since $\|\partial_z\phi_\sigma(\cdot-z)\|_1=E|Z|/\sigma\le1/\sigma\le1/\sigma_-$, using $2|Z|\le1+Z^2$ and [F8]. The relocated locations are separated by at least $\eta_n\sigma_-$. Around each take a centered cell of length $\ell_n=\eta_n\sigma_-/2$. In each component of $D$, split every intervening or end gap of length $g\ge\ell_n$ into $q=\lceil2g/\sigma_-\rceil$ equal subintervals. For large $n$, the end gaps have length at least $\ell_n$ because $K\subset\operatorname{int}D$, and gaps between atom-cells have length at least $\ell_n$ by lattice separation. If $q=1$, the subinterval length lies in $[\ell_n,\sigma_-/2]$; if $q\ge2$, then $g>\sigma_-/2$ and $q\le4g/\sigma_-$, so each subinterval has length in $[\sigma_-/4,\sigma_-/2]$. The resulting Borel partition $U_1,\ldots,U_N$ of $D$ has every cell length between $c\eta_n\sigma_-$ and $\sigma_-/2$, every atom-cell diameter at most $2\eta_n\sigma_-$, and $N\le C(m_n+\sigma_-^{-1})\le C\sigma_n^{-1}\log n$, where $m_n$ is the number of atoms. Let $w_j=\widetilde F_n(U_j)$, so $\sum_jw_j=1$. For all large $n$, $c\eta_n\sigma_n\le\alpha(U_j)\le1$ and $c\eta_n\sigma_n\ge c'\eta_n^2$. Also $N\eta_n\le C\sigma_n^7\log n\to0$. The residual cell is $U_0=\mathbb R\setminus D$, so $\alpha(U_0)$ is fixed, possibly zero. Apply [F3] with $a=c'$, $b=2$, and $\eta=\eta_n$; its constant may depend on this fixed residual mass. We obtain an event $E_n$ with $\Pi_{DP}(E_n)\ge e^{-C N\log(e/\eta_n)}\ge e^{-C\sigma_n^{-1}(\log n)^2}$, on which $F(U_0)\le3\eta_n$, $\sum_j|F(U_j)-w_j|\le3\eta_n$, and $F(U_j)\ge\eta_n^2/2$ for every $j$.

For $F$ in $E_n$, compare $p_{F,\sigma}$ with $p_{\widetilde F_n,\sigma}$, uniformly for $s_-\sigma_n\le\sigma\le s_+\sigma_n$. On atom cells, replacing $F|_{U_j}$ by its mass at the center costs at most $C\eta_n$ in $L^1$ by the [F7] location derivative bound and cell diameter. The event bounds make the total mass on gap cells and $U_0$ at most $C\eta_n$ and the sum of weight discrepancies at most $C\eta_n$. Since each normal density has $L^1$ norm one, $\|p_{F,\sigma}-p_{\widetilde F_n,\sigma}\|_1\le C\eta_n$. For every such $\sigma$, the relocation estimate in step 1.2 also gives $\|p_{\widetilde F_n,\sigma}-p_{F_n,\sigma}\|_1\le C\eta_n$. If $\sigma>\sigma_-$, completing the square gives $\phi_{\sigma_-}*\phi_v=\phi_\sigma$ for $v=\sqrt{\sigma^2-\sigma_-^2}$; at $\sigma=\sigma_-$ the identity is immediate. Convolution by a probability density contracts $L^1$ by Tonelli [F9], so $\|p_{F_n,\sigma}-p_{P_0,\sigma}\|_1\le\|p_{F_n,\sigma_-}-p_{P_0,\sigma_-}\|_1\le\eta_n$. Thus [F6] gives $h(p_{F,\sigma},p_{P_0,\sigma})\le C\sqrt{\eta_n}$, and the assumed bias bound gives $h(p_0,p_{F,\sigma})\le C(\sigma_n^2+\sqrt{\eta_n})\le C\sigma_n^2$.

For every $x\in K$, the interval $[x-\sigma_-,x+\sigma_-]$ contains a full cell $U_j$ because $D$ contains a fixed neighborhood of $K$ and all cells have length at most $\sigma_-/2$. On this interval $\phi_\sigma(x-z)\ge c/\sigma$ for $s_-\sigma_n\le\sigma\le s_+\sigma_n$. Thus [F1] and the cell-mass lower bound in step 1.2 give $p_{F,\sigma}(x)\ge c\eta_n^2/\sigma_n$. Since $p_0$ is bounded and vanishes outside $K$, $R_n:=\|p_0/p_{F,\sigma}\|_\infty\le C\sigma_n\eta_n^{-2}=C\sigma_n^{-15}$. Step 2.1 gives $h(p_0,p_{F,\sigma})\le C\sigma_n^2$, and the polynomial lower bound on $\sigma_n$ gives $1+\log^+R_n\le C\log n$. Apply [F4] to $p=p_0$ and $q=p_{F,\sigma}$ to obtain both local KL quantities at most $C\sigma_n^4(\log n)^2\le C\delta_n^2$.

The scale event $S\in[s_-,s_+]$ has probability $g>0$ and is independent of $F$. Thus the subset $E_n\times\{S\in[s_-,s_+]\}$ is contained in the displayed local KL/log-square set and has prior probability at least $g e^{-C\sigma_n^{-1}(\log n)^2}$. By the definition of $\delta_n$, $n\delta_n^2\ge\sigma_n^{-1}(\log n)^2$, so increasing $C_1$ absorbs $g$ and proves the required lower bound.

Assume AC. Let $p\in C^2(\mathbb R)$ be a nonnegative compactly supported probability density and suppose
$$J:=\int_{\{p>0\}}\frac{(p''(x))^2}{p(x)}\,dx<\infty.$$
For $\sigma>0$, set $q_\sigma=p*\phi_\sigma$, where $\phi_\sigma$ is the centered normal density with standard deviation $\sigma$. Then
$$\int\frac{(p-q_\sigma)^2}{q_\sigma}\,dx\le\frac49\sigma^4J,\qquad \mathrm{KL}(p\Vert q_\sigma)\le\frac49\sigma^4J,\qquad \int p\left[\log\frac p{q_\sigma}\right]^2dx\le\frac49\sigma^4J.$$
The logarithmic integrands are zero where $p=0$. No unimodality or uniform bound on $p/q_\sigma$ is assumed.

There is a universal constant $C$ such that, for $A,\sigma>0$,
$0<\eta<1/2$, and every probability measure $F$ supported on $[-A,A]$,
there is a discrete probability measure $F'$ on $[-A,A]$ with at most
$$C(A/\sigma\vee1)\log(e/\eta)$$
support points and
$$\|p_{F,\sigma}-p_{F',\sigma}\|_1\le\eta,\qquad \|p_{F,\sigma}-p_{F',\sigma}\|_\infty\le\eta/\sigma.$$

Assume AC, let $\alpha$ be a finite nonzero measure of total mass $m$, and
let $F\sim DP(\alpha)$. Consider a finite partition
$(U_0,U_1,\ldots,U_N)$ with $\alpha(U_0)=0$ or
$0<\alpha(U_0)\le m$. Write $\alpha_j=\alpha(U_j)$ for $j\ge1$, and assume
$$a\eta^b\le\alpha_j\le1\quad(1\le j\le N),\qquad 0<\eta<1/4,\qquad N\eta\le1/4,$$
for fixed $a,b>0$. For every $w=(w_1,\ldots,w_N)$ in the probability
simplex, there are constants $c,C>0$ depending only on $a,b,m,\alpha(U_0)$
such that
$$\Pr\!\left\{\sum_{j=1}^N|F(U_j)-w_j|+F(U_0)\le3\eta,\quad \min_{1\le j\le N}F(U_j)\ge\eta^2/2\right\}\ge C\exp\{-cN\log(e/\eta)\}.$$
For any compact $J\subset(0,m]$, the constants may instead depend only on
$a,b,m,J$ and are uniform over $\alpha(U_0)\in J$.
When $\alpha(U_0)=0$, the zero-base cell has $F(U_0)=0$ almost surely and is
omitted from the Dirichlet vector.

Let $\mathcal P(\mathbb R)$ be the probability measures on the Borel sets of
$\mathbb R$, equipped with the evaluation sigma-algebra, and let $\sigma>0$.
For $F\in\mathcal P(\mathbb R)$ define
$$p_{F,\sigma}(x):=\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{(x-z)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)F(dz).$$
Then $(F,\sigma,x)\mapsto p_{F,\sigma}(x)$ is jointly measurable,
$0<p_{F,\sigma}(x)\le(\sigma\sqrt{2\pi})^{-1}$ for every $(F,\sigma,x)$,
and $\int_{\mathbb R}p_{F,\sigma}(x)\,dx=1$. In particular it is the
Lebesgue density of the convolution of $F$ with $N(0,\sigma^2)$.

Assume AC. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma>0$, the normal law $N(m,\sigma^2)$
of [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]] has Lebesgue density
$$g_{m,\sigma}(y)=\frac1\sigma\frac{e^{-((y-m)/\sigma)^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}e^{-(y-m)^2/(2\sigma^2)}.$$

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

derivations.claim: Choose $0<s_-<s_+<\infty$ with $g:=G([s_-,s_+])>0$, possible because these compact intervals exhaust $(0,\infty)$. Set $b_n=\sigma_n$, $\tau=s_-b_n$, $B=a+6$ and $\eta=b_n^B$. For all large $n$, partition each nondegenerate component of $K$ into equal consecutive Borel intervals of lengths in $[\tau/8,\tau/4]$: use $\lceil4\ell/\tau\rceil$ pieces for a component of length $\ell$. Endpoints can be assigned arbitrarily because $P_0$ has a density. The support of a continuous density has no isolated points, so there are no isolated support components to treat. There are $O(b_n^{-1})$ coarse cells $I_k$, each of mass at least $c' b_n^a$. Translate the conditional probability $P_0(\cdot\mid I_k)$ to an interval centered at zero, apply [F2] at scale $\tau$, and translate back. Multiplying by $P_0(I_k)$ and summing gives a finite probability $F_n$ with at most $C b_n^{-1}\log(e/\eta)$ atoms in the closures of these cells, each carrying its original coarse-cell label, and $\|p_{F_n,\tau}-p_{P_0,\tau}\|_\infty\le\eta/\tau$. The total weight of atoms with label $k$ is exactly $P_0(I_k)$.

Put $\delta=\eta\tau$. Move each atom to a nearest point of the global lattice of mesh $\delta$ and merge atoms at the same location. Preserve its fractional label weights when merging. The resulting distinct locations $z_j$ are separated by at least $\delta$, with weights $w_j$ summing to one, and still number $N\le Cb_n^{-1}\log(e/\eta)$. Let $U_j=[z_j-\delta/4,z_j+\delta/4)$ and $U_0=\mathbb R\setminus\bigcup_{j=1}^NU_j$. These are disjoint partition cells. The base density is bounded above and below on a fixed compact neighborhood of $K$, so $c_0\eta\tau\le\alpha(U_j)\le C_0\eta\tau\le1$ eventually. Since $B>1$, $\eta\tau\ge c_1\eta^2$ and $N\eta\to0$. Also $\sum_j\alpha(U_j)\le C N\delta\to0$, so, writing $m=\alpha(\mathbb R)>0$, we have $\alpha(U_0)\in[m/2,m]$ eventually.

Apply [F3] with tolerance $\eta$ to get an event $E_n$ on which $\sum_j|F(U_j)-w_j|+F(U_0)\le3\eta$ and $\Pi_{DP}(E_n)\ge\exp\{-C b_n^{-1}(\log n)^2\}$. Its constants can be taken uniform in $n$: in the proof of [F3] the only residual-parameter factors are $\Gamma(m)/\Gamma(\alpha(U_0))$ and a lower bound $(\eta^2/2)^m$ for the residual power. The gamma ratio is bounded below on the fixed compact interval $[m/2,m]$, and the latter power already has fixed exponent $m$. The remaining constants use only the fixed bound $c_1\eta^2\le\alpha(U_j)\le1$. Finally $\log(e/\eta)\le C\log n$ by the polynomial lower bandwidth bound.

For $\tau\le\sigma\le s_+b_n$, the original discrete approximation still satisfies $\|p_{F_n,\sigma}-p_{P_0,\sigma}\|_\infty\le C\eta/b_n$. Indeed the Gaussian convolution identity $\phi_u*\phi_v=\phi_{\sqrt{u^2+v^2}}$ follows by completing the square and integrating; convolution with a probability kernel contracts the supremum norm by the triangle inequality. Use $u=\tau$, $v=\sqrt{\sigma^2-\tau^2}$, treating equality by the original approximation. Differentiating [F5] gives $\|\phi_\sigma'\|_\infty\le C\sigma^{-2}$. Atom relocation by at most $\delta/2$ therefore changes the mixture by at most $C\delta/\sigma^2\le C\eta/b_n$. For $F\in E_n$, replacing each $F|_{U_j}$ by its mass at $z_j$ costs at most the same derivative bound times $\delta/4$; the weight discrepancies and residual mass cost at most $3\eta\|\phi_\sigma\|_\infty$. Consequently, uniformly over $F\in E_n$ and $\tau\le\sigma\le s_+b_n$, one has $\|p_{F,\sigma}-p_{P_0,\sigma}\|_\infty\le C\eta/b_n$.

For any $x\in K$ choose a coarse cell whose closure contains $x$. Its length is at most $\tau/4$, so every original atom with that label, and every associated relocated atom-cell, lies in $[x-\tau,x+\tau]$ eventually. Let $J_x$ be the set of relocated atom indices carrying a positive fraction of this label's weight. Merging preserves the full label weight, so $\sum_{j\in J_x}w_j\ge P_0(I_k)\ge c' b_n^a$. The vector discrepancy on $E_n$ implies $F([x-\tau,x+\tau])\ge\sum_{j\in J_x}F(U_j)\ge c'b_n^a-3\eta\ge c'b_n^a/2$. On this neighborhood, [F5] is at least $c''/b_n$ for every $\tau\le\sigma\le s_+b_n$. Thus $p_{F,\sigma}(x)\ge c'''b_n^{a-1}$. The same argument directly with the coarse-cell mass under $P_0$ gives $p_{P_0,\sigma}(x)\ge c'''b_n^{a-1}$, after decreasing the constant.

Put $q=p_{P_0,\sigma}$ and $r=p_{F,\sigma}$. The mean-value theorem for the logarithm, whose derivative is given by [F6], and steps 4.1, 4.2 give $\sup_{x\in K}|\log(q(x)/r(x))|\le C\eta b_n^{-a}=Cb_n^6$. By [F1], $\mathrm{KL}(P_0\Vert Q)\le Cb_n^4$ and $P_0[\log(p_0/q)]^2\le Cb_n^4$ uniformly in these scales. Adding the bounded log perturbation proves $\mathrm{KL}(P_0\Vert P_{F,\sigma})\le Cb_n^4+Cb_n^6\le C'b_n^4$. The inequality $(u+v)^2\le2u^2+2v^2$ similarly gives $P_0[\log(p_0/r)]^2\le C'b_n^4$. All integrals exist by the displayed bounds, and integrands vanish off $\{p_0>0\}$.

The scale event $S\in[s_-,s_+]$ has fixed probability $g>0$ and is independent of $F$. Therefore $E_n$ times this event is contained in the displayed KL/log-square set and has probability at least $g\exp\{-C b_n^{-1}(\log n)^2\}$. Increase $C_2$ to absorb $g$. Since $nd_n^2\ge b_n^{-1}(\log n)^2$ and $d_n^2\ge b_n^4$, the consequent local-radius form follows as well. This proves all assertions without a unimodality hypothesis.
