The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$ be a standard Borel
space and let $\alpha$ be a finite nonzero measure on it. Then there is a
measurable random probability measure $G$ whose law on the evaluation
sigma-algebra of $\mathcal P(\mathsf X)$ is $DP(\alpha)$. For every finite
measurable partition $(A_1,\ldots,A_k)$, the unnormalized increments are
independent with
$\Gamma(A_j)\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(\alpha(A_j),1)$ when
$\alpha(A_j)>0$, and $\Gamma(A_j)=0$ almost surely when $\alpha(A_j)=0$.
Consequently the normalized masses have the finite-partition Dirichlet laws
in [[def-dirichlet-process]]. These laws determine the probability law on
$\mathcal P(\mathsf X)$ uniquely.

The construction uses the Poisson random measure with intensity
$$\mu(dx,dt)=\alpha(dx)t^{-1}e^{-t}\,dt\quad\text{on }\mathsf X\times(0,\infty),$$
and normalizes its weighted projection onto $\mathsf X$. It does not assume a
gamma-process existence theorem.

Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
([[def-probability-measure]]). Absolute continuity $P\ll Q$ has the convention
of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If
$P\not\ll Q$, define $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and
let $r=dP/dQ$ be a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative of its
Radon–Nikodym class; such a representative exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].
On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This
function is measurable: for $a\ge0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r>\exp(a)\}$, and for
$a<0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r=0\}\cup\{r>\exp(a)\}$, by the inverse and
monotonicity properties of the natural logarithm
([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]). These are
measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since
$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$ by
[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$
The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,
$$0\le \frac{\log s}{s}=\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{u}\le\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{\sqrt u}\le\frac2{\sqrt s}.$$
Thus $t\log t\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$; here $L=\log$ by
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and
[[def-integral-logarithm]]. On $(0,\infty)$, $\psi$ is a product of continuous
functions by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $\psi$ is continuous on
$[0,\infty)$ and $\psi(r)$ is measurable by
[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts
([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]],
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

For $0<t\le1$, the function $-t\log t$ has derivative $-\log t-1$ and
maximum $1/e$ at $t=1/e$: $e=\exp(1)>1$ by
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $1/e=\exp(-1)$ by
[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and $\log(1/e)=-1$ by
[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and the inverse definition. The mean value
theorem gives increase before and decrease after this point
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]],
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).
At $t=0$ the negative part is zero. Since $Q$ is a probability measure,
$$\int \psi(r)^-\,dQ\le\frac1e.$$
The change-of-measure identity of [[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]],
applied to $\ell^-$ gives $\int\ell^-\,dP=\int\psi(r)^-\,dQ\le1/e$,
so $\int\ell\,dP$ is well-defined; applying it to both positive and negative
parts gives
$$D(P\|Q)=\int\ell\,dP=\int\psi(r)\,dQ=\int r\log r\,dQ,$$
with $0\log0:=0$ and a finite negative part. Therefore the extended integral
is well-defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.

This convention is directional: the first argument must be absolutely
continuous with respect to the second for the integral formula to apply.

Assume AC. Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$ be standard Borel, let $\alpha$ be a
finite nonzero measure, draw $G\sim DP(\alpha)$, and, conditionally on $G$,
draw $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ with joint law $G^{\otimes n}$, where $n\ge1$. Then
$$K(x_1,\ldots,x_n;\,\cdot)=DP\!\left(\alpha+\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{x_i}\right)$$
is a measurable data-indexed posterior kernel version. It satisfies the
posterior disintegration identity on the evaluation sigma-algebra of
$\mathcal P(\mathsf X)$ and $\mathcal A^{\otimes n}$. On prior-predictive
null data sets its values are a version choice; the displayed formula is
well-defined there but is not asserted to be uniquely forced.

Assume AC. In the conditionally IID model
$G\sim DP(\alpha)$, $X_i\mid G\sim G$, the posterior version after
$x_{1:n}=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ has one-step predictive probability
$$\Pr(X_{n+1}\in A\mid X_{1:n}=x_{1:n})=\frac{\alpha(A)+\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf1_A(x_i)}{\alpha(\mathsf X)+n}$$
for every measurable $A$ and every data vector. The formula is a
data-indexed version on prior-predictive null data sets; those pointwise
values are not uniquely determined by the disintegration identity.

is a measurable data-indexed posterior kernel version. It satisfies the

$G\sim DP(\alpha)$, $X_i\mid G\sim G$, the posterior version after

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ be a measurable parameter space, $\Pi$ a prior probability measure on it, and $p_\theta$ a jointly measurable family of finite-valued probability densities relative to one fixed sigma-finite measure $\mu$. Let $P_0$ have finite-valued density $p_0$ relative to $\mu$, and let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be IID with law $P_0$. Assume the Axiom of Choice for the imported directional KL convention ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). The jointly measurable density family is explicit input, so no arbitrary-index selection of versions is used here. In the expression below, the weighted log terms are set to zero on $\{p_0=0\}$; on $\{p_0>0,p_\theta=0\}$ the log ratio is $-\infty$ and its square is $+\infty$. For $\epsilon_n>0$, define
$$K_n:=\left\{\theta:\mathrm{KL}(P_0\Vert P_\theta)\le\epsilon_n^2,\quad \int\left[\log\frac{p_\theta}{p_0}\right]^2p_0\,d\mu\le\epsilon_n^2\right\}.$$
Joint measurability and Tonelli make $K_n$ measurable, as verified below. If $\Pi(K_n)\ge e^{-Cn\epsilon_n^2}$ for $C>0$ and $\mathrm{KL}(P_0\Vert P_\theta)$ uses the direction in [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]], then, defining the ratio to be zero on the $P_0$-null set where $p_0=0$, the likelihood denominator
$$D_n:=\int_\Theta\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{p_\theta(X_i)}{p_0(X_i)}\,\Pi(d\theta)$$
is finite and positive $P_0^n$-almost surely and
$$P_0^n\!\left\{D_n\ge e^{-(C+2)n\epsilon_n^2}\right\}\ge1-\frac1{n\epsilon_n^2}.$$

Assume AC. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma>0$, the normal law $N(m,\sigma^2)$
of [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]] has Lebesgue density
$$g_{m,\sigma}(y)=\frac1\sigma\frac{e^{-((y-m)/\sigma)^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}e^{-(y-m)^2/(2\sigma^2)}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$ be a standard Borel space and let $\alpha$ be a
finite nonzero measure on it. Write $\mathcal P(\mathsf X)$ for the set of
probability measures on $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$, equipped with the
**evaluation sigma-algebra**
$$\sigma\bigl(\{G\mapsto G(A):A\in\mathcal A\}\bigr).$$
For a probability law $P$ on this space, let $G$ be the coordinate random
probability measure $G(\omega)=\omega$. Call $P$ a **Dirichlet-process law
with base measure** $\alpha$ if, for every finite measurable partition
$(A_1,\ldots,A_k)$ of $\mathsf X$, the vector
$(G(A_1),\ldots,G(A_k))$ has the Dirichlet distribution with parameters
$(\alpha(A_1),\ldots,\alpha(A_k))$ after zero-parameter cells are omitted;
each omitted zero-base cell has mass zero. If the partition has one
positive-parameter cell, its mass is one. The finite-partition specification
determines at most one law on the evaluation sigma-algebra. When such a law
exists, denote it by $DP(\alpha)$; the construction theorem on this page
proves existence.

The Dirichlet distribution here has the positive-parameter density and
one-category convention of [[def-dirichlet-distribution]]. The definition
asserts no weak topology, support statement, or density-contraction result.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$ be a standard Borel
space and let $\alpha$ be a finite nonzero measure on it. Then there is a
measurable random probability measure $G$ whose law on the evaluation
sigma-algebra of $\mathcal P(\mathsf X)$ is $DP(\alpha)$. For every finite
measurable partition $(A_1,\ldots,A_k)$, the unnormalized increments are

$\Gamma(A_j)\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(\alpha(A_j),1)$ when
$\alpha(A_j)>0$, and $\Gamma(A_j)=0$ almost surely when $\alpha(A_j)=0$.

The construction uses the Poisson random measure with intensity
$$\mu(dx,dt)=\alpha(dx)t^{-1}e^{-t}\,dt\quad\text{on }\mathsf X\times(0,\infty),$$
and normalizes its weighted projection onto $\mathsf X$. It does not assume a
gamma-process existence theorem.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]), let $F$ be its integral function
([[def-the-integral-function]]), and let $c \in [a,b]$ be a point at which $f$ is
continuous ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $F$ is differentiable at $c$ as a
function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]) and

$$F'(c) \;=\; f(c) .$$

At $c = a$ and $c = b$ this is the one-sided statement, which is what
[[def-derivative]] means at those points: every point of a nondegenerate interval
is a limit point of it, so $F'(c)$ is a meaningful symbol at every $c \in [a,b]$,
and the difference quotient is taken over $[a,b] \setminus \{c\}$.

**Consequently, if $f$ is continuous on the whole of $[a,b]$, then $F$ is a
primitive of $f$ there**: $F' = f$ at every point of $[a,b]$.

**Continuity at $c$ is a hypothesis and it cannot be dropped.** For an integrable
$f$ that is discontinuous at $c$, $F'(c)$ may fail to exist, and it may exist and
differ from $f(c)$; both are exhibited on the companion page, by
an integrable function with no primitive and by a false
statement about the integral function.

derivations.claim: The latent representation is $\theta_i\mid F\stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}\sim F$ and $X_i\mid\theta_i,\sigma\sim N(\theta_i,\sigma^2)$ independently. Use the test $\varphi_n=\mathbf1\{\text{some }X_i\notin I\}$. Its type-I error is zero. Write $\Phi(t)=\int_{-\infty}^t\phi(z)\,dz$; [F9] gives $\Phi'(t)=\phi(t)$. The normal formula [F5] is even and satisfies $\phi'(t)=-t\phi(t)$, so it decreases on $[0,\infty)$. For fixed $\theta$ and $\sigma$, set $g(\theta)=P(\theta+\sigma Z\in I)=\Phi((U-\theta)/\sigma)-\Phi((L-\theta)/\sigma)$. Then $g'(\theta)=\sigma^{-1}\left[\phi((L-\theta)/\sigma)-\phi((U-\theta)/\sigma)\right]$. For $\theta\le(L+U)/2$, $|L-\theta|\le|U-\theta|$, so $g'(\theta)\ge0$; for $\theta\ge(L+U)/2$ the inequality reverses and $g'(\theta)\le0$. Thus $g$ is maximized at the midpoint, where the component leakage is $2\Phi(-R/\sigma)$. Every component with $\sigma>s_n$ therefore puts probability at least $q_n=2\Phi(-R/s_n)$ outside $I$, and $P_{F,\sigma}^n(\varphi_n=0)\le(1-q_n)^n\le e^{-nq_n}$.

By [F8] the latent DP model is a measurable prior law. Introduce the latent locations $\theta_{1:n}$. Given these locations, $X_{1:n}$ and $\sigma$, the observation likelihood is independent of $F$, so [F1] gives the conditional law $DP(\alpha+\sum_i\delta_{\theta_i})$. Given this updated $F$, the next latent location has conditional law $F$; applying [F3] to that predictive draw gives $E[F(A)\mid\theta_{1:n},X_{1:n},\sigma]=\frac{\alpha(A)+\sum_i\mathbf1_A(\theta_i)}{\alpha(\mathbb R)+n}$ for every Borel set $A$. With $A=I_d^c$, conditional Markov inequality yields $\Pi_n(F(A)>\epsilon_n^2,\sigma\le s_n\mid X_{1:n})\le\frac{\alpha(A)+\sum_iP(\theta_i\in A,\sigma\le s_n\mid X_{1:n})}{\epsilon_n^2(\alpha(\mathbb R)+n)}.$

Fix an index $i$ and condition on $\theta_{-i},X_{1:n},\sigma$. The latent vector is exchangeable because its conditional law given $F$ is IID. Reordering $\theta_i$ last and applying [F2] shows its prior predictive law given $\theta_{-i}$ is $H_i=(\alpha+\sum_{k\ne i}\delta_{\theta_k})/(\alpha(\mathbb R)+n-1)$. Bayes' formula multiplies this measure by the likelihood $\phi_\sigma(X_i-t)$. Almost surely $X_i\in I$. On $A=I_d^c$, $|X_i-t|\ge d$, so the likelihood numerator is at most $C\sigma^{-1}e^{-d^2/(2\sigma^2)}$. For $\sigma\le s_n$, the denominator is at least the base-measure contribution $\frac{1}{\alpha(\mathbb R)+n-1}\int_{X_i-\sigma}^{X_i+\sigma}\phi_\sigma(X_i-t)\,\alpha(dt)\ge\frac{c}{\alpha(\mathbb R)+n-1},$ because the base density is bounded below near $I$ and $[X_i-\sigma,X_i+\sigma]$ lies there for all sufficiently large $n$. Consequently $P(\theta_i\in A\mid\theta_{-i},X_{1:n},\sigma)\le Cn\sigma^{-1}e^{-d^2/(2\sigma^2)}\le Cn s_n^{-1}e^{-d^2/(2s_n^2)},$ where $s^{-1}e^{-d^2/(2s^2)}$ is increasing on $0<s<d$.

Let $N_n^H$ be the likelihood-ratio numerator integrated over $\{\sigma>s_n\}$. By change of density and [F6], $E_0[(1-\varphi_n)N_n^H]\le e^{-nq_n}$. On the denominator event, [F7] therefore gives, for every $\zeta>0$, $P_0^n\{\Pi_n(\sigma>s_n\mid X_{1:n})>\zeta\}\le o(1)+\zeta^{-1}e^{(C_0+2)n\delta_n^2-nq_n}\longrightarrow0.$

Substitute the step 1.3 bound into step 1.2 and use $\alpha(A)\le\alpha(\mathbb R)$. The resulting upper bound is $\frac{\alpha(\mathbb R)}{\epsilon_n^2(\alpha(\mathbb R)+n)}+Cn\epsilon_n^{-2}s_n^{-1}e^{-d^2/(2s_n^2)}+\Pi_n(\sigma>s_n\mid X_{1:n}),$ which tends to zero by $n\epsilon_n^2\to\infty$, the second premise, and step 2.1. Thus the posterior probability of $F(I_d^c)>\epsilon_n^2$ tends to zero. Combining with step 2.1 proves the sieve-complement claim.

risk_review.notes: Reviewed all six steps and all twelve actual supplier interfaces, with complete current DP-update, predictive and denominator proofs. Clarified that the base density lower bound in the Statement is a positive constant; step 1.3 requires it, whereas merely being nonnegative is insufficient for that displayed denominator estimate. Removed the unsupported continuity adjective from Given; no continuity is used. Gaussian retention is maximal at the midpoint, giving the correct two-sided leakage. The latent full conditional is Gaussian likelihood times the predictive measure; positive base mass in [Xi-sigma,Xi+sigma] yields denominator c/(m+n-1), and its distant numerator is <=C sigma^-1 exp(-d^2/(2sigma^2)). Conditional Markov then gives the stated epsilon^-2 tail bound; the large-scale term is controlled by the denominator event. Both theorem and corollary consumers already assume positive continuous base density on a larger open interval, hence meet the clarified lower bound on their compact I.

This convention is directional: the first argument must be absolutely
continuous with respect to the second for the integral formula to apply.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$ be a standard Borel space and let $\alpha$ be a
finite nonzero measure on it. Write $\mathcal P(\mathsf X)$ for the set of
probability measures on $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$, equipped with the
**evaluation sigma-algebra**
$$\sigma\bigl(\{G\mapsto G(A):A\in\mathcal A\}\bigr).$$
For a probability law $P$ on this space, let $G$ be the coordinate random
probability measure $G(\omega)=\omega$. Call $P$ a **Dirichlet-process law
with base measure** $\alpha$ if, for every finite measurable partition
$(A_1,\ldots,A_k)$ of $\mathsf X$, the vector
$(G(A_1),\ldots,G(A_k))$ has the Dirichlet distribution with parameters
$(\alpha(A_1),\ldots,\alpha(A_k))$ after zero-parameter cells are omitted;
each omitted zero-base cell has mass zero. If the partition has one
positive-parameter cell, its mass is one. The finite-partition specification
determines at most one law on the evaluation sigma-algebra. When such a law
exists, denote it by $DP(\alpha)$; the construction theorem on this page
proves existence.

The Dirichlet distribution here has the positive-parameter density and
one-category convention of [[def-dirichlet-distribution]]. The definition
asserts no weak topology, support statement, or density-contraction result.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$ be a standard Borel
space and let $\alpha$ be a finite nonzero measure on it. Then there is a
measurable random probability measure $G$ whose law on the evaluation
sigma-algebra of $\mathcal P(\mathsf X)$ is $DP(\alpha)$. For every finite
measurable partition $(A_1,\ldots,A_k)$, the unnormalized increments are
independent with
$\Gamma(A_j)\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(\alpha(A_j),1)$ when
$\alpha(A_j)>0$, and $\Gamma(A_j)=0$ almost surely when $\alpha(A_j)=0$.
Consequently the normalized masses have the finite-partition Dirichlet laws
in [[def-dirichlet-process]]. These laws determine the probability law on
$\mathcal P(\mathsf X)$ uniquely.

The construction uses the Poisson random measure with intensity
$$\mu(dx,dt)=\alpha(dx)t^{-1}e^{-t}\,dt\quad\text{on }\mathsf X\times(0,\infty),$$
and normalizes its weighted projection onto $\mathsf X$. It does not assume a
gamma-process existence theorem.

Let $\mathcal P(\mathbb R)$ be the probability measures on the Borel sets of
$\mathbb R$, equipped with the evaluation sigma-algebra, and let $\sigma>0$.
For $F\in\mathcal P(\mathbb R)$ define
$$p_{F,\sigma}(x):=\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{(x-z)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)F(dz).$$
Then $(F,\sigma,x)\mapsto p_{F,\sigma}(x)$ is jointly measurable,
$0<p_{F,\sigma}(x)\le(\sigma\sqrt{2\pi})^{-1}$ for every $(F,\sigma,x)$,
and $\int_{\mathbb R}p_{F,\sigma}(x)\,dx=1$. In particular it is the
Lebesgue density of the convolution of $F$ with $N(0,\sigma^2)$.

Assume AC. Let $p_0$ be a bounded probability density supported on a compact
set $K\subset\mathbb R$. Let $\alpha$ be a finite nonzero measure with a
continuous density bounded below by a positive constant on a neighborhood of
$K$. Assume
$$h(p_0,p_0*\phi_\sigma)\le C\sigma^2$$
for all sufficiently small $\sigma>0$, where $\phi_\sigma$ is the centered
normal density with standard deviation $\sigma$. Let $F\sim DP(\alpha)$ and
let $S\sim G$ be independent, where $G$ is any probability measure on
$(0,\infty)$. Suppose $n^{-a_1}\lesssim\sigma_n\lesssim n^{-a_2}$ for
$0<a_2<a_1<1$. Set $\sigma=\sigma_nS$ and
$$\delta_n:=\max\{(n\sigma_n)^{-1/2}\log n,\ \sigma_n^2\log n\}.$$
Then, for some constant $C_1>0$ and all sufficiently large $n$,
$$\Pi_n\!\left\{(F,\sigma):\mathrm{KL}(P_0\Vert P_{F,\sigma})\le C_1\delta_n^2,\quad P_0\left[\log\frac{p_0}{p_{F,\sigma}}\right]^2\le C_1\delta_n^2\right\} \ge e^{-C_1n\delta_n^2}.$$
Here $p_{F,\sigma}$ is the density of [[lem-dirichlet-normal-mixture-density-well-defined]],
and all logarithmic integrands are set to zero on $\{p_0=0\}$.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ be a measurable parameter space, $\Pi$ a prior probability measure on it, and $p_\theta$ a jointly measurable family of finite-valued probability densities relative to one fixed sigma-finite measure $\mu$. Let $P_0$ have finite-valued density $p_0$ relative to $\mu$, and let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be IID with law $P_0$. Assume the Axiom of Choice for the imported directional KL convention ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). The jointly measurable density family is explicit input, so no arbitrary-index selection of versions is used here. In the expression below, the weighted log terms are set to zero on $\{p_0=0\}$; on $\{p_0>0,p_\theta=0\}$ the log ratio is $-\infty$ and its square is $+\infty$. For $\epsilon_n>0$, define
$$K_n:=\left\{\theta:\mathrm{KL}(P_0\Vert P_\theta)\le\epsilon_n^2,\quad \int\left[\log\frac{p_\theta}{p_0}\right]^2p_0\,d\mu\le\epsilon_n^2\right\}.$$
Joint measurability and Tonelli make $K_n$ measurable, as verified below. If $\Pi(K_n)\ge e^{-Cn\epsilon_n^2}$ for $C>0$ and $\mathrm{KL}(P_0\Vert P_\theta)$ uses the direction in [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]], then, defining the ratio to be zero on the $P_0$-null set where $p_0=0$, the likelihood denominator
$$D_n:=\int_\Theta\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{p_\theta(X_i)}{p_0(X_i)}\,\Pi(d\theta)$$
is finite and positive $P_0^n$-almost surely and
$$P_0^n\!\left\{D_n\ge e^{-(C+2)n\epsilon_n^2}\right\}\ge1-\frac1{n\epsilon_n^2}.$$

Assume AC. Let $p_0$ be supported on a compact interval $I=[L,U]$ with
$L<U$, let $F\sim DP(\alpha)$ for a finite nonzero base measure whose
density is bounded below by a positive constant on a neighborhood of $I$, and let $S\sim G$ be
independent with $\sigma=\sigma_nS$. Put $R=(U-L)/2$ and, for $d>0$,
$I_d=[L-d,U+d]$.
Observe IID data from $p_0$ under the location-mixture density
$p_{F,\sigma}$. Let $\epsilon_n,\delta_n>0$ with
$n\epsilon_n^2\to\infty$ and $n\delta_n^2\to\infty$. Suppose the local KL
and log-square prior-mass condition gives a denominator event
$$P_0^n\{D_n\ge e^{-C_0n\delta_n^2}\}\longrightarrow1,$$
where $D_n=\int\prod_i p_{F,\sigma}(X_i)/p_0(X_i)\,\Pi_n(dF,d\sigma)$.
Choose $s_n\to0$ and put $q_n=2\Phi(-R/s_n)$, where $\Phi$ is the
standard normal distribution function. If
$$nq_n-(C_0+2)n\delta_n^2\to\infty,\qquad n\epsilon_n^{-2}s_n^{-1}e^{-d^2/(2s_n^2)}\to0,$$
then the posterior complement of
$$\mathcal S_n:=\{(F,\sigma):\sigma\le s_n,\ F(I_d^c)\le\epsilon_n^2\}$$
converges to zero in $P_0^n$-probability.

Fix $A\ge1$ independently of $n$. The constants in the entropy estimates
and the required fixed $M_0$ may depend on $A$. Let $0<a_2<a_1<1$,
$n^{-a_1}\lesssim\sigma_n\lesssim n^{-a_2}$, and
$\gamma>1$. Suppose $G$ is a probability measure on $(0,\infty)$ satisfying
$G((0,s])\le C e^{-\beta s^{-\gamma}}$ for all sufficiently small $s>0$.
Let $s_n\to0$ with $s_n/\sigma_n\to\infty$. For integers $j$ with
$2^j\sigma_n\le s_n$, put $\widetilde r_n:=\min\{r_n,1/4\}$ and
$$\mathcal P_{n,j}:=\{p_{F,\sigma}:F([-A,A]^c)\le\widetilde r_n^2/8, \quad 2^j\sigma_n\le\sigma<2^{j+1}\sigma_n,\quad \sigma\le s_n\},$$
and let $\pi_{n,j}$ be the prior mass of the corresponding parameter band,
so $\pi_{n,j}\le G([2^j,2^{j+1}))$. Suppose $r_n>0$ and, for some fixed
sufficiently large $M_0$ (allowed to depend on $A$) and fixed
$\eta>\gamma/[2(\gamma-1)]$,
$$r_n\ge M_0\max\{(n\sigma_n)^{-1/2}\log n, n^{-1/2}\sigma_n^{-\eta}\}.$$
With $N_{n,j}=N(r_n,\mathcal P_{n,j},h)$, one has
$$e^{-nr_n^2}\sum_{j:2^j\sigma_n\le s_n}\sqrt{N_{n,j}\pi_{n,j}}\longrightarrow0.$$
If instead $G$ is supported on a compact subset of $(0,\infty)$, the same
conclusion holds under the first rate term alone.

Assume AC. For each $n$, let $\Pi_n$ be a prior on a measurable parameter
space $\Theta_n^*$, and let $p_\theta$ be a jointly measurable family of finite-valued densities
against one sigma-finite measure, and let $p_0$ be the true density for IID
data $X_1,\ldots,X_n$. Let $\epsilon_n,\delta_n>0$ satisfy
$\delta_n\le\epsilon_n$, $n\delta_n^2\to\infty$, and
$n\epsilon_n^2\to\infty$. Suppose for a constant $C_0>0$ that
$$\Pi_n\!\left\{\theta:\mathrm{KL}(P_0\Vert P_\theta)\le\delta_n^2,\quad P_0\left[\log\frac{p_0}{p_\theta}\right]^2\le\delta_n^2\right\}\ge e^{-C_0n\delta_n^2}.$$
Let $S_n\subseteq\Theta_n^*$ be a measurable sieve with
$\Pi_n(S_n^c\mid X_{1:n})\to0$ in $P_0^n$-probability. Partition it into
countably many measurable sets $S_{n,j}$, put $\pi_{n,j}=\Pi_n(S_{n,j})$,
and let $N_{n,j}=N(\epsilon_n,\{p_\theta:\theta\in S_{n,j}\},h)$ be the
finite covering number as defined in [[def-covering-packing-bracketing-number-and-metric-entropy]], with centers in that density class, whenever $\pi_{n,j}>0$. If
$$e^{-n\epsilon_n^2}\sum_{j:\pi_{n,j}>0}\sqrt{N_{n,j}\pi_{n,j}}\longrightarrow0,$$
then for every sufficiently large fixed $M$, the posterior mass of
$$\{\theta:h(p_\theta,p_0)>M\epsilon_n\}$$
converges to zero in $P_0^n$-probability.

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). It is
**dominated** by a supplied positive measure $\mu$ on
$(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ when $\mu$ is sigma-finite
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]) and
$P_\theta\ll\mu$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$
([[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]).
The dominating measure is part of the specified setup. This condition adds no
measurable structure on $\Theta$ and no measurability of
$\theta\mapsto P_\theta$.

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be dominated by the fixed sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$. For each
$\theta$, the Radon–Nikodym theorem gives the almost-everywhere class
$dP_\theta/d\mu$; a sigma-finite exhaustion for $\mu$ is also finite for the
probability measure $P_\theta$. Under AC, select simultaneously a
finite-valued measurable nonnegative representative $p_\theta$ from each
class. The nonnegative version exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].

For fixed observed $x\in\mathcal X$, the function
$$L_x:\Theta\to[0,+\infty),\qquad L_x(\theta):=p_\theta(x),$$
is the **likelihood at $x$**. This is a function on the parameter labels, not
a probability distribution on $\Theta$. No sigma-algebra on $\Theta$ or
measurability of $L_x$ is implied. Each density is determined only
$\mu$-almost everywhere; there is no canonical pointwise version and, for
arbitrary uncountable $\Theta$, no common exceptional null set is asserted.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $p,q:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ be measurable densities with $\int p\,d\mu=\int q\,d\mu=1$. They define probability laws $P(B)=\int_Bp\,d\mu$ and $Q(B)=\int_Bq\,d\mu$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **root-L2 Hellinger distance**, with the root-L2 normalization, is
$$h(P,Q):=\left(\int_{\mathsf X}(\sqrt p-\sqrt q)^2\,d\mu\right)^{1/2}.$$

The dominating measure $\mu$ is fixed throughout a use of this definition. Changing either density on a $\mu$-null set does not change the value, since the integrand changes only on a null set. This definition does not assert that separate choices of density versions are jointly measurable in an additional parameter.

derivations.claim: Put $d_n=\max\{(n\sigma_n)^{-1/2}\log n,\sigma_n^2\log n\}$. By [F3], choose $C_1\ge1$ so the prior mass is at least $e^{-C_1nd_n^2}$ on a set where both local quantities are at most $C_1d_n^2$. Set $\bar d_n=\sqrt{C_1}d_n$. Then the mass is at least $e^{-n\bar d_n^2}$ and both quantities are at most $\bar d_n^2$. By [F4], except on an event of probability at most $(n\bar d_n^2)^{-1}$, the likelihood denominator is at least $e^{-3n\bar d_n^2}$. Also $n\bar d_n^2\ge C_1\sigma_n^{-1}(\log n)^2\to\infty$.

Choose a compact interval $I=[L,U]$ containing $\operatorname{supp}(p_0)$ in its interior and contained in the open interval where the density of $\alpha$ is continuous and strictly positive. Such an interval exists because the support is compact; its base density is bounded below on $I$. Put $R=(U-L)/2>0$ and $\kappa=\max\{a_1,1-4a_2,0\}<1$. The polynomial bandwidth bounds give $n\bar d_n^2\le Cn^\kappa(\log n)^2$. Choose $s_n=c_0(\log n)^{-1/2}$ with $c_0$ large enough that for some $\theta<1-\kappa$, $q_n:=2\Phi(-R/s_n)\ge n^{-\theta}$ eventually: integrating the standard normal density on $[R/s_n,R/s_n+1]$ gives the claimed lower bound once $R^2/(2c_0^2)<\theta$. Hence $nq_n-5n\bar d_n^2\to\infty$. Set $r_n=M_0\epsilon_n$ for a fixed sufficiently large $M_0$, and $\xi_n=\min\{r_n,1/4\}/\sqrt8$. We have $n\xi_n^2\to\infty$ and $\xi_n^{-2}\le Cn$: if $r_n<1/4$, use $\epsilon_n\ge n^{-1/2}\log n$ for all large $n$, and otherwise $\xi_n$ is fixed. Choose $d>0$ with $d^2/(2c_0^2)>4$ and $A\ge1$ large enough that $I_d=[L-d,U+d]\subseteq[-A,A]$. Then $n\xi_n^{-2}s_n^{-1}e^{-d^2/(2s_n^2)}\to0$. Applying [F5] gives posterior concentration on $\{F(I_d^c)\le\xi_n^2,\sigma\le s_n\}$. Since $[-A,A]^c\subseteq I_d^c$, the larger sieve $S_n=\{F([-A,A]^c)\le\xi_n^2,\sigma\le s_n\}$ also has $\Pi_n(S_n^c\mid X_{1:n})\to0$.

Partition $S_n$ into dyadic scale bands $S_{n,j}=S_n\cap\{2^j\sigma_n\le\sigma<2^{j+1}\sigma_n\}$ for $2^j\sigma_n\le s_n$. Their prior masses are bounded by $G([2^j,2^{j+1}))$. Since $\xi_n^2=\min\{r_n,1/4\}^2/8$, [F6] applies at radius $r_n$ and gives $e^{-nr_n^2}\sum_j\sqrt{N(r_n,\{p_{F,\sigma}:(F,\sigma)\in S_{n,j}\},h) \,\Pi_n(S_{n,j})}\longrightarrow0.$ For compactly supported $G$, only finitely many bands have positive prior mass and the first rate term suffices.

If $G$ is compactly supported, put $\epsilon_n^{\mathrm c}=\max\{(n\sigma_n)^{-1/2}\log n,\sigma_n^2\log n\}$, $r_n^{\mathrm c}=M_0\epsilon_n^{\mathrm c}$ and $\xi_n^{\mathrm c}=\min\{r_n^{\mathrm c},1/4\}/\sqrt8$. Since $\sigma_n\to0$, $n(\epsilon_n^{\mathrm c})^2\ge\sigma_n^{-1}(\log n)^2\to\infty$ and $(\epsilon_n^{\mathrm c})^{-2}\le Cn$. Thus $n(\xi_n^{\mathrm c})^2\to\infty$ and $(\xi_n^{\mathrm c})^{-2}\le Cn$. Also $\bar d_n\le\sqrt{C_1}\epsilon_n^{\mathrm c}$. Retain $I,s_n,d,A$ from step 1.2: its denominator, leakage bound, and exponential factor do not depend on the target radius, so the hypotheses of [F5] hold with $\epsilon_n^{\mathrm c}$ and $\xi_n^{\mathrm c}$ in place of $\epsilon_n$ and $\xi_n$. It yields posterior sieve complement convergence for $S_n^{\mathrm c}=\{F([-A,A]^c)\le(\xi_n^{\mathrm c})^2,\sigma\le s_n\}$. The compact branch of [F6] supplies the weighted entropy condition at radius $r_n^{\mathrm c}$ using only the first rate term.

The prior is the measurable DP law from [F1], and [F2], [F8] give its jointly measurable density likelihoods. We have $\bar d_n\le\sqrt{C_1}\epsilon_n$, so increasing $M_0$ if necessary ensures $\bar d_n\le r_n$; also $n\bar d_n^2,nr_n^2\to\infty$. Thus [F3] supplies the local prior-mass condition for [F7]. For general $G$, steps 1.2 and 1.3 provide a sieve with vanishing posterior complement and its weighted entropy condition. If $G$ is compactly supported, step 2.1 instead provides these two conditions at radius $r_n^{\mathrm c}$, and its bound $\bar d_n\le\sqrt{C_1}\epsilon_n^{\mathrm c}$ allows $M_0$ to be chosen so $\bar d_n\le r_n^{\mathrm c}$. Apply [F7] with local radius $\bar d_n$ and target radius $r_n$ in the general case, or $r_n^{\mathrm c}$ in the compact case. It follows that for every sufficiently large fixed $M_1$, the posterior outside $M_1M_0\epsilon_n$ (respectively $M_1M_0\epsilon_n^{\mathrm c}$) tends to zero in $P_0^n$-probability. Since $M_1M_0$ can be any sufficiently large fixed constant, this proves the stated rates. The measurability and dominated-likelihood requirements are supplied by [F1], [F2], and [F8], and [F9] fixes the conclusion's metric convention.

Assume AC. Let $p_0$ be a finite-valued probability density on $\mathbb R$
with compact support. Assume $p_0\in C^2(\mathbb R)$ and, with the
integrands set to zero on $\{p_0=0\}$,
$$\int_{\{p_0>0\}}\left[\left(\frac{p_0''}{p_0}\right)^2+ \left(\frac{p_0'}{p_0}\right)^4\right]p_0\,dx<\infty,$$
and assume there is $C<\infty$ such that
$$h(p_0,p_0*\phi_\sigma)\le C\sigma^2$$
for all sufficiently small $\sigma>0$. Here $h$ is the root-L2 Hellinger
distance of [[def-hellinger-distance-between-density-laws]], and
$\phi_\sigma$ is the centered normal density with standard deviation
$\sigma$. Let $F\sim DP(\alpha)$, where $\alpha$ is a finite nonzero
measure with a continuous, strictly positive Lebesgue density on an open
interval containing $\operatorname{supp}(p_0)$, and independently let
$S\sim G$ on $(0,\infty)$. For $\sigma=\sigma_nS$, define
$$p_{F,\sigma}(x)=\int\phi_\sigma(x-z)F(dz),$$
and observe $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ IID from $p_0$. Suppose
$$n^{-a_1}\lesssim\sigma_n\lesssim n^{-a_2},\qquad 0<a_2<a_1<1,\qquad a_2\ge(4+\gamma)^{-1},$$
and, for some $\beta>0$ and $\gamma>1$,
$$G((0,s])\lesssim e^{-\beta s^{-\gamma}}\ (s\downarrow0),\qquad G((s,\infty))\lesssim e^{-\beta s^\gamma}\ (s\to\infty).$$
Here $u_n\lesssim v_n$ means $u_n\le Cv_n$ eventually for a fixed
constant $C$. For every fixed
$\eta>\gamma/[2(\gamma-1)]$, put
$$\epsilon_n=\max\left\{(n\sigma_n)^{-1/2}\log n, n^{-1/2}\sigma_n^{-\eta},\ \sigma_n^2\log n\right\}.$$
Then for every sufficiently large fixed $M$,
$$\Pi_n\!\left(h(p_{F,\sigma},p_0)>M\epsilon_n\mid X_{1:n}\right) \longrightarrow0$$
in $P_0^n$-probability. If $G$ is compactly supported in $(0,\infty)$,
the middle term $n^{-1/2}\sigma_n^{-\eta}$ may be omitted. The conclusion
is only in probability; it supplies no almost-sure contraction or generic
minimax-optimality assertion.

Assume AC. Let $p_0$ be supported on a compact interval $I=[L,U]$ with

$$P_0^n\{D_n\ge e^{-C_0n\delta_n^2}\}\longrightarrow1,$$

$$\mathcal S_n:=\{(F,\sigma):\sigma\le s_n,\ F(I_d^c)\le\epsilon_n^2\}$$
converges to zero in $P_0^n$-probability.

Fix $A\ge1$ independently of $n$. The constants in the entropy estimates
and the required fixed $M_0$ may depend on $A$. Let $0<a_2<a_1<1$,
$n^{-a_1}\lesssim\sigma_n\lesssim n^{-a_2}$, and

$n\epsilon_n^2\to\infty$. Suppose for a constant $C_0>0$ that
$$\Pi_n\!\left\{\theta:\mathrm{KL}(P_0\Vert P_\theta)\le\delta_n^2,\quad P_0\left[\log\frac{p_0}{p_\theta}\right]^2\le\delta_n^2\right\}\ge e^{-C_0n\delta_n^2}.$$

$\Pi_n(S_n^c\mid X_{1:n})\to0$ in $P_0^n$-probability. Partition it into
countably many measurable sets $S_{n,j}$, put $\pi_{n,j}=\Pi_n(S_{n,j})$,
and let $N_{n,j}=N(\epsilon_n,\{p_\theta:\theta\in S_{n,j}\},h)$ be the
finite covering number as defined in [[def-covering-packing-bracketing-number-and-metric-entropy]], with centers in that density class, whenever $\pi_{n,j}>0$. If
$$e^{-n\epsilon_n^2}\sum_{j:\pi_{n,j}>0}\sqrt{N_{n,j}\pi_{n,j}}\longrightarrow0,$$
then for every sufficiently large fixed $M$, the posterior mass of
$$\{\theta:h(p_\theta,p_0)>M\epsilon_n\}$$
converges to zero in $P_0^n$-probability.

Let $\mathcal P(\mathbb R)$ be the probability measures on the Borel sets of
$\mathbb R$, equipped with the evaluation sigma-algebra, and let $\sigma>0$.
For $F\in\mathcal P(\mathbb R)$ define
$$p_{F,\sigma}(x):=\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{(x-z)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)F(dz).$$

$0<p_{F,\sigma}(x)\le(\sigma\sqrt{2\pi})^{-1}$ for every $(F,\sigma,x)$,
and $\int_{\mathbb R}p_{F,\sigma}(x)\,dx=1$. In particular it is the
Lebesgue density of the convolution of $F$ with $N(0,\sigma^2)$.

Choose $d>0$ with $d^2/(2c_0^2)>4$ and a fixed $A\ge1$ large enough that $I_d=[L-d,U+d]\subseteq[-A,A]$. Then $n\xi_n^{-2}s_n^{-1}e^{-d^2/(2s_n^2)}\to0$, by the inverse-radius bound in step 2.1. Step 1.1 gives the local mass condition, step 3.1 gives the sieve complement, and step 4.1 gives the weighted entropy condition at target radius $r_n$. Assume AC. Let $p_0$ be a finite-valued probability density on $\mathbb R$
with compact support. Assume $p_0\in C^2(\mathbb R)$ and, with the
integrands set to zero on $\{p_0=0\}$,
$$\int_{\{p_0>0\}}\left[\left(\frac{p_0''}{p_0}\right)^2+ \left(\frac{p_0'}{p_0}\right)^4\right]p_0\,dx<\infty,$$
and assume there is $C<\infty$ such that
$$h(p_0,p_0*\phi_\sigma)\le C\sigma^2$$
for all sufficiently small $\sigma>0$. Here $h$ is the root-L2 Hellinger
distance of [[def-hellinger-distance-between-density-laws]], and
$\phi_\sigma$ is the centered normal density with standard deviation
$\sigma$. Let $F\sim DP(\alpha)$, where $\alpha$ is a finite nonzero
measure with a continuous, strictly positive Lebesgue density on an open
interval containing $\operatorname{supp}(p_0)$, and independently let
$S\sim G$ on $(0,\infty)$. For $\sigma=\sigma_nS$, define
$$p_{F,\sigma}(x)=\int\phi_\sigma(x-z)F(dz),$$
and observe $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ IID from $p_0$. Suppose
$$n^{-a_1}\lesssim\sigma_n\lesssim n^{-a_2},\qquad 0<a_2<a_1<1,\qquad a_2\ge(4+\gamma)^{-1},$$
and, for some $\beta>0$ and $\gamma>1$,
$$G((0,s])\lesssim e^{-\beta s^{-\gamma}}\ (s\downarrow0),\qquad G((s,\infty))\lesssim e^{-\beta s^\gamma}\ (s\to\infty).$$
Here $u_n\lesssim v_n$ means $u_n\le Cv_n$ eventually for a fixed
constant $C$. For every fixed
$\eta>\gamma/[2(\gamma-1)]$, put
$$\epsilon_n=\max\left\{(n\sigma_n)^{-1/2}\log n, n^{-1/2}\sigma_n^{-\eta},\ \sigma_n^2\log n\right\}.$$
Then for every sufficiently large fixed $M$,
$$\Pi_n\!\left(h(p_{F,\sigma},p_0)>M\epsilon_n\mid X_{1:n}\right) \longrightarrow0$$
in $P_0^n$-probability. If $G$ is compactly supported in $(0,\infty)$,
the middle term $n^{-1/2}\sigma_n^{-\eta}$ may be omitted. The conclusion
is only in probability; it supplies no almost-sure contraction or generic
minimax-optimality assertion.

derivations.claim: For large $n$, $n^{-1/4}\le\sigma_n\le n^{-1/6}$ because $n^{1/20}(\log n)^{2/5}\to\infty$ and $n^{-1/30}(\log n)^{2/5}\to0$. Thus $0<a_2<a_1<1$ and $a_2=(4+\gamma)^{-1}$. The compactly supported $G$ satisfies the lower scale-tail bound since $G(s)=0$ for $s<1$, and the upper tail is zero for $s\ge2$.

Direct calculation gives $(n\sigma_n)^{-1/2}\log n=n^{-2/5}(\log n)^{4/5}$ and $\sigma_n^2\log n=n^{-2/5}(\log n)^{4/5}$. Hence [F1] yields this Hellinger contraction upper bound in $P_0^n$-probability. It is not a minimax claim.

derivations.claim: The Pareto density integrates to one because $\int_2^\infty2s^{-2}ds=1$, so $G$ is a probability measure. For $s<1$, $G(s)=0$, which satisfies every required lower-tail upper bound near zero.
For $s\ge2$, the uniform component has no mass above $s$ and the Pareto survival function is $2/s$; the mixture weight $1/2$ therefore gives $1-G(s)=1/s$.

def-negative-sobolev-space-for-white-noi.claim:
Let $(\psi_{lk})$ be a countable complete orthonormal basis of the real Hilbert space $L^2([0,1])$ ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]], [[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). For a wavelet basis, index levels by $l\ge0$, let $K_l$ have $2^l$ indices, and put $a_l=2^l$ for $l\ge1$ and $a_0=2$ for the finite coarsest level. This finite-level convention only prevents a zero logarithmic weight and does not change any convergence criterion below. For a trigonometric basis, use its integer frequency index $l$, bounded multiplicities, and $a_l=\max(2,|l|)$.

Here an **$S$-regular wavelet basis** means a wavelet orthonormal basis whose members are $S$ times differentiable, with each derivative through order $S$ in $L^2([0,1])$, following the source convention. The weak BvM theorem below only uses the basis's completeness, orthonormality, and level counts.

For $\delta>0$, define $H(\delta)=H^{-1/2,\delta}_2$ to be the space of coefficient sequences $c=(c_{lk})$ with norm

$$\|c\|_{H(\delta)}^2:=\sum_{l,k}a_l^{-1}(\log a_l)^{-2\delta}|c_{lk}|^2<\infty.$$

Its inner product is the corresponding weighted coefficient inner product. Multiplying each coordinate by $a_l^{-1/2}(\log a_l)^{-\delta}$ identifies it isometrically with $\ell^2(I)$, where $I=\{(l,k):k\in K_l\}$ (or the corresponding trigonometric index set). This sequence space is complete: if $x^{(m)}$ is Cauchy, each coordinate converges to a scalar $x_i$; for every finite $F\subset I$, the Cauchy bound passes to the limit in $\sum_{i\in F}|x_i^{(m)}-x_i^{(n)}|^2$, so the supremum over finite $F$ shows $x^{(m)}\to x$ in $\ell^2(I)$. It is separable because finite-support sequences with rational coordinates form a countable dense set. Thus $H(\delta)$ is a separable Hilbert space without an additional choice assumption.

A function $f\in L^2([0,1])$ is identified with its coefficient sequence $c_{lk}=\langle f,\psi_{lk}\rangle$. For each finite set $F$ of indices, orthonormality makes $\sum_{(l,k)\in F}c_{lk}\psi_{lk}$ orthogonal to its residual in $L^2$, so the Pythagorean identity gives $\sum_F|c_{lk}|^2\le\|f\|_2^2$. Taking the supremum over finite $F$ and using the boundedness of the weights proves continuity of the coefficient map. If all coefficients of $f$ vanish, then $f$ is orthogonal to the linear span of the basis. Completeness makes this span dense, and continuity of $g\mapsto\langle f,g\rangle$ gives $\langle f,f\rangle=0$, hence $f=0$ in $L^2$. Applying this to the difference of two functions proves injectivity. Thus the coefficient map is a continuous linear embedding $L^2([0,1])\hookrightarrow H(\delta)$.

The weight trace $\sum_{l,k}a_l^{-1}(\log a_l)^{-2\delta}$ is finite exactly when $\delta>1/2$: for wavelets its tail is a constant multiple of $\sum_{l\ge1}l^{-2\delta}$, while for a trigonometric basis it is comparable to $\sum_{l\ge2}[l(\log l)^{2\delta}]^{-1}$. The product-prior theorem below uses the wavelet case.

citations.quote:
A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

Let $H$ be a real or complex inner-product space ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]), with inner
product linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second, and
with the induced length $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$. The definitions below
do not require completeness. When the term *Hilbert basis* is used, $H$ is
additionally assumed complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]).

**Orthonormal indexed family.** Let $I$ be any set. An indexed family
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ of vectors of $H$ is **orthonormal** when

$$\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}:=\begin{cases}1,&i=j,\\0,&i\ne j,\end{cases} \qquad\text{for all } i,j\in I .$$Because $1\ne 0$ in the scalar field, the family contains no zero vector: $\|e_i\|^2=\langle e_i,e_i\rangle=1$, so $\|e_i\|=1$ for every $i$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]); and the index map is injective, since $e_i=e_j$ with $i\ne j$ would give $0=\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=1$. Thus an orthonormal family is the same thing as an orthonormal set together with a labelling of it, and in the sequel no choice is hidden in passing between the two descriptions. **Orthonormal set.** A subset $S\subseteq H$ is **orthonormal** when every $s\in S$ has $\|s\|=1$ and $\langle s,t\rangle=0$ for all distinct $s,t\in S$. For such an $S$ the family $(e_s)_{s\in S}$ with $e_s:=s$ is orthonormal in the indexed sense, and the image of an orthonormal indexed family is an orthonormal set. Orthogonal means $\langle s,t\rangle=0$ ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]). **Independence and unique coefficients.** Let $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be orthonormal, let $F\subseteq I$ be finite, and let scalars $c_i$ satisfy $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i=0$. For each fixed $j\in F$, linearity in the first argument gives$$0=\Bigl\langle \sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i,\;e_j\Bigr\rangle=\sum_{i\in F}c_i\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=c_j ,$$

so every finite subfamily of an orthonormal family is linearly independent. In
particular the coefficients in a finite expansion are unique: if
$\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i=\sum_{i\in F}d_ie_i$, then applying the computation to
$c-d$ gives $c_i=d_i$ for every $i\in F$.

**Closed linear span and completeness.** The **span** of an indexed family is
the set of all finite linear combinations $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i$ with $F\subseteq I$
finite and scalars $c_i$; it is the smallest linear subspace of $H$ containing
every $e_i$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). Its closure in the induced norm is the
**closed linear span** of the family, the smallest closed linear subspace of $H$
containing every $e_i$. The family is **complete**, or is a **complete
orthonormal system**, when its closed linear span is all of $H$. A
**Hilbert basis**, or **orthonormal basis**, of $H$ is a complete orthonormal
family in $H$.

**The empty family.** The span of the empty family is $\{0\}$, which is already
closed, so the empty family is complete exactly when $H=\{0\}$. Thus the zero
Hilbert space always has a Hilbert basis, namely the empty one.

**Not a Hamel basis, and no order is assumed.** A Hilbert basis is a basis only
in the sense of closed linear span: for an infinite-dimensional $H$ the vectors
of $H$ are in general **not** finite linear combinations of a Hilbert basis, and
the expansion of an arbitrary vector is a norm limit of finite partial sums, not
a finite sum. No enumeration, ordering or countability of the index set is part
of the definition; the partial sums are indexed by the finite subsets of $I$,
ordered by inclusion, and that is the convention used on this page.

**Coefficient notation.** For orthonormal $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ and $x\in H$ the
scalars $\langle x,e_i\rangle$ are the **coefficients** of $x$ with respect to
the family. They are well defined for every $x$, without any assumption that
the family is complete.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Assume countable choice (in particular, the Axiom of Choice suffices). Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $1\le p\le\infty$. Then
$L^p(\mu)$, with the norm of
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]], is
complete. Equivalently, the metric induced by that norm is a complete metric in
the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]].

Moreover, if a sequence in $L^p(\mu)$ converges in norm, then some subsequence
admits measurable representatives converging almost everywhere in the sense of
[[def-convergence-almost-everywhere-relative-to-a-measure]].

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: For each finite $N$, orthonormality [F2] gives $\|f_N\|_H^2=\sum_{0\le l\le N}\sum_{k\in K_l}\sigma_l^2\xi_{lk}^2.$ The nonnegative partial sums increase to the full coefficient-square sum, so [F4] gives its expectation as the limit of the finite expectations, $\sum_{l\ge0}\sum_{k\in K_l}\sigma_l^2\mathbb E\xi_{lk}^2=m_2\sum_{l\ge0}2^l2^{-2l(\alpha+1/2)}=m_2\sum_{l\ge0}2^{-2\alpha l}<\infty,$ since the final series is geometric with ratio $2^{-2\alpha}<1$. If the coefficient-square sum were infinite on an event of probability $p>0$, its expectation would be at least $Rp$ for every $R>0$, contradicting finiteness. Thus that sum is finite almost surely.

On the probability-one event where that sum is finite, for $M>N$ orthonormality gives $\|f_M-f_N\|_H^2=\sum_{N<l\le M}\sum_{k\in K_l}\sigma_l^2\xi_{lk}^2.$ The right side tends to zero uniformly over $M>N$ as $N\to\infty$, since it is a tail of a convergent nonnegative series. Thus $(f_N)$ is Cauchy in $H$ and has a limit $f$ by completeness [F1]. When $H=L^2([0,1])$, completeness is supplied by [F5] under [A1]. The Cauchy event is measurable because it is a countable combination of conditions on the measurable distances $\|f_M-f_N\|_H$. On that event the pointwise limit is measurable as a limit into the separable metric space $H$; setting the limit equal to zero on the measurable complement gives a Borel $H$-valued random element.

The same monotone-convergence calculation in [F4] gives $\mathbb E\|f\|_H^2=\mathbb E\sum_{l\ge0}\sum_{k\in K_l}\sigma_l^2\xi_{lk}^2=m_2\sum_{l\ge0}2^{-2\alpha l}<\infty.$ This proves both the stated second-moment formula and the claimed well-definedness.

lem-bounded-lipschitz-metric-characteriz.claim:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(S,d)$ be a Polish space, and let $\mu_n,\mu$ be Borel probability measures on $S$. Define

$$\beta_{BL}(\nu,\rho):=\sup\left\{\left|\int g\,d\nu-\int g\,d\rho\right|:g:S\to\mathbb R,\ \|g\|_\infty\le1,\ \operatorname{Lip}_d(g)\le1\right\},$$

where $\operatorname{Lip}_d(g):=\sup_{x\ne y}|g(x)-g(y)|/d(x,y)$, with value $0$ when $S$ has at most one point. Then

$$\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\beta_{BL}(\mu_n,\mu)\longrightarrow0,$$

where $\Rightarrow$ is weak convergence of Borel probabilities ([[def-weak-convergence-of-borel-probability-measures]]). The implication from bounded-Lipschitz convergence to weak convergence is choice-free; the reverse implication below uses AC through Prokhorov's theorem.

citations.quote: For Borel probability measures $\mu_n,\mu$ on a metric space S, write $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$ if $\int f\,d\mu_n\to\int f\,d\mu$ for every bounded continuous real function f on S. Continuity is [[def-metric-continuity]]. Such f is Borel measurable (inverse images of open sets are open) and $\int|f|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\mu(S)<\infty$, so the integrals are finite in [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]. No completeness or coupling is required.

For Borel probabilities $\mu_n,\mu$ on a metric space S, the following are equivalent: (i) $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$; (ii) integrals converge for all bounded uniformly continuous real tests; (iii) $\limsup_n\mu_n(F)\le\mu(F)$ for every closed F; (iv) $\liminf_n\mu_n(G)\ge\mu(G)$ for every open G; (v) $\mu_n(A)\to\mu(A)$ for every Borel A with $\mu(\partial A)=0$.
Assume AC. A family $\mathcal A$ of Borel probabilities on a Polish space S is tight if and only if it is relatively sequentially compact for weak convergence.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

A topological space is **Polish** when it is separable ([[def-separable-space]]) and completely metrizable: its topology is induced by some complete metric ([[lem-complete-remetrisation]]). No particular compatible complete metric or countable dense subset is part of the structure.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ and let $\mathcal A=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. If finite measures $\mu$ and $
u$ on $(X,\mathcal A)$ agree on $\mathcal P$ and satisfy $\mu(X)=
u(X)$, then $\mu=
u$ on $\mathcal A$.

The total-mass equality is separate because this library's pi-system convention does not require $X\in\mathcal P$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Now assume $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$, and put $\mathcal A=\{\mu\}\cup\{\mu_n:n\ge1\}$. The functions $g_m$ decrease pointwise to $1_F$ and are bounded by the integrable constant function $1$ under the probability $\mu$. Let $(\psi_{lk})$ be a countable complete orthonormal basis of the real Hilbert space $L^2([0,1])$ ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]], [[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). For a wavelet basis, index levels by $l\ge0$, let $K_l$ have $2^l$ indices, and put $a_l=2^l$ for $l\ge1$ and $a_0=2$ for the finite coarsest level. This finite-level convention only prevents a zero logarithmic weight and does not change any convergence criterion below. For a trigonometric basis, use its integer frequency index $l$, bounded multiplicities, and $a_l=\max(2,|l|)$.

Here an **$S$-regular wavelet basis** means a wavelet orthonormal basis whose members are $S$ times differentiable, with each derivative through order $S$ in $L^2([0,1])$, following the source convention. The weak BvM theorem below only uses the basis's completeness, orthonormality, and level counts.

For $\delta>0$, define $H(\delta)=H^{-1/2,\delta}_2$ to be the space of coefficient sequences $c=(c_{lk})$ with norm

$$\|c\|_{H(\delta)}^2:=\sum_{l,k}a_l^{-1}(\log a_l)^{-2\delta}|c_{lk}|^2<\infty.$$

Its inner product is the corresponding weighted coefficient inner product. Multiplying each coordinate by $a_l^{-1/2}(\log a_l)^{-\delta}$ identifies it isometrically with $\ell^2(I)$, where $I=\{(l,k):k\in K_l\}$ (or the corresponding trigonometric index set). This sequence space is complete: if $x^{(m)}$ is Cauchy, each coordinate converges to a scalar $x_i$; for every finite $F\subset I$, the Cauchy bound passes to the limit in $\sum_{i\in F}|x_i^{(m)}-x_i^{(n)}|^2$, so the supremum over finite $F$ shows $x^{(m)}\to x$ in $\ell^2(I)$. It is separable because finite-support sequences with rational coordinates form a countable dense set. Thus $H(\delta)$ is a separable Hilbert space without an additional choice assumption.

A function $f\in L^2([0,1])$ is identified with its coefficient sequence $c_{lk}=\langle f,\psi_{lk}\rangle$. For each finite set $F$ of indices, orthonormality makes $\sum_{(l,k)\in F}c_{lk}\psi_{lk}$ orthogonal to its residual in $L^2$, so the Pythagorean identity gives $\sum_F|c_{lk}|^2\le\|f\|_2^2$. Taking the supremum over finite $F$ and using the boundedness of the weights proves continuity of the coefficient map. If all coefficients of $f$ vanish, then $f$ is orthogonal to the linear span of the basis. Completeness makes this span dense, and continuity of $g\mapsto\langle f,g\rangle$ gives $\langle f,f\rangle=0$, hence $f=0$ in $L^2$. Applying this to the difference of two functions proves injectivity. Thus the coefficient map is a continuous linear embedding $L^2([0,1])\hookrightarrow H(\delta)$.

The weight trace $\sum_{l,k}a_l^{-1}(\log a_l)^{-2\delta}$ is finite exactly when $\delta>1/2$: for wavelets its tail is a constant multiple of $\sum_{l\ge1}l^{-2\delta}$, while for a trigonometric basis it is comparable to $\sum_{l\ge2}[l(\log l)^{2\delta}]^{-1}$. The product-prior theorem below uses the wavelet case.

Assume countable choice for the $L^2$-valued prior construction. Let the wavelet product prior have independent coefficients $\theta_{lk}=\sigma_l\xi_{lk}$, where the $\xi_{lk}$ are IID with density $\varphi$. Observe the independent Gaussian sequence

$$X_{lk}=\theta_{0,lk}+n^{-1/2}Z_{lk},$$

where the $Z_{lk}$ have the standard normal density and are independent of the prior. Assume a data-indexed posterior kernel for the $L^2$-valued prior is supplied as part of this model. In the product white-noise model, for every finite set $J$ of coefficient indices its conditional law of $(\theta_j)_{j\in J}$ given the full data sequence $(X_j)$ is the product of the one-coordinate densities

$$p_{j,n}(t\mid X_j)=\frac{e^{-n(t-X_j)^2/2}\,\sigma_j^{-1}\varphi(t/\sigma_j)}{\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-n(s-X_j)^2/2}\,\sigma_j^{-1}\varphi(s/\sigma_j)\,ds},\qquad j\in J.$$

Here $j$ abbreviates a pair $(l,k)$ and $\sigma_j=\sigma_l$. For $J=\varnothing$, the formula denotes the unit law on the zero-dimensional one-point space. Each denominator is strictly positive and finite: the Gaussian factor is everywhere positive and at most $1$, while the prior density integrates to $1$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

If $\lambda\ge S_0$, let $R=hS_0$. For $|v|\le R$ one has $|r+v/\lambda|<\tau$, so $D_\lambda(z)\ge\frac{c_\varphi e^{z^2/2}}\lambda I_R(z),\qquad N_\lambda(z)\le\frac{C_\varphi e^{z^2/2}}\lambda J(z),$ where $I_R(z)=\int_{-R}^{R}e^{-(v-z)^2/2}\,dv$ and $J(z)=\int_{\mathbb R}v^2e^{-(v-z)^2/2}\,dv=\sqrt{2\pi}(1+z^2)$. Thus $nB_{lk}(X)\le(C_\varphi/c_\varphi)J(Z)/I_R(Z)$. For $|z|\le R$, integrate $I_R$ over the half-interval nearest $z$; for $|z|>R$, integrate over the half-interval adjacent to the nearer endpoint. The two ranges in steps 2.1 and 2.2 cover every $\lambda>0$; since $\sigma_l^2\le S_0^2/n$ in the first range, there is a single constant $C$ for which $\sup_{l,k}\mathbb E_{f_0}^{(n)}B_{lk}(X)\le C/n$.

Under the true law, $X_j/\sigma_j=r+Z_j/(\sqrt n\sigma_j)\to r$ in probability, and $b_n=(\sqrt n\sigma_j)^{-1}\to0$. By [F1], under [A1], the posterior density of $U_n=\sqrt n(\theta_j-X_j)$ is $p_n(u\mid X_j)=\frac{e^{-u^2/2}\varphi(X_j/\sigma_j+b_nu)}{c_n(X_j)},\qquad c_n(X_j)=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-v^2/2}\varphi(X_j/\sigma_j+b_nv)\,dv.$ For any deterministic sequence $x_n/\sigma_j\to r$, boundedness of $\varphi$ and [F2] give $c_n(x_n)\to\varphi(r)\sqrt{2\pi}>0$.

A second application of [F2] gives convergence in $L^1(du)$, hence convergence in total variation. Since $X_j/\sigma_j\to r$ in probability, if the total-variation convergence in probability failed, some subsequence would have error probability bounded below. Select a further subsequence for which $\mathbb P(|X_j/\sigma_j-r|>2^{-q})\le2^{-q}$ at its $q$th term; [F3] bounds each union of tail events by the corresponding geometric tail, which tends to zero, so the further subsequence converges almost surely to $r$, contradicting the deterministic conclusion.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $a<b$ and let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be
bounded and Riemann integrable. Then $f$ is Lebesgue measurable on $[a,b]$ and
is integrable there, and its Lebesgue integral equals its Riemann integral:
$$\int_{[a,b]} f\,d\lambda_1=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx.$$

This is the point at which the completeness of Lebesgue measure is used
essentially: the proof obtains a Borel function equal to $f$ almost everywhere,
and measurability of $f$ itself is then a completeness statement.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and define
$$\nu_f(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu \qquad (A\in\mathcal A).$$
Then $\nu_f$ is a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int g\,d(f\,d\mu)=\int gf\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $u, v : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at
every point of $[a,b]$ as functions on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]). Suppose
$u'$ and $v'$ are integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then $uv'$
and $u'v$ are integrable and

$$\int_a^b u\,v' \;=\; u(b)v(b) - u(a)v(a) \;-\; \int_a^b u'\,v .$$

**The integrability of $u'$ and $v'$ is a hypothesis, not a formality.** Without
it the two integrals in the display need not exist at all, and the identity is
then not false but ill-formed; that is
the false statement that deletes it on the companion
page. The hypothesis is automatic when $u$ and $v$ are continuously
differentiable, since a continuous function on $[a,b]$ is integrable
([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]).

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

derivations.claim: The positive continuous function $g$ is Borel measurable, since inverse images of open sets are open. For an integer $R\ge1$, substitute $x=\sqrt2\,t$ in the continuous compact-interval integral. The bridge in [F1] and then increasing truncation in [F2] give $\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-x^2/2}\,dx=\sqrt2\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_{-R/\sqrt2}^{R/\sqrt2}e^{-t^2}\,dt=\sqrt{2\pi}$. Thus [F2] makes $\gamma$ a probability. For $v>0$, compact substitutions in the same way show that its affine pushforward has the asserted half-line integrals of $g_{m,v}$; limits of compact intervals give the half-lines, and [F5] gives equality of the measures. For $v=0$ the affine map is constant, giving the Dirac law directly.

The CDF of $N(m,v)$ for $v>0$ is continuous, since $g_{m,v}$ is bounded and the integral over an interval of length $h$ is at most $|h|/\sqrt{2\pi v}$. It is strictly increasing because the positive continuous density has a positive minimum on every nondegenerate compact interval. For $Z$ with density $g$, $g'(x)=-xg(x)$, and integration by parts gives $\int_{-R}^R|x|g(x)dx=2(g(0)-g(R))$ and $\int_{-R}^Rx^2g(x)dx=\int_{-R}^Rg(x)dx-2Rg(R)$. The exponential series shows $g(R)\to0$ and $Rg(R)\to0$. Increasing truncation gives $\mathbb E|Z|<\infty$ and $\mathbb EZ^2=1$; symmetry gives $\mathbb EZ=0$. Expanding $m+\sqrt v Z$ gives the claimed mean and variance, also for $v=0$.

Let $U,V$ be independent centered density normal variables with variances $a,b>0$. Their sum has density $h(x)=\int_{\mathbb R}g_{0,a}(u)g_{0,b}(x-u)du$. Indeed, [F4] expresses $P(U+V\le x)$ as the nonnegative double integral of $\mathbf1_{u+t\le x}g_{0,a}(u)g_{0,b}(t)$; for each fixed $u$, a translation in the continuous half-line integral followed by Tonelli gives $\int_{-\infty}^xh(y)dy$. These half-line probabilities determine the law by [F5]. Completing the square gives $\frac{u^2}{a}+\frac{(x-u)^2}{b}=\frac{a+b}{ab}\left(u-\frac{ax}{a+b}\right)^2+\frac{x^2}{a+b}.$ The compact substitutions and increasing limits in step 1.1 therefore give $h(x)=g_{0,a+b}(x)$. If either variance is zero the corresponding variable is zero almost surely and the same conclusion is immediate. Scaling a coordinate by a negative coefficient gives the same density as scaling by its absolute value, by the symmetry of $g$. Finite induction, using mutual independence to separate the last coordinate from the preceding tuple, proves $S_m\sim N(0,v_m)$ with $v_m=\sum_{j\le m}c_j^2$.

If $v=0$, every coefficient is zero, so convergence in probability implies $S=0$ almost surely. Suppose $v>0$. Then $v_m\to v$ and eventually $v_m>0$. Write $\Phi$ for the continuous CDF of $\gamma$. For any $x\in\mathbb R$ and $\varepsilon>0$, convergence in probability and step 3.1 give $\Phi((x-\varepsilon)/\sqrt{v_m})-P(|S_m-S|>\varepsilon)\le P(S\le x)\le\Phi((x+\varepsilon)/\sqrt{v_m})+P(|S_m-S|>\varepsilon).$ First let $m\to\infty$, then $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. Continuity from step 2.1 gives $P(S\le x)=\Phi(x/\sqrt v)$ for every $x$. By [F5], $S$ has law $N(0,v)$. Almost sure convergence implies convergence in probability by dominated convergence on the indicators of $\{|S_m-S|>\varepsilon\}$, and $L^2$ convergence implies it by $\varepsilon^2P(|S_m-S|>\varepsilon)\le\mathbb E|S_m-S|^2$.
