where $\Rightarrow$ is weak convergence of Borel probabilities ([[def-weak-convergence-of-borel-probability-measures]]). The implication from bounded-Lipschitz convergence to weak convergence is choice-free; the reverse implication below uses AC through Prokhorov's theorem.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

derivations.claim: Choose a deterministic $b_n\to\infty$ sufficiently slowly that $b_n\sqrt d e_n\to0$ and $b_ne_nd^{2r+1}/\sqrt n\to0$ in the Gaussian case. Such a choice exists: the first unmultiplied expression tends to zero because $\alpha>1/2$, and the second is bounded by a logarithmic factor times $d^{2r-2\alpha+1/2}\to0$. Set $D_n=\{\|\theta-\theta_*\|_2\le b_ne_n\}$ in the quotient by constants used in [F1]. Then $\Pi(D_n\mid X^n)\to1$ in probability. On $D_n$, $\|\theta-\theta_*\|_\infty\le Cb_n\sqrt d e_n=o(1)$; hence $\|f-f_0\|_\infty=o(1)$ uniformly, and the densities are bounded above and away from zero. Write $\Pi_D$ for the posterior conditioned on $D_n$.

For $\gamma=\psi_{lk}$, $l\le L_n$, define $f_s=fe^{-s\gamma/\sqrt n}/P_fe^{-s\gamma/\sqrt n}$. For $|s|\le\sqrt{\lambda_l}$, Taylor expansion of the log moment generating function gives $s\sqrt n(P_f-P_n)\gamma=\ell_n(f_s)-\ell_n(f)+(s^2/2)\operatorname{Var}_f\gamma+R$, where $|R|\le C|s|^3\|\gamma\|_\infty/\sqrt n$. To justify the uniform remainder, differentiate $a\mapsto\log P_fe^{a\gamma}$ three times; its third derivative is the third centered moment under the tilted density, bounded by $C\|\gamma\|_\infty P_f\gamma^2$ when $|a|\|\gamma\|_\infty=o(1)$. On $D_n$, $P_f\gamma^2\le C$ by orthonormality and the density bound, while $\sqrt{L_n}2^{L_n/2}/\sqrt n\to0$. Thus $|R|\le Cs^2$ and $\operatorname{Var}_f\gamma\le C$. Here $\ell_n$ is the sum log likelihood.

The map $f\mapsto f_s$ is the quotient-coordinate translation $\theta\mapsto\theta-s(\gamma-\int\gamma)/\sqrt n$. On high wavelets it shifts one coordinate; low scaling directions involve only a fixed finite-dimensional block. In S1 the absolute log prior density ratio is at most $C|s|/(\sqrt n\sigma_l)\le C|s|$, since $2^{L_n(\alpha+1/2)}\le\sqrt n$. In S2 it is at most $C[|s|(|g_{0,lk}|+b_ne_n)/(\sqrt n\sigma_l^2)+s^2/(n\sigma_l^2)]$, with a bounded fixed low-block version. Uniformly in high $l\le L_n$, its coefficients are bounded: $|g_{0,lk}|\le C2^{-l(\alpha+1/2)}$, $b_ne_nd^{2r+1}/\sqrt n=o(1)$, and $d^{2r+1}/n=o(1)$. Changing variables in the numerator likelihood integral and discarding its transformed $D_n$ indicator therefore bounds that integral by $e^{C|s|+Cs^2}$ times the full posterior normalizer. Step 2.1 yields $E_{\Pi_D}e^{s\sqrt n(P_f-P_n)\psi_{lk}}\le Ce^{Cs^2+C|s|}/\Pi(D_n\mid X^n)$. No translation invariance of $D_n$ is used.

Put $Z_{lk}=\sqrt n\langle f-P_n,\psi_{lk}\rangle$ for $l\le L_n$ and $p_n=\Pi(D_n\mid X^n)$. Exponential Markov with $s=\pm\sqrt{\lambda_l}$ gives $\Pi_D\{|Z_{lk}|>u\sqrt{\lambda_l}\}\le Cp_n^{-1}e^{-\lambda_l(u-C)}$. Union over the at most $C2^l$ locations shows $E_{\Pi_D}\max_k|Z_{lk}|\le Cp_n^{-1}\sqrt{\lambda_l}$. Union also over levels and integrate in $u$ above a sufficiently large constant to obtain $E_{\Pi_D}\sup_{l\le L_n,k}|Z_{lk}|/\sqrt{\lambda_l}\le C/p_n$: the relevant integral is bounded by $Cp_n^{-1}\sum_{l\ge1}2^l\int_M^\infty e^{-l(u-C)}du$, plus a finite low-level term. Also the wavelet level bound and a geometric sum give $E_{\Pi_D}\|P_{L_n}(f-P_n)\|_\infty\le Cp_n^{-1}\sqrt{d\lambda_{L_n}/n}$.

Fix a finite linear combination $\gamma$ of wavelets and a fixed real $s$. Repeat step 2.1 with this bounded $\gamma$. Its remainder is now $o(1)$, and $\operatorname{Var}_f\gamma\to\operatorname{Var}_0\gamma$ uniformly on $D_n$. The prior translation involves finitely many fixed coordinates, and its density ratio tends to one uniformly on $D_n$: use the global S1 log-Lipschitz bound or the fixed Gaussian precision block and bounded quotient coordinates in S2. Let $A_s$ be the translated image of $D_n$. For large $n$, $A_s$ contains $D_n^-:=\{\|\theta-\theta_*\|_2\le b_ne_n/2\}$ because the translation has norm $O(n^{-1/2})=o(b_ne_n)$. Both $\Pi(D_n^-\mid X^n)$ and $\Pi(D_n\mid X^n)$ tend to one by [F1]. Bounding the translated integral above by the full normalizer and below by its integral on $D_n^-$ therefore gives $E_{\Pi_D}e^{s\sqrt n(P_f-P_n)\gamma}\to e^{s^2\operatorname{Var}_0(\gamma)/2}$ in probability.

Each empirical wavelet coordinate has variance at most $D_0/n$ and summands bounded by $C2^{l/2}$. Bernstein [F5] gives $\Pr\{|(P_n-P_0)\psi_{lk}|>C[\sqrt{t/n}+2^{l/2}t/n]\}\le2e^{-t}$. Choose $t=C'(l+1)+u$, union over $k$, and integrate over $u\ge0$ to get $E\max_k|(P_n-P_0)\psi_{lk}|\le C[\sqrt{\lambda_l/n}+2^{l/2}\lambda_l/n]$. Summing against $2^{l/2}$ yields $\|P_{L_n}(P_n-P_0)\|_\infty=O_P(\sqrt{d\lambda_{L_n}/n}+d\lambda_{L_n}/n)=O_P(\sqrt{d\lambda_{L_n}/n})$, since $d\lambda_{L_n}/n\to0$. Moreover $\|P_{L_n}f_0-f_0\|_\infty\le Cd^{-\alpha}\le C\sqrt{d\lambda_{L_n}/n}$ for both cutoffs. Consequently the posterior projected density error is tight at rate $a_n=\sqrt{d\lambda_{L_n}/n}$.

Here is the needed finite-dimensional Laplace continuity argument. Along any subsequence, extract a further subsequence on which the preceding transform convergences hold almost surely for every rational $s$ and every rational vector of finite-coordinate coefficients, using countability and convergence in probability. The transforms at the positive and negative coordinate unit vectors give tightness of these deterministic finite-dimensional laws by exponential Markov and a finite union bound. [F6] gives a weakly convergent further subsequence. For a fixed rational direction and rational $s$, its exponential is uniformly integrable: its second moment is bounded by the transform at $2s$, and Cauchy–Schwarz and Markov bound the expectation above any large cutoff. Truncation thus passes its transform to the weak limit. In each coordinate direction and then any rational linear direction, the limit has finite exponential moments of every rational order, and hence of every real order by bounding $e^{t|x|}$ by $e^{q x}+e^{-q x}$ for rational $q>|t|$. Its moment generating function is analytic: on every bounded complex disk its power series can be integrated term by term under $e^{q|x|}$. Equality with the Gaussian transform on the rationals therefore gives equality of all moments by the real power series at zero. Integrating the characteristic-function power series under the same exponential bound gives the Gaussian characteristic function. [F6] identifies every rational linear projection with the corresponding centered normal. Continuity of characteristic functions in their vector argument extends the identification to real vectors; [F6] then identifies the finite-dimensional law with the Gaussian projection of [F3]. Every weakly convergent further subsequence has that limit, so tightness implies weak convergence of the full deterministic subsequence, and [F7] gives bounded-Lipschitz convergence. The initial subsequence argument proves convergence in probability of the original random projected laws.

For the coefficients through $L_n$, step 4.1 and Markov give posterior tightness of $\sup_{l\le L_n,k}|Z_{lk}|/\sqrt{\lambda_l}$. Therefore for $J<L_n$, the $M(w)$ norm of the part with $J<l\le L_n$ is at most this variable times $\sup_{l>J}\sqrt{\lambda_l}/w_l$, which tends to zero as $J\to\infty$ by admissibility. This proves the required uniform projected posterior tail bound.

This projected rate controls the full supremum error. Put $h=\theta-\theta_*$, $f_*=e^{\theta_*}/\int e^{\theta_*}$, and $v=h-P_{f_*}h\in V_{L_n}$. Since $\int h=0$, $\|h\|_\infty\le2\|v\|_\infty$. Normalized exponential expansion gives $f-f_*=f_*v+R$ with $\|R\|_\infty\le C\|h\|_\infty^2$ on $D_n$. Also $\|f_*-f_0\|_\infty\le Cd^{-\alpha}$. For any fixed $0<\beta<\min(\alpha,1)$, $f_0$ is $\beta$-Hölder, so [F2] gives $\|P_{L_n}(f_0v)-f_0v\|_\infty\le Cd^{-\beta}\|v\|_\infty$. The lower bound $f_0\ge\rho_0$ and uniform boundedness of $P_{L_n}$ imply $c\|h\|_\infty\le\|P_{L_n}(f-f_0)\|_\infty+C d^{-\beta}\|h\|_\infty+C\|h\|_\infty^2+Cd^{-\alpha}$. Step 1.1 makes the two terms proportional to $\|h\|_\infty$ absorbable. It follows that $\|f-f_0\|_\infty\le C[\|P_{L_n}(f-f_0)\|_\infty+d^{-\alpha}]$ uniformly on $D_n$. Thus the full posterior supremum error is tight at rate $a_n$.

Choose $M_n\to\infty$ so slowly that $M_n\sqrt{\lambda_{L_n}}/w_{L_n}\to0$. Step 6.1 makes the posterior probability of $\|f-f_0\|_\infty>M_na_n$ tend to zero. On its complement, the $L^1$ wavelet bound and monotonicity of $w$ give $\sqrt n\|P_{>L_n}(f-f_0)\|_{M(w)}\le C\sqrt n2^{-L_n/2}w_{L_n}^{-1}M_na_n\le CM_n\sqrt{\lambda_{L_n}}/w_{L_n}\to0$. The truth coefficients satisfy $\sqrt n\|P_{>L_n}f_0\|_{M(w)}\le C\sqrt n d^{-\alpha-1/2}/w_{L_n}\le C\sqrt{\lambda_{L_n}}/w_{L_n}\to0$ for either cutoff. Hence the entire density tail above $L_n$ is negligible in posterior probability.

Each density is a finite exponential of bounded continuous functions, hence belongs to $L^2$; its coefficients, and those of $P_n(L_n)$, belong to $M_0(w)$. Removing $D_n$ changes posterior integrals of functions bounded by one by at most $2[1-\Pi(D_n\mid X^n)]=o_P(1)$. Step 5.2 supplies fixed finite-projection convergence to [F3], and steps 5.3, 7.1 supply the posterior-tail condition. Apply [F4] to conclude the asserted bounded-Lipschitz convergence in $M_0(w)$.

boundaries.reason: Statement: the IID density model is nonempty and each finite projection retains the fixed low scaling space.

boundaries.evidence: Proof 4.2, 5.2: gamma=0 and zero-variance constant directions have transform one and Dirac Gaussian limit; no variance division occurs.
Proof 5.2: the Laplace continuity argument covers a single scalar coordinate, and the fixed low-level cases use lambda_l=max(l,1) in 1.2–2.2.
Proof 5.2: singular finite bridge covariance is allowed because linear projections of variance zero are Dirac; F3 supplies the joint Borel Gaussian law.
Statement retains S1 alpha>1 and S2 alpha>1/2 with strict r<alpha-1/4. The integer-alpha exp composition is supplied by F2. Both cutoffs and interval boundary wavelets are covered.
Statement explicitly assumes full AC, used in F3 Gaussian construction and F6 Prokhorov/characteristic uniqueness; step 5.2 uses countable diagonal subsequences within that scope.

Statement asserts no converse for failed prior or truth hypotheses.

thm-type-s-density-weak-bvm-on-m0w.claim:
Assume AC. Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be IID on $[0,1]$ with density $0<\rho_0\le f_0\le D_0<\infty$, and suppose $g_0=\log f_0\in C^\alpha$. Use a sufficiently regular compactly supported boundary corrected orthonormal multiresolution wavelet basis satisfying [[lem-compact-wavelet-projection-kernel-and-commutator]], with regularity greater than $\alpha$, and let $V_L$ contain exactly its wavelet levels through $L$, including the fixed low scaling space and constants. Its regularity and vanishing moments satisfy the composition hypotheses in that lemma for some integer $m>\alpha$. Let $L_n$ be either of the two cutoff sequences in [[def-type-s-and-h-multiscale-density-priors]], fixed consistently for all $n$.

In Type-S1 take $\alpha>1$, $\sigma_l=2^{-l(\alpha+1/2)}$, and any coefficient probability density with globally Lipschitz logarithm. In Type-S2 take $\alpha>1/2$, Gaussian coefficients, and $\sigma_l=2^{-l(r+1/2)}$ with $0<r<\alpha-1/4$. Normalize $f=\exp(T)/\int\exp(T)$ as in that definition. For every admissible weight sequence $w$, the posterior satisfies
$$\beta_{BL,M_0(w)}\bigl(\mathcal L(\sqrt n(f-P_n(L_n))\mid X^n),\mathcal L(G_{P_0})\bigr)\longrightarrow0$$
in $P_0^n$-probability, where $P_n(L_n)$ has empirical wavelet coefficients through $L_n$ and zero coefficients above $L_n$, and $G_{P_0}$ is the Borel Gaussian bridge with covariance $P_0[(\psi_i-P_0\psi_i)(\psi_j-P_0\psi_j)]$.

risk_review.notes: Reviewed all eleven steps and the exact contraction, commutator, Bernstein, bridge, Prokhorov, Cramer–Wold, uniqueness and BL suppliers. The slow b_n exists because sqrt(d)e_n->0 and e_n d^(2r+1)/sqrt(n)->0 for r<alpha-1/4, including either cutoff. Translations act on quotient coordinates; the restricted posterior set need not be translation invariant for the upper exponential bound, while its shifted image contains the half-radius set for fixed-coordinate Laplace limits. Uniform prior ratios use global log-Lipschitz S1 bounds or the explicit S2 precision estimates. Rational-direction transforms and uniform exponential integrability identify finite Gaussian laws. The projected posterior maximum is tight after dividing by sqrt(l); the commutator plus positive f0 absorbs the small nonlinear log-density terms and yields full supremum contraction. Choosing M_n slowly relative to w_L/sqrt(L) removes the high-density tail. This independently justifies the locally broader scope rather than assuming the narrower published Theorem 3 (1310.2484 PDF p.14) proves it. No defect found; reader/refuter findings empty.

citations.quote:
Use the wavelet coefficient levels $(l,k)$ and multiplicities $|K_l|=2^l$ from [[def-negative-sobolev-space-for-white-noise]]. The same coefficient-space definition applies to the Haar system used for type-H histograms: detail levels $l\ge0$ have $2^l$ coefficients, and the single scaling coefficient is an additional finite coarsest coordinate, included in the norm with weight $1$. Finite projections always retain that scaling coordinate; this finite convention does not alter any tail assertion. Let $w=(w_l)$ be nondecreasing with $w_l\ge1$. Define
$$M(w)=\left\{x=(x_{lk}):\|x\|_{M(w)}:=\sup_l\frac{\max_{k\in K_l}|x_{lk}|}{w_l}<\infty\right\}$$
and its closed little-o subspace
$$M_0(w)=\left\{x\in M(w):\frac{\max_{k\in K_l}|x_{lk}|}{w_l}\longrightarrow0\text{ as }l\to\infty\right\},$$
with the same norm. Call $w$ admissible when $w_l/\sqrt l\to\infty$. The finite coarsest level is included in the norm and does not affect this limit. Elements are coefficient sequences; in particular, they need not be $L^2$ functions. [[lem-m0w-separable-and-projection-tails]] proves that $M_0(w)$ is a separable Banach space, that $L^2$ coefficient sequences embed in it, and that finite-level projections converge in its norm.

For every weight sequence in [[def-multiscale-coefficient-space-m0w]], $M_0(w)$ is a separable Banach space. If $P_J$ retains exactly the coefficients at levels $l\le J$, then $\|P_Jx\|_{M(w)}\le\|x\|_{M(w)}$ and $\|x-P_Jx\|_{M(w)}\to0$ for each $x\in M_0(w)$. Every square-summable coefficient sequence belongs to $M_0(w)$.

Let $(\psi_{lk})$ be a compactly supported wavelet basis of [[def-negative-sobolev-space-for-white-noise]]. The Haar basis with its finite scaling coordinate, as specified in [[def-multiscale-coefficient-space-m0w]], is also allowed. Assume each level-$l$ wavelet for $l\ge l_0$ has zero integral, uniformly bounded overlap, support length at most $C_0 2^{-l}$, and $\|\psi_{lk}\|_1\le C_0 2^{-l/2}$. Let $M_0(w)$ be as in [[def-multiscale-coefficient-space-m0w]], and suppose
$$S_w:=\sum_{l\ge l_0}w_l2^{-l/2}<\infty.$$
For $x\in M_0(w)$ define
$$Jx(t):=\sum_{l,k}x_{lk}\langle 1_{[0,t]},\psi_{lk}\rangle_{L^2},\qquad 0\le t\le1.$$
Then this series converges absolutely and uniformly in $t$, $Jx\in C([0,1])$, and $\|Jx-Jy\|_\infty\le C S_w\|x-y\|_{M(w)}$ after adding the finite coarsest-level constant to $C S_w$. If $x$ is the coefficient sequence of $f\in L^2$, then $Jx(t)=\int_0^t f(u)\,du$.

Let S,T be metric spaces, $g:S\to T$ measurable, and $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$. If the discontinuity set $D_g$ is $\mu$-null, then $g_*\mu_n\Rightarrow g_*\mu$. Consequently $X_n\Rightarrow X$ implies $g(X_n)\Rightarrow g(X)$ whenever $P_X(D_g)=0$.

Write $\mathbb Q$ for the canonical image of the rationals in $\mathbb R$ under the embedding of [[lem-rat-embeds-dense]].

Let $y\mapsto\Pi_y$ be a probability kernel on $\mathbb R$. For $u\in(0,1)$ put
$$F_y(t)=\Pi_y((-\infty,t]),\qquad q_u(y)=\inf\{r\in\mathbb Q:F_y(r)\ge u\}.$$The infimum is taken in $\mathbb R$; [[thm-infimum-property]] supplies it once the defining set is shown nonempty and bounded below. Then $q_u:\mathsf Y\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, and$$\Pi_y((-\infty,q_u(y)))\le u\le\Pi_y((-\infty,q_u(y)]).$$

Let $Q_n(y,\cdot)$ be data-indexed probability kernels on $\mathbb R$, let $Q$ be a fixed law with continuous CDF $F$, and suppose $\beta_{BL}(Q_n(y,\cdot),Q)\to0$ in probability. Fix $0<u<1$ and let $q=q_u(Q):=\inf\{r\in\mathbb Q:Q((-∞,r])\ge u\}$, using the canonical rational embedding. Assume $F$ is strictly increasing on some open interval containing $q$. Define $q_u(Q_n(y,\cdot))$ by the same convention. Then $q_u(Q_n)\to q$ in probability. The local strict-increase hypothesis permits CDFs, such as norms of nonnegative random elements, that are constant on part of $\mathbb R$.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ be measurable spaces and let $y\mapsto\Pi_y$ be a supplied posterior probability kernel. For $\alpha\in[0,1]$, a set-valued rule $C$ is **graph-measurable** when
$$\{(y,\theta)\in\mathsf Y\times\Theta:\theta\in C(y)\}\in\mathcal Y\otimes\mathcal T.$$
It is a **posterior credible set at level $1-\alpha$** when it is graph-measurable and
$$\Pi_y(C(y))\ge 1-\alpha\qquad\text{for every }y\text{ in its declared data domain}.$$
The posterior-mass function is measurable by integration of the indicator of the membership graph against the kernel. If a density is available relative to a specified dominating measure, a highest-posterior-density region selects parameter values with largest density; such regions need not be intervals and may be disconnected or nonunique.

For Borel probabilities $\mu_n,\mu$ on a metric space S, the following are equivalent: (i) $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$; (ii) integrals converge for all bounded uniformly continuous real tests; (iii) $\limsup_n\mu_n(F)\le\mu(F)$ for every closed F; (iv) $\liminf_n\mu_n(G)\ge\mu(G)$ for every open G; (v) $\mu_n(A)\to\mu(A)$ for every Borel A with $\mu(\partial A)=0$.

Assume AC. Let $P_0$ have a density $f_0$ on $[0,1]$ with $\|f_0\|_\infty\le B<\infty$. Let $(\psi_{lk})$ be an orthonormal, compactly supported wavelet basis with $2^l$ coefficients at level $l\ge1$, uniformly bounded overlap, and $\|\psi_{lk}\|_\infty\le C_0 2^{l/2}$. Suppose for some $\gamma>1/2$,
$$\max_k|\langle f_0,\psi_{lk}\rangle|\le C_f2^{-l(\gamma+1/2)}.$$
Let $w_l\ge1$ be nondecreasing and admissible in [[def-multiscale-coefficient-space-m0w]], and choose either cutoff regime
$$2^{L_n}\asymp n^{1/(2\gamma+1)}\quad\text{or}\quad 2^{L_n}\asymp(n/\log n)^{1/(2\gamma+1)}.$$
For IID $X_1,\ldots,X_n\sim P_0$, define the finite wavelet projection $P_n(L_n)$ by coefficients $\langle P_n(L_n),\psi_{lk}\rangle=P_n\psi_{lk}:=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\psi_{lk}(X_i)$ for $l\le L_n$ and zero for $l>L_n$, with the coarsest scaling coordinates projected as well. Let $G_{P_0}$ be a Borel centered Gaussian law on $M_0(w)$ whose coefficient covariance is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(G_{lk},G_{l'k'})=P_0[(\psi_{lk}-P_0\psi_{lk})(\psi_{l'k'}-P_0\psi_{l'k'})].$$
Then
$$\sqrt n\{P_n(L_n)-f_0\}\Rightarrow G_{P_0}\quad\text{in }M_0(w).$$

Let $(\psi_{lk})$ be a countable complete orthonormal basis of the real Hilbert space $L^2([0,1])$ ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]], [[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). For a wavelet basis, index levels by $l\ge0$, let $K_l$ have $2^l$ indices, and put $a_l=2^l$ for $l\ge1$ and $a_0=2$ for the finite coarsest level. This finite-level convention only prevents a zero logarithmic weight and does not change any convergence criterion below. For a trigonometric basis, use its integer frequency index $l$, bounded multiplicities, and $a_l=\max(2,|l|)$.

Here an **$S$-regular wavelet basis** means a wavelet orthonormal basis whose members are $S$ times differentiable, with each derivative through order $S$ in $L^2([0,1])$, following the source convention. The weak BvM theorem below only uses the basis's completeness, orthonormality, and level counts.

For $\delta>0$, define $H(\delta)=H^{-1/2,\delta}_2$ to be the space of coefficient sequences $c=(c_{lk})$ with norm

$$\|c\|_{H(\delta)}^2:=\sum_{l,k}a_l^{-1}(\log a_l)^{-2\delta}|c_{lk}|^2<\infty.$$

Its inner product is the corresponding weighted coefficient inner product. Multiplying each coordinate by $a_l^{-1/2}(\log a_l)^{-\delta}$ identifies it isometrically with $\ell^2(I)$, where $I=\{(l,k):k\in K_l\}$ (or the corresponding trigonometric index set). This sequence space is complete: if $x^{(m)}$ is Cauchy, each coordinate converges to a scalar $x_i$; for every finite $F\subset I$, the Cauchy bound passes to the limit in $\sum_{i\in F}|x_i^{(m)}-x_i^{(n)}|^2$, so the supremum over finite $F$ shows $x^{(m)}\to x$ in $\ell^2(I)$. It is separable because finite-support sequences with rational coordinates form a countable dense set. Thus $H(\delta)$ is a separable Hilbert space without an additional choice assumption.

A function $f\in L^2([0,1])$ is identified with its coefficient sequence $c_{lk}=\langle f,\psi_{lk}\rangle$. For each finite set $F$ of indices, orthonormality makes $\sum_{(l,k)\in F}c_{lk}\psi_{lk}$ orthogonal to its residual in $L^2$, so the Pythagorean identity gives $\sum_F|c_{lk}|^2\le\|f\|_2^2$. Taking the supremum over finite $F$ and using the boundedness of the weights proves continuity of the coefficient map. If all coefficients of $f$ vanish, then $f$ is orthogonal to the linear span of the basis. Completeness makes this span dense, and continuity of $g\mapsto\langle f,g\rangle$ gives $\langle f,f\rangle=0$, hence $f=0$ in $L^2$. Applying this to the difference of two functions proves injectivity. Thus the coefficient map is a continuous linear embedding $L^2([0,1])\hookrightarrow H(\delta)$.

The weight trace $\sum_{l,k}a_l^{-1}(\log a_l)^{-2\delta}$ is finite exactly when $\delta>1/2$: for wavelets its tail is a constant multiple of $\sum_{l\ge1}l^{-2\delta}$, while for a trigonometric basis it is comparable to $\sum_{l\ge2}[l(\log l)^{2\delta}]^{-1}$. The product-prior theorem below uses the wavelet case.

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

derivations.claim: The posterior draw $f$ and center $T_n$ are $L^2$-valued, so [F2] embeds $\sqrt n(f-T_n)$ in $M_0(w)$; [F1] supplies its norm. For an $L$-Lipschitz map $T$ between metric spaces and any admissible bounded 1-Lipschitz test $h$ on its target, $h\circ T/\max(1,L)$ is an admissible test on its domain. Therefore $\beta_{BL}(T_\#\nu,T_\#\rho)\le\max(1,L)\beta_{BL}(\nu,\rho).$ By [F3], $J$ is linear and Lipschitz with a finite constant $L_J$. The bound applied pointwise to the data-indexed laws in [A1] gives $\beta_{BL}(J_\#Q_n,J_\#G_{P_0})\to0$ in probability. Moreover, if $\ell:C([0,1])\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and linear, then $\ell\circ J$ is continuous and linear on $M_0(w)$. The centered Gaussian premise on $G_{P_0}$ says exactly that this scalar pushforward is centered normal, allowing zero variance. Thus $J_\#G_{P_0}$ is a centered Gaussian Borel law. In particular, for any finite $t_1,\ldots,t_m$ and real $a_1,\ldots,a_m$, the functional $x\mapsto\sum_i a_iJx(t_i)$ is continuous and linear, so the evaluation vector $(JG_{P_0}(t_i))_{i=1}^m$ is jointly centered Gaussian. This uses only the scalar Gaussian pushforward meaning of the premise, without characteristic-function uniqueness or a Gaussian existence theorem. To identify its covariance, let $p_J1_{[0,s]}$ be the finite wavelet projection of the indicator. The finite Gaussian coefficient covariance gives $\operatorname{Cov}(J(P_JG_{P_0})(s),J(P_JG_{P_0})(t))=P_0[(p_J1_{[0,s]}-P_0p_J1_{[0,s]})(p_J1_{[0,t]}-P_0p_J1_{[0,t]})].$ By [F11], $p_J1_{[0,s]}\to1_{[0,s]}$ in Lebesgue $L^2$; since $f_0\le B$, this is also convergence in $L^2(P_0)$. The variance of a difference of two finite projected Gaussian evaluations is the $P_0$-variance of the corresponding difference of projected indicators, so it tends to zero; hence those evaluations are Cauchy in $L^2$. They also converge almost surely to $JG_{P_0}(s)$ because $P_JG_{P_0}\to G_{P_0}$ in $M_0(w)$ and $J$ is continuous. The almost-sure and in-probability limits coincide: for any $\varepsilon>0$, the probability that they differ by more than $\varepsilon$ is bounded by the two probabilities that each sequence differs from its limit by more than $\varepsilon/2$, both tending to zero. The norm maps $x\mapsto\|x\|_{M(w)}$ and $F\mapsto\|F\|_\infty$ are 1-Lipschitz by the reverse triangle inequality. Applying the pushforward bound of step 1.1 first to the $M(w)$ norm and then to the supremum norm after $J$ gives bounded-Lipschitz convergence in probability of both posterior norm laws to their corresponding limit norm laws. For the projected empirical center $T_n=P_n(L_n)$, [F9] verifies [A2] under the smoothness and cutoff assumptions in [F9].

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be IID on $[0,1]$ with density $0<\rho_0\le f_0\le D_0<\infty$, and suppose $g_0=\log f_0\in C^\alpha$. Use a sufficiently regular compactly supported boundary corrected orthonormal multiresolution wavelet basis satisfying [[lem-compact-wavelet-projection-kernel-and-commutator]], with regularity greater than $\alpha$, and let $V_L$ contain exactly its wavelet levels through $L$, including the fixed low scaling space and constants. Its regularity and vanishing moments satisfy the composition hypotheses in that lemma for some integer $m>\alpha$. Let $L_n$ be either of the two cutoff sequences in [[def-type-s-and-h-multiscale-density-priors]], fixed consistently for all $n$.

In Type-S1 take $\alpha>1$, $\sigma_l=2^{-l(\alpha+1/2)}$, and any coefficient probability density with globally Lipschitz logarithm. In Type-S2 take $\alpha>1/2$, Gaussian coefficients, and $\sigma_l=2^{-l(r+1/2)}$ with $0<r<\alpha-1/4$. Normalize $f=\exp(T)/\int\exp(T)$ as in that definition. For every admissible weight sequence $w$, the posterior satisfies
$$\beta_{BL,M_0(w)}\bigl(\mathcal L(\sqrt n(f-P_n(L_n))\mid X^n),\mathcal L(G_{P_0})\bigr)\longrightarrow0$$
in $P_0^n$-probability, where $P_n(L_n)$ has empirical wavelet coefficients through $L_n$ and zero coefficients above $L_n$, and $G_{P_0}$ is the Borel Gaussian bridge with covariance $P_0[(\psi_i-P_0\psi_i)(\psi_j-P_0\psi_j)]$.

Assume AC. Use the type-H prior of [[def-type-s-and-h-multiscale-density-priors]], retaining its original conditions: $1/2<\alpha\le1$, $f_0\in C^\alpha([0,1])$, $0<\rho_0\le f_0\le D_0<\infty$, either original cutoff $L_n=j_n$ or $L_n=\ell_n$, and $c_1 2^{-L_na}\le a_{k,L_n}\le c_2$ for fixed positive $a,c_1,c_2$. Write $m_n=2^{L_n}$. In the Haar convention, the scaling function is $1$, the detail functions are
$$\psi_{lk}=2^{l/2}(\mathbf1_{I_{l+1,2k}}-\mathbf1_{I_{l+1,2k+1}}),\qquad l\ge0,\quad 0\le k<2^l,$$
and a histogram at resolution $L_n$ has only the scaling coordinate and levels $l<L_n$. Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be IID from $f_0$, let $N_{nk}=\sum_i\mathbf1_{I_{L_n,k}}(X_i)$, and define the empirical histogram
$$h_n(x)=m_n N_{nk}/n\quad\text{on }I_{L_n,k}.$$
Let $\Pi_n(\cdot\mid X^n)$ be the density posterior for the stated histogram prior. For every nondecreasing $w_l\ge1$ with $w_l/\sqrt{l+1}\to\infty$, its conditional law $Q_n$ of $\sqrt n(f-h_n)$ satisfies
$$\beta_{BL,M_0(w)}(Q_n,\mathcal L(G_{P_0}))\longrightarrow0$$
in $P_0^n$-probability, where the Borel centered Gaussian bridge $G_{P_0}$ is supplied by [[lem-density-gaussian-bridge-is-borel-on-m0w]] and has covariance $P_0[(\psi-P_0\psi)(\psi'-P_0\psi')]$. Its scaling coordinate is zero. This proves the type-H source-specific posterior BvM with the empirical projection center; no additional contraction, bias, or Dirichlet-parameter condition is imposed.

Let $V_L$ be the span of wavelets through level $L$ in a compactly supported orthonormal multiresolution basis on $[0,1]$, either boundary corrected or periodized. Assume constants belong to $V_L$, its dimension $d_L\asymp2^L$, and its orthonormal scaling functions $\phi_{Lk}$ have supremum norm at most $C2^{L/2}$, support diameter at most $C2^{-L}$, and uniformly bounded overlap. Periodized supports and distances are interpreted on the circle. Assume also $\sum_k|\psi_{lk}(x)|\le C2^{l/2}$ and $\|\psi_{lk}\|_1\le C2^{-l/2}$. Let $P_L$ denote the orthogonal projection onto $V_L$.

Then $P_L$ has a kernel $K_L$ satisfying $\sup_x\int|K_L(x,y)|dy\le C'$ and $K_L(x,y)=0$ when $\operatorname{dist}(x,y)>C'2^{-L}$. If $a$ is $\beta$-Hölder for $0<\beta\le1$, then
$$\|P_L(ah)-ah\|_\infty\le C'\|a\|_{C^\beta}2^{-\beta L}\|h\|_\infty,\qquad h\in V_L.$$
For the composition assertion, assume additionally an integer $m>\alpha$ such that $\|\psi_{lk}^{(q)}\|_\infty\le C_q2^{l(q+1/2)}$ for $0\le q\le m$, bounded overlap also for their derivatives, and vanishing moments through degree $m-1$ for the detail wavelets, including boundary wavelets; the finite low scaling functions are $C^m$. These are the usual sufficiently regular compact wavelet hypotheses. If a bounded function $g$ has coefficients bounded by $C_g2^{-l(\alpha+1/2)}$, with $\alpha>0$, and its wavelet expansion represents $g$ in $L^2$, then $\|g-P_Lg\|_\infty\le C''C_g2^{-\alpha L}$, up to equality of the continuous representatives. Under these additional derivative and cancellation hypotheses, $e^g$ also has coefficients bounded by $C_g^\prime2^{-l(\alpha+1/2)}$, including integer $\alpha$, and $g,e^g$ are $\beta$-Hölder for every $0<\beta<\min(\alpha,1)$. Moreover $\|h\|_\infty\le C''\sqrt{d_L}\|h\|_2$ for $h\in V_L$.

Assume AC. Let $P_0$ have a density $f_0$ on $[0,1]$ with $\|f_0\|_\infty\le B<\infty$. Let $(\psi_{lk})$ be an orthonormal, compactly supported wavelet basis with $2^l$ coefficients at level $l\ge1$, uniformly bounded overlap, and $\|\psi_{lk}\|_\infty\le C_0 2^{l/2}$. Suppose for some $\gamma>1/2$,
$$\max_k|\langle f_0,\psi_{lk}\rangle|\le C_f2^{-l(\gamma+1/2)}.$$
Let $w_l\ge1$ be nondecreasing and admissible in [[def-multiscale-coefficient-space-m0w]], and choose either cutoff regime
$$2^{L_n}\asymp n^{1/(2\gamma+1)}\quad\text{or}\quad 2^{L_n}\asymp(n/\log n)^{1/(2\gamma+1)}.$$
For IID $X_1,\ldots,X_n\sim P_0$, define the finite wavelet projection $P_n(L_n)$ by coefficients $\langle P_n(L_n),\psi_{lk}\rangle=P_n\psi_{lk}:=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\psi_{lk}(X_i)$ for $l\le L_n$ and zero for $l>L_n$, with the coarsest scaling coordinates projected as well. Let $G_{P_0}$ be a Borel centered Gaussian law on $M_0(w)$ whose coefficient covariance is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(G_{lk},G_{l'k'})=P_0[(\psi_{lk}-P_0\psi_{lk})(\psi_{l'k'}-P_0\psi_{l'k'})].$$
Then
$$\sqrt n\{P_n(L_n)-f_0\}\Rightarrow G_{P_0}\quad\text{in }M_0(w).$$

Assume AC. Let $P_0$ have density $0<\rho\le f_0\le D<\infty$ on $[0,1]$, and put $F_0(t)=\int_0^t f_0$. Use a complete real orthonormal wavelet basis, allowing the Haar basis with its finite scaling coordinate, and admissible weights $w$ as in [[def-multiscale-coefficient-space-m0w]]. Assume the wavelet geometry and summability conditions of [[lem-multiscale-primitive-map-to-continuous-cdfs]], and write $J:M_0(w)\to C([0,1])$ for its primitive map. Let $G$ be the Borel centered Gaussian bridge random element of [[lem-density-gaussian-bridge-is-borel-on-m0w]], with coefficient covariance

For a posterior draw $f$, write $F_f=Jf$ and $F_{T_n}=JT_n$, where $J$ is the primitive map of [[lem-multiscale-primitive-map-to-continuous-cdfs]]. Then the posterior law of $\sqrt n(F_f-F_{T_n})$ converges in bounded-Lipschitz distance on $C([0,1])$ to the $P_0$-Brownian bridge $B_{P_0}(t)$, with covariance $F_0(s\wedge t)-F_0(s)F_0(t)$.

For $0<\alpha<1$, let $R_n^M$ and $R_n^C$ be the posterior lower $1-\alpha$ quantiles of $\|\sqrt n(f-T_n)\|_{M(w)}$ and $\|\sqrt n(F_f-F_{T_n})\|_\infty$, respectively. The corresponding posterior balls
$$C_n^M=\{f:\|f-T_n\|_{M(w)}\le R_n^M/\sqrt n\},\qquad C_n^C=\{F:\|F-F_{T_n}\|_\infty\le R_n^C/\sqrt n\}$$
are measurable credible sets of posterior mass at least $1-\alpha$. Their frequentist coverage tends to $1-\alpha$, and the scaled radii converge to the respective $1-\alpha$ quantiles of $\|G_{P_0}\|_{M(w)}$ and $\|B_{P_0}\|_\infty$.

Suppose $\|f_0\|_{C^\gamma_\psi}<\infty$. Choose integers $j_n$ with $2^{j_n}\asymp(n/\log n)^{1/(2\gamma+1)}$ and let $u_n=w_{j_n}/\sqrt{j_n}\to\infty$. Intersect the credible ball with the coefficient smoothness ball:

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ be measurable spaces and let $y\mapsto\Pi_y$ be a supplied posterior probability kernel. For $\alpha\in[0,1]$, a set-valued rule $C$ is **graph-measurable** when
$$\{(y,\theta)\in\mathsf Y\times\Theta:\theta\in C(y)\}\in\mathcal Y\otimes\mathcal T.$$
It is a **posterior credible set at level $1-\alpha$** when it is graph-measurable and
$$\Pi_y(C(y))\ge 1-\alpha\qquad\text{for every }y\text{ in its declared data domain}.$$
The posterior-mass function is measurable by integration of the indicator of the membership graph against the kernel. If a density is available relative to a specified dominating measure, a highest-posterior-density region selects parameter values with largest density; such regions need not be intervals and may be disconnected or nonunique.

Let $\pi$ be a prior probability on $(E,\mathcal S)$ and let $Q:E\to T$ be a probability kernel dominated by a sigma-finite measure $\nu$ on $(T,\mathcal T)$, with specified nonnegative jointly measurable density $\ell:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$:
$$Q(\theta,B)=\int_B\ell(\theta,y)\,\nu(dy)\quad\text{for every }\theta\in E,\ B\in\mathcal T.$$

Define $m(y)=\int_E\ell(\theta,y)\,\pi(d\theta)$. Under the joint law with density $\ell$ relative to $\pi\times\nu$, a conditional law of the parameter given the observation is
$$K(y,A)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\int_A\ell(\theta,y)\,\pi(d\theta)}{m(y)},&0<m(y)<\infty,\\ \pi(A),&m(y)=0\text{ or }m(y)=\infty.\end{cases}$$

The observation marginal is $m\,d\nu$, and the filled fibres have marginal mass zero. This is a choice-free assertion about the explicit kernel and event identities.

derivations.claim: For data with $k$ successes, the likelihood is $\theta^k(1-\theta)^{n-k}$. It is bounded by $1$ and positive for $0<\theta<1$, so its integral against the uniform prior is finite and strictly positive. [F2] therefore gives the posterior density proportional to that likelihood. The sample space is finite for fixed $n$, so the interval rule's membership graph is a finite union of measurable slices. The posterior density is positive on $(0,1)$, making its CDF continuous and strictly increasing there; the posterior probability between its two quantiles is $(1-\alpha/2)-\alpha/2=1-\alpha$. Thus the rule is credible by [F1].

At $\theta_0=0$, the data are all zero with probability one, so the likelihood is $(1-\theta)^n$. Its normalizing integral is $\int_0^1(1-\theta)^n d\theta=1/(n+1)$, giving posterior density $(n+1)(1-\theta)^n$ and CDF $F_n(t)=1-(1-t)^{n+1}$. Solving $F_n(q_u)=u$ yields $q_u=1-(1-u)^{1/(n+1)}$. In particular $q_{\alpha/2}>0$, so $0\notin C_n$ for every $n$.

Because the truth is zero and all data are zero almost surely, [L1] gives frequentist coverage $P_0\{0\in C_n(X_1,\ldots,X_n)\}=0$. This contradicts the asserted lower bound $1-\alpha>0$ and exhibits failure at the boundary identified in [A1].

For type S use a fixed sufficiently regular compactly supported orthonormal multiresolution wavelet basis $(\psi_{lk})$ on $[0,1]$ as in [[def-negative-sobolev-space-for-white-noise]], with boundary correction, regularity greater than the truth smoothness $\alpha$, and $|K_l|=2^l$. The spaces $V_L$ spanned by the retained levels $l\le L$ contain constants and have orthonormal scaling bases with uniformly bounded overlap, support diameters at most $C2^{-L}$, and suprema at most $C2^{L/2}$; a fixed shift of the scaling-resolution index is absorbed in $C$. The wavelets likewise have uniformly bounded overlap, support diameters at most $C2^{-l}$, and suprema at most $C2^{l/2}$. For an integer $m>\alpha$, the detail wavelets have vanishing moments through degree $m-1$, and derivatives through order $m$ satisfy $\|\psi_{lk}^{(q)}\|_\infty\le C_q2^{l(q+1/2)}$, with uniformly bounded overlap of their supports; the fixed low scaling functions are $C^m$. These are the sufficiently regular compact multiresolution basis conditions in the source density theorem. For the density-model source results, every truth $f_0$ is a probability density satisfying $0<\rho_0\le f_0\le D_0<\infty$ for constants $\rho_0,D_0$. For $n\ge3$ and smoothness index $\alpha>0$, let $j_n$ and $\ell_n$ be the largest integers satisfying
$$2^{j_n}\le n^{1/(2\alpha+1)},\qquad 2^{\ell_n}\le(n/\log n)^{1/(2\alpha+1)}.$$
Choose one cutoff sequence $L_n\in\{j_n,\ell_n\}$ for all $n\ge3$; set any finite $L_n$ for $n=1,2$, which does not change asymptotic claims.

For a finite wavelet series $T_n=\sum_{l\le L_n}\sum_{k\in K_l}\sigma_l\xi_{lk}\psi_{lk}$, define $c(T_n)=\log\int_0^1e^{T_n(x)}dx$ and the normalized log-density $f_n(x)=e^{T_n(x)-c(T_n)}$.

The **type-S1 family** takes IID coefficients $\xi_{lk}$ with a continuous density $\varphi_H$ for which $\log\varphi_H$ is Lipschitz, and uses $\sigma_l=2^{-l(\alpha+1/2)}$. Its source theorem assumes $\log f_0$ has coefficient Hölder regularity $\alpha>1$ and $f_0$ is bounded above and bounded away from zero.

The **type-S2 family** takes IID standard-normal coefficients and uses $\sigma_l=2^{-l(r+1/2)}$, where $\alpha>1/2$ and $0<r<\alpha-1/4$. Here the truth regime is $\log f_0\in C^\alpha$ with positive finite density bounds. Equation (24) in the source specifies this prior-parameter range, but its Theorem 3 assumes $\alpha>1$ for both type-S families. The broader Gaussian truth range $\alpha>1/2$ is established separately by the local type-S posterior BvM theorem.

For the **type-H family**, use the Haar basis instead of the regular type-S wavelets: its scaling function is $1$ and $\psi_{lk}=2^{l/2}(1_{I_{l+1,2k}}-1_{I_{l+1,2k+1}})$ for $l\ge0$ and $0\le k<2^l$. The histogram space at resolution $L$ consists of the scaling coordinate and detail levels $l<L$; all detail coefficients at $l\ge L$ vanish. Partition $[0,1]$ into dyadic cells $I_{L_n,k}$ of length $2^{-L_n}$, draw $\omega=(\omega_k)_{k<2^{L_n}}\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(a_{0,L_n},\ldots,a_{2^{L_n}-1,L_n})$, and set $f_n=2^{L_n}\omega_k$ on cell $I_{L_n,k}$. The source assumptions are $c_1 2^{-L_na}\le a_{k,L_n}\le c_2$ for fixed positive $a,c_1,c_2$, and $f_0\in C^\alpha$ for $1/2<\alpha\le1$, together with the common positive finite density bounds above. The posterior asymptotic conclusions for these families are separate results.

Here $C^\alpha_\psi$ denotes the coefficient class with norm $\|g\|_{C^\alpha_\psi}:=\sup_{l,k}2^{l(\alpha+1/2)}|\langle g,\psi_{lk}\rangle|$. For sufficiently regular standard wavelets this is the usual Hölder scale (with the usual Zygmund interpretation at integer smoothness).

Use the wavelet coefficient levels $(l,k)$ and multiplicities $|K_l|=2^l$ from [[def-negative-sobolev-space-for-white-noise]]. The same coefficient-space definition applies to the Haar system used for type-H histograms: detail levels $l\ge0$ have $2^l$ coefficients, and the single scaling coefficient is an additional finite coarsest coordinate, included in the norm with weight $1$. Finite projections always retain that scaling coordinate; this finite convention does not alter any tail assertion. Let $w=(w_l)$ be nondecreasing with $w_l\ge1$. Define
$$M(w)=\left\{x=(x_{lk}):\|x\|_{M(w)}:=\sup_l\frac{\max_{k\in K_l}|x_{lk}|}{w_l}<\infty\right\}$$
and its closed little-o subspace
$$M_0(w)=\left\{x\in M(w):\frac{\max_{k\in K_l}|x_{lk}|}{w_l}\longrightarrow0\text{ as }l\to\infty\right\},$$
with the same norm. Call $w$ admissible when $w_l/\sqrt l\to\infty$. The finite coarsest level is included in the norm and does not affect this limit. Elements are coefficient sequences; in particular, they need not be $L^2$ functions. [[lem-m0w-separable-and-projection-tails]] proves that $M_0(w)$ is a separable Banach space, that $L^2$ coefficient sequences embed in it, and that finite-level projections converge in its norm.

Assume AC. Use either Type-S1, Type-S2 or Type-H with all the truth, basis, prior-scale, Dirichlet-parameter and cutoff conditions of [[def-type-s-and-h-multiscale-density-priors]]. In Type H take the empirical histogram $T_n=h_n$ at mesh $2^{-L_n}$, equivalently the Haar projection with scaling coordinate and details $l<L_n$.

For each $0<\eta<1$, the posterior multiscale and CDF balls of [[thm-cdf-and-multiscale-credible-band-calibration-from-bvm]], at posterior level $1-\eta$ and centered at these $T_n$, have posterior mass at least $1-\eta$ and frequentist coverage tending to $1-\eta$. Their scaled radii converge in probability to the positive finite $1-\eta$ quantiles of the corresponding Gaussian bridge norms. In particular, writing $F_h(t)=\int_0^t h(x)dx$, the posterior law of $\sqrt n(F_f-F_{T_n})$ converges in bounded-Lipschitz distance on $C([0,1])$ to the $P_0$-Brownian bridge law, in $P_0^n$-probability.

If additionally the coefficient smoothness and undersmoothing hypotheses of [[thm-multiscale-credible-band-holder-diameter]] hold, its intersection with the stated coefficient smoothness ball has the same limiting coverage and the diameter bound asserted there. Fix the real orthonormal wavelet basis and level weights $a_l$ of [[def-negative-sobolev-space-for-white-noise]]. For $0\le s<S$, define the basis Sobolev space
$$H^s_2=\left\{g\in L^2([0,1]):\sum_{l,k}a_l^{2s}|\langle g,\psi_{lk}\rangle|^2<\infty\right\}.$$
For $g\in H^s_2$, $s>1/2$, and $f\in L^2([0,1])$, define $L_g(f)=\langle f,g\rangle_{L^2}$. For $x=(x_{lk})\in H(\delta)$, the intended extension is the coefficient pairing $L_g(x)=\sum_{l,k}x_{lk}\langle g,\psi_{lk}\rangle$; [[lem-smooth-functional-extends-to-negative-sobolev-space]] proves that this series is absolutely convergent and defines a continuous linear functional on $H(\delta)$ for every $\delta>0$.

In the white-noise experiment $X^{(n)}=f_0+n^{-1/2}W$, fix $\delta>1/2$ so that the observation is $H(\delta)$-valued; $L_g(X^{(n)})$ means this continuous pairing with the $H(\delta)$-valued observation. It does not assert that $X^{(n)}$ is an $L^2$ function. The representer is nonzero when $g\ne0$; the corresponding white-noise variance is $\|g\|_2^2$.

Use the product-prior white-noise model and supplied posterior kernel of [[thm-weak-nonparametric-bernstein-von-mises-for-product-priors]], including its wavelet-basis, coefficient-density, truth, and countable-choice hypotheses. Let $g\in H^s_2$ for some $s>1/2$, with $g\ne0$, and put $\sigma_g=\|g\|_2$. Let $Q_n$ be the posterior law of $L_g(f)$ and let
$$C_{n,\alpha}=\left[q_{\alpha/2}(Q_n),q_{1-\alpha/2}(Q_n)\right],\qquad 0<\alpha<1.$$
Then
$$\beta_{BL,\mathbb R}\!\left(Q_n\circ[u\mapsto\sqrt n(u-L_g(X^{(n)}))]^{-1},N(0,\sigma_g^2)\right)\longrightarrow0$$
in $P_{f_0}^{(n)}$-probability. The interval $C_{n,\alpha}$ is posterior credible at level $1-\alpha$, and its frequentist coverage satisfies
$$P_{f_0}^{(n)}\{L_g(f_0)\in C_{n,\alpha}\}\longrightarrow1-\alpha.$$

Let $(\psi_{lk})$ be the S-regular wavelet basis in [[def-negative-sobolev-space-for-white-noise]], with $2^l$ coefficients at each level $l\ge0$. For $\alpha>0$, put $\sigma_l=2^{-l(\alpha+1/2)}$ and let the prior on $f=\sum_{l,k}\sigma_l\xi_{lk}\psi_{lk}$ have IID coefficients $\xi_{lk}$ with density $\varphi$. Assume countable choice for the $L^2$ prior construction supplied by [[lem-wavelet-product-prior-is-l2-valued]], and take the full posterior kernel as the supplied model input of [[lem-product-prior-coordinate-posterior-law]]. Let $f_0\in L^2([0,1])$, write $\theta_{0,lk}=\langle f_0,\psi_{lk}\rangle$ and $r_{lk}=\theta_{0,lk}/\sigma_l$, and suppose

$$\sup_{l,k}|r_{lk}|\le M<\tau,$$

where $\varphi$ is a probability density satisfying $\varphi(u)\le C_\varphi$ for every $u$, $\varphi(u)\ge c_\varphi>0$ for $|u|<\tau$, $\int u^2\varphi(u)\,du<\infty$, and $\varphi$ is continuous at each $r_{lk}$. The observation model is

$$dX^{(n)}(t)=f_0(t)\,dt+n^{-1/2}dW(t),\qquad 0\le t\le1,$$

with standard white noise $W$; in the stated basis this is the sequence experiment $X_{lk}=\theta_{0,lk}+n^{-1/2}Z_{lk}$ with independent standard normal coordinates. Let $\Pi_n(\cdot\mid X)$ be the product-coordinate posterior of [[lem-product-prior-coordinate-posterior-law]]. Let $N$ be the law of the canonical white noise in $H(\delta)$ and define

$$\widetilde\Pi_n:=\Pi_n(\cdot\mid X)\circ[f\mapsto\sqrt n(f-X)]^{-1},\qquad \beta_{BL,H(\delta)}(\mu,\nu):=\sup_{\substack{\|g\|_\infty\le1\\ \operatorname{Lip}_{H(\delta)}(g)\le1}}\left|\int g\,d\mu-\int g\,d\nu\right|.$$

For every $\delta>1/2$,

$$\beta_{BL,H(\delta)}(\widetilde\Pi_n,N)\longrightarrow0$$

in probability under the true white-noise law $P_{f_0}^{(n)}$. This is a bounded-Lipschitz weak BvM conclusion; it asserts neither total-variation convergence on all Borel subsets nor an $L^2$-valued Gaussian limit.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: The standard-normal coefficient density is bounded, continuous, strictly positive at every real value, and has finite second moment. By [A1], all wavelet coefficients of $g=1$ above a fixed finite level vanish; the remaining levels have finitely many coefficients. Therefore $\sum_{l,k}a_l^{2s}|g_{lk}|^2<\infty$ for every finite $s$, in particular for some $s>1/2$. Also $\|g\|_2=1$ and its pairing is $L_1(f)=\int_0^1f$.
Under $f_0=0$ and countable choice [F4], $\sqrt nL_1(X^{(n)})=L_1(W)$ is exactly $N(0,1)$. Applying [F2] with $g=1$ gives the scalar posterior BvM limit $N(0,1)$ and limiting coverage $1-\alpha$.

supplier_interfaces.excerpt:
Throughout, $\mathbb F$ is $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$ and families are indexed by
an arbitrary set $I$, with no enumeration or countability assumed. Finite real lists use [[def-finite-sum]], and sums over finite subsets use [[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]] in the additive monoid of the scalar field. Disjoint splitting is [[lem-finite-sum-reindexing-and-fubini]], and scalar modulus estimates use [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]; all suprema and infima of real sets below are
taken in the complete ordered field $\mathbb R$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) or in $[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$
([[def-extended-reals]], [[lem-extended-reals-complete]]).

**Sums of nonnegative families.** Let $(c_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family of
nonnegative reals and let $\operatorname{Fin}(I)$ be the set of finite subsets of
$I$, ordered by inclusion. Define

$$\sum_{i\in I}c_i:=\sup\Bigl\{\sum_{i\in F}c_i \;:\; F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)\Bigr\}\in[0,+\infty] .$$

The set of finite subsums is nonempty, since $\varnothing$ contributes the empty
sum $0$, so the supremum exists in $[0,+\infty]$; it is a real number exactly
when the finite subsums are bounded above in $\mathbb R$, and $+\infty$
otherwise. For finite $I$ the finite subsum at $I$ is the largest of all finite
subsums, because all terms are nonnegative, so the definition agrees with the
finite sum; in particular $\sum_{i\in I}c_i=0$ when every $c_i$ is $0$, and
$I=\varnothing$ gives the empty sum $0$.

**Splitting identity and small tails.** Fix a finite $F\subseteq I$. Every
finite $G\subseteq I$ splits as the disjoint union $(G\cap F)\cup(G\setminus F)$,
so $\sum_{i\in G}c_i=\sum_{i\in G\cap F}c_i+\sum_{i\in G\setminus F}c_i\le\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i$;
conversely the finite $G$ with $F\subseteq G$ satisfy
$\sum_{i\in G}c_i=\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in G\setminus F}c_i$. Taking suprema,
with the constant $\sum_{i\in F}c_i$ passing through the supremum,

$$\sum_{i\in I}c_i=\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i . \qquad (1)$$

Consequently, if $S:=\sum_{i\in I}c_i$ is finite, then for every real
$\varepsilon>0$ there is a finite $F\subseteq I$ with
$\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i<\varepsilon$: the finite subsums form a nonempty
bounded-above set with supremum $S$, so by the epsilon characterisation of the
supremum ([[lem-sup-epsilon]]) some finite $F$ has
$S-\varepsilon<\sum_{i\in F}c_i$, and (1) gives
$\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i=S-\sum_{i\in F}c_i<\varepsilon$. Such an $F$ is
called a **tail-control set** for $\varepsilon$.

**Sums of scalar families.** Now let $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family in $\mathbb F$
and put $s_F:=\sum_{i\in F}a_i$ for finite $F\subseteq I$. The set
$\operatorname{Fin}(I)$ with inclusion is a directed preorder: it is nonempty and
$F\cup G$ is a common upper bound of $F$ and $G$
([[def-directed-set-and-net]]). Hence $(s_F)_{F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)}$ is a
net in $\mathbb F$, the **finite-subset net** of the family, and the family is
**summable** when this net converges
([[def-net-convergence-and-cluster-point]]). The scalar metric is the usual real metric or [[def-complex-metric-convergence-and-continuity]]. These metric spaces are Hausdorff by [[thm-metric-hausdorff-separation]]. A net in $\mathbb F$ has at most one limit
([[thm-hausdorff-iff-net-limits-are-unique]]), so for a summable family the
limit is unique and we write $\sum_{i\in I}a_i:=\lim_F s_F$ for it. The family is
**absolutely summable** when $\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|<+\infty$ in the sense above.

**Every absolutely summable family is summable, in ZF.** Assume
$S:=\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|$ is finite and put $S_F:=\sum_{i\in F}|a_i|$ for finite
$F$. For finite $F,G\subseteq I$ the triangle inequality for finite sums and the
fact that a finite subsum is at most the whole nonnegative sum give

$$|s_F-s_G|\le\sum_{i\in F\triangle G}|a_i|\le S-S_{F\cap G} . \qquad (2)$$

Now fix a real $\varepsilon>0$, let $F_0$ be a tail-control set for
$\varepsilon$, and let $F,G\supseteq F_0$ be finite. Then $F\cap G\supseteq F_0$,
so $S-S_{F\cap G}\le S-S_{F_0}<\varepsilon$ and (2) gives
$|s_F-s_G|<\varepsilon$.

First suppose $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$. For each finite $F$ define
$A_F:=\inf\{s_G : G\supseteq F\}$ and $B_F:=\sup\{s_G : G\supseteq F\}$ over
finite $G$. Both are real numbers, because $|s_G|\le S_G\le S$, so the two sets
are nonempty and bounded, and $A_F\le B_F$. If $H\supseteq F$ then
$A_H\ge A_F$ and $B_H\le B_F$. Let $L:=\sup_FA_F$ and $U:=\inf_FB_F$.
Since $A_F\le s_{F\cup H}\le B_H$ for all finite $F,H$, we get $L\le U$.
Moreover, the preceding estimate holds for every pair $F,G\supseteq F_0$;
taking the supremum over $F$ and the infimum over $G$ gives
$B_{F_0}-A_{F_0}\le\varepsilon$. Hence
$0\le U-L\le B_{F_0}-A_{F_0}\le\varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon>0$, so
$L=U=:s$. If $F\supseteq F_0$, then both $s_F$ and $s$ lie in
$[A_{F_0},B_{F_0}]$, and therefore $|s_F-s|\le\varepsilon$.

If $\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, apply the real argument just proved to the families
$(\operatorname{Re}a_i)$ and $(\operatorname{Im}a_i)$. They are absolutely
summable because $|\operatorname{Re}a_i|,|\operatorname{Im}a_i|\le|a_i|$.
Their finite-subset nets converge to real numbers $r$ and $t$, respectively,
so $s_F\to r+it$ in $\mathbb C$. Thus every absolutely summable real or complex
family is summable. **No choice principle is used**: the construction uses only
two-sided suprema in $\mathbb R$.

**Linearity and absolute value.** If $(a_i)$ and $(b_i)$ are absolutely
summable and $\lambda\in\mathbb F$, then so are $(a_i+b_i)$ and
$(\lambda a_i)$, and

$$\sum_{i\in I}(a_i+b_i)=\sum_{i\in I}a_i+\sum_{i\in I}b_i,\qquad \sum_{i\in I}\lambda a_i=\lambda\sum_{i\in I}a_i,\qquad \Bigl|\sum_{i\in I}a_i\Bigr|\le\sum_{i\in I}|a_i| ,$$

because the corresponding identities hold for every finite subsum, both sides
are limits of the corresponding finite-subset nets, and addition, scalar
multiplication and the modulus are continuous. The splitting identity (1)
likewise passes to absolutely summable scalar families:
$\sum_{i\in I}a_i=\sum_{i\in F}a_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}a_i$ for every finite
$F$, because finite subsums over sets containing $F$ converge to the left-hand
side and equal the finite sum over $F$ plus the finite subsum of the tail, whose
net converges to the tail sum.

**The finite-dimensional Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.** Let $(u_k)_{0\le k<m}$ and $(v_k)_{0\le k<m}$ be scalar lists, for $m\in\mathbb N$ and let $t\in\mathbb R$. Every term of
$\sum_{k<m}(|u_k|-t|v_k|)^2$ is nonnegative, so for all real $t$

$$0\le\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2-2t\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|+t^2\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2 .$$

If $\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2>0$, substituting
$t=\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\bigr)/\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)$ gives
$\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\bigr)^2\le\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\bigr)\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)$;
if $\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2=0$ then every $v_k=0$ and both sides are $0$. In either case
$\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\le\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\bigr)^{1/2}\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)^{1/2}$
after taking square roots, and applying the modulus inequality for finite sums
to $u_k\overline{v_k}$ also gives

$$\Bigl|\sum_{k<m}u_k\overline{v_k}\Bigr|\le\Bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\Bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\Bigr)^{1/2} . \qquad (3)$$

**The space $\ell^2(I)$.** For a family $a=(a_i)_{i\in I}$ in $\mathbb F$ define
$Q(a):=\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|^2$. If $Q(a)$ is finite, set $\|a\|_2:=\sqrt{Q(a)}$, using the nonnegative real square root of [[thm-of-square-roots]]; if $Q(a)=+\infty$, set $\|a\|_2:=+\infty$. This is a case definition, not exponentiation of an extended real. Let

$$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F):=\{\,a=(a_i)_{i\in I} : \|a\|_2<+\infty\,\}.$$

The set $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is a vector space over $\mathbb F$: it contains the
zero family, is closed under scalar multiplication because
$\|\lambda a\|_2=|\lambda|\,\|a\|_2$, and is closed under addition because (3)
applied to finite subsums gives $\|a+b\|_2\le\|a\|_2+\|b\|_2<+\infty$. The same
inequality is the triangle inequality for $\|\cdot\|_2$, which is moreover
nonnegative, vanishes only for the zero family (an arbitrary sum of nonnegative
terms with supremum $0$ has every term $0$) and satisfies
$\|\lambda a\|_2=|\lambda|\,\|a\|_2$; thus $\|\cdot\|_2$ is a norm on
$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$. Finally the **pairing**
$\langle a,b\rangle:=\sum_{i\in I}a_i\overline{b_i}$ is well defined on
$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)\times\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$, because
$|a_i\overline{b_i}|=|a_i||b_i|$ has finite nonnegative sum by (3); it is linear
in the first variable, conjugate symmetric, positive definite, and satisfies
$\langle a,a\rangle=\|a\|_2^2$, all by the corresponding finite identities and
the linearity of the sum. Consequently $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is an inner-product
space, and $e_i\in\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ denotes the family that is $1$ at $i$ and
$0$ elsewhere. **Nothing here asserts that $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is complete**;
that follows later, from an orthonormal basis of a Hilbert space.

def-gaussian-sequence-hyperrectangle-cla.source_definition:
Write $\mathbb N_+=\{1,2,\ldots\}$. Let $\ell^2(\mathbb N_+,\mathbb R)$ be the real square-summable sequence space
from [[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]. For $\beta>0$
and $M>0$, the **Gaussian-sequence hyperrectangle** of smoothness index
$\beta$ and radius $M$ is
$$\Theta_\beta(M):= \left\{\theta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N_+,\mathbb R): \sup_{i\ge1}i^{1+2\beta}\theta_i^2\le M\right\}.$$
The definition uses a coordinatewise weighted bound. It is distinct from the
Sobolev ellipsoid $\{\theta:\sum_i i^{2\beta}\theta_i^2\le M\}$.

otherwise. For finite $I$ the finite subsum at $I$ is the largest of all finite
subsums, because all terms are nonnegative, so the definition agrees with the
finite sum; in particular $\sum_{i\in I}c_i=0$ when every $c_i$ is $0$, and
$I=\varnothing$ gives the empty sum $0$.

**Splitting identity and small tails.** Fix a finite $F\subseteq I$. Every
finite $G\subseteq I$ splits as the disjoint union $(G\cap F)\cup(G\setminus F)$,
so $\sum_{i\in G}c_i=\sum_{i\in G\cap F}c_i+\sum_{i\in G\setminus F}c_i\le\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i$;
conversely the finite $G$ with $F\subseteq G$ satisfy
$\sum_{i\in G}c_i=\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in G\setminus F}c_i$. Taking suprema,
with the constant $\sum_{i\in F}c_i$ passing through the supremum,

$$\sum_{i\in I}c_i=\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i . \qquad (1)$$

Consequently, if $S:=\sum_{i\in I}c_i$ is finite, then for every real
$\varepsilon>0$ there is a finite $F\subseteq I$ with
$\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i<\varepsilon$: the finite subsums form a nonempty
bounded-above set with supremum $S$, so by the epsilon characterisation of the
supremum ([[lem-sup-epsilon]]) some finite $F$ has
$S-\varepsilon<\sum_{i\in F}c_i$, and (1) gives
$\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i=S-\sum_{i\in F}c_i<\varepsilon$. Such an $F$ is
called a **tail-control set** for $\varepsilon$.

**Sums of scalar families.** Now let $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family in $\mathbb F$
and put $s_F:=\sum_{i\in F}a_i$ for finite $F\subseteq I$. The set
$\operatorname{Fin}(I)$ with inclusion is a directed preorder: it is nonempty and
$F\cup G$ is a common upper bound of $F$ and $G$
([[def-directed-set-and-net]]). Hence $(s_F)_{F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)}$ is a
net in $\mathbb F$, the **finite-subset net** of the family, and the family is
**summable** when this net converges
([[def-net-convergence-and-cluster-point]]). The scalar metric is the usual real metric or [[def-complex-metric-convergence-and-continuity]]. These metric spaces are Hausdorff by [[thm-metric-hausdorff-separation]]. A net in $\mathbb F$ has at most one limit
([[thm-hausdorff-iff-net-limits-are-unique]]), so for a summable family the
limit is unique and we write $\sum_{i\in I}a_i:=\lim_F s_F$ for it. The family is
**absolutely summable** when $\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|<+\infty$ in the sense above.

**Every absolutely summable family is summable, in ZF.** Assume
$S:=\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|$ is finite and put $S_F:=\sum_{i\in F}|a_i|$ for finite
$F$. For finite $F,G\subseteq I$ the triangle inequality for finite sums and the
fact that a finite subsum is at most the whole nonnegative sum give

$$|s_F-s_G|\le\sum_{i\in F\triangle G}|a_i|\le S-S_{F\cap G} . \qquad (2)$$

Now fix a real $\varepsilon>0$, let $F_0$ be a tail-control set for
$\varepsilon$, and let $F,G\supseteq F_0$ be finite. Then $F\cap G\supseteq F_0$,
so $S-S_{F\cap G}\le S-S_{F_0}<\varepsilon$ and (2) gives
$|s_F-s_G|<\varepsilon$.

First suppose $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$. For each finite $F$ define
$A_F:=\inf\{s_G : G\supseteq F\}$ and $B_F:=\sup\{s_G : G\supseteq F\}$ over
finite $G$. Both are real numbers, because $|s_G|\le S_G\le S$, so the two sets
are nonempty and bounded, and $A_F\le B_F$. If $H\supseteq F$ then
$A_H\ge A_F$ and $B_H\le B_F$. Let $L:=\sup_FA_F$ and $U:=\inf_FB_F$.
Since $A_F\le s_{F\cup H}\le B_H$ for all finite $F,H$, we get $L\le U$.
Moreover, the preceding estimate holds for every pair $F,G\supseteq F_0$;
taking the supremum over $F$ and the infimum over $G$ gives
$B_{F_0}-A_{F_0}\le\varepsilon$. Hence
$0\le U-L\le B_{F_0}-A_{F_0}\le\varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon>0$, so
$L=U=:s$. If $F\supseteq F_0$, then both $s_F$ and $s$ lie in
$[A_{F_0},B_{F_0}]$, and therefore $|s_F-s|\le\varepsilon$.

If $\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, apply the real argument just proved to the families
$(\operatorname{Re}a_i)$ and $(\operatorname{Im}a_i)$. They are absolutely
summable because $|\operatorname{Re}a_i|,|\operatorname{Im}a_i|\le|a_i|$.
Their finite-subset nets converge to real numbers $r$ and $t$, respectively,
so $s_F\to r+it$ in $\mathbb C$. Thus every absolutely summable real or complex
family is summable. **No choice principle is used**: the construction uses only
two-sided suprema in $\mathbb R$.

**Linearity and absolute value.** If $(a_i)$ and $(b_i)$ are absolutely
summable and $\lambda\in\mathbb F$, then so are $(a_i+b_i)$ and
$(\lambda a_i)$, and

$$\sum_{i\in I}(a_i+b_i)=\sum_{i\in I}a_i+\sum_{i\in I}b_i,\qquad \sum_{i\in I}\lambda a_i=\lambda\sum_{i\in I}a_i,\qquad \Bigl|\sum_{i\in I}a_i\Bigr|\le\sum_{i\in I}|a_i| ,$$

because the corresponding identities hold for every finite subsum, both sides
are limits of the corresponding finite-subset nets, and addition, scalar
multiplication and the modulus are continuous. The splitting identity (1)
likewise passes to absolutely summable scalar families:
$\sum_{i\in I}a_i=\sum_{i\in F}a_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}a_i$ for every finite
$F$, because finite subsums over sets containing $F$ converge to the left-hand
side and equal the finite sum over $F$ plus the finite subsum of the tail, whose
net converges to the tail sum.

**The finite-dimensional Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.** Let $(u_k)_{0\le k<m}$ and $(v_k)_{0\le k<m}$ be scalar lists, for $m\in\mathbb N$ and let $t\in\mathbb R$. Every term of
$\sum_{k<m}(|u_k|-t|v_k|)^2$ is nonnegative, so for all real $t$

$$0\le\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2-2t\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|+t^2\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2 .$$

If $\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2>0$, substituting
$t=\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\bigr)/\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)$ gives
$\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\bigr)^2\le\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\bigr)\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)$;
if $\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2=0$ then every $v_k=0$ and both sides are $0$. In either case
$\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\le\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\bigr)^{1/2}\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)^{1/2}$
after taking square roots, and applying the modulus inequality for finite sums
to $u_k\overline{v_k}$ also gives

$$\Bigl|\sum_{k<m}u_k\overline{v_k}\Bigr|\le\Bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\Bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\Bigr)^{1/2} . \qquad (3)$$

**The space $\ell^2(I)$.** For a family $a=(a_i)_{i\in I}$ in $\mathbb F$ define
$Q(a):=\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|^2$. If $Q(a)$ is finite, set $\|a\|_2:=\sqrt{Q(a)}$, using the nonnegative real square root of [[thm-of-square-roots]]; if $Q(a)=+\infty$, set $\|a\|_2:=+\infty$. This is a case definition, not exponentiation of an extended real. Let

$$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F):=\{\,a=(a_i)_{i\in I} : \|a\|_2<+\infty\,\}.$$

The set $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is a vector space over $\mathbb F$: it contains the
zero family, is closed under scalar multiplication because
$\|\lambda a\|_2=|\lambda|\,\|a\|_2$, and is closed under addition because (3)
applied to finite subsums gives $\|a+b\|_2\le\|a\|_2+\|b\|_2<+\infty$. The same
inequality is the triangle inequality for $\|\cdot\|_2$, which is moreover
nonnegative, vanishes only for the zero family (an arbitrary sum of nonnegative
terms with supremum $0$ has every term $0$) and satisfies
$\|\lambda a\|_2=|\lambda|\,\|a\|_2$; thus $\|\cdot\|_2$ is a norm on
$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$. Finally the **pairing**
$\langle a,b\rangle:=\sum_{i\in I}a_i\overline{b_i}$ is well defined on
$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)\times\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$, because
$|a_i\overline{b_i}|=|a_i||b_i|$ has finite nonnegative sum by (3); it is linear
in the first variable, conjugate symmetric, positive definite, and satisfies
$\langle a,a\rangle=\|a\|_2^2$, all by the corresponding finite identities and
the linearity of the sum. Consequently $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is an inner-product
space, and $e_i\in\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ denotes the family that is $1$ at $i$ and
$0$ elsewhere. **Nothing here asserts that $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is complete**;
that follows later, from an orthonormal basis of a Hilbert space.

boundaries.evidence: Definition restricts N to integers >=N_0>=1 and rho>=2, so the block [N,floor(rho N)] always contains N. The zero sequence shows the polished-tail class is nonempty.
For theta=0, both sums in the Definition are zero at every N, so 0<=L_0*0 holds. A zero block forces its corresponding tail to be zero because all terms are nonnegative.
Definition admits L_0=1 and N_0=1. At L_0=1, tail<=block and block<=tail force the mass beyond floor(rho N) to vanish for each tested N; the zero sequence still satisfies all tests.
Definition permits finite-support sequences and does not require positive tail energy. In particular, any sequence supported below N_0 has both tested sums zero at every N>=N_0.
Definition tests N=N_0 as well as all larger integers, includes rho=2 and L_0=1, and includes both block endpoints N and floor(rho N). No rho below 2 or N_0=0 is admitted.
Definition compares sums of a fixed real sequence for each specified integer N. It uses no chosen representatives or optimization selections; the zero sequence is an explicit class member.
Membership in Theta_pt(L_0,N_0,rho) means, by Definition, real ell^2 membership and the tail<=L_0 times block inequality for every integer N>=N_0. It does not impose a coordinatewise lower bound.

If a real square-summable sequence satisfies that inequality at every integer N>=N_0, the Definition includes it in the polished-tail class; no separate hyperrectangle or coordinatewise regularity condition is added.

def-polished-tail-class-for-gaussian-seq.source_definition:
Let $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ be the real square-summable sequence space
from [[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]. Fix
$L_0\ge1$, an integer $N_0\ge1$, and $\rho\ge2$. The **polished-tail class**
$\Theta_{\mathrm{pt}}(L_0,N_0,\rho)$ consists of the sequences
$\theta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ such that for every integer
$N\ge N_0$,
$$ \sum_{i=N}^{\infty}\theta_i^2 \le L_0\sum_{i=N}^{\lfloor\rho N\rfloor}\theta_i^2. $$
Thus each tail's total squared mass is controlled by the mass in the finite
block from $N$ through $\lfloor\rho N\rfloor$. The condition concerns block
energy; it is not a coordinatewise upper or lower bound.

supplier_interfaces.excerpt:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.
supplier_interfaces.use: Explicit assumed AC for normal laws and countable-product choice hypotheses.

supplier_interfaces.excerpt:
For measurable spaces $(E_i,\mathcal E_i)_{i\in I}$, put
$E=\prod_{i\in I}E_i$. For finite $F\subseteq I$, let
$\pi_F:E\to\prod_{i\in F}E_i$ be restriction to $F$ (the singleton empty
product when $F=\varnothing$). On $\prod_{i\in F}E_i$, write $q_i$ for the
$i$th coordinate map and define

$$\bigotimes_{i\in F}\mathcal E_i:=\sigma\{q_i^{-1}(A):i\in F,\ A\in\mathcal E_i\}.$$

For $F=\varnothing$ this is the two-set sigma-algebra on the singleton. If
$e:[n]\to F$ is any enumeration, coordinate relabelling identifies this
sigma-algebra with the recursively defined finite product sigma-algebra of
[[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]: both are
generated by the same coordinate inverse images. Thus the notation is
independent of the enumeration.

A **finite-coordinate cylinder** is $\pi_F^{-1}(A)$ for
$A\in\bigotimes_{i\in F}\mathcal E_i$. The **cylinder sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal C_I:=\sigma\{\pi_F^{-1}(A):F\subseteq I\text{ finite},\ A\in\bigotimes_{i\in F}\mathcal E_i\}.$$

This is the product sigma-algebra on the arbitrary product; the empty-support cylinder is either $\varnothing$ or $E$.
supplier_interfaces.use: Supplies the data product measurable space and its coordinate/cylinder conventions.

supplier_interfaces.excerpt: Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].
