Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ be a standard Borel parameter space
([[def-standard-borel-space]]). Let $\mathsf X$ be a set of possible observations,
and let $\ell:\Theta\times\mathsf X\to\mathbb R$ be a **loss** whose section
$\ell_x(\theta):=\ell(\theta,x)$ is $\mathcal T$-measurable for every
$x\in\mathsf X$. A **prior** is a probability measure $\pi$ on
$(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). A **temperature** is a
fixed scalar $w>0$ that multiplies the observed loss.

For $x\in\mathsf X$, define the normalizer
$$Z_w(\pi,x):=\int_\Theta \exp\{-w\ell_x(\theta)\}\,\pi(d\theta).$$
The integrand is measurable by continuity of the exponential and composition
of measurable maps ([[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]],
[[thm-composition-with-borel-functions-preserves-measurability]]). When
$0<Z_w(\pi,x)<\infty$, the **generalized Bayes loss update** (or **Gibbs loss
update**) is the set function
$$G_{w,\pi,x}(A):=\frac{1}{Z_w(\pi,x)}\int_A\exp\{-w\ell_x(\theta)\}\,\pi(d\theta),\qquad A\in\mathcal T.$$
It is a positive scalar multiple of the measure with density
$\exp\{-w\ell_x\}$ relative to $\pi$
([[def-measure-with-density]]).
If the normalizer is zero or infinite, this definition supplies no update.

Let $G_{w,\pi,x}$ be the update of
[[def-generalized-bayes-loss-update-and-temperature]], with prior probability
$\pi$ and normalizer $0<Z_w(\pi,x)<\infty$. Then $G_{w,\pi,x}$ is a
probability measure on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$.

Let $\mu$ be a sigma-finite positive measure.

1. If $\nu$ is a signed measure satisfying the hypothesis of [[thm-radon-nikodym-density-exists-and-is-unique-up-to-almost-everywhere-equality]] and $\nu\ll\mu$, the **Radon-Nikodym derivative** $d\nu/d\mu$ is the $\mu$-almost-everywhere equivalence class of measurable real-valued functions $f$ satisfying the measurable-set integral formula in that theorem.
2. Assuming the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), if $\nu$ is a finite complex measure and $\nu\ll\mu$, the **Radon-Nikodym derivative** $d\nu/d\mu$ is the $\mu$-almost-everywhere equivalence class of complex $L^1(\mu)$ functions $h$ satisfying
   $$\nu(E)=\int_E h\,d\mu\qquad(E\in\mathcal A),$$
   as given by [[cor-finite-complex-measures-admit-integrable-radon-nikodym-densities]].

In both cases the derivative is not a distinguished pointwise function: it is determined only up to $\mu$-almost-everywhere equality in the sense of [[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]].

Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
([[def-probability-measure]]). Absolute continuity $P\ll Q$ has the convention
of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If
$P\not\ll Q$, define $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and
let $r=dP/dQ$ be a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative of its
Radon–Nikodym class; such a representative exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].
On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This
function is measurable: for $a\ge0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r>\exp(a)\}$, and for
$a<0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r=0\}\cup\{r>\exp(a)\}$, by the inverse and
monotonicity properties of the natural logarithm
([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]). These are
measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since
$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$ by
[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$
The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,
$$0\le \frac{\log s}{s}=\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{u}\le\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{\sqrt u}\le\frac2{\sqrt s}.$$
Thus $t\log t\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$; here $L=\log$ by
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and
[[def-integral-logarithm]]. On $(0,\infty)$, $\psi$ is a product of continuous
functions by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $\psi$ is continuous on
$[0,\infty)$ and $\psi(r)$ is measurable by
[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts
([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]],
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

For $0<t\le1$, the function $-t\log t$ has derivative $-\log t-1$ and
maximum $1/e$ at $t=1/e$: $e=\exp(1)>1$ by
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $1/e=\exp(-1)$ by
[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and $\log(1/e)=-1$ by
[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and the inverse definition. The mean value
theorem gives increase before and decrease after this point
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]],
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).
At $t=0$ the negative part is zero. Since $Q$ is a probability measure,
$$\int \psi(r)^-\,dQ\le\frac1e.$$
The change-of-measure identity of [[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]],
applied to $\ell^-$ gives $\int\ell^-\,dP=\int\psi(r)^-\,dQ\le1/e$,
so $\int\ell\,dP$ is well-defined; applying it to both positive and negative
parts gives
$$D(P\|Q)=\int\ell\,dP=\int\psi(r)\,dQ=\int r\log r\,dQ,$$
with $0\log0:=0$ and a finite negative part. Therefore the extended integral
is well-defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.

This convention is directional: the first argument must be absolutely
continuous with respect to the second for the integral formula to apply.

Let $\mu$ be a positive measure and let $
u$ be a signed measure or a complex measure on the same measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$. We say that $
u$ is **absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu$**, and write
$$
u\ll\mu,$$
if every measurable $\mu$-null set is also $
u$-null:
$$\mu(E)=0\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 
u(E)=0\qquad(E\in\mathcal A).$$
Because every measurable subset of a $\mu$-null set is again $\mu$-null, this is equivalent to requiring $
u(F)=0$ for every measurable $F\subseteq E$ whenever $\mu(E)=0$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\lambda$ and $\mu$ be sigma-finite positive measures and let $\nu$ be a
signed measure or a finite complex measure on the same measurable space.
Assume there is an increasing measurable exhaustion $(X_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$
with $\bigcup_nX_n=X$, $\lambda(X_n)<+\infty$, $\mu(X_n)<+\infty$, and
$|\nu|(X_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$, and assume $\nu\ll\mu\ll\lambda$. Then
$$\frac{d\nu}{d\lambda}=\frac{d\nu}{d\mu}\frac{d\mu}{d\lambda}\qquad\lambda\text{-almost everywhere.}$$

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element, let
$\mathbb P_X$ be its law, and let $g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb R$ or
$g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb C$ be measurable.

1. If $g\ge0$, then
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$
2. If $g(X)$ is integrable, then $g$ is integrable with respect to
   $\mathbb P_X$ and the same formula holds:
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space and let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int f\,d\mu=0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad f=0 \text{ almost everywhere.}$$

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $X$ be a set and let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]). A **measure** on $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function

$$\mu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$$

such that:

1. $\mu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$,
   $$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k),$$
   where the right side is the nonnegative extended sum of [[def-nonnegative-extended-series]].

The second condition is **countable additivity**. It begins at index $0$ and includes the case in which some term or the total sum is $+\infty$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Let $g(\theta)=e^{-w\ell_x(\theta)}/Z$. By [F1]–[F2], $q$ is the probability measure with density $g$ relative to $\pi$. Since $\ell_x$ is real-valued, [F7] gives $g>0$ everywhere.

For $t>0$, put $u(t)=\log t-1+t^{-1}$. By [F10], $u'(t)=(t-1)/t^2$. If $0<t<1$, the mean value theorem on $[t,1]$ gives $u(t)>u(1)=0$; if $t>1$, it on $[1,t]$ gives $u(t)>u(1)=0$. Thus $\log t\ge1-t^{-1}$. Multiplying by $t>0$ gives $t\log t\ge t-1$, with equality only at $t=1$. At $t=0$ the inequality also holds under $0\log0:=0$.

The update is admissible: $q\ll\pi$ by [F1], and [F4], [F9] give $$D(q\|\pi)=\int\log g\,dq=-w\int\ell_x\,dq-\log Z,$$ which is finite by the loss-integrability hypothesis and $0<Z<\infty$. Thus $q\in\mathcal V$.

Fix $
u\in\mathcal V$. If $q(A)=0$, then for every integer $m\ge1$, [F8] and [F1] give $$0\le m^{-1}\pi(A\cap\{g\ge m^{-1}\})\le\int_Ag\,d\pi=q(A)=0.$$ Let $A_1=A\cap\{g\ge1\}$ and, for $m\ge2$, let $A_m=(A\cap\{g\ge m^{-1}\})\setminus(A\cap\{g\ge(m-1)^{-1}\})$. These sets are disjoint, each is $\pi$-null by the displayed bound, and their union is $A$ because $g>0$ everywhere. Countable additivity [F15] therefore gives $\pi(A)=0$. Hence $\pi\ll q$, and $
u\ll q$ follows from $
u\ll\pi$ and [F5].

The measures $
u,q,\pi$ are finite probabilities. The constant exhaustion $X_m=\Theta$ is therefore a common finite exhaustion, so [A1] and [F6] apply to $
u\ll q\ll\pi$. With $r=d
u/d\pi$ and $h=d
u/dq$, the chain rule gives $r=hg$ $\pi$-almost everywhere.

The Radon–Nikodym formula [F3] gives $
u(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,d\pi=0$ and likewise $
u(\{h=0\})=0$, so $r,h>0$ $
u$-almost everywhere. Since $D(
u\|\pi)<\infty$ and the negative part of the log-density integral is finite by [F4], $\log r$ is $
u$-integrable; $\log g$ is $
u$-integrable by $\int|\ell_x|\,d
u<\infty$. Using $r=hg$ from step 3.1, [F9], and $\log g=-w\ell_x-\log Z$, we obtain $$D(
u\|q)=\int\log h\,d
u =D(
u\|\pi)+w\int\ell_x\,d
u+\log Z.$$ The right-hand side is finite, so $D(
u\|q)<\infty$.

For $h=d
u/dq$, the density form of [F4] gives $$D(
u\|q)=\int\log h\,d
u=\int h\log h\,dq,$$ with $0\log0:=0$. The integral is finite by step 4.1.

Apply step 1.2 to $h$ and integrate under $q$. Since $\int h\,dq=
u(\Theta)=1$ and $q(\Theta)=1$, step 5.1 yields $$D(
u\|q)=\int h\log h\,dq\ge\int(h-1)\,dq=0.$$ If equality holds, the nonnegative function $h\log h-h+1$ has integral zero, so [F13] makes it zero $q$-almost everywhere. Step 1.2 then gives $h=1$ $q$-almost everywhere, and the Radon–Nikodym formula [F3] implies $
u=q$. Conversely, if $
u=q$, its Radon–Nikodym density relative to itself is $h=1$ $q$-almost everywhere, so [F4] and [F9] give $D(q\|q)=\int 1\log 1\,dq=0$. Thus equality holds exactly when $
u=q$.

By step 4.1 and [F12], $$J_w(
u)=D(
u\|q)-\log Z\ge-\log Z.$$ Step 2.1 gives $J_w(q)=-\log Z$, and step 6.1 shows equality is possible only for $
u=q$. Therefore $q$ is the unique minimizer and $J_w(
u)-J_w(q)=D(
u\|q)$.

boundaries.reason: Statement: the prior is a probability measure, which is impossible on an empty parameter space.

boundaries.evidence: step 6.1 proves the KL gap is nonnegative and is zero exactly at the update.
Statement: if Theta is a singleton, its only probability is the update; steps 1.1–7.1 remain valid and the minimizer is unique.
Statement: constant real loss sections satisfy the hypotheses; the density in step 1.1 is constant relative to pi and the same KL equality argument gives the unique minimizer.
Statement: Z is required to be finite and strictly positive and q must have finite absolute loss expectation; no zero/infinite-normalizer endpoint is claimed.
Fact A1 and step 3.1 identify the exact AC use in the supplied RN/KL interfaces; the remaining calculations use no additional selection.
step 6.1 proves that D(nu||q)=0 implies h=1 q-a.e. and hence nu=q.
step 6.1 also proves that nu=q gives h=1 q-a.e. and D(q||q)=0 by the KL definition.

risk_review.notes: Read every step 1.1–7.1 and all actual direct supplier statements/definitions. Strictly positive finite Gibbs density makes pi and q equivalent; the level-set null argument covers every positive value without a uniform lower bound. All three laws are finite, so the RN chain rule common exhaustion is Theta. AC is expressly carried through KL/RN representatives. Finite KL has finite negative log part; absolute loss integrability makes log g integrable, so log h=log r-log g entails finite KL(nu||q) without infinity-minus-infinity. The scalar inequality t log t>=t-1 includes t=0 (strict there), and equality of the integral forces h=1 q-a.e.; both equality directions are proved. Gibbs admissibility is checked rather than assumed. Constant losses/singletons return the prior; empty parameter spaces cannot admit a prior; zero/infinite Z and w=0 excluded. Bissiri et al. section 1.1 eqs. (7)–(8) and JMLR section 2.2 Theorem 1 are variational analogues, not replacements for these integrability qualifications. citations.quote:
Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ be a standard Borel parameter space
([[def-standard-borel-space]]). Let $\mathsf X$ be a set of possible observations,
and let $\ell:\Theta\times\mathsf X\to\mathbb R$ be a **loss** whose section
$\ell_x(\theta):=\ell(\theta,x)$ is $\mathcal T$-measurable for every
$x\in\mathsf X$. A **prior** is a probability measure $\pi$ on
$(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). A **temperature** is a
fixed scalar $w>0$ that multiplies the observed loss.

For $x\in\mathsf X$, define the normalizer
$$Z_w(\pi,x):=\int_\Theta \exp\{-w\ell_x(\theta)\}\,\pi(d\theta).$$
The integrand is measurable by continuity of the exponential and composition
of measurable maps ([[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]],
[[thm-composition-with-borel-functions-preserves-measurability]]). When
$0<Z_w(\pi,x)<\infty$, the **generalized Bayes loss update** (or **Gibbs loss
update**) is the set function
$$G_{w,\pi,x}(A):=\frac{1}{Z_w(\pi,x)}\int_A\exp\{-w\ell_x(\theta)\}\,\pi(d\theta),\qquad A\in\mathcal T.$$
It is a positive scalar multiple of the measure with density
$\exp\{-w\ell_x\}$ relative to $\pi$
([[def-measure-with-density]]).
If the normalizer is zero or infinite, this definition supplies no update.

Let $G_{w,\pi,x}$ be the update of
[[def-generalized-bayes-loss-update-and-temperature]], with prior probability
$\pi$ and normalizer $0<Z_w(\pi,x)<\infty$. Then $G_{w,\pi,x}$ is a
probability measure on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int g\,d(f\,d\mu)=\int gf\,d\mu.$$

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. The **measure with density $f$ relative
to $\mu$** is the measure
$$f\,d\mu:\mathcal A\to[0,+\infty],\qquad (f\,d\mu)(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu,$$
whose measure property is supplied by
[[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]].

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. If $0 \in S$ and $\sigma(n) \in S$ whenever $n \in S$, then $S = \mathbb{N}$. Equivalently (property form): if a property $P$ satisfies $P(0)$ and ($P(n) \Rightarrow P(\sigma(n))$) for all $n$, then $P(n)$ holds for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. This is the induction principle, the basis of proof by induction.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space and let
$f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ be measurable for the Borel sigma-algebra on
the extended real line. Products of functions use
$\odot_X$ from [[def-measurable-pointwise-extended-real-product]], and $cf$
abbreviates $\underline c\odot_X f$ for the constant function $\underline c$.
The magnitude function is $|f|=\max(f,-f)$ as in
[[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]]. Then:

1. $cf$ is measurable for every real scalar $c$;
2. $\max(f,g)$, $\min(f,g)$, $|f|$, $f^+$, and $f^-$ are measurable;
3. if the partial pointwise sum $f+g$ is defined at every point, then it is measurable;
4. the pointwise product $fg:=f\odot_X g$ is measurable.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

derivations.claim: For $n=0$, the cumulative loss is the empty sum zero. In the power series definition [F9] at zero, the zeroth term is $1$ and every positive-degree term vanishes, so its exponential weight is $1$. By [F4], $\int 1\,d\pi_0=\pi_0(\Theta)=1$. Thus the empty normalizer is the empty product one and the displayed formula is $\pi_0(A)=\pi_0(A)$.
For $n=1$, the claim is exactly the update definition [F1], with $z_1=\int e^{-w\ell_1}\,d\pi_0$. This normalizer is finite positive by hypothesis, so the update is a probability by [F2].

For $n\ge2$, suppose the formula holds at $n-1$, with cumulative normalizer $c_{n-1}=\prod_{i=1}^{n-1}z_i$ and density $f_{n-1}(\theta)=e^{-w\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\ell_i(\theta)}$ relative to $\pi_0$. The finite cumulative loss is measurable by repeated use of [F7], so [F1] gives measurability of $f_{n-1}$ and of $e^{-w\ell_n}$. Algebra and [F8] factor the cumulative exponential into $f_{n-1}e^{-w\ell_n}$. Then [F3] gives $$z_n=\int e^{-w\ell_n}\,d\pi_{n-1} =c_{n-1}^{-1}\int e^{-w\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ell_i}\,d\pi_0.$$ Thus the cumulative normalizer is $c_n=c_{n-1}z_n=\prod_{i=1}^n z_i$, which is finite and positive.

By [F1], [F3], and the same factorization [F8], for every measurable $A$, $$\pi_n(A)=z_n^{-1}\int_Ae^{-w\ell_n}\,d\pi_{n-1} =c_n^{-1}\int_Ae^{-w\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ell_i}\,d\pi_0.$$ This proves the induction step.

Define $Q(m)$ to be the claimed formula at $n=m+1$. Step 1.2 proves $Q(0)$. For any $m\in\mathbb N$, set $n=m+2\ge2$; steps 1.3–2.1 prove that the formula at $n-1=m+1$ implies it at $n=m+2$, hence $Q(m)$ implies $Q(m+1)$. Therefore [F6] gives the formula for every $n\ge1$; step 1.1 covers $n=0$. The initial $\pi_0$ is a probability by [F4], and every later $\pi_i$ is a probability by [F2]. The proof uses only fixed-temperature updates and the stated normalizers.

boundaries.evidence: Statement explicitly permits n=0. Proof 1.1 evaluates the empty loss sum as zero, exp(0)=1, its integral against pi_0 as one, and the empty product of normalizers as one; the resulting posterior is pi_0.
Statement: w and each sequential normalizer z_i are strictly positive; zero-temperature and zero-normalizer cases are excluded.
steps 1.1–1.2 give the n=0 and n=1 boundary cases explicitly.
steps 1.3–2.1 use only finite sums and exponential factorization; constant or zero losses are included in those identities.
steps 1.1–1.2 handle the finite-sequence endpoint n=0 and the base case n=1; steps 1.3–3.1 extend to all later finite n.
steps 1.1–3.1 use finite induction, integrals and algebra, with no choice of a point from a general family.

finite_checks.name: two-step density factorization
finite_checks.calculation: After step 1 the density is exp(-w ell_1)/z_1. Updating by exp(-w ell_2)/z_2 gives exp(-w(ell_1+ell_2))/(z_1 z_2), matching the cumulative formula and normalizer product.

risk_review.notes: Read steps 1.1–3.1 and all nine actual cited suppliers. For n=0, exp(0)=1, total prior mass and empty product are one. For n=1 the definition gives the base case. Inductively the prior density is f_(n-1)/c_(n-1); the text calls f_(n-1) the density but the displayed formula correctly includes its normalization. Real finite cumulative losses remain measurable; exponential addition and integration against the normalized density give z_n=c_(n-1)^(-1) integral exp(-w sum ell), hence c_n=product z_i in (0,infinity). The identical restricted-set computation proves equality for every measurable A. The shifted induction explicitly handles all n>=1. One common w is essential; no data independence, sampling law, choice, or infinite-data limit is assumed. Reader/refuter report no item defect. No repair needed.

citations.quote:
Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ be a standard Borel parameter space
([[def-standard-borel-space]]). Let $\mathsf X$ be a set of possible observations,
and let $\ell:\Theta\times\mathsf X\to\mathbb R$ be a **loss** whose section
$\ell_x(\theta):=\ell(\theta,x)$ is $\mathcal T$-measurable for every
$x\in\mathsf X$. A **prior** is a probability measure $\pi$ on
$(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). A **temperature** is a
fixed scalar $w>0$ that multiplies the observed loss.

For $x\in\mathsf X$, define the normalizer
$$Z_w(\pi,x):=\int_\Theta \exp\{-w\ell_x(\theta)\}\,\pi(d\theta).$$
The integrand is measurable by continuity of the exponential and composition
of measurable maps ([[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]],
[[thm-composition-with-borel-functions-preserves-measurability]]). When
$0<Z_w(\pi,x)<\infty$, the **generalized Bayes loss update** (or **Gibbs loss
update**) is the set function
$$G_{w,\pi,x}(A):=\frac{1}{Z_w(\pi,x)}\int_A\exp\{-w\ell_x(\theta)\}\,\pi(d\theta),\qquad A\in\mathcal T.$$
It is a positive scalar multiple of the measure with density
$\exp\{-w\ell_x\}$ relative to $\pi$
([[def-measure-with-density]]).
If the normalizer is zero or infinite, this definition supplies no update.

If $S$ is a nonempty at-most-countable set, then $(S,\mathcal P(S))$ is a
standard Borel space.

Recall that a natural number is a von Neumann natural
([[def-natural-numbers]]): $0 = \varnothing$ and $\sigma(n) = n \cup \{n\}$, so
that

$$n = \{\, m \in \mathbb{N} : m < n \,\} = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$$

is itself the set of its predecessors. Here $<$ is the order of
[[def-nat-order]], which is defined additively, so the displayed identity is a
theorem and not a convention: it is [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]], proved
immediately above. Let $A$ be a set, and let $\approx$ be equinumerosity
([[def-equinumerous]]).

- $A$ is **finite** if $A \approx n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
- $A$ is **countably infinite** if $A \approx \mathbb{N}$.
- $A$ is **at most countable** if it is finite or countably infinite.
- $A$ is **uncountable** if it is not at most countable.

The set of **natural numbers** is the **smallest inductive set**
([[def-inductive-set]]),

$$\mathbb{N} = \omega := \bigcap\,\{\, I : I \text{ is inductive} \,\},$$

which exists and is itself inductive by [[lem-omega-smallest-inductive]] (the
Axiom of Infinity, [[def-axiom-of-infinity]], supplies one inductive set to
intersect within, and Separation, [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]], makes the
intersection a set). On $\mathbb{N}$ we take

$$0 := \varnothing, \qquad \sigma(n) := n \cup \{n\},$$

the distinguished element and the successor function. Thus
$0 = \varnothing$, $1 = \{0\}$, $2 = \{0, 1\}$, $3 = \{0, 1, 2\}$, and in general
$n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ is the set of its predecessors.

Let $(\mu_k)$ be measures on one measurable space and let $c_k\in[0,+\infty]$. Each scalar multiple $c_k\mu_k$, defined by the zero, finite-positive, and positive-infinity branches of [[def-nonnegative-weighted-sum-of-measures]], is a measure. Every finite or countable weighted sum $\sum_kc_k\mu_k$ is also a measure.

Let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on a nonempty set $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]) and fix $x_0\in X$. The **Dirac set function at $x_0$** is

$$\delta_{x_0}(E):=\begin{cases}1,&x_0\in E,\\0,&x_0\notin E,\end{cases}\qquad E\in\mathcal A.$$

The two branches are exhaustive and disjoint. The fact that this set function is a probability measure is proved in [[prop-dirac-measure-is-a-probability-measure]].
For $x_0\in X$, the Dirac set function $\delta_{x_0}$ is a probability measure on every sigma-algebra on $X$.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. If $0 \in S$ and $\sigma(n) \in S$ whenever $n \in S$, then $S = \mathbb{N}$. Equivalently (property form): if a property $P$ satisfies $P(0)$ and ($P(n) \Rightarrow P(\sigma(n))$) for all $n$, then $P(n)$ holds for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. This is the induction principle, the basis of proof by induction.

Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$, where $\mathbb{R}$ is the ambient ordered field
([[def-ordered-field]], [[def-field]]).

**Natural exponents.** By the recursion theorem ([[thm-recursion]]) applied to
the set $\mathbb{R}$, the starting element $1$ and the function
$f(x) = x \cdot a$, there is a unique function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$,
written $n \mapsto a^n$, with

$$a^0 = 1, \qquad a^{n+1} = a^n \cdot a \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Thus $a^1 = a$, $a^2 = a \cdot a$, and so on. Note that this is defined for
**every** $a$, including $a = 0$.

**Negative exponents.** If $a \ne 0$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, set

$$a^{-n} := (a^n)^{-1}.$$

**Why that is legitimate.** The right-hand side presupposes that $a^n$ is
invertible, that is, that $a^n \ne 0$. This is a proof obligation and not an
observation, and it is discharged by claim 2 of [[lem-power-laws]]: for $a \ne 0$
in a field, $a^n \ne 0$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, proved there by induction on
$n$ from the fact that a field has no zero divisors ([[lem-of-no-zero-divisors]]).
That lemma is a statement *about* the operation introduced here, so it depends on
this definition and is recorded in this item's `justified_by` rather than in its
`deps` (SCHEMA §3). Given $a^n \ne 0$, the value $(a^n)^{-1}$ is a single
well-determined element, because multiplicative inverses in a field are unique
([[lem-of-inverse-unique]]).

**Integer exponents.** Every integer $m$ ([[def-integers]]) is either
$n$ or $-n$ for a unique natural $n$, where $n$ in these integer expressions denotes its image under the
embedding $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z}$ ([[lem-nat-embeds-int]],
[[def-int-operations]]). This too is a citation and not a slogan: the order on
$\mathbb{Z}$ is total ([[thm-int-ordered-ring]]), so $m \ge 0$ or $m < 0$; the
image of $\iota$ is exactly the set of nonnegative integers, and each of them is
$n$ for a unique natural $n$ ([[lem-nat-embeds-int]]); and if $m < 0$ then
$-m > 0$, by compatibility of the order with addition ([[thm-int-ordered-ring]]),
so $-m = n$ and $m = -n$, with $n$ unique because $\iota$ is
injective. The two clauses above therefore define $a^m$ for every
$m \in \mathbb{Z}$ whenever $a \ne 0$, and for every $m \in \mathbb{N}$ for
arbitrary $a$. The two exponent domains are disjoint: the natural clause
handles $m \ge 0$, including $m = 0$, while the negative clause requires
$n \ge 1$ and therefore handles only $m < 0$.

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges ([[def-series]]) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space. A measurable function
$s:X\to[0,+\infty)\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$
([[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]) is a
**nonnegative simple measurable function** when it has finite range.

Equivalently, there are pairwise disjoint measurable sets
$E_1,\dots,E_m\in\mathcal A$ and coefficients $c_1,\dots,c_m\in[0,+\infty)$
such that
$$s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\chi_{E_j}.$$
Any such display is a **simple representation** of $s$.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable
([[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]). Its
**nonnegative Lebesgue integral** is
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\left\{\int s\,d\mu:\ s \text{ is nonnegative simple and } 0\le s\le f\right\},$$
where the simple integral on the right is the one from
[[def-integral-of-a-nonnegative-simple-function]].

The set of admissible simple minorants is nonempty because it contains the zero
function, which is simple ([[def-nonnegative-simple-measurable-function]]).

Let $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\chi_{E_j}$ be a simple representation of a
nonnegative simple measurable function
([[def-nonnegative-simple-measurable-function]]) on a measure space
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$, so the $E_j\in\mathcal A$ are pairwise disjoint and
$c_j\ge0$. Its
**simple integral** is
$$\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mu(E_j),$$
where $\mu$ is the given measure ([[def-measure]]) and the convention
$0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ is fixed once and for all.

The next lemma proves that this value is independent of the chosen simple
representation.

If $s$ is a nonnegative simple measurable function, then its nonnegative
Lebesgue integral equals its simple integral:
$$\int s\,d\mu=\int_{\mathrm{simple}} s\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

The Cauchy-sequence reals $\mathbb{R}_C$ have the **least-upper-bound property**:
every nonempty $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}_C$ that is bounded above has a least upper
bound $\sup S \in \mathbb{R}_C$. Hence, together with [[thm-reals-ordered-field]],
$\mathbb{R}_C$ is a **complete ordered field** ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]).

Every complete ordered field $F$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) is Archimedean:
for every $x \in F$ there is a natural number $n \ge 1$ with $x < n \cdot 1_F$,
where $n \cdot 1_F$ is the canonical natural of the ordered field $F$
([[def-ordered-field]]). Equivalently, the canonical naturals are cofinal in $F$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]). The **absolute value** of
$x \in F$ is

$$|x| \;:=\; \begin{cases} x & \text{if } x \ge 0, \\ -x & \text{if } x < 0. \end{cases}$$

An **ordered field** is a field $F$ ([[def-field]]) together with a subset
$P \subseteq F$, the set of **positive** elements (the *positive cone*),
satisfying:

- **(O1) Trichotomy.** For each $x \in F$, exactly one of the following holds:
  $x \in P$, or $x = 0$, or $-x \in P$.
- **(O2) Closure.** If $x, y \in P$ then $x + y \in P$ and $x \cdot y \in P$.

We write $x > 0$ for $x \in P$ (read "$x$ is positive"), and define the order by

$$a < b \;:\Longleftrightarrow\; b - a \in P, \qquad a \le b \;:\Longleftrightarrow\; a < b \text{ or } a = b.$$

Thus $a > b$ means $b < a$, and $a \ge b$ means $b \le a$. An element $x$ with
$-x \in P$ (equivalently $x < 0$) is called **negative**.

In any ordered field $F$ with positive cone $P$, the multiplicative identity
satisfies $0 < 1$; that is, $1 \in P$.

Let $a, b, c : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be sequences of reals, let
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, with finite sums and
finite products as in [[def-finite-sum]]. Then:

1. **Additivity.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}(a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k<n} a_k + \sum_{k<n} b_k$.
2. **Scaling.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda a_k = \lambda \sum_{k<n} a_k$; in particular $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda = n\lambda$, where $n$ denotes the canonical field image $n\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ of the natural n ([[lem-of-q-embeds]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]).
3. **Splitting.** If $m \le n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k = \sum_{k<m} a_k + \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k$, and $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n} a_k = \Big(\prod_{k<m} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k\Big)$.
4. **Monotonicity.** If $a_k \le b_k$ for all $k < n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k \le \sum_{k<n} b_k$. In particular, if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\sum_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, every single term satisfies $a_j \le \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for $j < n$, and $\sum_{k<n} a_k = 0$ forces $a_k = 0$ for every $k < n$.
5. **Telescoping.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}\big(c_{k+1} - c_k\big) = c_n - c_0$.
6. **Products.** $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n}(a_k b_k) = \Big(\prod_{k<n} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k<n} b_k\Big)$; if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, and if $a_k > 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k > 0$.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field ([[def-real-numbers]]) and
a **sequence of reals** is a function $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$
([[def-sequence]]), written $(a_k)$; recall that $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$.

**Partial sums.** Let $(a_k)$ be a sequence of reals. Its **sequence of partial
sums** is

$$s_n \;:=\; \sum_{k < n} a_k \qquad (n \in \mathbb{N}),$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. In particular $s_0 = 0$, the empty sum, and
$s_{n+1} = s_n + a_n$ for every $n$, those being exactly the two recursion clauses
that define the finite sum. Note that $s_n$ is the sum of the $n$ terms
$a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$, so the index $n$ counts terms rather than naming the last
one.

**Convergence, the sum, divergence.** The **series** of $(a_k)$, written
$\sum a_k$, **converges** when the sequence $(s_n)$ of partial sums converges
([[def-real-limit]]), and then the **sum of the series** is

$$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} a_k \;:=\; \lim_{n} s_n .$$

The series **diverges** when $(s_n)$ does not converge. A convergent sequence of
reals has exactly one limit ([[lem-limit-unique]]), so the displayed symbol names
a single real number and nothing further has to be checked for it to be
well defined.

**Series with a general starting index.** Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $a$ be a
function on $\{\, k \in \mathbb{N} : k \ge m \,\}$, which we call a **family from
$m$** and write $(a_k)_{k \ge m}$. The series

$$\sum_{k \ge m} a_k$$

is by definition the series of the sequence $b_j := a_{j + m}$,
$j \in \mathbb{N}$, which is a genuine sequence of reals; it converges exactly
when that series converges, and its sum is then written
$\sum_{k = m}^{\infty} a_k$. Its partial sums are

$$\sum_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k \;=\; \sum_{j < n-m} a_{m+j} \qquad (n \ge m),$$

in the notation of [[def-finite-sum]], the value at $n = m$ being the empty sum
$0$. A sequence on $\mathbb{N}$ is the case $m = 0$, and the two readings of
$\sum a_k$ agree there, since $b_j = a_j$.

**This clause is not a convenience.** Sequences in this library are functions on
$\mathbb{N}$ and $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$ ([[def-sequence]]), while many of the
classical series are built from expressions that are undefined at the index $0$:
$1/k$, $1/k^{p}$ and $|a_k|^{1/k}$ all require $k \ge 1$. Writing such a series as
$\sum_{k \ge 1} a_k$ names an honest object, whereas writing it as a sequence on
$\mathbb{N}$ would require a value at an index where the defining expression has
none. Every statement on this page says which starting index it uses.

**Tail series.** For $N \in \mathbb{N}$, the **$N$-th tail series** of
$\sum a_k$ is $\sum_{k \ge N} a_k$, that is the series of the $N$-th tail
$a^{(N)}$ of [[def-sequence]], whose terms are $a^{(N)}_j = a_{j+N}$. The
$0$-th tail series is the series itself.

Let $(x_k)$ and $(y_k)$ be sequences of reals ([[def-sequence]]) converging to
$x$ and $y$ respectively ([[def-real-limit]]), and let $c \in \mathbb{R}$. Then

$$x_k + y_k \to x + y, \qquad c\,x_k \to c\,x, \qquad x_k - y_k \to x - y, \qquad x_k y_k \to x y,$$

and if in addition $y \ne 0$ and $y_k \ne 0$ for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$, then

$$\frac{1}{y_k} \to \frac{1}{y} \qquad \text{and} \qquad \frac{x_k}{y_k} \to \frac{x}{y}.$$

The quotient case rests on an eventual lower bound for $|y_k|$, proved below
rather than assumed: $|y_k| > |y|/2$ for all sufficiently large $k$.

Let $(a_k)$ be a sequence of reals with $a_k \ge 0$ for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$,
let $s_n = \sum_{k<n} a_k$ be its partial sums and let
$S = \{\, s_n : n \in \mathbb{N} \,\}$ be the range of $(s_n)$ ([[def-series]]).
Then:

1. $(s_n)$ is nondecreasing ([[def-monotone-sequence]]) and $s_n \ge 0$ for every
   $n$;
2. $\sum a_k$ converges **if and only if** $S$ is bounded above
   ([[def-bounded-set]]), and in that case
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} a_k \;=\; \sup S ,$$
   so in particular $s_n \le \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} a_k$ for every $n$;
3. if $S$ is not bounded above then $s_n \to +\infty$
   ([[def-divergence-to-infinity]]) and $\sum a_k$ diverges.

This is the theorem that makes the nonnegative theory work: for terms of one
sign, convergence is a boundedness question and no candidate limit is ever
needed. Every comparison test on this page is an application of it.

Let $a=(a_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ take values in $[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$ ([[def-extended-reals]]). Its **partial sums** are the unique sequence $(s_n)$ in $[0,+\infty]$ satisfying

$$s_0=0,\qquad s_{n+1}=s_n+a_n.$$

To apply [[thm-recursion]] with a fixed successor function, use the state space $\mathbb N\times[0,+\infty]$ and the self-map $T(n,s)=(n+1,s+a_n)$, starting from $(0,0)$. Recursion gives a unique state sequence; induction makes its first coordinate $n$, and its second coordinates are exactly the unique $(s_n)$ satisfying the displayed recurrence. Addition of two nonnegative extended reals is always defined, including when either is $+\infty$. The sequence $(s_n)$ is nondecreasing, and its **nonnegative extended sum** is

$$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}a_k:=\sup_{n\in\mathbb N}s_n\in[0,+\infty],$$

whose existence follows from completeness of the extended real line ([[lem-extended-reals-complete]]). More generally, for $m\in\mathbb N$,

$$\sum_{k\ge m}a_k:=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}a_{m+j}.$$

Finite sums use the same recursion: $\sum_{k<n}a_k=s_n$, so the empty sum at $n=0$ is $0$. A double sum such as $\sum_i\sum_j a_{ij}$ means that the inner nonnegative extended sum is formed first and the resulting nonnegative extended sequence is then summed.

Let $\mu$ be a measure and let $c\in[0,+\infty]$. Define the scalar set function $c\mu$ by three disjoint branches:

$$ (c\mu)(E):=\begin{cases}0,&c=0,\\c\,\mu(E),&0<c<+\infty,\\0,&c=+\infty\text{ and }\mu(E)=0,\\+\infty,&c=+\infty\text{ and }\mu(E)>0.\end{cases}$$

Thus neither the zero branch nor the infinite branch forms the undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

For measures $(\mu_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ on the same measurable space and weights $c_k\in[0,+\infty]$, their **countable weighted sum** is the pointwise set function

$$\left(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}c_k\mu_k\right)(E):=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(c_k\mu_k)(E),$$

using [[def-nonnegative-extended-series]]. Finite weighted sums are defined by the corresponding finite partial sum, with the empty weighted sum the zero set function. The fact that all these set functions are measures is [[thm-nonnegative-weighted-sums-of-measures]].

derivations.claim: The identity map shows $\mathbb N$ is equinumerous with itself, hence at-most-countable by [F3]; [F4] makes it nonempty. Therefore [F2] shows $(\Theta,\mathcal P(\Theta))$ is standard Borel.

Put $b=1/2$. Ordered-field arithmetic gives $0<b<1$, so [F21] gives $|b|=b<1$. The powers are positive: $b^0=1>0$ by [F10] and [F23], and if $b^k>0$, then $b^{k+1}=b^kb>0$ by [F10] and [F22]. Induction [F9] gives $a_k=b^{k+1}>0$ for every $k$.

By [F11], $\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}b^k=1/(1-b)$. For every $N$, recursion [F10] and finite-sum scaling [F24] give $$\sum_{k<N+1}a_k=\sum_{k<N+1}b^{k+1} =b\sum_{k<N+1}b^k.$$ The partial sums of $\sum b^k$ converge to $1/(1-b)$ by [F11] and [F25]; therefore [F26] gives $\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}a_k=b/(1-b)=1$. By [F27] and [F28], this usual series sum is also the nonnegative extended sum of the coefficients used in the weighted measure.

Since $a_k>0$, $\ell(k)=\log a_k$ is finite. Every inverse image of a Borel subset of $\mathbb R$ is a subset of $\mathbb N$, hence is in $\mathcal P(\mathbb N)$; therefore $\ell$ is measurable. By [F12]–[F13], $e^{-\ell(k)}=1/a_k$, so the normalizer is $Z=\int e^{-\ell}\,d\pi$.

By [F5] and [F7], $\pi=\sum_{k\ge0}a_k\delta_k$ is a measure. Its total mass is $$\pi(\Theta)=\sum_{k\ge0}a_k\delta_k(\Theta)=\sum_{k\ge0}a_k=1$$ by [F6], [F28], [F29], and step 2.1, so [F8] makes $\pi$ a probability. For each $k$, [F6] gives $\pi(\{k\})=a_k$.

For each $N\in\mathbb N$, set $$s_N:=\sum_{k=0}^{N}a_k^{-1}\mathbf1_{\{k\}}.$$ It is a nonnegative simple function by [F14], and $0\le s_N\le e^{-\ell}$: there is equality at $k\le N$, and for $k>N$ the left side is zero while $e^{-\ell(k)}>0$ by [F13]. By [F16]–[F17] and step 3.1, $$\int s_N\,d\pi=\sum_{k=0}^{N}a_k^{-1}\pi(\{k\})=N+1.$$ Thus [F18] yields $Z\ge N+1$ for every $N$.

If $Z$ were finite, [F19]–[F20] would give $N\in\mathbb N$, $N\ge1$, with $Z<N$. Step 4.1 gives $Z\ge N+1$, a contradiction. Since [F15] places $Z$ in $[0,+\infty]$, it follows that $Z=+\infty$. The finite-positive condition in [F1] therefore fails, so no generalized Bayes update is defined.

citations.quote:
If $S$ is a nonempty at-most-countable set, then $(S,\mathcal P(S))$ is a
standard Borel space.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on a nonempty set $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]) and fix $x_0\in X$. The **Dirac set function at $x_0$** is

$$\delta_{x_0}(E):=\begin{cases}1,&x_0\in E,\\0,&x_0\notin E,\end{cases}\qquad E\in\mathcal A.$$

The two branches are exhaustive and disjoint. The fact that this set function is a probability measure is proved in [[prop-dirac-measure-is-a-probability-measure]].
For $x_0\in X$, the Dirac set function $\delta_{x_0}$ is a probability measure on every sigma-algebra on $X$.

An **experiment** is a measurable space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, a set $\Theta$ of
parameter labels, and a family $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ of probability
measures on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ ([[def-measurable-space]],
[[def-probability-measure]]). The measures $P_\theta$ are the sampling laws.
If data under a parameter value are realized as a random element, its law is
the pushforward measure $P_X(B)=P(X^{-1}(B))$ from
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]; it is a probability measure by
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]].

The definition specifies the family of laws only. It supplies no sigma-algebra
on $\Theta$, no measurability condition on $\theta\mapsto P_\theta$, and no
common underlying probability space on which all observations must be realized.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ be a standard Borel parameter space
([[def-standard-borel-space]]). Let $\mathsf X$ be a set of possible observations,
and let $\ell:\Theta\times\mathsf X\to\mathbb R$ be a **loss** whose section
$\ell_x(\theta):=\ell(\theta,x)$ is $\mathcal T$-measurable for every
$x\in\mathsf X$. A **prior** is a probability measure $\pi$ on
$(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). A **temperature** is a
fixed scalar $w>0$ that multiplies the observed loss.

For $x\in\mathsf X$, define the normalizer
$$Z_w(\pi,x):=\int_\Theta \exp\{-w\ell_x(\theta)\}\,\pi(d\theta).$$
The integrand is measurable by continuity of the exponential and composition
of measurable maps ([[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]],
[[thm-composition-with-borel-functions-preserves-measurability]]). When
$0<Z_w(\pi,x)<\infty$, the **generalized Bayes loss update** (or **Gibbs loss
update**) is the set function
$$G_{w,\pi,x}(A):=\frac{1}{Z_w(\pi,x)}\int_A\exp\{-w\ell_x(\theta)\}\,\pi(d\theta),\qquad A\in\mathcal T.$$
It is a positive scalar multiple of the measure with density
$\exp\{-w\ell_x\}$ relative to $\pi$
([[def-measure-with-density]]).
If the normalizer is zero or infinite, this definition supplies no update.

Let $G_{w,\pi,x}$ be the update of
[[def-generalized-bayes-loss-update-and-temperature]], with prior probability
$\pi$ and normalizer $0<Z_w(\pi,x)<\infty$. Then $G_{w,\pi,x}$ is a
probability measure on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a
statistical experiment as in [[def-statistical-experiment]], and assume
$\Theta\ne\varnothing$. A **confidence-set procedure** is a map
$C:\mathcal X\to\mathcal P(\Theta)$, where
$\mathcal P(\Theta):=\{A:A\subseteq\Theta\}$, such that, for every
$\eta\in\Theta$, its
membership section
$$C_\eta:=\{x\in\mathcal X:\eta\in C(x)\}$$
belongs to $\mathcal A$. Its **coverage at $\theta$** is
$c_C(\theta):=P_\theta(C_\theta)$, and its **confidence level** is
$\inf_{\theta\in\Theta}c_C(\theta)$, the greatest lower bound of those
coverage values. For $0\le\alpha\le1$, it has coverage
at least $1-\alpha$ if $P_\theta(C_\theta)\ge1-\alpha$ for every
$\theta\in\Theta$.

Only membership sections need to be measurable; no sigma-algebra on the
parameter set is assumed. The parameter is fixed in the repeated-sampling
coverage probability.

derivations.claim: The parameter and data spaces are nonempty finite sets, so [F1] makes them standard Borel. The prior masses sum to one, hence [F2] makes $\pi$ a probability. [F3]–[F5] show the sampling laws define a statistical experiment. [F6]–[F8] give the normalizer $$Z=\frac1{100}e^{-1}+\frac{99}{100}e^0,$$ which is finite and positive. By [F7], the resulting update $q$ is a probability measure.

Since $-1<0$, [F9] gives $e^{-1}<e^0$. Both are positive by [F8], and $$Z=\frac1{100}e^{-1}+\frac{99}{100}e^0<e^0.$$ Therefore $$q(\{1\})=\frac{(99/100)e^0}{Z}>\frac{99}{100}>0.95.$$ Thus $C(x_0)=\{1\}$ is a posterior credible set of mass greater than $0.95$.

Regard $C$ as the data-to-set procedure with sole value $C(x_0)=\{1\}$. Its membership section for parameter $0$ is empty, and for parameter $1$ is $\{x_0\}$; both are measurable. The coverage definition [F10] therefore applies, and at true parameter $0$ it gives $$P_0\{x:C(x)\ni0\}=P_0(\varnothing)=0.$$ This is below $0.95$, refuting the proposed universal guarantee.

derivations.claim: The set $\Theta$ is nonempty and finite, so [F1] makes its power-set measurable space standard Borel. Since $0<p<1$, the masses $p$ and $1-p$ are positive and sum to one, so [F2] makes $\pi$ a probability. For every $t>0$, the two real loss values give positive finite weights $e^{-ta}$ and $e^{-tb}$ by [F6]; their prior-weighted sum is therefore finite and positive.

By [F3]–[F4], the update $q_t=G_{t,\pi,x_0}$ has masses $$q_t(0)=\frac{p e^{-ta}}{p e^{-ta}+(1-p)e^{-tb}},\qquad q_t(1)=\frac{(1-p)e^{-tb}}{p e^{-ta}+(1-p)e^{-tb}}.$$ Consequently its odds satisfy $$\frac{q_t(1)}{q_t(0)}=\frac{1-p}{p}e^{-t(b-a)}.$$.

For $\theta\in\Theta$, the unnormalized weight after replacing $\ell_{x_0}$ by $c\ell_{x_0}$ at temperature $w$ is $\pi(\theta)e^{-w c\ell_{x_0}(\theta)}= \pi(\theta)e^{-(cw)\ell_{x_0}(\theta)}$. These are exactly the unnormalized masses for $q_{cw}$. The two updates have the same finite positive normalizer by step 1.1, so their values on both singletons, and hence on every subset of $\Theta$, agree.

Because $b-a
e0$ and $t_1
e t_2$, the real numbers $-t_1(b-a)$ and $-t_2(b-a)$ differ. Injectivity in [F5] makes their exponentials different. Multiplication by the fixed positive factor $(1-p)/p$ preserves that difference, so step 2.1 gives distinct odds. On a two-point probability space the odds determine both singleton masses; therefore $q_{t_1}
e q_{t_2}$.

citations.quote:
If $S$ is a nonempty at-most-countable set, then $(S,\mathcal P(S))$ is a
standard Borel space.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

An **experiment** is a measurable space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, a set $\Theta$ of
parameter labels, and a family $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ of probability
measures on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ ([[def-measurable-space]],
[[def-probability-measure]]). The measures $P_\theta$ are the sampling laws.
If data under a parameter value are realized as a random element, its law is
the pushforward measure $P_X(B)=P(X^{-1}(B))$ from
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]; it is a probability measure by
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]].

The definition specifies the family of laws only. It supplies no sigma-algebra
on $\Theta$, no measurability condition on $\theta\mapsto P_\theta$, and no
common underlying probability space on which all observations must be realized.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ be a standard Borel parameter space
([[def-standard-borel-space]]). Let $\mathsf X$ be a set of possible observations,
and let $\ell:\Theta\times\mathsf X\to\mathbb R$ be a **loss** whose section
$\ell_x(\theta):=\ell(\theta,x)$ is $\mathcal T$-measurable for every
$x\in\mathsf X$. A **prior** is a probability measure $\pi$ on
$(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). A **temperature** is a
fixed scalar $w>0$ that multiplies the observed loss.

For $x\in\mathsf X$, define the normalizer
$$Z_w(\pi,x):=\int_\Theta \exp\{-w\ell_x(\theta)\}\,\pi(d\theta).$$
The integrand is measurable by continuity of the exponential and composition
of measurable maps ([[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]],
[[thm-composition-with-borel-functions-preserves-measurability]]). When
$0<Z_w(\pi,x)<\infty$, the **generalized Bayes loss update** (or **Gibbs loss
update**) is the set function
$$G_{w,\pi,x}(A):=\frac{1}{Z_w(\pi,x)}\int_A\exp\{-w\ell_x(\theta)\}\,\pi(d\theta),\qquad A\in\mathcal T.$$
It is a positive scalar multiple of the measure with density
$\exp\{-w\ell_x\}$ relative to $\pi$
([[def-measure-with-density]]).
If the normalizer is zero or infinite, this definition supplies no update.

Let $G_{w,\pi,x}$ be the update of
[[def-generalized-bayes-loss-update-and-temperature]], with prior probability
$\pi$ and normalizer $0<Z_w(\pi,x)<\infty$. Then $G_{w,\pi,x}$ is a
probability measure on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

Let $A$ and $B$ be events in a finite probability space with $\mathbb P(B)>0$. The **conditional probability of $A$ given $B$** is
$$\mathbb P(A\mid B):=\frac{\mathbb P(A\cap B)}{\mathbb P(B)}.$$
No value is assigned to $\mathbb P(A\mid B)$ when $\mathbb P(B)=0$.

derivations.claim: Both parameter and sample spaces are nonempty finite sets, so [F1] makes them standard Borel. The prior masses are nonnegative and sum to one; each pair of sampling probabilities is nonnegative and sums to one. By [F2] these are probability measures, and [F3] therefore gives the stated finite statistical experiment.

All four likelihoods are positive, so [F6] makes $\ell$ real-valued on $\Theta\times\mathsf X$. Each parameter section is measurable because the parameter sigma-algebra is the power set, satisfying the loss hypotheses of [F4] for every $y\in\mathsf X$. At $y=1$, the inverse relation in [F6] gives $e^{-\ell(\theta,1)}=e^{\log P_\theta(Y=1)}=P_\theta(Y=1)$. Hence the unnormalized weights are $$\pi(0)P_0(Y=1)=\frac1{12},\qquad \pi(1)P_1(Y=1)=\frac12,$$ and their normalizer is $Z=1/12+1/2=7/12$, finite and positive.
By [F4]–[F5], the update is a probability measure with $$q(0)=\frac{1/12}{7/12}=\frac17,\qquad q(1)=\frac{1/2}{7/12}=\frac67.$$.

Define the joint masses by $\Pr(\theta,y)=\pi(\theta)P_\theta(Y=y)$. The four masses are $1/4,1/12,1/6,1/2$ at $(0,0),(0,1),(1,0),(1,1)$, respectively; they sum to one, and $\Pr(Y=1)=7/12>0$. Applying [F7] to each parameter singleton gives $$\Pr(\theta=0\mid Y=1)=\frac{1/12}{7/12}=\frac17,\qquad \Pr(\theta=1\mid Y=1)=\frac{1/2}{7/12}=\frac67.$$ Thus the loss update equals the ordinary finite-model posterior at $y=1$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
([[def-probability-measure]]). Absolute continuity $P\ll Q$ has the convention
of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If
$P\not\ll Q$, define $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and
let $r=dP/dQ$ be a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative of its
Radon–Nikodym class; such a representative exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].
On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This
function is measurable: for $a\ge0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r>\exp(a)\}$, and for
$a<0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r=0\}\cup\{r>\exp(a)\}$, by the inverse and
monotonicity properties of the natural logarithm
([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]). These are
measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since
$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$ by
[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$
The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,
$$0\le \frac{\log s}{s}=\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{u}\le\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{\sqrt u}\le\frac2{\sqrt s}.$$
Thus $t\log t\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$; here $L=\log$ by
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and
[[def-integral-logarithm]]. On $(0,\infty)$, $\psi$ is a product of continuous
functions by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $\psi$ is continuous on
$[0,\infty)$ and $\psi(r)$ is measurable by
[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts
([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]],
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

For $0<t\le1$, the function $-t\log t$ has derivative $-\log t-1$ and
maximum $1/e$ at $t=1/e$: $e=\exp(1)>1$ by
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $1/e=\exp(-1)$ by
[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and $\log(1/e)=-1$ by
[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and the inverse definition. The mean value
theorem gives increase before and decrease after this point
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]],
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).
At $t=0$ the negative part is zero. Since $Q$ is a probability measure,
$$\int \psi(r)^-\,dQ\le\frac1e.$$
The change-of-measure identity of [[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]],
applied to $\ell^-$ gives $\int\ell^-\,dP=\int\psi(r)^-\,dQ\le1/e$,
so $\int\ell\,dP$ is well-defined; applying it to both positive and negative
parts gives
$$D(P\|Q)=\int\ell\,dP=\int\psi(r)\,dQ=\int r\log r\,dQ,$$
with $0\log0:=0$ and a finite negative part. Therefore the extended integral
is well-defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.

This convention is directional: the first argument must be absolutely
continuous with respect to the second for the integral formula to apply.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mu$ be a positive measure and let $
u$ be a signed measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. Assume there is an increasing measurable exhaustion $(X_n)$ with $ igcup_nX_n=X$, $\mu(X_n)<+\infty$, and $|
u|(X_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$. If $
u\ll\mu$, then there exists a measurable real-valued function $f$, unique up to $\mu$-almost-everywhere equality, such that
$$
u(E)=\int_Ef\,d\mu\qquad(E\in\mathcal A).$$
If in addition $|
u|(X)<+\infty$, then $f\in L^1(\mu)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $f\in L^1(\mathbb P)$
be real-valued, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval containing $f(x)$ for
almost every $x$, and let $\varphi:I\to\mathbb R$ be convex with
$\varphi\circ f\in L^1(\mathbb P)$. Then
$$\varphi\!\left(\int f\,d\mathbb P\right)\le\int\varphi(f)\,d\mathbb P.$$

For $x>0$, define the **integral logarithm**

$$L(x):=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t},$$

using the oriented integral when $x<1$
([[def-oriented-integral]]).

This is well defined. The function $t\mapsto1/t$ is continuous wherever
$t\neq0$ by the quotient clause of
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]]. For $x\neq1$ it is therefore continuous on the nondegenerate compact interval
with endpoints $1$ and $x$, hence Riemann integrable there by
[[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]], whose hypothesis is $a<b$. At $x=1$ the
interval is degenerate and that theorem does not apply; there
[[def-oriented-integral]] stipulates $\int_1^1f=0$, so $L(1)=0$ directly.

For every $x>0$,

$$L(x)=\log x.$$

For every $x>0$,

$$L'(x)=\frac1x,$$

and $L(1)=0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].
If $f:I\to\mathbb R$ is twice differentiable on an open interval, then $f$ is convex if and only if $f''(x)\ge0$ for every $x\in I$.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. **Nonnegativity.** If $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $\int_a^b f \ge 0$.
2. **Monotonicity.** If $f(x) \le g(x)$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $$\int_a^b f \;\le\; \int_a^b g .$$
3. **Two-sided bound.** If $m \le f(x) \le M$ for every $x \in [a,b]$, with
   $m, M$ real, then
   $$m\,(b-a) \;\le\; \int_a^b f \;\le\; M\,(b-a) .$$

**Equality in claim 1 does not force $f$ to vanish.** A nonnegative integrable
function with integral $0$ may be positive at infinitely many points; that is
[[fs-nonnegative-integrable-with-zero-integral-vanishes]] on the previous page's
companion. Under the additional hypothesis of continuity the conclusion does
hold, and that is [[thm-nonnegative-continuous-with-zero-integral-vanishes]]
below.

**Claim 2 is stated for $a < b$ and is not orientation-invariant.** With the
convention of [[def-oriented-integral]], $f \le g$ gives
$\int_u^v f \le \int_u^v g$ when $u \le v$ and the reverse inequality when
$u \ge v$, since both sides change sign together.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $a < c < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be bounded
([[def-bounded-set]]). Then:

1. $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]) **if and only if** its
   restrictions to $[a,c]$ and to $[c,b]$ are integrable;
2. and in that case
   $$\int_a^b f \;=\; \int_a^c f \;+\; \int_c^b f .$$
3. **Oriented form.** Let $\alpha < \beta$ be reals, let $f : [\alpha,\beta] \to
   \mathbb{R}$ be integrable, and let $u, v, w \in [\alpha,\beta]$ be arbitrary.
   Then, with the convention of [[def-oriented-integral]],
   $$\int_u^v f \;+\; \int_v^w f \;=\; \int_u^w f .$$

Claim 3 is where [[def-oriented-integral]] earns its place: it holds for every
arrangement of the three points, including the degenerate ones, and it is the
form used everywhere below.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space and let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int f\,d\mu=0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad f=0 \text{ almost everywhere.}$$

A **measure space** is a triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ in which $X$ is a set, $\mathcal A$ is a sigma-algebra on $X$, and $\mu$ is a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$ ([[def-measure]]). The members of $\mathcal A$ are the **measurable sets** of the space.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space ([[def-measure-space]]).

- The measure $\mu$ is **finite** if $\mu(X)<+\infty$.
- It is **sigma-finite** if there is a sequence $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$ such that $X=\bigcup_nE_n$ and $\mu(E_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$.
- It is **semifinite** if, whenever $E\in\mathcal A$ and $\mu(E)>0$, there is $F\in\mathcal A$ with $F\subseteq E$ and $0<\mu(F)<+\infty$.

The last condition is automatic when $0<\mu(E)<+\infty$, by taking $F=E$; its substantive case is $\mu(E)=+\infty$.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. The **measure with density $f$ relative
to $\mu$** is the measure
$$f\,d\mu:\mathcal A\to[0,+\infty],\qquad (f\,d\mu)(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu,$$
whose measure property is supplied by
[[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]].

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int g\,d(f\,d\mu)=\int gf\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

The **extended real line** is

$$\overline{\mathbb{R}} := \mathbb{R} \cup \{-\infty,+\infty\}$$

with the total order extending the usual order on $\mathbb{R}$ and satisfying
$-\infty < x < +\infty$ for every real $x$
([[def-extended-reals]]).

Its **Borel sigma-algebra** is the Borel sigma-algebra of that ordered
topological line in the sense of [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]. On this page it is
denoted $\mathcal{B}(\overline{\mathbb{R}})$ and is generated by the rays

$$\{\, (a,+\infty] : a \in \mathbb{R} \,\}.$$

In particular, $\{+\infty\}$ and $\{-\infty\}$ are Borel sets.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$, $(Y,\mathcal{B})$, and $(Z,\mathcal{C})$ be measurable
spaces. If $f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Y,\mathcal{B})$ is measurable and
$g : (Y,\mathcal{B}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable, then
$g \circ f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable.

In particular, if $f$ is measurable and $g$ is a Borel measurable function on
its codomain, then $g \circ f$ is measurable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space and let
$f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ be measurable for the Borel sigma-algebra on
the extended real line. Products of functions use
$\odot_X$ from [[def-measurable-pointwise-extended-real-product]], and $cf$
abbreviates $\underline c\odot_X f$ for the constant function $\underline c$.
The magnitude function is $|f|=\max(f,-f)$ as in
[[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]]. Then:

1. $cf$ is measurable for every real scalar $c$;
2. $\max(f,g)$, $\min(f,g)$, $|f|$, $f^+$, and $f^-$ are measurable;
3. if the partial pointwise sum $f+g$ is defined at every point, then it is measurable;
4. the pointwise product $fg:=f\odot_X g$ is measurable.

Let $f : X \to \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ with $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ as in
[[def-extended-reals]]. Its **positive part** and **negative part** are

$$f^+ := \max\{f,0\},\qquad f^- := \max\{-f,0\}.$$

All maxima, negations, and sums here are pointwise, using the total order,
reflection and partial addition of [[def-extended-reals]]. Both parts take
values in $[0,+\infty]$. For an extended-real-valued function, define the
**magnitude function** by $|f|(x):=\max\{f(x),-f(x)\}$. This is function notation;
it does not introduce an absolute-value operation into the scalar arithmetic of
that item. Likewise the notation $f^+-f^-$ below abbreviates the pointwise sum
$f^++(-f^-)$, whose definedness is verified here.

At each point at least one of $f^+$ and $f^-$ is zero. If $f(x)\ge0$, then
$f^+(x)=f(x)$ and $f^-(x)=0$; if $f(x)\le0$, then $f^+(x)=0$ and
$f^-(x)=-f(x)$. These cases include both infinite values and show that the
following sums are defined and satisfy

$$f=f^++(-f^-),\qquad |f|=f^++f^-.$$

Thus the familiar notation $f=f^+-f^-$ retains exactly these pointwise values;
no subtraction of two infinite nonzero values occurs.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) and let $x, y \in F$, with
$|x|$ the absolute value ([[def-abs-value]]). Then

$$|x| \ge 0; \quad |x| = 0 \iff x = 0; \quad -|x| \le x \le |x|; \quad |-x| = |x|; \quad |xy| = |x|\,|y|;$$

and, for every $c > 0$, one has $|x| < c \iff -c < x < c$.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$m \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; M \qquad \text{for every } x \in [a,b],$$

with $m, M$ real. Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]), so its Darboux sums
and integrals are defined ([[def-darboux-sums]], [[def-darboux-integral]]), and
for **every** partition $P$ of $[a,b]$ ([[def-partition-and-refinement]])

$$m(b-a) \;\le\; L(f,P) \;\le\; \underline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; \overline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; U(f,P) \;\le\; M(b-a) .$$

In particular, taking $f$ to be the constant function with value $c$:

$$\int_a^b c \;=\; c\,(b-a) ,$$

the constant function being integrable, with $L(f,P) = U(f,P) = c(b-a)$ for
every partition $P$.

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

derivations.claim: If $P\not\ll Q$, [F1] gives $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$ but $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$, nonnegativity is immediate. It remains to consider $P\ll Q$ with finite divergence; let $r=dP/dQ$.

Put $\varphi(0)=0$ and $\varphi(t)=t\log t$ for $t>0$. By [F5] and [F7], $\varphi''(t)=1/t>0$ for $t>0$, so [F8] makes $\varphi$ convex on $(0,\infty)$. Its continuity at zero is part of [F1]; taking limits in the convexity inequality as a positive endpoint tends to zero extends convexity to $[0,\infty)$.

Define $g(t):=t\log t-t+1$ for $t>0$ and $g(0):=1$. For $s>1$, set $c=(1+s)/2$. By [F11], $\log s=\int_1^cdu/u+\int_c^sdu/u$. On $[1,c]$, $1/u\le1$, while on $[c,s]$, $1/u\le1/c<1$; [F9] and [F24] give $\log s<s-1$. For $0<s<1$, set $c=(1+s)/2$. By [F11], $\log s=-\int_s^1du/u=-\left(\int_s^cdu/u+\int_c^1du/u\right)$. On $[s,c]$, $1/u\ge1/c>1$, and on $[c,1]$, $1/u\ge1$; [F9] and [F24] give $\log s<s-1$. The integrands and comparison constants are integrable on these compact intervals by [F10]. Equality holds at $s=1$. Applying this inequality to $s=1/t$ and using [F6] gives $t\log t\ge t-1$, strictly unless $t=1$. Hence $g\ge0$ and its only zero is $1$.

For the normalized-density clause on the measure space [F13], put $P:=q\,\mu$ and $Q:=\pi\,\mu$. By [F17], $\int\pi\,d\mu=Z^{-1}\int\gamma\,d\mu=1$; hence [F15] and [F14] make $P$ and $Q$ probability measures.

If $Q(E)=0$, [F15] gives $\int_E\pi\,d\mu=0$, hence $\int_E\gamma\,d\mu=0$ because $Z$ is finite and positive, using [F17]. By [F12], $\gamma=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $E$. The support hypothesis on $q$ then gives $P(E)=0$, so $P\ll Q$. Define $\rho:[0,\infty]\to[0,\infty]$ by $\rho(t)=1/t$ for finite $t>0$ and $\rho(0)=\rho(+\infty)=0$. For $a<0$, $\{\rho>a\}=[0,\infty]$; for $a=0$ it is $(0,\infty)$; and for $a>0$ it is $(0,1/a)$. These are Borel by [F18], so [F19] makes $\rho$ Borel. By [F20]–[F21], $r:=q\,\rho(\pi)$ is measurable and equals $q/\pi$ on $\{\pi>0\}$ and zero on $\{\pi=0\}$. For every measurable $E$, [F16] gives $$\int_E r\,dQ=\int_Er\pi\,d\mu=\int_Eq\,d\mu=P(E),$$ because $q=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $\{\pi=0\}$. Thus $r=dP/dQ$.

By [F2] with $E$ equal to the whole space, $\int r\,dQ=P(\Omega)=1$. The negative part of $r\log r$ is finite by [F1], so finiteness of $D(P\|Q)$ also makes its positive part finite. Thus $r$ and $r\log r$ are integrable with respect to the probability measure $Q$. The Radon–Nikodym representative here is the one whose selection is covered by [A1].

On the $P$-full-measure subset of $\{q>0\}$ where $\gamma>0$, we have $\pi=\gamma/Z>0$ and $\ell:=\log r=\log q-\log\gamma+\log Z$. Where $q=0$, the KL logarithm $\ell$ is defined to be zero. By [F23], $q|\ell|\le q|\log q|+q|\log\gamma|+q|\log Z|$ almost everywhere. The right-hand side has finite integral by the hypotheses and $\int q=1$; hence [F16] gives $\int|\ell|\,dP=\int q|\ell|\,d\mu<\infty$. By [F1], [F16], and [F22], applying [F16] to the positive and negative parts of $\ell$ gives $$D(P\|Q)=\int\log r\,dP =\int q(\log q-\log\gamma+\log Z)\,d\mu.$$ Using $\int q\,d\mu=1$ and rearranging proves the identity.

Apply [F3] on $(\Omega,\mathcal A,Q)$ to $r$ and $\varphi$. Steps 2.1 and 1.2 check its integrability and convexity hypotheses, and $\int r\,dQ=1$ by step 2.1. Therefore $$0=\varphi(1)=\varphi\!\left(\int r\,dQ\right) \le\int\varphi(r)\,dQ=D(P\|Q).$$

The representative $r$ is finite-valued and measurable by [F1], and $\varphi(r)$ is measurable there; the arithmetic measurability result [F21] therefore makes $g(r)=\varphi(r)-r+1$ measurable. It is nonnegative by step 1.3. By step 2.1, $r,\varphi(r)\in L^1(Q)$, and $1\in L^1(Q)$ because $Q$ is a probability measure. Linearity [F25] now gives $g(r)\in L^1(Q)$ and $$\int g(r)\,dQ=\int\varphi(r)\,dQ-\int r\,dQ+\int1\,dQ=D(P\|Q)-1+1=D(P\|Q).$$ Thus if $D(P\|Q)=0$, [F12] applies to the measurable nonnegative integrand and gives $g(r)=0$ $Q$-almost everywhere. By step 1.3, $r=1$ $Q$-almost everywhere, and the Radon–Nikodym identity [F2] gives $P(E)=Q(E)$ for every measurable $E$. Conversely, if $P=Q$ then $r=1$ almost everywhere and [F1] gives $D(P\|Q)=0$.
Step 2.2 identifies the normalized-density divergence as finite, and step 3.1 proves it is nonnegative. Therefore $\int q(\log\gamma-\log q)\,d\mu\le\log Z$, as claimed.
