Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$, $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$, and
$(\mathsf Z,\mathcal C)$ be measurable spaces (sets equipped with
sigma-algebras; [[def-measurable-space]]). Let $\nu$ and $\mu$ be sigma-finite
reference measures on the observation and latent spaces; each has a countable
measurable cover by sets of finite measure
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]). The finite product
sigma-algebra is generated by measurable rectangles
([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]). The product
reference measure $\nu\otimes\mu$ is the one supplied by
[[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]].

A **jointly measurable latent-variable density** is a specified function
$$p:\Theta\times\mathsf X\times\mathsf Z\longrightarrow[0,\infty]$$
measurable for $\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal C$ and normalized
on every parameter fibre:
$$\int_{\mathsf X\times\mathsf Z}p(\theta,x,z)\, (\nu\otimes\mu)(d(x,z))=1\qquad(\theta\in\Theta).$$
Here $x$ is the observed coordinate and $z$ the latent coordinate. The
observed marginal density is
$$m(\theta,x):=\int_{\mathsf Z}p(\theta,x,z)\,\mu(dz).$$
The valid-fibre set is
$V:=\{(\theta,x):0<m(\theta,x)<\infty\}$. Only on $V$ define the normalized
latent-fibre density
$$q(z\mid\theta,x):=\frac{p(\theta,x,z)}{m(\theta,x)}.$$
This definition requires a single jointly measurable density as an input.
[[def-likelihood-density]] supplies neither a sigma-algebra on $\Theta$ nor
joint parameter measurability from separately specified likelihood sections;
the joint measurability above is an additional hypothesis. Because $p$ is
already supplied as one joint function, this definition uses no choice axiom.
It does not assert that AC can turn separately specified pointwise likelihood
versions into a jointly measurable version. No quotient or pointwise
conditional density is asserted on a zero or infinite marginal fibre.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

Every complete ordered field $F$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) is Archimedean:
for every $x \in F$ there is a natural number $n \ge 1$ with $x < n \cdot 1_F$,
where $n \cdot 1_F$ is the canonical natural of the ordered field $F$
([[def-ordered-field]]). Equivalently, the canonical naturals are cofinal in $F$.

The **extended real line** is

$$\overline{\mathbb{R}} := \mathbb{R} \cup \{-\infty,+\infty\}$$

with the total order extending the usual order on $\mathbb{R}$ and satisfying
$-\infty < x < +\infty$ for every real $x$
([[def-extended-reals]]).

Its **Borel sigma-algebra** is the Borel sigma-algebra of that ordered
topological line in the sense of [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]. On this page it is
denoted $\mathcal{B}(\overline{\mathbb{R}})$ and is generated by the rays

$$\{\, (a,+\infty] : a \in \mathbb{R} \,\}.$$

In particular, $\{+\infty\}$ and $\{-\infty\}$ are Borel sets.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$, $(Y,\mathcal{B})$, and $(Z,\mathcal{C})$ be measurable
spaces. If $f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Y,\mathcal{B})$ is measurable and
$g : (Y,\mathcal{B}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable, then
$g \circ f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable.

In particular, if $f$ is measurable and $g$ is a Borel measurable function on
its codomain, then $g \circ f$ is measurable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space and let
$f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ be measurable for the Borel sigma-algebra on
the extended real line. Products of functions use
$\odot_X$ from [[def-measurable-pointwise-extended-real-product]], and $cf$
abbreviates $\underline c\odot_X f$ for the constant function $\underline c$.
The magnitude function is $|f|=\max(f,-f)$ as in
[[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]]. Then:

1. $cf$ is measurable for every real scalar $c$;
2. $\max(f,g)$, $\min(f,g)$, $|f|$, $f^+$, and $f^-$ are measurable;
3. if the partial pointwise sum $f+g$ is defined at every point, then it is measurable;
4. the pointwise product $fg:=f\odot_X g$ is measurable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space ([[def-measure-space]]).

- The measure $\mu$ is **finite** if $\mu(X)<+\infty$.
- It is **sigma-finite** if there is a sequence $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$ such that $X=\bigcup_nE_n$ and $\mu(E_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$.
- It is **semifinite** if, whenever $E\in\mathcal A$ and $\mu(E)>0$, there is $F\in\mathcal A$ with $F\subseteq E$ and $0<\mu(F)<+\infty$.

The last condition is automatic when $0<\mu(E)<+\infty$, by taking $F=E$; its substantive case is $\mu(E)=+\infty$.

derivations.claim: Fix $\theta$ and let $\mathcal D_\theta$ be the collection of subsets $E\subseteq\Theta\times\mathsf X\times\mathsf Z$ whose section $E_\theta:=\{(x,z):(\theta,x,z)\in E\}$ belongs to $\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal C$. Sections commute with complements and countable unions, so $\mathcal D_\theta$ is a sigma-algebra. It contains each measurable rectangle $T_0\times A_0\times C_0$, whose section is $A_0\times C_0$ if $\theta\in T_0$ and empty otherwise. By [F12], every product-measurable set has a measurable section. Applying this to preimages of Borel sets shows that $p_\theta(x,z):=p(\theta,x,z)$ is product-measurable. For complex $h$, first compose with the continuous Borel coordinate maps $\operatorname{Re},\operatorname{Im}:\mathbb C\to\mathbb R$; the same section argument makes both $\operatorname{Re}h_\theta$ and $\operatorname{Im}h_\theta$ measurable, hence $h_\theta$ is complex-measurable.

By [F13], choose a measurable exhaustion $Z_n\uparrow\mathsf Z$ with $\mu(Z_n)<\infty$. On $S:=\Theta\times\mathsf X$, the constant assignment $K(s,B):=\mu(B)$ is a measure kernel: each section is $\mu$ and each evaluation map is constant. The same exhaustion makes it uniformly sigma-finite by [F2].

For fixed $	heta$, step 1.1 makes $p_	heta$ product-measurable, so Tonelli [F4] gives $$\int_{\mathsf X}m(	heta,x)\,
u(dx)=\int_{\mathsf X	imes\mathsf Z}p_	heta(x,z)\,d(
u\otimes\mu)=1$$ by [F1]. Thus $m(	heta,\cdot)$ is a probability density. Also $E_	heta:=\{(x,z):p_	heta(x,z)=\infty\}$ is measurable. For every positive integer $n$, $n\mathbf1_{E_	heta}\le p_	heta$, so [F6] gives $n(
u\otimes\mu)(E_	heta)\le1$. Since this holds for every $n$, [F7] implies $(
u\otimes\mu)(E_	heta)=0$.

The function $p$ is nonnegative and product-measurable by [F1]. Under the finite-product identification $S\times\mathsf Z=(\Theta\times\mathsf X)\times\mathsf Z$ from [F12], apply [F3] to the constant kernel $K$ from step 1.2. It follows that $s\mapsto\int p(s,z)\,\mu(dz)=m(s)$ is measurable on $S$.

For fixed $	heta$, write $u_	heta=\operatorname{Re}h_	heta$ and $v_	heta=\operatorname{Im}h_	heta$. Define the finite-valued measurable function $\widetilde p_	heta:=p_	heta\mathbf1_{\{p_	heta<\infty\}}$ and then $$H_	heta:=u_	heta\widetilde p_	heta+i v_	heta\widetilde p_	heta.$$ By [F11] this is complex-valued product-measurable; it is defined to be zero on the null set where $p_	heta=\infty$. It agrees with $h_	heta p_	heta$ off that null set, and the assumed absolute integrability gives $\int|H_	heta|\,d(
u\otimes\mu)<\infty$. Fubini [F5] applies to this $L^1$ representative and gives $$\int_{\mathsf X	imes\mathsf Z}H_	heta\,d(
u\otimes\mu)=\int_{\mathsf X}\left(\int_{\mathsf Z}H_	heta(x,z)\,\mu(dz)ight)
u(dx)=\int_{\mathsf Z}\left(\int_{\mathsf X}H_	heta(x,z)\,
u(dx)ight)\mu(dz),$$ with its zero assignment on exceptional null sections. Since $H_	heta=hp$ almost everywhere on the fixed-$	heta$ product space, these are the asserted exchanges for $hp$.

Let $E:=\{x:m(\theta,x)=\infty\}$, measurable by step 2.2. For each positive integer $n$, $n\mathbf1_E\le m(\theta,\cdot)$, so [F6] and step 2.1 give $n\nu(E)\le1$. Since this holds for every $n$, [F7] forces $\nu(E)=0$. If $0<m(\theta,x)<\infty$, division by that scalar and the definition of $m$ give $\int q(z\mid\theta,x)\,\mu(dz)=m(\theta,x)/m(\theta,x)=1$. The valid-fibre set $V=m^{-1}((0,\infty))$ is measurable by step 2.2 and [F8]. For measurability, define $\rho:[0,\infty]\to[0,\infty]$ by $\rho(t)=1/t$ for finite $t>0$ and $\rho(0)=\rho(+\infty)=0$. For $a<0$, $\{\rho>a\}=[0,\infty]$; for $a=0$ it is $(0,\infty)$; and for $a>0$ it is $(0,1/a)$. These sets are Borel by [F8], so [F9] makes $\rho$ Borel. By [F10], $\rho\circ m$ is measurable on $\Theta\times\mathsf X$. Pulling it back along the measurable coordinate projection from the finite product space, which is measurable by [F12], gives a product-measurable function; multiplying by $p$ preserves measurability by [F11]. This product restricts to $q=p/m$ on $V\times\mathsf Z$, so $q$ is measurable on the valid-fibre set.
Steps 2.2, 2.1, 3.2, and 3.1 prove the marginal measurability, normalization, valid-fibre density, and integrable-exchange clauses.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be continuously
Fréchet differentiable. The gradient $\nabla f(x)$ is the vector of partial
derivatives in the Euclidean coordinates, with the convention of

Fix $x$ and write $g:=
abla f(x)$ and $d:=-g/L$. Define $\phi(s):=f(x+sd)$ on $[0,1]$. By [F2]–[F3], $\phi'(s)=\langle
abla f(x+sd),dangle$ on $(0,1)$. The gradient is continuous by [A1], so $\phi'$ is continuous and integrable by [F4]. Applying [F5] gives $$f(x-g/L)-f(x) =- rac1L\int_0^1\langle
abla f(x-sg/L),gangle\,ds.$$ By [A1] and [F6], $\|
abla f(x-sg/L)-g\|\le s\|g\|$, whence $\langle
abla f(x-sg/L),gangle\ge(1-s)\|g\|^2$. Integrating this bound gives $$f(x-g/L)\le f(x)- rac{\|g\|^2}{2L}.$$

By [A2], for every $y$, $$f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle+\frac\mu2\|y-x\|^2 =f(x)-\frac{\|g\|^2}{2\mu} +\frac\mu2\left\|y-x+\frac g\mu\right\|^2.$$ Taking $y=x^*$ and using nonnegativity of the square yields $\|g\|^2\ge2\mu(f(x)-f^*)$.

Apply steps 1.1 and 1.2 at $x=x_k$ and use [F1]. Then $$f(x_{k+1})-f^* \le f(x_k)-f^*-\frac{\|\nabla f(x_k)\|^2}{2L} \le\left(1-\frac\mu L\right)(f(x_k)-f^*).$$ The factor is nonnegative because $\mu\le L$.

The $k=0$ case is equality. For $k=1$, the result is step 2.1 whenever $x_1$ is generated. If $x_{k+1}$ is generated, then $x_k$ was generated and the algorithm made the $k$th update; multiplying the bound at $k$ by $1-\mu/L\ge0$ and applying step 2.1 proves it at $k+1$. Induction along generated iterates gives the claim for every generated $k\ge1$. If the stopping rule fires earlier, no later iterate is asserted.

1. **Nonnegativity.** If $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $\int_a^b f \ge 0$.
2. **Monotonicity.** If $f(x) \le g(x)$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $$\int_a^b f \;\le\; \int_a^b g .$$
3. **Two-sided bound.** If $m \le f(x) \le M$ for every $x \in [a,b]$, with
   $m, M$ real, then
   $$m\,(b-a) \;\le\; \int_a^b f \;\le\; M\,(b-a) .$$

**Equality in claim 1 does not force $f$ to vanish.** A nonnegative integrable
function with integral $0$ may be positive at infinitely many points; that is
[[fs-nonnegative-integrable-with-zero-integral-vanishes]] on the previous page's
companion. Under the additional hypothesis of continuity the conclusion does
hold, and that is [[thm-nonnegative-continuous-with-zero-integral-vanishes]]
below.

**Claim 2 is stated for $a < b$ and is not orientation-invariant.** With the
convention of [[def-oriented-integral]], $f \le g$ gives
$\int_u^v f \le \int_u^v g$ when $u \le v$ and the reverse inequality when
$u \ge v$, since both sides change sign together.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC and let $a,b\in\mathbb R$ and $\tau>0$. For the normal location
laws with common variance $\tau^2$,
$$D\bigl(N(a,\tau^2)\|N(b,\tau^2)\bigr)=\frac{(a-b)^2}{2\tau^2}.$$

Assume AC and use the directional convention of
[[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]. For probability measures $P,Q$ on one
measurable space, $D(P\|Q)\ge0$, and $D(P\|Q)=0$ if and only if $P=Q$.

There is also the following normalized-density identity. Let
$(\mathsf X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a sigma-finite measure space: it is a set
with a sigma-algebra and measure ([[def-measure-space]]), and there is a
countable measurable cover by sets of finite $\mu$-measure
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]). Let
$\gamma:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ be a finite-valued measurable function with
$Z:=\int\gamma\,d\mu\in(0,\infty)$, and put $\pi=\gamma/Z$. Let
$q:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ be a finite-valued measurable probability density,
so $\int q\,d\mu=1$, and suppose $q=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on
$\{\gamma=0\}$. Assume
$$\int q\bigl(|\log\gamma|+|\log q|\bigr)\,d\mu<\infty,$$
where each term with $q=0$ is defined to be zero. Then
$$\log Z =\int q(\log\gamma-\log q)\,d\mu +D(q\,\mu\|\pi\,\mu).$$
In particular, the first integral is at most $\log Z$. This identity concerns
normalized densities only; it does not assert posterior existence for an
unspecified statistical model.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be continuously
Fréchet differentiable. The gradient $\nabla f(x)$ is the vector of partial
derivatives in the Euclidean coordinates, with the convention of
[[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]; differentiability is the Fréchet
condition of [[def-real-frechet-derivative-on-real-and-complex-matrix-spaces]].

**Inputs:** an initial point $x_0\in U$; either a positive fixed-step
sequence $(t_k)_{k\ge0}$ or backtracking parameters $\alpha\in(0,1)$ and
$\beta\in(0,1)$; and an optional caller stopping predicate
$S(k,x,g)\in\{\mathrm{false},\mathrm{true}\}$, with
$S:\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\times U\times\mathbb R^d\to\{\mathrm{false},\mathrm{true}\}$.
If no predicate is supplied, use $S\equiv\mathrm{false}$. **Output:** when the
procedure stops, return the last valid iterate $x_k$ and the status
`stationary`, `caller-stop`, or `domain-failure`.
If no stopping status occurs, the sequence continues and there is no finite
return.
For example, an outer procedure's at-most-$M$-updates limit, for finite real
$M\ge0$, is implemented by $S(k,x,g):=(k+1>M)$.

At iteration $k$, where $k$ is the number of accepted updates so far and the
current iterate is $x_k$:

1. Compute $g_k:=\nabla f(x_k)$ and set $p_k:=-g_k$. If $g_k=0$, return
   $(x_k,\texttt{stationary})$.
2. If $S(k,x_k,g_k)$ is true, return $(x_k,\texttt{caller-stop})$. Check this
   predicate at the current iterate after its gradient is computed and before
   any step is selected.
3. In fixed-step mode, set $t=t_k$. If $x_k+tp_k\notin U$, return
   $(x_k,\texttt{domain-failure})$ without accepting that candidate.
4. In backtracking mode, start with $t=1$ and repeatedly replace $t$ by
   $\beta t$ until $x_k+tp_k\in U$ and
   $f(x_k+tp_k)\le f(x_k)+\alpha t\,\langle g_k,p_k\rangle$.
5. Set $x_{k+1}:=x_k+t p_k$ and continue at iteration $k+1$.

The fixed-step update map is $x\mapsto x-t_k\nabla f(x)$; at a stationary
point its value is $x$, which is the returned iterate. A backtracking search
that is reached at a nonstationary iterate is well-defined by
[[lem-armijo-backtracking-terminates-for-strict-descent-directions]]. The
procedure asserts no convergence or global-minimization property for an
arbitrary objective.

Let $d\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be twice
continuously Fréchet differentiable. Write $g(x)=\nabla f(x)$ and
$H(x)=\nabla^2 f(x)$ using [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] and
[[def-hessian-and-euclidean-critical-point]]. The Hessian is symmetric by
[[cor-hessian-is-symmetric]].

**Inputs:** $x_0\in U$, a Newton-decrement tolerance $\varepsilon>0$, and
line-search parameters $\alpha\in(0,1/2)$ and $\beta\in(0,1)$. **Output:**
when the procedure stops, return the last valid iterate $x_k$ and one of the
statuses `stationary`, `decrement`, or
`positive-definite solve unavailable`.
If none of these stopping conditions occurs, the sequence continues and there
is no finite return.

At iteration $k$ with current iterate $x_k$:

1. Compute $g_k:=g(x_k)$. If $g_k=0$, return
   $(x_k,\texttt{stationary})$.
2. If $H_k:=H(x_k)$ is not positive definite, return
   $(x_k,\texttt{positive-definite solve unavailable})$ without a Newton
   update. Otherwise compute its Cholesky factorization $H_k=L_kL_k^T$, solve
   $L_kw=-g_k$ and $L_k^Tp_k=w$, and set
   $$\lambda_k^2:=-\langle g_k,p_k\rangle=g_k^TH_k^{-1}g_k>0.$$
3. Before line search, if $\lambda_k^2/2\le\varepsilon$, return
   $(x_k,\texttt{decrement})$. This is the Newton-decrement stopping test.
4. Start with $t=1$ and repeatedly replace $t$ by $\beta t$ until
   $x_k+t p_k\in U$ and
   $f(x_k+t p_k)\le f(x_k)+\alpha t\,\langle g_k,p_k\rangle$.
5. Set $x_{k+1}:=x_k+t p_k$ and continue at iteration $k+1$.

The Cholesky factor exists and is unique when the symmetric Hessian is positive
definite by
[[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]].
Its positive diagonal makes both triangular solves unique. The backtracking
branch terminates whenever it is reached, since $g_k\ne0$ and $H_k$ is
positive definite, by
[[lem-armijo-backtracking-terminates-for-strict-descent-directions]]. This
procedure makes no global-optimality claim.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$, $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$, and
$(\mathsf Z,\mathcal C)$ be measurable spaces (sets equipped with
sigma-algebras; [[def-measurable-space]]). Let $\nu$ and $\mu$ be sigma-finite
reference measures on the observation and latent spaces; each has a countable
measurable cover by sets of finite measure
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]). The finite product
sigma-algebra is generated by measurable rectangles
([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]). The product
reference measure $\nu\otimes\mu$ is the one supplied by
[[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]].

A **jointly measurable latent-variable density** is a specified function
$$p:\Theta\times\mathsf X\times\mathsf Z\longrightarrow[0,\infty]$$
measurable for $\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal C$ and normalized
on every parameter fibre:
$$\int_{\mathsf X\times\mathsf Z}p(\theta,x,z)\, (\nu\otimes\mu)(d(x,z))=1\qquad(\theta\in\Theta).$$
Here $x$ is the observed coordinate and $z$ the latent coordinate. The
observed marginal density is
$$m(\theta,x):=\int_{\mathsf Z}p(\theta,x,z)\,\mu(dz).$$
The valid-fibre set is
$V:=\{(\theta,x):0<m(\theta,x)<\infty\}$. Only on $V$ define the normalized
latent-fibre density
$$q(z\mid\theta,x):=\frac{p(\theta,x,z)}{m(\theta,x)}.$$
This definition requires a single jointly measurable density as an input.
[[def-likelihood-density]] supplies neither a sigma-algebra on $\Theta$ nor
joint parameter measurability from separately specified likelihood sections;
the joint measurability above is an additional hypothesis. Because $p$ is
already supplied as one joint function, this definition uses no choice axiom.
It does not assert that AC can turn separately specified pointwise likelihood
versions into a jointly measurable version. No quotient or pointwise
conditional density is asserted on a zero or infinite marginal fibre.

Assume the hypotheses of
[[def-latent-variable-joint-and-observed-data-factorization]]. Then
$m(\theta,x)=\int p(\theta,x,z)\,\mu(dz)$ is jointly measurable in
$(\theta,x)$. For each fixed $\theta$, it is an observed-data probability
density: it is $\mathcal A$-measurable and
$$\int_{\mathsf X}m(\theta,x)\,\nu(dx)=1.$$
Consequently $m(\theta,x)<\infty$ for $\nu$-almost every $x$. On every valid
fibre $0<m(\theta,x)<\infty$, $q(z\mid\theta,x)=p(\theta,x,z)/m(\theta,x)$ is
a measurable $\mu$-density of total mass one. Finally, if $h:\Theta\times\mathsf X\times\mathsf Z\to\mathbb C$ is product
measurable and
$\int |h(\theta,x,z)|p(\theta,x,z)\,d(\nu\otimes\mu)<\infty$ for a fixed
$\theta$, Fubini permits exchanging the latent and observed integrals of
$hp$. No exchange is claimed without this absolute integrability.

derivations.claim: The map $p(x,j)=w_jf_j(x)$ is nonnegative and product measurable. With counting measure on the finite label set, $$\int_{\mathsf X\times\mathsf Z}p\,d(\nu\otimes\#) =\sum_{j=1}^J w_j\int_{\mathsf X}f_j\,d\nu =\sum_{j=1}^Jw_j=1.$$ It is therefore a complete-data probability density of the type in [F1].

Integrating over the label coordinate gives $m(x)=\int_{\mathsf Z}p(x,j)\,\#(dj)=\sum_{j=1}^Jw_jf_j(x)$. For $0<m(x)<\infty$, the conditional label mass is $q(j\mid x)=w_jf_j(x)/m(x)$ and its finite sum is $$\sum_{j=1}^Jq(j\mid x) =\frac{\sum_{j=1}^Jw_jf_j(x)}{m(x)}=1.$$
The joint density, its observed marginal, and its normalized positive finite fibres therefore have exactly the finite-mixture factorization claimed.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

**Inputs.** Supply a measurable parameter space $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$, sigma-finite measure spaces $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A,\nu)$ and $(\mathsf Z,\mathcal C,\mu)$, and a jointly measurable complete-data density $p(\theta,x,z)$ relative to $\nu\otimes\mu$ that integrates to one on each parameter fiber, as in [[def-latent-variable-joint-and-observed-data-factorization]]. This joint measurability is supplied explicitly and is not inferred from separate likelihood-density versions ([[def-likelihood-density]]). Also supply fixed observed data $x$, an initial value $\theta_0$, a mode `exact` or `generalized`, and a candidate selector that returns either a candidate or `unavailable` in finite time at each call. Require $0<m_{\theta_0}(x)<\infty$ and
$$\int q_{\theta_0}^x(z)\,|\log p(\theta_0,x,z)|\,\mu(dz)<\infty.$$

Write
$$m_\theta(x):=\int_{\mathsf Z}p(\theta,x,z)\,\mu(dz),\qquad q_\theta^x(z):=\frac{p(\theta,x,z)}{m_\theta(x)}$$
only when $0<m_\theta(x)<\infty$. By [[thm-observed-density-is-latent-marginal-under-tonelli]], $m_\theta$ is the observed-data density and $q_\theta^x$ is a probability density on every such fiber. The observed log likelihood is $\ell_x(\theta):=\log m_\theta(x)$ on those fibers.

At each valid iterate $\theta_t$, set $q_t:=q_{\theta_t}^x$ and define
$$Q(\theta\mid\theta_t):=\int_{\mathsf Z}\log p(\theta,x,z)\,q_t(z)\,\mu(dz)$$
only for candidates where this integral is finite. Use $\log0=-\infty$ and set $q_t|\log p|=0$ wherever $q_t=0$. The Q integral itself is choice-free. To test finite KL when $q_t\mu\ll q_\theta^x\mu$, assume AC as required by [[def-axiom-of-choice]] and [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]; when absolute continuity fails, $D=+\infty$ by that definition without AC. An **admissible candidate** $\theta$ also satisfies $0<m_\theta(x)<\infty$, $q_t\mu\ll q_\theta^x\mu$, and
$$D(q_t\mu\|q_\theta^x\mu)<\infty,$$
where the direction of $D$ is that of [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]. Require $\int q_t|\log p(\theta,x,\cdot)|\,d\mu<\infty$ for each candidate and $\int q_t|\log p(\theta_t,x,\cdot)|\,d\mu<\infty$ for the current iterate.

**Output.** Emit the iterate sequence beginning with $\theta_0$. If a stopping condition occurs after $T$ successful updates, return the finite list $(\theta_0,\ldots,\theta_T)$ and a status recording the first unavailable condition or selector result; do not append a failed candidate. If no stopping condition occurs, the emitted sequence is infinite and there is no finite stopping status.

**Procedure.** For $t=0,1,2,\ldots$, check that $0<m_{\theta_t}(x)<\infty$; if not, return the current list with status `stopped: invalid current marginal`. Form $q_t$ and $Q(\cdot\mid\theta_t)$ on admissible candidates. If $Q(\theta_t\mid\theta_t)$ is not finite, return with status `stopped: current Q is not finite`. Call the supplied selector. In **exact mode**, its candidate set must consist of admissible candidates and contain $\theta_t$; it returns an attained maximizer of $Q$ on that set, or `unavailable` if no attained maximum is available. In **generalized mode**, it returns any admissible $\theta_{t+1}$ with $Q(\theta_{t+1}\mid\theta_t)\ge Q(\theta_t\mid\theta_t)$, or `unavailable` if no such update is supplied. If the selector returns `unavailable`, return with status `stopped: no required update supplied`; otherwise append its candidate and continue. The procedure asserts no convergence or global-optimality property and makes no assertion for a candidate that loses current latent support.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $p(\theta,x,z)$ be a jointly measurable normalized complete-data density as in [[def-latent-variable-joint-and-observed-data-factorization]], and fix observed data $x$. Put $m_\theta(x)=\int p(\theta,x,z)\,\mu(dz)$. Let $\theta_t$ and $\theta$ satisfy $0<m_{\theta_t}(x),m_\theta(x)<\infty$. Define $q_t(z)=p(\theta_t,x,z)/m_{\theta_t}(x)$ and $q_\theta^x(z)=p(\theta,x,z)/m_\theta(x)$. Assume
$$q_t\mu\ll q_\theta^x\mu,\qquad \int q_t(z)\bigl(|\log p(\theta_t,x,z)|+|\log p(\theta,x,z)|\bigr)\,\mu(dz)<\infty,$$
and $D(q_t\mu\|q_\theta^x\mu)<\infty$. Use $\log0=-\infty$ and set $q_t|\log p|=0$ wherever $q_t=0$. Then, with $Q(\theta\mid\theta_t)=\int q_t(z)\log p(\theta,x,z)\,\mu(dz)$,
$$\ell_x(\theta)-\ell_x(\theta_t) =Q(\theta\mid\theta_t)-Q(\theta_t\mid\theta_t) +D(q_t\mu\|q_\theta^x\mu).$$
Consequently, any admissible update with $Q(\theta\mid\theta_t)\ge Q(\theta_t\mid\theta_t)$ does not decrease $\ell_x$. An exact M-step has this property when its maximum is attained over an admissible candidate set containing $\theta_t$. No equality-of-parameter conclusion is asserted when the KL divergence is zero.

([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]). The product
reference measure $\nu\otimes\mu$ is the one supplied by
[[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]].

of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If

([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and
let $r=dP/dQ$ be a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative of its

[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].

monotonicity properties of the natural logarithm

measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since

affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$

[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and

defined by the positive and negative parts

theorem gives increase before and decrease after this point

is well-defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.

derivations.claim: For every $\theta\in(0,1)$, summing $p_\theta(x,z)$ over $(x,z)\in\{0,1\}^2$ gives $(\theta+(1-\theta))^2=1$. At $x=1$, $m_\theta(1)=\theta$ and the conditional law of $Z$ is Bernoulli$(\theta)$, so the current law is Bernoulli$(1/2)$. Every candidate has positive finite marginal, the same two-point latent support, and $D(q_t\|q_\theta)=\frac12\log(1/(2\theta))+\frac12\log(1/(2(1-\theta)))$ is finite by [A1, F3]. Their complete-data log values are finite, so every $\theta\in(0,1)$ is admissible by [F4].

Averaging $\log p_\theta(1,Z)$ under that current conditional law gives $Q(\theta\mid1/2)=\frac32\log\theta+\frac12\log(1-\theta)=\frac12\log\bigl(\theta^3(1-\theta)\bigr)$. At $\theta=1/2$, this is $\log(1/4)$; at $\theta=7/10$, it is $\frac12\log(1029/10000)$. Their difference is $\frac12\log(1029/625)>0$, so the candidate strictly raises $Q$.

For $0<\theta<1$, $\frac{27}{256}-\theta^3(1-\theta)=(\theta-3/4)^2\bigl((\theta+1/4)^2+1/8\bigr)\ge0$, with equality only at $\theta=3/4$. Thus the exact maximizer of $Q$ is $3/4$, so $7/10$ is a genuinely nonmaximizing generalized step. The observed log-likelihood difference is $\log(7/10)-\log(1/2)=\log(7/5)>0$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma>0$, the normal law $N(m,\sigma^2)$
of [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]] has Lebesgue density
$$g_{m,\sigma}(y)=\frac1\sigma\frac{e^{-((y-m)/\sigma)^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}e^{-(y-m)^2/(2\sigma^2)}.$$

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$, $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$, and
$(\mathsf Z,\mathcal C)$ be measurable spaces (sets equipped with
sigma-algebras; [[def-measurable-space]]). Let $\nu$ and $\mu$ be sigma-finite
reference measures on the observation and latent spaces; each has a countable
measurable cover by sets of finite measure
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]). The finite product
sigma-algebra is generated by measurable rectangles
([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]). The product
reference measure $\nu\otimes\mu$ is the one supplied by
[[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]].

A **jointly measurable latent-variable density** is a specified function
$$p:\Theta\times\mathsf X\times\mathsf Z\longrightarrow[0,\infty]$$
measurable for $\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal C$ and normalized
on every parameter fibre:
$$\int_{\mathsf X\times\mathsf Z}p(\theta,x,z)\, (\nu\otimes\mu)(d(x,z))=1\qquad(\theta\in\Theta).$$
Here $x$ is the observed coordinate and $z$ the latent coordinate. The
observed marginal density is
$$m(\theta,x):=\int_{\mathsf Z}p(\theta,x,z)\,\mu(dz).$$
The valid-fibre set is
$V:=\{(\theta,x):0<m(\theta,x)<\infty\}$. Only on $V$ define the normalized
latent-fibre density
$$q(z\mid\theta,x):=\frac{p(\theta,x,z)}{m(\theta,x)}.$$
This definition requires a single jointly measurable density as an input.
[[def-likelihood-density]] supplies neither a sigma-algebra on $\Theta$ nor
joint parameter measurability from separately specified likelihood sections;
the joint measurability above is an additional hypothesis. Because $p$ is
already supplied as one joint function, this definition uses no choice axiom.
It does not assert that AC can turn separately specified pointwise likelihood
versions into a jointly measurable version. No quotient or pointwise
conditional density is asserted on a zero or infinite marginal fibre.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $p(\theta,x,z)$ be a jointly measurable normalized complete-data density as in [[def-latent-variable-joint-and-observed-data-factorization]], and fix observed data $x$. Put $m_\theta(x)=\int p(\theta,x,z)\,\mu(dz)$. Let $\theta_t$ and $\theta$ satisfy $0<m_{\theta_t}(x),m_\theta(x)<\infty$. Define $q_t(z)=p(\theta_t,x,z)/m_{\theta_t}(x)$ and $q_\theta^x(z)=p(\theta,x,z)/m_\theta(x)$. Assume
$$q_t\mu\ll q_\theta^x\mu,\qquad \int q_t(z)\bigl(|\log p(\theta_t,x,z)|+|\log p(\theta,x,z)|\bigr)\,\mu(dz)<\infty,$$
and $D(q_t\mu\|q_\theta^x\mu)<\infty$. Use $\log0=-\infty$ and set $q_t|\log p|=0$ wherever $q_t=0$. Then, with $Q(\theta\mid\theta_t)=\int q_t(z)\log p(\theta,x,z)\,\mu(dz)$,
$$\ell_x(\theta)-\ell_x(\theta_t) =Q(\theta\mid\theta_t)-Q(\theta_t\mid\theta_t) +D(q_t\mu\|q_\theta^x\mu).$$
Consequently, any admissible update with $Q(\theta\mid\theta_t)\ge Q(\theta_t\mid\theta_t)$ does not decrease $\ell_x$. An exact M-step has this property when its maximum is attained over an admissible candidate set containing $\theta_t$. No equality-of-parameter conclusion is asserted when the KL divergence is zero.

Under the hypotheses of [[thm-em-observed-log-likelihood-is-nondecreasing]] and [[thm-generalized-em-is-nondecreasing-under-q-ascent]], including AC, these are one-step inequalities for a fixed data fiber. They do not prove that the likelihood sequence is bounded, that parameter iterates converge, that a limit point is stationary, or that a stationary point is globally optimal. The exact M-step also requires an attained Q maximum; ascent itself does not supply one. These are limits of the stated ascent result, not additional convergence theorems.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim: For each fixed label pair the displayed density is continuous in $(\epsilon,y_1,y_2)$ on $(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^2$; the finite label space therefore makes it jointly measurable. For each observation coordinate, $\sum_{j=1}^2\int_{\mathbb R}\frac12\varphi_{a_j,s_j}(y)\,dy=1$ by [F1]. Lebesgue measure and finite counting measure are sigma-finite, so Tonelli [F5] gives integral $1\cdot1=1$ for the nonnegative two-coordinate product density. This verifies the requirements of [F2] directly. Summing over the two labels in each coordinate gives the observed joint density $g_\epsilon(y_1)g_\epsilon(y_2)$, so its value at $(0,1)$ is $L_\epsilon$.

At the two observations, $g_\epsilon(0)\ge\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2\pi}\,\epsilon}$ and $g_\epsilon(1)\ge\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2\pi}}$. Thus $L_\epsilon\ge1/(8\pi\epsilon)$. For every $M>0$, choosing $0<\epsilon<1/(8\pi M)$ gives $L_\epsilon>M$, so the likelihood is unbounded while each fixed-$\epsilon$ value is finite. No finite parameter attains a global maximum.

This is compatible with [F3]–[F4]: the ascent theorem only compares consecutive admissible iterates; it neither bounds the likelihood sequence nor supplies a parameter attaining its unbounded supremum.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$, $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$, and
$(\mathsf Z,\mathcal C)$ be measurable spaces (sets equipped with
sigma-algebras; [[def-measurable-space]]). Let $\nu$ and $\mu$ be sigma-finite
reference measures on the observation and latent spaces; each has a countable
measurable cover by sets of finite measure
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]). The finite product
sigma-algebra is generated by measurable rectangles
([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]). The product
reference measure $\nu\otimes\mu$ is the one supplied by
[[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]].

A **jointly measurable latent-variable density** is a specified function
$$p:\Theta\times\mathsf X\times\mathsf Z\longrightarrow[0,\infty]$$
measurable for $\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal C$ and normalized
on every parameter fibre:
$$\int_{\mathsf X\times\mathsf Z}p(\theta,x,z)\, (\nu\otimes\mu)(d(x,z))=1\qquad(\theta\in\Theta).$$
Here $x$ is the observed coordinate and $z$ the latent coordinate. The
observed marginal density is
$$m(\theta,x):=\int_{\mathsf Z}p(\theta,x,z)\,\mu(dz).$$
The valid-fibre set is
$V:=\{(\theta,x):0<m(\theta,x)<\infty\}$. Only on $V$ define the normalized
latent-fibre density
$$q(z\mid\theta,x):=\frac{p(\theta,x,z)}{m(\theta,x)}.$$
This definition requires a single jointly measurable density as an input.
[[def-likelihood-density]] supplies neither a sigma-algebra on $\Theta$ nor
joint parameter measurability from separately specified likelihood sections;
the joint measurability above is an additional hypothesis. Because $p$ is
already supplied as one joint function, this definition uses no choice axiom.
It does not assert that AC can turn separately specified pointwise likelihood
versions into a jointly measurable version. No quotient or pointwise
conditional density is asserted on a zero or infinite marginal fibre.

Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
([[def-probability-measure]]). Absolute continuity $P\ll Q$ has the convention
of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If
$P\not\ll Q$, define $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and
let $r=dP/dQ$ be a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative of its
Radon–Nikodym class; such a representative exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].
On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This
function is measurable: for $a\ge0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r>\exp(a)\}$, and for
$a<0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r=0\}\cup\{r>\exp(a)\}$, by the inverse and
monotonicity properties of the natural logarithm
([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]). These are
measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since
$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$ by
[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$
The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,
$$0\le \frac{\log s}{s}=\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{u}\le\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{\sqrt u}\le\frac2{\sqrt s}.$$
Thus $t\log t\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$; here $L=\log$ by
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and
[[def-integral-logarithm]]. On $(0,\infty)$, $\psi$ is a product of continuous
functions by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $\psi$ is continuous on
$[0,\infty)$ and $\psi(r)$ is measurable by
[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts
([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]],
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

For $0<t\le1$, the function $-t\log t$ has derivative $-\log t-1$ and
maximum $1/e$ at $t=1/e$: $e=\exp(1)>1$ by
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $1/e=\exp(-1)$ by
[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and $\log(1/e)=-1$ by
[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and the inverse definition. The mean value
theorem gives increase before and decrease after this point
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]],
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).
At $t=0$ the negative part is zero. Since $Q$ is a probability measure,
$$\int \psi(r)^-\,dQ\le\frac1e.$$
The change-of-measure identity of [[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]],
applied to $\ell^-$ gives $\int\ell^-\,dP=\int\psi(r)^-\,dQ\le1/e$,
so $\int\ell\,dP$ is well-defined; applying it to both positive and negative
parts gives
$$D(P\|Q)=\int\ell\,dP=\int\psi(r)\,dQ=\int r\log r\,dQ,$$
with $0\log0:=0$ and a finite negative part. Therefore the extended integral
is well-defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.

This convention is directional: the first argument must be absolutely
continuous with respect to the second for the integral formula to apply.

**Inputs.** Supply a measurable parameter space $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$, sigma-finite measure spaces $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A,\nu)$ and $(\mathsf Z,\mathcal C,\mu)$, and a jointly measurable complete-data density $p(\theta,x,z)$ relative to $\nu\otimes\mu$ that integrates to one on each parameter fiber, as in [[def-latent-variable-joint-and-observed-data-factorization]]. This joint measurability is supplied explicitly and is not inferred from separate likelihood-density versions ([[def-likelihood-density]]). Also supply fixed observed data $x$, an initial value $\theta_0$, a mode `exact` or `generalized`, and a candidate selector that returns either a candidate or `unavailable` in finite time at each call. Require $0<m_{\theta_0}(x)<\infty$ and
$$\int q_{\theta_0}^x(z)\,|\log p(\theta_0,x,z)|\,\mu(dz)<\infty.$$

Write
$$m_\theta(x):=\int_{\mathsf Z}p(\theta,x,z)\,\mu(dz),\qquad q_\theta^x(z):=\frac{p(\theta,x,z)}{m_\theta(x)}$$
only when $0<m_\theta(x)<\infty$. By [[thm-observed-density-is-latent-marginal-under-tonelli]], $m_\theta$ is the observed-data density and $q_\theta^x$ is a probability density on every such fiber. The observed log likelihood is $\ell_x(\theta):=\log m_\theta(x)$ on those fibers.

At each valid iterate $\theta_t$, set $q_t:=q_{\theta_t}^x$ and define
$$Q(\theta\mid\theta_t):=\int_{\mathsf Z}\log p(\theta,x,z)\,q_t(z)\,\mu(dz)$$
only for candidates where this integral is finite. Use $\log0=-\infty$ and set $q_t|\log p|=0$ wherever $q_t=0$. The Q integral itself is choice-free. To test finite KL when $q_t\mu\ll q_\theta^x\mu$, assume AC as required by [[def-axiom-of-choice]] and [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]; when absolute continuity fails, $D=+\infty$ by that definition without AC. An **admissible candidate** $\theta$ also satisfies $0<m_\theta(x)<\infty$, $q_t\mu\ll q_\theta^x\mu$, and
$$D(q_t\mu\|q_\theta^x\mu)<\infty,$$
where the direction of $D$ is that of [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]. Require $\int q_t|\log p(\theta,x,\cdot)|\,d\mu<\infty$ for each candidate and $\int q_t|\log p(\theta_t,x,\cdot)|\,d\mu<\infty$ for the current iterate.

**Output.** Emit the iterate sequence beginning with $\theta_0$. If a stopping condition occurs after $T$ successful updates, return the finite list $(\theta_0,\ldots,\theta_T)$ and a status recording the first unavailable condition or selector result; do not append a failed candidate. If no stopping condition occurs, the emitted sequence is infinite and there is no finite stopping status.

**Procedure.** For $t=0,1,2,\ldots$, check that $0<m_{\theta_t}(x)<\infty$; if not, return the current list with status `stopped: invalid current marginal`. Form $q_t$ and $Q(\cdot\mid\theta_t)$ on admissible candidates. If $Q(\theta_t\mid\theta_t)$ is not finite, return with status `stopped: current Q is not finite`. Call the supplied selector. In **exact mode**, its candidate set must consist of admissible candidates and contain $\theta_t$; it returns an attained maximizer of $Q$ on that set, or `unavailable` if no attained maximum is available. In **generalized mode**, it returns any admissible $\theta_{t+1}$ with $Q(\theta_{t+1}\mid\theta_t)\ge Q(\theta_t\mid\theta_t)$, or `unavailable` if no such update is supplied. If the selector returns `unavailable`, return with status `stopped: no required update supplied`; otherwise append its candidate and continue. The procedure asserts no convergence or global-optimality property and makes no assertion for a candidate that loses current latent support.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space. Let $\gamma:\Omega\to[0,\infty]$ be measurable and suppose
$$Z:=\int_\Omega\gamma\,d\mu\in(0,\infty).$$
Define the normalized target density $\pi:=\gamma/Z$. Then $\int\pi\,d\mu=1$. For a measurable probability density $q\ge0$ (that is, $\int_\Omega q\,d\mu=1$), write $q\ll_\mu\pi$ to mean $q=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $\{\pi=0\}$. This is a support condition on the two densities. It ensures that the induced probability measures $Q:=q\,\mu$ and $\Pi:=\pi\,\mu$ have $Q\ll\Pi$.

The normalization follows from positive-scalar homogeneity of the nonnegative integral:
$$\int\pi\,d\mu=Z^{-1}\int\gamma\,d\mu=1.$$
The induced density set functions are measures by [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]]. Their total masses are one: $Q(\Omega)=1$ by the probability-density hypothesis on $q$, and $\Pi(\Omega)=1$ by the preceding calculation. To verify the absolute-continuity claim, let $A\in\mathcal A$ satisfy $\Pi(A)=0$. Then $\int_A\pi\,d\mu=0$, so the zero-integral criterion gives $\pi=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $A$. The support condition then gives $q=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $A$, and hence $Q(A)=0$. The homogeneity and zero-integral criteria used here are [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]] and [[thm-nonnegative-integral-zero-iff-zero-almost-everywhere]].

Call $q$ **admissible** when $q\ll_\mu\pi$ and
$$\int_\Omega q\bigl(|\log\gamma|+|\log q|\bigr)\,d\mu<\infty.$$
Use the extended logarithm $\log0=-\infty$, agreeing with [[def-natural-logarithm]] on positive inputs. > Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

derivations.claim: Define $Q(A)=\int_A q\,d\mu$ and $\Pi(A)=\int_A\pi\,d\mu$. These are probability measures by [F1] and [F7]. If $\Pi(A)=0$, [F4] applied to $\pi\mathbf1_A$ gives $\pi=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $A$. Then [F1] gives $q=0$ almost everywhere on $A$, so $Q(A)=0$ and $Q\ll\Pi$. Define $r=q/\pi$ on $\{\pi>0\}$ and $r=0$ on $\{\pi=0\}$. For every measurable $A$, $\int_A r\,d\Pi=\int_{A\cap\{\pi>0\}}q\,d\mu=Q(A)$, so $r=dQ/d\Pi$.

On $\{q>0\}$, $\pi=\gamma/Z>0$ and $\log r=\log q-\log\gamma+\log Z$. The assumed absolute integrability and $\int q\,d\mu=1$ make all terms integrable. Hence $\int\log r\,dQ=\int q\log(q/\pi)\,d\mu=\log Z-\operatorname{ELBO}(q)$. This algebraic identity uses the explicit density ratio and no choice axiom.
By [A1] and [F5], the integral $\int\log r\,dQ$ is $D(Q\|\Pi)$ under the library convention. Rearranging step 2.1 gives $\log Z=\operatorname{ELBO}(q)+D(Q\|\Pi)$.
The measures $Q$ and $\Pi$ are probabilities, so [F6] gives $D(Q\|\Pi)\ge0$. Step 3.1 then yields $\operatorname{ELBO}(q)\le\log Z$.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.
Assume AC. The function $\phi(x)=e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}$ is positive and Borel measurable on $\mathbb R$, with Lebesgue integral one.

Assume AC. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma>0$, the normal law $N(m,\sigma^2)$
of [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]] has Lebesgue density
$$g_{m,\sigma}(y)=\frac1\sigma\frac{e^{-((y-m)/\sigma)^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}e^{-(y-m)^2/(2\sigma^2)}.$$

Assume AC. For $m\in\mathbb R$, $\sigma\ge0$, and a real random variable
$X$ with law $N(m,\sigma^2)$,
$$E[X]=m,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(X)=\sigma^2.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int g\,d(f\,d\mu)=\int gf\,d\mu.$$

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and
   $\lambda_n$ is a measure on it ([[def-measure]]);
2. the measure space $(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n), \lambda_n)$ is
   complete ([[def-complete-measure-space]]), and every $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   with $\lambda_n^*(S) = 0$ is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(S) = 0$;
3. every elementary set is Lebesgue measurable and
   $\lambda_n(A) = \mu_0(A)$ for every $A \in \mathcal{E}_n$; in particular
   $\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ for every half-open box $B$,
   $\lambda_n(\varnothing) = 0$ and $\lambda_n(\mathbb{R}^n) = +\infty$.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space ([[def-measure-space]]).

- The measure $\mu$ is **finite** if $\mu(X)<+\infty$.
- It is **sigma-finite** if there is a sequence $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$ such that $X=\bigcup_nE_n$ and $\mu(E_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$.
- It is **semifinite** if, whenever $E\in\mathcal A$ and $\mu(E)>0$, there is $F\in\mathcal A$ with $F\subseteq E$ and $0<\mu(F)<+\infty$.

The last condition is automatic when $0<\mu(E)<+\infty$, by taking $F=E$; its substantive case is $\mu(E)=+\infty$.

derivations.claim: Let $s=\sqrt\beta>0$ and $\phi(t)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-t^2/2}$. Direct algebra gives $\gamma_\rho(x,y)=\phi(x)g_{\rho x,\beta}(y)=\phi(y)g_{\rho y,\beta}(x)$. The target is nonnegative and measurable, and [F8] supplies the sigma-finite Lebesgue product spaces; Tonelli [F6] and [F3] show that it integrates to one and has both marginals $\phi$. By [F5], both marginal means are zero and both marginal variances are one. Since $|xy|\le(x^2+y^2)/2$, the cross moment is absolutely integrable. Fubini [F6], density integration [F7], and [F5] give $E[XY]=\int x\phi(x)(\rho x)dx=\rho$, because the conditional density $g_{\rho x,\beta}$ has mean $\rho x$. Thus the covariance is $\begin{pmatrix}1&\rho\\\rho&1\end{pmatrix}$.

For $m_j\in\mathbb R$ and $v_j>0$, [F4] makes $g_{m_j,v_j}$ probability densities with means $m_j$ and variances $v_j$. Tonelli [F6] gives $\int q=1$. The product density $q$ and target $\gamma_\rho$ are positive everywhere, so the support condition in [F1] holds. Their logarithms are quadratic; the second moments and $|xy|\le(x^2+y^2)/2$ make the absolute logarithms integrable under $q$, so $q$ is admissible. Fubini [F6], density integration [F7], and [F5] give $E_q[X^2]=m_1^2+v_1$, $E_q[Y^2]=m_2^2+v_2$, and $E_q[XY]=m_1m_2$.

From the displayed density, $\log\gamma_\rho=-\log(2\pi s)-(x^2-2\rho xy+y^2)/(2\beta)$. Also $-E_{g_{m_j,v_j}}\log g_{m_j,v_j}=\tfrac12\log(2\pi v_j)+\tfrac12$, by the moments in step 2.1. Substituting these expectations into [F2] gives $\operatorname{ELBO}(q)=C_\rho-\frac{m_1^2-2\rho m_1m_2+m_2^2+v_1+v_2}{2\beta}+\frac12\log v_1+\frac12\log v_2$, where $C_\rho$ is independent of $m_1,m_2,v_1,v_2$. The mean quadratic equals $(m_1-\rho m_2)^2+\beta m_2^2$, so its unique minimizing, hence ELBO-maximizing, means are $m_1=m_2=0$.

For each variance, the part depending on $v$ is $g(v)=-v/(2\beta)+(1/2)\log v$. Its derivative is $g'(v)=(\beta-v)/(2\beta v)$, positive for $0<v<\beta$ and negative for $v>\beta$. Thus the unique maximizer is $v=\beta$. Since $0<|\rho|<1$, $0<\beta<1$, proving strict variance underestimation.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space. Let $\gamma:\Omega\to[0,\infty]$ be measurable and suppose
$$Z:=\int_\Omega\gamma\,d\mu\in(0,\infty).$$
Define the normalized target density $\pi:=\gamma/Z$. Then $\int\pi\,d\mu=1$. For a measurable probability density $q\ge0$ (that is, $\int_\Omega q\,d\mu=1$), write $q\ll_\mu\pi$ to mean $q=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $\{\pi=0\}$. This is a support condition on the two densities. It ensures that the induced probability measures $Q:=q\,\mu$ and $\Pi:=\pi\,\mu$ have $Q\ll\Pi$.

The normalization follows from positive-scalar homogeneity of the nonnegative integral:
$$\int\pi\,d\mu=Z^{-1}\int\gamma\,d\mu=1.$$
The induced density set functions are measures by [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]]. Their total masses are one: $Q(\Omega)=1$ by the probability-density hypothesis on $q$, and $\Pi(\Omega)=1$ by the preceding calculation. To verify the absolute-continuity claim, let $A\in\mathcal A$ satisfy $\Pi(A)=0$. Then $\int_A\pi\,d\mu=0$, so the zero-integral criterion gives $\pi=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $A$. The support condition then gives $q=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $A$, and hence $Q(A)=0$. The homogeneity and zero-integral criteria used here are [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]] and [[thm-nonnegative-integral-zero-iff-zero-almost-everywhere]].

Call $q$ **admissible** when $q\ll_\mu\pi$ and
$$\int_\Omega q\bigl(|\log\gamma|+|\log q|\bigr)\,d\mu<\infty.$$
Use the extended logarithm $\log0=-\infty$, agreeing with [[def-natural-logarithm]] on positive inputs. Since $\int\gamma\,d\mu<\infty$ and $\int q\,d\mu=1$, both functions are finite $\mu$-almost everywhere: for either $f=\gamma$ or $f=q$, $\mu\{f=\infty\}\le n^{-1}\int f\,d\mu$ for every $n\ge1$. Interpret the weighted logarithmic terms on this measurable conull set and set them equal to zero on its measurable null complement, so the resulting functions remain measurable. In particular, set $q|\log\gamma|$, $q|\log q|$, $q\log\gamma$, and $q\log q$ equal to zero on $\{q=0\}$. On the set where $q>0$, admissibility implies $\gamma>0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere. Define the finite real number
$$\operatorname{ELBO}(q):=\int_\Omega q(\log\gamma-\log q)\,d\mu.$$
A **variational family** is a nonempty set of admissible densities. A maximizing member need not exist.

For a finite integer $m\ge1$, let $\Omega=\prod_{j=1}^m\Omega_j$, let each $(\Omega_j,\mathcal A_j,\mu_j)$ be sigma-finite, and let $\mu=\bigotimes_{j=1}^m\mu_j$. A **mean-field density** is a product $q(z)=\prod_{j=1}^m q_j(z_j)$ of probability densities $q_j$; it belongs to the admissible mean-field family only when the product satisfies the support and integrability conditions above. Tonelli gives $\int q\,d\mu=1$. The product form alone does not guarantee support or finite ELBO.

In a dominated Bayesian model, a posterior interpretation is available only with the model hypotheses and on fibers with finite positive evidence, as in [[thm-bayes-formula-for-dominated-kernels]] and [[thm-conditional-density-formula]]. In particular, [[def-likelihood-density]] supplies separate likelihood versions but does not assert joint measurability in parameter and data. Supply the single jointly measurable density $\gamma$ explicitly before using Tonelli or a posterior-kernel formula. No quotient is formed at zero or infinite normalizer.

spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int g\,d(f\,d\mu)=\int gf\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $f\in L^1(\mathbb P)$
be real-valued, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval containing $f(x)$ for
almost every $x$, and let $\varphi:I\to\mathbb R$ be convex with
$\varphi\circ f\in L^1(\mathbb P)$. Then
$$\varphi\!\left(\int f\,d\mathbb P\right)\le\int\varphi(f)\,d\mathbb P.$$

For all $x,y\in\mathbb R$ and $0\le t\le1$,
$$\exp((1-t)x+ty)\le(1-t)\exp x+t\exp y.$$
If $0<t<1$, equality holds exactly when $x=y$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space and let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int f\,d\mu=0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad f=0 \text{ almost everywhere.}$$

Put $\alpha=q_j\mu_j$ and $
u=v\mu_{-j}$. They are probabilities and the law with density $q$ is their product by [F1]–[F3]. A density is positive and finite almost surely under its own probability, since its zero set has mass zero and its infinite set has reference measure zero. Thus $A(x)=\log q_j(x)$ and $B(y)=\log v(y)$ are finite almost surely, and [F8] gives $\log q=A+B$ almost surely. Choose a finite integer $K$ for which $p:=
u(|B|\le K)>0$; such a $K$ exists because those events increase to a full-measure set. On that event $|A|\le|A+B|+K$, so product integration [F2]–[F3] yields $p\int|A|d\alpha\le\int|A+B|d(\alpha\otimes
u)+Kp<\infty$. Interchanging $A$ and $B$ and choosing an analogous positive-probability bounded event proves $\int|B|d
u<\infty$. Hence $H=\int B d
u$ is finite, including $H=0$ for the unit complementary factor.

By [F2] and $Z<\infty$, the marginal $G(x):=\int\gamma(x,y)d\mu_{-j}(y)$ is finite for $\mu_j$-almost every $x$. Fix such an $x$. Under $
u$, define $g(y)=\gamma(x,y)/v(y)$ on $\{0<v<\infty\}$; arbitrary values on its $
u$-null complement do not matter. Then $\int g d
u=\int_{\{0<v<\infty\}}\gamma(x,y)d\mu_{-j}(y)\le G(x)$ by [F3]. In particular $g$ is finite almost surely. Write $L=\log g$, allowing $L=-\infty$ at $g=0$. Its positive part is integrable since $\log^+g\le g$, and the defined expected-log convention and integrability of $B$ give $\int Ld
u=h_j(x)-H$ in the extended sense; in particular $h_j(x)$ cannot equal $+\infty$.

Let $L_n=\max(L,-n)$. Its negative part is bounded and its positive part is integrable by step 2.1, so $L_n$ is integrable. Also $e^{L_n}=\max(g,e^{-n})\le g+1$ is integrable. Apply [F4] with the convex exponential [F5] to obtain $\exp(\int L_n d
u)\le\int e^{L_n}d
u$. The negative parts increase to $L^-$, so [F6] gives $\int L_n d
u\downarrow\int Ld
u$, possibly $-\infty$. By [F7], the right side tends to $\int g d
u$, with domination $g+1$; continuity of the exponential and $e^{-\infty}=0$ therefore give $\exp(h_j(x)-H)\le\int g d
u\le G(x)$.

The inequality in step 3.1 holds for $\mu_j$-almost every $x$. Multiply it by $e^H$ and integrate using [F2] to obtain $c_j\le e^H\int Gd\mu_j=e^HZ<\infty$. Since $h_j$ is finite $\alpha$-almost surely, $e^{h_j}>0$ on an $\alpha$-full measurable set. If $c_j=0$, [F9] would make this set $\mu_j$-null, hence $\alpha$-null by [F3], contradicting $\alpha(\Omega_j)=1$. Thus $c_j>0$. This does not prove admissibility of the normalized replacement, which remains a separate requirement.

**Output:** The current admissible product density after at most $N$ full sweeps, together with a status indicating whether the requested sweeps completed or a coordinate update was unavailable.

For each sweep $t=1,\ldots,N$, visit coordinates in the fixed order $j=1,\ldots,m$. At coordinate $j$, keep $q_{-j}:=\prod_{k\ne j}q_k$ fixed; for $m=1$, the empty product reference space is a singleton with unit measure $\mu_{-j}$ and its density is $1$. Form the conditional log expectation
$$h_j(z_j):=\int_{\prod_{k\ne j}\Omega_k}\log\gamma(z_j,z_{-j})q_{-j}(z_{-j})\,d\mu_{-j}(z_{-j}).$$

$$c_j:=\int_{\Omega_j}e^{h_j(z_j)}\,\mu_j(dz_j).$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int g\,d(f\,d\mu)=\int gf\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the

4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
([[def-probability-measure]]). Absolute continuity $P\ll Q$ has the convention
of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If
$P\not\ll Q$, define $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and
let $r=dP/dQ$ be a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative of its
Radon–Nikodym class; such a representative exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].
On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This
function is measurable: for $a\ge0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r>\exp(a)\}$, and for
$a<0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r=0\}\cup\{r>\exp(a)\}$, by the inverse and
monotonicity properties of the natural logarithm
([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]). These are
measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since
$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$ by
[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$
The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,
$$0\le \frac{\log s}{s}=\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{u}\le\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{\sqrt u}\le\frac2{\sqrt s}.$$
Thus $t\log t\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$; here $L=\log$ by
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and
[[def-integral-logarithm]]. On $(0,\infty)$, $\psi$ is a product of continuous
functions by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $\psi$ is continuous on
$[0,\infty)$ and $\psi(r)$ is measurable by
[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts
([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]],
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

For $0<t\le1$, the function $-t\log t$ has derivative $-\log t-1$ and
maximum $1/e$ at $t=1/e$: $e=\exp(1)>1$ by
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $1/e=\exp(-1)$ by
[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and $\log(1/e)=-1$ by
[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and the inverse definition. The mean value
theorem gives increase before and decrease after this point
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]],
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).
At $t=0$ the negative part is zero. Since $Q$ is a probability measure,
$$\int \psi(r)^-\,dQ\le\frac1e.$$
The change-of-measure identity of [[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]],
applied to $\ell^-$ gives $\int\ell^-\,dP=\int\psi(r)^-\,dQ\le1/e$,
so $\int\ell\,dP$ is well-defined; applying it to both positive and negative
parts gives
$$D(P\|Q)=\int\ell\,dP=\int\psi(r)\,dQ=\int r\log r\,dQ,$$
with $0\log0:=0$ and a finite negative part. Therefore the extended integral
is well-defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.

This convention is directional: the first argument must be absolutely
continuous with respect to the second for the integral formula to apply.

[[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]. For probability measures $P,Q$ on one

$(\mathsf X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a sigma-finite measure space: it is a set
with a sigma-algebra and measure ([[def-measure-space]]), and there is a
countable measurable cover by sets of finite $\mu$-measure
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]). Let
$\gamma:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ be a finite-valued measurable function with
$Z:=\int\gamma\,d\mu\in(0,\infty)$, and put $\pi=\gamma/Z$. Let
$q:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ be a finite-valued measurable probability density,
so $\int q\,d\mu=1$, and suppose $q=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on
$\{\gamma=0\}$. Assume
$$\int q\bigl(|\log\gamma|+|\log q|\bigr)\,d\mu<\infty,$$
where each term with $q=0$ is defined to be zero. Then
$$\log Z =\int q(\log\gamma-\log q)\,d\mu +D(q\,\mu\|\pi\,\mu).$$
In particular, the first integral is at most $\log Z$. This identity concerns
normalized densities only; it does not assert posterior existence for an
unspecified statistical model.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Fix any admissible replacement $r_j$ and form $u=r_jq_{-j}$. Tonelli [F5] gives $\int u\,d\mu=1$, and the product rectangle formula [F4] gives $\mathbb P_u:=u\mu=\bigotimes_{k=1}^m(u_k\mu_k)$ is the product probability. Each coordinate density $u_k$ is positive and finite almost surely under its factor law; put $X_k=\log u_k(Z_k)$ and $S=\log u(Z)=\sum_{k=1}^mX_k$. By [F1], $\mathbb E_u|S|=\int u|\log u|d\mu<\infty$. Fix $j$ and put $R=\sum_{k\ne j}X_k$, which is finite almost surely under the product of the other factor laws. Since $\{|R|\le n\}$ increases to a full-measure set, choose an integer $K$ for which $p:=\mathbb P_u(|R|\le K)>0$. Product integration from [F5] and [F6] then gives $p\int u_j|\log u_j|d\mu_j=\int_{\{|R|\le K\}}|X_j|\,d\mathbb P_u\le\int|S|d\mathbb P_u+Kp<\infty$, using $|X_j|\le|S|+|R|$ on that event. Thus every factor log is integrable; the same argument applies to the current factor and to $q_j^*$ because their products are admissible.

For each admissible replacement $u_j$, [F1] makes $u\log\gamma$ absolutely integrable. Fubini [F7] applies also to $u|\log\gamma|$, so $\int u_j|h_j|d\mu_j<\infty$ and exchanging the $j$ and $-j$ integrals gives $\int u\log\gamma d\mu=\int u_jh_jd\mu_j$. By step 1.1, all factor log terms are integrable, so $\log u=\log u_j+\log q_{-j}$ almost surely and $\operatorname{ELBO}(u_jq_{-j})=\int u_jh_jd\mu_j-\int u_j\log u_jd\mu_j-\int q_{-j}\log q_{-j}d\mu_{-j}$. The final term is constant over coordinate replacements.

Write $q_j^*=e^{h_j}/c_j$. If $q_j^*=0$, then $h_j=-\infty$ almost everywhere on that set. For any admissible $r_j$, step 2.1 makes $\int r_j|h_j|d\mu_j<\infty$, hence $r_j=0$ almost everywhere there. Thus $r_j\mu_j\ll q_j^*\mu_j$. On $\{q_j^*>0\}$ the ratio $r_j/q_j^*$ is measurable, and for every measurable $A$, $\int_A(r_j/q_j^*)d(q_j^*\mu_j)=\int_{A\cap\{q_j^*>0\}}r_jd\mu_j=\int_Ar_jd\mu_j$, so it is the Radon–Nikodym density.

By [A1] and [F8], $D(r_j\mu_j\|q_j^*\mu_j)=\int r_j\log(r_j/q_j^*)d\mu_j=\int r_j\log r_jd\mu_j-\int r_jh_jd\mu_j+\log c_j$. All terms are finite by step 1.1 and step 2.1. Also $\int q_j^*h_j-\int q_j^*\log q_j^*=\log c_j$. Subtracting the ELBO expressions in step 2.1 therefore gives $\operatorname{ELBO}(q_j^*q_{-j})-\operatorname{ELBO}(r_jq_{-j})=D(r_j\mu_j\|q_j^*\mu_j)\ge0$ by [F9]. The current factor $q_j$ is itself an admissible replacement. Taking $r_j=q_j$ in step 3.2 proves that the update does not decrease ELBO.

By [F3], the procedure has at most $N$ sweeps and at most $m$ coordinate-update blocks in each sweep. An unavailable result returns immediately, so every run is either a prefix ending at that branch or a run through all $N$ sweeps. Since $N$ and $m$ are finite, under [A2] it returns after at most $Nm$ calls. The call-count complexity is therefore $O(Nm)$; no cost for evaluating an individual call is asserted.

derivations.claim: Fix any $c\in\mathbb R$. By the onto clause of [F5], choose $a>0$ with $\log a=c$. Define $\gamma_c=a\gamma$. Homogeneity [F4] gives $Z_c=\int\gamma_c d\mu=aZ$, so $\pi_c=\gamma_c/Z_c=\pi$ and both $Q$ and $\Pi$ remain unchanged. Since $\pi_c=\pi$, the support condition in [F1] is unchanged. On the q-support, $|\log\gamma_c|\le|\log\gamma|+|c|$, so the logarithmic integrability condition remains finite.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space. Let $\gamma:\Omega\to[0,\infty]$ be measurable and suppose
$$Z:=\int_\Omega\gamma\,d\mu\in(0,\infty).$$
Define the normalized target density $\pi:=\gamma/Z$. Then $\int\pi\,d\mu=1$. For a measurable probability density $q\ge0$ (that is, $\int_\Omega q\,d\mu=1$), write $q\ll_\mu\pi$ to mean $q=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $\{\pi=0\}$. This is a support condition on the two densities. It ensures that the induced probability measures $Q:=q\,\mu$ and $\Pi:=\pi\,\mu$ have $Q\ll\Pi$.

The normalization follows from positive-scalar homogeneity of the nonnegative integral:
$$\int\pi\,d\mu=Z^{-1}\int\gamma\,d\mu=1.$$
The induced density set functions are measures by [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]]. Their total masses are one: $Q(\Omega)=1$ by the probability-density hypothesis on $q$, and $\Pi(\Omega)=1$ by the preceding calculation. To verify the absolute-continuity claim, let $A\in\mathcal A$ satisfy $\Pi(A)=0$. Then $\int_A\pi\,d\mu=0$, so the zero-integral criterion gives $\pi=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $A$. The support condition then gives $q=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $A$, and hence $Q(A)=0$. The homogeneity and zero-integral criteria used here are [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]] and [[thm-nonnegative-integral-zero-iff-zero-almost-everywhere]].

Call $q$ **admissible** when $q\ll_\mu\pi$ and
$$\int_\Omega q\bigl(|\log\gamma|+|\log q|\bigr)\,d\mu<\infty.$$
Use the extended logarithm $\log0=-\infty$, agreeing with [[def-natural-logarithm]] on positive inputs. Since $\int\gamma\,d\mu<\infty$ and $\int q\,d\mu=1$, both functions are finite $\mu$-almost everywhere: for either $f=\gamma$ or $f=q$, $\mu\{f=\infty\}\le n^{-1}\int f\,d\mu$ for every $n\ge1$. Interpret the weighted logarithmic terms on this measurable conull set and set them equal to zero on its measurable null complement, so the resulting functions remain measurable. In particular, set $q|\log\gamma|$, $q|\log q|$, $q\log\gamma$, and $q\log q$ equal to zero on $\{q=0\}$. On the set where $q>0$, admissibility implies $\gamma>0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere. Define the finite real number
$$\operatorname{ELBO}(q):=\int_\Omega q(\log\gamma-\log q)\,d\mu.$$
A **variational family** is a nonempty set of admissible densities. A maximizing member need not exist.

For a finite integer $m\ge1$, let $\Omega=\prod_{j=1}^m\Omega_j$, let each $(\Omega_j,\mathcal A_j,\mu_j)$ be sigma-finite, and let $\mu=\bigotimes_{j=1}^m\mu_j$. A **mean-field density** is a product $q(z)=\prod_{j=1}^m q_j(z_j)$ of probability densities $q_j$; it belongs to the admissible mean-field family only when the product satisfies the support and integrability conditions above. Tonelli gives $\int q\,d\mu=1$. The product form alone does not guarantee support or finite ELBO.

In a dominated Bayesian model, a posterior interpretation is available only with the model hypotheses and on fibers with finite positive evidence, as in [[thm-bayes-formula-for-dominated-kernels]] and [[thm-conditional-density-formula]]. In particular, [[def-likelihood-density]] supplies separate likelihood versions but does not assert joint measurability in parameter and data. Supply the single jointly measurable density $\gamma$ explicitly before using Tonelli or a posterior-kernel formula. No quotient is formed at zero or infinite normalizer.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.
