A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be an experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). A **statistic** with target
measurable space $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ is a measurable map
$T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$, where measurability
means that $T^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal A$ for every $B\in\mathcal B$
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]). If
$\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal Y$ is an estimand ([[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]])
and its target set $\mathcal Y$ is equipped with $\mathcal B$, a statistic
$\widehat\psi$ with this same target space is an **estimator of $\psi$**.
The value $\widehat\psi(x)$ is the estimate at observed data $x$. Giving
$\mathcal Y$ a measurable structure is an additional choice; this definition
does not assert that $\psi$ is measurable as a function of the parameter.

Let $((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta))$ be a statistical experiment, where $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ is standard Borel, and let $T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ be a statistic with standard Borel target. Write $P_\theta^T=P_\theta\circ T^{-1}$. The statistic $T$ is **sufficient** if there is one probability kernel $K$ from $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ to $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ such that, for every $\theta\in\Theta$, $A\in\mathcal A$, and $C\in\mathcal B$,

$$P_\theta(A\cap T^{-1}(C))=\int_C K(y,A)\,P_\theta^T(dy).$$

Thus $K(T(x),A)$ is a common version of the conditional probability of $A$ given $T$, under every parameter. The kernel is fixed independently of $\theta$. Under AC, standard Borelness gives each law an individual conditional law through [[thm-existence-of-regular-conditional-distributions-for-standard-borel-targets]] and [[lem-regular-conditional-kernels-factor-through-a-standard-borel-conditioning-variable]]; sufficiency additionally asks that one kernel works across parameters.

A measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$ is **standard Borel** if there are a Polish space $P$ and a bijection $h:E\to P$ such that $A\in\mathcal E$ exactly when $h[A]$ is Borel in $P$. Thus the measurable structure is part of the datum; no particular compatible Polish topology on $E$ is selected.

A topological space is **Polish** when it is separable ([[def-separable-space]]) and completely metrizable: its topology is induced by some complete metric ([[lem-complete-remetrisation]]). No particular compatible complete metric or countable dense subset is part of the structure.

A topological space $X$ is **separable** if some at most countable subset $D\subseteq X$ is dense in $X$ ([[def-dense-top]], [[def-countable]]). Equivalently, every nonempty open subset of $X$ meets $D$.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

Every Cauchy sequence of real numbers ([[def-real-limit]]) converges to a real
number. Together with [[thm-reals-ordered-field]], this completes the
construction: $\mathbb{R}$ is a complete totally ordered field.
The proof uses no form of the axiom of choice.

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

**No choice principle is used.** The one place where a reader expects a choice,
"pick a representative $a/b$ of each rational", is exactly where
[[lem-rat-positive-denominator]] applies: every rational *has* a representative
with positive denominator, so the map $(a,b) \mapsto [(a,b)]$ defined on
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is already **surjective** onto $\mathbb{Q}$,
and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).

The map $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[def-real-numbers]]) is an embedding of ordered
fields. Every real is approximated by rationals: for $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and
rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $q \in \mathbb{Q}$ with
$|x - \hat q| < \hat\varepsilon$. Consequently, strictly between any two
reals lies a rational.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$. A von Neumann natural is the set of its
predecessors, $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), so it can be
used directly as an index set. Define

$$\mathbb{R}^n := \{\, x : x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\},$$

and write $x_k$ for $x(k)$, $k < n$. Two elements of $\mathbb{R}^n$ are equal
exactly when they agree at every $k < n$, functions being equal when they have
the same values. For $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^n$ put

$$d_1(x,y) := \sum_{k<n} |x_k - y_k|, \qquad d_2(x,y) := \sqrt{\ \sum_{k<n} (x_k - y_k)^2\ }, \qquad d_\infty(x,y) := \max\{\, |x_k - y_k| : k < n \,\}.$$

All three are well defined: the finite sums are those of [[def-finite-sum]]; the
sum of squares is nonnegative ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]], [[lem-of-square-positive]])
so it has a unique nonnegative square root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]); and
$\{|x_k - y_k| : k < n\}$ is a nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$, because
$n \ge 1$, so it has a maximum ([[lem-finite-set-has-max]], [[def-max-min]]).

**Then $d_1$, $d_2$ and $d_\infty$ are metrics on $\mathbb{R}^n$**
([[def-metric-space]]).

**Why $n \ge 1$.** For $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^0$ has exactly one element,
the empty function, and $d_1$ and $d_2$ are the empty sum $0$ and its root; but
$d_\infty$ would be the maximum of the empty set, which does not exist. The
hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is therefore not decoration, and it is carried by every
statement about $d_\infty$ in this library.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), let $x \in X$ and let
$r \in \mathbb{R}$ with $r > 0$ ([[def-real-order]]). Define

$$B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) < r \,\}, \qquad \bar B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) \le r \,\}, \qquad S(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) = r \,\}.$$

$B(x,r)$ is the **open ball**, $\bar B(x,r)$ the **closed ball** and $S(x,r)$ the
**sphere** of **centre** $x$ and **radius** $r$. The radius is always a strictly
positive real; a ball of radius $0$ or of negative radius is never written in
this library.

**Immediate consequences of the definitions.** For every $x \in X$ and $r > 0$:

- $x \in B(x,r)$, because $d(x,x) = 0 < r$ (axiom (M1) of [[def-metric-space]]);
  in particular open and closed balls are nonempty.
- $B(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, and
  $\bar B(x,r)$ is the disjoint union of $B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r)$, by trichotomy of
  the order of $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]):
  each $y$ satisfies exactly one of $d(x,y) < r$, $d(x,y) = r$, $d(x,y) > r$.
- If $0 < s \le r$ then $B(x,s) \subseteq B(x,r)$ and
  $\bar B(x,s) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, by transitivity of the order.
- Nonnegativity of the metric ([[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]) is what forces the
  radius convention, and it forces it for the **open** ball only: if $r \le 0$
  then $B(x,r) = \{y : d(x,y) < r\}$ is empty, because $d(x,y) \ge 0 \ge r$
  for every $y$. The other two sets behave differently at $r = 0$, and the
  convention $r > 0$ excludes them for uniformity rather than for emptiness:
  $\bar B(x,0) = S(x,0) = \{x\}$, since $d(x,y) \le 0$ together with
  $d(x,y) \ge 0$ gives $d(x,y) = 0$ and hence $y = x$ by (M1). For $r < 0$ all
  three sets are empty.

**A sphere may be empty, and so the three sets are not on a par.** For $r > 0$
the open and closed balls always contain $x$, but nothing in the definition
produces a point at distance exactly $r$ from $x$. If a metric takes only the
values $0$ and $1$, as the discrete metric on the companion page does, then
$S(x,2) = \emptyset$ while $B(x,2) = \bar B(x,2)$ is the whole space. So
nonemptiness of a sphere is never available by convention: where it is used, it
is proved.

**The ambient space is part of the notation.** $B(x,r)$ depends on $(X,d)$ and
not on $x$ and $r$ alone. When more than one space or more than one metric is in
play we write $B_X(x,r)$, or $B_d(x,r)$, and likewise for $\bar B$ and $S$. This
matters as soon as subspaces appear ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]): a
ball of a subspace is the trace on it of a ball of the ambient space, and the two
are different sets.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]).

A subset $U \subseteq X$ is **open in $(X,d)$** if for every $x \in U$ there is a
real $r > 0$ with $B(x,r) \subseteq U$ ([[def-metric-ball]]). A subset
$F \subseteq X$ is **closed in $(X,d)$** if its complement $X \setminus F$ is
open.

The collection

$$\mathcal{T}_d := \{\, U \subseteq X : U \text{ is open in } (X,d) \,\}$$

of all open subsets is the **metric topology** of $d$ on $X$. A subset of $X$
that is both open and closed is called **clopen**.

**Two sets are open for trivial reasons.** $\emptyset$ is open, because the
defining condition quantifies over no points; and $X$ is open, because
$B(x,r) \subseteq X$ for every $x$ and every $r > 0$. Consequently $X$ and
$\emptyset$ are also closed, and both are clopen.

**A neighbourhood of a point $x$** is any set containing an open set that
contains $x$; an **open neighbourhood** is an open set containing $x$. In a
metric space, a set is a neighbourhood of $x$ exactly when it contains some
ball $B(x,r)$ with $r>0$. Thus $U$ is open exactly when it is a neighbourhood of
each of its points, and metric balls suffice to test this condition.

**The metric, not the set, determines $\mathcal{T}_d$.** Two metrics on the same
set may have different metric topologies, and two different metrics may have the
same one; the systematic comparison is [[def-equivalent-metrics]].

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ be standard Borel spaces. Let $\Pi$ be a prior probability measure on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and let $K$ be a probability kernel from $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ to $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, as in [[def-bayesian-model-as-prior-and-sampling-kernel]]. Let $S:\mathsf Y\to\mathbb R^d$ be a measurable statistic for a fixed integer $d\ge1$, and fix an observed summary $s_0\in\mathbb R^d$. The Euclidean norm is $\|x\|_2=(\sum_{j=1}^d x_j^2)^{1/2}$.

$$M(A\times C)=\int_A K(\theta,S^{-1}(C))\,\Pi(d\theta).$$
The prior and simulator define a joint law by [[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]], and the change-of-variables formula identifies $M$ as the law after applying $S$ ([[thm-change-of-variables-for-expectation]]).

For $\epsilon\ge0$, define the closed tolerance ball
$$B_\epsilon(s_0)=\{s\in\mathbb R^d:\|s-s_0\|_2\le\epsilon\}.$$
Its prior-predictive acceptance probability is
$$p_\epsilon(s_0):=M(\Theta\times B_\epsilon(s_0))\in[0,1].$$
Only when $p_\epsilon(s_0)>0$ define the indicator ABC target by
$$\Pi_\epsilon(A\mid s_0):=\frac{M(A\times B_\epsilon(s_0))}{p_\epsilon(s_0)}\qquad(A\in\mathcal T).$$
This is exactly the conditional law of $\theta$ under the augmented event $S(Y)\in B_\epsilon(s_0)$. The denominator is finite because $M$ is a probability, and no quotient is assigned when the event has probability zero. This target is the posterior given a tolerance event, not in general the full-data posterior or the posterior given the exact summary.

The inputs are a proper prior $\Pi$ on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$, a simulator probability kernel $K(\theta,dy)$, a measurable summary statistic $S:\mathsf Y\to\mathbb R^d$, an observed summary $s_0$, and a tolerance $\epsilon\ge0$ as in [[def-approximate-bayesian-computation]]. The procedure is admissible when $p_\epsilon(s_0)>0$.

1. Draw a candidate parameter $\theta$ from $\Pi$.
2. Conditional on $\theta$, draw synthetic data $Y$ from $K(\theta,\cdot)$, independently of all earlier proposal-simulator pairs.
3. Compute $S(Y)$. If $\|S(Y)-s_0\|_2\le\epsilon$, return $\theta$ and stop. Otherwise repeat from step 1 with a fresh independent pair.

The output is one accepted parameter value. It does not itself assert a finite-run estimate or an accuracy bound for an empirical distribution of accepted values.

Use the model and notation of [[def-approximate-bayesian-computation]] and the procedure [[alg-abc-rejection]]. Let $B=B_\epsilon(s_0)$ and $p=M(\Theta\times B)>0$. Suppose the proposals and simulator outputs form an IID sequence $(\Theta_j,Y_j)_{j\ge1}$ with the prior-simulator joint law. Then the first accepted index
$$N:=\inf\{j\ge1:S(Y_j)\in B\}$$
is finite almost surely, and the accepted parameter has law
$$\mathbb P(\Theta_N\in A)=\frac{M(A\times B)}{p}=\Pi_\epsilon(A\mid s_0)\qquad(A\in\mathcal T).$$
Thus the accepted parameter has exactly the tolerance-conditioned target law. This statement does not identify that target with the full-data posterior or assert an expected proposal count.

Let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on a nonempty set $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]) and fix $x_0\in X$. The **Dirac set function at $x_0$** is

$$\delta_{x_0}(E):=\begin{cases}1,&x_0\in E,\\0,&x_0\notin E,\end{cases}\qquad E\in\mathcal A.$$

The two branches are exhaustive and disjoint. The fact that this set function is a probability measure is proved in [[prop-dirac-measure-is-a-probability-measure]].
For $x_0\in X$, the Dirac set function $\delta_{x_0}$ is a probability measure on every sigma-algebra on $X$.

derivations.claim: Give each finite set its discrete metric $d(x,x')=0$ for equality and $1$ otherwise. Since Cauchy means that tail distances are eventually below every positive radius, a Cauchy sequence is eventually constant at radius $1/2$; the metric is complete. Each finite set is countable and dense in itself, and its singletons are open, so its Borel sigma-algebra is the power set. The identity is a Borel isomorphism to this Polish presentation, so [F4] gives that $\Theta$ and $\mathsf Y$ are standard Borel. For $\mathbb R$, [F5] gives a complete usual metric and countable dense subset $\mathbb Q$; each metric ball is an ordinary open interval, so this metric induces the usual topology. Thus $\mathbb R$ is Polish and its usual Borel space is standard Borel by [F4].

The prior is proper. For each $\theta$, summing the likelihood over the eight binary triples gives $(\theta+(1-\theta))^3=1$, so $K$ is a probability kernel by [F1]. The count $S$ is measurable because its domain is finite.

For $k\in\{0,1,2,3\}$ let $F_k=\{y\in\mathsf Y:S(y)=k\}$ and define $Q(k,D)=|D\cap F_k|/\binom3k$. For $t\notin\{0,1,2,3\}$ set $Q(t,\cdot)=\delta_{(0,0,0)}$. Each value is a probability measure by [F7], and for fixed $D$ the map $t\mapsto Q(t,D)$ is Borel, so $Q$ is a probability kernel. For every $\theta$, $D\subseteq\mathsf Y$, and Borel $C\subseteq\mathbb R$, $K(\theta,D\cap S^{-1}(C))=\sum_{k\in C\cap\{0,1,2,3\}}|D\cap F_k|\theta^k(1-\theta)^{3-k}$ $=\sum_{k\in C\cap\{0,1,2,3\}}Q(k,D)\binom3k\theta^k(1-\theta)^{3-k}=\int_C Q(t,D)K_S(\theta,dt).$ This is the common-kernel criterion [F3], so $S$ is sufficient.

The full-data likelihood at $y_0=(1,1,0)$ is $\theta^2(1-\theta)$. The prior-weighted likelihoods at $1/3$ and $2/3$ are respectively $1/27$ and $2/27$, so their normalization gives posterior masses $1/3$ and $2/3$. For $0\le\epsilon<1$, the condition $|S(Y)-2|\le\epsilon$ is exactly $S(Y)=2$. Its likelihood is $3\theta^2(1-\theta)$, three times the full-data likelihood at either parameter; the prior-weighted masses are $1/9$ and $2/9$, giving the same normalized posterior.

The event in step 3.2 has positive prior-predictive probability $1/3$, so the ABC target is defined. By [F6], the rejection algorithm's accepted parameter has that target law; hence it equals the full-data posterior just computed. Explicitly, the summary likelihood differs from the full-data likelihood by the same positive factor $3$ at both parameters, which cancels from the finite posterior normalization in step 3.2; sufficiency itself was proved independently in step 3.1.

Epsilon=0 still selects S=2 with positive mass 1/3 in steps 3.2–4.1.
The common kernel includes singleton fibers k=0 and k=3 in step 3.1.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(Y_i)_{i\ge1}$ be a real IID sequence with $\mu=\mathbb E[Y_1]$ and $0<\sigma^2:=\operatorname{Var}(Y_1)<\infty$. Then
$$\sqrt n\,(\bar Y_n-\mu)\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma^2).$$

Let $(Y_i)_{i\ge1}$ be real IID random variables on one probability space, where IID means that the variables have a common law and are mutually independent ([[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]). When $\mathbb E|Y_1|<\infty$, write $\mu:=\mathbb E[Y_1]$ and define the Monte Carlo estimate of this expectation by the sample mean $\bar Y_n:=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nY_i$; this is the partial-sum convention of [[def-partial-sums-and-sample-means]]. For each $n\ge2$ and any realized finite real sample, define its sample variance and nonnegative square root by
$$s_n^2:=\frac1{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(Y_i-\bar Y_n)^2,\qquad s_n:=\sqrt{s_n^2}.$$
When $\mathbb E[Y_1^2]<\infty$, write $\sigma^2:=\operatorname{Var}(Y_1)$, using [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]. The population standard error of $\bar Y_n$ is $\sigma/\sqrt n$, and its plug-in estimate is $\widehat{se}_n:=s_n/\sqrt n$. Although the finite-sample quantity $s_n$ is defined for any finite real sample, its interpretation as an estimate of a finite population standard error is used here only under the finite-second-moment condition.

derivations.claim: By [F1], each output has mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$, so its first absolute moment and second moment are finite. Applying [F2] gives $\mathbb E[\bar Y_n]=\mu$ and $\operatorname{Var}(\bar Y_n)=\sigma^2/n$.
The finite-second-moment hypotheses of [F3] hold by [A1] and [F1]. Thus $s_n^2\to\sigma^2$ almost surely and, using the plug-in definition [F5], $\widehat{se}_n/(\sigma/\sqrt n)\to1$.
The sequence has positive finite variance and AC is assumed, so [F4] applies and gives $\sqrt n(\bar Y_n-\mu)\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma^2)$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

For $a>0$, the function $x\mapsto a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and
$$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$
For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with
$$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$

Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a > 0$ and let $r, s \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $r < s$
([[def-rat-order]]), with rational powers as in [[def-rational-power]].

1. **In the exponent.** If $a > 1$ then $a^{r} < a^{s}$; if $a = 1$ then $a^{r} = a^{s} = 1$; if $0 < a < 1$ then $a^{r} > a^{s}$.
2. **In the base.** If $r \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $r > 0$ and $0 < a < b$, then $a^{r} < b^{r}$; so $a \mapsto a^{r}$ is strictly increasing on $\{a \in \mathbb{R} : a > 0\}$.
3. **Comparison with $1$.** For rational $t > 0$: $a > 1$ implies $a^{t} > 1$, and $0 < a < 1$ implies $a^{t} < 1$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

1. Let $X$ be a real random variable, let $\mathbb P_X$ be its law, and let
   $F_X(x)=\mathbb P(X\le x)$. Then $F_X$ is nondecreasing and right-continuous,
   satisfies
   $$\lim_{x\to-\infty}F_X(x)=0,\qquad \lim_{x\to+\infty}F_X(x)=1,$$
   and obeys
   $$\mathbb P_X((a,b])=F_X(b)-F_X(a)\qquad(a<b).$$
2. Conversely, if $F:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is nondecreasing and
   right-continuous with
   $$\lim_{x\to-\infty}F(x)=0,\qquad \lim_{x\to+\infty}F(x)=1,$$
   then there is a unique Borel probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb R$ such
   that
   $$\mu((a,b])=F(b)-F(a)\qquad(a<b),$$
   equivalently
   $$F(x)=\mu((-\infty,x])\qquad(x\in\mathbb R).$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and let
$(S,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space. A **random element** of $S$ is a measurable
map
$$X:(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to(S,\Sigma)$$
in the sense of [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]].

When $S=\mathbb R$ and $\Sigma=\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$ from
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra]], the map $X$ is a **real random variable**.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

1. If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]=\int_0^\infty \mathbb P(X>t)\,dt,$$
   where the right-hand side may be $+\infty$.
2. If $X$ is an integrable real random variable, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]=\int_0^\infty \mathbb P(X>t)\,dt-\int_0^\infty \mathbb P(X<-t)\,dt.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $f : X \to \mathbb C$ be
measurable, and let $0<p<\infty$. Then
$$\int_X |f|^p\,d\mu = p\int_0^\infty t^{p-1}\mu(\{|f|>t\})\,dt = p\int_0^\infty t^{p-1}A_f(t)\,dt,$$
where either side may be $+\infty$.

For rational $p\ne1$ and $0<A<B$,
$$\int_A^B x^{-p}\,dx=\frac{B^{1-p}-A^{1-p}}{1-p}.$$
For $p=1$ and every positive integer $N$,
$$\int_1^{2^N}\frac{dx}{x}\ge\frac N2,\qquad \int_{2^{-N}}^1\frac{dx}{x}\ge\frac N2.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $a\in\mathbb R$ and let
$f:[a,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ be Riemann integrable on every compact interval
$[a,R]$ with $R>a$. If the improper Riemann integral
$$\int_a^\infty f(x)\,dx$$
converges in the sense of [[def-improper-integral-at-infinity]], then $f$ is
Lebesgue integrable on $[a,\infty)$ and
$$\int_{[a,\infty)} f\,d\lambda_1=\int_a^\infty f(x)\,dx.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $a<b$ and let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be
bounded and Riemann integrable. Then $f$ is Lebesgue measurable on $[a,b]$ and
is integrable there, and its Lebesgue integral equals its Riemann integral:
$$\int_{[a,b]} f\,d\lambda_1=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx.$$

This is the point at which the completeness of Lebesgue measure is used
essentially: the proof obtains a Borel function equal to $f$ almost everywhere,
and measurability of $f$ itself is then a completeness statement.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $n,m\ge1$. Every continuous map
$f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is Borel measurable in
the sense of [[def-borel-and-lebesgue-measurable-function-on-rn]].

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space and let
$f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ be measurable for the Borel sigma-algebra on
the extended real line. Products of functions use
$\odot_X$ from [[def-measurable-pointwise-extended-real-product]], and $cf$
abbreviates $\underline c\odot_X f$ for the constant function $\underline c$.
The magnitude function is $|f|=\max(f,-f)$ as in
[[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]]. Then:

1. $cf$ is measurable for every real scalar $c$;
2. $\max(f,g)$, $\min(f,g)$, $|f|$, $f^+$, and $f^-$ are measurable;
3. if the partial pointwise sum $f+g$ is defined at every point, then it is measurable;
4. the pointwise product $fg:=f\odot_X g$ is measurable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(Y_i)_{i\ge1}$ be a real IID sequence with $\mathbb E|Y_1|<\infty$, and set $\mu=\mathbb E[Y_1]$. Then $\mathbb E|\bar Y_n-\mu|\to0$, so $\bar Y_n\to\mu$ in probability; moreover, $\bar Y_n\to\mu$ almost surely.

Let $(Y_i)_{i\ge1}$ be real IID random variables on one probability space, where IID means that the variables have a common law and are mutually independent ([[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]). When $\mathbb E|Y_1|<\infty$, write $\mu:=\mathbb E[Y_1]$ and define the Monte Carlo estimate of this expectation by the sample mean $\bar Y_n:=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nY_i$; this is the partial-sum convention of [[def-partial-sums-and-sample-means]]. For each $n\ge2$ and any realized finite real sample, define its sample variance and nonnegative square root by
$$s_n^2:=\frac1{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(Y_i-\bar Y_n)^2,\qquad s_n:=\sqrt{s_n^2}.$$
When $\mathbb E[Y_1^2]<\infty$, write $\sigma^2:=\operatorname{Var}(Y_1)$, using [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]. The population standard error of $\bar Y_n$ is $\sigma/\sqrt n$, and its plug-in estimate is $\widehat{se}_n:=s_n/\sqrt n$. Although the finite-sample quantity $s_n$ is defined for any finite real sample, its interpretation as an estimate of a finite population standard error is used here only under the finite-second-moment condition.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element, let
$\mathbb P_X$ be its law, and let $g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb R$ or
$g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb C$ be measurable.

1. If $g\ge0$, then
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$
2. If $g(X)$ is integrable, then $g$ is integrable with respect to
   $\mathbb P_X$ and the same formula holds:
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

derivations.claim: For $x\ge1$, $x\mapsto x^{3/2}$ is strictly increasing by [F2], so its positive reciprocal $x^{-3/2}$ is decreasing; it is continuous by [F1]. Thus the displayed $F$ is nondecreasing and right-continuous, including at $x=1$ where its two formulas agree. For $x\ge1$, [F2] gives $x^{1/2}\ge1$, hence $0\le x^{-3/2}=x^{-1}x^{-1/2}\le x^{-1}$. Since $x^{-1}\to0$, $F(x)\to1$ as $x\to+\infty$; also $F(x)\to0$ as $x\to-\infty$. By [A1] and [F3], $F$ defines a Borel probability law $\mu$. Since $F(1)=0$, $\mu((-\infty,1])=0$ and hence $\mu([1,\infty))=1$. Restricting $\mu$ to $[1,\infty)$ gives a probability space on which the identity random variable $Y(x)=x$ is measurable by [F4], has CDF $F$, and satisfies $Y\ge1$.

If $0\le t<1$, $F(t)=0$ and hence $\mathbb P(Y>t)=1$. For $t\ge1$, the CDF gives $\mathbb P(Y>t)=1-F(t)=t^{-3/2}$. By the nonnegative expectation definition [F5] and layer-cake formula [F6], $\mathbb E[Y]=1+\int_1^\infty t^{-3/2}\,dt$. The function $t^{-3/2}$ is nonnegative and continuous on every compact $[1,R]$ by [F1]. For $R>1$, [F8] gives $\int_1^R t^{-3/2}\,dt=2(1-R^{-1/2})\to2$; [F9] identifies this finite improper integral with its Lebesgue value. Therefore $\mathbb E[Y]=3$.

Since $Y\ge1$ on the restricted space, $\mathbb P(|Y|>t)=\mathbb P(Y>t)$. By the nonnegative expectation definition [F5] and [F7] with $p=2$, $\mathbb E[Y^2]=1+2\int_1^\infty t^{-1/2}\,dt$. Extend $h(t)=t^{-1/2}$ from $[1,\infty)$ by $h(t)=1$ for $t<1$; it is continuous at $1$ and on both pieces, so [F11] makes it Borel. Since $[1,N]$ is Borel, [F12] makes each $h\mathbf1_{[1,N]}$ measurable. For each integer $N\ge2$, [F1] gives continuity of $t^{-1/2}$ on $[1,N]$, so [F17] makes it bounded and Riemann integrable there; [F8] and [F10] then give $\int_{[1,N]}t^{-1/2}\,d\lambda=2(\sqrt N-1)$. These values diverge because the natural numbers are unbounded. The truncations increase pointwise to $t^{-1/2}\mathbf1_{[1,\infty)}$, so [F13] gives $\int_{[1,\infty)}t^{-1/2}\,d\lambda=+\infty$. Hence $\mathbb E[Y^2]=+\infty$.

The given sequence has common law $\mu$. By [F11], the functions $y\mapsto|y|$ and $y\mapsto y^2$ are Borel; applying [F16] to these nonnegative functions gives $\mathbb E|Y_1|=\mathbb E|Y|=3$ and $\mathbb E[Y_1^2]=\mathbb E[Y^2]=+\infty$. Thus $Y_1$ is integrable, and [F16] applied to the identity gives $\mathbb E[Y_1]=\mathbb E[Y]=3$.

By step 4.1, $\mathbb E|Y_1|=3<\infty$, so [F14] proves strong and weak consistency of $\bar Y_n$. Step 4.1 shows $\mathbb E[Y_1^2]=+\infty$, so the finite-second-moment condition in [F15] fails and no finite population standard error $\sigma/\sqrt n$ is available. For each realized sample of size $n\ge2$, the empirical formula remains a statistic by [F15].

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X,P)$ be a probability space, let $q\ge1$ and $n\ge1$, and let $f:\mathsf X\to\mathbb R$ and $h=(h_1,\ldots,h_q):\mathsf X\to\mathbb R^q$ be measurable with $\int|f|\,dP<\infty$ and $\int|h_j|\,dP<\infty$ for every $j$; these are integrals in [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. For any integrable $g$ write $Pg:=\int_{\mathsf X}g\,dP$. Write $\mu=Pf$ and $\theta=Ph\in\mathbb R^q$, where $\theta$ is known, and use [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]] for variance and covariance. Given an IID sample $X_1,\ldots,X_n\sim P$ as in [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]] and a fixed coefficient $\beta\in\mathbb R^q$, the **control-variate estimator** is

$$\widehat\mu_\beta=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\bigl[f(X_i)-\beta^{\mathsf T}(h(X_i)-\theta)\bigr].$$

For one scalar control this is $n^{-1}\sum_i[f(X_i)-\beta(h(X_i)-\theta)]$. The coefficient is fixed independently of the production sample in this definition; a coefficient fitted from that same sample is treated separately.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability
space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. For each $i$, let
$g_i:(S_i,\Sigma_i)\to(T_i,\mathcal T_i)$ be measurable. Then the family
$(g_i\circ X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent.

Let $n\ge1$, let $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ be independent real random variables on a
common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then
   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$
   in $[0,+\infty]$. In this finite product of expectations, a zero factor
   makes the product zero even when another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise
   multiplication has its usual extended nonnegative meaning.
2. If every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable
   and the same factorization holds in $\mathbb R$.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element, let
$\mathbb P_X$ be its law, and let $g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb R$ or
$g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb C$ be measurable.

1. If $g\ge0$, then
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$
2. If $g(X)$ is integrable, then $g$ is integrable with respect to
   $\mathbb P_X$ and the same formula holds:
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ and $(Y_j)_{j\in J}$ be finite families of square-integrable real random variables on one common probability space. Then covariance is symmetric, and for real scalars $a_i,b_j$,
$$\operatorname{Cov}\!\left(\sum_{i\in I}a_iX_i,\sum_{j\in J}b_jY_j\right)=\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{j\in J}a_ib_j\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,Y_j).$$
This includes empty sums and constant summands. On a finite probability space all real random variables are square-integrable, so the original finite-space case is included with the same centered-product covariance.

derivations.claim: For $Z_i=f(X_i)-\beta^{\mathsf T}(h(X_i)-\theta)$, the expectation convention [F6] and linearity [F3] give $E Z_i=Pf-\beta^{\mathsf T}(Ph-\theta)=\mu$. Thus $E\widehat\mu_\beta=\mu$.
The $Z_i$ are the same measurable function of the IID variables $X_i$, so [F2] and [F4] make them IID.
By [F7]–[F8], the variance as a function of $\beta$ is $\operatorname{Var}_P(f)-2\beta^{\mathsf T}c+\beta^{\mathsf T}\Sigma\beta$.

Expanding the centered square of $n^{-1}\sum_i Z_i$, the diagonal terms contribute $n^{-2}n\operatorname{Var}(Z_1)$. For $i\ne j$, $Z_i-EZ_i$ and $Z_j-EZ_j$ are independent integrable variables, so [F5] factors their product expectation into zero. Hence $\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\mu_\beta)=n^{-1}\operatorname{Var}(Z_1)=n^{-1}\operatorname{Var}_P(f-\beta^{\mathsf T}h)$.

If $\Sigma$ is positive definite, substituting $c=\Sigma\beta^*$ and completing the square gives $\operatorname{Var}_P(f)-c^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}c+(\beta-\beta^*)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma(\beta-\beta^*)$. The last term is nonnegative and vanishes only at $\beta=\beta^*$; for $q=1$ the displayed scalar formula follows.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

Let $X,Y$ be square-integrable real random variables on one probability space.
Then
$$\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathbb E[X^2]-\mathbb E[X]^2,$$
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\mathbb E[XY]-\mathbb E[X]\mathbb E[Y].$$
Moreover, covariance is symmetric and bilinear on finite linear combinations.
On finite full-power-set probability spaces these formulas reduce to the
published finite identities.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element, let
$\mathbb P_X$ be its law, and let $g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb R$ or
$g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb C$ be measurable.

1. If $g\ge0$, then
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$
2. If $g(X)$ is integrable, then $g$ is integrable with respect to
   $\mathbb P_X$ and the same formula holds:
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability
space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

derivations.claim: In dimension one, let $\mu$ be the law of $U_1$. By [F7], the expectations defining the covariance are the corresponding $\mu$-integrals. Expanding those integrals using [F8] and applying [F3] gives $2\operatorname{Cov}(G(U_1),H(U_1))=\int\!\int (G(x)-G(y))(H(x)-H(y))\,\mu(dx)\mu(dy)$. The integrand is nonpositive for every $x,y$ because the two functions have opposite monotonicity, so the covariance is nonpositive. The two differences are square-integrable on $(\mathbb R^2,\mu\times\mu)$, so [F4] makes their product integrable and justifies the double integral.

Assume the claim holds for $d-1$ and first suppose $G,H$ are bounded. By [F2] the joint law is $\mu	imes
u$, where $\mu$ is the first $d-1$ coordinate laws and $
u$ is the law of $U_d$. The change-of-variables formula [F7] identifies expectations under the joint law with integrals against $\mu	imes
u$. Define $G_0(x)=\int G(x,z)\,
u(dz)$ and $H_0(x)=\int H(x,z)\,
u(dz)$. Fubini [F3] makes these measurable and bounded; they retain their respective coordinate monotonicities. For each fixed $x$, step 1.1 applied to the last coordinate gives $\operatorname{Cov}_
u(G(x,U_d),H(x,U_d))\le0$, and the induction hypothesis gives $\operatorname{Cov}_\mu(G_0,H_0)\le0$.

Expanding both sides by the covariance formula [F5], using expectation linearity [F8], the joint law identity [F7], and Fubini [F3] yields $\operatorname{Cov}(G(U),H(U))=\int \operatorname{Cov}_\nu(G(x,U_d),H(x,U_d))\,\mu(dx)+\operatorname{Cov}_\mu(G_0,H_0)\le0$. Thus the bounded case holds in dimension $d$, completing the induction.

For general square-integrable $G,H$, clamp each function to $[-m,m]$. The clamps remain coordinatewise monotone and bounded, with $|G_m|\le|G|$, $|H_m|\le|H|$, $|G_m-G|^2\le G^2$, and $|H_m-H|^2\le H^2$. Applying [F6] to the squared differences gives $L^2$ convergence, while $\|G_m\|_2\le\|G\|_2$ and $\|H_m\|_2\le\|H\|_2$. Cauchy–Schwarz [F4] shows that $E|G_m-G|$ and $E|H_m-H|$ tend to zero, and that $E|G_mH_m-GH|\le\|G_m-G\|_2\|H_m\|_2+\|G\|_2\|H_m-H\|_2$ tends to zero. Thus expectation linearity [F8] and the covariance identity [F5] imply $\operatorname{Cov}(G_m(U),H_m(U))\to\operatorname{Cov}(G(U),H(U))$. Each bounded covariance is nonpositive by step 3.1, so the limit is nonpositive.

Let $d,n\ge1$, let $\mathsf X$ be a measurable space, let $P$ be a probability law on $\mathsf X$, and let $f:\mathsf X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. On a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$, let $U_i=(U_{i1},\ldots,U_{id})$, $i=1,\ldots,n$, be IID random vectors whose coordinates are mutually independent and each have the uniform law on $[0,1]$, meaning $\mathbb P(U_{ij}\le t)=t$ for $0\le t\le1$. Let $T:[0,1]^d\to\mathsf X$ be measurable and satisfy $T(U_1)\sim P$. Define the reflected input $1-U_i=(1-U_{i1},\ldots,1-U_{id})$ and the antithetic estimator by

$$\widehat\mu_{\rm anti}=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{f(T(U_i))+f(T(1-U_i))}{2}.$$

The two outputs in each pair may be dependent; pairs with different indices are independent. The variance comparison in the theorem uses $2n$ function evaluations and compares with an ordinary mean of $2n$ independent $P$-draws. IID and mutual independence have the meanings of [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]], and variance/covariance use [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]].

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. For each $i$, let
$g_i:(S_i,\Sigma_i)\to(T_i,\mathcal T_i)$ be measurable. Then the family
$(g_i\circ X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent.

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ and $(Y_j)_{j\in J}$ be finite families of square-integrable real random variables on one common probability space. Then covariance is symmetric, and for real scalars $a_i,b_j$,
$$\operatorname{Cov}\!\left(\sum_{i\in I}a_iX_i,\sum_{j\in J}b_jY_j\right)=\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{j\in J}a_ib_j\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,Y_j).$$
This includes empty sums and constant summands. On a finite probability space all real random variables are square-integrable, so the original finite-space case is included with the same centered-product covariance.

Let $n\ge1$, let $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ be independent real random variables on a
common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then
   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$
   in $[0,+\infty]$. In this finite product of expectations, a zero factor
   makes the product zero even when another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise
   multiplication has its usual extended nonnegative meaning.
2. If every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable
   and the same factorization holds in $\mathbb R$.

Let $d\ge1$, let $U_1,\ldots,U_d$ be independent real random variables, and let $G,H:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be Borel functions with $E[G(U)^2]<\infty$ and $E[H(U)^2]<\infty$. A function is nondecreasing in coordinate $j$ when increasing only its $j$th input cannot decrease its value; nonincreasing is defined with the reverse inequality. Suppose $G$ is nondecreasing in each coordinate and $H$ is nonincreasing in each coordinate. Then $\operatorname{Cov}(G(U),H(U))\le0$.

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability
space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element, let
$\mathbb P_X$ be its law, and let $g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb R$ or
$g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb C$ be measurable.

1. If $g\ge0$, then
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$
2. If $g(X)$ is integrable, then $g$ is integrable with respect to
   $\mathbb P_X$ and the same formula holds:
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$

derivations.claim: For a uniform coordinate, $\mathbb P(U_{1j}=s)=0$ for every $s\in[0,1]$, since $\mathbb P(U_{1j}\le s)=s$ and the left limit of this cdf at $s$ is also $s$. Thus for $0\le t\le1$, $\mathbb P(1-U_{1j}\le t)=\mathbb P(U_{1j}\ge1-t)=1-\mathbb P(U_{1j}<1-t)=t$. By [F3], the reflected coordinates remain independent; [F4] then shows $1-U_1$ has the same product-uniform law as $U_1$. Therefore both $T(U_1)$ and $T(1-U_1)$ have law $P$. Applying [F10] to $f$ and $f^2$ identifies their means and variances as $\mu$ and $\sigma^2$, so $Y$ and $\widetilde Y$ have the same law, mean $\mu$, and variance $\sigma^2$.
The pair value $Z_i=[f(T(U_i))+f(T(1-U_i))]/2$ is a measurable function of $U_i$. Thus the $Z_i$ are IID by [F2]–[F3], each has mean $\mu$ by [F9], and their average is unbiased.

By [F5]–[F6], $\operatorname{Var}(Z_i)=[\operatorname{Var}(Y)+\operatorname{Var}(\widetilde Y)+2\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\widetilde Y)]/4=[\sigma^2+\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\widetilde Y)]/2$. For distinct $i,j$, the centered $Z_i,Z_j$ are independent, so [F7] gives zero covariance; expanding the centered square of their average therefore gives the stated variance divided by $n$.

The mean of $2n$ independent $P$-draws has variance $\sigma^2/(2n)$ by the same centered-square expansion and [F7]. Comparing this with step 2.1 gives the iff conditions for weak and strict variance reduction.

For each coordinate choose a monotonicity direction for $g$: define $S_j(v)=v_j$ in a nondecreasing coordinate and $S_j(v)=1-v_j$ in a nonincreasing coordinate; a constant coordinate may be assigned either direction. Then $S$ is a coordinatewise reflection map with $S(S(v))=v$ and $S(1-v)=1-S(v)$. By [F3] and [F4], $V=S(U_1)$ again has independent uniform coordinates, and $\phi=g\circ S$ is coordinatewise nondecreasing on $[0,1]^d$. Define the coordinatewise clamp $C:\mathbb R^d\to[0,1]^d$ by $C_j(x)=\min\{1,\max\{0,x_j\}\}$. It is continuous and nondecreasing in every coordinate, and $C(1-v)=1-C(v)$. Hence $\bar\phi:=\phi\circ C$ is a Borel coordinatewise nondecreasing function on $\mathbb R^d$, while $v\mapsto\bar\phi(1-v)$ is Borel and coordinatewise nonincreasing. On the cube these extensions equal $\phi(v)$ and $\phi(1-v)$, respectively; the identities for $S$ give $g(U_1)=\phi(V)$ and $g(1-U_1)=\phi(1-V)$. By step 1.1, these functions are square-integrable, so [F8] applies to $\bar\phi(V)$ and $\bar\phi(1-V)$ and gives $\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\widetilde Y)\le0$. In the stated ordered-subset case, $u\le v$ coordinatewise implies $T(u)\le T(v)$ and then $f(T(u))\le f(T(v))$, which makes $g$ nondecreasing and is the special case $S(v)=v$.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X,P)$ be a probability space, let $f:\mathsf X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable with $\int_{\mathsf X}|f|\,dP<\infty$, write $Pf=\int_{\mathsf X}f\,dP$, and let $H\ge1$ and $A_1,\ldots,A_H$ be a finite measurable partition of $\mathsf X$ with $p_h=P(A_h)>0$. Define the conditional stratum law by $P_h(B)=P(B\cap A_h)/p_h$ for $B\in\mathcal X$. Choose fixed integers $n_h\ge1$ and put $n=\sum_{h=1}^H n_h$. Draw mutually independent variables $X_{hj}$, with $X_{h1},\ldots,X_{hn_h}$ IID under $P_h$ as in [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]], and define $\bar f_h=n_h^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{n_h}f(X_{hj})$. Expectations and variances use [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]] and [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]. The **stratified Monte Carlo estimator** of $Pf$ is

$$\widehat\mu_{\rm strat}=\sum_{h=1}^H p_h\bar f_h.$$

The allocation $(n_1,\ldots,n_H)$ is part of the design. A variance comparison must specify it and the comparator.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element, let
$\mathbb P_X$ be its law, and let $g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb R$ or
$g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb C$ be measurable.

1. If $g\ge0$, then
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$
2. If $g(X)$ is integrable, then $g$ is integrable with respect to
   $\mathbb P_X$ and the same formula holds:
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability
space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

Let $n\ge1$, let $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ be independent real random variables on a
common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then
   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$
   in $[0,+\infty]$. In this finite product of expectations, a zero factor
   makes the product zero even when another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise
   multiplication has its usual extended nonnegative meaning.
2. If every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable
   and the same factorization holds in $\mathbb R$.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Let $(\mathcal F_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of sigma-algebras on a
probability space, and let $J_0,\dots,J_{m-1}\subseteq I$ be pairwise disjoint
index sets. For each $r<m$, define

$$\mathcal G_r:=\sigma\left(\bigcup_{i\in J_r}\mathcal F_i\right).$$

Then the sigma-algebras $\mathcal G_0,\dots,\mathcal G_{m-1}$ are independent.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space and let
$f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ be measurable for the Borel sigma-algebra on
the extended real line. Products of functions use
$\odot_X$ from [[def-measurable-pointwise-extended-real-product]], and $cf$
abbreviates $\underline c\odot_X f$ for the constant function $\underline c$.
The magnitude function is $|f|=\max(f,-f)$ as in
[[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]]. Then:

1. $cf$ is measurable for every real scalar $c$;
2. $\max(f,g)$, $\min(f,g)$, $|f|$, $f^+$, and $f^-$ are measurable;
3. if the partial pointwise sum $f+g$ is defined at every point, then it is measurable;
4. the pointwise product $fg:=f\odot_X g$ is measurable.

derivations.claim: For each $h$, [F1] gives $\int_{\mathsf X}f^2\,dP_h=p_h^{-1}\int_{A_h}f^2\,dP<\infty$. Since $|f|\le1+f^2$, $f$ is integrable under $P$ and every $P_h$. Thus [F3] gives $\mu_h=p_h^{-1}\int_{A_h}f\,dP$, and [F4] plus the finite partition identity yield $E\widehat\mu_{\rm strat}=\sum_h p_h\mu_h=\sum_h\int_{A_h}f\,dP=\int f\,dP=\mu$.

For fixed $h$, expand the centered square of $\bar f_h$. The diagonal terms give $\sigma_h^2/n_h$; for distinct draws the centered product expectation is zero by independence and [F5]. Thus $\operatorname{Var}(\bar f_h)=\sigma_h^2/n_h$.

Splitting $\int(f-\mu)^2dP$ over the partition and writing $f-\mu=(f-\mu_h)+(\mu_h-\mu)$ on $A_h$, the cross term integrates to zero since $\int_{A_h}(f-\mu_h)dP=p_hE_{P_h}(f-\mu_h)=0$. Therefore $\operatorname{Var}_P(f)=\sum_h p_h\sigma_h^2+\sum_h p_h(\mu_h-\mu)^2$.

By [F1] and [F7], the sigma-algebras generated by all individual draws are independent. Grouping them by stratum and applying [F8] shows that the sigma-algebras generated by the disjoint stratum blocks are independent. Each $\bar f_h$ is measurable with respect to its block sigma-algebra because it is a finite sum of measurable values of $f$, using [F9]; hence the stratum averages are independent. Applying [F5] to their centered products and expanding the variance of $\sum_h p_h\bar f_h$ gives $\sum_h p_h^2\sigma_h^2/n_h$.

Under $n_h=np_h$, step 3.1 becomes $n^{-1}\sum_h p_h\sigma_h^2$. The ordinary mean of $n$ IID $P$-draws has variance $\operatorname{Var}_P(f)/n$, by the same centered-square expansion as step 2.1. Step 2.2 shows the difference is $n^{-1}\sum_h p_h(\mu_h-\mu)^2\ge0$, proving the comparison.

For any integrable $g$ write $Pg:=\int_{\mathsf X}g\,dP$. Write $\mu=Pf$ and $\theta=Ph\in\mathbb R^q$, where $\theta$ is known, and use [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]] for variance and covariance. Given an IID sample $X_1,\ldots,X_n\sim P$ as in [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]] and a fixed coefficient $\beta\in\mathbb R^q$, the **control-variate estimator** is

$$\widehat\mu_\beta=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\bigl[f(X_i)-\beta^{\mathsf T}(h(X_i)-\theta)\bigr].$$

For one scalar control this is $n^{-1}\sum_i[f(X_i)-\beta(h(X_i)-\theta)]$. The coefficient is fixed independently of the production sample in this definition; a coefficient fitted from that same sample is treated separately.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$
For IID real $(X_n)_{n\ge1}$ with $\mathbb E|X_1|<\infty$, $S_n/n\to\mu=\mathbb EX_1$ almost surely.

If $X$ is a square-integrable real random variable and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(|X-\mathbb E[X]|\ge a)\le\frac{\operatorname{Var}(X)}{a^2}.$$

Let $n\ge1$, let $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ be independent real random variables on a
common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then
   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$
   in $[0,+\infty]$. In this finite product of expectations, a zero factor
   makes the product zero even when another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise
   multiplication has its usual extended nonnegative meaning.
2. If every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable
   and the same factorization holds in $\mathbb R$.

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability
space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element, let
$\mathbb P_X$ be its law, and let $g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb R$ or
$g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb C$ be measurable.

1. If $g\ge0$, then
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$
2. If $g(X)$ is integrable, then $g$ is integrable with respect to
   $\mathbb P_X$ and the same formula holds:
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. For each $i$, let
$g_i:(S_i,\Sigma_i)\to(T_i,\mathcal T_i)$ be measurable. Then the family
$(g_i\circ X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space and let
$f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ be measurable for the Borel sigma-algebra on
the extended real line. Products of functions use
$\odot_X$ from [[def-measurable-pointwise-extended-real-product]], and $cf$
abbreviates $\underline c\odot_X f$ for the constant function $\underline c$.
The magnitude function is $|f|=\max(f,-f)$ as in
[[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]]. Then:

1. $cf$ is measurable for every real scalar $c$;
2. $\max(f,g)$, $\min(f,g)$, $|f|$, $f^+$, and $f^-$ are measurable;
3. if the partial pointwise sum $f+g$ is defined at every point, then it is measurable;

derivations.claim: The entries $h_j(X_i)$, $f(X_i)$, $h_j(X_i)h_k(X_i)$, and $h_j(X_i)f(X_i)$ are measurable by [F11]. Since each $X_i$ has law $P$, applying the same measurable function to each gives a common law; [F10] preserves their mutual independence, so each resulting sequence is IID by [F2]. The fourth-moment hypothesis and [F8] make every product entry integrable, and [F9] identifies its expectation with the corresponding integral under $P$. Applying [F4] to these IID sequences gives $\bar h_n\to\theta$, $\bar f_n\to Pf$, $n^{-1}\sum_i h(X_i)h(X_i)^{\mathsf T}\to E_P[hh^{\mathsf T}]$, and $n^{-1}\sum_i h(X_i)f(X_i)\to E_P[hf]$ almost surely. The centered formulas therefore give $\widehat\Sigma_n\to\Sigma$ and $\widehat c_n\to c$ almost surely; positive definiteness of $\Sigma$ and continuity of determinant imply $\widehat\Sigma_n$ is eventually invertible almost surely. The fallback definition makes $\widehat\beta_n$ measurable: on the open nonsingular set the inverse entries are ratios of polynomial functions, and on its closed complement the value is constant.

Put $W_i=h(X_i)-\theta$ and $V_i=f(X_i)-Pf$. The finite fourth-moment assumptions imply finite fourth moments for every component of $W_i$ and for $V_i$; for example, $|x-a|^4\le8(|x|^4+|a|^4)$. Then [F8] gives finite second moments for every product $W_{ij}W_{ik}$ and $W_{ij}V_i$. Each centered coordinate and product is a fixed measurable function of $X_i$, so [F2] and [F10] make each sequence IID. By [F9] and [F7], $E W_i=0$, $E V_i=0$, and the product means are $\Sigma$ and $c$. Independence and [F6] give variance equal to the one-observation variance divided by $n$ for each sample average. Applying [F5] with $a=M/\sqrt n$ and taking a finite union over the fixed $q$ coordinates and matrix entries proves $\bar h_n-\theta=O_P(n^{-1/2})$, $\bar f_n-Pf=O_P(n^{-1/2})$, $n^{-1}\sum_iW_iW_i^{\mathsf T}-\Sigma=O_P(n^{-1/2})$, and $n^{-1}\sum_iW_iV_i-c=O_P(n^{-1/2})$. The identities $$\widehat\Sigma_n=\frac1n\sum_iW_iW_i^{\mathsf T}-(\bar h_n-\theta)(\bar h_n-\theta)^{\mathsf T},\qquad \widehat c_n=\frac1n\sum_iW_iV_i-(\bar h_n-\theta)(\bar f_n-Pf)$$ show that the centering corrections are $O_P(n^{-1})$. Thus $\widehat\Sigma_n-\Sigma$ and $\widehat c_n-c$ are jointly $O_P(n^{-1/2})$.

On the event that $\widehat\Sigma_n$ is invertible, $\widehat\beta_n-\beta^*=\widehat\Sigma_n^{-1}[(\widehat c_n-c)-(\widehat\Sigma_n-\Sigma)\beta^*]$, since $c=\Sigma\beta^*$. Step 1.1 and the adjugate-over-determinant formula show that the inverse converges to $\Sigma^{-1}$ almost surely on the eventually nonsingular set; extending it by zero on the singular event gives an $O_P(1)$ matrix sequence. Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose bounds for this inverse norm and for the bracket in step 1.2 after scaling by $\sqrt n$, with total failure probability less than $\varepsilon/2$. On their intersection the product is bounded after scaling by $\sqrt n$, so $\widehat\beta_n-\beta^*=O_P(n^{-1/2})$ there. The singular-event probability tends to zero by step 1.1; the fallback value $0$ therefore does not change this order in probability.

By the plug-in definition in the Statement and [F1] for the fixed coefficient $\beta^*$, subtracting the two estimators cancels $\bar f_n$ and leaves exactly $-(\widehat\beta_n-\beta^*)^{\mathsf T}(\bar h_n-\theta)$. Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose finite bounds for each factor after scaling by $\sqrt n$ so that the probability either bound fails is less than $\varepsilon/2$; on their intersection, Cauchy--Schwarz in $\mathbb R^q$ bounds $n$ times the absolute inner product by the product of those bounds. Thus the inner product is $O_P(n^{-1})$ by definition.

They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space, $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ a sub-sigma-algebra, and $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ integrable. A **conditional-expectation version of $X$ given $\mathcal G$** is a real, $\mathcal G$-measurable, integrable function $Y$ such that $\int_A Y\,dP=\int_A X\,dP$ for every $A\in\mathcal G$. No completeness of $\mathcal G$ is assumed.

Expectation means the integral of [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. Integrable representatives use [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]; quotient notation is introduced after uniqueness.

Let $n\ge1$, let $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ be independent real random variables on a
common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then
   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$
   in $[0,+\infty]$. In this finite product of expectations, a zero factor
   makes the product zero even when another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise
   multiplication has its usual extended nonnegative meaning.
2. If every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable
   and the same factorization holds in $\mathbb R$.

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability
space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element, let
$\mathbb P_X$ be its law, and let $g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb R$ or
$g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb C$ be measurable.

1. If $g\ge0$, then
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$
2. If $g(X)$ is integrable, then $g$ is integrable with respect to
   $\mathbb P_X$ and the same formula holds:
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

A family $(\mathcal F_i)_{i\in I}$ of sub-sigma-algebras of $\mathcal F$ is
**independent** when it is independent as a family of event classes in the
sense of [[def-independent-families-of-event-classes]].

A family $(A_i)_{i\in I}$ of events is **independent** when the singleton event
classes $\bigl(\{A_i\}\bigr)_{i\in I}$ are independent. Equivalently, for every
finite choice of distinct indices $i_0,\dots,i_{n-1}$,

$$\mathbb P\left(\bigcap_{k<n}A_{i_k}\right)=\prod_{k<n}\mathbb P(A_{i_k}).$$

For two events this reduces to the familiar identity
$\mathbb P(A\cap B)=\mathbb P(A)\mathbb P(B)$.

Let $n\ge1$, assume $P f^2<\infty$ and $P h_j^2<\infty$ for each component, and set $\mu=Pf$, $\theta=Ph$. Define the vector covariance matrix and cross-covariance vector by $\Sigma_{jk}=E_P[(h_j-\theta_j)(h_k-\theta_k)]$ and $c_j=E_P[(h_j-\theta_j)(f-\mu)]$. A matrix $\Sigma$ is positive definite when $v^{\mathsf T}\Sigma v>0$ for every nonzero $v$. For an IID sample $X_1,\ldots,X_n\sim P$ and a fixed $\beta\in\mathbb R^q$, the estimator in [[def-control-variate-estimator]] is unbiased and

$$\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\mu_\beta)=\frac1n\operatorname{Var}_P\bigl(f-\beta^{\mathsf T}h\bigr).$$

If $\Sigma$ is positive definite, the unique variance-minimizing vector coefficient and the minimum variance are

$$\beta^*=\Sigma^{-1}c,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(\widehat\mu_{\beta^*})=\frac1n\left(\operatorname{Var}_P(f)-c^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}c\right).$$

For a scalar control with $\operatorname{Var}_P(h)>0$, this reads $\beta^*=\operatorname{Cov}_P(f,h)/\operatorname{Var}_P(h)$. If controls are redundant, delete redundant directions or use the theorem only on a positive-definite covariance subspace; no inverse is asserted for a singular $\Sigma$.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X,P)$ be a probability space, let $q\ge1$ and $n\ge1$, and let $f:\mathsf X\to\mathbb R$ and $h=(h_1,\ldots,h_q):\mathsf X\to\mathbb R^q$ be measurable with $\int|f|\,dP<\infty$ and $\int|h_j|\,dP<\infty$ for every $j$; these are integrals in [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. Write $\mu=Pf$ and $\theta=Ph\in\mathbb R^q$, where $\theta$ is known, and use [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]] for variance and covariance. Given an IID sample $X_1,\ldots,X_n\sim P$ as in [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]] and a fixed coefficient $\beta\in\mathbb R^q$, the **control-variate estimator** is

$$\widehat\mu_\beta=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\bigl[f(X_i)-\beta^{\mathsf T}(h(X_i)-\theta)\bigr].$$

Let $d,n\ge1$, let $\mathsf X$ be a measurable space, let $P$ be a probability law on $\mathsf X$, and let $f:\mathsf X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. On a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$, let $U_i=(U_{i1},\ldots,U_{id})$, $i=1,\ldots,n$, be IID random vectors whose coordinates are mutually independent and each have the uniform law on $[0,1]$, meaning $\mathbb P(U_{ij}\le t)=t$ for $0\le t\le1$. Let $T:[0,1]^d\to\mathsf X$ be measurable and satisfy $T(U_1)\sim P$. Define the reflected input $1-U_i=(1-U_{i1},\ldots,1-U_{id})$ and the antithetic estimator by

$$\widehat\mu_{\rm anti}=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{f(T(U_i))+f(T(1-U_i))}{2}.$$

The two outputs in each pair may be dependent; pairs with different indices are independent. The variance comparison in the theorem uses $2n$ function evaluations and compares with an ordinary mean of $2n$ independent $P$-draws. IID and mutual independence have the meanings of [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]], and variance/covariance use [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]].

Use the setup of [[def-antithetic-randomized-sampling]], assume $E_P[f^2]<\infty$, and put $Y=f(T(U_1))$, $\widetilde Y=f(T(1-U_1))$, $\mu=E_Pf$, and $\sigma^2=\operatorname{Var}_P(f)$. Then $Y$ and $\widetilde Y$ have the same law and mean, and the antithetic estimator from $n$ independent input pairs is unbiased with

$$\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\mu_{\rm anti})=\frac{\sigma^2+\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\widetilde Y)}{2n}.$$

Compared with the ordinary mean of $2n$ independent draws from $P$, whose variance is $\sigma^2/(2n)$, antithetic sampling has no larger variance exactly when $\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\widetilde Y)\le0$, and has strictly smaller variance exactly when this covariance is negative. A sufficient condition is that $g=f\circ T$ is coordinatewise monotone on $[0,1]^d$ (each coordinate may have either monotonicity direction). In particular, when $\mathsf X$ is a subset of $\mathbb R^m$ with the order $x\le y$ defined by $x_j\le y_j$ for every coordinate, if $T$ is coordinatewise nondecreasing as a map into $\mathsf X$ and $f$ is nondecreasing for that order, then $g$ is coordinatewise nondecreasing.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X,P)$ be a probability space, let $f:\mathsf X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable with $\int_{\mathsf X}|f|\,dP<\infty$, write $Pf=\int_{\mathsf X}f\,dP$, and let $H\ge1$ and $A_1,\ldots,A_H$ be a finite measurable partition of $\mathsf X$ with $p_h=P(A_h)>0$. Define the conditional stratum law by $P_h(B)=P(B\cap A_h)/p_h$ for $B\in\mathcal X$. Choose fixed integers $n_h\ge1$ and put $n=\sum_{h=1}^H n_h$. Draw mutually independent variables $X_{hj}$, with $X_{h1},\ldots,X_{hn_h}$ IID under $P_h$ as in [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]], and define $\bar f_h=n_h^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{n_h}f(X_{hj})$. Expectations and variances use [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]] and [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]. The **stratified Monte Carlo estimator** of $Pf$ is

$$\widehat\mu_{\rm strat}=\sum_{h=1}^H p_h\bar f_h.$$

The allocation $(n_1,\ldots,n_H)$ is part of the design. A variance comparison must specify it and the comparator.

Use the setup of [[def-stratified-monte-carlo-estimator]] and suppose $\int_{\mathsf X} f^2\,dP<\infty$. Write $\mu=\int_{\mathsf X}f\,dP$, $\mu_h=E_{P_h}f$, and $\sigma_h^2=\operatorname{Var}_{P_h}(f)$. The estimator is unbiased and

$$\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\mu_{\rm strat})=\sum_{h=1}^H\frac{p_h^2\sigma_h^2}{n_h}.$$

If, additionally, each $np_h$ is a positive integer and the fixed allocation is proportional, $n_h=np_h$, then the variance is no larger than that of the ordinary IID sample mean of the same total size $n$:

$$\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\mu_{\rm strat})=\frac1n\sum_h p_h\sigma_h^2\le\frac{\operatorname{Var}_P(f)}n.$$

The comparison is only asserted for this proportional allocation; a general fixed allocation has the variance in the first display and need not beat the IID comparator.

For each $n\ge1$, assume $P|f|^4<\infty$ and $P|h_j|^4<\infty$ for each $j$. Set $\theta=Ph$, define $\Sigma_{jk}=E_P[(h_j-\theta_j)(h_k-\theta_k)]$ and $c_j=E_P[(h_j-\theta_j)(f-Pf)]$, and suppose $\Sigma$ is positive definite, meaning $v^{\mathsf T}\Sigma v>0$ for every nonzero vector $v$. Put $\beta^*=\Sigma^{-1}c$. Define $\bar f_n=n^{-1}\sum_i f(X_i)$, $\bar h_n=n^{-1}\sum_i h(X_i)$,

$$\widehat\Sigma_n=\frac1n\sum_i(h(X_i)-\bar h_n)(h(X_i)-\bar h_n)^{\mathsf T},\qquad \widehat c_n=\frac1n\sum_i(h(X_i)-\bar h_n)(f(X_i)-\bar f_n).$$

and let $\widehat\beta_n=\widehat\Sigma_n^{-1}\widehat c_n$ when $\widehat\Sigma_n$ is invertible and $0$ otherwise. Define the plug-in estimator pointwise by $\widehat\mu_{\widehat\beta_n}:=\bar f_n-\widehat\beta_n^{\mathsf T}(\bar h_n-\theta)$. For a scalar random sequence $R_n$, write $R_n=O_P(n^{-1})$ when $nR_n$ is bounded in probability: for each $\varepsilon>0$ some finite $M$ and $N$ satisfy $\mathbb P(|nR_n|>M)<\varepsilon$ for all $n\ge N$. For a fixed-dimensional vector or matrix, $O_P(a_n)$ means its Euclidean or Frobenius norm divided by $a_n$ is bounded in probability. Then

$$\widehat\mu_{\widehat\beta_n}-\widehat\mu_{\beta^*}=-(\widehat\beta_n-\beta^*)^{\mathsf T}(\bar h_n-\theta)=O_P(n^{-1}).$$

This result bounds only the same-sample coefficient-times-control-mean remainder; it does not assert that $\widehat\mu_{\widehat\beta_n}$ is unbiased.

Let $n,q\ge1$, let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be IID with law $P$, let $f,h_1,\ldots,h_q$ be integrable, and let $\theta=E_P h$ be known. Write $\mathcal X_n$ for the sigma-algebra generated by the production sample, namely the smallest sigma-algebra containing each event $\{X_i\in B\}$ for measurable $B$. Let $\mathcal P$ be a sigma-algebra generated by pilot data and assume $\mathcal P$ and $\mathcal X_n$ are independent in the sense of [[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]]. Let the $\mathcal P$-measurable coefficient $\widehat\beta\in\mathbb R^q$ satisfy $E\|\widehat\beta\|<\infty$. Then the random-coefficient control estimator

$$\widehat\mu_{\widehat\beta}=\frac1n\sum_i\left[f(X_i)-\widehat\beta^{\mathsf T}(h(X_i)-\theta)\right]$$

is integrable and $E[\widehat\mu_{\widehat\beta}\mid\mathcal P]=E_Pf$ almost surely. The first-moment condition on $\widehat\beta$ ensures the displayed estimator is integrable; no claim is made for an arbitrary nonintegrable pilot coefficient.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X,P)$ be a probability space, let $q\ge1$ and $n\ge1$, and let $f:\mathsf X\to\mathbb R$ and $h=(h_1,\ldots,h_q):\mathsf X\to\mathbb R^q$ be measurable with $\int|f|\,dP<\infty$ and $\int|h_j|\,dP<\infty$ for every $j$; these are integrals in [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. For any integrable $g$ write $Pg:=\int_{\mathsf X}g\,dP$. Write $\mu=Pf$ and $\theta=Ph\in\mathbb R^q$, where $\theta$ is known, and use [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]] for variance and covariance. Given an IID sample $X_1,\ldots,X_n\sim P$ as in [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]] and a fixed coefficient $\beta\in\mathbb R^q$, the **control-variate estimator** is

$$\widehat\mu_\beta=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\bigl[f(X_i)-\beta^{\mathsf T}(h(X_i)-\theta)\bigr].$$

For one scalar control this is $n^{-1}\sum_i[f(X_i)-\beta(h(X_i)-\theta)]$. The coefficient is fixed independently of the production sample in this definition; a coefficient fitted from that same sample is treated separately.

The independent pilot makes $\mathcal P$ independent of the sigma-algebra of the entire production sample, and $\widehat\beta=2V$ is $\mathcal P$-measurable and integrable by step 1.1.
