Let $X$ be a set. The **counting set function** on $\mathcal P(X)$ is

$$\#_X(E):=\begin{cases}|E|,&E\text{ is finite},\\+\infty,&E\text{ is infinite},\end{cases}$$

where finite means equinumerous with a natural number ([[def-countable]]) and $+\infty$ belongs to the extended real line ([[def-extended-reals]]). The two branches are exhaustive and disjoint. The fact that this set function is a measure, and hence deserves the name **counting measure**, is proved in [[prop-counting-measure-is-a-measure]].
For every set $X$, the counting set function $\#_X$ of [[def-counting-measure]] is a measure on $(X,\mathcal P(X))$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space. A measurable function
$s:X\to[0,+\infty)\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$
([[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]) is a
**nonnegative simple measurable function** when it has finite range.

Equivalently, there are pairwise disjoint measurable sets
$E_1,\dots,E_m\in\mathcal A$ and coefficients $c_1,\dots,c_m\in[0,+\infty)$
such that
$$s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\chi_{E_j}.$$
Any such display is a **simple representation** of $s$.

Let $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\chi_{E_j}$ be a simple representation of a
nonnegative simple measurable function
([[def-nonnegative-simple-measurable-function]]) on a measure space
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$, so the $E_j\in\mathcal A$ are pairwise disjoint and
$c_j\ge0$. Its
**simple integral** is
$$\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mu(E_j),$$
where $\mu$ is the given measure ([[def-measure]]) and the convention
$0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ is fixed once and for all.

The next lemma proves that this value is independent of the chosen simple
representation.

If $s$ is a nonnegative simple measurable function, then its nonnegative
Lebesgue integral equals its simple integral:
$$\int s\,d\mu=\int_{\mathrm{simple}} s\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $a=(a_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ take values in $[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$ ([[def-extended-reals]]). Its **partial sums** are the unique sequence $(s_n)$ in $[0,+\infty]$ satisfying

$$s_0=0,\qquad s_{n+1}=s_n+a_n.$$

To apply [[thm-recursion]] with a fixed successor function, use the state space $\mathbb N\times[0,+\infty]$ and the self-map $T(n,s)=(n+1,s+a_n)$, starting from $(0,0)$. Recursion gives a unique state sequence; induction makes its first coordinate $n$, and its second coordinates are exactly the unique $(s_n)$ satisfying the displayed recurrence. Addition of two nonnegative extended reals is always defined, including when either is $+\infty$. The sequence $(s_n)$ is nondecreasing, and its **nonnegative extended sum** is

$$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}a_k:=\sup_{n\in\mathbb N}s_n\in[0,+\infty],$$

whose existence follows from completeness of the extended real line ([[lem-extended-reals-complete]]). More generally, for $m\in\mathbb N$,

$$\sum_{k\ge m}a_k:=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}a_{m+j}.$$

Finite sums use the same recursion: $\sum_{k<n}a_k=s_n$, so the empty sum at $n=0$ is $0$. A double sum such as $\sum_i\sum_j a_{ij}$ means that the inner nonnegative extended sum is formed first and the resulting nonnegative extended sequence is then summed.

The Cauchy-sequence reals $\mathbb{R}_C$ have the **least-upper-bound property**:
every nonempty $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}_C$ that is bounded above has a least upper
bound $\sup S \in \mathbb{R}_C$. Hence, together with [[thm-reals-ordered-field]],
$\mathbb{R}_C$ is a **complete ordered field** ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]).

The relation of [[def-real-order]] is well defined and makes $\mathbb{R}$
([[thm-reals-field]]) a totally ordered field.

Every complete ordered field $F$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) is Archimedean:
for every $x \in F$ there is a natural number $n \ge 1$ with $x < n \cdot 1_F$,
where $n \cdot 1_F$ is the canonical natural of the ordered field $F$
([[def-ordered-field]]). Equivalently, the canonical naturals are cofinal in $F$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field, with field structure as in [[def-field]], and for
$n \ge 1$ let $n \cdot 1_F$ denote the canonical natural number
$\underbrace{1_F + \cdots + 1_F}_{n}$, defined recursively by $1 \cdot 1_F = 1_F$
and $(n+1) \cdot 1_F = n \cdot 1_F + 1_F$. Then for every $n \ge 1$:

- $n \cdot 1_F > 0$ and $(n+1) \cdot 1_F > n \cdot 1_F$;
- the map $n \mapsto n \cdot 1_F$ is strictly increasing, hence injective, on $\{1, 2, 3, \dots\}$;
- $(m+n) \cdot 1_F = m \cdot 1_F + n \cdot 1_F$ and $(mn) \cdot 1_F = (m \cdot 1_F)(n \cdot 1_F)$ for all $m, n \ge 1$.

derivations.claim: For each integer $m\ge1$, define $s_m(n)=\min\{f(n),m\}$ when $n<m$ and $s_m(n)=0$ when $n\ge m$. Every subset of $\mathbb N$ is measurable under [F1], so $s_m$ is measurable; its range is finite, hence it is simple by [F2]. For fixed $n$, the indicator $1_{n<m}$ is eventually one; if $f(n)<+\infty$, [F5] ensures the increasing canonical naturals eventually exceed $f(n)$, while if $f(n)=+\infty$ the capped values increase without bound. Thus $s_m(n)\uparrow f(n)$ for every $n$. Monotone convergence [F3] gives $\int f\,d\#=\lim_{m\to\infty}\int s_m\,d\#$.

By [F1] and [F2], for every $m\ge1$, $\int s_m\,d\#=\sum_{n<m}\min\{f(n),m\}\,\#(\{n\})=\sum_{n<m}\min\{f(n),m\}=:D_m.$ For each $n<m$, $\min\{f(n),m\}\le\min\{f(n),m+1\}$ and $D_{m+1}$ adds a nonnegative term, so $D_m$ is nondecreasing. Termwise $\min\{f(n),m\}\le f(n)$, so $D_m\le P_m\le\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}f(n)$ by [F4].

Fix $r\ge0$. If $P_r=+\infty$, some $f(n)=+\infty$ with $n<r$, so for every $m\ge r$ with $m>n$, $D_m\ge m$; the canonical naturals are unbounded by [F5], hence $\lim_mD_m=+\infty\ge P_r$. If $P_r<+\infty$, then each $f(n)$ for $n<r$ is finite. Write $\bar r=r\cdot1_{\mathbb R}$ and apply [F5] to $P_r+\bar r$ to choose an integer $m$ with $m\cdot1_{\mathbb R}>P_r+\bar r$. Then $m\ge r$ and $m>f(n)$ for every $n<r$, since nonnegative summands give $f(n)\le P_r$. Thus $D_m\ge P_r$, and monotonicity of $D_m$ again gives $\lim_mD_m\ge P_r$. Since this holds for every $r$, [F4] implies $\lim_mD_m\ge\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}f(n)$. Together with step 2.1's reverse bound, $\lim_mD_m=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}f(n)$.
Steps 1.1 and 2.1 identify the integral with $\lim_mD_m$, and step 3.1 identifies that limit with the nonnegative extended series. This proves the stated identity, including infinite values.

Let $(S,\mathcal S,\mu)$ be a measure space. The nonnegative measurable
functions $\tilde f,\tilde g:S\to[0,\infty)$ are the target and proposal
shapes, with
$$Z_f:=\int_S\tilde f\,d\mu\in(0,\infty),\qquad Z_g:=\int_S\tilde g\,d\mu\in(0,\infty).$$
The normalized densities $\bar f:=\tilde f/Z_f$ and $\bar g:=\tilde g/Z_g$
are measurable by closure under scalar multiplication
([[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]). Their
integrals are one by homogeneity of the nonnegative integral
([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]). Thus their
density measures are probability laws by
[[def-measure-with-density]] and [[def-probability-measure]]:
$$F(A):=Z_f^{-1}\int_A\tilde f\,d\mu,\qquad G(A):=Z_g^{-1}\int_A\tilde g\,d\mu\quad(A\in\mathcal S).$$
Assume a finite $c>0$ satisfies $\tilde f\le c\tilde g$ outside a common
$\mu$-null set. Use finite-valued representatives; values on that null set
do not affect $F$ or $G$.

The stochastic input is an ideal sequence of independent proposal draws
$Y_i$ with common law $G$ and independent auxiliary draws $U_i$ with common
law $\Lambda$, where $\Lambda$ is the uniform probability law on $(0,1)$:
$\Lambda(U\le t)=t$ for $0\le t\le1$. The two sequences are independent, so
the pairs $(Y_i,U_i)$ are IID in the sense of
[[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]. This contract
assumes exact draws; it makes no claim about a finite-precision pseudorandom
generator.

Define the measurable acceptance function
$$a(y):=\begin{cases} 0,&\tilde g(y)=0,\\ \min\!\left\{1,\dfrac{\tilde f(y)}{c\tilde g(y)}\right\},&\tilde g(y)>0. \end{cases}$$
It is measurable. The reciprocal extension $h:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$,
$h(t)=1/t$ for $t>0$ and $h(0)=0$, is Borel: for every real $r$, its strict
upper level set is $[0,\infty)$ if $r<0$, $(0,\infty)$ if $r=0$, and
$(0,1/r)$ if $r>0$. These are Borel sets in the subspace $[0,\infty)$ by
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra]], so the threshold characterization
[[thm-threshold-characterisations-of-real-and-extended-real-measurability]]
applies. Equivalently,
$a(y)=\min\{1,\tilde f(y)h(\tilde g(y))/c\}$. Arithmetic operations and Borel
composition preserve measurability by
[[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]] and
[[thm-composition-with-borel-functions-preserves-measurability]]. Where the
envelope holds and $\tilde g(y)>0$, this is exactly
$\tilde f(y)/(c\tilde g(y))$; where $\tilde g(y)=0$, $a(y)=0$. At an
exceptional point with $\tilde g(y)>0$ where the quotient exceeds $1$,
replacing it by $1$ does not change the test
$U_i\le\tilde f(y)/(c\tilde g(y))$, since $U_i\in(0,1)$.

**Procedure.** For $i=1,2,\ldots$, draw $(Y_i,U_i)$. If $U_i\le a(Y_i)$,
return $Y_i$ and stop; otherwise continue to the next pair. When
$\tilde f=f$ and $\tilde g=g$ are normalized densities, integrating
$f\le cg$ gives $c\ge1$, and the rule is the usual threshold $f(Y_i)/(cg(Y_i))$.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. The **measure with density $f$ relative
to $\mu$** is the measure
$$f\,d\mu:\mathcal A\to[0,+\infty],\qquad (f\,d\mu)(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu,$$
whose measure property is supplied by
[[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]].

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

If $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable and $\int f\,d\mu<+\infty$, then
$f(x)<+\infty$ for almost every $x$.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable
([[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]). Its
**nonnegative Lebesgue integral** is
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\left\{\int s\,d\mu:\ s \text{ is nonnegative simple and } 0\le s\le f\right\},$$
where the simple integral on the right is the one from
[[def-integral-of-a-nonnegative-simple-function]].

The set of admissible simple minorants is nonempty because it contains the zero
function, which is simple ([[def-nonnegative-simple-measurable-function]]).

Let $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\chi_{E_j}$ be a simple representation of a
nonnegative simple measurable function
([[def-nonnegative-simple-measurable-function]]) on a measure space
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$, so the $E_j\in\mathcal A$ are pairwise disjoint and
$c_j\ge0$. Its
**simple integral** is
$$\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mu(E_j),$$
where $\mu$ is the given measure ([[def-measure]]) and the convention
$0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ is fixed once and for all.

The next lemma proves that this value is independent of the chosen simple
representation.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. If $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ are measurable, then
$$\int(f+g)\,d\mu=\int f\,d\mu+\int g\,d\mu.$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element, let
$\mathbb P_X$ be its law, and let $g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb R$ or
$g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb C$ be measurable.

1. If $g\ge0$, then
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$
2. If $g(X)$ is integrable, then $g$ is integrable with respect to
   $\mathbb P_X$ and the same formula holds:
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int g\,d(f\,d\mu)=\int gf\,d\mu.$$

Let $(S,\mathcal S,\mu)$ be a measure space. The nonnegative measurable
functions $\tilde f,\tilde g:S\to[0,\infty)$ are the target and proposal
shapes, with
$$Z_f:=\int_S\tilde f\,d\mu\in(0,\infty),\qquad Z_g:=\int_S\tilde g\,d\mu\in(0,\infty).$$
The normalized densities $\bar f:=\tilde f/Z_f$ and $\bar g:=\tilde g/Z_g$
are measurable by closure under scalar multiplication
([[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]). Their
integrals are one by homogeneity of the nonnegative integral
([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]). Thus their
density measures are probability laws by
[[def-measure-with-density]] and [[def-probability-measure]]:
$$F(A):=Z_f^{-1}\int_A\tilde f\,d\mu,\qquad G(A):=Z_g^{-1}\int_A\tilde g\,d\mu\quad(A\in\mathcal S).$$
Assume a finite $c>0$ satisfies $\tilde f\le c\tilde g$ outside a common
$\mu$-null set. Use finite-valued representatives; values on that null set
do not affect $F$ or $G$.

The stochastic input is an ideal sequence of independent proposal draws
$Y_i$ with common law $G$ and independent auxiliary draws $U_i$ with common
law $\Lambda$, where $\Lambda$ is the uniform probability law on $(0,1)$:
$\Lambda(U\le t)=t$ for $0\le t\le1$. The two sequences are independent, so
the pairs $(Y_i,U_i)$ are IID in the sense of
[[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]. This contract
assumes exact draws; it makes no claim about a finite-precision pseudorandom
generator.

Define the measurable acceptance function
$$a(y):=\begin{cases} 0,&\tilde g(y)=0,\\ \min\!\left\{1,\dfrac{\tilde f(y)}{c\tilde g(y)}\right\},&\tilde g(y)>0. \end{cases}$$
It is measurable. The reciprocal extension $h:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$,
$h(t)=1/t$ for $t>0$ and $h(0)=0$, is Borel: for every real $r$, its strict
upper level set is $[0,\infty)$ if $r<0$, $(0,\infty)$ if $r=0$, and
$(0,1/r)$ if $r>0$. These are Borel sets in the subspace $[0,\infty)$ by
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra]], so the threshold characterization
[[thm-threshold-characterisations-of-real-and-extended-real-measurability]]
applies. Equivalently,
$a(y)=\min\{1,\tilde f(y)h(\tilde g(y))/c\}$. Arithmetic operations and Borel
composition preserve measurability by
[[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]] and
[[thm-composition-with-borel-functions-preserves-measurability]]. Where the
envelope holds and $\tilde g(y)>0$, this is exactly
$\tilde f(y)/(c\tilde g(y))$; where $\tilde g(y)=0$, $a(y)=0$. At an
exceptional point with $\tilde g(y)>0$ where the quotient exceeds $1$,
replacing it by $1$ does not change the test
$U_i\le\tilde f(y)/(c\tilde g(y))$, since $U_i\in(0,1)$.

**Procedure.** For $i=1,2,\ldots$, draw $(Y_i,U_i)$. If $U_i\le a(Y_i)$,
return $Y_i$ and stop; otherwise continue to the next pair. When
$\tilde f=f$ and $\tilde g=g$ are normalized densities, integrating
$f\le cg$ gives $c\ge1$, and the rule is the usual threshold $f(Y_i)/(cg(Y_i))$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space and let
$f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ be measurable for the Borel sigma-algebra on
the extended real line. Products of functions use
$\odot_X$ from [[def-measurable-pointwise-extended-real-product]], and $cf$
abbreviates $\underline c\odot_X f$ for the constant function $\underline c$.
The magnitude function is $|f|=\max(f,-f)$ as in
[[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]]. Then:

1. $cf$ is measurable for every real scalar $c$;
2. $\max(f,g)$, $\min(f,g)$, $|f|$, $f^+$, and $f^-$ are measurable;
3. if the partial pointwise sum $f+g$ is defined at every point, then it is measurable;
4. the pointwise product $fg:=f\odot_X g$ is measurable.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$, $(Y,\mathcal{B})$, and $(Z,\mathcal{C})$ be measurable
spaces. If $f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Y,\mathcal{B})$ is measurable and
$g : (Y,\mathcal{B}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable, then
$g \circ f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable.

In particular, if $f$ is measurable and $g$ is a Borel measurable function on
its codomain, then $g \circ f$ is measurable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

Let $X$ be a set and let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]). A **measure** on $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function

$$\mu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$$

such that:

1. $\mu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$,
   $$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k),$$
   where the right side is the nonnegative extended sum of [[def-nonnegative-extended-series]].

The second condition is **countable additivity**. It begins at index $0$ and includes the case in which some term or the total sum is $+\infty$.

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges ([[def-series]]) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]).

1. If $|r| < 1$ then $(r^k)$ is **null**, that is $r^k \to 0$
   ([[def-real-limit]]).
2. If $|r| > 1$ then $(|r|^k)$ **diverges to $+\infty$**
   ([[def-divergence-to-infinity]]).

Claim 2 is stated for $|r|^k$ and not for $r^k$ on purpose: for $r < -1$ the
terms $r^k$ alternate in sign and are unbounded, so they neither converge nor
diverge to $+\infty$; what is true of them is the statement about their absolute
values.

Both claims come from Bernoulli's inequality ([[lem-bernoulli-inequality]]) and
the Archimedean property. Nothing here needs the least-upper-bound property
except through [[thm-of-archimedean]] and [[cor-archimedean-reciprocal]].

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element. Its
**law** or **distribution** is the set function
$$\mathbb P_X:\Sigma\to[0,+\infty],\qquad \mathbb P_X(B):=\mathbb P(X^{-1}(B)).$$

Thus the law of $X$ records the probability of each measurable target set by
pulling it back to an event in the original probability space.

derivations.claim: By [F3], both shapes are finite outside null sets. Let $E_0$ be the measurable null union of those sets and the envelope exception from [A1]. For any nonnegative measurable $h$ supported on $E_0$, every simple minorant has all its positive level sets contained in $E_0$, so its simple integral is zero; hence $\int h\,d\mu=0$ by [F4]. For either shape $h$ and any measurable $A$, the decomposition $h\mathbf1_A=h\mathbf1_{A\setminus E_0}+h\mathbf1_{A\cap E_0}$ and additivity [F4] therefore give $\int_Ah\,d\mu=\int_A h\mathbf1_{S\setminus E_0}\,d\mu$. Products here use $0\cdot\infty=0$, and are measurable by [F9]. Replace each shape by $h\mathbf1_{S\setminus E_0}$; neither density measure nor any displayed integral changes. In particular $G(E_0)=0$. By [F13] and countable additivity [F11], the probability that any proposal hits $E_0$ is zero; changing the acceptance rule there leaves the output law unchanged. The new shapes are finite and satisfy $\tilde f\le c\tilde g$ everywhere, so $\tilde g=0$ implies $\tilde f=0$.

Fix $A\in\mathcal S$ and let $Q(A):=\mathbb P(Y_1\in A,\ U_1\le a(Y_1))$. By [F9] the event is measurable. By [F1] and [F6] the joint law of $(Y_1,U_1)$ is $G\otimes\Lambda$. Hence [F5] and [F13] give $Q(A)=\int_{S\times(0,1)}\mathbf1_A(y)\mathbf1_{\{u\le a(y)\}}\, (G\otimes\Lambda)(d(y,u)).$
Tonelli [F7] evaluates the last integral as $Q(A)=\int_A\Lambda((0,a(y)])\,G(dy)=\int_A a(y)\,G(dy),$ including $a(y)=0$ and $a(y)=1$, since $\Lambda((0,t])=t$ on $[0,1]$.

Apply [F8] to the proposal density $\tilde g/Z_g$ and the measurable function $\mathbf1_Aa$. Where $\tilde g>0$, the envelope makes $a=\tilde f/(c\tilde g)$; where $\tilde g=0$, [step 1.1] gives $\tilde f=0$. Therefore $Q(A)=\frac1{Z_g}\int_Aa\tilde g\,d\mu =\frac1{cZ_g}\int_A\tilde f\,d\mu.$

Taking $A=S$ in step 3.1 gives $p=Q(S)=Z_f/(cZ_g)>0$. Integrating the pointwise envelope and using [F10] gives $Z_f\le cZ_g$, so $p\le1$. For normalized densities, $Z_f=Z_g=1$, hence $p=1/c$ and $c\ge1$.

Put $q=1-p$. Independence of the proposal-uniform pairs [F1] gives $\mathbb P(N>m)=q^m$ for every $m\ge1$. Since $0\le q<1$, [F12] gives $q^m\to0$; the event $\{N=\infty\}$ is contained in every $\{N>m\}$, so $\mathbb P(N=\infty)=0$.

For each $k\ge1$, independence across trials gives $\mathbb P(N=k,\ Y_k\in A)=q^{k-1}Q(A).$ These events are disjoint, so countable additivity [F11] and the geometric series [F12] yield $\mathbb P(\text{the algorithm outputs a value in }A) =\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}q^{k-1}Q(A) =\frac{Q(A)}p =\frac1{Z_f}\int_A\tilde f\,d\mu.$ The almost-sure termination in step 5.1 makes this the full output law.

boundaries.evidence: Taking A=∅ in the accepted subdensity formula of step 3.1 gives zero accepted mass, and step 6.1 gives zero output mass.
The hypothesis Z_f>0 makes p>0 in step 4.1; a zero target normalizer is excluded by the Statement.
The p=1 case gives q=0 in step 5.1 and the geometric series in step 6.1 has only its first nonzero term.
The measure argument in steps 1.2–6.1 also applies to a one-point measurable space; no nondegeneracy premise appears in the Statement.
Step 2.1 explicitly covers acceptance thresholds a(y)=0 and a(y)=1; the uniform law gives masses 0 and 1.

Confirmed F4 domain defect: L1 requires complex-valued representatives, while original shapes may be infinite on a null set. Replaced F4 by simple-minorant null-support proof plus extended-nonnegative additivity; this works on arbitrary base measure spaces. Finite-a.e. supplier independently checked. Product-law/Tonelli is applied only to the two probability spaces, hence sigma-finite, with a measurable threshold indicator. The algorithm uses the same measurable acceptance region for each IID proposal-uniform pair, so mutual independence and common distribution in [F1] imply that the events $A_i$ are IID. By [F2], $\mathbb P(A_i)=p$ for every $i$. Therefore $\mathbb P(N>m)=q^m$ for $m\ge0$, and $\mathbb P(N=k)=\mathbb P(A_1^c\cap\cdots\cap A_{k-1}^c\cap A_k)=q^{k-1}p$ for each $k\ge1$.

For each $m\ge1$, the pointwise identity $N\wedge m=\sum_{j=1}^m\mathbf1_{\{N\ge j\}}$ holds, including on the null event $N=\infty$. By [F3], [F4], and step 1.1, $\mathbb E[N\wedge m]=\sum_{j=1}^m\mathbb P(N\ge j) =\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}q^j.$

The truncations $N\wedge m$ increase pointwise to $N$. By [F5] and then [F6], $\mathbb E[N]=\lim_{m\to\infty}\mathbb E[N\wedge m] =\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}q^j=\frac1{1-q}=\frac1p.$ This is finite because $p>0$.
Substituting $p=Z_f/(cZ_g)$ from [F2] gives $\mathbb E[N]=cZ_g/Z_f$; when $Z_f=Z_g=1$, this is $c$.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X,\mu)$ be a measure space. An **unnormalized target density** is a measurable function $\tilde p:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ with
$$Z_p:=\int_{\mathsf X}\tilde p\,d\mu\in(0,\infty).$$
The target probability measure is $\pi(dx)=\tilde p(x)\mu(dx)/Z_p$. A **proposal density** is a measurable $q:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ with $\int q\,d\mu=1$; write $Q(dx)=q(x)\mu(dx)$. The input integrand $f:\mathsf X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, and the input sample $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ is IID with law $Q$, in the sense of [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]. The normalizing constant $Z_p$ is known for this algorithm.

**Admissible conditions for an unbiased estimate:** $n\ge1$, $q>0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $\{x:f(x)\tilde p(x)\ne0\}$, and the random variable
$$Y:=\begin{cases}f(X_1)\tilde p(X_1)/(Z_pq(X_1)),&q(X_1)>0,\\0,&q(X_1)=0\end{cases}$$
is integrable under $Q$. The support condition makes the value on $q=0$ immaterial to the target integral.

**Well-defined weights:** The reciprocal map $r(s)=1/s$ for $s>0$ and $r(s)=0$ for $s\le0$ is Borel. Its composition with $q$, multiplied by the measurable inputs, makes the piecewise weight and weighted integrand measurable ([[thm-composition-with-borel-functions-preserves-measurability]], [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]).

**Procedure and output:** For each supplied draw $X_i$, set $Y_i=f(X_i)\tilde p(X_i)/(Z_pq(X_i))$ when $q(X_i)>0$ and set $Y_i=0$ otherwise. Return
$$\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}}:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nY_i.$$
Separate variance and central limit claims require the corresponding weighted second-moment hypothesis.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element, let
$\mathbb P_X$ be its law, and let $g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb R$ or
$g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb C$ be measurable.

1. If $g\ge0$, then
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$
2. If $g(X)$ is integrable, then $g$ is integrable with respect to
   $\mathbb P_X$ and the same formula holds:
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int g\,d(f\,d\mu)=\int gf\,d\mu.$$

Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Its positive and negative parts are
$$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$
they are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]] and
satisfy $f=f^+-f^-$ and $|f|=f^++f^-$.

The **Lebesgue integral of a real measurable function** is defined whenever at
most one of $\int f^+\,d\mu$ and $\int f^-\,d\mu$ is $+\infty$, in which case
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu.$$
The function is **integrable** when both integrals are finite, equivalently
when $\int|f|\,d\mu<+\infty$.

For a complex measurable function $h=u+iv$ with
$u=\operatorname{Re}h,\ v=\operatorname{Im}h$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]), define $h$ to be
**integrable** when $|h|$ is integrable, and then define
$$\int h\,d\mu:=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: Use [F5] with density $r=q$ for integration against $Q$ and with $r=\tilde p/Z_p$ for integration against $\pi$. For every $i$, apply the nonnegative case of [F2] to $|Y_i|$. Since $X_i$ has law $Q$, $\mathbb E_Q|Y_i|=\int_{\{q>0\}}\frac{|f(x)|\tilde p(x)}{Z_pq(x)}q(x)\,d\mu(x)=\frac1{Z_p}\int_{\{q>0\}}|f|\tilde p\,d\mu\le\frac1{Z_p}\int_{\mathsf X}|f|\tilde p\,d\mu<\infty.$ Thus $Y_i$ is $Q$-integrable. For any real measurable $h$ whose absolute integral is finite against $r\,d\mu$, apply [F5] separately to $h^+=\max(h,0)$ and $h^-=\max(-h,0)$: both product integrals are finite because $h^\pm\le|h|$. Subtracting their finite identities yields $\int h\,d(r\,d\mu)=\int hr\,d\mu$, since $(hr)^\pm=h^\pm r$ for $r\ge0$ (with the density convention $0\cdot\infty=0$). The integrable case of [F2] therefore gives $\mathbb E_Q[Y_i]=\int_{\{q>0\}}\frac{f(x)\tilde p(x)}{Z_pq(x)}q(x)\,d\mu(x)=\frac1{Z_p}\int_{\{q>0\}}f\tilde p\,d\mu.$ The support condition makes $f\tilde p=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $\{q=0\}$; hence this last integral equals $Z_p^{-1}\int_{\mathsf X}f\tilde p\,d\mu=\int f\,d\pi=\theta$.
By [F1], $\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}}=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nY_i$. Apply [F3] and step 1.1 to obtain $\mathbb E_Q[\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}}]=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbb E_Q[Y_i]=\theta$.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $\tilde p\ge0$ and $q\ge0$ be measurable densities with $Z_p=\int\tilde p\,d\mu\in(0,\infty)$ and $\int q\,d\mu=1$, and set $\pi(dx)=\tilde p(x)\mu(dx)/Z_p$ and $Q(dx)=q(x)\mu(dx)$. Let $f:\mathsf X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable with $\int|f|\tilde p\,d\mu<\infty$. Suppose $q>0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $\{f\tilde p\ne0\}$ and $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ are IID with law $Q$. For the ordinary importance sampling estimator in [[alg-importance-sampling]],
$$\mathbb E_Q[\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}}]=\int f\,d\pi.$$

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. For each $i$, let
$g_i:(S_i,\Sigma_i)\to(T_i,\mathcal T_i)$ be measurable. Then the family
$(g_i\circ X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

If $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is a finite pairwise-independent family of square-integrable real random variables on a common probability space, then
$$\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\sum_{i\in I}X_i\right)=\sum_{i\in I}\operatorname{Var}(X_i).$$
Pairwise independence, rather than mutual independence, is sufficient. In particular, the original finite-probability-space case is included, with pairwise atom independence as in the finite-valued convention. The empty sum has variance zero.

Let $X,Y$ be square-integrable real random variables on one probability space.
Then
$$\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathbb E[X^2]-\mathbb E[X]^2,$$
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\mathbb E[XY]-\mathbb E[X]\mathbb E[Y].$$
Moreover, covariance is symmetric and bilinear on finite linear combinations.
On finite full-power-set probability spaces these formulas reduce to the
published finite identities.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element, let
$\mathbb P_X$ be its law, and let $g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb R$ or
$g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb C$ be measurable.

1. If $g\ge0$, then
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$
2. If $g(X)$ is integrable, then $g$ is integrable with respect to
   $\mathbb P_X$ and the same formula holds:
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(Y_i)_{i\ge1}$ be a real IID sequence with $\mu=\mathbb E[Y_1]$ and $0<\sigma^2:=\operatorname{Var}(Y_1)<\infty$. Then
$$\sqrt n\,(\bar Y_n-\mu)\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma^2).$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space and let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int f\,d\mu=0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad f=0 \text{ almost everywhere.}$$

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int g\,d(f\,d\mu)=\int gf\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: By [F1], each $Y_i$ is obtained from $X_i$ by the same measurable weighted-integrand map and $\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}}=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nY_i$. Since the $X_i$ are IID, [F3] preserves independence and their common law under this map; [F4] therefore makes $(Y_i)$ IID.

Applying [F2] to a sample of size one gives $\mathbb E_QY_1=\theta$, and it also gives $\mathbb E_Q[\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}}]=\theta$ for the supplied sample. By step 1.1 every $Y_i$ has the same finite second moment and variance $\sigma^2$, and the finite family is pairwise independent. Thus [F5] gives $\operatorname{Var}_Q(\sum_{i=1}^nY_i)=n\sigma^2$ and $\operatorname{Var}_Q(\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}})=n^{-2}(n\sigma^2)=\sigma^2/n$.

Use [F11] with density $r=q$ for integration against $Q$. Applying [F6] to the nonnegative squared weighted integrand gives $\mathbb E_Q[Y_1^2]=Z_p^{-2}\int_{\{q>0\}}f(x)^2\tilde p(x)^2/q(x)\,d\mu(x)$. By [F5] and step 2.1, $\sigma^2=\mathbb E_Q[Y_1^2]-\theta^2$, proving the displayed variance formula.

For the CLT, use the given IID sequence $(X_i)_{i\ge1}$ and assume AC as in [A1]. The measurable transformation in step 1.1 now makes $(Y_i)_{i\ge1}$ IID. If $\sigma^2>0$, [F8] applies to the IID sequence from step 1.1 with mean $\theta$ from step 2.1 and yields the stated normal limit. If $\sigma^2=0$, [F7] gives $\mathbb E_Q[(Y_1-\theta)^2]=0$, so [F9] implies $Y_1=\theta$ $Q$-almost surely. By the common-law conclusion of step 1.1, each event $\{Y_i\ne\theta\}$ is null; for each fixed $n$, the union of the first $n$ such events is null. Thus $\bar Y_n=\theta$ almost surely for each $n$, and the centered sample mean has law $\delta_0=N(0,0)$ for every $n$ by [F10]. The variance argument in the preceding steps used no choice axiom.

citations.quote:
Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X,\mu)$ be a measure space. The unnormalized target density is a measurable $\tilde p\ge0$ with $0<Z_p=\int\tilde p\,d\mu<\infty$ and target $\pi(dx)=\tilde p(x)\mu(dx)/Z_p$. Let $q\ge0$ be a measurable proposal probability density against $\mu$, let $Q(dx)=q(x)\mu(dx)$, and let $f$ be a measurable real-valued integrand. The input $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ is an IID sample from $Q$ in the sense of [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]], with $n\ge1$. For target interpretation require $q>0$ $\pi$-almost everywhere. Write
$$W_i:=\begin{cases}\tilde p(X_i)/q(X_i),&q(X_i)>0,\\0,&q(X_i)=0.\end{cases}$$
This is a nonnegative unnormalized importance weight; the value on $q=0$ is immaterial under $Q$ and under the stated target support condition.

The reciprocal map that is $1/s$ for $s>0$ and $0$ for $s\le0$ is Borel. Its composition with $q$, multiplied by $\tilde p$, makes $W_i$ measurable by [[thm-composition-with-borel-functions-preserves-measurability]] and [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]].

**Procedure and output:** Compute $S_n=\sum_{i=1}^nW_i$. If $S_n=0$, return the status **no estimate: zero observed target weight**. If $S_n>0$, return
$$\hat\theta_{\mathrm{SN}}:=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^nW_if(X_i)}{S_n}.$$
For consistency require $\mathbb E_QW_1=Z_p\in(0,\infty)$ and $\mathbb E_Q[W_1|f(X_1)|]<\infty$. A ratio CLT and its Monte Carlo standard error require finite second moments of $W_1$ and $W_1f(X_1)$.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element, let
$\mathbb P_X$ be its law, and let $g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb R$ or
$g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb C$ be measurable.

1. If $g\ge0$, then
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$
2. If $g(X)$ is integrable, then $g$ is integrable with respect to
   $\mathbb P_X$ and the same formula holds:
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. For each $i$, let
$g_i:(S_i,\Sigma_i)\to(T_i,\mathcal T_i)$ be measurable. Then the family
$(g_i\circ X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $(Y_i)_{i\ge1}$ be a real IID sequence with $\mathbb E|Y_1|<\infty$, and set $\mu=\mathbb E[Y_1]$. Then $\mathbb E|\bar Y_n-\mu|\to0$, so $\bar Y_n\to\mu$ in probability; moreover, $\bar Y_n\to\mu$ almost surely.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$, $(Y,\mathcal{B})$, and $(Z,\mathcal{C})$ be measurable
spaces. If $f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Y,\mathcal{B})$ is measurable and
$g : (Y,\mathcal{B}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable, then
$g \circ f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable.

In particular, if $f$ is measurable and $g$ is a Borel measurable function on
its codomain, then $g \circ f$ is measurable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space and let
$f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ be measurable for the Borel sigma-algebra on
the extended real line. Products of functions use
$\odot_X$ from [[def-measurable-pointwise-extended-real-product]], and $cf$
abbreviates $\underline c\odot_X f$ for the constant function $\underline c$.
The magnitude function is $|f|=\max(f,-f)$ as in
[[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]]. Then:

1. $cf$ is measurable for every real scalar $c$;
2. $\max(f,g)$, $\min(f,g)$, $|f|$, $f^+$, and $f^-$ are measurable;
3. if the partial pointwise sum $f+g$ is defined at every point, then it is measurable;
4. the pointwise product $fg:=f\odot_X g$ is measurable.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $E$ be measurable with $\mu(E)=0$.
Then
$$\int_E f\,d\mu=0.$$

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X,\mu)$ be a measure space. The unnormalized target density is a measurable $\tilde p\ge0$ with $0<Z_p=\int\tilde p\,d\mu<\infty$ and target $\pi(dx)=\tilde p(x)\mu(dx)/Z_p$. Let $q\ge0$ be a measurable proposal probability density against $\mu$, let $Q(dx)=q(x)\mu(dx)$, and let $f$ be a measurable real-valued integrand. The input $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ is an IID sample from $Q$ in the sense of [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]], with $n\ge1$. For target interpretation require $q>0$ $\pi$-almost everywhere. Write
$$W_i:=\begin{cases}\tilde p(X_i)/q(X_i),&q(X_i)>0,\\0,&q(X_i)=0.\end{cases}$$
This is a nonnegative unnormalized importance weight; the value on $q=0$ is immaterial under $Q$ and under the stated target support condition.

The reciprocal map that is $1/s$ for $s>0$ and $0$ for $s\le0$ is Borel. Its composition with $q$, multiplied by $\tilde p$, makes $W_i$ measurable by [[thm-composition-with-borel-functions-preserves-measurability]] and [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]].

**Procedure and output:** Compute $S_n=\sum_{i=1}^nW_i$. If $S_n=0$, return the status **no estimate: zero observed target weight**. If $S_n>0$, return
$$\hat\theta_{\mathrm{SN}}:=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^nW_if(X_i)}{S_n}.$$
For consistency require $\mathbb E_QW_1=Z_p\in(0,\infty)$ and $\mathbb E_Q[W_1|f(X_1)|]<\infty$. A ratio CLT and its Monte Carlo standard error require finite second moments of $W_1$ and $W_1f(X_1)$.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element, let
$\mathbb P_X$ be its law, and let $g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb R$ or
$g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb C$ be measurable.

1. If $g\ge0$, then
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$
2. If $g(X)$ is integrable, then $g$ is integrable with respect to
   $\mathbb P_X$ and the same formula holds:
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be a finite integer. Let $(X_k)_{k\ge1}$ be iid $\mathbb R^d$-valued random vectors with $\mathbb E\|X_1\|^2<\infty$, mean m and covariance Sigma. Then $$n^{-1/2}\sum_{k=1}^n(X_k-m)\Rightarrow N_d(0,\Sigma).$$ The covariance may be singular.

Let $d,k\ge1$, let $r_n>0$ be deterministic with $r_n\to\infty$, and let $T_n$ be $\mathbb R^d$-valued random vectors with target $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$. Suppose $Z_n=r_n(T_n-\theta)\Rightarrow Z$ for an $\mathbb R^d$-valued random vector $Z$. All vector norms below are Euclidean.

If $g:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^k$ is Borel and there is a linear map $A:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^k$ such that
$$g(\theta+h)-g(\theta)=Ah+\rho_1(h),\qquad \frac{\|\rho_1(h)\|}{\|h\|}\longrightarrow0\quad(h\to0,\ h\ne0),$$
then
$$r_n\{g(T_n)-g(\theta)\}\Rightarrow AZ.$$

If, in addition, $A=0$ and there is a continuous symmetric bilinear map $H:\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^k$ such that
$$g(\theta+h)-g(\theta)=\frac12H[h,h]+\rho_2(h),\qquad \frac{\|\rho_2(h)\|}{\|h\|^2}\longrightarrow0\quad(h\to0,\ h\ne0),$$
then
$$r_n^2\{g(T_n)-g(\theta)\}\Rightarrow \frac12H[Z,Z].$$
For scalar-valued $g$, $H$ is the usual Hessian bilinear form. The second-order premise is a pointwise Peano expansion; continuous second derivatives on a neighborhood are not required.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X,\mu)$ be a measure space, $\tilde p\ge0$ a measurable target density with $Z_p=\int\tilde p\,d\mu\in(0,\infty)$, $\pi(dx)=\tilde p(x)\mu(dx)/Z_p$, and $q\ge0$ a measurable proposal probability density with $Q(dx)=q(x)\mu(dx)$. Assume $q>0$ $\pi$-almost everywhere. Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be IID with law $Q$, put $W_i=\tilde p(X_i)/q(X_i)$ for $q(X_i)>0$ and $W_i=0$ otherwise, and let $f:\mathsf X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Suppose
$$\mathbb E_QW_1=Z_p\in(0,\infty),\qquad \mathbb E_Q[W_1|f(X_1)|]<\infty.$$
Then the self-normalized estimate in [[alg-self-normalized-importance-sampling]] satisfies
$$\hat\theta_{\mathrm{SN},n}\longrightarrow\theta:=\int f\,d\pi\quad\text{almost surely}.$$
On a finite prefix where all observed weights vanish, the algorithm's no-estimate status is interpreted as the value $0$ for this convergence statement; almost surely that fallback is eventually unnecessary.
For IID real $(X_n)_{n\ge1}$ with $\mathbb E|X_1|<\infty$, $S_n/n\to\mu=\mathbb EX_1$ almost surely.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. For each $i$, let
$g_i:(S_i,\Sigma_i)\to(T_i,\mathcal T_i)$ be measurable. Then the family
$(g_i\circ X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be conjugate exponents. If $X$ and $Y$ are real random
variables in the spaces named by the corresponding clause of
[[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]], then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\|X\|_p\|Y\|_q.$$

In particular, $XY$ is integrable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space and let
$f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ be measurable for the Borel sigma-algebra on
the extended real line. Products of functions use
$\odot_X$ from [[def-measurable-pointwise-extended-real-product]], and $cf$
abbreviates $\underline c\odot_X f$ for the constant function $\underline c$.
The magnitude function is $|f|=\max(f,-f)$ as in
[[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]]. Then:

1. $cf$ is measurable for every real scalar $c$;
2. $\max(f,g)$, $\min(f,g)$, $|f|$, $f^+$, and $f^-$ are measurable;
3. if the partial pointwise sum $f+g$ is defined at every point, then it is measurable;
4. the pointwise product $fg:=f\odot_X g$ is measurable.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $E$ be measurable with $\mu(E)=0$.
Then
$$\int_E f\,d\mu=0.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int g\,d(f\,d\mu)=\int gf\,d\mu.$$

Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Its positive and negative parts are
$$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$
they are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]] and
satisfy $f=f^+-f^-$ and $|f|=f^++f^-$.

The **Lebesgue integral of a real measurable function** is defined whenever at
most one of $\int f^+\,d\mu$ and $\int f^-\,d\mu$ is $+\infty$, in which case
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu.$$
The function is **integrable** when both integrals are finite, equivalently
when $\int|f|\,d\mu<+\infty$.

For a complex measurable function $h=u+iv$ with
$u=\operatorname{Re}h,\ v=\operatorname{Im}h$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]), define $h$ to be
**integrable** when $|h|$ is integrable, and then define
$$\int h\,d\mu:=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$

Thus $\int_{\mathsf X}\tilde p|f|\,d\mu<\infty$. Subtracting their finite identities yields $\int h\,d(r\,d\mu)=\int hr\,d\mu$, since $(hr)^\pm=h^\pm r$ for $r\ge0$ (with the density convention $0\cdot\infty=0$). Applying [F7] to this map proves that the pairs $Z_i$ are independent; their laws agree because each $X_i$ has law $Q$ and the same map is applied, so they are IID by [F8]. Therefore [F3] and [A1] give $\sqrt n((\bar W_n,\bar V_n)-(Z_p,Z_p\theta))\Rightarrow N_2(0,\Sigma)$, where $\Sigma=\operatorname{Cov}_Q(Z_1)$.

Put $U_i=W_i^2(f(X_i)-\theta)^2$, $C_i=W_i^2(f(X_i)-\theta)$, and $B_i=W_i^2$. Their measurability follows from [F12]. Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element, let
$\mathbb P_X$ be its law, and let $g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb R$ or
$g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb C$ be measurable.

1. If $g\ge0$, then
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$
2. If $g(X)$ is integrable, then $g$ is integrable with respect to
   $\mathbb P_X$ and the same formula holds:
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$

Use the hypotheses and notation of [[thm-ordinary-importance-sampling-is-unbiased]]. Define
$$Y_i:=\begin{cases}f(X_i)\tilde p(X_i)/(Z_pq(X_i)),&q(X_i)>0,\\0,&q(X_i)=0\end{cases},\qquad \theta:=\int f\,d\pi,\qquad \sigma^2:=\operatorname{Var}_Q(Y_1).$$
If $\mathbb E_Q[Y_1^2]<\infty$, then $\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}}$ has finite variance and
$$\operatorname{Var}_Q(\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}})=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}=\frac1n\left(\frac1{Z_p^2}\int_{\{q>0\}}\frac{f(x)^2\tilde p(x)^2}{q(x)}\,d\mu(x)-\theta^2\right).$$
This finite-sample conclusion is choice-free. For the central limit conclusion, let $(X_i)_{i\ge1}$ be an IID sequence with law $Q$, and apply the estimator to its first $n$ draws for each $n\ge1$. If, in addition, AC holds, then
$$\sqrt n\bigl(\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}}-\theta\bigr)\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma^2).$$
No finite variance or normal-limit claim is made when the weighted second moment is infinite.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $\tilde p\ge0$ and $q\ge0$ be measurable densities with $Z_p=\int\tilde p\,d\mu\in(0,\infty)$ and $\int q\,d\mu=1$, and set $\pi(dx)=\tilde p(x)\mu(dx)/Z_p$ and $Q(dx)=q(x)\mu(dx)$. Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the

$$\int g\,d(f\,d\mu)=\int gf\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: On $\mathbb R$ with Lebesgue measure, take target density $p(x)=\tilde p(x)=\tfrac12e^{-|x|}$, proposal density $q(x)=e^{-2|x|}$, and $f(x)=1$. Direct integration gives $\int p=\tfrac12(\int_{-\infty}^0e^x\,dx+\int_0^\infty e^{-x}\,dx)=1$ and $\int q=2\int_0^\infty e^{-2x}\,dx=1$. Also $q(x)>0$ for every $x$, while $f=1$ has target mean $1$ and variance $0$.

Use [F7] with density $r=q$ for integration against $Q$. For every $x$, the importance weight is $W(x)=p(x)/q(x)=\tfrac12e^{|x|}$. By [F2], $\mathbb E_QW=\int_{\mathbb R}p(x)\,dx=1$ and $\mathbb E_Q[W^2]=\int_{\mathbb R}\frac14e^{2|x|}e^{-2|x|}\,dx=\int_{\mathbb R}\frac14\,dx=\infty$. The proposal has full target support, but the finite-second-moment hypothesis in [F3] fails.

By [F5], the ordinary estimate $\bar W_n=n^{-1}\sum_iW_i$ has mean $1$. For each finite $n$, nonnegativity gives $\bar W_n\ge W_1/n$, hence $W_1^2/n^2\le\bar W_n^2$. Monotonicity [F6] and step 2.1 imply $\mathbb E_Q[\bar W_n^2]\ge n^{-2}\mathbb E_Q[W_1^2]=\infty$. If its centered second moment were finite, the inequality $x^2\le2(x-1)^2+2$ would imply $\mathbb E_Q[\bar W_n^2]<\infty$, a contradiction. Thus the centered second moment is infinite, so the estimate does not have finite variance under [F4]. This refutes the sufficiency claim.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ be a measurable space, let $P$ be a probability
kernel on it, meaning that $P(x,\cdot)$ is a probability measure for each $x$
and $x\mapsto P(x,A)$ is measurable for each $A\in\mathcal X$
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and let $\pi$ be a
probability measure, that is a countably additive measure of total mass one
([[def-probability-measure]]). The product sigma-algebra
$\mathcal X\otimes\mathcal X$ is generated by measurable rectangles
([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]). The joint
flow measure of $(\pi,P)$ is the probability measure $\Lambda_{\pi,P}$ on
$(\mathsf X\times\mathsf X,\mathcal X\otimes\mathcal X)$ given, for each
$C\in\mathcal X\otimes\mathcal X$, by

$$\Lambda_{\pi,P}(C):=\int_{\mathsf X}P(x,C_x)\,\pi(dx),\qquad C_x:=\{y\in\mathsf X:(x,y)\in C\}.$$

Existence, countable additivity, and the nonnegative iterated-integral identity
for this measure follow from
[[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]]. Let $\tau(x,y):=(y,x)$ be
the coordinate-swap map. It is measurable because the preimage of a measurable
rectangle $A\times B$ is $B\times A$ and such rectangles generate the product
sigma-algebra. Define the transpose measure by
$\Lambda_{\pi,P}^{\top}(C):=\Lambda_{\pi,P}(\tau^{-1}(C))$.

The kernel $P$ is **reversible with respect to $\pi$** when
$$\Lambda_{\pi,P}=\Lambda_{\pi,P}^{\top}.$$
This definition uses equality of measures and requires no density, standard
Borel assumption, or prior assumption that $\pi$ is invariant.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be measurable spaces,
let $\pi$ be a probability measure on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$, and let
$K:\Theta\times\mathcal A\to[0,1]$ be a probability kernel. For
$C\in\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal A$, write
$C_\theta=\{x\in\mathcal X:(\theta,x)\in C\}$ and set
$$J(C)=\int_\Theta K(\theta,C_\theta)\,\pi(d\theta).$$
Then $J$ is a probability measure on the product sigma-algebra, and for every
nonnegative product-measurable $h$,
$$\int_{\Theta\times\mathcal X}h(\theta,x)\,J(d\theta,dx)=\int_\Theta\left(\int_\mathcal Xh(\theta,x)\,K(\theta,dx)\right)\pi(d\theta).$$
In particular, $J(A\times B)=\int_AK(\theta,B)\,\pi(d\theta)$ for
$A\in\mathcal T$ and $B\in\mathcal A$.

Let $K$ be a probability kernel on a measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and let $\pi$ be a
probability measure on $(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). The
probability measure $\pi$ is **invariant** for $K$, and $\pi$ is a
**stationary distribution** of $K$, when

$$(\pi K)(A):=\int_E K(x,A)\,\pi(dx)=\pi(A)\qquad\text{for every }A\in\mathcal E .$$

The set function $\pi K$ is again a probability measure: for fixed $A$ the map
$x\mapsto K(x,A)$ is measurable and lies in $[0,1]$, so the integral exists in
$[0,1]$; for pairwise disjoint $A_n\in\mathcal E$ the identity
$K(x,\bigcup_nA_n)=\sum_nK(x,A_n)$ of the measure $K(x,\cdot)$ and the
monotone convergence theorem for nonnegative functions
([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]) give
$\sigma$-additivity of $\pi K$; and $K(x,E)=1$ for every $x$ gives
$(\pi K)(E)=1$. Thus $(\pi K)(A)=\pi(A)$ is an identity between two probability
measures evaluated at $A$.

A $K$-chain whose initial law is $\pi$ is called **stationary** when
$\pi K=\pi$. Stationarity of the process is a statement about all of its
finite-dimensional laws and is proved, not assumed, from $\pi K=\pi$; see
[[thm-invariant-initial-law-makes-the-chain-stationary]].

On a countable state space $E$ with sigma-algebra $2^E$ and transition matrix
$p(x,y)=K(x,\{y\})$ ([[def-transition-matrix-and-n-step-transition-probabilities]]),
a measure on $E$ is its weighted sum of Dirac masses at singletons
([[thm-measures-on-countable-discrete-spaces-are-weighted-dirac-sums]]), so
invariance is equivalent to the matrix identity

$$\pi(y)=\sum_{x\in E}\pi(x)\,p(x,y)\qquad\text{for every }y\in E .$$

The definition fixes no irreducibility, aperiodicity or uniqueness hypothesis,
and it selects no conditional-expectation versions; the display defines a
single measure $\pi K$ and asserts an identity for it. A transient, periodic or
reducible chain may have several invariant probability measures or none.

([[def-probability-measure]]). The product sigma-algebra
$\mathcal X\otimes\mathcal X$ is generated by measurable rectangles
([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]). The joint

$(\mathsf X\times\mathsf X,\mathcal X\otimes\mathcal X)$ given, for each

$$\Lambda_{\pi,P}(C):=\int_{\mathsf X}P(x,C_x)\,\pi(dx),\qquad C_x:=\{y\in\mathsf X:(x,y)\in C\}.$$

rectangle $A\times B$ is $B\times A$ and such rectangles generate the product

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Throughout, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^n$ is written
$\lambda_n$ ([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]), and
$\mathbb Z\subseteq\mathbb R$ is the copy of the integers
([[def-integers]]).

**The torus.** Let $q:\mathbb R\to\mathbb T:=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ be the
canonical projection of the quotient of the additive group $\mathbb R$ by its
subgroup $\mathbb Z$, carrying the quotient topology
([[def-quotient-topology]], [[def-topological-space]]); we write
$[t]:=q(t)=t+\mathbb Z$. Thus $[s]=[t]$ exactly when $s-t\in\mathbb Z$. The map
$q$ is continuous ([[def-continuous-map-top]]), and $\mathbb T$ is a compact
Hausdorff space homeomorphic to the Euclidean unit circle.

**Fundamental domain.** Every class has exactly one representative in $[0,1)$:
for $t\in\mathbb R$ the integer part $n=\lfloor t\rfloor$ satisfies
$n\le t<n+1$, so $t-n\in[0,1)$ represents $[t]$ ([[lem-integer-part]]); and if
$s,t\in[0,1)$ satisfy $s-t\in\mathbb Z$, then $|s-t|<1$ forces $s=t$.
Consequently the map $[0,1)\to\mathbb T$, $t\mapsto[t]$, is a bijection.

**Topological checks.** The closed interval $[0,1]$ is compact by [[thm-heine-borel-r]] and maps onto $\mathbb T$, so the quotient is compact by [[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]. The map $t\mapsto(\cos 2\pi t,\sin 2\pi t)$ is continuous by [[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]] and [[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]], and is constant on quotient fibres by [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]]. It induces a continuous map $\varphi:\mathbb T\to S^1$ by [[thm-quotient-universal-property]]. The bijection of $[0,2\pi)$ with the circle in [[thm-sine-and-cosine-parametrize-the-unit-circle]], together with the unique representatives in $[0,1)$, makes $\varphi$ bijective. The Euclidean circle is Hausdorff by [[thm-metric-hausdorff-separation]], so the compact-to-Hausdorff clause of [[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]] makes $\varphi$ a homeomorphism. In particular $\mathbb T$ is Hausdorff.

The map $q$ is open: for an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R$, its saturation $q^{-1}[q[U]]=\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb Z}(U+k)$ is open. The images under $q$ of rational-endpoint open intervals form a countable base: if $q(t)\in V$ with $V$ open, choose such an interval containing $t$ and contained in $q^{-1}[V]$. Its image is an open neighbourhood contained in $V$.

**The measure.** For a Borel set $E\in\mathcal B(\mathbb T)$
([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]) the preimage $q^{-1}[E]$ is a Borel subset of
$\mathbb R$, because $q$ is continuous
([[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]]), hence Lebesgue
measurable ([[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]). Define

$$m_{\mathbb T}(E):=\lambda_1\bigl(q^{-1}[E]\cap[0,1)\bigr) ,$$

the value at $q^{-1}[E]$ of the same-ambient restriction of $\lambda_1$ to $[0,1)$
([[def-restriction-of-a-measure]]).

This is a measure on $\mathcal B(\mathbb T)$ by [[prop-restriction-is-a-measure]]:
the assignment $E\mapsto\lambda_1(q^{-1}[E]\cap[0,1))$ is the composition of the
restriction measure with the inverse image along $q$, and inverse images preserve
the empty set, complements and countable unions, while countable additivity is
that of $\lambda_1$. It is a **probability measure**:
$m_{\mathbb T}(\mathbb T)=\lambda_1([0,1))=1$
([[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]]). Thus
$(\mathbb T,\mathcal B(\mathbb T),m_{\mathbb T})$ is a probability measure space
([[def-measure-space]], [[def-measure]]).

**The integral.** For a Borel measurable $F:\mathbb T\to[0,+\infty]$, define

$$\int_{\mathbb T}F\,dm_{\mathbb T}:=\int_{[0,1)}F\circ q\,d\lambda_1 .$$

The defining integral is meaningful because $F\circ q$ is Borel
([[thm-composition-with-borel-functions-preserves-measurability]],
[[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]]). The assignment agrees with
$E\mapsto m_{\mathbb T}(E)$ on indicators, and it is additive and homogeneous on
finite nonnegative simple functions; for a sequence $0\le F_0\le F_1\le\cdots$
with $F_n\uparrow F$ pointwise the identity passes to the limit because
$F_n\circ q\uparrow F\circ q$ and monotone convergence holds for $\lambda_1$
([[thm-increasing-simple-approximation-of-a-nonnegative-measurable-function]],
[[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]). For real or complex integrable
$F$ the integral is defined by decomposition into nonnegative parts or into real
and imaginary parts, and it is linear
([[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]],
[[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]). In particular
$\int_{\mathbb T}1\,dm_{\mathbb T}=1$, and the same formula holds with $[0,1)$
replaced by any half-open interval $[a,a+1)$ or $(a,a+1]$, by the periodicity of
$q^{-1}[E]$ and the translation invariance of $\lambda_1$
([[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-and-measurability-are-translation-invariant]]).

**Translation invariance.** For $y\in\mathbb R$ the map
$\tau_y:\mathbb T\to\mathbb T$, $\tau_y([t]):=[t+y]$, is well defined (if
$s-t\in\mathbb Z$ then $(s+y)-(t+y)\in\mathbb Z$) and continuous, because it is
induced by the continuous map $t\mapsto q(t+y)$ from $\mathbb R$ to $\mathbb T$. This composite is constant on the fibres of $q$, since $q(t)=q(s)$ implies $q(t+y)=q(s+y)$ ([[thm-quotient-universal-property]]). It preserves
$m_{\mathbb T}$: write $y=n+r$ with $n=\lfloor y\rfloor$ and $r\in[0,1)$, put
$A:=q^{-1}[E]$ and use that $A-n=A$ and that
$A\cap[0,1)=\bigl(A\cap[0,r)\bigr)\cup\bigl(A\cap[r,1)\bigr)$ while
$A\cap[r,r+1)=\bigl(A\cap[r,1)\bigr)\cup\bigl((A\cap[0,r))+1\bigr)$, so that

$$m_{\mathbb T}(\tau_y^{-1}E)=\lambda_1\bigl((A-y)\cap[0,1)\bigr)=\lambda_1\bigl(A\cap[r,r+1)\bigr)=\lambda_1\bigl(A\cap[0,1)\bigr)=m_{\mathbb T}(E),$$

the middle equality by translation invariance of $\lambda_1$. Hence
$(\mathbb T,\mathcal B(\mathbb T),m_{\mathbb T},\tau_y)$ is a measure-preserving
system for every $y$, and the published integral-invariance theorem gives
$\int_{\mathbb T}F\circ\tau_y\,dm_{\mathbb T}=\int_{\mathbb T}F\,dm_{\mathbb T}$
for every measurable $F\ge0$ and every integrable $F$
([[def-measure-preserving-transformation-and-system]],
[[thm-integrals-are-invariant-under-measure-preserving-maps]]). This is the
**normalized Haar integral** of $\mathbb T$; abstract Haar theory is not
invoked.

**The finite torus.** For a natural $n\ge1$ put
$\mathbb T^n:=\mathbb R^n/\mathbb Z^n$ with the quotient topology of the
canonical projection $q_n$, and define

$$m_{\mathbb T^n}(E):=\lambda_n\bigl(q_n^{-1}[E]\cap[0,1)^n\bigr),\qquad \int_{\mathbb T^n}F\,dm_{\mathbb T^n}:=\int_{[0,1)^n}F\circ q_n\,d\lambda_n .$$

Coordinatewise integer parts give unique representatives in $[0,1)^n$, and the continuous quotient map sends the compact cube $[0,1]^n$ onto $\mathbb T^n$. Compactness of the cube follows from [[thm-heine-borel-r]] and [[thm-finite-products-of-compact-spaces]], and compactness of its image follows from [[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]. Preimages of Borel sets are Borel; disjoint preimages and countable additivity make the displayed set function a measure, and the box formula gives total mass one. The integral identity follows from indicators, increasing simple approximation and decomposition exactly as in one dimension. For translation invariance, discard the integer parts of the translation vector, split each coordinate of $[0,1)^n$ at its fractional part, and translate the resulting $2^n$ disjoint half-open boxes by integer vectors to partition the translated cube. The periodic preimage set is unchanged by these integer vectors; finite additivity and Lebesgue translation invariance give the same measure. Applying the indicator identity, simple approximation and decomposition gives the integral formula on any translated cube. The coordinate projections induce a continuous bijection
$\Phi:\mathbb T^n\to(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^n$ by the universal property. Its
domain is compact by the preceding check, while its codomain is a finite
product of Hausdorff spaces and hence Hausdorff ([[lem-products-preserve-t0-t1-and-hausdorff]]); the continuous-bijection
theorem therefore makes $\Phi$ a homeomorphism. Thus $\mathbb T^n$ carries the
finite product topology ([[def-product-topology]],
[[thm-finite-products-of-compact-spaces]],
[[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]), and its characters
$x\mapsto\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, are defined on this compact
Hausdorff space: replacing representatives by integer vectors leaves the exponential unchanged by [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]] and the trigonometric period. Finite products of the countable base above form a countable rectangular base. Hence every product-open set is a countable union of Borel rectangles. Conversely coordinate projections are continuous, so Borel rectangles are Borel in the product. Thus the product Borel sigma-algebra equals the Borel sigma-algebra of $\mathbb T^n$. On a product $A_0\times\cdots\times A_{n-1}$ of Borel subsets
of the factors, the defining fundamental-domain formula and repeated application of [[thm-lebesgue-product-measure-agrees-with-euclidean-lebesgue-on-borel-sets]] give
$m_{\mathbb T^n}(A_0\times\cdots\times A_{n-1})=\prod_jm_{\mathbb T}(A_j)$, so
$m_{\mathbb T^n}$ agrees on every measurable rectangle with the product measure
$m_{\mathbb T}\times\cdots\times m_{\mathbb T}$
([[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]]); both are probability measures,
and uniqueness of the product measure on sigma-finite spaces identifies them
on the entire Borel sigma-algebra
([[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]).
Fubini's theorem then computes iterated integrals of $L^1$ functions on
$\mathbb T^n$
([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

$$m_{\mathbb T}(\tau_y^{-1}E)=\lambda_1\bigl((A-y)\cap[0,1)\bigr)=\lambda_1\bigl(A\cap[r,r+1)\bigr)=\lambda_1\bigl(A\cap[0,1)\bigr)=m_{\mathbb T}(E),$$

$(\mathbb T,\mathcal B(\mathbb T),m_{\mathbb T},\tau_y)$ is a measure-preserving

$\int_{\mathbb T}F\circ\tau_y\,dm_{\mathbb T}=\int_{\mathbb T}F\,dm_{\mathbb T}$
for every measurable $F\ge0$ and every integrable $F$
([[def-measure-preserving-transformation-and-system]],
[[thm-integrals-are-invariant-under-measure-preserving-maps]]). This is the
**normalized Haar integral** of $\mathbb T$; abstract Haar theory is not
invoked.

**The finite torus.** For a natural $n\ge1$ put

Compactness of the cube follows from [[thm-heine-borel-r]] and [[thm-finite-products-of-compact-spaces]], and compactness of its image follows from [[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]. The integral identity follows from indicators, increasing simple approximation and decomposition exactly as in one dimension. For translation invariance, discard the integer parts of the translation vector, split each coordinate of $[0,1)^n$ at its fractional part, and translate the resulting $2^n$ disjoint half-open boxes by integer vectors to partition the translated cube. The periodic preimage set is unchanged by these integer vectors; finite additivity and Lebesgue translation invariance give the same measure. Applying the indicator identity, simple approximation and decomposition gives the integral formula on any translated cube. The coordinate projections induce a continuous bijection

domain is compact by the preceding check, while its codomain is a finite
product of Hausdorff spaces and hence Hausdorff ([[lem-products-preserve-t0-t1-and-hausdorff]]); the continuous-bijection
theorem therefore makes $\Phi$ a homeomorphism. Thus $\mathbb T^n$ carries the
finite product topology ([[def-product-topology]],
[[thm-finite-products-of-compact-spaces]],
[[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]), and its characters
$x\mapsto\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, are defined on this compact
Hausdorff space: replacing representatives by integer vectors leaves the exponential unchanged by [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]] and the trigonometric period. Finite products of the countable base above form a countable rectangular base. Hence every product-open set is a countable union of Borel rectangles. Conversely coordinate projections are continuous, so Borel rectangles are Borel in the product. Thus the product Borel sigma-algebra equals the Borel sigma-algebra of $\mathbb T^n$. On a product $A_0\times\cdots\times A_{n-1}$ of Borel subsets
of the factors, the defining fundamental-domain formula and repeated application of [[thm-lebesgue-product-measure-agrees-with-euclidean-lebesgue-on-borel-sets]] give
$m_{\mathbb T^n}(A_0\times\cdots\times A_{n-1})=\prod_jm_{\mathbb T}(A_j)$, so
$m_{\mathbb T^n}$ agrees on every measurable rectangle with the product measure
$m_{\mathbb T}\times\cdots\times m_{\mathbb T}$
([[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]]); both are probability measures,
and uniqueness of the product measure on sigma-finite spaces identifies them
on the entire Borel sigma-algebra
([[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]).
Fubini's theorem then computes iterated integrals of $L^1$ functions on
$\mathbb T^n$
([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

Throughout, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^n$ is written
$\lambda_n$ ([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]), and
$\mathbb Z\subseteq\mathbb R$ is the copy of the integers
([[def-integers]]).

**The torus.** Let $q:\mathbb R\to\mathbb T:=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ be the
canonical projection of the quotient of the additive group $\mathbb R$ by its
subgroup $\mathbb Z$, carrying the quotient topology

$q$ is continuous ([[def-continuous-map-top]]), and $\mathbb T$ is a compact
Hausdorff space homeomorphic to the Euclidean unit circle.

**Fundamental domain.** Every class has exactly one representative in $[0,1)$:
for $t\in\mathbb R$ the integer part $n=\lfloor t\rfloor$ satisfies
$n\le t<n+1$, so $t-n\in[0,1)$ represents $[t]$ ([[lem-integer-part]]); and if

It induces a continuous map $\varphi:\mathbb T\to S^1$ by [[thm-quotient-universal-property]]. The bijection of $[0,2\pi)$ with the circle in [[thm-sine-and-cosine-parametrize-the-unit-circle]], together with the unique representatives in $[0,1)$, makes $\varphi$ bijective. The Euclidean circle is Hausdorff by [[thm-metric-hausdorff-separation]], so the compact-to-Hausdorff clause of [[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]] makes $\varphi$ a homeomorphism. The map $q$ is open: for an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R$, its saturation $q^{-1}[q[U]]=\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb Z}(U+k)$ is open. Its image is an open neighbourhood contained in $V$.

([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]) the preimage $q^{-1}[E]$ is a Borel subset of

([[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]]), hence Lebesgue

$$m_{\mathbb T}(E):=\lambda_1\bigl(q^{-1}[E]\cap[0,1)\bigr) ,$$

([[def-restriction-of-a-measure]]).

the assignment $E\mapsto\lambda_1(q^{-1}[E]\cap[0,1))$ is the composition of the
restriction measure with the inverse image along $q$, and inverse images preserve
the empty set, complements and countable unions, while countable additivity is
that of $\lambda_1$. It is a **probability measure**:
$m_{\mathbb T}(\mathbb T)=\lambda_1([0,1))=1$
([[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]]). Thus
$(\mathbb T,\mathcal B(\mathbb T),m_{\mathbb T})$ is a probability measure space
([[def-measure-space]], [[def-measure]]).

**The integral.** For a Borel measurable $F:\mathbb T\to[0,+\infty]$, define

$$\int_{\mathbb T}F\,dm_{\mathbb T}:=\int_{[0,1)}F\circ q\,d\lambda_1 .$$

The defining integral is meaningful because $F\circ q$ is Borel
([[thm-composition-with-borel-functions-preserves-measurability]],

([[thm-increasing-simple-approximation-of-a-nonnegative-measurable-function]],
[[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]). For real or complex integrable

([[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]],

([[def-measure-preserving-transformation-and-system]],

invoked.

theorem therefore makes $\Phi$ a homeomorphism. Thus $\mathbb T^n$ carries the

Conversely coordinate projections are continuous, so Borel rectangles are Borel in the product. Thus the product Borel sigma-algebra equals the Borel sigma-algebra of $\mathbb T^n$. On a product $A_0\times\cdots\times A_{n-1}$ of Borel subsets
of the factors, the defining fundamental-domain formula and repeated application of [[thm-lebesgue-product-measure-agrees-with-euclidean-lebesgue-on-borel-sets]] give
$m_{\mathbb T^n}(A_0\times\cdots\times A_{n-1})=\prod_jm_{\mathbb T}(A_j)$, so
