The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

For $m,n\ge0$,
$$K^{m+n}=K^mK^n.$$ Assume Choice and let $X$ be a Markov chain with kernel $K$ relative to $(\mathcal F_n)$. For every bounded measurable real $f$, $$ \mathbb E[f(X_{m+n})\mid\mathcal F_m]=K^nf(X_m)\quad\text{a.s.} $$ Equivalently, for $A\in\mathcal E$, $$ \mathbb P(X_{m+n}\in A\mid\mathcal F_m)=K^n(X_m,A)\quad\text{a.s.} $$
Both assertions include $m=0$ and $n=0$.

Assume AC. For nonnegative measurable $X$ (possibly infinite), $E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ is the unique almost-sure class of nonnegative $\mathcal G$-measurable $Y$ satisfying $\int_A Y\,dP=\int_A X\,dP$ for every $A\in\mathcal G$. If $0\le X_n\uparrow X$ almost surely, then $E[X_n\mid\mathcal G]\uparrow E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. Every increasing integrable nonnegative approximation to $X$ gives the same class. For integrable real $V_n\downarrow V$ almost surely with $V_0,V\in L^1$, $E[V_n\mid\mathcal G]\downarrow E[V\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely.

Let $K$ be a probability kernel on a measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and let $\pi$ be a
probability measure on $(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). The
probability measure $\pi$ is **invariant** for $K$, and $\pi$ is a
**stationary distribution** of $K$, when

$$(\pi K)(A):=\int_E K(x,A)\,\pi(dx)=\pi(A)\qquad\text{for every }A\in\mathcal E .$$

The set function $\pi K$ is again a probability measure: for fixed $A$ the map
$x\mapsto K(x,A)$ is measurable and lies in $[0,1]$, so the integral exists in
$[0,1]$; for pairwise disjoint $A_n\in\mathcal E$ the identity
$K(x,\bigcup_nA_n)=\sum_nK(x,A_n)$ of the measure $K(x,\cdot)$ and the
monotone convergence theorem for nonnegative functions
([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]) give
$\sigma$-additivity of $\pi K$; and $K(x,E)=1$ for every $x$ gives
$(\pi K)(E)=1$. Thus $(\pi K)(A)=\pi(A)$ is an identity between two probability
measures evaluated at $A$.

A $K$-chain whose initial law is $\pi$ is called **stationary** when
$\pi K=\pi$. Stationarity of the process is a statement about all of its
finite-dimensional laws and is proved, not assumed, from $\pi K=\pi$; see
[[thm-invariant-initial-law-makes-the-chain-stationary]].

On a countable state space $E$ with sigma-algebra $2^E$ and transition matrix
$p(x,y)=K(x,\{y\})$ ([[def-transition-matrix-and-n-step-transition-probabilities]]),
a measure on $E$ is its weighted sum of Dirac masses at singletons
([[thm-measures-on-countable-discrete-spaces-are-weighted-dirac-sums]]), so
invariance is equivalent to the matrix identity

$$\pi(y)=\sum_{x\in E}\pi(x)\,p(x,y)\qquad\text{for every }y\in E .$$

The definition fixes no irreducibility, aperiodicity or uniqueness hypothesis,
and it selects no conditional-expectation versions; the display defines a
single measure $\pi K$ and asserts an identity for it. A transient, periodic or
reducible chain may have several invariant probability measures or none.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Assume AC for existence. For real $X,Y\in L^1(P)$ and $a,b\in\mathbb R$, $E[aX+bY\mid\mathcal G]=aE[X\mid\mathcal G]+bE[Y\mid\mathcal G]$. Conditional expectation is positive, preserves order and constants, satisfies $E(E[X\mid\mathcal G])=EX$, and $|E[X\mid\mathcal G]|\le E[|X|\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. Also $X<Y$ almost surely implies $E[X\mid\mathcal G]<E[Y\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely.

Assume AC. If $\phi:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is finite convex and both $X$ and $\phi(X)$ are integrable, then $\phi(E[X\mid\mathcal G])\le E[\phi(X)\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely; the left side is measurable and integrable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Assume AC for existence. If $X\in L^1(P)$ and $Z$ is bounded real $\mathcal G$-measurable, then $E[ZX\mid\mathcal G]=ZE[X\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. The identity also holds for finite real $\mathcal G$-measurable $Z$ whenever $ZX$ and $ZE[X\mid\mathcal G]$ are integrable. In fact $X,ZX\in L^1$ imply the latter integrability.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

derivations.claim: For bounded measurable $h$, [F1] with $n=1$ gives $\mathbb E[h(X_{k+1})\mid\mathcal F_k]=Ph(X_k)$. Kernel measurability [F5] makes the right side measurable.

Write $g=g^+-g^-$. By [F8], both parts are integrable. For $N\ge1$ let $g_N^\pm=g^\pm\wedge N$. These functions are bounded and increase to $g^\pm$. Step 1.1 gives the conditional kernel identity for each $g_N^\pm$; [F2] makes the conditional expectations increase to $\mathbb E[g^\pm(X_{k+1})\mid\mathcal F_k]$, while [F4] makes $Pg_N^\pm(X_k)\uparrow Pg^\pm(X_k)$. Invariance [F3], first for nonnegative simple functions and then by [F4], gives $\mathbb E[Pg^\pm(X_k)]=\pi(g^\pm)<\infty$; hence both limits are finite almost surely. Subtracting the two finite identities using [F6] proves $\mathbb E[g(X_{k+1})\mid\mathcal F_k]=Pg(X_k)$.

Apply the same argument to the nonnegative integrable function $g^2$: the truncations $g^2\wedge N$ increase to $g^2$, and invariance gives $\mathbb E[P(g^2)(X_k)]=\pi(g^2)<\infty$. Thus $\mathbb E[g(X_{k+1})^2\mid\mathcal F_k]=P(g^2)(X_k)$. These identities do not depend on the chosen representative: if two representatives differ on a measurable $\pi$-null set $A$, invariance gives $\pi(P1_A)=0$, hence $P(x,A)=0$ for $\pi$-almost every $x$; their kernel integrals agree there, and their evaluations at each $X_k$ agree almost surely.

By [F7] and step 2.2, $(Pg(X_k))^2\le P(g^2)(X_k)$ almost surely, so stationarity and [F3] imply $\mathbb E[(Pg(X_k))^2]\le\pi(g^2)$; therefore $D_{k+1}\in L^2$. Step 2.1, the preceding square-integrability bound, conditional linearity and [F9] for the $\mathcal F_k$-measurable factor $Pg(X_k)$ give $\mathbb E[D_{k+1}\mid\mathcal F_k]=0$. The product $g(X_{k+1})Pg(X_k)$ is integrable by the two $L^2$ bounds and [F10], so [F9] also gives its conditional expectation as $(Pg(X_k))^2$. Expanding the square and using step 2.2 now yields $\mathbb E[D_{k+1}^2\mid\mathcal F_k]=P(g^2)(X_k)-(Pg(X_k))^2$. Thus the sequence is a square-integrable martingale-difference sequence.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

For a probability kernel $K$ on $(E,\mathcal E)$, let $I$ be the identity
kernel $I(x,A)=1_A(x)$ and define
$$ K^0:=I,\qquad K^{n+1}:=K^nK, $$ where composition is in chronological order: $$ K^{n+1}(x,A)=\int_E K(y,A)K^n(x,dy). $$
The identity map makes $I$ a probability kernel, including on a one-point
space. Induction using the published kernel-composition lemma shows that every
$K^n$ is a probability kernel. Associativity makes products of several copies
of $K$ unambiguous. No conditional-expectation version is selected and no form
of Choice is used.

Let $K$ be a probability kernel on a measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and let $\pi$ be a
probability measure on $(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). The
probability measure $\pi$ is **invariant** for $K$, and $\pi$ is a
**stationary distribution** of $K$, when

$$(\pi K)(A):=\int_E K(x,A)\,\pi(dx)=\pi(A)\qquad\text{for every }A\in\mathcal E .$$

The set function $\pi K$ is again a probability measure: for fixed $A$ the map
$x\mapsto K(x,A)$ is measurable and lies in $[0,1]$, so the integral exists in
$[0,1]$; for pairwise disjoint $A_n\in\mathcal E$ the identity
$K(x,\bigcup_nA_n)=\sum_nK(x,A_n)$ of the measure $K(x,\cdot)$ and the
monotone convergence theorem for nonnegative functions
([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]) give
$\sigma$-additivity of $\pi K$; and $K(x,E)=1$ for every $x$ gives
$(\pi K)(E)=1$. Thus $(\pi K)(A)=\pi(A)$ is an identity between two probability
measures evaluated at $A$.

A $K$-chain whose initial law is $\pi$ is called **stationary** when
$\pi K=\pi$. Stationarity of the process is a statement about all of its
finite-dimensional laws and is proved, not assumed, from $\pi K=\pi$; see
[[thm-invariant-initial-law-makes-the-chain-stationary]].

On a countable state space $E$ with sigma-algebra $2^E$ and transition matrix
$p(x,y)=K(x,\{y\})$ ([[def-transition-matrix-and-n-step-transition-probabilities]]),
a measure on $E$ is its weighted sum of Dirac masses at singletons
([[thm-measures-on-countable-discrete-spaces-are-weighted-dirac-sums]]), so
invariance is equivalent to the matrix identity

$$\pi(y)=\sum_{x\in E}\pi(x)\,p(x,y)\qquad\text{for every }y\in E .$$

The definition fixes no irreducibility, aperiodicity or uniqueness hypothesis,
and it selects no conditional-expectation versions; the display defines a
single measure $\pi K$ and asserts an identity for it. A transient, periodic or
reducible chain may have several invariant probability measures or none.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
([[def-measurable-space]]). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ be a measurable space and let
$f : X \to [0,+\infty]$ be measurable. For $k \in \mathbb{N}$ define

$$s_k := \sum_{j=0}^{k2^k-1} j2^{-k}\, \mathbf{1}_{\{j2^{-k} \le f < (j+1)2^{-k}\}} + k\,\mathbf{1}_{\{f \ge k\}}.$$

Then each $s_k$ is a simple measurable function,

$$0 \le s_k \le s_{k+1} \le f,$$

and $s_k(x) \to f(x)$ for every $x \in X$. If $E \subseteq X$ is a set on which
$f \le M < +\infty$, then $s_k \to f$ uniformly on $E$.

derivations.claim: Let $\mathcal A_0$ be the algebra generated by $\{\{f<q\}:q\in\mathbb Q\}$. Inductively, let $\mathcal A_{j+1}$ be the algebra generated by $\mathcal A_j$ and all sets $\{x:P(x,A)>q\}$ with $A\in\mathcal A_j$ and $q\in\mathbb Q$. These are subsets in $\mathcal F$ by [F1] and [F6]. Each algebra is countable: enumerate its generators and then all finite Boolean expressions in them. This also explicitly enumerates $\mathcal A=\bigcup_{j\ge0}\mathcal A_j$. Put $\mathcal G=\sigma(\mathcal A)$. Since rational half-lines generate the real Borel sigma-field, $f$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable.

For $A\in\mathcal A$, all rational superlevel sets of $P(\cdot,A)$ belong to $\mathcal G$ by construction. The class $\mathcal D$ of $B\in\mathcal G$ for which $P(\cdot,B)$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable contains $\mathcal A$ and $X$. It is closed under complements because $P(x,B^c)=1-P(x,B)$ and under countable disjoint unions because $P(x,\bigcup_lB_l)=\sum_lP(x,B_l)$ is a measurable increasing limit. Thus $\mathcal D$ is a lambda-system, and [F2] gives $\mathcal D=\mathcal G$. The restriction $P_{\mathcal G}$ therefore is a probability kernel.

For every nonnegative $\mathcal G$-measurable $g$, integration against $P_{\mathcal G}(x,\cdot)$ agrees with integration against $P(x,\cdot)$: this holds for indicators by restriction, for nonnegative simple functions by finite additivity of the integral, and for general $g$ by [F7] and [F3]. Both integrals are allowed to be infinite. Induction in [F4], using this integration identity and step 2.1, gives $P_{\mathcal G}^n(x,B)=P^n(x,B)$ for every $B\in\mathcal G$, including $n=0$.

If $\pi$ is invariant, the same restriction identity for integrals gives $\int P_{\mathcal G}(x,B)(\pi|_{\mathcal G})(dx)=\int P(x,B)\pi(dx)=\pi(B)$ for $B\in\mathcal G$. This is invariance of $\pi|_{\mathcal G}$ by [F5]. All generating enumerations in step 1.1 were explicit, so this construction introduces no choice assumption.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge1$, let $Z\sim N_n(0,I_n)$ have independent standard-normal coordinates, and let $U\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ satisfy $U^TU=I_n$. Then $UZ$ also has independent $N(0,1)$ coordinates. Here $I_n$ is the identity matrix and $U$ is orthogonal.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Let $n\ge1$, let $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ be independent real random variables on a
common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then
   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$
   in $[0,+\infty]$. In this finite product of expectations, a zero factor
   makes the product zero even when another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise
   multiplication has its usual extended nonnegative meaning.
2. If every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable
   and the same factorization holds in $\mathbb R$.

derivations.claim: By [F1] choose an orthogonal matrix $O$ with $A=O\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n)O^T$. By [F2], $Z=O^TU$ has independent standard-normal coordinates. Integration by parts in the density [F3], with $ze^{-z^2/2}\to0$ at both infinities, gives $EZ_i^2=1$. Every absolute moment of $V_i=Z_i^2-1$ is finite: for an integer $k\ge1$, $|z^2-1|^k\le(1+z^2)^k$, and this polynomial is integrable against $e^{-z^2/2}$. Thus $EV_i=0$, $E(U^TAU)=\sum_i\lambda_i=\operatorname{tr}A$, and $U^TAU-\operatorname{tr}A=\sum_i\lambda_iV_i$.

Expand the even power $(\sum_i\lambda_iV_i)^{2r}$ over ordered tuples of $2r$ indices. By [F4], a term whose tuple has an index appearing exactly once has expectation zero. Group all other terms by the partition of their $2r$ positions into equal-index blocks. Such a partition has block sizes $k_1,\ldots,k_q\ge2$ with $\sum_a k_a=2r$. For each fixed partition, taking absolute values and dropping the restriction that different blocks have distinct indices bounds its contribution by $\prod_{a=1}^q E|V_1|^{k_a}\prod_{a=1}^q\sum_i|\lambda_i|^{k_a}$. All these quantities are finite by step 1.1.

Put $L=(\sum_i\lambda_i^2)^{1/2}$. If $L=0$, the centered form is identically zero and the bound holds. Otherwise $|\lambda_i|/L\le1$ and $\sum_i(|\lambda_i|/L)^2=1$, so for every integer $k\ge2$, $\sum_i|\lambda_i|^k\le L^k$. Consequently each partition contribution in step 2.1 is bounded by $L^{2r}\prod_a E|V_1|^{k_a}$. There are finitely many partitions of the fixed set of $2r$ positions; the sum of these moment products over the partitions without singleton blocks is a finite constant $C_r$ depending only on $r$.

Since $2r$ is even, the expanded power is the absolute $2r$th power. Summing the bounds of step 3.1 therefore gives $E|U^TAU-\operatorname{tr}A|^{2r}\le C_r L^{2r}$. Finally $L^2=\operatorname{tr}(A^2)=\sum_{i,k}A_{ik}^2$ by symmetry and orthogonal diagonalization. This proves the bound and the expectation assertion, including $A=0$, singular matrices and matrices of either sign.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC for existence. For real $X,Y\in L^1(P)$ and $a,b\in\mathbb R$, $E[aX+bY\mid\mathcal G]=aE[X\mid\mathcal G]+bE[Y\mid\mathcal G]$. Conditional expectation is positive, preserves order and constants, satisfies $E(E[X\mid\mathcal G])=EX$, and $|E[X\mid\mathcal G]|\le E[|X|\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. Also $X<Y$ almost surely implies $E[X\mid\mathcal G]<E[Y\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely.
Assume AC. For $1\le p\le\infty$, conditional expectation is a linear map from real $L^p(P)$ to real $L^p(P|_{\mathcal G})$ satisfying $\|E[X\mid\mathcal G]\|_p\le\|X\|_p$.

Assume AC for existence. If $\mathcal H\subseteq\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ and $X\in L^1(P)$, then $E[E[X\mid\mathcal G]\mid\mathcal H]=E[X\mid\mathcal H]$ and $E[E[X\mid\mathcal H]\mid\mathcal G]=E[X\mid\mathcal H]$ almost surely. Also, if a version of $E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ is $\mathcal H$-measurable, it is a version of $E[X\mid\mathcal H]$.

Assume AC for existence. If $X\in L^1(P)$ and $Z$ is bounded real $\mathcal G$-measurable, then $E[ZX\mid\mathcal G]=ZE[X\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. The identity also holds for finite real $\mathcal G$-measurable $Z$ whenever $ZX$ and $ZE[X\mid\mathcal G]$ are integrable. In fact $X,ZX\in L^1$ imply the latter integrability.

Assume countable choice (in particular, the Axiom of Choice suffices). Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $1\le p\le\infty$. Then
$L^p(\mu)$, with the norm of
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]], is
complete. Equivalently, the metric induced by that norm is a complete metric in
the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]].

Moreover, if a sequence in $L^p(\mu)$ converges in norm, then some subsequence
admits measurable representatives converging almost everywhere in the sense of
[[def-convergence-almost-everywhere-relative-to-a-measure]].

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

Assume AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $Y=(Y_n)_{n\ge0}$ be a real-valued
strictly stationary process with $\mathbb E|Y_0|<\infty$
([[def-stationary-process-and-canonical-shift]]), with canonical path law
$\mathbb P_Y$ and left shift $\theta$. Let
$\mathcal I=\{A:\theta^{-1}A=A\}$ be the strictly invariant sigma-algebra on
path space ([[def-strict-and-mod-null-invariant-sigma-algebras]]). Then

$$\frac1n\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}Y_k\ \longrightarrow\ \mathbb E_{\mathbb P_Y}[z_0\mid\mathcal I]\circ\Phi \qquad\text{almost surely and in }L^1(\mathbb P),$$

where $\Phi(\omega)=(Y_n(\omega))_{n\ge0}$ and the conditional expectation is
that of [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. If moreover the
canonical shift is ergodic ([[def-ergodic-measure-preserving-system]]), then
the limit is the constant $\mathbb EY_0$. For complex-valued processes the
assertions hold componentwise for real and imaginary parts.

A measure-preserving system is **ergodic for $\mu$** if each $E\in\mathcal I$ has $\mu(E)=0$ or $\mu(X\setminus E)=0$, with $\mathcal I$ as in [[def-strict-and-mod-null-invariant-sigma-algebras]]. For a probability system this means $\mu(E)\in\{0,1\}$. The definition is relative to the invariant measure; no probability assumption is implicit in the general null/conull formulation.

Assume AC. Let $(Z_{n,k},\mathcal F_{n,k})$ be a square-integrable martingale-difference array such that, for every $n$, $M_{n,m}$ and $\Gamma_{n,m}$ converge almost surely as $m\to\infty$ to finite limits $M_{n,\infty}$ and $\Gamma_{n,\infty}$. If
$$\Gamma_{n,\infty}\longrightarrow1\quad\text{in probability}$$
and, for every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$L_n(\varepsilon):=\sum_{k\ge1}\mathbb E[Z_{n,k}^2 1_{\{|Z_{n,k}|>\varepsilon\}}]\longrightarrow0,$$
then $M_{n,\infty}\Rightarrow N(0,1)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$
Let $1\le p<\infty$. If $X_n\to X$ in $L^p$, then $X_n\to X$ in probability.

Let $X_n$ and $Y_n$ be Borel-measurable random elements with values in a metric space $S$, on the same probability space for each $n$, and let $X$ be an $S$-valued Borel-measurable random element. Suppose $d(X_n,Y_n)$ is measurable and $P(d(X_n,Y_n)>\varepsilon)\to0$ for every $\varepsilon$>0. If $X_n\Rightarrow X$, then $Y_n\Rightarrow X$.

Let S,T be metric spaces, $g:S\to T$ measurable, and $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$. If the discontinuity set $D_g$ is $\mu$-null, then $g_*\mu_n\Rightarrow g_*\mu$. Consequently $X_n\Rightarrow X$ implies $g(X_n)\Rightarrow g(X)$ whenever $P_X(D_g)=0$.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

derivations.claim: For an integrable $Z$ and any integer $k$, the variable $\mathbb E[Z\mid\mathcal F_0]\circ T^k$ is $\mathcal F_k$ measurable because the pullback of $\mathcal F_0$ by $T^k$ is $\mathcal F_k$. Every event in $\mathcal F_k$ is the pullback of an event in $\mathcal F_0$, since $T$ is invertible and bimeasurable. Changing variables under the probability-preserving bijection $T^k$ proves that the integrals of this candidate and $Z\circ T^k$ agree over every $\mathcal F_k$ event. Uniqueness of conditional expectation therefore gives $\mathbb E[Z\circ T^k\mid\mathcal F_k]=\mathbb E[Z\mid\mathcal F_0]\circ T^k$ as almost-everywhere classes.

By summability and [F3], the partial sums defining $H_0$ are Cauchy in $L^2(\mathcal F_0)$ and have a limit there. Composition with $T^k$ is an $L^2$ isometry, so step 1.1 yields $H_k=\sum_{j\ge1}\mathbb E[X_{k+j}\mid\mathcal F_k]$ in $L^2$, with $H_k$ measurable in $\mathcal F_k$ and $\|H_k\|_2=\|H_0\|_2$. Representatives may be fixed for the countably many indices; discard a countable union of null sets for their identities.

By [F1], conditional expectation is continuous in $L^2$. Apply [F2]'s tower property to the partial sums in step 2.1 and pass to the $L^2$ limit to obtain $\mathbb E[H_k\mid\mathcal F_{k-1}]=\sum_{j\ge1}\mathbb E[X_{k+j}\mid\mathcal F_{k-1}]=H_{k-1}-\mathbb E[X_k\mid\mathcal F_{k-1}]$. Thus $D_k=X_k+H_k-H_{k-1}$ is square-integrable and $\mathcal F_k$ measurable, with $\mathbb E[D_k\mid\mathcal F_{k-1}]=0$. Also $D_k=D_1\circ T^{k-1}$, so the differences are stationary. Summing their defining identity gives $S_n=M_n+R_n$, where $M_n=\sum_{k=1}^nD_k$, $R_n=H_0-H_n$, and $\|R_n\|_2\le2\|H_0\|_2$. In particular $R_n/\sqrt n\to0$ in $L^2$ and hence in probability by [F8].

Put $q_0=\mathbb E[D_1^2\mid\mathcal F_0]$. It is nonnegative, integrable, and has expectation $\tau^2=\mathbb E[D_1^2]$ by [F1]. Step 1.1 gives $\mathbb E[D_k^2\mid\mathcal F_{k-1}]=q_0\circ T^{k-1}$. The map $\omega\mapsto(q_0(T^j\omega))_{j\ge0}$ intertwines $T$ with the canonical one-sided shift. Hence a shift-invariant event for this process pulls back to a $T$-invariant event modulo null sets, whose probability is zero or one by the assumed ergodicity. The process is stationary, integrable and ergodic, so [F5] gives $n^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^n\mathbb E[D_k^2\mid\mathcal F_{k-1}]\to\tau^2$ almost surely. The limiting variance is therefore a constant.

If $\tau^2>0$, let $Z_{n,k}=D_k/(\tau\sqrt n)$ for $1\le k\le n$, and let $Z_{n,k}=0$ for $k>n$; use the filtration $\mathcal F_{n,k}=\mathcal F_{\min(k,n)}$ for $k\ge0$. Step 3.1 makes each row a square-integrable martingale-difference row. The row sums and clocks are eventually constant, and step 4.1 shows their terminal clocks converge almost surely to $1$. For every $\varepsilon>0$, stationarity gives $\sum_{k\ge1}\mathbb E[Z_{n,k}^2\mathbf1_{\{|Z_{n,k}|>\varepsilon\}}]=\tau^{-2}\mathbb E[D_1^2\mathbf1_{\{|D_1|>\varepsilon\tau\sqrt n\}}]\to0$ by [F7]. Thus [F6] gives $M_n/(\tau\sqrt n)\Rightarrow N(0,1)$. Scaling and the perturbation in step 3.1 give $S_n/\sqrt n\Rightarrow N(0,\tau^2)$ by [F8].

If $\tau^2=0$, stationarity implies $\mathbb E[D_k^2]=0$ for every $k$, so $M_n=0$ almost surely. Step 3.1 gives $S_n/\sqrt n\to0$ in $L^2$ and hence in probability. The constant sequence $0$ has weak limit the point mass $N(0,0)$; [F8] transfers that limit to $S_n/\sqrt n$. This establishes the asserted CLT in both variance cases.

Suppose the additional covariance summability holds, and put $\gamma_j=\operatorname{Cov}(X_0,X_j)$. Stationarity and expansion of the finite square give $\operatorname{Var}(S_n)/n=\gamma_0+2\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}(1-j/n)\gamma_j\to\gamma_0+2\sum_{j\ge1}\gamma_j$, by [F7] on counting measure with summable dominator $|\gamma_j|$. For $i<j$, $D_i$ is $\mathcal F_{j-1}$ measurable, so [F2], [F4], and step 3.1 give $\mathbb E[D_iD_j]=0$. Therefore $\mathbb E[M_n^2]=n\tau^2$. The identity $S_n=M_n+R_n$ and [F4] imply $|\mathbb E[S_n^2]-n\tau^2|/n\le\|R_n\|_2^2/n+2\|R_n\|_2\tau/\sqrt n\to0$, since $\|R_n\|_2$ is bounded. All $S_n$ are centered, so [F9] identifies the two variance limits and proves the stated covariance formula, including $\tau^2=0$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be independent centered square-integrable real random variables. Suppose $b\ge0$ is finite and $|X_i|\le b$ almost surely for each $i$. Put $v=\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{Var}(X_i)$. For $t>0$, if $v>0$ then
$$\mathbb P\left(\left|\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\right|\ge t\right)\le 2\exp\!\left(-\frac{t^2}{2(v+bt/3)}\right),$$
and if $v=0$ then this probability is $0$.

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

Let $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be events in a probability space. If
$$\sum_{n=0}^\infty \mathbb P(A_n)<+\infty,$$
then
$$\mathbb P(A_n\ \mathrm{i.o.})=0.$$

No independence hypothesis is needed.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

derivations.claim: First assume independence and fix positive integers $A$ and $d$ with $d\ge0$. Choose $a$ strictly between $p$ and $q$, put $M_q=\mathbb E|Z_1|^q$, and, for dyadic integers $N=2^m\ge2$, put $b_N=N^{1/a}$, $\ell_N=\log N$, and $r_N=\lceil A N^{1/p}\ell_N^d\rceil$. The second moment $v=\mathbb E Z_1^2$ is finite since $|z|^2\le1+|z|^q$. If $v=0$, the nonnegative variable $Z_1^2$ has zero expectation and is zero almost surely: for each integer $h\ge1$, [F2] bounds $\mathbb P(Z_1^2\ge1/h)$ by zero, and the union of these events is $\{Z_1\ne0\}$. Equality of marginal laws and countable subadditivity make every $Z_k$ zero simultaneously almost surely. This proves the assertion in this case. Henceforth assume $v>0$.

The union bound and [F2] give $\mathbb P(\max_{k\le N}|Z_k|>b_N)\le M_qN^{1-q/a}$. Since $1-q/a<0$, these probabilities are summable over dyadic $N$. By [F3], eventually no one of the first $N$ variables is truncated at level $b_N$, almost surely along the dyadic horizons. Define $m_N=\mathbb E[Z_1\mathbf1_{\{|Z_1|\le b_N\}}]$ and $V_{N,k}=Z_k\mathbf1_{\{|Z_k|\le b_N\}}-m_N$. For each fixed $N$, these variables are independent and centered, $|V_{N,k}|\le2b_N$, and $\operatorname{Var}(V_{N,k})\le v$. Moreover centering of $Z_1$ gives $|m_N|\le\mathbb E[|Z_1|\mathbf1_{\{|Z_1|>b_N\}}]\le M_qb_N^{1-q}$.

For an interval of at most $r_N$ indices, [F1] bounds the tail of its $V_{N,k}$ sum by $2\exp(-x^2/[2(vr_N+2b_Nx/3)])$; if its actual variance is zero the bound still holds because the tail is zero. Set $x_N=C(\sqrt{r_N\ell_N}+b_N\ell_N)$, where $C\ge\max\{\sqrt{20v},40/3,1\}$. Then $2vr_N\le x_N^2/(10\ell_N)$ and $4b_Nx_N/3\le x_N^2/(10\ell_N)$, so the bound is at most $2e^{-5\ell_N}=2N^{-5}$. There are at most $N^2$ intervals with integer endpoints in $[0,N]$. The probability that any interval of length at most $r_N$ violates the bound $x_N$ is therefore at most $2N^{-3}$, summable over dyadic $N$. By [F3], all such interval sums are bounded by $x_N$ eventually almost surely.

On the eventual no-truncation event from step 2.1, every original interval sum differs from its centered truncated sum by at most $r_N|m_N|$. Now $\sqrt{r_N\ell_N}=o(N^{1/p})$ because $1/(2p)<1/p$, and $b_N\ell_N=o(N^{1/p})$ because $1/a<1/p$. Also $r_N|m_N|\le M_qr_NN^{(1-q)/a}=o(N^{1/p})$. Thus step 3.1 proves the claimed little-o bound at dyadic horizons. These comparisons follow by dividing by $N^{1/p}$: in each expression a strictly negative power of $N$ multiplies a fixed power of $\log N$, which tends to zero.

For $2^{m-1}<n\le2^m=N$, monotonicity of $n^{1/p}(\log n)^d$ gives $r_n\le r_N$, so every admissible interval for $n$ is included among those for $N$. Since $N^{1/p}\le2^{1/p}n^{1/p}$, step 4.1 proves the assertion at every horizon $n$. Intersect the probability-one events obtained for the countably many integer pairs $A\ge1,d\ge0$. For arbitrary real $A>0,d\ge0$, choose integers $A'\ge A$ and $d'\ge d$; when $n\ge3$, $\log n\ge1$ makes the real-parameter window no longer than the integer-parameter window. The conclusion therefore holds on one event for every $A,d$ in the Statement.

Under one-dependence, each parity subsequence is independent. Indeed, the sigma-algebra of any finite initial collection of even variables is contained in $\sigma(Z_1,\ldots,Z_{2h})$, which is independent of $Z_{2h+2}$ by the given separation; induction on the number of factors proves the finite rectangle factorization for all even variables. The identical argument applies to the odd variables. Both subsequences retain the common centered marginal and its $q$th moment. Apply step 5.1 to each subsequence and intersect their two probability-one events. An interval of at most $r_n$ original indices splits into one contiguous interval of each parity, each with at most $r_n$ terms and with its subsequence endpoints at most $n$. Each component is $o(n^{1/p})$ by the independent result, uniformly over the original intervals; their sum has the same bound. No independence between the parity subsequences is asserted or needed. All windows are nonempty by $i<j$; empty component windows contribute zero. This completes both dependence cases, including zero variance and every permitted window parameter.

boundaries.evidence: The maximum uses i<j; empty parity-component intervals are assigned zero in step 6.1.
Step 1.1 proves the zero-second-moment sequence is zero simultaneously almost surely.
Proof step 3.1. The Bernstein bound covers single-term intervals; r_n is a positive integer and n≥2.
Independent parity subsequences need not be independent of each other; step 6.1 uses only the triangle inequality between them.
The strict inequalities q>p>2 and choice p<a<q give every negative polynomial exponent in steps 2.1 and 4.1; n≥2 avoids log zero.
The open interval (p,q) contains a=(p+q)/2; integer ceilings supply the countable window parameters in step 5.1.

No converse or necessity of the moment condition is asserted.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. A real process
$B=(B_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **standard Brownian motion** if:

1. $B_0=0$ almost surely;
2. for every finite list $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_n$, the increments
   $B_{t_j}-B_{t_{j-1}}$ are mutually independent and have laws
   $N(0,t_j-t_{j-1})$; and
3. there is one measurable event $A$ with $P(A)=1$ such that
   $t\mapsto B_t(\omega)$ is continuous on $[0,\infty)$ for every
   $\omega\in A$.

By
[[lem-brownian-gaussian-covariance-is-equivalent-to-independent-stationary-normal-increments]],
the first two clauses are equivalent to saying that $B$ is a centered Gaussian
process with covariance $\min(s,t)$. Clause 3 is additional: it cannot be
recovered from finite-dimensional distributions alone.

No filtration is part of this definition. In particular, no completed or
right-continuous filtration and no Markov or martingale assertion is silently
imposed. Modifications and indistinguishability retain the distinct meanings in
[[def-law-modification-and-indistinguishability-of-processes]]. The cases
$n=0$, $t_1=0$, and zero-length increments are respectively vacuous or already
covered by $B_0=0$; the increment list itself is strictly increasing.

Choice is declared because the normal-law and Gaussian/increment-equivalence
interfaces construct and identify normal laws under AC. The continuity clause
selects no path and makes no additional use of choice.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ be a real process with
$X_0=0$ almost surely. The following are equivalent:

1. $X$ is a centered Gaussian process with
   $\operatorname{Cov}(X_s,X_t)=\min(s,t)$ for all $s,t\ge0$.
2. For every finite list $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_n$, the increments
   $X_{t_j}-X_{t_{j-1}}$, $1\le j\le n$, are mutually independent and have
   laws $N(0,t_j-t_{j-1})$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(U,V)$ be a jointly multivariate-normal real
vector with finite-dimensional blocks $U\in\mathbb R^p$ and
$V\in\mathbb R^q$, where $p,q\ge1$. If $\operatorname{Cov}(U_i,V_j)=0$ for every
$1\le i\le p$ and $1\le j\le q$, then $U$ and $V$ are independent. The
covariance matrix may be singular.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. The canonical centered Gaussian coordinate process
with covariance $E[X_sX_t]=\min(s,t)$ has a continuous modification $B$, and
$B$ is a standard Brownian motion. In particular, standard Brownian motion
exists.

Assume countable choice and dependent choice. For probability spaces
$(E_n,\mathcal E_n,\mu_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ there is a unique probability measure
$\mu$ on $\mathcal C_{\mathbb N}$ such that, for every finite $F$, its
$F$-coordinate marginal is $\bigotimes_{n\in F}\mu_n$.
Under the measure of [[thm-countable-product-of-probability-spaces]], the coordinate maps $X_n(x)=x_n$ have laws $\mu_n$ and are independent.

For a finite parameter $\lambda\ge0$, the **Poisson count law**
$\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)$ is the probability measure on
$\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ whose masses are
$$\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)\{k\}=e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^k}{k!},\qquad k\in\mathbb N_0,$$
when $\lambda>0$, and is the point mass at $0$ when $\lambda=0$. The
normalization and the moment and generating-function identities used below are
proved in [[lem-poisson-count-law-normalization-and-moments]]. The separate
extended convention for a Poisson point-process count on a Borel set of infinite
intensity is that the count equals $+\infty$ almost surely; it is not a finite
Poisson probability law.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$

Let $\varphi(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}$ and
$\overline\Phi(x)=\int_x^\infty\varphi(y)\,dy$ for $x\in\mathbb R$. Then for
every $x>0$
$$\frac{x\,\varphi(x)}{1+x^2}\ \le\ \overline\Phi(x)\ \le\ \frac{\varphi(x)}{x},$$
and consequently, for every $x>1$,
$$\Bigl(\frac1x-\frac1{x^3}\Bigr)\varphi(x)\ \le\ \overline\Phi(x)\ \le\ \frac{\varphi(x)}{x}.$$
Both bounds are sharp as $x\to\infty$ in the sense that the ratio of each side
to $\overline\Phi(x)$ tends to $1$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, let $B$ be a standard Brownian motion
[[def-brownian-motion]]. Use the everywhere-continuous, zero-start
representative fixed in [[thm-brownian-reflection-principle]]: replace the
path by zero outside a measurable probability-one event of continuity and
zero start, retaining the notation $B$. Let $t>0$ and
$M_t:=\sup_{0\le s\le t}B_s$. This is a finite nonnegative random variable:
continuity gives boundedness on $[0,t]$ and identifies its supremum with the
supremum over the countable dense set $(\mathbb Q\cap[0,t])\cup\{t\}$.
With
$\Phi$ the standard normal distribution function,
$\Phi(x)=N(0,1)((-\infty,x])$
[[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]]
[[def-cumulative-distribution-function-of-a-random-variable]], one has for
every $x\ge0$
$$P(M_t\le x)=2\Phi\!\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt t}\right)-1 .$$
Consequently $M_t$ has the same law as $|B_t|$, and on $x>0$ the law of $M_t$
has the density
$$f(x)=\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi t}}\,\exp\!\left(-\frac{x^2}{2t}\right).$$

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

Let $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be events in a probability space. If
$$\sum_{n=0}^\infty \mathbb P(A_n)<+\infty,$$
then
$$\mathbb P(A_n\ \mathrm{i.o.})=0.$$

No independence hypothesis is needed.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be convex and open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at every point. If $M\ge0$ satisfies $\|Df(z)v\|_2\le M\|v\|_2$ for every $z\in U$ and $v\in\mathbb R^m$, then

$$\|f(y)-f(x)\|_2\le M\|y-x\|_2\qquad(x,y\in U).$$

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

derivations.claim: Work on common full-measure events of Brownian continuity and the assumed clock paths. For each integer $K\ge0$, [F4] gives $\mathbb P(N(n)\le K)=e^{-\lambda n}\sum_{k=0}^K(\lambda n)^k/k!\to0$. The events $\{N(n)\le K\}$ decrease in $n$, so continuity of probability shows that $N(n)$ is unbounded almost surely after taking the countable union over $K$. By [A1] and [F3], extend the space by independent standard Brownian motions $(U_j)_{j\ge0}$, independent also of the original variables. They will supply continuous bridges; the original space and all its joint laws are preserved by this product extension.

We prove the necessary uniform clock bounds directly. If $X\sim\operatorname{Pois}(a)$, summing [F4]'s nonnegative series gives $\mathbb E e^{\theta(X-a)}=\exp(a(e^\theta-1-\theta))$ for every real $\theta$. For $|\theta|<3$, the exponential series and $k!\ge2\cdot3^{k-2}$ for $k\ge2$ imply $e^\theta-1-\theta\le\theta^2/[2(1-|\theta|/3)]$. Exponential Markov and the choice $\theta=x/(a+x/3)$, applied with either sign, therefore give $\mathbb P(|X-a|\ge x)\le2\exp(-x^2/[2(a+x/3)])$ when $a>0,x>0$; at $a=0$ the deviation is zero. With $a=\lambda(v-u)$ this implies $\mathbb P(|N(v)-N(u)-\lambda(v-u)|\ge x)\le2\exp(-c_\lambda\min\{x^2/(v-u),x\})$ for a constant $c_\lambda>0$ and integer $0\le u<v$. This derivation uses only the Poisson mass series and Markov, not a strong approximation theorem.

Partition the original time axis into macrointervals $[0,1],[1,2],[2,4],[4,8],\ldots$. For each macrointerval $I=[a,a+D]$, extract the root normal $R_I=(B(a+D)-B(a))/\sqrt D$. For every dyadic cell $J=[b,b+d]$ inside a macrointerval, of length $d\ge2$, extract its midpoint normal $G_J=2(B(b+d/2)-(B(b)+B(b+d))/2)/\sqrt d$. This is a countable iid standard-normal family, independent of $\mathcal G$. To verify independence, the midpoint contrast on $J$ has covariance zero with the endpoint increment on $J$ and with all Brownian evaluations outside its interior: for $t\le b$ the three covariance terms cancel, and for $t\ge b+d$ they are $2(b+d/2)-b-(b+d)=0$. Its variance is one by direct expansion of $\min(s,t)$. Two dyadic cells are either disjoint or nested; in the nested case, the larger cell's contrast uses only evaluations outside the smaller cell's interior or at its endpoints. Hence distinct contrasts and roots have zero covariance. Every finite family is jointly Gaussian by [F1], so repeated use of [F2] proves mutual independence.

For dyadic horizons $n=2^m$, write $\ell=\log(n+2)$. Applying step 1.2 with $x=K(\sqrt{(v-u)\ell}+\ell)$ and choosing a sufficiently large deterministic $K$ makes the probability at most $2(n+2)^{-6}$. There are at most $(n+1)^2$ integer intervals in $[0,n]$. The union bound and [F6] show that, almost surely eventually on dyadic horizons, every such interval satisfies $|N(v)-N(u)-\lambda(v-u)|\le K(\sqrt{(v-u)\ell}+\ell)$. Choose a deterministic $A>1$ sufficiently large. For every dyadic cell of length $d\ge A\ell$, its normalized half-counts $\alpha=L_J/(\lambda d)$ and $\beta=Q_J/(\lambda d)$ then lie in $[1/4,3/4]$. For every integer point $j$ in the cell, with $x=(j-b)/d$ and $z=(N(j)-N(b))/(\lambda d)$, one has $|z-x|+|\alpha-1/2|+|\beta-1/2|\le C\sqrt{\ell/d}$. Indeed the interval estimate gives this bound first with an additional term $C\ell/d$, which is at most another constant times $\sqrt{\ell/d}$ since $d\ge A\ell$. The same estimate implies that every integer interval of length at most $2A\ell$ has count increase at most $C\ell$. Constants here and below are deterministic and may depend on $\lambda,A,K$.

For a cell $J=[b,b+d]$ put $C_J=N(b+d)-N(b)$, with half-counts $L_J=N(b+d/2)-N(b)$ and $Q_J=C_J-L_J$ when $d\ge2$. Prescribe a $W$ increment $\sqrt{C_I}R_I$ over the count interval $[N(a),N(a+D)]$ of each macrointerval, starting from $W(0)=0$ and concatenating the macrointervals. Given both endpoint values for $J$, if $C_J>0$ prescribe its count-midpoint value as $W(N(b))+(L_J/C_J)(W(N(b+d))-W(N(b)))+\sqrt{L_JQ_J/C_J}\,G_J$. When $C_J=0$ all three count times agree and the midpoint value is that endpoint. When only one half-count is zero the displayed prescription also equals the appropriate existing endpoint. Recurse down to unit cells. For a unit cell $[j,j+1]$ of count length $c>0$, with left count time $h=N(j)$ and prescribed endpoint increment $Y$, fill its count interval continuously by $W(h+s)=W(h)+(s/c)Y+\sqrt c\,(U_j(s/c)-(s/c)U_j(1))$ for $0\le s\le c$. Zero-count leaves require no filling. Unboundedness from step 1.1 makes these intervals cover $[0,\infty)$. All operations depend measurably on finitely many integer counts and Gaussian evaluations for each fixed $W(t)$: partition by the first integer $j$ with $N(j)>t$ and its finite count history. The resulting countable pieces give measurable evaluations, including endpoints.

The tail bound in [F5] gives $\mathbb P(|G|>x)\le2e^{-x^2/2}$ for $x\ge1$. On $[0,n]$ the number of root and midpoint coefficients in step 2.1 is at most $2n$. A union bound with $x=K_1\sqrt\ell$, followed by [F6] with $K_1$ sufficiently large, shows that their maximum absolute value is $O(\sqrt\ell)$ almost surely eventually along dyadic horizons. Also [F5] and the union bound give, for Brownian $U$, $\mathbb P(\sup_{s\le h}|U(s)|>x)\le4e^{-x^2/(2h)}$ when $x/\sqrt h\ge1$. Therefore a bridge $U(s)-(s/h)U(h)$ over length $h$ has supremum tail bounded by $4e^{-x^2/(8h)}$ for $x/(2\sqrt h)\ge1$, since its supremum is at most twice that of $U$. These estimates also apply to translated Brownian increment paths by [F1].

Fix a deterministic finite count history. The Gaussian split used in step 3.1 is exact: if an interval has total increment $Y\sim N(0,c)$ and child lengths $l,r\ge0$, $l+r=c>0$, independent $G\sim N(0,1)$ gives child increments $Y_L=(l/c)Y+\sqrt{lr/c}\,G$ and $Y_R=Y-Y_L$. Their variances are $l,r$ and their covariance is $lr/c-lr/c=0$. Thus they are independent by [F2], with zero-length increments identically zero. Recursing proves independent normal increments of the prescribed count lengths over all nonzero unit leaves, also across macrointervals. For the independent bridge $\beta(s)=U_j(s)-sU_j(1)$, [F1] directly gives mean zero, continuous paths, endpoints zero, and covariance $\min(s,t)-st$. Filling a leaf as in step 3.1 therefore gives centered Gaussian increments whose covariance at offsets $s,t$ is $st/c+c(\min(s/c,t/c)-st/c^2)=\min(s,t)$. Different leaves have independent increment processes because their endpoint increments are independent and all bridge motions are independent. Summing these increments shows that, for every finite evaluation list, $W$ has centered Gaussian covariance $\min(s,t)$ on this fixed count history.

Fix a large dyadic horizon and a macrointerval $I=[a,a+D]\subseteq[0,n]$. If $D>A\ell$, stop its binary tree at cells with lengths in $[A\ell,2A\ell)$; if $D\le A\ell$, stop at the root. For an integer $j\in I$, consider the piecewise-linear interpolant of $B(j)-B(a)$ on this stopped grid, and the piecewise-linear interpolant of $\lambda^{-1/2}(W(N(j))-W(N(a)))$ on the corresponding count grid, evaluated at $N(j)$. Repeated midpoint interpolation from step 3.1 expands each interpolant in the same root normal and in the midpoint normals of its ancestor chain. In an active cell of length $d$ containing $j$ in its left half, the coefficients of its midpoint normal are respectively $\sqrt d\,x$ and $\sqrt d\,z\sqrt{\beta/[\alpha(\alpha+\beta)]}$, with $x,z,\alpha,\beta$ as in step 2.2. This follows by multiplying the left interpolation fraction $z/\alpha$ by $\lambda^{-1/2}\sqrt{L_JQ_J/C_J}$. In the right half the coefficients are obtained by replacing $(x,z,\alpha,\beta)$ by $(1-x,\alpha+\beta-z,\beta,\alpha)$. At a midpoint or endpoint these same formulas agree with the endpoint prescription.

For any finite list of evaluation times, partition the original space into countably many $\mathcal G$-events specifying a long enough finite integer count history to cover them. The Gaussian and added bridge variables are independent of $\mathcal G$; step 4.1 shows that on every such count configuration the resulting evaluation law is the same Brownian Gaussian law. Consequently, for any $A\in\mathcal G$ and any Borel set $H$ of that finite evaluation vector, summing over this partition gives $\mathbb P(A\cap\{(W(t_i))_i\in H\})=\mathbb P(A)\nu_H$, where $\nu_H$ is its Brownian probability. No regular conditional probability on the original space is needed. The construction has common continuous paths: count intervals have integer endpoints, finitely many nonzero intervals meet each bounded count-time interval, their bridges are continuous, and endpoint prescriptions agree. Thus [F1] makes $W$ standard Brownian. Continuous evaluations are limits of rational evaluations, and [F8] extends the factorization from rational cylinders to $\sigma(W(t):t\ge0)$. Therefore $W$ is independent of all of $\mathcal G$, not just of $N$.

The function $z\sqrt{\beta/[\alpha(\alpha+\beta)]}$ has uniformly bounded first derivatives for $1/4\le\alpha,\beta\le3/4$ and $0\le z\le2$: its displayed denominators are bounded away from zero, and differentiating gives only bounded products of these reciprocals and square roots. One may take a slightly larger open convex box still with positive $\alpha,\beta$ and use [F7]. At $(\alpha,\beta,z)=(1/2,1/2,x)$ its value is $x$. Hence step 2.2 bounds the midpoint coefficient discrepancy by $C\sqrt\ell$. The normalized right-half prefix differs from its deterministic value by at most another constant times $\sqrt{\ell/d}$, so the same bound applies there. The root coefficients for a large macrointerval are $\sqrt D\,x$ and $\sqrt D\,z/\sqrt{C_I/(\lambda D)}$; the same bounded-derivative argument and step 2.2 bound their discrepancy by $C\sqrt\ell$. By step 3.2, each shared Gaussian coefficient therefore contributes at most $C\ell$ to the interpolant difference. At most $1+\log_2 n$ coefficients occur on an ancestor chain, so the increment-interpolant error is $O(\ell^2)$.

We control the discarded bridge pieces uniformly. Each stopped cell has deterministic length at most $2A\ell$ and, on the count event from step 2.2, count length at most $C\ell$. The Brownian deviation from linear interpolation on a cell is a continuous bridge with the covariance computed in step 4.1, regardless of the endpoint values. Step 3.2 therefore bounds the probability that its supremum exceeds $K_2\ell$ by $4e^{-cK_2^2\ell}$. There are at most $n$ stopped cells. For the $W$ bridges the same estimate holds on every count history having these length bounds, by the conditional Gaussian calculation in steps 4.1, 5.1; summing over the count configurations gives the identical unconditional bound on the good count event. Choose $K_2$ large, add the summable failure probability of that count event, and apply [F6]. Thus all discarded $B$ and scaled $W$ bridge pieces are $O(\ell)$ almost surely eventually. This argument includes zero count length, whose bridge is identically zero.

A completed large macrointerval contributes only its root error $|\sqrt D-\sqrt{C_I/\lambda}|\,|R_I|\le C\ell$ by steps 2.2, 3.2. For a macrointerval of length at most $A\ell$, its entire $B$ increment supremum and its scaled $W$ increment supremum are $O(\ell)$ by the same reflection and count-history argument as step 6.1, applied without subtracting an interpolant. There are at most $1+\log_2 n$ macrointervals before time $n$. Add the root or small-macrointerval errors of the completed macrointervals, then the interpolant error from step 5.2 and the two leaf errors from step 6.1 in the last one. This gives $\max_{j\le n,\ j\in\mathbb N_0}|B(j)-\lambda^{-1/2}W(N(j))|=O(\ell^2)$ almost surely along dyadic horizons.

For real $t\in[j,j+1]$, Brownian reflection and a union bound over the $n$ unit intervals make $|B(t)-B(j)|=O(\sqrt\ell)$ uniformly eventually almost surely. Step 2.2 gives $N(j+1)-N(j)\le C\ell$. On every such count history, step 5.1 gives Brownian law for $W$, and reflection bounds its increment supremum on each $[N(j),N(j+1)]$ by $K_3\ell$ except on a probability bounded by $4ne^{-cK_3^2\ell}$; this is summable on dyadic horizons when $K_3$ is large. Integrating over the count configurations and using [F6] shows that these $W$ increments are uniformly $O(\ell)$. Monotonicity of $N$ places $N(t)$ in that count interval. Add these two bounds to step 7.1 to obtain the required real-time supremum on dyadic horizons. For any real $n\ge2$, the next dyadic horizon is less than $2n$, and its logarithm differs from $\log(n+2)$ by a bounded additive constant, proving the asserted bound at every horizon.

The finite initial time range is absorbed into the random constant: $B$ is bounded there by continuity, $N$ is bounded there by hypothesis, and $W$ is bounded on the corresponding compact count-time interval by continuity. Repeated or zero count times were treated in steps 3.1, 4.1. The restriction $\lambda>0$ is needed for the displayed scaling and the lower large-cell count bounds; no assertion is made at rate zero. Step 5.1 proves the full claimed independence, while steps 7.1, 8.1 prove the approximation. AC was used precisely through [F1]–[F3] and the product extension in step 1.1; all concentration, interpolation, and countable-event arguments are local.

boundaries.evidence: Empty or zero-count cells add no bridge; steps 3.1, 4.1 treat their prescriptions explicitly.
Statement and proof step 4.1. Rate λ=0 is expressly excluded; zero-length Poisson count intervals have identically zero increment and bridge.
Unit original-time leaves are explicitly filled with independent continuous Gaussian bridges in step 3.1.
Step 4.1 allows zero half-counts and singular Gaussian increments without division by a zero total count; no independence of W and B is asserted.
Proof steps 5.1 and 6.1. Common continuous paths agree at every glued count endpoint. Large-cell estimates require λ>0 and d≥A log(n+2); short cells use separate reflection bounds.
Proof step 1.1. AC is stated; Brownian existence and the actual countable-product suppliers provide the bridge copies on an extension preserving original joint laws.

boundaries.reason: The statement is a one-way existence/approximation claim, not a biconditional.
No converse to the Poisson or Brownian assumptions is asserted.

risk_review.notes: Checked steps 1.1–9.1: Poisson exponential concentration; Haar root/contrast independence; count-history measurable Gaussian splitting and bridge filling; count-independent Brownian finite-dimensional laws; large-cell Lipschitz errors O(log n) per level, small-cell bridge and root errors, dyadic summability and real-time interpolation. Zero counts handled by identical endpoints, positive lambda required, whole-environment independence follows by count partitions and rational cylinders. No KMT premise is used.

citations.quote:
Let $n\ge1$, let $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ be independent real random variables on a
common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then
   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$
   in $[0,+\infty]$. In this finite product of expectations, a zero factor
   makes the product zero even when another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise
   multiplication has its usual extended nonnegative meaning.
2. If every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable
   and the same factorization holds in $\mathbb R$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure

$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open and let $g_j:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ be holomorphic. Suppose the sequence of partial sums of $\sum_{j\ge0}g_j$ converges locally uniformly to $g$. Then $g$ is holomorphic, and for every natural $k$,

$$g^{(k)}=\sum_{j\ge0}g_j^{(k)},$$

where the derivative series converges locally uniformly.

If two holomorphic functions on a complex domain agree on a set with an accumulation point in the domain, then they agree everywhere on the domain.

Precisely, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C$ be a complex domain ([[def-complex-domain]]), let $f,g:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ be holomorphic, and suppose that some $a\in\Omega$ is an accumulation point of $\{z\in\Omega:f(z)=g(z)\}$. Then $f=g$ on $\Omega$. The requirement $a\in\Omega$ is essential.

$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

derivations.claim: Fix one centered bounded summand $X$ with covariance $D$, and put $M(z)=\mathbb E e^{z\cdot X}$. Its exponential series converges uniformly on every bounded complex set because $|X|\le B$, and the expectation of its absolute series is bounded by $e^{B|z|}$; thus termwise integration defines an entire function and its derivatives are the expectations of the corresponding polynomial factors times the exponential. Fix an absolute $b>0$ with $e^b-1\le1/2$. If $B|z|<b$, then $|M(z)-1|\le e^{B|z|}-1\le1/2$, so the convergent power series for $\log(1+(M(z)-1))$ supplies a single analytic logarithm vanishing at zero.

Completing the square in the density in [F4] shows $\mathbb E e^{h\cdot Z}=e^{h^TGh/2}$ for real $h$ and that its real tilt is $N_d(Gh,G)$. The same integral for complex $z$ converges absolutely on bounded complex sets: $e^{\operatorname{Re}(z)\cdot x}$ times the Gaussian density is a constant times a translated Gaussian density, which dominates its polynomial derivatives on smaller bounded sets. Its exponential series or differentiated integral therefore gives an entire function, and the real identity extends to complex arguments. To justify that last extension without a several-variable identity theorem, fix all but the first coordinate real and apply the one-variable identity theorem, then successively free each remaining coordinate. Thus the Gaussian cumulant is $z^TGz/2$ and has zero third derivative.

On this ball, writing subscripts for directional derivatives, the bounds $|e^{z\cdot X}|\le e^b$, $|u\cdot X|\le B|u|$, and $\mathbb E(v\cdot X)^2=v^TDv$ give $|M_u|\le e^bB|u|$, $|M_v|\le e^b\sqrt{v^TDv}$, $|M_{vv}|\le e^bv^TDv$, $|M_{uv}|\le e^bB|u|\sqrt{v^TDv}$, and $|M_{uvv}|\le e^bB|u|v^TDv$. These inequalities also hold when $D$ is singular: a direction with zero second moment has $v\cdot X=0$ almost surely.

Every real tilt exists because all bounded-summand moment generating functions and the Gaussian one are finite and strictly positive. Its density with respect to the original independent joint law factors as the product of the separately normalized tilt densities. Hence those summands remain independent under the tilt. Step 1.2 shows that the Gaussian factor retains covariance $G$, while each other factor has a characteristic function of modulus at most one because $|e^{it\cdot X_j}|=1$. Factorization and [F4] therefore give $|\varphi_h(t)|\le e^{-t^TGt/2}\le e^{-\gamma s|t|^2/2}$ for every real $h,t$.

Direct differentiation gives $(\log M)_{uvv}=M_{uvv}/M-(M_uM_{vv}+2M_vM_{uv})/M^2+2M_uM_v^2/M^3$. Since $|M|\ge1/2$, step 2.1 bounds this by $CB|u|v^TDv$ for one absolute finite $C$. Choose $C_0$ so that $C_0\ge C$ and $1/C_0<b$, and set $\tau=C_0B$. Each bounded summand therefore has the asserted derivative bound on $\tau|z|<1$, using its own covariance.

Substitute $u=\sqrt s\,t$ in each requested tail integral, using the constant Jacobian $s^{-d/2}$. For $|u|\ge a/\kappa$, $e^{-\gamma|u|^2/2}\le e^{-\gamma a^2/(4\kappa^2)}e^{-\gamma|u|^2/4}$. For every fixed $N$, the function $z\mapsto z^Ne^{-\gamma a^2z^2/4}$ is bounded on $z\ge1$ by differentiation, so the extracted exponential is at most $C_{a,N,\gamma}\kappa^N$. The integral of $e^{-\gamma|u|^2/4}$ is finite by the normal density normalization in [F4]; its product with $|u|$ is integrable as well, since $|u|e^{-\gamma|u|^2/8}$ is bounded and the remaining Gaussian is integrable. Using $|u\cdot v|\le|u||v|$ gives the two tail bounds, with an additional $s^{-1/2}|v|$ in the weighted bound. Taking the maximum of these constants over $d=1,2,3,4$ makes them uniform.

By independence [F1], the moment generating function of $S$ is the product of the factors in steps 1.1 and 1.2. On $\tau|z|<1$, its logarithm is the sum of the analytic logarithms just constructed, with value zero at zero. Since the covariances add and $\sum_j\operatorname{cov}(X_j)\le sI_d$, summing step 3.1 gives $|K_{uvv}(z)|\le\tau|u|\sum_jv^T\operatorname{cov}(X_j)v\le\tau s|u||v|^2$. This proves the analytic assertion, including the empty bounded sum.

If $AA^T=I_k$, the operator norm of $A$ is one: $A^T$ is an isometry and $|Ax|=\sup_{|v|=1}|v\cdot Ax|\le|x|$ by [F5]. Thus $AX_j$ remains bounded by $B$ and centered, its sum has covariance $sAA^T=sI_k$, and $AZ$ is Gaussian with covariance $AGA^T\ge\gamma sI_k$ by [F4]. Independence is preserved by applying measurable maps separately. All earlier steps therefore apply to $AS$ with the same $C_0$. The map $(x,y)\mapsto((x+y)/\sqrt2,(x-y)/\sqrt2)$ is orthogonal because it preserves $|x|^2+|y|^2$ by expansion; consequently its coordinate prefixes have the required row isometry property. This proves all assertions.

Let $Y=(Y_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a process on a probability space whose finite-dimensional laws are invariant under common nonnegative time shifts; call this strict stationarity. For $j\ge0$, set $\mathcal F_j^-:=\sigma(Y_0,\ldots,Y_j)$ and $\mathcal F_j^+:=\sigma(Y_j,Y_{j+1},\ldots)$. For $n\ge1$, define the **strong-mixing coefficient** by
$$\alpha_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{\substack{A\in\mathcal F_j^-\\B\in\mathcal F_{j+n}^+}}|\mathbb P(A\cap B)-\mathbb P(A)\mathbb P(B)|.$$

Define the **uniform-mixing coefficient** by
$$\phi_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{\substack{A\in\mathcal F_j^-\\\mathbb P(A)>0}}\ \sup_{B\in\mathcal F_{j+n}^+}|\mathbb P(B\mid A)-\mathbb P(B)|.$$

For square-integrable real random variables $U,V$ with positive variances, write
$$\operatorname{Corr}(U,V):=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(U,V)}{\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(U)\operatorname{Var}(V)}}.$$
For each $n\ge1$, let $\mathcal C_n$ consist of the triples $(j,U,V)$ such that $j\ge0$, $U,V$ are real and square-integrable, $U$ and $V$ are measurable with respect to $\mathcal F_j^-$ and $\mathcal F_{j+n}^+$ respectively, and both have positive variance. Define the **maximal-correlation coefficient** by
$$\rho_Y(n):=\sup\Bigl(\{0\}\cup\{|\operatorname{Corr}(U,V)|:(j,U,V)\in\mathcal C_n\}\Bigr),$$
where square-integrability is in the sense of [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]. Thus $\rho_Y(n)=0$ when there is no admissible pair, as for a constant process. The process is called strongly mixing, uniformly mixing, or rho-mixing, respectively, when the corresponding coefficient tends to zero. These coefficients are distinct conditions; no implication between them is included in this definition.

Assume Choice. Let $X$ be a $K$-chain and let
$H:E^{\mathbb N_0}\to\mathbb R$ be bounded and product-measurable. Then
$$h(x):=\mathbb E_x[H(X_0,X_1,\ldots)]$$ is $\mathcal E$-measurable and, for every $n\ge0$, $$ \mathbb E[H(X_n,X_{n+1},\ldots)\mid\mathcal F_n]=h(X_n)\quad\text{a.s.} $$

For $m,n\ge0$,
$$K^{m+n}=K^mK^n.$$ Assume Choice and let $X$ be a Markov chain with kernel $K$ relative to $(\mathcal F_n)$. For every bounded measurable real $f$, $$ \mathbb E[f(X_{m+n})\mid\mathcal F_m]=K^nf(X_m)\quad\text{a.s.} $$ Equivalently, for $A\in\mathcal E$, $$ \mathbb P(X_{m+n}\in A\mid\mathcal F_m)=K^n(X_m,A)\quad\text{a.s.} $$
Both assertions include $m=0$ and $n=0$.

Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
$(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **total variation
distance** is

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}\bigl|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\bigr| .$$

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in
$[-1,1]$, because both measures have total mass one; hence the set being
maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.
The empty event and the whole space give the values $0$ and
$|\mu(E)-\nu(E)|=0$, so the distance is zero when $\mu=\nu$, and it is symmetric
in $\mu$ and $\nu$. This convention carries no factor $1/2$ in the supremum;
it is therefore not the total variation norm of the signed measure $\mu-\nu$,
which is twice the quantity above when that signed measure is considered on a
measurable space where the decomposition is attained. On a countable state
space with its power-set sigma-algebra the supremum equals the half-$\ell^1$
sum $\tfrac12\sum_{x\in E}|\mu(\{x\})-\nu(\{x\})|$; that identity is proved in
[[lem-total-variation-half-l1-formula-on-a-countable-space]], not assumed here.

Assume AC for existence. If $X\in L^1(P)$ and $Z$ is bounded real $\mathcal G$-measurable, then $E[ZX\mid\mathcal G]=ZE[X\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. The identity also holds for finite real $\mathcal G$-measurable $Z$ whenever $ZX$ and $ZE[X\mid\mathcal G]$ are integrable. In fact $X,ZX\in L^1$ imply the latter integrability.

derivations.claim: Fix $n\ge1$, $j\ge0$, $A\in\mathcal F_j$, and a future event $B\in\sigma(X_{j+n},X_{j+n+1},\ldots)$. By [F2], for the path indicator defining $B$ there is a measurable $h:\mathsf X\to[0,1]$ with $\mathbb E[\mathbf1_B\mid\mathcal F_{j+n}]=h(X_{j+n})$. Applying [F3] and the tower property gives $\mathbb E[\mathbf1_B\mid\mathcal F_j]=P^nh(X_j)$. Stationarity gives $\mathbb P(B)=\pi(h)$.

For probability measures $\mu,
u$ and measurable $0\le h\le1$, the dyadic simple functions $h_m=2^{-m}\sum_{j=1}^{2^m}\mathbf1_{\{h\ge j2^{-m}\}}$ differ from $h$ by at most $2^{-m}$. Their integrals differ by at most $\|\mu-
u\|_{\mathrm{TV}}$, since each summand is an indicator and [F4] bounds its measure difference. Letting $m	o\infty$ proves $|\mu(h)-
u(h)|\le\|\mu-
u\|_{\mathrm{TV}}$.
Apply step 1.2 with $\mu=P^n(x,\cdot)$ and $\nu=\pi$. The given rate then yields $|P^nh(x)-\pi(h)|\le M(x)r^n$ for every $x$.

Using [F5], [F2], and [F3], $\displaystyle |\mathbb P(A\cap B)-\mathbb P(A)\mathbb P(B)|=|\mathbb E[\mathbf1_A(P^nh(X_j)-\pi(h))]|\le\mathbb E|P^nh(X_j)-\pi(h)|\le\pi(M)r^n.$ The first inequality uses $0\le\mathbf1_A\le1$; the last follows from the preceding pointwise bound and stationarity of $X_j$. Since $A,B,j$ were arbitrary, taking the supremum in [F1] proves the claim.
