The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $Y=(Y_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a process on a probability space whose finite-dimensional laws are invariant under common nonnegative time shifts; call this strict stationarity. For $j\ge0$, set $\mathcal F_j^-:=\sigma(Y_0,\ldots,Y_j)$ and $\mathcal F_j^+:=\sigma(Y_j,Y_{j+1},\ldots)$. For $n\ge1$, define the **strong-mixing coefficient** by
$$\alpha_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{\substack{A\in\mathcal F_j^-\\B\in\mathcal F_{j+n}^+}}|\mathbb P(A\cap B)-\mathbb P(A)\mathbb P(B)|.$$

Define the **uniform-mixing coefficient** by
$$\phi_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{\substack{A\in\mathcal F_j^-\\\mathbb P(A)>0}}\ \sup_{B\in\mathcal F_{j+n}^+}|\mathbb P(B\mid A)-\mathbb P(B)|.$$

For square-integrable real random variables $U,V$ with positive variances, write
$$\operatorname{Corr}(U,V):=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(U,V)}{\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(U)\operatorname{Var}(V)}}.$$
For each $n\ge1$, let $\mathcal C_n$ consist of the triples $(j,U,V)$ such that $j\ge0$, $U,V$ are real and square-integrable, $U$ and $V$ are measurable with respect to $\mathcal F_j^-$ and $\mathcal F_{j+n}^+$ respectively, and both have positive variance. Define the **maximal-correlation coefficient** by
$$\rho_Y(n):=\sup\Bigl(\{0\}\cup\{|\operatorname{Corr}(U,V)|:(j,U,V)\in\mathcal C_n\}\Bigr),$$
where square-integrability is in the sense of [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]. Thus $\rho_Y(n)=0$ when there is no admissible pair, as for a constant process. The process is called strongly mixing, uniformly mixing, or rho-mixing, respectively, when the corresponding coefficient tends to zero. These coefficients are distinct conditions; no implication between them is included in this definition.

Assume Choice. Let $X$ be a $K$-chain and let
$H:E^{\mathbb N_0}\to\mathbb R$ be bounded and product-measurable. Then
$$h(x):=\mathbb E_x[H(X_0,X_1,\ldots)]$$ is $\mathcal E$-measurable and, for every $n\ge0$, $$ \mathbb E[H(X_n,X_{n+1},\ldots)\mid\mathcal F_n]=h(X_n)\quad\text{a.s.} $$

For $m,n\ge0$,
$$K^{m+n}=K^mK^n.$$ Assume Choice and let $X$ be a Markov chain with kernel $K$ relative to $(\mathcal F_n)$. For every bounded measurable real $f$, $$ \mathbb E[f(X_{m+n})\mid\mathcal F_m]=K^nf(X_m)\quad\text{a.s.} $$ Equivalently, for $A\in\mathcal E$, $$ \mathbb P(X_{m+n}\in A\mid\mathcal F_m)=K^n(X_m,A)\quad\text{a.s.} $$
Both assertions include $m=0$ and $n=0$.

Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
$(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **total variation
distance** is

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}\bigl|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\bigr| .$$

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in
$[-1,1]$, because both measures have total mass one; hence the set being
maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.
The empty event and the whole space give the values $0$ and
$|\mu(E)-\nu(E)|=0$, so the distance is zero when $\mu=\nu$, and it is symmetric
in $\mu$ and $\nu$. This convention carries no factor $1/2$ in the supremum;
it is therefore not the total variation norm of the signed measure $\mu-\nu$,
which is twice the quantity above when that signed measure is considered on a
measurable space where the decomposition is attained. On a countable state
space with its power-set sigma-algebra the supremum equals the half-$\ell^1$
sum $\tfrac12\sum_{x\in E}|\mu(\{x\})-\nu(\{x\})|$; that identity is proved in
[[lem-total-variation-half-l1-formula-on-a-countable-space]], not assumed here.

Assume AC for existence. If $X\in L^1(P)$ and $Z$ is bounded real $\mathcal G$-measurable, then $E[ZX\mid\mathcal G]=ZE[X\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. The identity also holds for finite real $\mathcal G$-measurable $Z$ whenever $ZX$ and $ZE[X\mid\mathcal G]$ are integrable. In fact $X,ZX\in L^1$ imply the latter integrability.

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be an increasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$, so $E_n\subseteq E_{n+1}$. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\sup_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

No finiteness hypothesis is required.

Let $\mu$ be a measure and let $A\subseteq B$ be measurable with $\mu(A)<+\infty$. Then

$$\mu(B)=\mu(A)+\mu(B\setminus A).$$

If $\mu(B)<+\infty$, all terms are real and hence $\mu(B\setminus A)=\mu(B)-\mu(A)$. If $\mu(B)=+\infty$, then $\mu(B\setminus A)=+\infty$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

For a probability kernel $K$ on $(E,\mathcal E)$, let $I$ be the identity
kernel $I(x,A)=1_A(x)$ and define
$$ K^0:=I,\qquad K^{n+1}:=K^nK, $$ where composition is in chronological order: $$ K^{n+1}(x,A)=\int_E K(y,A)K^n(x,dy). $$
The identity map makes $I$ a probability kernel, including on a one-point
space. Induction using the published kernel-composition lemma shows that every
$K^n$ is a probability kernel. Associativity makes products of several copies
of $K$ unambiguous. No conditional-expectation version is selected and no form
of Choice is used.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

By [F2], the indicator of this future-path event has conditional expectation $h(X_{j+n})$ for a measurable $0\le h\le1$. Applying [F3] and the tower property gives $\mathbb E[\mathbf1_B\mid\mathcal F_j]=P^nh(X_j)$. Stationarity gives $\mathbb P(B)=\pi(h)$.

u$ and measurable $0\le h\le1$, the dyadic simple approximation $h_m=2^{-m}\sum_{r=1}^{2^m}\mathbf1_{\{h\ge r2^{-m}\}}$ differs from $h$ by at most $2^{-m}$. Each indicator integral difference is bounded by [F4], so the integrals of $h_m$ differ by at most $\|\mu-
u\|_{\mathrm{TV}}$. Letting $m	o\infty$ gives $|\mu(h)-
u(h)|\le\|\mu-
u\|_{\mathrm{TV}}$.

It contains $\mathcal C$ and is closed under complements because $\mathcal C$ is an algebra. For $A_i\in\mathcal D$ and $\varepsilon>0$, [F6] gives $N\ge1$ with $\mu_{n,x}((\bigcup_i A_i)\setminus(\bigcup_{i=1}^N A_i))<\varepsilon/2$. Choose $C_i\in\mathcal C$ with $\mu_{n,x}(A_i\triangle C_i)<\varepsilon/(2N)$ for $i\le N$. The finite union $C=\bigcup_{i=1}^NC_i$ belongs to $\mathcal C$ and $\mu_{n,x}((\bigcup_iA_i)\triangle C)<\varepsilon$ by finite subadditivity. Thus $\mathcal D$ is a sigma-algebra containing the generator $\mathcal C$, so $\mathcal D=\mathcal X$. Approximating each measurable $A$ in this way shows $d_n(x):=\sup_{C\in\mathcal C}|P^n(x,C)-\pi(C)|=\|P^n(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}$: the discrepancy for $A$ differs from that for an approximating $C$ by at most $P^n(x,A\triangle C)+\pi(A\triangle C)$. Since $\mathcal C$ is countable and each evaluation is measurable by [F8], $d_n$ is measurable; also $0\le d_n\le1$.

This bound is independent of $j,A,B$, so taking the supremum in [F1] proves $\alpha_X(n)\to0$.

$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

The summable sequence $|\gamma_k|$ dominates the summands, so [F5] gives $n^{-1}\operatorname{Var}(S_n)\to\gamma_0+2\sum_{k\ge1}\gamma_k=0$.

Since $\mathbb E[S_n]=0$, step 1.1 gives $\mathbb E[(S_n/\sqrt n)^2]=n^{-1}\operatorname{Var}(S_n)\to0$. This is convergence to zero in $L^2$; [F3] gives convergence in probability, and [F4] gives convergence in distribution to the point mass at zero, namely $N(0,0)$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $(X_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a stationary time-homogeneous Markov chain
with probability kernel $P$, invariant law $\pi$, and natural filtration
$\mathcal F_k=\sigma(X_0,\ldots,X_k)$. Let $g\in L^2(\pi)$ ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]) and fix a finite real measurable representative, also denoted by $g$. Define
$Pg(x)=\int g(y)P(x,dy)$ and $P(g^2)(x)=\int g(y)^2P(x,dy)$ on the
$\pi$-full measurable set where the respective integrals are finite, and set
these functions to zero on the exceptional set. Then, for each $k\ge0$,
$$\mathbb E[g(X_{k+1})\mid\mathcal F_k]=Pg(X_k).$$
$$\mathbb E[g(X_{k+1})^2\mid\mathcal F_k]=P(g^2)(X_k)\quad\text{a.s.}$$
Consequently, if $D_{k+1}=g(X_{k+1})-Pg(X_k)$, then $(D_{k+1})$ is a square-integrable martingale-difference sequence and
$$\mathbb E[D_{k+1}^2\mid\mathcal F_k]=P(g^2)(X_k)-(Pg(X_k))^2\quad\text{a.s.}$$

Assume AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $Y=(Y_n)_{n\ge0}$ be a real-valued
strictly stationary process with $\mathbb E|Y_0|<\infty$
([[def-stationary-process-and-canonical-shift]]), with canonical path law
$\mathbb P_Y$ and left shift $\theta$. Let
$\mathcal I=\{A:\theta^{-1}A=A\}$ be the strictly invariant sigma-algebra on
path space ([[def-strict-and-mod-null-invariant-sigma-algebras]]). Then

$$\frac1n\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}Y_k\ \longrightarrow\ \mathbb E_{\mathbb P_Y}[z_0\mid\mathcal I]\circ\Phi \qquad\text{almost surely and in }L^1(\mathbb P),$$

where $\Phi(\omega)=(Y_n(\omega))_{n\ge0}$ and the conditional expectation is
that of [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. If moreover the
canonical shift is ergodic ([[def-ergodic-measure-preserving-system]]), then
the limit is the constant $\mathbb EY_0$. For complex-valued processes the
assertions hold componentwise for real and imaginary parts.

Assume AC. Let $(Z_{n,k},\mathcal F_{n,k})$ be a square-integrable martingale-difference array such that, for every $n$, $M_{n,m}$ and $\Gamma_{n,m}$ converge almost surely as $m\to\infty$ to finite limits $M_{n,\infty}$ and $\Gamma_{n,\infty}$. If
$$\Gamma_{n,\infty}\longrightarrow1\quad\text{in probability}$$
and, for every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$L_n(\varepsilon):=\sum_{k\ge1}\mathbb E[Z_{n,k}^2 1_{\{|Z_{n,k}|>\varepsilon\}}]\longrightarrow0,$$
then $M_{n,\infty}\Rightarrow N(0,1)$.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Let $(X_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a stationary time-homogeneous Markov chain with invariant probability $\pi$, and let $f$ be real Borel with $\pi(f)=0$ and $\pi(f^2)<\infty$. For $k\ge0$, set $\gamma_k:=\operatorname{Cov}_{\pi}(f(X_0),f(X_k))$. When the Markov-chain CLT $n^{-1/2}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}f(X_k)\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_f^2)$ holds with finite variance parameter and $\sum_{k\ge1}|\gamma_k|<\infty$, the **covariance long-run variance** is
$$\sigma^2_{\mathrm{LR}}(f):=\gamma_0+2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\gamma_k.$$

This definition does not infer a CLT from covariance summability, or infer that a weak-limit variance equals the covariance sum. Whenever $\sigma^2_{\mathrm{LR}}(f)$ is used as the variance parameter in a CLT or MCSE claim, that equality must be established by the theorem being applied. For example, the local Poisson-equation theorem proves the equality under its square-integrable solution hypotheses.

Assume AC for existence. If $X\in L^1(P)$ and $Z$ is bounded real $\mathcal G$-measurable, then $E[ZX\mid\mathcal G]=ZE[X\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. The identity also holds for finite real $\mathcal G$-measurable $Z$ whenever $ZX$ and $ZE[X\mid\mathcal G]$ are integrable. In fact $X,ZX\in L^1$ imply the latter integrability.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $X_n$ and $Y_n$ be Borel-measurable random elements with values in a metric space $S$, on the same probability space for each $n$, and let $X$ be an $S$-valued Borel-measurable random element. Suppose $d(X_n,Y_n)$ is measurable and $P(d(X_n,Y_n)>\varepsilon)\to0$ for every $\varepsilon$>0. If $X_n\Rightarrow X$, then $Y_n\Rightarrow X$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$
Let $1\le p<\infty$. If $X_n\to X$ in $L^p$, then $X_n\to X$ in probability.

Assume Choice. For every probability measure $\mu$ and probability kernel $K$
on an arbitrary measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$, the canonical path space
$$ (E^{\mathbb N_0},\mathcal E^{\otimes\mathbb N_0}) $$
carries a unique probability $\mathbb P_\mu$ under which the coordinate maps
form a Markov chain with initial law $\mu$ and transition kernel $K$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space. A measurable self-map $T:X\to X$ is **measure preserving** if $\mu(T^{-1}E)=\mu(E)$ for every $E\in\mathcal A$. The quadruple $(X,\mathcal A,\mu,T)$ is a **measure-preserving system**; it is a probability system if $\mu(X)=1$. Here $T^{-1}E=\{x:T(x)\in E\}$ denotes an inverse image, whether or not $T$ is invertible. Neither completeness nor finiteness is implicit. The measure-space and measurable-map conventions are [[def-measure-space]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]].

A measure-preserving system is **ergodic for $\mu$** if each $E\in\mathcal I$ has $\mu(E)=0$ or $\mu(X\setminus E)=0$, with $\mathcal I$ as in [[def-strict-and-mod-null-invariant-sigma-algebras]]. For a probability system this means $\mu(E)\in\{0,1\}$. The definition is relative to the invariant measure; no probability assumption is implicit in the general null/conull formulation.

Let S,T be metric spaces, $g:S\to T$ measurable, and $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$. If the discontinuity set $D_g$ is $\mu$-null, then $g_*\mu_n\Rightarrow g_*\mu$. Consequently $X_n\Rightarrow X$ implies $g(X_n)\Rightarrow g(X)$ whenever $P_X(D_g)=0$.

derivations.claim: By [F1], each $D_{k+1}$ is a square-integrable martingale difference, so $\mathbb E[D_{k+1}\mid\mathcal F_k]=0$. Since $f=g-Pg$ $\pi$-almost everywhere and each $X_k$ has law $\pi$, the identity holds at every $X_k$ simultaneously outside a countable union of null events. Therefore $f(X_k)=g(X_k)-g(X_{k+1})+D_{k+1}$ almost surely.

Set $q(x)=P(g^2)(x)-(Pg(x))^2$ on the $\pi$-full set where these terms are finite, and set $q=0$ elsewhere. By [F1], $q(X_k)$ is the conditional variance of $D_{k+1}$, is nonnegative, and $\pi(q)=\mathbb E[D_1^2]=\tau_f^2$. Thus $q\in L^1(\pi)$. The process $(q(X_k))_{k\ge0}$ is a measurable factor of the stationary ergodic path process $(X_k)$: the inverse image of any shift-invariant event for $q(X)$ is shift-invariant for $X$. Hence it too is stationary and ergodic by [F10], and [F2] gives $n^{-1}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}q(X_k)\to\tau_f^2$ almost surely.

Stationarity and $g\in L^2(\pi)$ give $\mathbb E[(g(X_0)-g(X_n))^2/n]\le4\pi(g^2)/n\to0$. The $L^2$-norm of the endpoint divided by $\sqrt n$ therefore tends to zero, so [F9] gives convergence to zero in probability.
Summing step 1.1 for $k=0,\ldots,n-1$ cancels the intermediate $g(X_k)$ terms and yields $S_n:=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}f(X_k)=g(X_0)-g(X_n)+M_n$, where $M_n:=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}D_{k+1}$.

Suppose $\tau_f^2>0$. For row $n$, set $Z_{n,j}=D_j/\sqrt{n\tau_f^2}$ for $1\le j\le n$, set $Z_{n,j}=0$ for $j>n$, and use $\mathcal F_{n,j}=\mathcal F_{\min(j,n)}$ for every $j\ge0$. These are square-integrable martingale-difference rows by step 1.1. Their terminal variance clock is $\Gamma_{n,\infty}=(n\tau_f^2)^{-1}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}q(X_k)\to1$ almost surely by step 1.2. For every $\varepsilon>0$, stationarity of the transition pairs $(X_{j-1},X_j)$ gives $\sum_{j=1}^n\mathbb E[Z_{n,j}^2\mathbf1_{\{|Z_{n,j}|>\varepsilon\}}]=\tau_f^{-2}\mathbb E[D_1^2\mathbf1_{\{|D_1|>\varepsilon\sqrt{n\tau_f^2}\}}]\to0$ by [F8], since $D_1^2$ is integrable. Extending each row by zeros makes it an infinite array with the same terminal sum and clock. Therefore [F3] gives $M_n/\sqrt{n\tau_f^2}\Rightarrow N(0,1)$; scaling by $\tau_f$ using [F11] yields $M_n/\sqrt n\Rightarrow N(0,\tau_f^2)$.

If $\tau_f^2=0$, stationarity and [F1] imply $\mathbb E[D_{k+1}^2]=0$, so $D_{k+1}=0$ almost surely and hence $M_n=0$. By step 2.1, $S_n=g(X_0)-g(X_n)$. Step 1.3 shows $S_n/\sqrt n\to0$ in probability; [F7] then gives convergence to the point mass $N(0,0)$.
If $\tau_f^2>0$, step 2.2 gives $M_n/\sqrt n\Rightarrow N(0,\tau_f^2)$. Combining this with step 1.3, the decomposition in step 2.1, and [F7] gives $S_n/\sqrt n\Rightarrow N(0,\tau_f^2)$.

Assume additionally that the covariance series is absolutely convergent. Stationarity and expansion of the finite square give $n^{-1}\operatorname{Var}(S_n)=\gamma_0+2\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}(1-k/n)\gamma_k\to\gamma_0+2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\gamma_k$, where $\gamma_k=\operatorname{Cov}_{\pi}(f(X_0),f(X_k))$; [F8] applies to the series because $|\gamma_k|$ is summable. On the other hand, step 2.1 writes $S_n=R_n+M_n$ with $R_n=g(X_0)-g(X_n)$. For $i<j$, $D_{i+1}$ is $\mathcal F_j$-measurable and $\mathbb E[D_{j+1}\mid\mathcal F_j]=0$, so [F1, F6] give $\mathbb E[D_{i+1}D_{j+1}]=0$. Stationarity gives $\operatorname{Var}(M_n)=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\mathbb E[D_{j+1}^2]=n\tau_f^2$. Also $\operatorname{Var}(R_n)\le4\pi(g^2)$ and [F6] gives $|\operatorname{Cov}(R_n,M_n)|\le\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(R_n)\operatorname{Var}(M_n)}=O(\sqrt n)$. Dividing $\operatorname{Var}(S_n)=\operatorname{Var}(R_n)+\operatorname{Var}(M_n)+2\operatorname{Cov}(R_n,M_n)$ by $n$ therefore shows that its limit is $\tau_f^2$. Steps 3.1 and 3.2 give the CLT, so [F5] identifies its variance with the displayed covariance sum.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

For a probability kernel $P$ on $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ ([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), a measurable set $C$ is **$(m,\epsilon,\nu)$-small** if $m\ge1$ is an integer, $0<\epsilon\le1$, $\nu$ is a probability measure ([[def-probability-measure]]), and
$$P^m(x,A)\ge\epsilon\nu(A)\quad(x\in C,\ A\in\mathcal X).$$
The inequality is pointwise in $x$ and holds for every measurable $A$.

A **geometric drift inequality outside $C$** consists of a finite-valued measurable $V:\mathsf X\to[1,\infty)$, constants $0<\lambda<1$ and $0\le b<\infty$, and
$$PV(x):=\int V(y)P(x,dy)\le\lambda V(x)+b\,1_C(x)\quad(x\in\mathsf X).$$
The terms small set and drift are separate hypotheses; neither definition asserts the existence of the other.

When an invariant probability $\pi$ is specified ([[def-invariant-and-stationary-distribution-for-a-markov-kernel]]), an **extended geometric drift certificate finite $\pi$-almost everywhere** allows measurable $V:\mathsf X\to[1,+\infty]$ with $\pi(V<\infty)=1$ and the same pointwise inequality, interpreted in the nonnegative extended reals. This is a separate convention from the finite-valued drift function above. The geometric theorem treats this certificate on $E=\{V<\infty\}$; the original finite-valued convention gives the corresponding bound on the whole state space.

Assume Choice. For every probability measure $\mu$ and probability kernel $K$
on an arbitrary measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$, the canonical path space
$$ (E^{\mathbb N_0},\mathcal E^{\otimes\mathbb N_0}) $$
carries a unique probability $\mathbb P_\mu$ under which the coordinate maps
form a Markov chain with initial law $\mu$ and transition kernel $K$.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Assume Choice. Let $X$ be a $K$-chain, let
$\tau:\Omega\to\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$ be a stopping time, and let $H$ be a
bounded measurable path functional. Put $h(x)=\mathbb E_xH$ and define the
everywhere meaningful random variables
$$ Z_H:=\sum_{n\ge0}1_{\{\tau=n\}}H(X_n,X_{n+1},\ldots), \qquad R_h:=\sum_{n\ge0}1_{\{\tau=n\}}h(X_n). $$ Both are defined to be zero on $\{\tau=\infty\}$. Then $$ \mathbb E[Z_H\mid\mathcal F_\tau]=R_h\quad\text{a.s.} $$ This is the precise meaning of the usual eventwise notation $$ \mathbb E[1_{\{\tau<\infty\}}H(X_\tau,X_{\tau+1},\ldots)\mid\mathcal F_\tau] =1_{\{\tau<\infty\}}h(X_\tau): $$
no value $X_\infty$ is used. If $\tau<\infty$ almost surely, the indicators can
be omitted.

Assume Choice. Let $X$ be a $K$-chain and let
$H:E^{\mathbb N_0}\to\mathbb R$ be bounded and product-measurable. Then
$$h(x):=\mathbb E_x[H(X_0,X_1,\ldots)]$$ is $\mathcal E$-measurable and, for every $n\ge0$, $$ \mathbb E[H(X_n,X_{n+1},\ldots)\mid\mathcal F_n]=h(X_n)\quad\text{a.s.} $$

Assume AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $K$ be a probability kernel on a
measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$, let $\pi$ be an invariant probability for $K$
([[def-invariant-and-stationary-distribution-for-a-markov-kernel]]), and let
$X$ be a $K$-chain with initial law $\pi$
([[def-initial-distribution-of-a-markov-chain]]). Then every finite-dimensional
law of $X$ is invariant under every nonnegative integer time shift: for every
$r\ge1$, every $0\le n_1<\cdots<n_r$ and every $m\ge0$,

$$\mathcal L(X_{m+n_1},\ldots,X_{m+n_r})=\mathcal L(X_{n_1},\ldots,X_{n_r}).$$

Equivalently, the canonical path law
$\mathbb P_X:=\mathcal L\bigl((X_n)_{n\ge0}\bigr)$ on
$(E^{\mathbb N_0},\mathcal E^{\otimes\mathbb N_0})$ is invariant under the left
shift $\theta(z)_n=z_{n+1}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$
The sum of a complex power series is analytic on its open disc of convergence.
Every function analytic on an open set $U\subseteq\mathbb C$ is holomorphic on $U$.

If $f(z)=\sum_{n\ge0}c_n(z-a)^n$ has radius $R$, then for every $k\in\mathbb N$ and $|z-a|<R$,
$$f^{(k)}(z)=\sum_{n\ge k}\frac{n!}{(n-k)!}c_n(z-a)^{n-k}.$$
Every derived series has radius $R$.

Let $f$ be holomorphic on $D(a,R)$, let $0<r<R$, and let $\gamma(t)=a+r\exp(it)$ for $0\le t\le2\pi$. Define $f^{(0)}=f$ and, whenever it exists, $f^{(n+1)}=(f^{(n)})'$. Then every $f^{(n)}$ exists on $D(a,r)$ and, for every $z\in D(a,r)$ and $n\in\mathbb N$,

$$f^{(n)}(z)=\frac{n!}{2\pi i}\int_\gamma\frac{f(\zeta)}{(\zeta-z)^{n+1}}\,d\zeta.$$

In particular, every holomorphic function has complex derivatives of all orders locally.

Let $f$ be holomorphic on $D(a,R)$, let $0<r<R$, and suppose $M\ge0$ satisfies $|f(\zeta)|\le M$ whenever $|\zeta-a|=r$. If $c_n=f^{(n)}(a)/n!$ is the $n$th coefficient of the Taylor series of $f$ at $a$, then

$$|c_n|\le\frac{M}{r^n}\qquad(n\in\mathbb N).$$

If $|f(\zeta)|\le M$ on $|\zeta-a|=r$, then the $n$th Taylor coefficient $c_n$ satisfies $|c_n|\le M/r^n$.

Let $K$ be a probability kernel on a measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and let $\pi$ be a
probability measure on $(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). The
probability measure $\pi$ is **invariant** for $K$, and $\pi$ is a
**stationary distribution** of $K$, when

$$(\pi K)(A):=\int_E K(x,A)\,\pi(dx)=\pi(A)\qquad\text{for every }A\in\mathcal E .$$

The set function $\pi K$ is again a probability measure: for fixed $A$ the map
$x\mapsto K(x,A)$ is measurable and lies in $[0,1]$, so the integral exists in
$[0,1]$; for pairwise disjoint $A_n\in\mathcal E$ the identity
$K(x,\bigcup_nA_n)=\sum_nK(x,A_n)$ of the measure $K(x,\cdot)$ and the
monotone convergence theorem for nonnegative functions
([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]) give
$\sigma$-additivity of $\pi K$; and $K(x,E)=1$ for every $x$ gives
$(\pi K)(E)=1$. Thus $(\pi K)(A)=\pi(A)$ is an identity between two probability
measures evaluated at $A$.

A $K$-chain whose initial law is $\pi$ is called **stationary** when
$\pi K=\pi$. Stationarity of the process is a statement about all of its
finite-dimensional laws and is proved, not assumed, from $\pi K=\pi$; see
[[thm-invariant-initial-law-makes-the-chain-stationary]].

On a countable state space $E$ with sigma-algebra $2^E$ and transition matrix
$p(x,y)=K(x,\{y\})$ ([[def-transition-matrix-and-n-step-transition-probabilities]]),
a measure on $E$ is its weighted sum of Dirac masses at singletons
([[thm-measures-on-countable-discrete-spaces-are-weighted-dirac-sums]]), so
invariance is equivalent to the matrix identity

$$\pi(y)=\sum_{x\in E}\pi(x)\,p(x,y)\qquad\text{for every }y\in E .$$

The definition fixes no irreducibility, aperiodicity or uniqueness hypothesis,
and it selects no conditional-expectation versions; the display defines a
single measure $\pi K$ and asserts an identity for it. A transient, periodic or
reducible chain may have several invariant probability measures or none.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $Y=(Y_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a process on a probability space whose finite-dimensional laws are invariant under common nonnegative time shifts; call this strict stationarity. For $j\ge0$, set $\mathcal F_j^-:=\sigma(Y_0,\ldots,Y_j)$ and $\mathcal F_j^+:=\sigma(Y_j,Y_{j+1},\ldots)$. For $n\ge1$, define the **strong-mixing coefficient** by
$$\alpha_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{\substack{A\in\mathcal F_j^-\\B\in\mathcal F_{j+n}^+}}|\mathbb P(A\cap B)-\mathbb P(A)\mathbb P(B)|.$$

Define the **uniform-mixing coefficient** by
$$\phi_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{\substack{A\in\mathcal F_j^-\\\mathbb P(A)>0}}\ \sup_{B\in\mathcal F_{j+n}^+}|\mathbb P(B\mid A)-\mathbb P(B)|.$$

For square-integrable real random variables $U,V$ with positive variances, write
$$\operatorname{Corr}(U,V):=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(U,V)}{\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(U)\operatorname{Var}(V)}}.$$
For each $n\ge1$, let $\mathcal C_n$ consist of the triples $(j,U,V)$ such that $j\ge0$, $U,V$ are real and square-integrable, $U$ and $V$ are measurable with respect to $\mathcal F_j^-$ and $\mathcal F_{j+n}^+$ respectively, and both have positive variance. Define the **maximal-correlation coefficient** by
$$\rho_Y(n):=\sup\Bigl(\{0\}\cup\{|\operatorname{Corr}(U,V)|:(j,U,V)\in\mathcal C_n\}\Bigr),$$
where square-integrability is in the sense of [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]. Thus $\rho_Y(n)=0$ when there is no admissible pair, as for a constant process. The process is called strongly mixing, uniformly mixing, or rho-mixing, respectively, when the corresponding coefficient tends to zero. These coefficients are distinct conditions; no implication between them is included in this definition.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

1. If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]=\int_0^\infty \mathbb P(X>t)\,dt,$$
   where the right-hand side may be $+\infty$.
2. If $X$ is an integrable real random variable, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]=\int_0^\infty \mathbb P(X>t)\,dt-\int_0^\infty \mathbb P(X<-t)\,dt.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ and let $\mathcal A=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. If finite measures $\mu$ and $
u$ on $(X,\mathcal A)$ agree on $\mathcal P$ and satisfy $\mu(X)=
u(X)$, then $\mu=
u$ on $\mathcal A$.

The total-mass equality is separate because this library's pi-system convention does not require $X\in\mathcal P$.

derivations.claim: For a finite real $U$, write $T(t)=\mathbb P(|U|>t)$ for $t\ge0$. The tail tends to zero at infinity, is nonincreasing and is right-continuous. Thus $Q_U(u)$ is finite for $u>0$, is nonincreasing, and is Borel measurable. More precisely, $Q_U(u)>t$ if and only if $u<T(t)$: if $T(t)\le u$, then $t$ belongs to the set defining the infimum; if $T(t)>u$, right-continuity supplies an $\varepsilon>0$ with $T(t+\varepsilon)>u$, so that infimum exceeds $t$. Consequently Lebesgue measure on $(0,1)$ gives $\lambda\{u:Q_U(u)>t\}=T(t)$ for every $t\ge0$. The laws of $Q_U$ under $\lambda$ and of $|U|$ therefore agree on all closed left rays and both have total mass one. These rays form a pi-system and generate the Borel sigma-algebra: their differences give half-open intervals, and countable unions of those give all open intervals. By [F6] the laws agree, proving the stated integral identity. In particular $\int_0^1Q_U^2=\mathbb EU^2$.

Suppose first $U,V\ge0$ and $U,V\in L^2$. Their first moments and $\mathbb E(UV)$ are finite by [F3]. The threshold-indicator identities and [F5] give $\mathbb E(UV)=\int_0^\infty\int_0^\infty\mathbb P(U>s,V>t)\,ds\,dt$ and $\mathbb EU\mathbb EV=\int_0^\infty\int_0^\infty\mathbb P(U>s)\mathbb P(V>t)\,ds\,dt$. Both integrands have finite integrals, so their difference represents the covariance and the integral triangle inequality applies. The absolute threshold-indicator covariance is bounded by $a$, by $\mathbb P(U>s)$, and by $\mathbb P(V>t)$, since the joint probability and the product probability both lie between zero and either marginal probability.

Put $T_U(s)=\mathbb P(U>s)$ and $T_V(t)=\mathbb P(V>t)$. By [F5] and step 1.1, $\int_0^\infty\int_0^\infty\min\{a,T_U(s),T_V(t)\}\,ds\,dt=\int_0^a Q_U(u)Q_V(u)\,du.$ Indeed the minimum is $\int_0^a\mathbf1_{\{u<T_U(s)\}}\mathbf1_{\{u<T_V(t)\}}\,du$, and each inner threshold set has length its quantile. The right-hand side is finite by Cauchy–Schwarz on $(0,1)$ and the squared-quantile identity in step 1.1; this particular integral Cauchy–Schwarz inequality follows by integrating $(Q_U-cQ_V)^2\ge0$ and minimizing the resulting quadratic, with the zero-norm case immediate. Step 1.2 therefore proves the covariance bound with constant one for nonnegative $U,V$.

For real $U,V$, expand $\operatorname{Cov}(U^+-U^-,V^+-V^-)$ into four terms. Each nonnegative part has a tail quantile at most the corresponding absolute quantile, because its tail probabilities are smaller. The result of step 2.1 bounds each term by $\int_0^aQ_UQ_V$; the triangle inequality gives the asserted factor four. If $|U|\le A$ and $|V|\le B$, their absolute quantiles are bounded by $A,B$, so the bound becomes $4ABa$, including $a=0$ or either zero bound.

For complex $U,V$, expand $\mathbb E(UV)-\mathbb EU\mathbb EV$ into the four real bilinear covariance terms of their real and imaginary parts. Each real part is bounded in absolute value by $A$ or $B$, so step 3.1 and the complex triangle inequality give $16ABa$. Finally, for observations separated by $n$, both collection sigma-algebras are sub-sigma-algebras of the past and future fields appearing in [F1]; their event supremum is therefore at most $\alpha_Y(n)$. All assertions follow.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For any set $I$, standard-Borel coordinate spaces $(E_i,\mathcal E_i)$, and consistent finite-dimensional laws $(\mu_F)_{F\Subset I}$, there is a unique probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathcal C_I$ whose $F$-coordinate marginal is $\mu_F$ for each finite $F$.

Define the **uniform-mixing coefficient** by
$$\phi_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{\substack{A\in\mathcal F_j^-\\\mathbb P(A)>0}}\ \sup_{B\in\mathcal F_{j+n}^+}|\mathbb P(B\mid A)-\mathbb P(B)|.$$

$$\operatorname{Corr}(U,V):=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(U,V)}{\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(U)\operatorname{Var}(V)}}.$$
For each $n\ge1$, let $\mathcal C_n$ consist of the triples $(j,U,V)$ such that $j\ge0$, $U,V$ are real and square-integrable, $U$ and $V$ are measurable with respect to $\mathcal F_j^-$ and $\mathcal F_{j+n}^+$ respectively, and both have positive variance. Define the **maximal-correlation coefficient** by
$$\rho_Y(n):=\sup\Bigl(\{0\}\cup\{|\operatorname{Corr}(U,V)|:(j,U,V)\in\mathcal C_n\}\Bigr),$$
where square-integrability is in the sense of [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]. Thus $\rho_Y(n)=0$ when there is no admissible pair, as for a constant process. The process is called strongly mixing, uniformly mixing, or rho-mixing, respectively, when the corresponding coefficient tends to zero. These coefficients are distinct conditions; no implication between them is included in this definition.

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $1 \le p < \infty$. Then
every element of $L^p(\mu)$ can be approximated in $L^p$ by simple functions
whose supports have finite measure.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

A measure-preserving system is **ergodic for $\mu$** if each $E\in\mathcal I$ has $\mu(E)=0$ or $\mu(X\setminus E)=0$, with $\mathcal I$ as in [[def-strict-and-mod-null-invariant-sigma-algebras]]. For a probability system this means $\mu(E)\in\{0,1\}$. The definition is relative to the invariant measure; no probability assumption is implicit in the general null/conull formulation.

derivations.claim: For finite $F\subset\mathbb Z$, choose an integer $m\ge0$ with $F+m\subset\mathbb N_0$ and prescribe the law of $(X_i)_{i\in F}$ to be that of $(Y_{i+m})_{i\in F}$. If $m'$ is another permissible shift, stationarity compares the smaller shift with the larger one, so the law is independent of the choice. Restrictions are consistent because finitely many coordinate sets can be translated by one common shift. Every coordinate space is the standard Borel space $\mathbb R$, so [F1] gives $Q$. Its nonnegative restriction equals the process law of $Y$ on cylinders and hence everywhere by [F5]. Translating finite sets does not change their prescribed laws, so $Q\circ T^{-1}=Q$ by the same uniqueness argument. Both $T$ and its inverse are measurable because their coordinate maps are coordinates.

For any subset $I\subset\mathbb Z$, let $\mathcal A_I$ be the algebra of events depending on finitely many coordinates in $I$. Every event in $\sigma(X_i:i\in I)$ can be approximated in symmetric-difference probability by $\mathcal A_I$. Indeed, the approximable events are closed under complements. For a countable union, first replace that union by a finite subunion with arbitrarily small lost probability, using continuity from below, then approximate its finitely many constituent events and apply the union bound. Thus the approximable events form a sigma-algebra containing $\mathcal A_I$. By [F4], approximate an $L^2$ variable by simple functions, and approximate the finitely many indicator events of each simple function by $\mathcal A_I$ events. For an indicator the squared $L^2$ error is its symmetric-difference probability; finite summation gives the required arbitrarily small $L^2$ error for a simple function. Consequently every such variable has finite-coordinate $L^2$ approximants.

First suppose $U$ and $V$ depend on finitely many coordinates in $(-\infty,k]$ and $[k+n,\infty)$, respectively. Translate all coordinates by one integer $m\ge0$ so that the used past coordinates and the split $k+m$ are nonnegative. Their joint distribution is an original-process distribution by step 1.1. The translated variables are measurable in $\sigma(Y_0,\ldots,Y_{k+m})$ and $\sigma(Y_{k+m+n},Y_{k+m+n+1},\ldots)$, so [F2] proves the asserted covariance inequality when both variances are positive. A variable of variance zero equals its mean almost surely and has zero covariance, so the inequality holds then too. For arbitrary $U,V$, take step 1.2's finite-coordinate $L^2$ approximants. Their means, second moments, and covariances converge by [F3], so passage to the limit proves the same inequality.

Assume $\rho_Y(n)\to0$, and let $A$ satisfy $Q(A\mathbin\triangle T^{-1}A)=0$, with $p=Q(A)$. Given $\varepsilon>0$, step 1.2 supplies a finite-coordinate event $C$ with $Q(A\mathbin\triangle C)<\varepsilon$; enlarge its coordinate support to $[-m,m]$ for some $m\ge0$. For $n>2m$, $C$ is in $\mathcal F_m$ and $T^{-n}C$ is in $\mathcal G_{n-m}$. Step 2.1 applied to their indicators gives $|Q(C\cap T^{-n}C)-Q(C)^2|\le\rho_Y(n-2m)/4$, since every indicator variance is at most $1/4$. Invariance modulo null sets and measure preservation imply $Q(A\cap T^{-n}A)=p$. The intersection changes in probability by at most $2\varepsilon$ upon replacing both copies of $A$ by copies of $C$, and $|p^2-Q(C)^2|\le2\varepsilon$. Hence $|p-p^2|\le4\varepsilon+\rho_Y(n-2m)/4$. Let $n\to\infty$ and then $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ to obtain $p=p^2$. Therefore $p\in\{0,1\}$, proving [F6] and the stronger mod-null formulation claimed.

Assume AC. Fix $0<\gamma\le1$. Let $1\le d\le4$, $s>0$, $B>0$, and let $X_1,\ldots,X_m,Z$ be independent centered random vectors in $\mathbb R^d$, where $m\ge0$, $|X_j|\le B$ almost surely, and $Z\sim N_d(0,G)$. Suppose $S=Z+\sum_jX_j$ has covariance $sI_d$ and $G\ge\gamma sI_d$ in quadratic form order. There is an absolute constant $C_0\ge1$ such that, with $\tau=C_0B$, the logarithmic moment generating function
$$K(z)=\log\mathbb E e^{z\cdot S},\qquad K(0)=0,$$
has a single analytic branch on the complex Euclidean ball $\tau|z|<1$, and
$$|\partial_u\partial_v^2K(z)|\le\tau s|u||v|^2\qquad(u,v\in\mathbb R^d,\ \tau|z|<1).$$
Here $z\cdot S$ uses the complex bilinear dot product and $|z|^2=\sum_i|z_i|^2$. Every real exponential tilt $\mathbb P_h(d\omega)=e^{h\cdot S-K(h)}\mathbb P(d\omega)$ is defined, and its characteristic function satisfies
$$|\varphi_h(t)|:=|\mathbb E_h e^{it\cdot S}|\le e^{-\gamma s|t|^2/2}\qquad(t,h\in\mathbb R^d),$$
where $K(h)=\log\mathbb E e^{h\cdot S}$ for real $h$, also outside the analytic ball. Put $\kappa=\tau/\sqrt s$. For every fixed $a>0$ and integer $N\ge1$ there is a finite $C_{a,N,\gamma}$, uniform in $1\le d\le4$, such that, if $0<\kappa\le1$,
$$(2\pi)^{-d}\int_{|t|\ge a/\tau}|\varphi_h(t)|\,dt\le C_{a,N,\gamma}\kappa^Ns^{-d/2},$$
$$(2\pi)^{-d}\int_{|t|\ge a/\tau}|t\cdot v||\varphi_h(t)|\,dt\le C_{a,N,\gamma}\kappa^N|v|s^{-(d+1)/2}.$$
All assertions hold with the same $C_0$, $B$, $s$, and $\gamma$ for $AS$, where $A$ is any real $k\times d$ matrix with $1\le k\le d$ and $AA^T=I_k$. This includes every coordinate prefix, every orthogonal change of coordinates, and their compositions. In particular it covers the normalized joint sum and difference of two independent children by applying the assertion in their joint dimension, provided that dimension is at most four and the joint input satisfies the stated covariance assumptions.

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$, $m\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $\Sigma$ be a real symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then its law has Lebesgue density
$$f_{m,\Sigma}(x)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\det(\Sigma)^{-1/2} \exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(x-m)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-m)\right), \qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$

Assume AC. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then $$\Phi_X(t):=\mathbb E e^{it\cdot X}=\exp(it\cdot m-t^T\Sigma t/2)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R^d).$$ This transform uniquely determines the law, including singular Sigma.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$ and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$.

1. **Fundamental theorem, second part, in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

1. $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ with the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]) is a complete metric space
   ([[def-complete-metric-space]]).
2. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on
   $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ is complete.

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited and is not decoration.**
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] defines $\mathbb{R}^n$ and its three metrics only for
$n \ge 1$, because at $n = 0$ the metric $d_\infty$ would be a maximum over the
empty index set. Every statement about $\mathbb{R}^n$ in this library carries the
hypothesis, and this one does too.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Under any real tilt, write $S=Y+Z_h$, where the two terms are independent and $Z_h$ is Gaussian of covariance $G$ by [A1, F1]. Tonelli and translation of the Gaussian density show that $p_h(y)=\mathbb E_hq_G(y-Y-\mathbb E_hZ_h)$ is a probability density. It is strictly positive because its integrand is strictly positive, and is bounded by $(2\pi)^{-d/2}(\det G)^{-1/2}\le(2\pi\gamma s)^{-d/2}$. The Gaussian density and each of its first derivatives are bounded and continuous, so dominated convergence gives continuous first derivatives of this convolution. This proves the global assertions without a general vector inversion theorem.

Exponential moment differentiation identifies $K'(h)$ and $K''(h)$ with the tilted mean and covariance, respectively. To justify the differentiation, the bounded summands permit every polynomial factor, and the Gaussian square completion in [F1] makes all its polynomial moments integrable even after a slightly stronger real exponential; dominated convergence applies. For real $u,v,w$, polarization of the symmetric complex valued form $Q(v,w)=K_{uvw}(z)$ gives $|Q(v,w)|\le\tau s|u||v||w|$: apply $4Q(v,w)=Q(v+w,v+w)-Q(v-w,v-w)$ after replacing $v,w$ by $av,a^{-1}w$, and minimize the resulting bound $\tau s|u|(a^2|v|^2+a^{-2}|w|^2)/2$ over $a>0$. Integrating $K'''$ on the real segment from zero to $h$ therefore gives $\|K''(h)-sI\|\le\tau s|h|$. Hence $7sI/8\le D_h\le9sI/8$ for $\tau|h|\le1/8$.

We will also need its Fourier formula. Integrating the density of $N_d(0,G^{-1})$ against the character $e^{-it\cdot y}$ and using its characteristic function in [F2] gives $q_G(y)=(2\pi)^{-d}\int e^{-it\cdot y}e^{-t^TGt/2}\,dt$. The constants follow directly by inserting that density and multiplying by $(2\pi)^{-d/2}(\det G)^{-1/2}$. Insert this formula in step 1.1 and use absolute Fubini, dominated by the integrable Gaussian $e^{-t^TGt/2}$. Thus $p_h(y)=(2\pi)^{-d}\int e^{-it\cdot y}\varphi_h(t)\,dt$, and its derivative in direction $v$ is the same integral with factor $-i(t\cdot v)$. This differentiation is dominated because $|t\cdot v|e^{-\gamma s|t|^2/2}$ is integrable by [F1]. Centering or making an invertible linear change of coordinates gives the identical formulas for those transformed densities.

Fix this $h$ and center its law. Its cumulant is $K_h(z)=K(h+z)-K(h)-z\cdot\mu_h$. On $2\tau|z|<1$ the original analytic ball still contains $h+z$, since $\tau|h+z|<5/8$. Its third derivative is bounded by $\tau s|u||v|^2\le2\tau|u|v^TD_hv$. Whiten by $D_h^{-1/2}$, writing $W=D_h^{-1/2}(S-\mu_h)$ under this tilt and $L(a)=K_h(D_h^{-1/2}a)$. Then $L(0)=0$, $L'(0)=0$, $L''(0)=I$, and, with $\lambda=2\tau/\sqrt{\lambda_{\min}(D_h)}\le3\kappa$, it is analytic on $\lambda|a|<1$ and satisfies $|L_{uvv}(a)|\le\lambda|u||v|^2$. The centered Gaussian component of $W$ has covariance at least $(8\gamma/9)I$. Its covariance remains unchanged under every further real tilt; consequently all such tilted characteristic functions have modulus at most $e^{-(4\gamma/9)|t|^2}$.

Polarization as in step 1.2 and integration along $ta$, $0\le t\le1$, give $\|L''(a)-I\|\le\lambda|a|$, $|L'(a)-a|\le\lambda|a|^2/2$, and $|L(a)-|a|^2/2|\le\lambda|a|^3/6$ for real $a$ in the ball. For real $t$ the same last estimate along the complex segment $ist$ gives $L(it)=-|t|^2/2+R(t)$ with $|R(t)|\le\lambda|t|^3/6$: this uses only the real direction $t$ in each derivative and the factors $i^3$ from the segment parameter.

Put $b=D_h^{-1/2}x$, $r=|b|$. If $\lambda r\le1/16$, the map $T(a)=b-(L'(a)-a)$ sends the closed ball $|a|\le2r$ into itself by step 3.1, and its Lipschitz constant there is at most $2\lambda r\le1/8$. Starting at zero, its iterates are Cauchy since consecutive distances decrease geometrically; their limit exists by [F6], lies in the closed ball, and is a fixed point by continuity. Call it $a$. It satisfies $L'(a)=b$, $|a|\le2r$, and $|a-b|\le2\lambda r^2$. For $r=0$ take $a=0$. Thus no unproved global inverse assertion is needed for the saddlepoint.

Tilt $W$ further by the fixed parameter $a$. Its mean is $b$ and covariance $A=L''(a)$. Put $\epsilon=\lambda|a|\le2\lambda r$; step 3.1 gives $(1-\epsilon)I\le A\le(1+\epsilon)I$. Its cumulant centered at $b$ has third derivative bounded by a fixed multiple of $\lambda|u||v|^2$ on a complex ball of radius $c/\lambda$, because $a$ lies in the interior of the original analytic ball by step 4.1. Its characteristic modulus on all real frequencies is bounded by the same Gaussian $e^{-(4\gamma/9)|t|^2}$ from step 2.2. In what follows reduce the final constant $c_\gamma$ so that $\epsilon\le1/100$ and all these interior margins hold.

Let $\psi(t)$ be that last centered characteristic function and let $g_A=(2\pi)^{-d/2}(\det A)^{-1/2}$. For $|t|\le a_0/\lambda$, with a sufficiently small fixed $a_0>0$, the integrated third derivative estimate gives $\log\psi(t)=-t^TAt/2+E(t)$, $|E(t)|\le C\lambda|t|^3$, and $\operatorname{Re}\log\psi(t)\le-c|t|^2$. The elementary identity $e^z-e^w=(z-w)\int_0^1e^{(1-u)w+uz}\,du$ therefore gives $|\psi(t)-e^{-t^TAt/2}|\le C\lambda|t|^3e^{-c|t|^2}$ there. Its integral, and its integral after multiplication by $|t\cdot v|$, are bounded by $C\lambda$ and $C\lambda|v|$, respectively. To check the integrability explicitly, $|t|^je^{-c|t|^2/2}$ is bounded for each fixed $j$, by differentiation in $|t|$, and the remaining Gaussian is integrable by [F2]. Constants are uniform over $d\le4$ and $A$ in the displayed neighborhood of $I$.

Outside the ball of step 6.1, both $\psi$ and the Gaussian comparator have unweighted integral $O_\gamma(\lambda^2)$ and weighted integral $O_\gamma(\lambda^2|v|)$. Indeed their global bounds are $e^{-c_\gamma|t|^2}$; extract $e^{-c_\gamma a_0^2/(2\lambda^2)}$ and integrate the remaining Gaussian, also with $|t\cdot v|$. The extracted exponential is smaller than any prescribed fixed power of $\lambda$ because $z^je^{-cz^2}$ is bounded. This is the same direct Gaussian tail argument as [F1], and uses no smoothness condition on a lattice law. Combining this with step 6.1 and the Fourier formula of step 2.1 gives, for the density $f_a$ of the further tilted $W$, $|f_a(b)-g_A|\le C_\gamma\lambda,\qquad \sup_y|\partial_v f_a(y)|\le\left(\sqrt{2/\pi}\,g_A\sqrt{v^TA^{-1}v}+C_\gamma\lambda|v|\right).$ The Gaussian integral in the derivative bound is exact: transform by $A^{1/2}$ and rotate $A^{-1/2}v$ onto the first coordinate; the standard Gaussian first absolute moment is $\sqrt{2/\pi}$, from $\int_0^\infty t e^{-t^2/2}dt=1$.

The eigenvalue bounds in step 5.1 give $|\log\det A|\le C d\epsilon$ because $|\log(1+u)|\le2|u|$ for $|u|\le1/2$, by integrating $(1+u)^{-1}$. Thus $g_A$ is bounded above and away from zero, uniformly, and $\log(g_A/(2\pi)^{-d/2})=O(\lambda r)$. Step 7.1 and $|\log(1+u)|\le2|u|$ imply $f_a(b)>0$ and $\log\frac{f_a(b)}{(2\pi)^{-d/2}}=O_\gamma(\lambda(1+r)).$ We choose $c_\gamma$ small enough that all relative errors used here are at most $1/100$.

The exact exponential tilt density identity is $f(y)=f_a(y)e^{L(a)-a\cdot y}$, where $f$ is the original density of $W$. It initially follows almost everywhere from the definition of the tilt; both sides are continuous by step 1.1, so it holds everywhere, since a continuous nonzero difference would be nonzero on a ball of positive Lebesgue measure. Step 3.1 and $|a-b|\le2\lambda r^2$ give $L(a)-a\cdot b=-r^2/2+O(\lambda r^3).$ Indeed $|a|^2/2-a\cdot b=-|b|^2/2+|a-b|^2/2$, whose error is $O(\lambda^2r^4)=O(\lambda r^3)$ because $\lambda r$ is small. Combining this identity with step 8.1 proves $|\log(f(b)/q_I(b))|\le C_\gamma\lambda(1+r^3)$. The constant Jacobian for whitening cancels in the density ratio, and $\lambda\le3\kappa$ gives the stated moderate deviation bound.

Differentiate the exact identity in step 9.1 in direction $b$ at $y=b$, keeping $a$ fixed. It gives $\partial_b\log f(b)=(\partial_bf_a(b))/f_a(b)-a\cdot b$. By step 7.1, step 8.1, and $A=I+O(\lambda r)$, reduce $c_\gamma$ further so that $|\partial_bf_a(b)|/f_a(b)\le1.4r$; this is possible because its limiting coefficient is $\sqrt{2/\pi}<1$, the error is $O_\gamma(\lambda)$, and $A$ tends uniformly to $I$ as $\lambda r\to0$. Also step 4.1 gives $a\cdot b\ge r^2-2\lambda r^3\ge.99r^2$ after the same reduction. Hence $\partial_b\log f(b)\le1.4r-.99r^2\le-r^2/2$ for $r\ge7$. Whitening identifies this derivative with the derivative in direction $x$ in the Statement.

There are only finitely many smallness requirements above: bounds on $\kappa$, $\lambda r$, $\epsilon$, and fixed multiples depending only on $\gamma$ of $\lambda$. Since $\lambda\le3\kappa$, one sufficiently small positive $c_\gamma$ enforces all of them whenever $\kappa\le c_\gamma$ and $\kappa r\le c_\gamma$. All constants are uniform over dimensions one through four. Apply the same argument to a row isometry image using [F1]; its Gaussian component retains the same covariance lower bound, and every step applies in its own coordinates. This proves the remaining assertions.

there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that

Let $P$ be a probability kernel on an arbitrary measurable space $(X,\mathcal F)$, and let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. There is a countably generated sub-sigma-field $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ such that $f$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable and $P$, restricted to events in $\mathcal G$, is a probability kernel $P_{\mathcal G}$ on $(X,\mathcal G)$. For every $n\ge0$, $x\in X$, and $B\in\mathcal G$,
$$P_{\mathcal G}^n(x,B)=P^n(x,B).$$
If $\pi$ is invariant for $P$, then $\pi|_{\mathcal G}$ is invariant for $P_{\mathcal G}$.
Assume AC. Every standard-Borel space $(E,\mathcal S)$ is measurably isomorphic to a Borel subset of $[0,1]$, including $E=\varnothing$.
Every finite product of standard Borel spaces, with its finite product sigma-algebra, is standard Borel.

The measurable space $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$ with its usual
topology is standard Borel.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ and $g : X \to \overline{\mathbb{R}}$. Then $g$ is
$\sigma(f)$-measurable if and only if there is a Borel measurable function
$h : \mathbb{R} \to \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ such that

$$g = h \circ f.$$

Assume AC. Let $\lambda$ be a probability on $(E\times T,\mathcal S\otimes\mathcal T)$, where E and T are standard-Borel spaces, and let $\beta(B)=\lambda(E\times B)$ be its second marginal. There is a probability kernel $K:(T,\mathcal T)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ such that

$$\lambda(A\times B)=\int_B K(y,A)\,\beta(dy)\quad(A\in\mathcal S,\ B\in\mathcal T).$$

It is unique as a kernel outside a single measurable $\beta$-null set. For every nonnegative product-measurable $f:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$,

$$\int f(x,y)\,\lambda(d(x,y))=\int_T\left(\int_E f(x,y)K(y,dx)\right)\beta(dy).$$

In particular this applies to the joint law of random elements $(X,Y)$, with $\beta=P_Y$; the direction is the law of X given Y.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

Assume Choice. Let $X$ be a $K$-chain and let
$H:E^{\mathbb N_0}\to\mathbb R$ be bounded and product-measurable. Then
$$h(x):=\mathbb E_x[H(X_0,X_1,\ldots)]$$ is $\mathcal E$-measurable and, for every $n\ge0$, $$ \mathbb E[H(X_n,X_{n+1},\ldots)\mid\mathcal F_n]=h(X_n)\quad\text{a.s.} $$

Assume Choice. Let $(E_n,\mathcal E_n)_{n\ge0}$ be measurable spaces, let
$\mu_0$ be a probability measure on $E_0$, and, for each $n\ge0$, let $K_n$ be
a probability kernel from $E_0\times\cdots\times E_n$ to $E_{n+1}$. There is a
unique probability measure $P$ on
$$ \left(\prod_{n\ge0}E_n,\ \bigotimes_{n\ge0}\mathcal E_n\right) $$ whose finite-prefix laws are the prescribed iterated integrals $$ \mu_0(dx_0)K_0(x_0,dx_1)K_1(x_0,x_1,dx_2)\cdots K_{r-1}(x_0,\ldots,x_{r-1},dx_r). $$
In particular, if every $E_n=E$ and
$K_n(x_0,\ldots,x_n,A)=K(x_n,A)$, the coordinate process is a homogeneous
$K$-chain with initial law $\mu_0$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

The measurable space $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$ with its usual
topology is standard Borel.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. A countable product of Polish spaces is Polish, and every $G_\delta$ subspace of a Polish space is Polish.

A measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$ is **standard Borel** if there are a Polish space $P$ and a bijection $h:E\to P$ such that $A\in\mathcal E$ exactly when $h[A]$ is Borel in $P$. Thus the measurable structure is part of the datum; no particular compatible Polish topology on $E$ is selected.

Let $K$ be a probability kernel on a measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and let $\pi$ be a
probability measure on $(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). The
probability measure $\pi$ is **invariant** for $K$, and $\pi$ is a
**stationary distribution** of $K$, when

$$(\pi K)(A):=\int_E K(x,A)\,\pi(dx)=\pi(A)\qquad\text{for every }A\in\mathcal E .$$

The set function $\pi K$ is again a probability measure: for fixed $A$ the map
$x\mapsto K(x,A)$ is measurable and lies in $[0,1]$, so the integral exists in
$[0,1]$; for pairwise disjoint $A_n\in\mathcal E$ the identity
$K(x,\bigcup_nA_n)=\sum_nK(x,A_n)$ of the measure $K(x,\cdot)$ and the
monotone convergence theorem for nonnegative functions
([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]) give
$\sigma$-additivity of $\pi K$; and $K(x,E)=1$ for every $x$ gives
$(\pi K)(E)=1$. Thus $(\pi K)(A)=\pi(A)$ is an identity between two probability
measures evaluated at $A$.

A $K$-chain whose initial law is $\pi$ is called **stationary** when
$\pi K=\pi$. Stationarity of the process is a statement about all of its
finite-dimensional laws and is proved, not assumed, from $\pi K=\pi$; see
[[thm-invariant-initial-law-makes-the-chain-stationary]].

On a countable state space $E$ with sigma-algebra $2^E$ and transition matrix
$p(x,y)=K(x,\{y\})$ ([[def-transition-matrix-and-n-step-transition-probabilities]]),
a measure on $E$ is its weighted sum of Dirac masses at singletons
([[thm-measures-on-countable-discrete-spaces-are-weighted-dirac-sums]]), so
invariance is equivalent to the matrix identity

$$\pi(y)=\sum_{x\in E}\pi(x)\,p(x,y)\qquad\text{for every }y\in E .$$

The definition fixes no irreducibility, aperiodicity or uniqueness hypothesis,
and it selects no conditional-expectation versions; the display defines a
single measure $\pi K$ and asserts an identity for it. A transient, periodic or
reducible chain may have several invariant probability measures or none.

For a probability kernel $K$ on $(E,\mathcal E)$, let $I$ be the identity
kernel $I(x,A)=1_A(x)$ and define
$$ K^0:=I,\qquad K^{n+1}:=K^nK, $$ where composition is in chronological order: $$ K^{n+1}(x,A)=\int_E K(y,A)K^n(x,dy). $$
The identity map makes $I$ a probability kernel, including on a one-point
space. Induction using the published kernel-composition lemma shows that every
$K^n$ is a probability kernel. Associativity makes products of several copies
of $K$ unambiguous. No conditional-expectation version is selected and no form
of Choice is used.

derivations.claim: Define $\lambda=\tfrac12\pi+\tfrac12\sum_{k\ge0}2^{-k-1}\mu P^k.$ This is a probability by [F8], $\pi,\mu\ll\lambda$, and $\lambda P\ll\lambda$: if $\lambda(A)=0$, then $\pi(A)=0$ and $\mu P^k(A)=0$ for every $k$, which also makes $\lambda P(A)=0$. Thus $\lambda P^j\ll\lambda$ for every $j$. Apply [F2] to code the pair $(f,M)$ into one real observable, and apply [F1] to it. The resulting countably generated $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ is kernel-stable and contains both $f$ and $M$, since the coding has a Borel inverse.

Enumerate generators $A_j$ of $\mathcal G$ and set $c(x)=\sum_{j\ge1}2\cdot3^{-j}1_{A_j}(x)$, taking values in the closed Cantor subset $C$ of $[0,1]$. Its coordinate digits recover every $A_j$, so $\sigma(c)=\mathcal G$. The target $C$ is standard Borel by [F9]; no Borel-image assertion about $c(X)$ is needed. By [F3], write $f=\varphi_0\circ c$ and $M=m_0\circ c$ for Borel extended-real functions on $C$. Put $\lambda_c=c_*\lambda$, $\pi_c=c_*\pi$ and $\mu_c=c_*\mu$.

Push the probability $\lambda(dx)P(x,dy)$ to $(c(x),c(y))\in C^2$ and disintegrate by [F4], obtaining a Borel kernel $T:C\to C$. For each $B$ in a fixed countable generating algebra of $C$, kernel stability and [F3] factor $P(x,c^{-1}B)$ through $c(x)$. Its value is the conditional mean of $1_B(c(X_1))$ given $c(X_0)$ under this reference joint law. Hence $T(c(x),B)=P(x,c^{-1}B)$ for $\lambda$-almost every $x$. Intersect over the countable algebra and apply [F5] to obtain equality of these probability measures simultaneously on every Borel $B$, on one $\lambda$-full set. In particular $\lambda_cT=c_*(\lambda P)\ll\lambda_c$, and $\pi_cT=\pi_c$ because $\pi\ll\lambda$ and $\pi P=\pi$.

Iterating that kernel equality gives $T^n(c(x),\cdot)=c_*P^n(x,\cdot)$ for $\lambda$-almost every $x$, simultaneously for all $n\ge0$. At the induction step, $P(x,\cdot)$ avoids the preceding $\lambda$-null exceptional set for $\lambda$-almost every $x$, since $\lambda P\ll\lambda$; integration of a nonnegative Borel function of $c$ agrees under the two one-step measures by simple approximation and [F8]. The geometric hypothesis therefore implies $\|T^n(z,\cdot)-\pi_c\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le m_0(z)r^n$ for $\lambda_c$-almost every $z$, simultaneously for $n\ge1$.

On $C$ the total-variation supremum can be taken over its fixed countable generating algebra. Indeed, for any two probabilities, every Borel set is approximable in symmetric-difference measure by that algebra under their finite sum: the approximable sets form a sigma-field, using complements and first approximating a countable union by a finite union. Its probability difference is approximated too. Thus the supremum over the algebra equals the full supremum and is measurable as a function of the starting point. Let $B_0$ be the Borel set where all the bounds in step 4.1 hold and $\varphi_0,m_0$ are finite with $m_0\ge0$. It is $\lambda_c$-full by step 2.1 and the finiteness of $f,M$. Define $B_{j+1}=B_j\cap\{z:T(z,B_j)=1\}$ and $B=\bigcap_{j\ge0}B_j$. Absolute continuity $\lambda_cT\ll\lambda_c$ makes every $B_j$ full. If $z\in B$, continuity from above gives $T(z,B)=1$. Thus $B$ is nonempty, Borel, absorbing and $\lambda_c$-full; no Polish topology on $B$ is asserted.

Keep the factor space $S=C$, and define $T_*(z,\cdot)=T(z,\cdot)$ for $z\in B$ and $T_*(z,\cdot)=\pi_c$ otherwise. This is a Borel probability kernel. Set $\widehat\pi=\pi_c$ and $\widehat\mu=\mu_c$; both assign mass one to $B$, since they are absolutely continuous with respect to $\lambda_c$. Define $\varphi=\varphi_0$ and $\widehat M=m_0$ on $B$, and set both to zero on $C\setminus B$; these functions are finite measurable. Since $B$ is absorbing and $\pi_cT=\pi_c$, we have $\pi_cT_*=\pi_c$. For $z\in B$, the iterates of $T_*$ equal those of $T$, so the geometric bound holds by step 5.1. For $z\notin B$, $T_*^n(z,\cdot)=\pi_c$ for every $n\ge1$, so it holds with $\widehat M(z)=0$. Thus $T_*$ is the required kernel on the nonempty standard-Borel space $C$.

For an original chain with initial law $\mu$, every $X_k$ has law $\mu P^k\ll\lambda$. Thus step 3.1 and [F6], followed by conditioning on the coded past, show that $c(X_k)$ is a $T$-chain. Since every coded state belongs to $B$ almost surely, this is also a $T_*$-chain. Countably many time and algebra tests suffice; [F5] and bounded approximation extend them to every bounded Borel test. The code chain remains in $B$ almost surely and $f(X_k)=\varphi(c(X_k))$ simultaneously for every $k$. The same argument applies with initial law $\pi$. This proves the complete initial and stationary observation-path equalities and, by pushforward integration, every stated stationary moment identity.

The real observation-path space $\mathbb R^{\mathbb N_0}$ is standard Borel: its product topology is Polish by [F9], and its Borel sigma-algebra is the coordinate product sigma-algebra, since the real line has a countable base and finite-coordinate basic open sets form a countable base for this product. Disintegrate any specified joint law of this path and a standard-Borel auxiliary random element conditional on the path by [F4]. Evaluate that kernel at the actual original observation path and extend the original probability space by its kernel integral as in [F7]; explicitly, $P(d\omega)K((f(X_n(\omega)))_{n\ge0},dv)$ is countably additive by [F8] and has marginal $P$. Its observation/auxiliary joint law is exactly the specified law. This proves the lifting assertion without a conditional kernel on the original arbitrary state space.
