citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $P$ be a probability kernel with invariant probability $\pi$ on a measurable space $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$. Write $P^n(x,\cdot)$ for its $n$-step transition probability and use $\|\mu-\nu\|_{\mathrm{TV}}=\sup_{A\in\mathcal X}|\mu(A)-\nu(A)|$ for probability measures.

The chain is **geometrically ergodic** if there are a measurable finite function $M:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ and $r\in(0,1)$ such that
$$\|P^n(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le M(x)r^n\quad(x\in\mathsf X,\ n\ge1).$$

It is **uniformly ergodic** if this bound holds with $M$ bounded on $\mathsf X$. These are convergence-rate properties, not conclusions about a particular function's CLT or long-run variance. If a proof needs $\int M\,d\pi<\infty$, that integrability is an additional stated hypothesis unless a cited theorem establishes it.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ be a measurable space, let $P$ be a probability
kernel on it, meaning that $P(x,\cdot)$ is a probability measure for each $x$
and $x\mapsto P(x,A)$ is measurable for each $A\in\mathcal X$
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and let $\pi$ be a
probability measure, that is a countably additive measure of total mass one
([[def-probability-measure]]). The product sigma-algebra
$\mathcal X\otimes\mathcal X$ is generated by measurable rectangles
([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]). The joint
flow measure of $(\pi,P)$ is the probability measure $\Lambda_{\pi,P}$ on
$(\mathsf X\times\mathsf X,\mathcal X\otimes\mathcal X)$ given, for each
$C\in\mathcal X\otimes\mathcal X$, by

$$\Lambda_{\pi,P}(C):=\int_{\mathsf X}P(x,C_x)\,\pi(dx),\qquad C_x:=\{y\in\mathsf X:(x,y)\in C\}.$$

Existence, countable additivity, and the nonnegative iterated-integral identity
for this measure follow from
[[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]]. Let $\tau(x,y):=(y,x)$ be
the coordinate-swap map. It is measurable because the preimage of a measurable
rectangle $A\times B$ is $B\times A$ and such rectangles generate the product
sigma-algebra. Define the transpose measure by
$\Lambda_{\pi,P}^{\top}(C):=\Lambda_{\pi,P}(\tau^{-1}(C))$.

The kernel $P$ is **reversible with respect to $\pi$** when
$$\Lambda_{\pi,P}=\Lambda_{\pi,P}^{\top}.$$
This definition uses equality of measures and requires no density, standard
Borel assumption, or prior assumption that $\pi$ is invariant.

Assume AC. Let $(X_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a stationary time-homogeneous Markov chain
with probability kernel $P$, invariant law $\pi$, and natural filtration
$\mathcal F_k=\sigma(X_0,\ldots,X_k)$. Let $g\in L^2(\pi)$ ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]) and fix a finite real measurable representative, also denoted by $g$. Define
$Pg(x)=\int g(y)P(x,dy)$ and $P(g^2)(x)=\int g(y)^2P(x,dy)$ on the
$\pi$-full measurable set where the respective integrals are finite, and set
these functions to zero on the exceptional set. Then, for each $k\ge0$,
$$\mathbb E[g(X_{k+1})\mid\mathcal F_k]=Pg(X_k).$$
$$\mathbb E[g(X_{k+1})^2\mid\mathcal F_k]=P(g^2)(X_k)\quad\text{a.s.}$$
Consequently, if $D_{k+1}=g(X_{k+1})-Pg(X_k)$, then $(D_{k+1})$ is a square-integrable martingale-difference sequence and
$$\mathbb E[D_{k+1}^2\mid\mathcal F_k]=P(g^2)(X_k)-(Pg(X_k))^2\quad\text{a.s.}$$

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Assume Choice. Let $X$ be a $K$-chain and let
$H:E^{\mathbb N_0}\to\mathbb R$ be bounded and product-measurable. Then
$$h(x):=\mathbb E_x[H(X_0,X_1,\ldots)]$$ is $\mathcal E$-measurable and, for every $n\ge0$, $$ \mathbb E[H(X_n,X_{n+1},\ldots)\mid\mathcal F_n]=h(X_n)\quad\text{a.s.} $$

For $m,n\ge0$,
$$K^{m+n}=K^mK^n.$$ Assume Choice and let $X$ be a Markov chain with kernel $K$ relative to $(\mathcal F_n)$. For every bounded measurable real $f$, $$ \mathbb E[f(X_{m+n})\mid\mathcal F_m]=K^nf(X_m)\quad\text{a.s.} $$ Equivalently, for $A\in\mathcal E$, $$ \mathbb P(X_{m+n}\in A\mid\mathcal F_m)=K^n(X_m,A)\quad\text{a.s.} $$
Both assertions include $m=0$ and $n=0$.

Assume AC for existence. If $\mathcal H\subseteq\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ and $X\in L^1(P)$, then $E[E[X\mid\mathcal G]\mid\mathcal H]=E[X\mid\mathcal H]$ and $E[E[X\mid\mathcal H]\mid\mathcal G]=E[X\mid\mathcal H]$ almost surely. Also, if a version of $E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ is $\mathcal H$-measurable, it is a version of $E[X\mid\mathcal H]$.

Assume AC for existence. If $X\in L^1(P)$ and $Z$ is bounded real $\mathcal G$-measurable, then $E[ZX\mid\mathcal G]=ZE[X\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. The identity also holds for finite real $\mathcal G$-measurable $Z$ whenever $ZX$ and $ZE[X\mid\mathcal G]$ are integrable. In fact $X,ZX\in L^1$ imply the latter integrability.

Assume AC. If $\phi:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is finite convex and both $X$ and $\phi(X)$ are integrable, then $\phi(E[X\mid\mathcal G])\le E[\phi(X)\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely; the left side is measurable and integrable.

Let $Y=(Y_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a process on a probability space whose finite-dimensional laws are invariant under common nonnegative time shifts; call this strict stationarity. For $j\ge0$, set $\mathcal F_j^-:=\sigma(Y_0,\ldots,Y_j)$ and $\mathcal F_j^+:=\sigma(Y_j,Y_{j+1},\ldots)$. For $n\ge1$, define the **strong-mixing coefficient** by
$$\alpha_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{\substack{A\in\mathcal F_j^-\\B\in\mathcal F_{j+n}^+}}|\mathbb P(A\cap B)-\mathbb P(A)\mathbb P(B)|.$$

Define the **uniform-mixing coefficient** by
$$\phi_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{\substack{A\in\mathcal F_j^-\\\mathbb P(A)>0}}\ \sup_{B\in\mathcal F_{j+n}^+}|\mathbb P(B\mid A)-\mathbb P(B)|.$$

For square-integrable real random variables $U,V$ with positive variances, write
$$\operatorname{Corr}(U,V):=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(U,V)}{\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(U)\operatorname{Var}(V)}}.$$
For each $n\ge1$, let $\mathcal C_n$ consist of the triples $(j,U,V)$ such that $j\ge0$, $U,V$ are real and square-integrable, $U$ and $V$ are measurable with respect to $\mathcal F_j^-$ and $\mathcal F_{j+n}^+$ respectively, and both have positive variance. Define the **maximal-correlation coefficient** by
$$\rho_Y(n):=\sup\Bigl(\{0\}\cup\{|\operatorname{Corr}(U,V)|:(j,U,V)\in\mathcal C_n\}\Bigr),$$
where square-integrability is in the sense of [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]. Thus $\rho_Y(n)=0$ when there is no admissible pair, as for a constant process. The process is called strongly mixing, uniformly mixing, or rho-mixing, respectively, when the corresponding coefficient tends to zero. These coefficients are distinct conditions; no implication between them is included in this definition.

derivations.claim: On real $L^2(\pi)$ put $Tf=Pf$ and $H=\{f:\pi(f)=0\}$. By [F3], conditional Jensen and stationarity give $\|Tf\|_2^2\le\pi(f^2)$ and $\pi(Tf)=\pi(f)$. These identities also show that the operator is well defined on almost-everywhere classes. Thus $T$ is a contraction preserving $H$, and $T1=1$. For bounded $f,g$, [F2] gives $\langle f,Tg\rangle=\langle Tf,g\rangle$ by integrating $f(x)g(y)$ against the flow measure. Bounded truncation converges in $L^2$ by [F5], so contraction and [F4] extend this symmetry to all $L^2$ functions. Iterated kernel integration agrees with $T^k$; for bounded functions this is [F7], and contraction extends the identity to $L^2$ classes.

For probability measures $\mu,
u$ and $0\le a\le1$, approximate $a$ uniformly by $2^{-q}\sum_{i=1}^{2^q}1_{\{a\ge i2^{-q}\}}$. Each indicator integral difference is bounded by the event-supremum TV distance, so $|\mu(a)-
u(a)|\le\|\mu-
u\|_{\mathrm{TV}}$ on taking limits. Applying this to $a=(h+\|h\|_\infty)/(2\|h\|_\infty)$ for nonzero bounded measurable $h$, and separating $h=0$, gives $|P^kh(x)-\pi(h)|\le2\|h\|_\infty M(x)r^k$.

Put $C_m=\{M\le m\}$ for positive integers $m$. If bounded $h$ vanishes off $C_m$ and $f=h-\pi(h)$, symmetry and invariance give $\|T^kf\|_2^2=\langle f,T^{2k}f\rangle=\int h(x)(P^{2k}h(x)-\pi(h))\,\pi(dx)$ for $k\ge1$. Step 1.2 therefore gives $0\le\|T^kf\|_2^2\le2m\|h\|_\infty^2r^{2k}$. Write $A=\sqrt{2m}\|h\|_\infty<\infty$, so $\|T^kf\|_2\le Ar^k$. No integral of $M$ over the whole state space has been used.

For $u\in H$ and $a\ge1$, symmetry and [F4] give $\|T^au\|_2^2=\langle u,T^{2a}u\rangle\le\|u\|_2\|T^{2a}u\|_2$. Repeating with $a=1,2,4,\ldots,2^{\ell-1}$ yields $\|Tu\|_2\le\|u\|_2^{1-2^{-\ell}}\|T^{2^\ell}u\|_2^{2^{-\ell}}$. For the $f$ in step 2.1, if $f=0$ the bound $\|Tf\|_2\le r\|f\|_2$ is immediate; otherwise $A>0$ and the last display is at most $rA^{2^{-\ell}}\|f\|_2^{1-2^{-\ell}}$, tending to $r\|f\|_2$. Hence that bound holds for every such $f$.

For $u\in H$ choose a finite measurable representative and put $h_m=1_{C_m}\max(-m,\min(u,m))$. Finiteness of $M$ gives $h_m\to u$ almost everywhere and $|h_m-u|\le|u|$, so [F5] gives $h_m\to u$ in $L^2$. By [F4], $\pi(h_m)\to0$, and therefore $h_m-\pi(h_m)\to u$ in $L^2$. Applying step 3.1 to these centered functions and taking limits through the contraction $T$ gives $\|Tu\|_2\le r\|u\|_2$. Iteration on $H$ proves $\|T^nu\|_2\le r^n\|u\|_2$ for all $n\ge1$. This also covers $H=\{0\}$.

Fix $j\ge0$ and bounded centered real $U,V$ measurable respectively for $\mathcal F_j$ and $\sigma(X_{j+n},X_{j+n+1},\ldots)$. By [F6] there is bounded measurable $g$ such that $E[V\mid\mathcal F_{j+n}]=g(X_{j+n})$. Stationarity and [F9] give $\pi(g)=0$ and $\|g\|_2\le\|V\|_2$. The tower property and [F7] give $E[V\mid\mathcal F_j]=P^ng(X_j)$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $Y=(Y_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a process on a probability space whose finite-dimensional laws are invariant under common nonnegative time shifts; call this strict stationarity. For $j\ge0$, set $\mathcal F_j^-:=\sigma(Y_0,\ldots,Y_j)$ and $\mathcal F_j^+:=\sigma(Y_j,Y_{j+1},\ldots)$. For $n\ge1$, define the **strong-mixing coefficient** by
$$\alpha_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{\substack{A\in\mathcal F_j^-\\B\in\mathcal F_{j+n}^+}}|\mathbb P(A\cap B)-\mathbb P(A)\mathbb P(B)|.$$

Define the **uniform-mixing coefficient** by
$$\phi_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{\substack{A\in\mathcal F_j^-\\\mathbb P(A)>0}}\ \sup_{B\in\mathcal F_{j+n}^+}|\mathbb P(B\mid A)-\mathbb P(B)|.$$

For square-integrable real random variables $U,V$ with positive variances, write
$$\operatorname{Corr}(U,V):=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(U,V)}{\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(U)\operatorname{Var}(V)}}.$$
For each $n\ge1$, let $\mathcal C_n$ consist of the triples $(j,U,V)$ such that $j\ge0$, $U,V$ are real and square-integrable, $U$ and $V$ are measurable with respect to $\mathcal F_j^-$ and $\mathcal F_{j+n}^+$ respectively, and both have positive variance. Define the **maximal-correlation coefficient** by
$$\rho_Y(n):=\sup\Bigl(\{0\}\cup\{|\operatorname{Corr}(U,V)|:(j,U,V)\in\mathcal C_n\}\Bigr),$$
where square-integrability is in the sense of [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]. Thus $\rho_Y(n)=0$ when there is no admissible pair, as for a constant process. The process is called strongly mixing, uniformly mixing, or rho-mixing, respectively, when the corresponding coefficient tends to zero. These coefficients are distinct conditions; no implication between them is included in this definition.

Assume AC. Let $(Y_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a strictly stationary real sequence, with one-sided coefficients $\rho_Y(n)$ from [[def-mixing-coefficients-for-stationary-markov-chain]]. There is a shift-invariant probability $Q$ on the coordinate sigma-algebra of $\mathbb R^{\mathbb Z}$ such that its coordinate process $(X_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z}$ restricted to $k\ge0$ has the law of $Y$. The invertible left shift $T(x)_i=x_{i+1}$ preserves $Q$. Put $\mathcal F_k=\sigma(X_i:i\le k)$ and $\mathcal G_k=\sigma(X_i:i\ge k)$. For every integer $k$, every $n\ge1$, and real square-integrable $U$ measurable in $\mathcal F_k$ and $V$ measurable in $\mathcal G_{k+n}$,
$$|\operatorname{Cov}_Q(U,V)|\le\rho_Y(n)\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}_Q(U)\operatorname{Var}_Q(V)}.$$
If $\rho_Y(n)\to0$, then $T$ is ergodic: every event $A$ with $Q(A\mathbin\triangle T^{-1}A)=0$ has $Q(A)\in\{0,1\}$.

Assume AC. Real $L^2(\Omega,\mathcal G,P|_{\mathcal G})$ embeds isometrically as a closed subspace of real $L^2(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$. For $X\in L^2(P)$, $U=E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ is its orthogonal projection onto this subspace. It uniquely minimizes $E[(X-Z)^2]$ over $Z\in L^2(\mathcal G)$ as an almost-sure class.

Assume AC for existence. For real $X,Y\in L^1(P)$ and $a,b\in\mathbb R$, $E[aX+bY\mid\mathcal G]=aE[X\mid\mathcal G]+bE[Y\mid\mathcal G]$. Conditional expectation is positive, preserves order and constants, satisfies $E(E[X\mid\mathcal G])=EX$, and $|E[X\mid\mathcal G]|\le E[|X|\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. Also $X<Y$ almost surely implies $E[X\mid\mathcal G]<E[Y\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely.

Assume AC. Let $T$ be an invertible bimeasurable probability-preserving transformation on $(\Omega,\mathcal A,Q)$ such that $Q(A\mathbin\triangle T^{-1}A)=0$ implies $Q(A)\in\{0,1\}$. Let $X_0\in L^2(Q)$ be real and centered, put $X_k=X_0\circ T^k$ for $k\in\mathbb Z$, and put $\mathcal F_k=\sigma(X_i:i\le k)$. Suppose
$$\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\|\mathbb E[X_j\mid\mathcal F_0]\|_2<\infty.$$
Then the $L^2$ series $H_0=\sum_{j\ge1}\mathbb E[X_j\mid\mathcal F_0]$ converges. Put $H_k=H_0\circ T^k$ and $D_k=X_k+H_k-H_{k-1}$. The $D_k$ are stationary square-integrable martingale differences for $\mathcal F_k$, and for $n\ge1$,
$$S_n:=\sum_{k=1}^nX_k=\sum_{k=1}^nD_k+H_0-H_n,\qquad \|H_0-H_n\|_2\le2\|H_0\|_2.$$
With $\tau^2=\mathbb E[D_1^2]$,
$$S_n/\sqrt n\Rightarrow N(0,\tau^2),$$
including $\tau^2=0$. If additionally $\sum_{j\ge1}|\operatorname{Cov}(X_0,X_j)|<\infty$, then
$$\tau^2=\mathbb E[X_0^2]+2\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\operatorname{Cov}(X_0,X_j).$$

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

All second moments of the coordinates agree with those of $Y$.

Put $W_j=\mathbb E[X_j\mid\mathcal F_0]$ for $j\ge1$. By [F3], $W_j$ is centered and square-integrable and $\mathbb E[W_jX_j]=\mathbb E[W_j^2]$. Since $X$ and $Y$ have the same nonnegative-index law, the series is exactly $\sigma_Y^2$ and the finite sums have the original laws. Therefore the asserted nondegenerate and degenerate limits both hold for $Y$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. A real process
$B=(B_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **standard Brownian motion** if:

1. $B_0=0$ almost surely;
2. for every finite list $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_n$, the increments
   $B_{t_j}-B_{t_{j-1}}$ are mutually independent and have laws
   $N(0,t_j-t_{j-1})$; and
3. there is one measurable event $A$ with $P(A)=1$ such that
   $t\mapsto B_t(\omega)$ is continuous on $[0,\infty)$ for every
   $\omega\in A$.

By
[[lem-brownian-gaussian-covariance-is-equivalent-to-independent-stationary-normal-increments]],
the first two clauses are equivalent to saying that $B$ is a centered Gaussian
process with covariance $\min(s,t)$. Clause 3 is additional: it cannot be
recovered from finite-dimensional distributions alone.

No filtration is part of this definition. In particular, no completed or
right-continuous filtration and no Markov or martingale assertion is silently
imposed. Modifications and indistinguishability retain the distinct meanings in
[[def-law-modification-and-indistinguishability-of-processes]]. The cases
$n=0$, $t_1=0$, and zero-length increments are respectively vacuous or already
covered by $B_0=0$; the increment list itself is strictly increasing.

Choice is declared because the normal-law and Gaussian/increment-equivalence
interfaces construct and identify normal laws under AC. The continuity clause
selects no path and makes no additional use of choice.

Assume AC. For every positive integer $r$ there is a finite constant $C_r$, depending only on $r$, such that for every integer $n\ge1$, independent standard-normal variables $U_1,\ldots,U_n$, and real symmetric $n\times n$ matrix $A$,
$$E\left|U^TAU-\operatorname{tr}A\right|^{2r}\le C_r\left(\sum_{i,k=1}^n A_{ik}^2\right)^r.$$
In particular $E(U^TAU)=\operatorname{tr}A$. The matrix may be singular or indefinite.

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

Let $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be measurable sets in a measure space. If the nonnegative extended sum satisfies

$$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k)<+\infty,$$

then

$$\mu\left(\limsup_{k\to\infty}E_k\right)=0.$$

No independence hypothesis and no finiteness hypothesis on the whole space are required.

Let $\varphi(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}$ and
$\overline\Phi(x)=\int_x^\infty\varphi(y)\,dy$ for $x\in\mathbb R$. Then for
every $x>0$
$$\frac{x\,\varphi(x)}{1+x^2}\ \le\ \overline\Phi(x)\ \le\ \frac{\varphi(x)}{x},$$
and consequently, for every $x>1$,
$$\Bigl(\frac1x-\frac1{x^3}\Bigr)\varphi(x)\ \le\ \overline\Phi(x)\ \le\ \frac{\varphi(x)}{x}.$$
Both bounds are sharp as $x\to\infty$ in the sense that the ratio of each side
to $\overline\Phi(x)$ tends to $1$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $V$ be a normed space. For all $x,y\in V$,
$$\bigl|\|x\|-\|y\|\bigr|\le \|x-y\|.$$
In particular, the norm map is $1$-Lipschitz for the norm metric.

**Inputs:** Real outputs $y_1,\ldots,y_n$, an integer $n\ge2$, and an integer batch size $b$ with $1\le b<n$. For an MCMC run, $y_i=f(X_i)$ for the chosen real-valued observable $f$.

**Outputs:** The sample mean $\bar y_n$, the overlapping-batch-means estimate $\widehat{\sigma}^2_{\mathrm{OBM}}$, and its estimated Monte Carlo standard error.

1. Compute the sample mean
$$\bar y_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n y_i.$$

2. For each starting index $j=1,\ldots,n-b+1$, compute the overlapping batch mean
$$\bar y_j(b)=\frac1b\sum_{i=j}^{j+b-1}y_i.$$

3. Return the overlapping-batch-means variance estimate
$$\widehat{\sigma}^2_{\mathrm{OBM}}=\frac{nb}{(n-b)(n-b+1)}\sum_{j=1}^{n-b+1}\bigl(\bar y_j(b)-\bar y_n\bigr)^2.$$

4. Return the estimated Monte Carlo standard error
$$\widehat{\operatorname{MCSE}}(\bar y_n)=\sqrt{\widehat{\sigma}^2_{\mathrm{OBM}}/n}.$$

All sums are finite, the denominator is positive because $b<n$, and the variance estimate is nonnegative. The procedure always returns a number for the stated finite input. It does not by itself assert a CLT or consistency; consistency requires the hypotheses of the overlapping-batch-means theorem.

$$\operatorname{Corr}(U,V):=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(U,V)}{\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(U)\operatorname{Var}(V)}}.$$
For each $n\ge1$, let $\mathcal C_n$ consist of the triples $(j,U,V)$ such that $j\ge0$, $U,V$ are real and square-integrable, $U$ and $V$ are measurable with respect to $\mathcal F_j^-$ and $\mathcal F_{j+n}^+$ respectively, and both have positive variance. Define the **maximal-correlation coefficient** by
$$\rho_Y(n):=\sup\Bigl(\{0\}\cup\{|\operatorname{Corr}(U,V)|:(j,U,V)\in\mathcal C_n\}\Bigr),$$
where square-integrability is in the sense of [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]. Thus $\rho_Y(n)=0$ when there is no admissible pair, as for a constant process. The process is called strongly mixing, uniformly mixing, or rho-mixing, respectively, when the corresponding coefficient tends to zero. These coefficients are distinct conditions; no implication between them is included in this definition.

Let $\mathcal A,\mathcal B$ be sub-sigma-algebras of a probability space and put
$$a=\sup_{A\in\mathcal A,\,B\in\mathcal B}|\mathbb P(A\cap B)-\mathbb P(A)\mathbb P(B)|.$$
For any real random variable $U$, define its absolute tail quantile by
$$Q_U(u)=\inf\{t\ge0:\mathbb P(|U|>t)\le u\},\qquad 0<u<1.$$
This is a nonnegative nonincreasing Borel function and, for every nonnegative Borel function $\psi$,
$$\int_0^1\psi(Q_U(u))\,du=\mathbb E\psi(|U|).$$
If $U,V$ are square-integrable real random variables measurable respectively with respect to $\mathcal A,\mathcal B$, then
$$|\operatorname{Cov}(U,V)|\le4\int_0^a Q_U(u)Q_V(u)\,du.$$
In particular, if $|U|\le A$ and $|V|\le B$ almost surely, the right-hand side is at most $4ABa$. For complex $U,V$ with these bounds and the same measurability,
$$|\mathbb E(UV)-\mathbb EU\mathbb EV|\le16ABa.$$
For two collections of observations separated by $n$ time steps in a process $Y$, the coefficient $a$ of their sigma-algebras is at most $\alpha_Y(n)$ as defined in [[def-mixing-coefficients-for-stationary-markov-chain]]. An integral whose upper endpoint is zero is zero.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

If $\mathbb EX=0$ and $\mathbb EX^2=\sigma^2<\infty$, then $\varphi_X(t)=1-\sigma^2t^2/2+o(t^2)$ as $t\to0$. No third moment or choice axiom is assumed. The same scalar estimates give $0\le1-\cos u\le u^2/2$ for every real u. More precisely, for $r(u)=e^{iu}-1-iu+u^2/2$, $$|r(u)|\le \min(|u|^3/3,4u^2),\qquad |e^{iu}-1-iu|\le u^2.$$

Assume AC. If $X$ has law $N(m,\sigma^2)$ with $\sigma\ge0$, then $\varphi_X(t)=\exp(imt-\sigma^2t^2/2)$ for every real $t$. Moreover $\mathbb EX=m$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\sigma^2$, including $\sigma=0$.

Assume AC. For Borel probability laws $\mu_n$ and a specified Borel probability law $\mu$ on $\mathbb R$,
$$\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\varphi_{\mu_n}(t)\to\varphi_\mu(t)\ \text{for every }t\in\mathbb R.$$

derivations.claim: Put $\gamma_r=\operatorname{Cov}(Z_0,Z_r)$. By [F1]–[F2], $|\gamma_r|\le4B^2\alpha_Z(r)$ for $r\ge1$, so $D_Z<\infty$. Expanding the square of a sum indexed by a finite subset $I$ gives its diagonal terms $|I|\gamma_0$ and off-diagonal terms $2\gamma_{j-i}$ for pairs $i<j$ in $I$. For each fixed positive lag there are at most $|I|$ such pairs. Thus the asserted bound $\mathbb E(\sum_{i\in I}Z_i)^2\le D_Z|I|$ holds, also for $I=\varnothing$. For a consecutive block, the same expansion gives $\operatorname{Var}(T_n)/n=\gamma_0+2\sum_{r=1}^{n-1}(1-r/n)\gamma_r$. The summable majorant $2|\gamma_r|$ and [F4] imply convergence to the stated $\sigma_Z^2$, which is nonnegative as a limit of variances.

Extend the coefficient convention by $\alpha_Z(0)=1$. It is nonincreasing: increasing the separation restricts the future sigma-algebra in [F1]. For ordered indices $i\le j\le k\le l$, write $a=j-i$ and $c=l-k$. If $a>0$, centering of $Z_i$ and [F2] applied to $Z_i$ and $Z_jZ_kZ_l$ give $|\mathbb E Z_iZ_jZ_kZ_l|\le4B^4\alpha_Z(a)$; if $a=0$, the trivial bound $B^4$ suffices. Splitting off the centered last factor gives the same bound with $c$. Therefore $|\mathbb E Z_iZ_jZ_kZ_l|\le4B^4\alpha_Z(\max(a,c))$. There are at most $24$ orderings, at most $p$ choices each for the first index and the middle gap, and $2r+1$ pairs $(a,c)$ with maximum $r$. Hence $\mathbb ET_p^4\le96B^4p^2\sum_{r=0}^p(2r+1)\alpha_Z(r)=o(p^3).$ To justify the last limit, for each fixed $R$, $p^{-1}\sum_{r\le R}r\alpha_Z(r)\to0$, whereas $p^{-1}\sum_{R<r\le p}r\alpha_Z(r)\le\sum_{r>R}\alpha_Z(r)\to0$ as $R\to\infty$; the unweighted part divided by $p$ also tends to zero. Repeated indices are included by the convention at zero.

Set $\varepsilon_p=\mathbb ET_p^4/p^3$ and $\eta_n=\sup_{p\ge\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor}\varepsilon_p$. By step 1.2, $\eta_n\to0$. For sufficiently large $n$, define $h_n=\min(n^{1/8},\eta_n^{-1/4})$, interpreting the second entry as $+\infty$ if $\eta_n=0$, and ignore the finitely many earlier $n$. Then $h_n\to\infty$, $h_n=o(n^{1/4})$, and $h_n^2\eta_n\to0$. Put $p_n=\lceil\sqrt n h_n\rceil$, $q_n=\lfloor\sqrt n/h_n\rfloor$, and $k_n=\lfloor n/(p_n+q_n)\rfloor$. Thus $p_n,q_n\to\infty$, $p_n/n\to0$, $q_n/p_n\to0$, and $k_np_n/n\to1$. Retain $k_n$ consecutive blocks of length $p_n$, separated by discarded blocks of length $q_n$, and discard the final remainder. Their discarded index set $I_n$ has cardinality at most $k_nq_n+p_n+q_n=o(n)$. Step 1.1 gives $\|n^{-1/2}\sum_{i\in I_n}Z_i\|_2^2\le D_Z|I_n|/n\to0$, controlling all gaps together without asserting their independence.

Summability and monotonicity imply $r\alpha_Z(r)\to0$, since $\lfloor r/2\rfloor\alpha_Z(r)\le\sum_{s=\lfloor r/2\rfloor}^r\alpha_Z(s)$. For large $n$, $n/p_n\le\sqrt n/h_n\le2q_n$, so $k_n\alpha_Z(q_n)\le2q_n\alpha_Z(q_n)\to0$. Let $B_{n,j}$ denote the sum in retained block $j$. At a fixed real frequency $t$, put $U_j=e^{itB_{n,j}/\sqrt n}$. Both each factor and every partial product have modulus at most one. The partial product through block $j$ is measurable before the gap preceding block $j+1$, so [F2] bounds the discrepancy in factoring its expectation from $U_{j+1}$ by $16\alpha_Z(q_n)$. Telescoping these factorizations gives $\left|\mathbb E e^{it\sum_{j=1}^{k_n}B_{n,j}/\sqrt n}-\prod_{j=1}^{k_n}\mathbb E e^{itB_{n,j}/\sqrt n}\right|\le16(k_n-1)\alpha_Z(q_n)\longrightarrow0.$ This compares characteristic functions only and requires no independent copies or coupling construction.

Write $W_{n,j}=B_{n,j}/\sqrt n$. These variables are centered and each has the law of $T_{p_n}/\sqrt n$ by stationarity. Steps 1.1 and 2.1 imply $\sum_{j=1}^{k_n}\mathbb EW_{n,j}^2=(k_np_n/n)\operatorname{Var}(T_{p_n})/p_n\to\sigma_Z^2$. Also $\sum_{j=1}^{k_n}\mathbb EW_{n,j}^4=\frac{k_n\mathbb ET_{p_n}^4}{n^2}\le\frac{p_n^2}{n}\varepsilon_{p_n}\longrightarrow0,$ because $p_n^2/n=O(h_n^2)$ and $\varepsilon_{p_n}\le\eta_n$. For every $\delta>0$, the Lindeberg sum of these block marginals is at most $\delta^{-2}\sum_j\mathbb EW_{n,j}^4\to0$. Applying [F5] first to $|W|,W^2$ and then the finite-sum Cauchy–Schwarz inequality yields $\sum_j\mathbb E|W_{n,j}|^3\le(\sum_j\mathbb EW_{n,j}^2)^{1/2}(\sum_j\mathbb EW_{n,j}^4)^{1/2}\to0$. Finally $\max_j(\mathbb EW_{n,j}^2)^2\le\sum_j\mathbb EW_{n,j}^4\to0$. No uniform-integrability hypothesis or deterministic block bound tending to zero has been assumed.

For fixed $t$, [F6] gives $\mathbb Ee^{itW_{n,j}}=1-a_{n,j}+r_{n,j}$, where $a_{n,j}=t^2\mathbb EW_{n,j}^2/2\ge0$ and $\sum_j|r_{n,j}|\le |t|^3\sum_j\mathbb E|W_{n,j}|^3/3\to0$. Step 3.2 gives $\sum_ja_{n,j}\to t^2\sigma_Z^2/2$ and $\sum_ja_{n,j}^2\le(\max_ja_{n,j})\sum_ja_{n,j}\to0$. The elementary real Taylor bound $|1-a-e^{-a}|\le a^2/2$ for $a\ge0$ follows by integrating the second derivative $e^{-a}\le1$ twice. Since both $|\mathbb Ee^{itW_{n,j}}|$ and $e^{-a_{n,j}}$ are at most one, the product telescoping inequality now gives $\left|\prod_j\mathbb Ee^{itW_{n,j}}-e^{-\sum_ja_{n,j}}\right|\le\sum_j|r_{n,j}|+\frac12\sum_ja_{n,j}^2\longrightarrow0.$ Thus the product characteristic function tends to $e^{-t^2\sigma_Z^2/2}$.

The discarded normalized sum in step 2.1 tends to zero in $L^2$ and hence in $L^1$ by [F5]. The elementary bound $|e^{ix}-e^{iy}|\le|x-y|$, obtained by integrating the derivative of $e^{iu}$ along the real interval, makes its effect on each characteristic function tend to zero. Combine steps 3.1 and 4.1: $\mathbb Ee^{itT_n/\sqrt n}\to e^{-t^2\sigma_Z^2/2}$ for every real $t$. Under [A1], [F7] identifies this with the characteristic function of $N(0,\sigma_Z^2)$, and [F8] gives the asserted weak convergence. This remains valid for $\sigma_Z^2=0$; all finite-moment and discarded-set assertions were already proved in step 1.1.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $\mathcal A,\mathcal B$ be sub-sigma-algebras of a probability space and put
$$a=\sup_{A\in\mathcal A,\,B\in\mathcal B}|\mathbb P(A\cap B)-\mathbb P(A)\mathbb P(B)|.$$
For any real random variable $U$, define its absolute tail quantile by
$$Q_U(u)=\inf\{t\ge0:\mathbb P(|U|>t)\le u\},\qquad 0<u<1.$$
This is a nonnegative nonincreasing Borel function and, for every nonnegative Borel function $\psi$,
$$\int_0^1\psi(Q_U(u))\,du=\mathbb E\psi(|U|).$$
If $U,V$ are square-integrable real random variables measurable respectively with respect to $\mathcal A,\mathcal B$, then
$$|\operatorname{Cov}(U,V)|\le4\int_0^a Q_U(u)Q_V(u)\,du.$$
In particular, if $|U|\le A$ and $|V|\le B$ almost surely, the right-hand side is at most $4ABa$. For complex $U,V$ with these bounds and the same measurability,
$$|\mathbb E(UV)-\mathbb EU\mathbb EV|\le16ABa.$$
For two collections of observations separated by $n$ time steps in a process $Y$, the coefficient $a$ of their sigma-algebras is at most $\alpha_Y(n)$ as defined in [[def-mixing-coefficients-for-stationary-markov-chain]]. An integral whose upper endpoint is zero is zero.

Let $Y=(Y_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a process on a probability space whose finite-dimensional laws are invariant under common nonnegative time shifts; call this strict stationarity. For $j\ge0$, set $\mathcal F_j^-:=\sigma(Y_0,\ldots,Y_j)$ and $\mathcal F_j^+:=\sigma(Y_j,Y_{j+1},\ldots)$. For $n\ge1$, define the **strong-mixing coefficient** by
$$\alpha_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{\substack{A\in\mathcal F_j^-\\B\in\mathcal F_{j+n}^+}}|\mathbb P(A\cap B)-\mathbb P(A)\mathbb P(B)|.$$

Define the **uniform-mixing coefficient** by
$$\phi_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{\substack{A\in\mathcal F_j^-\\\mathbb P(A)>0}}\ \sup_{B\in\mathcal F_{j+n}^+}|\mathbb P(B\mid A)-\mathbb P(B)|.$$

For square-integrable real random variables $U,V$ with positive variances, write
$$\operatorname{Corr}(U,V):=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(U,V)}{\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(U)\operatorname{Var}(V)}}.$$
For each $n\ge1$, let $\mathcal C_n$ consist of the triples $(j,U,V)$ such that $j\ge0$, $U,V$ are real and square-integrable, $U$ and $V$ are measurable with respect to $\mathcal F_j^-$ and $\mathcal F_{j+n}^+$ respectively, and both have positive variance. Define the **maximal-correlation coefficient** by
$$\rho_Y(n):=\sup\Bigl(\{0\}\cup\{|\operatorname{Corr}(U,V)|:(j,U,V)\in\mathcal C_n\}\Bigr),$$
where square-integrability is in the sense of [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]. Thus $\rho_Y(n)=0$ when there is no admissible pair, as for a constant process. The process is called strongly mixing, uniformly mixing, or rho-mixing, respectively, when the corresponding coefficient tends to zero. These coefficients are distinct conditions; no implication between them is included in this definition.

For $m,n\ge0$,
$$K^{m+n}=K^mK^n.$$ Assume Choice and let $X$ be a Markov chain with kernel $K$ relative to $(\mathcal F_n)$. For every bounded measurable real $f$, $$ \mathbb E[f(X_{m+n})\mid\mathcal F_m]=K^nf(X_m)\quad\text{a.s.} $$ Equivalently, for $A\in\mathcal E$, $$ \mathbb P(X_{m+n}\in A\mid\mathcal F_m)=K^n(X_m,A)\quad\text{a.s.} $$
Both assertions include $m=0$ and $n=0$.

Assume AC. Let $(X_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a stationary time-homogeneous Markov chain
with probability kernel $P$, invariant law $\pi$, and natural filtration
$\mathcal F_k=\sigma(X_0,\ldots,X_k)$. Let $g\in L^2(\pi)$ ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]) and fix a finite real measurable representative, also denoted by $g$. Define
$Pg(x)=\int g(y)P(x,dy)$ and $P(g^2)(x)=\int g(y)^2P(x,dy)$ on the
$\pi$-full measurable set where the respective integrals are finite, and set
these functions to zero on the exceptional set. Then, for each $k\ge0$,
$$\mathbb E[g(X_{k+1})\mid\mathcal F_k]=Pg(X_k).$$
$$\mathbb E[g(X_{k+1})^2\mid\mathcal F_k]=P(g^2)(X_k)\quad\text{a.s.}$$
Consequently, if $D_{k+1}=g(X_{k+1})-Pg(X_k)$, then $(D_{k+1})$ is a square-integrable martingale-difference sequence and
$$\mathbb E[D_{k+1}^2\mid\mathcal F_k]=P(g^2)(X_k)-(Pg(X_k))^2\quad\text{a.s.}$$
Assume AC. For $1\le p\le\infty$, conditional expectation is a linear map from real $L^p(P)$ to real $L^p(P|_{\mathcal G})$ satisfying $\|E[X\mid\mathcal G]\|_p\le\|X\|_p$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space with $\mu(X)<\infty$.

1. If $1\le p<r<\infty$ and $f\in\mathcal L^r(\mu)$, then
   $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $$\|f\|_p\le\mu(X)^{1/p-1/r}\|f\|_r.$$
2. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $$\|f\|_p\le\mu(X)^{1/p}\|f\|_\infty.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $1\le p,q,r\le\infty$ satisfy

$$\frac1r=\frac1p+\frac1q,$$

with the convention $1/\infty=0$. If $f$ and $g$ lie in the corresponding
measurable-function spaces ($\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ or $L^\infty(\mu)$ according to
whether the exponent is finite or infinite), then $fg$ lies in the
corresponding space for $r$ and

$$\|fg\|_r\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $f,g\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$, then
   $$\|f+g\|_p\le\|f\|_p+\|g\|_p.$$
2. If $f,g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\|f+g\|_\infty\le\|f\|_\infty+\|g\|_\infty.$$

Assume countable choice (in particular, the Axiom of Choice suffices). Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $1\le p\le\infty$. Then
$L^p(\mu)$, with the norm of
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]], is
complete. Equivalently, the metric induced by that norm is a complete metric in
the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]].

Moreover, if a sequence in $L^p(\mu)$ converges in norm, then some subsequence
admits measurable representatives converging almost everywhere in the sense of
[[def-convergence-almost-everywhere-relative-to-a-measure]].

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

- For $0<p<\infty$, define an equivalence relation on $\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ by
  $$f\sim g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f-g\in\mathcal N(\mu),$$
  and write $L^p(\mu)$ for the set of classes $[f]$.
- For $p=\infty$, define the same relation on $L^\infty(\mu)$ and again write
  $L^\infty(\mu)$ for the set of classes.

Thus an element of $L^p(\mu)$ is an almost-everywhere equivalence class of
measurable representatives.

When $1\le p\le\infty$, the displayed set quotient agrees with the usual
quotient-vector-space construction of
[[def-quotient-vector-space-and-canonical-projection]].

For $0<p<1$, the same class notation is used; under its stated choice hypothesis, the later item
[[thm-the-l-p-distance-for-zero-less-p-less-one-is-a-complete-translation-invariant-metric]]
supplies the metric structure rather than a normed-space structure.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $K$ be a probability kernel on a measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and let $\pi$ be a
probability measure on $(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). The
probability measure $\pi$ is **invariant** for $K$, and $\pi$ is a
**stationary distribution** of $K$, when

$$(\pi K)(A):=\int_E K(x,A)\,\pi(dx)=\pi(A)\qquad\text{for every }A\in\mathcal E .$$

The set function $\pi K$ is again a probability measure: for fixed $A$ the map
$x\mapsto K(x,A)$ is measurable and lies in $[0,1]$, so the integral exists in
$[0,1]$; for pairwise disjoint $A_n\in\mathcal E$ the identity
$K(x,\bigcup_nA_n)=\sum_nK(x,A_n)$ of the measure $K(x,\cdot)$ and the
monotone convergence theorem for nonnegative functions
([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]) give
$\sigma$-additivity of $\pi K$; and $K(x,E)=1$ for every $x$ gives
$(\pi K)(E)=1$. Thus $(\pi K)(A)=\pi(A)$ is an identity between two probability
measures evaluated at $A$.

A $K$-chain whose initial law is $\pi$ is called **stationary** when
$\pi K=\pi$. Stationarity of the process is a statement about all of its
finite-dimensional laws and is proved, not assumed, from $\pi K=\pi$; see
[[thm-invariant-initial-law-makes-the-chain-stationary]].

On a countable state space $E$ with sigma-algebra $2^E$ and transition matrix
$p(x,y)=K(x,\{y\})$ ([[def-transition-matrix-and-n-step-transition-probabilities]]),
a measure on $E$ is its weighted sum of Dirac masses at singletons
([[thm-measures-on-countable-discrete-spaces-are-weighted-dirac-sums]]), so
invariance is equivalent to the matrix identity

$$\pi(y)=\sum_{x\in E}\pi(x)\,p(x,y)\qquad\text{for every }y\in E .$$

The definition fixes no irreducibility, aperiodicity or uniqueness hypothesis,
and it selects no conditional-expectation versions; the display defines a
single measure $\pi K$ and asserts an identity for it. A transient, periodic or
reducible chain may have several invariant probability measures or none.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ and $(Y_j)_{j\in J}$ be finite families of square-integrable real random variables on one common probability space. Then covariance is symmetric, and for real scalars $a_i,b_j$,
$$\operatorname{Cov}\!\left(\sum_{i\in I}a_iX_i,\sum_{j\in J}b_jY_j\right)=\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{j\in J}a_ib_j\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,Y_j).$$
This includes empty sums and constant summands. On a finite probability space all real random variables are square-integrable, so the original finite-space case is included with the same centered-product covariance.

derivations.claim: Invariance [F7], extended with [F6], gives $\pi P|h|=\pi|h|$ for integrable $h$, so the absolute kernel integral is finite off a measurable $\pi$-null set. A change of representative on a $\pi$-null set $A$ does not change its image class, since $\pi P1_A=\pi(A)=0$ implies $P1_A=0$ almost everywhere. For $h\in L^p$, [F3] gives $h\in L^2$, and [F2] identifies $Ph(X_0)$ with $\mathbb E[h(X_1)\mid X_0]$. Conditional contraction [F3] and stationarity give $\|Ph\|_p\le\|h\|_p$. The bounded iteration identity in [F2] extends to these $L^p$ classes by replacing $h$ with its bounded clipped truncations: their $L^p$ error tends to zero because the integrable tail $|h|^p1_{\{|h|>K\}}$ tends to zero, as follows from [F6] applied to its complementary truncations; conditional and kernel contractions pass this error to zero. Thus $P$ is a well-defined linear contraction on $L^p$, its iterates agree with the kernel iterates, and $P^nh(X_0)=\mathbb E[h(X_n)\mid X_0]$. This also proves $P^nf\in L^p$ before any covariance estimate is used.

Fix $n\ge1$, put $Z=P^nf$, and let $p'=p/(p-1)$ and $W_K(x)=\operatorname{sgn}(Z(x))|Z(x)|^{p-1}1_{\{|Z(x)|\le K\}}$ for integers $K\ge1$. This function is bounded, belongs to $L^2$, and satisfies $\|W_K\|_{p'}\le\|Z\|_p^{p-1}$. The centered $f(X_n)$ is in $L^2$ by [F3]. Step 1.1 and bounded conditional multiplication give $\mathbb E[W_K(X_0)f(X_n)]=\pi(W_KP^nf)=\pi(|Z|^p1_{\{|Z|\le K\}})$; since $\pi f=0$, this expectation is the covariance of $W_K(X_0)$ and $f(X_n)$. Bounded conditional multiplication here follows directly from the defining conditional expectation event identity, first for simple $W_K$ and then by uniform bounded approximation. Thus [F1] is applied only to square-integrable variables, even though $p'<2$.

Put $a=\alpha_X(n)$. The quantile identity in [F1] gives $\|Q_{W_K(X_0)}\|_{p'}=\|W_K\|_{p'}$ and $\|Q_{f(X_n)}\|_q=\|f\|_q$. Since $1/p'+1/q=1-\theta$, apply the product inequality [F4] to these two quantile functions in $L^{1/(1-\theta)}(0,1)$, and then Hölder with $1_{(0,a)}$, whose $L^{1/\theta}$ norm is $a^\theta$. Therefore [F1] and step 2.1 give $\pi(|Z|^p1_{\{|Z|\le K\}})\le4a^\theta\|Z\|_p^{p-1}\|f\|_q$. If $a=0$ the quantile integral and the right-hand side are zero. Let $K\to\infty$ using [F6]. If $\|Z\|_p=0$ the required bound is immediate; otherwise divide by $\|Z\|_p^{p-1}$ to obtain $\|P^nf\|_p\le4\alpha_X(n)^\theta\|f\|_q$. The restriction $p<q$ ensures $\theta>0$ and makes all Hölder exponents just used valid.

The geometric bound makes $\sum_{n\ge1}\alpha_X(n)^\theta\le C^\theta\sum_{n\ge1}r^{n\theta}<\infty$, including $C=0$. By step 3.1, [F4] makes $g_m=\sum_{n=0}^mP^nf$ a Cauchy sequence in $L^p$. Completeness [F5] gives $g_m\to g\in L^p$. The contraction in step 1.1 gives $Pg_m\to Pg$, while $g_m-Pg_m=f-P^{m+1}f\to f$ in $L^p$ by step 3.1. Thus $g-Pg=f$ as almost-everywhere classes. Choose the finite measurable representative supplied by [F5], setting it to zero on its measurable null exceptional set if necessary, and use the version convention from step 1.1 for $Pg$. These choices make the asserted almost-everywhere identity precise on the original sigma-algebra without completing the measure.

Apply [F1] directly to $f(X_0),f(X_n)$, both square-integrable. Their quantiles have common $L^q(0,1)$ norm $\|f\|_q$. Two applications of [F4], with reciprocal exponents $1/q,1/q,1-2/q$, yield $|c_n|\le4\alpha_X(n)^{1-2/q}\|f\|_q^2$. The exponent is positive because $q>2$; the geometric bound therefore gives $\sum_{n\ge1}|c_n|<\infty$. At a zero mixing coefficient the quantile integral is zero, so no division by that coefficient is needed.

Centering, stationarity and [F8] give $n^{-1}\mathbb E_\pi(\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}f(X_k))^2=\pi(f^2)+2\sum_{h=1}^{n-1}(1-h/n)c_h$. To pass to its limit, choose any finite $H$; the terms $h\le H$ converge individually to $c_h$, while the absolute value of either remaining weighted or limiting tail is at most $\sum_{h>H}|c_h|$, which tends to zero as $H\to\infty$ by step 4.2. The limit is the claimed finite covariance sum $v$. Each left-hand side is nonnegative, hence $v\ge0$. When $f=0$ almost everywhere all bounds and the choice $g=0$ hold directly; no claim of uniqueness of $g$ is made. The strict exponent range and all zero-mixing cases were handled in steps 3.1, 4.1, 4.2. AC is used through the Markov/conditional and completeness suppliers, not as an imported covariance or Poisson theorem.

boundaries.evidence: Statement and proof step 5.1. The probability space has total mass one; an empty state space cannot carry π. Covariance tails after a finite cutoff and finite sums with no terms contribute zero.
Steps 3.1 and 4.2 cover α_X(n)=0 without dividing by it; step 4.1 covers C=0, and step 5.1 explicitly covers f=0.
Proof steps 4.1 and 5.1. Kernel powers start at n=1 in the decay estimate; P^0f=f is included separately in the Poisson series. The n=1 variance expansion has an empty covariance tail.
Proof steps 2.1 and 3.1. The bounded dual test W_K is square-integrable even when p′<2. Zero ||P^nf||p is treated before division. g need not be unique.
Proof steps 3.1 and 4.2. q is finite and q>p>2. These strict inequalities make θ=1/p−1/q and 1−2/q positive and validate every Hölder exponent and geometric series.

Proof step 4.1. AC is explicit for conditional expectations and Lp completeness; finite measurable representatives are chosen on measurable null exceptional sets, without completing the underlying measure.

boundaries.reason: The statement is a one-way Poisson-solution and covariance estimate, not a biconditional.
No converse mixing or necessity assertion is made.

risk_review.notes: Checked quotient kernel contraction and iteration, bounded truncated dual W_K (essential because p prime<2), quantile Holder with theta=1/p-1/q>0, MCT and norm division only when nonzero. Geometric summability gives Lp Poisson series and telescoping; covariance Holder exponent 1-2/q>0 supplies absolute series and nonnegative variance limit. Handles C=0, zero mixing, f=0 without division.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Fix $0<\gamma\le1$. Let $1\le d\le4$, $s>0$, $B>0$, and let $X_1,\ldots,X_m,Z$ be independent centered random vectors in $\mathbb R^d$, where $m\ge0$, $|X_j|\le B$ almost surely, and $Z\sim N_d(0,G)$. Suppose $S=Z+\sum_jX_j$ has covariance $sI_d$ and $G\ge\gamma sI_d$ in quadratic form order. There is an absolute constant $C_0\ge1$ such that, with $\tau=C_0B$, the logarithmic moment generating function
$$K(z)=\log\mathbb E e^{z\cdot S},\qquad K(0)=0,$$
has a single analytic branch on the complex Euclidean ball $\tau|z|<1$, and
$$|\partial_u\partial_v^2K(z)|\le\tau s|u||v|^2\qquad(u,v\in\mathbb R^d,\ \tau|z|<1).$$
Here $z\cdot S$ uses the complex bilinear dot product and $|z|^2=\sum_i|z_i|^2$. Every real exponential tilt $\mathbb P_h(d\omega)=e^{h\cdot S-K(h)}\mathbb P(d\omega)$ is defined, and its characteristic function satisfies
$$|\varphi_h(t)|:=|\mathbb E_h e^{it\cdot S}|\le e^{-\gamma s|t|^2/2}\qquad(t,h\in\mathbb R^d),$$
where $K(h)=\log\mathbb E e^{h\cdot S}$ for real $h$, also outside the analytic ball. Put $\kappa=\tau/\sqrt s$. For every fixed $a>0$ and integer $N\ge1$ there is a finite $C_{a,N,\gamma}$, uniform in $1\le d\le4$, such that, if $0<\kappa\le1$,
$$(2\pi)^{-d}\int_{|t|\ge a/\tau}|\varphi_h(t)|\,dt\le C_{a,N,\gamma}\kappa^Ns^{-d/2},$$
$$(2\pi)^{-d}\int_{|t|\ge a/\tau}|t\cdot v||\varphi_h(t)|\,dt\le C_{a,N,\gamma}\kappa^N|v|s^{-(d+1)/2}.$$
All assertions hold with the same $C_0$, $B$, $s$, and $\gamma$ for $AS$, where $A$ is any real $k\times d$ matrix with $1\le k\le d$ and $AA^T=I_k$. This includes every coordinate prefix, every orthogonal change of coordinates, and their compositions. In particular it covers the normalized joint sum and difference of two independent children by applying the assertion in their joint dimension, provided that dimension is at most four and the joint input satisfies the stated covariance assumptions.

Assume AC and the hypotheses of [[lem-gaussian-anchored-sums-have-cumulant-and-fourier-bounds]], with $1\le d\le4$, fixed $\gamma>0$, $\tau=C_0B$, $\kappa=\tau/\sqrt s$, and logarithmic moment generating function $K$. Let $p_h$ denote the density of $S$ under the real exponential tilt with parameter $h$. Every such density exists, is continuously differentiable and strictly positive, and
$$\sup_y p_h(y)\le(2\pi\gamma s)^{-d/2}\qquad(h\in\mathbb R^d).$$
There are constants $c_\gamma>0$, $C_\gamma<\infty$, independent of $d,s,B,m$ and the summand laws, with the following property. If $\kappa\le c_\gamma$ and $\tau|h|\le1/8$, put $\mu_h=\mathbb E_hS$ and $D_h=\operatorname{cov}_h(S)$. Then
$$\tfrac78sI_d\le D_h\le\tfrac98sI_d.$$
For $x\in\mathbb R^d$ put $r=|D_h^{-1/2}x|$ and let $q_{D_h}(x)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}(\det D_h)^{-1/2}e^{-r^2/2}$. Whenever $\kappa r\le c_\gamma$,
$$\left|\log\frac{p_h(\mu_h+x)}{q_{D_h}(x)}\right|\le C_\gamma\kappa(1+r^3).$$
For $r\ge7$ in the same region,
$$\left.\frac{d}{dt}\log p_h(\mu_h+x+tx)\right|_{t=0}\le-\tfrac12r^2.$$
These assertions apply separately to every row isometry image in the supplier, including every required coordinate prefix and normalized joint child sum and difference. Their tilt parameter and covariance are taken in that image's own coordinates.

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$, $m\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $\Sigma$ be a real symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then its law has Lebesgue density
$$f_{m,\Sigma}(x)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\det(\Sigma)^{-1/2} \exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(x-m)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-m)\right), \qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Phi(x)=P(Z\le x)$ for $Z\sim N(0,1)$. Then $\Phi$ is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$, with $\lim_{x\to-\infty}\Phi(x)=0$ and $\lim_{x\to+\infty}\Phi(x)=1$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Let $(S,\Sigma)$ and $(T_i,\Tau_i)$ for $i<n$ be measurable spaces, with
$n<\infty$, and let $K_i:S\to T_i$ be probability kernels with the same
source. There is a unique probability kernel
$$K:S\to\prod_{i<n}T_i$$
whose evaluation on every measurable rectangle is
$$K(s,\prod_{i<n}B_i)=\prod_{i<n}K_i(s,B_i).$$
For $n=0$, the target is the empty-product singleton and $K$ is its point
mass. For $n>0$, the product sigma-algebra is the recursive finite product
sigma-algebra.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$ and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$.

1. **Fundamental theorem, second part, in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

1. $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ with the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]) is a complete metric space
   ([[def-complete-metric-space]]).
2. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on
   $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ is complete.

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited and is not decoration.**
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] defines $\mathbb{R}^n$ and its three metrics only for
$n \ge 1$, because at $n = 0$ the metric $d_\infty$ would be a maximum over the
empty index set. Every statement about $\mathbb{R}^n$ in this library carries the
hypothesis, and this one does too.

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

**No choice principle is used.** The one place where a reader expects a choice,
"pick a representative $a/b$ of each rational", is exactly where
[[lem-rat-positive-denominator]] applies: every rational *has* a representative
with positive denominator, so the map $(a,b) \mapsto [(a,b)]$ defined on
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is already **surjective** onto $\mathbb{Q}$,
and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).

Write $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ for the image of $\mathbb{Q}$ in $\mathbb{R}$
under the canonical embedding $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]), the
set usually written $\mathbb{Q}$ once the identification is made, and put
$X := \mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ for the irrationals. Then:

1. $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$, that is,
   $\overline{\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}} = \mathbb{R}$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]);
2. $X$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$;
3. every nonempty open subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is uncountable
   ([[def-countable]]).

Claim 2 is not a symmetry of claim 1: the rationals are dense because they are
*constructed* to approximate, whereas the irrationals are dense because there are
too many points in any interval for a countable set to exhaust it, which is why
claim 3 is proved alongside and used for it.

derivations.claim: Work with a fixed prefix of length $j\le4$ and write its dimension as $d$ during the proof. Its law satisfies [F1]–[F2]. Set $\sigma=\sqrt s$, $\epsilon=\tau/\sigma$, and normalize coordinates by $\sigma$. Its cumulant $f$ has mean zero, covariance $I$, and third derivatives bounded by $\epsilon|u||v|^2$. Polarization and [F6], integrating along a real segment, give $\|f''(a)-I\|\le\epsilon|a|$ and $|f'(a)-a|\le\epsilon|a|^2/2$. Fix a prefix $x'$, put $b=x'/\sigma$, $\delta=|b|$, and assume $\epsilon\delta$ sufficiently small. The map $a'\mapsto b-(\nabla'f(a',0)-a')$ sends $|a'|\le2\delta$ into itself and has Lipschitz constant at most $2\epsilon\delta<1/2$. Its iterates from zero have geometrically decreasing consecutive distances, hence converge by [F6] to a solution of $\nabla'f(a',0)=b$ with $|a'|\le2\delta$. For the empty prefix use $a'=0$. Put $a=(a',0)$ and let $y_0=\sigma\partial_df(a)$ be the physical last mean under this prefix tilt. The last mixed covariance row at zero vanishes; integrating its Hessian deviation yields $|y_0|\le C\tau\delta^2$. The physical tilt parameter is $h=a/\sigma$, so $\tau|h|\le2\epsilon\delta$ can be kept below $1/8$.

Let $p,p'$ be the joint and prefix densities. The Gaussian convolution representations in [F2] and [F4] give $\int_{\mathbb R}p(x',y)\,dy=p'(x')$ at every $x'$: integrate the Gaussian joint density over its last coordinate and then integrate the bounded-summand law. Both densities are everywhere positive. Thus $p(x',y)/p'(x')$ defines a probability density for each $x'$ and, by integration, a version of the conditional kernel. Denote tilted densities by $\bar p,\bar p'$. Since $h_d=0$, their exponential factors cancel exactly, and the density $v$ of $S_d-y_0$ conditional on $S'=x'$ is $v(u)=p(x',u+y_0)/p'(x')=\bar p(x',u+y_0)/\bar p'(x')$. The centered tilted covariance $C$ satisfies $\|C/s-I\|\le C\epsilon\delta$ by step 1.1. Apply [F2] to its full density at $(0,u)$ and prefix density at zero. The ratio of the matching Gaussian densities is a centered normal density with variance $\det C/\det C'=1/(C^{-1})_{dd}=s(1+O(\epsilon\delta))$; the determinant identity follows by eliminating the off-diagonal blocks in $C$. Consequently $\left|\log\frac{v(u)}{\phi_s(u)}\right|\le C\epsilon\left(1+\delta\left(1+\frac{u^2}{s}\right)+\frac{|u|^3}{s^{3/2}}\right)$ for $|u|\le c s/\tau$. Here $\phi_s$ is the density of $N(0,s)$, and the small constants also ensure all [F2] moderate bounds for the full centered tilt.

In standardized units set $g(t)=\sigma v(\sigma t)$ and let $\phi$ be the standard normal density. Step 2.1 implies, on $|t|\le c/\epsilon$, $|\log(g(t)/\phi(t))|\le C\epsilon(1+\delta+\delta t^2+|t|^3)$ and hence $c_1e^{-C_1t^2}\le g(t)\le C_1e^{-c_1t^2}$ after reducing $\epsilon$ and $\epsilon\delta$. There is also a global bound $g(t)\le C\exp[-c\min(t^2,|t|/\epsilon)]$. Indeed the standardized prefix-tilted law has prefix density at its mean bounded below by a positive constant by [F2]. Tilt its centered full law further by $q e_d$, where $|q|\le c/\epsilon$. Its full density is bounded above by a constant by the global part of [F2], while integration of its bounded Hessian gives a centered log mgf at most $Cq^2$. The density tilt identity therefore gives $g(t)\le C e^{Cq^2-qt}$ at every real $t$. Choosing $q=\operatorname{sign}(t)\min(|t|/(4C),c/(2\epsilon))$ proves the bound. The combined real tilt remains in a fixed smaller analytic ball, where the Hessian bound from step 1.1 applies; the global density bound in [F2] itself permits every real tilt.

We next convert the density estimate into a CDF displacement without a coupling theorem. Write $R(t)=\epsilon(1+\delta+\delta t+t^2)$ for $t\ge0$. Choose a fixed large $T\ge10$ and then a sufficiently large fixed $K$. Put $r(t)=KR(t)$ and $b=c_0/\epsilon$, with fixed $c_0$ sufficiently small. Reduce the allowed bounds on $\epsilon$ and $\epsilon\delta$ so that for $T/2\le t\le2b$ one has $0\le r(t)\le t/8$ and $0\le r'(t)\le1/2$; this is possible because $R'(t)\le2R(t)/t$ for $t\ge1$ and $r(t)/t\le C K\epsilon(1+\delta+t)$. Also choose $3b$ within the moderate interval of step 3.1. For $t\ge T$, the maps $f_\pm(t)=t\pm r(t)$ are increasing and their arguments are comparable with $t$. Since $(\log\phi)'(t)=-t$, step 3.1 bounds the logarithmic density error at either perturbed argument by $C tR(t)$, whereas the Gaussian log-density changes by at least a fixed positive multiple of $t r(t)$ in the favorable direction. The log Jacobians are at most $r'(t)$ and at least $-2r'(t)$, respectively. Since $r'(t)\le2r(t)/t$, first taking $T$ large and then $K$ large gives $g(f_+(t))f_+'(t)\le\phi(t)$ and $g(f_-(t))f_-'(t)\ge\phi(t)$. These comparisons follow by adding the three logarithmic contributions; the Jacobian contribution divided by $t r(t)$ is at most $4/t^2$, and the density-error contribution is at most $C/K$.

The inverse equations and monotonicity of $r$ imply $f_+^{-1}(z)\ge z-r(z)$ and $f_-^{-1}(z)\le z+r(2z)$ in the range below. Substituting $u=f_+(t)$ and $u=f_-(t)$ in the inequalities of step 4.1 gives, for $2T\le z\le b$, $\int_z^b g(u)\,du\le\int_{z-r(z)}^\infty\phi(u)\,du,\qquad \int_z^b g(u)\,du\ge\int_{z+r(2z)}^b\phi(u)\,du.$ Only a smaller range $z\le c_1/\epsilon$, with $c_1\ll c_0$, will be retained, so the lower integral has its endpoints in the stated order. The global tail estimate in step 3.1 and the Gaussian tail give $\int_b^\infty g+\int_b^\infty\phi\le C e^{-c b^2}$: split the first integral at a constant multiple of $1/\epsilon$ and integrate the Gaussian and exponential parts. Enlarge the shifts in the displayed inequalities to $3r(2z)$. Each extra Gaussian interval has mass at least $cR(z)e^{-Cz^2}\ge c\epsilon e^{-Cz^2}$. Choose $c_1$ so small that $C c_1^2<c c_0^2/2$. For sufficiently small $\epsilon$, uniformly for $2T\le z\le c_1/\epsilon$, that interval mass exceeds the discarded tail, since $\epsilon^{-1}\exp(-(c c_0^2-Cc_1^2)/\epsilon^2)\to0$. Thus the full tails have the corresponding inequalities with shift $C R(z)$; here $R(2z)\le4R(z)$. Reflecting $g,\phi$ proves the negative-tail version as well.

At $z=2T$ step 5.1 bounds the tail-probability difference by $C R(2T)$. For $|z|\le2T$, step 3.1 bounds the density-ratio error by $C a$, where $a=\epsilon(1+\delta)$; integrating over this fixed interval gives a CDF difference at most $C a$. The Gaussian density is bounded below by a fixed positive constant on $[-2T-1,2T+1]$, so a shift of length $C a$ in either direction dominates that difference, after reducing the allowed bound on $a$ to keep the shift within this compact interval. Since $R(|z|)\ge a$, this proves together with step 5.1, for the standardized conditional CDF $F_g$, $\Phi(z-C R(|z|))\le F_g(z)\le\Phi(z+C R(|z|))\qquad(|z|\le c/\epsilon).$ All constant choices are finite and made in the indicated order; reducing the common cutoff enforces every smallness requirement. Returning to physical units, the CDF $F_v$ of the centered conditional coordinate satisfies $\Phi_s(u-\rho(u))\le F_v(u)\le\Phi_s(u+\rho(u))$, where $\rho(u)=C\tau(1+\delta(1+|u|/\sigma)+u^2/s)$.

Every conditional density is positive and continuous by step 2.1, so its CDF is continuous, strictly increasing and has limits zero and one. Its inverse on $(0,1)$ is therefore unique. For a fresh $N(0,s)$ variable $Z$, [F3] implies that $\Phi_s(Z)$ is uniform: for $0<u<1$, the event $\Phi_s(Z)\le u$ is $Z\le\Phi_s^{-1}(u)$, of probability $u$. Thus the inverse-CDF map has the asserted conditional law. If $Y=T_j(x',Z)$ and $U=Y-y_0$, then $F_v(U)=\Phi_s(Z)$. Step 6.1 and strict monotonicity imply $|U-Z|\le\rho(U)$ whenever $U$ is moderate. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $P$ be a probability kernel with invariant probability $\pi$ on a measurable space $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$. Write $P^n(x,\cdot)$ for its $n$-step transition probability and use $\|\mu-\nu\|_{\mathrm{TV}}=\sup_{A\in\mathcal X}|\mu(A)-\nu(A)|$ for probability measures.

The chain is **geometrically ergodic** if there are a measurable finite function $M:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ and $r\in(0,1)$ such that
$$\|P^n(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le M(x)r^n\quad(x\in\mathsf X,\ n\ge1).$$

It is **uniformly ergodic** if this bound holds with $M$ bounded on $\mathsf X$. These are convergence-rate properties, not conclusions about a particular function's CLT or long-run variance. If a proof needs $\int M\,d\pi<\infty$, that integrability is an additional stated hypothesis unless a cited theorem establishes it.

Let $P$ be a probability kernel on an arbitrary measurable space $(X,\mathcal F)$, and let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. There is a countably generated sub-sigma-field $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ such that $f$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable and $P$, restricted to events in $\mathcal G$, is a probability kernel $P_{\mathcal G}$ on $(X,\mathcal G)$. For every $n\ge0$, $x\in X$, and $B\in\mathcal G$,
$$P_{\mathcal G}^n(x,B)=P^n(x,B).$$
If $\pi$ is invariant for $P$, then $\pi|_{\mathcal G}$ is invariant for $P_{\mathcal G}$.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ be countably generated, let $P$ be a probability kernel that is $\phi$-irreducible ([[def-phi-irreducible-chain]]), and let $\phi$ be a nonzero $\sigma$-finite irreducibility measure. Then there are an integer $m\ge1$, a measurable $C$ with $\phi(C)>0$, a probability $
u$ with $
u(C)>0$, and $\epsilon>0$ such that $P^m(x,\cdot)\ge\epsilon
u(\cdot)$ for every $x\in C$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $Q$ be a probability kernel on any measurable space $(X,\mathcal G)$, with invariant probability $\pi$. Let $C\in\mathcal G$ satisfy $\pi(C)>0$, and suppose
$$Q(x,\cdot)\ge\epsilon\nu(\cdot)\quad(x\in C),\qquad 0<\epsilon<1,$$
where $\nu$ is a probability measure. Suppose some $A<\infty$ and $0<\theta<1$ satisfy
$$|\nu Q^n(C)-\pi(C)|\le A\theta^n\quad(n\ge0).$$
For a $Q$-chain started at $x$, put $\sigma_C=\inf\{n\ge0:X_n\in C\}$. Then some $s>1$ makes
$$H(x)=\mathbb E_x[s^{\sigma_C}]\quad\text{measurable},\qquad \pi(H)<\infty,$$
where $s^\infty=\infty$. In particular $H$ is finite $\pi$-almost everywhere; finiteness at every state is not asserted.

For the same hypotheses, the split construction also has the following return and occupation properties. Put $w_1(x)=\epsilon1_C(x)$ and $w_0(x)=1-w_1(x)$. Define $K_{x,1}=\nu$, $K_{x,0}=(Q(x,\cdot)-\epsilon\nu)/(1-\epsilon)$ on $C$, and $K_{x,0}=Q(x,\cdot)$ off $C$. On $X\times\{0,1\}$ use the kernel
$$\widetilde Q((x,i),dy\times\{j\})=K_{x,i}(dy)w_j(y)$$
and invariant law $\widetilde\pi(dx,i)=w_i(x)\pi(dx)$. Its atom $\alpha=C\times\{1\}$ has mass $p=\epsilon\pi(C)>0$. If $Z_0$ has law $\kappa=\widetilde\pi(\cdot\mid\alpha)$ and $\tau=\inf\{n\ge1:Z_n\in\alpha\}$, then some $b>1$ satisfies
$$\mathbb E_\kappa b^\tau<\infty,$$
and for every nonnegative measurable $g$ on the split space,
$$\widetilde\pi(g)=p\,\mathbb E_\kappa\sum_{k=0}^{\tau-1}g(Z_k).$$
In particular $\tau<\infty$ almost surely and $\mathbb E_\kappa\tau=1/p$. These additional assertions use exactly the construction and hypotheses above; they do not assert an exponential entrance-time moment from every state.

Assume Choice. For every probability measure $\mu$ and probability kernel $K$
on an arbitrary measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$, the canonical path space
$$ (E^{\mathbb N_0},\mathcal E^{\otimes\mathbb N_0}) $$
carries a unique probability $\mathbb P_\mu$ under which the coordinate maps
form a Markov chain with initial law $\mu$ and transition kernel $K$.

Assume Choice. Let $X$ be a $K$-chain, let
$\tau:\Omega\to\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$ be a stopping time, and let $H$ be a
bounded measurable path functional. Put $h(x)=\mathbb E_xH$ and define the
everywhere meaningful random variables
$$ Z_H:=\sum_{n\ge0}1_{\{\tau=n\}}H(X_n,X_{n+1},\ldots), \qquad R_h:=\sum_{n\ge0}1_{\{\tau=n\}}h(X_n). $$ Both are defined to be zero on $\{\tau=\infty\}$. Then $$ \mathbb E[Z_H\mid\mathcal F_\tau]=R_h\quad\text{a.s.} $$ This is the precise meaning of the usual eventwise notation $$ \mathbb E[1_{\{\tau<\infty\}}H(X_\tau,X_{\tau+1},\ldots)\mid\mathcal F_\tau] =1_{\{\tau<\infty\}}h(X_\tau): $$
no value $X_\infty$ is used. If $\tau<\infty$ almost surely, the indicators can
be omitted.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ be a countably generated measurable space ([[def-measurable-space]]), $P$ a probability kernel ([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and $\phi$ a nonzero $\sigma$-finite measure ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]) on $\mathcal X$. Write $P^n$ for the $n$-fold kernel iterate. The kernel is **$\phi$-irreducible** if, for every $A\in\mathcal X$ with $\phi(A)>0$ and every $x\in\mathsf X$, there is an integer $n\ge1$ such that $P^n(x,A)>0$. Equivalently, the sum of these nonnegative probabilities over $n\ge1$ is positive. No recurrence or invariant law is part of this definition.

u$ on $C$, $

It supplies $s>1$ and a measurable $H(x)=\mathbb E_x[s^\sigma]$, where $\sigma=\inf\{j\ge0:X_{jm}\in C\}$, such that $\pi(H)<\infty$. Since $X_j\in C$, [F1] bounds its difference from $\pi(A)$ by $K_1r_0^{n-j}$; when $j=n$, use $|1_A(X_n)-\pi(A)|\le1\le K_1$. On $\{S>n\}$ use the bound $1$. Subtracting $\pi(A)$ on these two events gives $|P^n(x,A)-\pi(A)|\le\mathbb P_x(S>n)+K_1\mathbb E_x[r_0^{n-S};S\le n]\le(1+K_1)r_1^nH(x).$ For the final inequality, $r_1^{-S}\le s^\sigma$, and on $S\le n$ one has $r_0^{n-S}\le r_1^nr_1^{-S}$; on $S>n$, $1\le r_1^nr_1^{-S}$. The measurable set $N=\{H=\infty\}$ is $\pi$-null by step 3.1. Define $M_1(x)=(1+K_1)H(x)$ for $x\notin N$ and $M_1(x)=M_0(x)$ for $x\in N$.
