The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $(Z_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a centered strictly stationary real sequence, with $|Z_0|\le B$ almost surely for a finite $B$, and suppose
$$\sum_{r=1}^\infty\alpha_Z(r)<\infty.$$
Put $T_n=\sum_{k=1}^nZ_k$. Then its covariance series converges absolutely and
$$\sigma_Z^2=\mathbb EZ_0^2+2\sum_{r=1}^\infty\operatorname{Cov}(Z_0,Z_r)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\operatorname{Var}(T_n)}n\ge0.$$
Moreover
$$T_n/\sqrt n\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_Z^2),$$
including $\sigma_Z^2=0$. Writing $D_Z=\mathbb EZ_0^2+2\sum_{r\ge1}|\operatorname{Cov}(Z_0,Z_r)|$, every finite subset $I\subseteq\mathbb N_0$ satisfies
$$\mathbb E\left(\sum_{i\in I}Z_i\right)^2\le D_Z|I|.$$
The strong-mixing coefficient is that of [[def-mixing-coefficients-for-stationary-markov-chain]].

Let $\mathcal A,\mathcal B$ be sub-sigma-algebras of a probability space and put
$$a=\sup_{A\in\mathcal A,\,B\in\mathcal B}|\mathbb P(A\cap B)-\mathbb P(A)\mathbb P(B)|.$$
For any real random variable $U$, define its absolute tail quantile by
$$Q_U(u)=\inf\{t\ge0:\mathbb P(|U|>t)\le u\},\qquad 0<u<1.$$
This is a nonnegative nonincreasing Borel function and, for every nonnegative Borel function $\psi$,
$$\int_0^1\psi(Q_U(u))\,du=\mathbb E\psi(|U|).$$
If $U,V$ are square-integrable real random variables measurable respectively with respect to $\mathcal A,\mathcal B$, then
$$|\operatorname{Cov}(U,V)|\le4\int_0^a Q_U(u)Q_V(u)\,du.$$
In particular, if $|U|\le A$ and $|V|\le B$ almost surely, the right-hand side is at most $4ABa$. For complex $U,V$ with these bounds and the same measurability,
$$|\mathbb E(UV)-\mathbb EU\mathbb EV|\le16ABa.$$
For two collections of observations separated by $n$ time steps in a process $Y$, the coefficient $a$ of their sigma-algebras is at most $\alpha_Y(n)$ as defined in [[def-mixing-coefficients-for-stationary-markov-chain]]. An integral whose upper endpoint is zero is zero.

Let $X=(X_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a strictly stationary process on a measurable state
space and let $h$ be a measurable real-valued function. Put $Y_k=h(X_k)$.
Then $Y$ is strictly stationary and, for every $n\ge1$,
$$\alpha_Y(n)\le\alpha_X(n),\qquad \phi_Y(n)\le\phi_X(n),\qquad \rho_Y(n)\le\rho_X(n),$$
where the coefficients are as in
[[def-mixing-coefficients-for-stationary-markov-chain]].

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

Assume AC. If $X$ has law $N(m,\sigma^2)$ with $\sigma\ge0$, then $\varphi_X(t)=\exp(imt-\sigma^2t^2/2)$ for every real $t$. Moreover $\mathbb EX=m$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\sigma^2$, including $\sigma=0$.

Assume AC. For Borel probability laws $\mu_n$ and a specified Borel probability law $\mu$ on $\mathbb R$,
$$\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\varphi_{\mu_n}(t)\to\varphi_\mu(t)\ \text{for every }t\in\mathbb R.$$

Let $(Y_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a centered, strictly stationary, square-integrable real process ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), and put $\gamma_k=\operatorname{Cov}(Y_0,Y_k)$. If $\sum_{k\ge1}|\gamma_k|<\infty$ and
$$\gamma_0+2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\gamma_k=0,$$
then $n^{-1/2}\sum_{k=1}^nY_k\to0$ in $L^2$ and hence in distribution to $N(0,0)$.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Let $Y=(Y_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a process on a probability space whose finite-dimensional laws are invariant under common nonnegative time shifts; call this strict stationarity. For $j\ge0$, set $\mathcal F_j^-:=\sigma(Y_0,\ldots,Y_j)$ and $\mathcal F_j^+:=\sigma(Y_j,Y_{j+1},\ldots)$. For $n\ge1$, define the **strong-mixing coefficient** by
$$\alpha_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{\substack{A\in\mathcal F_j^-\\B\in\mathcal F_{j+n}^+}}|\mathbb P(A\cap B)-\mathbb P(A)\mathbb P(B)|.$$

Define the **uniform-mixing coefficient** by
$$\phi_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{\substack{A\in\mathcal F_j^-\\\mathbb P(A)>0}}\ \sup_{B\in\mathcal F_{j+n}^+}|\mathbb P(B\mid A)-\mathbb P(B)|.$$

For square-integrable real random variables $U,V$ with positive variances, write
$$\operatorname{Corr}(U,V):=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(U,V)}{\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(U)\operatorname{Var}(V)}}.$$
For each $n\ge1$, let $\mathcal C_n$ consist of the triples $(j,U,V)$ such that $j\ge0$, $U,V$ are real and square-integrable, $U$ and $V$ are measurable with respect to $\mathcal F_j^-$ and $\mathcal F_{j+n}^+$ respectively, and both have positive variance. Define the **maximal-correlation coefficient** by
$$\rho_Y(n):=\sup\Bigl(\{0\}\cup\{|\operatorname{Corr}(U,V)|:(j,U,V)\in\mathcal C_n\}\Bigr),$$
where square-integrability is in the sense of [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]. Thus $\rho_Y(n)=0$ when there is no admissible pair, as for a constant process. The process is called strongly mixing, uniformly mixing, or rho-mixing, respectively, when the corresponding coefficient tends to zero. These coefficients are distinct conditions; no implication between them is included in this definition.

derivations.claim: Write $Q=Q_{Y_0}$ for the absolute tail quantile in [F2], and put $w(u)=1+\sum_{r\ge1}\mathbf1_{\{u<\alpha_Y(r)\}}$ and $J=\int_0^1w(u)Q(u)^2\,du$. We first show in every stated regime that $J<\infty$ and $\sum_r\alpha_Y(r)<\infty$. In regime 1, $Q\le B$ and [F5] give $J\le B^2(1+\sum_r\alpha_Y(r))<\infty$. This regime also already follows directly from [F1].

In regime 2 put $p=2+\delta$ and $\theta=1-2/p=\delta/(2+\delta)\in(0,1)$. Holder's inequality [F6] with exponents $p/2$ and $p/(p-2)$, followed by the quantile identity [F2], gives $\int_0^{\alpha_Y(r)}Q(u)^2\,du\le\alpha_Y(r)^\theta\left(\int_0^1Q(u)^p\,du\right)^{2/p}=\alpha_Y(r)^\theta(\mathbb E|Y_0|^p)^{2/p}.$ Tonelli [F5] and the assumed summability yield $J<\infty$. Also $0\le\alpha_Y(r)\le1$ by its event definition, so $\alpha_Y(r)\le\alpha_Y(r)^\theta$, proving unweighted summability.

In regime 3, choose constants $C<\infty$ and $a\in(0,1)$ so $\alpha_Y(r)\le Ca^r$ outside a finite set of lags. Counting the positive integers satisfying $u<Ca^r$ shows $w(u)\le C_1+C_2\log(1/u)$ for $0<u<1$, with finite nonnegative constants $C_1,C_2$; also $\sum_r\alpha_Y(r)<\infty$. The elementary inequality $xv\le x\log^+x+e^v$ for $x,v\ge0$ follows for $x>0$ by maximizing $xv-x\log x+x$ as a function of $x$, whose maximum is $e^v$; $x=0$ is immediate. Set $x=Q(u)^2$ and $v=\tfrac12\log(1/u)$, then integrate and use [F2]: $\int_0^1Q(u)^2\log(1/u)\,du\le2\int_0^1Q(u)^2\log^+(Q(u)^2)\,du+2\int_0^1u^{-1/2}\,du=4\mathbb E[Y_0^2\log^+|Y_0|]+4<\infty.$ Together with the assumed second moment this proves $J<\infty$. Thus the two properties announced in step 1.1 hold in all three regimes, without imposing a power moment in regime 3.

Let $\gamma_r=\operatorname{Cov}(Y_0,Y_r)$. By [F2], [F12] and [F5], $\sum_{r\ge1}|\gamma_r|\le4\sum_{r\ge1}\int_0^{\alpha_Y(r)}Q(u)^2\,du=4\int_0^1(w(u)-1)Q(u)^2\,du<\infty.$ Set $D_Y=\gamma_0+2\sum_{r\ge1}|\gamma_r|$. Expanding a finite centered sum over $I\subseteq\mathbb N_0$ and counting at most $|I|$ pairs at each positive lag gives $\mathbb E(\sum_{i\in I}Y_i)^2\le D_Y|I|$. For consecutive sums the exact expression is $\operatorname{Var}(S_n)/n=\gamma_0+2\sum_{r=1}^{n-1}(1-r/n)\gamma_r$. The summable majorant and [F4] prove convergence to the stated $\sigma_Y^2$, which is nonnegative as a limit of nonnegative variances.

For an integer $M\ge1$ put $c_M(y)=\max(-M,\min(y,M))$, $Z_k^{(M)}=c_M(Y_k)-\mathbb Ec_M(Y_0)$, and $H_M(y)=y-c_M(y)$. Then $R_k^{(M)}=Y_k-Z_k^{(M)}=H_M(Y_k)-\mathbb EH_M(Y_0)$. Both processes are strictly stationary by [F3], and $Z^{(M)}$ is centered and bounded by $2M$. Its coefficients are bounded by $\alpha_Y$, whose sum is finite by steps 1.1, 2.1, 2.2. Thus [F1] gives an absolutely convergent covariance series with nonnegative sum $\sigma_M^2$, normalized variance convergence to $\sigma_M^2$, and $n^{-1/2}\sum_{k=1}^nZ_k^{(M)}\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_M^2)$.

Put $t_M=\mathbb P(|Y_0|>M)$ and let $Q_{H_M}$ be the absolute quantile of $H_M(Y_0)$. Since $|H_M(Y_0)|=(|Y_0|-M)_+\le|Y_0|$, monotonicity of tail probabilities gives $Q_{H_M}(u)\le Q(u)$, while $Q_{H_M}(u)=0$ for $u\ge t_M$ by its defining infimum. The centering in $R^{(M)}$ does not change any covariance, and $\operatorname{Var}(H_M(Y_0))\le\mathbb EH_M(Y_0)^2$. Applying [F2] to the raw, uncentered $H_M(Y_k)$, followed by [F5], therefore gives $D_{R^{(M)}}:=\mathbb E(R_0^{(M)})^2+2\sum_{r\ge1}|\operatorname{Cov}(R_0^{(M)},R_r^{(M)})|\le8\int_0^{t_M}w(u)Q(u)^2\,du=:e_M^2.$ Here the integrand is integrable by steps 1.1, 2.1, 2.2, and $t_M\to0$ because $Y_0$ is finite almost surely; hence [F4] makes $e_M\to0$. The same finite covariance expansion as in step 3.1 now gives $\sup_n\|n^{-1/2}\sum_{k=1}^nR_k^{(M)}\|_2\le e_M$. This bound uses the raw remainder quantile, without asserting that the centered remainder has that quantile.

The reverse triangle inequality for $L^2$ norms gives $|\|S_n/\sqrt n\|_2-\|n^{-1/2}\sum_{k=1}^nZ_k^{(M)}\|_2|\le e_M$ by step 4.1. This norm inequality follows by expanding a square and applying [F7] to its mixed term. Using the variance limits in steps 3.1 and 3.2 yields $|\sigma_Y-\sigma_M|\le e_M$, where the square roots are nonnegative. Therefore $\sigma_M\to\sigma_Y$.

For fixed real $t$, $|e^{ix}-e^{iy}|\le|x-y|$, obtained by integrating the unit-modulus derivative along the real interval, and [F7] give $|\mathbb Ee^{itS_n/\sqrt n}-\mathbb Ee^{it\sum_{k=1}^nZ_k^{(M)}/\sqrt n}|\le |t|e_M$. Under [A1], [F8]–[F9] prove $S_n/\sqrt n\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_Y^2)$. The case $\sigma_Y^2=0$ is also independently supplied by [F10] using absolute covariance summability from step 3.1. All three regimes and the degenerate case follow.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $Y=(Y_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a process on a probability space whose finite-dimensional laws are invariant under common nonnegative time shifts; call this strict stationarity. For $j\ge0$, set $\mathcal F_j^-:=\sigma(Y_0,\ldots,Y_j)$ and $\mathcal F_j^+:=\sigma(Y_j,Y_{j+1},\ldots)$. For $n\ge1$, define the **strong-mixing coefficient** by
$$\alpha_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{\substack{A\in\mathcal F_j^-\\B\in\mathcal F_{j+n}^+}}|\mathbb P(A\cap B)-\mathbb P(A)\mathbb P(B)|.$$

Define the **uniform-mixing coefficient** by
$$\phi_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{\substack{A\in\mathcal F_j^-\\\mathbb P(A)>0}}\ \sup_{B\in\mathcal F_{j+n}^+}|\mathbb P(B\mid A)-\mathbb P(B)|.$$

For square-integrable real random variables $U,V$ with positive variances, write
$$\operatorname{Corr}(U,V):=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(U,V)}{\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(U)\operatorname{Var}(V)}}.$$
For each $n\ge1$, let $\mathcal C_n$ consist of the triples $(j,U,V)$ such that $j\ge0$, $U,V$ are real and square-integrable, $U$ and $V$ are measurable with respect to $\mathcal F_j^-$ and $\mathcal F_{j+n}^+$ respectively, and both have positive variance. Define the **maximal-correlation coefficient** by
$$\rho_Y(n):=\sup\Bigl(\{0\}\cup\{|\operatorname{Corr}(U,V)|:(j,U,V)\in\mathcal C_n\}\Bigr),$$
where square-integrability is in the sense of [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]. Thus $\rho_Y(n)=0$ when there is no admissible pair, as for a constant process. The process is called strongly mixing, uniformly mixing, or rho-mixing, respectively, when the corresponding coefficient tends to zero. These coefficients are distinct conditions; no implication between them is included in this definition.

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $1 \le p < \infty$. Then
every element of $L^p(\mu)$ can be approximated in $L^p$ by simple functions
whose supports have finite measure.

Assume AC. Let $(Y_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a centered strictly stationary real sequence with $\mathbb E[Y_0^2]<\infty$. If
$$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\rho_Y(n)<\infty,$$
then the covariance series
$$\sigma_Y^2:=\mathbb E[Y_0^2]+2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\operatorname{Cov}(Y_0,Y_k)$$
converges absolutely and is nonnegative. If $\sigma_Y^2>0$, then for $S_n=\sum_{k=1}^nY_k$,
$$n^{-1/2}S_n\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_Y^2).$$
If $\sigma_Y^2=0$, [[lem-zero-long-run-variance-gives-degenerate-clt]] gives the degenerate normal limit.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

derivations.claim: Fix a gap $n\ge1$ and a split $k\ge0$, put $\mathcal A=\sigma(Y_0,\ldots,Y_k)$ and $\mathcal B=\sigma(Y_{k+n},Y_{k+n+1},\ldots)$, and put $\phi=\phi_Y(n)$. Take finite partitions $(A_i)$ in $\mathcal A$ and $(B_j)$ in $\mathcal B$. Write $a_i=\mathbb P(A_i)$, $b_j=\mathbb P(B_j)$, $p_{ij}=\mathbb P(A_i\cap B_j)$, and $d_{ij}=p_{ij}-a_ib_j$. For each fixed $i$ the $d_{ij}$ sum to zero. If $a_i>0$, their positive sum is $\mathbb P(A_i\cap B)-a_i\mathbb P(B)\le\phi a_i$ for $B=\bigcup_{j:d_{ij}>0}B_j$, by [F1]. Hence $\sum_j|d_{ij}|\le2\phi a_i$; when $a_i=0$, every $d_{ij}=0$ and the same bound holds. For each $j$, $|p_{ij}-a_ib_j|\le p_{ij}+a_ib_j$ gives $\sum_i|d_{ij}|\le2b_j$.

For simple $U=\sum_i u_i\mathbf1_{A_i}$ and $V=\sum_j v_j\mathbf1_{B_j}$, [F5] and finite Cauchy–Schwarz with weights $|d_{ij}|$ give $|\operatorname{Cov}(U,V)|=|\sum_{i,j}d_{ij}u_iv_j|\le(\sum_{i,j}|d_{ij}|u_i^2)^{1/2}(\sum_{i,j}|d_{ij}|v_j^2)^{1/2}\le2\sqrt\phi\,\|U\|_2\|V\|_2$, using step 1.1's row and column bounds. The finite Cauchy–Schwarz inequality here is also the probability-space inequality [F2] on a finite set, after normalizing the total weight; if all weights vanish the conclusion is immediate.

For arbitrary real square-integrable $\mathcal A$-measurable $U$ and $\mathcal B$-measurable $V$, choose simple approximants in their respective $L^2$ spaces using [F3]. Their means, norms and product expectations converge by [F2]; therefore step 2.1's inequality passes to the limit. Apply it to $U-\mathbb EU$ and $V-\mathbb EV$ to get $|\operatorname{Cov}(U,V)|\le2\sqrt\phi\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(U)\operatorname{Var}(V)}$. Taking the supremum over positive-variance variables and then splits in [F1] proves $\rho_Y(n)\le2\sqrt{\phi_Y(n)}$. No reversal of the conditioning direction of $\phi$ has been used.

Summation of step 3.1 gives $\sum_{n\ge1}\rho_Y(n)\le2\sum_{n\ge1}\sqrt{\phi_Y(n)}<\infty$. The given stationarity, centering, and second-moment assumptions are exactly those of [F4], so that theorem proves absolute convergence and nonnegativity of the displayed covariance series and $S_n/\sqrt n\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_Y^2)$ for positive or zero $\sigma_Y^2$. Thus every claimed conclusion holds.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Fix $0<\gamma\le1$. Let $1\le d\le4$, $s>0$, $B>0$, and let $X_1,\ldots,X_m,Z$ be independent centered random vectors in $\mathbb R^d$, where $m\ge0$, $|X_j|\le B$ almost surely, and $Z\sim N_d(0,G)$. Suppose $S=Z+\sum_jX_j$ has covariance $sI_d$ and $G\ge\gamma sI_d$ in quadratic form order. There is an absolute constant $C_0\ge1$ such that, with $\tau=C_0B$, the logarithmic moment generating function
$$K(z)=\log\mathbb E e^{z\cdot S},\qquad K(0)=0,$$
has a single analytic branch on the complex Euclidean ball $\tau|z|<1$, and
$$|\partial_u\partial_v^2K(z)|\le\tau s|u||v|^2\qquad(u,v\in\mathbb R^d,\ \tau|z|<1).$$
Here $z\cdot S$ uses the complex bilinear dot product and $|z|^2=\sum_i|z_i|^2$. Every real exponential tilt $\mathbb P_h(d\omega)=e^{h\cdot S-K(h)}\mathbb P(d\omega)$ is defined, and its characteristic function satisfies
$$|\varphi_h(t)|:=|\mathbb E_h e^{it\cdot S}|\le e^{-\gamma s|t|^2/2}\qquad(t,h\in\mathbb R^d),$$
where $K(h)=\log\mathbb E e^{h\cdot S}$ for real $h$, also outside the analytic ball. Put $\kappa=\tau/\sqrt s$. For every fixed $a>0$ and integer $N\ge1$ there is a finite $C_{a,N,\gamma}$, uniform in $1\le d\le4$, such that, if $0<\kappa\le1$,
$$(2\pi)^{-d}\int_{|t|\ge a/\tau}|\varphi_h(t)|\,dt\le C_{a,N,\gamma}\kappa^Ns^{-d/2},$$
$$(2\pi)^{-d}\int_{|t|\ge a/\tau}|t\cdot v||\varphi_h(t)|\,dt\le C_{a,N,\gamma}\kappa^N|v|s^{-(d+1)/2}.$$
All assertions hold with the same $C_0$, $B$, $s$, and $\gamma$ for $AS$, where $A$ is any real $k\times d$ matrix with $1\le k\le d$ and $AA^T=I_k$. This includes every coordinate prefix, every orthogonal change of coordinates, and their compositions. In particular it covers the normalized joint sum and difference of two independent children by applying the assertion in their joint dimension, provided that dimension is at most four and the joint input satisfies the stated covariance assumptions.

Assume AC and the hypotheses of [[lem-gaussian-anchored-sums-have-cumulant-and-fourier-bounds]]: $S=Z+\sum_{i=1}^mX_i\in\mathbb R^d$, $1\le d\le4$, the centered summands are independent, $|X_i|\le B$, $Z$ is Gaussian with covariance $G\ge\gamma sI_d$, and $\operatorname{cov}(S)=sI_d$, where $s,B>0$ and $0<\gamma\le1$. Put $\tau=C_0B$, with $C_0$ from that supplier, and let $\Phi_s$ be the CDF of $N(0,s)$. There are constants $c_\gamma>0$ and $C_\gamma<\infty$, independent of the summand laws, $m,d,s,B$, with the following properties.

For $1\le j\le d$, let $H_j(x',y)$ be the conditional CDF of $S_j$ given $S_{<j}=x'\in\mathbb R^{j-1}$ obtained by dividing the joint prefix density by its marginal density. These densities are strictly positive, so this defines a probability kernel at every $x'$, including prefixes of probability zero. Its quantile transport
$$T_j(x',z)=H_j(x',\cdot)^{-1}(\Phi_s(z))$$
is jointly Borel measurable and takes a fresh $N(0,s)$ variable to that conditional law. If $s\ge C_\gamma\tau^2$, then, with $y=T_j(x',z)$,
$$|y-z|\le C_\gamma\tau\left(1+\frac{|x'|^2+y^2}{s}\right)\quad\hbox{when }|x'|+|y|\le c_\gamma s/\tau,$$
and also
$$|T_j(x',z)-z|\le C_\gamma\tau\left(1+\frac{|x'|^2+z^2}{s}\right)\quad\hbox{when }|x'|+|z|\le c_\gamma s/\tau.$$
For $j=1$, the prefix is empty and its norm is zero. The resulting successive coordinate transport $R$ sends $N_d(0,sI_d)$ to the law of $S$ and satisfies
$$|R(g)-g|\le C_\gamma\tau\left(1+\frac{|R(g)|^2}{s}\right)\quad\hbox{when }|R(g)|\le c_\gamma s/\tau.$$

If $d=2a$ with $a\le2$, write $S=(P,D)$ with $P,D\in\mathbb R^a$. The last $a$ successive conditional transports give a jointly measurable $T_p$ taking a fresh $E\sim N_a(0,sI_a)$ to the conditional law of $D$ given $P=p$, and
$$|T_p(e)-e|\le C_\gamma\tau\left(1+\frac{|p|^2+|T_p(e)|^2}{s}\right)$$
when $s\ge C_\gamma\tau^2$ and $|p|,|T_p(e)|\le c_\gamma s/\tau$. The Gaussian reference bridge $E$ is independent of its Gaussian parent.

There is also the following scalar unequal-variance form. Let $L,R$ be independent centered scalar sums of independent variables bounded by $B$ and independent Gaussian terms, with variances $V_L,V_R\in[s/2,s]$, and with Gaussian component variances at least $\gamma V_L,\gamma V_R$, respectively. Put
$$W=V_L+V_R,\qquad w=V_L/W,\qquad v=V_LV_R/W,\qquad P=L+R,\qquad D=L-wP.$$
Then $W\in[s,2s]$, $w\in[1/3,2/3]$, $v\in[s/4,s/2]$. There is a jointly measurable transport taking a fresh $N(0,v)$ variable to $D$ conditional on $P=p$ with
$$|T_p(e)-e|\le C_\gamma\tau\left(1+\frac{p^2+T_p(e)^2}{s}\right)$$
when $s\ge C_\gamma\tau^2$ and $|p|,|T_p(e)|\le c_\gamma s/\tau$. The corresponding root transport from $N(0,W)$ to $P$ obeys the analogous bound with $|P|^2/s$. The reconstructed children are $L=wP+D$ and $R=(1-w)P-D$.

All these maps are jointly measurable in an additional measurable parameter whenever, on each fixed finite row length, the bounded input laws are probability kernels, their Gaussian covariance and $s$ are measurable functions, and the displayed hypotheses hold parameterwise. This includes countable arrays with different row lengths. No claim here asserts the conditional estimates for raw bounded laws without a positive Gaussian component.

For every natural $n\ge1$, let $\mathbb R^n$ be the set of functions
$x:n\to\mathbb R$ with its finite-product topology and Borel sigma-algebra
([[def-product-topology]], [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Then
$(\mathbb R^n,\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n))$ is standard Borel.

Assume AC. Let $\lambda$ be a probability on $(E\times T,\mathcal S\otimes\mathcal T)$, where E and T are standard-Borel spaces, and let $\beta(B)=\lambda(E\times B)$ be its second marginal. There is a probability kernel $K:(T,\mathcal T)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ such that

$$\lambda(A\times B)=\int_B K(y,A)\,\beta(dy)\quad(A\in\mathcal S,\ B\in\mathcal T).$$

It is unique as a kernel outside a single measurable $\beta$-null set. For every nonnegative product-measurable $f:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$,

$$\int f(x,y)\,\lambda(d(x,y))=\int_T\left(\int_E f(x,y)K(y,dx)\right)\beta(dy).$$

In particular this applies to the joint law of random elements $(X,Y)$, with $\beta=P_Y$; the direction is the law of X given Y.

Assume AC. Let $L,R,C,V$ be random elements in arbitrary measurable spaces. Suppose $L\perp\!\!\!\perp R\mid\sigma(C)$ and that the joint law of $(L,R,C,V)$ is obtained from the law of $(L,R,C)$ by a probability kernel $K(l,c,dv)$ depending only on $(l,c)$. Then
$$(L,V)\perp\!\!\!\perp R\mid\sigma(C),\qquad L\perp\!\!\!\perp R\mid\sigma(C,V).$$
No regular conditional law on an unspecified measurable space is assumed: $K$ is supplied in the hypotheses.

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

For every finite family of events $A_0,\ldots,A_{n-1}$,
$$\mathbb P\!\left(\bigcup_{i<n}A_i\right)\le\sum_{i<n}\mathbb P(A_i).$$
For $n=0$ both sides are $0$.

Assume AC. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then $$\Phi_X(t):=\mathbb E e^{it\cdot X}=\exp(it\cdot m-t^T\Sigma t/2)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R^d).$$ This transform uniquely determines the law, including singular Sigma.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$, $m\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $\Sigma$ be a real symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then its law has Lebesgue density
$$f_{m,\Sigma}(x)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\det(\Sigma)^{-1/2} \exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(x-m)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-m)\right), \qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

derivations.claim: It suffices to construct a coupling of row laws: by [F3] its joint law can be disintegrated given the raw row, and the measure $P(d\omega)K(X(\omega),dg)$ extends any original realization with that coupling law. This is a probability measure: for disjoint product-measurable events, countable additivity follows by monotone convergence inside the kernel integral. The original marginal remains $P$ because the kernel has total mass one. Pad the row to dyadic length $n=2^{\lceil\log_2N\rceil}$, with $n=1$ if $N=1$, by independent extra entries of the law of $X_1$. It suffices to control its first $N$ entries. Set $L=a\log(en)$, where the constant $a$ will depend only on $A$.

Every independent row of centered entries, each either one of the raw laws or $N_d(0,I_d)$, obeys a common Bernstein estimate. For a raw coordinate $Z$, $E|Z|^r\le B^{r-2}$ for $r\ge2$, so for $B|h|<1$ exponential-series expansion gives $\log Ee^{hZ}\le h^2/[2(1-B|h|)]$; the same inequality holds for a standard normal because its log mgf is $h^2/2$. For any block of $s$ entries, multiply the mgfs and apply [F5] to their exponential, using $h=u/(s+Bu)$ and both signs, and then the coordinate union bound. Thus for $t\ge1$, $\Pr\left(\left|\sum_{i\in I}Z_i\right|>C(\sqrt{st}+Bt)\right)\le4e^{-t}.$ The constant is uniform in $d\le2$ and in the individual row laws.

Consider a compressed dyadic row of length $m$, whose odd entries are Gaussian and whose even entries have their prescribed raw laws. For every aligned dyadic interval of length $s\ge4$, both halves contain half Gaussian slots. Its sum has covariance $sI_d$ and Gaussian covariance $(s/2)I_d$. Its joint normalized parent and difference $((U_L+U_R)/\sqrt2,(U_L-U_R)/\sqrt2)$ has covariance $(s/2)I_{2d}$ and Gaussian covariance $(s/4)I_{2d}$. Each bounded contribution to this joint vector has norm at most $B$. Hence [F1] applies with fixed Gaussian fraction $1/2$, also to all coordinate prefixes, and [F2] supplies root and bridge maps. Rescaling the normalized pair only changes universal constants. No identical-distribution assumption was used: each bounded contribution retains its own original index law.

Put $\tau=CB$, with a fixed $C$ covering [F2], and choose a fixed large $H$. Let $m_0$ be the least dyadic integer at least $H\tau^2L$. If $m\ge2m_0$, choose an independent Gaussian root $V_{\rm root}\sim N_d(0,mI_d)$ and independent Gaussian split primitives $Z_I\sim N_d(0,|I|I_d)$ for all dyadic $I$ of length greater than $m_0$. The root map constructs $U_{\rm root}$ from $V_{\rm root}$. Descending the tree, with $U_I,V_I$ present, let $D_I$ be the conditional bridge map of $Z_I$ given target parent $U_I$, and put $U_{I_L}=(U_I+D_I)/2,\quad U_{I_R}=(U_I-D_I)/2,\quad V_{I_L}=(V_I+Z_I)/2,\quad V_{I_R}=(V_I-Z_I)/2.$ The new primitive is independent of the exposed parents. Its Gaussian conditional law therefore does not depend on $U_I-V_I$. The target split has exactly the prescribed conditional law given $U_I$ by [F2].

At terminal blocks sample the entries of the mixed independent row by their regular conditional law given their sum $U_I$, with product kernels over distinct terminal blocks. Recover Gaussian entries given sum $V_I$ by fresh independent standard normals $h_i$ and the formula $g_i=V_I/m_0+h_i-m_0^{-1}\sum_{j\in I}h_j$. For the mixed row, independence of the original disjoint blocks implies that their conditional kernels given their sums factor: check the identity on products of block events by the disintegration formula and extend to all events by uniqueness of probability measures. Induction over the binary splits and then these terminal kernels recovers exactly the mixed row product law. For Gaussians, $(V_I+Z_I)/2$ and $(V_I-Z_I)/2$ have zero cross covariance and covariance $(|I|/2)I_d$; [F6] and induction give the Gaussian product law at each level and after terminal reconstruction. Thus the final two marginal rows have independent entries, despite their coupling.

Apply step 1.2 with $t=L$ to every dyadic mixed sum and to every prefix within a terminal block in either completed marginal row. There are at most $4m$ such vectors; their unconditional product marginal laws were proved in step 3.1. The union bound gives a good event of failure at most $Cm e^{-cL}$ on which each mixed sum satisfies $|U_I|\le C(\sqrt{|I|L}+\tau L)$ and each terminal residual is at most $C(\sqrt{m_0L}+\tau L)$. At an active split of size $s\ge2m_0$, $|D_I|\le|U_{I_L}|+|U_{I_R}|\le C(\sqrt{sL}+\tau L)$. Choose $H$ large enough that both $|U_I|,|D_I|\le cs/\tau$, using the bounds $C/\sqrt H+C/H$ for their ratios to $s/\tau$. Their normalized squares are at most $CL$. The same holds at the root. Consequently [F2] bounds the root and every split discrepancy by $C\tau L$.

At terminal boundaries write $E(k)=\sum_{i\le k}(Z_i-g_i)$. Its endpoint values are zero and $U_{\rm root}-V_{\rm root}$. At the midpoint $h$ of any active interval $[a,b]$, the split formulas give $E(h)=(E(a)+E(b))/2+(D_I-Z_I)/2$. Convexity of the Euclidean norm shows that adding one level increases the maximal boundary error by at most half the maximal split discrepancy at that level. There are at most $\log_2m$ levels. Adding the terminal residuals from step 4.1, and using $m_0<2H\tau^2L$, proves that one round's maximum prefix discrepancy is at most $C\tau L\log(en)$ except on probability $Cm e^{-cL}$. If $m<2m_0$, use instead an independent coupling of the full mixed and Gaussian rows; step 1.2 and a union bound over all their initial prefixes bound their discrepancy by $C(\sqrt{mL}+\tau L)\le C\tau L$, with the same failure bound. This also covers $m=1$ and arbitrarily large $B$.

Start with an independent Gaussian row of length $n$. Apply the round just proved to that row, putting its designated raw law in every even slot and retaining Gaussian odd slots. This is possible while preserving the existing row: disintegrate the coupling given its Gaussian marginal using [F3] and extend by that kernel. Freeze the newly raw entries. The output mixed marginal is a product law, so the retained Gaussian subsequence is independent of all frozen variables. Repeat on that subsequence using a kernel depending only on it; [F4] preserves independence from the frozen complement. At each stage every newly raw coordinate has the law originally designated for that particular original index. If the active length is less than $2m_0$, replace all its remaining slots by independent raw entries instead; step 5.1's terminal bound applies to the raw and Gaussian marginal prefix sums. After at most $\lceil\log_2n\rceil+1$ stages the final full row has exactly the prescribed product of the possibly different raw laws.

A prefix of the original row meets each active subsequence in an initial prefix, so triangle inequality bounds its total change by the sum of the stage maximum prefix errors. Each is at most $C\tau L\log(en)$ and there are at most $C\log(en)$ stages. The total error is therefore at most $C_AB\log^3(en)$. Use the same ambient $L=a\log(en)$ in every stage; since each active length is at most $n$, the total failure probability is at most $Cn\log(en)e^{-ca\log(en)}$. Choose $a$ large enough, depending only on $A$, that this is at most $N^{-A}$, including the finitely small lengths by increasing $a$ once. As $n<2N$ for $N>1$, $\log(en)\le C\log(eN)$. Restricting to the first $N$ coordinates and using step 1.1 proves the claimed estimate and the assertion about preserving an existing raw realization.

boundaries.evidence: Statement and proof step 1.3. The row length is positive; no empty maximum is asserted. Empty raw contribution sets in Gaussian-only subblocks are allowed by the Fourier supplier.
Proof steps 2.1 and 4.1. Zero coordinate values, zero root and split targets, and empty prefixes cause no division by those quantities; all scale denominators s, tau and B are positive.
Proof steps 1.1 and 5.1. N=1 and dimension one are covered by the terminal independent-product construction; the stated failure bound N^(-A)=1 is permitted.

Proof step 3.1. Raw laws may be atomic and their conditional laws singular. Only coarse blocks have Gaussian anchors; terminal laws are sampled by standard-Borel disintegration without density assumptions.

Proof steps 2.1 and 4.1. Every active size exceeds the dyadic stopping threshold, leaving the fixed moderate-region margin required by the quantile supplier. Equality in the bounded norm hypothesis is allowed.

Statement and proof steps 1.1 and 6.1. AC is explicitly assumed and its uses through Gaussian laws and standard-Borel disintegration are declared. The finite iterated kernel extensions preserve all existing marginals.

Above HB²L threshold target bounds yield O(BL) split errors; prefix interpolation and successive replacement each add O(log N), giving B log³(eN). citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ be a countably generated measurable space ([[def-measurable-space]]), $P$ a probability kernel ([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and $\phi$ a nonzero $\sigma$-finite measure ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]) on $\mathcal X$. Write $P^n$ for the $n$-fold kernel iterate. The kernel is **$\phi$-irreducible** if, for every $A\in\mathcal X$ with $\phi(A)>0$ and every $x\in\mathsf X$, there is an integer $n\ge1$ such that $P^n(x,A)>0$. Equivalently, the sum of these nonnegative probabilities over $n\ge1$ is positive. No recurrence or invariant law is part of this definition.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ be countably generated, let $P$ be a probability kernel that is $\phi$-irreducible ([[def-phi-irreducible-chain]]), and let $\phi$ be a nonzero $\sigma$-finite irreducibility measure. Then there are an integer $m\ge1$, a measurable $C$ with $\phi(C)>0$, a probability $
u$ with $
u(C)>0$, and $\epsilon>0$ such that $P^m(x,\cdot)\ge\epsilon
u(\cdot)$ for every $x\in C$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $Q$ be a probability kernel on any measurable space $(X,\mathcal G)$, with invariant probability $\pi$. Let $C\in\mathcal G$ satisfy $\pi(C)>0$, and suppose
$$Q(x,\cdot)\ge\epsilon\nu(\cdot)\quad(x\in C),\qquad 0<\epsilon<1,$$
where $\nu$ is a probability measure. Suppose some $A<\infty$ and $0<\theta<1$ satisfy
$$|\nu Q^n(C)-\pi(C)|\le A\theta^n\quad(n\ge0).$$
For a $Q$-chain started at $x$, put $\sigma_C=\inf\{n\ge0:X_n\in C\}$. Then some $s>1$ makes
$$H(x)=\mathbb E_x[s^{\sigma_C}]\quad\text{measurable},\qquad \pi(H)<\infty,$$
where $s^\infty=\infty$. In particular $H$ is finite $\pi$-almost everywhere; finiteness at every state is not asserted.

For the same hypotheses, the split construction also has the following return and occupation properties. Put $w_1(x)=\epsilon1_C(x)$ and $w_0(x)=1-w_1(x)$. Define $K_{x,1}=\nu$, $K_{x,0}=(Q(x,\cdot)-\epsilon\nu)/(1-\epsilon)$ on $C$, and $K_{x,0}=Q(x,\cdot)$ off $C$. On $X\times\{0,1\}$ use the kernel
$$\widetilde Q((x,i),dy\times\{j\})=K_{x,i}(dy)w_j(y)$$
and invariant law $\widetilde\pi(dx,i)=w_i(x)\pi(dx)$. Its atom $\alpha=C\times\{1\}$ has mass $p=\epsilon\pi(C)>0$. If $Z_0$ has law $\kappa=\widetilde\pi(\cdot\mid\alpha)$ and $\tau=\inf\{n\ge1:Z_n\in\alpha\}$, then some $b>1$ satisfies
$$\mathbb E_\kappa b^\tau<\infty,$$
and for every nonnegative measurable $g$ on the split space,
$$\widetilde\pi(g)=p\,\mathbb E_\kappa\sum_{k=0}^{\tau-1}g(Z_k).$$
In particular $\tau<\infty$ almost surely and $\mathbb E_\kappa\tau=1/p$. These additional assertions use exactly the construction and hypotheses above; they do not assert an exponential entrance-time moment from every state.

Assume AC. Let $\lambda$ be a probability on $(E\times T,\mathcal S\otimes\mathcal T)$, where E and T are standard-Borel spaces, and let $\beta(B)=\lambda(E\times B)$ be its second marginal. There is a probability kernel $K:(T,\mathcal T)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ such that

$$\lambda(A\times B)=\int_B K(y,A)\,\beta(dy)\quad(A\in\mathcal S,\ B\in\mathcal T).$$

It is unique as a kernel outside a single measurable $\beta$-null set. For every nonnegative product-measurable $f:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$,

$$\int f(x,y)\,\lambda(d(x,y))=\int_T\left(\int_E f(x,y)K(y,dx)\right)\beta(dy).$$

In particular this applies to the joint law of random elements $(X,Y)$, with $\beta=P_Y$; the direction is the law of X given Y.
Every finite product of standard Borel spaces, with its finite product sigma-algebra, is standard Borel.
Assume AC. Every standard-Borel space $(E,\mathcal S)$ is measurably isomorphic to a Borel subset of $[0,1]$, including $E=\varnothing$.

A measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$ is **standard Borel** if there are a Polish space $P$ and a bijection $h:E\to P$ such that $A\in\mathcal E$ exactly when $h[A]$ is Borel in $P$. Thus the measurable structure is part of the datum; no particular compatible Polish topology on $E$ is selected.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. A countable product of Polish spaces is Polish, and every $G_\delta$ subspace of a Polish space is Polish.

Assume Choice. For every probability measure $\mu$ and probability kernel $K$
on an arbitrary measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$, the canonical path space
$$ (E^{\mathbb N_0},\mathcal E^{\otimes\mathbb N_0}) $$
carries a unique probability $\mathbb P_\mu$ under which the coordinate maps
form a Markov chain with initial law $\mu$ and transition kernel $K$.

Assume countable choice and dependent choice. For probability spaces
$(E_n,\mathcal E_n,\mu_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ there is a unique probability measure
$\mu$ on $\mathcal C_{\mathbb N}$ such that, for every finite $F$, its
$F$-coordinate marginal is $\bigotimes_{n\in F}\mu_n$.

Assume Choice. Let $(E_n,\mathcal E_n)_{n\ge0}$ be measurable spaces, let
$\mu_0$ be a probability measure on $E_0$, and, for each $n\ge0$, let $K_n$ be
a probability kernel from $E_0\times\cdots\times E_n$ to $E_{n+1}$. There is a
unique probability measure $P$ on
$$ \left(\prod_{n\ge0}E_n,\ \bigotimes_{n\ge0}\mathcal E_n\right) $$ whose finite-prefix laws are the prescribed iterated integrals $$ \mu_0(dx_0)K_0(x_0,dx_1)K_1(x_0,x_1,dx_2)\cdots K_{r-1}(x_0,\ldots,x_{r-1},dx_r). $$
In particular, if every $E_n=E$ and
$K_n(x_0,\ldots,x_n,A)=K(x_n,A)$, the coordinate process is a homogeneous
$K$-chain with initial law $\mu_0$.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $f,g\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$, then
   $$\|f+g\|_p\le\|f\|_p+\|g\|_p.$$
2. If $f,g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\|f+g\|_\infty\le\|f\|_\infty+\|g\|_\infty.$$

Let $K$ be a probability kernel on a measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and let $\pi$ be a
probability measure on $(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). The
probability measure $\pi$ is **invariant** for $K$, and $\pi$ is a
**stationary distribution** of $K$, when

$$(\pi K)(A):=\int_E K(x,A)\,\pi(dx)=\pi(A)\qquad\text{for every }A\in\mathcal E .$$

The set function $\pi K$ is again a probability measure: for fixed $A$ the map
$x\mapsto K(x,A)$ is measurable and lies in $[0,1]$, so the integral exists in
$[0,1]$; for pairwise disjoint $A_n\in\mathcal E$ the identity
$K(x,\bigcup_nA_n)=\sum_nK(x,A_n)$ of the measure $K(x,\cdot)$ and the
monotone convergence theorem for nonnegative functions
([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]) give
$\sigma$-additivity of $\pi K$; and $K(x,E)=1$ for every $x$ gives
$(\pi K)(E)=1$. Thus $(\pi K)(A)=\pi(A)$ is an identity between two probability
measures evaluated at $A$.

A $K$-chain whose initial law is $\pi$ is called **stationary** when
$\pi K=\pi$. Stationarity of the process is a statement about all of its
finite-dimensional laws and is proved, not assumed, from $\pi K=\pi$; see
[[thm-invariant-initial-law-makes-the-chain-stationary]].

On a countable state space $E$ with sigma-algebra $2^E$ and transition matrix
$p(x,y)=K(x,\{y\})$ ([[def-transition-matrix-and-n-step-transition-probabilities]]),
a measure on $E$ is its weighted sum of Dirac masses at singletons
([[thm-measures-on-countable-discrete-spaces-are-weighted-dirac-sums]]), so
invariance is equivalent to the matrix identity

$$\pi(y)=\sum_{x\in E}\pi(x)\,p(x,y)\qquad\text{for every }y\in E .$$

The definition fixes no irreducibility, aperiodicity or uniqueness hypothesis,
and it selects no conditional-expectation versions; the display defines a
single measure $\pi K$ and asserts an identity for it. A transient, periodic or
reducible chain may have several invariant probability measures or none.

For a probability kernel $K$ on $(E,\mathcal E)$, let $I$ be the identity
kernel $I(x,A)=1_A(x)$ and define
$$ K^0:=I,\qquad K^{n+1}:=K^nK, $$ where composition is in chronological order: $$ K^{n+1}(x,A)=\int_E K(y,A)K^n(x,dy). $$
The identity map makes $I$ a probability kernel, including on a one-point
space. Induction using the published kernel-composition lemma shows that every
$K^n$ is a probability kernel. Associativity makes products of several copies
of $K$ unambiguous. No conditional-expectation version is selected and no form
of Choice is used.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

derivations.claim:
For every $\pi$-positive measurable set $A$, the geometric bound implies $P^n(x,A)>0$ for all sufficiently large $n$, for each $x$. Thus $P$ is $\pi$-irreducible. By [F4], a standard-Borel space has a countable generating algebra, so [F1] gives $m\ge1$, $D_0$ with $\pi(D_0)>0$, a probability $
u_0$ with $
u_0(D_0)>0$, and $\epsilon_0>0$ such that $P^m(x,\cdot)\ge\epsilon_0
u_0$ on $D_0$. Choose an integer $K$ so $C=D_0\cap\{M\le K\}$ is positive under both $\pi$ and $
u_0$, and restrict $
u_0$ to $\{M\le L\}$ for a finite integer $L\ge K$, then normalize. Decrease the minorization constant to $0<\epsilon<1$. With $Q=P^m$, the resulting probability $
u$ satisfies $Q(x,\cdot)\ge\epsilon
u$ on $C$, $
u(M)\le L$ and $\pi(C)>0$.

The bridge kernel has a jointly measurable uniform sampler. Code its standard-Borel word space into a Borel subset of $[0,1]$ by [F4]. Its distribution-function evaluations at rational cuts are measurable. The generalized inverse, defined by an infimum over those cuts, is jointly measurable in the endpoints and a uniform variable and has the coded probability law. Its output lies in the coded image almost surely for each endpoint; use a fixed valid word on the Borel complement and decode. For completeness, the word and sequence spaces here are standard Borel: code $S$ into a Borel subset $A\subseteq[0,1]$; $A^{\mathbb N}$ is Borel in the Polish cube by coordinate tests, and finite words are the Borel union of length-marked sequences with fixed trailing coordinates. The extra uniform sequences have the same property.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Fix $0<\gamma\le1$. Let $1\le d\le4$, $s>0$, $B>0$, and let $X_1,\ldots,X_m,Z$ be independent centered random vectors in $\mathbb R^d$, where $m\ge0$, $|X_j|\le B$ almost surely, and $Z\sim N_d(0,G)$. Suppose $S=Z+\sum_jX_j$ has covariance $sI_d$ and $G\ge\gamma sI_d$ in quadratic form order. There is an absolute constant $C_0\ge1$ such that, with $\tau=C_0B$, the logarithmic moment generating function
$$K(z)=\log\mathbb E e^{z\cdot S},\qquad K(0)=0,$$
has a single analytic branch on the complex Euclidean ball $\tau|z|<1$, and
$$|\partial_u\partial_v^2K(z)|\le\tau s|u||v|^2\qquad(u,v\in\mathbb R^d,\ \tau|z|<1).$$
Here $z\cdot S$ uses the complex bilinear dot product and $|z|^2=\sum_i|z_i|^2$. Every real exponential tilt $\mathbb P_h(d\omega)=e^{h\cdot S-K(h)}\mathbb P(d\omega)$ is defined, and its characteristic function satisfies
$$|\varphi_h(t)|:=|\mathbb E_h e^{it\cdot S}|\le e^{-\gamma s|t|^2/2}\qquad(t,h\in\mathbb R^d),$$
where $K(h)=\log\mathbb E e^{h\cdot S}$ for real $h$, also outside the analytic ball. Put $\kappa=\tau/\sqrt s$. For every fixed $a>0$ and integer $N\ge1$ there is a finite $C_{a,N,\gamma}$, uniform in $1\le d\le4$, such that, if $0<\kappa\le1$,
$$(2\pi)^{-d}\int_{|t|\ge a/\tau}|\varphi_h(t)|\,dt\le C_{a,N,\gamma}\kappa^Ns^{-d/2},$$
$$(2\pi)^{-d}\int_{|t|\ge a/\tau}|t\cdot v||\varphi_h(t)|\,dt\le C_{a,N,\gamma}\kappa^N|v|s^{-(d+1)/2}.$$
All assertions hold with the same $C_0$, $B$, $s$, and $\gamma$ for $AS$, where $A$ is any real $k\times d$ matrix with $1\le k\le d$ and $AA^T=I_k$. This includes every coordinate prefix, every orthogonal change of coordinates, and their compositions. In particular it covers the normalized joint sum and difference of two independent children by applying the assertion in their joint dimension, provided that dimension is at most four and the joint input satisfies the stated covariance assumptions.

Assume AC and the hypotheses of [[lem-gaussian-anchored-sums-have-cumulant-and-fourier-bounds]]: $S=Z+\sum_{i=1}^mX_i\in\mathbb R^d$, $1\le d\le4$, the centered summands are independent, $|X_i|\le B$, $Z$ is Gaussian with covariance $G\ge\gamma sI_d$, and $\operatorname{cov}(S)=sI_d$, where $s,B>0$ and $0<\gamma\le1$. Put $\tau=C_0B$, with $C_0$ from that supplier, and let $\Phi_s$ be the CDF of $N(0,s)$. There are constants $c_\gamma>0$ and $C_\gamma<\infty$, independent of the summand laws, $m,d,s,B$, with the following properties.

For $1\le j\le d$, let $H_j(x',y)$ be the conditional CDF of $S_j$ given $S_{<j}=x'\in\mathbb R^{j-1}$ obtained by dividing the joint prefix density by its marginal density. These densities are strictly positive, so this defines a probability kernel at every $x'$, including prefixes of probability zero. Its quantile transport
$$T_j(x',z)=H_j(x',\cdot)^{-1}(\Phi_s(z))$$
is jointly Borel measurable and takes a fresh $N(0,s)$ variable to that conditional law. If $s\ge C_\gamma\tau^2$, then, with $y=T_j(x',z)$,
$$|y-z|\le C_\gamma\tau\left(1+\frac{|x'|^2+y^2}{s}\right)\quad\hbox{when }|x'|+|y|\le c_\gamma s/\tau,$$
and also
$$|T_j(x',z)-z|\le C_\gamma\tau\left(1+\frac{|x'|^2+z^2}{s}\right)\quad\hbox{when }|x'|+|z|\le c_\gamma s/\tau.$$
For $j=1$, the prefix is empty and its norm is zero. The resulting successive coordinate transport $R$ sends $N_d(0,sI_d)$ to the law of $S$ and satisfies
$$|R(g)-g|\le C_\gamma\tau\left(1+\frac{|R(g)|^2}{s}\right)\quad\hbox{when }|R(g)|\le c_\gamma s/\tau.$$

If $d=2a$ with $a\le2$, write $S=(P,D)$ with $P,D\in\mathbb R^a$. The last $a$ successive conditional transports give a jointly measurable $T_p$ taking a fresh $E\sim N_a(0,sI_a)$ to the conditional law of $D$ given $P=p$, and
$$|T_p(e)-e|\le C_\gamma\tau\left(1+\frac{|p|^2+|T_p(e)|^2}{s}\right)$$
when $s\ge C_\gamma\tau^2$ and $|p|,|T_p(e)|\le c_\gamma s/\tau$. The Gaussian reference bridge $E$ is independent of its Gaussian parent.

There is also the following scalar unequal-variance form. Let $L,R$ be independent centered scalar sums of independent variables bounded by $B$ and independent Gaussian terms, with variances $V_L,V_R\in[s/2,s]$, and with Gaussian component variances at least $\gamma V_L,\gamma V_R$, respectively. Put
$$W=V_L+V_R,\qquad w=V_L/W,\qquad v=V_LV_R/W,\qquad P=L+R,\qquad D=L-wP.$$
Then $W\in[s,2s]$, $w\in[1/3,2/3]$, $v\in[s/4,s/2]$. There is a jointly measurable transport taking a fresh $N(0,v)$ variable to $D$ conditional on $P=p$ with
$$|T_p(e)-e|\le C_\gamma\tau\left(1+\frac{p^2+T_p(e)^2}{s}\right)$$
when $s\ge C_\gamma\tau^2$ and $|p|,|T_p(e)|\le c_\gamma s/\tau$. The corresponding root transport from $N(0,W)$ to $P$ obeys the analogous bound with $|P|^2/s$. The reconstructed children are $L=wP+D$ and $R=(1-w)P-D$.

All these maps are jointly measurable in an additional measurable parameter whenever, on each fixed finite row length, the bounded input laws are probability kernels, their Gaussian covariance and $s$ are measurable functions, and the displayed hypotheses hold parameterwise. This includes countable arrays with different row lengths. No claim here asserts the conditional estimates for raw bounded laws without a positive Gaussian component.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

Assume AC. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then $$\Phi_X(t):=\mathbb E e^{it\cdot X}=\exp(it\cdot m-t^T\Sigma t/2)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R^d).$$ This transform uniquely determines the law, including singular Sigma.

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$, $m\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $\Sigma$ be a real symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then its law has Lebesgue density
$$f_{m,\Sigma}(x)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\det(\Sigma)^{-1/2} \exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(x-m)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-m)\right), \qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Let $(S,\Sigma)$ and $(T_i,\Tau_i)$ for $i<n$ be measurable spaces, with
$n<\infty$, and let $K_i:S\to T_i$ be probability kernels with the same
source. There is a unique probability kernel
$$K:S\to\prod_{i<n}T_i$$
whose evaluation on every measurable rectangle is
$$K(s,\prod_{i<n}B_i)=\prod_{i<n}K_i(s,B_i).$$
For $n=0$, the target is the empty-product singleton and $K$ is its point
mass. For $n>0$, the product sigma-algebra is the recursive finite product
sigma-algebra.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Assume AC. Let $L,R,C,V$ be random elements in arbitrary measurable spaces. Suppose $L\perp\!\!\!\perp R\mid\sigma(C)$ and that the joint law of $(L,R,C,V)$ is obtained from the law of $(L,R,C)$ by a probability kernel $K(l,c,dv)$ depending only on $(l,c)$. Then
$$(L,V)\perp\!\!\!\perp R\mid\sigma(C),\qquad L\perp\!\!\!\perp R\mid\sigma(C,V).$$
No regular conditional law on an unspecified measurable space is assumed: $K$ is supplied in the hypotheses.

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

For every finite family of events $A_0,\ldots,A_{n-1}$,
$$\mathbb P\!\left(\bigcup_{i<n}A_i\right)\le\sum_{i<n}\mathbb P(A_i).$$
For $n=0$ both sides are $0$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $n\ge1$, let $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ be independent real random variables on a
common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then
   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$
   in $[0,+\infty]$. In this finite product of expectations, a zero factor
   makes the product zero even when another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise
   multiplication has its usual extended nonnegative meaning.
2. If every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable
   and the same factorization holds in $\mathbb R$.

derivations.claim: For a coordinate $Y$ of one centered atom, $E|Y|^r\le B^{r-2}EY^2$ for every integer $r\ge2$. Absolute exponential-series integration is legitimate because $\sum_r|hY|^r/r!\le e^{B|h|}$; [F6] permits summing its nonnegative absolute terms, and its positive and negative parts then give the signed series identity. For $B|h|<1$, centering cancels the linear term and $r!\ge2$ for $r\ge2$, so $\log Ee^{hY}\le Ee^{hY}-1\le\frac{h^2EY^2}{2(1-B|h|)}.$ A centered Gaussian coordinate has logarithmic mgf $h^2\operatorname{var}(Z)/2$, by completing the square in its positive-variance eigencoordinates using [F3] and [F4]; zero-variance coordinates vanish. Independence multiplies the finitely many atom and Gaussian mgfs. Since their variances add to each coordinate variance of $X_i$, at most $K$, any sum of $s$ entries, also with arbitrary matching Gaussian replacements, has coordinate log mgf at most $Ks h^2/[2(1-B|h|)]$. For a coordinate threshold $u>0$ use $h=u/(Ks+Bu)$ and exponential Markov for both signs. This gives tail at most $2\exp\{-u^2/[2(Ks+Bu)]\}$. The coordinate union bound therefore gives, uniformly in atom counts, $\Pr\!\left(\left|\sum_{i\in I}X_i\right|>C_K[\sqrt{st}+Bt]\right)\le C_K e^{-c_Kt},\qquad t\ge1.$ This holds for every contiguous interval in any compressed ordering.

Consider a dyadic mixed row whose odd entries are independent matching Gaussians and whose even entries have their raw laws. At a node of $s\ge4$ entries let its two child covariance matrices be $U,V$, put $W=U+V$, and, for its target child sums $S_L,S_R$, define $P=S_L+S_R,\qquad H=UW^{-1},\qquad D=S_L-HP,\qquad R=U-UW^{-1}U.$ Independence gives $\operatorname{cov}(P)=W$, $\operatorname{cov}(P,D)=U-WW^{-1}U=0$, and $\operatorname{cov}(D)=R$. The symmetric matrix $R$ equals $UW^{-1}V$ and has inverse $V^{-1}WU^{-1}=U^{-1}+V^{-1}$; hence it is positive definite without assuming commutation. Since each child has $s/2$ entries, [F3] gives $\tfrac s2I\le U,V\le\tfrac{Ks}2I,\qquad sI\le W\le KsI,\qquad \tfrac s4I\le R\le\tfrac{Ks}4I.$ The final inequalities follow by inverting, adding, and reinverting the quadratic form bounds.

The transformed pair $Q=\sqrt s\operatorname{diag}(W^{-1/2},R^{-1/2})(P,D)$ has covariance $sI_{2d}$. A raw atom $x$ in its left or right child contributes respectively $\sqrt s\bigl(W^{-1/2}x,R^{-1/2}VW^{-1}x\bigr),\qquad \sqrt s\bigl(W^{-1/2}x,-R^{-1/2}UW^{-1}x\bigr).$ Their norms are at most $C_KB$, since $\sqrt s\|W^{-1/2}\|\le1$, $\sqrt s\|R^{-1/2}\|\le2$, and $\|UW^{-1}\|,\|VW^{-1}\|\le K/2$. Each child contains half Gaussian entries, so its Gaussian covariance is at least $(s/4)I$, at least $\gamma$ times its total covariance with $\gamma=1/(2K)$. Congruence of quadratic forms therefore makes the Gaussian covariance of $Q$ at least $\gamma sI_{2d}$. All its bounded contributions are the independently transformed original atoms, and all Gaussian contributions combine into an independent Gaussian. Thus [F1] and [F2] apply directly to $Q$, including its coordinate prefixes. The conditioning is on its first $d$ coordinates. Undoing the separate parent and residual whitening, whose inverse norms are bounded by $C_K$, gives a transport of a fresh $E_I\sim N_d(0,R)$ to $D$ conditional on $P=p$, with error $|T_{I,p}(E_I)-E_I|\le C_KB\left(1+\frac{|p|^2+|T_{I,p}(E_I)|^2}{s}\right)$ when $s\ge C_KB^2$ and the two target norms are at most $c_Ks/B$. The root has the analogous transport from $N_d(0,W)$ with error $C_KB(1+|P|^2/s)$. There is no additional factor from the atom counts or from $\sqrt s$.

Temporarily take a dyadic current length $q\le2N$, set $L=a\log(eN)$, and let $q_0$ be the least dyadic integer at least $H_KB^2L$, with $H_K$ to be fixed. Suppose $q\ge2q_0$. Start with an independent Gaussian row having the individual covariances $D_i$. Its root sum and residuals $E_I=V_L-UW^{-1}V_I$ at the active nodes are mutually independent Gaussian vectors of covariances $W_{\rm root}$ and $R_I$: the cross covariances vanish, and independence follows recursively from [F4]. Apply the root transport in step 2.1 and then, descending the tree, set $D_I=T_{I,S_I}(E_I)$ and $S_L=UW^{-1}S_I+D_I,\quad S_R=VW^{-1}S_I-D_I,\quad V_L=UW^{-1}V_I+E_I,\quad V_R=VW^{-1}V_I-E_I.$ Stop at length $q_0$. Each fresh residual is independent of the already exposed parents, so every target split has exactly its prescribed conditional law. For Gaussians the child covariance is $UW^{-1}U+R=U$ and the cross covariance is $UW^{-1}V-R=0$, with the analogous right covariance $V$.

There is an explicit terminal target kernel, also measurable in any supplied environment. In a terminal mixed block let $\mu$ be the product law of its raw positions, let $s(r)$ be their sum, and let $G>0$ be the sum of the matching Gaussian-position covariances. Given the target block sum $u$, sample the raw-position vector from $\frac{q_G(u-s(r))\,\mu(dr)}{\int q_G(u-s(v))\,\mu(dv)}.$ The denominator is finite and strictly positive everywhere by [F4]. Fill the Gaussian positions conditional on their remaining sum $u-s(r)$: for their covariance matrices $C_j$ and fresh independent $h_j\sim N(0,C_j)$, put $H_0=\sum_jh_j$ and $g_j=C_jG^{-1}(u-s(r))+h_j-C_jG^{-1}H_0$. The residual vector has sum zero, zero cross covariance with $H_0$, and covariance blocks $\delta_{ij}C_i-C_iG^{-1}C_j$; thus [F4] identifies its Gaussian conditional law. Multiplying the posterior by the total-sum density and integrating in $u$ proves the original raw/Gaussian product law, first on rectangles and then by monotone approximation. This verifies the terminal conditional law at every sum, without choosing regular conditional versions. Independent terminal kernels and the split laws of step 3.1 consequently recover exactly the entire mixed row product law by induction through the disjoint binary blocks. The existing Gaussian row is unchanged, and already has its required product law.

Use step 1.1 and a union bound for every dyadic target sum and every within-terminal prefix in the completed target and Gaussian rows. There are at most $Cq$ such vectors. Except on probability $C_Kq e^{-c_KL}$, each target sum of size $s$ has norm at most $C_K(\sqrt{sL}+BL)$. The target residual is $D_I=VW^{-1}S_L-UW^{-1}S_R$, so its norm satisfies the same bound with a different $C_K$. At active sizes $s\ge2q_0$, choose $H_K$ large enough that these target norms are at most $c_Ks/B$; their ratios to $s/B$ are bounded by $C_K/\sqrt{H_K}+C_K/H_K$. Their squared norms divided by $s$ are at most $C_KL$. Step 2.1 therefore bounds the root discrepancy and every residual discrepancy $\delta_I=D_I-E_I$ by $C_KBL$. The within-terminal prefix norms are at most $C_K(\sqrt{q_0L}+BL)\le C_KBL$, since $q_0<2H_KB^2L$. No conditional concentration inside a terminal block has been assumed.

Write $e_I=S_I-V_I$. Its child equations are $e_L=UW^{-1}e_I+\delta_I$ and $e_R=VW^{-1}e_I-\delta_I$. For a prefix $P$ ending at a terminal boundary of $I$, let $C_P$ be the sum of its individual covariance matrices. Its discrepancy has the exact expansion $\sum_{i\in P}(X_i-G_i)=C_PW_I^{-1}e_I+\sum_{J\text{ on the boundary path}}M_{J,P}\delta_J.$ If the boundary lies in the left child, $M_{J,P}=C_{\rm partial\ left}W_{J_L}^{-1}$; if it lies in the right child, $M_{J,P}=I-C_{\rm partial\ right}W_{J_R}^{-1}$. To prove the formula, in the left case substitute the child's leading term $C_PU^{-1}e_L$ and cancel $U^{-1}U$; in the right case add $e_L$ to $C_QV^{-1}e_R$, obtaining leading coefficient $(U+C_Q)W^{-1}$ and residual coefficient $I-C_QV^{-1}$. Induction from terminal blocks proves the expansion. This cancellation uses the order $W_{\rm desc}W_{\rm parent}^{-1}W_{\rm parent}W_{\rm grandparent}^{-1}$ and never commutes two matrices. If a partial child has $r$ of its $h$ entries, its coefficient norm is at most $Kr/h\le K$. Hence $\|M_{J,P}\|\le1+K$ and $\|C_PW_I^{-1}\|\le K$. There are at most $\log_2q$ boundary ancestors. The expansion and step 5.1 give terminal-boundary error $C_KBL\log(eq)$; adding its terminal prefix residual gives the same bound for all prefixes.

If $q<2q_0$, couple a raw or mixed row independently to a matching Gaussian row. Their unconditional concentration bounds from step 1.1 and a union bound over prefixes give maximum discrepancy at most $C_K(\sqrt{qL}+BL)\le C_KBL$ except on probability $C_Kq e^{-c_KL}$. This covers the small sizes, including a row of one entry, and large $B$. Thus in all cases a mixed row can be coupled directly to an already realized matching Gaussian row with stage error at most $C_KBL\log(eq)$ and bad probability at most $C_Kq e^{-c_KL}$.

Pad the initial length $m$ to dyadic $q<2m$ by independent $N_d(0,I_d)$ entries; for $m=1$ take $q=1$. These added laws have empty atom sums and preserve all covariance bounds. Let $R^{(0)}$ be the matching independent Gaussian row, saved as the final reference row, and initially mark every position active. Inductively, the current full row consists of independent frozen raw entries and an independent active Gaussian row, all with the designated covariances. When its active length is at least $2q_0$, use that active Gaussian row and fresh terminal randomness in steps 3.1--6.1 to construct the target mixed row, with designated raw laws in even slots and matching Gaussian laws in odd slots. Replace the entire active row by this target row, including its odd coordinates, to obtain $R^{(j+1)}$ from $R^{(j)}$. Freeze the target evens and use the target Gaussian odds as the next active row. The extension kernel depends only on the previous active row, so [F7] makes the entire target independent of the previously frozen complement; its product marginal from step 4.1 makes its new raw evens independent of its Gaussian odds. This proves the induction. At active length below $2q_0$, replace every remaining active coordinate by independent designated raw entries using step 7.1 and stop. After at most $C\log(eN)$ stages, the final row $R^{(J)}$ has the intended raw product law. The saved row $R^{(0)}$ retains its Gaussian product law, although subsequent active Gaussian rows need not equal its corresponding coordinates.

Write $\Delta_j(k)=\sum_{i\le k}(R_i^{(j+1)}-R_i^{(j)})$. Frozen entries do not change at stage $j$, and every original prefix meets its active positions in an initial compressed prefix. Thus the stage estimate in steps 6.1--7.1 bounds $\max_k|\Delta_j(k)|$ by $C_KBL\log(eN)$ outside its stage bad event; this includes all changes to target Gaussian odds. The exact identity $\sum_{i\le k}(R_i^{(J)}-R_i^{(0)})=\sum_{j=0}^{J-1}\Delta_j(k)$ and triangle inequality therefore give total error at most $C_{A,K}B\log^3(eN)$. Each stage has the Gaussian input marginal and mixed target marginal used in its estimate by step 8.1, so its unconditional bad probability remains at most $C_Kq_j e^{-c_KL}$, where $q_j\le2N$ is its active length. With the same ambient $L=a\log(eN)$, a union bound over at most $C\log(eN)$ stages gives $C_KN\log(eN)e^{-c_Ka\log(eN)}$. Choose $a$ sufficiently large depending only on $A,K$ to make this at most $N^{-A}$ for all $N\ge1$. Taking $X=R^{(J)}$, $G=R^{(0)}$ and restricting to the first $m$ entries proves the numerical assertion.

For the parameter assertion, every entry law is a measurable kernel obtained by applying addition to the finite product of its supplied atom and Gaussian kernels, using [F5]. Covariance entries are measurable integrals. In dimensions one and two positive definite inverse square roots are continuous functions of their matrices: in dimension two, for $C>0$, $C^{1/2}=(C+\sqrt{\det C}\,I)/\sqrt{\operatorname{tr}C+2\sqrt{\det C}}$, as verified in an eigenbasis by [F3]; the semidefinite zero case is defined by zero and the formula extends continuously. Thus the Gaussian starts and all transforms in steps 1.2, 2.1 depend measurably on the parameter. Mixed transformed joint and prefix densities are Gaussian convolution integrals of their raw product kernels, so are jointly measurable by [F5] and strictly positive. Their conditional CDFs are measurable density-ratio integrals. The coordinate quantiles in [F2] are measurable rational infima of those CDFs; hence its root and residual maps are jointly measurable in the parameter and all spatial inputs. The terminal posterior in step 4.1 is likewise a measurable kernel with positive measurable denominator, followed by the explicit Gaussian bridge kernel. Finite kernel products and successive extensions preserve measurability: for one extension define its law by integrating the next kernel against the preceding law; [F5] gives measurable evaluations and [F6] gives countable additivity by monotone convergence of disjoint indicator sums. Iterating this finite construction gives a coupling kernel $Q_\theta$, and every previous marginal and probability bound holds at each parameter. No pointwise selection of conditional-law versions or coupling laws is used.

Proof steps 1.2, 2.1 and 4.1. Zero atoms and zero original Gaussian terms are allowed. The matrix inverses are only of block covariances W,R and Gaussian anchor aggregates, all explicitly positive definite.
Proof steps 7.1 and 9.1. m=N=1 and a one-entry active row are handled by the independent short-row coupling and Bernstein bound, with ambient log(eN)>=1.

Proof steps 1.1, 2.1 and 4.1. Individual atoms and original Gaussian terms may be degenerate. Their total entry covariances lie between I and KI; the mixed Gaussian anchors whiten to a fixed positive covariance fraction.
