The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $P$ be a probability kernel on an arbitrary measurable space $(X,\mathcal F)$, with invariant probability $\pi$, finite measurable $M:X\to[0,\infty)$ and $0<r<1$ satisfying
$$\|P^n(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le M(x)r^n\quad(x\in X,\ n\ge1).$$
Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be finite measurable. For each specified initial law $\mu$, there are a nonempty standard-Borel space $S$, a probability kernel $T$ on $S$, an invariant probability $\widehat\pi$, an initial probability $\widehat\mu$, and finite measurable functions $\varphi:S\to\mathbb R$ and $\widehat M:S\to[0,\infty)$ such that
$$\|T^n(z,\cdot)-\widehat\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le\widehat M(z)r^n\quad(z\in S,\ n\ge1).$$
The complete observation path $(f(X_n))_{n\ge0}$ of a $\mu$-started $P$-chain has the same law as $(\varphi(Y_n))_{n\ge0}$ of a $\widehat\mu$-started $T$-chain. The corresponding stationary observation paths also have the same law, and $\widehat\pi(|\varphi|^a)=\pi(|f|^a)$ for every $a>0$, with infinity allowed. The factor may depend on $\mu$.

Moreover, any joint law of that observation path with a random element of a standard-Borel space can be lifted to an extension preserving the entire original chain probability space and process.

Assume AC. Let $P$ be a probability kernel on a nonempty standard-Borel space $(S,\mathcal S)$, with invariant probability $\pi$, finite measurable $M:S\to[0,\infty)$ and $0<r<1$ such that
$$\|P^n(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le M(x)r^n\quad(x\in S,\ n\ge1).$$
Let $f:S\to\mathbb R$ be finite measurable, with $\pi(f)=0$ and $\pi(|f|^v)<\infty$ for some $v>1$. For every initial law, on an extension preserving the given chain there are an integer $m\ge1$, an almost surely finite delay $D\in m\mathbb N$, a standard-Borel seed space $E$, iid seeds $(U_j)_{j\ge0}$, and measurable finite-word and length functions $W:E^2\to\bigsqcup_{k\ge1}S^k$ and $L:E\to m\mathbb N$ with the following properties.

Put $T_0=D$ and $T_{j+1}=T_j+L(U_j)$. Almost surely, simultaneously for all $j\ge0$,
$$\bigl(X_{T_j},\ldots,X_{T_{j+1}-1}\bigr)=W(U_j,U_{j+1}).$$
Write $L_j=L(U_j)$, $Z_j=\sum_{t=T_j}^{T_{j+1}-1}f(X_t)$, and $H_j=\sum_{t=T_j}^{T_{j+1}-1}|f(X_t)|$. Then $Z_j=z(U_j,U_{j+1})$ and $H_j=h(U_j,U_{j+1})$ for measurable functions $z,h$, and
$$\mathbb E e^{aL_0}<\infty\text{ for some }a>0,\qquad 0<\mu_L:=\mathbb EL_0<\infty,$$
$$\mathbb EZ_0=0,\qquad \mathbb EH_0^q<\infty\quad(1\le q<v).$$
For every nonnegative measurable $b:S\to[0,\infty]$ the full-tour occupation identity is
$$\mathbb E\sum_{t=T_0}^{T_1-1}b(X_t)=\mu_L\pi(b).$$
For each specified initial law, the same $m$, iid seed law, $W,L$ and post-delay tour law can be used also for the invariant initial law $\pi$; only the finite initial segment and coupling change.

In particular $(L_j-\mu_L,Z_j)$ is an adjacent-iid centered vector sequence, while the lengths themselves are iid. Full tour words or rewards are not asserted to be iid. No moment of $D$ or of the initial finite prefix is required, and the construction uses a useful multistep split chosen from $P$ rather than requiring any supplied one-step minorization to have positive stationary mass.

Assume AC. Let $1\le d\le2$, let $(E,\mathcal E)$ be standard Borel, and let $(U_i)_{i\ge0}$ be iid $E$-valued random elements with law $\nu$. Let $h:E^2\to\mathbb R^d$ be measurable with
$$\mathbb E h(U_0,U_1)=0,\qquad \mathbb E|h(U_0,U_1)|^q<\infty$$
for some finite $q>2$. Put $X_i=h(U_i,U_{i+1})$, and define
$$\Gamma=\mathbb E[X_0X_0^T]+\mathbb E[X_0X_1^T]+\mathbb E[X_1X_0^T].$$
Then $\Gamma$ is positive semidefinite. For every fixed $2<p<q$, on an extension preserving the entire original process there are independent centered Gaussian vectors $G_i$ with covariance $\Gamma$ such that
$$\max_{1\le k\le n}\left|\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}(X_i-G_i)\right|=o(n^{1/p})\qquad\hbox{almost surely}.$$
The extension can also carry a standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion $B$ with $\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}G_i=\Gamma^{1/2}B(k)$ for every integer $k\ge0$. Singular $\Gamma$, including $\Gamma=0$, is allowed. Neither the Gaussian row nor $B$ is required to be independent of the original process.

Assume AC. Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be iid centered vectors in $\mathbb R^2$ with $E\|X_1\|^q<\infty$ for some $q>2$. For any fixed real numbers $2<p<a<q$, on an extension preserving the original process there are independent Gaussian vectors $G_i\sim N_2(0,\Sigma)$, where $\Sigma=EX_1X_1^T$, such that almost surely
$$\max_{1\le k\le n}\left\|\sum_{i=1}^k(X_i-G_i)\right\|=O\bigl(n^{1/a}[\log(en)]^3\bigr)=o(n^{1/p}).$$
The extension can also carry a standard two-dimensional Brownian motion $B$ with $\sum_{i=1}^kG_i=\Sigma^{1/2}B(k)$ for every integer $k\ge0$. Thus, in particular, the partial-sum Brownian approximation error is $O(n^{1/p}\log n)$ almost surely. Singular covariance, including $\Sigma=0$, is permitted. Neither $B$ nor $(G_i)$ is required to be independent of $(X_i)$.

Assume AC. Let $\mathcal G$ be a sigma-algebra on a probability space, let $\lambda>0$, and let $N=(N(t))_{t\ge0}$ be $\mathcal G$-measurable at each time. Suppose $N(0)=0$, its paths are nondecreasing right-continuous integer-valued functions finite on bounded intervals, its increments on disjoint time intervals are independent, and $N(t)-N(s)$ has law $\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda(t-s))$ for $0\le s<t$. Let $B$ be a standard Brownian motion independent of $\mathcal G$.

On an extension preserving the original probability space there is a standard Brownian motion $W$, independent of $\mathcal G$, such that
$$\sup_{0\le t\le n}\left|B(t)-\lambda^{-1/2}W(N(t))\right|=O((\log(n+2))^2)\qquad\text{almost surely as }n\to\infty.$$
The almost-sure bound has a finite random constant and a finite random starting index. In particular $W$ is independent of the entire Poisson clock; $W$ and $B$ are not asserted to be independent.

Fix $q>p>2$. Let $(Z_k)_{k\ge1}$ be identically distributed centered real random variables with $\mathbb E|Z_1|^q<\infty$. Assume either that they are independent, or that they are **one-dependent**, meaning that $\sigma(Z_1,\ldots,Z_k)$ and $\sigma(Z_{k+2},Z_{k+3},\ldots)$ are independent for every $k\ge1$. Put $S_0=0$ and $S_j=\sum_{k=1}^jZ_k$.

There is an event of probability one on which, for every $A>0$ and $d\ge0$, with $r_n=\lceil A n^{1/p}(\log n)^d\rceil$ for $n\ge2$,
$$\max_{\substack{0\le i<j\le n\\j-i\le r_n}}|S_j-S_i|=o(n^{1/p}).$$

Let $T>0$, $\theta>0$, and let $S=(0,T]$ carry its subspace topology and
Borel sigma-algebra. This space is Hausdorff as a subspace of $\mathbb R$;
rational intervals give a countable base; and each $x\in S$ has a compact
neighborhood $[x-\delta,x+\delta]\cap S$ for some $0<\delta<x$. Let $\ell$
be Lebesgue measure restricted to $S$. There exists a Poisson point process
on $S$ with intensity measure $\nu_\theta(B)=\theta\ell(B)$. Its total
count is finite almost surely, its event times have no ties almost surely,
and for every integer $m\ge0$ the joint density of the ordered event times
$$0<t_1<\cdots<t_m\le T,\qquad N(S)=m,$$
with respect to $m$-dimensional Lebesgue measure on the ordered simplex is
$$e^{-\theta T}\theta^m.$$
For $m>0$, conditional on $N(S)=m$, the ordered event times have density
$m!/T^m$. For $m=0$ the empty-pattern probability is $e^{-\theta T}$.

For a finite parameter $\lambda\ge0$, the **Poisson count law**
$\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)$ is the probability measure on
$\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ whose masses are
$$\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)\{k\}=e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^k}{k!},\qquad k\in\mathbb N_0,$$
when $\lambda>0$, and is the point mass at $0$ when $\lambda=0$. The
normalization and the moment and generating-function identities used below are
proved in [[lem-poisson-count-law-normalization-and-moments]]. The separate
extended convention for a Poisson point-process count on a Borel set of infinite
intensity is that the count equals $+\infty$ almost surely; it is not a finite
Poisson probability law.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$

The measurable space $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$ with its usual
topology is standard Borel.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. A countable product of Polish spaces is Polish, and every $G_\delta$ subspace of a Polish space is Polish.

Assume AC. Let $\lambda$ be a probability on $(E\times T,\mathcal S\otimes\mathcal T)$, where E and T are standard-Borel spaces, and let $\beta(B)=\lambda(E\times B)$ be its second marginal. There is a probability kernel $K:(T,\mathcal T)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ such that

$$\lambda(A\times B)=\int_B K(y,A)\,\beta(dy)\quad(A\in\mathcal S,\ B\in\mathcal T).$$

It is unique as a kernel outside a single measurable $\beta$-null set. For every nonnegative product-measurable $f:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$,

$$\int f(x,y)\,\lambda(d(x,y))=\int_T\left(\int_E f(x,y)K(y,dx)\right)\beta(dy).$$

In particular this applies to the joint law of random elements $(X,Y)$, with $\beta=P_Y$; the direction is the law of X given Y.

Assume Choice. Let $(E_n,\mathcal E_n)_{n\ge0}$ be measurable spaces, let
$\mu_0$ be a probability measure on $E_0$, and, for each $n\ge0$, let $K_n$ be
a probability kernel from $E_0\times\cdots\times E_n$ to $E_{n+1}$. There is a
unique probability measure $P$ on
$$ \left(\prod_{n\ge0}E_n,\ \bigotimes_{n\ge0}\mathcal E_n\right) $$ whose finite-prefix laws are the prescribed iterated integrals $$ \mu_0(dx_0)K_0(x_0,dx_1)K_1(x_0,x_1,dx_2)\cdots K_{r-1}(x_0,\ldots,x_{r-1},dx_r). $$
In particular, if every $E_n=E$ and
$K_n(x_0,\ldots,x_n,A)=K(x_n,A)$, the coordinate process is a homogeneous
$K$-chain with initial law $\mu_0$.

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

Let $\mu$ be a measure and let $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be measurable. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k).$$

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ one also has

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k<m}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k<m}\mu(E_k),$$

including $m=0$, where both sides are $0$.

Let $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be events in a probability space. If
$$\sum_{n=0}^\infty \mathbb P(A_n)<+\infty,$$
then
$$\mathbb P(A_n\ \mathrm{i.o.})=0.$$

No independence hypothesis is needed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. A real process
$B=(B_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **standard Brownian motion** if:

1. $B_0=0$ almost surely;
2. for every finite list $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_n$, the increments
   $B_{t_j}-B_{t_{j-1}}$ are mutually independent and have laws
   $N(0,t_j-t_{j-1})$; and
3. there is one measurable event $A$ with $P(A)=1$ such that
   $t\mapsto B_t(\omega)$ is continuous on $[0,\infty)$ for every
   $\omega\in A$.

By
[[lem-brownian-gaussian-covariance-is-equivalent-to-independent-stationary-normal-increments]],
the first two clauses are equivalent to saying that $B$ is a centered Gaussian
process with covariance $\min(s,t)$. Clause 3 is additional: it cannot be
recovered from finite-dimensional distributions alone.

No filtration is part of this definition. In particular, no completed or
right-continuous filtration and no Markov or martingale assertion is silently
imposed. Modifications and indistinguishability retain the distinct meanings in
[[def-law-modification-and-indistinguishability-of-processes]]. The cases
$n=0$, $t_1=0$, and zero-length increments are respectively vacuous or already
covered by $B_0=0$; the increment list itself is strictly increasing.

Choice is declared because the normal-law and Gaussian/increment-equivalence
interfaces construct and identify normal laws under AC. The continuity clause
selects no path and makes no additional use of choice.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(U,V)$ be a jointly multivariate-normal real
vector with finite-dimensional blocks $U\in\mathbb R^p$ and
$V\in\mathbb R^q$, where $p,q\ge1$. If $\operatorname{Cov}(U_i,V_j)=0$ for every
$1\le i\le p$ and $1\le j\le q$, then $U$ and $V$ are independent. The
covariance matrix may be singular.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. The canonical centered Gaussian coordinate process
with covariance $E[X_sX_t]=\min(s,t)$ has a continuous modification $B$, and
$B$ is a standard Brownian motion. In particular, standard Brownian motion
exists.

Assume countable choice and dependent choice. For probability spaces
$(E_n,\mathcal E_n,\mu_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ there is a unique probability measure
$\mu$ on $\mathcal C_{\mathbb N}$ such that, for every finite $F$, its
$F$-coordinate marginal is $\bigotimes_{n\in F}\mu_n$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, let $B$ be a standard Brownian motion
[[def-brownian-motion]]. Use the everywhere-continuous, zero-start
representative fixed in [[thm-brownian-reflection-principle]]: replace the
path by zero outside a measurable probability-one event of continuity and
zero start, retaining the notation $B$. Let $t>0$ and
$M_t:=\sup_{0\le s\le t}B_s$. This is a finite nonnegative random variable:
continuity gives boundedness on $[0,t]$ and identifies its supremum with the
supremum over the countable dense set $(\mathbb Q\cap[0,t])\cup\{t\}$.
With
$\Phi$ the standard normal distribution function,
$\Phi(x)=N(0,1)((-\infty,x])$
[[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]]
[[def-cumulative-distribution-function-of-a-random-variable]], one has for
every $x\ge0$
$$P(M_t\le x)=2\Phi\!\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt t}\right)-1 .$$
Consequently $M_t$ has the same law as $|B_t|$, and on $x>0$ the law of $M_t$
has the density
$$f(x)=\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi t}}\,\exp\!\left(-\frac{x^2}{2t}\right).$$

Let $\varphi(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}$ and
$\overline\Phi(x)=\int_x^\infty\varphi(y)\,dy$ for $x\in\mathbb R$. Then for
every $x>0$
$$\frac{x\,\varphi(x)}{1+x^2}\ \le\ \overline\Phi(x)\ \le\ \frac{\varphi(x)}{x},$$
and consequently, for every $x>1$,
$$\Bigl(\frac1x-\frac1{x^3}\Bigr)\varphi(x)\ \le\ \overline\Phi(x)\ \le\ \frac{\varphi(x)}{x}.$$
Both bounds are sharp as $x\to\infty$ in the sense that the ratio of each side
to $\overline\Phi(x)$ tends to $1$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $P$ be a probability kernel on a measurable space
$(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ with invariant probability $\pi$. Assume it is
$\phi$-irreducible
([[def-phi-irreducible-chain]]), aperiodic
([[def-general-state-aperiodic-markov-chain]]), and Harris recurrent relative
to its nonzero $\sigma$-finite irreducibility measure $\phi$
([[def-harris-recurrent-markov-chain]]). Suppose $P$ is geometrically
ergodic in the sense of
[[def-geometric-and-uniform-ergodicity-for-mcmc-clt]]. Then there exist a
measurable $M:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ with $\pi(M)<\infty$ and $r\in(0,1)$ such
that
$$\|P^n(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le M(x)r^n\quad(x\in\mathsf X,\ n\ge1).$$

In fact, the same conclusion holds assuming only AC, invariance of $\pi$, and the everywhere finite measurable common geometric-rate bound in [[def-geometric-and-uniform-ergodicity-for-mcmc-clt]], on the original arbitrary measurable space. The construction below derives the needed irreducibility on a restricted sigma-field directly from that bound.

Assume AC. Let $(X_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a stationary time-homogeneous Markov chain
with invariant probability $\pi$. Suppose there are a measurable
$M:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ with $\pi(M)<\infty$ and $r\in(0,1)$ such that
$$\|P^n(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le M(x)r^n\quad\text{for every }x\in\mathsf X,\ n\ge1.$$
Then the strong-mixing coefficient of the stationary process satisfies
$$\alpha_X(n)\le\pi(M)r^n\quad(n\ge1).$$

Let $X=(X_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a strictly stationary process on a measurable state
space and let $h$ be a measurable real-valued function. Put $Y_k=h(X_k)$.
Then $Y$ is strictly stationary and, for every $n\ge1$,
$$\alpha_Y(n)\le\alpha_X(n),\qquad \phi_Y(n)\le\phi_X(n),\qquad \rho_Y(n)\le\rho_X(n),$$
where the coefficients are as in
[[def-mixing-coefficients-for-stationary-markov-chain]].

Assume AC. Let $(Y_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a centered strictly stationary real sequence with $\mathbb E[Y_0^2]<\infty$, and define $S_n=\sum_{k=1}^nY_k$. Each of the following is sufficient:

1. There is $B<\infty$ with $|Y_0|\le B$ almost surely and $\sum_{n\ge1}\alpha_Y(n)<\infty$.
2. For some $\delta>0$, $\mathbb E|Y_0|^{2+\delta}<\infty$ and $\sum_{n\ge1}\alpha_Y(n)^{\delta/(2+\delta)}<\infty$.
3. For some $a\in(0,1)$, $\alpha_Y(n)=O(a^n)$ and $\mathbb E[Y_0^2\log^+|Y_0|]<\infty$, where $\log^+u=\max(0,\log u)$ for $u>0$ and $0\log^+0:=0$.

In each case the covariance series
$$\sigma_Y^2:=\mathbb E[Y_0^2]+2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\operatorname{Cov}(Y_0,Y_k)$$
converges absolutely and is nonnegative, and
$$n^{-1/2}S_n\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_Y^2).$$
This includes the degenerate law $N(0,0)$ when $\sigma_Y^2=0$, as in [[lem-zero-long-run-variance-gives-degenerate-clt]]. The coefficient $\alpha_Y$ and strict stationarity have the meanings in [[def-mixing-coefficients-for-stationary-markov-chain]].

Let $X_n$ and $Y_n$ be Borel-measurable random elements with values in a metric space $S$, on the same probability space for each $n$, and let $X$ be an $S$-valued Borel-measurable random element. Suppose $d(X_n,Y_n)$ is measurable and $P(d(X_n,Y_n)>\varepsilon)\to0$ for every $\varepsilon$>0. If $X_n\Rightarrow X$, then $Y_n\Rightarrow X$.

Assume AC. If $X$ has law $N(m,\sigma^2)$ with $\sigma\ge0$, then $\varphi_X(t)=\exp(imt-\sigma^2t^2/2)$ for every real $t$. Moreover $\mathbb EX=m$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\sigma^2$, including $\sigma=0$.

Let $(X_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a stationary time-homogeneous Markov chain with invariant probability $\pi$, and let $f$ be real Borel with $\pi(f)=0$ and $\pi(f^2)<\infty$. For $k\ge0$, set $\gamma_k:=\operatorname{Cov}_{\pi}(f(X_0),f(X_k))$. When the Markov-chain CLT $n^{-1/2}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}f(X_k)\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_f^2)$ holds with finite variance parameter and $\sum_{k\ge1}|\gamma_k|<\infty$, the **covariance long-run variance** is
$$\sigma^2_{\mathrm{LR}}(f):=\gamma_0+2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\gamma_k.$$

This definition does not infer a CLT from covariance summability, or infer that a weak-limit variance equals the covariance sum. Whenever $\sigma^2_{\mathrm{LR}}(f)$ is used as the variance parameter in a CLT or MCSE claim, that equality must be established by the theorem being applied. For example, the local Poisson-equation theorem proves the equality under its square-integrable solution hypotheses.

derivations.claim: Put $P_0=2+\delta$, $Q_0=2+\delta+\varepsilon$, and $f=g-\pi g$. The given moment makes $\pi|g|<\infty$, since $|g|\le1+|g|^{Q_0}$, and the finite-sum power inequality gives $\pi|f|^{Q_0}<\infty$. Choose $P_0<p<q<Q_0$ and set $b=1/p<1/P_0<1/2$. To obtain exactly the requested observation indices, apply [F1] to the chain starting at $X_1$, with its actual initial law, and observable $f$. This gives a standard-Borel factor retaining the full path $(f(X_1),f(X_2),\ldots)$, the stationary path and its moments, and an everywhere finite common geometric bound. Work on this factor until the original-space lift at the end. Apply [F2] there, retaining its finite prefix and integer delay $D$. Define $F(t)$ to be the sum of the first $\lfloor t\rfloor$ centered observations of the retained tail beginning at calendar position $D$, with the empty sum zero. This real-time tail process has cycle lengths $L_j$, centered rewards $Z_j$, envelopes $H_j$, and relative boundaries $T_0=0$, $T_k=\sum_{j<k}L_j$. Then $F(T_k)=\sum_{j<k}Z_j$, $\mathbb EH_0^q<\infty$, and $\mu=\mathbb EL_0\in[1,\infty)$. The pair $(Z_j,L_j-\mu)$ is a centered adjacent-iid vector in $L^q$; exponential length moments and $|Z_j|\le H_j$ verify its two coordinate moments. No iid assertion about the full tours is used.

Apply [F3] jointly to $(Z_j,L_j-\mu)$. Write its long-run covariance as $\Gamma=\begin{pmatrix}u&c\\c&s^2\end{pmatrix}\ge0$. Since the lengths are iid, $s^2=\operatorname{Var}(L_0)$; the reward and cross entries still include their actual lag-one terms. The Gaussian approximation gives a continuous centered Gaussian vector process $A$ of covariance $\min(t,r)\Gamma$ such that $\max_{k\le n}|F(T_k)-A_1(k)|=o(n^b)$ and $\max_{k\le n}|T_k-\mu k-A_2(k)|=o(n^b)$. For now suppose $s>0$. Put $a=c/s^2$ and $v^2=u-c^2/s^2\ge0$. Then $B_0=A_2/s$ is standard Brownian. If $v>0$, $B=(A_1-aA_2)/v$ is standard Brownian independent of the entire process $B_0$: each finite stack is jointly Gaussian and every cross-covariance is $(c-as^2)\min(t,r)=0$, so [F10] gives independence on finite rational-time cylinders and continuity extends it to all times. If $v=0$, the residual Gaussian process is zero on rational times almost surely and hence identically zero; adjoin an independent unused $B$. Thus, with independent $B,B_0$, we have $\max_{k\le n}|F(T_k)-a(T_k-\mu k)-vB(k)|=o(n^b)$ and $\max_{k\le n}|T_k-\mu k-sB_0(k)|=o(n^b)$. This regression uses the full $c=\Gamma_{12}$, not just the covariance inside a single cycle.

Define $\gamma=s^2/\mu$ and $\lambda=\mu^2/s^2$, so $\lambda\gamma=\mu$ and $\gamma\sqrt\lambda=s$. Choose any fixed $r>p$ and $r<a_1<q_1<\infty$. Apply [F4] to the centered iid scalar Poisson variables $C_i-\lambda$, embedded as $(C_i-\lambda,0)$, obtaining a joint law with a standard Brownian driver $B'_0$ and $\max_{k\le n}|\sum_{i=1}^kC_i-\lambda k-\sqrt\lambda B'_0(k)|=o(n^{1/r})$. Their moments of every order follow directly from the Poisson exponential series in [F7]. By [F8], disintegrate this joint law to a kernel for the entire count sequence given the integer driver sequence, and evaluate it at the already present $(B_0(k))_{k\ge0}$. This preserves all original variables and reproduces the asserted count/driver joint law. The kernel depends only on $B_0$ and is sampled using new randomness independent of everything earlier, so $B$ remains independent of the joint pair $(B_0,(C_i)_i)$. Conditional on $C_i=m$, insert $m$ independent uniform positions in $(i-1,i]$, independently over unit intervals and of earlier variables given the counts. By [F7] these are the exact finite-window Poisson laws. More explicitly, partitioning a unit interval into lengths $d_j$ gives multinomial conditional counts; summing their mass against $\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)$ yields the product $\prod_j e^{-\lambda d_j}(\lambda d_j)^{k_j}/k_j!$. Hence the resulting locally finite simple right-continuous clock $N$ has independent Poisson increments of rate $\lambda$, $N(k)=\sum_{i\le k}C_i$, and remains independent of $B$ jointly with $B_0$.

Two uniform bounds control the remaining calendar errors. By the common $q$th envelope moment and [F9], $\mathbb P(\max_{j\le C2^h}H_j>\eta2^{h/p})\le C'\eta^{-q}2^{h(1-q/p)}$, summable in $h$. Intersecting Borel–Cantelli events over positive rational $\eta$ and integer $C$ yields $\max_{j\le Cn}H_j=o(n^b)$ without any independence requirement. For any standard Brownian motion and fixed $A,C>0$, cover $[0,C2^h]$ by overlapping intervals of length $2A\cdot2^{hb}$. Every pair of times at distance at most $A\cdot2^{hb}$ lies in one such interval, and [F10] bounds the oscillation tail at $K\sqrt{2^{hb}h}$ by $4e^{-cK^2h}$. There are at most $C'2^{h(1-b)}+2$ intervals. Taking $K$ large and using [F9] gives the uniform modulus $O(n^{b/2}\sqrt{\log n})=o(n^b)$ for windows of length $An^b$; for fixed window length the same proof gives $O(\sqrt{\log n})$. All fixed integer $A,C$ can be placed on one event. Finally [F6] applies to the centered one-dependent rewards $Z_j$, so their partial-sum increments over at most $An^b$ consecutive cycle indices, among the first $Cn$ indices, are uniformly $o(n^b)$. A finite random bound for $A$ or $C$ is covered by their countably many integer choices.

We record the uniform estimates used for this clock and for Brownian motion. Summing the Poisson mass series gives $\mathbb E e^{\theta(N(v)-N(u)-\lambda(v-u))}=\exp(\lambda(v-u)(e^\theta-1-\theta))$. The exponential series and $k!\ge2\cdot3^{k-2}$ for $k\ge2$ give $e^\theta-1-\theta\le\theta^2/[2(1-|\theta|/3)]$ for $|\theta|<3$. Exponential Markov with parameter $x/(\lambda(v-u)+x/3)$ and either sign therefore bounds the increment deviation tail by $2\exp[-c_\lambda\min\{x^2/(v-u),x\}]$. On dyadic horizons $n$, take $x=K(\sqrt{(v-u)\log(n+2)}+\log(n+2))$ and union over the at most $(Cn+1)^2$ integer intervals in $[0,Cn]$. A sufficiently large deterministic $K$ makes the probabilities summable, so [F9] proves this bound for all such intervals eventually almost surely, for every positive integer $C$ by countable intersection. In particular unit counts are $O(\log n)$ uniformly, intervals of integer length at least $n^b$ have count increase at least $\lambda/2$ times their length eventually, and $N(t)/t\to\lambda$. Also [F10], a union bound and [F9] make all within-unit Brownian oscillations up to time $Cn$ be $O(\sqrt{\log n})$. These estimates require no independence between evaluation times and the Brownian motion. Consequently the integer coupling in step 3.1 extends to $\sup_{z\le n}|\gamma N(z)-\mu z-sB_0(z)|=o(n^b)$, and step 2.1 gives $\max_{k\le n}|T_k-\gamma N(k)|=o(n^b)$.

Let $m(t)=\max\{k:T_k\le t\}$ and $y(t)=\inf\{z:N(z)>t/\gamma\}$. Brownian reflection on dyadic horizons gives $\sup_{z\le n}|B_0(z)|=O(\sqrt{n\log n})=o(n)$; thus step 2.1 implies $T_k/k\to\mu$. Together with $N(z)/z\to\lambda$, this gives $m(t),y(t)=O(t)$, absorbing their finite initial values. Put $k=\lfloor y(t)\rfloor$. Monotonicity gives $\gamma N(k)\le t<\gamma N(k+1)$, except for an integer endpoint convention which is covered by shifting at most two indices. The unit-count bound in step 4.1 therefore gives $|\gamma N(k)-t|=O(\log n)$ uniformly for $t\le n$. On every required range of $O(n)$ indices, $|T_j-\gamma N(j)|\le n^b$ eventually by its little-o bound. Choose an integer $J$ with $\gamma\lambda J/2>4$. The lower-increment bound in step 4.1 makes a change of $\lceil Jn^b\rceil$ indices change $\gamma N$ by more than $2n^b+O(\log n)$ eventually. The corresponding $T$ values bracket $t$, using index zero at the lower boundary. Thus $\sup_{t\le n}|m(t)-y(t)|=O(n^b)$. The countable estimates for all deterministic horizon multipliers cover a finite random multiplier as well. This is a direct monotone inverse comparison, not an imported renewal approximation.

Let $E_i$ be the interarrival times of $N$. Their iid exponential law follows from [F7]: for $0<t_1<\cdots<t_k\le T$, sum its ordered density over all total counts $m\ge k$ and integrate the last $m-k$ ordered points above $t_k$. The simplex volume is $(T-t_k)^{m-k}/(m-k)!$, so the first-$k$ density is $e^{-\lambda T}\lambda^k\sum_{j\ge0}(\lambda(T-t_k))^j/j!=\lambda^ke^{-\lambda t_k}$. Increasing $T$ covers the whole ordered simplex. The spacing change of variables has determinant one and gives $\prod_{i=1}^k\lambda e^{-\lambda e_i}$ on positive spacings. Hence $\mathbb EE_i=1/\lambda$, $\operatorname{Var}(E_i)=1/\lambda^2$ and all moments are finite, by elementary exponential integration and integration by parts for integer moments, bounding other positive powers by the next integer power plus one. Apply [F4] to $(E_i-1/\lambda,0)$ with the same auxiliary exponent $r>p$, and glue its Brownian driver $V$ to the entire already realized arrival sequence by [F8], using a fresh kernel depending only on that sequence. Then $\max_{k\le n}|\sum_{i=1}^kE_i-k/\lambda-V(k)/\lambda|=o(n^{1/r})$. Since $y(t)=\sum_{i\le\lfloor t/\gamma\rfloor+1}E_i$, set $V_1(t)=\sqrt\gamma V(t/\gamma)$ and use step 4.1's within-unit Brownian bound to obtain $\sup_{t\le n}|y(t)-t/\mu-V_1(t)/(\lambda\sqrt\gamma)|=o(n^b)$. The clock sigma-algebra generated by $B_0,N,V_1$ and their fresh clock randomness remains independent of $B$: each new kernel depended on $B_0$ or on the clock alone and used randomness independent of earlier variables.

Apply [F5] to $B$, $N$ and this entire clock sigma-algebra. It supplies a standard Brownian motion $W^*$ independent of that sigma-algebra, hence independent of $V_1$, and $\sup_{z\le n}|B(z)-\lambda^{-1/2}W^*(N(z))|=O(\log^2(n+2))$. Define $G(t)=(v/\sqrt\lambda)W^*(t/\gamma)-(a\mu/(\lambda\sqrt\gamma))V_1(t)$. It is continuous centered Gaussian with independent stationary increments and variance per unit time $v^2/(\lambda\gamma)+a^2\mu^2/(\lambda^2\gamma)=(v^2+a^2s^2)/\mu=u/\mu$. Thus, when $u>0$, $G=\kappa W$ for a standard Brownian $W$ and $\kappa=\sqrt{u/\mu}$. When $u=0$, positive semidefiniteness forces $a=v=0$, so $G=0$ and adjoin an unused standard $W$. The case $v=0$ needs no residual normalization or nonzero Brownian coefficient.

For $y=y(t)$, the following exact decomposition has eight terms: $F(t)-G(t)=\sum_{i=1}^8\Phi_i(t)$, where $\Phi_1=F(t)-F(T_{m(t)})$, $\Phi_2=F(T_{m(t)})-F(T_{\lfloor y\rfloor})$, $\Phi_3=F(T_{\lfloor y\rfloor})-aT_{\lfloor y\rfloor}+a\mu y-vB(y)$, $\Phi_4=a(T_{\lfloor y\rfloor}-\gamma N(y))$, $\Phi_5=-a\mu(y-t/\mu-V_1(t)/(\lambda\sqrt\gamma))$, $\Phi_6=v(B(y)-\lambda^{-1/2}W^*(N(y)))$, $\Phi_7=(v/\sqrt\lambda)(W^*(N(y))-W^*(t/\gamma))$, and $\Phi_8=a(\gamma N(y)-t)$. Adding these expressions cancels every intermediate reward, clock and Gaussian evaluation and leaves exactly $F(t)-G(t)$. This verifies the signs and deterministic drift, including the bounded last term.

Uniformly for $t\le n$, the first term is $o(n^b)$ by the incomplete-cycle bound in [F2] and step 3.2. The second is $o(n^b)$ by the inverse comparison in step 5.1 and [F6]. The third is $o(n^b)$ by step 2.1 at $\lfloor y\rfloor$, the bounded fractional-part drift $a\mu(y-\lfloor y\rfloor)$, and the within-unit Brownian bound. The fourth is $o(n^b)$ by the length/Poisson comparison at $\lfloor y\rfloor$ and the $O(\log n)$ count increase between that point and $y$. The fifth is $o(n^b)$ by step 6.1, and the sixth is $O(\log^2 n)=o(n^b)$ by step 7.1. The strict inverse of the simple Poisson clock satisfies $N(y(t))=\lfloor t/\gamma\rfloor+1$, so its distance from $t/\gamma$ is at most one; step 3.2's fixed-window Brownian bound makes the seventh term $O(\sqrt{\log n})=o(n^b)$, while $|\Phi_8|\le|a|\gamma$. The indices $m(t),y(t)$ are $O(n)$ by step 5.1, so every approximation was evaluated inside its verified range. Therefore $\sup_{t\le n}|F(t)-\kappa W(t)|=o(n^b)$ for $s>0$.

If $s^2=0$, the iid lengths have variance zero, hence $L_j=\mu$ for every $j$ simultaneously almost surely. In particular $T_k=\mu k$; positive semidefiniteness of $\Gamma$ implies $c=0$. The joint approximation [F3] gives $F(T_k)=\sqrt u\,B(k)+o(n^b)$ uniformly for $k\le n$, with a standard Brownian $B$ when $u>0$, and an unused one when $u=0$. For $t\le n$, $m(t)=\lfloor t/\mu\rfloor$, so step 3.2's fixed-window modulus replaces $B(m(t))$ by $B(t/\mu)$ at error $o(n^b)$. The incomplete-tour bound is again $o(n^b)$. Thus $\sup_{t\le n}|F(t)-\sqrt u B(t/\mu)|=o(n^b)$. The process $W(t)=\sqrt\mu B(t/\mu)$ is standard Brownian by its continuous Gaussian covariance and increments, and the coefficient is the same $\kappa=\sqrt{u/\mu}$. This proves the tail approximation in every covariance case, including a zero residual or zero full Gaussian covariance, without inverting a singular matrix.

Restore the finite initial segment of [F2]. Let $A$ be its finite centered reward and $D$ its finite integer length. For $n\ge D$, the actual sum is $A+F(n-D)$. Keep the same standard Brownian motion $W$ and use $A+F(n-D)-\kappa W(n)=A+[F(n-D)-\kappa W(n-D)]+\kappa[W(n-D)-W(n)]$. The fixed-window Brownian estimates in step 3.2 hold on one event for every positive integer window length. On that event choose an integer at least the finite random $D$; then $\max_{D\le k\le n}|W(k-D)-W(k)|=O(\sqrt{\log n})$, regardless of any dependence of $D$ and $W$. Finitely many earlier indices contribute a finite maximum. Steps 9.1 and 10.1 therefore give the complete-path bound $\max_{k\le n}|\sum_{i=1}^k f(X_i)-\kappa W(k)|=o(n^b)$ in the factor construction. Neither a moment of the initial law nor an assertion that a randomly shifted Brownian path is standard has been used.

Identify $\kappa$ without making an unsupported second-moment inference from the almost-sure approximation. Use the same factor and fixed post-delay tour law under invariant initial law, as supplied in [F1]–[F2]. Steps 2.1, 3.1, 3.2, 4.1, 5.1, 6.1, 7.1, 8.1, 9.1, 10.1, 11.1 then give a CLT with variance $\kappa^2=u/\mu$: the approximation error divided by $\sqrt n$ tends to zero almost surely since $b<1/2$, and $\kappa W(n)/\sqrt n$ has exactly the centered normal law of variance $\kappa^2$ for each $n$; apply [F12]'s converging-together result. Independently, [F11] gives exponential stationary strong mixing of the original observations. Their $Q_0$th moment, with $Q_0>2$, satisfies [F12]'s moment regime because every positive power of an exponential rate is summable. Hence [F12] gives the stationary CLT with its absolutely convergent covariance-sum variance $\sigma_g^2$, the asymptotic variance in the Statement's convention. The stationary observation-path equality in [F1] makes these two limits refer to the same law. Uniqueness of centered normal characteristic functions, $e^{-t^2\kappa^2/2}=e^{-t^2\sigma_g^2/2}$, gives $\kappa^2=\sigma_g^2$. The assumed positivity therefore gives $\kappa=\sigma_g>0$. This argument uses no uniform-integrability assumption on the approximation error.

Finally preserve the actual original chain probability space. The factor construction gives a joint law of its real observation sequence and the rational-time coordinates of the final standard Brownian motion $W$. Both are standard-Borel real sequence spaces by [F8]. Use [F1]'s lifting assertion, or disintegrate this joint law and apply its conditional kernel at the actual sequence $(f(X_1),f(X_2),\ldots)$ by [F8]; this preserves the entire original probability space and reproduces that observation/Gaussian-coordinate joint law. The approximation event uses only these observations and integer driver coordinates, so it still has probability one. The rational coordinates extend to a continuous Brownian path on a common measurable full-measure event: for each positive integers $M,k$, some integer $l$ makes all rational pairs in $[0,M]$ at distance below $1/l$ have coordinate difference below $1/k$. This is a Borel condition and has probability one under the original Brownian rational law; completeness of $\mathbb R$ gives a unique consistent continuous extension on compact intervals. Every fixed real-time evaluation is the limit along a deterministic rational sequence, hence measurable; on the null failure event set the path to zero. Its finite-dimensional laws agree with standard Brownian laws by continuity, so [F10] identifies genuine standard Brownian motion on the extension. With $B=W$, steps 11.1, 12.1 give error $o(n^{1/p})$, and $p>P_0$ implies $n^{1/p}/(n^{1/P_0}\log n)\to0$. Choosing the finite eventual bound and starting index in this almost-sure comparison gives precisely the $C(\omega),N(\omega)$ in the Statement. AC was used through the stated local Gaussian, factor, tour and extension suppliers; the full moment range, arbitrary initial law, positive-variance convention and original observation indices are retained.

boundaries.evidence: Statement and proof steps 1.1 and 13.1. The state space carries an invariant probability and is nonempty. Empty partial sums, zero-count Poisson subintervals and initial finite index ranges are covered; the target is eventual in n.

The Statement retains σ_g>0. Internally, zero residual variance is handled in steps 2.1/3.3, zero length variance in step 10.1, and zero full Gaussian covariance before variance identification in step 12.1. No division by a zero variance is used.

Unit Poisson counts are interpolated with their actual conditional uniform event-time law in step 3.1; their O(log n) maximum and within-unit Brownian oscillations are proved in step 4.1. Tour lengths are positive integers and incomplete endpoint cycles are retained.

The joint Gaussian covariance may be singular. Regression uses full long-run Γ12; covariance-zero clock and reward directions are handled explicitly. Initial prefix dependence on tail seeds and Brownian driver is permitted: step 11.1 uses the same driver with a finite-window path bound.

Proof steps 1.1, 3.1 and 9.1. P0=2+δ<p<q<Q0=2+δ+ε makes b=1/p<1/P0<1/2. The scalar clock exponent r>p is chosen with all required Poisson/exponential moments, rather than claiming a logarithmic KMT rate. Strict inverse endpoint counts use floor(t/γ)+1 and the bounded eighth remainder.

Proof steps 1.1, 3.1 and 13.1. AC is explicit in the Facts and proposed axiom_use. The measurable factor preserves arbitrary initial observation laws, standard-Borel kernels glue the actual Gaussian drivers, and the final lift conditions only on real observations/rational Brownian coordinates; no arbitrary-state RCD is assumed.

boundaries.reason: The theorem is a one-way sufficient-condition assertion, not a biconditional.
No converse geometric-ergodicity, moment or strong-approximation claim is made.

risk_review.notes: Checked spare exponents P0<p<q<Q0, all-start standard-Borel factor and actual delayed adjacent-iid tours. Joint reward/length approximation uses full lag-one cross covariance; regression yields independent B,B0, with zero residual handled. Poisson counts coupled to B0 and exponential arrivals coupled to clock via separate kernels preserve independence from B; independent-clock composition yields W* independent of V1. Direct inverse comparison gives O(n^(1/p)) index error, controlled by moving-window reward bound. Eight-term calendar decomposition cancels exactly and each error is little-o; zero length variance branch explicit. Finite random delay handled by common deterministic-window Brownian modulus, not random shift law. Stationary CLT uniqueness identifies u/mu as actual covariance variance; rational-coordinate lift preserves entire original process.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume Choice. For every probability measure $\mu$ and probability kernel $K$
on an arbitrary measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$, the canonical path space
$$ (E^{\mathbb N_0},\mathcal E^{\otimes\mathbb N_0}) $$
carries a unique probability $\mathbb P_\mu$ under which the coordinate maps
form a Markov chain with initial law $\mu$ and transition kernel $K$.

Assume AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $K$ be a probability kernel on a
measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$, let $\pi$ be an invariant probability for $K$
([[def-invariant-and-stationary-distribution-for-a-markov-kernel]]), and let
$X$ be a $K$-chain with initial law $\pi$
([[def-initial-distribution-of-a-markov-chain]]). Then every finite-dimensional
law of $X$ is invariant under every nonnegative integer time shift: for every
$r\ge1$, every $0\le n_1<\cdots<n_r$ and every $m\ge0$,

$$\mathcal L(X_{m+n_1},\ldots,X_{m+n_r})=\mathcal L(X_{n_1},\ldots,X_{n_r}).$$

Equivalently, the canonical path law
$\mathbb P_X:=\mathcal L\bigl((X_n)_{n\ge0}\bigr)$ on
$(E^{\mathbb N_0},\mathcal E^{\otimes\mathbb N_0})$ is invariant under the left
shift $\theta(z)_n=z_{n+1}$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $P$ be a probability kernel on a measurable space
$(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ with invariant probability $\pi$. Assume it is
$\phi$-irreducible
([[def-phi-irreducible-chain]]), aperiodic
([[def-general-state-aperiodic-markov-chain]]), and Harris recurrent relative
to its nonzero $\sigma$-finite irreducibility measure $\phi$
([[def-harris-recurrent-markov-chain]]). Suppose $P$ is geometrically
ergodic in the sense of
[[def-geometric-and-uniform-ergodicity-for-mcmc-clt]]. Then there exist a
measurable $M:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ with $\pi(M)<\infty$ and $r\in(0,1)$ such
that
$$\|P^n(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le M(x)r^n\quad(x\in\mathsf X,\ n\ge1).$$

In fact, the same conclusion holds assuming only AC, invariance of $\pi$, and the everywhere finite measurable common geometric-rate bound in [[def-geometric-and-uniform-ergodicity-for-mcmc-clt]], on the original arbitrary measurable space. The construction below derives the needed irreducibility on a restricted sigma-field directly from that bound.

Assume AC. Let $(X_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a stationary time-homogeneous Markov chain
with invariant probability $\pi$. Suppose there are a measurable
$M:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ with $\pi(M)<\infty$ and $r\in(0,1)$ such that
$$\|P^n(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le M(x)r^n\quad\text{for every }x\in\mathsf X,\ n\ge1.$$
Then the strong-mixing coefficient of the stationary process satisfies
$$\alpha_X(n)\le\pi(M)r^n\quad(n\ge1).$$

Let $X=(X_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a strictly stationary process on a measurable state
space and let $h$ be a measurable real-valued function. Put $Y_k=h(X_k)$.
Then $Y$ is strictly stationary and, for every $n\ge1$,
$$\alpha_Y(n)\le\alpha_X(n),\qquad \phi_Y(n)\le\phi_X(n),\qquad \rho_Y(n)\le\rho_X(n),$$
where the coefficients are as in
[[def-mixing-coefficients-for-stationary-markov-chain]].

Assume AC. Let $(Y_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a centered strictly stationary real sequence with $\mathbb E[Y_0^2]<\infty$, and define $S_n=\sum_{k=1}^nY_k$. Each of the following is sufficient:

1. There is $B<\infty$ with $|Y_0|\le B$ almost surely and $\sum_{n\ge1}\alpha_Y(n)<\infty$.
2. For some $\delta>0$, $\mathbb E|Y_0|^{2+\delta}<\infty$ and $\sum_{n\ge1}\alpha_Y(n)^{\delta/(2+\delta)}<\infty$.
3. For some $a\in(0,1)$, $\alpha_Y(n)=O(a^n)$ and $\mathbb E[Y_0^2\log^+|Y_0|]<\infty$, where $\log^+u=\max(0,\log u)$ for $u>0$ and $0\log^+0:=0$.

In each case the covariance series
$$\sigma_Y^2:=\mathbb E[Y_0^2]+2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\operatorname{Cov}(Y_0,Y_k)$$
converges absolutely and is nonnegative, and
$$n^{-1/2}S_n\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_Y^2).$$
This includes the degenerate law $N(0,0)$ when $\sigma_Y^2=0$, as in [[lem-zero-long-run-variance-gives-degenerate-clt]]. The coefficient $\alpha_Y$ and strict stationarity have the meanings in [[def-mixing-coefficients-for-stationary-markov-chain]].

Let $(X_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a stationary time-homogeneous Markov chain with invariant probability $\pi$, and let $f$ be real Borel with $\pi(f)=0$ and $\pi(f^2)<\infty$. For $k\ge0$, set $\gamma_k:=\operatorname{Cov}_{\pi}(f(X_0),f(X_k))$. When the Markov-chain CLT $n^{-1/2}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}f(X_k)\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_f^2)$ holds with finite variance parameter and $\sum_{k\ge1}|\gamma_k|<\infty$, the **covariance long-run variance** is
$$\sigma^2_{\mathrm{LR}}(f):=\gamma_0+2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\gamma_k.$$

This definition does not infer a CLT from covariance summability, or infer that a weak-limit variance equals the covariance sum. Whenever $\sigma^2_{\mathrm{LR}}(f)$ is used as the variance parameter in a CLT or MCSE claim, that equality must be established by the theorem being applied. For example, the local Poisson-equation theorem proves the equality under its square-integrable solution hypotheses.

Let $P$ be a geometrically ergodic Markov chain with invariant probability
$\pi$, let $g$ be real Borel, and suppose there are $\delta,\varepsilon>0$
with $\pi(|g|^{2+\delta+\varepsilon})<\infty$. Suppose also that a
state-dependent one-step minorization
[[def-state-dependent-one-step-minorization]] holds. For the Flegal–Jones
strong invariance principle convention, assume its asymptotic standard
deviation satisfies $0<\sigma_g<\infty$. Then on a suitable extension of the
chain's probability space there are a standard Brownian motion $B$, a finite
random constant $C(\omega)$, and a finite random index $N(\omega)$ such that
for all $n\ge N(\omega)$,
$$\left|\sum_{i=1}^n(g(X_i)-\pi(g))-\sigma_g B(n)\right|\le C(\omega)n^{1/(2+\delta)}\log n$$
almost surely.

Assume AC. Let $P$ be a probability kernel on an arbitrary measurable space $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ with invariant probability $\pi$. Suppose its stationary Markov chain has strong-mixing coefficients $\alpha_X(n)\le Cr^n$ for $n\ge1$, with $0\le C<\infty$ and $0<r<1$. Let $f:\mathsf X\to\mathbb R$ be finite measurable with $\pi f=0$, $\pi|f|^q<\infty$ for a finite $q>2$, and suppose the absolutely convergent covariance sum is zero:
$$v:=\pi(f^2)+2\sum_{n\ge1}\operatorname{Cov}_\pi(f(X_0),f(X_n))=0.$$
Then for every $2<p<q$, under the stationary law,
$$\max_{0\le j\le n}\left|\sum_{k=0}^{j-1}f(X_k)\right|=o(n^{1/p})\qquad\text{almost surely}.$$
The empty sum at $j=0$ is zero. No ergodicity assumption is needed beyond the stated stationary mixing bound.

If additionally $\|P^n(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\to0$ for every $x\in\mathsf X$, the same assertion holds under every initial probability law, without a moment assumption on that law. In particular, it holds under every initial law whenever $P$ has an everywhere finite measurable common geometric total-variation envelope in the sense of [[def-geometric-and-uniform-ergodicity-for-mcmc-clt]] and $f$ has the stated moment, centering and zero covariance sum. No positive one-step minorization, irreducibility or Harris hypothesis is added to this last sufficient condition.

Assume AC. Let $Y_1,Y_2,\ldots$ be real random variables and $S_k=\sum_{i=1}^kY_i$, with $S_0=0$. Suppose on a probability-space extension with the original process as marginal there are a standard Brownian motion $B$, constants $\sigma\ge0$ and $0<\alpha<1/2$, and finite random constants $K,N$ such that almost surely
$$|S_k-\sigma B(k)|\le K k^\alpha\log k\qquad(k\ge N).$$
Let $(b_n)$ be deterministic positive integers with $b_n<n$ eventually and
$$\frac{b_n}{n}\to0,\qquad \sum_{n=2}^\infty(b_n/n)^c<\infty\quad\text{for some real }c\ge1,$$
$$\frac{b_n\log n}{n}\to0,\qquad\frac{n^{2\alpha}(\log n)^2}{b_n}\to0.$$
For the exact estimator of [[alg-overlapping-batch-means-mcse]], applied to $Y_1,\ldots,Y_n$,
$$\widehat\sigma_{\mathrm{OBM},n}^2=\frac{nb_n}{(n-b_n)(n-b_n+1)}\sum_{j=0}^{n-b_n}\left(\frac{S_{j+b_n}-S_j}{b_n}-\frac{S_n}{n}\right)^2\longrightarrow\sigma^2\quad\text{almost surely}.$$
No stationarity, independence of $B$ from $(Y_i)$, or monotonicity of $b_n$ or $n/b_n$ is required. The conclusion includes $\sigma=0$.

Let $\delta>0$ and let $(b_n)_{n\ge2}$ be positive integers. Say that the sequence satisfies the **Flegal–Jones OBM batch-size conditions for exponent $\delta$**, with the integer monotonicity correction described below, when $b_n<n$ for all sufficiently large $n$, $b_n\to\infty$, $n/b_n\to\infty$, and there is a constant $c\ge1$ such that
$$\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}(b_n/n)^c<\infty,$$
while
$$\frac{b_n}{n}\log n\to0,\qquad \frac{n^{2/(2+\delta)}(\log n)^3}{b_n}\to0,$$
there are $n_0\ge2$ and $c_1<\infty$ with $\log n/b_n\le c_1$ for all $n\ge n_0$, and
$$b_n^2n^{-2}\log\log n\to0,\qquad b_n^4n^{-3}\log\log n\to0.$$

These are all the numerical rate, summability and endpoint hypotheses of Flegal–Jones Theorem 2. The source additionally asks that both $b_n$ and $n/b_n$ be nondecreasing. Those two requirements are omitted here: for an integer sequence with $b_n<n$ eventually they are incompatible with $b_n\to\infty$. Indeed, ratio monotonicity would imply $n(b_{n+1}-b_n)\le b_n<n$, while integer monotonicity would force the nonnegative integer $b_{n+1}-b_n$ to be zero. Thus the literal source conditions would make $b_n$ eventually constant. The corrected interface preserves the intended floor-power batch sequences, and the Brownian quadratic-form proof of OBM consistency needs neither monotonicity assumption.

This is a sufficient-condition interface; failure of a condition does not imply inconsistency of the estimator.

For the floor-power sequence $b_n=\lfloor n^\nu\rfloor$, the intended source range $\delta>2/3$ and $2/(2+\delta)<\nu<3/4$ satisfies this corrected contract. Indeed, eventually $n^\nu/2\le b_n\le n^\nu$. Choose $c>\max\{1,1/(1-\nu)\}$ to bound the summability series by $\sum_n n^{-c(1-\nu)}<\infty$. The other displayed quantities are bounded respectively by $n^{\nu-1}\log n$, $2n^{2/(2+\delta)-\nu}(\log n)^3$, $2n^{-\nu}\log n$, $n^{2\nu-2}\log\log n$ and $n^{4\nu-3}\log\log n$, all tending to zero. Also $b_n\to\infty$, $n/b_n\to\infty$ and $b_n<n$ eventually. These checks establish the numerical contract without asserting the impossible simultaneous monotonicity.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and let $d\ge1$ be finite.

1. A standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion exists: one may take $d$
   independent copies of the constructed one-dimensional Brownian path and
   assemble them coordinatewise.
2. If $B$ is any standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion and $c>0$, then
   $$Y_t=c^{-1/2}B_{ct},\qquad t\ge0,$$
   is again standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion. Moreover, the random
   elements $B$ and $Y$ have the same law on $(\mathbb R^d)^{[0,\infty)}$
   equipped with its cylinder sigma-algebra.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

derivations.claim: Put $q=2+\delta+\varepsilon$, $\mu=\pi(g)$ and $f=g-\mu$. The moment hypothesis gives $\pi|g|<\infty$, since $|g|\le1+|g|^q$, so $\mu$ is finite. The elementary bound $|g-\mu|^q\le2^q(|g|^q+|\mu|^q)$ gives $\pi|f|^q<\infty$, and $\pi f=0$. For variance identification consider the canonical chain with initial law $\pi$, which is stationary by [F1]. The given geometric bound has an everywhere finite measurable common envelope, so the stronger arbitrary-measurable-space clause of [F2] supplies an integrable such envelope. By [F3], this stationary chain and its observation $f$ have a strong-mixing bound $\alpha_f(n)\le Cr^n$ with $C<\infty$ and $r\in(0,1)$. This construction is only for identifying the stationary covariance parameter; the observed initial law remains arbitrary.

Take $\eta=q-2=\delta+\varepsilon>0$. The geometric bound in step 1.1 makes $\sum_n\alpha_f(n)^{\eta/(2+\eta)}$ finite. Apply [F4] to the stationary observed sequence. Its covariance series is absolutely convergent, its sum $v=\pi(f^2)+2\sum_{k\ge1}\operatorname{Cov}_\pi(f(X_0),f(X_k))$ is finite and nonnegative, and its CLT has precisely variance $v$. Thus [F5] identifies $v=\sigma_g^2$, without using the stationary Harris-only formulation of a separate MCMC regime theorem. Write $\sigma=\sqrt v\ge0$ and $\alpha=1/(2+\delta)\in(0,1/2)$.

If $v>0$, the original $g$, the given $\delta,\varepsilon$, geometric ergodicity and supplied minorization meet [F6] with the finite positive standard deviation from step 2.1. Hence, for the original arbitrary initial law, on an extension there are a standard Brownian motion $B$ and finite random constants for which $|\sum_{i=1}^n f(X_i)-\sigma B(n)|=O(n^\alpha\log n)$ almost surely. The same approximation as in step 3.1 now holds, with zero Brownian coefficient. No division by $\sigma$ or implication from a degenerate CLT to an almost-sure rate is used.

In either variance branch the hypotheses of [F8] hold with this $\sigma,\alpha$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $K$ be a probability kernel on a measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and let $\pi$ be a
probability measure on $(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). The
probability measure $\pi$ is **invariant** for $K$, and $\pi$ is a
**stationary distribution** of $K$, when

$$(\pi K)(A):=\int_E K(x,A)\,\pi(dx)=\pi(A)\qquad\text{for every }A\in\mathcal E .$$

The set function $\pi K$ is again a probability measure: for fixed $A$ the map
$x\mapsto K(x,A)$ is measurable and lies in $[0,1]$, so the integral exists in
$[0,1]$; for pairwise disjoint $A_n\in\mathcal E$ the identity
$K(x,\bigcup_nA_n)=\sum_nK(x,A_n)$ of the measure $K(x,\cdot)$ and the
monotone convergence theorem for nonnegative functions
([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]) give
$\sigma$-additivity of $\pi K$; and $K(x,E)=1$ for every $x$ gives
$(\pi K)(E)=1$. Thus $(\pi K)(A)=\pi(A)$ is an identity between two probability
measures evaluated at $A$.

A $K$-chain whose initial law is $\pi$ is called **stationary** when
$\pi K=\pi$. Stationarity of the process is a statement about all of its
finite-dimensional laws and is proved, not assumed, from $\pi K=\pi$; see
[[thm-invariant-initial-law-makes-the-chain-stationary]].

On a countable state space $E$ with sigma-algebra $2^E$ and transition matrix
$p(x,y)=K(x,\{y\})$ ([[def-transition-matrix-and-n-step-transition-probabilities]]),
a measure on $E$ is its weighted sum of Dirac masses at singletons
([[thm-measures-on-countable-discrete-spaces-are-weighted-dirac-sums]]), so
invariance is equivalent to the matrix identity

$$\pi(y)=\sum_{x\in E}\pi(x)\,p(x,y)\qquad\text{for every }y\in E .$$

The definition fixes no irreducibility, aperiodicity or uniqueness hypothesis,
and it selects no conditional-expectation versions; the display defines a
single measure $\pi K$ and asserts an identity for it. A transient, periodic or
reducible chain may have several invariant probability measures or none.

Assume AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $K$ be a probability kernel on a
measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$, let $\pi$ be an invariant probability for $K$
([[def-invariant-and-stationary-distribution-for-a-markov-kernel]]), and let
$X$ be a $K$-chain with initial law $\pi$
([[def-initial-distribution-of-a-markov-chain]]). Then every finite-dimensional
law of $X$ is invariant under every nonnegative integer time shift: for every
$r\ge1$, every $0\le n_1<\cdots<n_r$ and every $m\ge0$,

$$\mathcal L(X_{m+n_1},\ldots,X_{m+n_r})=\mathcal L(X_{n_1},\ldots,X_{n_r}).$$

Equivalently, the canonical path law
$\mathbb P_X:=\mathcal L\bigl((X_n)_{n\ge0}\bigr)$ on
$(E^{\mathbb N_0},\mathcal E^{\otimes\mathbb N_0})$ is invariant under the left
shift $\theta(z)_n=z_{n+1}$.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

For real random variables $(X_n)$ and $X$, write $X_n\Rightarrow X$, or
$X_n\to X$ **in distribution**, when
$$F_{X_n}(x)\longrightarrow F_X(x)$$
at every continuity point $x$ of $F_X$. Here $F_X$ is the CDF from
[[def-cumulative-distribution-function-of-a-random-variable]] and continuity
points are those of [[def-atom-and-continuity-point-of-a-law]].

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ be a countably generated measurable space ([[def-measurable-space]]), $P$ a probability kernel ([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and $\phi$ a nonzero $\sigma$-finite measure ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]) on $\mathcal X$. Write $P^n$ for the $n$-fold kernel iterate. The kernel is **$\phi$-irreducible** if, for every $A\in\mathcal X$ with $\phi(A)>0$ and every $x\in\mathsf X$, there is an integer $n\ge1$ such that $P^n(x,A)>0$. Equivalently, the sum of these nonnegative probabilities over $n\ge1$ is positive. No recurrence or invariant law is part of this definition.

Let $P$ be $\phi$-irreducible with nonzero $\sigma$-finite irreducibility measure $\phi$. It is **Harris recurrent relative to $\phi$** if for every $A\in\mathcal X$ with $\phi(A)>0$ and every starting state $x$, the first hitting time $\tau_A=\inf\{n\ge0:X_n\in A\}$ satisfies $\Pr_x(\tau_A<\infty)=1$. This is an all-start almost-sure hitting property; it is stronger than $\phi$-irreducibility, which requires only positive probability at some finite time.

derivations.claim: Let $\mathsf X=\{0,1\}$, $P(0,\{0\})=P(1,\{1\})=1$, and let $\pi(\{0\})=\pi(\{1\})=1/2$. The identity kernel leaves $\pi$ invariant, so the chain initialized with $X_0\sim\pi$ is stationary by [F2]. Set $f(0)=-1$ and $f(1)=1$. Then $\pi(f)=0$ and $\pi(f^2)=1$.

The transition is deterministic, hence $X_k=X_0$ for every $k$ and $S_n:=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}f(X_k)=nf(X_0)$. Thus $S_n/\sqrt n=\sqrt n f(X_0)$ takes values $\pm\sqrt n$ with equal probabilities. For each fixed $t>0$, once $n>t^2$ its distribution function at $t$ is $1/2$, while any $N(0,\sigma^2)$ has distribution function strictly greater than $1/2$ at $t$ when $\sigma^2>0$ and equal to $1$ when $\sigma^2=0$. Since $t$ is a continuity point of every such normal law, [F4] rules out convergence to any normal distribution.

Choose $\phi=\pi$ and $A=\{1\}$. Then $\phi(A)=1/2>0$, but $P^n(0,A)=0$ for every $n\ge1$ because the chain stays at $0$. By [F5] the chain is not $\phi$-irreducible and is not Harris recurrent relative to $\phi$. This counterexample shows only that finite variance without an ergodicity assumption does not guarantee a root-$n$ CLT.

Let $\delta>0$ and let $(b_n)_{n\ge2}$ be positive integers. Say that the sequence satisfies the **Flegal–Jones OBM batch-size conditions for exponent $\delta$**, with the integer monotonicity correction described below, when $b_n<n$ for all sufficiently large $n$, $b_n\to\infty$, $n/b_n\to\infty$, and there is a constant $c\ge1$ such that
$$\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}(b_n/n)^c<\infty,$$
while
$$\frac{b_n}{n}\log n\to0,\qquad \frac{n^{2/(2+\delta)}(\log n)^3}{b_n}\to0,$$
there are $n_0\ge2$ and $c_1<\infty$ with $\log n/b_n\le c_1$ for all $n\ge n_0$, and
$$b_n^2n^{-2}\log\log n\to0,\qquad b_n^4n^{-3}\log\log n\to0.$$

These are all the numerical rate, summability and endpoint hypotheses of Flegal–Jones Theorem 2. The source additionally asks that both $b_n$ and $n/b_n$ be nondecreasing. Those two requirements are omitted here: for an integer sequence with $b_n<n$ eventually they are incompatible with $b_n\to\infty$. Indeed, ratio monotonicity would imply $n(b_{n+1}-b_n)\le b_n<n$, while integer monotonicity would force the nonnegative integer $b_{n+1}-b_n$ to be zero. Thus the literal source conditions would make $b_n$ eventually constant. The corrected interface preserves the intended floor-power batch sequences, and the Brownian quadratic-form proof of OBM consistency needs neither monotonicity assumption.

This is a sufficient-condition interface; failure of a condition does not imply inconsistency of the estimator.

For the floor-power sequence $b_n=\lfloor n^\nu\rfloor$, the intended source range $\delta>2/3$ and $2/(2+\delta)<\nu<3/4$ satisfies this corrected contract. Indeed, eventually $n^\nu/2\le b_n\le n^\nu$. Choose $c>\max\{1,1/(1-\nu)\}$ to bound the summability series by $\sum_n n^{-c(1-\nu)}<\infty$. The other displayed quantities are bounded respectively by $n^{\nu-1}\log n$, $2n^{2/(2+\delta)-\nu}(\log n)^3$, $2n^{-\nu}\log n$, $n^{2\nu-2}\log\log n$ and $n^{4\nu-3}\log\log n$, all tending to zero. Also $b_n\to\infty$, $n/b_n\to\infty$ and $b_n<n$ eventually. These checks establish the numerical contract without asserting the impossible simultaneous monotonicity.

**Inputs:** Real outputs $y_1,\ldots,y_n$, an integer $n\ge2$, and an integer batch size $b$ with $1\le b<n$. For an MCMC run, $y_i=f(X_i)$ for the chosen real-valued observable $f$.

**Outputs:** The sample mean $\bar y_n$, the overlapping-batch-means estimate $\widehat{\sigma}^2_{\mathrm{OBM}}$, and its estimated Monte Carlo standard error.

1. Compute the sample mean
$$\bar y_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n y_i.$$

2. For each starting index $j=1,\ldots,n-b+1$, compute the overlapping batch mean
$$\bar y_j(b)=\frac1b\sum_{i=j}^{j+b-1}y_i.$$

3. Return the overlapping-batch-means variance estimate
$$\widehat{\sigma}^2_{\mathrm{OBM}}=\frac{nb}{(n-b)(n-b+1)}\sum_{j=1}^{n-b+1}\bigl(\bar y_j(b)-\bar y_n\bigr)^2.$$

4. Return the estimated Monte Carlo standard error
$$\widehat{\operatorname{MCSE}}(\bar y_n)=\sqrt{\widehat{\sigma}^2_{\mathrm{OBM}}/n}.$$

All sums are finite, the denominator is positive because $b<n$, and the variance estimate is nonnegative. The procedure always returns a number for the stated finite input. It does not by itself assert a CLT or consistency; consistency requires the hypotheses of the overlapping-batch-means theorem.

> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $K$ be a probability kernel on a
measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$, let $\pi$ be an invariant probability for $K$
([[def-invariant-and-stationary-distribution-for-a-markov-kernel]]), and let
$X$ be a $K$-chain with initial law $\pi$
([[def-initial-distribution-of-a-markov-chain]]). Then every finite-dimensional
law of $X$ is invariant under every nonnegative integer time shift: for every
$r\ge1$, every $0\le n_1<\cdots<n_r$ and every $m\ge0$,

$$\mathcal L(X_{m+n_1},\ldots,X_{m+n_r})=\mathcal L(X_{n_1},\ldots,X_{n_r}).$$

Equivalently, the canonical path law
$\mathbb P_X:=\mathcal L\bigl((X_n)_{n\ge0}\bigr)$ on
$(E^{\mathbb N_0},\mathcal E^{\otimes\mathbb N_0})$ is invariant under the left
shift $\theta(z)_n=z_{n+1}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Assume AC. Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ have a supplied countable algebra $\mathcal C$ generating $\mathcal X$, and let $(X_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a stationary time-homogeneous Markov chain with invariant probability $\pi$. If
$$\|P^n(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\longrightarrow0\quad\text{for }\pi\text{-almost every }x,$$
then its stationary output process is strongly mixing:
$$\alpha_X(n)\longrightarrow0.$$

Let $Y=(Y_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a process on a probability space whose finite-dimensional laws are invariant under common nonnegative time shifts; call this strict stationarity. For $j\ge0$, set $\mathcal F_j^-:=\sigma(Y_0,\ldots,Y_j)$ and $\mathcal F_j^+:=\sigma(Y_j,Y_{j+1},\ldots)$. For $n\ge1$, define the **strong-mixing coefficient** by
$$\alpha_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{\substack{A\in\mathcal F_j^-\\B\in\mathcal F_{j+n}^+}}|\mathbb P(A\cap B)-\mathbb P(A)\mathbb P(B)|.$$

Define the **uniform-mixing coefficient** by
$$\phi_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{\substack{A\in\mathcal F_j^-\\\mathbb P(A)>0}}\ \sup_{B\in\mathcal F_{j+n}^+}|\mathbb P(B\mid A)-\mathbb P(B)|.$$

For square-integrable real random variables $U,V$ with positive variances, write
$$\operatorname{Corr}(U,V):=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(U,V)}{\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(U)\operatorname{Var}(V)}}.$$
For each $n\ge1$, let $\mathcal C_n$ consist of the triples $(j,U,V)$ such that $j\ge0$, $U,V$ are real and square-integrable, $U$ and $V$ are measurable with respect to $\mathcal F_j^-$ and $\mathcal F_{j+n}^+$ respectively, and both have positive variance. Define the **maximal-correlation coefficient** by
$$\rho_Y(n):=\sup\Bigl(\{0\}\cup\{|\operatorname{Corr}(U,V)|:(j,U,V)\in\mathcal C_n\}\Bigr),$$
where square-integrability is in the sense of [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]. Thus $\rho_Y(n)=0$ when there is no admissible pair, as for a constant process. The process is called strongly mixing, uniformly mixing, or rho-mixing, respectively, when the corresponding coefficient tends to zero. These coefficients are distinct conditions; no implication between them is included in this definition.

Assume AC. Let $(X_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a stationary time-homogeneous Markov chain with invariant probability $\pi$, natural filtration $\mathcal F_k$, and ergodic canonical path shift. Let $f$ be real Borel with $\pi(f)=0$ and $f\in L^2(\pi)$ ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). Suppose there is a measurable $g\in L^2(\pi)$ such that $f=g-Pg$ $\pi$-almost everywhere, where $Pg(x)=\int g(y)P(x,dy)$. Put $D_{k+1}:=g(X_{k+1})-Pg(X_k)$ and $\tau_f^2:=\mathbb E[D_1^2]$. Then for every $n\ge1$,
$$\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}f(X_k)=g(X_0)-g(X_n)+\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}D_{k+1},$$
and
$$\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}f(X_k)\Rightarrow N(0,\tau_f^2),$$
including the degenerate case $\tau_f^2=0$. If additionally $\sum_{k\ge1}|\operatorname{Cov}_{\pi}(f(X_0),f(X_k))|<\infty$, then
$$\tau_f^2=\pi(f^2)+2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\operatorname{Cov}_{\pi}(f(X_0),f(X_k)),$$
so this CLT's variance equals the covariance long-run variance of [[def-long-run-variance-for-stationary-markov-chain]].

Let $(X_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a stationary time-homogeneous Markov chain with invariant probability $\pi$, and let $f$ be real Borel with $\pi(f)=0$ and $\pi(f^2)<\infty$. For $k\ge0$, set $\gamma_k:=\operatorname{Cov}_{\pi}(f(X_0),f(X_k))$. When the Markov-chain CLT $n^{-1/2}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}f(X_k)\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_f^2)$ holds with finite variance parameter and $\sum_{k\ge1}|\gamma_k|<\infty$, the **covariance long-run variance** is
$$\sigma^2_{\mathrm{LR}}(f):=\gamma_0+2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\gamma_k.$$

This definition does not infer a CLT from covariance summability, or infer that a weak-limit variance equals the covariance sum. Whenever $\sigma^2_{\mathrm{LR}}(f)$ is used as the variance parameter in a CLT or MCSE claim, that equality must be established by the theorem being applied. For example, the local Poisson-equation theorem proves the equality under its square-integrable solution hypotheses.

Let $S\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ with Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal E$, let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a
probability space, and let $Y=(Y_n)_{n\ge0}$ be a stochastic process with each
$Y_n:\Omega\to S$ a random element
([[def-stochastic-process-and-finite-dimensional-distributions]]). The process
$Y$ is **strictly stationary** when every finite-dimensional law is unchanged
by a common nonnegative time shift: for every $r\ge1$, every
$0\le n_1<\cdots<n_r$ and every $m\ge0$,

$$\mathcal L(Y_{m+n_1},\ldots,Y_{m+n_r})=\mathcal L(Y_{n_1},\ldots,Y_{n_r}).$$

The **canonical path law** of $Y$ is the pushforward
$\mathbb P_Y=\mathcal L(Y)$ of $\mathbb P$ under the coordinate map
$\omega\mapsto(Y_n(\omega))_{n\ge0}$, a probability measure on the product
space $S^{\mathbb N_0}$ with its product sigma-algebra. The **left shift** is
$\theta(z)_n=z_{n+1}$ for $z=(z_n)_{n\ge0}\in S^{\mathbb N_0}$.

A strictly stationary process is called **ergodic** when the canonical shift $\theta$ is ergodic
for $\mathbb P_Y$ in the sense of
[[def-ergodic-measure-preserving-system]]. The shift-invariance needed for that
definition, namely that $\theta$ is measure preserving for $\mathbb P_Y$, is
proved below for strictly stationary $Y$, so in that case
$(S^{\mathbb N_0},\mathcal E^{\otimes\mathbb N_0},\mathbb P_Y,\theta)$ is a
probability measure-preserving system in the sense of
[[def-measure-preserving-transformation-and-system]].

Iterating the recursion gives $X_n=a^n x+\sum_{j=1}^n a^{n-j}\epsilon_j$ when $X_0=x$, so $P^n(x,\cdot)=N(a^nx,v_n)$ with $v_n=v(1-a^{2n})$. For each fixed $x$, $a^nx\to0$ and $v_n\to v$, so the Gaussian densities $p_n^x(y)$ converge pointwise to the density $p(y)$ of $N(0,v)$. For sufficiently large $n$, $v/2\le v_n\le v$ and $|a^nx|\le1$. On $|y|\le2$, $p_n^x(y)\le(\pi v)^{-1/2}$; on $|y|>2$, $|y-a^nx|\ge|y|/2$, hence $p_n^x(y)\le(\pi v)^{-1/2}e^{-y^2/(8v)}$. This gives one integrable majorant for $p_n^x$; with $p$ added it also dominates $|p_n^x-p|$. By [F2], $\int|p_n^x-p|\,dy\to0$. Therefore $\|P^n(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le\int|p_n^x-p|\,dy\to0$ for every $x$.
The Borel sigma-algebra of $\mathbb R$ has the countable generating algebra of finite unions of rational half-open intervals and rational rays. Applying [F3] to step 1.2 gives $\alpha_X(n)\to0$.

Let $E$ be an event invariant under every power of the canonical left shift and put $p=\mathbb P(E)$. Finite-coordinate cylinders form a generating pi-system. The events approximable in probability by such cylinders form a sigma-algebra: complements preserve symmetric-difference probability, and for a countable union one first truncates by continuity from below and then approximates the finitely many sets. Hence for every $\eta>0$ there are $j$ and $A\in\sigma(X_0,\ldots,X_j)$ with $\mathbb P(E\triangle A)<\eta$. For $m>j$, $B=\theta^{-m}E$ is measurable with respect to $\sigma(X_m,X_{m+1},\ldots)$, stationarity gives $\mathbb P(B)=p$, and shift invariance gives $E=B$. The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let U⊂R^n be open and Y:U→R^n be C¹. There is a unique maximal flow Φ on an open domain
D⊂R×U containing {0}×U, and Φ is jointly C¹. Its time slices are local C¹
diffeomorphisms with inverse Φ_{−t}; $\partial_t\Phi=Y(\Phi)$ and $D_p\Phi$ is the
unique solution V of $V′=DY(\Phi)V$, V(0)=I. Each regular point has a C¹ flow box. If Y
is C², Φ and those flow boxes are C²; the second state variation W satisfies
$W′=DY(\Phi)W+D²Y(\Phi)[Ve_i,Ve_j]$, W(0)=0. Individual trajectories of a C¹ field are
C² in time. A trajectory remaining in a compact K⊂⊂U cannot have a finite maximal
endpoint. These Euclidean conclusions use no full AC or DC.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $A$ be an $n\times n$ matrix and let $H$ be a direction matrix. Then

$$D\det(A)[H]=\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{adj}(A)H).$$

If $A$ is invertible, then

$$D\det(A)[H]=\det(A)\operatorname{tr}(A^{-1}H).$$

Let $F:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and suppose one $L\ge0$ satisfies $\|F(t,x)-F(t,y)\|_2\le L\|x-y\|_2$ for all $t,x,y$. Then every IVP for $x'=F(t,x)$ has a unique global solution.

Let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous on an open ODE domain, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an order-convex interval with at least two elements, and let $x,y:I\to\mathbb R^n$ solve $z'=F(t,z)$ with both graphs in $D$. Fix $t_0\in I$, and suppose that for every $t\in I$,

$$\|F(t,x(t))-F(t,y(t))\|_2\le L\|x(t)-y(t)\|_2.$$

Then

$$\|x(t)-y(t)\|_2\le e^{L|t-t_0|}\|x(t_0)-y(t_0)\|_2.$$

Coincident initial values give uniqueness on every common interval.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $n\ge 1$ and $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$; over $\mathbb R$ the same definition uses transpose
instead of conjugate transpose.

The matrix $A$ is **Hermitian positive definite** if $A=A^*$ and

$$x^*Ax>0$$for every nonzero vector $x\in \mathbb C^n$. A **Cholesky factorisation with positive diagonal** of $A$ is a factorisation$$A=LL^*,$$

where $L$ is lower triangular and every diagonal entry of $L$ is a positive real
number.

The Hermitian terminology matches
[[def-sesquilinear-and-hermitian-forms-over-a-field-with-involution]], and the
triangular terminology matches
[[def-triangular-and-diagonal-matrices-over-a-commutative-ring]].

Let $n\ge 1$ and let $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$, with the real case obtained by
restricting scalars to $\mathbb R$. Then the following are equivalent:

1. $A$ has a Cholesky factorisation $A=LL^*$ with $L$ lower triangular and
   positive real diagonal.
2. $A$ is Hermitian positive definite.

When these conditions hold, the factor $L$ is unique.

If $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$ is upper or lower triangular over a commutative ring, with $n\ge1$, then
$$\det(A)=\prod_{i<n}a_{ii}.$$

For $n\ge1$ and $A,B\in M_n(R)$ over a commutative ring,
$$\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B).$$

For every $n\ge1$ and every real matrix $A\in M_n(\mathbb R)$,
$$A\text{ is invertible}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\det(A)\ne0.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

If every partial derivative $\partial_jf_i(a)$ of $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ exists, the **Jacobian matrix** is $Jf(a)=(\partial_jf_i(a))_{i<n,j<m}$. For scalar-valued $f$, its **gradient** is

$$\nabla f(a):=(\partial_0f(a),\ldots,\partial_{m-1}f(a))\in\mathbb R^m,$$

with coordinates understood in the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]). The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

derivations.claim: By [F7], $M=LL^T$ where $L$ is lower triangular with strictly positive diagonal. Thus $\det L$ is the positive product of its diagonal entries, and $\det M=\det L\det(L^T)=(\det L)^2>0$; [F7] implies that $M$ is invertible, so $M^{-1}$ is well-defined and symmetric. Since $U\in C^2$, [F9] makes $F$ a $C^1$ vector field. By [F1] it has a unique maximal $C^1$ flow, and completeness as defined in the Statement makes every time slice $\Phi_t$ global with inverse $\Phi_{-t}$. Differentiating $\Phi_{-t}\circ\Phi_t=I$ by [F2] shows $D\Phi_t(z)$ is invertible. The derivative $A(t):=D\Phi_t(z)$ satisfies $A'(t)=DF(\Phi_t(z))A(t)$ by [F1].

Along a solution $z(t)=(q(t),p(t))$, [F2] and the displayed Hamilton equations give $$\frac d{dt}H(q(t),p(t))=\nabla U(q(t))^TM^{-1}p(t)+(M^{-1}p(t))^T(-\nabla U(q(t)))=0,$$ where symmetry of $M^{-1}$ identifies the derivative of the kinetic energy. Hence $H(\Phi_t(z))=H(z)$.

Suppose $\nabla U$ is globally $L$-Lipschitz. For $z=(q,p)$ and $w=(q',p')$, [F6] gives $$\|F(z)-F(w)\|_2^2\le\|M^{-1}\|_F^2\|p-p'\|_2^2+L^2\|q-q'\|_2^2\le C^2\|z-w\|_2^2.$$ Thus the time-independent field on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{2d}$ has global state-Lipschitz constant $C$.

By [F9], the variational matrix is $$DF(q,p)=\begin{pmatrix}0&M^{-1}\\-\nabla^2U(q)&0\end{pmatrix},$$ whose trace is zero. Since $A(t)$ is invertible by step 1.1, [F3] and the finite-sum trace identity $\operatorname{tr}(XY)=\sum_{i,j}X_{ij}Y_{ji}=\operatorname{tr}(YX)$ give $$\frac d{dt}\det A(t)=\det A(t)\operatorname{tr}(A(t)^{-1}DF(\Phi_t(z))A(t))=\det A(t)\operatorname{tr}(DF(\Phi_t(z)))=0.$$ Since $A(0)=I_{2d}$, $\det A(0)=1$, so $\det D\Phi_t(z)=1$ for all $t$.

Apply [F4] to obtain completeness and uniqueness in this globally Lipschitz case, and apply [F5] with the same $C$ to obtain the stated Gronwall stability estimate. This supplies a sufficient condition; no completeness is inferred from merely local Lipschitz continuity of $\nabla U$.

For each $t\in\mathbb R$, step 1.1 makes $\Phi_t:\mathbb R^{2d}\to\mathbb R^{2d}$ a global $C^1$ diffeomorphism. For any Lebesgue-measurable $E\subseteq\mathbb R^{2d}$, apply [F8] to $\mathbf1_E$ and use step 2.1 to get $\lambda_{2d}(\Phi_t^{-1}(E))=\int_{\mathbb R^{2d}}\mathbf1_E(\Phi_t(z))|\det D\Phi_t(z)|\,dz=\lambda_{2d}(E)$. Hence the exact flow preserves phase-space Lebesgue volume.
