citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $K$ be a probability kernel on a measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and let $\pi$ be a
probability measure on $(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). The
probability measure $\pi$ is **invariant** for $K$, and $\pi$ is a
**stationary distribution** of $K$, when

$$(\pi K)(A):=\int_E K(x,A)\,\pi(dx)=\pi(A)\qquad\text{for every }A\in\mathcal E .$$

The set function $\pi K$ is again a probability measure: for fixed $A$ the map
$x\mapsto K(x,A)$ is measurable and lies in $[0,1]$, so the integral exists in
$[0,1]$; for pairwise disjoint $A_n\in\mathcal E$ the identity
$K(x,\bigcup_nA_n)=\sum_nK(x,A_n)$ of the measure $K(x,\cdot)$ and the
monotone convergence theorem for nonnegative functions
([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]) give
$\sigma$-additivity of $\pi K$; and $K(x,E)=1$ for every $x$ gives
$(\pi K)(E)=1$. Thus $(\pi K)(A)=\pi(A)$ is an identity between two probability
measures evaluated at $A$.

A $K$-chain whose initial law is $\pi$ is called **stationary** when
$\pi K=\pi$. Stationarity of the process is a statement about all of its
finite-dimensional laws and is proved, not assumed, from $\pi K=\pi$; see
[[thm-invariant-initial-law-makes-the-chain-stationary]].

On a countable state space $E$ with sigma-algebra $2^E$ and transition matrix
$p(x,y)=K(x,\{y\})$ ([[def-transition-matrix-and-n-step-transition-probabilities]]),
a measure on $E$ is its weighted sum of Dirac masses at singletons
([[thm-measures-on-countable-discrete-spaces-are-weighted-dirac-sums]]), so
invariance is equivalent to the matrix identity

$$\pi(y)=\sum_{x\in E}\pi(x)\,p(x,y)\qquad\text{for every }y\in E .$$

The definition fixes no irreducibility, aperiodicity or uniqueness hypothesis,
and it selects no conditional-expectation versions; the display defines a
single measure $\pi K$ and asserts an identity for it. A transient, periodic or
reducible chain may have several invariant probability measures or none.

Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
$(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **total variation
distance** is

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}\bigl|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\bigr| .$$

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in
$[-1,1]$, because both measures have total mass one; hence the set being
maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.
The empty event and the whole space give the values $0$ and
$|\mu(E)-\nu(E)|=0$, so the distance is zero when $\mu=\nu$, and it is symmetric
in $\mu$ and $\nu$. This convention carries no factor $1/2$ in the supremum;
it is therefore not the total variation norm of the signed measure $\mu-\nu$,
which is twice the quantity above when that signed measure is considered on a
measurable space where the decomposition is attained. On a countable state
space with its power-set sigma-algebra the supremum equals the half-$\ell^1$
sum $\tfrac12\sum_{x\in E}|\mu(\{x\})-\nu(\{x\})|$; that identity is proved in
[[lem-total-variation-half-l1-formula-on-a-countable-space]], not assumed here.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ and $(\Gamma,\mathcal G)$ be nonempty measurable
spaces ([[def-measurable-space]]). Let $\pi$ be a probability measure on
$(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$, and let $(P_\gamma)_{\gamma\in\Gamma}$ be a jointly
measurable family of probability kernels on $\mathsf X$: for every
$A\in\mathcal X$, $(\gamma,x)\mapsto P_\gamma(x,A)$ is
$\mathcal G\otimes\mathcal X$-measurable and each $P_\gamma$ is a probability
kernel ([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]). Assume that $\pi$ is
invariant for every fixed kernel, meaning $\pi P_\gamma=\pi$
([[def-invariant-and-stationary-distribution-for-a-markov-kernel]]).

An **adaptive MCMC process** is a pair of measurable processes
$(X_n,\Gamma_n)_{n\ge0}$ with $X_n\in\mathsf X$, $\Gamma_n\in\Gamma$, and
natural filtration $\mathcal F_n=\sigma(X_0,\Gamma_0,\ldots,X_n,\Gamma_n)$,
such that for every $A\in\mathcal X$,
$$\mathbb P(X_{n+1}\in A\mid\mathcal F_n)=P_{\Gamma_n}(X_n,A)\quad\text{a.s.}$$
The update rule for $\Gamma_{n+1}$ may depend on the history through time
$n+1$; it is required only to make $\Gamma_{n+1}$ a measurable random variable.

For $n\ge0$, define the adaptation size
$$D_n:=\sup_{x\in\mathsf X}\lVert P_{\Gamma_{n+1}}(x,\cdot)-P_{\Gamma_n}(x,\cdot)\rVert_{\rm TV},$$
where total variation uses the convention
$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\rm TV}=\sup_{A\in\mathcal X}|\mu(A)-\nu(A)|$
([[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]]). Assume each $D_n$
is measurable; it lies in $[0,1]$. The process has **diminishing
adaptation** if $D_n\to0$ in probability as $n\to\infty$. This condition does
not require $\Gamma_n$ to converge.

Assume countable choice and dependent choice. For probability spaces
$(E_n,\mathcal E_n,\mu_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ there is a unique probability measure
$\mu$ on $\mathcal C_{\mathbb N}$ such that, for every finite $F$, its
$F$-coordinate marginal is $\bigotimes_{n\in F}\mu_n$.

Let $\mu$ be a measure and let $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be measurable. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k).$$

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ one also has

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k<m}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k<m}\mu(E_k),$$

including $m=0$, where both sides are $0$.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

derivations.claim: Since $\mathsf X$ and $\Gamma$ are finite discrete spaces, all kernel evaluations are jointly measurable. Every displayed matrix has probability rows, is symmetric, and has column sums one. Thus each is a probability kernel and $\pi P_i=\pi$ by [F1] and [F3]. For a two-state symmetric kernel with flip probability $q$, $(\delta_x-\pi)P=(1-2q)(\delta_x-\pi)$; induction gives $P^m(x,\cdot)-\pi=(1-2q)^m(\delta_x-\pi)$. For $P_0$ and $P_1$, $|1-2q|=4/5$, while $P_2=\Pi$ reaches $\pi$ in one step. Since $\lVert\delta_x-\pi\rVert_{\rm TV}=1/2$ by [F4], $$\sup_{x\in\mathsf X,\,i\in\{0,1,2\}}\lVert P_i^m(x,\cdot)-\pi\rVert_{\rm TV}\le\tfrac12(4/5)^m\quad(m\ge0).$$ The family is simultaneously uniformly ergodic.

For $k\in\mathbb N$, let $L_k=2^{2^k}$ and $s_k=\sum_{j<k}L_j$, the number of transitions before block $k$. Since $\sum_{j<k}L_j\le k2^{2^{k-1}}$, $$\frac{s_k}{L_k}\le k2^{-2^{k-1}}\longrightarrow0.$$

For each $k$, equip the finite space $$\Omega_k=\{0,\ldots,k\}\times\{1,\ldots,10\}^{L_k}$$ with its uniform probability measure. Write a coordinate as $(J_k,U_{k,0},\ldots,U_{k,L_k-1})$ and put $I_k=1_{\{J_k=0\}}$. Direct counting gives $\mathbb P(I_k=1)=1/(k+1)$; conditional on any value of $J_k$, the $U_{k,t}$ are independent and uniform on $\{1,\ldots,10\}$, with a law not depending on $J_k$. The countable product over $k\in\mathbb N$ exists by [F6] under [A1]–[A2].

In block $k$, for its first transition $n=s_k$ set $\Gamma_n=2$ and use $U_{k,0}$ to draw from $P_2$ (the next state is $0$ iff $U_{k,0}\le5$). For $n=s_k+t$ with $1\le t<L_k$, set $\Gamma_n=2$ if $I_k=0$; if $I_k=1$, set $\Gamma_n=0$ when $X_n=0$ and $\Gamma_n=1$ when $X_n=1$. Use $U_{k,t}$ to sample the selected matrix row: for $P_0$ use thresholds $9$ and $1$ for rows $0$ and $1$ respectively, for $P_1$ use thresholds $1$ and $9$, and for $P_2$ use threshold $5$; the next state is $0$ exactly when $U_{k,t}$ is at most the row's threshold. This recursively defines measurable $X_n$ and $\Gamma_n$. Each next $U_{k,t}$ is independent of the gate and earlier block coordinates by [F2] and the finite product counting in step 1.3; different blocks have the product marginals in [F6]. Therefore conditional on the history, $X_{n+1}$ has law $P_{\Gamma_n}(X_n,\cdot)$, so this is an adaptive MCMC process with the stated kernel family.

If $I_k=0$, every parameter in block $k$ is $2$, and the next block also starts with parameter $2$; hence $D_n=0$ at every transition whose current block has gate zero. If $I_k=1$, then $D_n\le1$. For each $n$ in block $k$, $$\mathbb P(D_n>0)\le\mathbb P(I_k=1)=1/(k+1)\longrightarrow0$$ as $n\to\infty$, because each block is finite and its index tends to infinity. Thus $D_n\to0$ in probability by [F5].

Conditional on $I_k=1$, for each $1\le t<L_k$ the active rule uses $P_0$ from state $0$ and $P_1$ from state $1$. In either case the next state is $0$ iff $U_{k,t}\le9$. Hence $$Z_{k,t}:=1_{\{X_{s_k+t+1}=0\}}=1_{\{U_{k,t}\le9\}}$$ are independent Bernoulli variables with success probability $p=9/10$.

Put $N_k=L_k-1$ and $\bar Z_k=N_k^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^{N_k}Z_{k,t}$. Under $I_k=1$, each centered variable $Z_{k,t}-p$ has mean zero and second moment $p(1-p)=9/100$; distinct centered variables have zero product expectation by the finite product law of the $U_{k,t}$. Expanding the square and using [F8]–[F9] gives $$\mathbb E[(\bar Z_k-p)^2\mid I_k=1]=\frac{9}{100N_k}.$$ Since $\bar Z_k<4/5$ implies $(\bar Z_k-p)^2>1/100$, Markov's inequality [F10] yields $$\mathbb P(\bar Z_k<4/5\mid I_k=1)\le\frac9{N_k}.$$

Let $H_k=\{I_k=1,\ \bar Z_k\ge4/5\}$. From steps 1.3 and 4.1, $$\mathbb P(H_k)\ge\frac1{k+1}\left(1-\frac9{L_k-1}\right)\ge\frac1{2(k+1)}$$ for all sufficiently large $k$, so $\sum_k\mathbb P(H_k)=\infty$. Each $H_k$ is a function only of coordinate $\Omega_k$, so [F6] makes these events independent. For any fixed $K$, $$\mathbb P\!\left(\bigcap_{k=K}^m H_k^c\right)=\prod_{k=K}^m(1-\mathbb P(H_k))\le\exp\!\left(-\sum_{k=K}^m\mathbb P(H_k)\right)\longrightarrow0.$$ Thus the probability of no $H_k$ after $K$ is zero; [F7] applied to the countable union over $K$ shows that infinitely many $H_k$ occur almost surely.

At the endpoint $n_k=s_k+L_k$ of any block with $H_k$, the active outputs $X_{s_k+2},\ldots,X_{s_k+L_k}$ contain at least $(4/5)(L_k-1)$ zeros. Therefore $$\frac1{n_k}\sum_{j=1}^{n_k}1_{\{X_j=0\}}\ge\frac{(4/5)(L_k-1)}{s_k+L_k}\longrightarrow\frac45$$ along the infinitely many such blocks, by step 1.2. But $\pi(1_{\{0\}})=1/2$. The strong law fails almost surely despite simultaneous uniform ergodicity and diminishing adaptation.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $K$ be a probability kernel on a measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and let $\pi$ be a
probability measure on $(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). The
probability measure $\pi$ is **invariant** for $K$, and $\pi$ is a
**stationary distribution** of $K$, when

$$(\pi K)(A):=\int_E K(x,A)\,\pi(dx)=\pi(A)\qquad\text{for every }A\in\mathcal E .$$

The set function $\pi K$ is again a probability measure: for fixed $A$ the map
$x\mapsto K(x,A)$ is measurable and lies in $[0,1]$, so the integral exists in
$[0,1]$; for pairwise disjoint $A_n\in\mathcal E$ the identity
$K(x,\bigcup_nA_n)=\sum_nK(x,A_n)$ of the measure $K(x,\cdot)$ and the
monotone convergence theorem for nonnegative functions
([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]) give
$\sigma$-additivity of $\pi K$; and $K(x,E)=1$ for every $x$ gives
$(\pi K)(E)=1$. Thus $(\pi K)(A)=\pi(A)$ is an identity between two probability
measures evaluated at $A$.

A $K$-chain whose initial law is $\pi$ is called **stationary** when
$\pi K=\pi$. Stationarity of the process is a statement about all of its
finite-dimensional laws and is proved, not assumed, from $\pi K=\pi$; see
[[thm-invariant-initial-law-makes-the-chain-stationary]].

On a countable state space $E$ with sigma-algebra $2^E$ and transition matrix
$p(x,y)=K(x,\{y\})$ ([[def-transition-matrix-and-n-step-transition-probabilities]]),
a measure on $E$ is its weighted sum of Dirac masses at singletons
([[thm-measures-on-countable-discrete-spaces-are-weighted-dirac-sums]]), so
invariance is equivalent to the matrix identity

$$\pi(y)=\sum_{x\in E}\pi(x)\,p(x,y)\qquad\text{for every }y\in E .$$

The definition fixes no irreducibility, aperiodicity or uniqueness hypothesis,
and it selects no conditional-expectation versions; the display defines a
single measure $\pi K$ and asserts an identity for it. A transient, periodic or
reducible chain may have several invariant probability measures or none.

Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
$(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **total variation
distance** is

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}\bigl|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\bigr| .$$

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in
$[-1,1]$, because both measures have total mass one; hence the set being
maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.
The empty event and the whole space give the values $0$ and
$|\mu(E)-\nu(E)|=0$, so the distance is zero when $\mu=\nu$, and it is symmetric
in $\mu$ and $\nu$. This convention carries no factor $1/2$ in the supremum;
it is therefore not the total variation norm of the signed measure $\mu-\nu$,
which is twice the quantity above when that signed measure is considered on a
measurable space where the decomposition is attained. On a countable state
space with its power-set sigma-algebra the supremum equals the half-$\ell^1$
sum $\tfrac12\sum_{x\in E}|\mu(\{x\})-\nu(\{x\})|$; that identity is proved in
[[lem-total-variation-half-l1-formula-on-a-countable-space]], not assumed here.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ and $(\Gamma,\mathcal G)$ be nonempty measurable
spaces ([[def-measurable-space]]). Let $\pi$ be a probability measure on
$(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$, and let $(P_\gamma)_{\gamma\in\Gamma}$ be a jointly
measurable family of probability kernels on $\mathsf X$: for every
$A\in\mathcal X$, $(\gamma,x)\mapsto P_\gamma(x,A)$ is
$\mathcal G\otimes\mathcal X$-measurable and each $P_\gamma$ is a probability
kernel ([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]). Assume that $\pi$ is
invariant for every fixed kernel, meaning $\pi P_\gamma=\pi$
([[def-invariant-and-stationary-distribution-for-a-markov-kernel]]).

An **adaptive MCMC process** is a pair of measurable processes
$(X_n,\Gamma_n)_{n\ge0}$ with $X_n\in\mathsf X$, $\Gamma_n\in\Gamma$, and
natural filtration $\mathcal F_n=\sigma(X_0,\Gamma_0,\ldots,X_n,\Gamma_n)$,
such that for every $A\in\mathcal X$,
$$\mathbb P(X_{n+1}\in A\mid\mathcal F_n)=P_{\Gamma_n}(X_n,A)\quad\text{a.s.}$$
The update rule for $\Gamma_{n+1}$ may depend on the history through time
$n+1$; it is required only to make $\Gamma_{n+1}$ a measurable random variable.

For $n\ge0$, define the adaptation size
$$D_n:=\sup_{x\in\mathsf X}\lVert P_{\Gamma_{n+1}}(x,\cdot)-P_{\Gamma_n}(x,\cdot)\rVert_{\rm TV},$$
where total variation uses the convention
$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\rm TV}=\sup_{A\in\mathcal X}|\mu(A)-\nu(A)|$
([[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]]). Assume each $D_n$
is measurable; it lies in $[0,1]$. The process has **diminishing
adaptation** if $D_n\to0$ in probability as $n\to\infty$. This condition does
not require $\Gamma_n$ to converge.

Use the adaptive MCMC setup of [[def-diminishing-adaptation]]. For
$\epsilon>0$, a state $x\in\mathsf X$, and a fixed parameter $\gamma\in\Gamma$,
define the convergence time
$$M_\epsilon(x,\gamma):=\inf\{m\in\mathbb N:m\ge1,\ \lVert P_\gamma^m(x,\cdot)-\pi\rVert_{\rm TV}\le\epsilon\},$$
with $\inf\varnothing=+\infty$. The power $P_\gamma^m$ is the $m$-fold
composition of the fixed kernel $P_\gamma$; it is not the adaptive transition
law. Assume $M_\epsilon(X_n,\Gamma_n)$ is measurable for each $n$ and
$\epsilon>0$.

For a specified initial probability law $\mu_0$ of $(X_0,\Gamma_0)$, the
adaptive process has **containment** if for every $\epsilon,\delta>0$ there is
an integer $N=N(\epsilon,\delta)$ such that
$$\mathbb P_{\mu_0}\!\left(M_\epsilon(X_n,\Gamma_n)\le N\right)\ge1-\delta\quad\text{for every }n\ge0.$$
A process initialized at the fixed pair $(x_*,\gamma_*)$ is the special case
$\mu_0=\delta_{(x_*,\gamma_*)}$. Thus containment says that
the fixed-kernel convergence times, evaluated at the current state and
parameter, form a sequence bounded in probability under the specified initial
law. It does not assert a uniform deterministic bound for every possible
state and parameter.

derivations.claim: Each row of $P_\gamma$ is a probability vector, and for fixed $x$ and $A$ the evaluation $P_\gamma(x,A)$ is affine in $\gamma$. Hence the family is jointly measurable on the stated finite discrete state space and Borel parameter space. Also $\pi P_\gamma=(1-\gamma)\pi+\gamma\pi=\pi$. The same projection identity $\Pi^2=\Pi$ gives $P_\gamma^m(x,\cdot)=(1-\gamma)^m\delta_x+\bigl(1-(1-\gamma)^m\bigr)\pi,$ so $\lVert P_\gamma^m(x,\cdot)-\pi\rVert_{\rm TV}=(1-\gamma)^m/2\to0$ for each fixed $\gamma$. Thus all individual kernels are ergodic for the common invariant target.
The difference of two successive rows is $(\Gamma_{n+1}-\Gamma_n)(\pi-\delta_x)$, so $D_n=|\Gamma_{n+1}-\Gamma_n|/2\to0$.

Let $r_0=1$ and $r_n=\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}(1-\Gamma_j)$. The law recursion $\mu_{n+1}=\mu_nP_{\Gamma_n}$ gives $\mu_n=r_n\delta_0+(1-r_n)\pi$. Since $\sum_j\Gamma_j=1/2$ and $\Gamma_j\le1/4$, the elementary bound $\log(1-u)\ge-2u$ for $0\le u\le1/2$ yields $r_n\ge\exp(-2\sum_j\Gamma_j)=e^{-1}$. Hence $\lVert\mu_n-\pi\rVert_{\rm TV}=r_n/2\ge e^{-1}/2$, so the marginal law does not converge to $\pi$.

For $\epsilon=1/4$, the formula in step 1.1 shows $M_\epsilon(x,\Gamma_n)\to\infty$ for both states as $\Gamma_n\to0$. Thus for every finite $N$, the probability of $M_\epsilon(X_n,\Gamma_n)\le N$ is eventually zero, contradicting containment in [F5].

flow measure of $(\pi,P)$ is the probability measure $\Lambda_{\pi,P}$ on
$(\mathsf X\times\mathsf X,\mathcal X\otimes\mathcal X)$ given, for each
$C\in\mathcal X\otimes\mathcal X$, by

$$\Lambda_{\pi,P}(C):=\int_{\mathsf X}P(x,C_x)\,\pi(dx),\qquad C_x:=\{y\in\mathsf X:(x,y)\in C\}.$$

Existence, countable additivity, and the nonnegative iterated-integral identity
for this measure follow from
[[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]]. Let $\tau(x,y):=(y,x)$ be
the coordinate-swap map. It is measurable because the preimage of a measurable
rectangle $A\times B$ is $B\times A$ and such rectangles generate the product
sigma-algebra. Define the transpose measure by
$\Lambda_{\pi,P}^{\top}(C):=\Lambda_{\pi,P}(\tau^{-1}(C))$.

The kernel $P$ is **reversible with respect to $\pi$** when
$$\Lambda_{\pi,P}=\Lambda_{\pi,P}^{\top}.$$
This definition uses equality of measures and requires no density, standard
Borel assumption, or prior assumption that $\pi$ is invariant.

conditions holds, then

derivations.claim: The matrix of $P_\gamma$ is $\begin{pmatrix}1-\gamma/2&\gamma/2\\\gamma/2&1-\gamma/2\end{pmatrix}.$ Its entries are continuous in $\gamma$, so the family is jointly measurable on the stated spaces; its rows are probability vectors by $0\le\gamma\le1$ and [F1]. The matrix is symmetric, and $\pi$ assigns equal mass to both states, so the four joint-flow atoms are symmetric under coordinate swap. Thus $P_\gamma$ is reversible by [F2], and $\pi$ is invariant by [F3].
The kernels satisfy $P_{\gamma'}(x,\cdot)-P_\gamma(x,\cdot)=(\gamma'-\gamma)(\pi-\delta_x)$, so $D_n=|\Gamma_{n+1}-\Gamma_n|/2\to0$. This is diminishing adaptation by [F5].

Since $\Pi^2=\Pi$ and $I\Pi=\Pi I=\Pi$, induction gives $P_\gamma^m=(1-\gamma)^mI+\bigl(1-(1-\gamma)^m\bigr)\Pi.$ For either state $x$, $\lVert\delta_x-\pi\rVert_{\rm TV}=1/2$, so $\lVert P_\gamma^m(x,\cdot)-\pi\rVert_{\rm TV}=(1-\gamma)^m/2\le2^{-m-1}$ uniformly in $x$ and $\gamma\in[1/2,1]$. Therefore the family is simultaneously uniformly ergodic.
Steps 2.1 and 1.2 verify the two hypotheses in alternative 1 of [F6]. Hence $\lVert\mathcal L(X_n)-\pi\rVert_{\rm TV}\to0$ for every initial state.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Fix $n \ge 1$ and let $\lambda_n^*$ be the Lebesgue outer set function on $\mathbb{R}^n$
([[def-lebesgue-outer-measure]]). A set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is
**Lebesgue measurable** when

$$\lambda_n^*(A) \;=\; \lambda_n^*(A \cap E) \;+\; \lambda_n^*(A \setminus E) \qquad \text{for every } A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n .$$

This formula makes sense before any outer-measure theorem is invoked. Under
countable choice, [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-is-an-outer-measure-agreeing-with-volume]]
makes $\lambda_n^*$ an outer measure, and the displayed condition is then exactly
Carathéodory measurability in the sense of [[def-caratheodory-measurable-set]].

The family of Lebesgue measurable sets is written $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$,
and **Lebesgue measure** is the restriction

$$\lambda_n \;:=\; \lambda_n^*\!\restriction_{\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)} .$$

On the real line the subscript is dropped and $\lambda := \lambda_1$.

The quantifier over every test set $A$ is part of the condition, and no
hypothesis on $E$ is imposed before it is tested. That
$\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra and that $\lambda_n$ is a complete
measure on it are not part of this definition: they are proved, under the Axiom
of Countable Choice, in [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]], which is
recorded in this item's `justified_by` because it is a statement about the
objects introduced here. Until that theorem the symbols $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$
and $\lambda_n$ name a family of sets and a restricted set function, nothing more.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and
   $\lambda_n$ is a measure on it ([[def-measure]]);
2. the measure space $(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n), \lambda_n)$ is
   complete ([[def-complete-measure-space]]), and every $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   with $\lambda_n^*(S) = 0$ is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(S) = 0$;
3. every elementary set is Lebesgue measurable and
   $\lambda_n(A) = \mu_0(A)$ for every $A \in \mathcal{E}_n$; in particular
   $\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ for every half-open box $B$,
   $\lambda_n(\varnothing) = 0$ and $\lambda_n(\mathbb{R}^n) = +\infty$.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then

$$\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n) \;\subseteq\; \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n) :$$

every Borel subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]) is Lebesgue
measurable ([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]). In
particular every open set, every closed set and every countable intersection of
open sets is Lebesgue measurable.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$, let
$\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Suppose $f$ and $g$ are continuous at
$c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then:

1. $f + g$, $\alpha f$ and $fg$ are continuous at $c$;
2. $|f|$, the function $x \mapsto |f(x)|$, is continuous at $c$;
3. $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, defined pointwise by
   $x \mapsto \max\{f(x), g(x)\}$ and $x \mapsto \min\{f(x), g(x)\}$
   ([[def-max-min]]), are continuous at $c$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is continuous at
   $c$ as a function on $A_0$.

Moreover, with no hypothesis at all:

5. every constant function $A \to \mathbb{R}$ and the identity
   $\mathrm{id} : A \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto x$, are continuous on $A$; hence
   so is $x \mapsto x^{n}$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$
   ([[def-integer-power]]), and hence so is every **polynomial function**
   $x \mapsto a_0 + a_1 x + \dots + a_n x^{n}$ with real coefficients.

Consequently, if $f$ and $g$ are continuous **on** $A$ then so are $f+g$,
$\alpha f$, $fg$, $|f|$, $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, and
$(f/g)|_{A_0}$ is continuous on $A_0$.

**Claim 4 is stated on $A_0$ because $f/g$ is not defined where $g$ vanishes**,
and $g$ may well vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$. The hypothesis is
$g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ nowhere zero"; what it buys is that $c$ itself lies in
the smaller domain, which is what makes continuity there mean anything.

**Nothing here is proved through a sequence.** Claims 1 and 4 are read off from
[[thm-algebra-of-function-limits]], which is itself proved from $\varepsilon$
and $\delta$, and claims 2, 3 and 5 are proved directly below. So no choice
principle is used anywhere in this item.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $n,m\ge1$. Every continuous map
$f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is Borel measurable in
the sense of [[def-borel-and-lebesgue-measurable-function-on-rn]].

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. The **measure with density $f$ relative
to $\mu$** is the measure
$$f\,d\mu:\mathcal A\to[0,+\infty],\qquad (f\,d\mu)(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu,$$
whose measure property is supplied by
[[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]].

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $a<b$ and let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be
bounded and Riemann integrable. Then $f$ is Lebesgue measurable on $[a,b]$ and
is integrable there, and its Lebesgue integral equals its Riemann integral:
$$\int_{[a,b]} f\,d\lambda_1=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx.$$

This is the point at which the completeness of Lebesgue measure is used
essentially: the proof obtains a Borel function equal to $f$ almost everywhere,
and measurability of $f$ itself is then a completeness statement.

For every $x\in\mathbb R$,

$$\frac{d}{dx}\arctan x=\frac1{1+x^2},\qquad \arctan x=\int_0^x\frac{dt}{1+t^2}.$$

For $|x|<1$,

$$\arctan x=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^n x^{2n+1}}{2n+1}.$$

At the endpoint, the ordinarily convergent alternating series satisfies

$$\frac\pi4=1-\frac13+\frac15-\frac17+\cdots.$$

Let $a < c < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be bounded
([[def-bounded-set]]). Then:

1. $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]) **if and only if** its
   restrictions to $[a,c]$ and to $[c,b]$ are integrable;
2. and in that case
   $$\int_a^b f \;=\; \int_a^c f \;+\; \int_c^b f .$$
3. **Oriented form.** Let $\alpha < \beta$ be reals, let $f : [\alpha,\beta] \to
   \mathbb{R}$ be integrable, and let $u, v, w \in [\alpha,\beta]$ be arbitrary.
   Then, with the convention of [[def-oriented-integral]],
   $$\int_u^v f \;+\; \int_v^w f \;=\; \int_u^w f .$$

Claim 3 is where [[def-oriented-integral]] earns its place: it holds for every
arrangement of the three points, including the degenerate ones, and it is the
form used everywhere below.

By [[lem-tangent-principal-branch-is-bijective]], tangent restricts to a
continuous strictly increasing bijection

$$\tan:(-\pi/2,\pi/2)\longrightarrow\mathbb R.$$

Its inverse is the **principal inverse tangent**

$$\arctan:\mathbb R\longrightarrow(-\pi/2,\pi/2).$$

Thus $\tan(\arctan y)=y$ for every real $y$, while
$\arctan(\tan x)=x$ precisely for $x$ in the displayed principal interval.
The inverse is continuous and strictly increasing by [[thm-continuous-inverse]].

For every real $x$, $\sin ^2x+\cos ^2x=1$, $\sin(-x)=-\sin x$, and $\cos(-x)=\cos x$. Wherever the displayed quotients are defined, $\tan(-x)=-\tan x$, $\cot(-x)=-\cot x$, $\sec(-x)=\sec x$, $\csc(-x)=-\csc x$, $1+\tan^2x=\sec^2x$, and $1+\cot^2x=\csc^2x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]], [[def-tangent-cotangent-secant-cosecant]].

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $\gamma$ be the unique smallest positive zero of cosine supplied by [[thm-cosine-has-a-smallest-positive-zero]]. Define
$$\pi:=2\gamma.$$

Thus $\pi>0$ and $\pi/2=\gamma$.

The **real numbers** are the quotient ring

$$\mathbb{R} := \mathcal{C} / \mathcal{N}$$

of the ring of Cauchy sequences ([[thm-cauchy-ring]]) by the ideal of null
sequences ([[lem-null-ideal]]). The class of $(a_n)$ is written
$[(a_n)]$. Each rational $q$ maps to the class $\hat q$ of the constant
sequence $(q, q, q, \dots)$.

The Cauchy-sequence reals $\mathbb{R}_C$ have the **least-upper-bound property**:
every nonempty $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}_C$ that is bounded above has a least upper
bound $\sup S \in \mathbb{R}_C$. Hence, together with [[thm-reals-ordered-field]],
$\mathbb{R}_C$ is a **complete ordered field** ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]).

Every complete ordered field $F$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) is Archimedean:
for every $x \in F$ there is a natural number $n \ge 1$ with $x < n \cdot 1_F$,
where $n \cdot 1_F$ is the canonical natural of the ordered field $F$
([[def-ordered-field]]). Equivalently, the canonical naturals are cofinal in $F$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

1. If $f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ are measurable and $f+g$ is defined
   pointwise, then $f+g$ is measurable.
2. If $c\in\mathbb R$ and $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, then $cf$ is
   measurable.
3. If $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, then $f^+=\max\{f,0\}$,
   $f^-=\max\{-f,0\}$, and $|f|=f^++f^-$ are measurable.
4. If $E\in\mathcal A$ and $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, then
   $f\chi_E$ is measurable, where this function equals $f$ on $E$ and $0$
   off $E$ (in particular, $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ here).
5. If $(f_n)$ is a sequence of measurable functions $X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$,
   then $\inf_n f_n$ is measurable; if moreover $f_n\uparrow f$ pointwise, then
   $f$ is measurable.

derivations.claim: Since $1+x^2\ge1$ and $\pi>0$ by [F9], the denominator in $f$ is positive. By [F2], $f$ is continuous and Borel measurable; [A1] and [F1] make it Lebesgue measurable. It is nonnegative, so [F3] defines the measure $\mu_C=f\,d\lambda$.

For each integer $n\ge1$, $f$ is continuous on $[-n,n]$, so [F4] permits evaluation of its Lebesgue integral by the Riemann integral. By [F5] and the evenness of $(1+x^2)^{-1}$, $\mu_C([-n,n])=\pi^{-1}\int_{-n}^n(1+x^2)^{-1}dx =(\arctan n-\arctan(-n))/\pi=2\arctan(n)/\pi$; the last equality follows from [F7].

The sequence $\arctan(n)$ is increasing and bounded above by $\pi/2$ by [F6]. For any $0<\varepsilon<\pi$, put $u=\pi/2-\varepsilon$ and $r=\tan u$. By [F10], all sufficiently large natural $n$ satisfy $n>r$, so strict increase and the inverse identity in [F6] give $\pi/2-\varepsilon=u<\arctan(n)<\pi/2$. This is the epsilon definition of $\arctan(n)\to\pi/2$.

The interval $[-n,n]$ is Borel and hence Lebesgue measurable by [F1]; [F11] makes $f\mathbf1_{[-n,n]}$ measurable. These nonnegative functions increase pointwise to $f$. By [F8], step 1.2, and step 1.3, $\mu_C(\mathbb R)=\int_{\mathbb R}f\,d\lambda =\lim_{n\to\infty}\mu_C([-n,n])=1$. Thus $\mu_C$ is a probability measure by [F9].

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $E$ be countable with sigma-algebra $2^E$, and let $K$ be a probability kernel on it. For $x,y\in E$, set

$$p(x,y):=K(x,\{y\}),\qquad p^{(n)}(x,y):=K^n(x,\{y\})\quad(n\in\mathbb N_0),$$

where $K^0$ is the identity kernel, so $p^{(0)}(x,y)=\mathbf 1_{\{x=y\}}$. By [[def-iterated-transition-kernels]], each $K^n$ is a probability kernel. Since measures on countable discrete spaces are their singleton-weighted sums ([[thm-measures-on-countable-discrete-spaces-are-weighted-dirac-sums]]), every row satisfies

$$\sum_{y\in E}p^{(n)}(x,y)=K^n(x,E)=1.$$

No conditional-expectation version or choice function is used in this matrix definition.

Let $K$ be a probability kernel on a measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and let $\pi$ be a
probability measure on $(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). The
probability measure $\pi$ is **invariant** for $K$, and $\pi$ is a
**stationary distribution** of $K$, when

$$(\pi K)(A):=\int_E K(x,A)\,\pi(dx)=\pi(A)\qquad\text{for every }A\in\mathcal E .$$

The set function $\pi K$ is again a probability measure: for fixed $A$ the map
$x\mapsto K(x,A)$ is measurable and lies in $[0,1]$, so the integral exists in
$[0,1]$; for pairwise disjoint $A_n\in\mathcal E$ the identity
$K(x,\bigcup_nA_n)=\sum_nK(x,A_n)$ of the measure $K(x,\cdot)$ and the
monotone convergence theorem for nonnegative functions
([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]) give
$\sigma$-additivity of $\pi K$; and $K(x,E)=1$ for every $x$ gives
$(\pi K)(E)=1$. Thus $(\pi K)(A)=\pi(A)$ is an identity between two probability
measures evaluated at $A$.

A $K$-chain whose initial law is $\pi$ is called **stationary** when
$\pi K=\pi$. Stationarity of the process is a statement about all of its
finite-dimensional laws and is proved, not assumed, from $\pi K=\pi$; see
[[thm-invariant-initial-law-makes-the-chain-stationary]].

On a countable state space $E$ with sigma-algebra $2^E$ and transition matrix
$p(x,y)=K(x,\{y\})$ ([[def-transition-matrix-and-n-step-transition-probabilities]]),
a measure on $E$ is its weighted sum of Dirac masses at singletons
([[thm-measures-on-countable-discrete-spaces-are-weighted-dirac-sums]]), so
invariance is equivalent to the matrix identity

$$\pi(y)=\sum_{x\in E}\pi(x)\,p(x,y)\qquad\text{for every }y\in E .$$

The definition fixes no irreducibility, aperiodicity or uniqueness hypothesis,
and it selects no conditional-expectation versions; the display defines a
single measure $\pi K$ and asserts an identity for it. A transient, periodic or
reducible chain may have several invariant probability measures or none.

Let $S\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ with Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal E$, let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a
probability space, and let $Y=(Y_n)_{n\ge0}$ be a stochastic process with each
$Y_n:\Omega\to S$ a random element
([[def-stochastic-process-and-finite-dimensional-distributions]]). The process
$Y$ is **strictly stationary** when every finite-dimensional law is unchanged
by a common nonnegative time shift: for every $r\ge1$, every
$0\le n_1<\cdots<n_r$ and every $m\ge0$,

$$\mathcal L(Y_{m+n_1},\ldots,Y_{m+n_r})=\mathcal L(Y_{n_1},\ldots,Y_{n_r}).$$

The **canonical path law** of $Y$ is the pushforward
$\mathbb P_Y=\mathcal L(Y)$ of $\mathbb P$ under the coordinate map
$\omega\mapsto(Y_n(\omega))_{n\ge0}$, a probability measure on the product
space $S^{\mathbb N_0}$ with its product sigma-algebra. The **left shift** is
$\theta(z)_n=z_{n+1}$ for $z=(z_n)_{n\ge0}\in S^{\mathbb N_0}$.

A strictly stationary process is called **ergodic** when the canonical shift $\theta$ is ergodic
for $\mathbb P_Y$ in the sense of
[[def-ergodic-measure-preserving-system]]. The shift-invariance needed for that
definition, namely that $\theta$ is measure preserving for $\mathbb P_Y$, is
proved below for strictly stationary $Y$, so in that case
$(S^{\mathbb N_0},\mathcal E^{\otimes\mathbb N_0},\mathbb P_Y,\theta)$ is a
probability measure-preserving system in the sense of
[[def-measure-preserving-transformation-and-system]].

Let $(X_n)_{n\ge0}$ be random elements of a measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$
on a common probability space, and let $h:E\to\mathbb R$ be measurable.
Suppose $Y_n:=h(X_n)$ is a strictly stationary real process in the sense of
[[def-stationary-process-and-canonical-shift]], and suppose
$0<\sigma_h^2:=\operatorname{Var}(Y_0)<\infty$ using
[[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]. For $k\ge1$, put

$$\rho_h(k):=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(Y_0,Y_k)}{\sigma_h^2}.$$

If $\sum_{k\ge1}|\rho_h(k)|<\infty$ and
$\tau_h:=1+2\sum_{k\ge1}\rho_h(k)>0$, define the theoretical
**functional-specific effective sample size** for an integer $n\ge1$ draws by
$\operatorname{ESS}_h(n):=n/\tau_h$. Here $Y_n$ is the scalar
functional whose Monte Carlo average is being assessed. When a central limit
theorem for that average has asymptotic variance
$\sigma_h^2\tau_h$, this definition is the iid sample size with the same
asymptotic variance. It does not assert that such a central limit theorem holds.
If the covariance series is not absolutely summable or $\tau_h\le0$, this
definition does not assign a finite positive effective sample size.

Assume the axiom of choice. Let $K$ be a probability kernel on $(E,\mathcal E)$,
let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P,(\mathcal F_n)_{n\ge0})$ be a filtered
probability space, and let $X=(X_n)_{n\ge0}$ be an adapted $E$-valued process.
We call $X$ a **time-homogeneous Markov chain with transition kernel $K$ relative
to $(\mathcal F_n)$** if, for every $n\ge0$ and $A\in\mathcal E$,
$$ \mathbb P(X_{n+1}\in A\mid\mathcal F_n)=K(X_n,A)\qquad\text{a.s.} $$
Here the left side is an almost-everywhere class of conditional-probability
versions. The right side is $\mathcal F_n$-measurable because
$x\mapsto K(x,A)$ is $\mathcal E$-measurable and $X_n$ is
$\mathcal F_n/\mathcal E$-measurable.

If $\mathcal F_n=\sigma(X_0,\ldots,X_n)$, we say simply that $X$ is a Markov
chain relative to its **natural filtration**. A chain relative to a larger
filtration is therefore a stronger assertion, not merely a change of notation.

Choice is used only through the library construction that supplies conditional
expectations, hence conditional probabilities, simultaneously as
almost-everywhere classes; this definition asserts no pointwise regular
conditional distribution.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

derivations.claim: Each row of $P$ is nonnegative and sums to one. The uniform law is invariant because each column also sums to one, so $\pi P=\pi$ by [F1] and [F2]. By [F5], the transition rule is time homogeneous. Repeated use of the Markov property gives, for times $n_1<\cdots<n_r$ and states $x_1,\ldots,x_r$, the path probability $\pi(x_1)\prod_{j=1}^{r-1}P^{n_{j+1}-n_j}(x_j,x_{j+1})$: the first marginal is $\pi$ because $\pi P=\pi$, and each later gap uses the corresponding matrix iterate. This expression depends only on the gaps, so a common time shift leaves every finite-dimensional law unchanged, which is strict stationarity by [F3].

Under $\pi$, $\mathbb E[Y_n]=0$ and $\operatorname{Var}(Y_n)=1$ by [F6]. Given $Y_n=1$, the next value is $1$ with probability $.9$ and $-1$ with probability $.1$; given $Y_n=-1$, the signs reverse. Thus $\mathbb E[Y_{n+1}\mid Y_n]=.8Y_n$. Iteration gives $\mathbb E[Y_{n+k}\mid Y_n]=.8^kY_n$. Since $\mathbb E Y_n=0$ and $\operatorname{Var}(Y_n)=1$, [F6] gives $\rho(k)=\mathbb E(Y_nY_{n+k})=.8^k$.
The sum is geometric, so $\tau=1+2\sum_{k\ge1}.8^k=1+2(.8/.2)=9$. By [F4], the ESS for $n$ unthinned transitions is $n/9$.

Keeping every tenth state gives retained lag-$j$ correlation $.8^{10j}$. Therefore $\tau_{10}=1+2\sum_{j\ge1}.8^{10j}=(1+.8^{10})/(1-.8^{10})\approx1.240$, and there are $n/10$ retained states. Its ESS is approximately $(n/10)/1.240=.0806n$, less than $n/9=.1111n$. The displayed lag-one correlation is lower, but the total information under a fixed transition budget is also lower.

Every row of $\Pi$ is $\pi$, hence $\pi\Pi=\pi$; linearity gives $\pi P=.99\pi K+.01\pi\Pi=\pi$.

statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

**Inputs:** $M\ge2$ scalar chains $x_{m,1},\ldots,x_{m,L}$ of equal length
$L\ge4$.

1. Let $N=\lfloor L/2\rfloor$. Replace each original chain by two chains: its
   first $N$ observations and its last $N$ observations. If $L$ is odd, discard
   the middle observation. There are now $M'=2M$ chains of length $N\ge2$.
2. For each split chain $j$, compute its mean $\bar x_j$ and sample variance
   $s_j^2=(N-1)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N(x_{j,i}-\bar x_j)^2$. Put
   $\bar x_{\cdot}=M'^{-1}\sum_j\bar x_j$,
   $W=M'^{-1}\sum_j s_j^2$, and
   $B=N(M'-1)^{-1}\sum_j(\bar x_j-\bar x_{\cdot})^2$.
3. If $W=0$, return **not estimable**. Otherwise return
   $$\widehat R_{\rm split}=\sqrt{\frac{\widehat V^+}{W}},\qquad \widehat V^+=\frac{N-1}{N}W+\frac{B}{N}.$$

This finite-sample formula is not clamped below at $1$; identical split-chain
means can therefore give a value slightly below $1$. Its interpretation as a
convergence diagnostic requires more than the arithmetic procedure itself.

**Inputs:** $M\ge2$ equal-length scalar chains with at least four observations
each. Let $S$ be the total number of pooled draws.

1. Apply [[def-blom-rank-normalization-for-pooled-draws]] to all pooled draws,
   split the transformed chains as in
   [[alg-split-rhat-from-multiple-chains]], and calculate the split statistic
   $R_z$ on the transformed values.
2. Compute the pooled median $m$ by sorting all $S$ draws and averaging the two
   central order statistics when $S$ is even (using the central order statistic
   when $S$ is odd). Fold each original draw to $|x_{m,n}-m|$, apply the same
   pooled rank-normal transformation to these folded values, split each folded
   chain, and calculate the split statistic $R_f$.
3. If either split calculation is not estimable, return **not estimable**.
   Otherwise return $\widehat R=\max\{R_z,R_f\}$.

The rank-normalized component addresses location and trend differences in a
finite output array; folding the absolute deviations makes the reported maximum
sensitive to scale differences as well. It is a diagnostic procedure, not a
proof of stationarity or convergence.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $Z$ have the standard normal law and let
$\Phi(x)=P(Z\le x)$ be its cumulative distribution function. Then $\Phi$ is
continuous and strictly increasing, with limits $0$ and $1$ at $-\infty$ and
$+\infty$, and $P(Z=x)=0$ for every $x\in\mathbb R$. For each $q\in(0,1)$
there is a unique real $z_q$ with
$\Phi(z_q)=q$, and
$$z_{1-q}=-z_q.$$

Let $\lambda$ be Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R$ and put
$f(x)=1/(\pi(1+x^2))$. Define the **standard Cauchy law** to be the measure
$\mu_C=f\,d\lambda$ given by [[def-measure-with-density]]. The proof below
verifies that this measure has total mass one, so it is a probability law.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int g\,d(f\,d\mu)=\int gf\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

If $s$ is a nonnegative simple measurable function, then its nonnegative
Lebesgue integral equals its simple integral:
$$\int s\,d\mu=\int_{\mathrm{simple}} s\,d\mu.$$

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

Let $\gamma$ be the unique smallest positive zero of cosine supplied by [[thm-cosine-has-a-smallest-positive-zero]]. Define
$$\pi:=2\gamma.$$

Thus $\pi>0$ and $\pi/2=\gamma$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$, let
$\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Suppose $f$ and $g$ are continuous at
$c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then:

1. $f + g$, $\alpha f$ and $fg$ are continuous at $c$;
2. $|f|$, the function $x \mapsto |f(x)|$, is continuous at $c$;
3. $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, defined pointwise by
   $x \mapsto \max\{f(x), g(x)\}$ and $x \mapsto \min\{f(x), g(x)\}$
   ([[def-max-min]]), are continuous at $c$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is continuous at
   $c$ as a function on $A_0$.

Moreover, with no hypothesis at all:

5. every constant function $A \to \mathbb{R}$ and the identity
   $\mathrm{id} : A \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto x$, are continuous on $A$; hence
   so is $x \mapsto x^{n}$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$
   ([[def-integer-power]]), and hence so is every **polynomial function**
   $x \mapsto a_0 + a_1 x + \dots + a_n x^{n}$ with real coefficients.

Consequently, if $f$ and $g$ are continuous **on** $A$ then so are $f+g$,
$\alpha f$, $fg$, $|f|$, $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, and
$(f/g)|_{A_0}$ is continuous on $A_0$.

**Claim 4 is stated on $A_0$ because $f/g$ is not defined where $g$ vanishes**,
and $g$ may well vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$. The hypothesis is
$g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ nowhere zero"; what it buys is that $c$ itself lies in
the smaller domain, which is what makes continuity there mean anything.

**Nothing here is proved through a sequence.** Claims 1 and 4 are read off from
[[thm-algebra-of-function-limits]], which is itself proved from $\varepsilon$
and $\delta$, and claims 2, 3 and 5 are proved directly below. So no choice
principle is used anywhere in this item.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $n,m\ge1$. Every continuous map
$f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is Borel measurable in
the sense of [[def-borel-and-lebesgue-measurable-function-on-rn]].

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then

$$\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n) \;\subseteq\; \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n) :$$

every Borel subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]) is Lebesgue
measurable ([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]). In
particular every open set, every closed set and every countable intersection of
open sets is Lebesgue measurable.

derivations.claim: Put $h(x):=x^2f(x)=x^2/(\pi(1+x^2))$, which is nonnegative and measurable by [F11]. For every finite $R>1$ and $x\in[1,R]$, $x^2/(1+x^2)\ge1/2$, so $(2\pi)^{-1}\mathbf1_{[1,R]}(x)\le h(x)$. By [F9] and [F10], $\int_{\mathbb R}h\,d\lambda\ge\int_{\mathbb R}(2\pi)^{-1}\mathbf1_{[1,R]}\,d\lambda=\frac{R-1}{2\pi}.$ These lower bounds are unbounded as $R\to\infty$, so $\int h\,d\lambda=+\infty$. Applying [F8] to the nonnegative measurable function $x\mapsto x^2$ gives $\int_{\mathbb R}x^2\,d\mu_C=\int_{\mathbb R}x^2f\,d\lambda=\int_{\mathbb R}h\,d\lambda=+\infty.$ Thus the Cauchy target is not square-integrable, and its population variance is not defined under [F1].

Splitting the arrays gives four length-four chains, two with values $(-1,-1,1,1)$ and two with $(1,1,3,3)$. Each has sample variance $4/3$; their means are $0,0,2,2$, with grand mean $1$. Hence $W=4/3$ and $B=(4/3)(1+1+1+1)=16/3$.

In the pooled sample, $-1,1,3$ have multiplicities $4,8,4$ and average ranks $2.5,8.5,14.5$. Their Blom probabilities are $17/130,1/2,113/130$. By [F7], the corresponding scores are $-a,0,a$ for $a=\Phi^{-1}(113/130)>0$. The four split-chain means are $-a/2,-a/2,a/2,a/2$, each variance is $a^2/3$, and the scale factors cancel in [F2]; the rank-normalized split statistic is again $\sqrt{7/4}$.
Therefore $\widehat V^+=(3/4)(4/3)+(1/4)(16/3)=7/3$, and the raw split statistic is $\sqrt{(7/3)/(4/3)}=\sqrt{7/4}$.

The pooled median is $1$, so the raw folds have values $0$ and $2$, each occurring eight times. Their average ranks are $4.5$ and $12.5$, with Blom probabilities $33/130$ and $97/130$. By [F7], their scores are $-b$ and $b$, where $b=\Phi^{-1}(97/130)>0$. Thus every folded score is $b$ times its raw fold minus $b$. A positive scaling and common translation multiply $W$ and $B$ by $b^2$ and leave $\widehat V^+/W$ unchanged. The raw folded split chains are $(2,2,0,0)$ and $(0,0,2,2)$; each has mean $1$ and sample variance $4/3$, so $B=0$ and the rank-normalized folded statistic is $\sqrt{3/4}$.
The maximum in [F3] is $\sqrt{7/4}$. The calculation detects this finite location shift, while step 1.1 shows why variance-based population reasoning is unavailable for the Cauchy target.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) and fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$. For
$0\le t\le T$, let
$(E_t,\mathcal E_t)$ be a standard-Borel state space; for $1\le t\le T$, let
$(F_t,\mathcal F_t)$ be a standard-Borel observation space
([[def-standard-borel-space]]), meaning a measurable space bimeasurably
isomorphic to a Polish space. A probability kernel has probability-measure
sections and measurable evaluations as in
[[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. Specify an initial probability
measure $\mu_0$ on $E_0$ (a measure of total mass one, as in
[[def-probability-measure]]), transition probability kernels $K_t$ from
$E_{t-1}$ to $E_t$, and observation probability kernels $G_t$ from $E_t$ to
$F_t$, for $1\le t\le T$.

The trajectory space, with the finite product sigma-algebra generated by
measurable coordinate rectangles
([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]), is
$$\mathcal Z_T=E_0\times E_1\times F_1\times\cdots\times E_T\times F_T,$$
with $\mathcal Z_0=E_0$. Its finite-horizon law $P_T$ is the unique probability
law whose ordered iterated kernel integral is
$$\mu_0(dx_0)\prod_{t=1}^T K_t(x_{t-1},dx_t)G_t(x_t,dy_t).$$
The product notation means successive integration in the displayed order; it
does not assert the existence of densities. Existence and uniqueness under AC
are proved in [[thm-finite-horizon-state-space-kernel-law-exists-uniquely]].
Every finite product trajectory space is standard Borel by
[[lem-finite-products-of-standard-borel-spaces-are-standard-borel]].

The initial and transition laws specify the state evolution, while each
$G_t$ specifies the observation law given the current state in this model.
State evolution by itself therefore does not specify a joint state-observation
law. No density or time-homogeneity assumption is imposed, and no strict
stationarity assumption (shift invariance of all finite-dimensional laws) is
required ([[def-strict-and-weak-stationarity-for-time-series]]). This is a
single law, not a parameter-indexed family. The model contract records a
proposed law and makes no claim that it adequately describes an application
([[def-scientific-statistical-model-contract]]).

Assume AC. Fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$, standard-Borel spaces
$E_0,\ldots,E_T$ and $F_1,\ldots,F_T$, an initial probability measure
$\mu_0$ on $E_0$, and transition and observation probability kernels
$K_t:E_{t-1}\to E_t$ and $G_t:E_t\to F_t$ for $1\le t\le T$, as in
[[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]. On the interleaved finite
product space
$$\mathcal Z_T=E_0\times E_1\times F_1\times\cdots\times E_T\times F_T,$$
there is a unique probability measure whose rectangle probabilities are the
ordered iterated kernel integrals
$$\mu_0(dx_0)\prod_{t=1}^T K_t(x_{t-1},dx_t)G_t(x_t,dy_t).$$
The product notation means successive integration in the displayed order.
For $T=0$, the assertion is the initial law $\mu_0$ on $E_0$.
Every finite product of standard Borel spaces, with its finite product sigma-algebra, is standard Borel.

Assume AC. Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ be a measurable random element with standard-Borel target, and let $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ be any sub-sigma-algebra. There exists a regular conditional distribution of $X$ given $\mathcal G$. Every section is a probability measure, including at exceptional sample points, and no countable-generation or completeness assumption on $\mathcal G$ is required.

For this necessarily nonempty target, the construction also supplies a bimeasurable bijection $c:E\to B$ onto a Borel set $B\subseteq[0,1]$, and a countable algebra $\mathcal A$ which generates $\mathcal S$, separates points, and determines finite measures.

Assume AC. Let $X$ and $Y$ take values in nonempty standard-Borel spaces $(E,\mathcal S)$ and $(T,\mathcal T)$ on a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$. Let $L$ be a specified regular conditional distribution of $X$ given $\sigma(Y)$, everywhere a probability kernel. There is a probability kernel $K:T\to E$ such that $L(\omega,\cdot)=K(Y(\omega),\cdot)$ simultaneously outside a single null set. In fact, with the stated everywhere-kernel convention, the construction below gives this equality for every $\omega$. Consequently K is a conditional law of X given Y.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ and $Y:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(T,\mathcal T)$ be measurable random elements. A **conditional law of X given Y** is a probability kernel $K:(T,\mathcal T)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ such that $\omega\mapsto K(Y(\omega),\cdot)$ is a regular conditional distribution of X given $\sigma(Y)$ in [[def-regular-conditional-distribution]]. Thus for every $A\in\mathcal S$ and $H\in\sigma(Y)$,
$$\int_H K(Y(\omega),A)\,dP=P(H\cap\{X\in A\}).$$

Composition with Y makes each evaluation $\sigma(Y)$-measurable, and every section remains a probability by [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. The notation $P(X\in A\mid Y=y)=K(y,A)$ refers to a chosen kernel; it is not a ratio involving the possibly zero probability $P(Y=y)$.

Write $P_Y(B)=P(Y^{-1}(B))$ for the law in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]. If a specified countable family $\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal S$ determines probability measures, two conditional laws K,L agree as measures outside a single $\mathcal T$-measurable $P_Y$-null set. Indeed for each $A\in\mathcal C$ the measurable discrepancy $D_A=\{y:K(y,A)\ne L(y,A)\}$ has null inverse image under Y by [[lem-conditional-expectation-is-unique-almost-surely]]. Hence $P_Y(D_A)=0$ by the law definition; the countable union $D$ is null by [[thm-finite-and-countable-subadditivity-of-measures]], and off D the determining property gives equality of measures. This uses a supplied determining family and makes no AC assertion about obtaining one.

Values on a measurable $P_Y$-null subset may be replaced by a specified fixed probability on E without changing these identities. The inverse image of that subset is measurable null, and all event evaluations are bounded, so the modified event integrals agree. Empty-event evaluations remain zero and whole-target evaluations remain one. Existence on standard-Borel spaces is proved separately; the definition alone does not assert a conditional kernel exists.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(T,\Tau)$ be a measurable random element and $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ a sub-sigma-algebra. A **regular conditional distribution of X given $\mathcal G$** is a probability kernel $K:(\Omega,\mathcal G)\to(T,\Tau)$ satisfying
$$\int_H K(\omega,A)\,P(d\omega)=P(H\cap\{X\in A\})\qquad(H\in\mathcal G,\ A\in\Tau).$$

“Probability kernel” has the pointwise meaning of [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]: every $K(\omega,\cdot)$ is a probability measure, and every evaluation is $\mathcal G$-measurable. Its evaluations lie in $[0,1]$ and are integrable. Thus the testing identity says exactly that $K(\cdot,A)$ is a conditional-expectation version of $1_{\{X\in A\}}$ in [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. Conversely, a probability kernel with these version identities satisfies the displayed definition.

The kernel requirement holds at every sample point. Separate eventwise choices of conditional-expectation versions do not imply it and do not by themselves provide one exceptional set valid for all A. When A is empty the testing identity is zero on both sides, and when A=T it is P(H) on both sides. This defines a property of a supplied kernel and makes no existence or AC assertion.

Assume AC and fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$ with a state-space model by
probability kernels as in
[[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]. If $T=0$, put $\Omega_T=E_0$;
otherwise put $\Omega_T=E_0\times E_1\times F_1\times\cdots\times E_T\times
F_T$. Let $\mathcal Z_T$ be the corresponding finite-product sigma-algebra
and write $(\Omega_T,\mathcal Z_T,P_T)$ for its finite-horizon probability
space. The law $P_T$ is the unique law supplied by
[[thm-finite-horizon-state-space-kernel-law-exists-uniquely]]. Let $X_t$ and
$Y_t$ be the coordinate random elements taking values in $E_t$ and $F_t$. For
$t\ge1$, write $Y_{1:t}:=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_t)$ and
$\mathsf F_{1:t}:=F_1\times\cdots\times F_t$ with its finite-product
sigma-algebra; let $\mathsf F_{1:0}$ be a singleton and $Y_{1:0}$ its constant
map. The factors are standard Borel, meaning measurably isomorphic to Polish
spaces ([[def-standard-borel-space]]), and their finite products are standard
Borel ([[lem-finite-products-of-standard-borel-spaces-are-standard-borel]]).

The **initial filtering kernel** $\pi_0:\mathsf F_{1:0}\to E_0$ assigns
$\mu_0$ to the unique empty history; it is the conditional law of $X_0$ given
the trivial history. For $1\le t\le T$, a **filtering kernel at time $t$** is
a probability kernel $\pi_t:\mathsf F_{1:t}\to E_t$ such that
$\omega\mapsto\pi_t(Y_{1:t}(\omega),\cdot)$ is a regular conditional
distribution of $X_t$ given $\sigma(Y_{1:t})$. For $1\le t\le T$, a
**predictive kernel at time $t$** is a probability kernel
$\pi_{t|t-1}:\mathsf F_{1:t-1}\to E_t$ whose composition with $Y_{1:t-1}$
is a regular conditional distribution of $X_t$ given
$\sigma(Y_{1:t-1})$. A **finite-horizon smoothing kernel** is a probability
kernel $\psi_T:\mathsf F_{1:T}\to E_0\times\cdots\times E_T$ whose
composition with $Y_{1:T}$ is a regular conditional distribution of the full
state path $(X_0,\ldots,X_T)$ given $\sigma(Y_{1:T})$. Here a regular
conditional distribution is an everywhere probability kernel satisfying the
conditional event identities in
[[def-regular-conditional-distribution]], and a conditional law given a
random element is its data-indexed kernel form in
