The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$, standard-Borel spaces
$E_0,\ldots,E_T$ and $F_1,\ldots,F_T$, an initial probability measure
$\mu_0$ on $E_0$, and transition and observation probability kernels
$K_t:E_{t-1}\to E_t$ and $G_t:E_t\to F_t$ for $1\le t\le T$, as in
[[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]. On the interleaved finite
product space
$$\mathcal Z_T=E_0\times E_1\times F_1\times\cdots\times E_T\times F_T,$$
there is a unique probability measure whose rectangle probabilities are the
ordered iterated kernel integrals
$$\mu_0(dx_0)\prod_{t=1}^T K_t(x_{t-1},dx_t)G_t(x_t,dy_t).$$
The product notation means successive integration in the displayed order.
For $T=0$, the assertion is the initial law $\mu_0$ on $E_0$.

Assume AC and fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$ with a state-space model by
probability kernels as in
[[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]. If $T=0$, put $\Omega_T=E_0$;
otherwise put $\Omega_T=E_0\times E_1\times F_1\times\cdots\times E_T\times
F_T$. Let $\mathcal Z_T$ be the corresponding finite-product sigma-algebra
and write $(\Omega_T,\mathcal Z_T,P_T)$ for its finite-horizon probability
space. The law $P_T$ is the unique law supplied by
[[thm-finite-horizon-state-space-kernel-law-exists-uniquely]]. Let $X_t$ and
$Y_t$ be the coordinate random elements taking values in $E_t$ and $F_t$. For
$t\ge1$, write $Y_{1:t}:=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_t)$ and
$\mathsf F_{1:t}:=F_1\times\cdots\times F_t$ with its finite-product
sigma-algebra; let $\mathsf F_{1:0}$ be a singleton and $Y_{1:0}$ its constant
map. The factors are standard Borel, meaning measurably isomorphic to Polish
spaces ([[def-standard-borel-space]]), and their finite products are standard
Borel ([[lem-finite-products-of-standard-borel-spaces-are-standard-borel]]).

The **initial filtering kernel** $\pi_0:\mathsf F_{1:0}\to E_0$ assigns
$\mu_0$ to the unique empty history; it is the conditional law of $X_0$ given
the trivial history. For $1\le t\le T$, a **filtering kernel at time $t$** is
a probability kernel $\pi_t:\mathsf F_{1:t}\to E_t$ such that
$\omega\mapsto\pi_t(Y_{1:t}(\omega),\cdot)$ is a regular conditional
distribution of $X_t$ given $\sigma(Y_{1:t})$. For $1\le t\le T$, a
**predictive kernel at time $t$** is a probability kernel
$\pi_{t|t-1}:\mathsf F_{1:t-1}\to E_t$ whose composition with $Y_{1:t-1}$
is a regular conditional distribution of $X_t$ given
$\sigma(Y_{1:t-1})$. A **finite-horizon smoothing kernel** is a probability
kernel $\psi_T:\mathsf F_{1:T}\to E_0\times\cdots\times E_T$ whose
composition with $Y_{1:T}$ is a regular conditional distribution of the full
state path $(X_0,\ldots,X_T)$ given $\sigma(Y_{1:T})$. Here a regular
conditional distribution is an everywhere probability kernel satisfying the
conditional event identities in
[[def-regular-conditional-distribution]], and a conditional law given a
random element is its data-indexed kernel form in
[[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]].

These kernels are versions: their values can be changed on a measurable set
of observation histories of probability zero without changing the conditional
identities. No density is assumed in these definitions. The state-space model
here is one fixed law. A parametric statistical model is instead a map
$\theta\mapsto P_\theta$ from a parameter set to probability laws; its
measurability is not asserted without a parameter sigma-algebra
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]).

Let $K$ be a specified regular conditional distribution of $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ given $\mathcal G$. For measurable $f:E\to[0,\infty]$, the measurable function $I_f(\omega)=\int f(x)K(\omega,dx)$ satisfies

$$\int_H I_f\,dP=\int_H f(X)\,dP\qquad(H\in\mathcal G).$$

This assertion is choice-free. Under AC, it says $I_f=E[f(X)\mid\mathcal G]$ as nonnegative almost-sure classes. If $f:E\to\mathbb R$ is measurable and $E|f(X)|<\infty$, put $D=\{I_{|f|}<\infty\}$. Then $D\in\mathcal G$, $P(D)=1$, and the signed integral on $D$, extended by zero off $D$, is a real integrable conditional-expectation version of $f(X)$. Its identification with the AC-based conditional-expectation class uses AC only for that class convention.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $\pi$ be a prior probability on $(E,\mathcal S)$ and let $Q:E\to T$ be a probability kernel dominated by a sigma-finite measure $\nu$ on $(T,\mathcal T)$, with specified nonnegative jointly measurable density $\ell:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$:
$$Q(\theta,B)=\int_B\ell(\theta,y)\,\nu(dy)\quad\text{for every }\theta\in E,\ B\in\mathcal T.$$

Define $m(y)=\int_E\ell(\theta,y)\,\pi(d\theta)$. Under the joint law with density $\ell$ relative to $\pi\times\nu$, a conditional law of the parameter given the observation is
$$K(y,A)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\int_A\ell(\theta,y)\,\pi(d\theta)}{m(y)},&0<m(y)<\infty,\\ \pi(A),&m(y)=0\text{ or }m(y)=\infty.\end{cases}$$

The observation marginal is $m\,d\nu$, and the filled fibres have marginal mass zero. This is a choice-free assertion about the explicit kernel and event identities.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element, let
$\mathbb P_X$ be its law, and let $g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb R$ or
$g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb C$ be measurable.

1. If $g\ge0$, then
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$
2. If $g(X)$ is integrable, then $g$ is integrable with respect to
   $\mathbb P_X$ and the same formula holds:
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Assume AC and a finite-horizon state-space model by standard-Borel state and
observation spaces, an initial probability measure, and transition and
observation probability kernels, as in
[[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]. Let $P_T$ be its finite-horizon
path law. The initial filtering kernel is $\pi_0=\mu_0$ on the singleton
empty-history space. For each $1\le t\le T$, data-indexed filtering and
predictive kernels from [[def-state-space-filtering-laws]] exist. A
data-indexed finite-horizon smoothing kernel for the full state path also
exists, including when $T=0$. The claim is existence of conditional versions
only; it asserts no density, filtering recursion, uniqueness on null
observation histories, or numerical approximation.

Assume AC and a finite-horizon model as in
[[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]. For each $1\le t\le T$, suppose
the observation kernel has a supplied product-measurable density
$g_t:E_t\times F_t\to[0,\infty]$ with respect to a sigma-finite measure
$\nu_t$ on $F_t$, normalized so that
$$G_t(x,B)=\int_Bg_t(x,y)\,\nu_t(dy),\qquad\int_{F_t}g_t(x,y)\,\nu_t(dy)=1$$
for every state $x$ and measurable $B\subseteq F_t$.

The procedure takes the initial law $\mu_0$, transition kernels $K_t$,
observation densities $g_t$ and measures $\nu_t$ as inputs. It defines
data-indexed prediction, evidence, and filtering functions on every
observation history as follows.

1. Initialize $\pi_0$ on the singleton empty-history space by
$\pi_0(*,A)=\mu_0(A)$.

2. For $t=1,\ldots,T$, each history $h\in\mathsf F_{1:t-1}$ and each
measurable state set $A\in\mathcal E_t$, form the predictive measure
$$\widehat\pi_t(h,A):=\int_{E_{t-1}}K_t(x,A)\,\pi_{t-1}(h,dx).$$

3. For each $y\in F_t$, calculate the evidence density
$$z_t(h,y):=\int_{E_t}g_t(x,y)\,\widehat\pi_t(h,dx).$$

4. Define the filtering measure at $(h,y)$ by
$$\pi_t(h,y,A):=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\int_Ag_t(x,y)\,\widehat\pi_t(h,dx)}{z_t(h,y)},&0<z_t(h,y)<\infty,\\[6pt]\widehat\pi_t(h,A),&z_t(h,y)=0\text{ or }z_t(h,y)=\infty.\end{cases}$$
Use $\pi_t$ as the input filtering function at the next time step.

The procedure returns the initialized filter $\pi_0=\mu_0$ and, for every
$1\le t\le T$, $\widehat\pi_t$, $z_t$, and $\pi_t$. It is an exact
measure-valued recursion; it makes no claim that the integrals have closed
forms or can be evaluated with finite computational cost.
[[thm-dominated-state-space-filtering-recursion]] proves that the returned
time-$t$ functions are predictive and filtering kernels for the specified
finite-horizon model.

derivations.claim: For $t=1$ use $\pi_0=\mu_0$; for $t>1$ use the filtering kernel supplied by [F11] under [A1], and define $\widehat\pi_t$ by the displayed mixture. Each section has mass $\int K_t(x,E_t)\pi_{t-1}(h,dx)=1$; countable additivity follows by applying [F10] to increasing partial sums for disjoint target sets, and measurability in $h$ follows from [F4].

Regard $(h,y)\mapsto\widehat\pi_t(h,dx)$ as a probability kernel constant in $y$. Product measurability of $(h,y,x)\mapsto g_t(x,y)$ and [F4] make $z_t$ and each numerator measurable. On $0<z_t<\infty$ the numerator is a finite measure of total mass $z_t$, so division gives a probability; off that set the predictive measure is a probability. Thus $\pi_t$ is an everywhere probability kernel with measurable evaluations, including zero and infinite fibers.

For a history rectangle $H$ and measurable $A\subseteq E_t$, inserting $K_t$ at the transition factor of [F1] gives $P_T(H\cap\{X_t\in A\})=E_{P_T}[\mathbf1_HK_t(X_{t-1},A)]$, since later kernels integrate to one; at $t=1$ this is the one-step transition integral. These are finite measures of $H$, so [F7]–[F8] extend equality from history rectangles to all $H\in\sigma(Y_{1:t-1})$. Then [F3] for the filtering kernel from [F11] turns the right side into $E_{P_T}[\mathbf1_H\widehat\pi_t(Y_{1:t-1},A)]$, proving that $\widehat\pi_t$ is predictive.

Fix $h$. The prior $\widehat\pi_t(h,\cdot)$ is a probability and $G_t$ has the specified jointly measurable normalized density, so [F6] gives observation marginal $z_t(h,y)\nu_t(dy)$ and conditional kernel $\pi_t(h,y,\cdot)$; the zero and infinite evidence fibers have zero marginal. In particular, $\int_C\pi_t(h,y,A)z_t(h,y)\nu_t(dy)=\int_A G_t(x,C)\widehat\pi_t(h,dx)$.

For a history rectangle $B$ and an observation set $C\in\mathcal F_t$, the path law [F1], predictive identity from step 2.2, and conditional integration [F3] applied to $x\mapsto\mathbf1_A(x)G_t(x,C)$ give $P_T(Y_{1:t-1}\in B,X_t\in A,Y_t\in C)=\int_B\int_A G_t(x,C)\,\widehat\pi_t(h,dx)P_{Y_{1:t-1}}(dh)$. By step 3.1 this is $\int_B\int_C\pi_t(h,y,A)z_t(h,y)\,\nu_t(dy)P_{Y_{1:t-1}}(dh)$. Taking $A=E_t$ and using $\pi_t(h,y,E_t)=1$ from step 2.1 identifies the law of $(Y_{1:t-1},Y_t)$ on history-observation rectangles with $P_{Y_{1:t-1}}(dh)z_t(h,y)\nu_t(dy)$; [F7]–[F8] extend this to the product sigma-algebra.

Step 2.1 makes $\pi_t(\cdot,\cdot,A)$ measurable and bounded. The joint-observation law just established and [F9] therefore give, on each history-observation rectangle $B\times C$, $E_{P_T}[\mathbf1_{\{Y_{1:t-1}\in B,Y_t\in C\}}\pi_t(Y_{1:t-1},Y_t,A)]=\int_B\int_C\pi_t(h,y,A)z_t(h,y)\,\nu_t(dy)P_{Y_{1:t-1}}(dh).$ By step 4.1 this is $P_T(Y_{1:t-1}\in B,X_t\in A,Y_t\in C)$. Such rectangles generate $\sigma(Y_{1:t})$ by [F7], and for fixed $A$ both sides are finite measures of the conditioning event, so [F8] extends the identity to every event in $\sigma(Y_{1:t})$. Thus $\pi_t$ is a filtering kernel; step 2.2 already proves prediction, and the procedure [F12] returns the claimed kernels.

Step 3.1 applies the dominated Bayes supplier on zero-evidence fibers and assigns the predictive probability filler; step 4.1 verifies the conditional identities.
Steps 1.1–2.1 show predictive and updated sections are everywhere probability measures, including the filler branches.
The Statement permits point-mass predictive laws; the mixture and dominated update remain probability-kernel formulas for such priors.
Step 1.1 starts at π₀=μ₀ and the statement applies each t=1,…,T, including the final horizon.
A1 and steps 1.1, 2.2, and 4.1 use AC through conditional-kernel existence; the supplied Bayes filler requires no further choice.

exists, including when $T=0$. The claim is existence of conditional versions

([[def-standard-borel-space]]), meaning a measurable space bimeasurably

sections and measurable evaluations as in
[[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. Specify an initial probability
measure $\mu_0$ on $E_0$ (a measure of total mass one, as in
[[def-probability-measure]]), transition probability kernels $K_t$ from
$E_{t-1}$ to $E_t$, and observation probability kernels $G_t$ from $E_t$ to

([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]), is

single law, not a parameter-indexed family. The model contract records a

([[def-scientific-statistical-model-contract]]).

Assume AC and a finite-horizon model as in
[[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]. For each $1\le t\le T$, suppose
the observation kernel has a supplied product-measurable density
$g_t:E_t\times F_t\to[0,\infty]$ with respect to a sigma-finite measure
$\nu_t$ on $F_t$, normalized so that
$$G_t(x,B)=\int_Bg_t(x,y)\,\nu_t(dy),\qquad\int_{F_t}g_t(x,y)\,\nu_t(dy)=1$$
for every state $x$ and measurable $B\subseteq F_t$.

observation densities $g_t$ and measures $\nu_t$ as inputs. It defines
data-indexed prediction, evidence, and filtering functions on every
observation history as follows.

1. Initialize $\pi_0$ on the singleton empty-history space by
$\pi_0(*,A)=\mu_0(A)$.

2. For $t=1,\ldots,T$, each history $h\in\mathsf F_{1:t-1}$ and each
measurable state set $A\in\mathcal E_t$, form the predictive measure
$$\widehat\pi_t(h,A):=\int_{E_{t-1}}K_t(x,A)\,\pi_{t-1}(h,dx).$$

3. For each $y\in F_t$, calculate the evidence density
$$z_t(h,y):=\int_{E_t}g_t(x,y)\,\widehat\pi_t(h,dx).$$

$$\pi_t(h,y,A):=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\int_Ag_t(x,y)\,\widehat\pi_t(h,dx)}{z_t(h,y)},&0<z_t(h,y)<\infty,\\[6pt]\widehat\pi_t(h,A),&z_t(h,y)=0\text{ or }z_t(h,y)=\infty.\end{cases}$$

derivations.claim: Let $g_t(i,j):=G_t(i,\{j\})$ for $i,j\in\{0,1\}$. Counting measure integrates by finite sums, so $\sum_jg_t(i,j)=G_t(i,\{0,1\})=1$ and $G_t(i,C)=\sum_{j\in C}g_t(i,j)$; every function on these finite discrete spaces is product-measurable. Thus [F2] applies. Since $\mu_0$ is uniform and each transition-matrix column sums to one, $X_1$ is uniform; hence $P(Y_1=1)=\frac12(\frac14+\frac34)=\frac12$, and Bayes' finite sum gives $P(X_1=0\mid Y_1=1)=\frac{(1/2)(1/4)}{1/2}=1/4$ and $P(X_1=1\mid Y_1=1)=3/4$.
Predicting through $M$ gives $P(X_2=0\mid Y_1=1)=\frac14\frac34+\frac34\frac14=\frac38$ and $P(X_2=1\mid Y_1=1)=\frac14\frac14+\frac34\frac34=\frac58$.

By the ordered path law [F3], for $i=0,1$ the conditional probability of $Y_2=0$ given $X_1=i,Y_1=1$ is $\sum_{j=0}^1M_{ij}G_2(j,\{0\})$; the factor $G_1(i,\{1\})$ cancels in this conditional probability because it depends only on the fixed state $i$ and event $Y_1=1$. These sums are $(3/4)(3/4)+(1/4)(1/4)=5/8$ for $i=0$ and $(1/4)(3/4)+(3/4)(1/4)=3/8$ for $i=1$. Multiplying by the time-1 filter $(1/4,3/4)$ gives conditional smoothing masses $(5/32,9/32)$; their sum is $7/16$, the conditional evidence in step 3.1, so the smoothing law of $X_1$ is $(5/14,9/14)$. The history event has positive probability by step 1.1 and step 3.1, so its conditional distribution is fixed by the event identities.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^2}\,dx=\sqrt\pi.$$

Let $n\ge 1$, let $E\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, and let $a\in\mathbb R^n$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). The **translate** of $E$ by $a$ is

$$E+a:=\{x+a:x\in E\}.$$

Translation by $a$ is the bijection $\tau_a(x)=x+a$, whose inverse is $\tau_{-a}$. In particular, $\varnothing+a=\varnothing$.

Let $n \ge 1$, let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $E + h$ be the translate of
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-translation-of-a-set-in-rn]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

**No choice principle is used.** Lebesgue outer measure is defined as an infimum
and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so
all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is
translation invariant.

Assume AC. Then countable choice holds. Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is serial on a nonempty set X and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\ge0}$ with $x_0=a$ and $x_n R x_{n+1}$ for every n. Thus the countable and dependent choices required by the probability-product suppliers are available under AC.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), let $c$ be a nonzero real and write
$cE := \{\, cx : x \in E \,\}$ for $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$, where
$(cx)_i := cx_i$. Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(cE) = |c|^{\,n}\,\lambda_n^*(E)$ for every subset $E$, the
   product being defined in $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ because $|c|^{\,n} > 0$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $cE$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(cE) = |c|^{\,n}\lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

At $c = -1$ the map is reflection in the origin and $|c|^{\,n} = 1$, so it
preserves outer measure, measurability and measure. The value $c = 0$ is
excluded because $0E$ is $\{0\}$ or $\varnothing$ and carries no information
about $E$.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then there is an increasing sequence of
nonnegative simple measurable functions $(s_n)$ such that $s_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x\in X$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $n,m\ge1$. Every continuous map
$f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is Borel measurable in
the sense of [[def-borel-and-lebesgue-measurable-function-on-rn]].

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then

$$\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n) \;\subseteq\; \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n) :$$

every Borel subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]) is Lebesgue
measurable ([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]). In
particular every open set, every closed set and every countable intersection of
open sets is Lebesgue measurable.

Let $m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
one has
$$\mathcal B(\mathbb R^m)\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n) = \mathcal B(\mathbb R^{m+n}).$$

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and
   $\lambda_n$ is a measure on it ([[def-measure]]);
2. the measure space $(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n), \lambda_n)$ is
   complete ([[def-complete-measure-space]]), and every $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   with $\lambda_n^*(S) = 0$ is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(S) = 0$;
3. every elementary set is Lebesgue measurable and
   $\lambda_n(A) = \mu_0(A)$ for every $A \in \mathcal{E}_n$; in particular
   $\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ for every half-open box $B$,
   $\lambda_n(\varnothing) = 0$ and $\lambda_n(\mathbb{R}^n) = +\infty$.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n$ is sigma-finite ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]):
   the cubes $(-k,k]^n$ are Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n\big((-k,k]^n\big) = (2k)^n < +\infty$, they increase with $k$, and
   their union over $k \in \mathbb{N}$ is $\mathbb{R}^n$.
2. Every bounded subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has $\lambda_n^*(E) < +\infty$; a bounded
   Lebesgue measurable set therefore has finite measure, and every compact
   subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is Lebesgue measurable of finite measure.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.
Let $\mu$ be a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. If $A,B\in\mathcal A$ and $A\subseteq B$, then $\mu(A)\le\mu(B)$.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $E$ be measurable with $\mu(E)=0$.
Then
$$\int_E f\,d\mu=0.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Equip all scalar state and observation spaces with $\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$, and let $
u_1$ be Lebesgue measure restricted to this sigma-algebra. By [A1] and [F4], Countable Choice is available. By [F13], $(-k,k]$ is a common finite-mass exhaustion, so both $
u_1$ and the constant measure kernel $L(x,B)=
u_1(B)$ are sigma-finite in the required sense. The constant evaluations are measurable. By [F10] and [F12], $(x,y)\mapsto f(y-x)$ is measurable for the product Borel sigma-algebra. By [F11], its one-variable Borel sections and the simple approximations used below are also Lebesgue measurable.

For a Borel set $B$, $P(x+Z\in B)=\int_{B-x}f(u)\,du=\int_Bf(y-x)\,dy$: [F3] gives the translated integral identity for indicators, finite sums give it for simple functions, and [F6] and [F11] extend it to nonnegative Borel functions. Thus the transition and observation sections are the probability laws $N(x,1)$ and have densities $f(x_1-x)$ and $f(y-x_1)$, whose integrals are one. For fixed Borel $B$, apply [F14] to the product-measurable integrand $\mathbf1_B(y)f(y-x)$ and the constant kernel $L$ from step 1.1. Its integral is Borel measurable in $x$. Hence these location families are probability kernels, and their product-measurable normalized densities with sigma-finite $\nu_1$ meet the premises of [F7] and [F8].

For every Borel set $B$, the path law [F8], step 2.1 and simple approximation [F6] give $P(X_1\in B)=\int_{\mathbb R}\int_B f(u)f(x-u)\,
u_1(dx)
u_1(du)$. The integrand $\mathbf1_B(x)f(u)f(x-u)$ is nonnegative and product-measurable, and both copies of $
u_1$ are sigma-finite by step 1.1. Thus [F16] gives $P(X_1\in B)=\int_B[\int_{\mathbb R}f(u)f(x-u)\,
u_1(du)]
u_1(dx)$. The predictive density is therefore $\int f(u)f(x-u)\,du= rac{e^{-x^2/4}}{2\pi}\int e^{-(u-x/2)^2}\,du= rac1{\sqrt{4\pi}}e^{-x^2/4}$ by [F2] and translation. This is the density of $N(0,2)$ by [F1], dilation [F5], and the simple-approximation argument [F6].

At $y=2$, the product density from step 3.1 has exponent $-x^2/4-(2-x)^2/2=-\frac34(x-\frac43)^2-\frac23$. By [F5] and [F6], $\int e^{-\frac34(x-4/3)^2}\,dx=2\sqrt{\pi/3}$, so $z_1(2)=\frac{e^{-2/3}}{\sqrt{8\pi^2}}2\sqrt{\pi/3}=\frac{e^{-2/3}}{\sqrt{6\pi}}\in(0,\infty)$.

Dividing the product density by the evidence in step 4.1 leaves $\frac1{\sqrt{4\pi/3}}e^{-\frac34(x-4/3)^2}$, the normal density with mean $4/3$ and variance $2/3$ by [F1,F5]; since $0<z_1(2)<\infty$, [F7] and [F9] identify it as the filtering-kernel value returned by the recursive procedure. The closed singleton $\{0\}$ is measurable by [F11]; [F13] and [F15] give $0\le a:=\lambda(\{0\})\le\lambda([0,1))=1$. citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC and fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$ with a state-space model by
probability kernels as in
[[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]. If $T=0$, put $\Omega_T=E_0$;
otherwise put $\Omega_T=E_0\times E_1\times F_1\times\cdots\times E_T\times
F_T$. Let $\mathcal Z_T$ be the corresponding finite-product sigma-algebra
and write $(\Omega_T,\mathcal Z_T,P_T)$ for its finite-horizon probability
space. The law $P_T$ is the unique law supplied by
[[thm-finite-horizon-state-space-kernel-law-exists-uniquely]]. Let $X_t$ and
$Y_t$ be the coordinate random elements taking values in $E_t$ and $F_t$. For
$t\ge1$, write $Y_{1:t}:=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_t)$ and
$\mathsf F_{1:t}:=F_1\times\cdots\times F_t$ with its finite-product
sigma-algebra; let $\mathsf F_{1:0}$ be a singleton and $Y_{1:0}$ its constant
map. The factors are standard Borel, meaning measurably isomorphic to Polish
spaces ([[def-standard-borel-space]]), and their finite products are standard
Borel ([[lem-finite-products-of-standard-borel-spaces-are-standard-borel]]).

The **initial filtering kernel** $\pi_0:\mathsf F_{1:0}\to E_0$ assigns
$\mu_0$ to the unique empty history; it is the conditional law of $X_0$ given
the trivial history. For $1\le t\le T$, a **filtering kernel at time $t$** is
a probability kernel $\pi_t:\mathsf F_{1:t}\to E_t$ such that
$\omega\mapsto\pi_t(Y_{1:t}(\omega),\cdot)$ is a regular conditional
distribution of $X_t$ given $\sigma(Y_{1:t})$. For $1\le t\le T$, a
**predictive kernel at time $t$** is a probability kernel
$\pi_{t|t-1}:\mathsf F_{1:t-1}\to E_t$ whose composition with $Y_{1:t-1}$
is a regular conditional distribution of $X_t$ given
$\sigma(Y_{1:t-1})$. A **finite-horizon smoothing kernel** is a probability
kernel $\psi_T:\mathsf F_{1:T}\to E_0\times\cdots\times E_T$ whose
composition with $Y_{1:T}$ is a regular conditional distribution of the full
state path $(X_0,\ldots,X_T)$ given $\sigma(Y_{1:T})$. Here a regular
conditional distribution is an everywhere probability kernel satisfying the
conditional event identities in
[[def-regular-conditional-distribution]], and a conditional law given a
random element is its data-indexed kernel form in
[[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]].

These kernels are versions: their values can be changed on a measurable set
of observation histories of probability zero without changing the conditional
identities. No density is assumed in these definitions. The state-space model
here is one fixed law. A parametric statistical model is instead a map
$\theta\mapsto P_\theta$ from a parameter set to probability laws; its
measurability is not asserted without a parameter sigma-algebra
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]).

Assume AC and a finite-horizon model as in
[[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]. For each $1\le t\le T$, let
$\nu_t$ be a sigma-finite measure on $(F_t,\mathcal F_t)$ and suppose the
observation kernel has a specified product-measurable density
$g_t:E_t\times F_t\to[0,\infty]$ with respect to $\mathcal E_t\otimes\mathcal F_t$:
$$G_t(x,B)=\int_B g_t(x,y)\,\nu_t(dy),\qquad\int_{F_t}g_t(x,y)\,\nu_t(dy)=1$$
for every state $x\in E_t$ and measurable $B\subseteq F_t$. For
$h\in\mathsf F_{1:t-1}$, let $\pi_{t-1}$ be the filtering kernel at time
$t-1$ from
[[def-state-space-filtering-laws]] when $t>1$, and for $t=1$ let $\pi_0$ be
the initial kernel $\mu_0$ on the singleton empty-history space. For
$A\in\mathcal E_t$, define the predictive kernel
$$\widehat\pi_t(h,A):=\int_{E_{t-1}}K_t(x,A)\,\pi_{t-1}(h,dx),$$
the evidence density
$$z_t(h,y):=\int_{E_t}g_t(x,y)\,\widehat\pi_t(h,dx),$$
and for $h\in\mathsf F_{1:t-1}$, $y\in F_t$, and $A\in\mathcal E_t$ define
the update
$$\pi_t(h,y,A):=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\int_Ag_t(x,y)\,\widehat\pi_t(h,dx)}{z_t(h,y)},&0<z_t(h,y)<\infty,\\[6pt]\widehat\pi_t(h,A),&z_t(h,y)=0\text{ or }z_t(h,y)=\infty.\end{cases}$$
Then $\widehat\pi_t$ is a predictive kernel for $X_t$ given $Y_{1:t-1}$,
and $\pi_t$ is a filtering kernel for $X_t$ given $Y_{1:t}$. For each fixed
history $h$, the observation marginal under the conditional version
determined by $\widehat\pi_t(h,\cdot)$ has density
$z_t(h,\cdot)$ with respect to $\nu_t$ and assigns zero mass to both
$\{y:z_t(h,y)=0\}$ and $\{y:z_t(h,y)=\infty\}$. Thus the formula never
divides by zero or infinity; values on those fibers are conditional-law
fillers. The statement is exact and finite-horizon and gives no numerical
approximation or long-time stability claim.

Assume AC. Fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$, standard-Borel spaces
$E_0,\ldots,E_T$ and $F_1,\ldots,F_T$, an initial probability measure
$\mu_0$ on $E_0$, and transition and observation probability kernels
$K_t:E_{t-1}\to E_t$ and $G_t:E_t\to F_t$ for $1\le t\le T$, as in
[[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]. On the interleaved finite
product space
$$\mathcal Z_T=E_0\times E_1\times F_1\times\cdots\times E_T\times F_T,$$
there is a unique probability measure whose rectangle probabilities are the
ordered iterated kernel integrals
$$\mu_0(dx_0)\prod_{t=1}^T K_t(x_{t-1},dx_t)G_t(x_t,dy_t).$$
The product notation means successive integration in the displayed order.
For $T=0$, the assertion is the initial law $\mu_0$ on $E_0$.

Assume AC and a finite-horizon model as in
[[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]. For each $1\le t\le T$, suppose
the observation kernel has a supplied product-measurable density
$g_t:E_t\times F_t\to[0,\infty]$ with respect to a sigma-finite measure
$\nu_t$ on $F_t$, normalized so that
$$G_t(x,B)=\int_Bg_t(x,y)\,\nu_t(dy),\qquad\int_{F_t}g_t(x,y)\,\nu_t(dy)=1$$
for every state $x$ and measurable $B\subseteq F_t$.

The procedure takes the initial law $\mu_0$, transition kernels $K_t$,
observation densities $g_t$ and measures $\nu_t$ as inputs. It defines
data-indexed prediction, evidence, and filtering functions on every
observation history as follows.

1. Initialize $\pi_0$ on the singleton empty-history space by
$\pi_0(*,A)=\mu_0(A)$.

2. For $t=1,\ldots,T$, each history $h\in\mathsf F_{1:t-1}$ and each
measurable state set $A\in\mathcal E_t$, form the predictive measure
$$\widehat\pi_t(h,A):=\int_{E_{t-1}}K_t(x,A)\,\pi_{t-1}(h,dx).$$

3. For each $y\in F_t$, calculate the evidence density
$$z_t(h,y):=\int_{E_t}g_t(x,y)\,\widehat\pi_t(h,dx).$$

4. Define the filtering measure at $(h,y)$ by
$$\pi_t(h,y,A):=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\int_Ag_t(x,y)\,\widehat\pi_t(h,dx)}{z_t(h,y)},&0<z_t(h,y)<\infty,\\[6pt]\widehat\pi_t(h,A),&z_t(h,y)=0\text{ or }z_t(h,y)=\infty.\end{cases}$$
Use $\pi_t$ as the input filtering function at the next time step.

The procedure returns the initialized filter $\pi_0=\mu_0$ and, for every
$1\le t\le T$, $\widehat\pi_t$, $z_t$, and $\pi_t$. It is an exact
measure-valued recursion; it makes no claim that the integrals have closed
forms or can be evaluated with finite computational cost.
[[thm-dominated-state-space-filtering-recursion]] proves that the returned
time-$t$ functions are predictive and filtering kernels for the specified
finite-horizon model.

derivations.claim: With counting measure on $F_1$, set $g_1(x,y)=G_1(x,\{y\})$; it is jointly measurable on the finite discrete spaces, sums to one over $y$, and gives $G_1(x,C)=\sum_{y\in C}g_1(x,y)$. The predictive state law is $\delta_0$, so the evidence is $z_1(a)=1$ and $z_1(b)=0$; the update at $a$ is $\delta_0$ and [F2] and [F4] make the update at $b$ the predictive filler $\delta_0$. The factorized law [F3] gives $P(Y_1=b)=0$.

Let $\rho$ be any probability measure on $E_1$ and define $q(a,\cdot)=\delta_0$ and $q(b,\cdot)=\rho$. This is a measurable probability kernel because the observation space is finite discrete. For every $A\subseteq\{0,1\}$ and $C\subseteq\{a,b\}$, the path law gives $P(X_1\in A,Y_1\in C)=\mathbf1_A(0)\mathbf1_C(a)$, while $E[\mathbf1_{\{Y_1\in C\}}q(Y_1,A)]=\mathbf1_C(a)\delta_0(A)+0\cdot\mathbf1_C(b)\rho(A)=\mathbf1_A(0)\mathbf1_C(a)$. These are all conditioning events in the finite observation space, so every probability $\rho$ at $b$ gives the same conditional identities.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ and $Y:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(T,\mathcal T)$ be measurable random elements. A **conditional law of X given Y** is a probability kernel $K:(T,\mathcal T)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ such that $\omega\mapsto K(Y(\omega),\cdot)$ is a regular conditional distribution of X given $\sigma(Y)$ in [[def-regular-conditional-distribution]]. Thus for every $A\in\mathcal S$ and $H\in\sigma(Y)$,
$$\int_H K(Y(\omega),A)\,dP=P(H\cap\{X\in A\}).$$

Composition with Y makes each evaluation $\sigma(Y)$-measurable, and every section remains a probability by [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. The notation $P(X\in A\mid Y=y)=K(y,A)$ refers to a chosen kernel; it is not a ratio involving the possibly zero probability $P(Y=y)$.

Write $P_Y(B)=P(Y^{-1}(B))$ for the law in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]. If a specified countable family $\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal S$ determines probability measures, two conditional laws K,L agree as measures outside a single $\mathcal T$-measurable $P_Y$-null set. Indeed for each $A\in\mathcal C$ the measurable discrepancy $D_A=\{y:K(y,A)\ne L(y,A)\}$ has null inverse image under Y by [[lem-conditional-expectation-is-unique-almost-surely]]. Hence $P_Y(D_A)=0$ by the law definition; the countable union $D$ is null by [[thm-finite-and-countable-subadditivity-of-measures]], and off D the determining property gives equality of measures. This uses a supplied determining family and makes no AC assertion about obtaining one.

Values on a measurable $P_Y$-null subset may be replaced by a specified fixed probability on E without changing these identities. The inverse image of that subset is measurable null, and all event evaluations are bounded, so the modified event integrals agree. Empty-event evaluations remain zero and whole-target evaluations remain one. Existence on standard-Borel spaces is proved separately; the definition alone does not assert a conditional kernel exists.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

A family $(\mathcal F_i)_{i\in I}$ of sub-sigma-algebras of $\mathcal F$ is
**independent** when it is independent as a family of event classes in the
sense of [[def-independent-families-of-event-classes]].

A family $(A_i)_{i\in I}$ of events is **independent** when the singleton event

finite choice of distinct indices $i_0,\dots,i_{n-1}$,

$$\mathbb P\left(\bigcap_{k<n}A_{i_k}\right)=\prod_{k<n}\mathbb P(A_{i_k}).$$

For two events this reduces to the familiar identity

“Probability kernel” has the pointwise meaning of [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]: every $K(\omega,\cdot)$ is a probability measure, and every evaluation is $\mathcal G$-measurable. Its evaluations lie in $[0,1]$ and are integrable. Thus the testing identity says exactly that $K(\cdot,A)$ is a conditional-expectation version of $1_{\{X\in A\}}$ in [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. The kernel requirement holds at every sample point. Separate eventwise choices of conditional-expectation versions do not imply it and do not by themselves provide one exceptional set valid for all A. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $m\ge1$ be finite, let $d_j\ge1$, and let
$Z_j$ for $1\le j\le m$ be mutually independent random elements of
$\mathbb R^{d_j}$. Suppose $Z_j\sim N_{d_j}(a_j,\Sigma_j)$, where each
$\Sigma_j$ is symmetric positive semidefinite. Put
$D=\sum_{j=1}^m d_j$, $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$,
$a=(a_1,\ldots,a_m)$, and
$\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(\Sigma_1,\ldots,\Sigma_m)$. Then
$$Z\sim N_D(a,\Sigma).$$
No covariance block needs to be invertible.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be non-negative. Then there exists a unique non-negative operator
$R:V\to V$ such that

$$R^2=T.$$

Assume AC. Let $X\in\mathbb R^d$ and $Y\in\mathbb R^m$, with $d,m\ge1$, be
jointly multivariate normal with mean $(a,b)$ and positive-semidefinite block
covariance
$$\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}A&C\\C^T&B\end{pmatrix},$$
where $B$ is positive definite. Then
$$S=A-CB^{-1}C^T$$
is positive semidefinite, and for every $y\in\mathbb R^m$ the probability law
$$K(y,\cdot)=N_d\!\left(a+CB^{-1}(y-b),S\right)$$
is defined. The map $K$ is a probability kernel and is a conditional law of
$X$ given $Y$: for all Borel $E\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ and
$F\subseteq\mathbb R^m$,
$$\mathbb P(X\in E,Y\in F)=\int_F K(y,E)\,\mathbb P_Y(dy).$$
The covariance $A$ and the conditional covariance $S$ may be singular.
Positive definiteness of $B$ is required; no pseudoinverse formula for
singular $B$ is asserted.

derivations.claim: By [F2], the stack $(U,q,r)$ is jointly Gaussian with mean $(m,0,0)$ and covariance $\operatorname{diag}(P,Q,R)$. For any $a\in\mathbb R^n$ and $b\in\mathbb R^p$, the scalar $a^TX+b^TY$ is a linear projection of this stack, so it is normal by [F1]; thus $(X,Y)$ is jointly Gaussian. Since $q$ is independent of $U$ and centered, $\operatorname{Cov}(X)=F\operatorname{Cov}(U)F^T+\operatorname{Cov}(q)=FPF^T+Q=P^-$. Since $Y=HX+r$ and $r$ is independent of $X$ and centered, $\mathbb E X=Fm$, $\mathbb E Y=HFm$, $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=P^-H^T$, and $\operatorname{Cov}(Y)=HP^-H^T+R=S$. Hence the block covariance is the one displayed in the Statement and is positive semidefinite as a covariance matrix. Also $P^-\succeq0$, since $u^TP^-u=(F^Tu)^TP(F^Tu)+u^TQu\ge0$ for every $u$.

Apply [F4] with $A=P^-$, $C=P^-H^T$, and $B=S$. The observed block is positive definite by hypothesis, and the joint block is positive semidefinite by step 1.1. The conditional mean is $Fm+P^-H^TS^{-1}(y-HFm)=Fm+K(y-HFm)$. Its covariance is $P^--P^-H^TS^{-1}HP^-=P^--KSK^T$, and [F4] makes it positive semidefinite and gives a conditional-law version for every $y$.

Since $S=HP^-H^T+R$ and $K=P^-H^TS^{-1}$, symmetry of $P^-$ and $S$ gives $KHP^-=P^-H^TK^T=KSK^T$. Expanding the Joseph expression yields $P^- -KHP^- -P^-H^TK^T+K(HP^-H^T+R)K^T=P^--KSK^T$. It is positive semidefinite because [F4] gives that covariance this property; independently, the Joseph expression is a sum of positive-semidefinite matrices. This proves the identity without inverting $P$, $Q$, or $R$.

the state dimension at time
$t$ be a positive integer $d_t$ for $0\le t\le T$, and the observation
dimension at time $t$ be a positive integer $p_t$ for $1\le t\le T$.
Choose deterministic matrices
$F_t\in\mathbb R^{d_t\times d_{t-1}}$ and
$H_t\in\mathbb R^{p_t\times d_t}$, a mean $m_0\in\mathbb R^{d_0}$, and
symmetric positive-semidefinite matrices, meaning $v^TPv\ge0$ for every
real vector $v$ of matching dimension,
$P_0\in\mathbb R^{d_0\times d_0}$,
$Q_t\in\mathbb R^{d_t\times d_t}$, and
$R_t\in\mathbb R^{p_t\times p_t}$. A **linear-Gaussian state-space model
with independent noises** is the general finite-horizon kernel model
([[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]) with initial law
$\mu_0=N_{d_0}(m_0,P_0)$ and transition and observation kernels

All Gaussian laws use the convention of
[[def-multivariate-normal-law]], which allows singular covariance matrices.

Its independent-noise representation consists of random vectors
$x_0,q_1,r_1,\ldots,q_T,r_T$ on a common probability space, with
$x_0\sim N_{d_0}(m_0,P_0)$, $q_t\sim N_{d_t}(0,Q_t)$,
$r_t\sim N_{p_t}(0,R_t)$, all mutually independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-random-elements]] (their generated sigma-algebras are
independent), and equations
$$x_t=F_t x_{t-1}+q_t,\qquad y_t=H_t x_t+r_t\qquad(1\le t\le T).$$
The local path-law theorem proves that every allowed parameter tuple has
such a finite representation, that its induced kernels are the displayed
$K_t,G_t$, and that its path law is the general kernel-product law.

This definition imposes the stated noise law and independence assumptions;
it does not establish their empirical adequacy. It supplies no filtering
algorithm, posterior recursion, or convergence claim. Any separate formula
that inverts an observed innovation covariance must assume that covariance is
positive definite at the point of inversion.

[[def-linear-gaussian-state-space-model-with-independent-noises]]. There is a
probability space carrying mutually independent Gaussian vectors

$x_t=F_t x_{t-1}+q_t$ and $y_t=H_t x_t+r_t$ induce the general kernel-product
law of [[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]. In the interleaved order
$Z_T=(x_0,x_1,y_1,\ldots,x_T,y_T)$, there is a deterministic matrix $M_T$
such that
$$Z_T=M_T W_T,\qquad W_T=(x_0,q_1,r_1,\ldots,q_T,r_T),$$
and
$$Z_T\sim N\!\left(M_T a_T,\ M_T\Sigma_T M_T^T\right),\qquad a_T=(m_0,0,\ldots,0),\quad \Sigma_T=\operatorname{diag}(P_0,Q_1,R_1,\ldots,Q_T,R_T).$$
The covariance may be singular.

Assume AC and fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$ with a state-space model by
probability kernels as in
[[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]. If $T=0$, put $\Omega_T=E_0$;
otherwise put $\Omega_T=E_0\times E_1\times F_1\times\cdots\times E_T\times
F_T$. Let $\mathcal Z_T$ be the corresponding finite-product sigma-algebra
and write $(\Omega_T,\mathcal Z_T,P_T)$ for its finite-horizon probability
space. The law $P_T$ is the unique law supplied by
[[thm-finite-horizon-state-space-kernel-law-exists-uniquely]]. Let $X_t$ and
$Y_t$ be the coordinate random elements taking values in $E_t$ and $F_t$. For
$t\ge1$, write $Y_{1:t}:=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_t)$ and
$\mathsf F_{1:t}:=F_1\times\cdots\times F_t$ with its finite-product
sigma-algebra; let $\mathsf F_{1:0}$ be a singleton and $Y_{1:0}$ its constant
map. The factors are standard Borel, meaning measurably isomorphic to Polish
spaces ([[def-standard-borel-space]]), and their finite products are standard
Borel ([[lem-finite-products-of-standard-borel-spaces-are-standard-borel]]).

The **initial filtering kernel** $\pi_0:\mathsf F_{1:0}\to E_0$ assigns
$\mu_0$ to the unique empty history; it is the conditional law of $X_0$ given
the trivial history. For $1\le t\le T$, a **filtering kernel at time $t$** is
a probability kernel $\pi_t:\mathsf F_{1:t}\to E_t$ such that
$\omega\mapsto\pi_t(Y_{1:t}(\omega),\cdot)$ is a regular conditional
distribution of $X_t$ given $\sigma(Y_{1:t})$. For $1\le t\le T$, a
**predictive kernel at time $t$** is a probability kernel
$\pi_{t|t-1}:\mathsf F_{1:t-1}\to E_t$ whose composition with $Y_{1:t-1}$

$\sigma(Y_{1:t-1})$. A **finite-horizon smoothing kernel** is a probability

composition with $Y_{1:T}$ is a regular conditional distribution of the full
state path $(X_0,\ldots,X_T)$ given $\sigma(Y_{1:T})$. Here a regular
conditional distribution is an everywhere probability kernel satisfying the
conditional event identities in
[[def-regular-conditional-distribution]], and a conditional law given a
random element is its data-indexed kernel form in
[[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]].

These kernels are versions: their values can be changed on a measurable set
of observation histories of probability zero without changing the conditional
identities. No density is assumed in these definitions. The state-space model
here is one fixed law. A parametric statistical model is instead a map
$\theta\mapsto P_\theta$ from a parameter set to probability laws; its
measurability is not asserted without a parameter sigma-algebra
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]).

observation spaces, an initial probability measure, and transition and
observation probability kernels, as in
[[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]. Let $P_T$ be its finite-horizon

independent of the random element $(X,Y)$, and let
$\kappa:H\to E$ be a supplied conditional law of $X$ given $Y$. For each
$h\in H$, form the product probability
$\Lambda(h,\cdot)=\kappa(h,\cdot)\otimes\mathcal L(Z)$ on
$\mathcal E\otimes\mathcal W$. Then $\Lambda$ is a conditional law of
$(X,Z)$ given $Y$. If $\Phi:E\times W\to V$ is measurable into a measurable
space $(V,\mathcal V)$, then
$$\Lambda^\Phi(h,C):=\Lambda(h,\Phi^{-1}(C))$$
is a conditional law of $\Phi(X,Z)$ given $Y$.

derivations.claim: The Euclidean state and observation spaces are standard Borel. By [F1], the finite path model uses Gaussian laws with the declared positive-semidefinite covariances; [F2] identifies its path law as jointly Gaussian, including when singular. The general existence result [F4] supplies the conditional-law setting, and [F3] fixes the initial filtering kernel as $\pi_0(*)=N_{d_0}(m_0,P_0)$ on the singleton empty history. This is a probability by [F9] and [F12], and is an RCD of $X_0$ given the trivial history because its event integral is exactly the $X_0$ marginal. The initial covariance is positive semidefinite by hypothesis. At every later step the algorithm is defined on its stated domain: $S_k\succ0$ has the Cholesky factor required by [F8].

Fix $k\in\{1,\ldots,T\}$ and assume inductively that the algorithm's $\pi_{k-1}$ is a filtering kernel with deterministic covariance $P_{k-1|k-1}\succeq0$. The vectors $X_{k-1}$ and $Y_{1:k-1}$ are measurable functions of $X_0,q_1,r_1,\ldots,q_{k-1},r_{k-1}$; by [F1,F13], the new pair $(q_k,r_k)$ is independent of that past. Apply [F5] with this past conditional law and push forward by $(x,q,r)\mapsto(F_kx+q,H_k(F_kx+q)+r)$. For each history $h$, the resulting conditional law of $(X_k,Y_k)$ is the one-step Gaussian block in [F6] with $m=m_{k-1|k-1}(h)$ and $P=P_{k-1|k-1}$. Its predicted covariance is positive semidefinite because $u^TP_{k|k-1}u=(F_k^Tu)^TP_{k-1|k-1}(F_k^Tu)+u^TQ_ku\ge0$. The positive-definite condition on $S_k$ allows [F7] to condition this block, for every $y_k$, with mean $m_{k|k-1}+P_{k|k-1}H_k^TS_k^{-1}v_k$ and covariance $P_{k|k-1}-P_{k|k-1}H_k^TS_k^{-1}H_kP_{k|k-1}$, exactly the algorithm's gain and update. The covariance is positive semidefinite by [F7]. To identify the computed gain, put $B_k=H_kP_{k|k-1}$. The algorithm's two triangular solves, applied columnwise, give $L_kU_k=B_k$ and $L_k^TK_k^T=U_k$. The diagonal entries of $L_k$ and $L_k^T$ are positive, so [F14] gives the unique solution of each column system. Therefore $S_kK_k^T=L_k(L_k^TK_k^T)=L_kU_k=B_k$; since $S_k\succ0$, this yields $K_k^T=S_k^{-1}B_k$, the gain in [F6]. The updated mean is affine in $(h,y_k)$ and the covariance is deterministic, so [F10] makes the Gaussian sections a measurable probability kernel.

Let $J_k(h,\cdot)$ be the conditional law of $(X_k,Y_k)$ given the previous history constructed in step 2.1, and let $M_k(h,\cdot)$ be its observation marginal. The one-step conditional identity [F7] gives $J_k(h,A\times B)=\int_B\pi_k(h,y_k,A)\,M_k(h,dy_k)$ for Borel state $A$ and observation set $B$. Integrating this identity over any Borel set $D$ of previous histories yields $\mathbb P(X_k\in A,Y_{1:k-1}\in D,Y_k\in B)=\int_D\int_B\pi_k(h,y_k,A)\,M_k(h,dy_k)\,\mathbb P_{Y_{1:k-1}}(dh)$. Since $M_k$ is the observation marginal of $J_k$, the iterated kernel is the joint law of $(Y_{1:k-1},Y_k)$ integrated against $\pi_k$. Thus this is the RCD identity on every rectangle $D\times B$; these rectangles form a pi-system generating the product history sigma-algebra, so [F11] extends the identity to all Borel history events. Therefore $\pi_k$ is a filtering kernel by [F3].

The base case is step 1.1, and steps 2.1–3.1 establish the induction step for every $k$, preserving positive semidefiniteness of the updated covariance. For $T=0$ only the base case applies. derivations.claim: Fix a history $h=y_{1:k}$. By [F3], the conditional law of $X_k$ is $N(m_{k|k}(h),P_{k|k})$. The next process noise is independent of the past by [F1], so [F4] extends this filtering kernel by $q_{k+1}$ and pushes it forward through $(x,q)\mapsto(x,F_{k+1}x+q)$. By [F5], $(X_k,q_{k+1})$ is jointly Gaussian, and the projection characterization in [F10] makes its linear image $(X_k,X_{k+1})$ jointly Gaussian. Its mean is $(m_{k|k},F_{k+1}m_{k|k})$, its state covariance is $P_{k|k}$, its cross-covariance is $P_{k|k}F_{k+1}^T$, and its next-state covariance is $P_{k+1|k}$. The latter block is positive definite by hypothesis. Apply [F6] with that observed block: the conditional mean and covariance are exactly the displayed $Q_k$ parameters, so $V_k\succeq0$. The history mean is affine by [F2], and representing each Gaussian section as a translate of fixed $N(0,V_k)$ plus [F8] gives joint measurability in $(h,x_{k+1})$. Thus $Q_k$ is an everywhere probability kernel.

Write $H=Y_{1:k}$, $V=X_{k+1}$, and $Z=Y_{k+1:T}$. By [F7], the full path law factors by taking the law of $(H,X_k)$, applying the transition kernel at $k+1$, and then a future observation kernel $R(V,dz)$ formed by the remaining transition and observation kernels. The first two factors disintegrate as $\pi_k(h,dx_k)K_{k+1}(x_k,dv)=\rho_k(h,dv)Q_k(h,v,dx_k)$ by step 1.1, where $\rho_k$ is the one-step predictive law. Substitution gives the joint factorization as the law of $H$ followed by $\rho_k$, $Q_k$, and $R$. The future kernel depends on the past only through $V$, and its iterated integrals are measurable by [F8].

For any Borel set $A$ of $X_k$ and any Borel set $D$ in the product space of $(H,V,Z)$, integrate $1_A(x_k)1_D(h,v,z)$ in the factorization from step 2.1. This gives $\mathbb P(X_k\in A,(H,V,Z)\in D)=\int_D Q_k(h,v,A)\,\mathbb P_{(H,V,Z)}(dh,dv,dz)$. This is the RCD event identity for $Q_k$ given $(H,V,Z)$; its kernel properties were established in step 1.1. Since $(H,Z)=Y_{1:T}$, it is also a version of the conditional law given $(Y_{1:T},X_{k+1})$. The factorization uses model kernels rather than observation densities, and the only inverse is of $P_{k+1|k}\succ0$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

For $0\le k\le T$, a **fixed-interval smoothing kernel for $X_k$** is an
everywhere-defined probability kernel
$$\psi_{k|T}:\mathsf Y_{1:T}\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{d_k}$$
whose composition with the full observation vector $Y_{1:T}$ is a regular
conditional distribution of $X_k$ given $\sigma(Y_{1:T})$. Thus it is the
single-time marginal smoothing law after all observations through time $T$
are supplied. The full-path smoothing kernel and its version convention are
defined in [[def-state-space-filtering-laws]].

This definition does not assert that such a kernel exists or is unique at
observation values in a null set. The theorem on this page constructs a
Gaussian version under its explicit forecast and innovation assumptions.

Assume AC. Let $(X_0,\ldots,X_T,Y_1,\ldots,Y_T)$ follow a finite-horizon
linear-Gaussian model as in
[[def-linear-gaussian-state-space-model-with-independent-noises]]. Suppose
the Kalman filter of [[alg-kalman-filter]] is admissible: every innovation
covariance $S_j$ it solves is positive definite. Fix $0\le k<T$, and let
$m_{k|k},P_{k|k}$ and $m_{k+1|k},P_{k+1|k}$ be the corresponding filtered
and one-step predicted quantities. Assume in addition that
$P_{k+1|k}\succ0$. Put
$$C_k=P_{k|k}F_{k+1}^TP_{k+1|k}^{-1},\qquad V_k=P_{k|k}-C_kP_{k+1|k}C_k^T.$$
Then $V_k\succeq0$, and the formula
$$Q_k(y_{1:k},x_{k+1},\cdot)=N\!\left(m_{k|k}(y_{1:k})+C_k(x_{k+1}-m_{k+1|k}(y_{1:k})),V_k\right)$$
defines an everywhere probability kernel. It is a conditional law of $X_k$
given $(Y_{1:k},X_{k+1})$ and also a version of the conditional law of
$X_k$ given $(Y_{1:T},X_{k+1})$ under the full finite-horizon model. Thus
future observations do not change this backward kernel once $X_{k+1}$ is
also given. The inverse is the ordinary inverse of the positive-definite
forecast covariance; no singular-forecast extension is asserted.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $m\ge1$ be finite, let $d_j\ge1$, and let
$Z_j$ for $1\le j\le m$ be mutually independent random elements of
$\mathbb R^{d_j}$. Suppose $Z_j\sim N_{d_j}(a_j,\Sigma_j)$, where each
$\Sigma_j$ is symmetric positive semidefinite. Put
$D=\sum_{j=1}^m d_j$, $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$,
$a=(a_1,\ldots,a_m)$, and
$\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(\Sigma_1,\ldots,\Sigma_m)$. Then
$$Z\sim N_D(a,\Sigma).$$
No covariance block needs to be invertible.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

For the computation, factor $P_{k+1|k}=L_kL_k^T$ with the unique
positive-diagonal Cholesky factor from
[[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]],
then compute the rows of $U_k$ in increasing order by
$$ (U_k)_{i,\cdot}=\frac{(F_{k+1}P_{k|k})_{i,\cdot}-\sum_{j=1}^{i-1}(L_k)_{ij}(U_k)_{j,\cdot}}{(L_k)_{ii}},\qquad i=1,\ldots,d_{k+1},$$
and compute the rows of $C_k^T$ in decreasing order by
$$ (C_k^T)_{i,\cdot}=\frac{(U_k)_{i,\cdot}-\sum_{j=i+1}^{d_{k+1}}(L_k)_{ji}(C_k^T)_{j,\cdot}}{(L_k)_{ii}},\qquad i=d_{k+1},\ldots,1.$$
These recurrences give $L_kU_k=F_{k+1}P_{k|k}$ and $L_k^TC_k^T=U_k$, so
$C_k=P_{k|k}F_{k+1}^TP_{k+1|k}^{-1}$; no inverse is formed in the procedure.

derivations.claim: At time $T$, the conditioning data for the forward filter are exactly $y_{1:T}$. By [F3], the terminal filter kernel $N(m_{T|T},P_{T|T})$ is an everywhere conditional-law version of $X_T$ given these data, with $P_{T|T}\succeq0$. It is therefore the base case for the fixed-interval smoothing kernels in [F4].

Suppose the Gaussian kernel $\psi_{k+1|T}(y,\cdot)$ is an RCD of $X_{k+1}$ given $Y_{1:T}=y$. Define $\psi_{k|T}(y,A)=\int Q_k(y_{1:k},x,A)\,\psi_{k+1|T}(y,dx)$ for each Borel state set $A$. This is a probability kernel by [F5]–[F6]. To verify its RCD identity, define $\nu(D)=\int\!\int 1_D(y,x)\,\psi_{k+1|T}(y,dx)\,\mathbb P_Y(dy)$ for Borel $D$ in the product of data and state spaces. Measurability follows from [F6]; for pairwise disjoint $D_n$, monotone convergence gives countable additivity, and $\nu$ has total mass one. Its rectangle values equal those of the actual joint law of $(Y_{1:T},X_{k+1})$ by the RCD identity for $\psi_{k+1|T}$. By [F8], the measures agree on every Borel set. Thus for any Borel data set $B$ and state set $A$, $\int_B\psi_{k|T}(y,A)\,\mathbb P_Y(dy)=\int_{B\times\mathbb R^{d_{k+1}}}Q_k(y_{1:k},x,A)\,\mathbb P_{(Y_{1:T},X_{k+1})}(dy,dx)=\mathbb P(X_k\in A,Y_{1:T}\in B)$, where the last equality is [F5] applied to the conditioning event $B\times\mathbb R^{d_{k+1}}$. Hence $\psi_{k|T}$ is the required RCD.

Write $P^-=P_{k+1|k}$ and $V_k=P_{k|k}-C_kP^-C_k^T$ as in [F5]. By [F13], row substitution gives $L_kU_k=F_{k+1}P_{k|k}$ and $L_k^TC_k^T=U_k$. Since $P^-=L_kL_k^T$, these equations yield $P^-C_k^T=F_{k+1}P_{k|k}$ and hence $C_k=P_{k|k}F_{k+1}^T(P^-)^{-1}$, exactly the gain in [F5]. On the product probability space carrying independent $U\sim N(0,V_k)$ and $W\sim N(m_{k+1|T},P_{k+1|T})$, the integral in step 2.1 is the law of $m_{k|k}+C_k(W-m_{k+1|k})+U$ by [F9]. The covariance matrices of $U$ and $W$ are positive semidefinite by [F5] and the induction hypothesis, so both Gaussian laws exist by [A1, F11]. The product coordinates are independent by [F12]; [F10] makes their stack jointly Gaussian, and its affine image is Gaussian by the projection characterization in [F11]. Independence makes the cross-covariance terms vanish, so its mean is $m_{k|k}+C_k(m_{k+1|T}-m_{k+1|k})$ and its covariance is $V_k+C_kP_{k+1|T}C_k^T=P_{k|k}+C_k(P_{k+1|T}-P^-)C_k^T$. This is exactly the smoother update in the statement and algorithm. The first covariance expression is positive semidefinite, so the updated covariance is positive semidefinite as well.

Starting from step 1.1, apply steps 2.1–3.1 for $k=T-1,T-2,\ldots,0$. The induction constructs an everywhere smoothing kernel at each time and identifies its mean and covariance with the algorithm output. When $T=0$ only the base case is needed. Positive definiteness is used only for the forecast inverses in [F5] and the forward innovation solves in [F2]; no singular forecast is inverted.
