citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) and fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$. Let
the state dimension at time
$t$ be a positive integer $d_t$ for $0\le t\le T$, and the observation
dimension at time $t$ be a positive integer $p_t$ for $1\le t\le T$.
Choose deterministic matrices
$F_t\in\mathbb R^{d_t\times d_{t-1}}$ and
$H_t\in\mathbb R^{p_t\times d_t}$, a mean $m_0\in\mathbb R^{d_0}$, and
symmetric positive-semidefinite matrices, meaning $v^TPv\ge0$ for every
real vector $v$ of matching dimension,
$P_0\in\mathbb R^{d_0\times d_0}$,
$Q_t\in\mathbb R^{d_t\times d_t}$, and
$R_t\in\mathbb R^{p_t\times p_t}$. A **linear-Gaussian state-space model
with independent noises** is the general finite-horizon kernel model
([[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]) with initial law
$\mu_0=N_{d_0}(m_0,P_0)$ and transition and observation kernels
$$K_t(x,\cdot)=N_{d_t}(F_t x,Q_t),\qquad G_t(x,\cdot)=N_{p_t}(H_t x,R_t).$$
All Gaussian laws use the convention of
[[def-multivariate-normal-law]], which allows singular covariance matrices.

Its independent-noise representation consists of random vectors
$x_0,q_1,r_1,\ldots,q_T,r_T$ on a common probability space, with
$x_0\sim N_{d_0}(m_0,P_0)$, $q_t\sim N_{d_t}(0,Q_t)$,
$r_t\sim N_{p_t}(0,R_t)$, all mutually independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-random-elements]] (their generated sigma-algebras are
independent), and equations
$$x_t=F_t x_{t-1}+q_t,\qquad y_t=H_t x_t+r_t\qquad(1\le t\le T).$$
The local path-law theorem proves that every allowed parameter tuple has
such a finite representation, that its induced kernels are the displayed
$K_t,G_t$, and that its path law is the general kernel-product law.

This definition imposes the stated noise law and independence assumptions;
it does not establish their empirical adequacy. It supplies no filtering
algorithm, posterior recursion, or convergence claim. Any separate formula
that inverts an observed innovation covariance must assume that covariance is
positive definite at the point of inversion.

Fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$, positive state dimensions $d_0,\ldots,d_T$,
and positive observation dimensions $p_1,\ldots,p_T$. The input is a
linear-Gaussian model from
[[def-linear-gaussian-state-space-model-with-independent-noises]], with
matrices $F_k\in\mathbb R^{d_k\times d_{k-1}}$ and
$H_k\in\mathbb R^{p_k\times d_k}$, initial mean $m_0$, and symmetric
positive-semidefinite covariances $P_0,Q_k,R_k$. Its state and observation
equations are
$$X_k=F_kX_{k-1}+q_k,\qquad Y_k=H_kX_k+r_k,$$
where $q_k\sim N(0,Q_k)$ and $r_k\sim N(0,R_k)$ are centered and mutually
independent across all times and of $X_0$.

The admissible data are vectors $y_k\in\mathbb R^{p_k}$ for which every
innovation covariance encountered below is positive definite. Positive
definite means $u^TS_ku>0$ for every nonzero $u\in\mathbb R^{p_k}$. The
algorithm returns predicted and updated means and covariances and the
innovation and gain at each time. Initialize
$$m_{0|0}=m_0,\qquad P_{0|0}=P_0.$$
For $k=1,\ldots,T$, perform:

1. Predict:
$$m_{k|k-1}=F_km_{k-1|k-1},\qquad P_{k|k-1}=F_kP_{k-1|k-1}F_k^T+Q_k.$$
2. Form the innovation and its covariance:
$$v_k=y_k-H_km_{k|k-1},\qquad S_k=H_kP_{k|k-1}H_k^T+R_k.$$
3. Factor $S_k=L_kL_k^T$ with lower-triangular $L_k$ having positive
diagonal, using
[[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]].
Solve $L_kU_k=H_kP_{k|k-1}$ and $L_k^TK_k^T=U_k$ by triangular solves. This
defines $K_k^T=S_k^{-1}H_kP_{k|k-1}$, hence
$K_k=P_{k|k-1}H_k^TS_k^{-1}$, without explicitly forming $S_k^{-1}$.
4. Update:
$$m_{k|k}=m_{k|k-1}+K_kv_k,\qquad P_{k|k}=P_{k|k-1}-K_kS_kK_k^T.$$

For $T=0$ the loop is empty and the returned pair is $(m_0,P_0)$. No
inverse of $P_0$, $Q_k$, or $R_k$ is used. This item defines the procedure
and makes no complexity, rounding-error, or numerical-stability claim.

Fix a finite-horizon linear-Gaussian model from
[[def-linear-gaussian-state-space-model-with-independent-noises]] and data
$y_{1:T}$ for which [[alg-kalman-filter]] is admissible. Its forward output
contains filtered means and covariances $m_{k|k},P_{k|k}$ and predicted means
and covariances $m_{k+1|k},P_{k+1|k}$. Assume each forecast covariance used
below is positive definite, meaning $u^TP_{k+1|k}u>0$ for every nonzero
$u\in\mathbb R^{d_{k+1}}$. Positive semidefinite means the same quadratic
form is nonnegative for every $u$.

The algorithm takes that forward output as input, initializes
$$m_{T|T}:=m_{T|T}^{\mathrm{filter}},\qquad P_{T|T}:=P_{T|T}^{\mathrm{filter}}$$
and for $k=T-1,T-2,\ldots,0$ performs the following steps:

1. Form the backward gain
$$C_k=P_{k|k}F_{k+1}^TP_{k+1|k}^{-1}.$$
For the computation, factor $P_{k+1|k}=L_kL_k^T$ with the unique
positive-diagonal Cholesky factor from
[[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]],
then compute the rows of $U_k$ in increasing order by
$$ (U_k)_{i,\cdot}=\frac{(F_{k+1}P_{k|k})_{i,\cdot}-\sum_{j=1}^{i-1}(L_k)_{ij}(U_k)_{j,\cdot}}{(L_k)_{ii}},\qquad i=1,\ldots,d_{k+1},$$
and compute the rows of $C_k^T$ in decreasing order by
$$ (C_k^T)_{i,\cdot}=\frac{(U_k)_{i,\cdot}-\sum_{j=i+1}^{d_{k+1}}(L_k)_{ji}(C_k^T)_{j,\cdot}}{(L_k)_{ii}},\qquad i=d_{k+1},\ldots,1.$$
These recurrences give $L_kU_k=F_{k+1}P_{k|k}$ and $L_k^TC_k^T=U_k$, so
$C_k=P_{k|k}F_{k+1}^TP_{k+1|k}^{-1}$; no inverse is formed in the procedure.
2. Update the smoothed mean and covariance:
$$m_{k|T}=m_{k|k}+C_k(m_{k+1|T}-m_{k+1|k})$$
$$P_{k|T}=P_{k|k}+C_k(P_{k+1|T}-P_{k+1|k})C_k^T$$

Return $(m_{k|T},P_{k|T})_{k=0}^T$. For $T=0$ the loop is empty and the
output is the initial filtered pair. The algorithm is undefined if a
forecast covariance to be solved is singular; it makes no pseudoinverse,
complexity, rounding-error, or numerical-stability claim. The theorem on
this page proves that the outputs are moments of the fixed-interval
conditional laws under these hypotheses.

Assume AC and fix a finite-horizon linear-Gaussian model
([[def-linear-gaussian-state-space-model-with-independent-noises]]) with
$P_0,Q_j,R_j\succeq0$. Run the forward Kalman filter on data $y_{1:T}$,
with every innovation covariance $S_j$ positive definite. Also assume that
every one-step forecast covariance $P_{k+1|k}$ is positive definite for
$0\le k<T$. Let $(m_{k|T},P_{k|T})_{k=0}^T$ be the output of
[[alg-rauch-tung-striebel-smoother]] applied to that forward output. Then,
for every $0\le k\le T$,
$$N_{d_k}(m_{k|T}(y_{1:T}),P_{k|T})$$
is an everywhere-defined fixed-interval smoothing kernel for $X_k$ in the
sense of [[def-fixed-interval-gaussian-smoothing-law]]. In particular,
$P_{k|T}\succeq0$. Singular initial, process, measurement, filtered, and
smoothed covariances are allowed; only the innovation matrices solved by the
filter and the forecast matrices inverted by this smoother must be positive
definite. The formulas select a conditional-law version at every data value;
other versions may differ on a set of observation data of probability zero.
No pseudoinverse result for a singular forecast is asserted.

derivations.claim: The first backward gain is $C_1=(2/3)/(5/3)=2/5$. Therefore $m_{1|2}=2/3+(2/5)(3/2-2/3)=1$ and $P_{1|2}=2/3+(2/5)(5/8-5/3)(2/5)=1/2$. The next gain is $C_0=1/2$, so $m_{0|2}=0+(1/2)(1-0)=1/2$ and $P_{0|2}=1+(1/2)(1/2-2)(1/2)=5/8$. The theorem [F4] identifies the resulting smoothing kernels as $N(1/2,5/8)$ for $X_0$, $N(1,1/2)$ for $X_1$, and $N(3/2,5/8)$ for $X_2$ at the selected data history.

boundaries.reason: The scalar example uses positive state and observation dimensions.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.1 and step 2.1 compute S_1=3 and S_2=8/3, both positive.
Step 3.1 applies the exact smoothing theorem to normalized Gaussian laws.
The example uses strictly positive prior and noise variances, so degeneracy is not part of this example.
Steps 1.1–3.1 cover the two forward times and backward steps k=1,0.
Statement A1 supplies the Gaussian-law convention; steps 1.1–3.1 use only finite exact arithmetic.

boundaries.reason: The Example evaluates forward and backward recursions at the fixed unit-variance random walk and observations (1,2), yielding three conditional Gaussian laws.
No inverse identification of the state-space model from the displayed smoothed moments is claimed; steps 1.1–3.1 are one concrete arithmetic verification.

finite_checks.result: Steps 1.1–3.1 compute the forward and backward gains and moments by exact rational arithmetic.

risk_review.notes: Read all three Verification steps and all six direct suppliers. Independently recomputed every forward and backward value using exact rational arithmetic: forecasts 2,5/3, innovations 3,8/3, filter gains 2/3,5/8, filtered means 2/3,3/2 and variances 2/3,5/8; backward gains 2/5,1/2 produce means (1/2,1,3/2) and variances (5/8,1/2,5/8). Both SPD assumptions hold at every solve. The final filter is the terminal smoother, and the initial state is explicitly included. The theorem supplies everywhere Gaussian versions at data (1,2), with no assertion of uniqueness on that null singleton. No limiting claim or extra AC use is involved.

Its independent-noise representation consists of random vectors
$x_0,q_1,r_1,\ldots,q_T,r_T$ on a common probability space, with
$x_0\sim N_{d_0}(m_0,P_0)$, $q_t\sim N_{d_t}(0,Q_t)$,
$r_t\sim N_{p_t}(0,R_t)$, all mutually independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-random-elements]] (their generated sigma-algebras are
independent), and equations
$$x_t=F_t x_{t-1}+q_t,\qquad y_t=H_t x_t+r_t\qquad(1\le t\le T).$$
The local path-law theorem proves that every allowed parameter tuple has
such a finite representation, that its induced kernels are the displayed
$K_t,G_t$, and that its path law is the general kernel-product law.

This definition imposes the stated noise law and independence assumptions;
it does not establish their empirical adequacy. It supplies no filtering
algorithm, posterior recursion, or convergence claim. Any separate formula
that inverts an observed innovation covariance must assume that covariance is
positive definite at the point of inversion.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$, positive state dimensions $d_0,\ldots,d_T$,
and positive observation dimensions $p_1,\ldots,p_T$. The input is a
linear-Gaussian model from
[[def-linear-gaussian-state-space-model-with-independent-noises]], with
matrices $F_k\in\mathbb R^{d_k\times d_{k-1}}$ and
$H_k\in\mathbb R^{p_k\times d_k}$, initial mean $m_0$, and symmetric
positive-semidefinite covariances $P_0,Q_k,R_k$. Its state and observation
equations are
$$X_k=F_kX_{k-1}+q_k,\qquad Y_k=H_kX_k+r_k,$$
where $q_k\sim N(0,Q_k)$ and $r_k\sim N(0,R_k)$ are centered and mutually
independent across all times and of $X_0$.

The admissible data are vectors $y_k\in\mathbb R^{p_k}$ for which every
innovation covariance encountered below is positive definite. Positive
definite means $u^TS_ku>0$ for every nonzero $u\in\mathbb R^{p_k}$. The
algorithm returns predicted and updated means and covariances and the
innovation and gain at each time. Initialize
$$m_{0|0}=m_0,\qquad P_{0|0}=P_0.$$
For $k=1,\ldots,T$, perform:

1. Predict:
$$m_{k|k-1}=F_km_{k-1|k-1},\qquad P_{k|k-1}=F_kP_{k-1|k-1}F_k^T+Q_k.$$
2. Form the innovation and its covariance:
$$v_k=y_k-H_km_{k|k-1},\qquad S_k=H_kP_{k|k-1}H_k^T+R_k.$$
3. Factor $S_k=L_kL_k^T$ with lower-triangular $L_k$ having positive
diagonal, using
[[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]].
Solve $L_kU_k=H_kP_{k|k-1}$ and $L_k^TK_k^T=U_k$ by triangular solves. This
defines $K_k^T=S_k^{-1}H_kP_{k|k-1}$, hence
$K_k=P_{k|k-1}H_k^TS_k^{-1}$, without explicitly forming $S_k^{-1}$.
4. Update:
$$m_{k|k}=m_{k|k-1}+K_kv_k,\qquad P_{k|k}=P_{k|k-1}-K_kS_kK_k^T.$$

For $T=0$ the loop is empty and the returned pair is $(m_0,P_0)$. No
inverse of $P_0$, $Q_k$, or $R_k$ is used. This item defines the procedure
and makes no complexity, rounding-error, or numerical-stability claim.

Fix a finite-horizon linear-Gaussian model from
[[def-linear-gaussian-state-space-model-with-independent-noises]] and data
$y_{1:T}$ for which [[alg-kalman-filter]] is admissible. Its forward output
contains filtered means and covariances $m_{k|k},P_{k|k}$ and predicted means
and covariances $m_{k+1|k},P_{k+1|k}$. Assume each forecast covariance used
below is positive definite, meaning $u^TP_{k+1|k}u>0$ for every nonzero
$u\in\mathbb R^{d_{k+1}}$. Positive semidefinite means the same quadratic
form is nonnegative for every $u$.

The algorithm takes that forward output as input, initializes
$$m_{T|T}:=m_{T|T}^{\mathrm{filter}},\qquad P_{T|T}:=P_{T|T}^{\mathrm{filter}}$$
and for $k=T-1,T-2,\ldots,0$ performs the following steps:

1. Form the backward gain
$$C_k=P_{k|k}F_{k+1}^TP_{k+1|k}^{-1}.$$
For the computation, factor $P_{k+1|k}=L_kL_k^T$ with the unique
positive-diagonal Cholesky factor from
[[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]],
then compute the rows of $U_k$ in increasing order by
$$ (U_k)_{i,\cdot}=\frac{(F_{k+1}P_{k|k})_{i,\cdot}-\sum_{j=1}^{i-1}(L_k)_{ij}(U_k)_{j,\cdot}}{(L_k)_{ii}},\qquad i=1,\ldots,d_{k+1},$$
and compute the rows of $C_k^T$ in decreasing order by
$$ (C_k^T)_{i,\cdot}=\frac{(U_k)_{i,\cdot}-\sum_{j=i+1}^{d_{k+1}}(L_k)_{ji}(C_k^T)_{j,\cdot}}{(L_k)_{ii}},\qquad i=d_{k+1},\ldots,1.$$
These recurrences give $L_kU_k=F_{k+1}P_{k|k}$ and $L_k^TC_k^T=U_k$, so
$C_k=P_{k|k}F_{k+1}^TP_{k+1|k}^{-1}$; no inverse is formed in the procedure.
2. Update the smoothed mean and covariance:
$$m_{k|T}=m_{k|k}+C_k(m_{k+1|T}-m_{k+1|k})$$
$$P_{k|T}=P_{k|k}+C_k(P_{k+1|T}-P_{k+1|k})C_k^T$$

Return $(m_{k|T},P_{k|T})_{k=0}^T$. For $T=0$ the loop is empty and the
output is the initial filtered pair. The algorithm is undefined if a
forecast covariance to be solved is singular; it makes no pseudoinverse,
complexity, rounding-error, or numerical-stability claim. The theorem on
this page proves that the outputs are moments of the fixed-interval
conditional laws under these hypotheses.

Assume AC and fix a finite-horizon linear-Gaussian state-space model
([[def-linear-gaussian-state-space-model-with-independent-noises]]) with
states $X_0,\ldots,X_T$, observations $Y_1,\ldots,Y_T$, and Borel observation
space $\mathsf Y_{1:T}=\mathbb R^{p_1}\times\cdots\times\mathbb R^{p_T}$,
with the empty product a singleton when $T=0$.
For $0\le k\le T$, a **fixed-interval smoothing kernel for $X_k$** is an
everywhere-defined probability kernel
$$\psi_{k|T}:\mathsf Y_{1:T}\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{d_k}$$
whose composition with the full observation vector $Y_{1:T}$ is a regular
conditional distribution of $X_k$ given $\sigma(Y_{1:T})$. Thus it is the
single-time marginal smoothing law after all observations through time $T$
are supplied. The full-path smoothing kernel and its version convention are
defined in [[def-state-space-filtering-laws]].

This definition does not assert that such a kernel exists or is unique at
observation values in a null set. The theorem on this page constructs a
Gaussian version under its explicit forecast and innovation assumptions.

derivations.claim: By [F2], $X_0=0$ and $q_1=0$ almost surely, so $X_1=0$ almost surely. The observation is $Y_1=r_1$ and the model covariances are positive semidefinite.

The forward recursion gives $P_{1|0}=1\cdot0\cdot1+0=0$ and $m_{1|0}=0$. Since $H_1=0$ and $R_1=1$, its innovation covariance is $S_1=1>0$, gain $K_1=0$, and filtered state remains $N(0,0)$. Thus the forward filter is admissible, while the RTS step would require the ordinary inverse of $P_{1|0}=0$, which does not exist by [F4]. No pseudoinverse substitution follows from that algorithm.

Define $\psi_{0|1}(y,\cdot)=\delta_0$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$. For any Borel sets $A,B\subseteq\mathbb R$, $\mathbb P(X_0\in A,Y_1\in B)=1_{\{0\in A\}}\mathbb P(Y_1\in B)=\int_B\delta_0(A)\,\mathbb P_{Y_1}(dy)$ by step 1.1. Hence this everywhere-defined kernel satisfies the RCD identity in [F5]; it is the fixed-interval smoothing law even though the ordinary RTS recursion is undefined.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

A measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$ is **standard Borel** if there are a Polish space $P$ and a bijection $h:E\to P$ such that $A\in\mathcal E$ exactly when $h[A]$ is Borel in $P$. Thus the measurable structure is part of the datum; no particular compatible Polish topology on $E$ is selected.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Assume Choice. Let $(E_n,\mathcal E_n)_{n\ge0}$ be measurable spaces, let
$\mu_0$ be a probability measure on $E_0$, and, for each $n\ge0$, let $K_n$ be
a probability kernel from $E_0\times\cdots\times E_n$ to $E_{n+1}$. There is a
unique probability measure $P$ on
$$ \left(\prod_{n\ge0}E_n,\ \bigotimes_{n\ge0}\mathcal E_n\right) $$ whose finite-prefix laws are the prescribed iterated integrals $$ \mu_0(dx_0)K_0(x_0,dx_1)K_1(x_0,x_1,dx_2)\cdots K_{r-1}(x_0,\ldots,x_{r-1},dx_r). $$
In particular, if every $E_n=E$ and
$K_n(x_0,\ldots,x_n,A)=K(x_n,A)$, the coordinate process is a homogeneous
$K$-chain with initial law $\mu_0$.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space and let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int f\,d\mu=0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad f=0 \text{ almost everywhere.}$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mu$ be a positive measure and let $
u$ be a signed measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. Assume there is an increasing measurable exhaustion $(X_n)$ with $ igcup_nX_n=X$, $\mu(X_n)<+\infty$, and $|
u|(X_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$. If $
u\ll\mu$, then there exists a measurable real-valued function $f$, unique up to $\mu$-almost-everywhere equality, such that
$$
u(E)=\int_Ef\,d\mu\qquad(E\in\mathcal A).$$
If in addition $|
u|(X)<+\infty$, then $f\in L^1(\mu)$.

Assume AC. Every standard-Borel space $(E,\mathcal S)$ has a countable algebra $\mathcal A$ which generates $\mathcal S$, separates points, and determines finite measures: if finite measures $\mu,\nu$ agree on $\mathcal A$, then $\mu=\nu$. In particular it determines probability measures.

Let $\mu$ be a sigma-finite positive measure and let $\nu$ be a signed measure or a finite complex measure with $\nu\ll\mu$. If $h$ is a representative of $d\nu/d\mu$, then
$$\nu(E)=\int_E h\,d\mu\qquad(E\in\mathcal A).$$
More generally, if
$$g=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf 1_{E_j}$$
is the canonical disjoint representation of a simple measurable function and $|\nu|(E_j)<+\infty$ for every $j$, then
$$\int g\,d\nu=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\int_{E_j} h\,d\mu.$$
In particular, whenever the Lebesgue integral of $gh$ is defined, one has
$$\int g\,d\nu=\int gh\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$, $(Y,\mathcal{B})$, and $(Z,\mathcal{C})$ be measurable
spaces. If $f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Y,\mathcal{B})$ is measurable and
$g : (Y,\mathcal{B}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable, then
$g \circ f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable.

In particular, if $f$ is measurable and $g$ is a Borel measurable function on
its codomain, then $g \circ f$ is measurable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces, and let
$$f : X \times Y \to \overline{\mathbb R}$$
be $(\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B,\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R}))$-measurable.
Then $f_x : Y \to \overline{\mathbb R}$ is $\mathcal B$-measurable for every
$x \in X$, and $f^y : X \to \overline{\mathbb R}$ is $\mathcal A$-measurable
for every $y \in Y$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and define
$$\nu_f(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu \qquad (A\in\mathcal A).$$
Then $\nu_f$ is a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$.

derivations.claim: Apply [F3] to $\lambda$ and each one-step kernel to obtain joint laws $P(dx,dy)=\lambda(dx)M(x,dy)$ and $Q(dx,dy)=\lambda(dx)R(x,dy)$. For any product-measurable $A$, the section integrals are measurable by [F4]. If $Q(A)=0$, then $R(x,A_x)=0$ for $\lambda$-almost every $x$ by [F5]; intersecting with the conull kernel-domination set gives $M(x,A_x)=0$ there, hence $P(A)=0$. Thus $P\ll Q$.

By [F6], choose a product-measurable density $h=dP/dQ$. On $N=\{h<0\}$, positivity of $P$ gives $0\le P(N)=\int_Nh\,dQ=-\int_Nh^-\,dQ$, so [F5] makes $h^-=0$ $Q$-almost everywhere on $N$. The Borel positive-part map preserves measurability by [F9], so replacing $h$ by $h^+=\max(h,0)$ leaves the density unchanged $Q$-almost everywhere and makes it nonnegative.

Let $\mathcal C$ be a countable measure-determining algebra on $F$ from [F7], containing $F$. For each $B\in\mathcal C$ and $D\in\mathcal E$, the rectangle laws and density identity [F8] give $\int_D M(x,B)\lambda(dx)=P(D\times B)=\int_D(\int_Bh(x,y)R(x,dy))\lambda(dx)$. Both integrands are measurable by [F2] and [F4] and integrable because their integrals over $E$ are at most one. Uniqueness of Radon–Nikodym densities in [F6] makes them equal $\lambda$-almost everywhere for each fixed $B$.

Intersect the conull sets from step 3.1 over the countable algebra $\mathcal C$. For each $x$ in the intersection, the section $h(x,\cdot)$ is measurable by [F10], so [F11] makes $B\mapsto\int_Bh(x,y)R(x,dy)$ a measure. The kernel section $M(x,\cdot)$ is a probability measure by [F2]. These two measures agree on $\mathcal C$ and have total mass one because $F\in\mathcal C$ and step 3.1 includes $B=F$. The measure-determining property [F7] makes them equal on every $B\in\mathcal F$, with the same exceptional null set for all $B$. Taking $r=h$ proves the assertion.

risk_review.notes: Independently checked steps 1.1–4.1 and all twelve cited prerequisite statements. Joint P and Q are probabilities; zero section integrals plus lambda-a.e. domination prove P << Q. Scalar RN applies to finite positive P and Q; positive-part modification is legitimate. Rectangle identities give equality of measurable section masses a.e. for each member of a countable determining algebra; including F ensures finite mass before applying uniqueness. Countable intersection gives one exceptional null set, independent of B. Empty F is excluded by a probability kernel from a lambda-probability source. AC is explicitly carried. No defect found.

citations.quote:
Input a particle count $N\ge1$, nonnegative finite weights $a_1,\ldots,a_N$, and a scheme label, either multinomial or residual. Let $A=\sum_{j=1}^Na_j$. If $A>0$, set $p_j=a_j/A$; if $A=0$, set $p_j=1/N$ for every $j$. Thus $p$ is always a probability vector.

- **Multinomial scheme.** Draw an index vector $(J_1,\ldots,J_N)\in\{1,\ldots,N\}^N$ with conditional mass $\mathbb P(J_1=j_1,\ldots,J_N=j_N\mid a)=\prod_{\ell=1}^Np_{j_\ell}$. Put $C_j=\#\{\ell:J_\ell=j\}$.
- **Residual scheme.** Put $q_j=\lfloor Np_j\rfloor$, $r_j=Np_j-q_j$, and $R=\sum_{j=1}^Nr_j=N-\sum_{j=1}^Nq_j$, an integer in $\{0,\ldots,N-1\}$. If $R=0$, put $C_j=q_j$. If $R>0$, draw $(K_1,\ldots,K_R)$ with conditional mass $\mathbb P(K_1=k_1,\ldots,K_R=k_R\mid a)=\prod_{\ell=1}^R(r_{k_\ell}/R)$ and put $C_j=q_j+\#\{\ell:K_\ell=j\}$.

For multinomial resampling, return the sampled vector $(J_1,\ldots,J_N)$ in its sampled order, together with its count vector $(C_1,\ldots,C_N)$; do not sort the sampled indices. For residual resampling, return the ancestor list containing exactly $C_j$ copies of index $j$, ordered by increasing index, together with its count vector. Each output is a length-$N$ list and a count vector summing to $N$. When all input weights vanish, the uniform fallback defines the procedure; any downstream normalizer already multiplied by this zero average remains zero.

derivations.claim: In the multinomial branch, $C_j=\sum_{\ell=1}^N\mathbf 1_{\{J_\ell=j\}}$ and each indicator has conditional expectation $p_j$ by the specified product mass. Linearity of a finite sum gives $\mathbb E[C_j\mid a]=Np_j$, including the uniform fallback.

In the residual branch, write $q_j=\lfloor Np_j\rfloor$ and $r_j=Np_j-q_j$. The remainder $R=\sum_jr_j=N-\sum_jq_j$ is an integer. If $R=0$, every $r_j=0$ and $C_j=q_j=Np_j$; if $R>0$, then $C_j=q_j+\sum_{\ell=1}^{R}\mathbf 1_{\{K_\ell=j\}}$ with each indicator having conditional expectation $r_j/R$, so $\mathbb E[C_j\mid a]=q_j+R(r_j/R)=Np_j$.
Steps 1.1 and 1.2 establish the same conditional expected-count identity for both schemes in the procedure, completing the assertion.

boundaries.reason: The Statement fixes N≥1, so its offspring-count index set is nonempty. Proof step 1.2 separately covers the permissible R=0 residual-draw list by C_j=Np_j.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.1 uses the uniform fallback for all-zero weights; step 1.2 handles R=0.
Statement: For N=1, p_1=1 and both count formulas give C_1=1.
Statement: The R=0 case gives deterministic counts when all Np_j are integers, including point-mass weights.
Step 1.2 treats R=0 separately from R>0, including zero fractional remainders.
Steps 1.1–1.2 use the specified finite categorical masses and linearity of finite indicator sums. The residual R=0 outcome is deterministic; no countable or arbitrary selection is invoked.

Assume AC and fix a finite horizon $T\in\mathbb N_0$. For each $0\le k\le T$, let $(\mathsf X_k,\mathcal X_k)$ be a standard Borel space. Let $\mu_0$ be a probability measure on $\mathsf X_0$, and for $1\le k\le T$ let $M_k:\mathsf X_{k-1}\rightsquigarrow\mathsf X_k$ be a probability kernel. A **potential** at time $k$ is a finite-valued nonnegative measurable function $G_k:\mathsf X_k\to[0,\infty)$. Write $\mathsf X_{0:t}=\prod_{k=0}^t\mathsf X_k$ with its finite-product sigma-algebra.

For each $0\le t\le T$, let $P_t^M$ be the finite path law with ordered kernel integral $\mu_0(dx_0)\prod_{k=1}^tM_k(x_{k-1},dx_k)$, supplied by Ionescu–Tulcea ([[thm-ionescu-tulcea-construction-of-a-markov-chain]]). The **unnormalized Feynman–Kac path measure** is
$$\gamma_t(A)=\int_{\mathsf X_{0:t}}\mathbf 1_A(x_{0:t})\prod_{k=0}^tG_k(x_k)\,P_t^M(dx_{0:t}),\qquad A\in\bigotimes_{k=0}^t\mathcal X_k.$$
Its **normalizer** is $Z_t=\gamma_t(\mathsf X_{0:t})=\gamma_t(1)\in[0,\infty]$. Only when $0<Z_t<\infty$ define the normalized path target $\pi_t^{\mathrm{FK}}=\gamma_t/Z_t$. The sequence $(\gamma_t)$ with its kernels and potentials is the Feynman–Kac flow.

State-space filtering kernels are conditional-law versions as in [[def-state-space-filtering-laws]]. A Feynman–Kac path target is not by itself an assertion that a pointwise conditional version has been selected at observation-null histories.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$, $(Y,\mathcal{B})$, and $(Z,\mathcal{C})$ be measurable
spaces. If $f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Y,\mathcal{B})$ is measurable and
$g : (Y,\mathcal{B}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable, then
$g \circ f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable.

In particular, if $f$ is measurable and $g$ is a Borel measurable function on
its codomain, then $g \circ f$ is measurable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space and let
$f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ be measurable for the Borel sigma-algebra on
the extended real line. Products of functions use
$\odot_X$ from [[def-measurable-pointwise-extended-real-product]], and $cf$
abbreviates $\underline c\odot_X f$ for the constant function $\underline c$.
The magnitude function is $|f|=\max(f,-f)$ as in
[[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]]. Then:

1. $cf$ is measurable for every real scalar $c$;
2. $\max(f,g)$, $\min(f,g)$, $|f|$, $f^+$, and $f^-$ are measurable;
3. if the partial pointwise sum $f+g$ is defined at every point, then it is measurable;
4. the pointwise product $fg:=f\odot_X g$ is measurable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int g\,d(f\,d\mu)=\int gf\,d\mu.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC and fix a finite horizon $T\in\mathbb N_0$. For each $0\le k\le T$, let $(\mathsf X_k,\mathcal X_k)$ be a standard Borel space. Let $\mu_0$ be a probability measure on $\mathsf X_0$, and for $1\le k\le T$ let $M_k:\mathsf X_{k-1}\rightsquigarrow\mathsf X_k$ be a probability kernel. For each $0\le t\le T$, let $P_t^M$ be the finite path law with ordered kernel integral $\mu_0(dx_0)\prod_{k=1}^tM_k(x_{k-1},dx_k)$, supplied by Ionescu–Tulcea ([[thm-ionescu-tulcea-construction-of-a-markov-chain]]). The **unnormalized Feynman–Kac path measure** is
$$\gamma_t(A)=\int_{\mathsf X_{0:t}}\mathbf 1_A(x_{0:t})\prod_{k=0}^tG_k(x_k)\,P_t^M(dx_{0:t}),\qquad A\in\bigotimes_{k=0}^t\mathcal X_k.$$
Its **normalizer** is $Z_t=\gamma_t(\mathsf X_{0:t})=\gamma_t(1)\in[0,\infty]$. Only when $0<Z_t<\infty$ define the normalized path target $\pi_t^{\mathrm{FK}}=\gamma_t/Z_t$. The sequence $(\gamma_t)$ with its kernels and potentials is the Feynman–Kac flow.

State-space filtering kernels are conditional-law versions as in [[def-state-space-filtering-laws]]. A Feynman–Kac path target is not by itself an assertion that a pointwise conditional version has been selected at observation-null histories.

Assume AC. Let $(E,\mathcal E)$ and $(F,\mathcal F)$ be standard Borel spaces, let $\lambda$ be a probability measure on $E$, and let $M$ and $R$ be probability kernels from $E$ to $F$. Suppose $M(x,\cdot)\ll R(x,\cdot)$ for $\lambda$-almost every $x$. Then there is an $(\mathcal E\otimes\mathcal F)$-measurable function $r:E\times F\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for $\lambda$-almost every $x$ and every $B\in\mathcal F$,
$$M(x,B)=\int_B r(x,y)\,R(x,dy).$$
The exceptional set in $x$ is a single null set, independent of $B$.

Assume Choice. Let $(E_n,\mathcal E_n)_{n\ge0}$ be measurable spaces, let
$\mu_0$ be a probability measure on $E_0$, and, for each $n\ge0$, let $K_n$ be
a probability kernel from $E_0\times\cdots\times E_n$ to $E_{n+1}$. There is a
unique probability measure $P$ on
$$ \left(\prod_{n\ge0}E_n,\ \bigotimes_{n\ge0}\mathcal E_n\right) $$ whose finite-prefix laws are the prescribed iterated integrals $$ \mu_0(dx_0)K_0(x_0,dx_1)K_1(x_0,x_1,dx_2)\cdots K_{r-1}(x_0,\ldots,x_{r-1},dx_r). $$
In particular, if every $E_n=E$ and
$K_n(x_0,\ldots,x_n,A)=K(x_n,A)$, the coordinate process is a homogeneous
$K$-chain with initial law $\mu_0$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mu$ be a positive measure and let $
u$ be a signed measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. Assume there is an increasing measurable exhaustion $(X_n)$ with $ igcup_nX_n=X$, $\mu(X_n)<+\infty$, and $|
u|(X_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$. If $
u\ll\mu$, then there exists a measurable real-valued function $f$, unique up to $\mu$-almost-everywhere equality, such that
$$
u(E)=\int_Ef\,d\mu\qquad(E\in\mathcal A).$$
If in addition $|
u|(X)<+\infty$, then $f\in L^1(\mu)$.

Let $\mu$ be a sigma-finite positive measure and let $\nu$ be a signed measure or a finite complex measure with $\nu\ll\mu$. If $h$ is a representative of $d\nu/d\mu$, then
$$\nu(E)=\int_E h\,d\mu\qquad(E\in\mathcal A).$$
More generally, if
$$g=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf 1_{E_j}$$
is the canonical disjoint representation of a simple measurable function and $|\nu|(E_j)<+\infty$ for every $j$, then
$$\int g\,d\nu=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\int_{E_j} h\,d\mu.$$
In particular, whenever the Lebesgue integral of $gh$ is defined, one has
$$\int g\,d\nu=\int gh\,d\mu.$$

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then there is an increasing sequence of
nonnegative simple measurable functions $(s_n)$ such that $s_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x\in X$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space and let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int f\,d\mu=0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad f=0 \text{ almost everywhere.}$$

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$, $(Y,\mathcal{B})$, and $(Z,\mathcal{C})$ be measurable
spaces. If $f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Y,\mathcal{B})$ is measurable and
$g : (Y,\mathcal{B}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable, then
$g \circ f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable.

In particular, if $f$ is measurable and $g$ is a Borel measurable function on
its codomain, then $g \circ f$ is measurable.

For each $0\le s\le t$, let $P_s^M$ and $Q_s$ be the target and proposal finite-prefix path laws supplied by [F3]. Initially choose a real-valued Radon–Nikodym representative $\widetildeho_0$ from [F4]. Since $\mu_0$ is positive, for $N_-:=\{\widetildeho_0<0\}$ its setwise identity gives $0\le\mu_0(N_-)=\int_{N_-}\widetildeho_0\,d
u_0\le0$. Thus $\int_{N_-}\widetildeho_0^-\,d
u_0=0$, and [F9] implies $\widetildeho_0^-=0$ $
u_0$-almost everywhere. Replace $\widetildeho_0$ by the measurable nonnegative version $ho_0=\max(\widetildeho_0,0)$; [F10] gives measurability and the modification preserves the setwise density identity. Hence $P_0^M\ll Q_0$ with base density $ho_0$; after weighting by $G_0$ in [F1], $\gamma_0$ has density $W_0=G_0ho_0$.

First record the nonnegative extension used below. If finite measures $P,Q$ satisfy $P(A)=\int_Au\,dQ$ for every measurable $A$, with $u\ge0$, choose by [F7] simple functions $g_n\uparrow g$ for any nonnegative measurable $g$. The simple-function identity in [F5] gives $\int g_n\,dP=\int g_nu\,dQ$ for each $n$; [F8] and monotone convergence of $g_nu$ give $\int g\,dP=\int gu\,dQ$, with infinity allowed. All measures to which this fact is applied below are probabilities, so the finite-level-set condition in [F5] holds.

Fix $1\le k\le t$ and assume $P_{k-1}^M\ll Q_{k-1}$ with density $D_{k-1}(x_{0:k-1})=\rho_0(x_0)\prod_{j=1}^{k-1}r_j(x_{j-1},x_j)$. For nonnegative product-measurable $h$, define $\psi(x_{0:k-1})=\int h(x_{0:k-1},x_k)M_k(x_{k-1},dx_k)$; [F6] makes $\psi$ measurable. For $Q_{k-1}$-almost every history, the kernel Radon–Nikodym identity and step 1.2 give $\psi(x_{0:k-1})=\int h(x_{0:k-1},x_k)r_k(x_{k-1},x_k)R_k(x_{k-1},dx_k)$. Step 1.2 also extends the induction density identity from sets to $\psi$, so ordered integration from [F3] gives $\begin{aligned} \int h\,dP_k^M &=\int\psi\,dP_{k-1}^M\\ &=\int D_{k-1}(x_{0:k-1})\,\psi(x_{0:k-1})\,Q_{k-1}(dx_{0:k-1})\\ &=\int h(x_{0:k})D_{k-1}(x_{0:k-1})r_k(x_{k-1},x_k)\,Q_k(dx_{0:k}). \end{aligned}$ Thus $P_k^M\ll Q_k$ with density $D_k=D_{k-1}r_k$. The kernel identity is needed only on a $Q_{k-1}$-conull set; the same is true for $P_{k-1}^M$ by the induction density, and changes on the exceptional set do not affect these nonnegative integrals.

Induction in step 2.1 gives the proposal density of every finite-horizon state path. The target measure $\gamma_s$ is obtained by integrating the nonnegative path potential $V_s=\prod_{j=0}^sG_j$ against $P_s^M$. Choose a measurable version $\rho_0=d\mu_0/d\nu_0$ and, using [[lem-jointly-measurable-radon-nikodym-derivatives-for-probability-kernels]], measurable versions $r_k(x,\cdot)=dM_k(x,\cdot)/dR_k(x,\cdot)$ for these preceding-state marginals.

Then $\gamma_s\ll Q_s$ for every $s\le t$, with product density
$$W_s(x_{0:s})=G_0(x_0)\rho_0(x_0)\prod_{k=1}^sG_k(x_k)r_k(x_{k-1},x_k).$$
That is, $\gamma_s(A)=\int_AW_s\,dQ_s$ for every measurable $A\subseteq\mathsf X_{0:s}$. If $0<Z_s<\infty$, the normalized path target has density $W_s/Z_s$ with respect to $Q_s$.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element, let
$\mathbb P_X$ be its law, and let $g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb R$ or
$g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb C$ be measurable.

1. If $g\ge0$, then
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$
2. If $g(X)$ is integrable, then $g$ is integrable with respect to
   $\mathbb P_X$ and the same formula holds:
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$
Assume AC. For every real integrable $X$ on $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ and every sub-sigma-algebra $\mathcal G$, a conditional-expectation version of $X$ given $\mathcal G$ exists.

Assume AC for existence. If $\mathcal H\subseteq\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ and $X\in L^1(P)$, then $E[E[X\mid\mathcal G]\mid\mathcal H]=E[X\mid\mathcal H]$ and $E[E[X\mid\mathcal H]\mid\mathcal G]=E[X\mid\mathcal H]$ almost surely. Also, if a version of $E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ is $\mathcal H$-measurable, it is a version of $E[X\mid\mathcal H]$.

Assume AC for the supplied existence theorem. Write $E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ for the unique class in $L^1(\Omega,\mathcal G,P|_{\mathcal G})$ consisting of conditional-expectation versions of $X$. A chosen real $\mathcal G$-measurable representative is a **version**. Equalities and inequalities involving these classes mean almost-sure equalities and inequalities.

Existence is [[thm-conditional-expectation-exists-by-radon-nikodym]] and uniqueness is [[lem-conditional-expectation-is-unique-almost-surely]], applied to [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. The quotient is [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]. If $X=X^{\ast}$ almost surely, [[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]] gives identical event integrals, so the output class is independent of the input representative. The [[def-axiom-of-choice]] assumption is inherited from RN existence.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Assume Choice. Let $(E_n,\mathcal E_n)_{n\ge0}$ be measurable spaces, let
$\mu_0$ be a probability measure on $E_0$, and, for each $n\ge0$, let $K_n$ be
a probability kernel from $E_0\times\cdots\times E_n$ to $E_{n+1}$. There is a
unique probability measure $P$ on
$$ \left(\prod_{n\ge0}E_n,\ \bigotimes_{n\ge0}\mathcal E_n\right) $$ whose finite-prefix laws are the prescribed iterated integrals $$ \mu_0(dx_0)K_0(x_0,dx_1)K_1(x_0,x_1,dx_2)\cdots K_{r-1}(x_0,\ldots,x_{r-1},dx_r). $$
In particular, if every $E_n=E$ and
$K_n(x_0,\ldots,x_n,A)=K(x_n,A)$, the coordinate process is a homogeneous
$K$-chain with initial law $\mu_0$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space and let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int f\,d\mu=0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad f=0 \text{ almost everywhere.}$$

Let $\mu$ be a sigma-finite positive measure and let $\nu$ be a signed measure or a finite complex measure with $\nu\ll\mu$. If $h$ is a representative of $d\nu/d\mu$, then
$$\nu(E)=\int_E h\,d\mu\qquad(E\in\mathcal A).$$
More generally, if
$$g=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf 1_{E_j}$$
is the canonical disjoint representation of a simple measurable function and $|\nu|(E_j)<+\infty$ for every $j$, then
$$\int g\,d\nu=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\int_{E_j} h\,d\mu.$$
In particular, whenever the Lebesgue integral of $gh$ is defined, one has
$$\int g\,d\nu=\int gh\,d\mu.$$

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then there is an increasing sequence of
nonnegative simple measurable functions $(s_n)$ such that $s_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x\in X$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$, $(Y,\mathcal{B})$, and $(Z,\mathcal{C})$ be measurable
spaces. If $f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Y,\mathcal{B})$ is measurable and
$g : (Y,\mathcal{B}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable, then
$g \circ f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable.

In particular, if $f$ is measurable and $g$ is a Borel measurable function on
its codomain, then $g \circ f$ is measurable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space and let
$f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ be measurable for the Borel sigma-algebra on
the extended real line. Products of functions use
$\odot_X$ from [[def-measurable-pointwise-extended-real-product]], and $cf$
abbreviates $\underline c\odot_X f$ for the constant function $\underline c$.
The magnitude function is $|f|=\max(f,-f)$ as in
[[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]]. Then:

1. $cf$ is measurable for every real scalar $c$;
2. $\max(f,g)$, $\min(f,g)$, $|f|$, $f^+$, and $f^-$ are measurable;
3. if the partial pointwise sum $f+g$ is defined at every point, then it is measurable;
4. the pointwise product $fg:=f\odot_X g$ is measurable.

Let $(S,\Sigma)$ and $(T_i,\Tau_i)$ for $i<n$ be measurable spaces, with
$n<\infty$, and let $K_i:S\to T_i$ be probability kernels with the same
source. There is a unique probability kernel
$$K:S\to\prod_{i<n}T_i$$
whose evaluation on every measurable rectangle is
$$K(s,\prod_{i<n}B_i)=\prod_{i<n}K_i(s,B_i).$$
For $n=0$, the target is the empty-product singleton and $K$ is its point
mass. For $n>0$, the product sigma-algebra is the recursive finite product
sigma-algebra.

derivations.claim: First, extend each setwise density identity needed here to nonnegative measurable integrands. If $P(A)=\int_Au\,dQ$ for every measurable $A$, with $u\ge0$, choose simple $g_n\uparrow g$ by [F15]. The simple-function identity [F14] gives $\int g_n\,dP=\int g_nu\,dQ$ for each $n$, and [F16] on both sides yields $\int g\,dP=\int gu\,dQ$, allowing infinity. This applies to the initial law pair and, for almost every preceding proposal state, to each transition-kernel pair in [F5]. At time zero, the algorithm gives $\widehat\gamma_0^N(\varphi)=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^NG_0(X_0^i)\rho_0(X_0^i)\varphi(X_0^i)$, with zero-weight terms interpreted by the nonnegative-integral convention $0\cdot\infty=0$. Each $X_0^i$ has law $\nu_0$, so [F6], finite-sum linearity [F7], and the just-proved extension give $\mathbb E[\widehat\gamma_0^N(\varphi)]=\int G_0\rho_0\varphi\,d\nu_0=\gamma_0(\varphi)$. The finite target integral makes this random variable integrable.

The finite procedure defines measurable transition kernels. The initial IID draws from $\nu_0$ form a finite product kernel by [F21]. At each later step, the previous normalized weights are measurable functions of the previous paths by [F17, F18, F19, F20]. The multinomial and residual laws are probability kernels on the finite ancestor-index set: normalization uses division on the Borel branch where the sum is positive, each floor map is Borel since $\{x:\lfloor x\rfloor=m\}=[m,m+1)$, and the $R=0$ or $R>0$ branches are Borel. Since $R$ takes only the values $0,\ldots,N-1$, each residual output-list probability is a finite sum over possible draw vectors of Borel product masses. For a fixed ancestor vector, the proposal law of the next particles is the finite product of the pullbacks of the $R_k$ kernels along measurable coordinate projections; [F17, F18, F19] make each pullback a probability kernel, and [F21] makes their product a probability kernel. The finite mixture over ancestor vectors is again a probability kernel by finite sums and products [F20]. Thus [F12] applies to the particle-system transitions.

Every time-zero particle path has law $Q_0$. Inductively, suppose each previous particle path avoids every fixed $Q_{k-1}$-null history set almost surely. If $Q_k(A)=0$, the pullback of $R_k$ to the history space is a probability kernel by step 1.2, and [F11] makes $x_{0:k-1}\mapsto R_k(x_{k-1},A_{x_{0:k-1}})$ measurable. The proposal path recursion [F12] and zero-integral criterion [F13] show it vanishes for $Q_{k-1}$-almost every history. The kernel-derivative exceptional parent-state set has a null preimage under the last-coordinate marginal of $Q_{k-1}$, so every stored path avoids that preimage; resampling copies only existing paths, and propagation therefore avoids $A$. Each initial or kernel derivative has reference integral one by [F5]; it is therefore finite almost everywhere for its reference law. The finite-valued potentials and the finite particle count then make all particle weights finite almost surely.

Write $\mathcal F_{k-1}$ for the previous particle histories and weights. Let $H_k$ be the integral of $\widehat\gamma_k^N(\varphi)$ against the algorithm's conditional finite-step transition law. By [F3], the expected number of children from parent $j$ is $N\bar w_{k-1}^j$. The algorithm gives $\widehat Z_k\bar w_k^i=\widehat Z_{k-1}a_k^i/N$ when the new weight sum is positive; when it is zero, both sides are zero. For each parent outside the exceptional proposal-marginal null set, [F18, F19, F20] make $x_k\mapsto G_k(x_k)\varphi(x_{0:k})$ nonnegative measurable; apply the simple-approximation extension in step 1.1 to it. The setwise identity in [F5] then gives $\int G_k\varphi\,r_k\,dR_k=\int G_k\varphi\,dM_k$, including infinite values. Integrating each child's incremental weight and summing the expected counts therefore gives $H_k=\widehat\gamma_{k-1}^N(g_k)$, where $g_k(x_{0:k-1})=\int G_k(x_k)\varphi(x_{0:k})M_k(x_{k-1},dx_k)$. If the previous normalizer estimate is zero, both sides vanish by the algorithm's zero-weight convention. Measurability follows from [F11]. This is initially a nonnegative conditional-kernel integral, not yet an $L^1$ conditional expectation.

By [F4], the target integral of $g_k$ is $\gamma_{k-1}(g_k)=\gamma_k(\varphi)<\infty$. The induction hypothesis therefore gives $\mathbb E[H_k]=\gamma_k(\varphi)$. For every prior event $B\in\mathcal F_{k-1}$, the ordered joint law of the prior histories and the algorithm's conditional finite-step transition law [F12], integrated with the nonnegative integrand $\mathbf1_B\widehat\gamma_k^N(\varphi)$, gives $\mathbb E[\mathbf1_B\widehat\gamma_k^N(\varphi)]=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_BH_k].$ This identity is valid before any integrability assumption, by nonnegative iterated integration. Taking $B=\Omega$ shows that $\widehat\gamma_k^N(\varphi)$ has finite expectation $\gamma_k(\varphi)$, so it is in $L^1$; $H_k$ is also in $L^1$ by its finite expectation. Thus the event identities and measurability make $H_k$ a version of $\mathbb E[\widehat\gamma_k^N(\varphi)\mid\mathcal F_{k-1}]$ by [F2] and [F10]. The tower property [F9] now yields $\mathbb E[\widehat\gamma_k^N(\varphi)]=\gamma_k(\varphi)$, completing the induction step.

Apply the established identity at $k=t$ to the constant function $\varphi=1$. Then $\widehat\gamma_t^N(1)=\widehat Z_t\widehat\pi_t^N(1)=\widehat Z_t$, while $\gamma_t(1)=Z_t$, proving the stated normalizer unbiasedness.

risk_review.notes: Reviewed all six steps, every cited interface and the reader preimage delta. Finite resampling probabilities, Borel floor/normalization branches, finite product proposal kernels and finite mixtures define the particle law. Null-history avoidance is proved for each fixed Q-null set before using marginal-a.e. derivative identities. Conditional expected offspring counts suffice for both schemes; child independence across ancestors is not assumed. The identity Zhat_k wbar_k^i = Zhat_(k-1) a_k^i/N handles the zero-sum branch exactly, and zero accumulated Zhat kills all subsequent mass. Nonnegative conditional-kernel integration precedes L1 conditional expectation, avoiding circular integrability. The induction applies to g_k because its gamma integral equals the finite gamma_k(phi); t=0 and phi=1 are valid. Infinite test values on target-null sets use zero-times-infinity and a.e. finite representatives before L1/tower. The N-in-N and 0<=t clarification agrees with the existing finite algorithm. No defect found; accept reader explicitization.

citations.quote:
Input a particle count $N\ge1$, nonnegative finite weights $a_1,\ldots,a_N$, and a scheme label, either multinomial or residual. Let $A=\sum_{j=1}^Na_j$. If $A>0$, set $p_j=a_j/A$; if $A=0$, set $p_j=1/N$ for every $j$. Thus $p$ is always a probability vector.

- **Multinomial scheme.** Draw an index vector $(J_1,\ldots,J_N)\in\{1,\ldots,N\}^N$ with conditional mass $\mathbb P(J_1=j_1,\ldots,J_N=j_N\mid a)=\prod_{\ell=1}^Np_{j_\ell}$. Put $C_j=\#\{\ell:J_\ell=j\}$.
- **Residual scheme.** Put $q_j=\lfloor Np_j\rfloor$, $r_j=Np_j-q_j$, and $R=\sum_{j=1}^Nr_j=N-\sum_{j=1}^Nq_j$, an integer in $\{0,\ldots,N-1\}$. If $R=0$, put $C_j=q_j$. If $R>0$, draw $(K_1,\ldots,K_R)$ with conditional mass $\mathbb P(K_1=k_1,\ldots,K_R=k_R\mid a)=\prod_{\ell=1}^R(r_{k_\ell}/R)$ and put $C_j=q_j+\#\{\ell:K_\ell=j\}$.

For multinomial resampling, return the sampled vector $(J_1,\ldots,J_N)$ in its sampled order, together with its count vector $(C_1,\ldots,C_N)$; do not sort the sampled indices. For residual resampling, return the ancestor list containing exactly $C_j$ copies of index $j$, ordered by increasing index, together with its count vector. Each output is a length-$N$ list and a count vector summing to $N$. When all input weights vanish, the uniform fallback defines the procedure; any downstream normalizer already multiplied by this zero average remains zero.

Fix $N\ge1$ and nonnegative input weights $a_1,\ldots,a_N$. Let $p$ be the normalized probability vector, with the uniform fallback when all weights vanish, and let $C_j$ be the offspring count from [[alg-multinomial-and-residual-offspring-resampling]]. Conditional on the input weights, for either scheme and every $1\le j\le N$,
$$\mathbb E[C_j\mid a_1,\ldots,a_N]=Np_j.$$
This assertion concerns the counts only; it gives no variance comparison for arbitrary weights.

derivations.claim: The vector is a probability vector, and $Np=(31/10,7/5,1/2,0,0)=(3.1,1.4,0.5,0,0)$. By [F2], both schemes therefore have those expected counts.

In multinomial resampling each count is a sum of five independent Bernoulli indicators with success probability $p_j$, so its variance is $5p_j(1-p_j)$. The first three marginal variances are $1.178$, $1.008$, and $0.45$; the last two are zero.

Residual resampling has deterministic floors $(3,1,0,0,0)$ and fractional remainders $(0.1,0.4,0.5,0,0)$, whose sum is $R=1$. It draws one extra index with these probabilities, so the marginal count variances are $0.1(0.9)=0.09$, $0.4(0.6)=0.24$, and $0.5(0.5)=0.25$ on the first three coordinates, with variance zero on the last two.

The expected counts agree componentwise, while for these weights each of the first three residual marginal variances is smaller than its multinomial counterpart, while the last two variances are zero in both schemes. This is a calculation for this input vector, not a general variance-ordering claim.

citations.quote:
Assume AC and fix a finite horizon $T\in\mathbb N_0$. For each $0\le k\le T$, let $(\mathsf X_k,\mathcal X_k)$ be a standard Borel space. Let $\mu_0$ be a probability measure on $\mathsf X_0$, and for $1\le k\le T$ let $M_k:\mathsf X_{k-1}\rightsquigarrow\mathsf X_k$ be a probability kernel. A **potential** at time $k$ is a finite-valued nonnegative measurable function $G_k:\mathsf X_k\to[0,\infty)$. Write $\mathsf X_{0:t}=\prod_{k=0}^t\mathsf X_k$ with its finite-product sigma-algebra.

For each $0\le t\le T$, let $P_t^M$ be the finite path law with ordered kernel integral $\mu_0(dx_0)\prod_{k=1}^tM_k(x_{k-1},dx_k)$, supplied by Ionescu–Tulcea ([[thm-ionescu-tulcea-construction-of-a-markov-chain]]). The **unnormalized Feynman–Kac path measure** is
$$\gamma_t(A)=\int_{\mathsf X_{0:t}}\mathbf 1_A(x_{0:t})\prod_{k=0}^tG_k(x_k)\,P_t^M(dx_{0:t}),\qquad A\in\bigotimes_{k=0}^t\mathcal X_k.$$
Its **normalizer** is $Z_t=\gamma_t(\mathsf X_{0:t})=\gamma_t(1)\in[0,\infty]$. Only when $0<Z_t<\infty$ define the normalized path target $\pi_t^{\mathrm{FK}}=\gamma_t/Z_t$. The sequence $(\gamma_t)$ with its kernels and potentials is the Feynman–Kac flow.

State-space filtering kernels are conditional-law versions as in [[def-state-space-filtering-laws]]. A Feynman–Kac path target is not by itself an assertion that a pointwise conditional version has been selected at observation-null histories.

Use the finite-horizon target and proposal setting of [[def-feynman-kac-path-targets-and-normalizers]]. For admissible inputs require $\mu_0\ll\nu_0$ and, for each $k\ge1$, $M_k(x,\cdot)\ll R_k(x,\cdot)$ for almost every $x$ under the last-coordinate marginal of the proposal path law $Q_{k-1}$. Select the joint measurable versions $\rho_0=d\mu_0/d\nu_0$ and $r_k(x,\cdot)=dM_k(x,\cdot)/dR_k(x,\cdot)$ supplied by [[thm-feynman-kac-path-radon-nikodym-weight]]. Fix $N\ge1$ and select either multinomial or residual resampling at each time. The algorithm returns a weighted empirical path measure and a normalizer estimate.

1. Draw $X_0^1,\ldots,X_0^N$ independently from $\nu_0$. Set $a_0^i=G_0(X_0^i)\rho_0(X_0^i)$ and $\widehat Z_0=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^Na_0^i$. If $\sum_i a_0^i>0$, put $\bar w_0^i=a_0^i/\sum_j a_0^j$; otherwise put $\bar w_0^i=1/N$. Each initial path is $X_{0:0}^i=X_0^i$.
2. For $k=1,\ldots,t$, do the following:
   1. Apply [[alg-multinomial-and-residual-offspring-resampling]] to the previous normalized weights $(\bar w_{k-1}^1,\ldots,\bar w_{k-1}^N)$, obtaining ancestor indices $A_k^1,\ldots,A_k^N$.
   2. Given the previous paths and these indices, draw $(X_k^1,\ldots,X_k^N)$ with joint conditional law $\bigotimes_{i=1}^N R_k(X_{k-1}^{A_k^i},\cdot)$ and set $X_{0:k}^i=(X_{0:k-1}^{A_k^i},X_k^i)$.
   3. Set $a_k^i=G_k(X_k^i)r_k(X_{k-1}^{A_k^i},X_k^i)$ and $\widehat Z_k=\widehat Z_{k-1}(N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^Na_k^i)$. If $\sum_i a_k^i>0$, put $\bar w_k^i=a_k^i/\sum_j a_k^j$; otherwise put $\bar w_k^i=1/N$.
3. Return $\widehat Z_t$ and the weighted empirical path probability measure $\widehat\pi_t^N=\sum_{i=1}^N\bar w_t^i\delta_{X_{0:t}^i}$. Its last-coordinate marginal is the corresponding empirical filtering approximation.

The all-zero fallback only defines a probability measure for reporting and future sampling. Once a zero average weight occurs, $\widehat Z$ remains zero. The procedure makes no finite-particle accuracy, consistency, or long-time stability claim.

The input convention is that $t\in\{0,\ldots,T\}$ is the requested horizon, $\nu_0$ is a proposal probability on $\mathsf X_0$, $R_k$ are proposal probability kernels for $1\le k\le t$, and $N\in\mathbb N$ with $N\ge1$. Thus the opening support condition ranges over $1\le k\le t$, and a resampling scheme is selected for each such $k$. Choose the finite-valued joint measurable versions $\rho_0$ and $r_k$ constructed in the proof of [[thm-feynman-kac-path-radon-nikodym-weight]].

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X,\mu)$ be a measure space. An **unnormalized target density** is a measurable function $\tilde p:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ with
$$Z_p:=\int_{\mathsf X}\tilde p\,d\mu\in(0,\infty).$$
The target probability measure is $\pi(dx)=\tilde p(x)\mu(dx)/Z_p$. A **proposal density** is a measurable $q:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ with $\int q\,d\mu=1$; write $Q(dx)=q(x)\mu(dx)$. The input integrand $f:\mathsf X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, and the input sample $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ is IID with law $Q$, in the sense of [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]. The normalizing constant $Z_p$ is known for this algorithm.

**Admissible conditions for an unbiased estimate:** $n\ge1$, $q>0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $\{x:f(x)\tilde p(x)\ne0\}$, and the random variable
$$Y:=\begin{cases}f(X_1)\tilde p(X_1)/(Z_pq(X_1)),&q(X_1)>0,\\0,&q(X_1)=0\end{cases}$$
is integrable under $Q$. The support condition makes the value on $q=0$ immaterial to the target integral.

Assume AC and fix a finite horizon $T\in\mathbb N_0$. For each $0\le k\le T$, let $(\mathsf X_k,\mathcal X_k)$ be a standard Borel space. Let $\mu_0$ be a probability measure on $\mathsf X_0$, and for $1\le k\le T$ let $M_k:\mathsf X_{k-1}\rightsquigarrow\mathsf X_k$ be a probability kernel. A **potential** at time $k$ is a finite-valued nonnegative measurable function $G_k:\mathsf X_k\to[0,\infty)$. Write $\mathsf X_{0:t}=\prod_{k=0}^t\mathsf X_k$ with its finite-product sigma-algebra.

For each $0\le t\le T$, let $P_t^M$ be the finite path law with ordered kernel integral $\mu_0(dx_0)\prod_{k=1}^tM_k(x_{k-1},dx_k)$, supplied by Ionescu–Tulcea ([[thm-ionescu-tulcea-construction-of-a-markov-chain]]). The **unnormalized Feynman–Kac path measure** is
$$\gamma_t(A)=\int_{\mathsf X_{0:t}}\mathbf 1_A(x_{0:t})\prod_{k=0}^tG_k(x_k)\,P_t^M(dx_{0:t}),\qquad A\in\bigotimes_{k=0}^t\mathcal X_k.$$
Its **normalizer** is $Z_t=\gamma_t(\mathsf X_{0:t})=\gamma_t(1)\in[0,\infty]$. Only when $0<Z_t<\infty$ define the normalized path target $\pi_t^{\mathrm{FK}}=\gamma_t/Z_t$. The sequence $(\gamma_t)$ with its kernels and potentials is the Feynman–Kac flow.

State-space filtering kernels are conditional-law versions as in [[def-state-space-filtering-laws]]. A Feynman–Kac path target is not by itself an assertion that a pointwise conditional version has been selected at observation-null histories.

Use the finite-horizon target and proposal setting of [[def-feynman-kac-path-targets-and-normalizers]]. For admissible inputs require $\mu_0\ll\nu_0$ and, for each $k\ge1$, $M_k(x,\cdot)\ll R_k(x,\cdot)$ for almost every $x$ under the last-coordinate marginal of the proposal path law $Q_{k-1}$. Select the joint measurable versions $\rho_0=d\mu_0/d\nu_0$ and $r_k(x,\cdot)=dM_k(x,\cdot)/dR_k(x,\cdot)$ supplied by [[thm-feynman-kac-path-radon-nikodym-weight]]. Fix $N\ge1$ and select either multinomial or residual resampling at each time. The algorithm returns a weighted empirical path measure and a normalizer estimate.

1. Draw $X_0^1,\ldots,X_0^N$ independently from $\nu_0$. Set $a_0^i=G_0(X_0^i)\rho_0(X_0^i)$ and $\widehat Z_0=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^Na_0^i$. If $\sum_i a_0^i>0$, put $\bar w_0^i=a_0^i/\sum_j a_0^j$; otherwise put $\bar w_0^i=1/N$. Each initial path is $X_{0:0}^i=X_0^i$.
2. For $k=1,\ldots,t$, do the following:
   1. Apply [[alg-multinomial-and-residual-offspring-resampling]] to the previous normalized weights $(\bar w_{k-1}^1,\ldots,\bar w_{k-1}^N)$, obtaining ancestor indices $A_k^1,\ldots,A_k^N$.
   2. Given the previous paths and these indices, draw $(X_k^1,\ldots,X_k^N)$ with joint conditional law $\bigotimes_{i=1}^N R_k(X_{k-1}^{A_k^i},\cdot)$ and set $X_{0:k}^i=(X_{0:k-1}^{A_k^i},X_k^i)$.
   3. Set $a_k^i=G_k(X_k^i)r_k(X_{k-1}^{A_k^i},X_k^i)$ and $\widehat Z_k=\widehat Z_{k-1}(N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^Na_k^i)$. If $\sum_i a_k^i>0$, put $\bar w_k^i=a_k^i/\sum_j a_k^j$; otherwise put $\bar w_k^i=1/N$.
3. Return $\widehat Z_t$ and the weighted empirical path probability measure $\widehat\pi_t^N=\sum_{i=1}^N\bar w_t^i\delta_{X_{0:t}^i}$. Its last-coordinate marginal is the corresponding empirical filtering approximation.

The all-zero fallback only defines a probability measure for reporting and future sampling. Once a zero average weight occurs, $\widehat Z$ remains zero. The procedure makes no finite-particle accuracy, consistency, or long-time stability claim.

The input convention is that $t\in\{0,\ldots,T\}$ is the requested horizon, $\nu_0$ is a proposal probability on $\mathsf X_0$, $R_k$ are proposal probability kernels for $1\le k\le t$, and $N\in\mathbb N$ with $N\ge1$. Thus the opening support condition ranges over $1\le k\le t$, and a resampling scheme is selected for each such $k$. Choose the finite-valued joint measurable versions $\rho_0$ and $r_k$ constructed in the proof of [[thm-feynman-kac-path-radon-nikodym-weight]].

Let $(S,\Sigma)$ and $(E,\mathcal E)$ be measurable spaces with $S\ne\varnothing$, and let $K:S\rightsquigarrow E$ be a probability kernel as in [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. Its **Dobrushin contraction coefficient** is
$$\delta(K):=\sup_{x,x'\in S}\lVert K(x,\cdot)-K(x',\cdot)\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}},$$
where $\lVert\cdot\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}$ is the event-supremum distance between probability laws in [[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]]. Thus $0\le\delta(K)\le1$. The coefficient measures the largest total-variation separation between two one-step output laws.

Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
$(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **total variation
distance** is

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}\bigl|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\bigr| .$$

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in
$[-1,1]$, because both measures have total mass one; hence the set being
maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.
The empty event and the whole space give the values $0$ and
$|\mu(E)-\nu(E)|=0$, so the distance is zero when $\mu=\nu$, and it is symmetric
in $\mu$ and $\nu$. This convention carries no factor $1/2$ in the supremum;
it is therefore not the total variation norm of the signed measure $\mu-\nu$,
which is twice the quantity above when that signed measure is considered on a
measurable space where the decomposition is attained. On a countable state
space with its power-set sigma-algebra the supremum equals the half-$\ell^1$
sum $\tfrac12\sum_{x\in E}|\mu(\{x\})-\nu(\{x\})|$; that identity is proved in
[[lem-total-variation-half-l1-formula-on-a-countable-space]], not assumed here.

derivations.claim: Fix $x,x'\in S$ and write $p=k_x$, $q=k_{x'}$. The assumed ordered-pair bound gives $p\le Cq$ almost everywhere, so $q\ge p/C$. Where $p\le q$, $\min(p,q)=p\ge p/C$; where $p>q$, the same inequality $p\le Cq$ gives $\min(p,q)=q\ge p/C$. Hence $\int\min(p,q)\,d\lambda\ge C^{-1}\int p\,d\lambda=C^{-1}$.

Let $A_+=\{z:p(z)\ge q(z)\}$. For every measurable $A$, $|\int_A(p-q)\,d\lambda|\le\int(p-q)^+\,d\lambda$. Since $\int(p-q)=0$, the positive and negative parts have equal integral, and $\int(p-q)^+\,d\lambda=1-\int\min(p,q)\,d\lambda$; equality is attained at $A_+$. Thus [F2] gives $\lVert K(x,\cdot)-K(x',\cdot)\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}=1-\int\min(p,q)\,d\lambda\le1-C^{-1}$ by step 1.1.
The bound in step 2.1 holds for every pair $x,x'$, so taking their supremum in [F1] proves $\delta(K)\le1-C^{-1}$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Fix a finite horizon $T$. At each $0\le t\le T$, let $\pi_t$ be a probability law on a measurable particle space $\Theta_t$. Let $\widetilde\pi_0$ be an initial proposal with $\pi_0\ll\widetilde\pi_0$, and fix $\upsilon_0=d\pi_0/d\widetilde\pi_0$. For $1\le t\le T$, let $k_t$ be a probability kernel from $\Theta_{t-1}$ to $\Theta_t$, and put
$$\widetilde\pi_t(A)=\int_{\Theta_{t-1}}k_t(x,A)\,\pi_{t-1}(dx).$$
Assume $\pi_t\ll\widetilde\pi_t$ and fix a nonnegative Radon–Nikodym version $\upsilon_t=d\pi_t/d\widetilde\pi_t$, so $\widetilde\pi_t(\upsilon_t)=1$. The BCS-41 sequential importance-resampling algorithm [[alg-sequential-importance-resampling]] is this scheme on path spaces when $k_t$ appends a proposal transition. Under the support and measurable versions of [[thm-feynman-kac-path-radon-nikodym-weight]], its normalized incremental weight is $\upsilon_t=(Z_{t-1}/Z_t)G_t r_t$ for $t\ge1$, and $\upsilon_0=G_0\rho_0/Z_0$ initially. The previous normalized target is already part of $\widetilde\pi_t$; one does not multiply by the full earlier path-weight product again.

For a measurable vector function $\phi:\Theta_t\to\mathbb R^d$, write $\mu(\phi)=\int\phi\,d\mu$ and
$$\operatorname{Cov}_{\mu}(\phi)=\int(\phi-\mu(\phi))(\phi-\mu(\phi))^\top\,d\mu,$$
when the second moment is finite. Also write $k_t\phi(x)=\int\phi(z)k_t(x,dz)$ and
$$\operatorname{Cov}_{k_t}(\phi)(x)=\int(\phi(z)-k_t\phi(x))(\phi(z)-k_t\phi(x))^\top k_t(x,dz).$$

The source recursive test classes are
$$\Phi_0^{(d)}=\{\phi:\widetilde\pi_0(\|\phi\|^2)<\infty\},$$
and, for $t\ge1$,
$$\Phi_t^{(d)}=\left\{\phi:\text{ for some }\delta>0,\ \widetilde\pi_t(\|\upsilon_t\phi\|^{2+\delta})<\infty\ \text{ and }\ x\mapsto k_t(\upsilon_t\phi)(x)\in\Phi_{t-1}^{(d)}\right\}.$$
Assume $1\in\Phi_t^{(1)}$ for every $t$. This is the source theorem's explicit normalizing-weight condition. For the recursive post-resampling CLTs proved on this page, use the stronger classes $\Psi_t^{(d)}$. At $t=0$, let $\Psi_0^{(d)}$ consist of the $\phi\in\Phi_0^{(d)}$ for which $\widetilde\pi_0(\|\upsilon_0(\phi-\pi_0(\phi))\|^2)<\infty$ and $\pi_0(\|\phi\|^2)<\infty$. The initial normalizing denominator needs only its finite first moment $\widetilde\pi_0(\upsilon_0)=1$. For $t\ge1$, let $\Psi_t^{(d)}$ consist of the $\phi\in\Phi_t^{(d)}$ for which $\pi_t(\|\phi\|^2)<\infty$ and $x\mapsto E_t(\phi-\pi_t(\phi))(x)\in\Psi_{t-1}^{(d)}$. Here $E_t h=k_t(\upsilon_t h)$ is the operator defined below. Only target second moments are required: fixed-tail truncation supplies the conditional selection Lindeberg condition without a target higher-moment assumption. The recursive target moments supply the offspring variance at every earlier selection used in the induction. The source $\Phi_t$ conditions alone need not imply them. The source condition $1\in\Phi_t$ and these recursive target moments are the stated hypotheses for the CLT induction; no higher initial normalizer moment is required.

Define the mutation covariance operators recursively. At time zero,
$$\widetilde V_0(\phi)=\operatorname{Cov}_{\widetilde\pi_0}(\phi).$$
For $t\ge1$,
$$\widetilde V_t(\phi)=\widehat V_{t-1}(k_t\phi)+\int\operatorname{Cov}_{k_t}(\phi)(x)\,\pi_{t-1}(dx).$$
The weighted-estimator covariance is
$$V_t(\phi)=\widetilde V_t\!\left(\upsilon_t(\phi-\pi_t(\phi))\right).$$
For a measurable vector function $h$ on $\Theta_t$, define the forward operator from $\Theta_{t-1}$ by
$$E_t h(x)=k_t(\upsilon_t h)(x)=\int\upsilon_t(z)h(z)\,k_t(x,dz).$$
For $k<t$, write $E_{k+1:t}=E_{k+1}\circ\cdots\circ E_t$; set $E_{t+1:t}$ to the identity operator.
For multinomial offspring resampling set
$$\widehat V_t^{\mathrm{multi}}(\phi)=V_t(\phi)+\operatorname{Cov}_{\pi_t}(\phi).$$
For residual offspring resampling, let $r(u)=u-\lfloor u\rfloor$. When $c_t=\widetilde\pi_t(r(\upsilon_t))>0$, define the formal source candidate
$$R_t^{\mathrm{cand}}(\phi)=\widetilde\pi_t\!\left(r(\upsilon_t)\phi\phi^\top\right)-\frac{\widetilde\pi_t(r(\upsilon_t)\phi)\,\widetilde\pi_t(r(\upsilon_t)\phi)^\top}{c_t}.$$
Set $R_t=R_t^{\mathrm{cand}}$ and $\widehat V_t^{\mathrm{res}}=V_t+R_t$ only when $\widetilde\pi_t(\upsilon_t\in\{1,2,\ldots\})=0$; then $c_t>0$ and the finite-sample floor discontinuities are avoided. If $\upsilon_t=1$ $\widetilde\pi_t$-almost everywhere, put $R_t=0$. Residual offspring are deterministic whenever all sampled weights equal one. In SIR this holds almost surely outside earlier zero-weight fallback events, whose probability tends to zero at a fixed horizon; the almost-everywhere condition alone does not prescribe weights on proposal-null states reached after a fallback. No residual covariance is assigned when $c_t=0$ but $\upsilon_t$ is not almost everywhere one: the finite-sample normalization can move positive integer weights across floor boundaries. The B-page counterexamples show why the general positive-integer-atom branch remains unassigned.

For $k=t$ this is $\|\bar\phi\|_\infty\le\Delta\phi$.
