derivations.claim: At time $0$, [F2] and the finite particle law [F7] give IID proposal particles with law $\widetilde\pi_0$. For $h\in L^1(\widetilde\pi_0)$, [F4] gives $\eta_0^N(h)\to\widetilde\pi_0(h)$. If $\phi\in L^1(\pi_0)$, then $\upsilon_0\phi$ is integrable under $\widetilde\pi_0$ and its integral is $\pi_0(\phi)$ by [F1]; also $\widetilde\pi_0(\upsilon_0)=1$. Applying [F4] to numerator and denominator and dividing on the event that the denominator is positive gives $\omega_0^N(\phi)\to\pi_0(\phi)$. That event has probability tending to one because the denominator average converges to $1$.

Fix $t\ge1$ and suppose the three convergences hold at $t-1$. First let $h$ be bounded. By [F2] and [F7], conditional on the selected parents, the $X_t^i$ are independent with laws $k_t(\check X_{t-1}^i,\cdot)$; measurability of $k_th$ follows from [F8]. Thus $\eta_t^N(h)-\check\eta_{t-1}^N(k_th)$ has conditional mean zero and conditional variance at most $\|h\|_\infty^2/N$. By [F5] this difference tends to zero in probability. Since $k_th$ is bounded and $\pi_{t-1}(k_th)=\widetilde\pi_t(h)$ by [F1], the induction hypothesis proves $\eta_t^N(h)\to\widetilde\pi_t(h)$.

The selected-law base at time zero follows as well. For bounded $\phi$, [F3] makes the conditional selected mean equal to $\omega_0^N(\phi)$. Under multinomial selection its conditional variance is at most $\|\phi\|_\infty^2/N$; under residual selection the deterministic floor counts have no variance and the at most $N$ remaining categorical draws give the same bound. By [F5] and step 1.1, $\check\eta_0^N(\phi)\to\pi_0(\phi)$ in probability. For integrable $\phi$, truncate at $M$. The conditional expected selected average of $|\phi|\mathbf1_{\{|\phi|>M\}}$ is its weighted empirical average by [F3], which converges to the target tail integral by step 1.1. Conditional Markov [F6], using $P(\text{tail average}>\epsilon)\le E[\min(1,\omega_0^N(\text{tail})/\epsilon)]$ and bounded continuity of $x\mapsto\min(1,x/\epsilon)$, makes the limiting tail probability vanish as $M\to\infty$. Combining with the bounded truncations proves the selected convergence for all $\pi_0$-integrable tests.

For general $h\in L^1(\widetilde\pi_t)$, let $h_M=h\mathbf1_{\{|h|\le M\}}$. The conditional mean of $\eta_t^N(|h-h_M|)$ is $Y_N=\check\eta_{t-1}^N(k_t|h-h_M|)$, measurable by [F8]. The function inside this last empirical average is integrable under $\pi_{t-1}$ and its integral is $a_M=\widetilde\pi_t(|h-h_M|)$. The induction hypothesis gives $Y_N\to a_M$ in probability. Conditional Markov [F6] bounds $P(\eta_t^N(|h-h_M|)>\epsilon)$ by $E[\min(1,Y_N/\epsilon)]$. For fixed $M$, bounded continuity of $y\mapsto\min(1,y/\epsilon)$ and convergence in probability to the constant $a_M$ imply that this expectation tends to $\min(1,a_M/\epsilon)$: for any $\eta>0$, split on $|Y_N-a_M|\le\eta$ and its complement, use continuity on the first event and convergence in probability on the second. Since $a_M\to0$ by integrability, the limiting tail probability vanishes. Applying the same truncation to the target integral and combining with step 1.2 proves the proposal empirical convergence for every integrable $h$.

Apply step 2.2 to $h=\upsilon_t$ and $h=\upsilon_t\phi$, where $\phi\in L^1(\pi_t)$. Their limiting integrals are $1$ and $\pi_t(\phi)$ by [F1]. The ratio consequently converges to $\pi_t(\phi)$ whenever its denominator is positive; the denominator-zero event has probability tending to zero because its normalized sum converges to $1$. The uniform fallback in [F2] on that event cannot change convergence in probability.

For bounded $\phi$, the conditional expectation of $\check\eta_t^N(\phi)$ is $\omega_t^N(\phi)$ by [F3]. In multinomial resampling the conditional variance is at most $\|\phi\|_\infty^2/N$. In residual resampling the deterministic floor counts contribute no variance, and the remaining $R\le N$ categorical draws give conditional variance at most $\|\phi\|_\infty^2/N$ as well. Chebyshev [F5] and step 3.1 prove $\check\eta_t^N(\phi)\to\pi_t(\phi)$ for bounded $\phi$.

For $\phi\in L^1(\pi_t)$, truncate to $\phi_M=\phi\mathbf1_{\{|\phi|\le M\}}$. By [F3], the conditional expected selected average of $|\phi-\phi_M|$ is exactly $\omega_t^N(|\phi-\phi_M|)$. Step 3.1 applied to this integrable tail and conditional Markov [F6] make the limiting probability of a tail deviation at most $\min(1,\pi_t(|\phi-\phi_M|)/\epsilon)$, which tends to zero as $M\to\infty$. Combining with step 4.1 proves the selected empirical convergence for all integrable $\phi$.

Steps 1.2, 2.2, 3.1, 4.1, and 5.1 establish the induction step from $t-1$ to $t$. Steps 1.1 and 2.1 give the base case, so the assertions hold for every fixed finite time. No conclusion is uniform in $t$.

$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by

derivations.claim: For every integrable $h$ on $\Theta_s$, the Radon–Nikodym identity [F1] gives $\pi_{s-1}(E_sh)=\pi_{s-1}(k_s(\upsilon_sh))=\widetilde\pi_s(\upsilon_sh)=\pi_s(h)$. Hence if $\pi_s(h)=0$, then $E_sh$ has mean zero under $\pi_{s-1}$.

For a square-integrable vector function $u$ on $\Theta_s$, expand $u-\widetilde\pi_s(u)=\bigl(u-k_su\bigr)+\bigl(k_su-\widetilde\pi_s(u)\bigr).$ The cross-covariance terms vanish after integrating the first factor conditionally against $k_s$, because $k_s(u-k_su)=0$. Therefore $\operatorname{Cov}_{\widetilde\pi_s}(u)=\int\operatorname{Cov}_{k_s}(u)(x)\,\pi_{s-1}(dx)+\operatorname{Cov}_{\pi_{s-1}}(k_su).$ For $u=\upsilon_s h$ with $\pi_s(h)=0$, its $\widetilde\pi_s$ mean is zero by step 1.1. Substituting the multinomial recursion from [F1] thus yields $V_s(h)=V_{s-1}(E_sh)+\widetilde\pi_s\!\left[\upsilon_s^2hh^\top\right].$

Starting with $h=\bar\phi$ at time $t$, apply step 1.1 to see that each backward iterate $E_{k+1:t}\bar\phi$ has $\pi_k$-mean zero. The recursive $\Psi$ condition also gives its finite target second moment at each such time. Repeated substitution of the one-step identity in step 2.1 gives one new term $\widetilde\pi_k[\upsilon_k^2(E_{k+1:t}\bar\phi)(E_{k+1:t}\bar\phi)^\top]$ at each $k=t,t-1,\ldots,1$, and the remaining initial term is $V_0(E_{1:t}\bar\phi)=\operatorname{Cov}_{\widetilde\pi_0}(\upsilon_0E_{1:t}\bar\phi)$. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $K:S\rightsquigarrow E$ be a probability kernel on a nonempty measurable source space. Suppose a sigma-finite measure $\lambda$ on $E$ and probability densities $k_x$ satisfy $K(x,A)=\int_A k_x\,d\lambda$ for every $x\in S$ and measurable $A\subseteq E$. If $C\ge1$ and, for every $x,x'\in S$, $k_x(z)\le Ck_{x'}(z)$ for $\lambda$-almost every $z$, then the Dobrushin coefficient from [[def-dobrushin-coefficient-for-probability-kernels]] obeys
$$\delta(K)\le1-C^{-1}.$$

Let $(S,\Sigma)$ and $(E,\mathcal E)$ be measurable spaces with $S\ne\varnothing$, and let $K:S\rightsquigarrow E$ be a probability kernel as in [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. Its **Dobrushin contraction coefficient** is
$$\delta(K):=\sup_{x,x'\in S}\lVert K(x,\cdot)-K(x',\cdot)\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}},$$
where $\lVert\cdot\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}$ is the event-supremum distance between probability laws in [[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]]. Thus $0\le\delta(K)\le1$. The coefficient measures the largest total-variation separation between two one-step output laws.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

1. If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]=\int_0^\infty \mathbb P(X>t)\,dt,$$
   where the right-hand side may be $+\infty$.
2. If $X$ is an integrable real random variable, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]=\int_0^\infty \mathbb P(X>t)\,dt-\int_0^\infty \mathbb P(X<-t)\,dt.$$

derivations.claim: Fix $k<t$. Define $Q_{j,t}h(x)$ by iterating the kernels $g_{j+1},\ldots,g_t$, multiplying by $f_{j+1},\ldots,f_t$, and evaluating $h$ at the final state. Put $H_{j,t}=Q_{j,t}1$ and $H_{t,t}=1$. Measurability follows from [F1], while probability normalization and the bounds on $f_s$ give $a^{t-j}\le H_{j,t}\le b^{t-j}$. Comparing the first transition row gives $H_{j,t}(x)\le C H_{j,t}(x')$ for $j<t$. Consequently $r_{k,t}:=H_{k,t}/\eta_k(H_{k,t})$ is positive, at most $C$, and has $\eta_k$-mean one.

For $j=k+1,\ldots,t$, set $L_{j,t}(x,dz)=g_j(z\mid x)f_j(z)H_{j,t}(z)\lambda(dz)/H_{j-1,t}(x)$. The recursion for $H$ shows that these are probability kernels, with strictly positive finite denominators. The ratio of two of their density rows is $[g_j(z\mid x)/g_j(z\mid x')][H_{j-1,t}(x')/H_{j-1,t}(x)]\le C^2$ by step 1.1. Thus [F3] gives $\delta(L_{j,t})\le1-C^{-2}=\rho$. Telescoping the $H$ factors in the product kernel $P_{k,t}=L_{k+1,t}\cdots L_{t,t}$ gives $P_{k,t}h=Q_{k,t}h/H_{k,t}$.

For any probability kernel $K$ and bounded real $h$ of positive oscillation, put $u=(h-\inf h)/\operatorname{osc}(h)$. Then $0\le u\le1$, and [F5] under each output law gives $K u(x)-K u(x')=\int_0^1[K(x,\{u>r\})-K(x',\{u>r\})]dr$. By [F4], its absolute value is at most $\delta(K)$. If the oscillation is zero, $K$ preserves the constant and the same oscillation bound is immediate. Hence $\operatorname{osc}(Kh)\le\delta(K)\operatorname{osc}(h)$. Iterating this inequality along the kernels in step 2.1 gives $\operatorname{osc}(P_{k,t}h)\le\rho^{t-k}\operatorname{osc}(h)$.

The filtering recursion and iterated integration [F2] yield $\eta_t h=\eta_k(Q_{k,t}h)/\eta_k(H_{k,t})$ and $\prod_{j=k+1}^tc_j=\eta_k(H_{k,t})$. Thus $E_{k+1:t}h=r_{k,t}P_{k,t}h$. Take $h=\psi-\eta_t\psi$. Then $\eta_k(r_{k,t}P_{k,t}h)=0$, and $r_{k,t}\eta_k$ is a probability by step 1.1. Therefore the global infimum of $P_{k,t}h$ is at most zero and its supremum is at least zero, so its sup norm is at most its oscillation. Step 3.1 bounds this by $\rho^{t-k}\operatorname{osc}(\psi)$; multiplying by $r_{k,t}\le C$ proves the claim. For $k=t$, the mean $\eta_t\psi$ lies between $\inf\psi$ and $\sup\psi$, giving the identity-case bound.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Fix a finite horizon $T$. At each $0\le t\le T$, let $\pi_t$ be a probability law on a measurable particle space $\Theta_t$. Let $\widetilde\pi_0$ be an initial proposal with $\pi_0\ll\widetilde\pi_0$, and fix $\upsilon_0=d\pi_0/d\widetilde\pi_0$. For $1\le t\le T$, let $k_t$ be a probability kernel from $\Theta_{t-1}$ to $\Theta_t$, and put
$$\widetilde\pi_t(A)=\int_{\Theta_{t-1}}k_t(x,A)\,\pi_{t-1}(dx).$$
Assume $\pi_t\ll\widetilde\pi_t$ and fix a nonnegative Radon–Nikodym version $\upsilon_t=d\pi_t/d\widetilde\pi_t$, so $\widetilde\pi_t(\upsilon_t)=1$. The BCS-41 sequential importance-resampling algorithm [[alg-sequential-importance-resampling]] is this scheme on path spaces when $k_t$ appends a proposal transition. Under the support and measurable versions of [[thm-feynman-kac-path-radon-nikodym-weight]], its normalized incremental weight is $\upsilon_t=(Z_{t-1}/Z_t)G_t r_t$ for $t\ge1$, and $\upsilon_0=G_0\rho_0/Z_0$ initially. The previous normalized target is already part of $\widetilde\pi_t$; one does not multiply by the full earlier path-weight product again.

For a measurable vector function $\phi:\Theta_t\to\mathbb R^d$, write $\mu(\phi)=\int\phi\,d\mu$ and
$$\operatorname{Cov}_{\mu}(\phi)=\int(\phi-\mu(\phi))(\phi-\mu(\phi))^\top\,d\mu,$$
when the second moment is finite. Also write $k_t\phi(x)=\int\phi(z)k_t(x,dz)$ and
$$\operatorname{Cov}_{k_t}(\phi)(x)=\int(\phi(z)-k_t\phi(x))(\phi(z)-k_t\phi(x))^\top k_t(x,dz).$$

The source recursive test classes are
$$\Phi_0^{(d)}=\{\phi:\widetilde\pi_0(\|\phi\|^2)<\infty\},$$
and, for $t\ge1$,
$$\Phi_t^{(d)}=\left\{\phi:\text{ for some }\delta>0,\ \widetilde\pi_t(\|\upsilon_t\phi\|^{2+\delta})<\infty\ \text{ and }\ x\mapsto k_t(\upsilon_t\phi)(x)\in\Phi_{t-1}^{(d)}\right\}.$$
Assume $1\in\Phi_t^{(1)}$ for every $t$. This is the source theorem's explicit normalizing-weight condition. For the recursive post-resampling CLTs proved on this page, use the stronger classes $\Psi_t^{(d)}$. At $t=0$, let $\Psi_0^{(d)}$ consist of the $\phi\in\Phi_0^{(d)}$ for which $\widetilde\pi_0(\|\upsilon_0(\phi-\pi_0(\phi))\|^2)<\infty$ and $\pi_0(\|\phi\|^2)<\infty$. The initial normalizing denominator needs only its finite first moment $\widetilde\pi_0(\upsilon_0)=1$. For $t\ge1$, let $\Psi_t^{(d)}$ consist of the $\phi\in\Phi_t^{(d)}$ for which $\pi_t(\|\phi\|^2)<\infty$ and $x\mapsto E_t(\phi-\pi_t(\phi))(x)\in\Psi_{t-1}^{(d)}$. Here $E_t h=k_t(\upsilon_t h)$ is the operator defined below. Only target second moments are required: fixed-tail truncation supplies the conditional selection Lindeberg condition without a target higher-moment assumption. The recursive target moments supply the offspring variance at every earlier selection used in the induction. The source $\Phi_t$ conditions alone need not imply them. The source condition $1\in\Phi_t$ and these recursive target moments are the stated hypotheses for the CLT induction; no higher initial normalizer moment is required.

Define the mutation covariance operators recursively. At time zero,
$$\widetilde V_0(\phi)=\operatorname{Cov}_{\widetilde\pi_0}(\phi).$$
For $t\ge1$,
$$\widetilde V_t(\phi)=\widehat V_{t-1}(k_t\phi)+\int\operatorname{Cov}_{k_t}(\phi)(x)\,\pi_{t-1}(dx).$$
The weighted-estimator covariance is
$$V_t(\phi)=\widetilde V_t\!\left(\upsilon_t(\phi-\pi_t(\phi))\right).$$
For a measurable vector function $h$ on $\Theta_t$, define the forward operator from $\Theta_{t-1}$ by
$$E_t h(x)=k_t(\upsilon_t h)(x)=\int\upsilon_t(z)h(z)\,k_t(x,dz).$$
For $k<t$, write $E_{k+1:t}=E_{k+1}\circ\cdots\circ E_t$; set $E_{t+1:t}$ to the identity operator.
For multinomial offspring resampling set
$$\widehat V_t^{\mathrm{multi}}(\phi)=V_t(\phi)+\operatorname{Cov}_{\pi_t}(\phi).$$
For residual offspring resampling, let $r(u)=u-\lfloor u\rfloor$. When $c_t=\widetilde\pi_t(r(\upsilon_t))>0$, define the formal source candidate
$$R_t^{\mathrm{cand}}(\phi)=\widetilde\pi_t\!\left(r(\upsilon_t)\phi\phi^\top\right)-\frac{\widetilde\pi_t(r(\upsilon_t)\phi)\,\widetilde\pi_t(r(\upsilon_t)\phi)^\top}{c_t}.$$
Set $R_t=R_t^{\mathrm{cand}}$ and $\widehat V_t^{\mathrm{res}}=V_t+R_t$ only when $\widetilde\pi_t(\upsilon_t\in\{1,2,\ldots\})=0$; then $c_t>0$ and the finite-sample floor discontinuities are avoided. If $\upsilon_t=1$ $\widetilde\pi_t$-almost everywhere, put $R_t=0$. Residual offspring are deterministic whenever all sampled weights equal one. In SIR this holds almost surely outside earlier zero-weight fallback events, whose probability tends to zero at a fixed horizon; the almost-everywhere condition alone does not prescribe weights on proposal-null states reached after a fallback. No residual covariance is assigned when $c_t=0$ but $\upsilon_t$ is not almost everywhere one: the finite-sample normalization can move positive integer weights across floor boundaries. The B-page counterexamples show why the general positive-integer-atom branch remains unassigned.

Input a particle count $N\ge1$, nonnegative finite weights $a_1,\ldots,a_N$, and a scheme label, either multinomial or residual. Let $A=\sum_{j=1}^Na_j$. If $A>0$, set $p_j=a_j/A$; if $A=0$, set $p_j=1/N$ for every $j$. Thus $p$ is always a probability vector.

- **Multinomial scheme.** Draw an index vector $(J_1,\ldots,J_N)\in\{1,\ldots,N\}^N$ with conditional mass $\mathbb P(J_1=j_1,\ldots,J_N=j_N\mid a)=\prod_{\ell=1}^Np_{j_\ell}$. Put $C_j=\#\{\ell:J_\ell=j\}$.
- **Residual scheme.** Put $q_j=\lfloor Np_j\rfloor$, $r_j=Np_j-q_j$, and $R=\sum_{j=1}^Nr_j=N-\sum_{j=1}^Nq_j$, an integer in $\{0,\ldots,N-1\}$. If $R=0$, put $C_j=q_j$. If $R>0$, draw $(K_1,\ldots,K_R)$ with conditional mass $\mathbb P(K_1=k_1,\ldots,K_R=k_R\mid a)=\prod_{\ell=1}^R(r_{k_\ell}/R)$ and put $C_j=q_j+\#\{\ell:K_\ell=j\}$.

For multinomial resampling, return the sampled vector $(J_1,\ldots,J_N)$ in its sampled order, together with its count vector $(C_1,\ldots,C_N)$; do not sort the sampled indices. For residual resampling, return the ancestor list containing exactly $C_j$ copies of index $j$, ordered by increasing index, together with its count vector. Each output is a length-$N$ list and a count vector summing to $N$. When all input weights vanish, the uniform fallback defines the procedure; any downstream normalizer already multiplied by this zero average remains zero.

Use the finite-horizon target, proposal and mutation sequence of [[def-smc-clt-function-classes-and-variance-recursions]], and run the SIR procedure of [[alg-sequential-importance-resampling]] with either multinomial or residual resampling at every selection. Let $X_t^{1:N}$ be the proposal particles after mutation and before correction, let $\eta_t^N=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N\delta_{X_t^i}$, and let
$$\omega_t^N=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^N\upsilon_t(X_t^i)\delta_{X_t^i}}{\sum_{i=1}^N\upsilon_t(X_t^i)}$$
when the denominator is positive, using the algorithm's uniform fallback otherwise. Let $\check\eta_t^N$ be the empirical probability measure of one offspring selection from $\omega_t^N$; for nonterminal times this is the population carried into the next mutation. For each fixed $t\le T$,
$$\eta_t^N(h)\xrightarrow{P}\widetilde\pi_t(h)\quad(h\in L^1(\widetilde\pi_t)),\qquad \omega_t^N(\phi)\xrightarrow{P}\pi_t(\phi),\qquad \check\eta_t^N(\phi)\xrightarrow{P}\pi_t(\phi)\quad(\phi\in L^1(\pi_t))$$
as $N\to\infty$. The terminal selection in $\check\eta_t^N$ is an auxiliary resampling output; it is not an extra finite-particle accuracy claim.
Assume AC. If a centered row-wise independent triangular array has finite second moments, $s_n>0$ and the Lindeberg condition, then $$s_n^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^{k_n}X_{n,k}\Rightarrow N(0,1).$$

If $X$ is a square-integrable real random variable and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(|X-\mathbb E[X]|\ge a)\le\frac{\operatorname{Var}(X)}{a^2}.$$

Let $(X_n)$ and $(Y_n)$ be real random variables on one probability space, and let $X$ be a real random variable (possibly on another space). If $X_n\Rightarrow X$ and $Y_n\to c$ in probability for $c\in\mathbb R$, then $X_n+Y_n\Rightarrow X+c$ and $X_nY_n\Rightarrow cX$. If $c\ne0$, define $Q_n=X_n/Y_n$ on $\{Y_n\ne0\}$ and give $Q_n$ any fixed value on $\{Y_n=0\}$. Then $Q_n\Rightarrow X/c$.

derivations.claim: Let $\mathcal F_N$ contain the corrected particles and their weights. By [F2], conditionally on $\mathcal F_N$ the selected values $Y_1^N,\ldots,Y_N^N$ are IID with law $\omega_t^N$. Their centered conditional variance is $s_N^2=\omega_t^N(\phi^2)-\omega_t^N(\phi)^2$, which converges in probability to $s^2=\operatorname{Var}_{\pi_t}(\phi)$ by [F1] and [F3].

Put $m_N=\omega_t^N(\phi)$ and $\xi_i^N=\phi(Y_i^N)-m_N$. By [F3], $m_N\to\pi_t\phi$ in probability, hence $m_N=O_P(1)$. For a fixed threshold $a>0$, choose fixed $K$ and then $R\ge K$. On $\{|m_N|\le K\}$ and for all sufficiently large $N$ with $a\sqrt N>R+K$, the event $|\phi(Y_i^N)-m_N|>a\sqrt N$ implies $|\phi(Y_i^N)|>R$, and $|\phi(Y_i^N)-m_N|^2\le4\phi(Y_i^N)^2$ there. Thus the conditional Lindeberg sum is at most $4\omega_t^N(\phi^2\mathbf1_{\{|\phi|>R\}})$ on that event. For fixed $R$, [F3] makes this upper bound converge to $4\pi_t(\phi^2\mathbf1_{\{|\phi|>R\}})$, which tends to zero as $R\to\infty$ by the finite target second moment. Given any error probability, first choose $K$ so that the probability of $|m_N|>K$ is small, then choose $R\ge K$ with this tail integral small, and finally let $N\to\infty$. This proves that the conditional Lindeberg sum tends to zero in probability using only target $L^2$.

Along any subsequence, choose a further subsequence on which $s_N\to s$ almost surely. If $s>0$, then eventually $s_N>s/2$; the normalized Lindeberg sum for draws divided by $s_N\sqrt N$ is bounded by step 2.1 at threshold $as/2$, divided by $s_N^2$. It therefore tends to zero in probability, and a further subsequence makes that convergence almost sure. Apply [F4] to obtain a standard-normal limit for the normalized row. Slutsky [F6] with $s_N\to s$ gives convergence of the conditional characteristic function of $N^{-1/2}\sum_i\xi_i^N$ to $e^{-u^2s^2/2}$. If $s=0$, conditional [F5] gives $P(|N^{-1/2}\sum_i\xi_i^N|>a\mid\mathcal F_N)\le\min(1,s_N^2/a^2)\to0$, giving the degenerate characteristic-function limit. The subsequence criterion therefore gives convergence in probability of these conditional characteristic functions along the full sequence.

The conditional characteristic functions are bounded by one, so their differences from $e^{-u^2s^2/2}$ converge to zero in $L^1$. For arbitrary real $v,u$, multiply the conditional resampling characteristic function at $u$ by the bounded factor $e^{iv\sqrt N(\omega_t^N(\phi)-\pi_t(\phi))}$ and take expectations. The resulting joint characteristic function tends to $e^{-v^2V/2}e^{-u^2s^2/2}$. Thus the resampling fluctuation is asymptotically independent of the weighted fluctuation, and their sum has variance $V+s^2$.

Statement: Step 3.1 explicitly treats target variance s²=0 with conditional Chebyshev, giving a degenerate resampling limit rather than dividing by zero.
Statement: N=1 gives one multinomial draw, but the asserted Gaussian behavior is a sequence limit as N→infinity, not a one-draw approximation.
Step 3.1 handles zero target variance by conditional Chebyshev; step 4.1 uses distinct arbitrary Fourier coefficients for full joint asymptotic independence.
Statement: The lemma fixes any time t, including t=0; step 1.1 conditions on corrected particles at that time and does not need an earlier mutation.
Statement: A1 records AC from finite particle laws and the limit supplier. Step 3.1 selects subsequences to apply the subsequence criterion under that assumed foundation.

For zero variance conditional Chebyshev supplies the degenerate limit. Subsequence selection (diagonal over rational thresholds) and bounded conditional characteristic functions give L1 convergence and joint independence from the weighted fluctuation; no extra target moment is used.

In SIR this holds almost surely outside earlier zero-weight fallback events, whose probability tends to zero at a fixed horizon; the almost-everywhere condition alone does not prescribe weights on proposal-null states reached after a fallback. No residual covariance is assigned when $c_t=0$ but $\upsilon_t$ is not almost everywhere one: the finite-sample normalization can move positive integer weights across floor boundaries. The B-page counterexamples show why the general positive-integer-atom branch remains unassigned.

Use the finite-horizon target and proposal setting of [[def-feynman-kac-path-targets-and-normalizers]]. For admissible inputs require $\mu_0\ll\nu_0$ and, for each $k\ge1$, $M_k(x,\cdot)\ll R_k(x,\cdot)$ for almost every $x$ under the last-coordinate marginal of the proposal path law $Q_{k-1}$. Select the joint measurable versions $\rho_0=d\mu_0/d\nu_0$ and $r_k(x,\cdot)=dM_k(x,\cdot)/dR_k(x,\cdot)$ supplied by [[thm-feynman-kac-path-radon-nikodym-weight]]. Fix $N\ge1$ and select either multinomial or residual resampling at each time. The algorithm returns a weighted empirical path measure and a normalizer estimate.

1. Draw $X_0^1,\ldots,X_0^N$ independently from $\nu_0$. Set $a_0^i=G_0(X_0^i)\rho_0(X_0^i)$ and $\widehat Z_0=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^Na_0^i$. If $\sum_i a_0^i>0$, put $\bar w_0^i=a_0^i/\sum_j a_0^j$; otherwise put $\bar w_0^i=1/N$. Each initial path is $X_{0:0}^i=X_0^i$.
2. For $k=1,\ldots,t$, do the following:
   1. Apply [[alg-multinomial-and-residual-offspring-resampling]] to the previous normalized weights $(\bar w_{k-1}^1,\ldots,\bar w_{k-1}^N)$, obtaining ancestor indices $A_k^1,\ldots,A_k^N$.
   2. Given the previous paths and these indices, draw $(X_k^1,\ldots,X_k^N)$ with joint conditional law $\bigotimes_{i=1}^N R_k(X_{k-1}^{A_k^i},\cdot)$ and set $X_{0:k}^i=(X_{0:k-1}^{A_k^i},X_k^i)$.
   3. Set $a_k^i=G_k(X_k^i)r_k(X_{k-1}^{A_k^i},X_k^i)$ and $\widehat Z_k=\widehat Z_{k-1}(N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^Na_k^i)$. If $\sum_i a_k^i>0$, put $\bar w_k^i=a_k^i/\sum_j a_k^j$; otherwise put $\bar w_k^i=1/N$.
3. Return $\widehat Z_t$ and the weighted empirical path probability measure $\widehat\pi_t^N=\sum_{i=1}^N\bar w_t^i\delta_{X_{0:t}^i}$. Its last-coordinate marginal is the corresponding empirical filtering approximation.

The all-zero fallback only defines a probability measure for reporting and future sampling. Once a zero average weight occurs, $\widehat Z$ remains zero. The procedure makes no finite-particle accuracy, consistency, or long-time stability claim.

Use the finite-horizon target, proposal and mutation sequence of [[def-smc-clt-function-classes-and-variance-recursions]], and run the SIR procedure of [[alg-sequential-importance-resampling]] with either multinomial or residual resampling at every selection. Let $X_t^{1:N}$ be the proposal particles after mutation and before correction, let $\eta_t^N=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N\delta_{X_t^i}$, and let
$$\omega_t^N=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^N\upsilon_t(X_t^i)\delta_{X_t^i}}{\sum_{i=1}^N\upsilon_t(X_t^i)}$$
when the denominator is positive, using the algorithm's uniform fallback otherwise. Let $\check\eta_t^N$ be the empirical probability measure of one offspring selection from $\omega_t^N$; for nonterminal times this is the population carried into the next mutation. For each fixed $t\le T$,
$$\eta_t^N(h)\xrightarrow{P}\widetilde\pi_t(h)\quad(h\in L^1(\widetilde\pi_t)),\qquad \omega_t^N(\phi)\xrightarrow{P}\pi_t(\phi),\qquad \check\eta_t^N(\phi)\xrightarrow{P}\pi_t(\phi)\quad(\phi\in L^1(\pi_t))$$
as $N\to\infty$. The terminal selection in $\check\eta_t^N$ is an auxiliary resampling output; it is not an extra finite-particle accuracy claim.
Assume AC. If a centered row-wise independent triangular array has finite second moments, $s_n>0$ and the Lindeberg condition, then $$s_n^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^{k_n}X_{n,k}\Rightarrow N(0,1).$$

Let $(X_n)$ and $(Y_n)$ be real random variables on one probability space, and let $X$ be a real random variable (possibly on another space). If $X_n\Rightarrow X$ and $Y_n\to c$ in probability for $c\in\mathbb R$, then $X_n+Y_n\Rightarrow X+c$ and $X_nY_n\Rightarrow cX$. If $c\ne0$, define $Q_n=X_n/Y_n$ on $\{Y_n\ne0\}$ and give $Q_n$ any fixed value on $\{Y_n=0\}$. Then $Q_n\Rightarrow X/c$.

If $X$ is a square-integrable real random variable and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(|X-\mathbb E[X]|\ge a)\le\frac{\operatorname{Var}(X)}{a^2}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: At $t=0$, the centered weighted numerator $Z=\upsilon_0(\phi-\pi_0\phi)$ has mean zero and finite second moment under the weighted-only assumptions; the $\Psi_0$ assumptions are sufficient for them. If its variance $\sigma_Z^2$ is positive, its IID row satisfies Lindeberg because $\sigma_Z^{-2}E[Z^2\mathbf1_{\{|Z|>a\sigma_Z\sqrt N\}}]\to0$ by [F7] for each $a>0$. Thus [F4] gives the IID CLT; if its variance is zero, [F6] gives convergence of its centered sample mean to zero. The denominator $\eta_0^N(\upsilon_0)$ converges to one by [F3], since $\widetilde\pi_0(\upsilon_0)=1$. Slutsky [F5] gives the ratio CLT with variance $V_0(\phi)$. For $p\ge1$, $|ax+by|^p\le2^{p-1}(|a|^p|x|^p+|b|^p|y|^p)$; choosing the smaller available positive $\delta$ therefore proves closure of $\Phi_t$ under finite linear combinations, by induction from $\Phi_0$. Kernel integration is linear on these integrable functions. The same inequality gives closure of the target and centered weighted $L^2$ conditions in $\Psi_t$, and its centered images combine linearly; induction proves closure of $\Psi_t$. If $\phi\in\Psi_t$, then $\psi=\upsilon_t(\phi-\pi_t\phi)$ has a finite proposal $2+\delta$ moment because $\phi,1\in\Phi_t$, and $k_t\psi=E_t(\phi-\pi_t\phi)\in\Psi_{t-1}$ by the recursive $\Psi_t$ condition.

For the mutation part, $k_t|\psi|^{2+\delta}$ is $\pi_{t-1}$-integrable, with integral $\widetilde\pi_t(|\psi|^{2+\delta})$. By [F3], $H_N=\check\eta_{t-1}^N(k_t|\psi|^{2+\delta})$ converges in probability to this finite value, so $H_N<\infty$ with probability tending to one. On this event condition on the selected parent paths $\check X_{t-1}^{1:N}$ and set $m_i=k_t\psi(\check X_{t-1}^i)$. Each parent has a finite conditional $2+\delta$ moment; under the product kernel in [F2], $D_{i,N}=\psi(X_t^i)-m_i$ are independent and centered. Their row variance is $s_N^2=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\operatorname{Var}_{k_t(\check X_{t-1}^i)}(\psi),$ which converges in probability to $\sigma^2=\pi_{t-1}(\operatorname{Var}_{k_t}(\psi))$ by [F3], since $\operatorname{Var}_{k_t}(\psi)\le k_t(\psi^2)$ is integrable by Jensen's inequality. The event removed has probability tending to zero and does not affect the distributional limits below. When $\sigma^2>0$, normalize the array by $s_N\sqrt N$, where $s_N^2$ is the displayed variance. For every $a>0$, the resulting conditional Lindeberg sum is at most $C_\delta a^{-\delta}N^{-\delta/2}s_N^{-(2+\delta)}\,H_N,$ where $C_\delta$ is a finite constant from $|a-b|^{2+\delta}\le2^{1+\delta}(|a|^{2+\delta}+|b|^{2+\delta})$ and Jensen's inequality. Since $s_N\to\sigma>0$ and $H_N$ converges in probability to a finite value, this conditional Lindeberg sum tends to zero.

Along any subsequence, choose a further subsequence on which $s_N\to\sigma$ almost surely. If $\sigma>0$, a further subsequence makes the normalized Lindeberg sums converge almost surely; [F4] gives a standard-normal limit for the normalized row, and Slutsky [F5] with $s_N\to\sigma$ gives the conditional characteristic-function limit $e^{-u^2\sigma^2/2}$. If $\sigma=0$, conditional [F6] gives $P\!\left(\left|N^{-1/2}\sum_iD_{i,N}\right|>a\,\middle|\,\check X_{t-1}^{1:N}\right)\le\min(1,s_N^2/a^2)\longrightarrow0$ for every $a>0$, yielding the same characteristic-function limit with variance zero. The subsequence criterion therefore gives convergence in probability of the conditional characteristic functions along the full sequence. They are bounded by one, so their $L^1$ differences from that limit also tend to zero.

The conditional mean part is $P_N=\sqrt N\left(\check\eta_{t-1}^N(k_t\psi)-\pi_{t-1}(k_t\psi)\right),$ and has the previous selected-population CLT by the hypothesis of the Statement. The total proposal error is $P_N+N^{-1/2}\sum_iD_{i,N}$. Multiplying the conditional characteristic function from step 2.1 by the bounded factor $e^{iuP_N}$ and integrating shows that its limit is the product of the previous Gaussian characteristic function and $e^{-u^2\sigma^2/2}$. Hence the two covariance contributions add, giving $\widetilde V_t(\psi)$.

For $\phi\in\Psi_t$, apply the mutation result to $\psi=\upsilon_t(\phi-\pi_t\phi)$ using step 1.1 and the preceding selected CLT for $k_t\psi\in\Psi_{t-1}$. By [F3], $\eta_t^N(\upsilon_t)\to\widetilde\pi_t(\upsilon_t)=1$ in probability, and the event of a zero denominator has probability tending to zero. On its complement, $\sqrt N\left(\omega_t^N(\phi)-\pi_t(\phi)\right)=\frac{\sqrt N\,\eta_t^N(\upsilon_t(\phi-\pi_t\phi))}{\eta_t^N(\upsilon_t)}.$ Slutsky [F5] gives the stated limit with covariance $\widetilde V_t(\upsilon_t(\phi-\pi_t\phi))=V_t(\phi)$. The fallback on a zero empirical weight sum changes the ratio only on an event whose probability tends to zero.

risk_review.notes: Accepted reader repairs: power inequality with minimum available delta proves recursive Phi/Psi linear closure; finite conditional 2+delta parent moments are isolated on H_N<infinity, whose probability tends to one by empirical convergence. Conditional variance is integrable; Lyapunov bound N^{-delta/2} H_N/s_N^{2+delta} gives Lindeberg. Zero variance uses Chebyshev, CF factorization adds parental variance, and ratio uses only denominator L1. Initial centered numerator L2 suffices. citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Fix a finite horizon $T$. At each $0\le t\le T$, let $\pi_t$ be a probability law on a measurable particle space $\Theta_t$. Let $\widetilde\pi_0$ be an initial proposal with $\pi_0\ll\widetilde\pi_0$, and fix $\upsilon_0=d\pi_0/d\widetilde\pi_0$. For $1\le t\le T$, let $k_t$ be a probability kernel from $\Theta_{t-1}$ to $\Theta_t$, and put
$$\widetilde\pi_t(A)=\int_{\Theta_{t-1}}k_t(x,A)\,\pi_{t-1}(dx).$$
Assume $\pi_t\ll\widetilde\pi_t$ and fix a nonnegative Radon–Nikodym version $\upsilon_t=d\pi_t/d\widetilde\pi_t$, so $\widetilde\pi_t(\upsilon_t)=1$. The BCS-41 sequential importance-resampling algorithm [[alg-sequential-importance-resampling]] is this scheme on path spaces when $k_t$ appends a proposal transition. Under the support and measurable versions of [[thm-feynman-kac-path-radon-nikodym-weight]], its normalized incremental weight is $\upsilon_t=(Z_{t-1}/Z_t)G_t r_t$ for $t\ge1$, and $\upsilon_0=G_0\rho_0/Z_0$ initially. The previous normalized target is already part of $\widetilde\pi_t$; one does not multiply by the full earlier path-weight product again.

For a measurable vector function $\phi:\Theta_t\to\mathbb R^d$, write $\mu(\phi)=\int\phi\,d\mu$ and
$$\operatorname{Cov}_{\mu}(\phi)=\int(\phi-\mu(\phi))(\phi-\mu(\phi))^\top\,d\mu,$$
when the second moment is finite. Also write $k_t\phi(x)=\int\phi(z)k_t(x,dz)$ and
$$\operatorname{Cov}_{k_t}(\phi)(x)=\int(\phi(z)-k_t\phi(x))(\phi(z)-k_t\phi(x))^\top k_t(x,dz).$$

The source recursive test classes are
$$\Phi_0^{(d)}=\{\phi:\widetilde\pi_0(\|\phi\|^2)<\infty\},$$
and, for $t\ge1$,
$$\Phi_t^{(d)}=\left\{\phi:\text{ for some }\delta>0,\ \widetilde\pi_t(\|\upsilon_t\phi\|^{2+\delta})<\infty\ \text{ and }\ x\mapsto k_t(\upsilon_t\phi)(x)\in\Phi_{t-1}^{(d)}\right\}.$$
Assume $1\in\Phi_t^{(1)}$ for every $t$. This is the source theorem's explicit normalizing-weight condition. For the recursive post-resampling CLTs proved on this page, use the stronger classes $\Psi_t^{(d)}$. At $t=0$, let $\Psi_0^{(d)}$ consist of the $\phi\in\Phi_0^{(d)}$ for which $\widetilde\pi_0(\|\upsilon_0(\phi-\pi_0(\phi))\|^2)<\infty$ and $\pi_0(\|\phi\|^2)<\infty$. The initial normalizing denominator needs only its finite first moment $\widetilde\pi_0(\upsilon_0)=1$. For $t\ge1$, let $\Psi_t^{(d)}$ consist of the $\phi\in\Phi_t^{(d)}$ for which $\pi_t(\|\phi\|^2)<\infty$ and $x\mapsto E_t(\phi-\pi_t(\phi))(x)\in\Psi_{t-1}^{(d)}$. Here $E_t h=k_t(\upsilon_t h)$ is the operator defined below. Only target second moments are required: fixed-tail truncation supplies the conditional selection Lindeberg condition without a target higher-moment assumption. The recursive target moments supply the offspring variance at every earlier selection used in the induction. The source $\Phi_t$ conditions alone need not imply them. The source condition $1\in\Phi_t$ and these recursive target moments are the stated hypotheses for the CLT induction; no higher initial normalizer moment is required.

Define the mutation covariance operators recursively. At time zero,
$$\widetilde V_0(\phi)=\operatorname{Cov}_{\widetilde\pi_0}(\phi).$$
For $t\ge1$,
$$\widetilde V_t(\phi)=\widehat V_{t-1}(k_t\phi)+\int\operatorname{Cov}_{k_t}(\phi)(x)\,\pi_{t-1}(dx).$$
The weighted-estimator covariance is
$$V_t(\phi)=\widetilde V_t\!\left(\upsilon_t(\phi-\pi_t(\phi))\right).$$
For a measurable vector function $h$ on $\Theta_t$, define the forward operator from $\Theta_{t-1}$ by
$$E_t h(x)=k_t(\upsilon_t h)(x)=\int\upsilon_t(z)h(z)\,k_t(x,dz).$$
For $k<t$, write $E_{k+1:t}=E_{k+1}\circ\cdots\circ E_t$; set $E_{t+1:t}$ to the identity operator.
For multinomial offspring resampling set
$$\widehat V_t^{\mathrm{multi}}(\phi)=V_t(\phi)+\operatorname{Cov}_{\pi_t}(\phi).$$
For residual offspring resampling, let $r(u)=u-\lfloor u\rfloor$. When $c_t=\widetilde\pi_t(r(\upsilon_t))>0$, define the formal source candidate
$$R_t^{\mathrm{cand}}(\phi)=\widetilde\pi_t\!\left(r(\upsilon_t)\phi\phi^\top\right)-\frac{\widetilde\pi_t(r(\upsilon_t)\phi)\,\widetilde\pi_t(r(\upsilon_t)\phi)^\top}{c_t}.$$
Set $R_t=R_t^{\mathrm{cand}}$ and $\widehat V_t^{\mathrm{res}}=V_t+R_t$ only when $\widetilde\pi_t(\upsilon_t\in\{1,2,\ldots\})=0$; then $c_t>0$ and the finite-sample floor discontinuities are avoided. If $\upsilon_t=1$ $\widetilde\pi_t$-almost everywhere, put $R_t=0$. Residual offspring are deterministic whenever all sampled weights equal one. In SIR this holds almost surely outside earlier zero-weight fallback events, whose probability tends to zero at a fixed horizon; the almost-everywhere condition alone does not prescribe weights on proposal-null states reached after a fallback. No residual covariance is assigned when $c_t=0$ but $\upsilon_t$ is not almost everywhere one: the finite-sample normalization can move positive integer weights across floor boundaries. The B-page counterexamples show why the general positive-integer-atom branch remains unassigned.

Input a particle count $N\ge1$, nonnegative finite weights $a_1,\ldots,a_N$, and a scheme label, either multinomial or residual. Let $A=\sum_{j=1}^Na_j$. If $A>0$, set $p_j=a_j/A$; if $A=0$, set $p_j=1/N$ for every $j$. Thus $p$ is always a probability vector.

- **Multinomial scheme.** Draw an index vector $(J_1,\ldots,J_N)\in\{1,\ldots,N\}^N$ with conditional mass $\mathbb P(J_1=j_1,\ldots,J_N=j_N\mid a)=\prod_{\ell=1}^Np_{j_\ell}$. Put $C_j=\#\{\ell:J_\ell=j\}$.
- **Residual scheme.** Put $q_j=\lfloor Np_j\rfloor$, $r_j=Np_j-q_j$, and $R=\sum_{j=1}^Nr_j=N-\sum_{j=1}^Nq_j$, an integer in $\{0,\ldots,N-1\}$. If $R=0$, put $C_j=q_j$. If $R>0$, draw $(K_1,\ldots,K_R)$ with conditional mass $\mathbb P(K_1=k_1,\ldots,K_R=k_R\mid a)=\prod_{\ell=1}^R(r_{k_\ell}/R)$ and put $C_j=q_j+\#\{\ell:K_\ell=j\}$.

For multinomial resampling, return the sampled vector $(J_1,\ldots,J_N)$ in its sampled order, together with its count vector $(C_1,\ldots,C_N)$; do not sort the sampled indices. For residual resampling, return the ancestor list containing exactly $C_j$ copies of index $j$, ordered by increasing index, together with its count vector. Each output is a length-$N$ list and a count vector summing to $N$. When all input weights vanish, the uniform fallback defines the procedure; any downstream normalizer already multiplied by this zero average remains zero.

Use the finite-horizon target, proposal and mutation sequence of [[def-smc-clt-function-classes-and-variance-recursions]], and run the SIR procedure of [[alg-sequential-importance-resampling]] with either multinomial or residual resampling at every selection. Let $X_t^{1:N}$ be the proposal particles after mutation and before correction, let $\eta_t^N=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N\delta_{X_t^i}$, and let
$$\omega_t^N=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^N\upsilon_t(X_t^i)\delta_{X_t^i}}{\sum_{i=1}^N\upsilon_t(X_t^i)}$$
when the denominator is positive, using the algorithm's uniform fallback otherwise. Let $\check\eta_t^N$ be the empirical probability measure of one offspring selection from $\omega_t^N$; for nonterminal times this is the population carried into the next mutation. For each fixed $t\le T$,
$$\eta_t^N(h)\xrightarrow{P}\widetilde\pi_t(h)\quad(h\in L^1(\widetilde\pi_t)),\qquad \omega_t^N(\phi)\xrightarrow{P}\pi_t(\phi),\qquad \check\eta_t^N(\phi)\xrightarrow{P}\pi_t(\phi)\quad(\phi\in L^1(\pi_t))$$
as $N\to\infty$. The terminal selection in $\check\eta_t^N$ is an auxiliary resampling output; it is not an extra finite-particle accuracy claim.
Assume AC. If a centered row-wise independent triangular array has finite second moments, $s_n>0$ and the Lindeberg condition, then $$s_n^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^{k_n}X_{n,k}\Rightarrow N(0,1).$$

If $X$ is a square-integrable real random variable and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(|X-\mathbb E[X]|\ge a)\le\frac{\operatorname{Var}(X)}{a^2}.$$

Let $(X_n)$ and $(Y_n)$ be real random variables on one probability space, and let $X$ be a real random variable (possibly on another space). If $X_n\Rightarrow X$ and $Y_n\to c$ in probability for $c\in\mathbb R$, then $X_n+Y_n\Rightarrow X+c$ and $X_nY_n\Rightarrow cX$. If $c\ne0$, define $Q_n=X_n/Y_n$ on $\{Y_n\ne0\}$ and give $Q_n$ any fixed value on $\{Y_n=0\}$. Then $Q_n\Rightarrow X/c$.

derivations.claim: Put $\bar u_N=\eta_t^N(u)$ and $b_i^N=r(u(X_t^i)/\bar u_N)$ on the event $\bar u_N>0$, whose probability tends to one by [F3]. If $u=1$ almost everywhere, exclude all earlier zero-weight fallback events; their union has probability tending to zero by [F3] and the fixed horizon. On the remaining event every proposal particle avoids proposal-null sets almost surely: initially particles have the proposal law, and inductively positive-weight selection avoids target-null sets, after which mutation avoids $\widetilde\pi_s$-null sets since $\widetilde\pi_s=\pi_{s-1}k_s$. Thus all sampled $u$ values equal one almost surely there, so residual selection is deterministic. The resampling fluctuation is zero outside an event of probability tending to zero, proving the constant-weight branch. In the other case, for the three tests $a=1,\phi,\phi^2$, where $\pi_t(\phi^2)<\infty$, one has $\frac1N\sum_i b_i^Na(X_t^i)\xrightarrow{P}\widetilde\pi_t(r(u)a).$ To verify this triangular empirical limit, fix $M$ and first restrict to $u\le M$ and $|\phi|\le M$. The compact $u$ interval meets only finitely many positive-integer discontinuities of $r$. Delete open $\gamma$-neighborhoods of those integers. On the remaining compact set, $r(u/\bar u_N)\to r(u)$ uniformly as $\bar u_N\to1$, and $|a|\le \max(1,M,M^2)$, so [F3] gives convergence of the restricted averages. Each deleted neighborhood has proposal integral of $|a|$ tending to zero as $\gamma\downarrow0$: it lies where $u\ge1/2$, and $\widetilde\pi_t(u|a|)=\pi_t(|a|)<\infty$; the no-atom condition gives the limit zero. [F3] controls its empirical average for each fixed $\gamma$. For the tails, when $\bar u_N\in[1/2,2]$, $b_i^N\le2u(X_t^i)$; hence the $|\phi|>M$ contribution is bounded by $2\eta_t^N(u|a|\mathbf1_{\{|\phi|>M\}})$, whose limit tends to zero by target integrability. On $u>M$, use $b_i^N\le1$ and $\widetilde\pi_t(|a|\mathbf1_{\{u>M\}})\le M^{-1}\pi_t(|a|)$, with [F3] again controlling the empirical average. The corresponding target tails obey the same bounds because $r(u)\le u$ and $r(u)\le1$. Taking first $N\to\infty$, then $\gamma\downarrow0$ and $M\to\infty$, proves the claim.

Taking $a=1$ in step 1.1 gives $N^{-1}\sum_i b_i^N\to c$. Here $c>0$: if $c=0$, then $u$ is integer-valued almost surely; the no-positive-integer-atom assumption would force $u=0$ almost surely, contradicting $\widetilde\pi_t(u)=1$. Thus the number $M_N=\sum_i b_i^N$ of residual draws diverges and $M_N/N\to c$. Their conditional sampling probabilities are $b_i^N/M_N$.

Let $m_N=M_N^{-1}\sum_i b_i^N\phi(X_t^i)$. Given the particles, the residual offspring contribution to the centered, $\sqrt N$-scaled empirical mean is $N^{-1/2}\sum_{\ell=1}^{M_N}(\phi(Y_\ell^N)-m_N)$, with IID conditional draws $Y_\ell^N$ from probabilities $b_i^N/M_N$. By step 1.1 its conditional variance converges in probability to $c\left\{\frac{\widetilde\pi_t(r(u)\phi^2)}c-\left(\frac{\widetilde\pi_t(r(u)\phi)}c\right)^2\right\}=R_t(\phi).$ The residual draw mean $m_N$ is bounded in probability by the $a=\phi$ limit in step 1.1 and $M_N/N\to c>0$. Fix a threshold $a_0>0$ and fixed $K$, then $R\ge K$. On $\{|m_N|\le K,\ \bar u_N\in[1/2,2]\}$, for sufficiently large $N$ with $a_0\sqrt N>R+K$, the conditional Lindeberg sum for $N^{-1/2}\sum_{\ell=1}^{M_N}(\phi(Y_\ell^N)-m_N)$ is at most $4N^{-1}\sum_i b_i^N\phi(X_t^i)^2\mathbf1_{\{|\phi(X_t^i)|>R\}}$. Since $b_i^N\le2u(X_t^i)$ on this event, it is at most $8\eta_t^N(u\phi^2\mathbf1_{\{|\phi|>R\}})$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Fix a finite horizon $T$. At each $0\le t\le T$, let $\pi_t$ be a probability law on a measurable particle space $\Theta_t$. Let $\widetilde\pi_0$ be an initial proposal with $\pi_0\ll\widetilde\pi_0$, and fix $\upsilon_0=d\pi_0/d\widetilde\pi_0$. For $1\le t\le T$, let $k_t$ be a probability kernel from $\Theta_{t-1}$ to $\Theta_t$, and put
$$\widetilde\pi_t(A)=\int_{\Theta_{t-1}}k_t(x,A)\,\pi_{t-1}(dx).$$
Assume $\pi_t\ll\widetilde\pi_t$ and fix a nonnegative Radon–Nikodym version $\upsilon_t=d\pi_t/d\widetilde\pi_t$, so $\widetilde\pi_t(\upsilon_t)=1$. The BCS-41 sequential importance-resampling algorithm [[alg-sequential-importance-resampling]] is this scheme on path spaces when $k_t$ appends a proposal transition. Under the support and measurable versions of [[thm-feynman-kac-path-radon-nikodym-weight]], its normalized incremental weight is $\upsilon_t=(Z_{t-1}/Z_t)G_t r_t$ for $t\ge1$, and $\upsilon_0=G_0\rho_0/Z_0$ initially. The previous normalized target is already part of $\widetilde\pi_t$; one does not multiply by the full earlier path-weight product again.

For a measurable vector function $\phi:\Theta_t\to\mathbb R^d$, write $\mu(\phi)=\int\phi\,d\mu$ and
$$\operatorname{Cov}_{\mu}(\phi)=\int(\phi-\mu(\phi))(\phi-\mu(\phi))^\top\,d\mu,$$
when the second moment is finite. Also write $k_t\phi(x)=\int\phi(z)k_t(x,dz)$ and
$$\operatorname{Cov}_{k_t}(\phi)(x)=\int(\phi(z)-k_t\phi(x))(\phi(z)-k_t\phi(x))^\top k_t(x,dz).$$

The source recursive test classes are
$$\Phi_0^{(d)}=\{\phi:\widetilde\pi_0(\|\phi\|^2)<\infty\},$$
and, for $t\ge1$,
$$\Phi_t^{(d)}=\left\{\phi:\text{ for some }\delta>0,\ \widetilde\pi_t(\|\upsilon_t\phi\|^{2+\delta})<\infty\ \text{ and }\ x\mapsto k_t(\upsilon_t\phi)(x)\in\Phi_{t-1}^{(d)}\right\}.$$
Assume $1\in\Phi_t^{(1)}$ for every $t$. This is the source theorem's explicit normalizing-weight condition. For the recursive post-resampling CLTs proved on this page, use the stronger classes $\Psi_t^{(d)}$. At $t=0$, let $\Psi_0^{(d)}$ consist of the $\phi\in\Phi_0^{(d)}$ for which $\widetilde\pi_0(\|\upsilon_0(\phi-\pi_0(\phi))\|^2)<\infty$ and $\pi_0(\|\phi\|^2)<\infty$. The initial normalizing denominator needs only its finite first moment $\widetilde\pi_0(\upsilon_0)=1$. For $t\ge1$, let $\Psi_t^{(d)}$ consist of the $\phi\in\Phi_t^{(d)}$ for which $\pi_t(\|\phi\|^2)<\infty$ and $x\mapsto E_t(\phi-\pi_t(\phi))(x)\in\Psi_{t-1}^{(d)}$. Here $E_t h=k_t(\upsilon_t h)$ is the operator defined below. Only target second moments are required: fixed-tail truncation supplies the conditional selection Lindeberg condition without a target higher-moment assumption. The recursive target moments supply the offspring variance at every earlier selection used in the induction. The source $\Phi_t$ conditions alone need not imply them. The source condition $1\in\Phi_t$ and these recursive target moments are the stated hypotheses for the CLT induction; no higher initial normalizer moment is required.

Define the mutation covariance operators recursively. At time zero,
$$\widetilde V_0(\phi)=\operatorname{Cov}_{\widetilde\pi_0}(\phi).$$
For $t\ge1$,
$$\widetilde V_t(\phi)=\widehat V_{t-1}(k_t\phi)+\int\operatorname{Cov}_{k_t}(\phi)(x)\,\pi_{t-1}(dx).$$
The weighted-estimator covariance is
$$V_t(\phi)=\widetilde V_t\!\left(\upsilon_t(\phi-\pi_t(\phi))\right).$$
For a measurable vector function $h$ on $\Theta_t$, define the forward operator from $\Theta_{t-1}$ by
$$E_t h(x)=k_t(\upsilon_t h)(x)=\int\upsilon_t(z)h(z)\,k_t(x,dz).$$
For $k<t$, write $E_{k+1:t}=E_{k+1}\circ\cdots\circ E_t$; set $E_{t+1:t}$ to the identity operator.
For multinomial offspring resampling set
$$\widehat V_t^{\mathrm{multi}}(\phi)=V_t(\phi)+\operatorname{Cov}_{\pi_t}(\phi).$$
For residual offspring resampling, let $r(u)=u-\lfloor u\rfloor$. When $c_t=\widetilde\pi_t(r(\upsilon_t))>0$, define the formal source candidate
$$R_t^{\mathrm{cand}}(\phi)=\widetilde\pi_t\!\left(r(\upsilon_t)\phi\phi^\top\right)-\frac{\widetilde\pi_t(r(\upsilon_t)\phi)\,\widetilde\pi_t(r(\upsilon_t)\phi)^\top}{c_t}.$$
Set $R_t=R_t^{\mathrm{cand}}$ and $\widehat V_t^{\mathrm{res}}=V_t+R_t$ only when $\widetilde\pi_t(\upsilon_t\in\{1,2,\ldots\})=0$; then $c_t>0$ and the finite-sample floor discontinuities are avoided. If $\upsilon_t=1$ $\widetilde\pi_t$-almost everywhere, put $R_t=0$. Residual offspring are deterministic whenever all sampled weights equal one. In SIR this holds almost surely outside earlier zero-weight fallback events, whose probability tends to zero at a fixed horizon; the almost-everywhere condition alone does not prescribe weights on proposal-null states reached after a fallback. No residual covariance is assigned when $c_t=0$ but $\upsilon_t$ is not almost everywhere one: the finite-sample normalization can move positive integer weights across floor boundaries. The B-page counterexamples show why the general positive-integer-atom branch remains unassigned.

Use the operators and multinomial variance recursion of [[def-smc-clt-function-classes-and-variance-recursions]] at every selection time. For $\phi\in\Psi_t^{(d)}$, put $\bar\phi=\phi-\pi_t(\phi)$. Then
$$V_t(\phi)=\sum_{k=0}^{t}\widetilde\pi_k\!\left[\upsilon_k^2\,E_{k+1:t}(\bar\phi)E_{k+1:t}(\bar\phi)^\top\right],$$
where the $k=t$ term uses $E_{t+1:t}\bar\phi=\bar\phi$. Each summand is a finite positive-semidefinite matrix under the stated class conditions.

Let $E_s$ be the forward operators of [[def-smc-clt-function-classes-and-variance-recursions]], and for bounded real $h$ put $\operatorname{osc}(h)=\sup h-\inf h$. Suppose there is one $\beta\in[0,1)$ such that
$$\operatorname{osc}(E_s h)\le\beta\operatorname{osc}(h)$$
for every $s$ and every bounded real $h$ with $\pi_s(h)=0$, with bounded measurable versions of $E_sh$. The stronger condition on every bounded $h$ is sufficient but is not necessary here. For bounded $\phi:\Theta_t\to\mathbb R$, put $\Delta\phi=\operatorname{osc}(\phi)$ and $\bar\phi=\phi-\pi_t(\phi)$. Then for every $0\le k\le t$,
$$\bigl\lVert E_{k+1:t}\bar\phi\bigr\rVert_\infty\le\beta^{t-k}\Delta\phi,$$
with $\beta^0=1$ and $E_{t+1:t}$ the identity. This condition concerns the actual SMC backward operators; it is not implied merely by mixing ratios of the proposal densities.

Let $\mathsf X$ be a nonempty standard-Borel space with a sigma-finite reference measure $\lambda$, and let $\eta_0$ be a probability on it. For $s\ge1$, supply jointly measurable, strictly positive finite densities $g_s(z\mid x)$ of probability transition kernels relative to $\lambda$, and measurable likelihood factors $f_s$ with $0<a\le f_s(z)\le b<\infty$. These specified versions satisfy, for one $C\ge1$ and every $s,x,x',z$,
$$g_s(z\mid x)\le Cg_s(z\mid x').$$
Define $c_s=\eta_{s-1}(g_sf_s)$, $\eta_s(h)=\eta_{s-1}(g_s(f_sh))/c_s$, and $E_sh(x)=g_s(f_sh)(x)/c_s$. They are the operators of [[def-smc-clt-function-classes-and-variance-recursions]] restricted to last-state tests in the corresponding filtering model. Put $\rho=1-C^{-2}$. For every bounded measurable real terminal test $\psi$ and $0\le k<t$,
$$\|E_{k+1:t}(\psi-\eta_t\psi)\|_\infty\le C\rho^{t-k}\operatorname{osc}(\psi).$$
For $k=t$ the identity image is bounded by $\operatorname{osc}(\psi)$; use $\rho^n=0$ for $n\ge1$ when $C=1$. This is a closed last-state-test assertion, not a contraction of arbitrary functions of the full stored path. Positivity, finiteness and the ratio bounds refer to the supplied pointwise density versions, not to unspecified unrelated null-set versions.

derivations.claim: Put $h_t=\phi-\pi_t(\phi)$ and $h_k=E_{k+1:t}h_t$ for $0\le k<t$, with $h_t$ itself at $k=t$. The multistep hypothesis supplies bounded versions of these centered images. By [F1], $\pi_k(h_k)=0$ and $E_kh_k=h_{k-1}$ for $1\le k\le t$. At $k=0$, boundedness and $\upsilon_0\le B$ almost everywhere give $h_0\in\Psi_0$. If $h_{k-1}\in\Psi_{k-1}$, then boundedness of $h_k$ and $\upsilon_k\le B$ almost everywhere give $\widetilde\pi_k(|\upsilon_k h_k|^{2+\delta})<\infty$ and $E_kh_k=h_{k-1}\in\Phi_{k-1}$, so $h_k\in\Phi_k$. Also $\pi_k(h_k^2)<\infty$ and $E_kh_k=h_{k-1}\in\Psi_{k-1}$, hence $h_k\in\Psi_k$. Induction gives $h_t\in\Psi_t$, so [F2] applies to $V_t(h_t)=V_t(\phi)$. Its summands are nonnegative and finite because $\upsilon_k\le B$ almost everywhere and each $h_k$ has a bounded version.

The multistep bound in the Statement makes the $k$th summand at most $B^2A^2\rho^{2(t-k)}(\Delta\phi)^2$. Summing the geometric series gives $V_t(\phi)\le A^2B^2(\Delta\phi)^2/(1-\rho^2)$. Applying [F3] yields the original one-step specialization.

In the filtering branch, the actual increment is $\upsilon_s(x,z)=g_s(z\mid x)f_s(z)/(c_sq_s(z\mid x))$, with $c_s=\eta_{s-1}(g_sf_s)\in[a,b]$. Hence $\upsilon_s\le Db/a$ for $s\ge1$; the initial bound gives $\upsilon_s\le B$ at every time. The last-state subspace is preserved by the filtering operators, and [F4] supplies its centered-image estimate with $A=C$, $\rho=1-C^{-2}$. Step 2.1 proves the displayed filtering bound; when $C=1$, all earlier images vanish and the same formula applies.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Fix a finite horizon $T$. At each $0\le t\le T$, let $\pi_t$ be a probability law on a measurable particle space $\Theta_t$. Let $\widetilde\pi_0$ be an initial proposal with $\pi_0\ll\widetilde\pi_0$, and fix $\upsilon_0=d\pi_0/d\widetilde\pi_0$. For $1\le t\le T$, let $k_t$ be a probability kernel from $\Theta_{t-1}$ to $\Theta_t$, and put
$$\widetilde\pi_t(A)=\int_{\Theta_{t-1}}k_t(x,A)\,\pi_{t-1}(dx).$$
Assume $\pi_t\ll\widetilde\pi_t$ and fix a nonnegative Radon–Nikodym version $\upsilon_t=d\pi_t/d\widetilde\pi_t$, so $\widetilde\pi_t(\upsilon_t)=1$. The BCS-41 sequential importance-resampling algorithm [[alg-sequential-importance-resampling]] is this scheme on path spaces when $k_t$ appends a proposal transition. Under the support and measurable versions of [[thm-feynman-kac-path-radon-nikodym-weight]], its normalized incremental weight is $\upsilon_t=(Z_{t-1}/Z_t)G_t r_t$ for $t\ge1$, and $\upsilon_0=G_0\rho_0/Z_0$ initially. The previous normalized target is already part of $\widetilde\pi_t$; one does not multiply by the full earlier path-weight product again.

For a measurable vector function $\phi:\Theta_t\to\mathbb R^d$, write $\mu(\phi)=\int\phi\,d\mu$ and
$$\operatorname{Cov}_{\mu}(\phi)=\int(\phi-\mu(\phi))(\phi-\mu(\phi))^\top\,d\mu,$$
when the second moment is finite. Also write $k_t\phi(x)=\int\phi(z)k_t(x,dz)$ and
$$\operatorname{Cov}_{k_t}(\phi)(x)=\int(\phi(z)-k_t\phi(x))(\phi(z)-k_t\phi(x))^\top k_t(x,dz).$$

The source recursive test classes are
$$\Phi_0^{(d)}=\{\phi:\widetilde\pi_0(\|\phi\|^2)<\infty\},$$
and, for $t\ge1$,
$$\Phi_t^{(d)}=\left\{\phi:\text{ for some }\delta>0,\ \widetilde\pi_t(\|\upsilon_t\phi\|^{2+\delta})<\infty\ \text{ and }\ x\mapsto k_t(\upsilon_t\phi)(x)\in\Phi_{t-1}^{(d)}\right\}.$$
Assume $1\in\Phi_t^{(1)}$ for every $t$. This is the source theorem's explicit normalizing-weight condition. For the recursive post-resampling CLTs proved on this page, use the stronger classes $\Psi_t^{(d)}$. At $t=0$, let $\Psi_0^{(d)}$ consist of the $\phi\in\Phi_0^{(d)}$ for which $\widetilde\pi_0(\|\upsilon_0(\phi-\pi_0(\phi))\|^2)<\infty$ and $\pi_0(\|\phi\|^2)<\infty$. The initial normalizing denominator needs only its finite first moment $\widetilde\pi_0(\upsilon_0)=1$. For $t\ge1$, let $\Psi_t^{(d)}$ consist of the $\phi\in\Phi_t^{(d)}$ for which $\pi_t(\|\phi\|^2)<\infty$ and $x\mapsto E_t(\phi-\pi_t(\phi))(x)\in\Psi_{t-1}^{(d)}$. Here $E_t h=k_t(\upsilon_t h)$ is the operator defined below. Only target second moments are required: fixed-tail truncation supplies the conditional selection Lindeberg condition without a target higher-moment assumption. The recursive target moments supply the offspring variance at every earlier selection used in the induction. The source $\Phi_t$ conditions alone need not imply them. The source condition $1\in\Phi_t$ and these recursive target moments are the stated hypotheses for the CLT induction; no higher initial normalizer moment is required.

Define the mutation covariance operators recursively. At time zero,
$$\widetilde V_0(\phi)=\operatorname{Cov}_{\widetilde\pi_0}(\phi).$$
For $t\ge1$,
$$\widetilde V_t(\phi)=\widehat V_{t-1}(k_t\phi)+\int\operatorname{Cov}_{k_t}(\phi)(x)\,\pi_{t-1}(dx).$$
The weighted-estimator covariance is
$$V_t(\phi)=\widetilde V_t\!\left(\upsilon_t(\phi-\pi_t(\phi))\right).$$
For a measurable vector function $h$ on $\Theta_t$, define the forward operator from $\Theta_{t-1}$ by
$$E_t h(x)=k_t(\upsilon_t h)(x)=\int\upsilon_t(z)h(z)\,k_t(x,dz).$$
For $k<t$, write $E_{k+1:t}=E_{k+1}\circ\cdots\circ E_t$; set $E_{t+1:t}$ to the identity operator.
For multinomial offspring resampling set
$$\widehat V_t^{\mathrm{multi}}(\phi)=V_t(\phi)+\operatorname{Cov}_{\pi_t}(\phi).$$

$$R_t^{\mathrm{cand}}(\phi)=\widetilde\pi_t\!\left(r(\upsilon_t)\phi\phi^\top\right)-\frac{\widetilde\pi_t(r(\upsilon_t)\phi)\,\widetilde\pi_t(r(\upsilon_t)\phi)^\top}{c_t}.$$

Fix a time $t$ in the finite-horizon SIR system of [[def-smc-clt-function-classes-and-variance-recursions]]. Assume the proposal empirical law converges in probability for every integrable test as in [[lem-smc-finite-horizon-empirical-law]], the weighted estimate has a finite-variance CLT
$$\sqrt N\{\omega_t^N(\phi)-\pi_t(\phi)\}\Rightarrow N(0,V),$$
and $\pi_t(\phi^2)<\infty$. Write $u=\upsilon_t$ and assume either $u=1$ $\widetilde\pi_t$-almost everywhere, or
$$\widetilde\pi_t(u\in\{1,2,\ldots\})=0.$$
In the second case $c=\widetilde\pi_t(r(u))>0$. Then, with
$$R_t(\phi)=\widetilde\pi_t(r(u)\phi^2)-\frac{\widetilde\pi_t(r(u)\phi)^2}{c},$$
where $R_t(\phi)=0$ in the constant-weight case,
$$\sqrt N\{\check\eta_t^N(\phi)-\omega_t^N(\phi)\}\Rightarrow N(0,R_t(\phi)),$$
asymptotically independently of the weighted-estimator fluctuation, and
$$\sqrt N\{\check\eta_t^N(\phi)-\pi_t(\phi)\}\Rightarrow N(0,V+R_t(\phi)).$$

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$ be a finite integer and $p_\theta(x)=\theta\cdot x$ for $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$. Borel probability laws on $\mathbb R^d$ are determined by all the laws $(p_\theta)_*\mu$. Moreover, if $(p_\theta)_*\mu_n\Rightarrow(p_\theta)_*\mu$ for every $\theta$ and a specified Borel probability law $\mu$, then $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$. If dimension zero is admitted, interpret $\mathbb R^0$ as the singleton empty tuple; both conclusions then hold as well.

Use the finite-horizon target, proposal and mutation sequence of [[def-smc-clt-function-classes-and-variance-recursions]], and run the SIR procedure of [[alg-sequential-importance-resampling]] with either multinomial or residual resampling at every selection. Let $X_t^{1:N}$ be the proposal particles after mutation and before correction, let $\eta_t^N=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N\delta_{X_t^i}$, and let
$$\omega_t^N=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^N\upsilon_t(X_t^i)\delta_{X_t^i}}{\sum_{i=1}^N\upsilon_t(X_t^i)}$$
when the denominator is positive, using the algorithm's uniform fallback otherwise. Let $\check\eta_t^N$ be the empirical probability measure of one offspring selection from $\omega_t^N$; for nonterminal times this is the population carried into the next mutation. For each fixed $t\le T$,
$$\eta_t^N(h)\xrightarrow{P}\widetilde\pi_t(h)\quad(h\in L^1(\widetilde\pi_t)),\qquad \omega_t^N(\phi)\xrightarrow{P}\pi_t(\phi),\qquad \check\eta_t^N(\phi)\xrightarrow{P}\pi_t(\phi)\quad(\phi\in L^1(\pi_t))$$
as $N\to\infty$. The terminal selection in $\check\eta_t^N$ is an auxiliary resampling output; it is not an extra finite-particle accuracy claim.

Fix $a\in\mathbb R^d$ and put $h=a^\top\phi$. The bound $|a^\top x|\le\|a\|\,\|x\|$ and linearity of each $E_s$ show from [F1] that $h\in\Psi_t^{(1)}$. We prove by induction on $s\le t$ the scalar assertion for every test in $\Psi_s^{(1)}$; at $s=t$ this includes $h$.

At time zero, let $h\in\Psi_0$. By [F2], the initial weighted ratio has CLT variance $V_0(h)$. The assumed residual-weight branch either has constant weight one, in which case selection is deterministic and $R_0(h)=0$, or has no positive-integer atom; in the latter case the target moment and weighted CLT meet [F3], which gives the selected CLT with its stated $R_0(h)$.

The base step 2.1 and induction steps 1.2, 2.2 prove both scalar limits at time $t$ for every $h\in\Psi_t$. Input a particle count $N\ge1$, nonnegative finite weights $a_1,\ldots,a_N$, and a scheme label, either multinomial or residual. Let $A=\sum_{j=1}^Na_j$. If $A>0$, set $p_j=a_j/A$; if $A=0$, set $p_j=1/N$ for every $j$. Thus $p$ is always a probability vector.

- **Multinomial scheme.** Draw an index vector $(J_1,\ldots,J_N)\in\{1,\ldots,N\}^N$ with conditional mass $\mathbb P(J_1=j_1,\ldots,J_N=j_N\mid a)=\prod_{\ell=1}^Np_{j_\ell}$. Put $C_j=\#\{\ell:J_\ell=j\}$.
- **Residual scheme.** Put $q_j=\lfloor Np_j\rfloor$, $r_j=Np_j-q_j$, and $R=\sum_{j=1}^Nr_j=N-\sum_{j=1}^Nq_j$, an integer in $\{0,\ldots,N-1\}$. If $R=0$, put $C_j=q_j$. If $R>0$, draw $(K_1,\ldots,K_R)$ with conditional mass $\mathbb P(K_1=k_1,\ldots,K_R=k_R\mid a)=\prod_{\ell=1}^R(r_{k_\ell}/R)$ and put $C_j=q_j+\#\{\ell:K_\ell=j\}$.

For multinomial resampling, return the sampled vector $(J_1,\ldots,J_N)$ in its sampled order, together with its count vector $(C_1,\ldots,C_N)$; do not sort the sampled indices. For residual resampling, return the ancestor list containing exactly $C_j$ copies of index $j$, ordered by increasing index, together with its count vector. Each output is a length-$N$ list and a count vector summing to $N$. When all input weights vanish, the uniform fallback defines the procedure; any downstream normalizer already multiplied by this zero average remains zero.

Fix $N\ge1$ and nonnegative input weights $a_1,\ldots,a_N$. Let $p$ be the normalized probability vector, with the uniform fallback when all weights vanish, and let $C_j$ be the offspring count from [[alg-multinomial-and-residual-offspring-resampling]]. Conditional on the input weights, for either scheme and every $1\le j\le N$,
$$\mathbb E[C_j\mid a_1,\ldots,a_N]=Np_j.$$
This assertion concerns the counts only; it gives no variance comparison for arbitrary weights.

derivations.claim: The two child indices are independent fair draws by [F1]. They choose the same parent with probability $(1/2)^2+(1/2)^2=1/2$. The expected number of distinct parents represented is $2\{1-(1-1/2)^2\}=3/2$, since each parent is selected at least once with probability $3/4$.

If both children select one parent, identity mutation leaves two copies of that same original ancestor. Every later resampling copies represented ancestors, so it cannot restore the lost ancestor. If both lineages remain, their survival through the next call requires different parent indices. By the stipulated independence across calls and step 1.1, this has conditional probability $1/2$ given the full preceding index history.

Starting from two lineages, the probability that no collapse occurs in $m$ successive resampling steps is $(1/2)^m$ by induction on $m$ using step 2.1. Hence the probability of a single represented ancestor is $1-2^{-m}\to1$, even though the expected offspring counts at each step remain $(1,1)$ by [F2].

boundaries.evidence: Statement: Two distinct initial ancestors and m≥1 resamplings are required; N=0 is outside the Example.
Statement: All weights are 1/2, so no zero weight occurs. Once one original lineage has zero representatives, identity mutation cannot restore it (step 2.1).
Statement: The Example fixes N=2, so N=1 is outside its witness. At the allowed m=1, step 3.1 gives collapse probability 1-1/2=1/2.
Statement: The absorbing collapsed configuration has two copies of one original ancestor, while both particle weights remain 1/2; step 2.1 shows why resampling cannot create a lost lineage.
Statement: At m=1, step 1.1 gives collapse probability 1/2; as m→infinity, step 3.1 gives 1-2^{-m}→1.

The Example specifies mutually independent uniform index pairs across calls; for each finite m their joint mass is 4^{-m} on the finite index-array space. Step 2.1 conditions on the entire past, and step 3.1 multiplies the resulting survival probabilities. No choice principle is used.

derivations.claim: The geometric proposal masses sum to one. Since $0<s<1/2$, $w_0$ is finite and positive, and $\sum_{n\ge0}p_nw_n=1$ by construction; hence $\pi_1$ is a probability law with density $w$ relative to $p$. The identity kernel gives $\widetilde\pi_1=p$.

For a separate initial-proposal witness, let $\Theta_0=\mathbb N_{\ge1}$, $\widetilde\pi_0\{n\}=2^{-n}$, $c=(\sum_{n\ge1}2^{-n/2})^{-1}$, and $\upsilon_0(n)=c2^{n/2}$. Then $\sum_n\widetilde\pi_0\{n\}\upsilon_0(n)=1$, so $\pi_0$ is a probability law and $\upsilon_0=d\pi_0/d\widetilde\pi_0$. Both $\phi$ and $1$ are bounded, hence belong to $\Phi_0$.

Choose $\delta=1$. For $n\ge1$, $w_n\phi(n)=w_n^{1/4}$, so $\sum p_n|w_n\phi(n)|^3=\sum_{n\ge1}p_nw_n^{3/4}<\infty$ and $\sum p_n|w_n\phi(n)|^2=\sum_{n\ge1}p_nw_n^{1/2}<\infty$. Thus $k_1(w\phi)=w\phi\in\Phi_0$ and $\phi\in\Phi_1$. Also $\sum p_nw_n^3<\infty$ and $k_1w=w\in\Phi_0$, so $1\in\Phi_1$.

Let $q=\pi_0(\phi)$. Positive proposal and target mass occur on both parities, so $0<q<1$. Input a particle count $N\ge1$, nonnegative finite weights $a_1,\ldots,a_N$, and a scheme label, either multinomial or residual. Let $A=\sum_{j=1}^Na_j$. If $A>0$, set $p_j=a_j/A$; if $A=0$, set $p_j=1/N$ for every $j$. Thus $p$ is always a probability vector.

- **Multinomial scheme.** Draw an index vector $(J_1,\ldots,J_N)\in\{1,\ldots,N\}^N$ with conditional mass $\mathbb P(J_1=j_1,\ldots,J_N=j_N\mid a)=\prod_{\ell=1}^Np_{j_\ell}$. Put $C_j=\#\{\ell:J_\ell=j\}$.
- **Residual scheme.** Put $q_j=\lfloor Np_j\rfloor$, $r_j=Np_j-q_j$, and $R=\sum_{j=1}^Nr_j=N-\sum_{j=1}^Nq_j$, an integer in $\{0,\ldots,N-1\}$. If $R=0$, put $C_j=q_j$. If $R>0$, draw $(K_1,\ldots,K_R)$ with conditional mass $\mathbb P(K_1=k_1,\ldots,K_R=k_R\mid a)=\prod_{\ell=1}^R(r_{k_\ell}/R)$ and put $C_j=q_j+\#\{\ell:K_\ell=j\}$.

derivations.claim: For $N$ IID proposal particles, let $M_N$ be the number at $A$ and $p_N=M_N/N$. The weighted empirical estimate is $S_N=\frac{2M_N}{2M_N+(2/3)(N-M_N)}=\frac{3p_N}{1+2p_N}.$ Since $M_N$ is binomial with parameters $(N,1/4)$, [F3] gives $\sqrt N(p_N-1/4)\Rightarrow N(0,3/16)$. The identity $\sqrt N(S_N-1/2)=2\sqrt N(p_N-1/4)/(1+2p_N)$ and [F4] yield $Z_N:=\sqrt N(S_N-1/2)\Rightarrow Z\sim N(0,1/3)$. Moreover, $Z_N>0$ exactly when $p_N>1/4$.

The limiting-weight candidate in [F1] gives $r(2)=0$ and $r(2/3)=2/3$. Because $\phi(B)=0$, both $\widetilde\pi_0(r(\upsilon_0)\phi^2)$ and $\widetilde\pi_0(r(\upsilon_0)\phi)$ are zero, so $R_0^{\mathrm{cand}}(\phi)=0$. If used as a universal residual CLT variance, it predicts a post-resampling Gaussian limit with variance $V_0(\phi)=\widetilde\pi_0[\upsilon_0^2(\phi-1/2)^2]=1/3$.

Put $\bar w_N=2/3+(4/3)p_N$ and $u_A=2/\bar w_N$, $u_B=(2/3)/\bar w_N$. On $1/4<p_N<1/3$, the normalized residual sizes are $u_A\in(1,2)$ and $u_B\in(0,1)$; hence each $A$ particle receives one deterministic child, each $B$ particle receives none, and $R=N-M_N$ children are sampled from the remainders. If $X_N$ is the number of residual children at $A$, then conditionally on the proposal sample, $X_N\sim\mathrm{Bin}(R,a_N)$ with $a_N=M_N(u_A-1)/R$. As $p_N\downarrow1/4$, $R/N\to3/4$ and $a_N\to1/3$.

On that event, the post-resampling mean is $(M_N+X_N)/N$ and its conditional mean is $S_N$. A Taylor expansion of the binomial characteristic function, uniform for $0\le a_N\le1$ and $R\le N$, gives $\mathbb E\!\left[\exp\!\left(iu\frac{X_N-Ra_N}{\sqrt N}\right)\middle|M_N\right]=\exp\!\left(-\frac{u^2}{2}\frac RN a_N(1-a_N)+O(N^{-1/2})\right).$ Thus, on the positive branch $p_N>1/4$, the extra resampling fluctuation has limiting variance $(3/4)(1/3)(2/3)=1/6$.

On the negative branch with $p_N<1/4$ and $p_N\to1/4$, one has $u_A\in(2,3)$ and $u_B\in(0,1)$. The floor for each $A$ particle is two, and its total fractional remainder is $M_N(u_A-2)=O_P(\sqrt N)$, because $u_A-2=2(1/\bar w_N-1)=O_P(|p_N-1/4|)$. Conditional variance of the residual $A$ count is at most this total remainder. Consequently the variance of $\sqrt N$ times the post-resampling proportion about its weighted conditional mean is $O_P(N^{-1/2})$, so the extra resampling fluctuation tends to zero in probability on the negative branch. The events $p_N\notin(1/5,1/3)$ have probability tending to zero by [F3].

Put $U_N=\sqrt N(\check\eta_0^N(\phi)-S_N)$, the post-resampling fluctuation centered at the weighted mean, and condition on the proposal count $M_N$. For any real $v,s$, steps 2.1, 2.2 and the negligible exceptional event show that $\mathbb E[e^{isU_N}\mid M_N]$ converges in probability to $e^{-s^2/12}$ when $Z_N>0$ and to $1$ when $Z_N<0$. Since $Z_N\Rightarrow Z$ and $P(Z=0)=0$, [F5] gives $\mathbb E[e^{ivZ_N+isU_N}]\longrightarrow\mathbb E\!\left[e^{ivZ}\left(\mathbf1_{\{Z>0\}}e^{-s^2/12}+\mathbf1_{\{Z<0\}}\right)\right].$ This is the joint characteristic function of $(Z,\mathbf1_{\{Z>0\}}W)$ for an independent $W\sim N(0,1/6)$, so the post-resampling limit is $Z+\mathbf1_{\{Z>0\}}W$. Its mean is zero and its third moment is $3\mathbb E[Z\mathbf1_{\{Z>0\}}]\mathbb E[W^2]>0$, so it is not Gaussian. This contradicts the variance-$1/3$ Gaussian predicted in step 1.2.

derivations.claim: For every pair of preceding states, both $g(x\mid x')/g(x\mid x'')$ and $q_t(x\mid x')/q_t(x\mid x'')$ equal $1$. The likelihood satisfies $0<1\le f(\ast\mid x)\le1$, and $\Delta\phi=1$. The filtering target at every $t\ge1$ has last-state law $\pi_t(X_t=1)=1/2$, while the proposal last-state law is $q_t$. Its normalized incremental Radon–Nikodym weight is $\upsilon_t(1)=1/(2\epsilon_t)$ and $\upsilon_t(0)=1/(2(1-\epsilon_t))$.

For every preceding path, the forward image of the centered test is $E_t(\phi-1/2)=\sum_{x=0}^1q_t(x\mid x_{t-1})\upsilon_t(x)(\mathbf1_{\{x=1\}}-1/2)=\sum_{x=0}^1g(x\mid x_{t-1})(\mathbf1_{\{x=1\}}-1/2)=0.$ Consequently $E_{k+1:t}(\phi-\pi_t\phi)=0$ for every $k<t$, so all earlier-time terms in [F2] vanish.

The remaining $k=t$ term in [F2] is $V_t(\phi)=\epsilon_t\left(\frac1{2\epsilon_t}\right)^2\frac14+(1-\epsilon_t)\left(\frac1{2(1-\epsilon_t)}\right)^2\frac14=\frac1{16\epsilon_t}+\frac1{16(1-\epsilon_t)}.$ Since $\epsilon_t=2^{-t-2}\downarrow0$, $V_t(\phi)\to\infty$ despite all the stated ratio, likelihood, and oscillation bounds.
