For a measurable vector function $\phi:\Theta_t\to\mathbb R^d$, write $\mu(\phi)=\int\phi\,d\mu$ and
$$\operatorname{Cov}_{\mu}(\phi)=\int(\phi-\mu(\phi))(\phi-\mu(\phi))^\top\,d\mu,$$
when the second moment is finite. Also write $k_t\phi(x)=\int\phi(z)k_t(x,dz)$ and
$$\operatorname{Cov}_{k_t}(\phi)(x)=\int(\phi(z)-k_t\phi(x))(\phi(z)-k_t\phi(x))^\top k_t(x,dz).$$

The source recursive test classes are
$$\Phi_0^{(d)}=\{\phi:\widetilde\pi_0(\|\phi\|^2)<\infty\},$$
and, for $t\ge1$,
$$\Phi_t^{(d)}=\left\{\phi:\text{ for some }\delta>0,\ \widetilde\pi_t(\|\upsilon_t\phi\|^{2+\delta})<\infty\ \text{ and }\ x\mapsto k_t(\upsilon_t\phi)(x)\in\Phi_{t-1}^{(d)}\right\}.$$
Assume $1\in\Phi_t^{(1)}$ for every $t$. This is the source theorem's explicit normalizing-weight condition. For the recursive post-resampling CLTs proved on this page, use the stronger classes $\Psi_t^{(d)}$. At $t=0$, let $\Psi_0^{(d)}$ consist of the $\phi\in\Phi_0^{(d)}$ for which $\widetilde\pi_0(\|\upsilon_0(\phi-\pi_0(\phi))\|^2)<\infty$ and $\pi_0(\|\phi\|^2)<\infty$. The initial normalizing denominator needs only its finite first moment $\widetilde\pi_0(\upsilon_0)=1$. For $t\ge1$, let $\Psi_t^{(d)}$ consist of the $\phi\in\Phi_t^{(d)}$ for which $\pi_t(\|\phi\|^2)<\infty$ and $x\mapsto E_t(\phi-\pi_t(\phi))(x)\in\Psi_{t-1}^{(d)}$. Here $E_t h=k_t(\upsilon_t h)$ is the operator defined below. Only target second moments are required: fixed-tail truncation supplies the conditional selection Lindeberg condition without a target higher-moment assumption. The recursive target moments supply the offspring variance at every earlier selection used in the induction. The source $\Phi_t$ conditions alone need not imply them. The source condition $1\in\Phi_t$ and these recursive target moments are the stated hypotheses for the CLT induction; no higher initial normalizer moment is required.

Define the mutation covariance operators recursively. At time zero,
$$\widetilde V_0(\phi)=\operatorname{Cov}_{\widetilde\pi_0}(\phi).$$
For $t\ge1$,
$$\widetilde V_t(\phi)=\widehat V_{t-1}(k_t\phi)+\int\operatorname{Cov}_{k_t}(\phi)(x)\,\pi_{t-1}(dx).$$
The weighted-estimator covariance is
$$V_t(\phi)=\widetilde V_t\!\left(\upsilon_t(\phi-\pi_t(\phi))\right).$$
For a measurable vector function $h$ on $\Theta_t$, define the forward operator from $\Theta_{t-1}$ by
$$E_t h(x)=k_t(\upsilon_t h)(x)=\int\upsilon_t(z)h(z)\,k_t(x,dz).$$
For $k<t$, write $E_{k+1:t}=E_{k+1}\circ\cdots\circ E_t$; set $E_{t+1:t}$ to the identity operator.
For multinomial offspring resampling set
$$\widehat V_t^{\mathrm{multi}}(\phi)=V_t(\phi)+\operatorname{Cov}_{\pi_t}(\phi).$$
For residual offspring resampling, let $r(u)=u-\lfloor u\rfloor$. When $c_t=\widetilde\pi_t(r(\upsilon_t))>0$, define the formal source candidate
$$R_t^{\mathrm{cand}}(\phi)=\widetilde\pi_t\!\left(r(\upsilon_t)\phi\phi^\top\right)-\frac{\widetilde\pi_t(r(\upsilon_t)\phi)\,\widetilde\pi_t(r(\upsilon_t)\phi)^\top}{c_t}.$$
Set $R_t=R_t^{\mathrm{cand}}$ and $\widehat V_t^{\mathrm{res}}=V_t+R_t$ only when $\widetilde\pi_t(\upsilon_t\in\{1,2,\ldots\})=0$; then $c_t>0$ and the finite-sample floor discontinuities are avoided. If $\upsilon_t=1$ $\widetilde\pi_t$-almost everywhere, put $R_t=0$. Residual offspring are deterministic whenever all sampled weights equal one. In SIR this holds almost surely outside earlier zero-weight fallback events, whose probability tends to zero at a fixed horizon; the almost-everywhere condition alone does not prescribe weights on proposal-null states reached after a fallback. No residual covariance is assigned when $c_t=0$ but $\upsilon_t$ is not almost everywhere one: the finite-sample normalization can move positive integer weights across floor boundaries. The B-page counterexamples show why the general positive-integer-atom branch remains unassigned.

Let $(S,\Sigma)$ and $(E,\mathcal E)$ be measurable spaces with $S\ne\varnothing$, and let $K:S\rightsquigarrow E$ be a probability kernel as in [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. Its **Dobrushin contraction coefficient** is
$$\delta(K):=\sup_{x,x'\in S}\lVert K(x,\cdot)-K(x',\cdot)\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}},$$
where $\lVert\cdot\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}$ is the event-supremum distance between probability laws in [[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]]. Thus $0\le\delta(K)\le1$. The coefficient measures the largest total-variation separation between two one-step output laws.

Let $K:S\rightsquigarrow E$ be a probability kernel on a nonempty measurable source space. Suppose a sigma-finite measure $\lambda$ on $E$ and probability densities $k_x$ satisfy $K(x,A)=\int_A k_x\,d\lambda$ for every $x\in S$ and measurable $A\subseteq E$. If $C\ge1$ and, for every $x,x'\in S$, $k_x(z)\le Ck_{x'}(z)$ for $\lambda$-almost every $z$, then the Dobrushin coefficient from [[def-dobrushin-coefficient-for-probability-kernels]] obeys
$$\delta(K)\le1-C^{-1}.$$

Let $\mathsf X$ be a nonempty standard-Borel space with a sigma-finite reference measure $\lambda$, and let $\eta_0$ be a probability on it. For $s\ge1$, supply jointly measurable, strictly positive finite densities $g_s(z\mid x)$ of probability transition kernels relative to $\lambda$, and measurable likelihood factors $f_s$ with $0<a\le f_s(z)\le b<\infty$. These specified versions satisfy, for one $C\ge1$ and every $s,x,x',z$,
$$g_s(z\mid x)\le Cg_s(z\mid x').$$
Define $c_s=\eta_{s-1}(g_sf_s)$, $\eta_s(h)=\eta_{s-1}(g_s(f_sh))/c_s$, and $E_sh(x)=g_s(f_sh)(x)/c_s$. They are the operators of [[def-smc-clt-function-classes-and-variance-recursions]] restricted to last-state tests in the corresponding filtering model. Put $\rho=1-C^{-2}$. For every bounded measurable real terminal test $\psi$ and $0\le k<t$,
$$\|E_{k+1:t}(\psi-\eta_t\psi)\|_\infty\le C\rho^{t-k}\operatorname{osc}(\psi).$$
For $k=t$ the identity image is bounded by $\operatorname{osc}(\psi)$; use $\rho^n=0$ for $n\ge1$ when $C=1$. This is a closed last-state-test assertion, not a contraction of arbitrary functions of the full stored path. Positivity, finiteness and the ratio bounds refer to the supplied pointwise density versions, not to unspecified unrelated null-set versions.

Use multinomial offspring resampling and the covariance $V_t$ of [[def-smc-clt-function-classes-and-variance-recursions]]. Suppose all normalized incremental weights satisfy $\upsilon_s\le B<\infty$ almost everywhere under their proposals, including $s=0$. For a chosen bounded real terminal test $\phi$ and every $0\le k\le t$, assume the bounded versions of its centered backward images satisfy
$$\|E_{k+1:t}(\phi-\pi_t\phi)\|_\infty\le A\rho^{t-k}\Delta\phi,$$
with fixed $A\ge1$ and $0\le\rho<1$, uniformly over the horizons considered; use $\rho^0=1$. Then
$$V_t(\phi)\le\frac{A^2B^2(\Delta\phi)^2}{1-\rho^2}.$$
The one-step centered oscillation condition of [[lem-smc-backward-operator-oscillation-bound]] gives the original specialization $A=1$, $\rho=\beta$ and bound $B^2(\Delta\phi)^2/(1-\beta^2)$.

There is a separate filtering-density sufficient branch. Use the strictly positive finite density versions, true-transition row-ratio bound $C\ge1$, likelihood bounds $0<a\le f_s\le b<\infty$ and normalized filtering operators in [[lem-smc-centered-filtering-feynman-kac-contraction]]. Additionally require strictly positive finite proposal densities $q_s(z\mid x)$ with $g_s(z\mid x)\le Dq_s(z\mid x)$ uniformly for a finite $D$, and an initial normalized weight $\upsilon_0\le B_{\rm init}<\infty$ under its proposal. Put $B=\max(B_{\rm init},Db/a)$ and $\rho=1-C^{-2}$. For bounded last-state tests $\phi(x_{0:t})=\psi(x_t)$, the bound holds with $A=C$:
$$V_t(\psi)\le\frac{B^2C^2(\operatorname{osc}\psi)^2}{1-(1-C^{-2})^2}.$$
This branch concerns the closed last-state test subspace and its backward images, not all path observables. Both bounds concern fixed-horizon CLT variances, uniform in the time index; neither is a finite-particle time-uniform error bound.

derivations.claim: Every transition row is $(1/2,1/2)$, so the target and proposal transitions coincide and the likelihood contributes no correction. By [F1], $\upsilon_s=1$, hence $B=1$, and $\pi_s$ is uniform for every $s\ge0$. Since the row does not depend on its predecessor, [F2] gives $\delta(K)=0$; its density rows are identical, so [F3] also applies with $C=1$.

On the closed last-state subspace the forward operator is $E_sh_s=Kh_s$, which maps a last-state test to its uniform average. The true transition and proposal density versions relative to counting measure are all $1/2$, so [F4] applies with $C=1$, $A=1$, and $\rho=0$. No contraction of arbitrary path-history functions is asserted. The test has $\Delta\phi=1$ and is centered by $1/2$. Every earlier backward image is zero; the final $k=t$ term in the variance expansion is $\operatorname{Var}_{\pi_t}(\phi)=1/4$. Hence $V_t(\phi)=1/4$ for every $t$.

Applying [F5] with $A=B=1$, $\rho=0$ and $\Delta\phi=1$ gives $V_t(\phi)\le1$, uniformly in $t$; the exact variance $1/4$ from step 1.2 satisfies the bound. This verifies a time-uniform asymptotic-variance result under explicit mixing and weight conditions.

$$V_t(\phi)=\sum_{k=0}^{t}\widetilde\pi_k\!\left[\upsilon_k^2\,E_{k+1:t}(\bar\phi)E_{k+1:t}(\bar\phi)^\top\right],$$
where the $k=t$ term uses $E_{t+1:t}\bar\phi=\bar\phi$. Each summand is a finite positive-semidefinite matrix under the stated class conditions.

Fix a finite horizon $t$ and use the target/proposal flow and classes $\Phi_s^{(d)},\Psi_s^{(d)}$ of [[def-smc-clt-function-classes-and-variance-recursions]], with $1\in\Phi_s^{(1)}$ for every $0\le s\le t$. Run the SIR procedure with multinomial resampling at each time. For $\phi\in\Psi_t^{(d)}$, let $\omega_t^N$ be the corrected weighted empirical law and $\check\eta_t^N$ the post-resampling empirical law. Then
$$\sqrt N\{\omega_t^N(\phi)-\pi_t(\phi)\}\Rightarrow\mathcal N_d(0,V_t(\phi)),\qquad \sqrt N\{\check\eta_t^N(\phi)-\pi_t(\phi)\}\Rightarrow\mathcal N_d(0,\widehat V_t^{\rm multi}(\phi)),$$
where $\widehat V_t^{\rm multi}(\phi)=V_t(\phi)+\operatorname{Cov}_{\pi_t}(\phi)$. The horizon is fixed as $N\to\infty$; the theorem asserts no time-uniform finite-particle accuracy.

derivations.claim: The identity kernel leaves the uniform law invariant and has incremental weight one. Thus [F1] gives $E_{k+1:t}(\phi-\pi_t\phi)=\phi-1/2$ for every $k\le t$. Since $(\phi-1/2)^2=1/4$ everywhere, each of the $t+1$ summands in [F2] equals $1/4$. Therefore $V_t(\phi)=(t+1)/4$.

By [F3], at every fixed $t$ the weighted estimate has a valid CLT with variance $(t+1)/4$, and the post-resampling estimate has variance $(t+2)/4$. Both variance sequences are unbounded as $t$ ranges over the integers. The fixed-horizon theorem therefore supplies no uniform-in-time variance bound or finite-particle accuracy guarantee.

Statement: At t=0 the variance is 1/4 and at t=1 it is 1/2 by step 1.1. No finite particle N is fixed; the cited CLT is an N→infinity statement.

Statement: At t=0, step 1.1 yields V_0=1/4 and step 2.1 selected variance 1/2; allowing fixed horizons t to vary makes both sequences unbounded.

citations.quote: A measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$ is **standard Borel** if there are a Polish space $P$ and a bijection $h:E\to P$ such that $A\in\mathcal E$ exactly when $h[A]$ is Borel in $P$. Thus the measurable structure is part of the datum; no particular compatible Polish topology on $E$ is selected.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.
Every finite product of standard Borel spaces, with its finite product sigma-algebra, is standard Borel.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

derivations.claim: By [F2], both finite path spaces carry their stated product sigma-algebras and the target path space is standard Borel. Fix a prefix $z_{0:t-1}$. The append map $j_{z_{0:t-1}}(z_t)=(z_{0:t-1},z_t)$ is measurable: the inverse image of a generating rectangle is either empty or the final-coordinate measurable set, and [F3] generates the target sigma-algebra from these rectangles. Thus $A\mapsto M_t(z_{t-1},j_{z_{0:t-1}}^{-1}(A))$ is the pushforward of the probability measure $M_t(z_{t-1},\cdot)$ and is a probability measure.

The projection $z_{0:t-1}\mapsto z_{t-1}$ is measurable, so composing each set-evaluation map $z_{t-1}\mapsto M_t(z_{t-1},B)$ with this projection gives a probability kernel from the prefix space to $\mathsf Z_t$. The function $(z_{0:t-1},z_t)\mapsto\mathbf1_A(z_{0:t-1},z_t)$ is product-measurable. By [F5], its integral against this composed kernel is measurable in the prefix. Together with step 1.1, this proves that $\overline M_t$ has probability-measure sections and measurable set evaluations, hence is a probability kernel. Iterating the definition appends each state using exactly $M_t$ because at each step the indicator is evaluated on the already fixed prefix and the new coordinate.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $Z_t$ take values in a standard-Borel space
$(\mathsf Z_t,\mathcal Z_t)$ and let $U_t\in\mathbb R^{d_t}$ for a finite
horizon $0\le t\le T$, where each $d_t$ is a positive integer. For
$1\le t\le T$, let $Y_t\in\mathbb R^{p_t}$ with each $p_t$ a positive
integer; observations begin at time $1$. The nonlinear
component has initial probability $\mu_0$ and transition probability kernels
$M_t(z_{t-1},dz_t)$; its transition does not depend on $U_{t-1}$. Given the
entire nonlinear path $z_{0:T}$, write $\mathsf Z_{0:t}=\prod_{s=0}^t\mathsf Z_s$
with its finite-product sigma-algebra and specify Borel maps
$$m_0:\mathsf Z_0\to\mathbb R^{d_0},\qquad P_0:\mathsf Z_0\to\mathbb R^{d_0\times d_0},$$
and, for $1\le t\le T$,
$$A_t:\mathsf Z_{0:t}\to\mathbb R^{d_t\times d_{t-1}},\quad Q_t:\mathsf Z_{0:t}\to\mathbb R^{d_t\times d_t},\quad C_t:\mathsf Z_{0:t}\to\mathbb R^{p_t\times d_t},\quad R_t:\mathsf Z_{0:t}\to\mathbb R^{p_t\times p_t}.$$
Require $P_0(z_0)$ and
$Q_t(z_{0:t})$ to be symmetric positive semidefinite, meaning
$v^TPv\ge0$ for every matching vector $v$, and $R_t(z_{0:t})$ to be
symmetric positive definite, meaning $v^TR_tv>0$ for every nonzero $v$. Conditional
on $Z_{0:T}=z_{0:T}$, the linear component and observations have the finite
linear-Gaussian model, with the transition and observation equations for
$1\le t\le T$:
$$U_0\sim N(m_0(z_0),P_0(z_0)),\qquad U_t=A_t(z_{0:t})U_{t-1}+\xi_t,\qquad Y_t=C_t(z_{0:t})U_t+\varepsilon_t,$$
where the centered Gaussian noises $\xi_t\sim N(0,Q_t(z_{0:t}))$ and
$\varepsilon_t\sim N(0,R_t(z_{0:t}))$ are mutually independent over time
and independent of $U_0$, under that conditional law. For every fixed path
$z_{0:T}$ these are exactly the hypotheses of
[[def-linear-gaussian-state-space-model-with-independent-noises]] with
deterministic matrices.

This hierarchical conditionally linear-Gaussian model is the input class for
the Rao–Blackwellized filter below: it samples the nonlinear path and keeps
the conditional Gaussian law of $U_t$ analytically. It does not include a
nonlinear transition whose law depends on $U_{t-1}$, nor does it assert that
the marginal nonlinear process remains Markov after conditioning on all
observations. Such models need their own marginal transition and backward
kernels. A state-space filtering or smoothing law is a data-indexed regular
conditional-distribution version as in
[[def-state-space-filtering-laws]]; no pointwise uniqueness on null data
histories is imposed.

Assume AC. Fix a finite-horizon model from
[[def-linear-gaussian-state-space-model-with-independent-noises]] with
state and observation equations
$$X_k=F_kX_{k-1}+q_k,\qquad Y_k=H_kX_k+r_k\qquad (1\le k\le T),$$
where $X_0\sim N_{d_0}(m_0,P_0)$, the centered Gaussian noises $q_k,r_k$ are
mutually independent across times and from $X_0$, and $P_0,Q_k,R_k$ are
symmetric positive semidefinite. Let the parameters and observations be
admissible for [[alg-kalman-filter]], so the recursively formed innovation
covariances
$$S_k=H_kP_{k|k-1}H_k^T+R_k$$
are positive definite for every $1\le k\le T$. Run that algorithm from
$m_{0|0}=m_0$ and $P_{0|0}=P_0$. Then, for each $0\le k\le T$, the map
$$\pi_k(y_{1:k},\cdot)=N_{d_k}(m_{k|k}(y_{1:k}),P_{k|k})$$
is an everywhere-defined filtering kernel for $X_k$ given $Y_{1:k}$ in the
sense of [[def-state-space-filtering-laws]]. The empty history at $k=0$ is a
singleton, and $\pi_0=N_{d_0}(m_0,P_0)$. In particular, these recursions
give an exact Gaussian conditional-law version at every observation history;
each $P_{k|k}$ is positive semidefinite. Singular initial, process,
measurement, predicted-state, and filtered-state covariances are allowed.
Equivalently, the covariance update can be written in Joseph form
$$P_{k|k}=(I-K_kH_k)P_{k|k-1}(I-K_kH_k)^T+K_kR_kK_k^T.$$
Only the innovation matrices being solved must be positive definite. No
pointwise uniqueness of a conditional-law version on null histories,
observation-density assumption, or numerical-stability claim is made.

Assume AC, and let $d,n,p$ be positive integers. Let $U\in\mathbb R^d$,
$q\in\mathbb R^n$, and $r\in\mathbb R^p$ be mutually independent Gaussian vectors with
$$U\sim N_d(m,P),\qquad q\sim N_n(0,Q),\qquad r\sim N_p(0,R),$$
where $P,Q,R$ are symmetric positive semidefinite. Let
$F\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$ and $H\in\mathbb R^{p\times n}$, and set
$$X=FU+q,\qquad Y=HX+r,\qquad P^-:=FPF^T+Q,\qquad S:=HP^-H^T+R.$$
If $S$ is positive definite, put $K:=P^-H^TS^{-1}$. Then $(X,Y)$ is jointly
Gaussian with mean $(Fm,HFm)$ and covariance
$$\begin{pmatrix}P^-&P^-H^T\\HP^-&S\end{pmatrix},$$
and for every $y\in\mathbb R^p$ an everywhere-defined conditional law is
$$\mathcal L(X\mid Y=y)=N_n\!\left(Fm+K(y-HFm),\,P^--KSK^T\right).$$
The conditional covariance is positive semidefinite even if $P$, $Q$, or
$R$ is singular. It also equals the Joseph expression
$$(I-KH)P^-(I-KH)^T+KRK^T.$$
No inverse of a state, process-noise, or measurement-noise covariance is
used.

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$, $m\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $\Sigma$ be a real symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then its law has Lebesgue density
$$f_{m,\Sigma}(x)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\det(\Sigma)^{-1/2} \exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(x-m)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-m)\right), \qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$

Let $(E,\mathcal S,\mu)$ and $(T,\mathcal T,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure spaces. Let a joint probability $\lambda$ on $E\times T$ have nonnegative product-measurable density $p:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$ relative to $\mu\times\nu$. A fixed probability $\rho$ on $(E,\mathcal S)$ is supplied. Put
$$m(y)=\int_E p(x,y)\,\mu(dx),\qquad D=\{y:0<m(y)<\infty\},$$
$$K(y,A)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\int_Ap(x,y)\,\mu(dx)}{m(y)},&y\in D,\\ \rho(A),&y\notin D.\end{cases}$$

Then K is an everywhere probability kernel from T to E. If $\beta$ is the second marginal of $\lambda$, then $\beta(D)=1$ and
$$\lambda(A\times B)=\int_B K(y,A)\,\beta(dy).$$

For any random elements X,Y with joint law $\lambda$, $K(Y,\cdot)$ is a regular conditional distribution of X given $\sigma(Y)$. These event identities require no AC. If interpreted with the library's conditional-expectation class existence convention, assume AC. Neither zero nor infinite marginal-density fibres are normalized by the displayed quotient.

Assume AC and fix a finite horizon $T\in\mathbb N_0$. For each $0\le k\le T$, let $(\mathsf X_k,\mathcal X_k)$ be a standard Borel space. Let $\mu_0$ be a probability measure on $\mathsf X_0$, and for $1\le k\le T$ let $M_k:\mathsf X_{k-1}\rightsquigarrow\mathsf X_k$ be a probability kernel. A **potential** at time $k$ is a finite-valued nonnegative measurable function $G_k:\mathsf X_k\to[0,\infty)$. Write $\mathsf X_{0:t}=\prod_{k=0}^t\mathsf X_k$ with its finite-product sigma-algebra.

For each $0\le t\le T$, let $P_t^M$ be the finite path law with ordered kernel integral $\mu_0(dx_0)\prod_{k=1}^tM_k(x_{k-1},dx_k)$, supplied by Ionescu–Tulcea ([[thm-ionescu-tulcea-construction-of-a-markov-chain]]). The **unnormalized Feynman–Kac path measure** is
$$\gamma_t(A)=\int_{\mathsf X_{0:t}}\mathbf 1_A(x_{0:t})\prod_{k=0}^tG_k(x_k)\,P_t^M(dx_{0:t}),\qquad A\in\bigotimes_{k=0}^t\mathcal X_k.$$
Its **normalizer** is $Z_t=\gamma_t(\mathsf X_{0:t})=\gamma_t(1)\in[0,\infty]$. Only when $0<Z_t<\infty$ define the normalized path target $\pi_t^{\mathrm{FK}}=\gamma_t/Z_t$. The sequence $(\gamma_t)$ with its kernels and potentials is the Feynman–Kac flow.

State-space filtering kernels are conditional-law versions as in [[def-state-space-filtering-laws]]. A Feynman–Kac path target is not by itself an assertion that a pointwise conditional version has been selected at observation-null histories.

Let $T\ge0$ be finite, let $(\mathsf Z_t,\mathcal Z_t)$ be standard-Borel
spaces for $0\le t\le T$, and for $1\le t\le T$ let
$M_t:\mathsf Z_{t-1}\rightsquigarrow\mathsf Z_t$ be probability kernels,
with the kernel convention of
[[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. For $1\le t\le T$, define the path-extension kernel
from $\mathsf Z_{0:t-1}$ to $\mathsf Z_{0:t}$ by
$$\overline M_t(z_{0:t-1},A)=\int_{\mathsf Z_t}\mathbf1_A(z_{0:t-1},z_t)M_t(z_{t-1},dz_t).$$
Then $\overline M_t$ is a probability kernel and $\mathsf Z_{0:t}$ is
standard Borel. Its ordered iterates append the nonlinear states with the
original transition law.

derivations.claim: Initially $P_{0|0}=P_0(z_0)$ is positive semidefinite. If $P_{t-1|t-1}$ is positive semidefinite, then $P_{t|t-1}=A_tP_{t-1|t-1}A_t^T+Q_t$ is positive semidefinite because $u^TP_{t|t-1}u=(A_t^Tu)^TP_{t-1|t-1}(A_t^Tu)+u^TQ_tu\ge0$. For every nonzero observation vector $a$, $a^TS_ta=(C_t^Ta)^TP_{t|t-1}(C_t^Ta)+a^TR_ta>0$, since the first term is nonnegative and $R_t$ is positive definite. Induction proves all innovation matrices meet the Kalman algorithm's domain.

By [F1], for this fixed path the conditional model is the deterministic finite-horizon model of [F2]. Step 1.1 verifies its positive-innovation hypothesis, so [F2] gives the exact conditional Gaussian filter at every observation history, including singular state covariances. At each time, [F3] gives the marginal observation law $N(C_tm_{t|t-1},S_t)$; applying [F4] yields the displayed density.

The coefficient functions are Borel by [F1]. Finite sums and products preserve Borel measurability, and matrix inversion and determinant are continuous on the positive-definite matrices established in step 1.1. The Kalman moment recursion and the displayed density are therefore Borel functions of the path. The covariance determinant is finite and positive and the exponential is finite and strictly positive, so $\ell_t$ has the claimed range.

For a fixed nonlinear path, step 2.1 gives the one-step conditional density $\ell_s$ of $Y_s$ given $Y_{1:s-1}$. By the defining event-integral identity for conditional densities, $p(y_{1:s}\mid z)=p(y_{1:s-1}\mid z)\ell_s(z_{0:s};y_{1:s})$ on finite-positive fibers; induction from the empty history, whose density is one, gives the product $\prod_{s=1}^t\ell_s$. By [F7], the ordered path-extension kernels are probability kernels on the standard-Borel path spaces and give the nonlinear path law. The joint law of $Z_{0:t}$ and $Y_{1:t}$ therefore has this product as its observation-density factor relative to that path law and Lebesgue observation measure. By [F5], conditioning on a history with finite positive evidence weights the nonlinear path law by this product and divides by its integral. Comparing with [F6] gives exactly the stated normalized Feynman–Kac path measure. This assertion is restricted to those finite-positive evidence fibers; null and infinite fibers are not normalized.

Step 1.1 explicitly permits positive-semidefinite, possibly singular state/process covariances.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC and fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$ with a state-space model by
probability kernels as in
[[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]. If $T=0$, put $\Omega_T=E_0$;
otherwise put $\Omega_T=E_0\times E_1\times F_1\times\cdots\times E_T\times
F_T$. Let $\mathcal Z_T$ be the corresponding finite-product sigma-algebra
and write $(\Omega_T,\mathcal Z_T,P_T)$ for its finite-horizon probability
space. The law $P_T$ is the unique law supplied by
[[thm-finite-horizon-state-space-kernel-law-exists-uniquely]]. Let $X_t$ and
$Y_t$ be the coordinate random elements taking values in $E_t$ and $F_t$. For
$t\ge1$, write $Y_{1:t}:=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_t)$ and
$\mathsf F_{1:t}:=F_1\times\cdots\times F_t$ with its finite-product
sigma-algebra; let $\mathsf F_{1:0}$ be a singleton and $Y_{1:0}$ its constant
map. The factors are standard Borel, meaning measurably isomorphic to Polish
spaces ([[def-standard-borel-space]]), and their finite products are standard
Borel ([[lem-finite-products-of-standard-borel-spaces-are-standard-borel]]).

The **initial filtering kernel** $\pi_0:\mathsf F_{1:0}\to E_0$ assigns
$\mu_0$ to the unique empty history; it is the conditional law of $X_0$ given
the trivial history. For $1\le t\le T$, a **filtering kernel at time $t$** is
a probability kernel $\pi_t:\mathsf F_{1:t}\to E_t$ such that
$\omega\mapsto\pi_t(Y_{1:t}(\omega),\cdot)$ is a regular conditional
distribution of $X_t$ given $\sigma(Y_{1:t})$. For $1\le t\le T$, a
**predictive kernel at time $t$** is a probability kernel
$\pi_{t|t-1}:\mathsf F_{1:t-1}\to E_t$ whose composition with $Y_{1:t-1}$
is a regular conditional distribution of $X_t$ given
$\sigma(Y_{1:t-1})$. A **finite-horizon smoothing kernel** is a probability
kernel $\psi_T:\mathsf F_{1:T}\to E_0\times\cdots\times E_T$ whose
composition with $Y_{1:T}$ is a regular conditional distribution of the full
state path $(X_0,\ldots,X_T)$ given $\sigma(Y_{1:T})$. Here a regular
conditional distribution is an everywhere probability kernel satisfying the
conditional event identities in
[[def-regular-conditional-distribution]], and a conditional law given a
random element is its data-indexed kernel form in
[[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]].

These kernels are versions: their values can be changed on a measurable set
of observation histories of probability zero without changing the conditional
identities. No density is assumed in these definitions. The state-space model
here is one fixed law. A parametric statistical model is instead a map
$\theta\mapsto P_\theta$ from a parameter set to probability laws; its
measurability is not asserted without a parameter sigma-algebra
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]).

Assume AC and a finite-horizon state-space model by standard-Borel state and
observation spaces, an initial probability measure, and transition and
observation probability kernels, as in
[[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]. Let $P_T$ be its finite-horizon
path law. The initial filtering kernel is $\pi_0=\mu_0$ on the singleton
empty-history space. For each $1\le t\le T$, data-indexed filtering and
predictive kernels from [[def-state-space-filtering-laws]] exist. A
data-indexed finite-horizon smoothing kernel for the full state path also
exists, including when $T=0$. The claim is existence of conditional versions
only; it asserts no density, filtering recursion, uniqueness on null
observation histories, or numerical approximation.

Assume AC and a finite-horizon model as in
[[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]. For each $1\le t\le T$, let
$\nu_t$ be a sigma-finite measure on $(F_t,\mathcal F_t)$ and suppose the
observation kernel has a specified product-measurable density
$g_t:E_t\times F_t\to[0,\infty]$ with respect to $\mathcal E_t\otimes\mathcal F_t$:
$$G_t(x,B)=\int_B g_t(x,y)\,\nu_t(dy),\qquad\int_{F_t}g_t(x,y)\,\nu_t(dy)=1$$
for every state $x\in E_t$ and measurable $B\subseteq F_t$. For
$h\in\mathsf F_{1:t-1}$, let $\pi_{t-1}$ be the filtering kernel at time
$t-1$ from
[[def-state-space-filtering-laws]] when $t>1$, and for $t=1$ let $\pi_0$ be
the initial kernel $\mu_0$ on the singleton empty-history space. For
$A\in\mathcal E_t$, define the predictive kernel
$$\widehat\pi_t(h,A):=\int_{E_{t-1}}K_t(x,A)\,\pi_{t-1}(h,dx),$$
the evidence density
$$z_t(h,y):=\int_{E_t}g_t(x,y)\,\widehat\pi_t(h,dx),$$
and for $h\in\mathsf F_{1:t-1}$, $y\in F_t$, and $A\in\mathcal E_t$ define
the update
$$\pi_t(h,y,A):=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\int_Ag_t(x,y)\,\widehat\pi_t(h,dx)}{z_t(h,y)},&0<z_t(h,y)<\infty,\\[6pt]\widehat\pi_t(h,A),&z_t(h,y)=0\text{ or }z_t(h,y)=\infty.\end{cases}$$
Then $\widehat\pi_t$ is a predictive kernel for $X_t$ given $Y_{1:t-1}$,
and $\pi_t$ is a filtering kernel for $X_t$ given $Y_{1:t}$. For each fixed
history $h$, the observation marginal under the conditional version
determined by $\widehat\pi_t(h,\cdot)$ has density
$z_t(h,\cdot)$ with respect to $\nu_t$ and assigns zero mass to both
$\{y:z_t(h,y)=0\}$ and $\{y:z_t(h,y)=\infty\}$. Thus the formula never
divides by zero or infinity; values on those fibers are conditional-law
fillers. The statement is exact and finite-horizon and gives no numerical
approximation or long-time stability claim.

Let $(E,\mathcal S,\mu)$ and $(T,\mathcal T,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure spaces. Let a joint probability $\lambda$ on $E\times T$ have nonnegative product-measurable density $p:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$ relative to $\mu\times\nu$. A fixed probability $\rho$ on $(E,\mathcal S)$ is supplied. Put
$$m(y)=\int_E p(x,y)\,\mu(dx),\qquad D=\{y:0<m(y)<\infty\},$$
$$K(y,A)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\int_Ap(x,y)\,\mu(dx)}{m(y)},&y\in D,\\ \rho(A),&y\notin D.\end{cases}$$

Then K is an everywhere probability kernel from T to E. If $\beta$ is the second marginal of $\lambda$, then $\beta(D)=1$ and
$$\lambda(A\times B)=\int_B K(y,A)\,\beta(dy).$$

For any random elements X,Y with joint law $\lambda$, $K(Y,\cdot)$ is a regular conditional distribution of X given $\sigma(Y)$. These event identities require no AC. If interpreted with the library's conditional-expectation class existence convention, assume AC. Neither zero nor infinite marginal-density fibres are normalized by the displayed quotient.

Assume AC. Fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$, standard-Borel spaces
$E_0,\ldots,E_T$ and $F_1,\ldots,F_T$, an initial probability measure
$\mu_0$ on $E_0$, and transition and observation probability kernels
$K_t:E_{t-1}\to E_t$ and $G_t:E_t\to F_t$ for $1\le t\le T$, as in
[[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]. On the interleaved finite
product space
$$\mathcal Z_T=E_0\times E_1\times F_1\times\cdots\times E_T\times F_T,$$
there is a unique probability measure whose rectangle probabilities are the
ordered iterated kernel integrals
$$\mu_0(dx_0)\prod_{t=1}^T K_t(x_{t-1},dx_t)G_t(x_t,dy_t).$$
The product notation means successive integration in the displayed order.
For $T=0$, the assertion is the initial law $\mu_0$ on $E_0$.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

derivations.claim: Fix $t<T$ and condition on $Y_{1:t}=y_{1:t}$. The conditional pair law of $(X_t,X_{t+1})$ is the ordered kernel integral $\eta_t(dx)M_{t+1}(x,dx')$ by [F3] and [F5]. In the density case this pair law has density $f_{t+1}(x'\mid x)$ with respect to $\eta_t\times\lambda_{t+1}$, and its second marginal has density $q_{t+1}(x')$. Applying [F4] gives the displayed $B_t$ on $D_{t+1}$ and the supplied filler $\eta_t$ off it. citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Use the finite-horizon target and proposal setting of [[def-feynman-kac-path-targets-and-normalizers]]. For admissible inputs require $\mu_0\ll\nu_0$ and, for each $k\ge1$, $M_k(x,\cdot)\ll R_k(x,\cdot)$ for almost every $x$ under the last-coordinate marginal of the proposal path law $Q_{k-1}$. Select the joint measurable versions $\rho_0=d\mu_0/d\nu_0$ and $r_k(x,\cdot)=dM_k(x,\cdot)/dR_k(x,\cdot)$ supplied by [[thm-feynman-kac-path-radon-nikodym-weight]]. Fix $N\ge1$ and select either multinomial or residual resampling at each time. The algorithm returns a weighted empirical path measure and a normalizer estimate.

1. Draw $X_0^1,\ldots,X_0^N$ independently from $\nu_0$. Set $a_0^i=G_0(X_0^i)\rho_0(X_0^i)$ and $\widehat Z_0=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^Na_0^i$. If $\sum_i a_0^i>0$, put $\bar w_0^i=a_0^i/\sum_j a_0^j$; otherwise put $\bar w_0^i=1/N$. Each initial path is $X_{0:0}^i=X_0^i$.
2. For $k=1,\ldots,t$, do the following:
   1. Apply [[alg-multinomial-and-residual-offspring-resampling]] to the previous normalized weights $(\bar w_{k-1}^1,\ldots,\bar w_{k-1}^N)$, obtaining ancestor indices $A_k^1,\ldots,A_k^N$.
   2. Given the previous paths and these indices, draw $(X_k^1,\ldots,X_k^N)$ with joint conditional law $\bigotimes_{i=1}^N R_k(X_{k-1}^{A_k^i},\cdot)$ and set $X_{0:k}^i=(X_{0:k-1}^{A_k^i},X_k^i)$.
   3. Set $a_k^i=G_k(X_k^i)r_k(X_{k-1}^{A_k^i},X_k^i)$ and $\widehat Z_k=\widehat Z_{k-1}(N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^Na_k^i)$. If $\sum_i a_k^i>0$, put $\bar w_k^i=a_k^i/\sum_j a_k^j$; otherwise put $\bar w_k^i=1/N$.
3. Return $\widehat Z_t$ and the weighted empirical path probability measure $\widehat\pi_t^N=\sum_{i=1}^N\bar w_t^i\delta_{X_{0:t}^i}$. Its last-coordinate marginal is the corresponding empirical filtering approximation.

The all-zero fallback only defines a probability measure for reporting and future sampling. Once a zero average weight occurs, $\widehat Z$ remains zero. The procedure makes no finite-particle accuracy, consistency, or long-time stability claim.

Input a particle count $N\ge1$, nonnegative finite weights $a_1,\ldots,a_N$, and a scheme label, either multinomial or residual. Let $A=\sum_{j=1}^Na_j$. If $A>0$, set $p_j=a_j/A$; if $A=0$, set $p_j=1/N$ for every $j$. Thus $p$ is always a probability vector.

- **Multinomial scheme.** Draw an index vector $(J_1,\ldots,J_N)\in\{1,\ldots,N\}^N$ with conditional mass $\mathbb P(J_1=j_1,\ldots,J_N=j_N\mid a)=\prod_{\ell=1}^Np_{j_\ell}$. Put $C_j=\#\{\ell:J_\ell=j\}$.
- **Residual scheme.** Put $q_j=\lfloor Np_j\rfloor$, $r_j=Np_j-q_j$, and $R=\sum_{j=1}^Nr_j=N-\sum_{j=1}^Nq_j$, an integer in $\{0,\ldots,N-1\}$. If $R=0$, put $C_j=q_j$. If $R>0$, draw $(K_1,\ldots,K_R)$ with conditional mass $\mathbb P(K_1=k_1,\ldots,K_R=k_R\mid a)=\prod_{\ell=1}^R(r_{k_\ell}/R)$ and put $C_j=q_j+\#\{\ell:K_\ell=j\}$.

For multinomial resampling, return the sampled vector $(J_1,\ldots,J_N)$ in its sampled order, together with its count vector $(C_1,\ldots,C_N)$; do not sort the sampled indices. For residual resampling, return the ancestor list containing exactly $C_j$ copies of index $j$, ordered by increasing index, together with its count vector. Each output is a length-$N$ list and a count vector summing to $N$. When all input weights vanish, the uniform fallback defines the procedure; any downstream normalizer already multiplied by this zero average remains zero.

Assume AC and fix a finite horizon $T\in\mathbb N_0$. For each $0\le k\le T$, let $(\mathsf X_k,\mathcal X_k)$ be a standard Borel space. Let $\mu_0$ be a probability measure on $\mathsf X_0$, and for $1\le k\le T$ let $M_k:\mathsf X_{k-1}\rightsquigarrow\mathsf X_k$ be a probability kernel. A **potential** at time $k$ is a finite-valued nonnegative measurable function $G_k:\mathsf X_k\to[0,\infty)$. Write $\mathsf X_{0:t}=\prod_{k=0}^t\mathsf X_k$ with its finite-product sigma-algebra.

For each $0\le t\le T$, let $P_t^M$ be the finite path law with ordered kernel integral $\mu_0(dx_0)\prod_{k=1}^tM_k(x_{k-1},dx_k)$, supplied by Ionescu–Tulcea ([[thm-ionescu-tulcea-construction-of-a-markov-chain]]). The **unnormalized Feynman–Kac path measure** is
$$\gamma_t(A)=\int_{\mathsf X_{0:t}}\mathbf 1_A(x_{0:t})\prod_{k=0}^tG_k(x_k)\,P_t^M(dx_{0:t}),\qquad A\in\bigotimes_{k=0}^t\mathcal X_k.$$
Its **normalizer** is $Z_t=\gamma_t(\mathsf X_{0:t})=\gamma_t(1)\in[0,\infty]$. Only when $0<Z_t<\infty$ define the normalized path target $\pi_t^{\mathrm{FK}}=\gamma_t/Z_t$. The sequence $(\gamma_t)$ with its kernels and potentials is the Feynman–Kac flow.

State-space filtering kernels are conditional-law versions as in [[def-state-space-filtering-laws]]. A Feynman–Kac path target is not by itself an assertion that a pointwise conditional version has been selected at observation-null histories.

Assume AC and the finite-horizon setup of [[def-feynman-kac-path-targets-and-normalizers]]. For $1\le k\le T$ and every nonnegative product-measurable $\varphi:\mathsf X_{0:k}\to[0,\infty]$,
$$\gamma_k(\varphi)=\int_{\mathsf X_{0:k-1}}\gamma_{k-1}(dx_{0:k-1})\int_{\mathsf X_k}G_k(x_k)\varphi(x_{0:k})M_k(x_{k-1},dx_k),$$
with equality in $[0,\infty]$.

For Borel probability measures $\mu_n,\mu$ on a metric space S, write $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$ if $\int f\,d\mu_n\to\int f\,d\mu$ for every bounded continuous real function f on S. Continuity is [[def-metric-continuity]]. Such f is Borel measurable (inverse images of open sets are open) and $\int|f|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\mu(S)<\infty$, so the integrals are finite in [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]. No completeness or coupling is required.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $t>0$. Then
$$\mu(\{f\ge t\})\le\frac1t\int f\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim:
At time zero, for any bounded continuous $h$, put $V_i=G_0(X_0^i)h(X_0^i)$. Expanding the squared centered sample average, the cross terms vanish by independence and the diagonal terms give $\mathbb E[(
u_0^N(G_0h)-\mu_0(G_0h))^2]\le C^2\|h\|_\infty^2/N$. The same calculation with $V_i=G_0(X_0^i)$ gives the denominator bound $C^2/N$. Applying [F5] to each squared error shows both averages converge in probability to their $\mu_0$ integrals. The denominator limit is at least $c$, so the ratio $\eta_0^N(h)=
u_0^N(G_0h)/
u_0^N(G_0)$ converges in probability to $\mu_0(G_0h)/\mu_0(G_0)=\eta_0(h)$.

Suppose $\eta_{t-1}^N(g)\to\eta_{t-1}(g)$ in probability for every bounded continuous $g$. Conditional on the previous particles, [F1]–[F2] make $X_t^1,\ldots,X_t^N$ IID with common law $\eta_{t-1}^N M_t$. For bounded continuous $h$, the squared error of their empirical average under this product law is the sum of $N$ diagonal centered terms divided by $N^2$; the cross terms vanish by independence, and each diagonal term is at most $\|h\|_\infty^2$. Thus its integral is at most $\|h\|_\infty^2/N$. Applying [F5] under the conditional product law and then integrating over the previous particles gives $\nu_t^N(h)-\eta_{t-1}^N(M_th)\to0$ in probability. The Feller hypothesis makes $M_th$ bounded continuous, so the induction hypothesis gives $\eta_{t-1}^N(M_th)\to\eta_{t-1}(M_th)$.

Apply step 1.2 to $h$ and $G_th$, both bounded continuous. Then $\eta_t^N(h)=\nu_t^N(G_th)/\nu_t^N(G_t)$; the denominator converges to $\eta_{t-1}(M_tG_t)\ge c$. The ratio therefore converges in probability to $\eta_{t-1}(M_t(G_th))/\eta_{t-1}(M_tG_t)=\eta_t(h)$ by [F3]. Induction from step 1.1 proves the assertion for each fixed $t\le T$. The lower bound $c$ rules out zero normalizers, while the upper bound $C$ gives the finite variance bounds used above.

$f_{t+1}(x'\mid x)$ relative to a declared sigma-finite measure
$\lambda_{t+1}$, meaning
$$M_{t+1}(x,A)=\int_A f_{t+1}(x'\mid x)\,\lambda_{t+1}(dx')$$
for each measurable $A$. For each $t<T$, define the predictive score with
zero-weight terms omitted:

If an exact filtering kernel $\eta_T$ and supplied backward conditional
kernels $B_t$ from
[[lem-smoothing-backward-kernel-bayes-factorization]] are available for
general transition kernels, there is a separate exact-kernel mode: draw
$S$ conditionally independent paths, each by drawing $X_T\sim\eta_T$ and then
drawing $X_t\sim B_t(X_{t+1},\cdot)$ successively backward. This mode uses
the actual kernels; it does not evaluate a transition density or a kernel on
particle singletons. It returns exact smoothing paths under the supplied
conditional versions wherever their factorization holds.

An optional all-marginals mode computes particle smoothing weights instead
of drawing paths. Initialize $\bar w_{T|T}^j=w_T^j$. For
$t=T-1,\ldots,0$, let $J_{t+1}=\{j:\bar w_{t+1|T}^j>0\}$. For each
$j\in J_{t+1}$ and $i$ with $w_t^i>0$, set
$$b_{t}^{i,j}=\frac{w_t^i f_{t+1}(x_{t+1}^j\mid x_t^i)}{q_{t+1}^N(x_{t+1}^j)};$$
set $b_t^{i,j}=0$ without evaluating the density if $j\notin J_{t+1}$ or
$w_t^i=0$. Update
$$\bar w_{t|T}^i=\sum_{j\in J_{t+1}}\bar w_{t+1|T}^j b_t^{i,j}.$$
For every active $j$, $(b_t^{i,j})_{i=1}^N$ is a probability vector, so the
raw updated values are nonnegative and already sum to one; explicit
normalization leaves them unchanged. Return
$\sum_i\bar w_{t|T}^i\delta_{x_t^i}$ as the approximate smoothed marginal at
time $t$. The algorithm makes no finite-particle accuracy, consistency, or
long-time stability claim.

derivations.claim: For any child value $x'$ at which a backward weight vector is required, the mode's admissibility condition gives $0<q_{t+1}^N(x')<\infty$. For each index with $w_t^i=0$ the algorithm sets its backward probability to zero without evaluating its density; for each positive-weight index the score is finite and nonnegative. Summing over $i$ therefore gives $\sum_{i:w_t^i>0}w_t^if_{t+1}(x'\mid x_t^i)/q_{t+1}^N(x')=1$. Thus each required backward vector is a probability vector.

Suppose $\sum_j\bar w_{t+1|T}^j=1$. For every $j$ with $\bar w_{t+1|T}^j>0$, admissibility makes its score sum finite positive, and the associated vector $(b_t^{i,j})_i$ sums to one by step 1.1. The raw update is $\bar w_{t|T}^i=\sum_{j:\bar w_{t+1|T}^j>0}\bar w_{t+1|T}^jb_t^{i,j}$. Summing over $i$ gives $\sum_{j:\bar w_{t+1|T}^j>0}\bar w_{t+1|T}^j=1$. Since $\bar w_{T|T}=w_T$ sums to one, backward induction proves every update is already normalized; zero smoothing-weight terms are never evaluated.

At each of the $T$ backward times for one sampled path, the algorithm evaluates $N$ transition scores and scans $N$ probabilities; terminal sampling also scans $N$ entries. Storing the path costs $O(T+1)$, so $S$ paths take $O(SN(T+1))$ operations. In the all-marginals recursion, initialization and output cost $O(N(T+1))$, while each backward time evaluates one transition score and performs bounded arithmetic for each of the $N^2$ past/future particle pairs. The total is $O(N(T+1)+N^2T)=O(N+N^2T)$ because $N\ge1$. For fixed $S$ this gives $O(N(T+1))$ path cost, and when $T\ge1$ the bounds reduce to $O(SNT)$ and $O(N^2T)$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $E_0,\ldots,E_T$ be compact metric spaces, let $\mu_0$ be a probability
on $E_0$, and let $M_t$ be a Feller probability kernel from $E_{t-1}$ to
$E_t$. Here **Feller** means that $x\mapsto M_t h(x):=\int h(x')M_t(x,dx')$
is continuous for every bounded continuous real $h$ on $E_t$. Let each
potential $G_t:E_t\to\mathbb R$ be continuous and satisfy fixed bounds
$0<c\le G_t(x)\le C<\infty$. Let $P_t^M$ be the Markov path law and
$Z_t=\int\prod_{s=0}^tG_s(x_s)\,P_t^M(dx_{0:t})$ the Feynman–Kac normalizer
from [[def-feynman-kac-path-targets-and-normalizers]]. Since $P_t^M$ is a
probability, $c^{t+1}\le Z_t\le C^{t+1}$, so the normalized path target exists.
For the initial law and transitions use the
bootstrap proposals $\nu_0=\mu_0$, $R_t=M_t$, initial potential $G_0$, and
multinomial resampling in
[[alg-sequential-importance-resampling]]. Write $\eta_t$ for the last-state
marginal of $\gamma_t/Z_t$ and
$\eta_t^N=\sum_iw_t^i\delta_{X_t^i}$ for the particle filter's current
weighted empirical measure. For every fixed $t\le T$,
$$\eta_t^N\Rightarrow\eta_t\quad\hbox{in probability as }N\to\infty,$$
where convergence in probability means that for every bounded continuous
$h:E_t\to\mathbb R$, $\int h\,d\eta_t^N\to\int h\,d\eta_t$ in probability.
This is a fixed-horizon, positive-bounded-potential result; it asserts no
time-uniform bound and no particle central limit theorem.

Assume AC, a finite-horizon Markov state-space model with standard-Borel
states, dominated observation kernels, and data-indexed filtering and
smoothing kernels as in
[[def-state-space-filtering-laws]]. Fix an observation history
$y_{1:T}$ in the full-measure set where the dominated filtering recursion
[[thm-dominated-state-space-filtering-recursion]] applies. Write $\eta_t$
for the filtering law of $X_t$ given $y_{1:t}$. Suppose the transition kernel
$M_{t+1}$ from time $t$ to $t+1$ has a product-measurable density
$f_{t+1}(x'\mid x)$ with respect to a sigma-finite measure $\lambda_{t+1}$,
meaning
$$M_{t+1}(x,A)=\int_A f_{t+1}(x'\mid x)\,\lambda_{t+1}(dx')$$
for every state $x$ and measurable set $A$.
Put
$$q_{t+1}(x')=\int f_{t+1}(x'\mid x)\,\eta_t(dx),\qquad D_{t+1}=\{x':0<q_{t+1}(x')<\infty\}.$$
The backward conditional kernel is
$$B_t(x',A)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\int_A f_{t+1}(x'\mid x)\,\eta_t(dx)}{q_{t+1}(x')},&x'\in D_{t+1},\\\eta_t(A),&x'\notin D_{t+1}.\end{cases}$$
It is a probability-kernel version of the conditional law of $X_t$ given
$X_{t+1}=x'$ and $y_{1:t}$. The finite-horizon smoothing kernel factors as
$$\psi_T(dx_{0:T})=\eta_T(dx_T)\prod_{t=T-1}^{0}B_t(x_{t+1},dx_t)$$
for observation-almost every full history, with the product interpreted as
successive backwards kernel integration. If the transition is supplied only
as a probability kernel, the same factorization uses a supplied regular
conditional kernel of $X_t$ given $(X_{t+1},Y_{1:t})$; no transition density
is asserted in that case. Null-history values remain version-dependent.

Fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$ and a requested path count $S\ge1$, used in
either mode below. In the **particle mode**, the inputs include a particle
count $N\ge1$ and normalized filtering clouds
$$\{(x_t^i,w_t^i):1\le i\le N\},\qquad w_t^i\ge0,\quad\sum_{i=1}^Nw_t^i=1,$$
for $0\le t\le T$, produced, for example, by
[[alg-sequential-importance-resampling]]. Each $x_t^i$ is the time-$t$
coordinate of its stored particle path. Write $M_{t+1}$ for the model
transition kernel and require a product-measurable density
$f_{t+1}(x'\mid x)$ relative to a declared sigma-finite measure
$\lambda_{t+1}$, meaning
$$M_{t+1}(x,A)=\int_A f_{t+1}(x'\mid x)\,\lambda_{t+1}(dx')$$
for each measurable $A$. For each $t<T$, define the predictive score with
zero-weight terms omitted:
$$q_{t+1}^N(x')=\sum_{i:w_t^i>0}w_t^i f_{t+1}(x'\mid x_t^i).$$
For particle-mode path sampling, define the set of reachable indices
recursively by $R_T=\{j:w_T^j>0\}$. Descending from $t=T-1$ to $0$, require
$q_{t+1}^N(x_{t+1}^j)\in(0,\infty)$ for every $j\in R_{t+1}$, and put
$$R_t=\bigcup_{j\in R_{t+1}}\{i:w_t^i>0,\ f_{t+1}(x_{t+1}^j\mid x_t^i)>0\}.$$
These are exactly the indices that can be drawn with positive probability at
the corresponding backward step. For the all-marginals mode below, require
instead that $q_{t+1}^N(x_{t+1}^j)\in(0,\infty)$ whenever the current
smoothing weight $\bar w_{t+1|T}^j$ is positive. Thus no denominator is
required for an omitted zero-weight term. At $T=0$ there are no denominator
conditions.

In particle mode, repeat independently for $s=1,\ldots,S$:

1. Draw $I_T^s$ from $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ with probabilities $w_T^i$ and set
   $\widetilde X_T^s=x_T^{I_T^s}$.
2. For $t=T-1,T-2,\ldots,0$, set $b_t^i=0$ without evaluating the density
   whenever $w_t^i=0$. For $w_t^i>0$, set
   $$b_t^i(\widetilde X_{t+1}^s)=\frac{w_t^i f_{t+1}(\widetilde X_{t+1}^s\mid x_t^i)}{q_{t+1}^N(\widetilde X_{t+1}^s)}.$$
   Draw $I_t^s$ from this probability vector, and set
   $\widetilde X_t^s=x_t^{I_t^s}$.
3. Return the tuple
   $$\widetilde X_{0:T}^s=(x_0^{I_0^s},\ldots,x_T^{I_T^s}).$$
   This is a draw from the particle backward approximation to the smoothing
   path law. The coordinates are selected by separate backward indices and
   need not be the stored forward ancestor history of any one particle.
The particle path-sampling output is the list
$\widetilde X_{0:T}^1,\ldots,\widetilde X_{0:T}^S$.

If an exact filtering kernel $\eta_T$ and supplied backward conditional
kernels $B_t$ from
[[lem-smoothing-backward-kernel-bayes-factorization]] are available for
general transition kernels, there is a separate exact-kernel mode: draw
$S$ conditionally independent paths, each by drawing $X_T\sim\eta_T$ and then
drawing $X_t\sim B_t(X_{t+1},\cdot)$ successively backward. This mode uses
the actual kernels; it does not evaluate a transition density or a kernel on
particle singletons. It returns exact smoothing paths under the supplied
conditional versions wherever their factorization holds.

An optional all-marginals mode computes particle smoothing weights instead
of drawing paths. Initialize $\bar w_{T|T}^j=w_T^j$. For
$t=T-1,\ldots,0$, let $J_{t+1}=\{j:\bar w_{t+1|T}^j>0\}$. For each
$j\in J_{t+1}$ and $i$ with $w_t^i>0$, set
$$b_{t}^{i,j}=\frac{w_t^i f_{t+1}(x_{t+1}^j\mid x_t^i)}{q_{t+1}^N(x_{t+1}^j)};$$
set $b_t^{i,j}=0$ without evaluating the density if $j\notin J_{t+1}$ or
$w_t^i=0$. Update
$$\bar w_{t|T}^i=\sum_{j\in J_{t+1}}\bar w_{t+1|T}^j b_t^{i,j}.$$
For every active $j$, $(b_t^{i,j})_{i=1}^N$ is a probability vector, so the
raw updated values are nonnegative and already sum to one; explicit
normalization leaves them unchanged. Return
$\sum_i\bar w_{t|T}^i\delta_{x_t^i}$ as the approximate smoothed marginal at
time $t$. The algorithm makes no finite-particle accuracy, consistency, or
long-time stability claim.

For Borel probability measures $\mu_n,\mu$ on a metric space S, write $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$ if $\int f\,d\mu_n\to\int f\,d\mu$ for every bounded continuous real function f on S. Continuity is [[def-metric-continuity]]. Such f is Borel measurable (inverse images of open sets are open) and $\int|f|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\mu(S)<\infty$, so the integrals are finite in [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]. No completeness or coupling is required.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $t>0$. Then
$$\mu(\{f\ge t\})\le\frac1t\int f\,d\mu.$$

Assume AC and a finite-horizon model as in
[[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]. For each $1\le t\le T$, let
$\nu_t$ be a sigma-finite measure on $(F_t,\mathcal F_t)$ and suppose the
observation kernel has a specified product-measurable density
$g_t:E_t\times F_t\to[0,\infty]$ with respect to $\mathcal E_t\otimes\mathcal F_t$:
$$G_t(x,B)=\int_B g_t(x,y)\,\nu_t(dy),\qquad\int_{F_t}g_t(x,y)\,\nu_t(dy)=1$$
for every state $x\in E_t$ and measurable $B\subseteq F_t$. For
$h\in\mathsf F_{1:t-1}$, let $\pi_{t-1}$ be the filtering kernel at time
$t-1$ from
[[def-state-space-filtering-laws]] when $t>1$, and for $t=1$ let $\pi_0$ be
the initial kernel $\mu_0$ on the singleton empty-history space. For
$A\in\mathcal E_t$, define the predictive kernel
$$\widehat\pi_t(h,A):=\int_{E_{t-1}}K_t(x,A)\,\pi_{t-1}(h,dx),$$
the evidence density
$$z_t(h,y):=\int_{E_t}g_t(x,y)\,\widehat\pi_t(h,dx),$$
and for $h\in\mathsf F_{1:t-1}$, $y\in F_t$, and $A\in\mathcal E_t$ define
the update
$$\pi_t(h,y,A):=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\int_Ag_t(x,y)\,\widehat\pi_t(h,dx)}{z_t(h,y)},&0<z_t(h,y)<\infty,\\[6pt]\widehat\pi_t(h,A),&z_t(h,y)=0\text{ or }z_t(h,y)=\infty.\end{cases}$$
Then $\widehat\pi_t$ is a predictive kernel for $X_t$ given $Y_{1:t-1}$,
and $\pi_t$ is a filtering kernel for $X_t$ given $Y_{1:t}$. For each fixed
history $h$, the observation marginal under the conditional version
determined by $\widehat\pi_t(h,\cdot)$ has density
$z_t(h,\cdot)$ with respect to $\nu_t$ and assigns zero mass to both
$\{y:z_t(h,y)=0\}$ and $\{y:z_t(h,y)=\infty\}$. Thus the formula never
divides by zero or infinity; values on those fibers are conditional-law
fillers. The statement is exact and finite-horizon and gives no numerical
approximation or long-time stability claim.

derivations.claim: For each $0\le t<T$, let $h$ be bounded continuous and let $x_n\to x$. Uniform continuity of $f_{t+1}$ on the compact product gives $\sup_{x'}|f_{t+1}(x'\mid x_n)-f_{t+1}(x'\mid x)|\to0$. Since $\lambda_{t+1}$ is a probability measure, $|M_{t+1}h(x_n)-M_{t+1}h(x)|\le\|h\|_\infty\sup_{x'}|f_{t+1}(x'\mid x_n)-f_{t+1}(x'\mid x)|\to0.$ Thus each transition is Feller.

By [F1] and [F6], for every $0\le t\le T$ the random filtering measure $\eta_t^N$ converges weakly in probability to the exact filtering law $\eta_t$ at the fixed observation history. For each $0\le t<T$, put $q_{t+1}(x')=\int f_{t+1}(x'\mid x)\eta_t(dx)$ and $q_{t+1}^N(x')=\int f_{t+1}(x'\mid x)\eta_t^N(dx)$. The density bounds imply $a\le q_{t+1}(x'),q_{t+1}^N(x')\le b$ for every $x'$, so every backward denominator used by the algorithm is finite positive.

Fix $0\le t<T$ and a continuous $h$ on $E_t$. The families $x\mapsto f_{t+1}(x'\mid x)$ and $x\mapsto h(x)f_{t+1}(x'\mid x)$ indexed by $x'\in E_{t+1}$ are uniformly bounded and equicontinuous: joint continuity on the compact product is uniformly continuous. For any $\epsilon>0$, a finite $\epsilon$-net of the compact parameter space gives a finite sup-norm net for each family. Weak convergence in probability from step 2.1 gives convergence of the integrals for every function in each finite net; since all measures have mass one, replacing a family member by a net function changes either integral by at most $\epsilon$. Letting $\epsilon\downarrow0$ proves uniform-in-$x'$ convergence of both numerators and denominators. Division is stable because all denominators are at least $a$, so $\sup_{x'}|B_t^N h(x')-B_th(x')|\to0$ in probability for the empirical and exact backward kernels. The exact function $B_th$ is continuous by dominated convergence.

For each $0\le t<T$, set $\omega_f(\delta)=\sup_{x,x',x'' : d(x',x'')\le\delta}|f_{t+1}(x'\mid x)-f_{t+1}(x''\mid x)|$, which tends to zero by uniform continuity. The exact and empirical backward kernels have densities $f_{t+1}(x'\mid x)/q_{t+1}(x')$ relative to $\eta_t$ and $f_{t+1}(x'\mid x)/q_{t+1}^N(x')$ relative to $\eta_t^N$, respectively. Using [F2]–[F3], $q,q^N\in[a,b]$ from step 2.1, and that both filtering measures have mass one, their total-variation distance at $x',x''$ is at most $\omega_f(\delta)(a^{-1}+ba^{-2})$. Indeed, if $H(u,x)$ is a continuous integrand indexed by remaining coordinates $u$, and $x'_u$ denotes the next-state coordinate in $u$, then the difference of its integrals at $u,u'$ is bounded by $\sup_x|H(u,x)-H(u',x)|+\|H\|_\infty\|B(\cdot\mid x'_u)-B(\cdot\mid x'_{u'})\|_{\rm TV}$; uniform continuity of $H$ and the displayed kernel bound make this tend uniformly to zero as $u'\to u$. Thus each backward integration preserves a common bound and modulus of equicontinuity over the remaining compact coordinates, uniformly over all particle clouds. Since $T$ is finite, iterating this estimate yields one such class for every section in the finite telescoping sum.

Telescope the finite backward product by replacing one empirical kernel at a time with its exact counterpart. The uniform moduli from step 3.2 put every possible section, over all clouds and remaining coordinates, in a uniformly bounded equicontinuous class on a compact metric space. Such a class has a finite sup-norm net: choose a finite $\delta$-net of the domain at a scale given by equicontinuity, quantize the bounded function values on those finitely many points, and retain one representative for each nonempty quantized pattern. Step 3.1 gives convergence for each fixed test in this finite net; since kernels are probabilities, the sup-norm approximation changes an integral difference by at most twice the net radius. The same finite-net argument and [F1] give convergence of the terminal empirical integrals uniformly over the resulting class. Thus every term in the finite telescoping sum tends to zero in probability, and the conditional path law $\widehat\psi_T^N$ converges weakly in the sense of [F4] to the exact product law $\psi_T$ in [F2].

Conditional on the particle clouds, the $S_N$ backward paths are IID with law $\widehat\psi_T^N$. Their conditional sample mean has variance at most $\|\Phi\|_\infty^2/S_N$. Applying [F5] to its squared centered deviation shows that its difference from $\widehat\psi_T^N(\Phi)$ converges to zero in probability because $S_N\to\infty$. Combining this with step 4.1 proves the second limit. If $S_N$ is fixed, this variance bound need not vanish, so no convergence of the path average is asserted.

The uniform lower density bound a>0 makes all exact and empirical backward denominators at least a in step 2.1.
The argument includes N=1 at finite N; convergence concerns the sequence N tending to infinity. The item statement and proof address this boundary case.

risk_review.notes: Read all six steps and all seven current direct dependencies. Joint continuous transition densities on compact products are uniformly continuous, giving the Feller property by integration against probability lambda. The bootstrap filter theorem applies with continuous G in [c,C]; dominated recursion and the stated good observation history identify the actual filters. Both true and empirical backward denominators lie in [a,b]. Finite parameter nets make density-weighted numerator/denominator convergence uniform in the next state, and division is stable at a>0. Step 3.2 controls variation in each backward kernel by the density modulus and q>=a; integrating sections preserves uniform bounds and equicontinuity independently of clouds. Step 4.1 gives the necessary finite sup-norm nets for those possibly random sections, so testwise filter convergence suffices for the finite product telescoping argument; no unjustified random-test substitution is used. Finally conditional IID path draws have squared-error bound ||Phi||^2/S_N, which vanishes only when S_N grows. T=0 reduces to the initial empirical measure and conditional sampling; deterministic singleton cases remain valid. No time-uniform or fixed-S empirical consistency is asserted. No defect or repair.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

For a finite horizon $T\ge0$, fix an integer lag $L\ge0$, a path count
$S\ge1$, and the normalized
filtering particle clouds and transition inputs required by
[[alg-particle-backward-simulator]]. For each time $t\in\{0,\ldots,T\}$,
put $s_t=\min(t+L,T)$. Independently for each $t$, run the particle backward
simulator using only the filtering clouds at times $0,\ldots,s_t$ and request
$S$ paths. Retain their time-$t$ coordinates $\widetilde X_t^{t,1},\ldots,
\widetilde X_t^{t,S}$ and return the empirical measure
$$\widehat\eta_{t|s_t}^{S}=\frac1S\sum_{r=1}^S\delta_{\widetilde X_t^{t,r}}.$$
In particle mode this empirical law approximates
$$\mathcal L(X_t\mid Y_{1:s_t}),$$
not the full smoothing law $\mathcal L(X_t\mid Y_{1:T})$ unless $s_t=T$ or
the two conditional laws happen to agree. The same procedure can use supplied
exact backward kernels when the model has no transition density; for each
$s_t$ it uses the supplied filtering kernel at $y_{1:s_t}$ and the backward
kernels for the corresponding prefix histories. On histories where these
kernels factor the truncated smoother, it samples that exact conditional law.

The procedure returns one truncated smoothing marginal per $t$. It does not
assert a bound on the lag bias, a forgetting rate, or convergence to the
full-data smoother for fixed $L$. Those conclusions require separate
conditions on the model.

Assume AC, a finite-horizon Markov state-space model with standard-Borel
states, dominated observation kernels, and data-indexed filtering and
smoothing kernels as in
[[def-state-space-filtering-laws]]. Fix an observation history
$y_{1:T}$ in the full-measure set where the dominated filtering recursion
[[thm-dominated-state-space-filtering-recursion]] applies. Write $\eta_t$
for the filtering law of $X_t$ given $y_{1:t}$. Suppose the transition kernel
$M_{t+1}$ from time $t$ to $t+1$ has a product-measurable density
$f_{t+1}(x'\mid x)$ with respect to a sigma-finite measure $\lambda_{t+1}$,
meaning
$$M_{t+1}(x,A)=\int_A f_{t+1}(x'\mid x)\,\lambda_{t+1}(dx')$$
for every state $x$ and measurable set $A$.
Put
$$q_{t+1}(x')=\int f_{t+1}(x'\mid x)\,\eta_t(dx),\qquad D_{t+1}=\{x':0<q_{t+1}(x')<\infty\}.$$
The backward conditional kernel is
$$B_t(x',A)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\int_A f_{t+1}(x'\mid x)\,\eta_t(dx)}{q_{t+1}(x')},&x'\in D_{t+1},\\\eta_t(A),&x'\notin D_{t+1}.\end{cases}$$
It is a probability-kernel version of the conditional law of $X_t$ given
$X_{t+1}=x'$ and $y_{1:t}$. The finite-horizon smoothing kernel factors as
$$\psi_T(dx_{0:T})=\eta_T(dx_T)\prod_{t=T-1}^{0}B_t(x_{t+1},dx_t)$$
for observation-almost every full history, with the product interpreted as
successive backwards kernel integration. If the transition is supplied only
as a probability kernel, the same factorization uses a supplied regular
conditional kernel of $X_t$ given $(X_{t+1},Y_{1:t})$; no transition density
is asserted in that case. Null-history values remain version-dependent.

Assume AC. Let $Z_t$ take values in a standard-Borel space
$(\mathsf Z_t,\mathcal Z_t)$ and let $U_t\in\mathbb R^{d_t}$ for a finite
horizon $0\le t\le T$, where each $d_t$ is a positive integer. For
$1\le t\le T$, let $Y_t\in\mathbb R^{p_t}$ with each $p_t$ a positive
integer; observations begin at time $1$. The nonlinear
component has initial probability $\mu_0$ and transition probability kernels
$M_t(z_{t-1},dz_t)$; its transition does not depend on $U_{t-1}$. Given the
entire nonlinear path $z_{0:T}$, write $\mathsf Z_{0:t}=\prod_{s=0}^t\mathsf Z_s$
with its finite-product sigma-algebra and specify Borel maps
$$m_0:\mathsf Z_0\to\mathbb R^{d_0},\qquad P_0:\mathsf Z_0\to\mathbb R^{d_0\times d_0},$$
and, for $1\le t\le T$,
$$A_t:\mathsf Z_{0:t}\to\mathbb R^{d_t\times d_{t-1}},\quad Q_t:\mathsf Z_{0:t}\to\mathbb R^{d_t\times d_t},\quad C_t:\mathsf Z_{0:t}\to\mathbb R^{p_t\times d_t},\quad R_t:\mathsf Z_{0:t}\to\mathbb R^{p_t\times p_t}.$$
Require $P_0(z_0)$ and
$Q_t(z_{0:t})$ to be symmetric positive semidefinite, meaning
$v^TPv\ge0$ for every matching vector $v$, and $R_t(z_{0:t})$ to be
symmetric positive definite, meaning $v^TR_tv>0$ for every nonzero $v$. Conditional
on $Z_{0:T}=z_{0:T}$, the linear component and observations have the finite
linear-Gaussian model, with the transition and observation equations for
$1\le t\le T$:
$$U_0\sim N(m_0(z_0),P_0(z_0)),\qquad U_t=A_t(z_{0:t})U_{t-1}+\xi_t,\qquad Y_t=C_t(z_{0:t})U_t+\varepsilon_t,$$
where the centered Gaussian noises $\xi_t\sim N(0,Q_t(z_{0:t}))$ and
$\varepsilon_t\sim N(0,R_t(z_{0:t}))$ are mutually independent over time
and independent of $U_0$, under that conditional law. For every fixed path
$z_{0:T}$ these are exactly the hypotheses of
[[def-linear-gaussian-state-space-model-with-independent-noises]] with
deterministic matrices.

This hierarchical conditionally linear-Gaussian model is the input class for
the Rao–Blackwellized filter below: it samples the nonlinear path and keeps
the conditional Gaussian law of $U_t$ analytically. It does not include a
nonlinear transition whose law depends on $U_{t-1}$, nor does it assert that
the marginal nonlinear process remains Markov after conditioning on all
observations. Such models need their own marginal transition and backward
kernels. A state-space filtering or smoothing law is a data-indexed regular
conditional-distribution version as in
[[def-state-space-filtering-laws]]; no pointwise uniqueness on null data
histories is imposed.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the model of
[[def-conditionally-linear-gaussian-state-space-model]] and fix a nonlinear
path $z_{0:T}$. Run [[alg-kalman-filter]] on the resulting deterministic
linear-Gaussian model for a fixed observation path $y_{1:T}$. Write
$m_{t|t-1},P_{t|t-1}$ and $m_{t|t},P_{t|t}$ for its predicted and updated
moments, and define
$$v_t=y_t-C_t(z_{0:t})m_{t|t-1},\qquad S_t=C_t(z_{0:t})P_{t|t-1}C_t(z_{0:t})^T+R_t(z_{0:t}).$$
Then $\mathcal L(U_t\mid Z_{0:T}=z_{0:T},Y_{1:t}=y_{1:t})$ has the Gaussian
version $N(m_{t|t},P_{t|t})$ for every $0\le t\le T$. At time $t\ge1$, the
conditional observation density given the nonlinear path and earlier
observations is
$$\ell_t(z_{0:t};y_{1:t})=(2\pi)^{-p_t/2}\det(S_t)^{-1/2}\exp\!\left(-\tfrac12v_t^TS_t^{-1}v_t\right).$$
Each $S_t$ is positive definite, each $P_{t|t}$ is positive semidefinite,
and $\ell_t$ is finite, strictly positive, and Borel in the nonlinear path.
For every $1\le t\le T$ whose observation evidence is finite positive, the
conditional density of $Y_{1:t}$ given the nonlinear path is
$\prod_{s=1}^t\ell_s(z_{0:s};y_{1:s})$. Consequently the conditional law of
$Z_{0:t}$ given $Y_{1:t}=y_{1:t}$ is the normalized Feynman–Kac path measure
with path-extension transitions induced by $M_s$, initial potential
$G_0\equiv1$, and potentials $G_s(z_{0:s})=\ell_s(z_{0:s};y_{1:s})$. At
$t=0$ it is the initial nonlinear law $\mu_0$.

Use the conditionally linear-Gaussian model of
[[def-conditionally-linear-gaussian-state-space-model]] and a fixed
observation path $y_{1:T}$. For each $0\le t\le T$, let $\bar P_t$ be the
nonlinear path law generated by $\mu_0$ and the path-extension kernels from
[[lem-nonlinear-path-extension-is-a-probability-kernel]], and
put
$$c_t(y_{1:t})=\int_{\mathsf Z_{0:t}}\prod_{s=1}^t\ell_s(z_{0:s};y_{1:s})\,\bar P_t(dz_{0:t}),\qquad c_0=1.$$
Here $\ell_s$ is the conditional observation density supplied by
[[lem-kalman-filter-is-exact-conditional-on-nonlinear-path]].
For the claim that the procedure targets the nonlinear filtering law at every
prefix, assume $0<c_t(y_{1:t})<\infty$ for every $t$; this is the finite-positive
normalizer condition for the normalized Feynman–Kac target. The Kalman
likelihood factorization identifies $c_t$ with the observation
evidence density and the normalized path target with the exact conditional
law of $Z_{0:t}$ given $Y_{1:t}=y_{1:t}$. The particle procedure itself uses
finite positive per-particle likelihoods, so each of
its empirical weight normalizers is finite positive. The particle state at
time $t$ is the full
nonlinear history $z_{0:t}$; finite products of the standard-Borel state
spaces are standard Borel. Its transition appends a draw
$z_t\sim M_t(z_{t-1},\cdot)$; the resulting path-extension probability
kernel and standard-Borel path space are supplied by
[[lem-nonlinear-path-extension-is-a-probability-kernel]]. Set the initial Feynman–Kac potential to
$G_0\equiv1$ and the time-$t$ potential to the conditional observation
density
$$G_t(z_{0:t})=\ell_t(z_{0:t};y_{1:t})$$
from [[lem-kalman-filter-is-exact-conditional-on-nonlinear-path]]. Use the
same path-extension kernel as target and proposal, so the initial and
transition Radon–Nikodym weights are identically one. Run
[[alg-sequential-importance-resampling]] with multinomial resampling to
approximate the filtering law of the nonlinear path. Each particle stores
alongside its path the conditional Gaussian moments of $U_t$.

Initialize $N\ge1$ particles by drawing $z_0^i\sim\mu_0$ independently,
setting $w_0^i=1/N$, $m_{0|0}^i=m_0(z_0^i)$, and
$P_{0|0}^i=P_0(z_0^i)$. For each $t=1,\ldots,T$:

1. Draw ancestor indices $J_t^1,\ldots,J_t^N$ independently with
   probabilities $(w_{t-1}^1,\ldots,w_{t-1}^N)$ and append independent
   transitions $z_t^i\sim M_t(z_{t-1}^{J_t^i},\cdot)$.
2. For each particle, abbreviate its appended path by $z_{0:t}^i$ and compute
   $$m_{t|t-1}^i=A_t(z_{0:t}^i)m_{t-1|t-1}^{J_t^i},\qquad P_{t|t-1}^i=A_t(z_{0:t}^i)P_{t-1|t-1}^{J_t^i}A_t(z_{0:t}^i)^T+Q_t(z_{0:t}^i).$$
   Form $v_t^i=y_t-C_t(z_{0:t}^i)m_{t|t-1}^i$ and
   $S_t^i=C_t(z_{0:t}^i)P_{t|t-1}^iC_t(z_{0:t}^i)^T+R_t(z_{0:t}^i)$.
3. Set the incremental weight to the finite positive Gaussian density
   $$a_t^i=(2\pi)^{-p_t/2}\det(S_t^i)^{-1/2}\exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(v_t^i)^T(S_t^i)^{-1}v_t^i\right),$$
   and normalize $w_t^i=a_t^i/\sum_j a_t^j$.
4. Update the conditional Gaussian moments by
   $$K_t^i=P_{t|t-1}^iC_t(z_{0:t}^i)^T(S_t^i)^{-1},\qquad m_{t|t}^i=m_{t|t-1}^i+K_t^iv_t^i,\qquad P_{t|t}^i=P_{t|t-1}^i-K_t^iS_t^i(K_t^i)^T.$$

The procedure returns the weighted nonlinear particle paths and the Gaussian
mixture
$$\widehat\pi_t^N(du_t,dz_{0:t})=\sum_{i=1}^Nw_t^iN(du_t;m_{t|t}^i,P_{t|t}^i)\,\delta_{z_{0:t}^i}(dz_{0:t}).$$
Its conditional mean is $\sum_iw_t^im_{t|t}^i$ and its conditional covariance
is $\sum_iw_t^i[P_{t|t}^i+(m_{t|t}^i-\bar m_t)(m_{t|t}^i-\bar m_t)^T]$,
where $\bar m_t=\sum_iw_t^im_{t|t}^i$. These are moments of the finite
mixture approximation; for finite $N$ the algorithm remains an approximation
to the full nonlinear filter. It makes no general variance-reduction,
convergence-rate, or long-time accuracy claim.

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$, $m\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $\Sigma$ be a real symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then its law has Lebesgue density
$$f_{m,\Sigma}(x)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\det(\Sigma)^{-1/2} \exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(x-m)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-m)\right), \qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$

derivations.claim: The state and observation noises are independent centered Gaussians, the conditional initial covariance is $1$, the process covariance is $1$, and the observation covariance is $1>0$. Thus the model satisfies [F1] and the exact conditional Kalman interface [F2].

Conditional on $Z_1=z$, prediction gives $m_{1|0}=0$ and $P_{1|0}=a_z^2+1$. Hence $P_{1|0}=1$ for $z=0$ and $P_{1|0}=2$ for $z=1$. The innovation is zero and the innovation variances are $S_0=2$ and $S_1=3$.

By [F4], the two conditional observation densities at zero are $\ell_0=(4\pi)^{-1/2}$ and $\ell_1=(6\pi)^{-1/2}$. Multiplying by the equal prior masses and normalizing gives $P(Z_1=0\mid Y_1=0)=\sqrt3/(\sqrt3+\sqrt2)$ and $P(Z_1=1\mid Y_1=0)=\sqrt2/(\sqrt3+\sqrt2)$.

The Kalman covariance update is $P_{1|1}=P_{1|0}R/(P_{1|0}+R)$ here, so the two conditional posterior variances are $1/2$ and $2/3$; both conditional means remain zero. Mixing these exact conditional Gaussians with the mode probabilities from step 2.1 gives the displayed posterior. The filter in [F3] uses these same per-mode likelihoods and Gaussian components; only its finite particle approximation to the mode weights is random.

The two mode components are explicitly enumerated, so each conditional state dimension is one. The item statement and proof address this boundary case.
The nonlinear transition is deterministic but is a valid probability kernel; step 1.1 covers it.
The single observation update at t=1 is computed in steps 1.2, 2.1 and 3.1.
The finite two-mode arithmetic and Gaussian formulas make no selections. The item statement and proof address this boundary case.
