citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC and fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$ with a state-space model by
probability kernels as in
[[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]. If $T=0$, put $\Omega_T=E_0$;
otherwise put $\Omega_T=E_0\times E_1\times F_1\times\cdots\times E_T\times
F_T$. Let $\mathcal Z_T$ be the corresponding finite-product sigma-algebra
and write $(\Omega_T,\mathcal Z_T,P_T)$ for its finite-horizon probability
space. The law $P_T$ is the unique law supplied by
[[thm-finite-horizon-state-space-kernel-law-exists-uniquely]]. Let $X_t$ and
$Y_t$ be the coordinate random elements taking values in $E_t$ and $F_t$. For
$t\ge1$, write $Y_{1:t}:=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_t)$ and
$\mathsf F_{1:t}:=F_1\times\cdots\times F_t$ with its finite-product
sigma-algebra; let $\mathsf F_{1:0}$ be a singleton and $Y_{1:0}$ its constant
map. The factors are standard Borel, meaning measurably isomorphic to Polish
spaces ([[def-standard-borel-space]]), and their finite products are standard
Borel ([[lem-finite-products-of-standard-borel-spaces-are-standard-borel]]).

The **initial filtering kernel** $\pi_0:\mathsf F_{1:0}\to E_0$ assigns
$\mu_0$ to the unique empty history; it is the conditional law of $X_0$ given
the trivial history. For $1\le t\le T$, a **filtering kernel at time $t$** is
a probability kernel $\pi_t:\mathsf F_{1:t}\to E_t$ such that
$\omega\mapsto\pi_t(Y_{1:t}(\omega),\cdot)$ is a regular conditional
distribution of $X_t$ given $\sigma(Y_{1:t})$. For $1\le t\le T$, a
**predictive kernel at time $t$** is a probability kernel
$\pi_{t|t-1}:\mathsf F_{1:t-1}\to E_t$ whose composition with $Y_{1:t-1}$
is a regular conditional distribution of $X_t$ given
$\sigma(Y_{1:t-1})$. A **finite-horizon smoothing kernel** is a probability
kernel $\psi_T:\mathsf F_{1:T}\to E_0\times\cdots\times E_T$ whose
composition with $Y_{1:T}$ is a regular conditional distribution of the full
state path $(X_0,\ldots,X_T)$ given $\sigma(Y_{1:T})$. Here a regular
conditional distribution is an everywhere probability kernel satisfying the
conditional event identities in
[[def-regular-conditional-distribution]], and a conditional law given a
random element is its data-indexed kernel form in
[[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]].

These kernels are versions: their values can be changed on a measurable set
of observation histories of probability zero without changing the conditional
identities. No density is assumed in these definitions. The state-space model
here is one fixed law. A parametric statistical model is instead a map
$\theta\mapsto P_\theta$ from a parameter set to probability laws; its
measurability is not asserted without a parameter sigma-algebra
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]).

Assume AC, a finite-horizon Markov state-space model with standard-Borel
states, dominated observation kernels, and data-indexed filtering and
smoothing kernels as in
[[def-state-space-filtering-laws]]. Fix an observation history
$y_{1:T}$ in the full-measure set where the dominated filtering recursion
[[thm-dominated-state-space-filtering-recursion]] applies. Write $\eta_t$
for the filtering law of $X_t$ given $y_{1:t}$. Suppose the transition kernel
$M_{t+1}$ from time $t$ to $t+1$ has a product-measurable density
$f_{t+1}(x'\mid x)$ with respect to a sigma-finite measure $\lambda_{t+1}$,
meaning
$$M_{t+1}(x,A)=\int_A f_{t+1}(x'\mid x)\,\lambda_{t+1}(dx')$$
for every state $x$ and measurable set $A$.
Put
$$q_{t+1}(x')=\int f_{t+1}(x'\mid x)\,\eta_t(dx),\qquad D_{t+1}=\{x':0<q_{t+1}(x')<\infty\}.$$
The backward conditional kernel is
$$B_t(x',A)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\int_A f_{t+1}(x'\mid x)\,\eta_t(dx)}{q_{t+1}(x')},&x'\in D_{t+1},\\\eta_t(A),&x'\notin D_{t+1}.\end{cases}$$
It is a probability-kernel version of the conditional law of $X_t$ given
$X_{t+1}=x'$ and $y_{1:t}$. The finite-horizon smoothing kernel factors as
$$\psi_T(dx_{0:T})=\eta_T(dx_T)\prod_{t=T-1}^{0}B_t(x_{t+1},dx_t)$$
for observation-almost every full history, with the product interpreted as
successive backwards kernel integration. If the transition is supplied only
as a probability kernel, the same factorization uses a supplied regular
conditional kernel of $X_t$ given $(X_{t+1},Y_{1:t})$; no transition density
is asserted in that case. Null-history values remain version-dependent.

Fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$ and a requested path count $S\ge1$, used in
either mode below. In the **particle mode**, the inputs include a particle
count $N\ge1$ and normalized filtering clouds
$$\{(x_t^i,w_t^i):1\le i\le N\},\qquad w_t^i\ge0,\quad\sum_{i=1}^Nw_t^i=1,$$
for $0\le t\le T$, produced, for example, by
[[alg-sequential-importance-resampling]]. Each $x_t^i$ is the time-$t$
coordinate of its stored particle path. Write $M_{t+1}$ for the model
transition kernel and require a product-measurable density
$f_{t+1}(x'\mid x)$ relative to a declared sigma-finite measure
$\lambda_{t+1}$, meaning
$$M_{t+1}(x,A)=\int_A f_{t+1}(x'\mid x)\,\lambda_{t+1}(dx')$$
for each measurable $A$. For each $t<T$, define the predictive score with
zero-weight terms omitted:
$$q_{t+1}^N(x')=\sum_{i:w_t^i>0}w_t^i f_{t+1}(x'\mid x_t^i).$$
For particle-mode path sampling, define the set of reachable indices
recursively by $R_T=\{j:w_T^j>0\}$. Descending from $t=T-1$ to $0$, require
$q_{t+1}^N(x_{t+1}^j)\in(0,\infty)$ for every $j\in R_{t+1}$, and put
$$R_t=\bigcup_{j\in R_{t+1}}\{i:w_t^i>0,\ f_{t+1}(x_{t+1}^j\mid x_t^i)>0\}.$$
These are exactly the indices that can be drawn with positive probability at
the corresponding backward step. For the all-marginals mode below, require
instead that $q_{t+1}^N(x_{t+1}^j)\in(0,\infty)$ whenever the current
smoothing weight $\bar w_{t+1|T}^j$ is positive. Thus no denominator is
required for an omitted zero-weight term. At $T=0$ there are no denominator
conditions.

In particle mode, repeat independently for $s=1,\ldots,S$:

1. Draw $I_T^s$ from $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ with probabilities $w_T^i$ and set
   $\widetilde X_T^s=x_T^{I_T^s}$.
2. For $t=T-1,T-2,\ldots,0$, set $b_t^i=0$ without evaluating the density
   whenever $w_t^i=0$. For $w_t^i>0$, set
   $$b_t^i(\widetilde X_{t+1}^s)=\frac{w_t^i f_{t+1}(\widetilde X_{t+1}^s\mid x_t^i)}{q_{t+1}^N(\widetilde X_{t+1}^s)}.$$
   Draw $I_t^s$ from this probability vector, and set
   $\widetilde X_t^s=x_t^{I_t^s}$.
3. Return the tuple
   $$\widetilde X_{0:T}^s=(x_0^{I_0^s},\ldots,x_T^{I_T^s}).$$
   This is a draw from the particle backward approximation to the smoothing
   path law. The coordinates are selected by separate backward indices and
   need not be the stored forward ancestor history of any one particle.
The particle path-sampling output is the list
$\widetilde X_{0:T}^1,\ldots,\widetilde X_{0:T}^S$.

If an exact filtering kernel $\eta_T$ and supplied backward conditional
kernels $B_t$ from
[[lem-smoothing-backward-kernel-bayes-factorization]] are available for
general transition kernels, there is a separate exact-kernel mode: draw
$S$ conditionally independent paths, each by drawing $X_T\sim\eta_T$ and then
drawing $X_t\sim B_t(X_{t+1},\cdot)$ successively backward. This mode uses
the actual kernels; it does not evaluate a transition density or a kernel on
particle singletons. It returns exact smoothing paths under the supplied
conditional versions wherever their factorization holds.

An optional all-marginals mode computes particle smoothing weights instead
of drawing paths. Initialize $\bar w_{T|T}^j=w_T^j$. For
$t=T-1,\ldots,0$, let $J_{t+1}=\{j:\bar w_{t+1|T}^j>0\}$. For each
$j\in J_{t+1}$ and $i$ with $w_t^i>0$, set
$$b_{t}^{i,j}=\frac{w_t^i f_{t+1}(x_{t+1}^j\mid x_t^i)}{q_{t+1}^N(x_{t+1}^j)};$$
set $b_t^{i,j}=0$ without evaluating the density if $j\notin J_{t+1}$ or
$w_t^i=0$. Update
$$\bar w_{t|T}^i=\sum_{j\in J_{t+1}}\bar w_{t+1|T}^j b_t^{i,j}.$$
For every active $j$, $(b_t^{i,j})_{i=1}^N$ is a probability vector, so the
raw updated values are nonnegative and already sum to one; explicit
normalization leaves them unchanged. Return
$\sum_i\bar w_{t|T}^i\delta_{x_t^i}$ as the approximate smoothed marginal at
time $t$. The algorithm makes no finite-particle accuracy, consistency, or
long-time stability claim.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC and fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$ with a state-space model by
probability kernels as in
[[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]. If $T=0$, put $\Omega_T=E_0$;
otherwise put $\Omega_T=E_0\times E_1\times F_1\times\cdots\times E_T\times
F_T$. Let $\mathcal Z_T$ be the corresponding finite-product sigma-algebra
and write $(\Omega_T,\mathcal Z_T,P_T)$ for its finite-horizon probability
space. The law $P_T$ is the unique law supplied by
[[thm-finite-horizon-state-space-kernel-law-exists-uniquely]]. Let $X_t$ and
$Y_t$ be the coordinate random elements taking values in $E_t$ and $F_t$. For
$t\ge1$, write $Y_{1:t}:=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_t)$ and
$\mathsf F_{1:t}:=F_1\times\cdots\times F_t$ with its finite-product
sigma-algebra; let $\mathsf F_{1:0}$ be a singleton and $Y_{1:0}$ its constant
map. The factors are standard Borel, meaning measurably isomorphic to Polish
spaces ([[def-standard-borel-space]]), and their finite products are standard
Borel ([[lem-finite-products-of-standard-borel-spaces-are-standard-borel]]).

The **initial filtering kernel** $\pi_0:\mathsf F_{1:0}\to E_0$ assigns
$\mu_0$ to the unique empty history; it is the conditional law of $X_0$ given
the trivial history. For $1\le t\le T$, a **filtering kernel at time $t$** is
a probability kernel $\pi_t:\mathsf F_{1:t}\to E_t$ such that
$\omega\mapsto\pi_t(Y_{1:t}(\omega),\cdot)$ is a regular conditional
distribution of $X_t$ given $\sigma(Y_{1:t})$. For $1\le t\le T$, a
**predictive kernel at time $t$** is a probability kernel
$\pi_{t|t-1}:\mathsf F_{1:t-1}\to E_t$ whose composition with $Y_{1:t-1}$
is a regular conditional distribution of $X_t$ given
$\sigma(Y_{1:t-1})$. A **finite-horizon smoothing kernel** is a probability
kernel $\psi_T:\mathsf F_{1:T}\to E_0\times\cdots\times E_T$ whose
composition with $Y_{1:T}$ is a regular conditional distribution of the full
state path $(X_0,\ldots,X_T)$ given $\sigma(Y_{1:T})$. Here a regular
conditional distribution is an everywhere probability kernel satisfying the
conditional event identities in
[[def-regular-conditional-distribution]], and a conditional law given a
random element is its data-indexed kernel form in
[[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]].

These kernels are versions: their values can be changed on a measurable set
of observation histories of probability zero without changing the conditional
identities. No density is assumed in these definitions. The state-space model
here is one fixed law. A parametric statistical model is instead a map
$\theta\mapsto P_\theta$ from a parameter set to probability laws; its
measurability is not asserted without a parameter sigma-algebra
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]).

For a finite horizon $T\ge0$, fix an integer lag $L\ge0$, a path count
$S\ge1$, and the normalized
filtering particle clouds and transition inputs required by
[[alg-particle-backward-simulator]]. For each time $t\in\{0,\ldots,T\}$,
put $s_t=\min(t+L,T)$. Independently for each $t$, run the particle backward
simulator using only the filtering clouds at times $0,\ldots,s_t$ and request
$S$ paths. Retain their time-$t$ coordinates $\widetilde X_t^{t,1},\ldots,
\widetilde X_t^{t,S}$ and return the empirical measure
$$\widehat\eta_{t|s_t}^{S}=\frac1S\sum_{r=1}^S\delta_{\widetilde X_t^{t,r}}.$$
In particle mode this empirical law approximates
$$\mathcal L(X_t\mid Y_{1:s_t}),$$
not the full smoothing law $\mathcal L(X_t\mid Y_{1:T})$ unless $s_t=T$ or
the two conditional laws happen to agree. The same procedure can use supplied
exact backward kernels when the model has no transition density; for each
$s_t$ it uses the supplied filtering kernel at $y_{1:s_t}$ and the backward
kernels for the corresponding prefix histories. On histories where these
kernels factor the truncated smoother, it samples that exact conditional law.

The procedure returns one truncated smoothing marginal per $t$. It does not
assert a bound on the lag bias, a forgetting rate, or convergence to the
full-data smoother for fixed $L$. Those conclusions require separate
conditions on the model.

Assume AC, a finite-horizon Markov state-space model with standard-Borel
states, dominated observation kernels, and data-indexed filtering and
smoothing kernels as in
[[def-state-space-filtering-laws]]. Fix an observation history
$y_{1:T}$ in the full-measure set where the dominated filtering recursion
[[thm-dominated-state-space-filtering-recursion]] applies. Write $\eta_t$
for the filtering law of $X_t$ given $y_{1:t}$. Suppose the transition kernel
$M_{t+1}$ from time $t$ to $t+1$ has a product-measurable density
$f_{t+1}(x'\mid x)$ with respect to a sigma-finite measure $\lambda_{t+1}$,
meaning
$$M_{t+1}(x,A)=\int_A f_{t+1}(x'\mid x)\,\lambda_{t+1}(dx')$$
for every state $x$ and measurable set $A$.
Put
$$q_{t+1}(x')=\int f_{t+1}(x'\mid x)\,\eta_t(dx),\qquad D_{t+1}=\{x':0<q_{t+1}(x')<\infty\}.$$
The backward conditional kernel is
$$B_t(x',A)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\int_A f_{t+1}(x'\mid x)\,\eta_t(dx)}{q_{t+1}(x')},&x'\in D_{t+1},\\\eta_t(A),&x'\notin D_{t+1}.\end{cases}$$
It is a probability-kernel version of the conditional law of $X_t$ given
$X_{t+1}=x'$ and $y_{1:t}$. The finite-horizon smoothing kernel factors as
$$\psi_T(dx_{0:T})=\eta_T(dx_T)\prod_{t=T-1}^{0}B_t(x_{t+1},dx_t)$$
for observation-almost every full history, with the product interpreted as
successive backwards kernel integration. If the transition is supplied only
as a probability kernel, the same factorization uses a supplied regular
conditional kernel of $X_t$ given $(X_{t+1},Y_{1:t})$; no transition density
is asserted in that case. Null-history values remain version-dependent.

Assume AC and a finite-horizon Markov state-space model with standard-Borel
state and observation spaces. Supply the exact filtering and backward
conditional kernels of
[[lem-smoothing-backward-kernel-bayes-factorization]]. Fix an observation
history in the full-measure set on which their factorization holds for every
prefix horizon $s\le T$. In the exact-kernel mode of
[[alg-fixed-lag-particle-smoother]], fix an integer lag $L\ge0$ and
$t\in\{0,\ldots,T\}$, and set
$s=\min(t+L,T)$. Each returned path's time-$t$ coordinate has conditional
law $\mathcal L(X_t\mid Y_{1:s})$ (for the supplied conditional versions),
so, for any requested $S\ge1$, the empirical measure of its $S$ returned
time-$t$ coordinates is a Monte Carlo estimate of that marginal. The target
equals the full smoothing marginal only when later
observations do not change the conditional law; increasing the particle count
cannot remove a difference caused by truncating the observation history.

derivations.claim: Since $Y_1$ is constant, conditioning on $Y_1$ leaves the prior law of $X_0$ unchanged. The time-$0$ target for lag $1$ uses $s_0=\min(0+1,2)=1$, so [F2] and [F4] give the lagged law $\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2)$.

For each $b\in\{0,1\}$, the event $Y_2=b$ has probability $1/2$. On this event, $X_0=X_1=X_2=b$ surely. Thus the full smoothing path law is $\delta_{(b,b,b)}$, and its time-$0$ marginal is $\mathcal L(X_0\mid Y_1=0,Y_2=b)=\delta_b$.

For $A=\{b\}$, the probabilities under the lagged law and the full smoothing marginal at time $0$ are $1/2$ and $1$, respectively; for any subset $A\subseteq\{0,1\}$ their probability difference has absolute value at most $1/2$. Hence $\sup_A|\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2)(A)-\delta_b(A)|=1/2$. This difference is between the truncated and full targets at time $0$, so particle-count growth alone cannot remove it.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Fix observations $y_{1:T}$, a standard-Borel parameter space $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$,
a prior probability $\pi_0$, and the finite-horizon Feynman–Kac path model in
[[def-feynman-kac-path-targets-and-normalizers]]. Write
$$L_\theta(y_{1:T})=\gamma_{\theta,T}(1),\qquad C=\int_\Theta L_\theta(y_{1:T})\,\pi_0(d\theta).$$
Require every prefix normalizer $0<Z_{\theta,t}<\infty$ for $t=0,\ldots,T$
and $\pi_0$-almost every $\theta$, together with $0<C<\infty$; then the
parameter posterior is
$$\pi_y(d\theta)=C^{-1}L_\theta(y_{1:T})\,\pi_0(d\theta).$$

For fixed particle count $N\ge1$, let $U$ contain the full output of
[[alg-sequential-importance-resampling]] at $\theta$ and a terminal index
$K\in\{1,\ldots,N\}$ drawn conditionally with its final normalized weight.
Let $m_\theta(du)$ be this measurable auxiliary-variable probability kernel and
let $\widehat L_\theta(U)=\widehat Z_T$ be jointly measurable and nonnegative
in $(\theta,U)$. The required interface is
$$\int\widehat L_\theta(u)\,m_\theta(du)=L_\theta(y_{1:T});$$
[[thm-sequential-particle-estimator-is-unbiased]] supplies this identity under
its finite-horizon support and integrability hypotheses. Define the extended
target probability by
$$\widetilde\pi(d\theta,du)=C^{-1}\pi_0(d\theta)m_\theta(du)\widehat L_\theta(u).$$

Given current $(\theta,U)$, propose $\theta'\sim R(\theta,\cdot)$ and then
$U'\sim m_{\theta'}$. Apply the general Metropolis–Hastings construction
[[alg-metropolis-hastings-kernel]] to this proposal kernel and target
$\widetilde\pi$. On rejection retain the entire current pair $(\theta,U)$,
including its stored likelihood estimate and selected path index. When $\pi_0$
and $R$ have densities $p_0$ and $r$, and the current extended target density
is positive, the acceptance probability is
$$1\wedge\frac{p_0(\theta')\widehat L_{\theta'}(U')r(\theta\mid\theta')}{p_0(\theta)\widehat L_\theta(U)r(\theta'\mid\theta)}.$$
For the displayed density-ratio formula, initialize at a current state where
$p_0(\theta)\widehat L_\theta(U)>0$. The density-free version uses the
accepted-flow Radon–Nikodym construction in the cited general-state algorithm;
it does not evaluate a pointwise prior mass or require this density condition.
Proposed zero estimates are rejected.
The input is the current extended state $(\theta,U)$; output the proposed
extended state $(\theta',U')$ on acceptance and retain $(\theta,U)$ on
rejection.

The selected path stored in $U$ is part of the auxiliary state. Refreshing its
estimate after rejection defines the different Monte Carlo within Metropolis
procedure, not this algorithm.

Assume AC and the finite-horizon setup of [[def-feynman-kac-path-targets-and-normalizers]] and [[alg-sequential-importance-resampling]]. Fix $N\in\mathbb N$ with $N\ge1$ and $0\le t\le T$. Suppose every prefix normalizer satisfies $0<Z_k<\infty$ for $0\le k\le t$. For any nonnegative measurable $\varphi:\mathsf X_{0:t}\to[0,\infty]$ with $\gamma_t(\varphi)<\infty$, define $\widehat\gamma_t^N(\varphi)=\int\varphi\,d(\widehat Z_t\widehat\pi_t^N)$. Then
$$\mathbb E[\widehat\gamma_t^N(\varphi)]=\gamma_t(\varphi).$$
In particular, with $\varphi=1$, the product-of-average-incremental-weights estimator in the algorithm satisfies $\mathbb E[\widehat Z_t]=Z_t$. At each time either multinomial or residual offspring resampling may be used. The theorem asserts no unbiasedness for the normalized empirical measure $\widehat\pi_t^N$ by itself.

Assume AC. The **Metropolis–Hastings procedure** takes as input a standard-Borel
space $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ ([[def-standard-borel-space]]), a target
probability measure $\pi$ ([[def-probability-measure]]), and a probability
kernel $Q$ from $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ to itself
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]).

1. On the product sigma-algebra ([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]),
form the proposal-flow measure $\mu$ ([[def-measure]]) on
$\mathsf X\times\mathsf X$ by
$$\mu(C)=\int_{\mathsf X}Q(x,C_x)\,\pi(dx),\qquad C_x=\{y:(x,y)\in C\}.$$
This is a probability measure by [[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]].
Let $\tau(x,y)=(y,x)$ and set $\mu^{\mathsf T}(C)=\mu(\tau^{-1}C)$.

2. Set $\eta=\mu\wedge\mu^{\mathsf T}$, the greatest measure dominated by both
flows. Put $\lambda_0=\mu+\mu^{\mathsf T}$, which is a finite measure by
[[thm-nonnegative-weighted-sums-of-measures]], and choose nonnegative measurable
representatives $f=d\mu/d\lambda_0$ and $g=d\mu^{\mathsf T}/d\lambda_0$
with $f+g=1$ everywhere after modification on a $\lambda_0$-null set. Define
$$\alpha(x,y)=\begin{cases}\min\{1,g(x,y)/f(x,y)\},&f(x,y)>0,\\1,&f(x,y)=0.\end{cases}$$
This is a jointly measurable version of $d\eta/d\mu$ taking values in $[0,1]$.

3. For $x\in\mathsf X$, compute the integrated acceptance probability
$$a(x)=\int_{\mathsf X}\alpha(x,y)\,Q(x,dy)$$
and rejection probability $r(x)=1-a(x)$.

4. Return the transition rule
$$P(x,A)=\int_{\mathsf X}\mathbf1_A(y)\alpha(x,y)\,Q(x,dy)+\mathbf1_A(x)r(x),\qquad A\in\mathcal X.$$
The second term retains every rejected proposal as a self-transition.

The item [[lem-common-submeasure-and-bounded-radon-nikodym-density]] proves the
common-submeasure construction and density-version claims in step 2.

Assume AC and the hypotheses of [[alg-metropolis-hastings-kernel]]. Its output
$P$ is a probability kernel, the joint measure
$J_P(dx,dy)=\pi(dx)P(x,dy)$ is symmetric under $(x,y)\mapsto(y,x)$, and $\pi$
is invariant for $P$. Symmetry of this joint measure is reversibility. No
irreducibility, uniqueness, convergence-rate, or central limit theorem
conclusion is asserted.

Let $K$ be a probability kernel on a measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and let $\pi$ be a
probability measure on $(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). The
probability measure $\pi$ is **invariant** for $K$, and $\pi$ is a
**stationary distribution** of $K$, when

$$(\pi K)(A):=\int_E K(x,A)\,\pi(dx)=\pi(A)\qquad\text{for every }A\in\mathcal E .$$

The set function $\pi K$ is again a probability measure: for fixed $A$ the map
$x\mapsto K(x,A)$ is measurable and lies in $[0,1]$, so the integral exists in
$[0,1]$; for pairwise disjoint $A_n\in\mathcal E$ the identity
$K(x,\bigcup_nA_n)=\sum_nK(x,A_n)$ of the measure $K(x,\cdot)$ and the
monotone convergence theorem for nonnegative functions
([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]) give
$\sigma$-additivity of $\pi K$; and $K(x,E)=1$ for every $x$ gives
$(\pi K)(E)=1$. Thus $(\pi K)(A)=\pi(A)$ is an identity between two probability
measures evaluated at $A$.

A $K$-chain whose initial law is $\pi$ is called **stationary** when
$\pi K=\pi$. Stationarity of the process is a statement about all of its
finite-dimensional laws and is proved, not assumed, from $\pi K=\pi$; see
[[thm-invariant-initial-law-makes-the-chain-stationary]].

On a countable state space $E$ with sigma-algebra $2^E$ and transition matrix
$p(x,y)=K(x,\{y\})$ ([[def-transition-matrix-and-n-step-transition-probabilities]]),
a measure on $E$ is its weighted sum of Dirac masses at singletons
([[thm-measures-on-countable-discrete-spaces-are-weighted-dirac-sums]]), so
invariance is equivalent to the matrix identity

$$\pi(y)=\sum_{x\in E}\pi(x)\,p(x,y)\qquad\text{for every }y\in E .$$

The definition fixes no irreducibility, aperiodicity or uniqueness hypothesis,
and it selects no conditional-expectation versions; the display defines a
single measure $\pi K$ and asserts an identity for it. A transient, periodic or
reducible chain may have several invariant probability measures or none.

derivations.claim: Integrating [F1] first in $u$ gives $C^{-1}\pi_0(d\theta)\mathbb E_{m_\theta}\widehat L_\theta=C^{-1}L_\theta\pi_0(d\theta)$ by [F2]. Its total mass is $C^{-1}\int L_\theta\,d\pi_0=1$, so $\widetilde\pi$ is a probability and its parameter marginal is $\pi_y$.

For a measurable set $B$ of parameter-path pairs, summing over the terminal index gives $\widetilde\pi\{(\theta,X^K_{0:T})\in B\}=C^{-1}\int\pi_0(d\theta)\,\mathbb E\!\left[\widehat Z_T\sum_{k=1}^NW_T^k1_B(\theta,X^k_{0:T})\right]=C^{-1}\int\pi_0(d\theta)\,\gamma_{\theta,T}(B_\theta)$, because the sum is the weighted empirical path integral in [F2]. Thus the selected path marginal is the joint posterior.

The proposal in [F1] is a probability kernel because it is the composition of the probability kernel $R$ and the auxiliary probability kernels $m_{\theta'}$. Applying [F3] to this target and proposal defines the PMMH accept/reject rule, which is a probability kernel by [F4]; in the common-density case the factors $m_\theta(u)$ cancel between the target and proposal ratios, leaving exactly the displayed ratio in [[alg-pmmh]]. On rejection, [F3] retains the current extended state.

By [F4], this extended-space kernel is reversible and invariant for $\widetilde\pi$. Applying the measurable coordinate projections $(\theta,u)\mapsto\theta$ and $(\theta,u)\mapsto(\theta,X^K_{0:T})$ to the invariant law gives the exact marginals in steps 1.1 and 2.1, in the sense of [F5].

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ be a standard-Borel parameter space with a prior
$\pi_0$. Use common standard-Borel state spaces and a jointly measurable
parameterized target/proposal family: the initial and transition target and
proposal laws are probability kernels in $\theta$ and their state arguments,
the potentials are jointly measurable, and the chosen Radon–Nikodym weight
versions are jointly measurable. Thus $\theta\mapsto\gamma_{\theta,T}$ and
$\theta\mapsto\psi_\theta$ are measure and probability kernels, and the SIR
weights and normalizer are jointly measurable in $(\theta,U)$. The prior-kernel
law $\pi_0(d\theta)\psi_\theta(du)$ is a probability measure by
[[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]].

Use the finite-horizon state path model and proposal support conditions in
[[def-feynman-kac-path-targets-and-normalizers]],
[[thm-feynman-kac-path-radon-nikodym-weight]], and
[[alg-sequential-importance-resampling]]. Select the multinomial resampling
branch, returning ancestor indices in sampled order. Residual resampling is not
the labeled particle law used by this genealogical construction. Write
$\gamma_{\theta,T}$ for the Feynman–Kac path measure at parameter $\theta$ and
set $L_\theta=\gamma_{\theta,T}(1)$. Assume $0<L_\theta<\infty$ for
$\pi_0$-almost every $\theta$, and
$$C=\int L_\theta\,\pi_0(d\theta),\qquad 0<C<\infty.$$
For a fixed particle count $N\ge2$, write
$$U=(X_0^{1:N},A_1^{1:N},X_1^{1:N},\ldots,A_T^{1:N},X_T^{1:N})$$
for the full particle system and ancestor indices generated by
[[alg-sequential-importance-resampling]]. Its forward probability law at
parameter $\theta$ is $\psi_\theta(du)$. The algorithm defines the product
normalizer estimate $\widehat Z_T(U)$ and final normalized weights
$W_T^1(U),\ldots,W_T^N(U)$; $K$ is a terminal particle index. The path
$X_{0:T}^{K}$ means the states on the ancestral lineage of particle $K$,
traced through the arrays $A_1^{1:N},\ldots,A_T^{1:N}$.

More explicitly, relative to counting measure on ancestor arrays and the
ordered SIR proposal-kernel integrals for the states,
$$\psi_\theta(du)=\prod_{i=1}^N\nu_{\theta,0}(dx_0^i)\prod_{t=1}^T\prod_{i=1}^N\left[W_{t-1}^{A_t^i}(U)R_{\theta,t}(X_{t-1}^{A_t^i},dx_t^i)\right].$$
Each factor $W_{t-1}^{A_t^i}(U)$ is the categorical mass of that ancestor
choice; no state transition density is assumed for the genealogical variant.

The genealogical particle Gibbs extended target is the measure
$$\varphi_N(d\theta,du,k)=C^{-1}\pi_0(d\theta)\,\psi_\theta(du)\,\widehat Z_T(u)W_T^k(u),\qquad k\in\{1,\ldots,N\}.$$
The selected state is $(\theta,X_{0:T}^{K})$. The zero-weight fallback in the
particle algorithm defines $W_T$ everywhere; when $\widehat Z_T=0$ the extended
target assigns the configuration zero mass.

The measure is a probability and has the exact joint smoothing posterior as
its selected $(\theta,X_{0:T}^{K})$ marginal by
[[thm-particle-gibbs-selected-path-marginal]].

Use the finite-horizon target and proposal setting of [[def-feynman-kac-path-targets-and-normalizers]]. For admissible inputs require $\mu_0\ll\nu_0$ and, for each $k\ge1$, $M_k(x,\cdot)\ll R_k(x,\cdot)$ for almost every $x$ under the last-coordinate marginal of the proposal path law $Q_{k-1}$. Select the joint measurable versions $\rho_0=d\mu_0/d\nu_0$ and $r_k(x,\cdot)=dM_k(x,\cdot)/dR_k(x,\cdot)$ supplied by [[thm-feynman-kac-path-radon-nikodym-weight]]. Fix $N\ge1$ and select either multinomial or residual resampling at each time. The algorithm returns a weighted empirical path measure and a normalizer estimate.

1. Draw $X_0^1,\ldots,X_0^N$ independently from $\nu_0$. Set $a_0^i=G_0(X_0^i)\rho_0(X_0^i)$ and $\widehat Z_0=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^Na_0^i$. If $\sum_i a_0^i>0$, put $\bar w_0^i=a_0^i/\sum_j a_0^j$; otherwise put $\bar w_0^i=1/N$. Each initial path is $X_{0:0}^i=X_0^i$.
2. For $k=1,\ldots,t$, do the following:
   1. Apply [[alg-multinomial-and-residual-offspring-resampling]] to the previous normalized weights $(\bar w_{k-1}^1,\ldots,\bar w_{k-1}^N)$, obtaining ancestor indices $A_k^1,\ldots,A_k^N$.
   2. Given the previous paths and these indices, draw $(X_k^1,\ldots,X_k^N)$ with joint conditional law $\bigotimes_{i=1}^N R_k(X_{k-1}^{A_k^i},\cdot)$ and set $X_{0:k}^i=(X_{0:k-1}^{A_k^i},X_k^i)$.
   3. Set $a_k^i=G_k(X_k^i)r_k(X_{k-1}^{A_k^i},X_k^i)$ and $\widehat Z_k=\widehat Z_{k-1}(N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^Na_k^i)$. If $\sum_i a_k^i>0$, put $\bar w_k^i=a_k^i/\sum_j a_k^j$; otherwise put $\bar w_k^i=1/N$.
3. Return $\widehat Z_t$ and the weighted empirical path probability measure $\widehat\pi_t^N=\sum_{i=1}^N\bar w_t^i\delta_{X_{0:t}^i}$. Its last-coordinate marginal is the corresponding empirical filtering approximation.

The all-zero fallback only defines a probability measure for reporting and future sampling. Once a zero average weight occurs, $\widehat Z$ remains zero. The procedure makes no finite-particle accuracy, consistency, or long-time stability claim.

The input convention is that $t\in\{0,\ldots,T\}$ is the requested horizon, $\nu_0$ is a proposal probability on $\mathsf X_0$, $R_k$ are proposal probability kernels for $1\le k\le t$, and $N\in\mathbb N$ with $N\ge1$. Thus the opening support condition ranges over $1\le k\le t$, and a resampling scheme is selected for each such $k$. Choose the finite-valued joint measurable versions $\rho_0$ and $r_k$ constructed in the proof of [[thm-feynman-kac-path-radon-nikodym-weight]].

Assume AC and the setup of [[def-feynman-kac-path-targets-and-normalizers]] through a fixed horizon $t\le T$. Let $\nu_0$ be a proposal probability on $\mathsf X_0$, and for $1\le k\le t$ let $R_k:\mathsf X_{k-1}\rightsquigarrow\mathsf X_k$ be proposal probability kernels. Define $Q_s(dx_{0:s})=\nu_0(dx_0)\prod_{k=1}^sR_k(x_{k-1},dx_k)$. Suppose $\mu_0\ll\nu_0$, and for each $k$ suppose $M_k(x,\cdot)\ll R_k(x,\cdot)$ for almost every $x$ under the last-coordinate marginal of $Q_{k-1}$. Choose a measurable version $\rho_0=d\mu_0/d\nu_0$ and, using [[lem-jointly-measurable-radon-nikodym-derivatives-for-probability-kernels]], measurable versions $r_k(x,\cdot)=dM_k(x,\cdot)/dR_k(x,\cdot)$ for these preceding-state marginals.

Then $\gamma_s\ll Q_s$ for every $s\le t$, with product density
$$W_s(x_{0:s})=G_0(x_0)\rho_0(x_0)\prod_{k=1}^sG_k(x_k)r_k(x_{k-1},x_k).$$
That is, $\gamma_s(A)=\int_AW_s\,dQ_s$ for every measurable $A\subseteq\mathsf X_{0:s}$. If $0<Z_s<\infty$, the normalized path target has density $W_s/Z_s$ with respect to $Q_s$.

Assume AC and fix a finite horizon $T\in\mathbb N_0$. For each $0\le k\le T$, let $(\mathsf X_k,\mathcal X_k)$ be a standard Borel space. Let $\mu_0$ be a probability measure on $\mathsf X_0$, and for $1\le k\le T$ let $M_k:\mathsf X_{k-1}\rightsquigarrow\mathsf X_k$ be a probability kernel. A **potential** at time $k$ is a finite-valued nonnegative measurable function $G_k:\mathsf X_k\to[0,\infty)$. Write $\mathsf X_{0:t}=\prod_{k=0}^t\mathsf X_k$ with its finite-product sigma-algebra.

For each $0\le t\le T$, let $P_t^M$ be the finite path law with ordered kernel integral $\mu_0(dx_0)\prod_{k=1}^tM_k(x_{k-1},dx_k)$, supplied by Ionescu–Tulcea ([[thm-ionescu-tulcea-construction-of-a-markov-chain]]). The **unnormalized Feynman–Kac path measure** is
$$\gamma_t(A)=\int_{\mathsf X_{0:t}}\mathbf 1_A(x_{0:t})\prod_{k=0}^tG_k(x_k)\,P_t^M(dx_{0:t}),\qquad A\in\bigotimes_{k=0}^t\mathcal X_k.$$
Its **normalizer** is $Z_t=\gamma_t(\mathsf X_{0:t})=\gamma_t(1)\in[0,\infty]$. Only when $0<Z_t<\infty$ define the normalized path target $\pi_t^{\mathrm{FK}}=\gamma_t/Z_t$. The sequence $(\gamma_t)$ with its kernels and potentials is the Feynman–Kac flow.

State-space filtering kernels are conditional-law versions as in [[def-state-space-filtering-laws]]. A Feynman–Kac path target is not by itself an assertion that a pointwise conditional version has been selected at observation-null histories.

$0<C=\int L_\theta\,\pi_0(d\theta)<\infty$. Then $\varphi_N$ in
[[def-particle-gibbs-extended-target]] is a probability measure and its

$$C^{-1}\pi_0(d\theta)\gamma_{\theta,T}(dx_{0:T}),$$

Assume AC. Let $\lambda$ be a probability on $(E\times T,\mathcal S\otimes\mathcal T)$, where E and T are standard-Borel spaces, and let $\beta(B)=\lambda(E\times B)$ be its second marginal. There is a probability kernel $K:(T,\mathcal T)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ such that

$$\lambda(A\times B)=\int_B K(y,A)\,\beta(dy)\quad(A\in\mathcal S,\ B\in\mathcal T).$$

It is unique as a kernel outside a single measurable $\beta$-null set. For every nonnegative product-measurable $f:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$,

$$\int f(x,y)\,\lambda(d(x,y))=\int_T\left(\int_E f(x,y)K(y,dx)\right)\beta(dy).$$

In particular this applies to the joint law of random elements $(X,Y)$, with $\beta=P_Y$; the direction is the law of X given Y.

derivations.claim: Since the only $K$-dependent factor in [F1] is $W_T^K$, and the final normalized weights sum to one, $\varphi_N(K=k\mid\theta,U)=W_T^k$.

Fix a selected index $K$ and trace its lineage $b_0,\ldots,b_T$. On the positive-mass support of [F1], write $\bar w_t=N^{-1}\sum_iw_t^i$, so $\widehat Z_TW_T^K=(\prod_{t=0}^{T-1}\bar w_t)w_T^{b_T}/N$. In the forward density [F2], the selected lineage contributes $\prod_{t=1}^TW_{t-1}^{b_{t-1}}R_t(x_{t-1}^{b_{t-1}},dx_t^{b_t})$ and its initial proposal $\nu_0(dx_0^{b_0})$. Substituting $W_{t-1}^{b_{t-1}}=w_{t-1}^{b_{t-1}}/(N\bar w_{t-1})$ cancels each $\bar w_{t-1}$, leaving the selected path factor $N^{-(T+1)}\nu_0(dx_0^{b_0})w_0^{b_0}\prod_{t=1}^TR_t(x_{t-1}^{b_{t-1}},dx_t^{b_t})w_t^{b_t}$. If any average weight is zero, [F1] assigns the configuration zero extended-target mass, so its conditional law need not be specified there.

By the initial and transition Radon–Nikodym weight identities in [F4], the selected path factor in step 2.1 equals $N^{-(T+1)}\gamma_{\theta,T}(dx_{0:T}^{b})$. All remaining factors are exactly the conditional SIR laws for the non-reference particles and ancestors in [F3]. Thus, conditional on the selected path and lineage, the remaining particle variables have the stated conditional-particle-filter law; the same factorization makes the lineage indices uniform given the selected path.

By [F5], the extended target is a probability on a standard-Borel product. Apply [F6] to the particle system conditional on its retained parameter-path-lineage variables. The normalized factorization in step 3.1 identifies its conditional kernel outside a single measurable marginal-null set; pull their exceptional events back to the common extended-state space and take the finite union over lineages and update blocks. This union has target mass zero. Its conditional probability given the retained parameter-path-lineage is therefore zero outside a measurable marginal-null set, by the defining integral identity in [F6]; remove that set to obtain $D$ in [F3]. The same restriction excludes infinite or zero denominators on the positive extended-target support. On the exceptional set the algorithm uses the identity transition on the retained state, so it remains an everywhere measurable probability kernel without claiming pointwise Radon–Nikodym identities at null reference values.

In the coordinates consisting of the selected path $x^b$, its lineage $b$, and the remaining particle variables $U_{-b}$, the factorization in step 3.1 gives the conditional law of $(\theta,U_{-b})$ given $(x^b,b)$. Its leading factor is $\pi_0(d\theta)\gamma_{\theta,T}(dx^b)/(C N^{T+1})$; the factor $N^{-(T+1)}$ makes $b$ uniform given $x^b$ and independent of $\theta$, while the conditional law of $U_{-b}$ given $(\theta,x^b,b)$ is exactly the conditional-particle-filter law in [F3]. Thus the posterior draw of $\theta$ given $x^b$, followed by regeneration of $U_{-b}$ with that filter, samples the joint conditional law of $(\theta,U_{-b})$ given $(x^b,b)$. This is a conditional-block update; the parameter draw alone is not asserted to be conditional on the old full particle system.

The block in step 4.2 is the conditional law of $(\theta,U_{-b})$ given the retained $(x^b,b)$, so replacing that block preserves $\varphi_N$ by the defining conditional-probability identity. By step 1.1, the subsequent draw of $K$ given the regenerated particle system is its conditional law $\mathrm{Categorical}(W_T^{1:N})$ and also preserves $\varphi_N$. The exceptional-state identity modification changes the target integral only on a target-null set by step 4.1. Therefore their composition preserves $\varphi_N$, whose selected marginal is the exact posterior by [F5].

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the finite-horizon Feynman–Kac model and proposal support conditions in
[[def-feynman-kac-path-targets-and-normalizers]] and
[[thm-feynman-kac-path-radon-nikodym-weight]]. Use the multinomial SIR law with ancestor indices in sampled order. Residual resampling is not included in this labeled-density construction. For this variant, additionally
assume that the initial target law has a measurable density $\mu_{\theta,0}$,
each target transition $M_{\theta,t}$ has a jointly measurable density
$f_{\theta,t}(x_t\mid x_{t-1})$, and each proposal transition $R_{\theta,t}$ has
a density $q_{\theta,t}(x_t\mid x_{t-1})$, all with respect to declared
sigma-finite coordinate reference measures. Let $q_{\theta,0}$ be the proposal
initial density with respect to the initial coordinate reference measure.
Retain the proper-prior and positive-finite-evidence assumptions of
[[def-particle-gibbs-extended-target]]. Then
the path measure has density
$$\gamma_{\theta,T}(x_{0:T})=\mu_{\theta,0}(x_0)G_0(x_0)\prod_{t=1}^Tf_{\theta,t}(x_t\mid x_{t-1})G_t(x_t).$$
Require positive finite denominators in the backward probabilities below on
the extended-target support.

Write $U$ for all SIR particles and ancestor indices, $\psi_\theta(u)$ for
their forward joint density, and $j=(j_0,\ldots,j_T)$ for a sequence of
particle indices. Let $x^j_{0:T}$ be the path formed from states
$X_t^{j_t}$, without requiring $A_t^{j_t}=j_{t-1}$. For
$t=0,\ldots,T-1$, define
$$B_t^i(z;U)=\frac{W_t^i f_{\theta,t+1}(z\mid X_t^i)}{\sum_{\ell=1}^NW_t^\ell f_{\theta,t+1}(z\mid X_t^\ell)}.$$
The backward-simulation extended target is
$$\varphi_N^{\rm BS}(d\theta,du,j)=\frac{\pi_0(d\theta)\,\gamma_{\theta,T}(x^j_{0:T})}{C\,N^{T+1}}\frac{\psi_\theta(u)}{q_{\theta,0}(X_0^{j_0})\prod_{t=1}^TW_{t-1}^{A_t^{j_t}}q_{\theta,t}(X_t^{j_t}\mid X_{t-1}^{A_t^{j_t}})}\prod_{t=1}^TB_{t-1}^{A_t^{j_t}}(X_t^{j_t};U).$$
where the displayed expression is a density with respect to the common
particle reference measures, counting measure on ancestor and selected indices,
and the prior measure on $\theta$. The complete SIR forward density
$\psi_\theta$ includes the normalized ancestor probabilities and proposal
densities for every particle. This is the backward-simulation extension of the
particle Gibbs target; its exact selected-path marginal and Gibbs conditionals
are proved in
[[thm-particle-gibbs-backward-simulation-sweep-is-gibbs]].

Use the density, support, and positive-denominator hypotheses of
[[def-particle-gibbs-backward-simulation-extended-target]]. Select multinomial resampling with ancestor indices in sampled order. Fix $N\ge2$. Before updating, require the retained parameter-path-index triple $(\theta,x^j_{0:T},j)$ to be in $D_{\rm BS}$, the set fixed in the Conditional-version convention of [[def-particle-gibbs-backward-simulation-extended-target]]; otherwise return the unchanged extended state. If a required ratio is undefined or nonfinite, or a required denominator or normalizing sum is zero or nonfinite during a sweep, return the old retained state. A finite zero density ratio is valid: assign that particle zero weight and continue. The factorization theorem proves that the stated failures have conditional probability zero on the designated full-measure set.

A backward-simulation sweep takes the current extended state $(\theta,U,j)$,
where $j=(j_0,\ldots,j_T)$ selects the reference path
$x^*_{0:T}=x^j_{0:T}$ from $U$. It returns the updated extended state $(\theta',U',J)$
and selected path $x^J_{0:T}$. First draw $\theta'$ from its exact posterior
full conditional given $x^*_{0:T}$ and the observations. If
$(\theta',x^*,j)$ is outside $D_{\rm BS}$, return the old extended state.

The initial proposal, non-reference resampling and propagation, and SIR
weight updates use [[alg-conditional-particle-gibbs]] in its density setting.
Because $j$ is a backward index sequence rather than an ancestral lineage, the
reference particle's ancestor is sampled from $B$ below instead of being fixed
to the preceding reference index.

1. Initialize the conditional auxiliary particle filter at time $0$: set
   $X_0^{j_0}=x_0^*$ and independently draw $X_0^i\sim q_{\theta',0}$ for
   $i\ne j_0$. For each $i$, compute the SIR initial weight
   $a_0^i=\mu_{\theta',0}(X_0^i)G_0(X_0^i)/q_{\theta',0}(X_0^i)$. If
   $\sum_i a_0^i>0$, set $W_0^i=a_0^i/\sum_\ell a_0^\ell$; otherwise use the
   SIR zero-weight convention $W_0^i=1/N$.
2. For $t=1,\ldots,T$, do the following in order:
   1. For each $i\ne j_t$, draw $A_t^i$ categorically with probabilities
      $W_{t-1}^{1:N}$ and then draw $X_t^i\sim
      q_{\theta',t}(\cdot\mid X_{t-1}^{A_t^i})$.
   2. Set $X_t^{j_t}=x_t^*$ and draw its ancestor $A_t^{j_t}$ categorically
      with probabilities $B_{t-1}^{1:N}(x_t^*;U')$.
   3. For every $i$, compute
      $a_t^i=G_t(X_t^i)f_{\theta',t}(X_t^i\mid
      X_{t-1}^{A_t^i})/q_{\theta',t}(X_t^i\mid
      X_{t-1}^{A_t^i})$. If $\sum_i a_t^i>0$, set
      $W_t^i=a_t^i/\sum_\ell a_t^\ell$; otherwise use the SIR zero-weight
      convention $W_t^i=1/N$.
3. Draw $J_T$ categorically with probabilities $W_T^{1:N}$. For
   $t=T-1,T-2,\ldots,0$, draw $J_t$ with probabilities
   $B_t^{1:N}(X_{t+1}^{J_{t+1}};U')$. Return the updated extended state and
   selected path.

The zero-weight conventions above define normalized weights as in
[[alg-sequential-importance-resampling]]. Retain zero individual density ratios,
importance weights, and backward probabilities. If a required ratio is undefined
or nonfinite, a backward-probability denominator is zero or nonfinite, or a
weight sum is zero or nonfinite, return the old extended state as specified above.
On the designated good set these exceptional events have conditional
probability zero. For $T=0$, Step 2 is empty and Step 3 draws $J_0$ from $W_0$.

The conditional auxiliary particle filter and the backward simulator are the
two particle-coordinate conditionals of
[[def-particle-gibbs-backward-simulation-extended-target]]. Their Gibbs
interpretation and exact posterior marginal are separate proved properties.

Assume AC and the setup of [[def-feynman-kac-path-targets-and-normalizers]] through a fixed horizon $t\le T$. Let $\nu_0$ be a proposal probability on $\mathsf X_0$, and for $1\le k\le t$ let $R_k:\mathsf X_{k-1}\rightsquigarrow\mathsf X_k$ be proposal probability kernels. Define $Q_s(dx_{0:s})=\nu_0(dx_0)\prod_{k=1}^sR_k(x_{k-1},dx_k)$. Suppose $\mu_0\ll\nu_0$, and for each $k$ suppose $M_k(x,\cdot)\ll R_k(x,\cdot)$ for almost every $x$ under the last-coordinate marginal of $Q_{k-1}$. Choose a measurable version $\rho_0=d\mu_0/d\nu_0$ and, using [[lem-jointly-measurable-radon-nikodym-derivatives-for-probability-kernels]], measurable versions $r_k(x,\cdot)=dM_k(x,\cdot)/dR_k(x,\cdot)$ for these preceding-state marginals.

Then $\gamma_s\ll Q_s$ for every $s\le t$, with product density
$$W_s(x_{0:s})=G_0(x_0)\rho_0(x_0)\prod_{k=1}^sG_k(x_k)r_k(x_{k-1},x_k).$$
That is, $\gamma_s(A)=\int_AW_s\,dQ_s$ for every measurable $A\subseteq\mathsf X_{0:s}$. If $0<Z_s<\infty$, the normalized path target has density $W_s/Z_s$ with respect to $Q_s$.

Assume AC and fix a finite horizon $T\in\mathbb N_0$. For each $0\le k\le T$, let $(\mathsf X_k,\mathcal X_k)$ be a standard Borel space. Let $\mu_0$ be a probability measure on $\mathsf X_0$, and for $1\le k\le T$ let $M_k:\mathsf X_{k-1}\rightsquigarrow\mathsf X_k$ be a probability kernel. A **potential** at time $k$ is a finite-valued nonnegative measurable function $G_k:\mathsf X_k\to[0,\infty)$. Write $\mathsf X_{0:t}=\prod_{k=0}^t\mathsf X_k$ with its finite-product sigma-algebra.

For each $0\le t\le T$, let $P_t^M$ be the finite path law with ordered kernel integral $\mu_0(dx_0)\prod_{k=1}^tM_k(x_{k-1},dx_k)$, supplied by Ionescu–Tulcea ([[thm-ionescu-tulcea-construction-of-a-markov-chain]]). The **unnormalized Feynman–Kac path measure** is
$$\gamma_t(A)=\int_{\mathsf X_{0:t}}\mathbf 1_A(x_{0:t})\prod_{k=0}^tG_k(x_k)\,P_t^M(dx_{0:t}),\qquad A\in\bigotimes_{k=0}^t\mathcal X_k.$$
Its **normalizer** is $Z_t=\gamma_t(\mathsf X_{0:t})=\gamma_t(1)\in[0,\infty]$. Only when $0<Z_t<\infty$ define the normalized path target $\pi_t^{\mathrm{FK}}=\gamma_t/Z_t$. The sequence $(\gamma_t)$ with its kernels and potentials is the Feynman–Kac flow.

State-space filtering kernels are conditional-law versions as in [[def-state-space-filtering-laws]]. A Feynman–Kac path target is not by itself an assertion that a pointwise conditional version has been selected at observation-null histories.

Assume AC. Let $\lambda$ be a probability on $(E\times T,\mathcal S\otimes\mathcal T)$, where E and T are standard-Borel spaces, and let $\beta(B)=\lambda(E\times B)$ be its second marginal. There is a probability kernel $K:(T,\mathcal T)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ such that

$$\lambda(A\times B)=\int_B K(y,A)\,\beta(dy)\quad(A\in\mathcal S,\ B\in\mathcal T).$$

It is unique as a kernel outside a single measurable $\beta$-null set. For every nonnegative product-measurable $f:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$,

$$\int f(x,y)\,\lambda(d(x,y))=\int_T\left(\int_E f(x,y)K(y,dx)\right)\beta(dy).$$

In particular this applies to the joint law of random elements $(X,Y)$, with $\beta=P_Y$; the direction is the law of X given Y.

derivations.claim: Write $w_t^i$ for the unnormalized importance weight of particle $i$ using its actual ancestor $A_t^i$. On the proposal-support set in [F3], $q_{\theta,0}(X_0^i)w_0^i=\mu_{\theta,0}(X_0^i)G_0(X_0^i)$ and $q_{\theta,t}(X_t^i\mid X_{t-1}^{A_t^i})w_t^i=G_t(X_t^i)f_{\theta,t}(X_t^i\mid X_{t-1}^{A_t^i})$. These product identities include zero weights and zero transition densities; they require no division by an alternative-parent transition density. Put $S_t=\sum_iw_t^i$ and $H_t(z)=\sum_iw_{t-1}^if_{\theta,t}(z\mid X_{t-1}^i)$. Whenever the prescribed normalizers are positive and finite, $W_t^i=w_t^i/S_t$ and $B_{t-1}^i(z;U)=w_{t-1}^if_{\theta,t}(z\mid X_{t-1}^i)/H_t(z)$.

Fix a backward index sequence $j$ and its reference path. Expanding the forward density $\psi_\theta$ in [F1] and canceling the selected initial proposal and each selected joint ancestor-proposal factor gives $\varphi_N^{\rm BS}(d\theta,du,j)=\frac{\pi_0(d\theta)\gamma_{\theta,T}(dx^j_{0:T})}{C N^{T+1}}\prod_{i\ne j_0}q_{\theta,0}(x_0^i)\prod_{t=1}^T\left[\prod_{i\ne j_t}\left(W_{t-1}^{A_t^i}q_{\theta,t}(x_t^i\mid x_{t-1}^{A_t^i})\right)\right]\prod_{t=1}^TB_{t-1}^{A_t^{j_t}}(x_t^{j_t};U)$. The bracketed factors are exactly the non-reference resample-and-propagate law and the categorical backward ancestor law in [F2]. For target-almost every retained path, its initial target factor and all its potentials are positive. The reference initial weight is therefore positive on the supplied proposal-support set. Inductively, a reference ancestor drawn from $B$ has positive preceding weight and transition density, so its new importance weight is positive there as well. Thus each weight sum remains positive; zero individual free-particle weights cause no failure. The prescribed support and finite-denominator conventions exclude the remaining exceptional ratios almost everywhere. Each categorical or proposal factor then integrates to one, so this is the normalized conditional auxiliary particle filter.

Fix $(\theta,U)$ on its forward-support set with positive finite required normalizers. In [F1], cancel each selected ancestor probability against the numerator of its backward factor, then use the product identities in step 1.1 to absorb each potential into the actual-parent weight. The extended density becomes $\frac{\pi_0(d\theta)\psi_\theta(u)}{CN^{T+1}}w_0^{j_0}\prod_{t=1}^T\frac{w_t^{j_t}f_{\theta,t}(X_t^{j_t}\mid X_{t-1}^{j_{t-1}})}{H_t(X_t^{j_t})/S_{t-1}}=\frac{\pi_0(d\theta)\psi_\theta(u)}{CN^{T+1}}\left(\prod_{t=0}^TS_t\right)W_T^{j_T}\prod_{t=1}^TB_{t-1}^{j_{t-1}}(X_t^{j_t};U)$. This equality merely regroups products; no weight or transition density is divided out. A zero selected weight or path-transition factor gives zero mass on both sides. Index sequences encountering a zero backward denominator likewise have zero mass: a positive terminal weight has a positive actual-parent factor, and a positive backward draw recursively has positive preceding weight. Set these zero-mass terms to zero as prescribed by [F1]. The prefactor is independent of $j$, and summing the remaining factors from $j_0$ through $j_T$ gives one by their categorical normalization. Thus the index conditional is exactly the backward simulator in [F2], including $T=0$, when the product is empty.

By step 1.2, for each fixed $j$ the other particle variables have a normalized conditional law. The leading factor is $C^{-1}\pi_0(d\theta)\gamma_{\theta,T}(dx^j)/N^{T+1}$ by [F4]. There are $N^{T+1}$ index sequences, so integrating the remaining variables and summing over them gives total mass one and selected $(\theta,x^*)$ marginal $C^{-1}\pi_0(d\theta)\gamma_{\theta,T}(dx^*)$.

The standard-Borel state and particle spaces permit [F5] to be applied to the probability target in step 2.2. The normalized factorizations in steps 1.2 and 2.1 identify its conditional kernels outside measurable marginal-null sets. Pull exceptional events back to the common extended-state space and take their finite union over index sequences and sweep blocks; its target mass is zero. By the conditional integral identity in [F5], its conditional probability given the retained variables is zero outside a measurable marginal-null set. Removing this set gives the good set specified in [F1]–[F2]. On its complement the algorithm retains the old state; undefined ratio or normalization events within a conditional factorization have zero conditional mass on this good set. Thus the stated formulas and their measurable fallback define conditional-law versions almost everywhere, without assuming arbitrary reference points admit valid density ratios.

In coordinates consisting of the selected path $x^j$, its index sequence $j$, and the remaining particle variables $U_{-j}$, the factorization in step 1.2 shows that the conditional law of $(\theta,U_{-j})$ given $(x^j,j)$ is obtained by first drawing $\theta$ from its posterior full conditional given $x^j$ and then drawing $U_{-j}$ from the conditional auxiliary-particle-filter law. The factor $N^{-(T+1)}$ is constant in $\theta$ and $x^j$, so the old particle system has been marginalized in this joint conditional block. Thus the first two updates in the algorithm, parameter draw and filter regeneration, together preserve the extended target. By step 2.1, the following backward-index draw is the conditional law of $j$ given $(\theta,U)$ and also preserves that target. The exceptional-state identity modifications do not change its integral by step 3.1, and the selected marginal in step 2.2 remains exact.

Fix observations $y_{1:T}$, a standard-Borel parameter space $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$,
a prior probability $\pi_0$, and the finite-horizon Feynman–Kac path model in
[[def-feynman-kac-path-targets-and-normalizers]]. Write
$$L_\theta(y_{1:T})=\gamma_{\theta,T}(1),\qquad C=\int_\Theta L_\theta(y_{1:T})\,\pi_0(d\theta).$$
Require every prefix normalizer $0<Z_{\theta,t}<\infty$ for $t=0,\ldots,T$
and $\pi_0$-almost every $\theta$, together with $0<C<\infty$; then the
parameter posterior is
$$\pi_y(d\theta)=C^{-1}L_\theta(y_{1:T})\,\pi_0(d\theta).$$

For fixed particle count $N\ge1$, let $U$ contain the full output of
[[alg-sequential-importance-resampling]] at $\theta$ and a terminal index
$K\in\{1,\ldots,N\}$ drawn conditionally with its final normalized weight.
Let $m_\theta(du)$ be this measurable auxiliary-variable probability kernel and
let $\widehat L_\theta(U)=\widehat Z_T$ be jointly measurable and nonnegative
in $(\theta,U)$. The required interface is
$$\int\widehat L_\theta(u)\,m_\theta(du)=L_\theta(y_{1:T});$$
[[thm-sequential-particle-estimator-is-unbiased]] supplies this identity under
its finite-horizon support and integrability hypotheses. Define the extended
target probability by
$$\widetilde\pi(d\theta,du)=C^{-1}\pi_0(d\theta)m_\theta(du)\widehat L_\theta(u).$$

Given current $(\theta,U)$, propose $\theta'\sim R(\theta,\cdot)$ and then
$U'\sim m_{\theta'}$. Apply the general Metropolis–Hastings construction
[[alg-metropolis-hastings-kernel]] to this proposal kernel and target
$\widetilde\pi$. On rejection retain the entire current pair $(\theta,U)$,
including its stored likelihood estimate and selected path index. When $\pi_0$
and $R$ have densities $p_0$ and $r$, and the current extended target density
is positive, the acceptance probability is
$$1\wedge\frac{p_0(\theta')\widehat L_{\theta'}(U')r(\theta\mid\theta')}{p_0(\theta)\widehat L_\theta(U)r(\theta'\mid\theta)}.$$

$p_0(\theta)\widehat L_\theta(U)>0$. The density-free version uses the
accepted-flow Radon–Nikodym construction in the cited general-state algorithm;
it does not evaluate a pointwise prior mass or require this density condition.
Proposed zero estimates are rejected.
The input is the current extended state $(\theta,U)$; output the proposed
extended state $(\theta',U')$ on acceptance and retain $(\theta,U)$ on
rejection.

At each iteration draw a fresh $U\sim m_\theta$, propose

derivations.claim: Under MCWM, a move $0\to1$ accepts with conditional probabilities $1/2$ and $1$ for the two proposed estimates. Thus $P(0,1)=(1/2)(1/2)+(1/2)(1)=3/4$.

Fix $N\ge2$, a finite horizon $T$, a parameter $\theta$, and a reference
trajectory $x^*_{0:T}$ with a reference lineage of particle indices
$b_0,\ldots,b_T\in\{1,\ldots,N\}$. Use the proposal kernels, incremental
weights, and normalized resampling weights of
[[alg-sequential-importance-resampling]]. Use multinomial resampling with indices in sampled order. Require target-path domination as in [[thm-feynman-kac-path-radon-nikodym-weight]] and a retained $(\theta,x^*,b)$ in the measurable full-measure good set $D$ of [[def-particle-gibbs-extended-target]]. The formulas are conditional-law versions for posterior-almost every reference path; membership in topological support alone is insufficient. Outside $D$, return status “unavailable” and leave the retained parameter-path-lineage state unchanged in the sweep. If an arithmetic operation in a sampled particle system is undefined or a required normalizing sum is zero/nonfinite, also return “unavailable” and retain the old state; on $D$ these events have conditional probability zero by the factorization theorem.

At fixed $\theta$, use the parameter-specific proposal kernels and weights in
[[alg-sequential-importance-resampling]], writing its normalized resampling
weights $\bar w_t^i$ as $W_t^i$. The input is $(\theta,x^*_{0:T},b_{0:T})$;
the output is the conditional particle system, its normalized weights, its
ancestry arrays, and either a successful status or “unavailable”.

1. At time $0$, draw each $X_0^i$ for $i\ne b_0$ independently from $\nu_0$
   and set $X_0^{b_0}=x_0^*$. Compute the SIR initial weights
   $a_0^i=G_0(X_0^i)\rho_0(X_0^i)$ and set
   $\widehat Z_0=N^{-1}\sum_i a_0^i$. If $\sum_i a_0^i>0$, put
   $W_0^i=a_0^i/\sum_j a_0^j$; otherwise use the SIR zero-weight convention
   $W_0^i=1/N$. A zero or nonfinite normalizing sum makes the sweep unavailable
   and returns the unchanged retained state.
2. For $t=1,\ldots,T$, for every $i\ne b_t$ draw an ancestor $A_t^i$ from the
   categorical distribution with probabilities $W_{t-1}^{1:N}$ and then draw
   $X_t^i$ from the proposal kernel conditional on $X_{t-1}^{A_t^i}$. Set
   $A_t^{b_t}=b_{t-1}$ and $X_t^{b_t}=x_t^*$. Compute the SIR incremental
   weights $a_t^i=G_t(X_t^i)r_t(X_{t-1}^{A_t^i},X_t^i)$ and update
   $\widehat Z_t=\widehat Z_{t-1}(N^{-1}\sum_i a_t^i)$. If the weight sum is
   positive, put $W_t^i=a_t^i/\sum_j a_t^j$; otherwise use the SIR zero-weight
   convention $W_t^i=1/N$. A zero or nonfinite normalizing sum makes the sweep
   unavailable and returns the unchanged retained state.
3. Return the conditional particle system, its normalized weights, and its
   ancestry arrays.

For a joint parameter-path sweep, retain the current selected path $x^*$ and
its lineage $b$, draw $\theta'$ from its exact posterior full conditional
given $x^*$, and apply Steps 1–3 at $\theta'$. This parameter draw followed by
conditional-particle-filter regeneration is one joint conditional-block
update. Then draw $K'\sim\mathrm{Categorical}(W_T^{1:N})$ and trace its
ancestry to obtain the next selected path. Output the new extended state
$(\theta',U',K')$ together with that path. The correctness of this sweep is a
separate result.

Under [[def-particle-gibbs-extended-target]] and
[[alg-conditional-particle-gibbs]], for $\varphi_N$-almost every extended
state the conditional law of the terminal index $K$ given $(\theta,U)$ is
$\mathrm{Categorical}(W_T^{1:N})$. For posterior-almost every retained parameter-trajectory-lineage value, the remaining particles and
ancestor indices have exactly the conditional-particle-filter law in
[[alg-conditional-particle-gibbs]]. In a joint sweep, the parameter draw from
its posterior full conditional given the selected path, followed by
regeneration of the remaining particles and ancestors from the
conditional-particle-filter law, is the joint conditional-block update of
those variables given the retained selected path and lineage. The terminal
index is then drawn from its categorical conditional given the particle
system. These two updates preserve the extended target; the measurable
exceptional-state identity fallback specified by the algorithm is included.
The selected marginal is the exact joint parameter-path posterior. This
invariance does not assert fast mixing.

derivations.claim: The importance weights are $w(0)=(99/100)/(1/100)=99$ and $w(1)=(1/100)/(99/100)=1/99$. From reference state $0$, the free particle is $1$ with probability $99/100$ and is selected with probability $(1/99)/(99+1/99)=1/9802$. Therefore $P(0,1)=99/980200$.
From reference state $1$, the free particle is $0$ with probability $1/100$ and is selected with probability $99/(99+1/99)=9801/9802$. Therefore $P(1,0)=9801/980200$.

The detailed-balance flows agree: $(99/100)P(0,1)=9801/98020000=(1/100)P(1,0)$, consistent with the exact invariance in [F2]. Yet the probability of leaving state $0$ is only $99/980200<1/9000$, so exact invariance alone gives no useful lower bound on movement.

Assume AC and the setup of [[def-feynman-kac-path-targets-and-normalizers]] through a fixed horizon $t\le T$. Let $\nu_0$ be a proposal probability on $\mathsf X_0$, and for $1\le k\le t$ let $R_k:\mathsf X_{k-1}\rightsquigarrow\mathsf X_k$ be proposal probability kernels. Define $Q_s(dx_{0:s})=\nu_0(dx_0)\prod_{k=1}^sR_k(x_{k-1},dx_k)$. Suppose $\mu_0\ll\nu_0$, and for each $k$ suppose $M_k(x,\cdot)\ll R_k(x,\cdot)$ for almost every $x$ under the last-coordinate marginal of $Q_{k-1}$. Choose a measurable version $\rho_0=d\mu_0/d\nu_0$ and, using [[lem-jointly-measurable-radon-nikodym-derivatives-for-probability-kernels]], measurable versions $r_k(x,\cdot)=dM_k(x,\cdot)/dR_k(x,\cdot)$ for these preceding-state marginals.

Then $\gamma_s\ll Q_s$ for every $s\le t$, with product density
$$W_s(x_{0:s})=G_0(x_0)\rho_0(x_0)\prod_{k=1}^sG_k(x_k)r_k(x_{k-1},x_k).$$
That is, $\gamma_s(A)=\int_AW_s\,dQ_s$ for every measurable $A\subseteq\mathsf X_{0:s}$. If $0<Z_s<\infty$, the normalized path target has density $W_s/Z_s$ with respect to $Q_s$.

Let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be conjugate exponents. If $X$ and $Y$ are real random
variables in the spaces named by the corresponding clause of
[[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]], then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\|X\|_p\|Y\|_q.$$

In particular, $XY$ is integrable.

derivations.claim: By [A1], all $X_{N,i}$ have the same distribution and every distinct pair has the same covariance. By [A3] and [F1], $\mathbb E X_{N,1}\to\mathbb E U$; the same $L^2$ convergence and $\mathbb E U^2<\infty$ give $\sup_N\|X_{N,1}\|_2<\infty$.

Write $X_i=X_{N,i}$ and $U_i=U_{N,i}$. The identity $X_1X_2-U_1U_2=(X_1-U_1)X_2+U_1(X_2-U_2)$ and [F1] give $|\operatorname{Cov}(X_1,X_2)-\operatorname{Cov}(U_1,U_2)|\le \|X_1-U_1\|_2\|X_2\|_2+\|U_1\|_2\|X_2-U_2\|_2+|\mathbb EX_1\mathbb EX_2-\mathbb EU_1\mathbb EU_2|.$ By exchangeability the two $L^2$ differences have the same norm and both means converge as in step 1.1. Thus [A2]–[A3] imply $\operatorname{Cov}(X_{N,1},X_{N,2})\to0$.

Expanding the variance and using [A1] yields $\operatorname{Var}(\bar X_N)=N^{-1}\operatorname{Var}(X_{N,1})+(1-N^{-1})\operatorname{Cov}(X_{N,1},X_{N,2})\longrightarrow0,$ because the first variance is uniformly bounded by step 1.1 and the second term tends to zero by step 2.1. Also $\mathbb E\bar X_N=\mathbb E X_{N,1}\to\mathbb E U$ by step 1.1. Hence $\mathbb E|\bar X_N-\mathbb E U|^2=\operatorname{Var}(\bar X_N)+|\mathbb E\bar X_N-\mathbb E U|^2\to0$.

For each integer $N\ge2$, let $(X_{N,i},U_{N,i})_{i=1}^N$ be a jointly exchangeable row of real random pairs: its law is invariant when the same permutation is applied to every index. Assume that $U_{N,1},\ldots,U_{N,N}$ are pairwise uncorrelated, all have the law of a fixed square-integrable random variable $U$, and
$$\|X_{N,1}-U_{N,1}\|_2:=\bigl(\mathbb E|X_{N,1}-U_{N,1}|^2\bigr)^{1/2}\longrightarrow0.$$
Here $\operatorname{Cov}(V,W):=\mathbb E[(V-\mathbb EV)(W-\mathbb EW)]$. Then the empirical mean $\bar X_N=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N X_{N,i}$ converges to $\mathbb E U$ in $L^2$, meaning $\mathbb E|\bar X_N-\mathbb E U|^2\to0$, and hence in probability.

Let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be conjugate exponents. If $X$ and $Y$ are real random
variables in the spaces named by the corresponding clause of
[[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]], then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\|X\|_p\|Y\|_q.$$

In particular, $XY$ is integrable.

derivations.claim: Holder's inequality [F2] on a probability space gives $\|X_{N,1}-U_{N,1}\|_2\le\|X_{N,1}-U_{N,1}\|_4$. Apply [F1] to each coordinate to obtain $\bar X_N\to\mathbb EU$ in probability.

Fix coordinates $r,s\in\{1,\ldots,d\}$ and set $V_{N,i}=X_{N,i,r}X_{N,i,s}$ and $W_{N,i}=U_{N,i,r}U_{N,i,s}$. The rows $(V_{N,i},W_{N,i})$ are jointly exchangeable. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) and fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$. Let
the state dimension at time
$t$ be a positive integer $d_t$ for $0\le t\le T$, and the observation
dimension at time $t$ be a positive integer $p_t$ for $1\le t\le T$.
Choose deterministic matrices
$F_t\in\mathbb R^{d_t\times d_{t-1}}$ and
$H_t\in\mathbb R^{p_t\times d_t}$, a mean $m_0\in\mathbb R^{d_0}$, and
symmetric positive-semidefinite matrices, meaning $v^TPv\ge0$ for every
real vector $v$ of matching dimension,
$P_0\in\mathbb R^{d_0\times d_0}$,
$Q_t\in\mathbb R^{d_t\times d_t}$, and
$R_t\in\mathbb R^{p_t\times p_t}$. A **linear-Gaussian state-space model
with independent noises** is the general finite-horizon kernel model
([[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]) with initial law
$\mu_0=N_{d_0}(m_0,P_0)$ and transition and observation kernels
$$K_t(x,\cdot)=N_{d_t}(F_t x,Q_t),\qquad G_t(x,\cdot)=N_{p_t}(H_t x,R_t).$$
All Gaussian laws use the convention of
[[def-multivariate-normal-law]], which allows singular covariance matrices.

Its independent-noise representation consists of random vectors
$x_0,q_1,r_1,\ldots,q_T,r_T$ on a common probability space, with
$x_0\sim N_{d_0}(m_0,P_0)$, $q_t\sim N_{d_t}(0,Q_t)$,
$r_t\sim N_{p_t}(0,R_t)$, all mutually independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-random-elements]] (their generated sigma-algebras are
independent), and equations
$$x_t=F_t x_{t-1}+q_t,\qquad y_t=H_t x_t+r_t\qquad(1\le t\le T).$$
The local path-law theorem proves that every allowed parameter tuple has
such a finite representation, that its induced kernels are the displayed
$K_t,G_t$, and that its path law is the general kernel-product law.

This definition imposes the stated noise law and independence assumptions;
it does not establish their empirical adequacy. It supplies no filtering
algorithm, posterior recursion, or convergence claim. Any separate formula
that inverts an observed innovation covariance must assume that covariance is
positive definite at the point of inversion.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $m\ge1$ be finite, let $d_j\ge1$, and let
$Z_j$ for $1\le j\le m$ be mutually independent random elements of
$\mathbb R^{d_j}$. Suppose $Z_j\sim N_{d_j}(a_j,\Sigma_j)$, where each
$\Sigma_j$ is symmetric positive semidefinite. Put
$D=\sum_{j=1}^m d_j$, $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$,
$a=(a_1,\ldots,a_m)$, and
$\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(\Sigma_1,\ldots,\Sigma_m)$. Then
$$Z\sim N_D(a,\Sigma).$$
No covariance block needs to be invertible.

Fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$, positive state dimensions $d_0,\ldots,d_T$,
and positive observation dimensions $p_1,\ldots,p_T$. The input is a
linear-Gaussian model from
[[def-linear-gaussian-state-space-model-with-independent-noises]], with
matrices $F_k\in\mathbb R^{d_k\times d_{k-1}}$ and
$H_k\in\mathbb R^{p_k\times d_k}$, initial mean $m_0$, and symmetric
positive-semidefinite covariances $P_0,Q_k,R_k$. Its state and observation
equations are
$$X_k=F_kX_{k-1}+q_k,\qquad Y_k=H_kX_k+r_k,$$
where $q_k\sim N(0,Q_k)$ and $r_k\sim N(0,R_k)$ are centered and mutually
independent across all times and of $X_0$.

The admissible data are vectors $y_k\in\mathbb R^{p_k}$ for which every
innovation covariance encountered below is positive definite. Positive
definite means $u^TS_ku>0$ for every nonzero $u\in\mathbb R^{p_k}$. The
algorithm returns predicted and updated means and covariances and the
innovation and gain at each time. Initialize
$$m_{0|0}=m_0,\qquad P_{0|0}=P_0.$$
For $k=1,\ldots,T$, perform:

1. Predict:
$$m_{k|k-1}=F_km_{k-1|k-1},\qquad P_{k|k-1}=F_kP_{k-1|k-1}F_k^T+Q_k.$$
2. Form the innovation and its covariance:
$$v_k=y_k-H_km_{k|k-1},\qquad S_k=H_kP_{k|k-1}H_k^T+R_k.$$
3. Factor $S_k=L_kL_k^T$ with lower-triangular $L_k$ having positive
diagonal, using
[[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]].
Solve $L_kU_k=H_kP_{k|k-1}$ and $L_k^TK_k^T=U_k$ by triangular solves. This
defines $K_k^T=S_k^{-1}H_kP_{k|k-1}$, hence
$K_k=P_{k|k-1}H_k^TS_k^{-1}$, without explicitly forming $S_k^{-1}$.
4. Update:
$$m_{k|k}=m_{k|k-1}+K_kv_k,\qquad P_{k|k}=P_{k|k-1}-K_kS_kK_k^T.$$

For $T=0$ the loop is empty and the returned pair is $(m_0,P_0)$. No
inverse of $P_0$, $Q_k$, or $R_k$ is used. This item defines the procedure
and makes no complexity, rounding-error, or numerical-stability claim.

Assume AC. Fix a finite-horizon model from
[[def-linear-gaussian-state-space-model-with-independent-noises]] with
state and observation equations
$$X_k=F_kX_{k-1}+q_k,\qquad Y_k=H_kX_k+r_k\qquad (1\le k\le T),$$
where $X_0\sim N_{d_0}(m_0,P_0)$, the centered Gaussian noises $q_k,r_k$ are
mutually independent across times and from $X_0$, and $P_0,Q_k,R_k$ are
symmetric positive semidefinite. Let the parameters and observations be
admissible for [[alg-kalman-filter]], so the recursively formed innovation
covariances
$$S_k=H_kP_{k|k-1}H_k^T+R_k$$
are positive definite for every $1\le k\le T$. Run that algorithm from
$m_{0|0}=m_0$ and $P_{0|0}=P_0$. Then, for each $0\le k\le T$, the map
$$\pi_k(y_{1:k},\cdot)=N_{d_k}(m_{k|k}(y_{1:k}),P_{k|k})$$
is an everywhere-defined filtering kernel for $X_k$ given $Y_{1:k}$ in the
sense of [[def-state-space-filtering-laws]]. The empty history at $k=0$ is a
singleton, and $\pi_0=N_{d_0}(m_0,P_0)$. In particular, these recursions
give an exact Gaussian conditional-law version at every observation history;
each $P_{k|k}$ is positive semidefinite. Singular initial, process,
measurement, predicted-state, and filtered-state covariances are allowed.
Equivalently, the covariance update can be written in Joseph form
$$P_{k|k}=(I-K_kH_k)P_{k|k-1}(I-K_kH_k)^T+K_kR_kK_k^T.$$
Only the innovation matrices being solved must be positive definite. No
pointwise uniqueness of a conditional-law version on null histories,
observation-density assumption, or numerical-stability claim is made.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

derivations.claim: At $k=0$, the analysis members are iid with law $N(m_0,P_0)$ by their initialization, so the claim holds at the base time.

Assume the induction hypothesis: the members at time $k-1$ are iid with law $N(m_{k-1|k-1},P_{k-1|k-1})$. Each forecast is an affine image of the independent Gaussian pair $(U_{N,i}^{a,k-1},q_{N,i}^k)$. By [F2] the pair is jointly Gaussian; every scalar projection of its affine image is a scalar Gaussian projection, so [F5] makes the forecasts iid Gaussian with mean $m^f=F_km_{k-1|k-1}$ and covariance $P^f=F_kP_{k-1|k-1}F_k^T+Q_k$.

Since $P^f\succeq0$ and $R_k\succ0$, $S=H_kP^fH_k^T+R_k\succ0$, so $K=P^fH_k^TS^{-1}$ is defined. The independent Gaussian pair $(U_{N,i}^{f,k},y_k+\eta_{N,i}^k)$ and [F2] show that $U_{N,i}^{a,k}=A U_{N,i}^{f,k}+K(y_k+\eta_{N,i}^k)$, with $A=I-KH_k$, is Gaussian. Its mean is $m^f+K(y_k-H_km^f)$ and its covariance is $AP^fA^T+KR_kK^T=P^f-KSK^T,$ because $KS K^T=P^fH_k^TK^T=KH_kP^f$. These are precisely the Kalman update parameters in [F3].

For distinct member indices the pairs of forecast and perturbed observation are independent by the input independence and the induction hypothesis; applying the same deterministic affine update separately to each pair preserves independence. Therefore the updated members are iid with the Gaussian law from step 3.1. By [A1] and [F4] that law is the exact filtering law at the fixed data.

The initialization in step 1.1 is the base case, and step 4.1 proves the claim at time $k$ from the induction hypothesis at time $k-1$. Induction therefore gives the asserted iid exact filtering law for every $k\le T$.

Fix an ensemble size $N\ge2$, forecast map $\Psi$, observation map $G$, datum $y\in\mathbb R^p$, and observation covariance $\Gamma\succ0$. The input is a state ensemble $x^1,\ldots,x^N\in\mathbb R^d$, forecast-error draws $\xi^i$ that are independent across members and of the input ensemble, each with the caller-specified additive model-error law, and observation perturbations $\eta^i\sim N_p(0,\Gamma)$ under [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]. The observation perturbations are independent across members and independent of the forecast ensemble and forecast-error draws.

1. Forecast each member: $\widehat x^i=\Psi(x^i)+\xi^i$.

2. Form predicted observations $z^i=G(\widehat x^i)$, means $\bar x=N^{-1}\sum_i\widehat x^i$, $\bar z=N^{-1}\sum_i z^i$, and empirical covariance blocks
$$C_{xz}=N^{-1}\sum_i(\widehat x^i-\bar x)(z^i-\bar z)^T,\qquad C_{zz}=N^{-1}\sum_i(z^i-\bar z)(z^i-\bar z)^T.$$
The divisor-$N$ convention is part of this algorithm.

3. Form $S_N=C_{zz}+\Gamma$. Since $C_{zz}$ is positive semidefinite and $\Gamma$ is positive definite, $S_N$ is positive definite. Factor it by Cholesky and solve $S_NK_N^T=C_{xz}^T$ by triangular solves.

4. Update every member using its perturbed datum:
$$x^{a,i}=\widehat x^i+K_N(y+\eta^i-z^i).$$

Return the updated ensemble and its empirical mean and covariance. When $G(x)=Hx$, $C_{xz}=C_xH^T$ and $C_{zz}=HC_xH^T$, giving the usual sample-covariance Kalman gain. This item specifies the perturbed-observation variant; deterministic square-root updates are different finite-ensemble procedures. Finite ensembles in nonlinear models are approximations and carry no general posterior-exactness claim.

derivations.claim: Fix a permutation $\sigma$ of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$. Applying it to the input states and errors permutes the forecast states and predicted observations by the same $\sigma$. Their empirical means are unchanged, while the sums defining $C_{xz}$ and $C_{zz}$ are unchanged because they only reorder their summands. Therefore $S_N$ and the common gain $K_N$ are unchanged.

With the same $K_N$, the update at permuted index $i$ is exactly the original updated state at index $\sigma(i)$, since its datum perturbation and reference variable are permuted along with that member. Thus the full updated tuple under $\sigma$ is a permutation of the original updated tuple. Its law is unchanged by [A1], which is joint exchangeability.

Statement: Step 1.1 fixes an arbitrary finite permutation and step 2.1 applies equivariance. This uses no selection from arbitrary nonempty families.
