Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

Let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be conjugate exponents. If $X$ and $Y$ are real random
variables in the spaces named by the corresponding clause of
[[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]], then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\|X\|_p\|Y\|_q.$$

In particular, $XY$ is integrable.

derivations.claim: By [A1] and [F2]–[F3], each Gaussian vector is an affine image of finitely many standard normals. For every finite $p$, the integral of $|x|^p e^{-x^2/2}$ is finite because for sufficiently large $|x|$, $|x|^p\le e^{x^2/4}$ and $e^{-x^2/4}$ is integrable; bounded intervals contribute a finite integral. Finite-dimensional triangle inequalities then give finite moments for each vector input, with laws independent of $N$ and $i$. This proves the asserted state bound at $k=0$.

Assume the induction hypothesis that at time $k-1$ the state moments are bounded uniformly in $N,i$ at every finite order. The forecast formula in [F1] is a fixed linear map plus a Gaussian process-error draw. The triangle inequality and $ (a+b)^p\le2^{p-1}(a^p+b^p)$ for $a,b\ge0$ therefore give uniform bounds at every order for the forecast members $X_{N,i}^{f,k}$.

Write the forecast sample covariance as $C_N=N^{-1}\sum_iX_iX_i^T-\bar X\bar X^T$. Since $\|xx^T\|_{\rm op}=\|x\|^2$, Jensen's inequality for finite averages bounds the $p$th moment of the first term by $N^{-1}\sum_i\mathbb E\|X_i\|^{2p}$ and bounds $\mathbb E\|\bar X\|^{2p}$ by the same average. Thus [F1] and the forecast bounds in step 2.1 give $\sup_N\mathbb E\|C_N\|_{\rm op}^p<\infty$ for every finite $p$.

The matrix $H_kC_NH_k^T$ is positive semidefinite, so $S_N=H_kC_NH_k^T+R_k$ has quadratic form at least that of $R_k$. Let $r_k>0$ be the least eigenvalue of $R_k$, which exists by [F4]. Every eigenvalue of $S_N$ is at least $r_k$, hence $\|S_N^{-1}\|_{\rm op}\le r_k^{-1}$. It follows from $K_N=C_NH_k^TS_N^{-1}$ and step 3.1 that $\sup_N\mathbb E\|K_N\|_{\rm op}^p<\infty$ at every finite order.

Let $D_i=y_k+\eta_{N,i}^k$. The update in [F1] gives $\|X_{N,i}^{a,k}\|\le\|X_{N,i}^{f,k}\|+\|K_N\|_{\rm op}\|H_kX_{N,i}^{f,k}\|+\|K_N\|_{\rm op}\|D_i\|$. Apply [F5] with exponent pair $(2,2)$ to the middle product; for the last product use that $D_i$ is independent of $K_N$ and has finite Gaussian moments. The forecast, gain, and perturbation bounds in steps 2.1 and 4.1 therefore bound the $p$th moment of the updated state uniformly in $N,i$. This proves the induction step at time $k$.

Step 1.1 proves the state bound at time zero. For each $k\in\{1,\ldots,T\}$, step 5.1 derives both the state and gain bounds at time $k$ from the state bound at time $k-1$. Finite induction therefore proves the state bounds for every $0\le k\le T$ and the gain bounds for every $1\le k\le T$, for each finite $p$.

Induct simultaneously over all finite moment orders: a pth updated-state bound may use the 2pth forecast and gain bounds, already obtained at the same step from all previous-time moments. Jensen bounds covariance moments by forecast 2p moments; spectral decomposition gives ||(HC_NH^T+R_k)^-1||<=1/lambda_min(R_k), independently of N and i. citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

For integers $d,p\ge1$, given a forecast mean $m^f\in\mathbb R^d$, fixed background covariance $B\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$, linear observation matrix $H\in\mathbb R^{p\times d}$, datum $y\in\mathbb R^p$, and observation-error covariance $\Gamma\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$, require $B$ and $\Gamma$ symmetric positive definite. Define the 3DVAR objective
$$J(u)=\tfrac12(u-m^f)^TB^{-1}(u-m^f)+\tfrac12(y-Hu)^T\Gamma^{-1}(y-Hu).$$
Form $S=HBH^T+\Gamma$. It is positive definite because for every $z\ne0$,
$$z^TSz=(H^Tz)^TB(H^Tz)+z^T\Gamma z>0.$$
Factor $S=LL^T$ with the unique positive-diagonal Cholesky factor from [[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]]. Solve $LW=HB$ and $L^TK^T=W$; thus $K^T=S^{-1}HB$ without explicitly forming $S^{-1}$. Return the analysis point
$$m^a=m^f+K(y-Hm^f).$$
For a sequential 3DVAR filter, first set $m^f_{j+1}=\Psi_j(m^a_j)$, then apply this update with the fixed matrices $B,H,\Gamma$ and observation $y_{j+1}$. The routine returns a point estimate only. Its unique-minimizer and Gaussian-MAP properties are established separately; no analysis covariance is returned.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional inner product spaces and let $b\in W$. A vector $x\in V$ minimises $\lVert Tx-b\rVert$ if and only if

$$T^*(Tx-b)=0,$$

equivalently $T^*Tx=T^*b$. Minimisers exist, and if $x_0$ is one minimiser, then the full set of minimisers is $x_0+\ker T$.

Let $n\ge 1$ and let $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$, with the real case obtained by
restricting scalars to $\mathbb R$. Then the following are equivalent:

1. $A$ has a Cholesky factorisation $A=LL^*$ with $L$ lower triangular and
   positive real diagonal.
2. $A$ is Hermitian positive definite.

When these conditions hold, the factor $L$ is unique.

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$, $m\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $\Sigma$ be a real symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then its law has Lebesgue density
$$f_{m,\Sigma}(x)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\det(\Sigma)^{-1/2} \exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(x-m)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-m)\right), \qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$

Let $\pi$ be a prior probability on $(E,\mathcal S)$ and let $Q:E\to T$ be a probability kernel dominated by a sigma-finite measure $\nu$ on $(T,\mathcal T)$, with specified nonnegative jointly measurable density $\ell:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$:
$$Q(\theta,B)=\int_B\ell(\theta,y)\,\nu(dy)\quad\text{for every }\theta\in E,\ B\in\mathcal T.$$

Define $m(y)=\int_E\ell(\theta,y)\,\pi(d\theta)$. Under the joint law with density $\ell$ relative to $\pi\times\nu$, a conditional law of the parameter given the observation is
$$K(y,A)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\int_A\ell(\theta,y)\,\pi(d\theta)}{m(y)},&0<m(y)<\infty,\\ \pi(A),&m(y)=0\text{ or }m(y)=\infty.\end{cases}$$

The observation marginal is $m\,d\nu$, and the filled fibres have marginal mass zero. This is a choice-free assertion about the explicit kernel and event identities.

Fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$, positive state dimensions $d_0,\ldots,d_T$,
and positive observation dimensions $p_1,\ldots,p_T$. The input is a
linear-Gaussian model from
[[def-linear-gaussian-state-space-model-with-independent-noises]], with
matrices $F_k\in\mathbb R^{d_k\times d_{k-1}}$ and
$H_k\in\mathbb R^{p_k\times d_k}$, initial mean $m_0$, and symmetric
positive-semidefinite covariances $P_0,Q_k,R_k$. Its state and observation
equations are
$$X_k=F_kX_{k-1}+q_k,\qquad Y_k=H_kX_k+r_k,$$
where $q_k\sim N(0,Q_k)$ and $r_k\sim N(0,R_k)$ are centered and mutually
independent across all times and of $X_0$.

The admissible data are vectors $y_k\in\mathbb R^{p_k}$ for which every
innovation covariance encountered below is positive definite. Positive
definite means $u^TS_ku>0$ for every nonzero $u\in\mathbb R^{p_k}$. The
algorithm returns predicted and updated means and covariances and the
innovation and gain at each time. Initialize
$$m_{0|0}=m_0,\qquad P_{0|0}=P_0.$$
For $k=1,\ldots,T$, perform:

1. Predict:
$$m_{k|k-1}=F_km_{k-1|k-1},\qquad P_{k|k-1}=F_kP_{k-1|k-1}F_k^T+Q_k.$$
2. Form the innovation and its covariance:
$$v_k=y_k-H_km_{k|k-1},\qquad S_k=H_kP_{k|k-1}H_k^T+R_k.$$
3. Factor $S_k=L_kL_k^T$ with lower-triangular $L_k$ having positive
diagonal, using
[[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]].
Solve $L_kU_k=H_kP_{k|k-1}$ and $L_k^TK_k^T=U_k$ by triangular solves. This
defines $K_k^T=S_k^{-1}H_kP_{k|k-1}$, hence
$K_k=P_{k|k-1}H_k^TS_k^{-1}$, without explicitly forming $S_k^{-1}$.
4. Update:
$$m_{k|k}=m_{k|k-1}+K_kv_k,\qquad P_{k|k}=P_{k|k-1}-K_kS_kK_k^T.$$

For $T=0$ the loop is empty and the returned pair is $(m_0,P_0)$. No
inverse of $P_0$, $Q_k$, or $R_k$ is used. This item defines the procedure
and makes no complexity, rounding-error, or numerical-stability claim.

Assume AC. Fix a finite-horizon model from
[[def-linear-gaussian-state-space-model-with-independent-noises]] with
state and observation equations
$$X_k=F_kX_{k-1}+q_k,\qquad Y_k=H_kX_k+r_k\qquad (1\le k\le T),$$
where $X_0\sim N_{d_0}(m_0,P_0)$, the centered Gaussian noises $q_k,r_k$ are
mutually independent across times and from $X_0$, and $P_0,Q_k,R_k$ are
symmetric positive semidefinite. Let the parameters and observations be
admissible for [[alg-kalman-filter]], so the recursively formed innovation
covariances
$$S_k=H_kP_{k|k-1}H_k^T+R_k$$
are positive definite for every $1\le k\le T$. Run that algorithm from
$m_{0|0}=m_0$ and $P_{0|0}=P_0$. Then, for each $0\le k\le T$, the map
$$\pi_k(y_{1:k},\cdot)=N_{d_k}(m_{k|k}(y_{1:k}),P_{k|k})$$
is an everywhere-defined filtering kernel for $X_k$ given $Y_{1:k}$ in the
sense of [[def-state-space-filtering-laws]]. The empty history at $k=0$ is a
singleton, and $\pi_0=N_{d_0}(m_0,P_0)$. In particular, these recursions
give an exact Gaussian conditional-law version at every observation history;
each $P_{k|k}$ is positive semidefinite. Singular initial, process,
measurement, predicted-state, and filtered-state covariances are allowed.
Equivalently, the covariance update can be written in Joseph form
$$P_{k|k}=(I-K_kH_k)P_{k|k-1}(I-K_kH_k)^T+K_kR_kK_k^T.$$
Only the innovation matrices being solved must be positive definite. No
pointwise uniqueness of a conditional-law version on null histories,
observation-density assumption, or numerical-stability claim is made.

derivations.claim: For $z\ne0$, $z^TSz=(H^Tz)^TB(H^Tz)+z^T\Gamma z>0$, so $S\succ0$ and $K$ is defined. The inverses $B^{-1}$ and $\Gamma^{-1}$ are positive definite: for nonzero $v$, $v^TB^{-1}v=(B^{-1}v)^TB(B^{-1}v)>0$, and the same argument applies to $\Gamma$. By [F3], choose Cholesky factors $B^{-1}=L_BL_B^T$ and $\Gamma^{-1}=L_\Gamma L_\Gamma^T$. Define $T u=(L_B^Tu,L_\Gamma^THu)$ and $b=(L_B^Tm^f,L_\Gamma^Ty)$. Then $2J(u)=\|Tu-b\|^2$. The first block $L_B^T$ is invertible, hence $\ker T=\{0\}$.

The normal equation in [F2] is $B^{-1}(u-m^f)+H^T\Gamma^{-1}(Hu-y)=0$. Let $\delta=y-Hm^f$ and $u=m^f+BH^TS^{-1}\delta=m^a$. Then $B^{-1}(u-m^f)=H^TS^{-1}\delta$, while $y-Hu=(I-HBH^TS^{-1})\delta=\Gamma S^{-1}\delta$. Substitution gives the normal equation. By [F2] this $u$ minimizes $J$, and because $\ker T=\{0\}$ it is the unique minimizer.

Under the Gaussian prior and independent Gaussian observation-error model, [F4] gives a prior density proportional to $\exp[-\tfrac12(u-m^f)^TB^{-1}(u-m^f)]$ and a jointly continuous likelihood density proportional to $\exp[-\tfrac12(y-Hu)^T\Gamma^{-1}(y-Hu)]$. The likelihood is strictly positive and bounded above by its finite Gaussian normalizing constant; hence its prior integral is finite and positive. Bayes' formula [F5] makes the posterior density proportional to $e^{-J(u)}$; its unique maximum is therefore the unique minimizer from step 2.1.

Apply [F6] to the one-step model with forecast covariance $B$, identity transition, zero process covariance, and observation covariance $\Gamma$. Its innovation covariance is $S\succ0$ by step 1.1, so the output mean is $m^f+K(y-Hm^f)=m^a$. By [F7] this is the mean of the exact conditional Gaussian law.

derivations.claim: Set $e_j=m_j-v_j^\dagger$. By [F1], the observation equation, and $v_{j+1}^\dagger=\Psi(v_j^\dagger)$, $e_{j+1}=F(m_j)-F(v_j^\dagger)+K\epsilon_j.$ The contraction bound [A1], triangle inequality, and [F2] give $\|e_{j+1}\|\le a\|e_j\|+\kappa\epsilon.$

Put $c=\kappa\epsilon$. Repeated substitution in step 1.1 gives, for each $n\ge1$, $\|e_n\|\le a^n\|e_0\|+c\sum_{r=0}^{n-1}a^r=a^n\|e_0\|+c\frac{1-a^n}{1-a}.$ For $a=0$ the finite sum is $1$ and the same expression holds for every $n\ge1$. Since $0\le a<1$, $a^n\to0$, so taking the limit superior proves the bound.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) and fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$. Let
the state dimension at time
$t$ be a positive integer $d_t$ for $0\le t\le T$, and the observation
dimension at time $t$ be a positive integer $p_t$ for $1\le t\le T$.
Choose deterministic matrices
$F_t\in\mathbb R^{d_t\times d_{t-1}}$ and
$H_t\in\mathbb R^{p_t\times d_t}$, a mean $m_0\in\mathbb R^{d_0}$, and
symmetric positive-semidefinite matrices, meaning $v^TPv\ge0$ for every
real vector $v$ of matching dimension,
$P_0\in\mathbb R^{d_0\times d_0}$,
$Q_t\in\mathbb R^{d_t\times d_t}$, and
$R_t\in\mathbb R^{p_t\times p_t}$. A **linear-Gaussian state-space model
with independent noises** is the general finite-horizon kernel model
([[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]) with initial law
$\mu_0=N_{d_0}(m_0,P_0)$ and transition and observation kernels
$$K_t(x,\cdot)=N_{d_t}(F_t x,Q_t),\qquad G_t(x,\cdot)=N_{p_t}(H_t x,R_t).$$
All Gaussian laws use the convention of
[[def-multivariate-normal-law]], which allows singular covariance matrices.

Its independent-noise representation consists of random vectors
$x_0,q_1,r_1,\ldots,q_T,r_T$ on a common probability space, with
$x_0\sim N_{d_0}(m_0,P_0)$, $q_t\sim N_{d_t}(0,Q_t)$,
$r_t\sim N_{p_t}(0,R_t)$, all mutually independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-random-elements]] (their generated sigma-algebras are
independent), and equations
$$x_t=F_t x_{t-1}+q_t,\qquad y_t=H_t x_t+r_t\qquad(1\le t\le T).$$
The local path-law theorem proves that every allowed parameter tuple has
such a finite representation, that its induced kernels are the displayed
$K_t,G_t$, and that its path law is the general kernel-product law.

This definition imposes the stated noise law and independence assumptions;
it does not establish their empirical adequacy. It supplies no filtering
algorithm, posterior recursion, or convergence claim. Any separate formula
that inverts an observed innovation covariance must assume that covariance is
positive definite at the point of inversion.

Fix an ensemble size $N\ge2$, forecast map $\Psi$, observation map $G$, datum $y\in\mathbb R^p$, and observation covariance $\Gamma\succ0$. The input is a state ensemble $x^1,\ldots,x^N\in\mathbb R^d$, forecast-error draws $\xi^i$ that are independent across members and of the input ensemble, each with the caller-specified additive model-error law, and observation perturbations $\eta^i\sim N_p(0,\Gamma)$ under [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]. The observation perturbations are independent across members and independent of the forecast ensemble and forecast-error draws.

1. Forecast each member: $\widehat x^i=\Psi(x^i)+\xi^i$.

2. Form predicted observations $z^i=G(\widehat x^i)$, means $\bar x=N^{-1}\sum_i\widehat x^i$, $\bar z=N^{-1}\sum_i z^i$, and empirical covariance blocks
$$C_{xz}=N^{-1}\sum_i(\widehat x^i-\bar x)(z^i-\bar z)^T,\qquad C_{zz}=N^{-1}\sum_i(z^i-\bar z)(z^i-\bar z)^T.$$
The divisor-$N$ convention is part of this algorithm.

3. Form $S_N=C_{zz}+\Gamma$. Since $C_{zz}$ is positive semidefinite and $\Gamma$ is positive definite, $S_N$ is positive definite. Factor it by Cholesky and solve $S_NK_N^T=C_{xz}^T$ by triangular solves.

4. Update every member using its perturbed datum:
$$x^{a,i}=\widehat x^i+K_N(y+\eta^i-z^i).$$

Return the updated ensemble and its empirical mean and covariance. When $G(x)=Hx$, $C_{xz}=C_xH^T$ and $C_{zz}=HC_xH^T$, giving the usual sample-covariance Kalman gain. This item specifies the perturbed-observation variant; deterministic square-root updates are different finite-ensemble procedures. Finite ensembles in nonlinear models are approximations and carry no general posterior-exactness claim.

Fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$, positive state dimensions $d_0,\ldots,d_T$,
and positive observation dimensions $p_1,\ldots,p_T$. The input is a
linear-Gaussian model from
[[def-linear-gaussian-state-space-model-with-independent-noises]], with
matrices $F_k\in\mathbb R^{d_k\times d_{k-1}}$ and
$H_k\in\mathbb R^{p_k\times d_k}$, initial mean $m_0$, and symmetric
positive-semidefinite covariances $P_0,Q_k,R_k$. Its state and observation
equations are
$$X_k=F_kX_{k-1}+q_k,\qquad Y_k=H_kX_k+r_k,$$
where $q_k\sim N(0,Q_k)$ and $r_k\sim N(0,R_k)$ are centered and mutually
independent across all times and of $X_0$.

The admissible data are vectors $y_k\in\mathbb R^{p_k}$ for which every
innovation covariance encountered below is positive definite. Positive
definite means $u^TS_ku>0$ for every nonzero $u\in\mathbb R^{p_k}$. The
algorithm returns predicted and updated means and covariances and the
innovation and gain at each time. Initialize
$$m_{0|0}=m_0,\qquad P_{0|0}=P_0.$$
For $k=1,\ldots,T$, perform:

1. Predict:
$$m_{k|k-1}=F_km_{k-1|k-1},\qquad P_{k|k-1}=F_kP_{k-1|k-1}F_k^T+Q_k.$$
2. Form the innovation and its covariance:
$$v_k=y_k-H_km_{k|k-1},\qquad S_k=H_kP_{k|k-1}H_k^T+R_k.$$
3. Factor $S_k=L_kL_k^T$ with lower-triangular $L_k$ having positive
diagonal, using
[[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]].
Solve $L_kU_k=H_kP_{k|k-1}$ and $L_k^TK_k^T=U_k$ by triangular solves. This
defines $K_k^T=S_k^{-1}H_kP_{k|k-1}$, hence
$K_k=P_{k|k-1}H_k^TS_k^{-1}$, without explicitly forming $S_k^{-1}$.
4. Update:
$$m_{k|k}=m_{k|k-1}+K_kv_k,\qquad P_{k|k}=P_{k|k-1}-K_kS_kK_k^T.$$

For $T=0$ the loop is empty and the returned pair is $(m_0,P_0)$. No
inverse of $P_0$, $Q_k$, or $R_k$ is used. This item defines the procedure
and makes no complexity, rounding-error, or numerical-stability claim.

Assume AC. Fix a finite-horizon model from
[[def-linear-gaussian-state-space-model-with-independent-noises]] with
state and observation equations
$$X_k=F_kX_{k-1}+q_k,\qquad Y_k=H_kX_k+r_k\qquad (1\le k\le T),$$
where $X_0\sim N_{d_0}(m_0,P_0)$, the centered Gaussian noises $q_k,r_k$ are
mutually independent across times and from $X_0$, and $P_0,Q_k,R_k$ are
symmetric positive semidefinite. Let the parameters and observations be
admissible for [[alg-kalman-filter]], so the recursively formed innovation
covariances
$$S_k=H_kP_{k|k-1}H_k^T+R_k$$
are positive definite for every $1\le k\le T$. Run that algorithm from
$m_{0|0}=m_0$ and $P_{0|0}=P_0$. Then, for each $0\le k\le T$, the map
$$\pi_k(y_{1:k},\cdot)=N_{d_k}(m_{k|k}(y_{1:k}),P_{k|k})$$
is an everywhere-defined filtering kernel for $X_k$ given $Y_{1:k}$ in the
sense of [[def-state-space-filtering-laws]]. The empty history at $k=0$ is a
singleton, and $\pi_0=N_{d_0}(m_0,P_0)$. In particular, these recursions
give an exact Gaussian conditional-law version at every observation history;
each $P_{k|k}$ is positive semidefinite. Singular initial, process,
measurement, predicted-state, and filtered-state covariances are allowed.
Equivalently, the covariance update can be written in Joseph form
$$P_{k|k}=(I-K_kH_k)P_{k|k-1}(I-K_kH_k)^T+K_kR_kK_k^T.$$
Only the innovation matrices being solved must be positive definite. No
pointwise uniqueness of a conditional-law version on null histories,
observation-density assumption, or numerical-stability claim is made.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ be independent real random variables on a
common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then
   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$
   in $[0,+\infty]$. In this finite product of expectations, a zero factor
   makes the product zero even when another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise
   multiplication has its usual extended nonnegative meaning.
2. If every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable
   and the same factorization holds in $\mathbb R$.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $t>0$. Then
$$\mu(\{f\ge t\})\le\frac1t\int f\,d\mu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $m\ge1$ be finite, let $d_j\ge1$, and let
$Z_j$ for $1\le j\le m$ be mutually independent random elements of
$\mathbb R^{d_j}$. Suppose $Z_j\sim N_{d_j}(a_j,\Sigma_j)$, where each
$\Sigma_j$ is symmetric positive semidefinite. Put
$D=\sum_{j=1}^m d_j$, $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$,
$a=(a_1,\ldots,a_m)$, and
$\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(\Sigma_1,\ldots,\Sigma_m)$. Then
$$Z\sim N_D(a,\Sigma).$$
No covariance block needs to be invertible.

Fix the perturbed-observation update of [[alg-ensemble-kalman-filter]]. A row of random inputs is **exchangeable** if its joint law is invariant under every common permutation of the member indices. If the forecast states, forecast errors, observation perturbations, and any reference-member variables form an exchangeable input row, then the updated states together with those reference variables are exchangeable.

Let $d\ge1$. For each $N\ge2$, let $(X_{N,i},U_{N,i})_{i=1}^N$ be jointly exchangeable random pairs in $\mathbb R^d$. Assume that $U_{N,1},\ldots,U_{N,N}$ are iid with the law of a fixed $U$, $\mathbb E\|U\|^4<\infty$, and $\|X_{N,1}-U_{N,1}\|_4\to0$. Define
$$\bar X_N=N^{-1}\sum_iX_{N,i},\qquad C_N=N^{-1}\sum_i(X_{N,i}-\bar X_N)(X_{N,i}-\bar X_N)^T.$$
Here $\operatorname{Cov}(U):=\mathbb E[(U-\mathbb EU)(U-\mathbb EU)^T]$. Then $\bar X_N\to\mathbb EU$ and $C_N\to\operatorname{Cov}(U)$ in probability, entry by entry.

Assume AC and the finite-horizon linear-Gaussian model of [[def-linear-gaussian-state-space-model-with-independent-noises]], with $R_k\succ0$ for $1\le k\le T$. Fix the observation values $y_{1:T}$. For each $N$, initialize $U_{N,i}^{a,0}$ iid with the model's $N(m_0,P_0)$ prior. At each time use independent per-member noises $q_{N,i}^k\sim N(0,Q_k)$ and $\eta_{N,i}^k\sim N(0,R_k)$, independent across $i,k$ and from the preceding ensemble, and form
$$U_{N,i}^{f,k}=F_kU_{N,i}^{a,k-1}+q_{N,i}^k,\qquad U_{N,i}^{a,k}=U_{N,i}^{f,k}+K_k(y_k+\eta_{N,i}^k-H_kU_{N,i}^{f,k}),$$
where $K_k=P_{k|k-1}H_k^T(H_kP_{k|k-1}H_k^T+R_k)^{-1}$ is the deterministic gain from [[alg-kalman-filter]]. Then, for every $k\le T$, the analysis members $U_{N,1}^{a,k},\ldots,U_{N,N}^{a,k}$ are iid with law $N(m_{k|k},P_{k|k})$, the exact Kalman filtering law at the fixed data $y_{1:k}$.

Fix a finite horizon linear-Gaussian model from [[def-linear-gaussian-state-space-model-with-independent-noises]], with each observation covariance $R_k\succ0$. Run the perturbed-observation procedure of [[alg-ensemble-kalman-filter]] with iid Gaussian initial members and independent Gaussian process and observation perturbations having the model's laws. For every finite $p\ge1$, there are constants $c_{k,p}$ for $0\le k\le T$ and $b_{k,p}$ for $1\le k\le T$, independent of ensemble size $N\ge2$ and member index $i$, such that
$$\sup_{N,i}\mathbb E\|X_{N,i}^{a,k}\|^p\le c_{k,p}\quad(0\le k\le T),\qquad \sup_N\mathbb E\|K_N^k\|_{\rm op}^p\le b_{k,p}\quad(1\le k\le T).$$
Here $\|\cdot\|_{\rm op}$ is the Euclidean operator norm. The claim is for each fixed finite horizon, not a bound uniform in $k$ as the horizon grows.

Let $1\le q<s<\infty$. Suppose random vectors $Z_n,Z$ in a fixed finite-dimensional Euclidean space satisfy $Z_n\to Z$ in probability, $\mathbb E\|Z\|^s<\infty$, and $\sup_n\mathbb E\|Z_n\|^s<\infty$. Then $\mathbb E\|Z_n-Z\|^q\to0$.

derivations.claim: Couple the EnKF members with a reference ensemble by using the same iid initial vectors, process-error draws, and perturbed observations. At time $0$, $X_{N,i}^{a,0}=U_{N,i}^{a,0}$, so the paired row is exchangeable and the memberwise difference is zero in every finite $L^p$.

Fix $k\in\{1,\ldots,T\}$ and assume the induction hypothesis: the paired analysis row $(X_{N,i}^{a,k-1},U_{N,i}^{a,k-1})_{i=1}^N$ is exchangeable and $\|X_{N,1}^{a,k-1}-U_{N,1}^{a,k-1}\|_p\to0$ for every finite $p$. Couple the forecasts with the same $q_{N,i}^k$; then $X_{N,i}^{f,k}-U_{N,i}^{f,k}=F_k(X_{N,i}^{a,k-1}-U_{N,i}^{a,k-1})$. Thus forecast differences tend to zero in every finite $L^p$. The independent iid process-error and observation-perturbation rows have permutation-invariant laws and are independent of the paired analysis row; their product with that row is permutation-invariant, and the same forecast map is applied to each member. Hence the forecast pair row with its perturbations is exchangeable. By [F8] and [F1], each reference forecast is Gaussian, with mean and covariance $m^f=F_km_{k-1|k-1}$ and $P^f=F_kP_{k-1|k-1}F_k^T+Q_k$ as in [F3]; independence across members follows from the independent per-member inputs.

Apply [L2] to the forecast pair row with $p=4$. The reference forecast covariance is $P_{k|k-1}$ by [F1] and [F3], so $C_N^{f,k}\to P_{k|k-1}$ in probability. Since $R_k\succ0$, both $S_N=H_kC_N^{f,k}H_k^T+R_k$ and $S=H_kP_{k|k-1}H_k^T+R_k$ dominate $R_k$ in quadratic form. [F5] bounds both inverse operator norms by $1/\lambda_{\min}(R_k)$. The identity $S_N^{-1}-S^{-1}=S_N^{-1}(S-S_N)S^{-1}$ therefore gives $K_N^k=C_N^{f,k}H_k^TS_N^{-1}\to K_k=P_{k|k-1}H_k^TS^{-1}$ in probability.

Let $D_{N,i}^k=y_k+\eta_{N,i}^k$. Subtracting the reference update from the EnKF update yields $X_{N,i}^{a,k}-U_{N,i}^{a,k}=(I-K_N^kH_k)(X_{N,i}^{f,k}-U_{N,i}^{f,k})+(K_N^k-K_k)(D_{N,i}^k-H_kU_{N,i}^{f,k}).$ The first factor in the first product is bounded in probability because $K_N^k\to K_k$ in probability. The first factor in the second product tends to zero in probability, while $D_{N,i}^k-H_kU_{N,i}^{f,k}$ has a fixed finite-moment Gaussian law. Splitting on whether this latter norm exceeds an arbitrary $M$ shows the product tends to zero in probability. The same bounded-in-probability argument for the first product gives $X_{N,1}^{a,k}-U_{N,1}^{a,k}\to0$ in probability. By [L1], the updated paired row is exchangeable.

The uniform moment bounds [L4] and the Gaussian reference law [L3] give a uniform bound on $\mathbb E\|X_{N,1}^{a,k}-U_{N,1}^{a,k}\|^s$ for every finite $s$. Apply [L5] with any $s>p$ to the probability convergence in step 4.1; the memberwise difference tends to zero in $L^p$ for every finite $p$. Together, the preceding steps establish the induction hypothesis at time $k$.

At any fixed $k$, the paired row is exchangeable, the reference members are iid with law $\pi_k$ by [L3], and [F4] identifies that Kalman law with the exact filtering law at the fixed data. At $k=0$, the memberwise difference is identically zero by step 1.1, hence tends to zero in $L^4$; for $k\ge1$, it tends to zero in $L^4$ by step 5.1. The sample-moment result [L2] gives the claimed mean and covariance convergence. For bounded Lipschitz $\varphi$, the empirical-average difference is at most $\operatorname{Lip}(\varphi)N^{-1}\sum_i\|X_{N,i}^{a,k}-U_{N,i}^{a,k}\|$; its expectation tends to zero by exchangeability and the $L^1$ convergence in step 1.1 when $k=0$ and step 5.1 when $k\ge1$, so the pointwise bound $\mathbb P(W\ge t)\le t^{-1}\mathbb EW$ from [F7] makes it vanish in probability. For the iid reference average, independence [F6] makes all distinct centered cross terms have expectation zero, so its variance is $\operatorname{Var}(\varphi(U_{N,1}^{a,k}))/N\le\|\varphi\|_\infty^2/N$. Apply [F7] to its squared centered deviation at threshold $\epsilon^2$ to obtain convergence in probability to $\int\varphi\,d\pi_k$. This proves the limits for each fixed $k$.

Step 1.1 is the base case, and for every $k\ge1$ the four induction steps establish the induction hypothesis at time $k$ from time $k-1$. Thus the coupling bounds hold through $T$, and step 6.1 gives the three asserted limits for every fixed $k\le T$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Fix an ensemble size $N\ge2$, forecast map $\Psi$, observation map $G$, datum $y\in\mathbb R^p$, and observation covariance $\Gamma\succ0$. The input is a state ensemble $x^1,\ldots,x^N\in\mathbb R^d$, forecast-error draws $\xi^i$ that are independent across members and of the input ensemble, each with the caller-specified additive model-error law, and observation perturbations $\eta^i\sim N_p(0,\Gamma)$ under [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]. The observation perturbations are independent across members and independent of the forecast ensemble and forecast-error draws.

1. Forecast each member: $\widehat x^i=\Psi(x^i)+\xi^i$.

2. Form predicted observations $z^i=G(\widehat x^i)$, means $\bar x=N^{-1}\sum_i\widehat x^i$, $\bar z=N^{-1}\sum_i z^i$, and empirical covariance blocks
$$C_{xz}=N^{-1}\sum_i(\widehat x^i-\bar x)(z^i-\bar z)^T,\qquad C_{zz}=N^{-1}\sum_i(z^i-\bar z)(z^i-\bar z)^T.$$
The divisor-$N$ convention is part of this algorithm.

3. Form $S_N=C_{zz}+\Gamma$. Since $C_{zz}$ is positive semidefinite and $\Gamma$ is positive definite, $S_N$ is positive definite. Factor it by Cholesky and solve $S_NK_N^T=C_{xz}^T$ by triangular solves.

4. Update every member using its perturbed datum:
$$x^{a,i}=\widehat x^i+K_N(y+\eta^i-z^i).$$

Return the updated ensemble and its empirical mean and covariance. When $G(x)=Hx$, $C_{xz}=C_xH^T$ and $C_{zz}=HC_xH^T$, giving the usual sample-covariance Kalman gain. This item specifies the perturbed-observation variant; deterministic square-root updates are different finite-ensemble procedures. Finite ensembles in nonlinear models are approximations and carry no general posterior-exactness claim.

derivations.claim: The event $A=\{-0.1<X_1<0.1,\ 3<X_2<3.1\}$ has positive probability: each interval has positive probability by [F1], and the variables are independent. On $A$, $X_2-X_1>2.9$, so step 1.1 gives $C_2>2.9^2/4=2.1025>1$. The true variance of $N(0,1)$ is $1$ by [F2]; hence the finite-ensemble covariance differs from it with positive probability.

The ensemble is finite and admissible; no asymptotic or degenerate-Gaussian density claim is made. Inherited AC is explicit.

In **strong-constraint 4DVAR**, choose the initial state $u_0$ and generate $u_t=\Psi_{t-1}(u_{t-1})$ for $1\le t\le T$. Minimize the trajectory objective
$$J_s(u_0)=\tfrac12\|u_0-m_b\|_{B^{-1}}^2+\tfrac12\sum_{t=1}^T\|y_t-G_t(u_t)\|_{\Gamma_t^{-1}}^2.$$

derivations.claim: Since $u_1=\Psi(u_0)=u_0$, the one-variable objective from [F1] is $J(u)=\tfrac12u^2+\tfrac12(1-u^2)^2=\tfrac12-\tfrac12u^2+\tfrac12u^4.$

Differentiating gives $J'(u)=u(2u^2-1)$. Its only stationary points are $0$ and $\pm1/\sqrt2$. The derivative changes from negative to positive at each of $\pm1/\sqrt2$, so both are strict local minima. The objective is even, $J(\pm1/\sqrt2)=3/8<J(0)=1/2$, and $J(u)\to\infty$ as $|u|\to\infty$. Every global minimum is therefore attained at a stationary point, and these two distinct points are both global minimizers. Thus the minimizer is not unique, so an iterative routine's finite definition gives no guarantee that it returns a designated unique solution.

Statement: At u=0, J=1/2 and J′=0; step 2.1 compares it with J(±1/sqrt(2))=3/8, so the stationary zero is not a minimum.
Example: its one-step window T=1 is an allowed boundary case.
Statement: B=Gamma_1=1 are nonsingular. Symmetry produces two equal global minima despite those positive covariances, as calculated in step 2.1.
Statement: The witness is T=1 with identity model map; it is an admitted one-step strong-constraint window, not a zero-window extension.
Statement: Step 2.1 explicitly identifies both minima ±1/sqrt(2); no arbitrary choice of one minimizer is required.

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$, $m\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $\Sigma$ be a real symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then its law has Lebesgue density
$$f_{m,\Sigma}(x)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\det(\Sigma)^{-1/2} \exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(x-m)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-m)\right), \qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$

Let $\pi$ be a prior probability on $(E,\mathcal S)$ and let $Q:E\to T$ be a probability kernel dominated by a sigma-finite measure $\nu$ on $(T,\mathcal T)$, with specified nonnegative jointly measurable density $\ell:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$:
$$Q(\theta,B)=\int_B\ell(\theta,y)\,\nu(dy)\quad\text{for every }\theta\in E,\ B\in\mathcal T.$$

Define $m(y)=\int_E\ell(\theta,y)\,\pi(d\theta)$. Under the joint law with density $\ell$ relative to $\pi\times\nu$, a conditional law of the parameter given the observation is
$$K(y,A)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\int_A\ell(\theta,y)\,\pi(d\theta)}{m(y)},&0<m(y)<\infty,\\ \pi(A),&m(y)=0\text{ or }m(y)=\infty.\end{cases}$$

The observation marginal is $m\,d\nu$, and the filled fibres have marginal mass zero. This is a choice-free assertion about the explicit kernel and event identities.

Fix an ensemble size $N\ge2$, forecast map $\Psi$, observation map $G$, datum $y\in\mathbb R^p$, and observation covariance $\Gamma\succ0$. The input is a state ensemble $x^1,\ldots,x^N\in\mathbb R^d$, forecast-error draws $\xi^i$ that are independent across members and of the input ensemble, each with the caller-specified additive model-error law, and observation perturbations $\eta^i\sim N_p(0,\Gamma)$ under [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]. The observation perturbations are independent across members and independent of the forecast ensemble and forecast-error draws.

1. Forecast each member: $\widehat x^i=\Psi(x^i)+\xi^i$.

2. Form predicted observations $z^i=G(\widehat x^i)$, means $\bar x=N^{-1}\sum_i\widehat x^i$, $\bar z=N^{-1}\sum_i z^i$, and empirical covariance blocks
$$C_{xz}=N^{-1}\sum_i(\widehat x^i-\bar x)(z^i-\bar z)^T,\qquad C_{zz}=N^{-1}\sum_i(z^i-\bar z)(z^i-\bar z)^T.$$
The divisor-$N$ convention is part of this algorithm.

3. Form $S_N=C_{zz}+\Gamma$. Since $C_{zz}$ is positive semidefinite and $\Gamma$ is positive definite, $S_N$ is positive definite. Factor it by Cholesky and solve $S_NK_N^T=C_{xz}^T$ by triangular solves.

4. Update every member using its perturbed datum:
$$x^{a,i}=\widehat x^i+K_N(y+\eta^i-z^i).$$

Return the updated ensemble and its empirical mean and covariance. When $G(x)=Hx$, $C_{xz}=C_xH^T$ and $C_{zz}=HC_xH^T$, giving the usual sample-covariance Kalman gain. This item specifies the perturbed-observation variant; deterministic square-root updates are different finite-ensemble procedures. Finite ensembles in nonlinear models are approximations and carry no general posterior-exactness claim.

derivations.claim: The predicted observations of both ensemble members equal $1$, so their empirical observation variance is $0$. Their empirical state-observation cross-covariance is also $0$, because the observation deviations are both zero. By [F5] and $\gamma>0$, the gain is zero; the update is therefore $x^{a,1}=-1$, $x^{a,2}=1$ for every perturbation realization. The updated empirical variance remains $1$.

By [A1], [F1], and [F3], the prior and Gaussian likelihood have densities. The likelihood is positive and bounded, so its prior integral is finite and positive; Bayes' formula [F4] makes the posterior density proportional to the even function $e^{-x^2/2}w(x^2)$, where $w(t)=e^{-t^2/(2\gamma)}$. The posterior mean is therefore zero by symmetry. Put $T=X^2$. Since $\mathbb ET=1$ by [F2], $\mathbb E[(T-1)w(T)]=\mathbb E[(T-1)(w(T)-w(1))]<0.$ The equality uses $\mathbb E(T-1)=0$. The inequality holds because $w$ is strictly decreasing on $[0,\infty)$, so the integrand is negative whenever $T\ne1$; the standard normal density gives $\mathbb P(T=1)=0$. The integrand is integrable since $0<w\le1$ and $\mathbb ET<\infty$. Thus the posterior variance is $\operatorname{Var}(X\mid Y=0)=\frac{\mathbb E[T w(T)]}{\mathbb E[w(T)]}<1.$ The finite EnKF ensemble variance from step 1.1 is $1$, so this admissible nonlinear finite-ensemble update does not equal the exact posterior law.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) and fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$. Let
the state dimension at time
$t$ be a positive integer $d_t$ for $0\le t\le T$, and the observation
dimension at time $t$ be a positive integer $p_t$ for $1\le t\le T$.
Choose deterministic matrices
$F_t\in\mathbb R^{d_t\times d_{t-1}}$ and
$H_t\in\mathbb R^{p_t\times d_t}$, a mean $m_0\in\mathbb R^{d_0}$, and
symmetric positive-semidefinite matrices, meaning $v^TPv\ge0$ for every
real vector $v$ of matching dimension,
$P_0\in\mathbb R^{d_0\times d_0}$,
$Q_t\in\mathbb R^{d_t\times d_t}$, and
$R_t\in\mathbb R^{p_t\times p_t}$. A **linear-Gaussian state-space model
with independent noises** is the general finite-horizon kernel model
([[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]) with initial law
$\mu_0=N_{d_0}(m_0,P_0)$ and transition and observation kernels
$$K_t(x,\cdot)=N_{d_t}(F_t x,Q_t),\qquad G_t(x,\cdot)=N_{p_t}(H_t x,R_t).$$
All Gaussian laws use the convention of
[[def-multivariate-normal-law]], which allows singular covariance matrices.

Its independent-noise representation consists of random vectors
$x_0,q_1,r_1,\ldots,q_T,r_T$ on a common probability space, with
$x_0\sim N_{d_0}(m_0,P_0)$, $q_t\sim N_{d_t}(0,Q_t)$,
$r_t\sim N_{p_t}(0,R_t)$, all mutually independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-random-elements]] (their generated sigma-algebras are
independent), and equations
$$x_t=F_t x_{t-1}+q_t,\qquad y_t=H_t x_t+r_t\qquad(1\le t\le T).$$
The local path-law theorem proves that every allowed parameter tuple has
such a finite representation, that its induced kernels are the displayed
$K_t,G_t$, and that its path law is the general kernel-product law.

This definition imposes the stated noise law and independence assumptions;
it does not establish their empirical adequacy. It supplies no filtering
algorithm, posterior recursion, or convergence claim. Any separate formula
that inverts an observed innovation covariance must assume that covariance is
positive definite at the point of inversion.

For integers $d,p\ge1$, given a forecast mean $m^f\in\mathbb R^d$, fixed background covariance $B\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$, linear observation matrix $H\in\mathbb R^{p\times d}$, datum $y\in\mathbb R^p$, and observation-error covariance $\Gamma\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$, require $B$ and $\Gamma$ symmetric positive definite. Define the 3DVAR objective
$$J(u)=\tfrac12(u-m^f)^TB^{-1}(u-m^f)+\tfrac12(y-Hu)^T\Gamma^{-1}(y-Hu).$$
Form $S=HBH^T+\Gamma$. It is positive definite because for every $z\ne0$,
$$z^TSz=(H^Tz)^TB(H^Tz)+z^T\Gamma z>0.$$
Factor $S=LL^T$ with the unique positive-diagonal Cholesky factor from [[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]]. Solve $LW=HB$ and $L^TK^T=W$; thus $K^T=S^{-1}HB$ without explicitly forming $S^{-1}$. Return the analysis point
$$m^a=m^f+K(y-Hm^f).$$
For a sequential 3DVAR filter, first set $m^f_{j+1}=\Psi_j(m^a_j)$, then apply this update with the fixed matrices $B,H,\Gamma$ and observation $y_{j+1}$. The routine returns a point estimate only. Its unique-minimizer and Gaussian-MAP properties are established separately; no analysis covariance is returned.

Let $d,p\ge1$, $m^f\in\mathbb R^d$, $y\in\mathbb R^p$, $H\in\mathbb R^{p\times d}$, and symmetric positive-definite $B\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ and $\Gamma\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$. Put $S=HBH^T+\Gamma$, $K=BH^TS^{-1}$, and
$$J(u)=\tfrac12(u-m^f)^TB^{-1}(u-m^f)+\tfrac12(y-Hu)^T\Gamma^{-1}(y-Hu).$$
The 3DVAR analysis $m^a=m^f+K(y-Hm^f)$ from [[alg-three-dimensional-variational-assimilation]] is the unique global minimizer of $J$. If $m^f,B$ are the mean and covariance of a Gaussian forecast and the observation model is $Y=HX+r$ with independent $r\sim N_p(0,\Gamma)$, then $m^a$ is the unique maximum-a-posteriori point of the posterior density. It is also the mean update of the exact one-step Kalman filter with identity state transition, zero process covariance, and datum $y$.

Fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$, positive state dimensions $d_0,\ldots,d_T$,
and positive observation dimensions $p_1,\ldots,p_T$. The input is a
linear-Gaussian model from
[[def-linear-gaussian-state-space-model-with-independent-noises]], with
matrices $F_k\in\mathbb R^{d_k\times d_{k-1}}$ and
$H_k\in\mathbb R^{p_k\times d_k}$, initial mean $m_0$, and symmetric
positive-semidefinite covariances $P_0,Q_k,R_k$. Its state and observation
equations are
$$X_k=F_kX_{k-1}+q_k,\qquad Y_k=H_kX_k+r_k,$$
where $q_k\sim N(0,Q_k)$ and $r_k\sim N(0,R_k)$ are centered and mutually
independent across all times and of $X_0$.

The admissible data are vectors $y_k\in\mathbb R^{p_k}$ for which every
innovation covariance encountered below is positive definite. Positive
definite means $u^TS_ku>0$ for every nonzero $u\in\mathbb R^{p_k}$. The
algorithm returns predicted and updated means and covariances and the
innovation and gain at each time. Initialize
$$m_{0|0}=m_0,\qquad P_{0|0}=P_0.$$
For $k=1,\ldots,T$, perform:

1. Predict:
$$m_{k|k-1}=F_km_{k-1|k-1},\qquad P_{k|k-1}=F_kP_{k-1|k-1}F_k^T+Q_k.$$
2. Form the innovation and its covariance:
$$v_k=y_k-H_km_{k|k-1},\qquad S_k=H_kP_{k|k-1}H_k^T+R_k.$$
3. Factor $S_k=L_kL_k^T$ with lower-triangular $L_k$ having positive
diagonal, using
[[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]].
Solve $L_kU_k=H_kP_{k|k-1}$ and $L_k^TK_k^T=U_k$ by triangular solves. This
defines $K_k^T=S_k^{-1}H_kP_{k|k-1}$, hence
$K_k=P_{k|k-1}H_k^TS_k^{-1}$, without explicitly forming $S_k^{-1}$.
4. Update:
$$m_{k|k}=m_{k|k-1}+K_kv_k,\qquad P_{k|k}=P_{k|k-1}-K_kS_kK_k^T.$$

For $T=0$ the loop is empty and the returned pair is $(m_0,P_0)$. No
inverse of $P_0$, $Q_k$, or $R_k$ is used. This item defines the procedure
and makes no complexity, rounding-error, or numerical-stability claim.

Assume AC. Fix a finite-horizon model from
[[def-linear-gaussian-state-space-model-with-independent-noises]] with
state and observation equations
$$X_k=F_kX_{k-1}+q_k,\qquad Y_k=H_kX_k+r_k\qquad (1\le k\le T),$$
where $X_0\sim N_{d_0}(m_0,P_0)$, the centered Gaussian noises $q_k,r_k$ are
mutually independent across times and from $X_0$, and $P_0,Q_k,R_k$ are
symmetric positive semidefinite. Let the parameters and observations be
admissible for [[alg-kalman-filter]], so the recursively formed innovation
covariances
$$S_k=H_kP_{k|k-1}H_k^T+R_k$$
are positive definite for every $1\le k\le T$. Run that algorithm from
$m_{0|0}=m_0$ and $P_{0|0}=P_0$. Then, for each $0\le k\le T$, the map
$$\pi_k(y_{1:k},\cdot)=N_{d_k}(m_{k|k}(y_{1:k}),P_{k|k})$$
is an everywhere-defined filtering kernel for $X_k$ given $Y_{1:k}$ in the
sense of [[def-state-space-filtering-laws]]. The empty history at $k=0$ is a
singleton, and $\pi_0=N_{d_0}(m_0,P_0)$. In particular, these recursions
give an exact Gaussian conditional-law version at every observation history;
each $P_{k|k}$ is positive semidefinite. Singular initial, process,
measurement, predicted-state, and filtered-state covariances are allowed.
Equivalently, the covariance update can be written in Joseph form
$$P_{k|k}=(I-K_kH_k)P_{k|k-1}(I-K_kH_k)^T+K_kR_kK_k^T.$$
Only the innovation matrices being solved must be positive definite. No
pointwise uniqueness of a conditional-law version on null histories,
observation-density assumption, or numerical-stability claim is made.

Use the prior and simulator setup of [[def-approximate-bayesian-computation]]:
standard-Borel parameter and data spaces $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and
$(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, a prior probability $\Pi$, a probability kernel
$K(\theta,\cdot)$, a measurable summary map $S:\mathsf Y\to\mathbb R^d$ with
$d\ge1$, an observed summary $s_0\in\mathbb R^d$, and tolerance
$\epsilon\ge0$. Let
$$B_\epsilon(s_0)=\{s\in\mathbb R^d:\|s-s_0\|_2\le\epsilon\},\qquad A_\epsilon=S^{-1}(B_\epsilon(s_0)).$$
The **prior-simulator joint law** $H$ on the product sigma-algebra
$(\Theta\times\mathsf Y,\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal Y)$ is
$$H(C)=\int_\Theta K(\theta,C_\theta)\,\Pi(d\theta),\qquad C_\theta=\{y:(\theta,y)\in C\},$$
which is a probability measure by
[[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]]. The finite product is standard
Borel by [[lem-finite-products-of-standard-borel-spaces-are-standard-borel]].
Put
$$h_\epsilon(\theta,y)=\mathbf1_{A_\epsilon}(y),\qquad Z_\epsilon=\int_{\Theta\times\mathsf Y}h_\epsilon\,dH =\int_\Theta K(\theta,A_\epsilon)\,\Pi(d\theta).$$
Thus $0\le Z_\epsilon\le1$, and $Z_\epsilon$ is the prior-predictive probability
$p_\epsilon(s_0)$ in [[def-approximate-bayesian-computation]]. Only when
$Z_\epsilon>0$ define the **augmented ABC tolerance target**
$$\widetilde\Pi_\epsilon(C)=\frac{1}{Z_\epsilon}\int_C h_\epsilon\,dH \qquad(C\in\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal Y).$$
It is the prior-simulator joint law conditioned on the summary-tolerance event.
Its parameter marginal is identified in
[[lem-abc-augmented-target-has-tolerance-posterior-marginal]]. The definition
does not assert that summary reduction or a positive tolerance preserves the
full-data posterior.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ be standard Borel spaces. Let $\Pi$ be a prior probability measure on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and let $K$ be a probability kernel from $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ to $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, as in [[def-bayesian-model-as-prior-and-sampling-kernel]]. Let $S:\mathsf Y\to\mathbb R^d$ be a measurable statistic for a fixed integer $d\ge1$, and fix an observed summary $s_0\in\mathbb R^d$. The Euclidean norm is $\|x\|_2=(\sum_{j=1}^d x_j^2)^{1/2}$.

Under the prior-simulator joint law, first draw $\theta\sim\Pi$ and then $Y\sim K(\theta,\cdot)$. The summary-predictive probability measure $M$ on $\Theta\times\mathbb R^d$ is the law of $(\theta,S(Y))$; on measurable rectangles it is
$$M(A\times C)=\int_A K(\theta,S^{-1}(C))\,\Pi(d\theta).$$
The prior and simulator define a joint law by [[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]], and the change-of-variables formula identifies $M$ as the law after applying $S$ ([[thm-change-of-variables-for-expectation]]).

For $\epsilon\ge0$, define the closed tolerance ball
$$B_\epsilon(s_0)=\{s\in\mathbb R^d:\|s-s_0\|_2\le\epsilon\}.$$
Its prior-predictive acceptance probability is
$$p_\epsilon(s_0):=M(\Theta\times B_\epsilon(s_0))\in[0,1].$$
Only when $p_\epsilon(s_0)>0$ define the indicator ABC target by
$$\Pi_\epsilon(A\mid s_0):=\frac{M(A\times B_\epsilon(s_0))}{p_\epsilon(s_0)}\qquad(A\in\mathcal T).$$
This is exactly the conditional law of $\theta$ under the augmented event $S(Y)\in B_\epsilon(s_0)$. The denominator is finite because $M$ is a probability, and no quotient is assigned when the event has probability zero. This target is the posterior given a tolerance event, not in general the full-data posterior or the posterior given the exact summary.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be measurable spaces,
let $\pi$ be a probability measure on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$, and let
$K:\Theta\times\mathcal A\to[0,1]$ be a probability kernel. For
$C\in\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal A$, write
$C_\theta=\{x\in\mathcal X:(\theta,x)\in C\}$ and set
$$J(C)=\int_\Theta K(\theta,C_\theta)\,\pi(d\theta).$$
Then $J$ is a probability measure on the product sigma-algebra, and for every
nonnegative product-measurable $h$,
$$\int_{\Theta\times\mathcal X}h(\theta,x)\,J(d\theta,dx)=\int_\Theta\left(\int_\mathcal Xh(\theta,x)\,K(\theta,dx)\right)\pi(d\theta).$$
In particular, $J(A\times B)=\int_AK(\theta,B)\,\pi(d\theta)$ for
$A\in\mathcal T$ and $B\in\mathcal A$.

derivations.claim: For each $A\in\mathcal T$, [F1] and the rectangle formula [F3] give $\widetilde\Pi_\epsilon(A\times\mathsf Y)=Z_\epsilon^{-1}\int_AK(\theta,A_\epsilon)\Pi(d\theta)$.

Since $A_\epsilon=S^{-1}(B_\epsilon(s_0))$, [F2] gives $M(A\times B_\epsilon(s_0))=\int_AK(\theta,A_\epsilon)\Pi(d\theta)$ and $p_\epsilon(s_0)=Z_\epsilon$; substitution into [F2] makes step 1.1 exactly $\Pi_\epsilon(A\mid s_0)$ for every measurable $A$, so the parameter marginal is the tolerance posterior.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Use the prior and simulator setup of [[def-approximate-bayesian-computation]]:
standard-Borel parameter and data spaces $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and
$(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, a prior probability $\Pi$, a probability kernel
$K(\theta,\cdot)$, a measurable summary map $S:\mathsf Y\to\mathbb R^d$ with
$d\ge1$, an observed summary $s_0\in\mathbb R^d$, and tolerance
$\epsilon\ge0$. Let
$$B_\epsilon(s_0)=\{s\in\mathbb R^d:\|s-s_0\|_2\le\epsilon\},\qquad A_\epsilon=S^{-1}(B_\epsilon(s_0)).$$
The **prior-simulator joint law** $H$ on the product sigma-algebra
$(\Theta\times\mathsf Y,\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal Y)$ is
$$H(C)=\int_\Theta K(\theta,C_\theta)\,\Pi(d\theta),\qquad C_\theta=\{y:(\theta,y)\in C\},$$
which is a probability measure by
[[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]]. The finite product is standard
Borel by [[lem-finite-products-of-standard-borel-spaces-are-standard-borel]].
Put
$$h_\epsilon(\theta,y)=\mathbf1_{A_\epsilon}(y),\qquad Z_\epsilon=\int_{\Theta\times\mathsf Y}h_\epsilon\,dH =\int_\Theta K(\theta,A_\epsilon)\,\Pi(d\theta).$$
Thus $0\le Z_\epsilon\le1$, and $Z_\epsilon$ is the prior-predictive probability
$p_\epsilon(s_0)$ in [[def-approximate-bayesian-computation]]. Only when
$Z_\epsilon>0$ define the **augmented ABC tolerance target**
$$\widetilde\Pi_\epsilon(C)=\frac{1}{Z_\epsilon}\int_C h_\epsilon\,dH \qquad(C\in\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal Y).$$
It is the prior-simulator joint law conditioned on the summary-tolerance event.
Its parameter marginal is identified in
[[lem-abc-augmented-target-has-tolerance-posterior-marginal]]. The definition
does not assert that summary reduction or a positive tolerance preserves the
full-data posterior.

Fix $\epsilon\ge0$ with $Z_\epsilon>0$ and let
$\widetilde\Pi_\epsilon$ be the target in
[[def-abc-augmented-tolerance-target]]. The state is
$x=(\theta,y)\in\Theta\times\mathsf Y$, a standard-Borel product by
[[lem-finite-products-of-standard-borel-spaces-are-standard-borel]], and
admissible initial states satisfy
$y\in A_\epsilon$. As proposal inputs take a parameter probability kernel
$q(\theta,d\theta')$ and the simulator kernel $K(\theta',dy')$ from
[[def-abc-augmented-tolerance-target]], such that
$$Q((\theta,y),d\theta',dy')=q(\theta,d\theta')K(\theta',dy')$$
is a probability kernel on the augmented state space. Construct the transition
kernel $P_\epsilon$ by applying
[[alg-metropolis-hastings-kernel]] with target
$\widetilde\Pi_\epsilon$ and proposal $Q$. Each iteration proposes a new
parameter from $q$, simulates new data from $K$, applies the general
Metropolis–Hastings accepted-flow rule, and retains the current augmented state
after rejection.

This definition uses one fixed tolerance and the augmented state
$(\theta,y)$. It does not claim irreducibility, uniqueness of a stationary law,
convergence, a mixing rate, or recovery of the full-data posterior.

Assume AC. The **Metropolis–Hastings procedure** takes as input a standard-Borel
space $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ ([[def-standard-borel-space]]), a target
probability measure $\pi$ ([[def-probability-measure]]), and a probability
kernel $Q$ from $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ to itself
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]).

1. On the product sigma-algebra ([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]),
form the proposal-flow measure $\mu$ ([[def-measure]]) on
$\mathsf X\times\mathsf X$ by
$$\mu(C)=\int_{\mathsf X}Q(x,C_x)\,\pi(dx),\qquad C_x=\{y:(x,y)\in C\}.$$
This is a probability measure by [[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]].
Let $\tau(x,y)=(y,x)$ and set $\mu^{\mathsf T}(C)=\mu(\tau^{-1}C)$.

2. Set $\eta=\mu\wedge\mu^{\mathsf T}$, the greatest measure dominated by both
flows. Put $\lambda_0=\mu+\mu^{\mathsf T}$, which is a finite measure by
[[thm-nonnegative-weighted-sums-of-measures]], and choose nonnegative measurable
representatives $f=d\mu/d\lambda_0$ and $g=d\mu^{\mathsf T}/d\lambda_0$
with $f+g=1$ everywhere after modification on a $\lambda_0$-null set. Define
$$\alpha(x,y)=\begin{cases}\min\{1,g(x,y)/f(x,y)\},&f(x,y)>0,\\1,&f(x,y)=0.\end{cases}$$
This is a jointly measurable version of $d\eta/d\mu$ taking values in $[0,1]$.

3. For $x\in\mathsf X$, compute the integrated acceptance probability
$$a(x)=\int_{\mathsf X}\alpha(x,y)\,Q(x,dy)$$
and rejection probability $r(x)=1-a(x)$.

4. Return the transition rule
$$P(x,A)=\int_{\mathsf X}\mathbf1_A(y)\alpha(x,y)\,Q(x,dy)+\mathbf1_A(x)r(x),\qquad A\in\mathcal X.$$
The second term retains every rejected proposal as a self-transition.

The item [[lem-common-submeasure-and-bounded-radon-nikodym-density]] proves the
common-submeasure construction and density-version claims in step 2.

Assume AC and the hypotheses of [[alg-metropolis-hastings-kernel]]. Its output
$P$ is a probability kernel, the joint measure
$J_P(dx,dy)=\pi(dx)P(x,dy)$ is symmetric under $(x,y)\mapsto(y,x)$, and $\pi$
is invariant for $P$. Symmetry of this joint measure is reversibility. No
irreducibility, uniqueness, convergence-rate, or central limit theorem
conclusion is asserted.

derivations.claim: By [F1], $\widetilde\Pi_\epsilon$ is a probability target on the product state space; by [F2], the proposal is a probability kernel and the returned kernel is exactly the general Metropolis–Hastings output for this target and proposal.

The state space is standard Borel and [A1] supplies AC, so [F3] applies to the target and proposal identified in step 1.1; it gives reversibility and invariance of $P_\epsilon$ with respect to $\widetilde\Pi_\epsilon$, with no irreducibility or convergence assertion.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Use the prior and simulator setup of [[def-approximate-bayesian-computation]]:
standard-Borel parameter and data spaces $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and
$(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, a prior probability $\Pi$, a probability kernel
$K(\theta,\cdot)$, a measurable summary map $S:\mathsf Y\to\mathbb R^d$ with
$d\ge1$, an observed summary $s_0\in\mathbb R^d$, and tolerance
$\epsilon\ge0$. Let
$$B_\epsilon(s_0)=\{s\in\mathbb R^d:\|s-s_0\|_2\le\epsilon\},\qquad A_\epsilon=S^{-1}(B_\epsilon(s_0)).$$
The **prior-simulator joint law** $H$ on the product sigma-algebra
$(\Theta\times\mathsf Y,\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal Y)$ is
$$H(C)=\int_\Theta K(\theta,C_\theta)\,\Pi(d\theta),\qquad C_\theta=\{y:(\theta,y)\in C\},$$
which is a probability measure by
[[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]]. The finite product is standard
Borel by [[lem-finite-products-of-standard-borel-spaces-are-standard-borel]].
Put
$$h_\epsilon(\theta,y)=\mathbf1_{A_\epsilon}(y),\qquad Z_\epsilon=\int_{\Theta\times\mathsf Y}h_\epsilon\,dH =\int_\Theta K(\theta,A_\epsilon)\,\Pi(d\theta).$$
Thus $0\le Z_\epsilon\le1$, and $Z_\epsilon$ is the prior-predictive probability
$p_\epsilon(s_0)$ in [[def-approximate-bayesian-computation]]. Only when
$Z_\epsilon>0$ define the **augmented ABC tolerance target**
$$\widetilde\Pi_\epsilon(C)=\frac{1}{Z_\epsilon}\int_C h_\epsilon\,dH \qquad(C\in\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal Y).$$
It is the prior-simulator joint law conditioned on the summary-tolerance event.
Its parameter marginal is identified in
[[lem-abc-augmented-target-has-tolerance-posterior-marginal]]. The definition
does not assert that summary reduction or a positive tolerance preserves the
full-data posterior.

Fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$, $N\ge1$, a positive nonincreasing tolerance
schedule $\epsilon_0\ge\epsilon_1\ge\cdots\ge\epsilon_T>0$, and assume
$Z_{\epsilon_t}>0$ for every $t$. Let
$\widetilde\Pi_{\epsilon_t}$ be the normalized augmented target from
[[def-abc-augmented-tolerance-target]]. The parameter proposal at stage $t$
is a probability kernel $Q_t(\theta,d\theta')$ on $\Theta$.

For each $t\ge1$, write the previous weighted population as
$$Z_{t-1}=((\theta_{t-1}^i,y_{t-1}^i)_{i=1}^N,(W_{t-1}^i)_{i=1}^N)$$
in the standard-Borel space
$$E_N=(\Theta\times\mathsf Y)^N\times[0,1]^N,$$
where $[0,1]$ has its Borel sigma-algebra and is standard Borel because the
closed interval with the Euclidean metric is Polish. Thus $E_N$ is standard
Borel by [[lem-finite-products-of-standard-borel-spaces-are-standard-borel]].
Let $\lambda_{t-1}$ be the law of $Z_{t-1}$ conditional on the algorithm
reaching stage $t$, when that event has positive probability. For
$z=((\theta_i,y_i)_{i=1}^N,(w_i)_{i=1}^N)\in E_N$, define the probability
kernel $\phi_t^N$ by
$$\phi_t^N(z,B)=\begin{cases} \sum_{i=1}^Nw_iQ_t(\theta_i,B),&\sum_iw_i=1,\\[2pt] \frac1N\sum_{i=1}^NQ_t(\theta_i,B),&\sum_iw_i\ne1. \end{cases}$$
For each fixed measurable $B\subseteq\Theta$, $z\mapsto Q_t(\theta_i,B)$
and $z\mapsto w_i$ are measurable. For nonnegative measurable $u,v$ on
$E_N$, the superlevel sets satisfy
$$\{uv>a\}=E_N\ (a<0),\qquad \{uv>a\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q,\ q>0}(\{u>q\}\cap\{v>a/q\})\ (a\ge0),$$
so each product $w_iQ_t(\theta_i,B)$ is measurable. Finite sums and scalar
multiples are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]],
making the branch condition and both branch evaluations measurable. Each
branch is a convex combination of probability measures, so
[[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]] gives a probability kernel.
The second branch only extends the kernel to ambient states outside the
algorithm; every actual previous population has normalized weights and uses
the proposal mixture in the first branch. Require
$\Pi\ll\phi_t^N(z,\cdot)$ for $\lambda_{t-1}$-almost every $z$ at every
stage that is reached with positive probability. Apply
[[lem-jointly-measurable-radon-nikodym-derivatives-for-probability-kernels]]
to the constant kernel $z\mapsto\Pi$ and the kernel $\phi_t^N$ to obtain a
product-measurable derivative on $E_N\times\Theta$. Set its value to zero
where it is infinite; since its integral is one for $\lambda_{t-1}$-almost
every $z$, this gives a finite-valued product-measurable version
$r_t^N(z,\theta)=d\Pi/d\phi_t^N(z,\cdot)(\theta)$ for almost every
previous population.

At stage $0$, draw $(\theta_i,y_i)$ independently from the prior-simulator
law $H$, and set $a_0^i=\mathbf1_{A_{\epsilon_0}}(y_i)$. If
$\sum_i a_0^i=0$, stop and report finite-particle degeneracy; otherwise
normalize these weights to obtain $W_0^i$ and report the weighted empirical
measure
$$\widehat\Pi_0^N=\sum_{i=1}^NW_0^i\delta_{(\theta_i,y_i)}.$$

For each $t=1,\ldots,T$, form the proposal mixture
$$\phi_t^N(\cdot)=\sum_{i=1}^N W_{t-1}^iQ_t(\theta_{t-1}^i,\cdot).$$
Draw $N$ ancestor indices from the previous weights using the multinomial
branch of [[alg-multinomial-and-residual-offspring-resampling]]. Conditional
on those ancestors, independently draw one perturbed parameter from its
$Q_t$ kernel and one datum from $K$ for each child. For a candidate
$(\theta_t^j,y_t^j)$ set
$$a_t^j=\mathbf1_{A_{\epsilon_t}}(y_t^j)r_t^N(Z_{t-1},\theta_t^j).$$
If $\sum_j a_t^j=0$, stop and report finite-particle degeneracy; do not report
a normalized target estimate. If the sum is positive, set
$W_t^j=a_t^j/\sum_k a_t^k$ and report the weighted empirical measure
$\widehat\Pi_t^N=\sum_jW_t^j\delta_{(\theta_t^j,y_t^j)}$.

If a stage degenerates, return that status and no normalized estimate for the
stage or any later target. If every stage through $T$ succeeds, return
$\widehat\Pi_T^N$; in particular, when $T=0$ the returned estimate is
$\widehat\Pi_0^N$.

The mixture support condition is stage-specific and must hold almost surely
under the law of the actual previous population. The algorithm makes no
finite-$N$ accuracy, mixing, or posterior-recovery claim.

Assume AC. Let $(E,\mathcal E)$ and $(F,\mathcal F)$ be standard Borel spaces, let $\lambda$ be a probability measure on $E$, and let $M$ and $R$ be probability kernels from $E$ to $F$. Suppose $M(x,\cdot)\ll R(x,\cdot)$ for $\lambda$-almost every $x$. Then there is an $(\mathcal E\otimes\mathcal F)$-measurable function $r:E\times F\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for $\lambda$-almost every $x$ and every $B\in\mathcal F$,
$$M(x,B)=\int_B r(x,y)\,R(x,dy).$$
The exceptional set in $x$ is a single null set, independent of $B$.

Let $\mu$ be a sigma-finite positive measure and let $\nu$ be a signed measure or a finite complex measure with $\nu\ll\mu$. If $h$ is a representative of $d\nu/d\mu$, then
$$\nu(E)=\int_E h\,d\mu\qquad(E\in\mathcal A).$$
More generally, if
$$g=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf 1_{E_j}$$
is the canonical disjoint representation of a simple measurable function and $|\nu|(E_j)<+\infty$ for every $j$, then
$$\int g\,d\nu=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\int_{E_j} h\,d\mu.$$
In particular, whenever the Lebesgue integral of $gh$ is defined, one has
$$\int g\,d\nu=\int gh\,d\mu.$$

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then there is an increasing sequence of
nonnegative simple measurable functions $(s_n)$ such that $s_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x\in X$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Input a particle count $N\ge1$, nonnegative finite weights $a_1,\ldots,a_N$, and a scheme label, either multinomial or residual. Let $A=\sum_{j=1}^Na_j$. If $A>0$, set $p_j=a_j/A$; if $A=0$, set $p_j=1/N$ for every $j$. Thus $p$ is always a probability vector.

- **Multinomial scheme.** Draw an index vector $(J_1,\ldots,J_N)\in\{1,\ldots,N\}^N$ with conditional mass $\mathbb P(J_1=j_1,\ldots,J_N=j_N\mid a)=\prod_{\ell=1}^Np_{j_\ell}$. Put $C_j=\#\{\ell:J_\ell=j\}$.
- **Residual scheme.** Put $q_j=\lfloor Np_j\rfloor$, $r_j=Np_j-q_j$, and $R=\sum_{j=1}^Nr_j=N-\sum_{j=1}^Nq_j$, an integer in $\{0,\ldots,N-1\}$. If $R=0$, put $C_j=q_j$. If $R>0$, draw $(K_1,\ldots,K_R)$ with conditional mass $\mathbb P(K_1=k_1,\ldots,K_R=k_R\mid a)=\prod_{\ell=1}^R(r_{k_\ell}/R)$ and put $C_j=q_j+\#\{\ell:K_\ell=j\}$.

For multinomial resampling, return the sampled vector $(J_1,\ldots,J_N)$ in its sampled order, together with its count vector $(C_1,\ldots,C_N)$; do not sort the sampled indices. For residual resampling, return the ancestor list containing exactly $C_j$ copies of index $j$, ordered by increasing index, together with its count vector. Each output is a length-$N$ list and a count vector summing to $N$. When all input weights vanish, the uniform fallback defines the procedure; any downstream normalizer already multiplied by this zero average remains zero.

Fix $N\ge1$ and nonnegative input weights $a_1,\ldots,a_N$. Let $p$ be the normalized probability vector, with the uniform fallback when all weights vanish, and let $C_j$ be the offspring count from [[alg-multinomial-and-residual-offspring-resampling]]. Conditional on the input weights, for either scheme and every $1\le j\le N$,
$$\mathbb E[C_j\mid a_1,\ldots,a_N]=Np_j.$$
This assertion concerns the counts only; it gives no variance comparison for arbitrary weights.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be measurable spaces,
let $\pi$ be a probability measure on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$, and let
$K:\Theta\times\mathcal A\to[0,1]$ be a probability kernel. For
$C\in\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal A$, write
$C_\theta=\{x\in\mathcal X:(\theta,x)\in C\}$ and set
$$J(C)=\int_\Theta K(\theta,C_\theta)\,\pi(d\theta).$$
Then $J$ is a probability measure on the product sigma-algebra, and for every
nonnegative product-measurable $h$,
$$\int_{\Theta\times\mathcal X}h(\theta,x)\,J(d\theta,dx)=\int_\Theta\left(\int_\mathcal Xh(\theta,x)\,K(\theta,dx)\right)\pi(d\theta).$$
In particular, $J(A\times B)=\int_AK(\theta,B)\,\pi(d\theta)$ for
$A\in\mathcal T$ and $B\in\mathcal A$.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

1. If $f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ are measurable and $f+g$ is defined
   pointwise, then $f+g$ is measurable.
2. If $c\in\mathbb R$ and $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, then $cf$ is
   measurable.
3. If $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, then $f^+=\max\{f,0\}$,
   $f^-=\max\{-f,0\}$, and $|f|=f^++f^-$ are measurable.
4. If $E\in\mathcal A$ and $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, then
   $f\chi_E$ is measurable, where this function equals $f$ on $E$ and $0$
   off $E$ (in particular, $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ here).
5. If $(f_n)$ is a sequence of measurable functions $X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$,
   then $\inf_n f_n$ is measurable; if moreover $f_n\uparrow f$ pointwise, then
   $f$ is measurable.

derivations.claim: Each initial draw $X_0^j$ has law $H$ and weight $a_0^j=\mathbf1_{A_{\epsilon_0}}(Y_0^j)$, so definition of $\gamma_0$ gives $\mathbb E[a_0^jf(X_0^j)]=\int f\mathbf1_{A_{\epsilon_0}}\,dH=\gamma_0(f)$; linearity of the finite average proves the identity.

Fix $t$ with positive probability of reaching stage $t$, and let $\lambda_{t-1}$ be the conditional law of the previous population. By [F3], the constant kernel $z\mapsto\Pi$ and the proposal-mixture kernel $\phi_t^N$ have a product-measurable density $h(z,\theta)$; by [F4], its finite version $r_t^N(z,\theta)$ is a derivative for $\lambda_{t-1}$-almost every $z$. By [F10], $g_f(\theta)=\int_{\mathsf Y}\mathbf1_{A_{\epsilon_t}}(y)f(\theta,y)K(\theta,dy)$ is measurable and bounded. Choose simple functions $s_n\uparrow g_f$ by [F6]; each $s_n$ is a finite sum of measurable indicators, so $s_n(\theta)r_t^N(z,\theta)$ is measurable by [F11]. For almost every $z$, applying the setwise RN identity [F5] to the level sets of $s_n$ gives $\int s_n(\theta)r_t^N(z,\theta)\,\phi_t^N(z,d\theta)=\int s_n\,d\Pi.$ Since $r_t^N$ is finite and nonnegative, [F6] and monotone convergence give $\int g_f(\theta)r_t^N(z,\theta)\,\phi_t^N(z,d\theta)=\int g_f\,d\Pi.$ The right side is $\int f\mathbf1_{A_{\epsilon_t}}\,dH=\gamma_t(f)$ by the iterated-integral formula [F9] and target definition [F1]. Thus the one-candidate conditional proposal expectation equals $\gamma_t(f)$ for $\lambda_{t-1}$-almost every previous population.

Given parent $i$, each child has law $Q_t(\theta_{t-1}^i,d\theta)K(\theta,dy)$; the multinomial expected count is $NW_{t-1}^i$ by [F8]. Conditional on the previous population $z$, summing contributions over parents and dividing by $N$ gives the one-candidate expectation under $\phi_t^N(z,d\theta)K(\theta,dy)$ with weight $\mathbf1_{A_{\epsilon_t}}(y)r_t^N(z,\theta)$. Step 1.2 makes this $\gamma_t(f)$ for $\lambda_{t-1}$-almost every $z$, proving the conditional identity.

For candidate weights $a_j=\mathbf1_{A_{\epsilon_t}}(y_j)r_t^N(Z_{t-1},\theta_j)$ with $\sum_ja_j>0$, [F8] gives conditional offspring-count means $Na_j/\sum_ka_k$; hence for bounded measurable $f$, $\mathbb E[\frac1N\sum_jC_jf(\theta_t^j,y_t^j)\mid(\theta_t^i,y_t^i,a_i)_{i=1}^N]=\sum_ja_jf(\theta_t^j,y_t^j)/\sum_ka_k$, the weighted empirical mean. If the total weight is zero, [F2] reports degeneracy and makes no normalized-target claim.

Use the prior and simulator setup of [[def-approximate-bayesian-computation]]:
standard-Borel parameter and data spaces $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and
$(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, a prior probability $\Pi$, a probability kernel
$K(\theta,\cdot)$, a measurable summary map $S:\mathsf Y\to\mathbb R^d$ with
$d\ge1$, an observed summary $s_0\in\mathbb R^d$, and tolerance
$\epsilon\ge0$. Let
$$B_\epsilon(s_0)=\{s\in\mathbb R^d:\|s-s_0\|_2\le\epsilon\},\qquad A_\epsilon=S^{-1}(B_\epsilon(s_0)).$$
The **prior-simulator joint law** $H$ on the product sigma-algebra
$(\Theta\times\mathsf Y,\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal Y)$ is
$$H(C)=\int_\Theta K(\theta,C_\theta)\,\Pi(d\theta),\qquad C_\theta=\{y:(\theta,y)\in C\},$$
which is a probability measure by
[[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]]. The finite product is standard
Borel by [[lem-finite-products-of-standard-borel-spaces-are-standard-borel]].
Put
$$h_\epsilon(\theta,y)=\mathbf1_{A_\epsilon}(y),\qquad Z_\epsilon=\int_{\Theta\times\mathsf Y}h_\epsilon\,dH =\int_\Theta K(\theta,A_\epsilon)\,\Pi(d\theta).$$
Thus $0\le Z_\epsilon\le1$, and $Z_\epsilon$ is the prior-predictive probability
$p_\epsilon(s_0)$ in [[def-approximate-bayesian-computation]]. Only when
$Z_\epsilon>0$ define the **augmented ABC tolerance target**
$$\widetilde\Pi_\epsilon(C)=\frac{1}{Z_\epsilon}\int_C h_\epsilon\,dH \qquad(C\in\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal Y).$$
It is the prior-simulator joint law conditioned on the summary-tolerance event.
Its parameter marginal is identified in
[[lem-abc-augmented-target-has-tolerance-posterior-marginal]]. The definition
does not assert that summary reduction or a positive tolerance preserves the
full-data posterior.

Fix $\epsilon\ge0$ with $Z_\epsilon>0$ and let
$\widetilde\Pi_\epsilon$ be the target in
[[def-abc-augmented-tolerance-target]]. The state is
$x=(\theta,y)\in\Theta\times\mathsf Y$, a standard-Borel product by
[[lem-finite-products-of-standard-borel-spaces-are-standard-borel]], and
admissible initial states satisfy
$y\in A_\epsilon$. As proposal inputs take a parameter probability kernel
$q(\theta,d\theta')$ and the simulator kernel $K(\theta',dy')$ from
[[def-abc-augmented-tolerance-target]], such that
$$Q((\theta,y),d\theta',dy')=q(\theta,d\theta')K(\theta',dy')$$
is a probability kernel on the augmented state space. Construct the transition
kernel $P_\epsilon$ by applying
[[alg-metropolis-hastings-kernel]] with target
$\widetilde\Pi_\epsilon$ and proposal $Q$. Each iteration proposes a new
parameter from $q$, simulates new data from $K$, applies the general
Metropolis–Hastings accepted-flow rule, and retains the current augmented state
after rejection.

This definition uses one fixed tolerance and the augmented state
$(\theta,y)$. It does not claim irreducibility, uniqueness of a stationary law,
convergence, a mixing rate, or recovery of the full-data posterior.

Assume AC. The **Metropolis–Hastings procedure** takes as input a standard-Borel
space $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ ([[def-standard-borel-space]]), a target
probability measure $\pi$ ([[def-probability-measure]]), and a probability
kernel $Q$ from $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ to itself
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]).

1. On the product sigma-algebra ([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]),
form the proposal-flow measure $\mu$ ([[def-measure]]) on
$\mathsf X\times\mathsf X$ by
$$\mu(C)=\int_{\mathsf X}Q(x,C_x)\,\pi(dx),\qquad C_x=\{y:(x,y)\in C\}.$$
This is a probability measure by [[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]].
Let $\tau(x,y)=(y,x)$ and set $\mu^{\mathsf T}(C)=\mu(\tau^{-1}C)$.

2. Set $\eta=\mu\wedge\mu^{\mathsf T}$, the greatest measure dominated by both
flows. Put $\lambda_0=\mu+\mu^{\mathsf T}$, which is a finite measure by
[[thm-nonnegative-weighted-sums-of-measures]], and choose nonnegative measurable
representatives $f=d\mu/d\lambda_0$ and $g=d\mu^{\mathsf T}/d\lambda_0$
with $f+g=1$ everywhere after modification on a $\lambda_0$-null set. Define
$$\alpha(x,y)=\begin{cases}\min\{1,g(x,y)/f(x,y)\},&f(x,y)>0,\\1,&f(x,y)=0.\end{cases}$$
This is a jointly measurable version of $d\eta/d\mu$ taking values in $[0,1]$.

3. For $x\in\mathsf X$, compute the integrated acceptance probability
$$a(x)=\int_{\mathsf X}\alpha(x,y)\,Q(x,dy)$$
and rejection probability $r(x)=1-a(x)$.

4. Return the transition rule
$$P(x,A)=\int_{\mathsf X}\mathbf1_A(y)\alpha(x,y)\,Q(x,dy)+\mathbf1_A(x)r(x),\qquad A\in\mathcal X.$$
The second term retains every rejected proposal as a self-transition.

The item [[lem-common-submeasure-and-bounded-radon-nikodym-density]] proves the
common-submeasure construction and density-version claims in step 2.

derivations.claim: For $0\le\epsilon\le\tfrac12$, the tolerance interval has length $2\epsilon$, so the singleton prior gives $Z_\epsilon=2\epsilon$; for $\epsilon>\tfrac12$ it covers all of $[0,1]$, so $Z_\epsilon=1$.

Fix $\epsilon>0$ and write $h(x)$ for the tolerance indicator of the datum in the augmented state $x$. Relative to $H(dx)H(dy)$, the forward and transposed flows have densities $h(x)/Z_\epsilon$ and $h(y)/Z_\epsilon$. Choose $f(x,y)=h(x)/(h(x)+h(y))$ and $g(x,y)=h(y)/(h(x)+h(y))$ when $h(x)+h(y)>0$, and $f=g=1/2$ otherwise. These are measurable, sum to one everywhere, and multiplying them by the density $(h(x)+h(y))/Z_\epsilon$ of $\mu+\mu^{\mathsf T}$ recovers the two flow densities; hence they are valid representatives for [F3].

At every admissible current state $x$, $h(x)=1$, so these representatives give $f(x,y)>0$, $g(x,y)/f(x,y)=h(y)$ and thus $\alpha(x,y)=h(y)$. Consequently the acceptance probability is $\int h(y)H(dy)=Z_\epsilon$, equal to $2\epsilon\to0$ for $0<\epsilon\le\tfrac12$ and to $1$ for $\epsilon>\tfrac12$. At $\epsilon=0$, $Z_0=0$ and [F1] assigns no target. The pointwise acceptance calculation uses the specified representatives, rather than arbitrary modifications on flow-null sets.
