derivations.claim: The accepted prior-simulator masses are $H(0,0)=1/4$, $H(0,1)=1/4$, $H(1,0)=1/8$, and $H(1,1)=1/4$, while $(1,2)$ has mass $1/8$ outside the tolerance; hence $Z_\epsilon=7/8$.
Dividing those four accepted masses by $7/8$ gives augmented masses $(2/7,2/7,1/7,2/7)$ and, by [F2], parameter marginal $(4/7,3/7)$.

Given exact data $Y=0$, the prior-weighted likelihood masses are $1/4$ at $\theta=0$ and $1/8$ at $\theta=1$, so the exact posterior is $(2/3,1/3)$, different from $(4/7,3/7)$ because the tolerance summary merges $Y=0$ with $Y=1$.

For accepted current and proposed states, the forward flow is $\widetilde\Pi_\epsilon(dx)H(dy)=\tfrac87H(dx)H(dy)$, symmetric under swap, so [F5] accepts; for proposal $(1,2)$ the transposed flow is zero and the proposal is rejected. Thus $P(x,B)=H(B\cap A_\epsilon)+\tfrac18\mathbf1_B(x)=\tfrac78\widetilde\Pi_\epsilon(B)+\tfrac18\mathbf1_B(x)$ for accepted $x$, and integration gives $\widetilde\Pi_\epsilon P(B)=\widetilde\Pi_\epsilon(B)$, verifying stationarity consistently with [F4].

Use the prior and simulator setup of [[def-approximate-bayesian-computation]]:
standard-Borel parameter and data spaces $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and
$(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, a prior probability $\Pi$, a probability kernel
$K(\theta,\cdot)$, a measurable summary map $S:\mathsf Y\to\mathbb R^d$ with
$d\ge1$, an observed summary $s_0\in\mathbb R^d$, and tolerance
$\epsilon\ge0$. Let
$$B_\epsilon(s_0)=\{s\in\mathbb R^d:\|s-s_0\|_2\le\epsilon\},\qquad A_\epsilon=S^{-1}(B_\epsilon(s_0)).$$
The **prior-simulator joint law** $H$ on the product sigma-algebra
$(\Theta\times\mathsf Y,\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal Y)$ is
$$H(C)=\int_\Theta K(\theta,C_\theta)\,\Pi(d\theta),\qquad C_\theta=\{y:(\theta,y)\in C\},$$
which is a probability measure by
[[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]]. The finite product is standard
Borel by [[lem-finite-products-of-standard-borel-spaces-are-standard-borel]].
Put
$$h_\epsilon(\theta,y)=\mathbf1_{A_\epsilon}(y),\qquad Z_\epsilon=\int_{\Theta\times\mathsf Y}h_\epsilon\,dH =\int_\Theta K(\theta,A_\epsilon)\,\Pi(d\theta).$$
Thus $0\le Z_\epsilon\le1$, and $Z_\epsilon$ is the prior-predictive probability
$p_\epsilon(s_0)$ in [[def-approximate-bayesian-computation]]. Only when
$Z_\epsilon>0$ define the **augmented ABC tolerance target**
$$\widetilde\Pi_\epsilon(C)=\frac{1}{Z_\epsilon}\int_C h_\epsilon\,dH \qquad(C\in\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal Y).$$
It is the prior-simulator joint law conditioned on the summary-tolerance event.
Its parameter marginal is identified in
[[lem-abc-augmented-target-has-tolerance-posterior-marginal]]. The definition
does not assert that summary reduction or a positive tolerance preserves the
full-data posterior.

Fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$, $N\ge1$, a positive nonincreasing tolerance
schedule $\epsilon_0\ge\epsilon_1\ge\cdots\ge\epsilon_T>0$, and assume
$Z_{\epsilon_t}>0$ for every $t$. Let
$\widetilde\Pi_{\epsilon_t}$ be the normalized augmented target from
[[def-abc-augmented-tolerance-target]]. The parameter proposal at stage $t$
is a probability kernel $Q_t(\theta,d\theta')$ on $\Theta$.

For each $t\ge1$, write the previous weighted population as
$$Z_{t-1}=((\theta_{t-1}^i,y_{t-1}^i)_{i=1}^N,(W_{t-1}^i)_{i=1}^N)$$
in the standard-Borel space
$$E_N=(\Theta\times\mathsf Y)^N\times[0,1]^N,$$
where $[0,1]$ has its Borel sigma-algebra and is standard Borel because the
closed interval with the Euclidean metric is Polish. Thus $E_N$ is standard
Borel by [[lem-finite-products-of-standard-borel-spaces-are-standard-borel]].
Let $\lambda_{t-1}$ be the law of $Z_{t-1}$ conditional on the algorithm
reaching stage $t$, when that event has positive probability. For
$z=((\theta_i,y_i)_{i=1}^N,(w_i)_{i=1}^N)\in E_N$, define the probability
kernel $\phi_t^N$ by
$$\phi_t^N(z,B)=\begin{cases} \sum_{i=1}^Nw_iQ_t(\theta_i,B),&\sum_iw_i=1,\\[2pt] \frac1N\sum_{i=1}^NQ_t(\theta_i,B),&\sum_iw_i\ne1. \end{cases}$$
For each fixed measurable $B\subseteq\Theta$, $z\mapsto Q_t(\theta_i,B)$
and $z\mapsto w_i$ are measurable. For nonnegative measurable $u,v$ on
$E_N$, the superlevel sets satisfy
$$\{uv>a\}=E_N\ (a<0),\qquad \{uv>a\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q,\ q>0}(\{u>q\}\cap\{v>a/q\})\ (a\ge0),$$
so each product $w_iQ_t(\theta_i,B)$ is measurable. Finite sums and scalar
multiples are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]],
making the branch condition and both branch evaluations measurable. Each
branch is a convex combination of probability measures, so
[[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]] gives a probability kernel.
The second branch only extends the kernel to ambient states outside the
algorithm; every actual previous population has normalized weights and uses
the proposal mixture in the first branch. Require
$\Pi\ll\phi_t^N(z,\cdot)$ for $\lambda_{t-1}$-almost every $z$ at every
stage that is reached with positive probability. Apply
[[lem-jointly-measurable-radon-nikodym-derivatives-for-probability-kernels]]
to the constant kernel $z\mapsto\Pi$ and the kernel $\phi_t^N$ to obtain a
product-measurable derivative on $E_N\times\Theta$. Set its value to zero
where it is infinite; since its integral is one for $\lambda_{t-1}$-almost
every $z$, this gives a finite-valued product-measurable version
$r_t^N(z,\theta)=d\Pi/d\phi_t^N(z,\cdot)(\theta)$ for almost every
previous population.

At stage $0$, draw $(\theta_i,y_i)$ independently from the prior-simulator
law $H$, and set $a_0^i=\mathbf1_{A_{\epsilon_0}}(y_i)$. If
$\sum_i a_0^i=0$, stop and report finite-particle degeneracy; otherwise
normalize these weights to obtain $W_0^i$ and report the weighted empirical
measure
$$\widehat\Pi_0^N=\sum_{i=1}^NW_0^i\delta_{(\theta_i,y_i)}.$$

For each $t=1,\ldots,T$, form the proposal mixture
$$\phi_t^N(\cdot)=\sum_{i=1}^N W_{t-1}^iQ_t(\theta_{t-1}^i,\cdot).$$
Draw $N$ ancestor indices from the previous weights using the multinomial
branch of [[alg-multinomial-and-residual-offspring-resampling]]. Conditional
on those ancestors, independently draw one perturbed parameter from its
$Q_t$ kernel and one datum from $K$ for each child. For a candidate
$(\theta_t^j,y_t^j)$ set
$$a_t^j=\mathbf1_{A_{\epsilon_t}}(y_t^j)r_t^N(Z_{t-1},\theta_t^j).$$
If $\sum_j a_t^j=0$, stop and report finite-particle degeneracy; do not report
a normalized target estimate. If the sum is positive, set
$W_t^j=a_t^j/\sum_k a_t^k$ and report the weighted empirical measure
$\widehat\Pi_t^N=\sum_jW_t^j\delta_{(\theta_t^j,y_t^j)}$.

If a stage degenerates, return that status and no normalized estimate for the
stage or any later target. If every stage through $T$ succeeds, return
$\widehat\Pi_T^N$; in particular, when $T=0$ the returned estimate is
$\widehat\Pi_0^N$.

The mixture support condition is stage-specific and must hold almost surely
under the law of the actual previous population. The algorithm makes no
finite-$N$ accuracy, mixing, or posterior-recovery claim.

Assume the setup of [[alg-abc-sequential-smc]] and put
$$\gamma_t(d\theta,dy)=\Pi(d\theta)K(\theta,dy)\mathbf1_{A_{\epsilon_t}}(y), \qquad \pi_t=\gamma_t/Z_{\epsilon_t}=\widetilde\Pi_{\epsilon_t}.$$
For a measure $\mu$, write $\mu(f)=\int f\,d\mu$ for bounded nonnegative
measurable $f$. For every bounded nonnegative product-measurable
$f:\Theta\times\mathsf Y\to[0,\infty)$, let
$X_0^j=(\Theta_0^j,Y_0^j)$, $1\le j\le N$, be the initial $N$ independent
prior-simulator draws with law $H$ and weights
$a_0^j=\mathbf1_{A_{\epsilon_0}}(Y_0^j)$ satisfy
$$\mathbb E\!\left[\frac1N\sum_{j=1}^Na_0^jf(X_0^j)\right]=\gamma_0(f).$$
For each $1\le t\le T$ reached with positive probability, let
$Z_{t-1}=((\Theta_{t-1}^i,Y_{t-1}^i)_{i=1}^N,(W_{t-1}^i)_{i=1}^N)$ be the
previous population and let $\lambda_{t-1}$ be its law conditional on reaching
stage $t$. Use the standard-Borel population space and probability kernel
$\phi_t^N(z,\cdot)$ from [[alg-abc-sequential-smc]], and assume
$\Pi\ll\phi_t^N(z,\cdot)$ for $\lambda_{t-1}$-almost every $z$. The kernel
Radon–Nikodym lemma
[[lem-jointly-measurable-radon-nikodym-derivatives-for-probability-kernels]]
then supplies a product-measurable derivative; use the finite-valued version
specified in [[alg-abc-sequential-smc]] after changing infinite values to zero.
Write this version as
$r_t^N(z,\theta)=d\Pi/d\phi_t^N(z,\cdot)(\theta)$ for almost every $z$.
Put $a_t^j=\mathbf1_{A_{\epsilon_t}}(Y_t^j)r_t^N(Z_{t-1},\Theta_t^j)$ for
the candidates produced by multinomial ancestor resampling, perturbation, and
simulation. For every bounded nonnegative product-measurable
$f:\Theta\times\mathsf Y\to[0,\infty)$,
$$\mathbb E\!\left[\frac1N\sum_{j=1}^Na_t^jf(\Theta_t^j,Y_t^j)\,\middle|\,\text{previous population}\right] =\gamma_t(f)\quad\text{almost surely on reaching stage }t.$$
In particular, the average weight is conditionally unbiased for
$Z_{\epsilon_t}$. If candidates with positive total weight are resampled by
the multinomial or residual scheme from normalized weights, then for every
bounded measurable $f$ their conditional empirical mean equals the weighted

Fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$, $N\ge1$, a positive nonincreasing tolerance
schedule $\epsilon_0\ge\epsilon_1\ge\cdots\ge\epsilon_T>0$, and assume
$Z_{\epsilon_t}>0$ for every $t$. Let
$\widetilde\Pi_{\epsilon_t}$ be the normalized augmented target from
[[def-abc-augmented-tolerance-target]]. The parameter proposal at stage $t$
is a probability kernel $Q_t(\theta,d\theta')$ on $\Theta$.

For each $t\ge1$, write the previous weighted population as
$$Z_{t-1}=((\theta_{t-1}^i,y_{t-1}^i)_{i=1}^N,(W_{t-1}^i)_{i=1}^N)$$
in the standard-Borel space
$$E_N=(\Theta\times\mathsf Y)^N\times[0,1]^N,$$
where $[0,1]$ has its Borel sigma-algebra and is standard Borel because the
closed interval with the Euclidean metric is Polish. Thus $E_N$ is standard
Borel by [[lem-finite-products-of-standard-borel-spaces-are-standard-borel]].
Let $\lambda_{t-1}$ be the law of $Z_{t-1}$ conditional on the algorithm
reaching stage $t$, when that event has positive probability. For
$z=((\theta_i,y_i)_{i=1}^N,(w_i)_{i=1}^N)\in E_N$, define the probability
kernel $\phi_t^N$ by
$$\phi_t^N(z,B)=\begin{cases} \sum_{i=1}^Nw_iQ_t(\theta_i,B),&\sum_iw_i=1,\\[2pt] \frac1N\sum_{i=1}^NQ_t(\theta_i,B),&\sum_iw_i\ne1. \end{cases}$$
For each fixed measurable $B\subseteq\Theta$, $z\mapsto Q_t(\theta_i,B)$
and $z\mapsto w_i$ are measurable. For nonnegative measurable $u,v$ on
$E_N$, the superlevel sets satisfy
$$\{uv>a\}=E_N\ (a<0),\qquad \{uv>a\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q,\ q>0}(\{u>q\}\cap\{v>a/q\})\ (a\ge0),$$
so each product $w_iQ_t(\theta_i,B)$ is measurable. Finite sums and scalar
multiples are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]],
making the branch condition and both branch evaluations measurable. Each
branch is a convex combination of probability measures, so
[[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]] gives a probability kernel.
The second branch only extends the kernel to ambient states outside the
algorithm; every actual previous population has normalized weights and uses
the proposal mixture in the first branch. Require
$\Pi\ll\phi_t^N(z,\cdot)$ for $\lambda_{t-1}$-almost every $z$ at every
stage that is reached with positive probability. Apply
[[lem-jointly-measurable-radon-nikodym-derivatives-for-probability-kernels]]
to the constant kernel $z\mapsto\Pi$ and the kernel $\phi_t^N$ to obtain a
product-measurable derivative on $E_N\times\Theta$. Set its value to zero
where it is infinite; since its integral is one for $\lambda_{t-1}$-almost
every $z$, this gives a finite-valued product-measurable version
$r_t^N(z,\theta)=d\Pi/d\phi_t^N(z,\cdot)(\theta)$ for almost every
previous population.

At stage $0$, draw $(\theta_i,y_i)$ independently from the prior-simulator
law $H$, and set $a_0^i=\mathbf1_{A_{\epsilon_0}}(y_i)$. If
$\sum_i a_0^i=0$, stop and report finite-particle degeneracy; otherwise
normalize these weights to obtain $W_0^i$ and report the weighted empirical
measure
$$\widehat\Pi_0^N=\sum_{i=1}^NW_0^i\delta_{(\theta_i,y_i)}.$$

For each $t=1,\ldots,T$, form the proposal mixture
$$\phi_t^N(\cdot)=\sum_{i=1}^N W_{t-1}^iQ_t(\theta_{t-1}^i,\cdot).$$
Draw $N$ ancestor indices from the previous weights using the multinomial
branch of [[alg-multinomial-and-residual-offspring-resampling]]. Conditional
on those ancestors, independently draw one perturbed parameter from its
$Q_t$ kernel and one datum from $K$ for each child. For a candidate
$(\theta_t^j,y_t^j)$ set
$$a_t^j=\mathbf1_{A_{\epsilon_t}}(y_t^j)r_t^N(Z_{t-1},\theta_t^j).$$
If $\sum_j a_t^j=0$, stop and report finite-particle degeneracy; do not report
a normalized target estimate. If the sum is positive, set
$W_t^j=a_t^j/\sum_k a_t^k$ and report the weighted empirical measure
$\widehat\Pi_t^N=\sum_jW_t^j\delta_{(\theta_t^j,y_t^j)}$.

If a stage degenerates, return that status and no normalized estimate for the
stage or any later target. If every stage through $T$ succeeds, return
$\widehat\Pi_T^N$; in particular, when $T=0$ the returned estimate is
$\widehat\Pi_0^N$.

The mixture support condition is stage-specific and must hold almost surely
under the law of the actual previous population. The algorithm makes no
finite-$N$ accuracy, mixing, or posterior-recovery claim.

Assume the setup of [[alg-abc-sequential-smc]] and put
$$\gamma_t(d\theta,dy)=\Pi(d\theta)K(\theta,dy)\mathbf1_{A_{\epsilon_t}}(y), \qquad \pi_t=\gamma_t/Z_{\epsilon_t}=\widetilde\Pi_{\epsilon_t}.$$
For a measure $\mu$, write $\mu(f)=\int f\,d\mu$ for bounded nonnegative
measurable $f$. For every bounded nonnegative product-measurable
$f:\Theta\times\mathsf Y\to[0,\infty)$, let
$X_0^j=(\Theta_0^j,Y_0^j)$, $1\le j\le N$, be the initial $N$ independent
prior-simulator draws with law $H$ and weights
$a_0^j=\mathbf1_{A_{\epsilon_0}}(Y_0^j)$ satisfy

previous population and let $\lambda_{t-1}$ be its law conditional on reaching
stage $t$. Use the standard-Borel population space and probability kernel
$\phi_t^N(z,\cdot)$ from [[alg-abc-sequential-smc]], and assume
$\Pi\ll\phi_t^N(z,\cdot)$ for $\lambda_{t-1}$-almost every $z$. The kernel
Radon–Nikodym lemma

then supplies a product-measurable derivative; use the finite-valued version
specified in [[alg-abc-sequential-smc]] after changing infinite values to zero.

$r_t^N(z,\theta)=d\Pi/d\phi_t^N(z,\cdot)(\theta)$ for almost every $z$.

the candidates produced by multinomial ancestor resampling, perturbation, and
simulation. For every bounded nonnegative product-measurable
$f:\Theta\times\mathsf Y\to[0,\infty)$,
$$\mathbb E\!\left[\frac1N\sum_{j=1}^Na_t^jf(\Theta_t^j,Y_t^j)\,\middle|\,\text{previous population}\right] =\gamma_t(f)\quad\text{almost surely on reaching stage }t.$$

$Z_{\epsilon_t}$. If candidates with positive total weight are resampled by
the multinomial or residual scheme from normalized weights, then for every
bounded measurable $f$ their conditional empirical mean equals the weighted
candidate empirical mean in expectation. No unbiasedness is asserted for the
self-normalized finite-$N$ estimate, and a finite sample may have zero total
weight or fail to represent positive target mass.

Throughout this page $\mathbb{N}$ is the set of von Neumann naturals
([[def-natural-numbers]]): $0 = \varnothing$, $\sigma(n) = n \cup \{n\}$, and
$n = \{\, m \in \mathbb{N} : m < n \,\}$ is itself the set of its predecessors,
the order being the additive order of [[def-nat-order]] identified with
membership in [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]. Write $A \approx B$ when a
bijection $A \to B$ exists ([[def-equinumerous]],
[[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]). A set $A$ is **finite** when
$A \approx n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-countable]]).

**Definition.** Let $A$ be a finite set. Then there is **exactly one**
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $A \approx n$, and we write

$$\lvert A\rvert := \text{that } n,$$

the **cardinality**, or number of elements, of $A$. The notation $\lvert A\rvert$
is defined for finite $A$ only, and its value is a natural number.

**Why exactly one, which is the whole content of the definition.** At least one
such $n$ exists: that is literally what "$A$ is finite" says. At most one exists:
if $A \approx n$ and $A \approx m$ with $n, m \in \mathbb{N}$, then $n \approx A$,
because the inverse of a bijection is a bijection, and hence $n \approx m$,
because a composition of bijections is a bijection
([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]); and $n \approx m$ forces $n = m$ by
claim 3 of [[lem-pigeonhole]]. So $\lvert A\rvert$ names a single natural number
and not a family of choices.

**Four consequences, proved here because everything on this page uses them.**

**(a) $\lvert n\rvert = n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.** The identity map
$\mathrm{id}_n$ is a bijection $n \to n$, so $n \approx n$; thus $n$ is finite and
the unique natural equinumerous with it is $n$ itself.

**(b) $\lvert\varnothing\rvert = 0$, and a finite $A$ satisfies
$\lvert A\rvert = 0$ if and only if $A = \varnothing$.** Since $0 = \varnothing$,
part (a) gives $\lvert\varnothing\rvert = 0$. Conversely, if $\lvert A\rvert = 0$
then there is a bijection $f : A \to \varnothing$; were some $a \in A$, the value
$f(a)$ would be an element of $\varnothing$, and $\varnothing$ has none, so
$A = \varnothing$.

**(c) Transport along a bijection.** If $A$ is finite and $f : A \to B$ is a
bijection, then $B$ is finite and $\lvert B\rvert = \lvert A\rvert$. Indeed
$B \approx A$ through $f^{-1}$ and $A \approx \lvert A\rvert$, so
$B \approx \lvert A\rvert$ by transitivity.

**(d) Equality of cardinalities is equinumerosity.** For finite $A$ and $B$:
$\lvert A\rvert = \lvert B\rvert$ if and only if $A \approx B$. If the
cardinalities agree then $A \approx \lvert A\rvert = \lvert B\rvert \approx B$;
conversely $A \approx B$ gives $\lvert B\rvert = \lvert A\rvert$ by (c).

Let $A$ and $B$ be finite sets and write

$$A^{B} := \{\, f : f \text{ is a function } B \to A \,\}.$$

Then $A^{B}$ is finite and $\lvert A^{B}\rvert = \lvert A\rvert^{\lvert B\rvert}$,
the power being the $\mathbb{N}$-valued exponentiation of [[def-nat-power]].

Both degenerate cases are covered and neither is a stipulation. If
$B = \varnothing$ there is exactly one function $B \to A$, the empty function, so
$\lvert A^{\varnothing}\rvert = 1 = \lvert A\rvert^{0}$ **even when
$A = \varnothing$**. If $A = \varnothing$ and $B \ne \varnothing$ there is no
function at all, so $\lvert A^{B}\rvert = 0 = 0^{\lvert B\rvert}$ with
$\lvert B\rvert \ge 1$.

Let $A$ be a finite set ([[def-countable]]) and let $B \subseteq A$. Then:

1. $B$ is finite;
2. $\lvert B\rvert \le \lvert A\rvert$ ([[def-finite-cardinality]]);
3. $\lvert B\rvert = \lvert A\rvert$ if and only if $B = A$;
4. every injection $f : A \to A$ is a bijection, and every surjection
   $f : A \to A$ is a bijection.

Clause 3 is the finite form of the Dedekind statement: a finite set is not
equinumerous with a proper subset of itself. Clause 4 is its working form, and
**finiteness is exactly the hypothesis that fails in general**: the successor map
is an injection of $\mathbb{N}$ into itself that is not surjective, which is the
false statement recorded on this page's companion.

A **finite probability space** is a pair $(\Omega,w)$ consisting of a finite set $\Omega$ and a function $w:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ such that $w(\omega)\ge0$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$ and
$$\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1.$$
The elements of $\Omega$ are **outcomes**. Every subset $A\subseteq\Omega$ is an **event**, and its probability is
$$\mathbb P(A):=\sum_{\omega\in A}w(\omega).$$

An outcome of weight zero remains an outcome. Thus an event can be nonempty and still have probability zero.

derivations.claim: Let $B=\{0,1\}$. The shift $j\mapsto j-1$ is a bijection from the conventional index set $[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}$ to the von Neumann natural $n=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$; for $n=0$ both sets are empty. Thus $[n]$ is finite by [F1]. The set $B$ is bijective with $2$, so it is finite as well. For each $I\in\mathcal S_{n,r}$ define its indicator function $\chi_I:[n]\to B$ by $\chi_I(j)=1$ if $j\in I$ and $0$ otherwise. The map $I\mapsto\chi_I$ is injective because equal indicator functions have equal inverse images of $\{1\}$. Its image is a subset of the finite set $B^{[n]}$, which is finite by [F2] and [F3]. Therefore some natural $k$ is bijective with this image; composing that bijection with $I\mapsto\chi_I$ makes $\mathcal S_{n,r}$ bijective with $k$, so [F1] makes it finite.

If $r=0$, then $\varnothing\in\mathcal S_{n,r}$. If $r>0$, then $\{1,\ldots,r\}\subseteq[n]$ because $r\le n$, and the shift $j\mapsto j-1$ is a bijection from $\{1,\ldots,r\}$ to the von Neumann natural $r$; hence this subset has cardinality $r$ by [F1, F5], so $\{1,\ldots,r\}\in\mathcal S_{n,r}$. Thus $\mathcal S_{n,r}$ is nonempty. By [F5], its cardinality $M:=|\mathcal S_{n,r}|$ is defined; by [F6] and nonemptiness, $M\ge1$. Give each $I\in\mathcal S_{n,r}$ weight $q(I)=1/M$. These weights are nonnegative and their finite sum is $M(1/M)=1$.

The outcome set is finite by step 1.1 and its weights satisfy the conditions in step 1.2, so [F4] makes $(\mathcal S_{n,r},q)$ a finite probability space. The argument includes $n=0$, $r=0$, and $r=n$.

Let $(\mathcal Z,\mathcal F)$ be a measurable unit space ([[def-measurable-space]]), let $n\ge1$, and fix an observed ordered tuple $z_1,\ldots,z_n\in\mathcal Z$. Its **empirical measure** is the set function
$$P_n:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{z_i},\qquad P_n(A)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n1\{z_i\in A\}\quad(A\in\mathcal F),$$
where $\delta_{z_i}$ is the Dirac set function from [[def-dirac-measure]]. Repeated observations contribute once for each index at which they occur. The statement that $P_n$ is a probability measure is established in [[lem-empirical-measure-is-a-probability-measure]].
For $x_0\in X$, the Dirac set function $\delta_{x_0}$ is a probability measure on every sigma-algebra on $X$.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

derivations.claim: For any $A\in\mathcal F$, the finite sum in [F1] is nonnegative by [F2]. Also $P_n(\varnothing)=0$ and $P_n(\mathcal Z)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n1=1$.

Let $(A_k)_{k\ge1}$ be pairwise disjoint members of $\mathcal F$. For each fixed $i$, at most one term $\delta_{z_i}(A_k)$ is nonzero, and countable additivity in [F2] gives $\delta_{z_i}(\bigcup_k A_k)=\sum_k\delta_{z_i}(A_k)$. Because the sum over $i$ is finite and there are at most $n$ nonzero terms in the resulting double sum, we may regroup to obtain $P_n(\bigcup_k A_k)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_k\delta_{z_i}(A_k)=\sum_k\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{z_i}(A_k)=\sum_kP_n(A_k)$. Thus $P_n$ is countably additive.
By step 1.1, $P_n$ has total mass $1$, and by step 1.2 it is countably additive and vanishes on the empty set. Therefore it is a measure of total mass $1$, hence a probability measure by [F3].

**Input.** Let $n\ge1$, let $(\mathcal Z,\mathcal F)$ be the declared measurable space of sampling units, and fix the observed ordered tuple $z=(z_1,\ldots,z_n)$. Let $P_n$ be its empirical probability measure from [[def-empirical-measure]] and [[lem-empirical-measure-is-a-probability-measure]]. Declare a sample sigma-algebra $\mathcal F_n$ on the ordered tuple space $\mathcal Z^n$ and provide a statistic $T_n:(\mathcal Z^n,\mathcal F_n)\to(\mathbb R^q,\mathcal B_q)$, where $q\ge1$ is finite and $\mathcal B_q$ is the declared target sigma-algebra; "statistic" has the measurable-map meaning in [[def-statistic-and-estimator]].

Write $[n]:=\{1,\ldots,n\}$ for the indexing set.

**Procedure.** Draw indices $I_1,\ldots,I_n$ independently and uniformly from $[n]$, so repeated indices are allowed. Set $Z_j^*:=z_{I_j}$ for $j=1,\ldots,n$. Return the bootstrap tuple $(Z_1^*,\ldots,Z_n^*)$ and the replicate $T_n(Z_1^*,\ldots,Z_n^*)$. Generate further replicates by repeating the index draws with fresh randomness. These are resampling units only when the tuple entries satisfy the unit contract in [[def-resampling-sampling-unit-contract]].

The conditional IID law of the draws is proved in [[thm-bootstrap-draws-are-conditionally-iid-empirical-law]]. This algorithm does not claim that its conditional law consistently approximates any sampling law; such validity requires separate hypotheses and a separate theorem.

A **finite probability space** is a pair $(\Omega,w)$ consisting of a finite set $\Omega$ and a function $w:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ such that $w(\omega)\ge0$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$ and
$$\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1.$$
The elements of $\Omega$ are **outcomes**. Every subset $A\subseteq\Omega$ is an **event**, and its probability is
$$\mathbb P(A):=\sum_{\omega\in A}w(\omega).$$

An outcome of weight zero remains an outcome. Thus an event can be nonempty and still have probability zero.

Let $(\mathcal Z,\mathcal F)$ be a measurable unit space ([[def-measurable-space]]), let $n\ge1$, and fix an observed ordered tuple $z_1,\ldots,z_n\in\mathcal Z$. Its **empirical measure** is the set function
$$P_n:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{z_i},\qquad P_n(A)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n1\{z_i\in A\}\quad(A\in\mathcal F),$$
where $\delta_{z_i}$ is the Dirac set function from [[def-dirac-measure]]. Repeated observations contribute once for each index at which they occur. The statement that $P_n$ is a probability measure is established in [[lem-empirical-measure-is-a-probability-measure]].

Let $A$ and $B$ be finite sets and write

$$A^{B} := \{\, f : f \text{ is a function } B \to A \,\}.$$

Then $A^{B}$ is finite and $\lvert A^{B}\rvert = \lvert A\rvert^{\lvert B\rvert}$,
the power being the $\mathbb{N}$-valued exponentiation of [[def-nat-power]].

Both degenerate cases are covered and neither is a stipulation. If
$B = \varnothing$ there is exactly one function $B \to A$, the empty function, so
$\lvert A^{\varnothing}\rvert = 1 = \lvert A\rvert^{0}$ **even when
$A = \varnothing$**. If $A = \varnothing$ and $B \ne \varnothing$ there is no
function at all, so $\lvert A^{B}\rvert = 0 = 0^{\lvert B\rvert}$ with
$\lvert B\rvert \ge 1$.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and let
$(S,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space. A **random element** of $S$ is a measurable
map
$$X:(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to(S,\Sigma)$$
in the sense of [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]].

When $S=\mathbb R$ and $\Sigma=\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$ from
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra]], the map $X$ is a **real random variable**.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element. Its
**law** or **distribution** is the set function
$$\mathbb P_X:\Sigma\to[0,+\infty],\qquad \mathbb P_X(B):=\mathbb P(X^{-1}(B)).$$

Thus the law of $X$ records the probability of each measurable target set by
pulling it back to an event in the original probability space.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

A family $(\mathcal F_i)_{i\in I}$ of sub-sigma-algebras of $\mathcal F$ is
**independent** when it is independent as a family of event classes in the
sense of [[def-independent-families-of-event-classes]].

A family $(A_i)_{i\in I}$ of events is **independent** when the singleton event
classes $\bigl(\{A_i\}\bigr)_{i\in I}$ are independent. Equivalently, for every
finite choice of distinct indices $i_0,\dots,i_{n-1}$,

$$\mathbb P\left(\bigcap_{k<n}A_{i_k}\right)=\prod_{k<n}\mathbb P(A_{i_k}).$$

For two events this reduces to the familiar identity
$\mathbb P(A\cap B)=\mathbb P(A)\mathbb P(B)$.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Throughout this page $\mathbb{N}$ is the set of von Neumann naturals
([[def-natural-numbers]]): $0 = \varnothing$, $\sigma(n) = n \cup \{n\}$, and
$n = \{\, m \in \mathbb{N} : m < n \,\}$ is itself the set of its predecessors,
the order being the additive order of [[def-nat-order]] identified with
membership in [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]. Write $A \approx B$ when a
bijection $A \to B$ exists ([[def-equinumerous]],
[[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]). A set $A$ is **finite** when
$A \approx n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-countable]]).

**Definition.** Let $A$ be a finite set. Then there is **exactly one**
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $A \approx n$, and we write

$$\lvert A\rvert := \text{that } n,$$

the **cardinality**, or number of elements, of $A$. The notation $\lvert A\rvert$
is defined for finite $A$ only, and its value is a natural number.

**Why exactly one, which is the whole content of the definition.** At least one
such $n$ exists: that is literally what "$A$ is finite" says. At most one exists:
if $A \approx n$ and $A \approx m$ with $n, m \in \mathbb{N}$, then $n \approx A$,
because the inverse of a bijection is a bijection, and hence $n \approx m$,
because a composition of bijections is a bijection
([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]); and $n \approx m$ forces $n = m$ by
claim 3 of [[lem-pigeonhole]]. So $\lvert A\rvert$ names a single natural number
and not a family of choices.

**Four consequences, proved here because everything on this page uses them.**

**(a) $\lvert n\rvert = n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.** The identity map
$\mathrm{id}_n$ is a bijection $n \to n$, so $n \approx n$; thus $n$ is finite and
the unique natural equinumerous with it is $n$ itself.

**(b) $\lvert\varnothing\rvert = 0$, and a finite $A$ satisfies
$\lvert A\rvert = 0$ if and only if $A = \varnothing$.** Since $0 = \varnothing$,
part (a) gives $\lvert\varnothing\rvert = 0$. Conversely, if $\lvert A\rvert = 0$
then there is a bijection $f : A \to \varnothing$; were some $a \in A$, the value
$f(a)$ would be an element of $\varnothing$, and $\varnothing$ has none, so
$A = \varnothing$.

**(c) Transport along a bijection.** If $A$ is finite and $f : A \to B$ is a
bijection, then $B$ is finite and $\lvert B\rvert = \lvert A\rvert$. Indeed
$B \approx A$ through $f^{-1}$ and $A \approx \lvert A\rvert$, so
$B \approx \lvert A\rvert$ by transitivity.

**(d) Equality of cardinalities is equinumerosity.** For finite $A$ and $B$:
$\lvert A\rvert = \lvert B\rvert$ if and only if $A \approx B$. If the
cardinalities agree then $A \approx \lvert A\rvert = \lvert B\rvert \approx B$;
conversely $A \approx B$ gives $\lvert B\rvert = \lvert A\rvert$ by (c).

1. $B$ is finite;
2. $\lvert B\rvert \le \lvert A\rvert$ ([[def-finite-cardinality]]);
3. $\lvert B\rvert = \lvert A\rvert$ if and only if $B = A$;
4. every injection $f : A \to A$ is a bijection, and every surjection

derivations.claim: The shift $j\mapsto j-1$ is a bijection from $[n]$ to the von Neumann natural $n$. By [F10]–[F12], $[n]$ is finite with cardinality $n$. Let $\Omega_n=\{f:[n]\to[n]\}$, the set of index vectors. By [F4], $|\Omega_n|=n^n$. Assign weight $n^{-n}$ to each $\omega\in\Omega_n$. The weights are nonnegative and sum to $n^n n^{-n}=1$, so [F2] gives a finite probability space $(\Omega_n,w)$ whose event sigma-algebra contains every subset. Each coordinate map $I_j(\omega)=\omega(j)$ and record map $Z_j^*(\omega)=z_{\omega(j)}$ is measurable, because every preimage is a subset of $\Omega_n$; hence each $Z_j^*$ is a random element of $(\mathcal Z,\mathcal F)$ by [F6].

For $A_j\in\mathcal F$, put $B_j:=\{i\in[n]:z_i\in A_j\}$. Each $B_j$ is a subset of the finite set $[n]$, so [F13] makes it finite. The event $\{Z_j^*\in A_j\text{ for every }j\}$ consists of the functions $g:[n]\to[n]$ with $g(j)\in B_j$ for every $j$. The shift $\tau:[n]\to n$, $\tau(j)=j-1$, from step 1.1 has inverse $\rho:n\to[n]$, $\rho(k)=k+1$; thus $g\mapsto g\circ\rho$ is a bijection from this event's index functions onto $\prod_{k<n}B_{k+1}$. By [F5] this set has cardinality $\prod_{k<n}|B_{k+1}|$, which is the same product as $\prod_{j=1}^n|B_j|$ under that reindexing. Its probability under the uniform weights is therefore $\prod_{k<n}(|B_{k+1}|/n)=\prod_{j=1}^n(|B_j|/n)$. Taking all events except the $j$th to be $\mathcal Z$ gives $\mathbb P^*(Z_j^*\in A_j)=|B_j|/n=P_n(A_j)$ by [F3] and [F7]. Hence the joint event probability is the product of its marginal probabilities.

The one-coordinate case of step 2.1 gives each $Z_j^*$ law $P_n$. To check independence for any finite subfamily indexed by $J\subseteq[n]$, take arbitrary $A_j\in\mathcal F$ for $j\in J$ and set $A_j=\mathcal Z$ for every omitted coordinate. Since $P_n(\mathcal Z)=1$ and $\mathbb P^*(Z_j^*\in\mathcal Z)=1$, step 2.1 then gives $\mathbb P^*(\bigcap_{j\in J}\{Z_j^*\in A_j\})=\prod_{j\in J}P_n(A_j)$. This is the finite-intersection factorization in [F8], so the coordinate random elements are independent. They have a common measurable target and the same law, hence they are IID by [F9].

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]) with a declared sampling or assignment mechanism. A **sampling unit** is one indexed unit that the declared mechanism treats as an indivisible draw or assignment object. Its **unit record** contains the complete observed data attached to that unit, including repeated measurements or labels that the analysis keeps together. Examples of sampling units are individuals, matched pairs, clusters, time blocks, and treatment-assignment units.

The declared mechanism also specifies a measurable unit-record space $(\mathcal Z,\mathcal F)$ and represents each unit record as an element of $\mathcal Z$. The record space may be the whole data space or one record-valued component of it; the convention is part of the experiment's sampling or assignment contract.

A **resampling unit** is the complete unit record or predeclared group of records that one draw of a resampling procedure selects. A procedure is **unit-compatible for a stated target** when it declares which records are sampled together and does not split a bundle whose joint sampling or assignment dependence is part of that target's data-generating design. Unit compatibility describes the procedure's input and dependence contract; it does not itself establish exact or asymptotic validity. A validity claim requires a separate theorem with hypotheses matched to the sampling or assignment law, target, and resample-size regime.

The conditional bootstrap law of observed units is a law on resampled data records given the fixed observations. When defined, a Bayesian posterior is instead a conditional law on parameter values under a specified prior and joint parameter-data model. They have different state spaces and are not identified by this definition. In particular, neither law determines the other.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same

$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Let $N\ge1$, and let $\mathcal I=\{1,\ldots,N\}$ index the fixed
experimental units at the actual treatment-assignment level. Let
$\mathcal Z$ be a nonempty finite set of allowed assignments. If treatment
is assigned to clusters, each cluster is one indexed unit; no separate
probability-sampling unit is present. The index $i$ identifies that unit,
and no visit or repeated-measurement index is modeled here.

A known assignment law is a function $p:\mathcal Z\to[0,1]$ satisfying
$\sum_{z\in\mathcal Z}p(z)=1$, so $(\mathcal Z,p)$ is a finite probability
space ([[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]]); assignments of probability
zero may remain in $\mathcal Z$. A **potential-outcome schedule** is a function
$\theta:\mathcal I\times\mathcal Z\to\mathbb R$, with
$Y_i(z):=\theta(i,z)$. The schedule and the units are fixed; the assignment
$Z$ is the only randomness supplied by the design, and the observed response
vector is $Y_\theta(Z)=(Y_i(Z))_{i\in\mathcal I}$. The schedule is defined
for every allowed assignment, including zero-probability assignments, and
may depend on the full assignment vector, so no no-interference assumption is
implicit. The scientific statistical model contract
[[def-scientific-statistical-model-contract]] requires the observation space,
units, quantity status, observation mechanism, support, conditioning
convention, and adequacy assumptions to be recorded; this model specifies
those fields as follows.

To express this as a statistical experiment, take the data space
$\mathcal X=\mathcal Z\times\mathbb R^{\mathcal I}$ with its full power-set
sigma-algebra, which is a sigma-algebra by [[def-sigma-algebra]] and makes
$\mathcal X$ a measurable space ([[def-measurable-space]]), and parameter
set $\Theta=\mathbb R^{\mathcal I\times\mathcal Z}$. For each $\theta\in\Theta$
let $P_\theta$ be the law
([[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]) of the deterministic
observation map $O_\theta(z)=(z,Y_\theta(z))$ from $(\mathcal Z,p)$. The map
is measurable because its domain has the full power set, in the preimage
sense of [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]], and its law
is a probability measure by
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]]. Thus
$((\mathcal X,2^{\mathcal X}),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ is an
experiment in the sense of [[def-statistical-experiment]]. The assignment
law asserts no response-error model, Gaussian law, superpopulation
randomization, or sampling representativeness beyond the stated finite
assignment mechanism. Its finite full-measure support set is
$$S_\theta:=\{(z,Y_\theta(z)):z\in\mathcal Z,\ p(z)>0\},$$
since $P_\theta(S_\theta)=\sum_{z:p(z)>0}p(z)=1$. The record contains the
assigned vector and every unit's response; missing or censored outcomes and
repeated visits require a separately declared observation mechanism. The
inferential target is the assignment-invariance hypothesis for these $N$
units, not an estimand for a wider population.

Inference in this page holds $\mathcal I$ and $\theta$ fixed and averages
over the declared law $p$; it does not condition on the realized assignment.
The status of the quantities is explicit: $\theta$ and all
$Y_i(z)$ are fixed, $Z$ is random, $(Z,Y_\theta(Z))$ is observed, and
potential responses under unassigned vectors are fixed but latent. The
assignment set, weights, and implemented randomization protocol are
design-controlled and should be checked against protocol records. Assignment
logs and response records are empirically assessable, but those checks do not
prove that the declared law generated the data. Potential outcomes under
unassigned vectors are fixed and latent in the realized record. This does
not imply nonidentifiability from the observed-data law: for each $z$ with
$p(z)>0$, the law assigns mass $p(z)$ to $(z,Y_\theta(z))$, and therefore
determines $Y_\theta(z)$. Assignment invariance on this positive-probability
set is **empirically assessable**, and the theorem tests the stronger
invariance hypothesis on all allowed assignments. Values at assignments
with $p(z)=0$, and restrictions on those values, are **substantively
untestable** from this law, since changing them leaves $P_\theta$ unchanged.
One realized assignment does not reveal responses at other assignments.
These classifications do not make the design or scientific model
empirically true.

In the finite randomized treatment-assignment model
[[def-finite-randomized-treatment-assignment-model]], a schedule satisfies
the **Fisher sharp null** when for each unit $i$ there is a value $y_i$ such that
$Y_i(z)=y_i$ for every allowed assignment $z$. The full vector
$y=(y_i)_{i\in\mathcal I}$ is then imputable under every assignment.

A **predeclared ordering score** is a real-valued statistic
$T:\mathcal Z\times\mathbb R^{\mathcal I}\to\mathbb R$
([[def-statistic-and-estimator]]) fixed before the
assignment and outcomes are inspected. Its upper-tail ordering includes ties:
assignment $z'$ is at least as extreme as $z$ when $T(z',y)\ge T(z,y)$.
For a signed score $S$ and fixed null center $s_0$, the corresponding
two-sided ordering is explicitly $T(z,y)=|S(z,y)-s_0|$. The center is part
of the predeclared ordering; the sharp null alone does not force $s_0=0$
for an arbitrary signed score. A lower-tail ordering is represented by
using $-S$ as the score. A statistic in this setting is a measurable map in
the sense of [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]; the full power-set data
sigma-algebra makes every such real-valued map measurable.

In a finite randomized treatment-assignment model, fix any real-valued
predeclared ordering score $T(z,y)$. For observed data $(z,y)$ define
$$p_{\rm rand}(z,y):=\sum_{z'\in\mathcal Z}p(z')1\{T(z',y)\ge T(z,y)\}.$$
Let $\lambda$ be the uniform probability measure on the Borel subsets of
$[0,1]$. For each $\theta$, equip $\mathcal X\times[0,1]$ with the product
sigma-algebra $2^{\mathcal X}\otimes\mathcal B([0,1])$ and define
$$\widetilde P_\theta(E):=\sum_{z\in\mathcal Z}p(z)\,\lambda\bigl(\{u\in[0,1]:((z,Y_\theta(z)),u)\in E\}\bigr).$$
Let $U$ be the $[0,1]$ coordinate on this extension. Define
$$p^+(z,y,U):=\sum_{z'\in\mathcal Z}p(z')1\{T(z',y)>T(z,y)\}+U\sum_{z'\in\mathcal Z}p(z')1\{T(z',y)=T(z,y)\}.$$
For every schedule satisfying the Fisher sharp null and every
$u\in[0,1]$,
$$P_\theta\!\left(p_{\rm rand}(Z,Y_\theta(Z))\le u\right)\le u,$$
whereas the added randomization gives
$$\widetilde P_\theta\!\left(p^+(Z,Y_\theta(Z),U)\le u\right)=u.$$
Thus $p_{\rm rand}$ is a valid finite-sample p-value for the sharp null,
and randomized ties give an exactly uniform p-value when the additional
independent uniform randomizer is used. For a two-sided test, take
$T(z,y)=|S(z,y)-s_0|$ with its center $s_0$ fixed in advance. The result
uses the actual, possibly unequal assignment probabilities; random
assignment supplies no Gaussian error law, and this theorem makes no
validity claim under the weak zero-average-effect null from
[[def-finite-population-average-treatment-effect-and-weak-null]] unless it
is also Fisher-sharp.

**Input.** Let $n\ge1$, let $(\mathcal Z,\mathcal F)$ be the declared measurable space of sampling units, and fix the observed ordered tuple $z=(z_1,\ldots,z_n)$. Let $P_n$ be its empirical probability measure from [[def-empirical-measure]] and [[lem-empirical-measure-is-a-probability-measure]]. Declare a sample sigma-algebra $\mathcal F_n$ on the ordered tuple space $\mathcal Z^n$ and provide a statistic $T_n:(\mathcal Z^n,\mathcal F_n)\to(\mathbb R^q,\mathcal B_q)$, where $q\ge1$ is finite and $\mathcal B_q$ is the declared target sigma-algebra; "statistic" has the measurable-map meaning in [[def-statistic-and-estimator]].

Write $[n]:=\{1,\ldots,n\}$ for the indexing set.

**Procedure.** Draw indices $I_1,\ldots,I_n$ independently and uniformly from $[n]$, so repeated indices are allowed. Set $Z_j^*:=z_{I_j}$ for $j=1,\ldots,n$. Return the bootstrap tuple $(Z_1^*,\ldots,Z_n^*)$ and the replicate $T_n(Z_1^*,\ldots,Z_n^*)$. Generate further replicates by repeating the index draws with fresh randomness. These are resampling units only when the tuple entries satisfy the unit contract in [[def-resampling-sampling-unit-contract]].

The conditional IID law of the draws is proved in [[thm-bootstrap-draws-are-conditionally-iid-empirical-law]]. This algorithm does not claim that its conditional law consistently approximates any sampling law; such validity requires separate hypotheses and a separate theorem.

Fix $n\ge1$, write $[n]:=\{1,\ldots,n\}$, let $(\mathcal Z,\mathcal F)$ be a measurable unit space, and fix an observed tuple $z=(z_1,\ldots,z_n)$. Let $P_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{z_i}$ be its empirical probability measure. For the bootstrap algorithm [[alg-n-out-of-n-bootstrap-from-empirical-law]], equip the conditional index vector $(I_1,\ldots,I_n)$ with the finite uniform law on $\Omega_n:=\{f:[n]\to[n]\}$ and set $Z_j^*=z_{I_j}$. For every $A_1,\ldots,A_n\in\mathcal F$,
$$\mathbb P^*(Z_1^*\in A_1,\ldots,Z_n^*\in A_n)=\prod_{j=1}^nP_n(A_j).$$
Thus, conditional on the fixed observed tuple, $Z_1^*,\ldots,Z_n^*$ are independent random elements with common law $P_n$ ([[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]).

Consider the no-interference binary-treatment submodel of
[[def-finite-randomized-treatment-assignment-model]] in which the allowed
assignment set is $\{0,1\}^{\mathcal I}$ and unit $i$'s response under
assignment vector $z$ is $Y_i(z)=Y_i(z_i)$ for fixed real potential responses
$Y_i(0)$ and $Y_i(1)$. For the fixed units, define the
**finite-population average treatment effect** by
$$\tau_F:=\frac1N\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}\bigl(Y_i(1)-Y_i(0)\bigr).$$
The **weak zero-average-effect null** is the hypothesis $\tau_F=0$; it
constrains the average of the unit-level effects, not each effect separately.
The Fisher sharp null in this submodel, defined in
[[def-fisher-sharp-null-and-predeclared-test-orderings]], requires
$Y_i(1)=Y_i(0)$ for every unit. No probability distribution on the fixed
potential responses is part of either definition.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]) with a declared sampling or assignment mechanism. A **sampling unit** is one indexed unit that the declared mechanism treats as an indivisible draw or assignment object. Its **unit record** contains the complete observed data attached to that unit, including repeated measurements or labels that the analysis keeps together. Examples of sampling units are individuals, matched pairs, clusters, time blocks, and treatment-assignment units.

The declared mechanism also specifies a measurable unit-record space $(\mathcal Z,\mathcal F)$ and represents each unit record as an element of $\mathcal Z$. The record space may be the whole data space or one record-valued component of it; the convention is part of the experiment's sampling or assignment contract.

A **resampling unit** is the complete unit record or predeclared group of records that one draw of a resampling procedure selects. A procedure is **unit-compatible for a stated target** when it declares which records are sampled together and does not split a bundle whose joint sampling or assignment dependence is part of that target's data-generating design. Unit compatibility describes the procedure's input and dependence contract; it does not itself establish exact or asymptotic validity. A validity claim requires a separate theorem with hypotheses matched to the sampling or assignment law, target, and resample-size regime.

The conditional bootstrap law of observed units is a law on resampled data records given the fixed observations. When defined, a Bayesian posterior is instead a conditional law on parameter values under a specified prior and joint parameter-data model. They have different state spaces and are not identified by this definition. In particular, neither law determines the other.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). A **p-value
statistic** is a statistic $p:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$, where $[0,1]$ carries the
trace of the Borel sigma-algebra, meaning
$\{B\cap[0,1]:B\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\}$
([[def-statistic-and-estimator]],
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]).

For a nonempty null hypothesis $\Theta_0\subseteq\Theta$, the statistic is a
**valid p-value for $\Theta_0$** if it is superuniform under every null law:
$$P_\theta(\{x:p(x)\le u\})\le u\qquad\text{for every }\theta\in\Theta_0\text{ and }u\in[0,1].$$
The variable $p(X)$ is the observed p-value when the data are $X$. The
validity condition is distributional; measurability alone does not imply it.

Let $(\mathcal Z,\mathcal F)$ be a measurable unit space ([[def-measurable-space]]), let $n\ge1$, and fix an observed ordered tuple $z_1,\ldots,z_n\in\mathcal Z$. Its **empirical measure** is the set function
$$P_n:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{z_i},\qquad P_n(A)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n1\{z_i\in A\}\quad(A\in\mathcal F),$$
where $\delta_{z_i}$ is the Dirac set function from [[def-dirac-measure]]. Repeated observations contribute once for each index at which they occur. The statement that $P_n$ is a probability measure is established in [[lem-empirical-measure-is-a-probability-measure]].

derivations.claim: Define $T(z,y)=\sum_{i:z_i=1}y_i-\sum_{i:z_i=0}y_i$. The sharp-null schedule fixes $y=(0,2)$, so $T(z^{(1)},y)=-2$ and $T(z^{(2)},y)=2$.

The design randomization law therefore assigns probability $1/2$ to each of $-2$ and $2$. Its inclusive upper-tail p-value is $1$ at $z^{(1)}$ and $1/2$ at $z^{(2)}$, a superuniform distribution under the assignment law, so [F8] identifies it as valid for this null; [F3] also gives the general validity statement.

The observed unit values are $(0,2)$, so [F9] gives empirical mass $1/2$ to each. By [F4] and [F5], an ordered size-two bootstrap pair takes $(0,0),(0,2),(2,0),(2,2)$ with probabilities $1/4$ each. The same difference score has bootstrap law with masses $1/2$ at $0$ and $1/4$ at each of $-2,2$, which differs from the design law in step 2.1.

The two laws have different state spaces and sampling mechanisms: one resamples assignments under a known design, the other resamples observed unit records conditional on those records. By [F7], a Bayesian posterior, when defined, is instead a conditional law on parameter values under a specified prior and joint model; this example supplies no such prior or posterior. By [F6], its sharp-null calculation also asserts no validity under the weaker average-effect null.

citations.quote: Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

If $(X_k)_{k\ge1}$ are IID real random variables and $\mathbb E|X_1|<\infty$, then, with $S_n=\sum_{k=1}^nX_k$ and $\mu=\mathbb EX_1$,
$$\mathbb E|S_n/n-\mu|\longrightarrow0.$$
Consequently $S_n/n\to\mu$ in probability.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. For each $i$, let
$g_i:(S_i,\Sigma_i)\to(T_i,\mathcal T_i)$ be measurable. Then the family
$(g_i\circ X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent.

derivations.claim: For each coordinate $j$, the sequence $(X_{ij})_i$ is IID by [F1] and [F4], and is integrable since $\mathbb E|X_{1j}|\le 1+\mathbb E|X_{1j}|^2<\infty$. For each pair $j,k$, $(X_{ij}X_{ik})_i$ is also IID by [F1] and [F4], and is integrable because $2|X_{1j}X_{1k}|\le X_{1j}^2+X_{1k}^2$. Apply [F3] to each of these finitely many sequences. This gives $\bar X_{n,j}\to\mu_j$ and $n^{-1}\sum_iX_{ij}X_{ik}\to\mathbb E[X_{1j}X_{1k}]$ in probability.

For each $j,k$, expand $\widehat\Sigma_{n,jk}=\frac1n\sum_iX_{ij}X_{ik}-\bar X_{n,j}\bar X_{n,k}.$ Step 1.1 makes the right side converge in probability to $\mathbb E[X_{1j}X_{1k}]-\mu_j\mu_k=\Sigma_{jk}$; the same step gives the claimed mean convergence. Since $d$ is finite, entrywise convergence holds simultaneously in probability.

citations.quote:
Fix integers $d,n\ge1$ and observed vectors $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R^d$, with the Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d)$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Their empirical law is the set function
$$P_n(A)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n 1\{x_i\in A\},\qquad A\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d).$$

Let $\mathsf I_n=\{\omega:[n]\to[n]\}$ be the finite set of index vectors. By [[thm-cardinality-of-a-set-of-functions]], it has $n^n$ elements. Give each index vector mass $n^{-n}$; the weights sum to one, so this is a finite probability space in the sense of [[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]]. For $j=1,\ldots,n$, let $I_j(\omega)=\omega(j)$ and put $X_j^*(\omega)=x_{I_j(\omega)}$. The **ideal size-$n$ empirical bootstrap law conditional on the data** is the pushforward of this finite uniform law under
$\omega\longmapsto (x_{\omega(1)},\ldots,x_{\omega(n)}).$
Thus conditional probabilities are finite averages over the $n^n$ index tuples. The empirical law is a probability measure, and the bootstrap coordinates are conditionally IID with that law, by the well-definedness results listed in justified_by.

For random observations $X_1,\ldots,X_n$, write $\bar X_n=n^{-1}\sum_iX_i$ coordinatewise, so each coordinate is the scalar sample mean in [[def-partial-sums-and-sample-means]]. Write $P_n=n^{-1}\sum_i\delta_{X_i}$, using the Dirac measure [[def-dirac-measure]], and let $\bar X_n^*$ be the bootstrap mean. If $g:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ is Borel ([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]), then
$$\hat\theta_n=g(\bar X_n),\qquad \hat\theta_n^*=g(\bar X_n^*).$$
When $X_i$ are IID ([[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]) with finite second moment, write $\mu_j=\mathbb E X_{1j}$ and $\Sigma_{jk}=\mathbb E[(X_{1j}-\mu_j)(X_{1k}-\mu_k)]$ ([[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]), and set $\theta=g(\mu)$. The functions of the data above are Borel statistics and estimators in the sense of [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]; coordinatewise arithmetic preserves measurability ([[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]). No bootstrap validity or interval coverage is part of this definition. For $n\ge2$, the delete-one mean and plug-in statistic are
$$\bar X_{n,(-i)}=\frac1{n-1}\sum_{j\ne i}X_j,\qquad \hat\theta_{n,(-i)}=g(\bar X_{n,(-i)}).$$

Let $X$ be a set and let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]). A **measure** on $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function

$$\mu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$$

such that:

1. $\mu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$,
   $$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k),$$
   where the right side is the nonnegative extended sum of [[def-nonnegative-extended-series]].

The second condition is **countable additivity**. It begins at index $0$ and includes the case in which some term or the total sum is $+\infty$.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $a=(a_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ take values in $[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$ ([[def-extended-reals]]). Its **partial sums** are the unique sequence $(s_n)$ in $[0,+\infty]$ satisfying

$$s_0=0,\qquad s_{n+1}=s_n+a_n.$$

To apply [[thm-recursion]] with a fixed successor function, use the state space $\mathbb N\times[0,+\infty]$ and the self-map $T(n,s)=(n+1,s+a_n)$, starting from $(0,0)$. Recursion gives a unique state sequence; induction makes its first coordinate $n$, and its second coordinates are exactly the unique $(s_n)$ satisfying the displayed recurrence. Addition of two nonnegative extended reals is always defined, including when either is $+\infty$. The sequence $(s_n)$ is nondecreasing, and its **nonnegative extended sum** is

$$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}a_k:=\sup_{n\in\mathbb N}s_n\in[0,+\infty],$$

whose existence follows from completeness of the extended real line ([[lem-extended-reals-complete]]). More generally, for $m\in\mathbb N$,

$$\sum_{k\ge m}a_k:=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}a_{m+j}.$$

Finite sums use the same recursion: $\sum_{k<n}a_k=s_n$, so the empty sum at $n=0$ is $0$. A double sum such as $\sum_i\sum_j a_{ij}$ means that the inner nonnegative extended sum is formed first and the resulting nonnegative extended sequence is then summed.

derivations.claim: Formula [F1] gives $P_n(\varnothing)=0$ and $P_n(\mathbb R^d)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n1=1$.

Let $(A_k)_{k\ge1}$ be pairwise disjoint Borel sets. For each fixed $i$, at most one indicator $1\{x_i\in A_k\}$ is nonzero. Therefore $P_n\!\left(\bigcup_{k\ge1}A_k\right)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{k\ge1}1\{x_i\in A_k\} =\sum_{k\ge1}\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n1\{x_i\in A_k\} =\sum_{k\ge1}P_n(A_k).$ The interchange is between a finite sum and a nonnegative series; by [F4] both are the supremum of the corresponding finite partial sums, so finite distributivity gives the equality.
Steps 1.1 and 1.2 verify the empty-set and countable-additivity clauses in [F2], and step 1.1 gives total mass one. Thus [F3] makes $P_n$ a probability measure.

boundaries.evidence: Statement explicitly requires n>=1. At n1 the law is a single point mass; at n0 the coefficient1/n is undefined, so no empty empirical probability law is asserted. Proof1.1 separately verifies P_n(emptyset)=0.
Statement: the data points may equal zero; all finite point masses still sum to one.
Statement: n=1 gives the Dirac probability measure at the sole observation.
Statement: repeated or identical observations produce a probability measure with the corresponding combined atom mass.

Statement varies finite data points and positive integer n, not an interval probability level. Repeated or coincident points, including n1, simply produce point-mass multiplicities; there is no omitted lower/upper tuning endpoint.
Statement: Proof: only finite sums and nonnegative series are used; no choice principle is used.

citations.quote:
Let $d\ge1$ be finite and let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be IID $\mathbb R^d$-valued random vectors with $\mathbb E\|X_1\|^2<\infty$. Put $\mu_j=\mathbb E X_{1j}$ and $\Sigma_{jk}=\mathbb E[(X_{1j}-\mu_j)(X_{1k}-\mu_k)]$, the coordinate covariance entries from [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]. Define
$$\bar X_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i,\qquad \widehat\Sigma_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\bar X_n)(X_i-\bar X_n)^T.$$
Then $\bar X_n\to\mu$ in probability and every entry of $\widehat\Sigma_n$ converges in probability to the corresponding entry of $\Sigma$.

Let $\mu$ be a measure and let $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be measurable. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k).$$

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ one also has

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k<m}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k<m}\mu(E_k),$$

including $m=0$, where both sides are $0$.

Fix integers $d,n\ge1$ and observed vectors $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R^d$, with the Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d)$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Their empirical law is the set function
$$P_n(A)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n 1\{x_i\in A\},\qquad A\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d).$$

Let $\mathsf I_n=\{\omega:[n]\to[n]\}$ be the finite set of index vectors. By [[thm-cardinality-of-a-set-of-functions]], it has $n^n$ elements. Give each index vector mass $n^{-n}$; the weights sum to one, so this is a finite probability space in the sense of [[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]]. For $j=1,\ldots,n$, let $I_j(\omega)=\omega(j)$ and put $X_j^*(\omega)=x_{I_j(\omega)}$. The **ideal size-$n$ empirical bootstrap law conditional on the data** is the pushforward of this finite uniform law under
$\omega\longmapsto (x_{\omega(1)},\ldots,x_{\omega(n)}).$
Thus conditional probabilities are finite averages over the $n^n$ index tuples. The empirical law is a probability measure, and the bootstrap coordinates are conditionally IID with that law, by the well-definedness results listed in justified_by.

For random observations $X_1,\ldots,X_n$, write $\bar X_n=n^{-1}\sum_iX_i$ coordinatewise, so each coordinate is the scalar sample mean in [[def-partial-sums-and-sample-means]]. Write $P_n=n^{-1}\sum_i\delta_{X_i}$, using the Dirac measure [[def-dirac-measure]], and let $\bar X_n^*$ be the bootstrap mean. If $g:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ is Borel ([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]), then
$$\hat\theta_n=g(\bar X_n),\qquad \hat\theta_n^*=g(\bar X_n^*).$$
When $X_i$ are IID ([[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]) with finite second moment, write $\mu_j=\mathbb E X_{1j}$ and $\Sigma_{jk}=\mathbb E[(X_{1j}-\mu_j)(X_{1k}-\mu_k)]$ ([[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]), and set $\theta=g(\mu)$. The functions of the data above are Borel statistics and estimators in the sense of [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]; coordinatewise arithmetic preserves measurability ([[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]). No bootstrap validity or interval coverage is part of this definition. For $n\ge2$, the delete-one mean and plug-in statistic are
$$\bar X_{n,(-i)}=\frac1{n-1}\sum_{j\ne i}X_j,\qquad \hat\theta_{n,(-i)}=g(\bar X_{n,(-i)}).$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $U \subseteq X$ be open in a real Banach space $X$, and let $Y$, $Z$, $W$ be
real Banach spaces. Then:

1. **Sum rule.** If $f_1, f_2 : U \to Y$ are Fréchet differentiable at $x \in U$
   and $a, b \in \mathbb R$, then $af_1+bf_2$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$
   with $D(af_1+bf_2)(x) = a\,Df_1(x) + b\,Df_2(x)$.
2. **Bounded-bilinear product rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ and $g : U \to Z$ are
   Fréchet differentiable at $x$, and $B : Y \times Z \to W$ is bounded
   bilinear, then $U \ni u \mapsto B(f(u),g(u))$ is Fréchet differentiable at
   $x$ and

$$D\bigl(B(f,g)\bigr)(x)h = B\bigl(Df(x)h,\ g(x)\bigr) + B\bigl(f(x),\ Dg(x)h\bigr) \qquad (h \in X).$$

3. **Chain rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$, if
   $W_0 \subseteq Y$ is an open set with $f[U] \subseteq W_0$, and if
   $g : W_0 \to Z$ is Fréchet differentiable at $f(x)$, then
   $g \circ f$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$ and
   $$D(g \circ f)(x) = Dg\bigl(f(x)\bigr)\,Df(x).$$

No continuity of any derivative map is assumed; these are pointwise statements
about one $x$ at a time.

derivations.claim: On $E_n$, define $\varphi_i(t)=g(\bar X_n-t(X_i-\bar X_n)/(n-1))$ for $0\le t\le1$. By [F4] there is $\tau_i\in(0,1)$ at which this derivative equals $\varphi_i(1)-\varphi_i(0)$. On every outcome define the measurable algebraic remainder $e_{n,i}:=\hat\theta_{n,(-i)}-\hat\theta_n+a^T(X_i-\bar X_n)/(n-1)$. On $E_n$ the mean-value identity expresses this remainder as $-\frac{(\nabla g(\bar X_n-\tau_i(X_i-\bar X_n)/(n-1))-a)^T(X_i-\bar X_n)}{n-1}$, so $|e_{n,i}|\le\omega_n\|X_i-\bar X_n\|/(n-1)$. The points $\tau_i$ are used only for this pointwise identity and bound; no measurable selection is needed. Since $\mathbb P(E_n)\to1$, the expansion with the stated bound holds with probability tending to one.

The algebraic definition of $e_{n,i}$ gives $p_{n,i}=\hat\theta_n+a^T(X_i-\bar X_n)-(n-1)e_{n,i}$. On $E_n$, the bound in step 2.1 makes the average squared error in the statement at most $\omega_n^2\,\frac1n\sum_i\|X_i-\bar X_n\|^2,$ which tends to zero in probability by step 1.1. Since $\mathbb P(E_n^c)\to0$, the stated convergence in probability follows.

The algebraic definition of $e_{n,i}$ gives, after averaging over $i$ and using $\sum_i(X_i-\bar X_n)=0$, $$nV_{J,n}=\frac1{n-1}\sum_i\left(a^T(X_i-\bar X_n)-(n-1)(e_{n,i}-\bar e_n)\right)^2,$$ where $\bar e_n=n^{-1}\sum_ie_{n,i}$. The leading quadratic term is $\frac1{n-1}\sum_i\{a^T(X_i-\bar X_n)\}^2=\frac n{n-1}a^T\widehat\Sigma_n a\longrightarrow a^T\Sigma a$ by [F1]. On $E_n$, the normalized squared error term is bounded by $(n-1)\sum_i(e_{n,i}-\bar e_n)^2\le(n-1)\sum_i e_{n,i}^2\le\omega_n^2\frac1{n-1}\sum_i\|X_i-\bar X_n\|^2\longrightarrow0.$ If $\psi_i=a^T(X_i-\bar X_n)$ and $r_i=(n-1)(e_{n,i}-\bar e_n)$, then on $E_n$ the absolute cross term is at most $2\sqrt{\left(\frac1{n-1}\sum_i\psi_i^2\right)\left(\frac1{n-1}\sum_i r_i^2\right)},$ which tends to zero because the first factor converges to the finite $a^T\Sigma a$ and the second to zero. Since $\mathbb P(E_n^c)\to0$, these bounds prove the jackknife variance limit in probability.

boundaries.evidence: Statement requires n>=2: each deletion retains n-1>=1 observations and both n and n-1 denominators are positive. The n0/n1 deletion formulas are outside the claim.

Statement excludes a^T Sigma a=0 by strict positivity. Proof1.1 uses any epsilon>0 for the tail bound, so epsilon²n>0 with n>=2; deletion denominators n-1>=1 are also nonzero. Zero secant remainders or zero finite sample variance may occur and their bounds in Proof3.1–4.1 remain valid without dividing by those quantities.

boundaries.reason: Statement: n=1 is outside the delete-one domain.
Statement: a zero projected variance is excluded by the strict positivity hypothesis.

boundaries.evidence: Statement has integer n>=2 and an open neighborhood ofmu, with no interval-valued tuning parameter. Proof2.1 handles deletion secants on the closed segment[0,1] by the mean-value theorem; its endpoints are the full and deleted means.
Statement: Proof: the mean-value theorem is applied for the finitely many i=1,...,n; finite choice suffices and no arbitrary-index choice is used.

boundaries.reason: Statement gives pseudovalue linearization and jackknife variance convergence under neighborhood C1 regularity and finite second moments. Steps 2.1 and 4.1 establish this sufficient result through deletion secants.

Statement expressly distinguishes neighborhood C1 from differentiability at the mean, but asserts no converse recovering C1 from jackknife consistency. Step 4.1 only bounds the errors using the given regularity.

risk_review.notes: Reviewed all four steps and all seven prerequisite statements. Finite second moment bounds max_i ||X_i||/n in probability and empirical second moments. On E_n all deletion segments stay in a compact ball inside U; rational supremum defines a measurable modulus tending to zero. The scalar MVT and chain rule give the secant remainder without a measurable selection of tau_i. Averaged squared pseudovalue error is bounded by modulus squared times empirical second moment; centering reduces the quadratic error, and Cauchy-Schwarz removes the cross term. n>=2 and local C1 (stronger than differentiability at mu) are explicit. No AC use or claim of BCa coverage is present.

Let $A$ and $B$ be finite sets and write

$$A^{B} := \{\, f : f \text{ is a function } B \to A \,\}.$$

Then $A^{B}$ is finite and $\lvert A^{B}\rvert = \lvert A\rvert^{\lvert B\rvert}$,
the power being the $\mathbb{N}$-valued exponentiation of [[def-nat-power]].

Both degenerate cases are covered and neither is a stipulation. If
$B = \varnothing$ there is exactly one function $B \to A$, the empty function, so
$\lvert A^{\varnothing}\rvert = 1 = \lvert A\rvert^{0}$ **even when
$A = \varnothing$**. If $A = \varnothing$ and $B \ne \varnothing$ there is no
function at all, so $\lvert A^{B}\rvert = 0 = 0^{\lvert B\rvert}$ with
$\lvert B\rvert \ge 1$.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
([[def-measurable-space]]). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ be a measurable space and let $E \subseteq X$. The
indicator function

$$\mathbf{1}_E(x) := \begin{cases} 1, & x \in E,\\ 0, & x \notin E \end{cases}$$

is measurable as a map $X \to \mathbb{R}$ if and only if $E \in \mathcal{A}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space and let
$f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ be measurable for the Borel sigma-algebra on
the extended real line. Products of functions use
$\odot_X$ from [[def-measurable-pointwise-extended-real-product]], and $cf$
abbreviates $\underline c\odot_X f$ for the constant function $\underline c$.
The magnitude function is $|f|=\max(f,-f)$ as in
[[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]]. Then:

1. $cf$ is measurable for every real scalar $c$;
2. $\max(f,g)$, $\min(f,g)$, $|f|$, $f^+$, and $f^-$ are measurable;
3. if the partial pointwise sum $f+g$ is defined at every point, then it is measurable;
4. the pointwise product $fg:=f\odot_X g$ is measurable.

Let $X$ be a real random variable. Its **cumulative distribution function** is
the function
$$F_X:\mathbb R\to[0,1],\qquad F_X(x):=\mathbb P(X\le x)=\mathbb P_X((-\infty,x]).$$

The second expression is the same quantity written in terms of the law
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] of $X$.

If $f:X\to Y$ is continuous between topological spaces, then
$f^{-1}[B]\in\mathcal B(X)$ for every $B\in\mathcal B(Y)$.

derivations.claim: Fix an outcome and let $u_1<\cdots<u_m$ be the distinct values among the finite list $(R_{n,\omega})_{\omega\in\mathsf I_n}$. Write $F_n^*(u_j^-)=n^{-n}\#\{\eta:R_{n,\eta}<u_j\}$. On $[u_j,u_{j+1})$, $F_n^*$ is constant at $F_n^*(u_j)$ and $G$ is nondecreasing, so the absolute difference is bounded by the larger of its two endpoint errors, $|F_n^*(u_j)-G(u_j)|$ and $|F_n^*(u_{j+1}^-)-G(u_{j+1})|$. For $t<u_1$, the error is at most $|F_n^*(u_1^-)-G(u_1)|$; for $t\ge u_m$, it is at most $|F_n^*(u_m)-G(u_m)|$. Each left-limit error is approached as $t\uparrow u_j$, and each right-value error occurs at $u_j$. Therefore $D_n=\max_{\omega\in\mathsf I_n}\max\{|F_n^*(R_{n,\omega})-G(R_{n,\omega})|,\ |F_n^*(R_{n,\omega}^-)-G(R_{n,\omega})|\}$, where $F_n^*(r^-)=n^{-n}\#\{\eta:R_{n,\eta}<r\}$.

For each fixed tuple $\omega$, $R_{n,\omega}$ is a finite linear combination of measurable coordinates, hence measurable by [F2]. Thus each comparison event $\{R_{n,\eta}\le R_{n,\omega}\}$ or $\{R_{n,\eta}<R_{n,\omega}\}$ is measurable by applying [F2] to the measurable difference and its Borel half-line. Consequently $F_n^*(R_{n,\omega})$ and $F_n^*(R_{n,\omega}^-)$ are measurable finite sums; $G(R_{n,\omega})$ is measurable by [F4]. The finite maximum in step 1.1 is measurable by [F2], so $D_n$ is measurable.

$g_i:(S_i,\Sigma_i)\to(T_i,\mathcal T_i)$ be measurable. Then the family
$(g_i\circ X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent.

derivations.claim: For subsets $C_1,\ldots,C_n\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$, the product-uniform index law gives $\mathbb P^*(I_1\in C_1,\ldots,I_n\in C_n)=\frac{\prod_{j=1}^n|C_j|}{n^n} =\prod_{j=1}^n\frac{|C_j|}{n}.$ Thus the coordinate indices are independent and each is uniform on $\{1,\ldots,n\}$.

For each $j$, the map $i\mapsto x_i$ from the finite discrete index set to $\mathbb R^d$ is measurable, and its pushforward of the uniform law assigns $A\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d)$ mass $n^{-1}\sum_i1\{x_i\in A\}=P_n(A)$. Applying [F3] to the independent indices shows the values $X_j^*=x_{I_j}$ are independent; their common law is $P_n$, which is a probability law by [F2].

Statement: n=1 gives a one-point index space and one bootstrap coordinate with law P1.
Statement: identical data are allowed; independence and identical distribution still hold for point-mass coordinates.

Statement uses the finite-index bootstrap definition. Step 1.1 counts uniform labels from 1 through n, including both extreme labels, and step 2.1 pushes this law to the data; there is no continuous interval endpoint parameter.
Statement: Proof: the index vector space and all event counts are finite; no arbitrary choice is used.
