citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Fix integers $d,n\ge1$ and observed vectors $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R^d$, with the Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d)$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Their empirical law is the set function
$$P_n(A)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n 1\{x_i\in A\},\qquad A\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d).$$

Let $\mathsf I_n=\{\omega:[n]\to[n]\}$ be the finite set of index vectors. By [[thm-cardinality-of-a-set-of-functions]], it has $n^n$ elements. Give each index vector mass $n^{-n}$; the weights sum to one, so this is a finite probability space in the sense of [[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]]. For $j=1,\ldots,n$, let $I_j(\omega)=\omega(j)$ and put $X_j^*(\omega)=x_{I_j(\omega)}$. The **ideal size-$n$ empirical bootstrap law conditional on the data** is the pushforward of this finite uniform law under
$\omega\longmapsto (x_{\omega(1)},\ldots,x_{\omega(n)}).$
Thus conditional probabilities are finite averages over the $n^n$ index tuples. The empirical law is a probability measure, and the bootstrap coordinates are conditionally IID with that law, by the well-definedness results listed in justified_by.

For random observations $X_1,\ldots,X_n$, write $\bar X_n=n^{-1}\sum_iX_i$ coordinatewise, so each coordinate is the scalar sample mean in [[def-partial-sums-and-sample-means]]. Write $P_n=n^{-1}\sum_i\delta_{X_i}$, using the Dirac measure [[def-dirac-measure]], and let $\bar X_n^*$ be the bootstrap mean. If $g:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ is Borel ([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]), then
$$\hat\theta_n=g(\bar X_n),\qquad \hat\theta_n^*=g(\bar X_n^*).$$
When $X_i$ are IID ([[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]) with finite second moment, write $\mu_j=\mathbb E X_{1j}$ and $\Sigma_{jk}=\mathbb E[(X_{1j}-\mu_j)(X_{1k}-\mu_k)]$ ([[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]), and set $\theta=g(\mu)$. The functions of the data above are Borel statistics and estimators in the sense of [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]; coordinatewise arithmetic preserves measurability ([[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]). No bootstrap validity or interval coverage is part of this definition. For $n\ge2$, the delete-one mean and plug-in statistic are
$$\bar X_{n,(-i)}=\frac1{n-1}\sum_{j\ne i}X_j,\qquad \hat\theta_{n,(-i)}=g(\bar X_{n,(-i)}).$$
For fixed data $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R^d$, the coordinates of the finite-index bootstrap sample in [[def-iid-empirical-bootstrap-sample]] are independent and each has law $P_n$.

Let $d\ge1$ be finite and let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be IID $\mathbb R^d$-valued random vectors with $\mathbb E\|X_1\|^2<\infty$. Put $\mu_j=\mathbb E X_{1j}$ and $\Sigma_{jk}=\mathbb E[(X_{1j}-\mu_j)(X_{1k}-\mu_k)]$, the coordinate covariance entries from [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]. Define
$$\bar X_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i,\qquad \widehat\Sigma_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\bar X_n)(X_i-\bar X_n)^T.$$
Then $\bar X_n\to\mu$ in probability and every entry of $\widehat\Sigma_n$ converges in probability to the corresponding entry of $\Sigma$.

For each integer $n\ge1$, let $k_n\ge1$ be a finite integer and let $X_{n,1},\ldots,X_{n,k_n}$ be integrable real random variables on a probability space $(\Omega_n,\mathcal F_n,\mathbb P_n)$. The family is a **centered triangular array** when $\mathbb E_nX_{n,k}=0$ for every admissible pair $(n,k)$. It is **row-wise independent** when, for each fixed n and all Borel sets $B_1,\ldots,B_{k_n}$, $$\mathbb P_n\!\left(\bigcap_{k=1}^{k_n}\{X_{n,k}\in B_k\}\right)=\prod_{k=1}^{k_n}\mathbb P_n(X_{n,k}\in B_k).$$ Taking unused $B_k$ equal to the real line gives the same factorization for each subfamily; by [[thm-rectangle-criterion-for-independent-random-elements]], this is exactly independence in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Random variables and integrability have the meanings in [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]] and [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. There is no independence requirement between different rows. The spaces may differ with n; assertions about row sums compare their laws. A single-entry row is independent automatically, and deterministic zero entries are allowed. Empty rows are excluded by $k_n\ge1$. This definition makes no existence or choice assumption.

For a centered triangular array as in [[def-row-wise-independent-centered-triangular-array]], suppose every entry has finite second moment. Write $$v_{n,k}=\mathbb E_nX_{n,k}^2=\operatorname{Var}_n(X_{n,k}),\qquad s_n^2=\sum_{k=1}^{k_n}v_{n,k}.$$ Variance is defined in [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]. Every term is finite and nonnegative, so the finite sum and its nonnegative square root s_n exist. Whenever $s_n>0$, define $$L_n(\varepsilon)=s_n^{-2}\sum_{k=1}^{k_n}\mathbb E_n\!\left[X_{n,k}^2\mathbf1_{\{|X_{n,k}|>\varepsilon s_n\}}\right]\quad(\varepsilon>0).$$ The **Lindeberg condition** is $L_n(\varepsilon)\to0$ for every fixed $\varepsilon>0$, with $s_n>0$ for all n under consideration. The event is measurable because absolute value is continuous and the entries are measurable; products are measurable by [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]. Its nonnegative integrand is bounded by $X_{n,k}^2$, so its expectation exists and is finite by [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]] and [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. In particular $0\le L_n(\varepsilon)\le1$.

For $Y_{n,k}=X_{n,k}/s_n$, scalar homogeneity gives $\sum_k\mathbb E_nY_{n,k}^2=1$. The equality $|Y_{n,k}|>\varepsilon\Longleftrightarrow |X_{n,k}|>\varepsilon s_n$ gives $$L_n(\varepsilon)=\sum_k\mathbb E_n[Y_{n,k}^2\mathbf1_{\{|Y_{n,k}|>\varepsilon\}}].$$ Thus the normalized and unnormalized conditions are exactly equivalent, not merely asymptotic. The cutoff uses strict inequality; equality at the threshold is excluded. A zero-variance row is allowed in the initial variance definition, but its normalization and Lindeberg expression above are undefined. No independence or choice is needed to define these quantities.
Assume AC. If a centered row-wise independent triangular array has finite second moments, $s_n>0$ and the Lindeberg condition, then $$s_n^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^{k_n}X_{n,k}\Rightarrow N(0,1).$$

For real random variables $(X_n)$ and $X$, write $X_n\Rightarrow X$, or
$X_n\to X$ **in distribution**, when
$$F_{X_n}(x)\longrightarrow F_X(x)$$
at every continuity point $x$ of $F_X$. Here $F_X$ is the CDF from
[[def-cumulative-distribution-function-of-a-random-variable]] and continuity
points are those of [[def-atom-and-continuity-point-of-a-law]].

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

Let $\mu$ be a measure and let $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be measurable. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k).$$

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ one also has

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k<m}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k<m}\mu(E_k),$$

including $m=0$, where both sides are $0$.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Phi(x)=P(Z\le x)$ for $Z\sim N(0,1)$. Then $\Phi$ is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$, with $\lim_{x\to-\infty}\Phi(x)=0$ and $\lim_{x\to+\infty}\Phi(x)=1$.

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]]), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
([[def-metric-uniform-continuity]]).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
([[thm-lebesgue-number-lemma]]).
Every nonempty subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ has a least element: there is $\ell \in S$ with $\ell \le s$ for all $s \in S$.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) and let
$\varepsilon \in F$ with $\varepsilon > 0$. Then there is a natural number
$n \ge 1$ such that

$$\frac{1}{n \cdot 1_F} < \varepsilon ,$$

where $n \cdot 1_F$ is the canonical natural of $F$ ([[thm-of-archimedean]]) and
$1/(n \cdot 1_F)$ is its multiplicative inverse ([[def-field]]). As is standard
we abbreviate $n \cdot 1_F$ to $n$ and write the conclusion $1/n < \varepsilon$.

This is the **reciprocal form** of the Archimedean property.
[[thm-of-archimedean]] on its own delivers only the assertion that the canonical
naturals are cofinal, $x < n \cdot 1_F$; the form actually used in analysis, that
the reciprocals of the naturals get below every positive bound, is the statement
above, and it is recorded separately so that no proof has to reconstruct the
inversion step in passing.

Let $n,d\ge1$, let $(X_1,\ldots,X_n)$ be a measurable $(\mathbb R^d)^n$-valued random vector, and fix $a\in\mathbb R^d$. For each finite index tuple $\omega=(i_1,\ldots,i_n)\in\mathsf I_n=\{1,\ldots,n\}^n$, define the projected centered bootstrap-mean value
$$R_{n,\omega}=\sqrt n\,a^T\!\left(\frac1n\sum_{\ell=1}^n X_{i_\ell}-\bar X_n\right),\qquad \bar X_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i.$$
The finite-index conditional bootstrap CDF is
$$F_n^*(t)=n^{-n}\sum_{\omega\in\mathsf I_n}1\{R_{n,\omega}\le t\}.$$
For every fixed continuous cumulative distribution function $G:\mathbb R\to[0,1]$, the supremum
$$D_n=\sup_{t\in\mathbb R}|F_n^*(t)-G(t)|$$
is a measurable real random variable.
If $X_n\to X$ almost surely, then $X_n\to X$ in probability.

derivations.claim: Put $Y_i=a^T(X_i-\mu)$ and $\bar Y_n=n^{-1}\sum_iY_i$. Its variance is $\sigma^2$. By [F2], the empirical variance $s_n^2=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(Y_i-\bar Y_n)^2=a^T\widehat\Sigma_n a$ converges in probability to $\sigma^2>0$, while $\bar Y_n\to0$ in probability and $n^{-1}\sum_iY_i^2\to\sigma^2$ in probability.

For $t>0$, define the unnormalized empirical tail quantity $T_n(t)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(Y_i-\bar Y_n)^2\,1\{|Y_i-\bar Y_n|>t\sqrt n\}.$ On $|\bar Y_n|\le t\sqrt n/2$, the indicator implies $|Y_i|>t\sqrt n/2$, and $T_n(t)\le 2\,\frac1n\sum_iY_i^2\,1\{|Y_i|>t\sqrt n/2\} +2\bar Y_n^2\,\frac1n\sum_i1\{|Y_i|>t\sqrt n/2\}.$ The expectation of the first term tends to zero by [F7], so [F8] makes it converge to zero in probability. The second empirical tail fraction is at most $4(t^2n)^{-1}(n^{-1}\sum_iY_i^2)$; hence its product with $2\bar Y_n^2$ tends to zero in probability by [F2]. The complement event has probability tending to zero by [F2], so $T_n(t)\to0$ in probability for every $t>0$.

Conditionally on the data, the row variables $Z_{n\ell}^*=n^{-1/2}a^T(X_\ell^*-\bar X_n)$, $1\le\ell\le n$, are independent and centered by [F1]. They are finite conditional rows of the type in [F3], with total variance $s_n^2$. By [F4], when $s_n>0$ their normalized Lindeberg quantity at threshold $\varepsilon>0$ is $s_n^{-2}T_n(\varepsilon s_n)$. On $s_n\ge\sigma/2$, this is at most $4\sigma^{-2}T_n(\varepsilon\sigma/2)$, which tends to zero in probability by step 1.2; also $s_n^2\to\sigma^2$ in probability by [F2].

Take any subsequence, indexed $(n_k)_{k\ge1}$. Recursively, after $k_0=0$, let $k_j$ be the least integer $k>k_{j-1}$ for which $\mathbb P(|s_{n_k}^2-\sigma^2|>1/j)+\sum_{r=1}^j\mathbb P(T_{n_k}(1/r)>1/j)<2^{-j}$. For fixed $j$, each of these finitely many probabilities tends to zero as $k\to\infty$ by [F2] and step 1.2, so the qualifying set is nonempty; [F12] gives its least index.

Let $E_j$ be the union of the variance-deviation event and the $j$ tail events at index $k_j$. By [F9], $\mathbb P(E_j)<2^{-j}$ and $\mathbb P(\bigcup_{j\ge m}E_j)\le\sum_{j\ge m}2^{-j}=2^{1-m}$. The event that infinitely many $E_j$ occur is contained in every such tail union, so its probability is zero. Off this null event, $s_{n_{k_j}}^2\to\sigma^2$ and, for every fixed $r\ge1$, $T_{n_{k_j}}(1/r)\to0$. For any $t>0$, choose $r$ with $1/r<t$ by [F13]; since $T_n$ is nonincreasing, $0\le T_{n_{k_j}}(t)\le T_{n_{k_j}}(1/r)\to0$.

Along almost every selected data path, $s_{n_{k_j}}\to\sigma>0$, and for every $\varepsilon>0$ the Lindeberg quantity is eventually bounded by $4\sigma^{-2}T_{n_{k_j}}(\varepsilon\sigma/2)\to0$. Thus the deterministic conditional rows satisfy [F5], giving $\sum_{\ell=1}^{n_{k_j}}Z_{n_{k_j},\ell}^*/s_{n_{k_j}}\Rightarrow N(0,1)$. Every starting subsequence has a further subsequence with this almost-sure conditional convergence.

Along each data sequence from step 4.1, put $m_j=n_{k_j}$ and let $H_j$ be the conditional CDF of $\sum_{\ell=1}^{m_j}Z_{m_j,\ell}^*/s_{m_j}$, discarding finitely many rows before $s_{m_j}>0$. By [F6], $H_j(t)\to\Phi(t)$ for every real $t$. Fix $x\in\mathbb R$ and $h>0$. Since $s_{m_j}\to\sigma>0$, eventually $x/\sigma-h\le x/s_{m_j}\le x/\sigma+h$, so monotonicity gives $H_j(x/\sigma-h)\le F_{m_j}^*(x)=H_j(x/s_{m_j})\le H_j(x/\sigma+h)$. Letting $j\to\infty$ and then $h\downarrow0$, continuity in [F10] yields $F_{m_j}^*(x)\to\Phi(x/\sigma)=\Phi_\sigma(x)$. To make this uniform, fix $\eta>0$, choose $R$ with $\Phi_\sigma(-R)<\eta$ and $1-\Phi_\sigma(R)<\eta$, and partition $[-R,R]$ into finitely many intervals on which $\Phi_\sigma$ varies by less than $\eta$, using [F11]. Monotonicity of each conditional CDF bounds its error between grid points by the endpoint errors plus $\eta$; outside $[-R,R]$ the two tail probabilities add at most $2\eta$ plus endpoint errors. The maximum grid error tends to zero, and then $\eta\downarrow0$ proves almost-sure uniform CDF convergence along the selected subsequence. Since $D_n$ is measurable by [F14], this is almost-sure convergence of real random variables.

If $D_n$ did not converge to zero in probability, there would be $\delta,\varepsilon>0$ and a subsequence on which $\mathbb P(D_n>\delta)\ge\varepsilon$. Applying the subsequence construction in step 2.2 and its consequences in steps 3.1–5.1 gives a further subsequence with $D_n\to0$ almost surely by step 5.1. By [F15], this is convergence in probability, contradicting the lower bound.

boundaries.reason: Statement: the CLT concerns rows n tending to infinity, with n>=1.
Statement: the projected variance sigma^2 is required to be positive.

boundaries.evidence: Statement: a finite initial row such as n=1 is permitted but does not affect the asymptotic assertion.

boundaries.reason: Statement: zero projected variance is excluded, although the full covariance matrix may be singular.

boundaries.evidence: Statement takes the supremum over every real CDF argumentx. Proof5.1 explicitly controls both infinite tails outside[-R,R] and finite partition endpoints, so no extra CDF endpoint regime is missing.
Statement: Assumption A1: AC is explicit and is used through the Lindeberg-Feller theorem; the bootstrap index space itself is finite.

boundaries.reason: Statement proves uniform conditional Gaussian CDF convergence with finite second moment and strictly positive projected variance. Steps 4.1–6.1 use conditional Lindeberg rows and subsequences to establish the sufficient implication.

Statement does not recover finite second moments or positive variance from validity of an arbitrary bootstrap approximation. The positive variance specifically licenses the normalization at step 2.1; necessity is not claimed.

risk_review.notes: Independently read all eight proof steps and all twenty direct prerequisite statements, including the full finite-index IID proof. Finite second moment controls empirical projected tails by dominated convergence and Markov. The least-index recursion simultaneously selects variance and cutoffs 1/r; summable bad-event bounds give pathwise convergence for every threshold by monotonicity. Positive limiting variance makes normalization legal after finitely many rows, and Lindeberg-Feller allows varying finite row spaces. Deterministic scaling gives the unnormalized normal limit; continuity, tail truncation and a finite grid give uniform CDF convergence. The finite-supremum lemma supplies measurable D_n. Step 6.1 correctly uses 2.2 and 3.1-5.1, and the subsequence contradiction proves convergence in probability. AC is explicitly inherited from LF and normal suppliers; the least-index selection itself uses no AC. Washington ch8b §4 Theorem 4.1 and full proof, PDF p14, were independently read as source context. Degenerate data rows can occur for small n; sigma^2>0 ensures eventual positivity on each selected path.

then
$$r_n\{g(T_n)-g(\theta)\}\Rightarrow AZ.$$

If, in addition, $A=0$ and there is a continuous symmetric bilinear map $H:\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^k$ such that
$$g(\theta+h)-g(\theta)=\frac12H[h,h]+\rho_2(h),\qquad \frac{\|\rho_2(h)\|}{\|h\|^2}\longrightarrow0\quad(h\to0,\ h\ne0),$$
then
$$r_n^2\{g(T_n)-g(\theta)\}\Rightarrow \frac12H[Z,Z].$$
For scalar-valued $g$, $H$ is the usual Hessian bilinear form. The second-order premise is a pointwise Peano expansion; continuous second derivatives on a neighborhood are not required.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be IID $\mathbb R^d$-valued vectors with $\mathbb E\|X_1\|^2<\infty$, mean $\mu$, and covariance $\Sigma$. Fix $a\in\mathbb R^d$ such that $\sigma^2=a^T\Sigma a>0$. For the finite-index empirical bootstrap in [[def-iid-empirical-bootstrap-sample]], let $\bar X_n^*$ be the bootstrap mean and define the conditional CDF
$$F_n^*(x)=\mathbb P^*\!\left(\sqrt n\,a^T(\bar X_n^*-\bar X_n)\le x\mid X_1,\ldots,X_n\right).$$
Then
$$D_n:=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R}\left|F_n^*(x)-\Phi_\sigma(x)\right|\longrightarrow0\quad\text{in probability},$$
where $\Phi_\sigma$ is the CDF of $N(0,\sigma^2)$. The assumption $\sigma^2>0$ is needed for the normalized Lindeberg–Feller step.

Let $d\ge1$ be finite and let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be IID $\mathbb R^d$-valued random vectors with $\mathbb E\|X_1\|^2<\infty$. Put $\mu_j=\mathbb E X_{1j}$ and $\Sigma_{jk}=\mathbb E[(X_{1j}-\mu_j)(X_{1k}-\mu_k)]$, the coordinate covariance entries from [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]. Define
$$\bar X_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i,\qquad \widehat\Sigma_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\bar X_n)(X_i-\bar X_n)^T.$$
Then $\bar X_n\to\mu$ in probability and every entry of $\widehat\Sigma_n$ converges in probability to the corresponding entry of $\Sigma$.

Let all random vectors with index $n$ be defined on a common probability space for that $n$; the spaces may vary with $n$. In any fixed finite-dimensional Euclidean space, the following rules hold:

1. If $U_n=o_P(1)$ and $V_n=o_P(1)$, then $U_n+V_n=o_P(1)$. If $U_n=O_P(1)$ and $V_n=O_P(1)$, then $U_n+V_n=O_P(1)$.
2. For positive integers $p,q,r$, let $B:\mathbb R^p\times\mathbb R^q\to\mathbb R^r$ be a fixed map for which there is a constant $C\ge0$ with $\|B(u,v)\|_2\le C\|u\|_2\|v\|_2$ for all $u,v$. Assume in each application that $B(U_n,V_n)$ is a random vector on the same probability space as $U_n,V_n$, for every $n$. If $U_n=o_P(1)$ and $V_n=O_P(1)$, or conversely, then $B(U_n,V_n)=o_P(1)$. If both are $O_P(1)$, then $B(U_n,V_n)=O_P(1)$.
3. If $X_n\Rightarrow X$ in $\mathbb R^d$, then $X_n=O_P(1)$.

The last conclusion is finite-dimensional boundedness in probability. No independence or Axiom of Choice is assumed.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

For real random variables $(X_n)$ and $X$, write $X_n\Rightarrow X$, or
$X_n\to X$ **in distribution**, when
$$F_{X_n}(x)\longrightarrow F_X(x)$$
at every continuity point $x$ of $F_X$. Here $F_X$ is the CDF from
[[def-cumulative-distribution-function-of-a-random-variable]] and continuity
points are those of [[def-atom-and-continuity-point-of-a-law]].

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Phi(x)=P(Z\le x)$ for $Z\sim N(0,1)$. Then $\Phi$ is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$, with $\lim_{x\to-\infty}\Phi(x)=0$ and $\lim_{x\to+\infty}\Phi(x)=1$.

Let $U$ be an open subset of a real matrix space $\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ or of
a complex matrix space $\mathbb C^{m\times n}$ viewed as a real vector space,
and let $F:U\to W$ take values in a finite-dimensional real normed vector
space $(W,\|\,\cdot\,\|_W)$.
We say that $F$ is **real Fr\'echet differentiable** at $A\in U$ if there is a
real-linear map $L$ such that

$$\frac{\|F(A+H)-F(A)-L[H]\|_W}{\|H\|_F}\longrightarrow0\qquad(H\to0,\ H\ne0).$$

That map $L$ is the **real Fr\'echet derivative** of $F$ at $A$ and is denoted
$DF(A)$.

derivations.claim: By [F2], $Z_n:=\sqrt n(\bar X_n-\mu)\Rightarrow Z$ for $Z\sim N_d(0,\Sigma)$.

Put $H_n^*=\sqrt n(\bar X_n^*-\bar X_n)$ and $V_n^*=a^TH_n^*$. By [F4], the conditional CDF of $V_n^*$ converges uniformly in probability to $\Phi_\sigma$. Also $\mathbb E^*(\|H_n^*\|^2\mid X_1,\ldots,X_n)=\operatorname{tr}(\widehat\Sigma_n).$ By [F5], this trace converges in probability to $\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)$. For any $M>0$, $\mathbb P^*(\|H_n^*\|>M\mid X_1,\ldots,X_n)\le \frac{\operatorname{tr}(\widehat\Sigma_n)}{M^2}$ by [F9]. Given $\eta>0$, choose $K>\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)$; with probability tending to one the trace is at most $K$, and then choosing $M^2>K/\eta$ makes this conditional tail at most $\eta$. Thus $H_n^*$ is bounded in conditional probability, in probability. By [F2] and [F6], $Z_n$ is bounded in probability, so $Z_n+H_n^*=\sqrt n(\bar X_n^*-\mu)$ is also bounded in conditional probability, in probability.
Apply [F3] with $r_n=\sqrt n$ and derivative $a^T$. Then $\sqrt n\{g(\bar X_n)-g(\mu)\}\Rightarrow a^TZ$, and [F7] identifies this law as $N(0,\sigma^2)$. This proves the sampling limit.

By [F11], $g(\mu+h)=g(\mu)+a^Th+r(h)$ with $|r(h)|/\|h\|\to0$. Fix $\varepsilon,\eta>0$. By [F6], choose $R_0$ so that $\limsup_n\mathbb P(\|Z_n\|>R_0)<\eta$. The conditional tightness established in step 1.2 gives $R_1$ such that, for all sufficiently large $n$, the data probability that $\mathbb P^*(\|H_n^*\|>R_1\mid X_1,\ldots,X_n)>\eta$ is below $\eta$. On the complementary data event and $\|Z_n\|\le R_0$, the conditional probability that $\|\sqrt n(\bar X_n^*-\mu)\|>R_0+R_1$ is at most $\eta$. Put $R=R_0+R_1$ and choose $\delta>0$ so $|r(h)|\le \varepsilon\|h\|/(4R)$ for $0<\|h\|<\delta$. For $n$ large enough that $R/\sqrt n<\delta$, the true remainder $\sqrt n|r(\bar X_n-\mu)|$ is at most $\varepsilon/4$ on $\|Z_n\|\le R_0$ (enlarge $R$ to at least $R_0$), and the bootstrap remainder $\sqrt n|r(\bar X_n^*-\mu)|$ is at most $\varepsilon/4$ whenever its root norm is at most $R$. The exceptional data probability has limiting upper bound at most $2\eta$, and the exceptional conditional probability is at most $\eta$ on the remaining data event. Letting $\eta\downarrow0$ proves that the difference of these two remainders is $o_{P^*}(1)$ in probability. Consequently $\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n^*-\hat\theta_n)=V_n^*+\Delta_n^*,$ where $\mathbb P^*(|\Delta_n^*|>\eta\mid X_1,\ldots,X_n)\to0$ in probability for every $\eta>0$.

Fix $x\in\mathbb R$ and $h>0$. With $G_n^*$ the conditional CDF of the left side in step 2.2 and $F_n^*$ that of $V_n^*$, the event inclusion gives $F_n^*(x-h)-q_n(h)\le G_n^*(x)\le F_n^*(x+h)+q_n(h),$ where $q_n(h)=\mathbb P^*(|\Delta_n^*|>h\mid X_1,\ldots,X_n)$. By [F4] and step 2.2, for each fixed $h$ these bounds converge in probability to $\Phi_\sigma(x-h)$ and $\Phi_\sigma(x+h)$. Given any tolerance, [F10] lets us choose $h$ so both constants differ from $\Phi_\sigma(x)$ by less than that tolerance; convergence of the bounds then gives $G_n^*(x)\to\Phi_\sigma(x)$ in probability. By [F8], this is conditional weak convergence in probability to the same first-order law as the sampling limit in step 2.1.

Fix integers $d,n\ge1$ and observed vectors $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R^d$, with the Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d)$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Their empirical law is the set function
$$P_n(A)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n 1\{x_i\in A\},\qquad A\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d).$$

Let $\mathsf I_n=\{\omega:[n]\to[n]\}$ be the finite set of index vectors. By [[thm-cardinality-of-a-set-of-functions]], it has $n^n$ elements. Give each index vector mass $n^{-n}$; the weights sum to one, so this is a finite probability space in the sense of [[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]]. For $j=1,\ldots,n$, let $I_j(\omega)=\omega(j)$ and put $X_j^*(\omega)=x_{I_j(\omega)}$. The **ideal size-$n$ empirical bootstrap law conditional on the data** is the pushforward of this finite uniform law under
$\omega\longmapsto (x_{\omega(1)},\ldots,x_{\omega(n)}).$
Thus conditional probabilities are finite averages over the $n^n$ index tuples. The empirical law is a probability measure, and the bootstrap coordinates are conditionally IID with that law, by the well-definedness results listed in justified_by.

For random observations $X_1,\ldots,X_n$, write $\bar X_n=n^{-1}\sum_iX_i$ coordinatewise, so each coordinate is the scalar sample mean in [[def-partial-sums-and-sample-means]]. Write $P_n=n^{-1}\sum_i\delta_{X_i}$, using the Dirac measure [[def-dirac-measure]], and let $\bar X_n^*$ be the bootstrap mean. If $g:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ is Borel ([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]), then
$$\hat\theta_n=g(\bar X_n),\qquad \hat\theta_n^*=g(\bar X_n^*).$$
When $X_i$ are IID ([[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]) with finite second moment, write $\mu_j=\mathbb E X_{1j}$ and $\Sigma_{jk}=\mathbb E[(X_{1j}-\mu_j)(X_{1k}-\mu_k)]$ ([[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]), and set $\theta=g(\mu)$. The functions of the data above are Borel statistics and estimators in the sense of [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]; coordinatewise arithmetic preserves measurability ([[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]). No bootstrap validity or interval coverage is part of this definition. For $n\ge2$, the delete-one mean and plug-in statistic are
$$\bar X_{n,(-i)}=\frac1{n-1}\sum_{j\ne i}X_j,\qquad \hat\theta_{n,(-i)}=g(\bar X_{n,(-i)}).$$

derivations.claim: By [F2], $\bar X_{n,(-i)}=\bar X_n-(X_i-\bar X_n)/(n-1)$. Averaging over $i$ gives $\bar\theta_{n,(-)}=\bar X_n$, since $\sum_i(X_i-\bar X_n)=0$.

Substitution into [F1] gives $p_{n,i}=X_i$ and $V_{J,n}=\frac{n-1}{n}\sum_i\left(\frac{\bar X_n-X_i}{n-1}\right)^2 =\frac1{n(n-1)}\sum_i(X_i-\bar X_n)^2.$ Thus $V_{J,n}=s_n^2/n$, where $s_n^2=(n-1)^{-1}\sum_i(X_i-\bar X_n)^2$ is the unbiased sample variance.

Input a nonempty finite list $y_1,\ldots,y_B\in\mathbb R$ and $p\in[0,1]$. Sort the values with multiplicity as $y_{(1)}\le\cdots\le y_{(B)}$. If $p=0$, set $k=1$; if $p>0$, let $k$ be the least integer in $\{1,\ldots,B\}$ with $k\ge Bp$. Return
$$Q_B(p)=y_{(k)}.$$
This is the lower inverse empirical-CDF quantile, with the explicit endpoint convention $Q_B(0)=y_{(1)}$ and $Q_B(1)=y_{(B)}$. Repeated values remain repeated; no interpolation is performed. An empty list or a value of $p$ outside $[0,1]$ is inadmissible.

Input a nonempty list of $B$ bootstrap estimates $\hat\theta_1^*,\ldots,\hat\theta_B^*$ generated under the empirical bootstrap law in [[def-iid-empirical-bootstrap-sample]], and $0<\alpha<1$. Let $Q_B$ be [[alg-lower-empirical-bootstrap-quantile]] and set $p=\alpha/2$. Return
$$[Q_B(p),\,Q_B(1-p)].$$
This finite-$B$ procedure uses the declared lower empirical-quantile convention. It defines endpoints only; it asserts no coverage guarantee.

Input the observed estimate $\hat\theta$, a nonempty list of $B$ bootstrap estimates $\hat\theta_1^*,\ldots,\hat\theta_B^*$ generated under [[def-iid-empirical-bootstrap-sample]], and $0<\alpha<1$. Let $Q_B$ be [[alg-lower-empirical-bootstrap-quantile]] and set $p=\alpha/2$. Return
$$[2\hat\theta-Q_B(1-p),\,2\hat\theta-Q_B(p)].$$
This is the reflected bootstrap-quantile interval under the declared finite-sample quantile convention. It makes no coverage claim.

List the $27$ conditional median values with multiplicity: twenty zeros and seven ones. With $\alpha=1/3$, [F2] gives $Q_{27}(1/6)=0$ and $Q_{27}(5/6)=1$. Thus [F3] returns $[0,1]$, while [F4] with observed median $0$ returns $[-1,0]$. These are the outputs under the specified tie and quantile conventions.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be IID $\mathbb R^d$-valued vectors with $\mathbb E\|X_1\|^2<\infty$, mean $\mu$, and covariance $\Sigma$. Fix $a\in\mathbb R^d$ such that $\sigma^2=a^T\Sigma a>0$. For the finite-index empirical bootstrap in [[def-iid-empirical-bootstrap-sample]], let $\bar X_n^*$ be the bootstrap mean and define the conditional CDF
$$F_n^*(x)=\mathbb P^*\!\left(\sqrt n\,a^T(\bar X_n^*-\bar X_n)\le x\mid X_1,\ldots,X_n\right).$$
Then
$$D_n:=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R}\left|F_n^*(x)-\Phi_\sigma(x)\right|\longrightarrow0\quad\text{in probability},$$
where $\Phi_\sigma$ is the CDF of $N(0,\sigma^2)$. The assumption $\sigma^2>0$ is needed for the normalized Lindeberg–Feller step.
Assume AC. Let $(X_k)_{k\ge1}$ be iid real random variables with mean $m$ and variance $0<\sigma^2<\infty$. Then $$\frac{\sum_{k=1}^nX_k-nm}{\sigma\sqrt n}\ \Rightarrow\ N(0,1).$$

Let S,T be metric spaces, $g:S\to T$ measurable, and $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$. If the discontinuity set $D_g$ is $\mu$-null, then $g_*\mu_n\Rightarrow g_*\mu$. Consequently $X_n\Rightarrow X$ implies $g(X_n)\Rightarrow g(X)$ whenever $P_X(D_g)=0$.

Let $(X_n)$ and $(Y_n)$ be real random variables on one probability space, and let $X$ be a real random variable (possibly on another space). If $X_n\Rightarrow X$ and $Y_n\to c$ in probability for $c\in\mathbb R$, then $X_n+Y_n\Rightarrow X+c$ and $X_nY_n\Rightarrow cX$. If $c\ne0$, define $Q_n=X_n/Y_n$ on $\{Y_n\ne0\}$ and give $Q_n$ any fixed value on $\{Y_n=0\}$. Then $Q_n\Rightarrow X/c$.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Phi(x)=P(Z\le x)$ for $Z\sim N(0,1)$. Then $\Phi$ is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$, with $\lim_{x\to-\infty}\Phi(x)=0$ and $\lim_{x\to+\infty}\Phi(x)=1$.

derivations.claim: By [F2], $Z_n=\sqrt n\,\bar X_n\Rightarrow Z$ with $Z\sim N(0,1)$. Since absolute value is continuous, [F3] gives $\sqrt n|\bar X_n|\Rightarrow |Z|$. The limiting CDF of $|Z|$ is continuous at $0$ and equals $\mathbb P(|Z|\le0)=0$.

Let $V_n^*=\sqrt n(\bar X_n^*-\bar X_n)$. Its conditional CDF $F_n^*$ satisfies $D_n:=\sup_t|F_n^*(t)-\Phi(t)|\to0$ in probability by [F1]. The bootstrap root for $g(x)=|x|$ is $R_n^*=\sqrt n(|\bar X_n^*|-|\bar X_n|)=|Z_n+V_n^*|-|Z_n|.$ For fixed data value $Z_n=z\ge0$, the event $R_n^*\le0$ is $-2z\le V_n^*\le0$; for $z<0$, it is $0\le V_n^*\le-2z$.

For any interval $[u,v]$, the difference between its conditional bootstrap probability and its standard normal probability is at most $2D_n$: use $F_n^*(v)-F_n^*(u-)$ and take left limits in the uniform CDF bound, using continuity of $\Phi$. Therefore $Q_n:=\mathbb P^*(R_n^*\le0\mid X_1,\ldots,X_n)=\Phi(2|Z_n|)-\frac12+o_{\mathbb P}(1).$ Indeed, the normal mass of either interval in step 1.2 is $\Phi(2|z|)-1/2$. By [F3] and [F4], $Q_n\Rightarrow \Phi(2|Z|)-1/2$. This limit is positive with positive probability because $\mathbb P(|Z|\ge1)>0$ and [F5] gives $\Phi(2)-1/2>0$. Thus $Q_n$ does not converge in probability to zero.

If the conditional bootstrap law consistently estimated the sampling law of $\sqrt n|\bar X_n|$, its conditional CDF at the continuity point $0$ would converge in probability to the sampling limit CDF there, namely zero by step 1.1 and [F5]. Step 2.1 contradicts this. The failure occurs because $g(x)=|x|$ is not differentiable at the true mean $0$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Fix integers $d,n\ge1$ and observed vectors $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R^d$, with the Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d)$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Their empirical law is the set function
$$P_n(A)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n 1\{x_i\in A\},\qquad A\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d).$$

Let $\mathsf I_n=\{\omega:[n]\to[n]\}$ be the finite set of index vectors. By [[thm-cardinality-of-a-set-of-functions]], it has $n^n$ elements. Give each index vector mass $n^{-n}$; the weights sum to one, so this is a finite probability space in the sense of [[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]]. For $j=1,\ldots,n$, let $I_j(\omega)=\omega(j)$ and put $X_j^*(\omega)=x_{I_j(\omega)}$. The **ideal size-$n$ empirical bootstrap law conditional on the data** is the pushforward of this finite uniform law under
$\omega\longmapsto (x_{\omega(1)},\ldots,x_{\omega(n)}).$
Thus conditional probabilities are finite averages over the $n^n$ index tuples. The empirical law is a probability measure, and the bootstrap coordinates are conditionally IID with that law, by the well-definedness results listed in justified_by.

For random observations $X_1,\ldots,X_n$, write $\bar X_n=n^{-1}\sum_iX_i$ coordinatewise, so each coordinate is the scalar sample mean in [[def-partial-sums-and-sample-means]]. Write $P_n=n^{-1}\sum_i\delta_{X_i}$, using the Dirac measure [[def-dirac-measure]], and let $\bar X_n^*$ be the bootstrap mean. If $g:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ is Borel ([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]), then
$$\hat\theta_n=g(\bar X_n),\qquad \hat\theta_n^*=g(\bar X_n^*).$$
When $X_i$ are IID ([[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]) with finite second moment, write $\mu_j=\mathbb E X_{1j}$ and $\Sigma_{jk}=\mathbb E[(X_{1j}-\mu_j)(X_{1k}-\mu_k)]$ ([[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]), and set $\theta=g(\mu)$. The functions of the data above are Borel statistics and estimators in the sense of [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]; coordinatewise arithmetic preserves measurability ([[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]). No bootstrap validity or interval coverage is part of this definition. For $n\ge2$, the delete-one mean and plug-in statistic are
$$\bar X_{n,(-i)}=\frac1{n-1}\sum_{j\ne i}X_j,\qquad \hat\theta_{n,(-i)}=g(\bar X_{n,(-i)}).$$

Assume AC. Let $X_i$ be IID $\mathbb R^d$-valued vectors with $\mathbb E\|X_1\|^2<\infty$, mean $\mu$, and covariance $\Sigma$. Let $g:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be Borel and Fréchet differentiable at $\mu$, with derivative $a^T$, and assume
$$0<\sigma^2:=a^T\Sigma a<\infty.$$
Set $\theta=g(\mu)$, $\hat\theta_n=g(\bar X_n)$, and $\hat\theta_n^*=g(\bar X_n^*)$ for the finite-index empirical bootstrap in [[def-iid-empirical-bootstrap-sample]]. Then
$$\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta)\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma^2),$$
and, for every fixed $x\in\mathbb R$,
$$\mathbb P^*\!\left(\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n^*-\hat\theta_n)\le x\mid X_1,\ldots,X_n\right)\longrightarrow\Phi_\sigma(x)\quad\text{in probability},$$
where $\Phi_\sigma$ is the CDF of $N(0,\sigma^2)$. Thus the ideal conditional bootstrap law and the sampling law have the same first-order limit with the stated centering and $\sqrt n$ scaling. This theorem does not imply coverage of any interval algorithm.

derivations.claim: Here $g(x)=x$ is Borel and differentiable everywhere with derivative $a=1$. Thus $a^T\Sigma a=\operatorname{Var}(X_1)=\sigma^2\in(0,\infty)$, so all assumptions of [F2] hold.

Since $\hat\theta_n=\bar X_n$ and $\hat\theta_n^*=\bar X_n^*$ by [F1], [F2] gives $\sqrt n(\bar X_n-\mu)\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma^2)$ and the conditional law of $\sqrt n(\bar X_n^*-\bar X_n)$ converges weakly in probability to the same normal law. This is first-order distributional validity only.

Let $X$ be a real random variable. Its **cumulative distribution function** is
the function
$$F_X:\mathbb R\to[0,1],\qquad F_X(x):=\mathbb P(X\le x)=\mathbb P_X((-\infty,x]).$$

The second expression is the same quantity written in terms of the law
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] of $X$.

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a decreasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$. If $\mu(E_{n_0})<+\infty$ for some $n_0$, then

$$\mu\left(\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\inf_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be an increasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$, so $E_n\subseteq E_{n+1}$. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\sup_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

No finiteness hypothesis is required.

derivations.claim: For $u\in(0,1)$ the quantile set $\{x:F(x)\ge u\}$ is nonempty and bounded below because the events $\{X\le k\}$ increase to the whole space and $\{X\le-k\}$ decrease to the empty set; [F2]–[F3] give the CDF limits $1$ and $0$ at the two tails. If $q=q_F(u)$, then for every $r>0$ there is $x<q+r$ with $F(x)\ge u$, so $F(q+r)\ge u$. The events $\{X\le q+1/k\}$ decrease to $\{X\le q\}$; by [F2], $F(q)=\lim_kF(q+1/k)\ge u$. Also, for every $x<q$, $F(x)<u$ by the definition of infimum.

If $\alpha_2=0$, the event is vacuous because $q_G(1)=+\infty$. Otherwise, if $1-\alpha_2-\varepsilon\le0$, the lower bound is nonpositive and is trivial. In the remaining case, every $x$ with $G(x)\ge1-\alpha_2$ satisfies $F(x)\ge1-\alpha_2-\varepsilon$, so $q_F(1-\alpha_2-\varepsilon)\le q_G(1-\alpha_2)$. Step 1.1 gives $F(q_F(1-\alpha_2-\varepsilon))\ge1-\alpha_2-\varepsilon$, and monotonicity of $F$ proves the first probability bound.

If $\alpha_1=0$, the event is vacuous because $q_G(0)=-\infty$. If $\alpha_1+\varepsilon\ge1$, the lower bound is nonpositive and is trivial. Otherwise, each $x$ with $F(x)\ge\alpha_1+\varepsilon$ has $G(x)\ge\alpha_1$, whence $q_G(\alpha_1)\le q_F(\alpha_1+\varepsilon)$. For every $y<q_F(\alpha_1+\varepsilon)$, step 1.1 gives $F(y)<\alpha_1+\varepsilon$. The events $\{X\le q_F(\alpha_1+\varepsilon)-1/k\}$ increase to $\{X<q_F(\alpha_1+\varepsilon)\}$; [F3] therefore gives $\mathbb P\{X<q_F(\alpha_1+\varepsilon)\}\le\alpha_1+\varepsilon$. This proves the second bound.

The stated replacement on $N$ preserves measurable evaluations and gives CDF paths everywhere. For $u\in(0,1)$, $q_{\widehat G}(u)$ is measurable because $\{q_{\widehat G}(u)<a\}=\bigcup_{r\in\mathbb Q,\,r<a}\{\widehat G(r)\ge u\}$; the endpoint quantiles are constant, so the coverage event is measurable. Also $E:=\{\sup_x|\widehat G(x)-F(x)|\le\varepsilon/2\}$ is measurable because $|\widehat G-F|$ is right-continuous for every outcome and its supremum over $\mathbb R$ equals its supremum over $\mathbb Q$. If $\alpha_1+\alpha_2+\varepsilon+\delta\ge1$, part 3 is the trivial nonnegative lower bound. Otherwise, on $E$, when $\alpha_1>0$ the pointwise order implies $q_{\widehat G}(\alpha_1)\le q_F(\alpha_1+\varepsilon/2)$; hence the lower-tail failure on $E$ is contained in $\{X<q_F(\alpha_1+\varepsilon/2)\}$ and has probability at most $\alpha_1+\varepsilon/2$ by step 2.2. If $\alpha_1=0$, this tail is empty. Similarly, when $\alpha_2>0$, $q_F(1-\alpha_2-\varepsilon/2)\le q_{\widehat G}(1-\alpha_2)$; hence the upper-tail failure on $E$ is contained in $\{X>q_F(1-\alpha_2-\varepsilon/2)\}$, whose probability is at most $\alpha_2+\varepsilon/2$ by step 1.1. If $\alpha_2=0$, that tail is empty. A union bound and $\mathbb P(E^c)\le\delta$ give the claimed coverage bound; no independence between $E$ and $X$ is needed because each intersection with $E$ is bounded by the corresponding unconditional tail event.

Let $X$ be a real random variable. Its **cumulative distribution function** is
the function
$$F_X:\mathbb R\to[0,1],\qquad F_X(x):=\mathbb P(X\le x)=\mathbb P_X((-\infty,x]).$$

The second expression is the same quantity written in terms of the law
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] of $X$.

Let $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be compact ([[def-open-cover-r]]) and let
$f : K \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $K$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$
is uniformly continuous on $K$ ([[def-uniform-continuity-real]]).

**This theorem is stated twice in this library, on purpose.** Its metric-space
twin is [[thm-heine-cantor-metric]], proved there from the cover machinery of
metric spaces; the proof below uses the open-cover definition of compactness
in $\mathbb{R}$ directly. That the two
statements are the same statement in two vocabularies is
[[lem-real-and-metric-notions-agree]], clauses 1, 2 and 5, immediately above.

**Choice-free proof.** The argument below uses the open-cover definition of compactness directly. It considers every continuity neighbourhood at once and extracts only a finite subcover, so no countable or global choice function is selected.

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a decreasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$. If $\mu(E_{n_0})<+\infty$ for some $n_0$, then

$$\mu\left(\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\inf_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be an increasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$, so $E_n\subseteq E_{n+1}$. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\sup_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

No finiteness hypothesis is required.

derivations.claim: The stated replacement on each measurable null set preserves measurable evaluations and their pointwise convergence in probability, and gives CDF paths everywhere. Consequently $\sup_x|G_n(x)-F(x)|$ equals the supremum over rational $x$ for every outcome, by right-continuity, and is measurable. Fix $0<\eta<1/2$. The events defining a CDF increase to the whole space as $x\to+\infty$ and decrease to the empty set as $x\to-\infty$; [F3]–[F4] therefore give its tail limits. Choose $L<R$ with $F(L)<\eta$ and $1-F(R)<\eta$. By [F2], $F$ is uniformly continuous on $[L,R]$, so choose a finite partition $L=x_0<\cdots<x_k=R$ for which every increment $F(x_{j+1})-F(x_j)<\eta$.

Pointwise convergence at the finitely many grid points implies that, with probability tending to one, $|G_n(x_j)-F(x_j)|\le\eta$ for every $j$. On this event, monotonicity of both CDFs bounds their difference on each $[x_j,x_{j+1}]$ by $3\eta$. For $x<L$, both CDF values lie between $0$ and their values at $L$, so their difference is at most $2\eta$; for $x>R$, apply the same argument to the complementary tails using their values at $R$. Hence $\sup_x|G_n(x)-F(x)|\le3\eta$ with probability tending to one. Since $\eta>0$ was arbitrary, the supremum converges to zero in probability.

For $p\in[0,1]$, a **Bernoulli$(p)$ random variable** takes the value $1$ with probability $p$ and $0$ with probability $1-p$.

For $n\in\mathbb N$, a **binomial$(n,p)$ random variable** is a sum $X=\sum_{i<n}X_i$ of $n$ mutually independent Bernoulli$(p)$ variables. When $n=0$, this is the constant zero random variable.

Work on a common probability space; the independent Bernoulli variables used to represent a binomial sum are independent in the sense of [[def-independent-random-elements]]. The original finite-space atom-independence convention is included.

If $X$ is Bernoulli$(p)$, then $\mathbb E[X]=p$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=p(1-p)$. If $S$ is binomial$(n,p)$, then
$$\mathbb E[S]=np,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(S)=np(1-p).$$
These formulas include $p=0$, $p=1$, and $n=0$.

If $X$ is a square-integrable real random variable and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(|X-\mathbb E[X]|\ge a)\le\frac{\operatorname{Var}(X)}{a^2}.$$

For Borel probabilities $\mu$,$
u$ on a metric space S, put $F^{[\varepsilon]}=\{x:d(x,F)\le\varepsilon\}$ for nonempty closed F, and $\varnothing^{[\varepsilon]}=\varnothing$. Define $\pi(\mu,
u)$ as the infimum of $\varepsilon$>0 such that, for every closed F, both $\mu(F)\le
u(F^{[\varepsilon]})+\varepsilon$ and $
u(F)\le\mu(F^{[\varepsilon]})+\varepsilon$. The admissible set contains every $\varepsilon$>=1 and is bounded below by zero, so its real infimum exists by [[thm-infimum-property]]. Enlargements are closed because distance to a nonempty set is continuous. [[lem-distance-to-set-is-lipschitz]] The metric assertion is proved in the following lemma.

derivations.claim: If $p=q$, the laws coincide. Suppose $p\le q$. For each $i$, give $(B_i,C_i)\in\{0,1\}^2$ probabilities $p$ at $(1,1)$, $q-p$ at $(0,1)$, $1-q$ at $(0,0)$, and zero at $(1,0)$, and take $n$ independent copies of this finite pair. Then $B_i\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)$, $C_i\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(q)$, and $D_i:=C_i-B_i\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(q-p)$; the pairs are independent across $i$. Thus $S_{n,q}-S_{n,p}=n^{-1/2}\sum_i(D_i-(q-p))$, whose mean is zero and whose variance, by [F2], is $(q-p)(1-q+p)\le q-p$. If $q<p$, interchange the two parameters and change the sign of the difference; its variance is $|p-q|(1-|p-q|)\le|p-q|$.

Put $r=|p-q|$ and $\varepsilon=r^{1/3}$ for $r>0$. By [F3] and step 1.1, the coupling just constructed satisfies $\mathbb P(|S_{n,p}-S_{n,q}|>\varepsilon)\le r/\varepsilon^2=\varepsilon$. For any closed set $A$, the event $\{S_{n,p}\in A,\ |S_{n,p}-S_{n,q}|\le\varepsilon\}$ is contained in $\{S_{n,q}\in A^{[\varepsilon]}\}$, so $\mu_{n,p}(A)\le\mu_{n,q}(A^{[\varepsilon]})+\varepsilon$. Interchanging $p$ and $q$ gives the reverse inequality. Hence $\varepsilon$ is admissible in [F4], so the infimum defining $\pi$ is at most $\varepsilon$. For $r=0$ the laws coincide and their distance is zero by [F4]. This proves the bound for every endpoint case as well.

Let $n\ge1$ be an integer, let $(\mathcal Z,\mathcal C)$ be a measurable observation space, let $P$ be a probability law on it, and let $Z_1,\ldots,Z_n$ be IID $P$-distributed sampling units ([[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]). For each $1\le k\le n$, let $T_k$ be a measurable real-valued statistic and write $\widehat\theta_k=T_k(Z_1,\ldots,Z_k)$; the target is a scalar $\theta(P)$ and $a_k>0$ is its declared normalization at sample size $k$. The empirical law
$$P_n:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{Z_i}$$
is a probability law by [[lem-finite-empirical-measure-is-a-probability-law]].

For an integer $1\le m\le n$, the **m-out-of-n bootstrap** draws $Z_1^*,\ldots,Z_m^*$ conditionally IID from $P_n$ and computes
$$R_{m,n}^{*}:=a_m\bigl(T_m(Z_1^*,\ldots,Z_m^*)-\widehat\theta_n\bigr).$$
The conditional distribution of this root given the observed sample is the bootstrap approximation. The ordinary n-out-of-n bootstrap is the case $m=n$ and uses $a_n$.

For $1\le m<n$, **subsampling without replacement** chooses a subset $I=\{i_1<\cdots<i_m\}$ uniformly from the $\binom{n}{m}$ subsets of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ and computes
$$R_{m,n}^{\mathrm{sub}}:=a_m\bigl(T_m(Z_{i_1},\ldots,Z_{i_m})-\widehat\theta_n\bigr).$$
Its conditional law is the uniform distribution over those subsets. With replacement and without replacement are distinct conditional laws, even though both use the same declared statistic $T_m$.

The asymptotic regime considered on this page has integer $m=m_n\to\infty$ and $m_n/n\to0$. The resampled root uses the actual size-$m$ scale $a_m$; validity does not follow merely from this regime. For inference based on a centered root, the scale ratio $a_m/a_n\to0$ is an additional root-specific centering condition when it is used. A design with dependent sampling units requires a separate design-matched resampling procedure. This definition does not identify a bootstrap law with a Bayesian posterior or a design-randomization law. Extrapolation from several resample sizes is not asserted here; it requires a separate proof of the source-specific regular expansion and remainder regime.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $X$ be a real random variable. Its **cumulative distribution function** is
the function
$$F_X:\mathbb R\to[0,1],\qquad F_X(x):=\mathbb P(X\le x)=\mathbb P_X((-\infty,x]).$$

The second expression is the same quantity written in terms of the law
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] of $X$.

For Borel probability measures $\mu_n,\mu$ on a metric space S, write $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$ if $\int f\,d\mu_n\to\int f\,d\mu$ for every bounded continuous real function f on S. Continuity is [[def-metric-continuity]]. Such f is Borel measurable (inverse images of open sets are open) and $\int|f|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\mu(S)<\infty$, so the integrals are finite in [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]. No completeness or coupling is required.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

derivations.claim: Almost surely $M_n\le1$, so $R_n\le0$ and $0\le h\le1$ with support in $[-1/2,1/2]$. The uniform CDF gives $\mathbb E[h(R_n)]\le\mathbb P(|R_n|\le1/2)=\mathbb P(M_n\ge1-1/(2n))=1-(1-1/(2n))^n$. By [F5], $\log(1-u)/u\to-1$ as $u\downarrow0$: the integral formula gives $-\log(1-u)/u=u^{-1}\int_{1-u}^1dt/t$, an average of $1/t$ over an interval shrinking to $1$. The maximum observation is unique almost surely because the uniform law has no atoms. Let $n\ge1$ be an integer, let $(\mathcal Z,\mathcal C)$ be a measurable observation space, let $P$ be a probability law on it, and let $Z_1,\ldots,Z_n$ be IID $P$-distributed sampling units ([[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]). For each $1\le k\le n$, let $T_k$ be a measurable real-valued statistic and write $\widehat\theta_k=T_k(Z_1,\ldots,Z_k)$; the target is a scalar $\theta(P)$ and $a_k>0$ is its declared normalization at sample size $k$. The empirical law
$$P_n:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{Z_i}$$
is a probability law by [[lem-finite-empirical-measure-is-a-probability-law]].

For an integer $1\le m\le n$, the **m-out-of-n bootstrap** draws $Z_1^*,\ldots,Z_m^*$ conditionally IID from $P_n$ and computes
$$R_{m,n}^{*}:=a_m\bigl(T_m(Z_1^*,\ldots,Z_m^*)-\widehat\theta_n\bigr).$$
The conditional distribution of this root given the observed sample is the bootstrap approximation. The ordinary n-out-of-n bootstrap is the case $m=n$ and uses $a_n$.

For $1\le m<n$, **subsampling without replacement** chooses a subset $I=\{i_1<\cdots<i_m\}$ uniformly from the $\binom{n}{m}$ subsets of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ and computes
$$R_{m,n}^{\mathrm{sub}}:=a_m\bigl(T_m(Z_{i_1},\ldots,Z_{i_m})-\widehat\theta_n\bigr).$$
Its conditional law is the uniform distribution over those subsets. With replacement and without replacement are distinct conditional laws, even though both use the same declared statistic $T_m$.

The asymptotic regime considered on this page has integer $m=m_n\to\infty$ and $m_n/n\to0$. The resampled root uses the actual size-$m$ scale $a_m$; validity does not follow merely from this regime. For inference based on a centered root, the scale ratio $a_m/a_n\to0$ is an additional root-specific centering condition when it is used. A design with dependent sampling units requires a separate design-matched resampling procedure. This definition does not identify a bootstrap law with a Bayesian posterior or a design-randomization law. Extrapolation from several resample sizes is not asserted here; it requires a separate proof of the source-specific regular expansion and remainder regime.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $X$ be a real random variable. Its **cumulative distribution function** is
the function
$$F_X:\mathbb R\to[0,1],\qquad F_X(x):=\mathbb P(X\le x)=\mathbb P_X((-\infty,x]).$$

The second expression is the same quantity written in terms of the law
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] of $X$.

For $p\in[0,1]$, a **Bernoulli$(p)$ random variable** takes the value $1$ with probability $p$ and $0$ with probability $1-p$.

For $n\in\mathbb N$, a **binomial$(n,p)$ random variable** is a sum $X=\sum_{i<n}X_i$ of $n$ mutually independent Bernoulli$(p)$ variables. When $n=0$, this is the constant zero random variable.

Work on a common probability space; the independent Bernoulli variables used to represent a binomial sum are independent in the sense of [[def-independent-random-elements]]. The original finite-space atom-independence convention is included.

If $X$ is Bernoulli$(p)$, then $\mathbb E[X]=p$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=p(1-p)$. If $S$ is binomial$(n,p)$, then
$$\mathbb E[S]=np,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(S)=np(1-p).$$
These formulas include $p=0$, $p=1$, and $n=0$.

If $X$ is a square-integrable real random variable and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(|X-\mathbb E[X]|\ge a)\le\frac{\operatorname{Var}(X)}{a^2}.$$

Let $F$ be a continuous CDF and $(G_n)$ random CDFs, meaning that each $G_n(x)$ is a measurable real random variable and, for every outcome, $x\mapsto G_n(x)$ is a right-continuous CDF. Suppose that for each fixed $x\in\mathbb R$, $G_n(x)\to F(x)$ in probability. Then
$$\sup_{x\in\mathbb R}|G_n(x)-F(x)|\longrightarrow0$$
in probability.

If the initial paths are CDFs only outside specified measurable null sets $N_n$, first set $G_n(x)=\mathbf1_{\{x\ge0\}}$ on $N_n$. All suprema in the conclusion refer to these everywhere-CDF versions; no completeness of the probability space is assumed.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

derivations.claim: For a size-$k$ IID uniform sample, $\mathbb P\{k(M_k-1)\le x\}=0$ for $x<-k$, equals $(1+x/k)^k$ for $-k\le x<0$, and is $1$ for $x\ge0$. For fixed $x<0$, [F10] gives $k\log(1+x/k)\to x$, so these CDFs converge to $F(x)=e^x$; for $x\ge0$ they equal $1$. The limiting CDF is continuous, including at zero.

Fix $x<0$ and put $c=-x>0$, $D_n=1-M_n$, and $K_n(c)=\#\{i:X_i>M_n-c/m\}$. For fixed $t>0$ and all sufficiently large $m$, each indicator $1\{X_i>1-t/m\}$ is Bernoulli$(t/m)$, and the indicators are independent by [F2]; hence $N_n(t):=\#\{i:X_i>1-t/m\}$ is binomial by [F4]. By [F5]–[F6], $mN_n(t)/n\to t$ in probability, since its mean is $t$ and its variance is $t(m/n)(1-t/m)\to0$. Also $mD_n\to0$ in probability, since for each $\eta>0$ and large $m$, $\mathbb P(mD_n>\eta)=(1-\eta/m)^n$. By [F10], $\log(1-u)=-\int_{1-u}^1dt/t\le-u$ for $0<u<1$, so this probability is at most $e^{-\eta n/m}\to0$.

For any $0<\eta<c$, on $mD_n\le\eta$ the interval from $1$ down to $M_n-c/m$ has width between $c/m$ and $(c+\eta)/m$, so $N_n(c)\le K_n(c)\le N_n(c+\eta)$. Fix $\rho>0$ and choose $0<\eta<\min(c,\rho/3)$. Step 1.2 gives $mN_n(c)/n\to c$ and $mN_n(c+\eta)/n\to c+\eta$, while $P(mD_n>\eta)\to0$; the sandwich therefore gives $mK_n(c)/n\to c$ and $K_n(c)/n\to0$ in probability. For $u_n=K_n(c)/n$, the integral identity in [F10] gives $|\log(1-u_n)+u_n|\le u_n^2/(1-u_n)$ when $u_n<1$. Since $mu_n\to c$ and $u_n\to0$, $m u_n^2/(1-u_n)\to0$, hence $(1-u_n)^m\to e^{-c}$. By [F1], the conditional with-replacement CDF is $P^*(R_{m,n}^{*}\le x)=(1-K_n(c)/n)^m\to e^{-c}=e^x$.

For subsampling, the conditional probability that every selected observation is at most $M_n-c/m$ is $P^*(R_{m,n}^{\mathrm{sub}}\le x)=\binom{n-K_n(c)}m/\binom nm=\prod_{j=0}^{m-1}(1-u_{n,j})$, where $u_{n,j}=K_n(c)/(n-j)$; this formula holds on $n-K_n(c)\ge m$, an event whose probability tends to one by step 2.1 and $m/n\to0$.

We have $\max_{j<m}u_{n,j}\le(K_n(c)/n)/(1-m/n)\to0$ in probability, and $\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}u_{n,j}=(mK_n(c)/n)\cdot m^{-1}\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}n/(n-j)\to c$, because the average factor lies between $1$ and $(1-m/n)^{-1}\to1$. Therefore $\sum_j u_{n,j}^2\le(\max_j u_{n,j})\sum_j u_{n,j}\to0$.
With probability tending to one, all $u_{n,j}<1$; [F10] and $|\log(1-u)+u|\le u^2/(1-u)$ then show $\sum_j\log(1-u_{n,j})\to-c$, so the product in step 3.1 tends to $e^{-c}=e^x$.

For $x\ge0$, both resampled maxima are at most $M_n$, so both conditional CDFs equal $1$. Step 1.1 gives the continuous sampling-root limit $F$, while steps 2.1 and 4.1 prove pointwise convergence for negative $x$; [F7] upgrades each method's conditional CDF convergence to uniform convergence in probability. Step 1.1 also identifies $F$ as the limiting CDF of the actual size-$m$ sampling root, which is the first-order target specified in the statement. The use of the actual size-$m$ scale is essential in steps 2.1–4.1. [F1, F7, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 3.2, step 4.1] ∎

**The m-regime alone is insufficient.** Take the singleton class $\mathcal P=\{P\}$ with $P=\delta_0$, target $\theta(P)=0$, statistic $T_k(z_1,\ldots,z_k)=1/k$, and normalization $a_k=k$. Let $m_n=\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor$. For all $n\ge4$, $1\le m_n<n$, and $m_n\to\infty$, $m_n/n\to0$, and $a_{m_n}/a_n=m_n/n\to0$. The actual size-$n$ and size-$m_n$ roots are both identically $1$, so their CDFs $J_{n,P}$ and $H_{m_n,P}$ coincide exactly. For either resampling method, every resampled statistic is $1/m_n$, so $\widehat H_{m,n}$ is the point-mass CDF at $1-m_n/n$. With $\alpha_1=\alpha_2=1/4$, both quantiles equal $1-m_n/n$ and $I_n=\{m_n/n^2\}$. Since $m_n/n^2>0$, the coverage of $\theta(P)=0$ is zero for every $n\ge4$. Thus uniform CDF approximation of the actual m-root by the feasible resampling root, and the associated quantile coverage guarantee, do not follow from the m-regime even when the actual n-root and m-root laws coincide.

boundaries.reason: The asymptotic regime has positive integer sample sizes and m>=1 eventually.

boundaries.evidence: Step 5.1 gives the conditional CDF value at x=0.
Step 5.1 proves both conditional CDFs equal one for every x>=0.
Steps 2.1–4.1 cover finite-support conditional laws, including zero atoms and without-replacement subsets.
Steps 1.1 and 5.1 handle the root-law CDF at zero and on the nonnegative half-line.

The theorem proves convergence for the displayed uniform model and m-regime; it gives no necessary-and-sufficient characterization of valid regimes.
It does not assert that every sequence yielding validity must satisfy the displayed m-regime.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a
statistical experiment as in [[def-statistical-experiment]], and assume
$\Theta\ne\varnothing$. A **confidence-set procedure** is a map
$C:\mathcal X\to\mathcal P(\Theta)$, where
$\mathcal P(\Theta):=\{A:A\subseteq\Theta\}$, such that, for every
$\eta\in\Theta$, its
membership section
$$C_\eta:=\{x\in\mathcal X:\eta\in C(x)\}$$
belongs to $\mathcal A$. Its **coverage at $\theta$** is
$c_C(\theta):=P_\theta(C_\theta)$, and its **confidence level** is
$\inf_{\theta\in\Theta}c_C(\theta)$, the greatest lower bound of those
coverage values. For $0\le\alpha\le1$, it has coverage
at least $1-\alpha$ if $P_\theta(C_\theta)\ge1-\alpha$ for every
$\theta\in\Theta$.

Only membership sections need to be measurable; no sigma-algebra on the
parameter set is assumed. The parameter is fixed in the repeated-sampling
coverage probability.

For a cumulative distribution function $F$ and $u\in(0,1)$, define the generalized quantile $q_F(u):=\inf\{x\in\mathbb R:F(x)\ge u\}$, and put $q_F(0):=-\infty$ and $q_F(1):=+\infty$. Let $X$ be a real random variable with CDF $F$. In part 3, a **random CDF** $\widehat G$ means that each $\widehat G(x)$ is measurable and, for every outcome, $x\mapsto\widehat G(x)$ is a right-continuous CDF. If the initial paths are CDFs only outside a specified measurable null set $N$, first set $\widehat G(x)=\mathbf1_{\{x\ge0\}}$ on $N$; all suprema and quantiles in part 3 use this everywhere-CDF version. No completeness of the probability space is assumed. For $\varepsilon,\delta\ge0$ and $0\le\alpha_1,\alpha_2<1$ with $\alpha_1+\alpha_2<1$, the following hold.

1. If $G$ is a CDF and $\sup_x(G(x)-F(x))\le\varepsilon$, then $\mathbb P\{X\le q_G(1-\alpha_2)\}\ge1-\alpha_2-\varepsilon$.
2. If $G$ is a CDF and $\sup_x(F(x)-G(x))\le\varepsilon$, then $\mathbb P\{X\ge q_G(\alpha_1)\}\ge1-\alpha_1-\varepsilon$.
3. If $\widehat G$ is a random CDF and $\mathbb P\{\sup_x|\widehat G(x)-F(x)|\le\varepsilon/2\}\ge1-\delta$, then
$$\mathbb P\{q_{\widehat G}(\alpha_1)\le X\le q_{\widehat G}(1-\alpha_2)\}\ge1-\alpha_1-\alpha_2-\varepsilon-\delta.$$

The endpoints $\alpha_i=0$ use the extended quantiles and make the corresponding tail event vacuous. No continuity of $F$ or absence of atoms at the target quantiles is required.

Let $X$ be a real random variable. Its **cumulative distribution function** is
the function
$$F_X:\mathbb R\to[0,1],\qquad F_X(x):=\mathbb P(X\le x)=\mathbb P_X((-\infty,x]).$$

The second expression is the same quantity written in terms of the law
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] of $X$.

derivations.claim: By [F2], under each fixed $P$ the IID observations have joint sampling law $P^{\otimes n}$. By [F5], $J_{n,P}$ is the CDF of the actual root $R_{n,P}$ under that law. Fix $\eta>0$. The two root-law limsup conditions imply that, for all sufficiently large $n$ and every $P\in\mathcal P$, both one-sided differences between $H_{m,P}$ and $J_{n,P}$ are at most $\eta/2$. The feasible-root condition gives numbers $\delta_n\to0$ such that, uniformly in $P$, the event $E_{n,P}:=\{\sup_x|\widehat H_{m,n}(x)-H_{m,P}(x)|\le\eta/2\}$ has probability at least $1-\delta_n$. On this event, the triangle inequality gives $\sup_x|\widehat H_{m,n}(x)-J_{n,P}(x)|\le\eta$.

To see that neither root-law comparison follows from the m-regime, take $\mathcal P=\{\delta_0\}$, $\theta(P)=0$, $a_k=k$, and the measurable constant statistic $T_k=\mathbf1_{\{k\text{ is odd}\}}/k$. Let $m_n=\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor$. Then $a_{m_n}/a_n=m_n/n\to0$, $J_{n,P}=\delta_{\mathbf1_{\{n\text{ is odd}\}}}$, and $H_{m_n,P}=\delta_{\mathbf1_{\{m_n\text{ is odd}\}}}$. For every sufficiently large even $m$, the block $m^2\le n<(m+1)^2$ contains odd $n$, giving $H_{m_n,P}=\delta_0$, $J_{n,P}=\delta_1$, and $\sup_x(H_{m_n,P}(x)-J_{n,P}(x))=1$. For every sufficiently large odd $m$, the same block contains even $n$, giving $H_{m_n,P}=\delta_1$, $J_{n,P}=\delta_0$, and $\sup_x(J_{n,P}(x)-H_{m_n,P}(x))=1$. Each root-law comparison can therefore fail under the stated m-regime, even with $a_m/a_n\to0$.

Apply [F4], part 3, with $F=J_{n,P}$, $\widehat G=\widehat H_{m,n}$, CDF error $2\eta$, and exceptional-event probability $\delta_n$. Step 1.1 supplies the event on which the CDF error is at most $\eta$, so the lemma's pointwise tail inclusions bound the joint miss event without assuming independence of $R_{n,P}$ and that event. The root interval $[q_{\widehat H_{m,n}}(\alpha_1),q_{\widehat H_{m,n}}(1-\alpha_2)]$ therefore misses $R_{n,P}$ with probability at most $\alpha_1+\alpha_2+2\eta+\delta_n$, uniformly in $P$.

Suppose only the first root-law limsup condition and the feasible-root condition hold. For any $\eta>0$, all sufficiently large $n$ satisfy $H_{m,P}(x)-J_{n,P}(x)\le\eta/2$ uniformly in $P,x$, and on an event $E_{n,P}$ of probability at least $1-\delta_n$ we have $\widehat H_{m,n}(x)-H_{m,P}(x)\le\eta/2$ for all $x$. Hence on $E_{n,P}$, $\widehat H_{m,n}-J_{n,P}\le\eta$. If $\alpha_2+\eta<1$, quantile ordering in [F4] gives $q_{J_{n,P}}(1-\alpha_2-\eta)\le q_{\widehat H_{m,n}}(1-\alpha_2)$. Thus the joint failure event $\{R_{n,P}>q_{\widehat H_{m,n}}(1-\alpha_2)\}\cap E_{n,P}$ is contained in $\{R_{n,P}>q_{J_{n,P}}(1-\alpha_2-\eta)\}$, whose probability is at most $\alpha_2+\eta$ by [F4]; adding $P(E_{n,P}^c)\le\delta_n$ bounds total failure. Letting $n\to\infty$ and then $\eta\downarrow0$ proves uniform asymptotic coverage at least $1-\alpha_2$ for the lower confidence bound; if $\alpha_2+\eta\ge1$, the intermediate lower bound is trivial. For the second assertion, if only the second root-law condition holds, then on the same event $J_{n,P}-\widehat H_{m,n}\le\eta$. When $\alpha_1+\eta<1$, [F4] gives $q_{\widehat H_{m,n}}(\alpha_1)\le q_{J_{n,P}}(\alpha_1+\eta)$. The joint failure event $\{R_{n,P}<q_{\widehat H_{m,n}}(\alpha_1)\}\cap E_{n,P}$ is contained in $\{R_{n,P}<q_{J_{n,P}}(\alpha_1+\eta)\}$, whose probability is at most $\alpha_1+\eta$ by [F4]; adding the complement probability and letting $\eta\downarrow0$ proves uniform asymptotic coverage at least $1-\alpha_1$ for the upper confidence bound. If $\alpha_1+\eta\ge1$, the intermediate lower bound is trivial.

By the definition of $\mathcal C_n$, $P\in\mathcal C_n$ exactly when $\theta(P)\in I_n$. Since $a_n>0$, this is algebraically equivalent to $q_{\widehat H}(\alpha_1)\le a_n(\widehat\theta_n-\theta(P))\le q_{\widehat H}(1-\alpha_2)$. It is the coverage event in [F3]. Thus its uniform lower bound is $1-\alpha_1-\alpha_2-2\eta-\delta_n$. Take the liminf in $n$, then let $\eta\downarrow0$, to obtain the stated inequality. The proof uses no independence between the two tail events.

To see that feasible-root control can fail even when both root-law comparisons hold exactly, take $\mathcal P=\{P\}$ with $P=\delta_0$, $\theta(P)=0$, $T_k(z_1,\ldots,z_k)=1/k$, and $a_k=k$, again with $m_n=\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor$. For all $n\ge4$, $1\le m_n<n$, $m_n\to\infty$, $m_n/n\to0$, and $a_{m_n}/a_n=m_n/n\to0$. The actual size-$n$ and size-$m_n$ roots are both identically $1$, so $J_{n,P}=H_{m_n,P}$. For either resampling method, every resampled statistic is $1/m_n$, hence $\widehat H_{m,n}=\delta_{1-m_n/n}$. Its sup-CDF distance from $H_{m_n,P}=\delta_1$ is $1$, so feasible-root control fails. With $\alpha_1=\alpha_2=1/4$, both quantiles equal $1-m_n/n$ and $I_n=\{m_n/n^2\}$, which excludes $\theta(P)=0$; coverage is zero for every $n\ge4$.
