The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $n\ge1$ be an integer, let $(\mathcal Z,\mathcal C)$ be a measurable observation space, let $P$ be a probability law on it, and let $Z_1,\ldots,Z_n$ be IID $P$-distributed sampling units ([[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]). For each $1\le k\le n$, let $T_k$ be a measurable real-valued statistic and write $\widehat\theta_k=T_k(Z_1,\ldots,Z_k)$; the target is a scalar $\theta(P)$ and $a_k>0$ is its declared normalization at sample size $k$. The empirical law
$$P_n:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{Z_i}$$
is a probability law by [[lem-finite-empirical-measure-is-a-probability-law]].

For an integer $1\le m\le n$, the **m-out-of-n bootstrap** draws $Z_1^*,\ldots,Z_m^*$ conditionally IID from $P_n$ and computes
$$R_{m,n}^{*}:=a_m\bigl(T_m(Z_1^*,\ldots,Z_m^*)-\widehat\theta_n\bigr).$$
The conditional distribution of this root given the observed sample is the bootstrap approximation. The ordinary n-out-of-n bootstrap is the case $m=n$ and uses $a_n$.

For $1\le m<n$, **subsampling without replacement** chooses a subset $I=\{i_1<\cdots<i_m\}$ uniformly from the $\binom{n}{m}$ subsets of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ and computes
$$R_{m,n}^{\mathrm{sub}}:=a_m\bigl(T_m(Z_{i_1},\ldots,Z_{i_m})-\widehat\theta_n\bigr).$$
Its conditional law is the uniform distribution over those subsets. With replacement and without replacement are distinct conditional laws, even though both use the same declared statistic $T_m$.

The asymptotic regime considered on this page has integer $m=m_n\to\infty$ and $m_n/n\to0$. The resampled root uses the actual size-$m$ scale $a_m$; validity does not follow merely from this regime. For inference based on a centered root, the scale ratio $a_m/a_n\to0$ is an additional root-specific centering condition when it is used. A design with dependent sampling units requires a separate design-matched resampling procedure. This definition does not identify a bootstrap law with a Bayesian posterior or a design-randomization law. Extrapolation from several resample sizes is not asserted here; it requires a separate proof of the source-specific regular expansion and remainder regime.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

For real random variables $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ on one probability space, define
$$S_0=0,\qquad S_n=\sum_{k=1}^nX_k,\qquad \overline X_n=S_n/n\quad(n\ge1).$$
For a triangular array with finite row length $r_n\ge0$, write $S_n=\sum_{k=1}^{r_n}X_{n,k}$. An empty row has sum zero. These are finite sums in [[def-finite-sum]], with its index shifted by one. Each sum and each sample mean is a real random variable by [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]] and [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]. No independence, common law, or integrability is implicit.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Assume AC. For $m\in\mathbb R$, $\sigma\ge0$, and a real random variable
$X$ with law $N(m,\sigma^2)$,
$$E[X]=m,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(X)=\sigma^2.$$

Assume AC. Let $n\ge1$, and let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be mutually independent real random variables on one probability space, each with law $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ for a fixed $\mu\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$. Then $\bar X_n=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nX_i$ has law $N(\mu,\sigma^2/n)$. If $\sigma>0$, then for every $\mu_0\in\mathbb R$,
$$\frac{\sqrt n(\bar X_n-\mu_0)}{\sigma}\sim N\!\left(\frac{\sqrt n(\mu-\mu_0)}{\sigma},1\right).$$

Let $d,k\ge1$, let $r_n>0$ be deterministic with $r_n\to\infty$, and let $T_n$ be $\mathbb R^d$-valued random vectors with target $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$. Suppose $Z_n=r_n(T_n-\theta)\Rightarrow Z$ for an $\mathbb R^d$-valued random vector $Z$. All vector norms below are Euclidean.

If $g:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^k$ is Borel and there is a linear map $A:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^k$ such that
$$g(\theta+h)-g(\theta)=Ah+\rho_1(h),\qquad \frac{\|\rho_1(h)\|}{\|h\|}\longrightarrow0\quad(h\to0,\ h\ne0),$$
then
$$r_n\{g(T_n)-g(\theta)\}\Rightarrow AZ.$$

If, in addition, $A=0$ and there is a continuous symmetric bilinear map $H:\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^k$ such that
$$g(\theta+h)-g(\theta)=\frac12H[h,h]+\rho_2(h),\qquad \frac{\|\rho_2(h)\|}{\|h\|^2}\longrightarrow0\quad(h\to0,\ h\ne0),$$
then
$$r_n^2\{g(T_n)-g(\theta)\}\Rightarrow \frac12H[Z,Z].$$
For scalar-valued $g$, $H$ is the usual Hessian bilinear form. The second-order premise is a pointwise Peano expansion; continuous second derivatives on a neighborhood are not required.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be IID $\mathbb R^d$-valued vectors with $\mathbb E\|X_1\|^2<\infty$, mean $\mu$, and covariance $\Sigma$. Fix $a\in\mathbb R^d$ such that $\sigma^2=a^T\Sigma a>0$. For the finite-index empirical bootstrap in [[def-iid-empirical-bootstrap-sample]], let $\bar X_n^*$ be the bootstrap mean and define the conditional CDF
$$F_n^*(x)=\mathbb P^*\!\left(\sqrt n\,a^T(\bar X_n^*-\bar X_n)\le x\mid X_1,\ldots,X_n\right).$$
Then
$$D_n:=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R}\left|F_n^*(x)-\Phi_\sigma(x)\right|\longrightarrow0\quad\text{in probability},$$
where $\Phi_\sigma$ is the CDF of $N(0,\sigma^2)$. The assumption $\sigma^2>0$ is needed for the normalized Lindeberg–Feller step.

Let $F$ be a continuous CDF and $(G_n)$ random CDFs, meaning that each $G_n(x)$ is a measurable real random variable and, for every outcome, $x\mapsto G_n(x)$ is a right-continuous CDF. Suppose that for each fixed $x\in\mathbb R$, $G_n(x)\to F(x)$ in probability. Then
$$\sup_{x\in\mathbb R}|G_n(x)-F(x)|\longrightarrow0$$
in probability.

If the initial paths are CDFs only outside specified measurable null sets $N_n$, first set $G_n(x)=\mathbf1_{\{x\ge0\}}$ on $N_n$. All suprema in the conclusion refer to these everywhere-CDF versions; no completeness of the probability space is assumed.

For Borel probability measures $\mu_n,\mu$ on a metric space S, write $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$ if $\int f\,d\mu_n\to\int f\,d\mu$ for every bounded continuous real function f on S. Continuity is [[def-metric-continuity]]. Such f is Borel measurable (inverse images of open sets are open) and $\int|f|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\mu(S)<\infty$, so the integrals are finite in [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]. No completeness or coupling is required.

For Borel probabilities $\mu_n,\mu$ on a metric space S, the following are equivalent: (i) $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$; (ii) integrals converge for all bounded uniformly continuous real tests; (iii) $\limsup_n\mu_n(F)\le\mu(F)$ for every closed F; (iv) $\liminf_n\mu_n(G)\ge\mu(G)$ for every open G; (v) $\mu_n(A)\to\mu(A)$ for every Borel A with $\mu(\partial A)=0$.

Let $X$ be a real random variable. Its **cumulative distribution function** is
the function
$$F_X:\mathbb R\to[0,1],\qquad F_X(x):=\mathbb P(X\le x)=\mathbb P_X((-\infty,x]).$$

The second expression is the same quantity written in terms of the law
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] of $X$.

derivations.claim: By [F2], the data form an IID sequence, and [F3] identifies $\bar X_n$ as its arithmetic sample mean. By [F4], $Z_n=\sqrt n\bar X_n$ is standard normal for every $n$. For $g_2(\mu)=\mu^2$, the derivative at zero vanishes and the second derivative is $2$, so [F5] gives the second-order scale $R_{n,2}=Z_n^2\Rightarrow Z^2$; directly, its law is exactly that of $Z^2$ for every $n$. For $g_1(\mu)=|\mu|$, the first-order delta premise fails at zero, and directly $R_{n,1}=|Z_n|$ has the law of $|Z|$ for every $n$. For $t>0$, the density bound in [F4] gives $P(|Z|\le t)\le2t/\sqrt{2\pi}$ and $P(Z^2\le t)\le2\sqrt t/\sqrt{2\pi}$; for $t<0$ both probabilities are zero. Therefore both true-root CDFs are continuous at zero and equal zero there. Their constant-law sequences converge weakly by [F8], and [F9] gives the same CDF limit at this continuity point.

By [F1], the bootstrap draws are conditionally IID from the empirical law and $W_n^*$ is the centered, $\sqrt n$-scaled empirical-bootstrap mean. By [F10], $G_n^*$ is the CDF of this conditional root law. The specialized supplier fact [F6] and the local CDF lemma [F7] give $\Delta_n:=\sup_x|G_n^*(x)-\Phi(x)|\to0$ in probability. For a realized value $z=Z_n$, the event $R_{n,1}^*\le0$ is $|z+W_n^*|\le|z|$, and the event $R_{n,2}^*\le0$ is $(z+W_n^*)^2\le z^2$; both are the same interval event, with $W_n^*\in[-2z,0]$ if $z\ge0$ and $W_n^*\in[0,-2z]$ if $z<0$. A uniform CDF error $\Delta_n$ also bounds the error at left limits, since $\Phi$ is continuous. Thus each conditional probability differs by at most $2\Delta_n$ from its standard-normal value $\Phi(2|Z_n|)-\frac12$.

Put $b:=\Phi(2)-\frac12>0$ and $c=b/2$. On $A_n:=\{|Z_n|\ge1\}$, whose probability is the fixed positive number $P(|Z|\ge1)$ by [F4], the normal interval probability in step 1.2 is at least $b$. On the additional event $\Delta_n\le b/4$, both conditional root CDFs at zero are therefore at least $c$. The true roots have the laws of $|Z|$ and $Z^2$ for every $n$ by [F4]. Their atom at zero is zero, and the standard-normal density is bounded by $(2\pi)^{-1/2}$, so for every $d>0$, $\mathbb E[h_d(|Z|)]\le P(|Z|<d)\le2d/\sqrt{2\pi}$ and $\mathbb E[h_d(Z^2)]\le P(|Z|<\sqrt d)\le2\sqrt d/\sqrt{2\pi}$, where $h_d(t)=1$ for $t\le0$, $h_d(t)=1-t/d$ for $0<t<d$, and $h_d(t)=0$ for $t\ge d$. Choose $d$ so both expectations are below $c/2$. For either bootstrap root, $\mathbb E^*[h_d(R_{n,j}^*)]\ge P^*(R_{n,j}^*\le0)\ge c$ on that event, while its true test integral is below $c/2$. The event has probability at least $P(|Z|\ge1)-P(\Delta_n>b/4)$, whose limit is positive. Thus the conditional integral of a bounded continuous test function fails to converge in probability to the true integral, contradicting conditional weak consistency.

citations.quote: For each integer $n\ge1$, let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be IID with the uniform law on $[0,1]$, let $M_n=\max_{i\le n}X_i$, and set the support endpoint $\theta=1$. The sampling root is $R_n=n(M_n-1)$. For the ordinary n-out-of-n bootstrap, draw $n$ observations IID from the empirical law $P_n$ and set $R_n^*=n(M_n^*-M_n)$. Here weak conditional consistency means that for every bounded continuous real function $f$, the conditional expectation $\mathbb E^*[f(R_n^*)]$ converges in probability to $\mathbb E[f(R_n)]$. With $h(x)=(1-2|x|)_+$, a bounded continuous function, the conditional bootstrap expectation $\mathbb E^*[h(R_n^*)]$ stays asymptotically separated from $\mathbb E[h(R_n)]$. Therefore the ordinary bootstrap is not weakly conditionally consistent at this support endpoint.
citations.proof_quote: The maximum observation is unique almost surely because the uniform law has no atoms. Conditional on the data, each bootstrap draw selects that maximal observation with probability $1/n$, independently across draws, so $\mathbb P^*(R_n^*=0)=1-(1-1/n)^n$. Since $h(0)=1$ and $h\ge0$, $\mathbb E^*[h(R_n^*)]\ge1-(1-1/n)^n\to1-e^{-1}$. [F1, F2, algebra]

citations.proof_quote: For a size-$k$ IID uniform sample, $\mathbb P\{k(M_k-1)\le x\}=0$ for $x<-k$, equals $(1+x/k)^k$ for $-k\le x<0$, and is $1$ for $x\ge0$. Work on a common probability space; the independent Bernoulli variables used to represent a binomial sum are independent in the sense of [[def-independent-random-elements]]. The original finite-space atom-independence convention is included.

If $X$ is Bernoulli$(p)$, then $\mathbb E[X]=p$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=p(1-p)$. If $S$ is binomial$(n,p)$, then
$$\mathbb E[S]=np,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(S)=np(1-p).$$
These formulas include $p=0$, $p=1$, and $n=0$.

If $X$ is a square-integrable real random variable and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(|X-\mathbb E[X]|\ge a)\le\frac{\operatorname{Var}(X)}{a^2}.$$

For $n\ge1$ and $p\in[0,1]$, let $\mu_{n,p}$ be the law of
$$S_{n,p}:=\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^n(B_i(p)-p),$$
where $B_1(p),\ldots,B_n(p)$ are IID Bernoulli$(p)$. For every $p,q\in[0,1]$,
$$\pi(\mu_{n,p},\mu_{n,q})\le |p-q|^{1/3},$$
where $\pi$ is the Levy–Prokhorov metric. The bound is uniform in the sample size and choice-free.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a
statistical experiment as in [[def-statistical-experiment]], and assume
$\Theta\ne\varnothing$. A **confidence-set procedure** is a map
$C:\mathcal X\to\mathcal P(\Theta)$, where
$\mathcal P(\Theta):=\{A:A\subseteq\Theta\}$, such that, for every
$\eta\in\Theta$, its
membership section
$$C_\eta:=\{x\in\mathcal X:\eta\in C(x)\}$$
belongs to $\mathcal A$. Its **coverage at $\theta$** is
$c_C(\theta):=P_\theta(C_\theta)$, and its **confidence level** is
$\inf_{\theta\in\Theta}c_C(\theta)$, the greatest lower bound of those
coverage values. For $0\le\alpha\le1$, it has coverage
at least $1-\alpha$ if $P_\theta(C_\theta)\ge1-\alpha$ for every
$\theta\in\Theta$.

Only membership sections need to be measurable; no sigma-algebra on the
parameter set is assumed. The parameter is fixed in the repeated-sampling
coverage probability.

For Borel probabilities $\mu$,$
u$ on a metric space S, put $F^{[\varepsilon]}=\{x:d(x,F)\le\varepsilon\}$ for nonempty closed F, and $\varnothing^{[\varepsilon]}=\varnothing$. Define $\pi(\mu,
u)$ as the infimum of $\varepsilon$>0 such that, for every closed F, both $\mu(F)\le
u(F^{[\varepsilon]})+\varepsilon$ and $
u(F)\le\mu(F^{[\varepsilon]})+\varepsilon$. The admissible set contains every $\varepsilon$>=1 and is bounded below by zero, so its real infimum exists by [[thm-infimum-property]]. Enlargements are closed because distance to a nonempty set is continuous. [[lem-distance-to-set-is-lipschitz]] The metric assertion is proved in the following lemma.

For Borel probability measures $\mu_n,\mu$ on a metric space S, write $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$ if $\int f\,d\mu_n\to\int f\,d\mu$ for every bounded continuous real function f on S. Continuity is [[def-metric-continuity]]. Such f is Borel measurable (inverse images of open sets are open) and $\int|f|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\mu(S)<\infty$, so the integrals are finite in [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]. No completeness or coupling is required.
Assume AC. For Borel probabilities on a separable metric space, $\pi(\mu_n,\mu)\to0$ if and only if $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$. Completeness is not required.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a nonempty class of IID laws on a measurable observation space. For $P\in\mathcal P$, let $\theta(P)\in\mathbb R$ be a target, let $\widehat\theta_k$ be a measurable estimator at every sample size $k$, and let $a_k>0$ be deterministic. Put
$$R_{n,P}=a_n(\widehat\theta_n-\theta(P)),\qquad J_{n,P}(x)=P^{\otimes n}(R_{n,P}\le x),$$
and define $H_{m,P}$ as the CDF of the actual size-$m$ root $a_m(\widehat\theta_m-\theta(P))$. Let $m=m_n$ be integers with $1\le m_n<n$ for all sufficiently large $n$, $m_n\to\infty$, and $m_n/n\to0$; for centered resampling roots, assume $a_m/a_n\to0$. Let $\widehat H_{m,n}$ be the conditional CDF of either $a_m(\widehat\theta^*_{m,n}-\widehat\theta_n)$ for the m-out-of-n bootstrap or $a_m(\widehat\theta_{I,m}-\widehat\theta_n)$ for uniform subsampling without replacement, as defined in [[def-m-out-of-n-bootstrap-and-subsampling]], with each evaluation measurable and almost surely right-continuous sample paths.

Suppose the following exact root-law and feasible-root conditions hold:
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty}\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}\sup_x\{H_{m,P}(x)-J_{n,P}(x)\}\le0,\qquad \limsup_{n\to\infty}\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}\sup_x\{J_{n,P}(x)-H_{m,P}(x)\}\le0,$$
and for every $\eta>0$,
$$\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}P^{\otimes n}\!\left(\sup_x|\widehat H_{m,n}(x)-H_{m,P}(x)|>\eta\right)\longrightarrow0.$$
For $0\le\alpha_1,\alpha_2$ with $\alpha_1+\alpha_2<1$, define
$$I_n=\left[\widehat\theta_n-\frac{q_{\widehat H_{m,n}}(1-\alpha_2)}{a_n},\ \widehat\theta_n-\frac{q_{\widehat H_{m,n}}(\alpha_1)}{a_n}\right].$$
Assume the interval endpoints are measurable functions of the data and set $\mathcal C_n=\{Q\in\mathcal P:\theta(Q)\in I_n\}$. Then
$$\liminf_{n\to\infty}\inf_{P\in\mathcal P}P^{\otimes n}\{P\in\mathcal C_n\}\ge1-\alpha_1-\alpha_2.$$
If only the first one-sided root-law comparison is assumed, together with feasible-root control, the upper root quantile gives the corresponding one-sided lower confidence bound; if only the second root-law comparison is assumed, again with feasible-root control, the lower root quantile gives the one-sided upper confidence bound. The m-regime alone does not imply any of these CDF conditions. Weak convergence of root laws alone is not a substitute for the stated uniform comparisons and feasible-root control.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

For a cumulative distribution function $F$ and $u\in(0,1)$, define the generalized quantile $q_F(u):=\inf\{x\in\mathbb R:F(x)\ge u\}$, and put $q_F(0):=-\infty$ and $q_F(1):=+\infty$. Let $X$ be a real random variable with CDF $F$. In part 3, a **random CDF** $\widehat G$ means that each $\widehat G(x)$ is measurable and, for every outcome, $x\mapsto\widehat G(x)$ is a right-continuous CDF. If the initial paths are CDFs only outside a specified measurable null set $N$, first set $\widehat G(x)=\mathbf1_{\{x\ge0\}}$ on $N$; all suprema and quantiles in part 3 use this everywhere-CDF version. No completeness of the probability space is assumed. For $\varepsilon,\delta\ge0$ and $0\le\alpha_1,\alpha_2<1$ with $\alpha_1+\alpha_2<1$, the following hold.

1. If $G$ is a CDF and $\sup_x(G(x)-F(x))\le\varepsilon$, then $\mathbb P\{X\le q_G(1-\alpha_2)\}\ge1-\alpha_2-\varepsilon$.
2. If $G$ is a CDF and $\sup_x(F(x)-G(x))\le\varepsilon$, then $\mathbb P\{X\ge q_G(\alpha_1)\}\ge1-\alpha_1-\varepsilon$.
3. If $\widehat G$ is a random CDF and $\mathbb P\{\sup_x|\widehat G(x)-F(x)|\le\varepsilon/2\}\ge1-\delta$, then
$$\mathbb P\{q_{\widehat G}(\alpha_1)\le X\le q_{\widehat G}(1-\alpha_2)\}\ge1-\alpha_1-\alpha_2-\varepsilon-\delta.$$

The endpoints $\alpha_i=0$ use the extended quantiles and make the corresponding tail event vacuous. No continuity of $F$ or absence of atoms at the target quantiles is required.

A topological space $X$ is **separable** if some at most countable subset $D\subseteq X$ is dense in $X$ ([[def-dense-top]], [[def-countable]]). Equivalently, every nonempty open subset of $X$ meets $D$.

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

**No choice principle is used.** The one place where a reader expects a choice,
"pick a representative $a/b$ of each rational", is exactly where
[[lem-rat-positive-denominator]] applies: every rational *has* a representative
with positive denominator, so the map $(a,b) \mapsto [(a,b)]$ defined on
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is already **surjective** onto $\mathbb{Q}$,
and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).

Write $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ for the image of $\mathbb{Q}$ in $\mathbb{R}$
under the canonical embedding $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]), the
set usually written $\mathbb{Q}$ once the identification is made, and put
$X := \mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ for the irrationals. Then:

1. $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$, that is,
   $\overline{\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}} = \mathbb{R}$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]);
2. $X$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$;
3. every nonempty open subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is uncountable
   ([[def-countable]]).

Claim 2 is not a symmetry of claim 1: the rationals are dense because they are
*constructed* to approximate, whereas the irrationals are dense because there are
too many points in any interval for a countable set to exhaust it, which is why
claim 3 is proved alongside and used for it.

derivations.claim: Under $P_p$, $\bar X_n$ has law $\operatorname{Binomial}(n,p)/n$. Conditional on the sample, the bootstrap observations are IID Bernoulli$(\bar X_n)$, so their centered root law is $\mu_{n,\bar X_n}$, while the true root law is $\mu_{n,p}$. By [F7], $\pi(\mathcal L^*(R_{n,p}^*),\mathcal L(R_{n,p}))\le|\bar X_n-p|^{1/3}$.

Fix $\lambda>0$, take $p_n=1-\lambda/n$ for $n>\lambda$, and let $q_n$ be the conditional $(1-\alpha)$-quantile of $R_{n,p_n}^*$. Define the lower interval $I_n=[\bar X_n-q_n/\sqrt n,1]\cap[0,1]$. It is measurable because the data take only finitely many values, and $p_n\in I_n$ is exactly the coverage event for root threshold $q_n$.

From [F5], $\operatorname{Var}_p(\bar X_n)=p(1-p)/n\le1/(4n)$. For each $\epsilon>0$, Chebyshev's inequality [F6] and step 1.1 give $\sup_{p\in[0,1]}P_p\{\pi(\mathcal L^*(R_{n,p}^*),\mathcal L(R_{n,p}))>\epsilon\}\le\sup_pP_p\{|\bar X_n-p|>\epsilon^3\}\le1/(4n\epsilon^6)\to0$. By [F15], $\mathbb R$ is a separable metric space, so [F11] shows this is uniform closeness in a metric that induces weak convergence.

On the event $X_1=\cdots=X_n=1$, the empirical law is $\delta_1$, every bootstrap root is zero, and [F14] gives $q_n=0$ because $1-\alpha\in(0,1)$; then $I_n=\{1\}$ and $p_n\notin I_n$. This event has probability $p_n^n=(1-\lambda/n)^n$. By the integral formula in [F13], $n\log(1-\lambda/n)=-n\int_{1-\lambda/n}^1dt/t\to-\lambda$, since the integrand converges uniformly to $1$ on that shrinking interval; exponentiating gives $p_n^n\to e^{-\lambda}$. Hence $\limsup_nP_{p_n}(p_n\in I_n)\le1-e^{-\lambda}<1-\alpha$, so $\liminf_n\inf_{p\in[0,1]}P_p(p\in I_n)<1-\alpha$.

Steps 1.1 and 2.1 establish uniform weak-metric closeness, while steps 1.2 and 2.2 show the coverage failure. Thus weak-metric closeness alone does not imply uniform quantile coverage or the stronger root-CDF and feasible-root conditions in [F12]. The coupling and coverage calculation use no choice; AC enters only through the metric-to-weak-topology equivalence [F11].

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. For each integer $n\ge1$, let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be IID $N(0,1)$ and let $\bar X_n=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nX_i$. At $\mu=0$, which is the boundary value of the nonnegative ranges of $g_1(\mu)=|\mu|$ and $g_2(\mu)=\mu^2$, consider these two functionals. For the ordinary bootstrap, draw $X_1^*,\ldots,X_n^*$ conditionally IID from the empirical law and write $W_n^*=\sqrt n(\bar X_n^* -\bar X_n)$ with conditional CDF $G_n^*$. The conditional empirical-bootstrap CLT [[thm-conditional-iid-bootstrap-clt-for-empirical-law]], specialized to $d=1$, $a=1$, and $\sigma^2=1$, gives $G_n^*(x)\to\Phi(x)$ in probability for every fixed $x$, where $\Phi$ is the standard normal CDF. Here conditional weak consistency means that the conditional integral of every bounded continuous test function converges in probability to its sampling-law integral.

Then the ordinary bootstrap is inconsistent for both correctly centered roots
$$R_{n,1}=\sqrt n\,|\bar X_n|,\qquad R_{n,1}^*=\sqrt n\,(|\bar X_n^*|-|\bar X_n|),$$
and
$$R_{n,2}=n\bar X_n^2,\qquad R_{n,2}^*=n\bigl((\bar X_n^*)^2-\bar X_n^2\bigr).$$
In both cases the true root CDF is continuous at zero with value zero, whereas the conditional bootstrap root CDF at zero stays away from zero with positive probability. The first functional is nonsmooth at the boundary; the second has zero first derivative there, so its nondegenerate sampling root is on the second-order scale.

Let $n\ge1$ be an integer, let $(\mathcal Z,\mathcal C)$ be a measurable observation space, let $P$ be a probability law on it, and let $Z_1,\ldots,Z_n$ be IID $P$-distributed sampling units ([[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]). For each $1\le k\le n$, let $T_k$ be a measurable real-valued statistic and write $\widehat\theta_k=T_k(Z_1,\ldots,Z_k)$; the target is a scalar $\theta(P)$ and $a_k>0$ is its declared normalization at sample size $k$. The empirical law
$$P_n:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{Z_i}$$
is a probability law by [[lem-finite-empirical-measure-is-a-probability-law]].

For an integer $1\le m\le n$, the **m-out-of-n bootstrap** draws $Z_1^*,\ldots,Z_m^*$ conditionally IID from $P_n$ and computes
$$R_{m,n}^{*}:=a_m\bigl(T_m(Z_1^*,\ldots,Z_m^*)-\widehat\theta_n\bigr).$$
The conditional distribution of this root given the observed sample is the bootstrap approximation. The ordinary n-out-of-n bootstrap is the case $m=n$ and uses $a_n$.

For $1\le m<n$, **subsampling without replacement** chooses a subset $I=\{i_1<\cdots<i_m\}$ uniformly from the $\binom{n}{m}$ subsets of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ and computes
$$R_{m,n}^{\mathrm{sub}}:=a_m\bigl(T_m(Z_{i_1},\ldots,Z_{i_m})-\widehat\theta_n\bigr).$$
Its conditional law is the uniform distribution over those subsets. With replacement and without replacement are distinct conditional laws, even though both use the same declared statistic $T_m$.

The asymptotic regime considered on this page has integer $m=m_n\to\infty$ and $m_n/n\to0$. The resampled root uses the actual size-$m$ scale $a_m$; validity does not follow merely from this regime. For inference based on a centered root, the scale ratio $a_m/a_n\to0$ is an additional root-specific centering condition when it is used. A design with dependent sampling units requires a separate design-matched resampling procedure. This definition does not identify a bootstrap law with a Bayesian posterior or a design-randomization law. Extrapolation from several resample sizes is not asserted here; it requires a separate proof of the source-specific regular expansion and remainder regime.

derivations.claim: Under AC and the IID standard-normal model in [F1], the boundary mean is zero. The target for $|\mu|$ is zero and $|\cdot|$ is not differentiable there; the target for $\mu^2$ is also zero and its first derivative vanishes. The root normalizations are respectively $\sqrt n$ and $n$.

The ordinary bootstrap roots therefore are $\sqrt n(|\bar X_n^*|-|\bar X_n|)$ and $n((\bar X_n^*)^2-\bar X_n^2)$, as follows from the centering and size-$n$ scale in [F2]. Theorem [F1] proves that each conditional CDF fails at the continuity point zero, despite the nondegenerate true limits $|Z|$ and $Z^2$.

definition_review.source_exact:
Let $E,F$ be normed spaces, let $D\subseteq E$, let $\theta\in D$, and let $E_0\subseteq E$ be a linear subspace. A map $\Psi:D\to F$ is **Hadamard differentiable at $\theta$, tangentially to $E_0$** if there is a continuous linear map $\Psi'_\theta:E_0\to F$ such that, for every sequence $t_m>0$ with $t_m\to0$, and every sequence $h_m\to h\in E_0$ for which $\theta+t_mh_m\in D$,

$$\frac{\Psi(\theta+t_mh_m)-\Psi(\theta)}{t_m}\longrightarrow \Psi'_\theta(h)\quad\hbox{in }F.$$

The subspace is part of the hypothesis: directions outside $E_0$ are not covered by this definition.

Definition at b=1 draws n IID empirical records; at b=n it has N=k=1 and returns the input in its original order. When b divides n, exactly k full blocks are retained.

**Input:** a finite sequence $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ in a measurable space, with $n\ge1$, and an integer block length $b$ satisfying $1\le b\le n$. Set $N=n-b+1$ and $k=\lceil n/b\rceil$.

**Randomization:** draw $J_1,\ldots,J_k$ independently and uniformly from $\{1,\ldots,N\}$.

**Output:** in order $s=1,\ldots,k$, append the block $x_{J_s},x_{J_s+1},\ldots,x_{J_s+b-1}$, then retain the first $n$ entries of the concatenation. Thus the final selected block is truncated to its first $r=n-b\lfloor n/b\rfloor$ entries when $r>0$. Conditional expectation given the input sequence means expectation over the indices $J_s$ alone.

definition_review.source_exact:
**Input:** observations $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ in a real Hilbert space $H$, and an integer block length $b$ with $1\le b\le n$.

**Output:** a pseudo-series $X_1^*,\ldots,X_n^*$, generated by [[alg-overlapping-block-resampling]]: within each selected block retain the original order and concatenate blocks in their draw order, truncating only the last block when $b\nmid n$. The conditional bootstrap sample mean is $\bar X_n^*=n^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^nX_t^*$. Its conditional center is $E^*\bar X_n^*$, where $E^*$ averages over the independent uniform block starts while the observations remain fixed.

This algorithm specifies the resampling law only. It does not assert that the conditional law approximates the sampling law for any data-generating process or block-length regime.

Under [[def-resampling-sampling-unit-contract]], take each observation $x_t$ to be a complete time-indexed unit record. Each draw selects an ordered group of $b$ consecutive records; the output retains every record of each complete block and only the initial $r=n-b\lfloor n/b\rfloor$ records of the final block when $r>0$. Thus selected length-$b$ groups are not declared indivisible sampling units. Unit compatibility for a stated target requires that block boundaries and final truncation do not split any bundle declared indivisible by that target's sampling or assignment design. This is the sampling-unit interface, not a bootstrap-validity result.

boundaries.evidence: Definition requires 1<=b<=n and W_b>0, hence at least one weight and candidate start. An empty final prefix when b divides n contributes nothing and is not appended as an extra block.
Definition excludes W_b=0 before normalizing. Zero observations are allowed: all residuals and tapered pseudo-observations are zero, with the positive a_b denominator still well-defined.
Definition at b=1 evaluates w(1/2)>0, so W_1=w(1/2) and a_1*w_1(1)=1; it pointwise resamples the sample-centered records. If n=1 also, that record is zero.
Definition permits constant observations, whose residuals vanish. An identically zero window is inadmissible because it violates both midpoint-neighbourhood positivity and W_b>0.
Definition uses midpoint arguments strictly between 0 and 1, allowing windows vanishing at 0 and 1; b=n gives one deterministic tapered candidate with no random-start variation.
Definition forms every candidate weight deterministically from supplied w and uses finitely many uniform starts; it selects no arbitrary representatives from an infinite family.

boundaries.reason: The taper prescription provides inputs, centering, weights and resampling instructions and expressly withholds validity; it contains no necessary-and-sufficient theorem.
The Definition draws no inference from a covariance or sampling limit back to a taper choice, so there is no reverse direction of a validity characterization.

definition_review.evidence: Read support, symmetry, midpoint and monotonicity assumptions, strict norm admissibility, sample centering, scaling, final-prefix convention and sampling-unit interpretation.
definition_review.source_exact:
**Input:** observations $Y_1,\ldots,Y_n$ in a real Hilbert space $H$, an integer $1\le b\le n$, and a window $w:\mathbb R\to[0,1]$ that vanishes off $[0,1]$, is positive on a neighbourhood of $1/2$, satisfies $w(1-u)=w(u)$, and is nondecreasing on $[0,1/2]$. Put $w_b(r)=w((r-\tfrac12)/b)$ for $1\le r\le b$, $W_b=(\sum_{r=1}^bw_b(r)^2)^{1/2}$, and $a_b=\sqrt b/W_b$. The procedure is admissible only when $W_b>0$.

**Center and taper:** set $\bar Y_n=n^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^nY_t$ and $R_t=Y_t-\bar Y_n$. For each start $j\in\{1,\ldots,n-b+1\}$, form the block

$$\bigl(a_bw_b(1)R_j,\ldots,a_bw_b(b)R_{j+b-1}\bigr).$$

**Resample:** use the independent uniform block starts from [[alg-overlapping-block-resampling]], multiply each selected centered observation by its within-block taper and the factor $a_b$, concatenate in draw order, and retain the first $n$ entries. The conditional bootstrap mean is centered by its own conditional expectation when used to approximate the sampling law of $\sqrt n\,\bar Y_n$.

The factor $a_b$ compensates for the window's squared-weight sum in the block-sum variance calculation; this definition alone gives no bootstrap validity result.

For a dependent time series, the selected length-$b$ consecutive run is the resampling unit under [[def-resampling-sampling-unit-contract]]. The taper changes each unit record's within-block weight but the whole block is selected and resampled together; validity remains a separate theorem.

citations.quote:
**Input:** observations $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ in a real Hilbert space $H$, and an integer block length $b$ with $1\le b\le n$.

**Output:** a pseudo-series $X_1^*,\ldots,X_n^*$, generated by [[alg-overlapping-block-resampling]]: within each selected block retain the original order and concatenate blocks in their draw order, truncating only the last block when $b\nmid n$. The conditional bootstrap sample mean is $\bar X_n^*=n^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^nX_t^*$. Its conditional center is $E^*\bar X_n^*$, where $E^*$ averages over the independent uniform block starts while the observations remain fixed.

This algorithm specifies the resampling law only. It does not assert that the conditional law approximates the sampling law for any data-generating process or block-length regime.

Under [[def-resampling-sampling-unit-contract]], take each observation $x_t$ to be a complete time-indexed unit record. Each draw selects an ordered group of $b$ consecutive records; the output retains every record of each complete block and only the initial $r=n-b\lfloor n/b\rfloor$ records of the final block when $r>0$. Thus selected length-$b$ groups are not declared indivisible sampling units. Unit compatibility for a stated target requires that block boundaries and final truncation do not split any bundle declared indivisible by that target's sampling or assignment design. This is the sampling-unit interface, not a bootstrap-validity result.

derivations.claim: Write $n=kb+r$, $0\le r<b$. The sum of the first $n$ bootstrap observations is the sum of $k$ complete selected block sums and, if $r>0$, the first $r$ entries of one additional selected block. Conditional on the data, these $k+\mathbf 1_{\{r>0\}}$ contributions are independent, and the centered covariance of each complete contribution is $C_b$, while that of the partial contribution is $C_r$ by uniformity of its start.

The covariance of a sum of independent centered Hilbert-valued random elements is the sum of their covariance operators: expanding the tensor product leaves only diagonal terms, since each off-diagonal expected tensor is the tensor of a zero mean with a zero mean. Dividing the sum by $n$ to obtain $\bar X_n^*$, and multiplying its covariance by $n$, gives $(kC_b+C_r)/n$.

boundaries.evidence: Statement has n>=b>=1 and N=n-b+1>=1; the prefix r=0 is the permitted empty sum and is assigned C_0=0, so step 1.1 omits that contribution.
Statement sets C_0=0; when all observed x_t are zero, every S_j and C_q vanishes and step 2.1 gives zero on both sides.
Statement review: For n=b=1 the covariance identity has one full block, no remainder, and reduces to that block empirical covariance; see step 2.1.
Statement permits identical candidate block sums, so C_b or C_r may be zero; step 2.1 adds these zero covariances without any positivity division.
Statement allows b=1 and b=n. For b=n, N=k=1 and r=0, so the sole candidate block is deterministic and C_b=0.
Statement samples only finitely many independent uniform starts from {1,...,N}; step 1.1 expands a finite product law and uses no arbitrary choice function.

The sum of the first $n$ tapered bootstrap observations is the sum of $k$ complete tapered block sums and, if $r>0$, the first $r$ tapered entries of one additional block. Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be monotone, that is
nondecreasing or nonincreasing on $[a,b]$ ([[def-monotone-function]]). Then $f$
is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann integrable on $[a,b]$
([[def-darboux-integral]]).

Moreover, for the uniform partition $U_N$ of $[a,b]$ into $N \ge 1$ parts
([[def-partition-and-refinement]]),

$$U(f,U_N) - L(f,U_N) \;=\; \bigl|f(b) - f(a)\bigr| \cdot \frac{b-a}{\iota(N)} ,$$

where $\iota(N)$ is the canonical natural of $N$ in $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-canonical-natural]]). The right-hand side is an **equality**, not an
estimate: the sum $\sum_{i<N}(M_i - m_i)$ telescopes exactly, because on each
subinterval a monotone function attains its extremes at the two endpoints.

No continuity is assumed, and none holds in general: a nondecreasing function may
be discontinuous at every rational
([[thm-monotone-with-prescribed-discontinuity-set]]), and the companion page of
this pair works out the integral of the floor function, the simplest
discontinuous monotone integrand.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) and let
$\varepsilon \in F$ with $\varepsilon > 0$. Then there is a natural number
$n \ge 1$ such that

$$\frac{1}{n \cdot 1_F} < \varepsilon ,$$

where $n \cdot 1_F$ is the canonical natural of $F$ ([[thm-of-archimedean]]) and
$1/(n \cdot 1_F)$ is its multiplicative inverse ([[def-field]]). As is standard
we abbreviate $n \cdot 1_F$ to $n$ and write the conclusion $1/n < \varepsilon$.

This is the **reciprocal form** of the Archimedean property.
[[thm-of-archimedean]] on its own delivers only the assertion that the canonical
naturals are cofinal, $x < n \cdot 1_F$; the form actually used in analysis, that
the reciprocals of the naturals get below every positive bound, is the statement
above, and it is recorded separately so that no proof has to reconstruct the
inversion step in passing.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be bounded
([[def-bounded-set]]). Then $f$ is Darboux integrable on $[a,b]$
([[def-darboux-integral]]) **if and only if**

$$\text{for every real } \varepsilon > 0 \text{ there is a partition } P \text{ of } [a,b] \text{ with } U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$$

([[def-darboux-sums]], [[def-partition-and-refinement]]).

**This is the criterion every later integrability proof on this page uses.** It
replaces a statement about a supremum and an infimum over all partitions, which
cannot be checked directly, by the exhibition of a **single** partition for each
$\varepsilon$. The criterion says nothing about the value of the integral; that
separate lower-and-upper-sum estimate places the integral between $L(f,P)$ and
$U(f,P)$ for the same $P$.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be bounded
([[def-bounded-set]]) and let $I \in \mathbb{R}$. The following are equivalent.

1. **(Darboux)** $f$ is Darboux integrable on $[a,b]$ with
   $\int_a^b f = I$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).
2. **(Riemann)** For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real $\delta > 0$
   such that
   $$\bigl|\,S(f,P,\xi) - I\,\bigr| \;<\; \varepsilon$$
   for **every** tagged partition $(P,\xi)$ of $[a,b]$ with $\|P\| < \delta$
   ([[def-tagged-partition-and-riemann-sum]], [[def-partition-and-refinement]]).

**The quantifier over tagged partitions is universal, and that is the content.**
Condition 2 constrains every tagged partition of small mesh at once, tags
included; it is not a statement about one sequence of tagged partitions, and it
cannot be weakened to one. The companion page of this pair exhibits a
non-integrable function whose Riemann sums are constant along such a sequence.

**Boundedness is a hypothesis of both conditions as stated here.** Condition 1
presupposes it, since the Darboux sums of an unbounded function do not exist
([[def-darboux-sums]]); condition 2 makes sense for unbounded $f$ as well, and
in fact implies boundedness, but that implication is not proved here and is not
used: every application on this page starts from a bounded $f$.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be bounded
([[def-bounded-set]]). Write $\mathcal{P}$ for the set of all partitions of
$[a,b]$ ([[def-partition-and-refinement]]) and put

$$\mathcal{L} \;:=\; \{\, L(f,P) \ : \ P \in \mathcal{P} \,\}, \qquad \mathcal{U} \;:=\; \{\, U(f,P) \ : \ P \in \mathcal{P} \,\}$$

for the sets of lower and of upper Darboux sums ([[def-darboux-sums]]).

### Both extrema exist

**$\mathcal{P}$ is nonempty**: the pair $(1, t)$ with $t_0 := a$ and $t_k := b$
for $k \ge 1$ is a partition of $[a,b]$, since $a < b$. So $\mathcal{L}$ and
$\mathcal{U}$ are nonempty.

**$\mathcal{L}$ is bounded above and $\mathcal{U}$ is bounded below.** Fix any
$Q \in \mathcal{P}$. By claim 2 of [[lem-refinement-inequalities]],
$L(f,P) \le U(f,Q)$ for every $P \in \mathcal{P}$, so $U(f,Q)$ is an upper bound
of $\mathcal{L}$; and $L(f,Q) \le U(f,P)$ for every $P$, so $L(f,Q)$ is a lower
bound of $\mathcal{U}$.

Hence a nonempty set bounded above has a supremum
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) and a nonempty set bounded below has an infimum
([[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]]), each unique ([[lem-sup-unique]]).
The **lower** and **upper Darboux integrals** of $f$ over $[a,b]$ are the real
numbers

$$\underline{\int_a^b} f \;:=\; \sup \mathcal{L} \;=\; \sup_{P} L(f,P), \qquad \overline{\int_a^b} f \;:=\; \inf \mathcal{U} \;=\; \inf_{P} U(f,P) .$$

### The lower integral never exceeds the upper one

$$\underline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; \overline{\int_a^b} f .$$

Indeed, for each fixed $Q \in \mathcal{P}$ the number $U(f,Q)$ is an upper bound
of $\mathcal{L}$, so the least upper bound satisfies
$\underline{\int_a^b} f \le U(f,Q)$. As $Q$ was arbitrary, $\underline{\int_a^b}f$
is a lower bound of $\mathcal{U}$, and the greatest lower bound satisfies
$\underline{\int_a^b} f \le \overline{\int_a^b} f$ ([[def-infimum]]).

Moreover, for **every** partition $P$,

$$L(f,P) \;\le\; \underline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; \overline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; U(f,P) ,$$

the outer inequalities because a member of a set is at most its supremum and at
least its infimum.

### Integrability

$f$ is **Darboux integrable on $[a,b]$**, and on this page simply
**integrable**, when

$$\underline{\int_a^b} f \;=\; \overline{\int_a^b} f ,$$

and then the common value is written

$$\int_a^b f \qquad \text{or} \qquad \int_a^b f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x ,$$

the **integral of $f$ over $[a,b]$**. It is a single well-determined real
number, being the common value of two numbers each of which is unique
([[lem-sup-unique]]). Without the displayed equality the symbol $\int_a^b f$ is
not defined and is never written.

**The inequality above is the whole difficulty.** By the previous paragraph
integrability is *never* a question of one integral exceeding the other, only of
the gap $\overline{\int_a^b} f - \underline{\int_a^b} f \ge 0$ being $0$; and by
[[thm-riemann-criterion]] that gap is $0$ exactly when a single partition can be
found making $U(f,P) - L(f,P)$ small. Whether that is possible is settled
completely, in terms of the discontinuities of $f$, by
[[thm-lebesgue-criterion]].

**"Riemann integrable" means the same thing here.** The definition above is
Darboux's. Riemann's own definition, in terms of tagged partitions of small
mesh, is [[def-tagged-partition-and-riemann-sum]], and the two define the same
class of functions with the same integral by [[thm-darboux-equals-riemann]].
Until that theorem is proved the two phrases are kept apart; after it they are
used interchangeably, as they are throughout the literature.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be **bounded**
([[def-bounded-set]]), so that there is a real $M \ge 0$ with $|f(x)| \le M$ for
every $x \in [a,b]$, and let $P = (n,t)$ be a partition of $[a,b]$ with
subintervals $I_i = [t_i, t_{i+1}]$ and lengths $\Delta_i = t_{i+1} - t_i$ for
$i < n$ ([[def-partition-and-refinement]]).

### The two extreme values on a subinterval

For $i < n$ put

$$m_i \;:=\; \inf f[I_i], \qquad M_i \;:=\; \sup f[I_i], \qquad f[I_i] \;=\; \{\, f(x) : x \in I_i \,\} .$$

**Both exist.** The set $f[I_i]$ is nonempty, because $t_i < t_{i+1}$ makes $I_i$
nonempty ([[def-interval]]), and it is bounded, because $|f(x)| \le M$ for every
$x$ ([[def-bounded-set]]). A nonempty set bounded above has a supremum
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) and a nonempty set bounded below has an infimum
([[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]]); each is unique, so the notations
$\inf f[I_i]$ and $\sup f[I_i]$ name single real numbers ([[lem-sup-unique]]).

**They bracket the values, and each other.** For $x \in I_i$,

$$-M \;\le\; m_i \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; M_i \;\le\; M ,$$

the outer inequalities because $-M$ is a lower bound and $M$ an upper bound of
$f[I_i]$, and the middle ones by the definitions of infimum and supremum. In
particular $m_i \le M_i$ and $M_i - m_i \le 2M$.

The dependence of $m_i$ and $M_i$ on $f$ and on $P$ is suppressed in the
notation, as is customary; where two partitions are in play the sums below carry
the partition and the extreme values are written out.

### The two Darboux sums

$$L(f,P) \;:=\; \sum_{i<n} m_i \,\Delta_i, \qquad U(f,P) \;:=\; \sum_{i<n} M_i \,\Delta_i ,$$

the finite sums of [[def-finite-sum]], indexed by $i \in \mathbb{N}$ with
$i < n$. Both are real numbers, being finite sums of reals, and

$$L(f,P) \;\le\; U(f,P) ,$$

by monotonicity of finite sums, clause 4 of [[lem-finite-sum-laws]], since
$m_i \Delta_i \le M_i \Delta_i$ for every $i < n$: multiplying $m_i \le M_i$ by
$\Delta_i > 0$ preserves the inequality ([[def-ordered-field]]).

### The gap on a subinterval is the oscillation there

For every $i < n$,

$$M_i - m_i \;=\; \omega_f(I_i) \;=\; \sup\{\, |f(x) - f(y)| \ : \ x, y \in I_i \,\} ,$$

the oscillation of $f$ on the set $I_i$ ([[def-oscillation]]). The supremum is a
real number here rather than an extended one, because $f$ is bounded
([[def-oscillation]], [[def-extended-reals]]). The identity is proved in two
inequalities.

*The oscillation is at most the gap.* For $x, y \in I_i$ both $f(x)$ and $f(y)$
lie in $[m_i, M_i]$, so $f(x) - f(y) \le M_i - m_i$ and
$f(y) - f(x) \le M_i - m_i$, whence $|f(x) - f(y)| \le M_i - m_i$
([[lem-of-abs-value]]). So $M_i - m_i$ is an upper bound of the set whose
supremum is $\omega_f(I_i)$.

*The gap is at most the oscillation.* Let $\varepsilon > 0$ be real. By the
$\varepsilon$-characterisations of the supremum and the infimum
([[lem-sup-epsilon]], [[lem-inf-epsilon]]) there are $x, y \in I_i$ with
$f(x) > M_i - \varepsilon/2$ and $f(y) < m_i + \varepsilon/2$; then

$$|f(x) - f(y)| \;\ge\; f(x) - f(y) \;>\; (M_i - m_i) - \varepsilon ,$$

so $\omega_f(I_i) > (M_i - m_i) - \varepsilon$. As $\varepsilon > 0$ was
arbitrary, $\omega_f(I_i) \ge M_i - m_i$: otherwise
$\varepsilon := (M_i - m_i) - \omega_f(I_i)$ would be positive and give
$\omega_f(I_i) > \omega_f(I_i)$.

This identity is what connects the Darboux machinery to the pointwise
oscillation of [[def-oscillation]], and it is the hinge of
[[thm-lebesgue-criterion]].

For $a>0$, the function $x\mapsto a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and
$$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$
For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with
$$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$

derivations.claim: Put $g=w^2$. On $[0,1/2]$, $g$ is bounded and nondecreasing; symmetry makes it bounded and nonincreasing on $[1/2,1]$. For each $N\ge1$, combine the uniform $N$-part partitions of these two half-intervals. By [F2], the Darboux gap on each half is at most $1/(2N)$, since $0\le g\le1$; the gap on the combined partition is their sum and is at most $1/N$. By [F3], choose $N$ with $1/N<\varepsilon$ for each $\varepsilon>0$; [F4] therefore gives Riemann integrability of $g$ on $[0,1]$.

Choose $0<\delta<1/2$ so that $[1/2-\delta,1/2+\delta]$ lies inside the neighbourhood where $w$ is positive, and put $c=w(1/2-\delta)>0$. Monotonicity on the left half and symmetry imply $g(u)\ge c^2$ throughout this central interval, while $g\ge0$ on $[0,1]$. The partition with endpoints $0,1/2-\delta,1/2+\delta,1$ therefore has lower sum at least $2\delta c^2$. By [F6], $I_w\ge2\delta c^2>0$.
Let $I_w=\int_0^1g(u)\,du$. The uniform partition into $b$ parts with midpoint tags has mesh $1/b\to0$, and its Riemann sum is exactly $W_b^2/b$. By [F3], [F5] and step 1.1, $W_b^2/b\to I_w$.
Since $W_b^2/b\to I_w>0$, it is positive and bounded away from zero for all sufficiently large $b$. For those $b$, $a_b=(W_b^2/b)^{-1/2}$, so [F7] gives $a_b\to I_w^{-1/2}$.

boundaries.evidence: Statement uses b>=1, so the weight vector is nonempty; the window is positive near 1/2, and step 1.2 supplies a nonempty central interval giving I_w>0.
By steps 1.2 and 3.1 and the Statement, I_w is strictly positive and eventual W_b positivity follows; finite b may still have W_b=0.

risk_review.notes: Read steps 1.1–3.1. Squaring preserves monotonicity on each half; their Darboux gaps add to at most 1/N. Positivity on an actual central neighbourhood supplies a positive lower sum, including possibly discontinuous windows. Midpoint sums converge by the tagged Riemann criterion, then reciprocal square-root continuity applies only once the norm is positive. No claim is made for small b with zero norm.

definition_review.source_exact:
**Input:** a fixed number $K\ge2$ of observed series $Y_{i,1},\ldots,Y_{i,n_i}$ in a real Hilbert space $H$, positive integer sample sizes $n_i$, total size $M=\sum_{i=1}^K n_i$, integer block lengths $1\le b_i\le n_i$, and a mode, moving or tapered. For tapered mode also supply an admissible window with positive block norm at each $b_i$. Put

$$\bar Y_i=\frac1{n_i}\sum_{t=1}^{n_i}Y_{i,t},\qquad \bar Y_P=\frac1M\sum_{i=1}^K n_i\bar Y_i,\qquad R_{i,t}=Y_{i,t}-\bar Y_i.$$

For each series $i=1,\ldots,K$, let $N_i=n_i-b_i+1$ and $k_i=\lceil n_i/b_i\rceil$. For every candidate start $j=1,\ldots,N_i$ and position $r=1,\ldots,b_i$, define the following arrays. In moving mode set $A_{i,j,r}=R_{i,j+r-1}$. In tapered mode set $A_{i,j,r}=a_{b_i}w_{b_i}(r)R_{i,j+r-1}$, with $a_{b_i}$ and $w_{b_i}$ as in [[alg-tapered-block-bootstrap]]. For each $i=1,\ldots,K$ and $s=1,\ldots,k_i$, draw independent uniform starts $J_{i,s}\in\{1,\ldots,N_i\}$, using the index law of [[alg-overlapping-block-resampling]]. For each within-block position define

$$c_{i,r}=\frac1{N_i}\sum_{j=1}^{N_i}A_{i,j,r}.$$

**Output:** for each $i$, a pseudo-series $Y^*_{i,1},\ldots,Y^*_{i,n_i}$. In the order $s=1,\ldots,k_i$, retain the positions $r=1,\ldots,q_{i,s}$, where $q_{i,s}=\min\{b_i,n_i-(s-1)b_i\}$, and set

$$Y^*_{i,(s-1)b_i+r}=\bar Y_P+A_{i,J_{i,s},r}-c_{i,r}.$$

Thus a divisible sample uses $k_i$ complete blocks; otherwise only the first $n_i-b_i\lfloor n_i/b_i\rfloor$ positions of the final block are retained. This centers each resampled residual position by its own conditional average, then gives every pseudo-series the same pooled location $\bar Y_P$. All block starts are conditionally independent across blocks and across series.

derivations.claim: Fix $i,s,r$. Uniformity of $J_{i,s}$ gives $E^*A_{i,J_{i,s},r}-c_{i,r}=\frac1{N_i}\sum_{j=1}^{N_i}A_{i,j,r}-c_{i,r}=0$. Therefore $E^*Y^*_{i,(s-1)b_i+r}=\bar Y_P$, including positions in a truncated final block.

The bootstrap mean $\bar Y_i^*$ is the average of exactly $n_i$ such pseudo-observations. Linearity of the finite conditional expectation gives $E^*\bar Y_i^*=\bar Y_P$ for every $i$. The common conditional mean proves the stated null imposition.

Let $E,F$ be normed spaces, let $D\subseteq E$, let $\theta\in D$, and let $E_0\subseteq E$ be a linear subspace. A map $\Psi:D\to F$ is **Hadamard differentiable at $\theta$, tangentially to $E_0$** if there is a continuous linear map $\Psi'_\theta:E_0\to F$ such that, for every sequence $t_m>0$ with $t_m\to0$, and every sequence $h_m\to h\in E_0$ for which $\theta+t_mh_m\in D$,

$$\frac{\Psi(\theta+t_mh_m)-\Psi(\theta)}{t_m}\longrightarrow \Psi'_\theta(h)\quad\hbox{in }F.$$

The subspace is part of the hypothesis: directions outside $E_0$ are not covered by this definition.

Let $E$ be a separable complete metric space, let $\mathcal D_n$ be the sigma-algebra generated by the observed data at sample size $n$, and let $Z_n^*$ be a bootstrap random element whose remaining randomness is the resampling randomization. Write $\mathcal L^*(Z_n^*)$ for its conditional Borel probability law given $\mathcal D_n$. Supply as part of the data a metric $d_w$ on Borel probability measures on $E$ such that $d_w(\mu_n,\mu)\to0$ exactly when $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$ in the sense of [[def-weak-convergence-of-borel-probability-measures]]. Assume the displayed metric distance is a measurable real random variable. For a fixed Borel probability measure $\mu$ on $E$, we say that $Z_n^*$ converges conditionally weakly in probability to $\mu$ when

$$d_w\!\left(\mathcal L^*(Z_n^*),\mu\right)\longrightarrow 0\quad\hbox{in probability}.$$

The metric is supplied as a hypothesis; this definition makes no metric-existence assertion. It applies to separable complete metric spaces, including separable Banach spaces, their closed linear subspaces and finite products.

For Borel probabilities $\mu_n,\mu$ on a metric space S, the following are equivalent: (i) $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$; (ii) integrals converge for all bounded uniformly continuous real tests; (iii) $\limsup_n\mu_n(F)\le\mu(F)$ for every closed F; (iv) $\liminf_n\mu_n(G)\ge\mu(G)$ for every open G; (v) $\mu_n(A)\to\mu(A)$ for every Borel A with $\mu(\partial A)=0$.

Let S,T be metric spaces, $g:S\to T$ measurable, and $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$. If the discontinuity set $D_g$ is $\mu$-null, then $g_*\mu_n\Rightarrow g_*\mu$. Consequently $X_n\Rightarrow X$ implies $g(X_n)\Rightarrow g(X)$ whenever $P_X(D_g)=0$.

$X_n\to X$ in probability if and only if every subsequence of $(X_n)$ has a
further subsequence converging almost surely to $X$.

Let $\mathcal B$ be the Borel sigma-algebra of $[0,1]$, generated by intervals with rational endpoints; let $dt$ be Lebesgue measure restricted to $\mathcal B$, and set $H=L^2([0,1],\mathcal B,dt;\mathbb R)$, with inner product $\langle x,y\rangle_H=\int_0^1x(u)y(u)\,du$. We use the quotient-by-null-functions convention for $L^2$ ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). The measure space is finite and countably generated, so under Countable Choice $H$ is separable ([[thm-l-p-of-a-sigma-finite-countably-generated-measure-space-is-separable]], [[def-countable-choice]], [[def-separable-space]]); [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]] verifies that this real pairing makes the quotient a Hilbert space.

Let $(S,\mathcal S,\nu)$ be a probability space and $(\delta_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ an independent identically distributed family of $S$-valued random elements with law $\nu$ ([[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]], [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]], [[def-independent-random-elements]]). A **causal Bernoulli shift** with innovation law $\nu$ is a process
$$X_t=f(\delta_t,\delta_{t-1},\delta_{t-2},\ldots),\qquad t\in\mathbb Z,$$
where $f:S^{\mathbb N_0}\to H$ is measurable from the product sigma-algebra $\mathcal S^{\otimes\mathbb N_0}$ to the Borel sigma-algebra of $H$. This product-measurability formulation is meaningful for a merely measurable innovation space $S$.

On an independent product extension, take replacement innovations $\delta'_{t,m,k}$, indexed by $t\in\mathbb Z$, $m\in\mathbb N_0$, and integers $k\le t-m$, all with law $\nu$, mutually independent, and independent of the original innovations. Such a countable family and its product with the original probability space exist under Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]], [[cor-countable-independent-copies-exist]], [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]). For $m\ge1$ define
$$X_{t,m}=f(\delta_t,\ldots,\delta_{t-m+1},\delta'_{t,m,t-m},\delta'_{t,m,t-m-1},\ldots),$$
and define the full replacement $X_{t,0}=f(\delta'_{t,0,t},\delta'_{t,0,t-1},\ldots)$. Each $X_{t,m}$ has the same marginal law as $X_t$; for fixed $m\ge1$ the sequence $(X_{t,m})_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ is strictly stationary and $m$-dependent because its original-innovation windows have length $m$ and its replacement arrays are independent across $t$.

For every fixed $m\ge0$, the joint process $(X_t,X_{t,m})_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ is strictly stationary: shifting all indices relabels a family of mutually independent innovations with the same law and commutes with the defining measurable maps. Consequently $D_{t,m}:=X_t-X_{t,m}$ is stationary and $\|D_{t,m}\|_{L^2(H)}=\delta_m$ for every $t$.

Write $\|X\|_{L^2(H)}=(\mathbb E\|X\|_H^2)^{1/2}$ and
$$\delta_m=\|X_0-X_{0,m}\|_{L^2(H)},\qquad m\ge0.$$
The process is **$L^2$-$m$-approximable** when
$$\mathbb E\|X_0\|_H^2<\infty\qquad\hbox{and}\qquad\sum_{m\ge1}\delta_m<\infty.$$
The same marginal law gives $\delta_0\le2\|X_0\|_{L^2(H)}<\infty$. For a Bochner-integrable $H$-valued random element $Y$, write $\mathbb E_B Y=\int Y\,d\mathbb P$; the moment condition makes $X_t$ and every $X_{t,m}$ Bochner integrable ([[def-bochner-integrable-function]], [[thm-bochner-integrability-criterion]]).

Here **strict stationarity** means invariance of every finite-dimensional law under integer shifts. A process is **$m$-dependent** if, for every $a\in\mathbb Z$, the sigma-algebras generated by $(X_s)_{s\le a}$ and $(X_s)_{s\ge a+m+1}$ are independent ([[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]]). The stated input windows for $X_{t,m}$ are disjoint across these two index ranges, so they satisfy this definition.

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let $H=L^2([0,1],dt;\mathbb R)$,
let $(X_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ be a centered causal Bernoulli shift as in
[[def-l2-m-approximable-causal-bernoulli-shift]], and suppose it is
$L^2$-$m$-approximable. Write $\sigma=(\mathbb E\|X_0\|_H^2)^{1/2}$,
let $S_1(H)$ be the trace-class Banach space with trace norm $\|\cdot\|_1$
([[def-trace-class-operator]], [[thm-trace-class-is-a-two-sided-banach-operator-ideal]]),
write $\mathbb E_B$ for a Bochner integral, and define $x\otimes y:H\to H$ by
$(x\otimes y)h=\langle h,y\rangle_Hx$. The Bochner series
$$ \Gamma=\mathbb E_B[X_0\otimes X_0]+ \sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\bigl(\mathbb E_B[X_0\otimes X_j] +\mathbb E_B[X_j\otimes X_0]\bigr) $$
converges absolutely in trace norm to a positive self-adjoint trace-class
operator. For $S_n=\sum_{t=1}^nX_t$, the Bochner covariance operators
$\Gamma_n=n^{-1}\mathbb E_B[S_n\otimes S_n]$ satisfy
$\|\Gamma_n-\Gamma\|_1\to0$. If $\boxtimes$ is the product-kernel class from
[[lem-real-l-two-kernel-operator-is-bounded-and-rank-one-compatible]], then
$$ \kappa_j=\mathbb E_B[X_0\boxtimes X_j],\qquad \widetilde\kappa_j=\mathbb E_B[X_j\boxtimes X_0] $$
are well-defined elements of $K=L^2([0,1]^2,dt\times dt;\mathbb R)$, and
$$ c=\kappa_0+\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}(\kappa_j+\widetilde\kappa_j) $$
converges absolutely in $K$ and satisfies $T_c=\Gamma$. Equivalently, $c$ is
the design's long-run covariance-kernel series interpreted as an
$L^2([0,1]^2)$ equivalence class; no pointwise representatives are fixed.

Let $(\mathcal F_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of sigma-algebras on a
probability space, and let $J_0,\dots,J_{m-1}\subseteq I$ be pairwise disjoint
index sets. For each $r<m$, define

$$\mathcal G_r:=\sigma\left(\bigcup_{i\in J_r}\mathcal F_i\right).$$

Then the sigma-algebras $\mathcal G_0,\dots,\mathcal G_{m-1}$ are independent.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. For each $i$, let
$g_i:(S_i,\Sigma_i)\to(T_i,\mathcal T_i)$ be measurable. Then the family

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ and $K$
be Hilbert spaces over the same real or complex scalar field and let $T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be compact
([[def-compact-linear-operator]]). Then $T$ is trace class
([[def-trace-class-operator]]) if and only if there are families
$(u_j)_{j\ge1}$ in $H$ and $(v_j)_{j\ge1}$ in $K$, indexed by the positive
integers, with
$$\sum_{j\ge1}\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\|<+\infty$$
such that the zero-based sequence of finite-rank operators defined by $R_0=0$
and
$$R_m:=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\langle\cdot,u_j\rangle v_j\qquad(m\ge1)$$
