   are bounded linear operators on Hilbert spaces $H_0,L$, then
   $ATB\in\mathcal S_1(H_0,L)$ and
   $$\|ATB\|_1\le\|A\|\,\|T\|_1\,\|B\| ;$$
3. $(\mathcal S_1(H,K),\|\cdot\|_1)$ is a Banach space: every
   $\|\cdot\|_1$-Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ has a limit in
   $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ to which it converges in $\|\cdot\|_1$
   ([[def-banach-space]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]],
   [[def-metric-space]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be a **self-adjoint positive** trace-class operator
([[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]],
[[def-trace-class-operator]]), so that $\langle Tx,x\rangle\ge0$ for every
$x\in H$. Let $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots>0$ be the positive eigenvalues of
$T$ listed with multiplicity
([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]) and let
$(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$ be the zero-padded singular-value sequence
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]). Then
$s_n(T)=\lambda_n$ for every $n$, and
$$\operatorname{tr}(T)=\sum_{n\ge1}\lambda_n=\|T\|_1 ,$$
where the sum is over the positive eigenvalues with multiplicity and the
equalities are also valid in the finite-rank case (then $\lambda_n:=0$ for
$n$ beyond the rank). This is the positive compact self-adjoint case only; it is
**not** Lidskii's theorem for arbitrary trace-class operators, which is not
claimed here.

If $f:\Omega\to X$ is Bochner integrable, then for every measurable $E$,

$$\left\|\int_E f\,d\mu\right\|\leq\int_E\|f\|\,d\mu.$$

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $H$ be a real Hilbert space and let $(e_k)$ be a finite or countable
orthonormal family whose finite linear span is dense in $H$. Here
orthonormal means $\langle e_j,e_k\rangle_H=1$ when $j=k$ and $0$ otherwise;
density means every $x\in H$ is arbitrarily close in norm to a finite linear
combination of the $e_k$. For $x\in H$, define
$$P_Nx=\sum_{k\le N}\langle x,e_k\rangle_H e_k,$$
using all basis vectors once $N$ reaches the size of a finite family. Then
$P_Nx\to x$ in norm and
$$\|x\|_H^2=\lim_{N\to\infty}\sum_{k\le N}|\langle x,e_k\rangle_H|^2.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $H$ be a real or
complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let $T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be a
compact self-adjoint operator ([[def-compact-linear-operator]],
[[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]). Then $T$ has a
Hilbert basis ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]])
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$
([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]): one may take the union
of orthonormal bases of the finitely many-dimensional nonzero eigenspaces with a
Hilbert basis of $\ker T$. If $\ker T=\{0\}$ no vectors from the kernel are
needed, and if all nonzero eigenspaces are absent (that is $T=0$) the union is a
Hilbert basis of $H=\ker T$.

**Input:** observations $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ in a real Hilbert space $H$, and an integer block length $b$ with $1\le b\le n$.

**Output:** a pseudo-series $X_1^*,\ldots,X_n^*$, generated by [[alg-overlapping-block-resampling]]: within each selected block retain the original order and concatenate blocks in their draw order, truncating only the last block when $b\nmid n$. The conditional bootstrap sample mean is $\bar X_n^*=n^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^nX_t^*$. Its conditional center is $E^*\bar X_n^*$, where $E^*$ averages over the independent uniform block starts while the observations remain fixed.

This algorithm specifies the resampling law only. It does not assert that the conditional law approximates the sampling law for any data-generating process or block-length regime.

Under [[def-resampling-sampling-unit-contract]], take each observation $x_t$ to be a complete time-indexed unit record. Each draw selects an ordered group of $b$ consecutive records; the output retains every record of each complete block and only the initial $r=n-b\lfloor n/b\rfloor$ records of the final block when $r>0$. Thus selected length-$b$ groups are not declared indivisible sampling units. Unit compatibility for a stated target requires that block boundaries and final truncation do not split any bundle declared indivisible by that target's sampling or assignment design. This is the sampling-unit interface, not a bootstrap-validity result.

**Input:** observations $Y_1,\ldots,Y_n$ in a real Hilbert space $H$, an integer $1\le b\le n$, and a window $w:\mathbb R\to[0,1]$ that vanishes off $[0,1]$, is positive on a neighbourhood of $1/2$, satisfies $w(1-u)=w(u)$, and is nondecreasing on $[0,1/2]$. Put $w_b(r)=w((r-\tfrac12)/b)$ for $1\le r\le b$, $W_b=(\sum_{r=1}^bw_b(r)^2)^{1/2}$, and $a_b=\sqrt b/W_b$. The procedure is admissible only when $W_b>0$.

**Center and taper:** set $\bar Y_n=n^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^nY_t$ and $R_t=Y_t-\bar Y_n$. For each start $j\in\{1,\ldots,n-b+1\}$, form the block

$$\bigl(a_bw_b(1)R_j,\ldots,a_bw_b(b)R_{j+b-1}\bigr).$$

**Resample:** use the independent uniform block starts from [[alg-overlapping-block-resampling]], multiply each selected centered observation by its within-block taper and the factor $a_b$, concatenate in draw order, and retain the first $n$ entries. The conditional bootstrap mean is centered by its own conditional expectation when used to approximate the sampling law of $\sqrt n\,\bar Y_n$.

The factor $a_b$ compensates for the window's squared-weight sum in the block-sum variance calculation; this definition alone gives no bootstrap validity result.

For a dependent time series, the selected length-$b$ consecutive run is the resampling unit under [[def-resampling-sampling-unit-contract]]. The taper changes each unit record's within-block weight but the whole block is selected and resampled together; validity remains a separate theorem.

Let $w$ satisfy the taper conditions in [[alg-tapered-block-bootstrap]]. As the positive integer $b\to\infty$, $w^2$ is Riemann integrable on $[0,1]$, and

$$\frac{1}{b}\sum_{j=1}^b w\!\left(\frac{j-\tfrac12}{b}\right)^2\longrightarrow I_w:=\int_0^1 w(u)^2\,du>0.$$

Consequently, $W_b>0$ for all sufficiently large $b$ and $a_b=\sqrt b/W_b\to I_w^{-1/2}$.

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $X,Y$ be Banach spaces, let $T:X\to Y$ be bounded and linear, and let $f$
be Bochner integrable. Then $T\circ f$ is Bochner integrable and, for every
measurable $E$,

$$T\left(\int_Ef\,d\mu\right)=\int_E Tf\,d\mu.$$

Let $n\ge1$, let $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ be independent real random variables on a
common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then
   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$
   in $[0,+\infty]$. In this finite product of expectations, a zero factor
   makes the product zero even when another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise
   multiplication has its usual extended nonnegative meaning.
2. If every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable
   and the same factorization holds in $\mathbb R$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: For $h\ge1$, $X_{h,h}$ is independent of $X_0$: its retained original innovation indices are $1,\ldots,h$, and its replacement array is independent of all inputs to $X_0$. Its mean is zero. The tensor $X_0\otimes X_{h,h}$ is Bochner integrable by [F1], [F3]–[F4], and the rank-one norm identity. For arbitrary $f,g\in H$, [F6] gives $\langle \mathbb E_B[X_0\otimes X_{h,h}]f,g\rangle=E[\langle f,X_{h,h}\rangle\langle X_0,g\rangle]=0$, hence $\mathbb E_B[X_0\otimes X_{h,h}]=0$. Thus $\|E[X_0\otimes X_h]\|_1\le\sigma\delta_h$ by [F3]–[F4]. For every finite real coefficient sequence $(u_t)$, expansion and $2|u_tu_{t+h}|\le u_t^2+u_{t+h}^2$ therefore give $E\|\sum_tu_tX_t\|^2\le K\sum_tu_t^2$. This proves the prefix bound. The same argument after applying $R=I-P$ gives $|E\langle RX_0,RX_h\rangle|\le\alpha_P\delta_h$, since $\|R\|\le1$ and projection preserves independence and centering. It proves the asserted projected prefix bound. Along complete basis projections, $\alpha_{P_d}\to0$ by norm convergence and dominated convergence, with dominating squared norm $\|X_0\|^2$.

Put $D_{t,m}=X_t-X_{t,m}$. For $h\ge1$, $X_{h,h}$ is independent of $D_{0,m}$, so [F6] and Cauchy–Schwarz bound $|E\langle D_{0,m},X_h\rangle|\le\delta_m\delta_h$. If $h\ge m$, $X_{h,m}$ is independent of $D_{0,m}$, while for $1\le h<m$, Cauchy–Schwarz bounds $|E\langle D_{0,m},X_{h,m}\rangle|$ by $\delta_m\sigma$. Consequently the individual lag bounds are $|E\langle D_{0,m},D_{h,m}\rangle|\le\delta_m(\delta_h+\sigma)$ for $h<m$ and $\le\delta_m\delta_h$ for $h\ge m$. Negative-lag scalar covariances equal their positive counterparts by stationarity. Expanding any bounded-weight block and bounding each $|c_{b,\ell}c_{b,\ell+h}|$ by $A^2$ gives $\sup_{j,b}E\|b^{-1/2}\sum_{\ell=1}^bc_{b,\ell}D_{j+\ell-1,m}\|^2\le A^2\varepsilon_m^2$, where $\varepsilon_m^2=\delta_m^2+2\delta_m\sum_{h\ge1}\delta_h+2\sigma(m-1)\delta_m\to0$. The convergence uses precisely the assumed $m\delta_m\to0$ and summability.

Minkowski's inequality in $L^2(H)$ and the finite-coefficient bound in step 1.1 give $\|N^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^NX_{j+\ell-1}\|_{L^2(H)}\le\sqrt{K/N}$ for each $\ell$. Hence $\|\bar Z_{n,b}\|_{L^2(H)}\le b^{-1/2}\sum_{\ell=1}^b|c_{b,\ell}|\sqrt{K/N}\le A\sqrt{Kb/N}$, as claimed. Minkowski here follows by expanding a finite squared norm and applying Cauchy–Schwarz to each cross term.

Fix $m$. Write $Y_t=X_{t,m}$ and define $V_t=Y_t\mathbf1_{\{\|Y_t\|\le M\}}-E[Y_0\mathbf1_{\{\|Y_0\|\le M\}}]$. This is centered, stationary and $m$-dependent, with $\|V_t\|\le2M$. Put $\eta_{m,M}=\|Y_0-V_0\|_{L^2(H)}$. Since $EY_0=0$, $\eta_{m,M}\le2\|Y_0\mathbf1_{\{\|Y_0\|>M\}}\|_{L^2(H)}\to0$ by dominated convergence. The centered residual $Y-V$ is $m$-dependent, so its covariances vanish at distances greater than $m$ by [F6], and all remaining scalar covariances have absolute value at most $\eta_{m,M}^2$. Hence its normalized weighted block has second moment at most $A^2(2m+1)\eta_{m,M}^2$. With $Z^V_{j,b}=b^{-1/2}\sum_{\ell=1}^bc_{b,\ell}V_{j+\ell-1}$, step 1.2 and Minkowski give $\sup_{j,b}\|Z_{j,b}-Z^V_{j,b}\|_{L^2(H)}\le d_{m,M}:=A\varepsilon_m+A\sqrt{2m+1}\eta_{m,M}$. Choose first $m$ and then $M$ to make this arbitrarily small.

For independent centered Hilbert elements $U_1,\ldots,U_q$ bounded by $L$, write $\|\sum_iU_i\|^2=\sum_i\|U_i\|^2+2\sum_{i<j}\langle U_i,U_j\rangle$. On squaring, every term containing an index exactly once has expectation zero, by integrating that independent centered element first using [F6]. In particular all mixed terms between the two sums vanish; among products of two inner products only identical pairs survive. Cauchy–Schwarz then gives $E\|\sum_iU_i\|^4\le\sum_iE\|U_i\|^4+6\sum_{i<j}E\|U_i\|^2E\|U_j\|^2\le3q^2L^4$; the empty sum is zero. Partition the $b$ summands defining $\sqrt b Z^V_{j,b}$ into $p=m+1$ residue classes. Inside each class their input innovation sets are disjoint, hence they are jointly independent by [F2]. Applying the proved bound to the class sizes $q_s$ and using $\|\sum_{s=1}^pu_s\|^4\le p^3\sum_s\|u_s\|^4$ and $\sum_sq_s^2\le b^2$ gives $\sup_{j,b}E\|Z^V_{j,b}\|^4\le3p^3A^4(2M)^4=:C_{m,M}$. Thus fourth moments are used only for bounded truncations.

The rank-one identity and Cauchy–Schwarz imply both $\sup_{j,b}E|\|Z_{j,b}\|^2-\|Z^V_{j,b}\|^2|\le d_{m,M}(2A\sqrt K+d_{m,M})$ and $\sup_{j,b}E\|Z_{j,b}\otimes Z_{j,b}-Z^V_{j,b}\otimes Z^V_{j,b}\|_1\le d_{m,M}(2A\sqrt K+d_{m,M})$. Here use $\|Z_{j,b}\|_{L^2}\le A\sqrt K$ and $\|u\otimes u-v\otimes v\|_1\le\|u-v\|(\|u\|+\|v\|)$. The squared truncated blocks are uniformly integrable by step 3.1 and Markov's inequality. For nonnegative $F,G$, splitting at $G>L/2$ proves $E[F\mathbf1_{\{F>L\}}]\le2E|F-G|+E[G\mathbf1_{\{G>L/2\}}]$. Apply this with the two squared block norms, then let $L\to\infty$ and $d_{m,M}\to0$. This proves the asserted uniform integrability for $Z$.

Fix $m,M$ and set $Q_n^V=N^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^NZ^V_{j,b}\otimes Z^V_{j,b}$ and $B_n=EQ_n^V$. For fixed unit vectors $e,f$, the real variables $\langle Z^V_{j,b},e\rangle\langle Z^V_{j,b},f\rangle$ have second moments at most $C_{m,M}$. When two starts differ by more than $b+m$, the blocks use disjoint original innovations and disjoint replacement arrays, so these variables are independent by [F2]. Expanding the variance of their empirical mean and factoring the independent cross terms by [F6] therefore gives $E|\langle(Q_n^V-B_n)f,e\rangle|^2\le C_{m,M}(2(b+m)+1)/N\to0$, since $b/n\to0$. For any fixed finite-rank orthogonal projection $P$ of rank $d$, expansion in an orthonormal basis of its range and the rank-one norm bound show $\|P(Q_n^V-B_n)P\|_1\le\sum_{u,v\le d}|\langle(Q_n^V-B_n)e_v,e_u\rangle|$. Thus its expectation tends to zero.

Choose complete basis projections $P_d$ and put $R_d=I-P_d$. For any square-integrable $H$-valued $U$, the operator $T=E[U\otimes U]$ satisfies $\|T-PTP\|_1\le E\|RU\|^2+2\sqrt{E\|PU\|^2 E\|RU\|^2}$: expand its four $P,R$ corners, use the rank-one norm inequality on each off-diagonal corner, and use positivity for the $R$ corner. The same inequality holds for an empirical average, using its finite empirical expectation. For the $V$ blocks, finite dependence and covariance expansion give $E\|R_dZ^V_{j,b}\|^2\le A^2(2m+1)E\|R_dV_0\|^2=:t_d\to0$ by dominated convergence. Also $\sup_{j,b}E\|Z^V_{j,b}\|^2\le (A\sqrt K+d_{m,M})^2=:C$. Applying the corner inequality to $Q_n^V$ and $B_n$, and then Cauchy–Schwarz to expectations, yields $E\|Q_n^V-B_n\|_1\le E\|P_d(Q_n^V-B_n)P_d\|_1+2t_d+4\sqrt{Ct_d}$. Send $n\to\infty$ by step 4.2, then $d\to\infty$. This proves trace-norm concentration locally, without inferring trace-norm convergence from coordinate convergence alone.

Define $Q_n=N^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^NZ_{j,b}\otimes Z_{j,b}$. By step 4.1, $E\|Q_n-Q_n^V\|_1$ and $\|EQ_n-B_n\|_1$ are each at most $d_{m,M}(2A\sqrt K+d_{m,M})$. The triangle inequality and step 5.1 therefore give $\limsup_n E\|Q_n-EQ_n\|_1\le2d_{m,M}(2A\sqrt K+d_{m,M})$. First send $M\to\infty$ for each fixed $m$, then send $m\to\infty$. It follows that $E\|Q_n-EQ_n\|_1\to0$. This concentration conclusion required only the uniform bound on weights.

Now impose the squared normalization and fixed-lag autocorrelation hypotheses. Extend each weight vector by zero. Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|q_b(h)|\le1$. With $C_h=E[X_0\otimes X_h]$, stationarity gives $EQ_n=C_0+\sum_{h=1}^{b-1}q_b(h)(C_h+C_h^*)$. The series is absolutely convergent in trace norm by step 1.1. On each finite set of lags $q_b(h)\to1$, and the remaining trace-norm tail is uniformly bounded by its summable covariance tail. Thus $EQ_n\to\Gamma$ in trace norm. Step 6.1 gives $E\|Q_n-\Gamma\|_1\to0$. The empirically centered covariance equals $Q_n-\bar Z_{n,b}\otimes\bar Z_{n,b}$, whose difference from $Q_n$ has expected trace norm $E\|\bar Z_{n,b}\|^2\le A^2Kb/N\to0$ by step 2.1. This proves the asserted $L^1$ limit and its probability consequence by Markov's inequality.

MBB has $q_b(h)=(1-h/b)_+$ and squared normalization exactly. For TBB the squared normalization is also exact and the coefficients are bounded eventually by [F5]. Extend its nonnegative unimodal coefficients by zero to all integers; the total variation is at most $2A$. Telescoping gives $\sum_{\ell\in\mathbb Z}|c_{b,\ell+h}-c_{b,\ell}|\le2Ah$, so $|q_b(h)-q_b(0)|\le2A^2h/b\to0$. This uses exactly the midpoint coefficients of the algorithm and requires no continuity of the taper. All proved limits and uniform-integrability conclusions apply after any finite initial set of block sizes is discarded. The moment and projection conclusions, covariance limit, and claimed specializations are now established.

boundaries.evidence: Statement includes q=0: the prefix sum is empty and both moment bounds read 0<=0. For fixed h>=b the lag-weight sum is empty and equals zero; the fixed-h limit is taken only as b grows.
Steps 1.1, 1.2 and 7.1 include the zero process: all variances, replacement bounds and covariance operators are zero, with no division by them.
Step 1.1 includes prefix q=1 and block b=1 in the finite moment inequalities; the covariance limit separately requires b tending to infinity.
Steps 3.1, 4.1, 4.2, 5.1, 6.1, 7.1 use covariance positivity and trace bounds without a nonsingularity assumption; finite-rank and zero limiting covariance are included.
Steps 1.1 and 8.1 cover q=0 and q=b, exterior zero weights, midpoint taper positions and discontinuous monotone tapers.
Statement and A1 explicitly assume AC for the replacement-extension and complete-basis constructions; steps 1.1 and 5.1 use the supplied complete basis.

Reverse equivalence review: uniform block moments and trace-norm convergence of normalized weighted overlapping covariance is asserted as a one-direction conclusion or worked verification; no converse equivalence is asserted.

risk_review.notes: Reviewed every step including difference lags h<m and h>=m. The error epsilon_m tends to zero using m delta_m and summability. For fixed m then M, bounded finite-dependent truncations have uniform fourth moments by independent residue classes; fourth moments are not assumed of X. Uniform L2 approximation yields UI and tensor L1 approximation. Finite-coordinate concentration alone is supplemented by explicit projection-tail corner estimates before trace-norm concentration. Fixed-lag weight convergence and summable trace covariance yield the expectation limit; b/N controls empirical centering. TBB total variation <=2A proves fixed-lag correlation without window continuity. Empty residue classes, q=0, zero covariance and positive eventual taper norms are covered; AC use is declared.

citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(X_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ be a centered $L^2$-$m$-approximable causal Bernoulli shift in $H=L^2([0,1];\mathbb R)$ under [[def-l2-m-approximable-causal-bernoulli-shift]], and suppose additionally that $m\delta_m\to0$. Put $\sigma=\|X_0\|_{L^2(H)}$, let $\Gamma$ be its long-run covariance operator, and put

$$K=\sigma^2+2\sigma\sum_{h\ge1}\delta_h.$$

For every integer $b\ge1$, let $c_{b,1},\ldots,c_{b,b}$ be deterministic real weights, uniformly bounded in absolute value by $A<\infty$. Define

$$Z_{j,b}=b^{-1/2}\sum_{\ell=1}^b c_{b,\ell}X_{j+\ell-1}.$$

Then $\{\|Z_{j,b}\|_H^2:j\in\mathbb Z,b\ge1\}$ is uniformly integrable, and for $0\le q\le b$,

$$E\left\|\sum_{\ell=1}^q c_{b,\ell}X_{j+\ell-1}\right\|_H^2\le A^2Kq.$$

If $P$ is any finite-rank orthogonal projection, $R=I-P$ and $\alpha_P=\|RX_0\|_{L^2(H)}$, then also

$$E\left\|\sum_{\ell=1}^q c_{b,\ell}RX_{j+\ell-1}\right\|_H^2\le A^2q\left(\alpha_P^2+2\alpha_P\sum_{h\ge1}\delta_h\right).$$

For $n\ge b$, set $N=n-b+1$ and $\bar Z_{n,b}=N^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^NZ_{j,b}$. Then

$$E\|\bar Z_{n,b}\|_H^2\le A^2Kb/N.$$

Suppose further that $b=b_n\to\infty$, $b_n/n\to0$, and the weights satisfy

$$b^{-1}\sum_{\ell=1}^bc_{b,\ell}^2=1,\qquad q_b(h):=b^{-1}\sum_{\ell=1}^{b-h}c_{b,\ell}c_{b,\ell+h}\longrightarrow1\quad\text{for every fixed }h\ge0.$$

The centered overlapping-block covariance then satisfies the stronger $L^1$ trace-norm limit

$$E\left\|N^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^N(Z_{j,b}-\bar Z_{n,b})\otimes(Z_{j,b}-\bar Z_{n,b})-\Gamma\right\|_1\longrightarrow0.$$

In particular it converges in probability in trace norm. Both the MBB weights $c_{b,\ell}=1$ and the actual TBB weights $c_{b,\ell}=a_bw((\ell-\tfrac12)/b)$ satisfy these weight hypotheses for all sufficiently large $b$. For any complete finite or countable orthonormal basis and its initial-coordinate projections $P_d$, the projection-tail coefficient $\alpha_{P_d}^2+2\alpha_{P_d}\sum_{h\ge1}\delta_h$ tends to zero as $d\to\infty$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H=L^2([0,1],dt;\mathbb R)$ and let
$(X_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ be a centered, $L^2$-$m$-approximable causal
Bernoulli shift as defined in
[[def-l2-m-approximable-causal-bernoulli-shift]], with Bochner mean
$\mathbb E_BX_0=0$. Let $\Gamma$ be its long-run covariance operator from
[[lem-long-run-covariance-is-trace-class]], and let $G$ be a centered
$H$-valued Gaussian random element with covariance $\Gamma$, whose existence
is given by [[lem-positive-trace-class-covariance-defines-hilbert-gaussian]].
Then, for $S_n=\sum_{t=1}^nX_t$,
$$n^{-1/2}S_n\ \Rightarrow\ G$$
in the weak topology of Borel probability measures on $H$. The covariance
kernel is the $L^2([0,1]^2)$ equivalence class $c$ in the long-run covariance
lemma, and its integral operator is $T_c=\Gamma$. This is a CLT for the
$H$-valued sample sums; it is not a functional CLT for the time-indexed
partial-sum process.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $H$ be a real or
complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let $T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be a
compact self-adjoint operator ([[def-compact-linear-operator]],
[[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]). Then $T$ has a
Hilbert basis ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]])
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$
([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]): one may take the union
of orthonormal bases of the finitely many-dimensional nonzero eigenspaces with a
Hilbert basis of $\ker T$. If $\ker T=\{0\}$ no vectors from the kernel are
needed, and if all nonzero eigenspaces are absent (that is $T=0$) the union is a
Hilbert basis of $H=\ker T$.

If $\mathbb EX=0$ and $\mathbb EX^2=\sigma^2<\infty$, then $\varphi_X(t)=1-\sigma^2t^2/2+o(t^2)$ as $t\to0$. No third moment or choice axiom is assumed. The same scalar estimates give $0\le1-\cos u\le u^2/2$ for every real u. More precisely, for $r(u)=e^{iu}-1-iu+u^2/2$, $$|r(u)|\le \min(|u|^3/3,4u^2),\qquad |e^{iu}-1-iu|\le u^2.$$

Assume AC. If $X$ has law $N(m,\sigma^2)$ with $\sigma\ge0$, then $\varphi_X(t)=\exp(imt-\sigma^2t^2/2)$ for every real $t$. Moreover $\mathbb EX=m$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\sigma^2$, including $\sigma=0$.

For real $a,b,t$, $\varphi_{aX+b}(t)=e^{itb}\varphi_X(at)$. For a finite mutually independent family $(X_j)_{j=1}^n$ of real random variables, $\varphi_{\sum_jX_j}(t)=\prod_j\varphi_{X_j}(t)$. The empty sum has characteristic function one.

Assume AC. For Borel probability laws $\mu_n$ and a specified Borel probability law $\mu$ on $\mathbb R$,
$$\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\varphi_{\mu_n}(t)\to\varphi_\mu(t)\ \text{for every }t\in\mathbb R.$$

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$ be a finite integer and $p_\theta(x)=\theta\cdot x$ for $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$. Borel probability laws on $\mathbb R^d$ are determined by all the laws $(p_\theta)_*\mu$. Moreover, if $(p_\theta)_*\mu_n\Rightarrow(p_\theta)_*\mu$ for every $\theta$ and a specified Borel probability law $\mu$, then $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$. If dimension zero is admitted, interpret $\mathbb R^0$ as the singleton empty tuple; both conclusions then hold as well.

$X_n\to X$ in probability if and only if every subsequence of $(X_n)$ has a
further subsequence converging almost surely to $X$.

If $X_n\to X$ in probability, then some subsequence $X_{n_k}$ converges to
$X$ almost surely.

For Borel probabilities $\mu_n,\mu$ on a metric space S, the following are equivalent: (i) $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$; (ii) integrals converge for all bounded uniformly continuous real tests; (iii) $\limsup_n\mu_n(F)\le\mu(F)$ for every closed F; (iv) $\liminf_n\mu_n(G)\ge\mu(G)$ for every open G; (v) $\mu_n(A)\to\mu(A)$ for every Borel A with $\mu(\partial A)=0$.
Assume AC. For Borel probabilities on a separable metric space, $\pi(\mu_n,\mu)\to0$ if and only if $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$. Completeness is not required.

Let $E$ be a separable complete metric space, let $\mathcal D_n$ be the sigma-algebra generated by the observed data at sample size $n$, and let $Z_n^*$ be a bootstrap random element whose remaining randomness is the resampling randomization. Write $\mathcal L^*(Z_n^*)$ for its conditional Borel probability law given $\mathcal D_n$. Supply as part of the data a metric $d_w$ on Borel probability measures on $E$ such that $d_w(\mu_n,\mu)\to0$ exactly when $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$ in the sense of [[def-weak-convergence-of-borel-probability-measures]]. Assume the displayed metric distance is a measurable real random variable. For a fixed Borel probability measure $\mu$ on $E$, we say that $Z_n^*$ converges conditionally weakly in probability to $\mu$ when

$$d_w\!\left(\mathcal L^*(Z_n^*),\mu\right)\longrightarrow 0\quad\hbox{in probability}.$$

The metric is supplied as a hypothesis; this definition makes no metric-existence assertion. It applies to separable complete metric spaces, including separable Banach spaces, their closed linear subspaces and finite products.

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$, $K$
and $L$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces ([[def-hilbert-space]]). Then:

1. the trace-class operators $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]])
   form a linear subspace of $\mathcal B(H,K)$ on which $\|\cdot\|_1$ is a norm,
   and
   $$\|T\|\le\|T\|_1\qquad\text{for every }T\in\mathcal S_1(H,K)$$
   ([[def-operator-norm]]);
2. if $T\in\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ and $A\in\mathcal B(K,L)$, $B\in\mathcal B(H_0,H)$
   are bounded linear operators on Hilbert spaces $H_0,L$, then
   $ATB\in\mathcal S_1(H_0,L)$ and
   $$\|ATB\|_1\le\|A\|\,\|T\|_1\,\|B\| ;$$
3. $(\mathcal S_1(H,K),\|\cdot\|_1)$ is a Banach space: every
   $\|\cdot\|_1$-Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ has a limit in
   $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ to which it converges in $\|\cdot\|_1$
   ([[def-banach-space]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]],
   [[def-metric-space]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ and $K$
be Hilbert spaces over the same real or complex scalar field and let $T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be compact
([[def-compact-linear-operator]]). Then $T$ is trace class
([[def-trace-class-operator]]) if and only if there are families
$(u_j)_{j\ge1}$ in $H$ and $(v_j)_{j\ge1}$ in $K$, indexed by the positive
integers, with
$$\sum_{j\ge1}\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\|<+\infty$$
such that the zero-based sequence of finite-rank operators defined by $R_0=0$
and
$$R_m:=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\langle\cdot,u_j\rangle v_j\qquad(m\ge1)$$
converges to $T$ in operator norm ([[def-operator-norm]],
[[def-metric-convergence]]).  Here the displayed scalar series is, under the
library convention, the series of the sequence
$(\|u_{m+1}\|\,\|v_{m+1}\|)_{m\in\mathbb N}$. In that case
$$\|T\|_1=\inf\Bigl\{\sum_{j\ge1}\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\|:\ R_m\to T\ \text{in operator norm}\Bigr\},$$
the infimum being over all such **nuclear representations** of $T$, with the
same zero-based shift understood in every displayed sum, and the
infimum is attained: using its positive-integer index set and padding finite rank by zeros,
the singular-value series
$T=\sum_{j\in J}s_j\langle\cdot,e_j\rangle f_j$ is a nuclear representation with
sum $\|T\|_1$.

Throughout, $H$ and $K$ are real or complex Hilbert spaces with the pairing
linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-hilbert-space]]), $T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ is a bounded linear operator
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]) of
operator norm $\|T\|$ ([[def-operator-norm]]), and $E$ is a **Hilbert basis**
of $H$, that is, a complete orthonormal subset of $H$
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]).
The basis $E$ is **supplied as data**; the definitions below are stated
relative to it.

**The Hilbert–Schmidt square-sum.** The family $(\|Te\|^2)_{e\in E}$ consists of
nonnegative real numbers and is indexed by the arbitrary set $E$. Its sum is the
supremum of the finite subsums,

$$s_E(T):=\sum_{e\in E}\|Te\|^2:=\sup\Bigl\{\sum_{e\in F}\|Te\|^2 \;:\; F\subseteq E \text{ finite}\Bigr\}\in[0,+\infty],$$

in the finite-subset-supremum convention of
[[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]; the empty finite
subset contributes the empty sum $0$, so the supremum is over a nonempty
set and exists in $[0,+\infty]$. No enumeration, ordering or countability of
$E$ is used or asserted, and no choice is performed: the supremum ranges over
the set of finite subsets of the fixed index set $E$. For finite $E$ the
supremum is the ordinary finite sum over $E$, because all terms are
nonnegative.

**Hilbert–Schmidt relative to a basis.** The operator $T$ is
**Hilbert–Schmidt relative to $E$** when $s_E(T)<+\infty$, that is, when the
finite subsums are bounded above in $\mathbb R$. In that case the
**Hilbert–Schmidt norm of $T$ relative to $E$** is the nonnegative square root

$$\|T\|_{HS,E}:=\Bigl(\sum_{e\in E}\|Te\|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\in[0,+\infty).$$

When $s_E(T)=+\infty$, no Hilbert–Schmidt norm relative to $E$ is defined, and
$T$ is not Hilbert–Schmidt relative to $E$.

**Degenerate and extreme cases.** The zero operator satisfies $s_E(0)=0$ for
every basis $E$, so it is Hilbert–Schmidt relative to every basis with norm
$0$. If $H=\{0\}$ then the empty family is a Hilbert basis of $H$, the only
finite subset is empty, and $s_\varnothing(T)=0$ for the only linear operator
$T:\{0\}\to K$; that operator is Hilbert–Schmidt relative to the empty basis
with norm $0$. If $H$ is finite dimensional and $E$ is finite, $s_E(T)$ is an
ordinary finite sum of the squared norms $\|Te\|^2$, and $T$ is automatically
Hilbert–Schmidt relative to $E$.

**The basis is part of the notation.** The symbol $\|T\|_{HS,E}$ keeps the
basis in the subscript on purpose. Until the next result is proved, the phrase
"$T$ is Hilbert–Schmidt" is never used without a specified Hilbert basis, and
nothing here asserts that a Hilbert basis of $H$ exists: the existence of $E$
is a hypothesis of the definition, and the question of whether the finiteness
of $s_E(T)$ and the value $\|T\|_{HS,E}$ depend on $E$ is taken up in
[[thm-hilbert-schmidt-norm-is-basis-independent]]. In particular this
definition makes no basis-existence claim and no comparison with the operator
norm $\|T\|$; every such statement is proved later, where its own hypotheses
are displayed.

**Notation.** For a finite $F\subseteq E$ we write
$s_F(T):=\sum_{e\in F}\|Te\|^2$ for the finite subsum, so that
$s_E(T)=\sup\{s_F(T):F\subseteq E \text{ finite}\}$.

Let $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be an orthonormal family in a real or complex inner-product
space $H$ ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]),
let $F\subseteq I$ be finite, and for $x\in H$ put

$$P_Fx:=\sum_{i\in F}\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i .$$Then: 1. $P_Fx$ lies in the span of $\{e_i : i\in F\}$, and $\|P_Fx\|^2=\sum_{i\in F}|\langle x,e_i\rangle|^2$; 2. the residual $x-P_Fx$ is orthogonal to every $e_j$ with $j\in F$, hence to every vector of the span of $\{e_i : i\in F\}$; 3. $\|x-P_Fx\|^2=\|x\|^2-\sum_{i\in F}|\langle x,e_i\rangle|^2$, and therefore the **finite Bessel inequality** holds:$$\sum_{i\in F}|\langle x,e_i\rangle|^2\le\|x\|^2 ;$$4. $P_Fx$ is the unique best approximation to $x$ from the span of $\{e_i : i\in F\}$: for every $y$ in that span,$$\|x-y\|^2=\|x-P_Fx\|^2+\|P_Fx-y\|^2\ge\|x-P_Fx\|^2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if $y=P_Fx$.

At $F=\varnothing$ the sum defining $P_Fx$ is empty, so $P_Fx=0$ and the
identities read $\|x\|^2=\|x\|^2$.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: First, for a nuclear representation $T=\sum_j\langle\cdot,u_j\rangle v_j$ and an orthogonal projection $R$, its absolutely convergent trace has $|\operatorname{tr}(RTR)|\le\sum_j\|u_j\|\|v_j\|$. For every finite orthonormal set $E$, Minkowski and Bessel give $(\sum_{e\in E}\|Te\|^2)^{1/2}\le\sum_j\|v_j\|(\sum_{e\in E}|\langle e,u_j\rangle|^2)^{1/2}\le\sum_j\|u_j\|\|v_j\|$. Infinite nuclear sums follow from their summable tails. Taking the nuclear infimum proves $|\operatorname{tr}(RTR)|\le\|T\|_1$ and $\|T\|_{\mathrm{HS}}\le\|T\|_1$ by [F5]. Subtraction of $M_n$ replaces $B_{j,q}$ by $B_{j,q}-s_qM_n$, where $s_q=\sum_{\ell=1}^qc_{b,\ell}$ does not depend on $j$. It changes $\bar B_q$ by exactly the same amount. Thus every centered block is unchanged. Independence of the starts gives $\operatorname{Cov}^*(Z_n^*)=(kC_b+C_r)/n$. Positivity and the rank-one trace formula give $E\operatorname{tr}C_r\le E\|B_{1,r}\|^2\le Dr$, so $E\|C_r/n\|_1\le Db/n\to0$. Since $kb/n\to1$, [F1] now gives the asserted trace-norm covariance limit. The conditional squared norm of the centered remainder has expectation $\operatorname{tr}(C_r/n)$ and therefore its unconditional expectation tends to zero at rate $O(b/n)$.

Set $U_j=B_{j,b}/\sqrt b$, $\bar U=\bar B_b/\sqrt b$, and $V_j=U_j-\bar U$. For any vectors $x,y$ and $a>0$, splitting according as the larger summand exceeds $a/2$ gives $\|x+y\|^2\mathbf1_{\{\|x+y\|>a\}}\le4\|x\|^2\mathbf1_{\{\|x\|>a/2\}}+4\|y\|^2\mathbf1_{\{\|y\|>a/2\}}$. Consequently, for each $\varepsilon>0$, the conditional Lindeberg sum of the $k$ complete blocks is at most $L_n(\varepsilon)=\frac{kb}{nN}\sum_{j=1}^N\|V_j\|^2\mathbf1_{\{\|V_j\|>\varepsilon\sqrt{n/b}\}},\qquad E L_n(\varepsilon)\le4E\!\left[\|U_1\|^2\mathbf1_{\{\|U_1\|>(\varepsilon/2)\sqrt{n/b}\}}\right]+4E\|\bar U\|^2\longrightarrow0.$ Here $n/b\to\infty$, stationarity makes the expected empirical uncentered tail equal to that of $U_1$, and [F1] supplies uniform integrability and $E\|\bar U\|^2\to0$. Hence $L_n(\varepsilon)\to0$ in probability by [F5].

Take any subsequence. Apply [F4] diagonally to the scalar trace-norm covariance error, $\operatorname{tr}(C_r/n)$, and $L_n(1/j)$ for positive integers $j$. There is a further subsequence on which all tend to zero almost surely. Fix a data outcome in this probability-one event. For any $a\in H$, let $\xi_n=\langle a,B_{J_1,b}-\bar B_b\rangle/\sqrt n$ and $v_n=kE^*\xi_n^2$. Step 1.1 and remainder negligibility give $v_n\to\langle\Gamma a,a\rangle$, and the norm Lindeberg bounds imply $kE^*[\xi_n^2\mathbf1_{\{|\xi_n|>\rho\}}]\to0$ for every $\rho>0$. The Taylor bound in [F3], split at $\rho$, gives $k\left|E^*e^{i\xi_n}-1+\tfrac12E^*\xi_n^2\right|\le (\rho/3)v_n+4kE^*[\xi_n^2\mathbf1_{\{|\xi_n|>\rho\}}].$ Let $n\to\infty$ and then $\rho\downarrow0$. Thus $k(E^*e^{i\xi_n}-1)\to-\langle\Gamma a,a\rangle/2$ and $k|E^*e^{i\xi_n}-1|^2\to0$, since $k\to\infty$. The convergent power-series expansion $\log(1+z)=z+O(|z|^2)$ near zero proves $(E^*e^{i\xi_n})^k\to\exp(-\langle\Gamma a,a\rangle/2)$. The remainder's characteristic function tends to one because its conditional mean is zero and [F3], [F6] give $|E^*e^{i\langle a,R_n\rangle}-1|\le E^*\langle a,R_n\rangle^2\le\|a\|_H^2\operatorname{tr}(C_r/n)\to0$, where $R_n=n^{-1/2}(B_{J_{k+1},r}-\bar B_r)$. Replacing $a$ by $ta$ covers every real frequency. Therefore [F3] gives weak convergence of every finite-dimensional projection of the conditional law to that of $G$, on this fixed outcome; no positive lower bound on any variance was used.

On the same outcome let $T_n=\operatorname{Cov}^*(Z_n^*)$. For every fixed $d$, conditional centering and [F5] give $E^*\|R_dZ_n^*\|^2=\operatorname{tr}(R_dT_nR_d)\to\operatorname{tr}(R_d\Gamma R_d)$. If $\phi$ is bounded uniformly continuous, put $M=\sup|\phi|$ and $\omega_\phi(h)=\sup_{\|x-y\|\le h}|\phi(x)-\phi(y)|$. Markov gives $|E^*\phi(Z_n^*)-E^*\phi(P_dZ_n^*)|\le\omega_\phi(h)+2Mh^{-2}\operatorname{tr}(R_dT_nR_d).$ The analogous bound for $G$ uses $\operatorname{tr}(R_d\Gamma R_d)$. Step 3.1 gives convergence of the projected expectations. Take the limit superior in $n$, then $d\to\infty$, and finally $h\downarrow0$. All such test expectations converge, so [F4] gives weak convergence of the full conditional laws on this outcome. Thus their distance to the law of $G$ in the metric of [F4] tends to zero almost surely on the extracted subsequence. The subsequence characterization proves convergence in probability along the original sequence.

To verify tightness explicitly, empirical centering decreases each projected second moment. By [F1] and independence, $E E^*\|R_dZ_n^*\|^2\le\frac{k b+r}{n}D_d=D_d.$ The same bound without projection is $D$. Enlarge constants to cover any finitely many initial admissible block lengths. Given $\varepsilon,\eta>0$, choose $R$ and increasing integers $d_j$ so that $D/R^2<\varepsilon\eta/4$ and $j^2D_{d_j}<\varepsilon\eta\,2^{-j-2}$. The closed set $K=\{x\in H:\|x\|\le R,\ \|R_{d_j}x\|\le1/j\text{ for every }j\ge1\}$ is compact: for any radius choose $j$ with $1/j$ smaller than half the radius, and a finite net for the bounded ball in $P_{d_j}H$; this gives a finite net for $K$, and closedness in complete $H$ gives compactness. Markov and the union bound yield $E P^*(Z_n^*\notin K)<\varepsilon\eta/2$, and then $P\{P^*(Z_n^*\notin K)>\varepsilon\}<\eta/2$. This proves the stated conditional tightness, and steps 1.1-4.1 establish all the other assertions.

boundaries.evidence: Statement explicitly sets B_j,0=bar B_0=C_0=0; r=0 therefore contributes an empty zero prefix. Candidate starts remain nonempty because n>=b on the admissible tail.
Steps 1.1 and 3.1 include zero covariance; characteristic functions converge to one and no variance is divided out.
Statement includes b=1 at finite rows and a one-point start set if b=n, but neither can persist when b->infinity and b/sqrt(n)->0; the asymptotic number of complete blocks diverges.
Step 3.1 treats every projection variance, including zero, through its characteristic function and does not standardize by that variance.
Step 1.1 covers r=0 with C_0=0 and every 0<r<b using the same N candidate starts, with E tr(C_r/n) bounded by Db/n.
Statement, A1 and F2 explicitly assume AC for the Gaussian and complete eigenbasis. Step 3.1 uses only countably many scalar subsequence conditions; step 5.1 chooses integer cutoffs.

Reverse equivalence review: the centered independent-block conditional CLT including its final prefix is asserted as a one-direction conclusion or worked verification; no converse equivalence is asserted.

risk_review.notes: Read steps 1.1–5.1. Nuclear bounds control trace and Hilbert-Schmidt norm; common data shifts cancel exactly. Prefix covariance is O(b/n); UI yields conditional Lindeberg without extra moments. A single countable subsequence extraction controls covariance and every reciprocal threshold, then the characteristic-function expansion proves all finite projections, including variance zero. Trace tails upgrade to full weak convergence. The explicit compact set from projection-tail bounds proves conditional tightness, not just bounded norms. Finite-mixture atom laws justify metric measurability. AC is explicit and covers basis/Gaussian suppliers.

citations.quote:
**Input:** a fixed integer $K\ge2$ of observed series $Y_{i,1},\ldots,Y_{i,n_i}$ in a real Hilbert space $H$, positive integer sample sizes $n_i$, total size $M=\sum_{i=1}^K n_i$, integer block lengths $1\le b_i\le n_i$, and a mode, moving or tapered. For tapered mode also supply an admissible window with positive block norm at each $b_i$. Put

$$\bar Y_i=\frac1{n_i}\sum_{t=1}^{n_i}Y_{i,t},\qquad \bar Y_P=\frac1M\sum_{i=1}^K n_i\bar Y_i,\qquad R_{i,t}=Y_{i,t}-\bar Y_i.$$

For each series $i=1,\ldots,K$, let $N_i=n_i-b_i+1$ and $k_i=\lceil n_i/b_i\rceil$. For every candidate start $j=1,\ldots,N_i$ and position $r=1,\ldots,b_i$, define the following arrays. In moving mode set $A_{i,j,r}=R_{i,j+r-1}$. In tapered mode set $A_{i,j,r}=a_{b_i}w_{b_i}(r)R_{i,j+r-1}$, with $a_{b_i}$ and $w_{b_i}$ as in [[alg-tapered-block-bootstrap]]. For each $i=1,\ldots,K$ and $s=1,\ldots,k_i$, draw independent uniform starts $J_{i,s}\in\{1,\ldots,N_i\}$, using the index law of [[alg-overlapping-block-resampling]]. For each within-block position define

$$c_{i,r}=\frac1{N_i}\sum_{j=1}^{N_i}A_{i,j,r}.$$

**Output:** for each $i$, a pseudo-series $Y^*_{i,1},\ldots,Y^*_{i,n_i}$. In the order $s=1,\ldots,k_i$, retain the positions $r=1,\ldots,q_{i,s}$, where $q_{i,s}=\min\{b_i,n_i-(s-1)b_i\}$, and set

$$Y^*_{i,(s-1)b_i+r}=\bar Y_P+A_{i,J_{i,s},r}-c_{i,r}.$$

Thus a divisible sample uses $k_i$ complete blocks; otherwise only the first $n_i-b_i\lfloor n_i/b_i\rfloor$ positions of the final block are retained. This centers each resampled residual position by its own conditional average, then gives every pseudo-series the same pooled location $\bar Y_P$. All block starts are conditionally independent across blocks and across series.

For fixed data and either mode of [[alg-k-sample-null-constrained-block-bootstrap]], every pseudo-observation in every series has conditional expectation $\bar Y_P$. Consequently, for each $i$,

$$E^*\bar Y_i^*=\bar Y_P,$$

so the conditional mean functions of the $K$ pseudo-series are equal.

Let $E$ be a separable complete metric space, let $\mathcal D_n$ be the sigma-algebra generated by the observed data at sample size $n$, and let $Z_n^*$ be a bootstrap random element whose remaining randomness is the resampling randomization. Write $\mathcal L^*(Z_n^*)$ for its conditional Borel probability law given $\mathcal D_n$. Supply as part of the data a metric $d_w$ on Borel probability measures on $E$ such that $d_w(\mu_n,\mu)\to0$ exactly when $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$ in the sense of [[def-weak-convergence-of-borel-probability-measures]]. Assume the displayed metric distance is a measurable real random variable. For a fixed Borel probability measure $\mu$ on $E$, we say that $Z_n^*$ converges conditionally weakly in probability to $\mu$ when

$$d_w\!\left(\mathcal L^*(Z_n^*),\mu\right)\longrightarrow 0\quad\hbox{in probability}.$$

The metric is supplied as a hypothesis; this definition makes no metric-existence assertion. It applies to separable complete metric spaces, including separable Banach spaces, their closed linear subspaces and finite products.

Let S,T be metric spaces, $g:S\to T$ measurable, and $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$. If the discontinuity set $D_g$ is $\mu$-null, then $g_*\mu_n\Rightarrow g_*\mu$. Consequently $X_n\Rightarrow X$ implies $g(X_n)\Rightarrow g(X)$ whenever $P_X(D_g)=0$.

For Borel probability measures $\mu_n,\mu$ on a metric space S, write $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$ if $\int f\,d\mu_n\to\int f\,d\mu$ for every bounded continuous real function f on S. Continuity is [[def-metric-continuity]]. Such f is Borel measurable (inverse images of open sets are open) and $\int|f|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\mu(S)<\infty$, so the integrals are finite in [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]. No completeness or coupling is required.

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a decreasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$. If $\mu(E_{n_0})<+\infty$ for some $n_0$, then

$$\mu\left(\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\inf_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

$X_n\to X$ in probability if and only if every subsequence of $(X_n)$ has a
further subsequence converging almost surely to $X$.

For Borel probabilities $\mu_n,\mu$ on a metric space S, the following are equivalent: (i) $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$; (ii) integrals converge for all bounded uniformly continuous real tests; (iii) $\limsup_n\mu_n(F)\le\mu(F)$ for every closed F; (iv) $\liminf_n\mu_n(G)\ge\mu(G)$ for every open G; (v) $\mu_n(A)\to\mu(A)$ for every Borel A with $\mu(\partial A)=0$.

derivations.claim: Since every pseudo-series has conditional mean $\bar Y_P$ by [F1]-[F2], that common location cancels in every contrast. Direct substitution gives $L_MU_M^*=\bigl(\sqrt M(\bar Y_i^*-\bar Y_K^*)\bigr)_{i=1}^{K-1}$ and $L_MU_M=\bigl(\sqrt M(\bar Y_i-\bar Y_K)\bigr)_{i=1}^{K-1}$. Thus the two statistics use the same contrast map; under the null the common population mean also cancels from $L_MU_M$.

Endow the finite products with their Hilbert product norms. The coefficients in $L_M$ converge to those of $L_\theta$, hence $a_M=\|L_M-L_\theta\|_{\mathrm{op}}\to0$. For $R>0$, the function $\chi_R(z)=\min\{1,\max\{0,\|z\|-R\}\}$ is bounded and continuous, vanishes when $\|z\|\le R$, and equals one when $\|z\|\ge R+1$. Thus [F5] and the given weak convergence imply $\limsup_M\Pr(\|U_M\|\ge R+1)\le E\chi_R(G)\le\Pr(\|G\|>R)\longrightarrow0\quad(R\to\infty).$ The last limit follows from continuity from above since $G$ has finite norm. Given $\delta>0$, eventually $a_M(R+1)\le\delta$, so $\Pr(\|(L_M-L_\theta)U_M\|>\delta)\le\Pr(\|U_M\|>R+1)$. First take the limit superior in $M$ and then let $R\to\infty$. Hence $(L_M-L_\theta)U_M\to0$ in probability, without a compact-tightness or AC premise. For the conditional discrepancy, every supplied compact $C\subset H^K$ is norm bounded, say by $R_C$. For arbitrary $\epsilon,\eta>0$, conditional tightness supplies such a $C$ with $\limsup_M\Pr\{\Pr^*(U_M^*\notin C)>\epsilon\}<\eta$. Eventually $a_MR_C\le\delta$, so $\Pr^*(\|(L_M-L_\theta)U_M^*\|>\delta)\le\Pr^*(U_M^*\notin C)$. Since $\eta$ is arbitrary, each conditional discrepancy probability tends to zero in probability.

By [F4], $L_\theta U_M\Rightarrow L_\theta G$. For a closed $B\subset H^{K-1}$, the sampling probability of $L_MU_M\in B$ is at most the discrepancy probability from step 2.1 plus $\Pr(L_\theta U_M\in B^\delta)$, where $B^\delta$ is the closed $\delta$-neighbourhood. Apply [F6] and let $\delta\downarrow0$ to obtain $L_MU_M\Rightarrow L_\theta G$. For the conditional version, combine the input weak-metric distance, truncated at one, with the weighted sum $\sum_{j\ge1}2^{-j}\Pr^*(\|(L_M-L_\theta)U_M^*\|>1/j)$. This scalar tends to zero in probability by truncation of the geometric tail and step 2.1. Every subsequence therefore has a further subsequence on which it tends to zero almost surely by [F6]. On each such outcome, [F4] gives weak convergence of the fixed-map conditional laws, and the same closed-neighbourhood inequality proves weak convergence of the varying-map conditional laws to $\mathcal L(L_\theta G)$.

Apply [F4] to $\Psi$ for the sampling convergence and, on every almost-sure subsequence outcome of step 3.1, for conditional convergence. Every bounded continuous $f:S\to\mathbb R$ then has convergent conditional expectations on those outcomes; [F6] gives their convergence in probability along the whole sequence. When the supplied output weak-convergence metric is available on separable complete $S$, the same outcome-wise weak convergence says its distance to the fixed limiting law tends to zero. Applying [F6] to that measurable scalar distance proves the metric conditional conclusion as well.

citations.quote:
Let $\mathcal B$ be the Borel sigma-algebra of $[0,1]$, generated by intervals with rational endpoints; let $dt$ be Lebesgue measure restricted to $\mathcal B$, and set $H=L^2([0,1],\mathcal B,dt;\mathbb R)$, with inner product $\langle x,y\rangle_H=\int_0^1x(u)y(u)\,du$. We use the quotient-by-null-functions convention for $L^2$ ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). The measure space is finite and countably generated, so under Countable Choice $H$ is separable ([[thm-l-p-of-a-sigma-finite-countably-generated-measure-space-is-separable]], [[def-countable-choice]], [[def-separable-space]]); [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]] verifies that this real pairing makes the quotient a Hilbert space.

Let $(S,\mathcal S,\nu)$ be a probability space and $(\delta_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ an independent identically distributed family of $S$-valued random elements with law $\nu$ ([[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]], [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]], [[def-independent-random-elements]]). A **causal Bernoulli shift** with innovation law $\nu$ is a process
$$X_t=f(\delta_t,\delta_{t-1},\delta_{t-2},\ldots),\qquad t\in\mathbb Z,$$
where $f:S^{\mathbb N_0}\to H$ is measurable from the product sigma-algebra $\mathcal S^{\otimes\mathbb N_0}$ to the Borel sigma-algebra of $H$. This product-measurability formulation is meaningful for a merely measurable innovation space $S$.

On an independent product extension, take replacement innovations $\delta'_{t,m,k}$, indexed by $t\in\mathbb Z$, $m\in\mathbb N_0$, and integers $k\le t-m$, all with law $\nu$, mutually independent, and independent of the original innovations. Such a countable family and its product with the original probability space exist under Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]], [[cor-countable-independent-copies-exist]], [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]). For $m\ge1$ define
$$X_{t,m}=f(\delta_t,\ldots,\delta_{t-m+1},\delta'_{t,m,t-m},\delta'_{t,m,t-m-1},\ldots),$$
and define the full replacement $X_{t,0}=f(\delta'_{t,0,t},\delta'_{t,0,t-1},\ldots)$. Each $X_{t,m}$ has the same marginal law as $X_t$; for fixed $m\ge1$ the sequence $(X_{t,m})_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ is strictly stationary and $m$-dependent because its original-innovation windows have length $m$ and its replacement arrays are independent across $t$.

For every fixed $m\ge0$, the joint process $(X_t,X_{t,m})_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ is strictly stationary: shifting all indices relabels a family of mutually independent innovations with the same law and commutes with the defining measurable maps. Consequently $D_{t,m}:=X_t-X_{t,m}$ is stationary and $\|D_{t,m}\|_{L^2(H)}=\delta_m$ for every $t$.

Write $\|X\|_{L^2(H)}=(\mathbb E\|X\|_H^2)^{1/2}$ and
$$\delta_m=\|X_0-X_{0,m}\|_{L^2(H)},\qquad m\ge0.$$
The process is **$L^2$-$m$-approximable** when
$$\mathbb E\|X_0\|_H^2<\infty\qquad\hbox{and}\qquad\sum_{m\ge1}\delta_m<\infty.$$
The same marginal law gives $\delta_0\le2\|X_0\|_{L^2(H)}<\infty$. For a Bochner-integrable $H$-valued random element $Y$, write $\mathbb E_B Y=\int Y\,d\mathbb P$; the moment condition makes $X_t$ and every $X_{t,m}$ Bochner integrable ([[def-bochner-integrable-function]], [[thm-bochner-integrability-criterion]]).

Here **strict stationarity** means invariance of every finite-dimensional law under integer shifts. A process is **$m$-dependent** if, for every $a\in\mathbb Z$, the sigma-algebras generated by $(X_s)_{s\le a}$ and $(X_s)_{s\ge a+m+1}$ are independent ([[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]]). The stated input windows for $X_{t,m}$ are disjoint across these two index ranges, so they satisfy this definition.

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(f_n)$ be nonnegative measurable functions. Then
$$\int \liminf_{n\to\infty}f_n\,d\mu\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int f_n\,d\mu.$$

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

Let $\mu$ be a measure and let $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be measurable. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k).$$

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ one also has

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k<m}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k<m}\mu(E_k),$$

including $m=0$, where both sides are $0$.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

derivations.claim: Fix $m$. Write the innovation input as $(A,B)$, with $A$ its first $m$ coordinates and $B$ its remaining tail. Its law is a product by [F2]. The replacement uses $(A,B')$, where $B,B'$ have the same tail law and are independent of one another and of $A$. To construct the conditional mean without assuming a vector conditional-expectation theorem, take finite-valued measurable approximants $f_j(A,B)$ to the filter $f(A,B)$ with $\|f_j-f\|_{L^2(H)}\le2^{-2j}$. They exist explicitly: include zero in a fixed dense sequence in $H$, use the first nearest point among its first $N$ points, and let $N$ increase. The error is at most $\|f\|$ and tends pointwise to zero, so [F3] gives $L^2$ convergence; choose the first $N$ achieving the indicated bound. For each finite-valued $f_j$, its tail average $g_j(A)=\int f_j(A,b)\,\nu_{\rm tail}(db)$ is a finite linear combination of measurable section probabilities, hence is measurable by [F2]. Convexity of the squared Hilbert norm for finite averages, extended by simple scalar integration, gives $\mathbb E\|g_j-g_k\|^2\le\mathbb E\|f_j-f_k\|^2$.

The last inequality implies $\sum_j\mathbb E\|g_{j+1}-g_j\|<\infty$, by [F3] and the chosen error bounds. Tonelli [F2] makes the sum of these norms finite almost surely. Completeness of $H$ gives a measurable pointwise limit $g_m$, set to zero on the null complement. Fatou [F3], applied to $\|g_j-g_k\|^2$ as $k\to\infty$, gives $g_j\to g_m$ in $L^2(H)$. In particular $g_m$ is square integrable. For finite-valued $\mathcal F_m$-measurable $Y$, finite sums and the section-integral identity give $\mathbb E\langle f_j(A,B),Y\rangle=\mathbb E\langle g_j(A),Y\rangle$. Pass to the limit by Cauchy–Schwarz. Approximate any square-integrable $\mathcal F_m$-measurable $Y$ by its finite nearest-point approximants as in step 1.1, and pass to the limit again. Thus $\mathbb E\langle X-g_m,Y\rangle=0$ for every such $Y$, which is the conditional-mean identity and implies $\mathbb E\|X-Y\|^2=\mathbb E\|X-g_m\|^2+\mathbb E\|g_m-Y\|^2.$ This proves the stated minimization, without a regular conditional law on the innovation space.

Conditional product integration for the two copies of the finite-valued $f_j$ gives $\mathbb E\langle f_j(A,B),f_j(A,B')\rangle=\mathbb E\|g_j(A)\|^2$. Passing to the $L^2$ limits by [F3] and Hilbert-space Cauchy–Schwarz [F4] gives $\mathbb E\langle X,X_{0,m}\rangle=\mathbb E\|g_m\|^2$. The two copies have the same second moment by [F1]. Expanding their squared difference therefore yields $\delta_m^2=2(\mathbb E\|X\|^2-\mathbb E\|g_m\|^2)=2\mathbb E\|X-g_m\|^2$, the final equality also following from step 2.1 with $Y=g_m$. The sigma-fields increase with $m$, so every $\mathcal F_m$-measurable competitor is an $\mathcal F_{m+1}$-measurable competitor. The minimum residual squared norm cannot increase; hence $\delta_{m+1}\le\delta_m$.

For $m\ge2$, monotonicity gives $\lfloor m/2\rfloor\delta_m\le\sum_{j=\lceil m/2\rceil}^{m}\delta_j$. If the full nonnegative series is summable, its right-hand tail tends to zero. Since $m/\lfloor m/2\rfloor\le3$, this implies $m\delta_m\to0$. Thus the rate-separation example requested in the former design cannot exist under the actual independent-tail replacement convention. This is a proved implication, not an absence of a known counterexample.

Write $\|X\|_{L^2(H)}=(\mathbb E\|X\|_H^2)^{1/2}$ and
$$\delta_m=\|X_0-X_{0,m}\|_{L^2(H)},\qquad m\ge0.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H=L^2([0,1],dt;\mathbb R)$ and let
$(X_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ be a centered, $L^2$-$m$-approximable causal
Bernoulli shift as defined in
[[def-l2-m-approximable-causal-bernoulli-shift]], with Bochner mean
$\mathbb E_BX_0=0$. Let $\Gamma$ be its long-run covariance operator from
[[lem-long-run-covariance-is-trace-class]], and let $G$ be a centered
$H$-valued Gaussian random element with covariance $\Gamma$, whose existence
is given by [[lem-positive-trace-class-covariance-defines-hilbert-gaussian]].
Then, for $S_n=\sum_{t=1}^nX_t$,
$$n^{-1/2}S_n\ \Rightarrow\ G$$
in the weak topology of Borel probability measures on $H$. The covariance
kernel is the $L^2([0,1]^2)$ equivalence class $c$ in the long-run covariance
lemma, and its integral operator is $T_c=\Gamma$. This is a CLT for the
$H$-valued sample sums; it is not a functional CLT for the time-indexed
partial-sum process.

**Input:** observations $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ in a real Hilbert space $H$, and an integer block length $b$ with $1\le b\le n$.

**Output:** a pseudo-series $X_1^*,\ldots,X_n^*$, generated by [[alg-overlapping-block-resampling]]: within each selected block retain the original order and concatenate blocks in their draw order, truncating only the last block when $b\nmid n$. The conditional bootstrap sample mean is $\bar X_n^*=n^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^nX_t^*$. Its conditional center is $E^*\bar X_n^*$, where $E^*$ averages over the independent uniform block starts while the observations remain fixed.

This algorithm specifies the resampling law only. It does not assert that the conditional law approximates the sampling law for any data-generating process or block-length regime.

Under [[def-resampling-sampling-unit-contract]], take each observation $x_t$ to be a complete time-indexed unit record. Each draw selects an ordered group of $b$ consecutive records; the output retains every record of each complete block and only the initial $r=n-b\lfloor n/b\rfloor$ records of the final block when $r>0$. Thus selected length-$b$ groups are not declared indivisible sampling units. Unit compatibility for a stated target requires that block boundaries and final truncation do not split any bundle declared indivisible by that target's sampling or assignment design. This is the sampling-unit interface, not a bootstrap-validity result.

Fix a positive integer $n$, observations $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in H$, and an integer block length $b$ with $1\le b\le n$. Put $N=n-b+1$, $k=\lfloor n/b\rfloor$, and $r=n-kb$. For $q\in\{b\}$, and also $q=r$ when $r>0$, define

$$S_j^{(q)}=\sum_{\ell=1}^q x_{j+\ell-1},\qquad \bar S_q=N^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^N S_j^{(q)},\qquad C_q=N^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^N(S_j^{(q)}-\bar S_q)\otimes(S_j^{(q)}-\bar S_q).$$

Set $C_0=0$. If $\bar X_n^*$ is the mean produced by [[alg-moving-block-bootstrap]], then its conditional covariance operator is

$$n\,\operatorname{Cov}^*(\bar X_n^*)=\frac{kC_b+C_r}{n},$$

where the $C_r$ term is zero when $r=0$. Here $\operatorname{Cov}^*(Z)=E^*[(Z-E^*Z)\otimes(Z-E^*Z)]$.

$$K=\sigma^2+2\sigma\sum_{h\ge1}\delta_h.$$

For every integer $b\ge1$, let $c_{b,1},\ldots,c_{b,b}$ be deterministic real weights, uniformly bounded in absolute value by $A<\infty$. Define

$$Z_{j,b}=b^{-1/2}\sum_{\ell=1}^b c_{b,\ell}X_{j+\ell-1}.$$

Then $\{\|Z_{j,b}\|_H^2:j\in\mathbb Z,b\ge1\}$ is uniformly integrable, and for $0\le q\le b$,

$$E\left\|\sum_{\ell=1}^q c_{b,\ell}X_{j+\ell-1}\right\|_H^2\le A^2Kq.$$

If $P$ is any finite-rank orthogonal projection, $R=I-P$ and $\alpha_P=\|RX_0\|_{L^2(H)}$, then also

$$E\left\|\sum_{\ell=1}^q c_{b,\ell}RX_{j+\ell-1}\right\|_H^2\le A^2q\left(\alpha_P^2+2\alpha_P\sum_{h\ge1}\delta_h\right).$$

$$E\|\bar Z_{n,b}\|_H^2\le A^2Kb/N.$$

$$b^{-1}\sum_{\ell=1}^bc_{b,\ell}^2=1,\qquad q_b(h):=b^{-1}\sum_{\ell=1}^{b-h}c_{b,\ell}c_{b,\ell+h}\longrightarrow1\quad\text{for every fixed }h\ge0.$$

$$E\left\|N^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^N(Z_{j,b}-\bar Z_{n,b})\otimes(Z_{j,b}-\bar Z_{n,b})-\Gamma\right\|_1\longrightarrow0.$$

Both the MBB weights $c_{b,\ell}=1$ and the actual TBB weights $c_{b,\ell}=a_bw((\ell-\tfrac12)/b)$ satisfy these weight hypotheses for all sufficiently large $b$. Assume AC and all the process and weight hypotheses of [[lem-weighted-overlapping-block-moment-and-covariance-limits]], including squared normalization and convergence of each fixed-lag weight autocorrelation to one. Let $b=b_n\to\infty$ with $b/\sqrt n\to0$, $N=n-b+1$, $k=\lfloor n/b\rfloor$, $r=n-kb$, and

$$B_{j,q}=\sum_{\ell=1}^q c_{b,\ell}X_{j+\ell-1},\qquad \bar B_q=N^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^NB_{j,q},\qquad C_q=N^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^N(B_{j,q}-\bar B_q)\otimes(B_{j,q}-\bar B_q),$$

with $B_{j,0}=\bar B_0=C_0=0$. Conditional on the observations choose independent uniform starts $J_1,\ldots,J_{k+1}$ in $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ and set

$$Z_n^*=n^{-1/2}\left\{\sum_{s=1}^k(B_{J_s,b}-\bar B_b)+(B_{J_{k+1},r}-\bar B_r)\right\}.$$

Then, for the centered Hilbert Gaussian $G$ of covariance $\Gamma$,

$$\mathcal L^*(Z_n^*)\Rightarrow\mathcal L(G)\quad\hbox{in probability},\qquad \left\|\operatorname{Cov}^*(Z_n^*)-\Gamma\right\|_1\longrightarrow0\quad\hbox{in probability}.$$

Trace-norm convergence implies convergence in Hilbert-Schmidt norm as well. The conditional laws are tight in probability: for every $\varepsilon,\eta>0$ there is a deterministic compact $K\subset H$ such that $\limsup_nP\{P^*(Z_n^*\notin K)>\varepsilon\}<\eta$. The complete blocks satisfy conditional Lindeberg, and the final partial block has $E E^*\|n^{-1/2}(B_{J_{k+1},r}-\bar B_r)\|^2=O(b/n)$. Replacing every $X_t$ by $X_t-M_n$ for any common data-dependent $M_n\in H$ leaves $Z_n^*$ and all its conditional covariances unchanged.

Use the actual independent-tail replacement construction of [[def-l2-m-approximable-causal-bernoulli-shift]], and put $X=X_0$, $\mathcal F_m=\sigma(\delta_0,\ldots,\delta_{-m+1})$ and $\delta_m=(\mathbb E\|X-X_{0,m}\|_H^2)^{1/2}$. There is an $\mathcal F_m$-measurable square-integrable conditional mean $g_m$ such that
$$\delta_m^2=2\mathbb E\|X-g_m\|_H^2.$$
The conditional mean minimizes $\mathbb E\|X-Y\|_H^2$ over all square-integrable $\mathcal F_m$-measurable $H$-valued $Y$. Consequently $\delta_{m+1}\le\delta_m$ for every $m\ge1$, and
$$\sum_{m\ge1}\delta_m<\infty\quad\Longrightarrow\quad m\delta_m\longrightarrow0.$$
In particular no process under this replacement definition has summable replacement errors while failing the displayed rate condition.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Take $c_{b,\ell}=1$ for $1\le\ell\le b$. These weights are bounded by one, have $b^{-1}\sum_\ell c_{b,\ell}^2=1$, and for each fixed $h\ge0$ have $b^{-1}\sum_{\ell=1}^{b-h}c_{b,\ell}c_{b,\ell+h}=(1-h/b)_+\to1$. By [F5], the process satisfies the rate needed in [F4], and the given block regime supplies its remaining asymptotic condition.

Write $n=kb+r$, $0\le r<b$. Subtracting the conditional mean from the sum of the $k$ complete sampled blocks and the sampled length-$r$ prefix gives exactly the variable $Z_n^*$ in the conditional-block supplier. The candidate starts for both block sizes are the same $N=n-b+1$ starts, as required by [F3]. Hence [F4] gives the asserted conditional law and trace-norm covariance convergence. The Hilbert-Schmidt conclusion follows from $\|T\|_{\mathrm{HS}}\le\|T\|_1$; the covariance in question is exactly $n\operatorname{Cov}^*(\bar X_n^*)$ by [F3]. The remainder has expected conditional squared norm $O(b/n)$, so no divisibility condition is used.

Fix the sampling-law Gaussian $G$ supplied by [F2]. The conditional-block result [F4] applies with this same centered Gaussian, whose covariance is $\Gamma$. This proves both stated limits. [F2, F4, step 2.1] ∎

Let $\mathcal B$ be the Borel sigma-algebra of $[0,1]$, generated by intervals with rational endpoints; let $dt$ be Lebesgue measure restricted to $\mathcal B$, and set $H=L^2([0,1],\mathcal B,dt;\mathbb R)$, with inner product $\langle x,y\rangle_H=\int_0^1x(u)y(u)\,du$. We use the quotient-by-null-functions convention for $L^2$ ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). The measure space is finite and countably generated, so under Countable Choice $H$ is separable ([[thm-l-p-of-a-sigma-finite-countably-generated-measure-space-is-separable]], [[def-countable-choice]], [[def-separable-space]]); [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]] verifies that this real pairing makes the quotient a Hilbert space.

Let $(S,\mathcal S,\nu)$ be a probability space and $(\delta_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ an independent identically distributed family of $S$-valued random elements with law $\nu$ ([[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]], [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]], [[def-independent-random-elements]]). A **causal Bernoulli shift** with innovation law $\nu$ is a process
$$X_t=f(\delta_t,\delta_{t-1},\delta_{t-2},\ldots),\qquad t\in\mathbb Z,$$
where $f:S^{\mathbb N_0}\to H$ is measurable from the product sigma-algebra $\mathcal S^{\otimes\mathbb N_0}$ to the Borel sigma-algebra of $H$. This product-measurability formulation is meaningful for a merely measurable innovation space $S$.

On an independent product extension, take replacement innovations $\delta'_{t,m,k}$, indexed by $t\in\mathbb Z$, $m\in\mathbb N_0$, and integers $k\le t-m$, all with law $\nu$, mutually independent, and independent of the original innovations. Such a countable family and its product with the original probability space exist under Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]], [[cor-countable-independent-copies-exist]], [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]). For $m\ge1$ define
$$X_{t,m}=f(\delta_t,\ldots,\delta_{t-m+1},\delta'_{t,m,t-m},\delta'_{t,m,t-m-1},\ldots),$$
and define the full replacement $X_{t,0}=f(\delta'_{t,0,t},\delta'_{t,0,t-1},\ldots)$. Each $X_{t,m}$ has the same marginal law as $X_t$; for fixed $m\ge1$ the sequence $(X_{t,m})_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ is strictly stationary and $m$-dependent because its original-innovation windows have length $m$ and its replacement arrays are independent across $t$.

For every fixed $m\ge0$, the joint process $(X_t,X_{t,m})_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ is strictly stationary: shifting all indices relabels a family of mutually independent innovations with the same law and commutes with the defining measurable maps. Consequently $D_{t,m}:=X_t-X_{t,m}$ is stationary and $\|D_{t,m}\|_{L^2(H)}=\delta_m$ for every $t$.

Write $\|X\|_{L^2(H)}=(\mathbb E\|X\|_H^2)^{1/2}$ and
$$\delta_m=\|X_0-X_{0,m}\|_{L^2(H)},\qquad m\ge0.$$
The process is **$L^2$-$m$-approximable** when
$$\mathbb E\|X_0\|_H^2<\infty\qquad\hbox{and}\qquad\sum_{m\ge1}\delta_m<\infty.$$
The same marginal law gives $\delta_0\le2\|X_0\|_{L^2(H)}<\infty$. For a Bochner-integrable $H$-valued random element $Y$, write $\mathbb E_B Y=\int Y\,d\mathbb P$; the moment condition makes $X_t$ and every $X_{t,m}$ Bochner integrable ([[def-bochner-integrable-function]], [[thm-bochner-integrability-criterion]]).

Here **strict stationarity** means invariance of every finite-dimensional law under integer shifts. A process is **$m$-dependent** if, for every $a\in\mathbb Z$, the sigma-algebras generated by $(X_s)_{s\le a}$ and $(X_s)_{s\ge a+m+1}$ are independent ([[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]]). The stated input windows for $X_{t,m}$ are disjoint across these two index ranges, so they satisfy this definition.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H=L^2([0,1],dt;\mathbb R)$ and let
$(X_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ be a centered, $L^2$-$m$-approximable causal
Bernoulli shift as defined in
[[def-l2-m-approximable-causal-bernoulli-shift]], with Bochner mean
$\mathbb E_BX_0=0$. Let $\Gamma$ be its long-run covariance operator from
[[lem-long-run-covariance-is-trace-class]], and let $G$ be a centered
$H$-valued Gaussian random element with covariance $\Gamma$, whose existence
is given by [[lem-positive-trace-class-covariance-defines-hilbert-gaussian]].
Then, for $S_n=\sum_{t=1}^nX_t$,
$$n^{-1/2}S_n\ \Rightarrow\ G$$
in the weak topology of Borel probability measures on $H$. The covariance
kernel is the $L^2([0,1]^2)$ equivalence class $c$ in the long-run covariance
lemma, and its integral operator is $T_c=\Gamma$. This is a CLT for the
$H$-valued sample sums; it is not a functional CLT for the time-indexed
partial-sum process.

**Input:** observations $Y_1,\ldots,Y_n$ in a real Hilbert space $H$, an integer $1\le b\le n$, and a window $w:\mathbb R\to[0,1]$ that vanishes off $[0,1]$, is positive on a neighbourhood of $1/2$, satisfies $w(1-u)=w(u)$, and is nondecreasing on $[0,1/2]$. Put $w_b(r)=w((r-\tfrac12)/b)$ for $1\le r\le b$, $W_b=(\sum_{r=1}^bw_b(r)^2)^{1/2}$, and $a_b=\sqrt b/W_b$. The procedure is admissible only when $W_b>0$.

**Center and taper:** set $\bar Y_n=n^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^nY_t$ and $R_t=Y_t-\bar Y_n$. For each start $j\in\{1,\ldots,n-b+1\}$, form the block

$$\bigl(a_bw_b(1)R_j,\ldots,a_bw_b(b)R_{j+b-1}\bigr).$$

**Resample:** use the independent uniform block starts from [[alg-overlapping-block-resampling]], multiply each selected centered observation by its within-block taper and the factor $a_b$, concatenate in draw order, and retain the first $n$ entries. The conditional bootstrap mean is centered by its own conditional expectation when used to approximate the sampling law of $\sqrt n\,\bar Y_n$.

The factor $a_b$ compensates for the window's squared-weight sum in the block-sum variance calculation; this definition alone gives no bootstrap validity result.

For a dependent time series, the selected length-$b$ consecutive run is the resampling unit under [[def-resampling-sampling-unit-contract]]. The taper changes each unit record's within-block weight but the whole block is selected and resampled together; validity remains a separate theorem.

Fix a positive integer $n$, observations $Y_1,\ldots,Y_n\in H$, an integer block length $b$ with $1\le b\le n$ and $W_b>0$, and the taper and scale $w_b,a_b$ from [[alg-tapered-block-bootstrap]]. Set $R_t=Y_t-\bar Y_n$, $N=n-b+1$, $k=\lfloor n/b\rfloor$, and $r=n-kb$. For $q=b$, and also $q=r$ when $r>0$, define the tapered partial block sum

$$T_j^{(q)}=a_b\sum_{\ell=1}^q w_b(\ell)R_{j+\ell-1},\qquad \bar T_q=N^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^N T_j^{(q)},\qquad V_q=N^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^N(T_j^{(q)}-\bar T_q)\otimes(T_j^{(q)}-\bar T_q).$$

Set $V_0=0$. If $\bar X_n^*$ is the tapered bootstrap mean, then

$$n\,\operatorname{Cov}^*(\bar X_n^*)=\frac{kV_b+V_r}{n},$$

with the $V_r$ term zero when $r=0$.

Let $w$ satisfy the taper conditions in [[alg-tapered-block-bootstrap]]. As the positive integer $b\to\infty$, $w^2$ is Riemann integrable on $[0,1]$, and

$$\frac{1}{b}\sum_{j=1}^b w\!\left(\frac{j-\tfrac12}{b}\right)^2\longrightarrow I_w:=\int_0^1 w(u)^2\,du>0.$$

Consequently, $W_b>0$ for all sufficiently large $b$ and $a_b=\sqrt b/W_b\to I_w^{-1/2}$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(X_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ be a centered $L^2$-$m$-approximable causal Bernoulli shift in $H=L^2([0,1];\mathbb R)$ under [[def-l2-m-approximable-causal-bernoulli-shift]], and suppose additionally that $m\delta_m\to0$. Put $\sigma=\|X_0\|_{L^2(H)}$, let $\Gamma$ be its long-run covariance operator, and put

$$K=\sigma^2+2\sigma\sum_{h\ge1}\delta_h.$$

For every integer $b\ge1$, let $c_{b,1},\ldots,c_{b,b}$ be deterministic real weights, uniformly bounded in absolute value by $A<\infty$. Define

$$Z_{j,b}=b^{-1/2}\sum_{\ell=1}^b c_{b,\ell}X_{j+\ell-1}.$$

Then $\{\|Z_{j,b}\|_H^2:j\in\mathbb Z,b\ge1\}$ is uniformly integrable, and for $0\le q\le b$,

$$E\left\|\sum_{\ell=1}^q c_{b,\ell}X_{j+\ell-1}\right\|_H^2\le A^2Kq.$$

If $P$ is any finite-rank orthogonal projection, $R=I-P$ and $\alpha_P=\|RX_0\|_{L^2(H)}$, then also

$$E\left\|\sum_{\ell=1}^q c_{b,\ell}RX_{j+\ell-1}\right\|_H^2\le A^2q\left(\alpha_P^2+2\alpha_P\sum_{h\ge1}\delta_h\right).$$

For $n\ge b$, set $N=n-b+1$ and $\bar Z_{n,b}=N^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^NZ_{j,b}$. Then

$$E\|\bar Z_{n,b}\|_H^2\le A^2Kb/N.$$

Suppose further that $b=b_n\to\infty$, $b_n/n\to0$, and the weights satisfy

$$b^{-1}\sum_{\ell=1}^bc_{b,\ell}^2=1,\qquad q_b(h):=b^{-1}\sum_{\ell=1}^{b-h}c_{b,\ell}c_{b,\ell+h}\longrightarrow1\quad\text{for every fixed }h\ge0.$$

The centered overlapping-block covariance then satisfies the stronger $L^1$ trace-norm limit

$$E\left\|N^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^N(Z_{j,b}-\bar Z_{n,b})\otimes(Z_{j,b}-\bar Z_{n,b})-\Gamma\right\|_1\longrightarrow0.$$

In particular it converges in probability in trace norm. Both the MBB weights $c_{b,\ell}=1$ and the actual TBB weights $c_{b,\ell}=a_bw((\ell-\tfrac12)/b)$ satisfy these weight hypotheses for all sufficiently large $b$. For any complete finite or countable orthonormal basis and its initial-coordinate projections $P_d$, the projection-tail coefficient $\alpha_{P_d}^2+2\alpha_{P_d}\sum_{h\ge1}\delta_h$ tends to zero as $d\to\infty$.

Assume AC and all the process and weight hypotheses of [[lem-weighted-overlapping-block-moment-and-covariance-limits]], including squared normalization and convergence of each fixed-lag weight autocorrelation to one. Let $b=b_n\to\infty$ with $b/\sqrt n\to0$, $N=n-b+1$, $k=\lfloor n/b\rfloor$, $r=n-kb$, and

$$B_{j,q}=\sum_{\ell=1}^q c_{b,\ell}X_{j+\ell-1},\qquad \bar B_q=N^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^NB_{j,q},\qquad C_q=N^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^N(B_{j,q}-\bar B_q)\otimes(B_{j,q}-\bar B_q),$$

with $B_{j,0}=\bar B_0=C_0=0$. Conditional on the observations choose independent uniform starts $J_1,\ldots,J_{k+1}$ in $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ and set

$$Z_n^*=n^{-1/2}\left\{\sum_{s=1}^k(B_{J_s,b}-\bar B_b)+(B_{J_{k+1},r}-\bar B_r)\right\}.$$

Then, for the centered Hilbert Gaussian $G$ of covariance $\Gamma$,

$$\mathcal L^*(Z_n^*)\Rightarrow\mathcal L(G)\quad\hbox{in probability},\qquad \left\|\operatorname{Cov}^*(Z_n^*)-\Gamma\right\|_1\longrightarrow0\quad\hbox{in probability}.$$

Trace-norm convergence implies convergence in Hilbert-Schmidt norm as well. The conditional laws are tight in probability: for every $\varepsilon,\eta>0$ there is a deterministic compact $K\subset H$ such that $\limsup_nP\{P^*(Z_n^*\notin K)>\varepsilon\}<\eta$. The complete blocks satisfy conditional Lindeberg, and the final partial block has $E E^*\|n^{-1/2}(B_{J_{k+1},r}-\bar B_r)\|^2=O(b/n)$. Replacing every $X_t$ by $X_t-M_n$ for any common data-dependent $M_n\in H$ leaves $Z_n^*$ and all its conditional covariances unchanged.

Use the actual independent-tail replacement construction of [[def-l2-m-approximable-causal-bernoulli-shift]], and put $X=X_0$, $\mathcal F_m=\sigma(\delta_0,\ldots,\delta_{-m+1})$ and $\delta_m=(\mathbb E\|X-X_{0,m}\|_H^2)^{1/2}$. There is an $\mathcal F_m$-measurable square-integrable conditional mean $g_m$ such that
$$\delta_m^2=2\mathbb E\|X-g_m\|_H^2.$$
The conditional mean minimizes $\mathbb E\|X-Y\|_H^2$ over all square-integrable $\mathcal F_m$-measurable $H$-valued $Y$. Consequently $\delta_{m+1}\le\delta_m$ for every $m\ge1$, and
$$\sum_{m\ge1}\delta_m<\infty\quad\Longrightarrow\quad m\delta_m\longrightarrow0.$$
In particular no process under this replacement definition has summable replacement errors while failing the displayed rate condition.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
