derivations.claim: Set $c_{b,\ell}=a_bw((\ell-1/2)/b)$ and extend this finite sequence by zero on all other integer indices. The exact normalization gives $b^{-1}\sum_\ell c_{b,\ell}^2=1$, and [F4] bounds its maximum by a constant $A$ for sufficiently large $b$. Symmetry and monotonicity of $w$ make the sequence nonnegative and unimodal, including the possible equal central pair; hence its discrete total variation, including both exterior zero tails, is at most $2A$. For every fixed integer $h\ge1$, telescoping $h$ successive shifts gives $\sum_{\ell\in\mathbb Z}|c_{b,\ell+h}-c_{b,\ell}|\le2Ah$. Therefore $\left|b^{-1}\sum_{\ell=1}^{b-h}c_{b,\ell}c_{b,\ell+h}-1\right|\le\frac{A}{b}\sum_{\ell\in\mathbb Z}|c_{b,\ell+h}-c_{b,\ell}|\le\frac{2A^2h}{b}\longrightarrow0.$ This verifies every weight hypothesis of [F5], even for discontinuous monotone tapers. By [F6], the process satisfies the replacement-error rate needed by [F5].

For each full or partial weighted block, replacing $Y_t$ by $Y_t-\bar Y_n$ subtracts $(\sum_{\ell=1}^qc_{b,\ell})\bar Y_n$ from every candidate block with $q$ entries. Its empirical conditional center over the $N=n-b+1$ starts subtracts the same vector, so all conditionally centered block sums agree exactly with those formed from $Y_t$. Thus $\sqrt n(\bar Y_n^*-E^*\bar Y_n^*)$ is precisely $Z_n^*$ in [F5], with the full-taper prefix weights on its last $r=n-b\lfloor n/b\rfloor$ entries.

Apply [F5] with the sampling-law Gaussian $G$ supplied by [F2]. It gives conditional weak convergence to that same $G$, conditional tightness, and convergence of the exact covariance $n\operatorname{Cov}^*(\bar Y_n^*)$ in trace norm, which implies its stated Hilbert-Schmidt convergence. The final prefix has expected conditional squared norm $O(b/n)$ and is negligible without requiring $b\mid n$. Its limiting covariance $\Gamma$ is the sampling target in [F2], completing both claims. [F2, F3, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

**Input:** observations $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ in a real Hilbert space $H$, and an integer block length $b$ with $1\le b\le n$.

**Output:** a pseudo-series $X_1^*,\ldots,X_n^*$, generated by [[alg-overlapping-block-resampling]]: within each selected block retain the original order and concatenate blocks in their draw order, truncating only the last block when $b\nmid n$. The conditional bootstrap sample mean is $\bar X_n^*=n^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^nX_t^*$. Its conditional center is $E^*\bar X_n^*$, where $E^*$ averages over the independent uniform block starts while the observations remain fixed.

This algorithm specifies the resampling law only. It does not assert that the conditional law approximates the sampling law for any data-generating process or block-length regime.

Under [[def-resampling-sampling-unit-contract]], take each observation $x_t$ to be a complete time-indexed unit record. Each draw selects an ordered group of $b$ consecutive records; the output retains every record of each complete block and only the initial $r=n-b\lfloor n/b\rfloor$ records of the final block when $r>0$. Thus selected length-$b$ groups are not declared indivisible sampling units. Unit compatibility for a stated target requires that block boundaries and final truncation do not split any bundle declared indivisible by that target's sampling or assignment design. This is the sampling-unit interface, not a bootstrap-validity result.

derivations.claim: At the first position of a selected block, the conditional average over starts is $(0+1+2)/3=1$. At the second position it is $(1+2+3)/3=2$.

The output mean is the average of two first-position values and two second-position values, so its conditional expectation is $(1+2)/2=3/2$, which equals the observed sample mean. The resampled blocks preserve each adjacent pair inside its chosen block; only the join between blocks can alter adjacency.

Example has three distinct blocks, so each start is random; the conditional sample mean takes values 1/2,1,3/2,2,5/2 and is not deterministic.
Example candidate starts are 1,2,3; start 3 selects (2,3) and ends exactly at the fourth observation, with no wraparound.

**Input:** observations $Y_1,\ldots,Y_n$ in a real Hilbert space $H$, an integer $1\le b\le n$, and a window $w:\mathbb R\to[0,1]$ that vanishes off $[0,1]$, is positive on a neighbourhood of $1/2$, satisfies $w(1-u)=w(u)$, and is nondecreasing on $[0,1/2]$. Put $w_b(r)=w((r-\tfrac12)/b)$ for $1\le r\le b$, $W_b=(\sum_{r=1}^bw_b(r)^2)^{1/2}$, and $a_b=\sqrt b/W_b$. The procedure is admissible only when $W_b>0$.

**Center and taper:** set $\bar Y_n=n^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^nY_t$ and $R_t=Y_t-\bar Y_n$. For each start $j\in\{1,\ldots,n-b+1\}$, form the block

$$\bigl(a_bw_b(1)R_j,\ldots,a_bw_b(b)R_{j+b-1}\bigr).$$

**Resample:** use the independent uniform block starts from [[alg-overlapping-block-resampling]], multiply each selected centered observation by its within-block taper and the factor $a_b$, concatenate in draw order, and retain the first $n$ entries. The conditional bootstrap mean is centered by its own conditional expectation when used to approximate the sampling law of $\sqrt n\,\bar Y_n$.

The factor $a_b$ compensates for the window's squared-weight sum in the block-sum variance calculation; this definition alone gives no bootstrap validity result.

For a dependent time series, the selected length-$b$ consecutive run is the resampling unit under [[def-resampling-sampling-unit-contract]]. The taper changes each unit record's within-block weight but the whole block is selected and resampled together; validity remains a separate theorem.

Let $w$ satisfy the taper conditions in [[alg-tapered-block-bootstrap]]. As the positive integer $b\to\infty$, $w^2$ is Riemann integrable on $[0,1]$, and

$$\frac{1}{b}\sum_{j=1}^b w\!\left(\frac{j-\tfrac12}{b}\right)^2\longrightarrow I_w:=\int_0^1 w(u)^2\,du>0.$$

Consequently, $W_b>0$ for all sufficiently large $b$ and $a_b=\sqrt b/W_b\to I_w^{-1/2}$.

derivations.claim: The scaled within-block weights are therefore $(\sqrt{3/11},3\sqrt{3/11},\sqrt{3/11})$. Their squared sum is $\frac{3+27+3}{11}=3$, equal to $b$, as required by the normalization $a_b^2W_b^2=b$.

**Input:** a finite sequence $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ in a measurable space, with $n\ge1$, and an integer block length $b$ satisfying $1\le b\le n$. Set $N=n-b+1$ and $k=\lceil n/b\rceil$.

**Randomization:** draw $J_1,\ldots,J_k$ independently and uniformly from $\{1,\ldots,N\}$.

**Output:** in order $s=1,\ldots,k$, append the block $x_{J_s},x_{J_s+1},\ldots,x_{J_s+b-1}$, then retain the first $n$ entries of the concatenation. Thus the final selected block is truncated to its first $r=n-b\lfloor n/b\rfloor$ entries when $r>0$. Conditional expectation given the input sequence means expectation over the indices $J_s$ alone.

derivations.claim: Since $n^{1/3}\le b_n<n^{1/3}+1$, $b_n\to\infty$, and $b_n$ is a positive integer. For every integer $n\ge1$, $n^{1/3}\le n$; since $n$ itself is an integer, taking the least integer above $n^{1/3}$ gives $b_n\le n$. Thus the block length is admissible at every positive sample size.
Dividing the same bounds by $\sqrt n$ gives $0\le b_n/\sqrt n<n^{-1/6}+n^{-1/2}\to0$. Thus $b_n^{-1}+b_nn^{-1/2}\to0$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Assume AC. If $X$ has law $N(m,\sigma^2)$ with $\sigma\ge0$, then $\varphi_X(t)=\exp(imt-\sigma^2t^2/2)$ for every real $t$. Moreover $\mathbb EX=m$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\sigma^2$, including $\sigma=0$.

For real $a,b,t$, $\varphi_{aX+b}(t)=e^{itb}\varphi_X(at)$. For a finite mutually independent family $(X_j)_{j=1}^n$ of real random variables, $\varphi_{\sum_jX_j}(t)=\prod_j\varphi_{X_j}(t)$. The empty sum has characteristic function one.

Assume AC. Two Borel probability laws on $\mathbb R$ with equal characteristic functions are equal. In particular a real random variable has a real-valued characteristic function if and only if its law is symmetric under $x\mapsto-x$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. If $0\le s,t$ and a real random variable
$X_t-X_s$ has law $N(0,|t-s|)$, then, for every integer $m\ge1$,
$$E|X_t-X_s|^{2m}=c_m|t-s|^m,$$
where
$$c_m=E|Z|^{2m}=(2m-1)!!=1\cdot3\cdots(2m-1)<\infty$$
for $Z\sim N(0,1)$. In particular, when $m\ge2$, this is the moment hypothesis
of the one-parameter Kolmogorov criterion with
$\alpha=2m$, $\beta=m-1$, and $C_T=c_m$.

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

**Output:** a pseudo-series $X_1^*,\ldots,X_n^*$, generated by [[alg-overlapping-block-resampling]]: within each selected block retain the original order and concatenate blocks in their draw order, truncating only the last block when $b\nmid n$. The conditional bootstrap sample mean is $\bar X_n^*=n^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^nX_t^*$. Its conditional center is $E^*\bar X_n^*$, where $E^*$ averages over the independent uniform block starts while the observations remain fixed.

**Input:** a finite sequence $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ in a measurable space, with $n\ge1$, and an integer block length $b$ satisfying $1\le b\le n$. Set $N=n-b+1$ and $k=\lceil n/b\rceil$.

**Randomization:** draw $J_1,\ldots,J_k$ independently and uniformly from $\{1,\ldots,N\}$.

**Output:** in order $s=1,\ldots,k$, append the block $x_{J_s},x_{J_s+1},\ldots,x_{J_s+b-1}$, then retain the first $n$ entries of the concatenation. Thus the final selected block is truncated to its first $r=n-b\lfloor n/b\rfloor$ entries when $r>0$. Conditional expectation given the input sequence means expectation over the indices $J_s$ alone.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(\mathcal F_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of sigma-algebras on a
probability space, and let $J_0,\dots,J_{m-1}\subseteq I$ be pairwise disjoint
index sets. For each $r<m$, define

$$\mathcal G_r:=\sigma\left(\bigcup_{i\in J_r}\mathcal F_i\right).$$

Then the sigma-algebras $\mathcal G_0,\dots,\mathcal G_{m-1}$ are independent.

Let $n\ge1$, let $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ be independent real random variables on a
common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then
   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$
   in $[0,+\infty]$. In this finite product of expectations, a zero factor
   makes the product zero even when another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise
   multiplication has its usual extended nonnegative meaning.
2. If every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable
   and the same factorization holds in $\mathbb R$.

Assume countable choice (in particular, the Axiom of Choice suffices). Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $1\le p\le\infty$. Then
$L^p(\mu)$, with the norm of
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]], is
complete. Equivalently, the metric induced by that norm is a complete metric in
the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]].

Moreover, if a sequence in $L^p(\mu)$ converges in norm, then some subsequence
admits measurable representatives converging almost everywhere in the sense of
[[def-convergence-almost-everywhere-relative-to-a-measure]].

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

For Borel probabilities $\mu_n,\mu$ on a metric space S, the following are equivalent: (i) $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$; (ii) integrals converge for all bounded uniformly continuous real tests; (iii) $\limsup_n\mu_n(F)\le\mu(F)$ for every closed F; (iv) $\liminf_n\mu_n(G)\ge\mu(G)$ for every open G; (v) $\mu_n(A)\to\mu(A)$ for every Borel A with $\mu(\partial A)=0$.

Let $X=(X_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ be a real-valued stochastic process on one
probability space, so each $X_t$ is a real random variable and each finite
tuple has its pushforward law
([[def-stochastic-process-and-finite-dimensional-distributions]],
[[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]],
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]).
We call $X$ a **time series** here because its index set is $\mathbb Z$.

The process is **strictly stationary** when for every integer $r\ge1$, every
$t_1,\ldots,t_r\in\mathbb Z$, and every shift $m\in\mathbb Z$,
$$\mathcal L(X_{t_1+m},\ldots,X_{t_r+m})=\mathcal L(X_{t_1},\ldots,X_{t_r}).$$
This condition concerns the full finite-dimensional laws and imposes no moment
condition by itself.

The process is **weakly stationary** when $E[|X_t|^2]<\infty$ for every
$t\in\mathbb Z$, its mean $\mu:=E[X_t]$ is independent of $t$, and for every
$h\in\mathbb Z$ the covariance
$$\gamma(h):=\operatorname{Cov}(X_{t+h},X_t)$$
is independent of $t$. Expectation, variance, and covariance have the meanings
in [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]] and
[[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]. Strict stationarity alone therefore
does not supply the moment hypotheses needed for covariance or sample-mean
claims.

derivations.claim: For $J\ge1$ let $X_{t,J}=\sum_{j=0}^{J-1}2^{-j}\varepsilon_{t-j}$. For $K>J$, independence, centering and [F12] give $E|X_{t,K}-X_{t,J}|^2=\sigma^2\sum_{j=J}^{K-1}4^{-j}$, so the partial sums are $L^2$-Cauchy and have a limit by [F13]. Also [F9] and [F2], [F6] give $E\sum_{j\ge0}2^{-j}|\varepsilon_{t-j}|=2E|\varepsilon_0|<\infty$, so the series converges absolutely almost surely. The $L^2$ limit and the almost-sure series are both probability limits of these partial sums: [F14] applied to squared $L^2$ errors proves the first assertion, and [F10] applied to indicators of tail events proves the second. For each $\epsilon>0$, the triangle inequality bounds the probability that the two limits differ by more than $\epsilon$ by the sum of the two partial-sum error probabilities at threshold $\epsilon/2$; letting $J\to\infty$ gives zero, so the limits agree almost surely. By [F6], the expectations of the partial sums converge to $E X_0=0$, and continuity of the $L^2$ norm gives $v:=E X_0^2=\lim_J E X_{0,J}^2=\sigma^2\sum_{j\ge0}4^{-j}=4\sigma^2/3$. For any finite set of times, the finite truncation vector has the same law after a common time shift by [F1]; its coordinates converge almost surely to the series vector, so bounded uniformly continuous test expectations pass to the limit by [F10]. [F15] gives equality of the limiting vector laws, proving strict stationarity in the sense of [F16].

The characteristic function of $X_{0,J}$ is $\exp\{-t^2\sigma^2\sum_{j=0}^{J-1}4^{-j}/2\}$ by [F3] and [F2]. By the a.s. convergence in step 1.1 and [F10], these characteristic functions converge to $\exp(-t^2v/2)$; [F4] identifies $X_0\sim N(0,v)$. Thus [F5] gives $E X_0^4=3v^2$.

For $h\ge1$, the recursion gives $X_h=2^{-h}X_0+\eta_h$, where $\eta_h=\sum_{j=0}^{h-1}2^{-j}\varepsilon_{h-j}$. The variable $X_0$ is measurable with respect to the past innovation sigma-algebra and $\eta_h$ with respect to the disjoint sigma-algebra generated by $\varepsilon_1,\ldots,\varepsilon_h$, so [F11] makes them independent. [F12] gives $E\eta_h=0$, $E\eta_h^2=v(1-4^{-h})$, and $E[X_0^2\eta_h^2]=EX_0^2E\eta_h^2$. Thus $\gamma(h):=E(X_0X_h)=2^{-h}v$. Expanding the product of squares, the cross term vanishes because $E\eta_h=0$ and independence, and $EX_0^4=3v^2$ by step 2.1; by the covariance definition [F7], $\operatorname{Cov}(X_0^2,X_h^2)=2v^2 4^{-h}=2\gamma(h)^2$.

By [F8], conditional on the observations each of the $n$ draws is uniform on the observed values, so its mean is $\bar X_n$ and its variance is $n^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^n(X_t-\bar X_n)^2$. [F12] factors the cross terms in the variance of their mean, giving $\operatorname{Var}^*\!\left(\sqrt n(\bar X_n^*-\bar X_n)\right)=n^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^n(X_t-\bar X_n)^2$. Stationarity and step 3.1 give $\operatorname{Var}(n^{-1}\sum_tX_t^2)\le\frac2n(v^2+2\sum_{h\ge1}\gamma(h)^2)\to0$: the lag-zero covariance is $E X_0^4-v^2=2v^2$, and the positive-lag covariances are $2\gamma(h)^2$. Also $E\bar X_n^2=\frac1n\sum_{|h|<n}(1-|h|/n)\gamma(|h|)\to0$ because $\sum_{h\in\mathbb Z}|\gamma(h)|<\infty$. Markov [F14] applied to squared deviations gives $n^{-1}\sum_tX_t^2\to v$ in probability and $\bar X_n^2\to0$ in probability. Therefore $n^{-1}\sum_t(X_t-\bar X_n)^2=n^{-1}\sum_tX_t^2-\bar X_n^2\to v$ in probability.

Counting pairs at each lag gives $\operatorname{Var}(\sqrt n\,\bar X_n)=\sum_{|h|<n}(1-|h|/n)\gamma(|h|)$. Absolute summability of $\gamma$ gives the limit $\gamma(0)+2\sum_{h\ge1}\gamma(h)=v(1+2\sum_{h\ge1}2^{-h})=3v=4\sigma^2$, whereas the conditional bootstrap variance tends to $v=4\sigma^2/3$ by step 4.1. The finite, unequal limits refute the universal variance-consistency claim. This calculation makes no broader assertion about every possible distributional metric.

citations.quote:
**Input:** a fixed integer $K\ge2$ of observed series $Y_{i,1},\ldots,Y_{i,n_i}$ in a real Hilbert space $H$, positive integer sample sizes $n_i$, total size $M=\sum_{i=1}^K n_i$, integer block lengths $1\le b_i\le n_i$, and a mode, moving or tapered. For tapered mode also supply an admissible window with positive block norm at each $b_i$. Put

$$\bar Y_i=\frac1{n_i}\sum_{t=1}^{n_i}Y_{i,t},\qquad \bar Y_P=\frac1M\sum_{i=1}^K n_i\bar Y_i,\qquad R_{i,t}=Y_{i,t}-\bar Y_i.$$

For each series $i=1,\ldots,K$, let $N_i=n_i-b_i+1$ and $k_i=\lceil n_i/b_i\rceil$. For every candidate start $j=1,\ldots,N_i$ and position $r=1,\ldots,b_i$, define the following arrays. In moving mode set $A_{i,j,r}=R_{i,j+r-1}$. In tapered mode set $A_{i,j,r}=a_{b_i}w_{b_i}(r)R_{i,j+r-1}$, with $a_{b_i}$ and $w_{b_i}$ as in [[alg-tapered-block-bootstrap]]. For each $i=1,\ldots,K$ and $s=1,\ldots,k_i$, draw independent uniform starts $J_{i,s}\in\{1,\ldots,N_i\}$, using the index law of [[alg-overlapping-block-resampling]]. For each within-block position define

$$c_{i,r}=\frac1{N_i}\sum_{j=1}^{N_i}A_{i,j,r}.$$

**Output:** for each $i$, a pseudo-series $Y^*_{i,1},\ldots,Y^*_{i,n_i}$. In the order $s=1,\ldots,k_i$, retain the positions $r=1,\ldots,q_{i,s}$, where $q_{i,s}=\min\{b_i,n_i-(s-1)b_i\}$, and set

$$Y^*_{i,(s-1)b_i+r}=\bar Y_P+A_{i,J_{i,s},r}-c_{i,r}.$$

Thus a divisible sample uses $k_i$ complete blocks; otherwise only the first $n_i-b_i\lfloor n_i/b_i\rfloor$ positions of the final block are retained. This centers each resampled residual position by its own conditional average, then gives every pseudo-series the same pooled location $\bar Y_P$. All block starts are conditionally independent across blocks and across series.

For fixed data and either mode of [[alg-k-sample-null-constrained-block-bootstrap]], every pseudo-observation in every series has conditional expectation $\bar Y_P$. Consequently, for each $i$,

$$E^*\bar Y_i^*=\bar Y_P,$$

so the conditional mean functions of the $K$ pseudo-series are equal.

derivations.claim: Here $M=7$, $\bar Y_P=(6+52)/7=58/7$, $N_1=2$, $N_2=3$, and $k_1=k_2=2$. The first residual series is $(-2,0,2)$; its candidate blocks are $(-2,0)$ and $(0,2)$, with position averages $(-1,1)$. After subtracting those averages the two candidates are $(-1,-1)$ and $(1,1)$. The second residual series is $(-3,-1,1,3)$; its candidates are $(-3,-1),(-1,1),(1,3)$, also with position averages $(-1,1)$, and become $(-2,-2),(0,0),(2,2)$.

Let $V_1,V_2$ be independent uniforms on $\{-1,1\}$ and $W_1,W_2$ independent uniforms on $\{-2,0,2\}$, all four independent. The outputs are $(58/7+V_1,58/7+V_1,58/7+V_2)$ and $(58/7+W_1,58/7+W_1,58/7+W_2,58/7+W_2)$. The first output retains only the first entry of its final block. Since all four offsets have mean zero, $E^*\bar Y_1^*=E^*\bar Y_2^*=58/7$, explicitly realizing [F2] despite the unequal observed means and unequal sample sizes.

Let $\mathcal B$ be the Borel sigma-algebra of $[0,1]$, generated by intervals with rational endpoints; let $dt$ be Lebesgue measure restricted to $\mathcal B$, and set $H=L^2([0,1],\mathcal B,dt;\mathbb R)$, with inner product $\langle x,y\rangle_H=\int_0^1x(u)y(u)\,du$. We use the quotient-by-null-functions convention for $L^2$ ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). The measure space is finite and countably generated, so under Countable Choice $H$ is separable ([[thm-l-p-of-a-sigma-finite-countably-generated-measure-space-is-separable]], [[def-countable-choice]], [[def-separable-space]]); [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]] verifies that this real pairing makes the quotient a Hilbert space.

Let $(S,\mathcal S,\nu)$ be a probability space and $(\delta_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ an independent identically distributed family of $S$-valued random elements with law $\nu$ ([[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]], [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]], [[def-independent-random-elements]]). A **causal Bernoulli shift** with innovation law $\nu$ is a process
$$X_t=f(\delta_t,\delta_{t-1},\delta_{t-2},\ldots),\qquad t\in\mathbb Z,$$
where $f:S^{\mathbb N_0}\to H$ is measurable from the product sigma-algebra $\mathcal S^{\otimes\mathbb N_0}$ to the Borel sigma-algebra of $H$. This product-measurability formulation is meaningful for a merely measurable innovation space $S$.

On an independent product extension, take replacement innovations $\delta'_{t,m,k}$, indexed by $t\in\mathbb Z$, $m\in\mathbb N_0$, and integers $k\le t-m$, all with law $\nu$, mutually independent, and independent of the original innovations. Such a countable family and its product with the original probability space exist under Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]], [[cor-countable-independent-copies-exist]], [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]). For $m\ge1$ define
$$X_{t,m}=f(\delta_t,\ldots,\delta_{t-m+1},\delta'_{t,m,t-m},\delta'_{t,m,t-m-1},\ldots),$$
and define the full replacement $X_{t,0}=f(\delta'_{t,0,t},\delta'_{t,0,t-1},\ldots)$. Each $X_{t,m}$ has the same marginal law as $X_t$; for fixed $m\ge1$ the sequence $(X_{t,m})_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ is strictly stationary and $m$-dependent because its original-innovation windows have length $m$ and its replacement arrays are independent across $t$.

For every fixed $m\ge0$, the joint process $(X_t,X_{t,m})_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ is strictly stationary: shifting all indices relabels a family of mutually independent innovations with the same law and commutes with the defining measurable maps. Consequently $D_{t,m}:=X_t-X_{t,m}$ is stationary and $\|D_{t,m}\|_{L^2(H)}=\delta_m$ for every $t$.

Write $\|X\|_{L^2(H)}=(\mathbb E\|X\|_H^2)^{1/2}$ and
$$\delta_m=\|X_0-X_{0,m}\|_{L^2(H)},\qquad m\ge0.$$
The process is **$L^2$-$m$-approximable** when
$$\mathbb E\|X_0\|_H^2<\infty\qquad\hbox{and}\qquad\sum_{m\ge1}\delta_m<\infty.$$
The same marginal law gives $\delta_0\le2\|X_0\|_{L^2(H)}<\infty$. For a Bochner-integrable $H$-valued random element $Y$, write $\mathbb E_B Y=\int Y\,d\mathbb P$; the moment condition makes $X_t$ and every $X_{t,m}$ Bochner integrable ([[def-bochner-integrable-function]], [[thm-bochner-integrability-criterion]]).

Here **strict stationarity** means invariance of every finite-dimensional law under integer shifts. A process is **$m$-dependent** if, for every $a\in\mathbb Z$, the sigma-algebras generated by $(X_s)_{s\le a}$ and $(X_s)_{s\ge a+m+1}$ are independent ([[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]]). The stated input windows for $X_{t,m}$ are disjoint across these two index ranges, so they satisfy this definition.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H=L^2([0,1])$, and let $(X_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ be a centered causal Bernoulli shift that is $L^2$-$m$-approximable under [[def-l2-m-approximable-causal-bernoulli-shift]]. Write

$$\delta_m=\bigl(E\|X_0-X_{0,m}\|_H^2\bigr)^{1/2}.$$

By [[lem-independent-tail-replacement-errors-are-monotone]], the summability in the stated process definition implies $m\delta_m\to0$. For each $n$, let $b_n$ be an integer with $b_n\to\infty$ and $b_n/\sqrt n\to0$. For all sufficiently large $n$, these conditions give $1\le b_n\le n$; apply [[alg-moving-block-bootstrap]] to $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ on this admissible tail. All limits below concern that tail. Let $\Gamma$ be the long-run covariance operator from [[thm-hilbert-valued-clt-for-l2-m-approximable-bernoulli-shifts]], and let $\bar X_n^*=n^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^nX_t^*$. Then

$$\mathcal L^*\!\left(\sqrt n(\bar X_n^*-E^*\bar X_n^*)\right)\Rightarrow\mathcal L(G)\quad\hbox{in probability},$$

and

$$\left\|n\,\operatorname{Cov}^*(\bar X_n^*)-\Gamma\right\|_{\mathrm{HS}}\longrightarrow0\quad\hbox{in probability},$$

where $G$ is the centered $H$-valued Gaussian with covariance $\Gamma$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H=L^2([0,1])$, and let $(Y_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ be a centered causal Bernoulli shift that is $L^2$-$m$-approximable under [[def-l2-m-approximable-causal-bernoulli-shift]]. Write

$$\delta_m=\bigl(E\|Y_0-Y_{0,m}\|_H^2\bigr)^{1/2}.$$

By [[lem-independent-tail-replacement-errors-are-monotone]], the summability in the stated process definition implies $m\delta_m\to0$. Let the integers $b_n\to\infty$ with $b_n/\sqrt n\to0$. Let the taper satisfy the support, positivity-near-$1/2$, symmetry and monotonicity conditions in [[alg-tapered-block-bootstrap]]. For all sufficiently large $n$, $1\le b_n\le n$ and $W_{b_n}>0$, the latter by [[lem-taper-window-l2-normalization]]. Apply that algorithm to $Y_1,\ldots,Y_n$ only on this admissible tail; all limits below concern that tail. Write $\bar Y_n^*=n^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^nY_t^*$ for the resulting bootstrap mean. Let $\Gamma$ be the long-run covariance operator from [[thm-hilbert-valued-clt-for-l2-m-approximable-bernoulli-shifts]]. Then

$$\mathcal L^*\!\left(\sqrt n(\bar Y_n^*-E^*\bar Y_n^*)\right)\Rightarrow\mathcal L(G)\quad\hbox{in probability},$$

and

$$\left\|n\,\operatorname{Cov}^*(\bar Y_n^*)-\Gamma\right\|_{\mathrm{HS}}\longrightarrow0\quad\hbox{in probability},$$

where $G$ is centered Gaussian with covariance $\Gamma$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: The filter $f(s_0,s_1,\ldots)=s_0e$ is measurable: it is the coordinate projection followed by a map from the finite innovation space to $H$. We have $EX_t=0$ and $E\|X_t\|_H^2=1$. For every $m\ge1$, the retained current innovation gives $X_{t,m}=X_t$ exactly, so $\delta_m=0$. Thus both $\sum_{m\ge1}\delta_m<\infty$ and $m\delta_m\to0$ hold. Independence and identical laws follow directly because each $X_t$ depends only on its own IID innovation.

The integer lengths satisfy $1\le\lceil n^{1/3}\rceil\le n$, $b_n\to\infty$ and $b_n/\sqrt n\le n^{-1/6}+n^{-1/2}\to0$. The window vanishes off $[0,1]$, takes values in $[0,1]$, is positive near $1/2$, symmetric, and nondecreasing on $[0,1/2]$. Every midpoint weight equals one, so $W_{b_n}=\sqrt{b_n}>0$ and $a_{b_n}=1$. All assumptions of both theorems are therefore met, giving their stated conditional law and covariance limits for this IID example.

citations.quote:
Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]), let
$\varnothing\ne\Theta_0\subseteq\Theta$, and let $G$ be a finite group
([[def-group]]) acting on $\mathcal X$ by a left action
([[def-group-action]]). Require that each map $x\mapsto g\cdot x$ is
measurable from $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ to itself and that
$T:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]).

For $\theta\in\Theta_0$, the null law is **invariant under the action** when
$P_\theta(\{x:g\cdot x\in A\})=P_\theta(A)$ for every $g\in G$ and
$A\in\mathcal A$. Equivalently, $g\cdot X$ and $X$ have the same law when
$X\sim P_\theta$. The setup defines the action and score whether or not this
invariance condition holds; the validity theorem below assumes it for every
null parameter.

The data space need not be finite, and the action need not be free. Group
elements, including distinct elements that send $x$ to the same point, remain
distinct transformations in every group average. On a finite data space with
the full power-set sigma-algebra, if every null law is invariant, the setup specializes to
[[def-finite-group-randomization-test]].

In a setup as in [[def-measurable-finite-group-permutation-setup]], the
**inclusive full-orbit upper-tail p-value** at $x\in\mathcal X$ is
$$p_{\mathrm{orb}}(x):=\frac{\#\{g\in G:T(g\cdot x)\ge T(x)\}}{|G|}.$$
If $U$ is independent of the data and uniform on $[0,1]$, meaning
$\mathbb P(U\le u)=u$ for every $u\in[0,1]$, the **tie-randomized full-orbit
p-value** is
$$p_{\mathrm{tie}}(x,U):=\frac{\#\{g\in G:T(g\cdot x)>T(x)\}+U\,\#\{g\in G:T(g\cdot x)=T(x)\}}{|G|}.$$
Independence is in the sense of
[[def-independent-random-elements]]. Each count is over group elements with
multiplicity, so nonfree actions are handled without replacing $|G|$ by the
number of distinct orbit points.

On the finite-space special case with invariant null laws, these formulas are the inclusive and
tie-randomized ranks of [[def-orbit-rank-p-value]]. The null-law validity
argument is supplied separately from this definition.

Let $a_1,\ldots,a_m\in\mathbb R$ with $m\ge1$. Let $J$ be uniform on $\{1,\ldots,m\}$ and let $U$ be independent of $J$ and uniform on $[0,1]$. Set
$$R_0:=\frac{\#\{i:a_i\ge a_J\}}{m},\qquad R_U:=\frac{\#\{i:a_i>a_J\}+U\#\{i:a_i=a_J\}}{m}.$$
Then $R_U$ is uniform on $[0,1]$, while $R_0$ is superuniform: $P(R_0\le u)\le u$ for every $u\in[0,1]$.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Let $\Omega$ be a nonempty finite set. Its **uniform probability space** assigns every $\omega\in\Omega$ the weight $1/|\Omega|$. Thus every event $A\subseteq\Omega$ has
$$\mathbb P(A)=\frac{|A|}{|\Omega|}.$$
Nonemptiness is required so that the denominator is positive.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). A **p-value
statistic** is a statistic $p:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$, where $[0,1]$ carries the
trace of the Borel sigma-algebra, meaning
$\{B\cap[0,1]:B\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\}$
([[def-statistic-and-estimator]],
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]).

For a nonempty null hypothesis $\Theta_0\subseteq\Theta$, the statistic is a
**valid p-value for $\Theta_0$** if it is superuniform under every null law:
$$P_\theta(\{x:p(x)\le u\})\le u\qquad\text{for every }\theta\in\Theta_0\text{ and }u\in[0,1].$$
The variable $p(X)$ is the observed p-value when the data are $X$. The
validity condition is distributional; measurability alone does not imply it.

Let $p$ be a valid p-value for a nonempty null hypothesis $\Theta_0$ in a
statistical experiment. For every $\alpha\in[0,1]$, the deterministic test
with rejection function
$$\varphi_\alpha(x)=\mathbf 1_{\{p(x)\le\alpha\}}$$
satisfies
$$P_\theta(p(X)\le\alpha)=E_\theta[\varphi_\alpha(X)]\le\alpha \qquad(\theta\in\Theta_0).$$
Consequently, whenever a nonempty alternative hypothesis
$\Theta_1\subseteq\Theta\setminus\Theta_0$ is specified, this test has size
at most $\alpha$ and hence level $\alpha$ in the sense of
[[def-test-size-and-power]].

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]) and let
$(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a measurable **action space**: a set of available
actions equipped with a sigma-algebra of action events, hence a measurable
space ([[def-measurable-space]]). A **randomized procedure** (or
randomized decision rule) is a probability kernel $K$ from
$(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ to $(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$, in the pointwise sense
of [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. Thus $K(x,\cdot)$ is a
probability measure on $(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ for every $x\in\mathcal X$,
and $x\mapsto K(x,B)$ is $\mathcal A$-measurable for every $B\in\mathcal G$.
After observing $x$, the procedure assigns probability $K(x,B)$ to taking an
action in $B$. The kernel is specified without reference to the unknown
parameter. This definition imposes no measurable structure on $\Theta$. The
kernel is the specification of the procedure; no representation by a separate
random seed is asserted for arbitrary measurable action spaces.

A **randomized test** is a randomized procedure with binary action space
whose action set is $\{0,1\}$, equipped with its full sigma-algebra
$2^{\{0,1\}}$ (the power set, which is a sigma-algebra by
[[def-sigma-algebra]]), where $1$ means reject and $0$ means do not reject
([[def-randomized-procedure-as-a-markov-kernel]]). Its **test function** is
$$\varphi(x)=K(x,\{1\}),\qquad x\in\mathcal X.$$
Since $K(x,\cdot)$ is a probability measure and $\{0\},\{1\}$ partition the
action set, $K(x,\{0\})+K(x,\{1\})=1$. Thus $\varphi(x)\in[0,1]$ and
$1-\varphi(x)=K(x,\{0\})$ is the probability of not rejecting. Give $[0,1]$
the trace of the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,+\infty]$, namely
$\{C\cap[0,1]:C\in\mathcal B([0,+\infty])\}$. By
[[lem-procedure-action-law-is-measurable]], $x\mapsto K(x,\{1\})$ is
measurable; since it has range in $[0,1]$, its preimage of $C\cap[0,1]$ equals
its preimage of $C$ and is measurable for every such $C$. Hence $\varphi$ is a
measurable map in the preimage sense of
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]. Its value is the
rejection probability after observing $x$.
The convention $1=\text{reject}$ is fixed here. No null or alternative
hypothesis is part of this definition.

Let $\mathsf E=((X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a
statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]) and let
$\varphi:X\to[0,1]$ be measurable, where $[0,1]$ has its Borel sigma-algebra.
On the binary action space $\{0,1\}$ with its full sigma-algebra, define
$$K(x,B)=\varphi(x)\mathbf 1_B(1)+(1-\varphi(x))\mathbf 1_B(0)\qquad (B\subseteq\{0,1\}).$$
Then $K$ is a probability kernel and hence a randomized procedure; its
randomized-test function under the convention $1=\mathrm{reject}$ is
$\varphi$.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). Let
$\Theta_0,\Theta_1$ be nonempty disjoint subsets of $\Theta$, called the null
and alternative hypotheses. A hypothesis is **simple** when it is a singleton
and **composite** when it has at least two elements.

For a randomized test with test function
$\varphi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$ ([[def-randomized-test]]), its **power function**
is
$$\beta(\theta):=E_\theta[\varphi(X)]\qquad(\theta\in\Theta).$$
Its **size** is
$$\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_0}\beta(\theta),$$
and it has **level $\alpha$** when this supremum is at most
$\alpha\in[0,1]$. The expectations exist and lie in $[0,1]$ because
$0\le\varphi\le1$ and each $P_\theta$ is a probability measure
([[def-probability-measure]],
[[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]).
The supremum exists because $\Theta_0$ is nonempty, the values lie in
$[0,1]$, and $\mathbb R$ has the least-upper-bound property
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]).

For the binary action $a\in\{0,1\}$, where $1$ means reject, the
**zero-one error loss** is $1$ when $a=1$ and $\theta\in\Theta_0$, or when
$a=0$ and $\theta\in\Theta_1$, and is $0$ otherwise. The decision-rule risk
from [[def-loss-function-and-risk]] integrates this loss against the action
kernel and data law. For each fixed $\theta$, its section on the binary
action space is measurable. The risk identities proved in
[[lem-test-zero-one-loss-risk-identities]] show that risk equals
$\beta(\theta)$ on $\Theta_0$ and $1-\beta(\theta)$ on $\Theta_1$. Thus size
is the worst null error risk, and power is the rejection probability under
each alternative parameter.

derivations.claim: For each $g\in G$, $x\mapsto T(g\cdot x)$ is measurable by [F1]. For measurable real functions $f,h$, $\{f>h\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q}\{f>q\}\cap\{h<q\}$, so strict comparisons are measurable; equality sets are complements of the union of the two opposite strict comparisons. Finite sums show that both rank counts are measurable. The identity belongs to $G$, so the tied count is at least one and both p-value formulas take values in $[0,1]$. For the joint tie-rank formula, partition the data space by the finitely many possible integer pairs $(N_>,N_=)$; on each part it is an affine function of $U$, so it is jointly measurable.

Fix $\theta\in\Theta_0$ and let $H$ be uniform on $G$, independent of $(X,U)$. For each fixed $h\in G$, invariance gives $h\cdot X\overset d=X$. Averaging over the finite law of $H$ therefore gives $(H\cdot X,U)\overset d=(X,U)$, so replacing $X$ by $H\cdot X$ does not change either p-value distribution.

Fix $x$ and form the finite list $a_g=T(g\cdot x)$ indexed by $g\in G$, retaining repeated values and repeated orbit points. At $H=h$, the transformed list at $h\cdot x$ is $T((gh)\cdot x)$ as $g$ ranges over $G$. Right multiplication $g\mapsto gh$ is a bijection of $G$, and the observed value $T(h\cdot x)$ is the entry indexed by $h$. Thus $p_{\mathrm{orb}}(h\cdot x)$ is the inclusive upper rank of a uniform index in $(a_g)_{g\in G}$, while $p_{\mathrm{tie}}(h\cdot x,U)$ is its independently tie-randomized rank.

By [F3], conditional on each fixed $x$, the first rank in step 2.1 is superuniform and the second is uniform. Averaging over $X$ preserves these bounds. The distributional equality in step 1.2 transfers them from $H\cdot X$ back to $X$, proving both displayed claims for this $\theta$. Since $\theta$ was arbitrary in $\Theta_0$, the claims hold under every null law. No orbit quotient or freeness assumption is used.

By [F6], $p_{\mathrm{orb}}$ is a valid p-value; [F7] gives its level-$\alpha$ cutoff test when an alternative is specified. For the tied test put $N_>(x)=\#\{g:T(g\cdot x)>T(x)\}$ and $N_=(x)=\#\{g:T(g\cdot x)=T(x)\}$. Its conditional rejection probability is $\phi_\alpha(x)=\min\{1,\max\{0,(|G|\alpha-N_>(x))/N_=(x)\}\}$, because $p_{\mathrm{tie}}(x,U)\le\alpha$ exactly when $U\le(|G|\alpha-N_>(x))/N_=(x)$, with the threshold clipped to $[0,1]$. The counts are measurable by step 1.1 and $N_=(x)\ge1$, so [F8] makes $\phi_\alpha$ a randomized test. Its null rejection probability equals $\mathbb P_\theta(p_{\mathrm{tie}}(X,U)\le\alpha)=\alpha$ by step 3.1, and [F9] identifies its size as $\alpha$ when a nonempty disjoint alternative is specified. The argument uses only a finite uniform group index and the stated uniform tie randomizer; it uses no choice axiom.

Measurable comparisons and finite count-pair partition establish joint measurability; H independent of (X,U), null invariance and the bijection g -> gh transfer the finite-multiset rank lemma without an orbit quotient. The lemma proves uniformity by tie-block interval lengths and inclusive superuniformity by initial-block sums. Checked |G|=1, constant scores, nonfree actions, zero-mass points and u/alpha=0,1. The equality-block denominator is positive; the clipped rejection function gives exact null probability alpha, with size language conditional on a nonempty disjoint alternative. No AC. be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]), let
$\varnothing\ne\Theta_0\subseteq\Theta$, and let $G$ be a finite group
([[def-group]]) acting on $\mathcal X$ by a left action
([[def-group-action]]). Require that each map $x\mapsto g\cdot x$ is
measurable from $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ to itself and that
$T:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]).

For $\theta\in\Theta_0$, the null law is **invariant under the action** when
$P_\theta(\{x:g\cdot x\in A\})=P_\theta(A)$ for every $g\in G$ and
$A\in\mathcal A$. Equivalently, $g\cdot X$ and $X$ have the same law when
$X\sim P_\theta$. The setup defines the action and score whether or not this
invariance condition holds; the validity theorem below assumes it for every
null parameter.

The data space need not be finite, and the action need not be free. Group
elements, including distinct elements that send $x$ to the same point, remain
distinct transformations in every group average. On a finite data space with
the full power-set sigma-algebra, if every null law is invariant, the setup specializes to
[[def-finite-group-randomization-test]].

**Input:** a measurable finite-group setup
[[def-measurable-finite-group-permutation-setup]], an observed $x$, an
integer $B\ge0$, and one of the two simulation designs below. Simulated
transformations are independent of $X$.

1. **With replacement.** Draw $g_1,\ldots,g_B$ independently and uniformly
   from $G$. Set $g_0=e$, the identity, and return
   $$\widehat p_{B,\mathrm{wr}}(x):=\frac{1+\sum_{b=1}^{B}\mathbf 1\{T(g_b\cdot x)\ge T(x)\}}{B+1}.$$
   A simulated draw may itself equal $e$; it is still counted in addition to
   the distinguished identity.
2. **Without replacement.** Require $B\le |G|-1$. Draw a subset $S$ uniformly
   from the $B$-element subsets of $G\setminus\{e\}$, and return
   $$\widehat p_{B,\mathrm{wor}}(x):=\frac{\#\{g\in\{e\}\cup S:T(g\cdot x)\ge T(x)\}}{B+1}.$$
   This is a uniform-subset design; the selected transformations are distinct
   and the identity is adjoined.

In either design, a cutoff rule rejects when the returned value is at most
$\alpha\in[0,1]$. For $B=0$ the only transformation is the distinguished
identity and the returned value is $1$. Validity under an invariant null law,
including ties, is a separate theorem on this page.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Let $\Omega$ be a nonempty finite set. Its **uniform probability space** assigns every $\omega\in\Omega$ the weight $1/|\Omega|$. Thus every event $A\subseteq\Omega$ has
$$\mathbb P(A)=\frac{|A|}{|\Omega|}.$$
Nonemptiness is required so that the denominator is positive.

Let $a_1,\ldots,a_m\in\mathbb R$ with $m\ge1$. Let $J$ be uniform on $\{1,\ldots,m\}$ and let $U$ be independent of $J$ and uniform on $[0,1]$. Set
$$R_0:=\frac{\#\{i:a_i\ge a_J\}}{m},\qquad R_U:=\frac{\#\{i:a_i>a_J\}+U\#\{i:a_i=a_J\}}{m}.$$
Then $R_U$ is uniform on $[0,1]$, while $R_0$ is superuniform: $P(R_0\le u)\le u$ for every $u\in[0,1]$.

Let $\mathsf E,\Theta_0,G,T$ be as in
[[def-measurable-finite-group-permutation-setup]], and suppose every null law
$P_\theta$, $\theta\in\Theta_0$, is invariant under the action. Let
$p_{\mathrm{orb}}$ and $p_{\mathrm{tie}}$ be as in
[[def-measurable-finite-group-orbit-pvalues]]. Then, for every
$u\in[0,1]$ and every $\theta\in\Theta_0$,
$$P_\theta(p_{\mathrm{orb}}(X)\le u)\le u,\qquad \mathbb P_\theta(p_{\mathrm{tie}}(X,U)\le u)=u,$$
where $U$ is independent uniform on $[0,1]$. Thus $p_{\mathrm{orb}}$ is a
valid p-value; its cutoff has null rejection probability at most $\alpha$,
and hence size at most $\alpha$ when a nonempty disjoint alternative is
specified. The tie-randomized cutoff is a randomized test with rejection
probability exactly $\alpha$ under each null law. These level and size
statements use [[def-test-size-and-power]].

On finite sample spaces, the first two distributional claims specialize to
[[thm-finite-group-randomization-validity]] and use the same multiplicity
convention as [[def-orbit-rank-p-value]]. The proof below supplies the
measurable-space extension rather than importing it from that finite-space
supplier.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). A **p-value
statistic** is a statistic $p:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$, where $[0,1]$ carries the
trace of the Borel sigma-algebra, meaning
$\{B\cap[0,1]:B\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\}$
([[def-statistic-and-estimator]],
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]).

For a nonempty null hypothesis $\Theta_0\subseteq\Theta$, the statistic is a
**valid p-value for $\Theta_0$** if it is superuniform under every null law:
$$P_\theta(\{x:p(x)\le u\})\le u\qquad\text{for every }\theta\in\Theta_0\text{ and }u\in[0,1].$$
The variable $p(X)$ is the observed p-value when the data are $X$. The
validity condition is distributional; measurability alone does not imply it.

Let $p$ be a valid p-value for a nonempty null hypothesis $\Theta_0$ in a
statistical experiment. For every $\alpha\in[0,1]$, the deterministic test
with rejection function
$$\varphi_\alpha(x)=\mathbf 1_{\{p(x)\le\alpha\}}$$
satisfies
$$P_\theta(p(X)\le\alpha)=E_\theta[\varphi_\alpha(X)]\le\alpha \qquad(\theta\in\Theta_0).$$
Consequently, whenever a nonempty alternative hypothesis
$\Theta_1\subseteq\Theta\setminus\Theta_0$ is specified, this test has size
at most $\alpha$ and hence level $\alpha$ in the sense of
[[def-test-size-and-power]].

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]) and let
$(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a measurable **action space**: a set of available
actions equipped with a sigma-algebra of action events, hence a measurable
space ([[def-measurable-space]]). A **randomized procedure** (or
randomized decision rule) is a probability kernel $K$ from
$(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ to $(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$, in the pointwise sense
of [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. Thus $K(x,\cdot)$ is a
probability measure on $(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ for every $x\in\mathcal X$,
and $x\mapsto K(x,B)$ is $\mathcal A$-measurable for every $B\in\mathcal G$.
After observing $x$, the procedure assigns probability $K(x,B)$ to taking an
action in $B$. The kernel is specified without reference to the unknown
parameter. This definition imposes no measurable structure on $\Theta$. The
kernel is the specification of the procedure; no representation by a separate
random seed is asserted for arbitrary measurable action spaces.

A **randomized test** is a randomized procedure with binary action space
whose action set is $\{0,1\}$, equipped with its full sigma-algebra
$2^{\{0,1\}}$ (the power set, which is a sigma-algebra by
[[def-sigma-algebra]]), where $1$ means reject and $0$ means do not reject
([[def-randomized-procedure-as-a-markov-kernel]]). Its **test function** is
$$\varphi(x)=K(x,\{1\}),\qquad x\in\mathcal X.$$
Since $K(x,\cdot)$ is a probability measure and $\{0\},\{1\}$ partition the
action set, $K(x,\{0\})+K(x,\{1\})=1$. Thus $\varphi(x)\in[0,1]$ and
$1-\varphi(x)=K(x,\{0\})$ is the probability of not rejecting. Give $[0,1]$
the trace of the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,+\infty]$, namely
$\{C\cap[0,1]:C\in\mathcal B([0,+\infty])\}$. By
[[lem-procedure-action-law-is-measurable]], $x\mapsto K(x,\{1\})$ is
measurable; since it has range in $[0,1]$, its preimage of $C\cap[0,1]$ equals
its preimage of $C$ and is measurable for every such $C$. Hence $\varphi$ is a
measurable map in the preimage sense of
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]. Its value is the
rejection probability after observing $x$.
The convention $1=\text{reject}$ is fixed here. No null or alternative
hypothesis is part of this definition.

Let $\mathsf E=((X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a
statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]) and let
$\varphi:X\to[0,1]$ be measurable, where $[0,1]$ has its Borel sigma-algebra.
On the binary action space $\{0,1\}$ with its full sigma-algebra, define
$$K(x,B)=\varphi(x)\mathbf 1_B(1)+(1-\varphi(x))\mathbf 1_B(0)\qquad (B\subseteq\{0,1\}).$$
Then $K$ is a probability kernel and hence a randomized procedure; its
randomized-test function under the convention $1=\mathrm{reject}$ is
$\varphi$.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). Let
$\Theta_0,\Theta_1$ be nonempty disjoint subsets of $\Theta$, called the null
and alternative hypotheses. A hypothesis is **simple** when it is a singleton
and **composite** when it has at least two elements.

For a randomized test with test function
$\varphi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$ ([[def-randomized-test]]), its **power function**
is
$$\beta(\theta):=E_\theta[\varphi(X)]\qquad(\theta\in\Theta).$$
Its **size** is
$$\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_0}\beta(\theta),$$
and it has **level $\alpha$** when this supremum is at most
$\alpha\in[0,1]$. The expectations exist and lie in $[0,1]$ because
$0\le\varphi\le1$ and each $P_\theta$ is a probability measure
([[def-probability-measure]],
[[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]).
The supremum exists because $\Theta_0$ is nonempty, the values lie in
$[0,1]$, and $\mathbb R$ has the least-upper-bound property
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]).

For the binary action $a\in\{0,1\}$, where $1$ means reject, the
**zero-one error loss** is $1$ when $a=1$ and $\theta\in\Theta_0$, or when
$a=0$ and $\theta\in\Theta_1$, and is $0$ otherwise. The decision-rule risk
from [[def-loss-function-and-risk]] integrates this loss against the action
kernel and data law. For each fixed $\theta$, its section on the binary
action space is measurable. The risk identities proved in
[[lem-test-zero-one-loss-risk-identities]] show that risk equals
$\beta(\theta)$ on $\Theta_0$ and $1-\beta(\theta)$ on $\Theta_1$. Thus size
is the worst null error risk, and power is the rejection probability under
each alternative parameter.

An **experiment** is a measurable space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, a set $\Theta$ of
parameter labels, and a family $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ of probability
measures on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ ([[def-measurable-space]],
[[def-probability-measure]]). The measures $P_\theta$ are the sampling laws.
If data under a parameter value are realized as a random element, its law is
the pushforward measure $P_X(B)=P(X^{-1}(B))$ from
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]; it is a probability measure by
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]].

The definition specifies the family of laws only. It supplies no sigma-algebra
on $\Theta$, no measurability condition on $\theta\mapsto P_\theta$, and no
common underlying probability space on which all observations must be realized.

derivations.claim: For the selected design, $\mathcal W$ is finite. Every $A\in\mathcal A\otimes2^{\mathcal W}$ has measurable sections $A_w=\{x:(x,w)\in A\}$. The displayed finite sum $\widetilde P_\theta(A)=\sum_w\nu(w)P_\theta(A_w)$ is nonnegative with total mass one. For disjoint $A_n$, each section $(\bigcup_nA_n)_w$ is the disjoint union of $(A_n)_w$, so countable additivity of $P_\theta$ and the finite sum over $w$ give countable additivity of $\widetilde P_\theta$. Thus [F11] makes this a joint statistical experiment. For measurable real functions $f,h$, $\{f\ge h\}$ is measurable because $\{f<h\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q}\{f<q\}\cap\{h>q\}$. Therefore each section $x\mapsto p_B(x,w)$ is measurable. Since $\mathcal W$ is finite, each sublevel set of $p_B$ is a finite union of measurable sections $A_w\times\{w\}$, so $p_B$ is measurable on the joint space. The distinguished identity contributes one tied-or-higher value, so $1/(B+1)\le p_B\le1$; at $B=0$, $W=\{e\}$ and $p_B=1$.

First use the with-replacement design. Represent $W$ by its $B+1$ generating positions to choose an independent uniform position $J$, and write $H$ for the entry at that position. The unordered multiset $WH^{-1}$ has the same law as $W$: if $J$ is the identity position it is unchanged; if $J=j>0$, right multiplication by $H^{-1}=g_j^{-1}$ makes position $j$ equal to $e$, makes the former identity position $g_j^{-1}$ uniform on $G$, and leaves the other $B-1$ draws conditionally independent uniform on $G$. Thus, after order is ignored, there is again one distinguished identity and $B$ IID uniform group elements.

Now use the without-replacement design and put $w=B+1$. The possible sets $W$ are the $w$-element subsets of $G$ containing $e$, all equally likely. Given $W$, choose $H$ uniformly from its $w$ elements. The map $(W,H)\mapsto(WH^{-1},H)$ is a bijection from pairs with $e\in W$, $|W|=w$, $H\in W$ onto pairs $(S,h)$ with $e\in S$, $|S|=w$, $h^{-1}\in S$: its inverse is $(S,h)\mapsto(Sh,h)$. Each fixed $S$ in the image has exactly $w$ possible $h$, so $WH^{-1}$ has the same uniform-subset law as $W$.

Since $X$ is independent of $(W,J)$ and each fixed $H\in G$ preserves its null law, conditioning on $(W,J)$ gives $H\cdot X\overset d=X$. By step 1.2, $WH^{-1}$ has the same design law as $W$, so $(H\cdot X,WH^{-1})$ and $(X,W)$ have the same joint law. Now fix $x$ and a labelled presentation of a with-replacement multiset $W$ before drawing $J$. The value $p_B(H\cdot x,WH^{-1})$ counts, with multiplicity, the entries $w\in W$ for which $T(w\cdot x)\ge T(H\cdot x)$, because $(wH^{-1})\cdot(H\cdot x)=w\cdot x$. As $J$ is uniform over the $B+1$ positions, this is the inclusive upper rank of a uniform position in the score multiset $(T(w\cdot x))_{w\in W}$. By [F5] this rank is superuniform conditional on $x,W$; averaging and using the joint-law equality transfers the bound to $p_B(X,W)$. This proves the with-replacement case, with ties and duplicate transformations counted by position.

The auxiliary pair $(W,H)$ is independent of $X$. For each fixed value of that pair, invariance gives $H\cdot X\overset d=X$; step 1.3 gives $WH^{-1}$ the same design law as $W$. Hence $(H\cdot X,WH^{-1})$ and $(X,W)$ have the same joint law. To bound the transformed p-value, fix $x,W$ before drawing $H$. Conditional on $W$, $H$ is uniform over its $B+1$ elements, and $p_B(H\cdot x,WH^{-1})$ is the inclusive upper rank of that selected position in $(T(g\cdot x))_{g\in W}$, since $(gH^{-1})\cdot(H\cdot x)=g\cdot x$. By [F5] this rank is superuniform conditional on $x,W$; averaging and using the joint-law equality transfers the bound to $p_B(X,W)$. This is a separate uniform-subset proof.

By [F7], the superuniform bounds in steps 2.1 and 2.2 make $p_B$ a valid p-value on the joint experiment. For each observed $x$, the probability over the finite simulation design of rejection is $\phi_\alpha(x)=\sum_{w\in\mathcal W}\nu(w)\mathbf1\{p_B(x,w)\le\alpha\}$, a finite average of measurable indicators by step 1.1. By [F9], $\phi_\alpha$ defines a binary randomized test on the original experiment. Its null rejection probability is $E_\theta[\phi_\alpha(X)]=\widetilde P_\theta(p_B\le\alpha)\le\alpha$, the rejection probability of the joint-experiment threshold test covered by [F8]. Thus, when a nonempty disjoint alternative is specified, [F10] gives size at most $\alpha$ and hence level $\alpha$. When $B=|G|-1$ without replacement, the only possible set is $W=G$, so the formula agrees with [F6]. No choice axiom is used.

risk_review.notes: Reviewed all six steps and F1-F11 independently against the current algorithm, setup, finite-rank lemma and test suppliers. For fixed selected j>0, (g_j^{-1},(g_i g_j^{-1})_{i != j}) is jointly uniform: conditioning on g_j gives the same product-uniform law for the other coordinates, hence independence from g_j^{-1}. Discarding order preserves the identity-adjoined multiset law; it need not preserve a distinguished-first ordered list. For subsets the inverse (S,h)->(Sh,h) has exactly B+1 preimages over every S, proving the separate design law. Null invariance conditional on the finite auxiliary sample makes transformed data independent of the recentered design, so the joint-law transfer and conditional uniform-position rank bound are valid on arbitrary measurable data spaces. Checked B=0, singleton groups, duplicate identity draws, constant scores, nonfree actions, u=0,1 and B=|G|-1 without replacement. Finite rejection averaging yields the randomized kernel; no AC or conditional-orbit disintegration. Hemerik-Goeman v3 Theorem 2 pp.11-12 and section 3.4 pp.15-16 support this argument; Katsevich section 3.2.4.2 equations (3.19)-(3.20) supplies the formula in its independence-null setting. citations.quote:
Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]), let
$\varnothing\ne\Theta_0\subseteq\Theta$, and let $G$ be a finite group
([[def-group]]) acting on $\mathcal X$ by a left action
([[def-group-action]]). Require that each map $x\mapsto g\cdot x$ is
measurable from $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ to itself and that
$T:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]).

For $\theta\in\Theta_0$, the null law is **invariant under the action** when
$P_\theta(\{x:g\cdot x\in A\})=P_\theta(A)$ for every $g\in G$ and
$A\in\mathcal A$. Equivalently, $g\cdot X$ and $X$ have the same law when
$X\sim P_\theta$. The setup defines the action and score whether or not this
invariance condition holds; the validity theorem below assumes it for every
null parameter.

The data space need not be finite, and the action need not be free. Group
elements, including distinct elements that send $x$ to the same point, remain
distinct transformations in every group average. On a finite data space with
the full power-set sigma-algebra, if every null law is invariant, the setup specializes to
[[def-finite-group-randomization-test]].

In a setup as in [[def-measurable-finite-group-permutation-setup]], the
**inclusive full-orbit upper-tail p-value** at $x\in\mathcal X$ is
$$p_{\mathrm{orb}}(x):=\frac{\#\{g\in G:T(g\cdot x)\ge T(x)\}}{|G|}.$$
If $U$ is independent of the data and uniform on $[0,1]$, meaning
$\mathbb P(U\le u)=u$ for every $u\in[0,1]$, the **tie-randomized full-orbit
p-value** is
$$p_{\mathrm{tie}}(x,U):=\frac{\#\{g\in G:T(g\cdot x)>T(x)\}+U\,\#\{g\in G:T(g\cdot x)=T(x)\}}{|G|}.$$
Independence is in the sense of
[[def-independent-random-elements]]. Each count is over group elements with
multiplicity, so nonfree actions are handled without replacing $|G|$ by the
number of distinct orbit points.

On the finite-space special case with invariant null laws, these formulas are the inclusive and
tie-randomized ranks of [[def-orbit-rank-p-value]]. The null-law validity
argument is supplied separately from this definition.

Let $\mathsf E,\Theta_0,G,T$ be as in
[[def-measurable-finite-group-permutation-setup]], and suppose every null law
$P_\theta$, $\theta\in\Theta_0$, is invariant under the action. Let
$p_{\mathrm{orb}}$ and $p_{\mathrm{tie}}$ be as in
[[def-measurable-finite-group-orbit-pvalues]]. Then, for every
$u\in[0,1]$ and every $\theta\in\Theta_0$,
$$P_\theta(p_{\mathrm{orb}}(X)\le u)\le u,\qquad \mathbb P_\theta(p_{\mathrm{tie}}(X,U)\le u)=u,$$
where $U$ is independent uniform on $[0,1]$. Thus $p_{\mathrm{orb}}$ is a
valid p-value; its cutoff has null rejection probability at most $\alpha$,
and hence size at most $\alpha$ when a nonempty disjoint alternative is
specified. The tie-randomized cutoff is a randomized test with rejection
probability exactly $\alpha$ under each null law. These level and size
statements use [[def-test-size-and-power]].

On finite sample spaces, the first two distributional claims specialize to
[[thm-finite-group-randomization-validity]] and use the same multiplicity
convention as [[def-orbit-rank-p-value]]. The proof below supplies the
measurable-space extension rather than importing it from that finite-space
supplier.

A **finite probability space** is a pair $(\Omega,w)$ consisting of a finite set $\Omega$ and a function $w:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ such that $w(\omega)\ge0$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$ and
$$\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1.$$
The elements of $\Omega$ are **outcomes**. Every subset $A\subseteq\Omega$ is an **event**, and its probability is
$$\mathbb P(A):=\sum_{\omega\in A}w(\omega).$$

An outcome of weight zero remains an outcome. Thus an event can be nonempty and still have probability zero.

**Input:** a measurable finite-group setup
[[def-measurable-finite-group-permutation-setup]], an observed $x$, an
integer $B\ge0$, and one of the two simulation designs below. Simulated
transformations are independent of $X$.

1. **With replacement.** Draw $g_1,\ldots,g_B$ independently and uniformly
   from $G$. Set $g_0=e$, the identity, and return
   $$\widehat p_{B,\mathrm{wr}}(x):=\frac{1+\sum_{b=1}^{B}\mathbf 1\{T(g_b\cdot x)\ge T(x)\}}{B+1}.$$
   A simulated draw may itself equal $e$; it is still counted in addition to
   the distinguished identity.
2. **Without replacement.** Require $B\le |G|-1$. Draw a subset $S$ uniformly
   from the $B$-element subsets of $G\setminus\{e\}$, and return
   $$\widehat p_{B,\mathrm{wor}}(x):=\frac{\#\{g\in\{e\}\cup S:T(g\cdot x)\ge T(x)\}}{B+1}.$$
   This is a uniform-subset design; the selected transformations are distinct
   and the identity is adjoined.

In either design, a cutoff rule rejects when the returned value is at most
$\alpha\in[0,1]$. For $B=0$ the only transformation is the distinguished
identity and the returned value is $1$. Validity under an invariant null law,
including ties, is a separate theorem on this page.

derivations.claim: All four masses are nonnegative and sum to $(q+(1-q))^2=1$, so [F4] makes them a finite probability law. The swap fixes $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$ and exchanges $(0,1)$ with $(1,0)$, which have equal mass. Thus $P_q(s^{-1}A)=P_q(A)$ for every $A\subseteq\Omega$, and the group action is invariant for every $q\in[0,1]$.

The subset $S$ is uniform and independent of $X$ by the Example, so it satisfies the without-replacement design premise in [F5]. In the $\mathbb Z/6\mathbb Z$ example, addition by any fixed group element permutes the six equally likely outcomes, so the null law is invariant. If $X=0$, only the identity in $W$ has score at least $T(X)=1$, and the without-replacement p-value is $1/3$. If $X\ne0$, then $T(X)=0$ and every element of $W$ has score at least zero, so the p-value is $1$. Its distribution is therefore $1/3$ with probability $1/6$ and $1$ with probability $5/6$; its CDF is superuniform.

At $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$, both transformed scores are $0$, giving $p_{\mathrm{orb}}=1$ and $p_{\mathrm{tie}}=U$. At $(1,0)$ the two scores are $1,-1$, giving $p_{\mathrm{orb}}=1/2$ and $p_{\mathrm{tie}}=U/2$. At $(0,1)$ they are $-1,1$, giving $p_{\mathrm{orb}}=1$ and $p_{\mathrm{tie}}=(1+U)/2$.

Put $a=q(1-q)$. Then $p_{\mathrm{orb}}=1/2$ with probability $a$ and equals $1$ otherwise. Its CDF is $0$ for $u<1/2$, $a\le1/4\le u$ for $1/2\le u<1$, and $1$ at $u=1$, so it is superuniform. For $0\le u\le1/2$, the tie-randomized CDF is $2au+(1-2a)u=u$: the $(1,0)$ branch contributes $2au$, the $(0,1)$ branch contributes zero except at a probability-zero endpoint, and the tied branches contribute $(1-2a)u$. For $1/2\le u\le1$, it is $a+a(2u-1)+(1-2a)u=u$. Thus $p_{\mathrm{tie}}$ is uniform, in agreement with [F3].

In the weak mean-difference example, $E[X]=E[Y]=0$. But the coordinate swap sends $(1,0)$ to $(0,1)$, and the product law assigns these points probabilities $P(X=1)Q(Y=0)=1/4$ and $P(X=0)Q(Y=1)=0$, respectively. Hence this weak null does not make the pooled law invariant under the swap, so the invariant-null premise of [F3] cannot be inferred from equality of means.

Step 1.1 checks the four-point law by finite arithmetic; no choice is used.

citations.quote:
Let $N\ge1$, and let $\mathcal I=\{1,\ldots,N\}$ index the fixed
experimental units at the actual treatment-assignment level. Let
$\mathcal Z$ be a nonempty finite set of allowed assignments. If treatment
is assigned to clusters, each cluster is one indexed unit; no separate
probability-sampling unit is present. The index $i$ identifies that unit,
and no visit or repeated-measurement index is modeled here.

A known assignment law is a function $p:\mathcal Z\to[0,1]$ satisfying
$\sum_{z\in\mathcal Z}p(z)=1$, so $(\mathcal Z,p)$ is a finite probability
space ([[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]]); assignments of probability
zero may remain in $\mathcal Z$. A **potential-outcome schedule** is a function
$\theta:\mathcal I\times\mathcal Z\to\mathbb R$, with
$Y_i(z):=\theta(i,z)$. The schedule and the units are fixed; the assignment
$Z$ is the only randomness supplied by the design, and the observed response
vector is $Y_\theta(Z)=(Y_i(Z))_{i\in\mathcal I}$. The schedule is defined
for every allowed assignment, including zero-probability assignments, and
may depend on the full assignment vector, so no no-interference assumption is
implicit. The scientific statistical model contract
[[def-scientific-statistical-model-contract]] requires the observation space,
units, quantity status, observation mechanism, support, conditioning
convention, and adequacy assumptions to be recorded; this model specifies
those fields as follows.

To express this as a statistical experiment, take the data space
$\mathcal X=\mathcal Z\times\mathbb R^{\mathcal I}$ with its full power-set
sigma-algebra, which is a sigma-algebra by [[def-sigma-algebra]] and makes
$\mathcal X$ a measurable space ([[def-measurable-space]]), and parameter
set $\Theta=\mathbb R^{\mathcal I\times\mathcal Z}$. For each $\theta\in\Theta$
let $P_\theta$ be the law
([[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]) of the deterministic
observation map $O_\theta(z)=(z,Y_\theta(z))$ from $(\mathcal Z,p)$. The map
is measurable because its domain has the full power set, in the preimage
sense of [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]], and its law
is a probability measure by
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]]. Thus
$((\mathcal X,2^{\mathcal X}),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ is an
experiment in the sense of [[def-statistical-experiment]]. The assignment
law asserts no response-error model, Gaussian law, superpopulation
randomization, or sampling representativeness beyond the stated finite
assignment mechanism. Its finite full-measure support set is
$$S_\theta:=\{(z,Y_\theta(z)):z\in\mathcal Z,\ p(z)>0\},$$
since $P_\theta(S_\theta)=\sum_{z:p(z)>0}p(z)=1$. The record contains the
assigned vector and every unit's response; missing or censored outcomes and
repeated visits require a separately declared observation mechanism. The
inferential target is the assignment-invariance hypothesis for these $N$
units, not an estimand for a wider population.

Inference in this page holds $\mathcal I$ and $\theta$ fixed and averages
over the declared law $p$; it does not condition on the realized assignment.
The status of the quantities is explicit: $\theta$ and all
$Y_i(z)$ are fixed, $Z$ is random, $(Z,Y_\theta(Z))$ is observed, and
potential responses under unassigned vectors are fixed but latent. The
assignment set, weights, and implemented randomization protocol are
design-controlled and should be checked against protocol records. Assignment
logs and response records are empirically assessable, but those checks do not
prove that the declared law generated the data. Potential outcomes under
unassigned vectors are fixed and latent in the realized record. This does
not imply nonidentifiability from the observed-data law: for each $z$ with
$p(z)>0$, the law assigns mass $p(z)$ to $(z,Y_\theta(z))$, and therefore
determines $Y_\theta(z)$. Assignment invariance on this positive-probability
set is **empirically assessable**, and the theorem tests the stronger
invariance hypothesis on all allowed assignments. Values at assignments
with $p(z)=0$, and restrictions on those values, are **substantively
untestable** from this law, since changing them leaves $P_\theta$ unchanged.
One realized assignment does not reveal responses at other assignments.
These classifications do not make the design or scientific model
empirically true.

In the finite randomized treatment-assignment model
[[def-finite-randomized-treatment-assignment-model]], a schedule satisfies
the **Fisher sharp null** when for each unit $i$ there is a value $y_i$ such that
$Y_i(z)=y_i$ for every allowed assignment $z$. The full vector
$y=(y_i)_{i\in\mathcal I}$ is then imputable under every assignment.

A **predeclared ordering score** is a real-valued statistic
$T:\mathcal Z\times\mathbb R^{\mathcal I}\to\mathbb R$
([[def-statistic-and-estimator]]) fixed before the
assignment and outcomes are inspected. Its upper-tail ordering includes ties:
assignment $z'$ is at least as extreme as $z$ when $T(z',y)\ge T(z,y)$.
For a signed score $S$ and fixed null center $s_0$, the corresponding
two-sided ordering is explicitly $T(z,y)=|S(z,y)-s_0|$. The center is part
of the predeclared ordering; the sharp null alone does not force $s_0=0$
for an arbitrary signed score. A lower-tail ordering is represented by
using $-S$ as the score. A statistic in this setting is a measurable map in
the sense of [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]; the full power-set data
sigma-algebra makes every such real-valued map measurable.

In a finite randomized treatment-assignment model, fix any real-valued
predeclared ordering score $T(z,y)$. For observed data $(z,y)$ define
$$p_{\rm rand}(z,y):=\sum_{z'\in\mathcal Z}p(z')1\{T(z',y)\ge T(z,y)\}.$$
Let $\lambda$ be the uniform probability measure on the Borel subsets of
$[0,1]$. For each $\theta$, equip $\mathcal X\times[0,1]$ with the product
sigma-algebra $2^{\mathcal X}\otimes\mathcal B([0,1])$ and define
$$\widetilde P_\theta(E):=\sum_{z\in\mathcal Z}p(z)\,\lambda\bigl(\{u\in[0,1]:((z,Y_\theta(z)),u)\in E\}\bigr).$$
Let $U$ be the $[0,1]$ coordinate on this extension. Define
$$p^+(z,y,U):=\sum_{z'\in\mathcal Z}p(z')1\{T(z',y)>T(z,y)\}+U\sum_{z'\in\mathcal Z}p(z')1\{T(z',y)=T(z,y)\}.$$
For every schedule satisfying the Fisher sharp null and every
$u\in[0,1]$,
$$P_\theta\!\left(p_{\rm rand}(Z,Y_\theta(Z))\le u\right)\le u,$$
whereas the added randomization gives
$$\widetilde P_\theta\!\left(p^+(Z,Y_\theta(Z),U)\le u\right)=u.$$
Thus $p_{\rm rand}$ is a valid finite-sample p-value for the sharp null,
and randomized ties give an exactly uniform p-value when the additional
independent uniform randomizer is used. For a two-sided test, take
$T(z,y)=|S(z,y)-s_0|$ with its center $s_0$ fixed in advance. The result
uses the actual, possibly unequal assignment probabilities; random
assignment supplies no Gaussian error law, and this theorem makes no
validity claim under the weak zero-average-effect null from
[[def-finite-population-average-treatment-effect-and-weak-null]] unless it
is also Fisher-sharp.

Let $\mathsf E,\Theta_0,G,T$ be as in
[[def-measurable-finite-group-permutation-setup]], and suppose every null law
$P_\theta$, $\theta\in\Theta_0$, is invariant under the action. Let
$p_{\mathrm{orb}}$ and $p_{\mathrm{tie}}$ be as in
[[def-measurable-finite-group-orbit-pvalues]]. Then, for every
$u\in[0,1]$ and every $\theta\in\Theta_0$,
$$P_\theta(p_{\mathrm{orb}}(X)\le u)\le u,\qquad \mathbb P_\theta(p_{\mathrm{tie}}(X,U)\le u)=u,$$
where $U$ is independent uniform on $[0,1]$. Thus $p_{\mathrm{orb}}$ is a
valid p-value; its cutoff has null rejection probability at most $\alpha$,
and hence size at most $\alpha$ when a nonempty disjoint alternative is
specified. The tie-randomized cutoff is a randomized test with rejection
probability exactly $\alpha$ under each null law. These level and size
statements use [[def-test-size-and-power]].

On finite sample spaces, the first two distributional claims specialize to
[[thm-finite-group-randomization-validity]] and use the same multiplicity
convention as [[def-orbit-rank-p-value]]. The proof below supplies the
measurable-space extension rather than importing it from that finite-space
supplier.

Consider the no-interference binary-treatment submodel of
[[def-finite-randomized-treatment-assignment-model]] in which the allowed
assignment set is $\{0,1\}^{\mathcal I}$ and unit $i$'s response under
assignment vector $z$ is $Y_i(z)=Y_i(z_i)$ for fixed real potential responses
$Y_i(0)$ and $Y_i(1)$. For the fixed units, define the
**finite-population average treatment effect** by
$$\tau_F:=\frac1N\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}\bigl(Y_i(1)-Y_i(0)\bigr).$$
The **weak zero-average-effect null** is the hypothesis $\tau_F=0$; it
constrains the average of the unit-level effects, not each effect separately.
The Fisher sharp null in this submodel, defined in
[[def-fisher-sharp-null-and-predeclared-test-orderings]], requires
$Y_i(1)=Y_i(0)$ for every unit. No probability distribution on the fixed
potential responses is part of either definition.

derivations.claim: The assignment weights are nonnegative and sum to one. Under the sharp null the same fixed response vector $y$ is available at both assignments, so the two score values in the Example are imputable before observing $Z$. The published weighted randomization theorem [F3] therefore applies to this schedule and this predeclared ordering.
If $Z=a$, the only assignment with score at least $1$ is $a$, so $p_{\mathrm{rand}}(a,y)=0.9$. If $Z=b$, both assignments have score at least $0$, so $p_{\mathrm{rand}}(b,y)=0.9+0.1=1$.

The p-value is $0.9$ with probability $0.9$ and $1$ with probability $0.1$. Its CDF is $0$ for $u<0.9$, $0.9\le u$ for $0.9\le u<1$, and $1$ at $u=1$, hence it is superuniform. The assignment law is not invariant under the swap $a\leftrightarrow b$, since the two assignment masses differ, so the group-invariance theorem [F4] is not the justification here. This example uses the Fisher sharp null and makes no claim under the weaker average-effect null [F5].
