Let $(X,d)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $F \subseteq X$ be closed in $X$
([[def-metric-topology]]). Then $F$ is a compact subset of $X$: the metric
subspace $(F, d_F)$ is a compact metric space
([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]).

No choice principle is used.

Let $(X, d_X)$ and $(Y, d_Y)$ be metric spaces ([[def-metric-space]]), let
$f : X \to Y$ be a function and let $a \in X$.

$f$ is **continuous at $a$** if for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that

$$d_X(x,a) < \delta \;\Longrightarrow\; d_Y\big(f(x), f(a)\big) < \varepsilon \qquad \text{for all } x \in X .$$

$f$ is **continuous** (globally, or on $X$) if it is continuous at every point of
$X$.

**The same condition in balls.** Since $d_X(x,a) < \delta$ says $x \in B_X(a,\delta)$
and $d_Y(f(x),f(a)) < \varepsilon$ says $f(x) \in B_Y(f(a),\varepsilon)$
([[def-metric-ball]]), continuity at $a$ reads: for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there
is $\delta > 0$ with

$$f\big[B_X(a,\delta)\big] \subseteq B_Y\big(f(a), \varepsilon\big).$$

Both forms are used below and are the same statement written twice.

**Both metrics matter, and both are named.** Continuity is a property of the
triple $(d_X, d_Y, f)$, not of $f$ alone. When several metrics on the same
underlying sets are in play, as in [[def-equivalent-metrics]], the metrics are
always written out.

**Quantifier order.** The $\delta$ is allowed to depend on $\varepsilon$ **and on
the point $a$**. Requiring one $\delta$ to work at every point simultaneously is
a strictly stronger condition, uniform continuity; it is defined on a later page
of this library, and at this point in the reading order it is written out in full
where needed ([[def-equivalent-metrics]]).

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), with open sets as in
[[def-metric-topology]] and balls as in [[def-metric-ball]].

- An **open cover** of $(X,d)$ is a family $\mathcal{U}$ of open subsets of $X$
  with $X = \bigcup \mathcal{U}$, where
  $\bigcup \mathcal{U} = \{\, x \in X : x \in U \text{ for some } U \in \mathcal{U} \,\}$.
- A **subcover** of $\mathcal{U}$ is a subfamily
  $\mathcal{V} \subseteq \mathcal{U}$ that is itself an open cover.
- A family $\mathcal{V}$ of sets is **finite** when $\mathcal{V} = \emptyset$ or
  there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and sets $V_0, \dots, V_n$ with
  $\mathcal{V} = \{V_0, \dots, V_n\}$; repetitions in the list are allowed and
  harmless.
- $(X,d)$ is **compact** when every open cover of it has a finite subcover: for
  every open cover $\mathcal{U}$, either $X = \emptyset$ and the empty subfamily
  covers it, or there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and
  $U_0, \dots, U_n \in \mathcal{U}$ with
  $$X = U_0 \cup \dots \cup U_n .$$
- A subset $A \subseteq X$ is a **compact subset** of $X$ when the metric
  subspace $(A, d_A)$ is a compact metric space, $d_A$ being the restriction of
  $d$ to $A \times A$ ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]).

**Compactness of a subset is defined intrinsically, and only intrinsically.**
The last clause speaks about the subspace $(A,d_A)$ and its own open sets, not
about families of open subsets of the ambient $X$. The two readings do agree,
but that is a theorem and not a convention: it is
[[lem-compactness-is-intrinsic]], and no item of this library may use the
ambient reading without citing it. Taking the intrinsic reading as the
definition is what makes "compact" a property of the metric space $(A,d_A)$
alone, so that a set compact in one ambient space is compact in every other one
containing it isometrically.

**The empty space is compact**, since the empty subfamily of any family covers
it; this is the reason the clause above is written with the two cases. The
one-point space is compact too, and so is every space listed as
$\{x_0, \dots, x_n\}$: given a cover, each $x_i$ lies in some member, and
finitely many members chosen in this way already cover.

**The finiteness convention, and how it is used both ways.** "Finite" above is
the listing form, matching the finite lists of
[[def-finite-intersection-property]]. It agrees with the definition of
finiteness by equinumerosity with a natural number ([[def-countable]]), and
both directions of the agreement are available and are used below:

- A nonempty finite set $F$ in the sense of [[def-countable]] satisfies
  $F \approx m$ for some $m \ge 1$, and a bijection $m \to F$ is exactly a
  listing $F = \{a_0, \dots, a_{m-1}\}$.
- Conversely a set listed as $A = \{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$, that is the image of a
  function $a$ with domain $\sigma(n)$, is finite in the sense of
  [[def-countable]]: the map sending $x \in A$ to the least $i \le n$ with
  $a_i = x$ is an injection of $A$ into $\sigma(n)$, so $A$ is equinumerous with
  a subset of $\mathbb{N}$ bounded above, and such a subset is finite
  ([[lem-subset-of-countable]]).

Neither direction uses a choice principle: the second selects nothing, taking a
least index instead.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) constructed in this
library ([[def-real-numbers]]) and carrying its order ([[def-real-order]]).

Let $X$ be a set. A **metric** on $X$ is a function
$d : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $x, y, z \in X$:

- **(M1) Separation.** $d(x,y) = 0$ if and only if $x = y$.
- **(M2) Symmetry.** $d(x,y) = d(y,x)$.
- **(M3) Triangle inequality.** $d(x,z) \le d(x,y) + d(y,z)$.

A **metric space** is a pair $(X,d)$ consisting of a set $X$ and a metric $d$ on
it. The elements of $X$ are its **points** and $d(x,y)$ is the **distance** from
$x$ to $y$. When only one metric is in play we write $X$ for $(X,d)$; when
several are, the metric is always named.

**The values of a metric are real numbers.** The codomain is $\mathbb{R}$, so
$d(x,y)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and every
inequality above is an inequality there. No infinite value is permitted;
[[rem-metric-axiom-conventions]] records why extended metrics are not treated in
this library.

**Nonnegativity is deliberately absent from the axiom list.** Many texts add a
fourth axiom $d(x,y) \ge 0$. It is redundant: (M1), (M2) and (M3) already force
it, as [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]] proves. Nothing below assumes it before that
lemma is available.

**Pseudometric.** A **pseudometric** on $X$ is a function
$p : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying (M2), (M3) and the weakening

- **(M1') Reflexivity.** $p(x,x) = 0$ for every $x \in X$

of (M1). A pseudometric may therefore assign distance $0$ to two distinct
points. Every metric is a pseudometric, and a pseudometric is a metric exactly
when $p(x,y) = 0$ forces $x = y$.

**Ultrametric.** An **ultrametric** on $X$ is a metric $d$ that in addition
satisfies

- **(M3') Strong triangle inequality.** $d(x,z) \le \max\{d(x,y), d(y,z)\}$

for all $x, y, z \in X$, where the maximum is that of a two-element subset of
$\mathbb{R}$, which exists and is one of the two elements
([[def-max-min]], [[lem-finite-set-has-max]]). An **ultrametric space** is a pair
$(X,d)$ with $d$ an ultrametric.

derivations.claim: By [F2], $q_s$ attains a minimum $c$ on $\Theta$. Hence $M_s=\{\theta\in\Theta:q_s(\theta)=c\}$ is nonempty.

The set $M_s$ is closed in $\Theta$. Indeed, if $\theta\notin M_s$, then $q_s(\theta)>c$; take $\varepsilon=(q_s(\theta)-c)/2>0$. By [F4], some $\delta>0$ makes $d(\eta,\theta)<\delta$ imply $|q_s(\eta)-q_s(\theta)|<\varepsilon$, and therefore $q_s(\eta)>c$. This ball misses $M_s$, so every point of its complement has a neighborhood in that complement.
By [F3], $M_s$ is compact.

Set $M_0:=M_s$. For $k=1,\ldots,p$, suppose $M_{k-1}$ is nonempty compact. The coordinate map $\pi_k(x)=x_k$ is continuous because $|\pi_k(x)-\pi_k(y)|\le\|x-y\|_2$. By [F2], it attains a minimum $a_k$ on $M_{k-1}$. Define $M_k:=\{x\in M_{k-1}:x_k=a_k\}$; this set is nonempty. It is closed in $M_{k-1}$: for $x_k\ne a_k$, a ball of radius $|x_k-a_k|/2$ around $x$ misses $M_k$ by the same coordinate inequality. Hence [F3] makes $M_k$ compact. Finite induction constructs nonempty compact $M_1,\ldots,M_p$.

The nonempty set $M_p$ contains a vector whose $k$th coordinate is $a_k$ for each $k$, so it contains at most one vector and is a singleton. For any $x\in M_s$, take the first coordinate $k$ at which $x_k\ne a_k$, if one exists. Then $x\in M_{k-1}$ and the definition of $a_k$ gives $x_k>a_k$. Thus the unique element of $M_p$ is lexicographically no larger than every member of $M_s$, and is the unique lexicographically least minimizer.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Let $n\ge 1$ and let $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$, with the real case obtained by
restricting scalars to $\mathbb R$. Then the following are equivalent:

1. $A$ has a Cholesky factorisation $A=LL^*$ with $L$ lower triangular and
   positive real diagonal.
2. $A$ is Hermitian positive definite.

When these conditions hold, the factor $L$ is unique.

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$, $m\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $\Sigma$ be a real symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then its law has Lebesgue density
$$f_{m,\Sigma}(x)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\det(\Sigma)^{-1/2} \exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(x-m)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-m)\right), \qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$

supplier_interfaces.excerpt:
Assume AC only as required by the synthetic-likelihood definition and its Gaussian-density supplier ([[def-axiom-of-choice]] [[def-synthetic-likelihood]] [[thm-nondegenerate-multivariate-normal-law-has-density]]). IID means common law and mutual independence as in [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]. Each real coordinate sequence uses the arithmetic sample-mean definition in [[def-iid-monte-carlo-estimators]]; covariance uses centered second moments as in [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]].

**Inputs:** A parameter $\theta$, observed data $y$, a summary statistic $S:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^d$ satisfying the contract of [[def-synthetic-likelihood]], an integer simulation count $m\ge2$, and a simulator that returns $m$ mutually independent observations with common law $P_\theta$.

**Output:** Either the finite-simulation plug-in synthetic-likelihood value at $S(y)$, or the explicit result **unavailable**.

1. Simulate $Y_1,\ldots,Y_m$ and compute $S_i:=S(Y_i)$. For each coordinate $j$, compute $\bar S_{m,j}:=m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m S_{i,j}$; this is the scalar Monte Carlo sample mean of [[def-iid-monte-carlo-estimators]] applied to the IID coordinate sequence.
2. Set $\bar S_m:=(\bar S_{m,1},\ldots,\bar S_{m,d})^T$ and compute
   $$
   \widehat\Sigma_m:=(m-1)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m(S_i-\bar S_m)(S_i-\bar S_m)^T.
   $$
3. If $\widehat\Sigma_m$ is not positive definite, stop and return **unavailable**. Do not add a ridge term or otherwise modify the covariance.
4. If $\widehat\Sigma_m$ is positive definite, take its unique Cholesky factor $L$ with positive diagonal by [[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]]. Return
   $$
   (2\pi)^{-d/2}\det(\widehat\Sigma_m)^{-1/2}
   \exp\!\left[-\tfrac12(S(y)-\bar S_m)^T\widehat\Sigma_m^{-1}(S(y)-\bar S_m)\right],
   $$
   the Gaussian density formula in [[def-synthetic-likelihood]] evaluated at the simulated mean and covariance, using [[thm-nondegenerate-multivariate-normal-law-has-density]].

This algorithm evaluates one parameter value. It does not optimize over $\theta$ and asserts no unbiasedness, convergence, consistency, posterior calibration, or optimizer property.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a statistical experiment and let $S:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^d$ be a statistic, meaning a measurable map to its declared Borel target as in [[def-statistic-and-estimator]], where $d\ge1$ is finite. Expectations are Lebesgue integrals under $P_\theta$ as in [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]], and variances and covariances use centered second moments as in [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]. For every $\theta\in\Theta$, assume
$$\mathbb E_\theta\!\left[\|S\|_2^2\right]<\infty,\qquad \|x\|_2^2:=\sum_{j=1}^d x_j^2.$$
The **binding mean** and **summary covariance** are the pointwise-defined quantities
$$b_j(\theta):=\mathbb E_\theta[S_j],\qquad \Sigma_{jk}(\theta):=\mathbb E_\theta\!\left[(S_j-b_j(\theta))(S_k-b_k(\theta))\right]\quad(1\le j,k\le d).$$
Each covariance entry is finite since $2|uv|\le u^2+v^2$ and the coordinates are square-integrable. The matrix is symmetric and positive semidefinite because for $a\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$a^T\Sigma(\theta)a=\mathbb E_\theta\!\left[(a^T(S-b(\theta)))^2\right]\ge0.$$
No measurability or continuity of $\theta\mapsto b(\theta)$ or $\theta\mapsto\Sigma(\theta)$ follows from these pointwise definitions.

Assume AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). If $\Sigma(\theta)$ is positive definite, the **ideal Gaussian synthetic likelihood** for observed data $y\in\mathcal X$ is the Gaussian density evaluated at its summary, as supplied by [[def-multivariate-normal-law]] and [[thm-nondegenerate-multivariate-normal-law-has-density]],
$$g_{\mathrm{SL}}(y\mid\theta):=\varphi_d\!\left(S(y);b(\theta),\Sigma(\theta)\right)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\det(\Sigma(\theta))^{-1/2}\exp\!\left[-\tfrac12(S(y)-b(\theta))^T\Sigma(\theta)^{-1}(S(y)-b(\theta))\right].$$
Here $\varphi_d(\,\cdot\,;m,\Sigma)$ is the Lebesgue density of $N_d(m,\Sigma)$. If $\Sigma(\theta)$ is singular, this positive-definite-covariance density is not defined by this item.

Let $Q_\theta:=P_\theta\circ S^{-1}$ be the pushforward law of the statistic under $P_\theta$ as in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]. For $m\ge2$, let $S_1,\ldots,S_m$ be IID simulated summaries with common law $Q_\theta$, where IID means a common law and mutual independence as in [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]. Set
$$\bar S_m:=m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m S_i,\qquad \widehat\Sigma_m:=(m-1)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m(S_i-\bar S_m)(S_i-\bar S_m)^T.$$
The **finite-simulation plug-in synthetic likelihood** is the random quantity
$$\widehat g_{\mathrm{SL},m}(y\mid\theta):=\varphi_d(S(y);\bar S_m,\widehat\Sigma_m).$$
when $\widehat\Sigma_m$ is positive definite, and is **unavailable** otherwise. The finite plug-in quantity is a function of simulated summaries; it is not defined as an unbiased estimator of the ideal Gaussian density.

The exact experiment’s likelihood density, when the experiment is dominated as in [[def-dominated-statistical-experiment]] and given a pointwise density as in [[def-likelihood-density]], and this Gaussian summary approximation are different objects. The latter density-selection interface assumes AC and does not assert a common exceptional null set across an arbitrary parameter set; the present definition adds no parameter-indexed measurability. This definition makes no claim that the actual summary law is Gaussian, that $g_{\mathrm{SL}}$ equals an exact likelihood, or that it yields posterior calibration, consistency, a Bernstein–von Mises theorem, or coverage. No optimizer or optimizer convergence property is included.

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$, $m\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $\Sigma$ be a real symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then its law has Lebesgue density
$$f_{m,\Sigma}(x)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\det(\Sigma)^{-1/2} \exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(x-m)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-m)\right), \qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be an experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). A **statistic** with target
measurable space $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ is a measurable map
$T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$, where measurability
means that $T^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal A$ for every $B\in\mathcal B$
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]). If
$\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal Y$ is an estimand ([[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]])
and its target set $\mathcal Y$ is equipped with $\mathcal B$, a statistic
$\widehat\psi$ with this same target space is an **estimator of $\psi$**.
The value $\widehat\psi(x)$ is the estimate at observed data $x$. Giving
$\mathcal Y$ a measurable structure is an additional choice; this definition
does not assert that $\psi$ is measurable as a function of the parameter.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element. Its
**law** or **distribution** is the set function
$$\mathbb P_X:\Sigma\to[0,+\infty],\qquad \mathbb P_X(B):=\mathbb P(X^{-1}(B)).$$

Thus the law of $X$ records the probability of each measurable target set by
pulling it back to an event in the original probability space.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

derivations.claim: The identity summary has mean $p$ and variance $p(1-p)>0$, so its ideal Gaussian synthetic likelihood is the density $g_p(x)=(2\pi p(1-p))^{-1/2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{(x-p)^2}{2p(1-p)}\right)$.

For $x\in(1/4,3/4)$ and $p\in(0,1)$, $|x-p|<1$. Hence $g_p(x)\ge c_p:=(2\pi p(1-p))^{-1/2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{1}{2p(1-p)}\right)>0$. The Gaussian law therefore assigns $(1/4,3/4)$ probability at least $c_p/2>0$, since this interval has Lebesgue length $1/2$.

The true summary law is supported on $\{0,1\}$, so it assigns $(1/4,3/4)$ probability zero. It differs from the Gaussian law in step 2.1. Thus the Gaussian synthetic likelihood is not the exact likelihood of this non-Gaussian summary model.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a statistical experiment and let $S:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^d$ be a statistic, meaning a measurable map to its declared target as in [[def-statistic-and-estimator]], with finite second moment under each $P_\theta$. Expectations are integrated against the law as in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] and [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]], and covariance uses the centered second moment as in [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]. The **moment binding function** for this page is
$$b:\Theta\to\mathbb R^d,\qquad b(\theta):=\mathbb E_\theta[S].$$
The name refers here to the mean of the declared summary vector; classical indirect inference also uses bindings defined by auxiliary-model estimators, which are a different interface.

The summary-law map is itself a parametric model in the sense of [[def-parametric-statistical-model]]:
$$Q:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathbb R^d),\qquad Q_\theta(B):=P_\theta(\{x:S(x)\in B\})$$
for each Borel set $B\subseteq\mathbb R^d$. It records the full law of the summary, whereas $b$ records only its mean.

For the finite-dimensional minimum-distance target, assume $p\ge1$, a nonempty compact parameter set $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ with its Euclidean subspace metric ([[def-metric-compactness]] [[def-metric-space]]), a binding map $b$ continuous from this metric to the Euclidean metric on $\mathbb R^d$ ([[def-metric-continuity]]), and a fixed summary vector $s\in\mathbb R^d$ (either the observed summary or a specified deterministic probability limit). Define
$$q_s(\theta):=\|b(\theta)-s\|_2^2.$$
Here $\|\cdot\|_2$ is the Euclidean norm. Require $q_s:\Theta\to\mathbb R$ to be continuous as part of this target’s admissible input contract. Its minimizer set is
$$M_s:=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\theta\in\Theta}q_s(\theta)=\{\theta\in\Theta:q_s(\theta)=\inf_{\eta\in\Theta}q_s(\eta)\}.$$
The **indirect-inference target** $\theta^{\mathrm{II}}(s)$ is the lexicographically least member of $M_s$: among all minimizers, minimize the first coordinate; among those, minimize the second; continue through coordinate $p$. The target is well-defined under exactly the stated compactness and continuity contract by [[thm-indirect-inference-target-exists-with-lexicographic-tie-break]].

For moment-based parameter recovery, the proposed limiting summary must satisfy $s=b(\theta_0)$ for some $\theta_0\in\Theta$. The **moment-identification condition at $\theta_0$** is
$$\{\theta\in\Theta:b(\theta)=b(\theta_0)\}=\{\theta_0\}.$$
Global moment identification means that $b$ is injective. Identifiability of $b$ as an estimand in [[def-identifiability-of-an-estimand]] is weaker: equality of sampling laws already implies equality of these means and does not ensure parameter recovery.

If the method instead compares the full summary laws, parameter identification requires injectivity of $\theta\mapsto Q_\theta$. By [[def-identifiability-of-an-estimand]] and [[thm-identifiability-iff-constant-on-equivalence-classes]], this is exactly identifiability of the identity estimand in the summary experiment. These identification conditions are additional assumptions for parameter recovery; the minimum-distance target and its tie rule do not require them.

No consistency theorem for an estimated minimizer follows from this target definition. Such a theorem needs additional hypotheses controlling sampling, simulation error, separation of the population target and the optimizer; the plan does not assert those hypotheses here.

Let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ be the nonempty compact parameter set of [[def-binding-function-and-indirect-inference-target]], and fix an admissible $s$ for which its objective $q_s:\Theta\to\mathbb R$ is continuous. Then
$$M_s:=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\theta\in\Theta}q_s(\theta)$$
is a nonempty compact set and has a unique lexicographically least element. Thus the target selector specified in [[def-binding-function-and-indirect-inference-target]] exists.

An estimand $\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0$ is **identifiable** in a parametric
model $\mathsf P$ when
$$
P_\theta=P_\eta\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\psi(\theta)=\psi(\eta)\qquad(\theta,\eta\in\Theta),
$$
or equivalently when $\psi$ is constant on each set of parameter values with
the same sampling law ([[def-parametric-statistical-model]],
[[def-observational-equivalence]], [[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]]).
The model is **identifiable** when its identity target
$\operatorname{id}_\Theta:\Theta\to\Theta$ is identifiable, equivalently
when $\mathsf P$ is injective.

Let $\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be a parametric
model, let $\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0$ be an estimand, and set
$\mathcal M:=\mathsf P(\Theta)$, the set of laws in the model. For
$\theta\in\Theta$, write
$$
[\theta]_\sim:=\{\eta\in\Theta:\eta\sim\theta\}.
$$
Then the following are equivalent: **(i)** $\psi$ is identifiable; **(ii)**
$\psi$ is constant on every observational equivalence class $[\theta]_\sim$;
and **(iii)** there is a unique function $\bar\psi:\mathcal M\to\mathcal T_0$
such that $\psi=\bar\psi\circ\mathsf P$.

The factorization is a statement about sets and functions. It asserts no
measurable structure or measurable factor map.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element. Its
**law** or **distribution** is the set function
$$\mathbb P_X:\Sigma\to[0,+\infty],\qquad \mathbb P_X(B):=\mathbb P(X^{-1}(B)).$$

Thus the law of $X$ records the probability of each measurable target set by
pulling it back to an event in the original probability space.

derivations.claim: Under either point-mass law, $S(Y)=Y^2=1$ surely. Thus $b(-1)=b(1)=1$.
The original laws differ: $P_{-1}(\{-1\})=1$ but $P_1(\{-1\})=0$. Therefore the parameter identity is identifiable in the original experiment.
For the observed summary $s=1$, $q_1$ is the constant continuous function zero on the finite compact set $\Theta$, so $M_1=\{-1,1\}$. The target’s lexicographic rule selects $-1$.

By the pushforward-law definition [F5], both summary laws assign probability one to $\{1\}$, so the summary-law map is not injective and the parameter identity is not identifiable from this summary. The moment target therefore does not recover the sign, even though the raw experiment distinguishes it.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Assume AC only as required by the synthetic-likelihood definition and its Gaussian-density supplier ([[def-axiom-of-choice]] [[def-synthetic-likelihood]] [[thm-nondegenerate-multivariate-normal-law-has-density]]). IID means common law and mutual independence as in [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]. This algorithm states the vector sample mean and covariance directly; covariance uses centered second moments as in [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]].

**Inputs:** A parameter $\theta$, observed data $y$, a summary statistic $S:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^d$ satisfying the contract of [[def-synthetic-likelihood]], an integer simulation count $m\ge2$, and a simulator that returns $m$ mutually independent observations with common law $P_\theta$.

**Output:** Either the finite-simulation plug-in synthetic-likelihood value at $S(y)$, or the explicit result **unavailable**.

1. Simulate $Y_1,\ldots,Y_m$ and compute $S_i:=S(Y_i)$. For each coordinate $j$, compute $\bar S_{m,j}:=m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m S_{i,j}$.
2. Set $\bar S_m:=(\bar S_{m,1},\ldots,\bar S_{m,d})^T$ and compute
   $$\widehat\Sigma_m:=(m-1)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m(S_i-\bar S_m)(S_i-\bar S_m)^T.$$
3. If $\widehat\Sigma_m$ is not positive definite, stop and return **unavailable**. Do not add a ridge term or otherwise modify the covariance.
4. If $\widehat\Sigma_m$ is positive definite, take its unique Cholesky factor $L$ with positive diagonal by [[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]]. Return the plug-in Gaussian density $(2\pi)^{-d/2}\det(\widehat\Sigma_m)^{-1/2}\exp\!\left[-\tfrac12(S(y)-\bar S_m)^T\widehat\Sigma_m^{-1}(S(y)-\bar S_m)\right]$ from [[def-synthetic-likelihood]] and [[thm-nondegenerate-multivariate-normal-law-has-density]].

This algorithm evaluates one parameter value. It does not optimize over $\theta$ and asserts no unbiasedness, convergence, consistency, posterior calibration, or optimizer property.

For any two simulated vectors $z_1,z_2\in\mathbb R^2$, put $\bar z=(z_1+z_2)/2$ and define the Bessel-corrected sample covariance
$$\widehat\Sigma:=\sum_{i=1}^2(z_i-\bar z)(z_i-\bar z)^T.$$
Then $\widehat\Sigma$ is not positive definite.

Assume AC only as required by the synthetic-likelihood definition and its Gaussian-density supplier ([[def-axiom-of-choice]] [[def-synthetic-likelihood]] [[thm-nondegenerate-multivariate-normal-law-has-density]]). IID means common law and mutual independence as in [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]. This algorithm states the vector sample mean and covariance directly; covariance uses centered second moments as in [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]].

**Inputs:** A parameter $\theta$, observed data $y$, a summary statistic $S:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^d$ satisfying the contract of [[def-synthetic-likelihood]], an integer simulation count $m\ge2$, and a simulator that returns $m$ mutually independent observations with common law $P_\theta$.

**Output:** Either the finite-simulation plug-in synthetic-likelihood value at $S(y)$, or the explicit result **unavailable**.

1. Simulate $Y_1,\ldots,Y_m$ and compute $S_i:=S(Y_i)$. For each coordinate $j$, compute $\bar S_{m,j}:=m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m S_{i,j}$.
2. Set $\bar S_m:=(\bar S_{m,1},\ldots,\bar S_{m,d})^T$ and compute
   $$\widehat\Sigma_m:=(m-1)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m(S_i-\bar S_m)(S_i-\bar S_m)^T.$$
3. If $\widehat\Sigma_m$ is not positive definite, stop and return **unavailable**. Do not add a ridge term or otherwise modify the covariance.
4. If $\widehat\Sigma_m$ is positive definite, take its unique Cholesky factor $L$ with positive diagonal by [[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]]. Return the plug-in Gaussian density $(2\pi)^{-d/2}\det(\widehat\Sigma_m)^{-1/2}\exp\!\left[-\tfrac12(S(y)-\bar S_m)^T\widehat\Sigma_m^{-1}(S(y)-\bar S_m)\right]$ from [[def-synthetic-likelihood]] and [[thm-nondegenerate-multivariate-normal-law-has-density]].

This algorithm evaluates one parameter value. It does not optimize over $\theta$ and asserts no unbiasedness, convergence, consistency, posterior calibration, or optimizer property.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a statistical experiment and let $S:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^d$ be a statistic, meaning a measurable map to its declared Borel target as in [[def-statistic-and-estimator]], where $d\ge1$ is finite. Expectations are Lebesgue integrals under $P_\theta$ as in [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]], and variances and covariances use centered second moments as in [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]. For every $\theta\in\Theta$, assume
$$\mathbb E_\theta\!\left[\|S\|_2^2\right]<\infty,\qquad \|x\|_2^2:=\sum_{j=1}^d x_j^2.$$
The **binding mean** and **summary covariance** are the pointwise-defined quantities
$$b_j(\theta):=\mathbb E_\theta[S_j],\qquad \Sigma_{jk}(\theta):=\mathbb E_\theta\!\left[(S_j-b_j(\theta))(S_k-b_k(\theta))\right]\quad(1\le j,k\le d).$$
Each covariance entry is finite since $2|uv|\le u^2+v^2$ and the coordinates are square-integrable. The matrix is symmetric and positive semidefinite because for $a\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$a^T\Sigma(\theta)a=\mathbb E_\theta\!\left[(a^T(S-b(\theta)))^2\right]\ge0.$$
No measurability or continuity of $\theta\mapsto b(\theta)$ or $\theta\mapsto\Sigma(\theta)$ follows from these pointwise definitions.

Assume AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). If $\Sigma(\theta)$ is positive definite, the **ideal Gaussian synthetic likelihood** for observed data $y\in\mathcal X$ is the Gaussian density evaluated at its summary, as supplied by [[def-multivariate-normal-law]] and [[thm-nondegenerate-multivariate-normal-law-has-density]],
$$g_{\mathrm{SL}}(y\mid\theta):=\varphi_d\!\left(S(y);b(\theta),\Sigma(\theta)\right)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\det(\Sigma(\theta))^{-1/2}\exp\!\left[-\tfrac12(S(y)-b(\theta))^T\Sigma(\theta)^{-1}(S(y)-b(\theta))\right].$$
Here $\varphi_d(\,\cdot\,;m,\Sigma)$ is the Lebesgue density of $N_d(m,\Sigma)$. If $\Sigma(\theta)$ is singular, this positive-definite-covariance density is not defined by this item.

Let $Q_\theta:=P_\theta\circ S^{-1}$ be the pushforward law of the statistic under $P_\theta$ as in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]. For $m\ge2$, let $S_1,\ldots,S_m$ be IID simulated summaries with common law $Q_\theta$, where IID means a common law and mutual independence as in [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]. Set
$$\bar S_m:=m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m S_i,\qquad \widehat\Sigma_m:=(m-1)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m(S_i-\bar S_m)(S_i-\bar S_m)^T.$$
The **finite-simulation plug-in synthetic likelihood** is the random quantity
$$\widehat g_{\mathrm{SL},m}(y\mid\theta):=\varphi_d(S(y);\bar S_m,\widehat\Sigma_m).$$
when $\widehat\Sigma_m$ is positive definite, and is **unavailable** otherwise. The finite plug-in quantity is a function of simulated summaries; it is not defined as an unbiased estimator of the ideal Gaussian density.

The exact experiment’s likelihood density, when the experiment is dominated as in [[def-dominated-statistical-experiment]] and given a pointwise density as in [[def-likelihood-density]], and this Gaussian summary approximation are different objects. The latter density-selection interface assumes AC and does not assert a common exceptional null set across an arbitrary parameter set; the present definition adds no parameter-indexed measurability. This definition makes no claim that the actual summary law is Gaussian, that $g_{\mathrm{SL}}$ equals an exact likelihood, or that it yields posterior calibration, consistency, a Bernstein–von Mises theorem, or coverage. No optimizer or optimizer convergence property is included.

derivations.claim: Each coordinate has mean zero and variance one, while the cross moment is zero. Hence the population summary covariance is $I_2$, positive definite.
By independence and the four equally likely support points, $P(Z_1=Z_2)=4(1/4)^2=1/4$. On this event the sample covariance is the zero matrix.

The event $Z_1=(1,1)$ and $Z_2=(-1,-1)$ has probability $1/16$. On it, $\bar Z_2=(0,0)$ and $\widehat\Sigma_2=\begin{pmatrix}2&2\\2&2\end{pmatrix}$, which differs from the zero matrix in step 1.2. Thus the sample covariance is a nonconstant random matrix.

By [F3], every two-simulation covariance here is not positive definite, so [F4] makes the finite plug-in synthetic likelihood unavailable for every outcome despite the positive-definite population covariance in step 1.1.

citations.quote: A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
$(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **total variation
distance** is

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}\bigl|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\bigr| .$$

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in
$[-1,1]$, because both measures have total mass one; hence the set being
maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.
The empty event and the whole space give the values $0$ and
$|\mu(E)-\nu(E)|=0$, so the distance is zero when $\mu=\nu$, and it is symmetric
in $\mu$ and $\nu$. This convention carries no factor $1/2$ in the supremum;
it is therefore not the total variation norm of the signed measure $\mu-\nu$,
which is twice the quantity above when that signed measure is considered on a
measurable space where the decomposition is attained. On a countable state
space with its power-set sigma-algebra the supremum equals the half-$\ell^1$
sum $\tfrac12\sum_{x\in E}|\mu(\{x\})-\nu(\{x\})|$; that identity is proved in
[[lem-total-variation-half-l1-formula-on-a-countable-space]], not assumed here.

If $s$ is a nonnegative simple measurable function, then its nonnegative
Lebesgue integral equals its simple integral:
$$\int s\,d\mu=\int_{\mathrm{simple}} s\,d\mu.$$

Let $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\chi_{E_j}$ be a simple representation of a
nonnegative simple measurable function
([[def-nonnegative-simple-measurable-function]]) on a measure space
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$, so the $E_j\in\mathcal A$ are pairwise disjoint and
$c_j\ge0$. Its
**simple integral** is
$$\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mu(E_j),$$
where $\mu$ is the given measure ([[def-measure]]) and the convention
$0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ is fixed once and for all.

The next lemma proves that this value is independent of the chosen simple
representation.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. If $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ are measurable, then
$$\int(f+g)\,d\mu=\int f\,d\mu+\int g\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Its positive and negative parts are
$$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$
they are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]] and
satisfy $f=f^+-f^-$ and $|f|=f^++f^-$.

The **Lebesgue integral of a real measurable function** is defined whenever at
most one of $\int f^+\,d\mu$ and $\int f^-\,d\mu$ is $+\infty$, in which case
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu.$$
The function is **integrable** when both integrals are finite, equivalently
when $\int|f|\,d\mu<+\infty$.

For a complex measurable function $h=u+iv$ with
$u=\operatorname{Re}h,\ v=\operatorname{Im}h$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]), define $h$ to be
**integrable** when $|h|$ is integrable, and then define
$$\int h\,d\mu:=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) and let
$\varepsilon \in F$ with $\varepsilon > 0$. Then there is a natural number
$n \ge 1$ such that

$$\frac{1}{n \cdot 1_F} < \varepsilon ,$$

where $n \cdot 1_F$ is the canonical natural of $F$ ([[thm-of-archimedean]]) and
$1/(n \cdot 1_F)$ is its multiplicative inverse ([[def-field]]). As is standard
we abbreviate $n \cdot 1_F$ to $n$ and write the conclusion $1/n < \varepsilon$.

This is the **reciprocal form** of the Archimedean property.
[[thm-of-archimedean]] on its own delivers only the assertion that the canonical
naturals are cofinal, $x < n \cdot 1_F$; the form actually used in analysis, that
the reciprocals of the naturals get below every positive bound, is the statement
above, and it is recorded separately so that no proof has to reconstruct the
inversion step in passing.

derivations.claim: If $M=0$, then $f=0$ and $g=0$ pointwise, so both claims hold. To prove the nonnegative claim for an arbitrary finite bound $L>0$, let $w:E\to\mathbb R$ be measurable with $0\le w\le L$, fix an integer $n\ge1$, put $\Delta=L/n$, and define $A_k=\{x:w(x)\ge k\Delta\}$ for $1\le k\le n$ and $s_n=\Delta\sum_{k=1}^n\mathbf1_{A_k}$. The sets are measurable, $s_n$ is nonnegative simple, and $0\le w-s_n\le\Delta$ pointwise.

By [F3]–[F5], $\int s_n\,dP=\Delta\sum_{k=1}^nP(A_k)$ and likewise for $Q$, so $|\int s_n\,dP-\int s_n\,dQ|\le n\Delta\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}=L\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}$. Also $0\le\int(w-s_n)\,dP\le\Delta$ and $0\le\int(w-s_n)\,dQ\le\Delta$, because $w-s_n\le\Delta$ and both measures have mass one. The triangle inequality therefore gives $|\int w\,dP-\int w\,dQ|\le L\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}+2L/n$.

Given any $\eta>0$, choose $n$ by [F7] with $1/n<\eta/(2L)$. The estimate in step 2.1 then gives $|\int w\,dP-\int w\,dQ|<L\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}+\eta$. If the bound by $L\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}$ failed, choosing $\eta$ to be half the positive excess would contradict this inequality. Taking $w=g$ and $L=M$ proves the stated nonnegative case when $M>0$.

For the signed case with $M>0$, let $h=f+M$. Then $h$ is measurable and $0\le h\le2M$, so step 3.1 with $w=h$ and $L=2M$ gives $|\int h\,dP-\int h\,dQ|\le2M\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}$. Also $|f|\le M$, so [F1], [F3]–[F5] give $\int|f|\,dP\le M$ and $\int|f|\,dQ\le M$; hence $f$ is integrable under both measures by [F6]. The constant $M$ has integral $M$ under each probability measure, so linearity [F6] gives $\int f\,dP-\int f\,dQ=\int h\,dP-\int h\,dQ$. This proves the signed case.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) constructed in this
library ([[def-real-numbers]]) and carrying its order ([[def-real-order]]).

Let $X$ be a set. A **metric** on $X$ is a function
$d : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $x, y, z \in X$:

- **(M1) Separation.** $d(x,y) = 0$ if and only if $x = y$.
- **(M2) Symmetry.** $d(x,y) = d(y,x)$.
- **(M3) Triangle inequality.** $d(x,z) \le d(x,y) + d(y,z)$.

A **metric space** is a pair $(X,d)$ consisting of a set $X$ and a metric $d$ on
it. The elements of $X$ are its **points** and $d(x,y)$ is the **distance** from
$x$ to $y$. When only one metric is in play we write $X$ for $(X,d)$; when
several are, the metric is always named.

**The values of a metric are real numbers.** The codomain is $\mathbb{R}$, so
$d(x,y)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and every
inequality above is an inequality there. No infinite value is permitted;
[[rem-metric-axiom-conventions]] records why extended metrics are not treated in
this library.

**Nonnegativity is deliberately absent from the axiom list.** Many texts add a
fourth axiom $d(x,y) \ge 0$. It is redundant: (M1), (M2) and (M3) already force
it, as [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]] proves. Nothing below assumes it before that
lemma is available.

**Pseudometric.** A **pseudometric** on $X$ is a function
$p : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying (M2), (M3) and the weakening

- **(M1') Reflexivity.** $p(x,x) = 0$ for every $x \in X$

of (M1). A pseudometric may therefore assign distance $0$ to two distinct
points. Every metric is a pseudometric, and a pseudometric is a metric exactly
when $p(x,y) = 0$ forces $x = y$.

**Ultrametric.** An **ultrametric** on $X$ is a metric $d$ that in addition
satisfies

- **(M3') Strong triangle inequality.** $d(x,z) \le \max\{d(x,y), d(y,z)\}$

for all $x, y, z \in X$, where the maximum is that of a two-element subset of
$\mathbb{R}$, which exists and is one of the two elements
([[def-max-min]], [[lem-finite-set-has-max]]). An **ultrametric space** is a pair
$(X,d)$ with $d$ an ultrametric.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space as in [[def-probability-measure]], let $\theta\in\mathbb R$ be a fixed target, and let $m\in\mathbb N\cup\{0\}$. Take $r_1,\ldots,r_m$ and $\widetilde r$ to be real random variables on this space, meaning measurable maps $(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$ as in [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]. Set $r_0(\omega):=\theta$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$. Deterministic values are included by using a one-point probability space. The reference chain $r_0,r_1,\ldots,r_m$ must put every quantity on the same scale and state which ideal analysis stage each transition represents. Define the signed stage errors pointwise by
$$e_j:=r_j-r_{j-1}\qquad(1\le j\le m)$$
and the final numerical error
$$e_{\mathrm{fp}}:=\widetilde r-r_m.$$

Each error is measurable because finite sums and differences of measurable real-valued functions are measurable ([[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]).

When the stages are present, $e_1$ may record data-sampling error, a later transition may record a bootstrap or permutation approximation, a discretized target may record numerical-model bias, and a finite simulation may record computation-randomization error. The labels describe the declared adjacent references; they do not by themselves assert that errors are independent, centered, unbiased, or even random. If a stage is absent, omit it or set its two adjacent references equal. If no floating-point computation is involved, set $\widetilde r=r_m$.

For a probability statement about these errors, the required joint probability law and any conditioning convention must also be specified. For example, fixing the observed data and varying independent randomizations concerns computation error conditional on those data; it does not include variation across new data samples. A deterministic quadrature rule has no replicate-based error estimate unless an actual randomization is added. Any numerical roundoff bound must state its arithmetic and normal-range hypotheses.

Let $\theta=r_0,r_1,\ldots,r_m,\widetilde r$ be the finite scalar reference chain and returned value of [[def-statistical-and-computational-error-ledger]], with $m\ge0$. Then, pointwise,
$$\widetilde r-\theta=\sum_{j=1}^{m}(r_j-r_{j-1})+(\widetilde r-r_m),$$
and consequently
$$|\widetilde r-\theta|\le\sum_{j=1}^{m}|r_j-r_{j-1}|+|\widetilde r-r_m|.$$
The sum is empty when $m=0$. No independence, unbiasedness, or distributional assumption is needed.

Let $E_1,\ldots,E_m$ be square-integrable real random variables on one probability space, where $m\ge1$. Write $b_j=\mathbb E E_j$. Then
$$\mathbb E\left[\left(\sum_{j=1}^{m}E_j\right)^2\right]=\left(\sum_{j=1}^{m}b_j\right)^2+\sum_{j=1}^{m}\operatorname{Var}(E_j)+2\sum_{1\le j<k\le m}\operatorname{Cov}(E_j,E_k).$$
The correction to the sum of component variances is exactly $(\sum_j b_j)^2+2\sum_{j<k}\operatorname{Cov}(E_j,E_k)$. Thus the mean square equals the sum of component variances exactly when this combined correction is zero. In particular, if the total bias is zero, pairwise independence suffices.

derivations.claim: We prove by induction on $m$ that $d(T_0,T_m)\le\sum_{j=1}^{m}d(T_{j-1},T_j)$. For $m=0$ both sides are zero; for $m=1$ this is equality. If it holds through $m$, then the triangle inequality [F1] gives $d(T_0,T_{m+1})\le d(T_0,T_m)+d(T_m,T_{m+1})\le\sum_{j=1}^{m+1}d(T_{j-1},T_j)$.

Apply the triangle inequality once more to $T_0,T_m,\widehat T$ and then step 1.1 to bound $d(T_0,\widehat T)$ by the displayed sum. For a scalar chain, [F2] specifies the same-scale adjacent errors and [F3] gives their exact signed telescope; when the terms are square-integrable, [F4] explains why squaring them retains bias and covariance terms rather than giving an automatic variance sum.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].
Let $\mu$ be a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. If $A,B\in\mathcal A$ and $A\subseteq B$, then $\mu(A)\le\mu(B)$.

Let $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\chi_{E_j}$ be a simple representation of a
nonnegative simple measurable function
([[def-nonnegative-simple-measurable-function]]) on a measure space
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$, so the $E_j\in\mathcal A$ are pairwise disjoint and
$c_j\ge0$. Its
**simple integral** is
$$\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mu(E_j),$$
where $\mu$ is the given measure ([[def-measure]]) and the convention
$0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ is fixed once and for all.

The next lemma proves that this value is independent of the chosen simple
representation.

If $s$ is a nonnegative simple measurable function, then its nonnegative
Lebesgue integral equals its simple integral:
$$\int s\,d\mu=\int_{\mathrm{simple}} s\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

A bounded function on a nondegenerate rectangle is Darboux integrable with
value $I$ if and only if all tagged grid sums converge with mesh to $I$.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^2}\,dx=\sqrt\pi.$$

Let $c < d$ be reals and let $\varphi : [c,d] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable
at every point of $[c,d]$ as a function on $[c,d]$ ([[def-derivative]]), with
$\varphi'$ integrable on $[c,d]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex with at least two elements
([[def-interval]]) with $\varphi[\,[c,d]\,] \subseteq J$, and let $f : J \to
\mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $J$ ([[def-continuity-real]]).

Then $(f\circ\varphi)\,\varphi'$ is integrable on $[c,d]$ and

$$\int_{\varphi(c)}^{\varphi(d)} f \;=\; \int_c^d (f\circ\varphi)\,\varphi' ,$$

the left-hand integral being the oriented one of [[def-oriented-integral]].

**Neither injectivity nor monotonicity of $\varphi$ is assumed**, and that is
exactly why the left-hand side is written with oriented limits: $\varphi(d)$ may
lie below $\varphi(c)$, and $\varphi$ may return to the same value many times.
The proof runs through a primitive of $f$ and the chain rule, and no inverse
function is ever formed.

**Continuity of $f$ is a hypothesis and cannot be weakened to integrability.**
With $f$ merely integrable the composite $f \circ \varphi$ need not be
integrable at all, so the right-hand side need not exist; that is
the false statement that weakens it on the companion page.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $u, v : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at
every point of $[a,b]$ as functions on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]). Suppose
$u'$ and $v'$ are integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then $uv'$
and $u'v$ are integrable and

$$\int_a^b u\,v' \;=\; u(b)v(b) - u(a)v(a) \;-\; \int_a^b u'\,v .$$

**The integrability of $u'$ and $v'$ is a hypothesis, not a formality.** Without
it the two integrals in the display need not exist at all, and the identity is
then not false but ill-formed; that is
the false statement that deletes it on the companion
page. The hypothesis is automatic when $u$ and $v$ are continuously
differentiable, since a continuous function on $[a,b]$ is integrable
([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]).

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ and every real $a>0$,
$$\frac{x^m}{\exp(ax)}\longrightarrow0\qquad(x\to+\infty).$$

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

derivations.claim: Every compact box has finite supplied measure, since it is contained in a larger half-open box. A bounded coordinate face has measure zero: enclose it in a half-open slab of arbitrary positive thickness $\eta$, with the other side lengths fixed and positive. Its measure is at most $C\eta$ by the given volume formula and [F2], and so must be zero. In dimension one this says that singletons are null. Consequently compact boxes have their usual volumes, and disjointifying a finite grid of closed cells only removes null faces.

For a nonnegative bounded Borel Riemann integrand $h$ on $Q$, take the infimum and supremum of $h$ on each cell of any finite grid. The corresponding disjoint-cell simple functions bound $h$, and [F2] and step 1.1 make their integrals exactly the lower and upper Darboux sums. By [F3] and [F4], the integral of $h$ is squeezed to its Riemann value. For signed bounded $h$, add a finite constant to make it nonnegative and subtract that constant's finite integral using [F3]. This proves the compact comparison. For nonnegative Borel $H$ on the whole space, $H\mathbf1_{[-n,n]^d}\uparrow H$, so [F5] gives the cutoff assertion. The grids, extrema, and cutoff sequence are finite or explicitly specified; no countable selection is used.

Put $\phi(t)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-t^2/2}$. It is continuous and Borel by [F1] and [F7]. On $[-n,n]$, proper substitution $t=\sqrt2u$ in [F6] computes its Riemann integral. As $n\to\infty$, [F6]'s improper Gaussian value makes this tend to one. Step 2.1 identifies each compact integral with its supplied-measure integral, and [F5] gives $\int\phi\,d\lambda_1=1$.

Since $\phi'=-t\phi$ by [F7], compact integration by parts [F6] gives $\int_{-n}^nt^2\phi(t)dt=\int_{-n}^n\phi(t)dt-2n\phi(n).$ All functions and derivatives here are continuous, so the proper integral hypotheses hold by [F4]. Also $n\phi(n)\to0$: for $n\ge1$, $n^2/2\ge n/2$, hence $0\le ne^{-n^2/2}\le ne^{-n/2}\to0$ by [F7]. Apply step 2.1 and monotone convergence [F5] to the nonnegative $t^2\phi(t)$ cutoffs. Step 3.1 then gives $\int t^2\phi(t)\,d\lambda_1=1$.

The bound $|t|\le1+t^2$ and steps 3.1, 4.1 make $|t|\phi(t)$ integrable. On each symmetric compact interval, the Riemann integral of $t\phi(t)$ is zero by oddness, using the proper substitution $t=-u$. Step 2.1 transfers these compact integrals to the supplied measure. Dominated convergence [F5], with majorant $|t|\phi(t)$, yields $\int t\phi(t)\,d\lambda_1=0$.

Fix $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma=\sqrt v>0$. On the explicitly specified intervals $[m-\sigma n,m+\sigma n]$, proper substitution $x=m+\sigma t$ gives compact integrals of $g_{m,v}$, $(x-m)^2g_{m,v}$ and $(x-m)g_{m,v}$ equal to the corresponding integrals of $\phi$, $\sigma^2t^2\phi$ and $\sigma t\phi$ on $[-n,n]$. Step 2.1 and monotone convergence give mass one and centered second moment $\sigma^2=v$. Since $|x-m|\le1+(x-m)^2$, the centered first moment is absolutely integrable, and the same dominated-cutoff argument as step 5.1 gives centered mean zero. Linearity then gives raw mean $m$. This proves both claims for the supplied measures without constructing any new measure or invoking a choice-dependent normal-law supplier.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Fix a measurable parameter space $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$, a prior probability measure $\Pi_0$ on it, observed data $x$, and an explicitly supplied $\mathcal T$-measurable likelihood version $\ell_x:\Theta\to[0,\infty)$. Define the evidence
$$Z_x:=\int_\Theta \ell_x\,d\Pi_0.$$
When $0<Z_x<\infty$, the **exact inferential target** is the probability measure
$$\Pi_x(A):=\frac{1}{Z_x}\int_A\ell_x\,d\Pi_0\qquad(A\in\mathcal T).$$
The measure is well-defined by the indefinite-integral construction
[[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]]. This is a fixed-data definition: [[def-likelihood-density]] selects, under AC, a measurable data-space density representative $p_\theta$ for each parameter $\theta$, but does not guarantee measurability of $\theta\mapsto p_\theta(x)$. Here the fixed-data likelihood version and its parameter measurability are supplied explicitly; no posterior is assigned when the evidence is zero or infinite.

For approximation accounting, declare a metric space $(\mathcal M,d)$ and a finite chain of elements $T_0,T_1,\ldots,T_m,\widehat T\in\mathcal M$, where $m\ge1$ and $T_1=\Pi_x$ whenever the exact target is included. The first distance $d(T_0,T_1)$ is the declared reference-to-target discrepancy; later adjacent distances and $d(T_m,\widehat T)$ are approximation and computation discrepancies on the same metric scale. For probability measures on a common measurable space, total variation may be used with the event-supremum convention of [[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]]. For scalar random quantities on one probability space, the statistical and computational stages are the same-scale signed differences defined in [[def-statistical-and-computational-error-ledger]]. This notation does not assert independence, unbiasedness, convergence, or that any numerical method attains a global optimum.

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). It is
**dominated** by a supplied positive measure $\mu$ on
$(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ when $\mu$ is sigma-finite
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]) and
$P_\theta\ll\mu$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$
([[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]).
The dominating measure is part of the specified setup. This condition adds no
measurable structure on $\Theta$ and no measurability of
$\theta\mapsto P_\theta$.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
([[def-measurable-space]]). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

An **experiment** is a measurable space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, a set $\Theta$ of
parameter labels, and a family $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ of probability
measures on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ ([[def-measurable-space]],
[[def-probability-measure]]). The measures $P_\theta$ are the sampling laws.
If data under a parameter value are realized as a random element, its law is
the pushforward measure $P_X(B)=P(X^{-1}(B))$ from
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]; it is a probability measure by
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]].

The definition specifies the family of laws only. It supplies no sigma-algebra
on $\Theta$, no measurability condition on $\theta\mapsto P_\theta$, and no
common underlying probability space on which all observations must be realized.

For an experiment on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, let
$\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ denote the set of all probability measures
on that measurable space. Its **parametric statistical model** is the parameter
map
$$
\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\qquad \mathsf P(\theta)=P_\theta,
$$
regarded together with its parameter set and sample space
([[def-statistical-experiment]]). The map need not be injective. Unless a
measurable structure on $\Theta$ is supplied separately, no measurability of
$\mathsf P$ is asserted.

In a parametric model $\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$,
two parameter values $\theta,\eta\in\Theta$ are **observationally
equivalent**, written $\theta\sim\eta$, if and only if
$$
P_\theta=P_\eta,
$$
that is, $P_\theta(A)=P_\eta(A)$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]). Equivalent parameter values therefore
give exactly the same sampling law. No distinctness of $\theta$ and $\eta$ is
required.

For a parametric model with parameter set $\Theta$, an **estimand** or
**parameter target** is a specified function
$$
\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0,
$$
where $\mathcal T_0$ is a set of target values
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]). This definition imposes no measurable
structure on $\Theta$ or $\mathcal T_0$ and does not require $\psi$ to determine
the full parameter value.

An estimand $\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0$ is **identifiable** in a parametric
model $\mathsf P$ when
$$
P_\theta=P_\eta\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\psi(\theta)=\psi(\eta)\qquad(\theta,\eta\in\Theta),
$$
or equivalently when $\psi$ is constant on each set of parameter values with
the same sampling law ([[def-parametric-statistical-model]],
[[def-observational-equivalence]], [[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]]).
The model is **identifiable** when its identity target
$\operatorname{id}_\Theta:\Theta\to\Theta$ is identifiable, equivalently
when $\mathsf P$ is injective.

Let $d\ge1$ and let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be compact, Lebesgue measurable,
and of positive Lebesgue measure. Let $a:K\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable with
$\int_K a\,d\lambda_d<\infty$. Let $h:K\to\mathbb R$ be continuous and have
a unique maximizer $\hat\theta$ in the interior of $K$. Assume $a$ is
continuous at $\hat\theta$ with $0<a(\hat\theta)<\infty$. Suppose $h$ is $C^3$ on an
open neighborhood $U\subseteq K$ of $\hat\theta$, and put
$H:=-D^2h(\hat\theta)$ using the Hessian convention of
[[def-hessian-and-euclidean-critical-point]]. Assume $H$ is symmetric positive
definite in the sense of
[[def-cholesky-factorisation-with-positive-diagonal]].
For $x\in\mathbb R^d$ and $r>0$, write
$B(x,r):=\{\theta\in\mathbb R^d:\|\theta-x\|_2<r\}$ and
$\overline B(x,r):=\{\theta\in\mathbb R^d:\|\theta-x\|_2\le r\}$.
Assume there are
$r_0,c,r_1,\eta>0$ such that $\overline B(\hat\theta,r_0)\subseteq U\cap K$,
$$h(\theta)\le h(\hat\theta)-c\|\theta-\hat\theta\|_2^2 \quad(\theta\in\overline B(\hat\theta,r_0)),$$
and
$$h(\theta)\le h(\hat\theta)-\eta \quad(\theta\in K\setminus B(\hat\theta,r_1)).$$
All integrals are the nonnegative Lebesgue integral of
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]].
For $I_n:=\int_K a(\theta)e^{nh(\theta)}\,d\lambda_d(\theta)$, as the
positive integer $n\to\infty$,
$$I_n\sim a(\hat\theta)e^{nh(\hat\theta)}\left(\frac{2\pi}{n}\right)^{d/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{\det H}},$$
where $u_n\sim v_n$ means $u_n/v_n\to1$. No relative $O(n^{-1})$ remainder
is asserted.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\ge1$ be an integer and let $H\in M_d(\mathbb R)$,
the square-matrix space of [[def-matrix-space]],
be symmetric positive definite in the sense of
[[def-cholesky-factorisation-with-positive-diagonal]]. Let $\lambda_d$ denote
the Lebesgue measure of
[[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]. Interpret the
displayed integral as the nonnegative Lebesgue integral of
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]].
$$\int_{\mathbb R^d}\exp\!\left(-\frac12 u^{\mathsf T}Hu\right)\,d\lambda_d(u) =\frac{(2\pi)^{d/2}}{\sqrt{\det H}}.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be an increasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$, so $E_n\subseteq E_{n+1}$. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\sup_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

No finiteness hypothesis is required.

Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
$(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **total variation
distance** is

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}\bigl|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\bigr| .$$

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in
$[-1,1]$, because both measures have total mass one; hence the set being
maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.
The empty event and the whole space give the values $0$ and
$|\mu(E)-\nu(E)|=0$, so the distance is zero when $\mu=\nu$, and it is symmetric
in $\mu$ and $\nu$. This convention carries no factor $1/2$ in the supremum;
it is therefore not the total variation norm of the signed measure $\mu-\nu$,
which is twice the quantity above when that signed measure is considered on a
measurable space where the decomposition is attained. On a countable state
space with its power-set sigma-algebra the supremum equals the half-$\ell^1$
sum $\tfrac12\sum_{x\in E}|\mu(\{x\})-\nu(\{x\})|$; that identity is proved in
[[lem-total-variation-half-l1-formula-on-a-countable-space]], not assumed here.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then

$$\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n) \;\subseteq\; \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n) :$$

every Borel subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]) is Lebesgue
measurable ([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]). In
particular every open set, every closed set and every countable intersection of
open sets is Lebesgue measurable.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

Let $Y$ be a subspace of a topological space $X$. Then

$$\mathcal B(Y)=\mathcal B(X)|_Y.$$

The Cauchy-sequence reals $\mathbb{R}_C$ have the **least-upper-bound property**:
every nonempty $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}_C$ that is bounded above has a least upper
bound $\sup S \in \mathbb{R}_C$. Hence, together with [[thm-reals-ordered-field]],
$\mathbb{R}_C$ is a **complete ordered field** ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]).

The relation of [[def-real-order]] is well defined and makes $\mathbb{R}$
([[thm-reals-field]]) a totally ordered field.

Every complete ordered field $F$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) is Archimedean:
for every $x \in F$ there is a natural number $n \ge 1$ with $x < n \cdot 1_F$,
where $n \cdot 1_F$ is the canonical natural of the ordered field $F$
([[def-ordered-field]]). Equivalently, the canonical naturals are cofinal in $F$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) and let $x, y \in F$, with
$|x|$ the absolute value ([[def-abs-value]]). Then

$$|x| \ge 0; \quad |x| = 0 \iff x = 0; \quad -|x| \le x \le |x|; \quad |-x| = |x|; \quad |xy| = |x|\,|y|;$$

and, for every $c > 0$, one has $|x| < c \iff -c < x < c$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field. For $a, b \ge 0$:

$$a < b \iff a^2 < b^2, \qquad a \le b \iff a^2 \le b^2.$$

More generally, for arbitrary $a, b \in F$, $a^2 < b^2 \iff |a| < |b|$.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

derivations.claim: On $\Theta$, $0\le(\theta^2-1)^2\le9$, so $0<p_{n,\theta}(0)\le1/2$. Also $3/16\le p_{n,\theta}(1)\le5/16$, hence $p_{n,\theta}(2)\ge1-1/2-5/16=3/16$; the three entries are nonnegative and sum to one. Thus each $P_{n,\theta}$ is a probability measure on $\mathcal X$. Since $p_{n,\theta}(1)=1/4+\theta/32$ is injective, $P_{n,\theta}=P_{n,\eta}$ implies $\theta=\eta$, so the identity estimand is identifiable by [F2].

The Borel sets of $\Theta$ are Lebesgue measurable, $\lambda([-2,2])=4$, and $\ell_{n,0}(\theta)=p_{n,\theta}(0)$ is continuous and satisfies $\tfrac12e^{-9n}\le\ell_{n,0}(\theta)\le\tfrac12$. Therefore $\Pi_0$ is a probability measure, $\ell_{n,0}$ is measurable, and $0<\tfrac12e^{-9n}\le Z_n=\int\ell_{n,0}\,d\Pi_0\le\tfrac12<\infty$. By [F1], $\Pi_n$ is the exact posterior target with density proportional to $e^{-n(\theta^2-1)^2}$ relative to $\Pi_0$.

The phase $h$ has exactly two global maxima, at $\theta=\pm1$, because $(\theta^2-1)^2=0$ exactly there and is positive elsewhere. Direct differentiation gives $h''(\theta)=4-12\theta^2$, so $h''(\pm1)=-8$; each local negative Hessian is full rank, but [F3]'s unique-maximum hypothesis fails. Writing $t=1+u$ gives $h(1+u)=-(2u+u^2)^2=-4u^2-4u^3-u^4$, so its quadratic term at $+1$ is $-4u^2$. The one-mode Laplace density is therefore proportional to $e^{-4nu^2}$, exactly the stated $q_n$, and integrates to one by [A1, F4].

Under the affine change $z=\sqrt{8n}(t-1)$, [F5] sends $Q_n((0,\infty))$ to the standard normal probability of $(-\sqrt{8n},\infty)$. These sets are increasing. Given any $z\in\mathbb R$, choose $n>z^2/8$ by [F9]; positivity and monotonicity of the square root then give $\sqrt{8n}>|z|$, so their union is all of $\mathbb R$. Continuity from below [F6] therefore gives $Q_n((0,\infty))\to1$.

Define $w_n(t)=e^{-n(t^2-1)^2}\mathbf1_{[-2,2]}(t)$ on $\mathbb R$; it is a nonnegative even Borel function. Apply [F5] to the reflection diffeomorphism $T(t)=-t$ on $\mathbb R$, using the function $w_n\mathbf1_{(0,\infty)}$: the unnormalized integrals of $w_n$ over $(0,\infty)$ and $(-\infty,0)$ are equal. The singleton $\{0\}$ has Lebesgue measure zero by [F8], so these two integrals split the prior-weighted posterior normalizer equally. Thus $\overline\Pi_n((0,\infty))=\Pi_n((0,\infty))=1/2$.

Using event $(0,\infty)$ in [F7], $\lVert Q_n-\overline\Pi_n\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}\ge|Q_n((0,\infty))-\overline\Pi_n((0,\infty))|$, whose right side tends to $1/2$ by steps 2.1 and 2.2. Thus $\liminf_{n\to\infty}\lVert Q_n-\overline\Pi_n\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}\ge1/2$, proving that the local curvature at one mode misses persistent posterior mass at the other.

This is a fixed-data definition: [[def-likelihood-density]] selects, under AC, a measurable data-space density representative $p_\theta$ for each parameter $\theta$, but does not guarantee measurability of $\theta\mapsto p_\theta(x)$. Here the fixed-data likelihood version and its parameter measurability are supplied explicitly; no posterior is assigned when the evidence is zero or infinite.

For approximation accounting, declare a metric space $(\mathcal M,d)$ and a finite chain of elements $T_0,T_1,\ldots,T_m,\widehat T\in\mathcal M$, where $m\ge1$ and $T_1=\Pi_x$ whenever the exact target is included. The first distance $d(T_0,T_1)$ is the declared reference-to-target discrepancy; later adjacent distances and $d(T_m,\widehat T)$ are approximation and computation discrepancies on the same metric scale. For probability measures on a common measurable space, total variation may be used with the event-supremum convention of [[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]].
